# GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA
## THE MOST ACUTE PHILOSOPHER,
### AND A PRINCIPAL FOLLOWER OF THE PLATONIC SCHOOL
->ALL HIS EXTANT WORKS:<-
->Recently illustrated by the genius and labor of most distinguished men,<-
->and purged of countless errors. These are as follows:<-

->THE LIFE OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA, most elegantly written by<-
->Gianfrancesco, son of the illustrious Prince Galeotto Pico.<-

<term>Heptaplus</term> (a mystical sevenfold explanation) on the Work of the Six Days of Genesis.
A Prayer to God in elegiac verse.
Defense of the Thirteen Questions.
A Treatise on Being and the One, divided into various objections and responses.
A most elegant Oration on the Loftiness and Dignity of Man <note>This famous speech is often called the "Manifesto of the Renaissance."</note>.

Two books of his Letters.
Testimonies of his life and teaching.
An Exposition of the psalm "Preserve me, O Lord."
Twelve books of Disputations against Astrologers.
A poem on the wood of the cross by Caecilius Cyprian, Bishop of Carthage.

---

->LIKEWISE, THE NAMES OF THE MOST DISTINGUISHED MEN<-
->*who wrote letters regarding all his works are these:*<-

| | |
| :--- | :--- |
| Giovanni Pico della Mirandola | Filippo Beroaldo |
| Gianfrancesco Pico, son of Count Galeotto | Battista Guarino |
| Ermolao Barbaro | Cristoforo Landino |
| Angelo Poliziano | Alessandro Cortesi |
| Brother Battista the Carmelite <note>Also known as Battista Mantovano, a famous Neo-Latin poet.</note> | Bartolomeo Fonte |
| Matteo Bosso of Verona | Marsilio Ficino <note>The leader of the Florentine Platonic Academy.</note> |
| Girolamo Donato | Baccio Ugolini |
| Roberto Salviati | Giuliano Maggio the Neapolitan |

---

->*To all these have recently been added the Conclusions, which he himself,*<-
->*while he lived, attempted to defend with the greatest praise from all.*<-

->FINALLY, A MOST COMPREHENSIVE INDEX HAS BEEN ADDED TO ALL THESE.<-

That Plato nowhere implied that the One is superior to Being, but rather that they are equal. leaf 40
By the testimony of Parmenides, Dionysius, and Simplicius, it is proved that Being and the One are reciprocal and equal. leaf 41
How you can say something is superior to Being is declared. leaf 41
By what means we may ascend through four steps to the darkness in which God dwells. leaf 41
He resolves the argument of the Platonists concerning prime matter. leaf 42

First, the preface: likewise that astrology has been condemned by philosophers, prophets, emperors, and popes; and what sort of men those were who wrote on astrology. leaf 75. Homer.

<column-break/>

Second: The uselessness and falsity of the profession in general; the ignorance and lack of diligence of the professors of our time. Also why they sometimes predict the truth when the profession itself is false. But not only that:

Third: Reasons approving the truth of astrology are brought forward, then they are diluted and turned back. We resolve:

Fourth: That what astrologers believe does not come from the heavens; likewise, that what does not come from the heavens is not signified by it; that "interrogations" <note>In astrology, "interrogations" are questions asked of the stars to find lost objects or predict outcomes.</note> are empty. This is ours.

Fifth: The great orbs, Saturnian revolutions, and great conjunctions are eliminated. But many:

Sixth: The houses, signs, aspects, obsessions, and combustions are destroyed; as are retrogradations, the head and tail of the dragon <note>The lunar nodes where eclipses occur.</note>, <term>antiscia</term> <note>Shadow-points or reflections of planets across the solstice points.</note>, presiding and obeying signs. Exaltations of the trine or triplicities, faces, terms, <term>dodecatemoria</term> <note>Subdivisions of a zodiac sign into twelve parts.</note>, novenae, <term>monomoriae</term> <note>Single-degree divisions of the zodiac.</note>, properties of degrees, parts, and <term>climacteric years</term> <note>Critical years in a person's life, thought by astrologers to be governed by the planet Saturn.</note>. We have exceeded:

Seventh: It is contained that the beginnings of fate, whether particular or universal, of a man or of any other thing, are not well understood. Also, the time when something is to happen is wrongly defined by "directions" or another way; and the manifold error regarding fixed stars. Thus far:

Eighth: That the number of spheres is uncertain; and whatever is established, the error of astrologers is certain. Also concerning errors about the difference of images and signs; also about invisible images. Among all:

Ninth: It is contained concerning the uncertainty of the birth hour and other beginnings, and of the errors in the division of houses, signs, places, planets, the motion of the seventh sphere, and directions. It has been demonstrated:

Tenth: The reasons of astrologers with which they strive to strengthen their dogmas are reduced to five kinds; and all these are shown to be ineffective and utterly ridiculous. For many now:

Eleventh: That astrology cannot be obtained through experience, or if any experience can be compared, it has not yet been obtained. If nature:

Twelfth: That it was not obtained through revelation. Likewise where it was born, increased, nourished, and how it was propagated. If by fables:

->Table of chapters for the Twelve Books.<-

The first book is not divided into several chapters, but in one chapter it casts down astrology by the authority of philosophers, prophets, emperors, and popes. leaf 76

In the second book are contained the uselessness and falsity of the profession; the ignorance and lack of diligence of the professors.

Chapter 1: That this art is uncertain even by the judgment of its own principles. leaf 79

Chapter 2: That auspices, which they call "elections," are useless by the testimony of one astrologer, by reason, and by experience. leaf 80

Chapter 3: That astrology is not useful in deciding what is to be done or what is to be avoided. leaf 80

Chapter 4: That astrology is not useful to religion, as <term>Roger Bacon</term> and <term>Pierre d’Ailly</term> <note>Medieval thinkers who, unlike Pico, believed astrology could be used to interpret religious history.</note> thought. leaf 80

Chapter 5: How harmful astrology is and how pestilential to the Christian religion. leaf 81

Chapter 6: That this art is deceptive, if it exists at all, both for many reasons and because of the differing opinions of astrologers. leaf 81

Chapter 7: On the ignorance of the astrologers of our age. leaf 82

Chapter 8: On the lack of diligence of the astrologers of our age, which is so great that even if astrology were true, they themselves could not be truthful. leaf 83

Chapter 9: That what astrologers say rarely happens, which is shown by both external and domestic examples. leaf 83

Chapter 10: Why astrologers sometimes predict true things. leaf 83

<meta>This page continues the table of contents (Tabula) from the previous section. It outlines the specific arguments Pico della Mirandola uses to dismantle the foundations of astrology in Books 3, 4, and 5. This text is from his seminal work, *Disputations Against Divinatory Astrology*.</meta>

-># TABLE OF DISPUTATIONS<-

[Signature M]

<warning>Slight foxing and ink bleed from the back of the page is visible; there is minor fading on the left margin near the binding.</warning>

The third book contains the arguments favoring astrologers and their refutation. Page 84

**Chapter 1.** What was discussed in the preceding book and what is to be done next, and in what order. page 84
**Chapter 2.** Whatever reasons by which astrology seems to be able to be strengthened. page 84
**Chapter 3.** The first reason is turned back on itself, and it is shown that the heavens are a universal cause and not to be related to the very variety of individuals.
**Chapter 4.** How the heavens act through motion and light, and how they are the universal cause of the elements, meteorological phenomena, minerals, and living things.
**Chapter 5.** That besides the common influence of motion and light, there is no power peculiar to the celestial bodies.
**Chapter 6.** That the light of the moon, just like that of the sun, is vital; and neither produces cold or humidity except by accident <note>original: "per accidens"; a philosophical term meaning indirectly or as a side effect rather than by its essential nature</note>.
**Chapter 7.** That the dogmas of the astrologers cannot be defended as <term>Ibn Ezra<note>Abraham Ibn Ezra (Auenazra), a 12th-century scholar whose astrological works were highly influential in the Latin West.</note></term> thought if all stars are considered hot.
**Chapter 8.** An objection against what has been said.
**Chapter 9.** The objection is resolved and it is shown that neither the specific nor the individual differences of things depend on the motion of the heavens.
**Chapter 10.** That stars other than the sun and moon either have no effect on us, or certainly very little.
**Chapter 11.** By what means the same stars can act on us differently at different times.
**Chapter 12.** What variety of effects can be traced back to the heavens and what cannot.
**Chapter 13.** That the sun performs many things which astrologers think are done by other stars.
**Chapter 14.** How the power of the moon varies and that certain days of the moon are observed without superstition. page 97
**Chapter 15.** That the tides of the sea can be attributed to another cause than the moon; and even if they are so attributed, astrology is not helped by it. page 98
**Chapter 16.** The opinion of Galen <note>A prominent Greek physician whose theories dominated Western medicine for centuries.</note> concerning <term>critical days<note>original: "creticis diebus"; days in a disease's progress where a significant change or "crisis" was expected.</note></term>, referring them to the moon, is refuted. 99
**Chapter 17.** That the periods of the <term>humors<note>The four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) believed to control health and temperament.</note></term> are not to be referred to the movements of the stars. 101
**Chapter 18.** That the misfortune of an eight-month birth is not to be ascribed to Saturn. 101
**Chapter 19.** Why sailors, doctors, and farmers predict the truth more often than astrologers. 101
**Chapter 20.** That not all things predicted by astrologers depend on the primary qualities <note>The basic qualities of hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note>. 101
**Chapter 21.** Neither the harms of the elements nor the damage to our bodies are from the heavens. 102
**Chapter 22.** That the variety of intellects and characters does not depend entirely on the primary qualities. 102
**Chapter 23.** Neither wars nor external events depend on the primary qualities. 102
**Chapter 24.** That occult powers <note>Hidden or supernatural forces.</note> do not exist in the celestial bodies through which they might produce the hidden properties of lower things; but only heat and life-giving light. 103
**Chapter 25.** If its own proper power is granted to each star, it is nevertheless a universal one. 103
**Chapter 26.** The epilogue of this book, with the rejection of certain arguments of the astrologers by turning them back against those arguing. 104
**Chapter 27.** 104

The fourth book contains a discussion of the heavens' efficiency and significance. 105

**Chapter 1.** What method was observed in disputing and is to be observed hereafter: and that even if that which the theologians grant most fully were given to the astrologers, astrology would still be nothing. 105
**Chapter 2.** That fortuitous <note>Random or chance</note> events are not from the heavens. 105

<column-break/>

**Chapter 3.** How God is the cause of fortuitous things: how angels, how the heavens, how we ourselves, and how fortune. 105
**Chapter 4.** That if anything is done by us which seems to exceed our powers, it is not to be referred to the heavens, but rather either to angels or to God; and therein much about fate and how divine providence does not take away our liberty. 106
**Chapter 5.** That neither the past nor things pertaining to others can be foreseen from any constellation. 107
**Chapter 6.** That future events far distant in time cannot be produced by a present constellation. 108
**Chapter 7.** Concerning "auspices" which they call "elections" <note>The practice of choosing an astrologically "lucky" time to begin an endeavor.</note>: how vain and impossible the astrologers' opinion is. 108
**Chapter 8.** That astrologers subject our minds to the heavens, although they try to hide this, being shrewd as they are. 109
**Chapter 9.** That human morals are not created by the heavens. 109
**Chapter 10.** That bad laws, just like good ones, are not subject to the heavens. 109
**Chapter 11.** That physical dispositions are not produced by the heavens. 109
**Chapter 12.** That the heavens cannot be a sign of that thing for which they are not the cause. 110
**Chapter 13.** Whether the stars are signs or causes, that part of astrology which concerns <term>interrogations<note>The practice of casting a chart to answer a specific question.</note></term> is nothing. 110
**Chapter 14.** That divine miracles are neither performed nor signified by the heavens; but miracles are indicated by miracles, just as natural things are indicated by natural things. 110
**Chapter 15.** That no constellation can be understood by the Star of the Magi; and an explanation of certain scriptures which might seem to the unskilled to support astrology. 111
**Chapter 16.** That things which exceed the powers of nature, even regarding what they contain that is natural in themselves, cannot be signified by the heavens. 111

The fifth book contains a refutation of those constellations to which they ascribe the great events of human affairs.

**Chapter 1.** That the decrees of astrologers concerning great conjunctions are usefully refuted, and those who wish to judge great changes of lower things through them are caught as liars. 112
**Chapter 2.** By what ways astrologers pass judgment on grander things, and a rejection of the "great orbs." 112
**Chapter 3.** That the Saturnian revolutions, an invention of <term>Abu Ma'shar<note>original: "Aboafaris"; a 9th-century Persian astrologer influential in the medieval West.</note></term>, are contrary to both history and reason. 112
**Chapter 4.** The order of things to be said, and the differing opinions of astrologers regarding great conjunctions. 113
**Chapter 5.** That planets joined in great conjunctions have no more power than when separate; and those great conjunctions are a new invention born from a bad understanding of <term>Ptolemy<note>The 2nd-century author of the *Tetrabiblos*, the foundational text of Western astrology.</note></term>. 113
**Chapter 6.** That the principal astrologers used mean <note>Average or mathematical</note> conjunctions rather than true ones; then other errors of theirs concerning the same. 114
**Chapter 7.** What order is to be kept, and that <term>Pierre d'Ailly<note>original: "Alliacensem"; a French cardinal who wrote on the "concordance" of astrology and history.</note></term> thought one thing at one time and another at another. 114
**Chapter 8.** That the timing of events is not to be sought from astrology, as d'Ailly thought, but from history. 115
**Chapter 9.** The summary of d'Ailly's opinion in the book which he titled *On the Concordance of Astrology and History*. 115
**Chapter 10.** That d'Ailly erred in many ways: and even if whatever he supposes were granted, he still does not achieve what he wants. 115
**Chapter 11.** That concerning the conjunction of the Flood, the astrologers differed both among themselves and from the truth; and even if they were given whatever they ask, they still do not prove what they contend. 115
**Chapter 12.** How delirious <term>Abraham the Jew<note>Abraham Ibn Ezra.</note></term> was concerning the conjunction of Moses and the prophecy of the Messiah. 116
**Chapter 13.** That the Christian law is ascribed by various people to various mean conjunctions, even without astrological reason. 116
**Chapter 14.** That the <term>geniture<note>A birth horoscope.</note></term> of Jesus which is commonly cited is not true, nor is it indicated by it that He would die a violent death, or that He is a great prophet. 117

-># TABLE OF DISPUTATIONS<-

**Chapter 15.** What <term>Albumasar<note>Abu Ma'shar, a highly influential 9th-century Persian astrologer.</note></term> said about Muhammad <note>original: "maumethe"</note> has been found false by experience.
**Chapter 16.** That in the prophecy of the Antichrist some have already appeared as liars, and others will be liars in the future.
**Chapter 17.** How weakly the astrologers prove there can only be six religions; likewise that the law of the Hebrews should be called "Jovian" <note>governed by Jupiter</note> or "Solar" rather than "Saturnian."
***
->The sixth book contains the refutation of those things by which they claim the celestial influences vary.<-

**Chapter 1.** In what order one must proceed in tearing down the foundations of the astrologers: likewise that it is impossible for all the stars to ever be restored to the same positions in which they once were <note>This refers to the "Great Year," a theoretical cycle where all planets return to a starting point, which Pico argues is mathematically impossible.</note>.
**Chapter 2.** By what means astrologers say the influences of the stars vary, and how altogether absurd their claims are in every respect.
**Chapter 3.** How the <term>Houses<note>The twelve divisions of the sky in a natal chart, distinct from the signs of the zodiac.</note></term> of the astrologers rely on no foundation, and how astrologers fight among themselves in explaining their powers.
**Chapter 4.** Concerning the twelve signs, that they were fabricated by mathematicians for the ease of calculation: likewise that the astrologers have erred in many ways regarding them. 119
**Chapter 5.** What the opinion of the astrologers is regarding <term>Aspects<note>The geometric angles between planets, such as squares or trines.</note></term>, and how little it is based on reason. 120
**Chapter 6.** Various theories of the aspects are recited and refuted. 121
**Chapter 7.** What deceived them: and that no experience has been gained concerning the aspects. 121
**Chapter 8.** That the things said about "obsession" <note>being "besieged" or hemmed in by malevolent planets</note> conflict with those said about aspects. 122
**Chapter 9.** That planets positioned under the rays of the sun are not badly affected, nor "combust" <note>the astrological term for a planet weakened by being too close to the sun</note> as the astrologers claim. 122
**Chapter 10.** If we wish to follow reason and even the authority of certain astrologers, <term>Retrograde<note>When a planet appears to move backward in the sky.</note></term> planets seem stronger than those moving direct. 122
**Chapter 11.** That the <term>Head and Tail<note>The Lunar Nodes (Caput and Cauda Draconis), the points where the moon's path crosses the sun's path.</note></term> are intersections of imaginary circles with no natural power of the aforementioned kind, which the ancients did not use in predicting: nor do the moderns agree on their powers. 122
**Chapter 12.** The origin of <term>Antiscia<note>Points in the zodiac that are equidistant from the solstice points.</note></term>: that Ptolemy did not use them in presaging and how much <term>Firmicus Maternus<note>A 4th-century Roman lawyer and astrologer.</note></term> and <term>Haly<note>Haly Abenragel, an 11th-century Arab astrologer.</note></term> erred in these matters. 123
**Chapter 13.** That the astrologers were equally deceived regarding "commanding" and "obeying" signs. 123
**Chapter 14.** Refutation of the reasons which certain astrologers assigned for the "exaltations" <note>specific signs where a planet is thought to have maximum power</note> of the planets. 123
**Chapter 15.** The reasons of the astrologers concerning <term>Trigons<note>Also called triplicities; groups of three signs belonging to the same element (Fire, Earth, Air, Water).</note></term> and the masters of the trigons: and in passing, the gender of the signs is refuted. 124
**Chapter 16.** Concerning "faces," "terms," <term>Dodecatemoria<note>The division of a single zodiac sign into twelve smaller parts.</note></term>, the Babylonian ninths, and the "monomiris": how little they agree even with the testimony of Ptolemy himself. 125
**Chapter 17.** Concerning feminine, bright, and dark degrees: and other things of that kind which Ptolemy despised, nor do other astrologers agree on them. 125
**Chapter 18.** From whence the <term>Parts<note>Also known as "Arabic Parts" or "Lots," mathematical points calculated from the positions of other planets.</note></term> arose and how much the astrologers fight among themselves in measuring them. 126
**Chapter 19.** The opinion on the Dodecatemoria is exploded, and their Egyptian authors are rejected along with their <term>Climacteric Years<note>Specific years in a person's life (multiples of 7 or 9) thought to be especially dangerous.</note></term>. 126
***
->The seventh book contains the discussion on the initial hour, "directions," and fixed stars. 127<-

**Chapter 1.** What has been discussed so far: and what is to be discussed in this book. 127
**Chapter 2.** That the "fatal hour" is ambiguous, if indeed there were one in all things which are completed not in a moment but over time: and in men

<column-break/>

especially, in whom the <term>Horoscope<note>original: "genitura"; the birth chart or the moment of birth.</note></term> seems to have little strength. 127
**Chapter 3.** That <term>Ptolemy<note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century author of the *Tetrabiblos*, the "bible" of traditional astrology.</note></term> attributed more to conception than to birth, to which the reasoning of Ptolemy convinces us that nothing should be attributed. 127
**Chapter 4.** By what ways astrologers track "universal events," and how little they are based on reason. 128
**Chapter 5.** That the astrologer does not predict in which region of the world a certain fate will occur: since it is uncertain among them which region is subject to which sign or planet. 120
**Chapter 6.** That a single beginning cannot be established upon which the fates of the whole year depend, as different beginnings of the year are established by different people; and according to the Hebrews, the year begins in autumn rather than in spring. 128
**Chapter 7.** Concerning <term>Directions<note>A predictive technique where one degree of movement in the sky is equated to one year of life.</note></term> and other ways by which they define the timing of future events: how little they agree and how much the astrologers differ among themselves in these. 129

->The eighth book contains the discussion on the number of spheres, the difference between constellations and signs, and invisible images. 132<-

**Chapter 2.** If there is another sphere above the eighth, the old astrology is false: if there is none, the new is false: which, even if there is a ninth, must necessarily collapse entirely. 132

# GIOVANNI FRANCESCO PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA
## TO LUDOVICO MARIA SFORZA VISCONTI ANGLUS <note>original: "VICECO MITI ANGLO"; This refers to the Sforza family's claim of descent from the Visconti and the legendary figure Anglus, common in the titulature of the Dukes of Milan.</note>
### DUKE OF THE MILANESE, SENDS MANY GREETINGS.

-><image-desc>Decorative woodcut headpiece consisting of symmetrical scrolling foliage and floral motifs.</image-desc><-

<margin>admonition</margin>
<image-desc>Ornate woodcut initial 'Q' containing a miniature portrait of a man, possibly a scholar or saint, seated in a landscape with trees and distant hills.</image-desc>Those who have handed down the lives of illustrious men written for the reading of posterity, most illustrious Prince, have done so for various reasons. Some acted so that the names of those to whom they were bound by blood or to whom they owed a debt of education would not fade away through consuming antiquity, but would be entirely rescued from the injury of oblivion; Pliny showed this kind of piety toward his uncle Pliny <note>Pliny the Younger and Pliny the Elder</note>, and Porphyry toward his teacher Plotinus. Others, however, did this very thing even more purposefully—not so much for the eternal memory of the deceased as to provide a model for the lives of those still living. For this reason, we find that the tireless studies, most exact morals, and most famous works of Hilarion, Jerome, Athanasius, Antony, Martin, Severus, Paulinus, and Ambrose <note>A list of Church Fathers and Saints whose biographies served as moral guides.</note> were committed to paper. From these, the glory of God has spread through the world, and men are even now spurred toward living well and blessedly by both their teaching and their character. Enticed by their examples, I thought I would be doing something worthwhile if I were to pursue the life of Giovanni Pico <note>The author's uncle, the famous philosopher Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494).</note> with my pen.
<margin>praise</margin>
I do this partly to fulfill a debt of service to my uncle—who was also my teacher, and by whose spiritual benefits I have been enriched and overwhelmed—and partly to present to our own and future ages a man worthy of admiration. By his example, mortals can be instructed in frugality and warned of impending death, but also be abundantly enriched in learning. For among the widely learned men of our time (not to mention antiquity), he held the first place beyond all risk of doubt. This may be an enviable word to say, but it is undoubtedly true. This will not seem strange to those who have explored him "inside and under the skin" (as the saying goes), nor to those who 
<margin>eloquence</margin>
shall eventually learn that he knew five languages <note>Pico was famous for studying Latin, Greek, Hebrew, Arabic, and Aramaic.</note>, was a master of human and divine philosophy, and had drunk deeply from every discipline in use among mortals—and indeed had unearthed some from the shadows and even devised others—before he had even completed his eleventh three-year cycle <note>original: "undena trieteride"; A trieterid is a three-year period. 11 x 3 = 33. Pico died at age 31.</note>.
<margin>credibility</margin>
Full testimony will be provided by those commentaries, never sufficiently celebrated for their merits, which are now coming forth into the public: 
<margin>Heptaplus</margin>
the *Heptaplus* <note>Pico’s mystical seven-fold explanation of the six days of creation in Genesis.</note>, the *Apology* <note>Pico's defense of his 900 theses against charges of heresy.</note>, and the treatise *On Being and the One*, and several others. All are so brilliant by their own nature and commended by the judgments of so many wise men that anyone who condemns them, or approves them less, or does not exalt them with the highest praises, immediately brings judgment against himself, or falls under suspicion of a malicious mind that is ignorant of literature. As many may envy him as may admire him, or as the very few may imitate him, or as no one may find fault with him. His remaining writings will be published in the following order: especially
<margin>astrological</margin>
the refutations of the astrological plague. These were composed with great labor, and have been expected and demanded with many sighs by men of well-ordered minds. They have been reduced by us with great effort into a single body from a torn copy that was ripped into many parts. They will soon be released so that, as quickly as possible, they may illuminate with their life-giving splendor eyes that are dimmed and infected by the foul vapor of superstitions. If you taste these books occasionally when you are at leisure from handling the business of the state, you will become certain beyond all controversy that the dogmas of the astrologers are the purest nonsense and like the dreams of those in a delirium. Their deceptions are exposed by these 
<margin>monuments</margin>
monuments <note>A classical way of referring to enduring literary works.</note>. Once these have been read and understood, the professors of that vanity—who, imitating the frogs of our land, have croaked for a long time—will fall silent like the Macedonian frogs <note>An ancient proverb: frogs in certain parts of Macedonia were said to be silent.</note>, unless they fall into open madness. I remember that I perhaps testified to this to you in some part while we were debating this matter. In the meantime, look upon these works with a willing mind; I decided they should be dedicated to no one more than to you. I did this so you might recognize that my loyalty and respect for you—which you saw and tested while I earned my wages in your service—has not only not been forgotten, but perseveres and increases daily. I thought I would be doing something not unpleasing to you, since the dignity of these books is such that the greatest kings have always considered it honorable and glorious to have them inscribed to themselves. It remains for me, with the love I have for you, to exhort you to 
<margin>justice</margin>
perform the duties of two-fold justice, and to invite you to constantly remember (which is always the duty of a most prudent prince) that your reign is not so much an honor as it is an <term>onus</term> <note>burden</note> <term>q</term><note>Abbreviation for "quod" or "quia" (that/because).</note>; so that, having looked around at the impediments that beset both a man and a prince, you may be able to overcome them with the most moderate passions and earn for yourself eternal happiness. Farewell, most famous Prince. At Mirandola, on the Kalends of March <note>March 1st</note>, 1496.

<meta>This page begins the formal biography of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, written by his nephew Gianfrancesco. It transitions from the previous page's dedication to the Duke of Milan into the narrative of Pico's life, starting with his lineage, miraculous birth, and early education.</meta>

# THE LIFE OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA, A MAN OF THE MOST CONSUMMATE SKILL IN EVERY KIND OF DISCIPLINE,
## PUBLISHED BY GIOVANNI FRANCESCO, SON OF THE ILLUSTRIOUS PRINCE
### GALEOTTO PICO.

---

Having begun to write the life of my uncle Giovanni, I consider it my first duty to tell my readers (lest they suspect me of speaking out of favor or flattery, as either a nephew or a student) that nothing here is granted to friendship, nothing to family, and nothing repaid with false praise for the great benefits he bestowed upon me. Indeed, my narrative is as far removed from adulation as the necessity of flattering was absent; I have taken great care lest those reading me think I have either lied or been too vehement in my praises. Had I committed to writing everything I had conceived of him, there might perhaps have been a danger that his own sublime virtues, or those who defend them, could prove me too sparse in my account. One can see the truth of this from the fact that many of the most refined writings of the learned men of our age—indeed, of the leaders among them—have not only provided the richest testimony to what I am about to say, but while he still lived, and after he exchanged this light for a better one, they surpassed me in their heraldry of his character and learning. I have ordered some of these to be inscribed at the end of this book, after his own commentaries, so that a firmer faith might be placed in witnesses who are not of his own kin.

<margin>Paternal lineage.</margin>
Leaving aside his paternal lineage (although it is recorded in memory that he drew his origins from the Emperor Constantine through his great-grandson Pico, from whom the surname of the entire family is derived), we shall begin at the time of his birth. This is partly because he perhaps brought no less honor to the family than he received from it, and partly because I have chosen to reveal the specific gifts of his mind and the rest of the sequence of his life and death, which I have either drawn from my own eyes and ears or received from the most serious witnesses. I have set aside the four hundred years of the deeds of his ancestors that could be recounted. In the year 1463 after the birth of the Virgin <note>1463 AD</note>, while Pope Pius II was the supreme head of the Church and Frederick III held the reins of the Roman Empire, his mother Julia, from the noble Boiardo family, gave birth to him, her last child, for her husband Giovanni Francesco. She had already born Galeotto the elder (from whom I was sired) and Antonio Maria, as well as two sisters. One of these sisters, as the wife of Leonello, gave birth to Alberto Pio (one of the princes of Carpi) and is now the consort of Prince Rodolfo Gonzaga. The other, after the death of her first husband, Prince Pino Ordelaffi of Forlì, entered a second marriage with the Count of Monteagano.

<margin>
Mother Julia.
Giovanni Francesco, the father.
Galeotto and Antonio Maria, brothers.
Alberto Pio.
</margin>
<margin>A prodigy</margin>
A great prodigy appeared before his birth. A circular flame was seen to stand above the chamber of the laboring mother and then soon vanish. This perhaps suggested to us that he would be most similar in the perfection of his intellect to the circular figure <note>The circle was considered the most perfect geometric shape in Renaissance philosophy.</note>, he who was brought forth among mortals at that same hour, and that he would be celebrated everywhere across the entire globe for the excellence of his name. His mind was always to seek heavenly things like fire, and his fiery eloquence, in harmony with his flaming mind, was destined to celebrate with all its strength our God (who is a consuming fire), but then to be hidden by death, just as that flame vanished. Indeed, we read that unusual signs have sometimes preceded or followed the births of the most learned and holy men, as if the divine will were separating the cradles of these infants from the throng of others and indicating they were born for the greatest deeds. Thus, to omit others:

<column-break/>

<margin>Ambrose.</margin>
A swarm of bees hovered over the mouth of the great Ambrose <note>St. Ambrose of Milan</note>; they entered it, and then exiting and flying very high, hiding themselves among the clouds, they escaped the sight of his father and the others present. Paulinus, making much of this omen in his writings, argued that it showed him to be a speaker of oracles who would announce heavenly gifts and raise the minds of men from the earth to heaven.

<margin>Form and build of the body.</margin>
His appearance was distinguished and noble: he was of tall and lofty stature, with soft flesh. His face was beautiful overall, with a pale complexion interspersed with a becoming redness; his eyes were grey and alert, and his hair was blond and natural. His teeth were also white and even. Brought to teachers and discipline under his mother's authority, he cultivated the study of the humanities with such an ardent spirit that he was soon—and not without merit—to be ranked among the chief poets and orators of that time.

<margin>Swift intellect.</margin>
In learning, he was indeed most swift, endowed with such a ready intellect that, having heard a poem once, he could recite it both forwards and in reverse order, to the wonder of everyone; he retained it with a most tenacious memory. This usually happens the opposite way for others: for it often happens by nature that those who have a swift intellect do not have a strong memory, while those who perceive with labor become more tenacious of what they have perceived.

When he was fourteen years old, by the command of his mother, who strongly desired him to be initiated into the sacred rites, he moved to Bologna for the purpose of learning Pontifical Law <note>Canon Law</note>. After he had tasted this for two years, seeing that it rested on mere traditions, he turned elsewhere. Yet he did not leave without a harvest of good fruit: for even as a boy, and a very tender one at that, he compiled a certain "Epitome" or "Breviary" from the letters of the Popes (which they call Decretals). In this, he concluded all the meanings of those sanctions as concisely as possible—a work of no small weight even for seasoned professors.

<margin>A boy skilled in Pontifical Law.</margin>
But as an eager explorer of the secrets of nature, leaving these worn paths, he devoted himself entirely to the speculation of the intellect and to philosophy, both human and divine. For the sake of acquiring this, he traveled through the literary gymnasiums not only of Italy but also of the Gauls <note>France, specifically the University of Paris</note>, searching out the famous teachers of that time with the same scrupulousness as Plato and Apollonius. He spent such untiring labor on these studies that he was, and was considered to be, at once both a consummate theologian and a philosopher while still beardless.

He had already spent seven years among them when, eager for human praise and glory (for he did not yet burn with divine love, as will become clear), he traveled to Rome. There, wishing to show how much envy would later await him from the most eminent men, he proposed nine hundred questions on dialectics, mathematics, natural, and divine things.

<margin>Nine hundred conclusions proposed at Rome for dispute.</margin>
These were drawn not only from the stores of the Latins and excerpted from the cabinets of the Greeks, but even unearthed from the mysteries of the Hebrews, and tracked down from the secrets of the Chaldeans and Arabs. He also wove into those questions many things concerning the ancient and somewhat obscure philosophy of Pythagoras, Trismegistus <note>Hermes Trismegistus</note>, and Orpheus, and many things concerning the Kabbalah <note>Cabala</note>—that is, the reception of the secret dogmas of the Hebrews, which Origen and Hilary among our own people specifically mention.

<margin>Origen, Hilary.</margin>
He also included many things concerning "natural magic," which he taught was separated by a great distance from impious and wicked magic. This he proved most elegantly by the testimony of many. Nor were seventy-two new physical and metaphysical dogmas lacking—his own inventions and meditations, adapted to elucidate any questions of philosophy. To these, he annexed a new method of philosophizing through numbers. He posted all of these at once in public places so they might be more easily spread, promising that he would pay the expenses of those who traveled to Rome from remote lands for the sake of debating. But because of the grudge of detractors (which always, like fire, seeks high places), he could never bring it about that...

<meta>This page continues the biography of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, shifting from his early education to the great controversy in Rome regarding his nine hundred theses. It describes the opposition he faced, his written defense (the Apologia), his moral transformation, and his subsequent devotion to sacred scripture.</meta>

# THE LIFE OF GIOVANNI PICO OF MIRANDOLA

<margin>Detractors and the envious</margin>
...until a day for the debate could be appointed. For this reason, he remained in Rome for a year. During this time, his detractors did not dare to attack him openly or in a free examination; instead, they attempted to undermine him through tricks and hidden plots, stabbing at him with the weapons of secrecy, driven by a poisonous and corrupt envy. (Indeed, many were of the opinion that they were moved to such malice for this reason: it was thought that many who had applied themselves to literary pursuits out of ambition or greed feared their own reputations would be tarnished if this young man—endowed with the ancestral wealth he had gathered and great learning—were to risk his reputation and intellect in the primary city of the world, discussing natural and divine matters and many things that had been inaccessible to our people for many centuries, like a fertile field flourishing in its first bloom.) When they realized they could achieve nothing against his learning with honest means, they brought forth the engines of slander. Out of his nine hundred questions, they cried out that thirteen were suspect of heresy. To these detractors, some others perhaps joined themselves—men whose ears were unaccustomed to such questions—who attacked him perhaps less out of erudition than out of a pious but misguided zeal for the faith and under the pretext of religion. Nevertheless, many celebrated doctors of theology had previously approved and signed these same questions as pious and blameless. Among this group <margin>Bonfranciscus, Bishop of Reggio</margin> was Bonfranciscus, the Bishop of Reggio, a man of all-encompassing learning, the sharpest judgment, and distinguished gravity of character, who was serving at that time in Rome as the ambassador to the Pope for the Duke of Ferrara. Those loudmouths attempted nothing against him, perhaps fearing they could not shake his reputation, since whatever he handled he submitted to the correction of Holy Mother Church and the Pope. 

But Pico, not enduring this damage to his reputation, <margin>The Apologia</margin> published his *Apologia* <note>original: "Apologiam"; a formal written defense of his ideas</note>, a work certainly varied and elegant, filled with the knowledge of many things worth knowing, which he composed in only twenty nights of study. In this edition, it was seen clearer than light that not only could his conclusions be understood in a Catholic sense, but that those who had previously barked against them were to be convicted of insolence and ignorance. As a most Christian man, he committed the book itself and whatever he might write in the future to the judgment of Mother Church and its most holy leader. He was fully persuaded that this ought to be done either expressly or tacitly, as if he were quoting that saying of Augustine: <margin>I can err, but not be a heretic</margin> *“I am able to err, but I cannot be a heretic,”* <note>original: "Errare possum haereticus esse non possum"</note> since the former is a human trait, while the latter belongs to a perverse and obstinate will. 

But when Pope Innocent VIII <margin>Pope Innocent VIII</margin> learned through the publication of the *Apologia* that those conclusions, which had previously been infested by slanders, had been interpreted in a Catholic sense and relieved of the mark of crime; and when several people to whom the examination of the conclusions had been entrusted reported that traps could be set for the faithful if some of those questions (which lay there in a raw and unrefined state, according to the manner of debate) were to wander about everywhere, he forbade the reading of the booklet <margin>Alexander VI</margin> in which they were contained. All of this can be clearly seen through the Decree (which they call a "Brief") of Pope Alexander VI, under whom we now live, which we have decided to hand over to the printers to be transcribed along with the *Apologia* itself. 

Indeed, at the very end of the *Apologia*, Pico had already done by his own reasoning what the Pope later provided by authority. For he had entreated his friends and enemies, the learned and the unlearned, <margin>Note</margin> to read the *Apologia*, but to keep the booklet of theses for private meetings, as it contained many things not to be spread everywhere in the streets, <margin>Alexander and Averroes</margin> but to be undertaken for dispute in secret gatherings among the learned and the few. Following the scholastic exercise in the manner of the academies, he had proposed many impious dogmas of the ancient philosophers—namely Alexander <note>likely Alexander of Aphrodisias</note>, Averroes, and many others—which he had always asserted, professed, and preached, both publicly and privately, to be as far from true and right philosophy as they were from the paths of faith. And speaking in this manner about that booklet of nine hundred conclusions, he concluded his defensive work: "Therefore, let those who hate me not read those things because they are mine; let those who love me not read them because from those things which are mine, they might think

<column-break/>

<margin>The goodness of God</margin> of many things which are not ours." Furthermore, he judged it to be an effect of the immense goodness of God, which draws good even out of evil (as he related to me), that the slander falsely inflicted by spiteful men should correct his true errors. It shone upon him as a most splendid beam of light while he was wandering in the darkness, so that he might behold how far he had drifted from the path of truth. 

<margin>Freed from general vanity and lustful affection</margin> For previously, he had been both desirous of glory and kindled by vain love, moved by womanly allurements. Indeed, many women, on account of the beauty of his body and the grace of his face—to which were added his learning, ample riches, and nobility of birth—burned with love for him. Not shrinking from their devotion, he had for a little while neglected the way of life and slipped into delights. <margin>Conversion of his soul to God</margin> But truly awakened by those events, he restrained his mind which was dissolving in luxury and turned it toward Christ. He exchanged feminine flatteries for the joys of the heavenly fatherland. Neglecting the "glorious air" <note>worldly fame or reputation</note> which he had sought, he began to seek with his whole mind the glory of God and the utility of the Church. He so composed his character that from then on he could be approved even by the judgment of an enemy. 

When the glorious report of him began immediately to fly through both neighboring and remote lands, many of the philosophers who were considered the most learned flocked to him, as if to a "market of the good arts" (as Cicero says), <margin>Cicero</margin> either to stir up literary contests or (for those who possessed a more upright mind) to hear and hold fast the healthy dogmas of right living. These were sought after all the more because they flowed from a man who was most learned and equally noble, and who had once followed the devious windings of luxurious softness. For those things seem to have the greatest weight in instilling moral discipline into the minds of listeners which are both good by their own nature and proceed from a teacher who has turned to the paths of justice from the distorted and crooked path of lusts. 

<margin>Love poems burned; Study of sacred letters</margin> He had toyed with love in elegiac verse, which, having been composed in five books, he committed to the flames for the sake of religion. He likewise toyed with many things in Italian rhymes <note>original: "Rhithmis... Hetruscis"; Tuscan/Italian verses</note>, which a similar fire consumed. Then, embracing the Sacred Letters with the most burning zeal, he immediately offered in the temple of God—as if the first fruits of his harvest—his work on the six days of Genesis and the day of rest, the *Heptaplus*, being then twenty-eight years old. <margin>At age 28 he offered the work of 6 days and the Heptaplus</margin> It was a work perfect in genius and elaborated with industry, most full of the sublime dogmas of the philosophers and the most profound mysteries of our Christian theology. It was connected by a seven-fold varied narration, with a seven-fold number of chapters assigned to each seven-fold exposition, matching the name of the book perfectly. Yet, because of the things unearthed from the bosom of nature, the difficult unrolling of divine questions, the most hidden meanings of the Prophet <note>Moses, the traditional author of Genesis</note>, and the elegance of its speech, it does not offer itself everywhere to those unrefined in philosophy and eloquence. Rather, the use of that precious and rare furniture is prepared for the few. Noticing this himself, he made a charming mention of this matter at the end of the same preface. 

As soon as he <margin>What he declared about sacred letters; Paul's epistles, which he said surpassed all writings</margin> first tasted the Sacred Letters, he exulted with joy, finding in them not only true wisdom but also true eloquence. To omit many things, he used to say that they surpassed the writings of everyone else in eloquence, specifically citing the works of Cicero himself and Demosthenes, the primary masters of speaking. This was not because they were "singed with curling irons" <note>a metaphor for overly artificial or ornate style</note> or stuffed with gathered-up pigments and ringlets, but so that they might smell and taste of true, solid eloquence, supported by true sentiments and true art. They were, to say it briefly, not deliberately stuffed with the "wealth of the Egyptians" <note>a common metaphor for using pagan learning in Christian service</note>. Furthermore, <margin>The words of the Old Law; Augustine, Septimius, Eusebius, Cassiodorus, Tertullian</margin> he preached that all the words of the Old Law were full of the most consummate science and wisdom. Although Augustine (in his book *On Christian Doctrine*), Tertullian, Eusebius, and Cassiodorus clearly show this and affirm that the grammarians, rhetoricians, orators, and all the ancient philosophers drank the streams of their eloquence and learning from the fountains of the Divine Scriptures, he himself put forward other reasons for this gift, part of which he expressed in the introductions to the most celebrated *Heptaplus*...

<meta>This page continues the biography of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola by his nephew, Gianfrancesco Pico. # THE LIFE OF GIOVANNI PICO OF MIRANDOLA

<margin>The book *On Being and the One* was completed in the second year after the *Heptaplus*.</margin>
...and it is worth seeing in the very preface of that second exposition. Amidst so many continuous unfoldings of the Divine Law <note>This refers to his deep study of the Bible and Jewish mysticism</note>, in the second year after the publication of the *Heptaplus* <note>Pico's famous commentary on the seven days of the creation in Genesis</note>, he also completed a small work titled *On Being and the One*, divided into ten chapters. It is brief in its physical size, but vast in its intellectual power. It is sprinkled throughout with the deepest doctrines of the philosophers and with theological insights. In it, he demonstrates that "Being" is not superior to "the One," but that they correspond to each other and are equal in scope. He reviewed the controversy held on this matter by the followers of Plato and Aristotle, asserting that those Academics who contended for the opposite had not truly grasped Plato's dogma. He intended to show that there was no lack of commonality in meaning between Aristotle and Plato regarding the One and Being—as with everything else in general—even if their words seemed to disagree. In the final chapter of the work, he turns the entire dispute toward the instruction of life and the improvement of morals, doing so no less ingeniously than religiously.

<margin>Note.</margin>
Against this work, Antonio of Faenza <margin>Antonio of Faenza.</margin>, an outstanding philosopher of the time, brought forth some objections in four letters. Pico himself responded to three of them; however, to the fourth—either because it was not faithfully delivered, or because he thought it could be answered from what he had already written, or for some other cause which we must believe was just—he made no mention of it that I know of. After he departed this life, I myself took up the duty of responding, so that an opportunity would not be given to the malevolent to bark falsehoods, or to the unlearned to believe something sinister. I took the greatest care to show that, from Pico's own previous statements, a response had already been largely provided.

<margin>Some Platonic matters.</margin>
We have also seen several Platonic works arranged by him in the vernacular tongue <note>The "vernacular" refers to Italian, as opposed to the scholarly Latin</note>. In these, many things are found that serve to unravel the theology of the ancients, and many things reflecting the hidden wisdom of the sages buried in riddles and writings. Perhaps, having found greater leisure, we will attempt to render these into Latin, lest the towering doctrine of such a man regarding these most accessible matters be carried only before the eyes of the common people. Thus far concerning the completed labors which he had sent out before his death.

<margin>The Old Testament interpreted.</margin>
These were like messengers and forerunners of the even more magnificent works he had conceived and was proceeding with. For he was already illuminating the Old Testament with the torches of interpretation, being prepared to perform the same service for the New. He brought forth not only those meanings which the literal sequence of the text could carry, but on those sites which were to bear the three high levels of divine eloquence, he built further. He compared the Greek and Hebrew explanations with the discordant readings of our own Latin codices. But this was foremost in his mind: among all the projects he had conceived in the genre of commentary, it sat most deeply within him that he would not merely bring forward the dogmas of others—since those were already possessed, read, and known—but would instead set forth his own discoveries and meditations, so that he might satisfy hungry souls seeking truth with his own resources, not those of others, to the best of his ability.

<margin>The book *On the Truth of Jerome’s Translation*; the book *On the True Calculation of Times*.</margin>
After this, being proficient in the Hebrew idiom, he published a small book on the truth of Jerome's translation <note>St. Jerome's Latin Vulgate</note> against the slanders of the Jews. He also wrote a defense for the Seventy Translators <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek version of the Old Testament</note> regarding the Psalms against the same critics, as well as a book on the true calculation of time. Finally, he had turned his mind toward defeating the seven enemies of the Church. For whoever obeys neither Christ nor His Church is consequently His enemy: either as an impious person who receives no dogma to be believed; or if he serves false idols and worships demons under these images; or if he observes the Mosaic law after the ritual of the most lost Jews; or follows the unspeakable Muhammad, enslaved to his detestable decrees; or lives a Christian life in hearing only, not in works and a sincere mind, perverting the evangelical teachings and not consenting to the Catholic Church, kicking back with an obstinate heart; or accepts the Gospels not with a chaste faith, but one adulterated and profaned by various superstitions; or even if he has received the faith with solid, clear, and constant belief, he opposes it by his works. These seven he had summoned to the encounter, like leaders under whom the rest are contained as common soldiers, intending to fight them with their own weapons. Against the impious philosophers, who, depressed by the yoke of no religion and addicted to no deity, worship only natural reasons, he fought with those same reasons.

<column-break/>

Against the Jews, he fought most powerfully with the declarations of the Old Testament and the specific authorities of the Jewish schools. With the Muslims, he joined battle relying on the Quran. He prostrated the worshipers of idols with many wounds, and no fewer against those ensnared by vain superstitions—especially those who worship divinatory astrology. He had sharply criticized these with both true philosophy and the specific arguments of the astrologers. In twelve completed books (out of thirteen destined for this purpose), he had pursued their delusions. Finally, he had exploded, one by one, hydromancy, geomancy, pyromancy, divination by entrails, and other vanities of that kind. But he directed his battle line specifically against the prophesying astrologers, and had aimed his battering ram with all his strength, since other superstitions catch at their futiliies and supports for their errors from those dogmas—either weighing the moments of an inspected birth <note>Casting a natal horoscope</note>, or in choosing hours, or seeking the "favorable" influences of hexagons or triangles <note>Astrological aspects: sextiles and trines</note>, and other such things that even the mad Orestes <note>A classical reference to Orestes, who was driven mad by the Furies</note> would not approach. Nor was he content to have utterly overturned all astrology; he wished to show that the astrologers of our time, being mostly ignorant of the Greek language, had made astrology (the vainest of all professions) even vainer, if such a thing can be said, through perverse translations.

<margin>Ptolemy’s *Centiloquium* translated from Greek into Latin.</margin>
While writing against these people, as if doing something else, he translated the "Fruits" of Ptolemy, which the common people call the *Centiloquium* <note>A collection of 100 astrological aphorisms</note>, from the Greek language into Latin and honored it with a most elegant exposition. In this book, he demonstrates that more errors (so to speak) than words are contained in that common translation, which the lazy followers of the art nevertheless always guarded in secret like a precious treasure. Regarding those who think wrongly of the faith of Christ and do not obey the commands of Mother Church—whom we call by the common name "heretics"—he had attacked them with both the New Testament and outstanding arguments in a magnificent rebuke. Almost ninety heresies are publicly known; but he, having searched everything, found two hundred, which he proposed not only to eliminate and put to flight individually, but also to teach how they had drawn or twisted their errors from philosophy that had not been rightly understood. Finally, he had vehemently turned against those Christians whose faith is seen without works. He had also diligently explored how it could be that men believe there is a fire established in the center of the earth—by which the bodies of the damned and other things are to suffer eternal punishment—and other such unimaginable tortures of both soul and body, as well as the immense joys of the seen Deity by which souls joined to bodies are blessed, and yet they are not obedient to the words of the Church which compel belief. Instead, they everywhere rave in vice and lean into piling up riches, fearing nothing less than punishment and seeking nothing less than the kingdom of God. He attempted to apply suitable help according to the quality of the diseases: namely, to cauterize foul and naturally impure diseases with sharp and bitter medicines; but for those wounds infected with lesser malice and depravity that desired to be scarred over, he wished to soothe them with gentle and peaceful comforts; and for those who had attained health but feared a relapse, he prepared the most wholesome potions and celebrated antidotes. He had begun many other works by which it could be hoped that the study of philosophy would flourish again in general, with errors eliminated and barbarism exploded. Among these, the most prominent was the concord of Plato and Aristotle.

<margin>The Concord of Plato and Aristotle.</margin>
This concord he had already begun and was soon to complete, if life had remained as a companion for a few more years. For he had nourished philosophy from its infancy with milk, and had brought it through to its adulthood in our own times. So much so, that a philosopher of our age would have nothing more to desire in Greek, Latin, or barbarian codices. He would have cited the watery Thales, the fiery Heraclitus, and Democritus surrounded by atoms; Orpheus also, and Pythagoras, and other ancients would have come together in the Academy by his help and favor. Finally, the princes of philosophy—namely, Plato, packed in the veils of fables and mathematical coverings, and Aristotle, fortified by motions—would have sanctioned the faith of future friendship with their right hands joined.

...had established. Between Averroes and Avicenna <note>Averroes and Avicenna were influential Islamic philosophers whose interpretations of Aristotle often conflicted</note>, and also between Thomas Aquinas and Duns Scotus—who have been in conflict for a long time—he would have obtained, if not a total peace, then at least a truce in many matters. For in most of their controversies, if one examines the differing words more attentively and weighs them more exactly, and if a person, searching scrupulously and carrying the search inward to the deepest hiding places and the profound inner chambers of the mind, penetrates the matter, they will find beyond any ambiguity a union of meanings despite the separate and fighting words. The crowd of "Moderns" <note>The "Neoterici," or later Scholastic theologians of the medieval period</note> would have been both honored for their merits and corrected for their faults. Thus, being entirely dedicated to God, he defended the Church with whatever weapons he could. He drew out the truth which lies hidden (as they say) in the well of Democritus <note>A classical proverb suggesting that truth is buried deep and hard to find</note>, and he utterly cut down and uprooted the unyielding grass of ignorance by which the minds of many are choked, as well as the budding, destructive weeds. 

But approaching death rendered the labor of so many and such great vigils, and the birth of his refined nighttime studies, almost empty. This was the primary reason why he left behind many commentaries that were unfinished—even if for the most part they were worked out and smoothed down—because he was writing, essentially, only for himself and not for us. For he possessed such a swift genius in composing and such a fast hand in writing that, although he previously drew the most beautiful literary characters, it happened that through the habit of excessive speed in composing, he was scarcely able to read what he himself had written. He was also accustomed to writing here and there, sometimes obliterating old notes with new ones added on top. For that reason, I have found some things worn out and deleted, some things written only in snatches and fragments; in short, everything was so confused and disordered that they might be thought of as "forests" or "mixtures" <note>Metaphors for unorganized collections of notes</note>. From his seven-fold book <note>The *Heptaplus*</note>, which he had titled against the enemies of the Church, that part which especially attacks the soothsaying astrologers and casters of horoscopes was brought "from the anvil to the file" <note>A Latin idiom meaning a work was polished and refined from its rough state</note> as the saying goes. We drew this out with no small labor and no mediocre care from a manuscript that was blotted and almost torn to pieces. In this work, he demonstrates himself to be a supreme philosopher, a supreme theologian, a supreme orator, and a most sharp defender of the Church of Christ, endowed with an incomparable genius, which is seen in all his commentaries. 

I also found with me certain small things not yet "turned on the lathe" <note>Not yet finished or perfected</note>. Only an interpretation of the Lord’s Prayer, and about fifty brief rules for living well—truly too short and unexplained, which he certainly would have expanded into many chapters had he lived. He had also composed two prayers to God: one in elegiac rhythm and the other in a graver meter, so that he could sometimes soothe his mind when it was exhausted by studies by singing to the lyre. <margin>Highly cultivated in music.</margin> For in the first years of his youth, he had so cultivated every kind of musical art that the melodies he devised and the harmonies he noted down with their proper arrangements were considered famous. We also saw many things in his chests, though disordered, from which I thought something useful could be compiled, especially an explanation of the Psalms. But also about fifty letters <margin>Letters of many kinds.</margin> published at different times—some familiar, some doctrinal, some exhortatory—emerged along with the speech he would have given in Rome if the disputation had taken place. This speech does not merely reflect the most perceptive genius and most abundant learning of a young man not yet in his twenty-fourth year (which all his writings do), but it provides us with the richest testimony of his most fertile eloquence. He always used a style that was highly <margin>An approved character of speaking.</margin> commendable, not one that was borrowed, but one that was multi-formed according to his genius and the variety of subjects. Even if he had mixed together the entire "perfume-cabinet" of Isocrates <note>Isocrates was a Greek orator known for a polished, "sweet" style</note> as they say, he nevertheless preserved the ornaments of purity and becoming majesty. For those celebrated genres of speaking— <margin>Genres of speaking.</margin> three of which Gellius describes and four of which Macrobius describes—are easily gathered from his commentaries: the "copious" style in which Cicero is said to dominate; the "brief" style ascribed to Sallust; <margin>Copious, Brief, Dry, Florid and Rich.</margin> the "dry" style given to Fronto; and the "rich and florid" style in which they say Pliny and Symmachus took delight. But perhaps Brutus would not have called this "copious" style weak, nor would Sallust have called it immoderate. A speaker will easily detect with right judgment Fronto’s "dryness" 

<column-break/>

moistened, Sallust’s "brevity" extended, and Pliny’s "florid richness" carried out into a wider field. Add to these the "milky fountain" of Livy, perhaps without the "Paduosity" <note>A jab at Livy's regional Paduan dialect, mentioned by ancient critics</note> (as that author says), with many "little flowers" of Apuleius added. But he did not <margin>As Jerome says.</margin> exercise himself here in philosophy borrowed from the Greeks, nor in "Attic Nights" <note>A reference to Aulus Gellius's miscellany</note>, nor in "fictional Saturnalia" <note>A reference to Macrobius's work</note> fabricated almost to praise Virgil’s Aeneid, nor in Roman history, nor in mere natural history void of the highest and most difficult speculations. Instead, he labored in understanding the fabric of the world, in attacking the enemies of the most holy Catholic Church, and he wore himself out in eliminating the astrologers. He worked in investigating theological questions and in the harmony of Aristotle and Plato; he devoted his efforts to advising and encouraging his friends. 

Indeed, he was so far from affecting this eloquence of which we speak that he instead condemned those who, searching too scrupulously for painted allurements, applied all the strength of their genius to investigating the origins of words. <margin>Speed of reading.</margin> All these things turned many people more readily toward admiration of him because he had spent a long and very devoted time among the writings of those who did not profess the Latin language to be filled with the flowers of eloquence. Let the excessive lovers of antiquity endure these things with an even mind; for Hermolaus Barbarus, Baptista the Carmelite, Marsilio Ficino, Matteo Bosso, and many other most learned and eloquent men have related these things about him—more concisely and briefly perhaps, but more truly than those more learned than I. He both read through and excerpted from vast libraries of both Latin and Greek authors with incredible speed. And (if the opportunity was given) he passed over no commentaries unread. 

He had attained so much knowledge of the ancient Doctors of the Church that it is difficult to believe even in one who had spent his entire life only in unrolling their works. Regarding the "Modern" <note>Scholastic</note> theologians who used the style commonly called the "Parisian" style, such judgment resided in him that if anyone suddenly asked him to clarify some abstruse and poorly explained question from one of them, he would open it up with such fertility of genius and unlock it with such skill that you would say he had all the sayings of that doctor before his eyes and ready for use. He recognized all the "families" <note>Schools of thought</note> in the same way; he had examined all the sects, and you should not believe he was so addicted to any one of them (as is the custom of our people) that he despised the others. For he himself was so instructed and so minded from his tender years that he sought the truth in them and honored it wherever it shone forth; once found, he venerated it in whoever it was, stripped of private affection. Yet what he thought of each of them—those who are generally considered the leaders—can be seen in the preface to his *Apology*, when he recounted the properties and peculiar praises of the "barbarous," Greek, and Latin philosophers. 

When mention was made during conversation about those philosophers or theologians who wrote in the French manner of disputing, he was accustomed to praise <margin>Thomas Aquinas.</margin> Thomas Aquinas above all others, as one resting on a more solid base of truth than the others. He also calls him the "splendor of our theology" in his *Heptaplus*. When asked about this very frequently, even by me, he gave the same answer. Nor should certain things contained in his *Apology* that were to be disputed persuade anyone to the contrary—things that otherwise openly contradict the opinions of Thomas—since at that time he was a very young man, eager for glory, and in that most celebrated city <note>Rome</note>, in the manner of <margin>Gorgias of Leontini.</margin> Gorgias of Leontini <note>A famous ancient Greek Sophist</note>, he was hunting for the fame of his side by defending whatever parts he could. Add to this that out of ten thousand propositions, failing to agree with—or even opposing—only three or four does not prove the contrary. Furthermore, he was most skilled in disputing and applied frequent and very great effort to literary contests while his mind was fervent. By his objecting, they could easily have detected the <margin>Scotus's sharpness, Aureolus.</margin> sharpness and vigilance of Scotus, the stinging wit of Francis <note>Likely Francis of Meyronnes</note>, and the copiousness and multitude of Aureolus; nor were those knots lacking, complicated with many-fold twists, supported not so much by tickling subtleties as by gravity. By his responding, you would have seen the strength and power of Thomas and the breadth of Albert <note>Albert the Great</note>. But he had long ago sent a message of dismissal to these conflicts, and more and more...
