<margin>Ercole d'Este</margin>
...he had grown to loathe that task daily, and he refused it to such an extent that he even resisted the requests of Ercole d'Este, the Duke of Ferrara <note>Ercole I d'Este (1431–1505) was a major patron of the arts and a supporter of the reformer Savonarola</note>, as well as his messengers and his own reputation. When the general synod of the Preaching Friars <note>The Dominicans</note> was held at Ferrara, he was reluctant to engage in debate, though he did not find it difficult. However, yielding to the many entreaties of that prince, whose love for him was no small thing, he finally complied. From this, people were unsure whether he appeared more skillful or more eloquent, more learned or more kind. From the mouth of the debater, there always shone such a cheerful spirit that he seemed to be discussing a pleasant and gentle matter rather than something sharp and difficult. Because of this, those who hung on his every word were moved to a wonderful love for him. But a frequent
<margin>Adage</margin>
adage of his was that such a task belonged to the dialectician, not the philosopher. He also used to say that those disputations were beneficial which were conducted with a calm mind to track down and investigate the truth in private places and away from witnesses. But he believed those held in public were most harmful, being done to show off learning or to catch the breeze of common favor and the applause of the unlearned. He judged it almost impossible for the desire for honor—which drives those wandering, public debaters—not to be joined by an inseparable bond to a desire for the shame and confusion of the opponent, which is a lethal wound to the soul and a deadly poison to charity. Nothing was hidden from him
<margin>The snares of the sophists. The Swinesheadian trifles were not unknown to him.</margin>
that pertained to the little traps and quibbles of the sophists, and the "Swinesheadian trifles" <note>original: "suisseticas quisquillias." This refers to Richard Swineshead, known as "The Calculator," a 14th-century English logician whose complex mathematical logic was often criticized by Renaissance humanists as useless hair-splitting</note> which are called "calculations." These are mathematical commentaries applied to natural speculations that are rather futile, if not to say tiresome. But even though he was learned in these and had read such writings—which perhaps Italy does not fully know (for no path of literature could be found so trackless and inaccessible that it had not been traversed and thoroughly explored by his footsteps)—he nevertheless seemed to hate and detest them. In my judgment, he noticed that their common use served only to bring infamy upon colleagues and to undermine memory during rebuttal; but for finding the truth, to which he thought untiring effort should be devoted, they contributed either nothing or very little. But lest I write too much and delay the reader, I will summarize briefly. One man may shine in eloquence but be dishonored by ignorance of the secrets of nature.
Another may know foreign languages but not be skilled in the universal decrees of the philosophers. Another may have read the inventions of the ancients but not composed new doctrines. Knowledge is sought by another only for the sake of men and human glory, not for the benefit of the Christian republic. But Pico had embraced all these things with such equal zeal that they seemed to flow into him in troops and heaps; he was not like many who, excelling in one thing, do not participate in all. Rather, he had progressed so far in all sciences that whichever one you considered in him, you would have judged that he had chosen it as his own particular specialty. These things were even more admirable because he had been moved by the force of his own genius and love of truth, as if without a teacher; so that we might say of him what Epicurus said of himself: that he was his own master.
<margin>Five causes of such wonderful effects.</margin>
To produce such wonderful effects in so small a space of time, I have found that five causes converged: incredible genius, a most tenacious memory, ample resources (with which he was aided in purchasing books in our own, Greek, and foreign languages),
<margin>Seven thousand gold coins spent in acquiring books.</margin>
(for I recall it being reported to me that he spent seven thousand gold pieces <note>A staggering sum for the 15th century, equivalent to millions of dollars today</note> up to that day in acquiring volumes of every kind of literature for himself), constant and indefatigable study, and finally, contempt for earthly things. If that ancient age of the Spartans had produced him, if we believe Aristotle, it would have called him a "divine man." But now I think the virtues of the intellect should be left aside, and the noble parts of his soul which regard actions must be pursued. His morals must be brought most exactly into the public view, so that his soul’s flame for God may become known, his wealth bestowed upon the needy may be praised, and so that those who are finally devoted to the divine law may find an abundant occasion to give thanks to the Author of all good things.

<column-break/>

<margin>Bestowal to the poor.</margin>
Three years before he died, so that he could live in deep peace, free from the cares of ruling and secure in wherever the scepter might fall, he handed over all the patrimony he possessed in Mirandola and Concordia—that is, a third part of them—to me, whether as a gift or a sale I do not know. This act was later confirmed with imperial liberality by Maximilian the August <note>Emperor Maximilian I (1459–1519)</note>, who is our king and, so to speak, immediate lord (for we have recognized no other for as many centuries as Mirandola and Concordia have been built, except whoever successively sits upon the royal or imperial throne of the Romans). Whatever money he had received from this business he partly distributed to the poor and partly spent on buying lands from which he and his household might be supported; specifically, he purchased the "Corbulae" in the territory of Ferrara for many thousands of gold coins. He likewise distributed many silver vessels and pieces of precious furniture for the
<margin>A modest table.</margin>
use of the poor. He was content with a modest table, yet retaining something of his former elegance in terms of the dishes and silver vessels. Each day at the appointed hours, he poured out prayers to God. He always gave money to any poor people he encountered. Not content with that, he gave a great deal of money to Girolamo Benivieni <note>A Florentine poet and close friend of Pico and Savonarola</note>, a literate citizen of Florence whom he loved greatly for his vast charity and integrity of character, instructing him to always help the needy with his [Pico's] own money. He also gave young women money for their dowries, telling Benivieni to report to him as soon as the money was spent so he could replace it immediately. He had delegated this task to him so that, through a faithful intermediary, he could more easily relieve the calamities and miseries of the poor citizens which might have remained hidden from him. He also very often (which I think should not be passed over knowingly) gave alms from his own body. We know that many (to use the words of Jerome) have reached out
<margin>Jerome</margin>
a hand to the needy but were overcome by the pleasure and allure of the flesh. But he, especially on those days which represent the suffering and death of Christ for the sake of our salvation, in memory of that supreme benefit and for the expiation of sins, would beat his own flesh.
<margin>His own body struck with whips.</margin>
And with my own eyes (may all things return to the glory of God), I often saw the whip. He was always of a cheerful and calm countenance, and of such a mild nature that he testified, even in the hearing of many, that he had never been disturbed by anger.
<margin>A cheerful face. A mild nature. Constancy of mind. Knowledge of five languages.</margin>
I remember him saying during a conversation that he believed he could not be moved to anger by any event (even if things went very badly), unless certain papers were destroyed in which his nighttime labors and hidden vigils were packed. But when he realized that he was working for God, the Best and Greatest, and His Church, and that he had dedicated all his works, studies, and actions to Him, and that nothing could happen unless He either ordered it or permitted it, he was confident that he would not be saddened. O happy mind, which could no longer be cast down by any adversity nor (as will become clear) be puffed up by any advantages! Certainly, his skill in universal philosophy did not make him arrogant, nor did his knowledge of the Hebrew, Chaldean, and Arabic languages, in addition to Latin and Greek. Ample riches did not inflate him, nor did the nobility of his lineage; the beauty and elegance of his body, and the great license to sin afforded by that soft and spacious way of the world, could not call him back. What, then, could be so admirable that it could pervert his mind? What, I say, could be above him who (to
<margin>Seneca</margin>
use the words of Seneca) was above fortune? Since he at all times despised fortune, whether it was puffed up by favorable winds or humbled by adverse blasts, his mind was joined to Christ and the citizens of the heavenly homeland by a spiritual glue. This is clearly perceived by this argument: while he saw not a few in our time (alas, the grief!) bidding for and auctioning off the offices and dignities of the Church, seeking them, demanding them, sighing for them, and buying them most strenuously, he himself—when they were offered by two kings through messengers (most grave witnesses are present, and I am a witness)—rejected them, responding that he did not wish to be initiated into sacred orders. Indeed, when one man promised he would give him worldly dignities and ample revenues if he would come to his king, Pico, seeing that he was an angel who would not be left with nowhere to hide, and that all refuges had been taken away, gave him such an answer that he might understand he did not seek dignities or riches...

# THE LIFE OF GIOVANNI PICO OF MIRANDOLA

<margin>Wealth neglected for the sake of God and study.</margin>
...or to seek riches. Rather, so that he might be free for God and his studies, he neglected them. In Ferrara, when some of his friends urged Pandolfo Collenuccio of Pesaro <note>A famous lawyer and historian of the time</note>—a man of sharp intellect and wide reading with whom Pico was very close—to assist Pico by whatever means possible in seeking the dignity of the Cardinalate, or certainly to embrace it if the Pope should offer it (which many thought likely to happen), Pico, with his characteristic greatness of soul, immediately ordered that this prophetic response be sent by letter: *My thoughts are not your thoughts* <note>original: "Non sunt cogitationes meæ: cogitationes uestræ," a quote from the Book of Isaiah 55:8</note>. Perhaps he was reflecting on the goods of the Church—the greatest part of which is owed by hereditary right to the poor—and felt that one ought not to maintain magnificent displays. He also kept before his eyes the examples of the holiest men:
<margin>Ambrose, Augustine, Martin</margin>
specifically Ambrose, Augustine, and Martin <note>St. Ambrose, St. Augustine, and St. Martin of Tours, all of whom famously resisted being made bishops</note>, and others who fled the dignity of the episcopacy when it was offered. For a long time before they died, they rejected that office. Furthermore, he had read that the most holy Celestine <note>Pope Celestine V, who famously abdicated the papacy in 1294 to return to a hermit's life</note> had abdicated not only from the Cardinalate itself but even from the supreme power of the High Pontificate,
<margin>Celestine.</margin>
shaking off that burden from the shoulders of the whole Christian commonwealth. It was a burden indeed, though for those who undertake it, a very great reward is prepared—that is, for those who are unwilling and who embrace it only for the sake of obeying and helping others. He was most convinced that for a philosopher, praise did not consist in accumulating wealth or seeking honors, but in refusing them. By refusing shadowy glory, one attains the true glory that always accompanies virtue like an inseparable companion and follower. Human glory
<margin>Despiser of human glory.</margin>
he held as almost nothing. He often said that fame would benefit the living somewhat, but the dead not at all. We recognized that he valued his own learning only insofar as it served the utility of the Church and the elimination and explosion of opposing errors. We also perceived that he had reached such a goal of perfection that he cared little if his commentaries were published without his own name, provided that they brought the same benefit to men as they would have under Pico's name. He decided to concern himself very little with other books except for the Old and New Testaments, intending to spend the rest of his life always turning them over in his mind—unless public utility spurred him on, seeing as
<margin>Note.</margin>
so many great things he had conceived and brought forth were not only being demanded by everyone everywhere but were being pulled from him prematurely. He valued even the smallest bit of devotion toward God from a simple old man or old woman more than all his own knowledge of human and divine
<margin>True Christian instruction.</margin>
matters. He very often advised his friends during conversation that they should notice how much mortal things labor and totter, and how fleeting and flowing is this life we live, while how firm and stable is that which we shall be in the future. Whether we are thrust down to the underworld or raised up to the heavens, he urged them to turn and incite their minds to loving God. He believed this work outweighed any knowledge we could have in this life. He carried this out most clearly in his book *On Being and the One* <note>original: "de ente et uno," one of Pico's most famous philosophical works</note>, when he turned to Angelo Poliziano <note>A renowned Renaissance poet and scholar, and Pico's close friend</note>, to whom he dedicated the book, and spoke these words during the disputation:

<margin>Pico's judgment on loving and knowing in this life.</margin>
"But see, my Angelo, what madness holds us: we can love God while we are in the body more than we can either speak of Him or know Him. By loving Him, we benefit ourselves more, we labor less, and we obey Him more; yet we always prefer, through knowledge, never to find what we seek, rather than to possess through love that which would be found in vain without love." That saying of Saint Francis was also
<margin>A praise frequently on his lips.</margin>
frequently on his lips: "A man knows as much as he works." <note>A common Franciscan aphorism emphasizing that true knowledge is expressed through action/charity</note>. Otherwise, his liberality <note>generosity</note> alone exceeded all bounds; he was so far from placing any care in earthly things that he was even stained with the blemish of
<margin>Excessive liberality.</margin>
carelessness. We find he was often warned by his friends not to despise wealth entirely, asserting that it brought shame upon him when it became common knowledge—whether true or false—that he had given his stewards the opportunity for theft. Never-

<column-break/>

-theless, that mind, which was always intent on contemplating and searching out the designs of all nature, could not easily lower itself to weigh these lowest and most abject matters. I remember while I was staying with him in Ferrara, a caterer presented a small page seeking approval of expenses. Seeing this, Pico was struck with wonder and asked him if he had set his mind to that which he had neglected in times past. His friend replied that he had not only requested it of Pico but insisted he undertake the duty, which Pico had done to comply with their custom—though with no more care than he had before. Furthermore, when his primary steward approached him to ask that he order an audit of the money he had handled for many years, so that he might put his own mind at rest, and brought such books before him, we heard that Pico replied with these words: "I know that I could have been cheated by you very often, and still could be. Therefore, there is no need for a balancing of these expenses. If I owe you, I will pay the coins as soon as possible. If you owe me, pay back the debt either now, if you can, or in the future, if you lack the means." He always treated his friends with great indulgence, using such speech when encouraging them to live well. I knew a man who, while relying on Pico's learning and fame,
<margin>Benevolence toward friends.</margin>
spoke with him; when the conversation turned to morals, he was so moved by just two of Pico's words that he deserted the path of vice and reformed his character. The words were as follows: "If we held before our eyes the death of Christ suffered for love of us, and likewise thought of our own death, we would beware of vices." He showed admirable modesty and kindness toward those
<margin>Two very healthy remedies against vice.</margin>
whom he felt bound to himself not by power or fortune, but by love and learning. He was accustomed to love those who showed even a little skill in literature or at least an aptitude and diligence for the study of the good arts. For similarity is the cause of love, and toward a wise 
<margin>Similarity is the cause of love.</margin>
man (as Philostratus <note>A Greek sophist of the Roman Empire</note> says Apollonius said), there is a certain affinity. It is not doubted that a man perceives knowledge insofar as he is a man, but he attains perfect goodness beyond that, and therefore other upright people must be loved. Otherwise, nothing was more intolerable to him than (to use the words of Horace) *the proud thresholds of powerful citizens* <note>original: "superba ciuium potentiorum limina," a reference to Horace's Epodes 2.7-8</note>. He also loathed the 
<margin>Horace.</margin>
military service of the age and the bond of marriage. When asked in conversation which burden would be lighter to bear—if forced by necessity and given the choice—he hesitated a little, wavering and smiling slightly, then replied: "Marriage," for it did not have as much connection to slavery and danger as the burden of military service. He loved freedom beyond measure, which both his 
<margin>Freedom of the mind.</margin>
nature and his philosophical studies suggested to him. For this reason, we believe he remained a wanderer for the most part and never chose a permanent home for himself, although he stayed often in Florence and sometimes in Ferrara. I think he made the former city his domicile because there, after Bologna, he had first cultivated the study of letters, and its prince <note>Lorenzo de' Medici (the Magnificent)</note> loved him wonderfully. He was also joined by a kind of affinity, as I was born from his sister, Blanca Maria d'Este <note>Blanca Maria d'Este was Pico's sister-in-law (wife of Galeotto Pico), but here Gianfrancesco is explaining his own lineage; Blanca Maria was the daughter of Niccolò III d'Este</note>.
<margin>Blanca Maria d'Este.</margin>
Nor was Ferrara too far from his homeland, as it is only thirty miles east of Mirandola. He loved and inhabited the other city [Florence] either for the pleasantness of the air, the sweetness of many friends, or the subtlety of the intellects there. Among these, he bound two especially to himself with a literary love: Angelo Poliziano,
<margin>Angelo Poliziano.</margin>
a man most learned in Greek and Latin, full of the flowers of various literatures, and almost the protector of the Roman tongue; and the other, Marsilio Ficino <note>The leading figure of the Platonic Academy in Florence</note>, a Florentine redolent with all kinds of literature.
<margin>Marsilio Ficino.</margin>
But the greatest of those now living was the Platonist [Ficino], whose works in claiming the Academy for himself Pico had used. He was not very fond of the external worship of latria <note>Supreme worship offered to God alone</note>—we are not speaking of that which the Church commands to be observed (for we saw him keep this before his eyes)—but we mention those ceremonies which some people perform while neglecting the true worship of God, which is in the spirit...

# THE LIFE OF GIOVANNI PICO OF MIRANDOLA

<margin>Ercole d'Este</margin>
He had grown weary of such duties <note>referring to public disputations</note> day by day, to the point that he refused them—even when Ercole d'Este, Duke of Ferrara, his envoys, and Pico himself were most earnestly requested to participate. When the general synod of the Friars Preachers <note>The Dominicans</note> was being held at Ferrara, he did not find it difficult to debate. Although he had long been reluctant to comply, he eventually yielded to the many requests of that prince, for whom he had no small affection. From this, it was debated whether he appeared more skillful or more eloquent, more learned or more kind. From the mouth of the disputant, such a cheerful spirit was always evident that he seemed to be discussing a pleasant and peaceful matter rather than a sharp or difficult one. Consequently, those who hung on his every word were moved to a wonderful love for him. But he had a frequent <margin>Adage.</margin> adage: that such a task belonged to the logician, not the philosopher. He also said that those disputations were beneficial which were carried out with a calm mind to track down and investigate the truth in private places, away from spectators. However, he believed those were very harmful which were done in public to show off learning or to catch the breeze of the common folk and the applause of the unlearned. He considered it almost impossible for those "front-wandering" <note>wandering or public-facing</note> disputers, driven by a desire for honor, not to be bound by an inseparable link to the desire for their opponent's infamy and confusion—a lethal wound to the soul and a deadly poison to charity. Nothing was hidden from him regarding the "captious traps" and trivialities of the sophists and the <margin>Sophistical traps. Suissetic trifles known to him.</margin> "Suissetic trifles" <note>referring to the complex logical "Calculations" of Richard Swineshead, known as 'The Calculator'</note> which are called *calculations*. These are mathematical commentaries applied to natural philosophy with thoughts more subtle—if not to say more troublesome—than necessary. But although he was learned in them and had read such writings (which perhaps Italy did not fully know, for no path of literature was so inaccessible that it had not been thoroughly explored by his footsteps), he seemed to hate and detest them. In my judgment, he noticed that their common use served only to bring infamy to colleagues and to undermine memory in replying, while contributing little or nothing to finding the truth, to which he believed unwearied effort should be devoted. But lest I go on too long and detain the reader, I will summarize briefly. One man may shine in eloquence but be disgraced by ignorance of the secrets of nature. Another may know foreign languages but not the universal decrees of the philosophers. Another may read the inventions of the ancients but devise no new doctrines. For some, knowledge is sought only for the sake of men and human glory, not for the benefit of the Christian republic or divine matters. But Pico had embraced all these with equal zeal, so that they seemed to flow into him in troops and heaps. He was not like many who excel in one thing but do not participate in all; rather, he had progressed so far in all sciences that whichever one you considered in him, you would judge that he had chosen it as his own special and peculiar field. These things were all the more admirable because he had attained them by the force of his own genius and love of truth, almost without a teacher. Thus we might say of him what Epicurus said of himself: that he had been his own master. <margin>Five causes of such wonderful effects.</margin> To produce such wonderful effects in so short a time, I have found five causes that coincided: incredible genius, a most tenacious memory, ample wealth (which helped him buy books in our own, Greek, and foreign languages), <margin>Seven thousand gold coins spent on purchasing books.</margin> for I recall it being reported to me that he had spent seven thousand gold coins up to that day in acquiring volumes of every kind of literature for himself, constant and indefatigable study, and finally, contempt for earthly things. If the ancient age of the Spartans had produced this man, he would have been called "divine," if we believe Aristotle's criteria. But now, it seems the virtues of the intellect should be left behind, and the noble parts of his soul regarding actions must be followed, and his most exact morals brought into the public eye. Thus his soul, inflamed toward God, may become known; his riches distributed to the needy may be praised; and for those who are at last devoted to the divine law, a most abundant occasion may be provided to return thanks to the Author of all good things.

<column-break/>

Three years before he died, so that he might live in deep peace and security, setting aside the cares of ruling, he handed over all the estates he possessed in Mirandola and Concordia—that is, a third part of them—to me, whether as a gift or a sale I do not know. This act was later confirmed with imperial liberality by Maximilian the August <note>Emperor Maximilian I</note>, who is our King and immediate Lord (for we have recognized no other for as many centuries as Mirandola and Concordia have been built, except whoever successively sat on the royal or imperial throne of the Romans). Whatever money he received from this transaction he partly <margin>Distribution to the poor.</margin> gave to the poor, and partly spent on buying lands from which he and his household might be supported; specifically, he purchased estates in the territory of Ferrara for many thousands of gold coins. Likewise, he distributed many silver vessels and parts of his precious furniture for the use of the poor. He was content with a modest table, which nevertheless retained something of his former elegance regarding the courses and the <margin>A modest table.</margin> silver vessels. Every day at the appointed hours, he poured out prayers to God. He always gave money to the poor if any came his way; and not content with that, he had commissioned Girolamo Benivieni—a literate citizen of Florence whom he loved greatly for his great charity and integrity of character—to always help the needy with Pico's own money. He also provided dowries for young women to be married, and he told Benivieni to report to him immediately so that he could restore the spent coins as soon as possible. He had delegated this duty to him so that he might more easily relieve the calamities and miseries of the poor citizens through a faithful intermediary, things that might have otherwise remained hidden from him. He also frequently gave (which I think should not be passed over in silence) alms from his own body. We know that many (to use the words of Jerome) <margin>Jerome.</margin> stretched out a hand to the needy but were overcome by the pleasure and allurements of the flesh. But he, especially on those days which represent the torture and death of Christ for the sake of our salvation, would strike his own flesh in memory of that supreme benefit and for the expiation of sins; <margin>His own body beaten with whips.</margin> and with my own eyes I often saw the whip (may all things return to the glory of God). He was always of a cheerful and peaceful countenance, and of such a mild nature that he testified, even in the hearing of many, that he had never been disturbed. <margin>Cheerful face. Mild nature. Constancy of mind. Knowledge of five languages.</margin> I recall him saying in conversation that he believed he could not be moved to anger by any event (even if things went very badly), unless certain chests were lost in which his late-night studies and labors were stored. But when he realized that he was working for the best and greatest God and His Church, and had dedicated all his works, studies, and actions to Him—and that this could not happen unless by His command or permission—he was confident that he would not be saddened. O happy mind, which could now be cast down by no adversity, nor (as will become clear) be puffed up by any advantages! Certainly, his skill in universal philosophy, and his knowledge of the Hebrew, Chaldean, and Arabic languages beyond Latin and Greek, had not made him arrogant. Ample riches had not inflated him; nobility of birth, beauty of body, and elegance had not. Nor could the great license for sinning recall him to that soft and wide path of the many. What then could be so remarkable that it could pervert the peace of his mind? What, I say, could be above him, who (to use the words of Seneca) <margin>Seneca.</margin> was "above fortune"? Since he sometimes despised her, neither swollen by her favorable breezes nor humbled by her adverse blasts, his mind was joined by a spiritual glue to Christ and the citizens of the heavenly fatherland. This is clearly perceived even by this argument: while he saw many of our time (alas!) bidding for and auctioning off the offices and dignities of the Church—not a few seeking, demanding, sighing for, and most earnestly buying them—he himself rejected them when offered by two kings through intermediaries. Witnesses are present, most grave witnesses; I myself heard him respond that he did not wish to be initiated into holy orders, and so he refused. <margin>Dignities offered by two kings and rejected.</margin> To another who promised secular dignities and ample revenues if he would come to the king's court, he gave such an answer—realizing that he had not been left an angel into whom he had hidden himself, and that everything had been taken away—that the man understood Pico did not seek dignities or riches...

<margin>Wealth neglected for the sake of God and study.</margin>
...or to seek after riches. Rather, so that he might be free for God and his studies, he neglected them. In Ferrara, certain friends—including Pandolfo Collenuccio of Pesaro, a legal expert, a man of sharp wit and wide reading with whom Pico was very intimate—had urged Pandolfo to persuade him by whatever means possible to seek the dignity of the cardinalate. Or at least, if the Pope were to offer it (as many thought would happen), he should embrace it. Pandolfo attempted this with some hesitation, for he was not unaware that Pico preferred anything else over being entangled in such honors. Pico himself, with the greatness of soul that he possessed, immediately ordered that prophetic response be sent by letter: 

> "My thoughts are not your thoughts." <note>original: "non sunt cogitationes meę: cogitationes uestrę," quoting Isaiah 55:8.</note>

He perhaps considered that regarding the goods of the Church—the greatest part of which is owed to the poor by hereditary right—it was not fitting to lead a life of magnificent display. He also kept the examples of the holiest men before his eyes: 
<margin>Ambrose, Augustine, Martin</margin>
namely Ambrose, Augustine, Martin, and others who fled from the offered dignity of a bishopric. For a long time, they refused that office before they finally undertook it. Moreover, he had read that the most holy 
<margin>Celestine.</margin>
Celestine <note>Pope Celestine V, who famously resigned the Papacy in 1294.</note> had abdicated not only from the cardinalate itself but from the supreme power of the high pontificate, shaking the burden from his shoulders for the sake of the whole Christian republic. It was a burden indeed, for which a great reward is prepared for those who undertake it—provided they do so unwillingly, embracing it only for the sake of obedience and helping others. It was his firm conviction, as a philosopher, that one should not pile up riches, nor seek honors, but rather refuse them. By refusing shadowy glory, one attains true glory, which always follows virtue like an inseparable companion and attendant. 
<margin>A contemner of human glory.</margin>
He held human glory as almost nothing. He often said that fame would be of some use to the living, but of none at all to the dead. We recognize that he valued his own learning only as much as it contributed to the benefit of the Church and to the elimination and explosion of opposing errors. Furthermore, we perceive that he reached such a goal of perfection that he cared little if his commentaries were published without his own 
<margin>Note.</margin>
name, provided that the very thing they would have achieved under Pico's name brought benefit to mankind. He decided to be affected by no other books more than the Old and New Testaments, and to spend the remainder of his life always turning them over, unless public utility spurred him otherwise. He saw that so many and such great things which he had conceived and brought to birth were not only being 
<margin>The true training of a Christian mind.</margin>
demanded by everyone everywhere, but were being required prematurely. He valued the smallest, tiniest bit of devotion toward God from a simple woman or an old crone more than all his own knowledge of human and divine affairs. He very often warned his close friends in 
<margin>What he judged concerning loving and knowing God in this life.</margin>
conversation: that they should notice how mortal things labor and falter, and how fleeting and fluid is the life we live, yet how firm and stable is what we shall be—whether we are thrust down to the depths or raised up to the heavens. He exhorted them to turn and incite their minds toward loving God, a work he judged to outweigh any knowledge we can have in this life. He also executed this most clearly in his book *On Being and the One* <note>original: "de ente & uno," Pico's famous philosophical treatise.</note> when, in the midst of the disputation, he turned to Angelo Poliziano, to whom he dedicated the book, and spoke these words:

> "But see, my Angelo, what madness holds us: while we are in the body, we can love God more than we can either speak of or know Him. In loving Him, we benefit ourselves more, labor less, and obey Him more. Yet we always prefer, through knowledge, never to find what we seek, rather than to possess through love that which, without love, would even be found in vain."

That saying of Saint Francis:
<margin>A praise he frequently had on his lips. Excessive liberality.</margin>
> "A man knows only as much as he puts into practice," <note>original: "tantum scit homo quantum operatur."</note>

was also frequent on his lips. However, in his liberality <note>Generosity with money and resources.</note> alone did he exceed moderation. He was so far from giving any care to earthly things that he was even stained by the vice of negligence. We have learned that he was often warned by his friends not to utterly despise riches, asserting that it brought him shame since it would become common knowledge—whether true or false—that he had provided an opportunity for his managers to steal, yet 

<column-break/>

nevertheless, that mind which was always fixed on contemplating and searching out the designs of all nature could not easily lower itself to weigh these lowest and most abject matters. I remember while I was staying with him in Ferrara, a steward presented him with a small page seeking approval for expenses. Upon seeing this, I stood amazed; when I asked him if he had finally applied his mind to that which he had neglected in times past, a friend replied that he had not only been asked but required to undertake this duty, which he had done to comply with custom, though with as much care as he had previously shown. Furthermore, when his primary manager had interrupted him to ask that he order an audit of the money he had handled for many years, so that he might settle his accounts more securely, and had brought such books before him, we heard him reply with these words: "I know that I have been able to be cheated by you very often, and still could be. Therefore, there is no need for a weighing of these expenses. If I owe you, I will pay the coins as soon as possible. If you owe me, pay back the debt now if you can, or in the future if the means are not present." He always treated his friends with great indulgence, 
<margin>Kindness toward friends.</margin>
to whom he used to speak as an exhorter to living well. I knew a man who, relying on Pico's learning and fame, spoke with him; when the conversation turned to morals, he was so moved by just two of Pico's words that he deserted the path of vice and reformed his character. The words were of this sort: "If we kept before our eyes the death of Christ, 
<margin>Two most healthy remedies against vice.</margin>
suffered for love of us, and likewise thought of our own death, we would beware of vices." He showed admirable modesty and courtesy toward those who were proven not by power or fortune, but whom he felt bound to win over by love and learning. He was accustomed to love those who possessed even a small amount of literacy, or at least those he saw were industrious and fit for the study of the liberal arts. 
<margin>Likeness is the cause of love.</margin>
For likeness is the cause of love, and toward a wise man (as Apollonius says in Philostratus), there is a certain kinship. It is not doubted that a man should perceive the knowledge by which he is a man, but further, that he should pursue perfect goodness and love other upright men. Moreover, nothing was more intolerable to him than (to use the words of Horace) "the proud thresholds of powerful citizens." 
<margin>Horace.</margin>
He also loathed the military service of the world and the bond of marriage. When asked jokingly which burden seemed lighter to bear—forced by necessity or given a choice—he hesitated a little, nodding, and with a slight smile replied: marriage, for it did not have as much of a connection to slavery and danger as the burden of military service. 
<margin>Freedom of the mind.</margin>
For he loved liberty beyond measure, which both his nature and his studies of philosophy had suggested. Because of this, they say he was mostly a wanderer, and never chose a permanent seat for himself, although he stayed often in Florence and sometimes in Ferrara. Some thought he had established the latter city as his domicile because he had first cultivated the study of letters there after Bologna, and its prince loved him wonderfully, 
<margin>Blancha Maria Estensis.</margin>
being joined to him as if by kinship—seeing as I was born of his sister, namely Blancha Maria Estensis <note>Blanca Maria d'Este, mother of the author, Gianfrancesco Pico.</note>—and also because it was not too far from his homeland, since Ferrara is only thirty miles east of Mirandola. The other city <note>Florence</note> he loved greatly and inhabited for the subtlety of its character. Among these people, he bound two to himself especially with a literary love: Angelo 
<margin>Angelo Poliziano.</margin>
Poliziano, a man most learned in Greek and Latin, filled with the flowers of various literatures, and almost the champion of the Roman tongue; and the other, 
<margin>Marsilio Ficino.</margin>
Marsilio Ficino, a Florentine redolent with every kind of literature, but the greatest Platonist among those now living, whose labor he had used in mastering the Academic works. He was not very fond of the cult of outward worship—we do not speak of that which the Church commands to be observed (for we saw him keep this before his eyes), but we make mention of those ceremonies which some people perform, neglecting the true worship of God, which is in spirit...

# THE LIFE OF GIOVANNI PICO OF MIRANDOLA

->VITA IOAN. PICI MIRAN.<-

<margin>Fervor of love for God.</margin>
...should be worshipped in ritual and truth, they pursue and move forward. But with internal affections, he pursued God with the most fervent love. At times, that alacrity of spirit almost fainted and fell away; yet, taking up strength with a greater effort, I remember him burning so much from God toward God that once, when we were walking in long paths in a certain orchard in Ferrara, talking about the love of Christ, he broke out into words of this kind: "I tell you this, kept in the secret of my heart. Once I have finished and completed certain studies, I shall distribute what hopes remain to me to the needy, and, armed with the crucifix, with bare feet, wandering the world through cities and towns, I shall preach Christ." I later learned that he changed this proposal and decided to devote himself to the Order of Preachers <note>The Dominicans</note>; meanwhile, he was hurrying the publication of the works he had conceived and begun.

<margin>The year of his death: 1494, at age 32.</margin>
But in the year 1494 of our redemption, while he was completing the thirty-second year of his age and staying in Florence, he was seized by a most treacherous fever. It raged so much through his humors and viscera that he disdained no kind of medicine applied to him, yet it forced him to satisfy the debt of nature within thirteen days. But regarding how he conducted himself in his illness, although I was far from him at that time, 

<margin>How he behaved in his illness; the death of a Christian man is to be praised.</margin>
I shall not cease to tell what I received from the most serious witnesses who were present. For instance, after receiving the sacrament of the Eucharist, when the sign of the crucified Christ was offered to him, so that he might take full draughts of love before exhaling his soul—in memory of that ineffable Passion for the sake of our salvation—it served as a very strong defense against any adversity and a most powerful bulwark against wicked demons. Soon after, when an elder asked him whether he firmly believed 

<margin>The image of God.</margin>
that this was the image of the true God and true man—who, as God, was begotten before time and the ages by God the Father, to whom He is equal in all things; and who, by the Holy Spirit, who is also God from Him and the Father (which three are one), remaining co-eternal, was conceived in time in the womb of Mary, ever virgin; who suffered hunger, thirst, labors, heat, and vigils; and who finally, to wash away our filth contracted from the seed of Adam and to open the great gate of heaven, embraced the human race with the greatest charity and most willingly poured out His most precious blood upon the altar of the cross; and other such things usually recounted—he responded that he not only believed it, but was certain of it. And likewise, 

<margin>Alberto Pio. Alexander of Aphrodisias. Themistius.</margin>
with Alberto Pio, his sister's son—whom we mentioned at the beginning of this life, a young man distinguished in character and the study of the liberal arts—he declared that fortitude is taken from physical contemplations against the fear of death, in the same way that Alexander of Aphrodisias and Themistius do in the proem to their books on natural philosophy. 

<margin>Averroes.</margin>
He soon employed a sentiment of Averroes <note>A famous Islamic philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were central to Renaissance study.</note> when Alberto was trying to make the boundaries of death more peaceable: he replied in this manner, that the mind was not pacified by that reason alone, nor was an end put to the tortures of death, but rather by this most of all: that an end was now being put to his offenses against God, since he judged that a shorter time of life would not contain more frequent offenses against God. And furthermore, it was revealed by several most approved witnesses from the college of preachers, and by Alberto himself cited a little before:

<margin>The Queen of Heaven visited the sick man at night.</margin>
That the Queen of Heaven <note>The Virgin Mary</note> came to him at night, fragrant with a wondrous odor, and refreshed all his limbs crushed and contracted by that fever, promising that he would not yield to death entirely. He began to lie in his bed with a cheerful and calm face while he was sick. And amidst the stings of death which he sustained, he was accustomed to speak as if he saw the heavens opened to him; and receiving all who greeted him and promised their help (as is the custom) with the most charming speech, he both welcomed and kissed them. We have also been informed that he asked forgiveness from all his servants if he had perhaps been troublesome to any of them; for these servants, he had provided in his will a year prior: for some, food and clothing while they lived, and for others, money to be paid out according to their merits. He appointed the poor of the Florentine hospital <term>xenodochei</term> <note>A hospital or hostel for the poor and strangers.</note> as his heirs for those things which could not be moved,

<column-break/>

<margin>His death affected all ranks of men with distress.</margin>
but for movable goods, he named his brother Antonio Maria. Indeed, how much distress his death caused to the lowest and highest ranks of all people is witnessed by the princes, cities, and peoples of Italy. Witnessed too by those kings whom we cited above. Witnessed again by the kindness and grace of Charles, King of the Gauls <note>Charles VIII of France</note>, which must not be passed over in silence: when it was announced to him as he arrived in Florence (on his way to Rome to conquer the Kingdom of Naples) that Pico was laboring under a grave illness, he immediately sent two doctors to him, who were still performing the office of legates, to visit and help him. He also gave letters which we have both seen and read, signed by his own hand, full of both humanity and those promises which both the most benevolent mind of a high-spirited king and the distinguished virtues of the sick man demanded. For Pico was then most well-known to him by fame and joined by a certain familiarity, for he had been honorably received by the King in Gaul while visiting Paris. Just as he lived as one to be admired by the whole world and for many centuries, so he decreed that his death, no less famous and unheard of, should be celebrated. Wherefore, I think those things should be related at present which I heard with my own ears while I was in the sacred building called Santa Reparata in Florence (where I had gone, though not in time, having learned of his infirmity), listening to Girolamo Savonarola of Ferrara, of the Order of Preachers—a man most learned in theology, most distinguished, and most famous for sanctity—holding sacred sermons to the Florentine people.

<margin>Apuleius. Words of Brother Girolamo.</margin>
But first, it is my plan to warn those ignorant of sacred letters, in the words of Apuleius <note>A 2nd-century Roman writer.</note>: let them not, with thick ears and an obstinate heart, think those things to be lies which seem strange to the hearing, or unrefined to the sight, or certainly arduous beyond the reach of thought; for if they explore them a little more deeply, they will find them not only evident to the understanding, but also most easy in the doing. He, therefore, declaiming from the pulpit, suggested to all who were present what I am about to say: "A secret must be opened to you, O Florence, which is as true as that proverb frequent among you, the Gospel of John. I would have remained silent, truly; but I am compelled to speak, and He who can command me has ordered that I make these things public. Furthermore, I think there was no one among you who did not know Giovanni Pico della Mirandola. He was heaped with great benefits and great graces by God and endowed with multifaceted learning; perhaps to no mortal did such a famous genius fall. The Church suffered a great loss in him. I would judge that if a longer space of life had been granted to him, he would have excelled all who died these eight hundred years past because of the monuments of writings he would have left behind. He was accustomed to turn to me to make secrets public, from which I knew he was summoned by internal locutions from God to religion <note>Meaning he was called to join a monastic order.</note>; wherefore, desiring to obey these inspirations, he had proposed to comply more than once. But, ungrateful for divine benefits, he either declined the labors because he was called by the senses (for he was of a delicate temperament), or, thinking that religion needed his works, he deferred it for a time—this, however, I say not as certain truth, but as my own conjecture and presumption. Because of this, for two years I threatened him with a scourge if he should negligently execute the work God had proposed for him to perform. I confess I asked God repeatedly that he might be struck a little so that he might finally take the path shown to him from on high. I did not seek this by which he was struck down; I had not thought God had decreed this: that he should leave this life and lose part of the distinguished crown prepared in heaven, and that he should not fully attain the fame and celebrity of name which he would have had to the highest degree if he had lived. But the most kind Judge behaved most mercifully toward him. And because of the alms bestowed upon the poor with a large and most effusive hand, 

<margin>Alms. State of the soul.</margin>
and the prayers which were most insistently poured out to God, it was brought about that his soul does not yet exult in the bosom of the Father above the heavens, nor is it deputed to the lower regions to be tortured with perpetual torments. But, delivered for a time to the purgatorial fire, it pays temporary penalties. This I would most willingly say in this place so that those who knew him, and especially those who were heaped with his benefits..."

It also records Girolamo Savonarola's famous funeral sermon, claiming Pico's soul was in Purgatory for hesitating to join the Dominican order.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the narrative following the death of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola in 1494. It focuses on the public response in Florence, specifically a sermon by the friar Girolamo Savonarola regarding Pico’s spiritual fate, and concludes with an epitaph and a poem attributed to St. Cyprian.</meta>

# THE LIFE OF GIOVANNI PICO OF MIRANDOLA

->VITA IOAN. PICI MIRAN.<-
<sig>* * ij</sig>

...should be aided by their supreme votes. These and many other things the man of God <note>Girolamo Savonarola</note> asserted with a clear voice. He added that it had not been hidden from him that, on account of lies of this sort—if any were mixed in—the preachers of the word of God would be made worthy of eternal punishment. He also added that for several days these matters had been entirely discovered by him. But because of the words which he affirmed the virgin had spoken to the sick man, he stood wavering and feared for a long time that he had been mocked by the work of demons, since the virgin's promise was frustrated by Pico's death. However, it became known to him that the deceased had been deceived by an "equivocation of death."

<margin>A double death.</margin>
For while she had spoken of the second and eternal death, he had believed she meant the first and temporary one. If anyone should say that this man <note>Savonarola</note> either lied out of hypocrisy, or was mocked by phantasms, or circumvented by the trickery of demons, that person must—unless they hold a poor view of the faith or are of unsound mind—confess that God has revealed in many ways, and is still able to reveal to the living, the happiness or misery of those who have poured out their souls. At the same time, He makes those to whom these things are openly revealed certain that they are not being mocked by unseen things or specters, but that the things they perceive and see with their mind or eyes are true.

<margin>Praise of the learning and integrity of Brother Jerome.</margin>
Indeed, no one except the malevolent would deny that a man of such great learning and authority, of such great probity and prudence—whose shorthand theorems on Aristotelian philosophy, public warnings, most brilliant interpretations of the sacred word, and predictions of future events (which almost all of Italy knows happened exactly as described) have long since provided the most witnessed proof of a most holy life—pronounced these things as true and to be held as unshakable to so many thousands of people in the principal temple of such a celebrated city. Add to this that while I was inquiring somewhat into this business, I heard that a man who had been present at the sermon went to the preacher and, so that those things he had made public might have more strength, reported that the deceased had appeared to him surrounded by fire, and confessed that he was still paying the penalty for ingratitude. Furthermore, a certain nun, famous for many noble prophecies—who, while he was alive, predicted many future things to him that happened precisely—uttered this one thing two years before he departed from life: that at the "time of the lilies," by the work and encouragement of Brother Jerome (of whom we have made mention), he would dedicate himself to the college of the Friars Preachers <note>The Dominican Order</note>. At the same time, she said that a certain Florentine family (which they call the Medicean <note>original: "paetiam", likely a corruption of "Mediceam"</note>), then in exile, would return to their fatherland. Many to whom this report had come were speaking about this "nomenclature of lilies," thinking she spoke of the springtime when lilies bloom. But it was discovered that this "lily" was the King of the Gauls <note>Charles VIII of France, whose heraldry featured the fleur-de-lis</note>, who, on the day before Pico was to take his religious vows (for he had so vowed before he died), and four days after that exiled family betook themselves into their father's city, entered Florence with a great retinue while making his way through Etruria <note>Tuscany</note> to claim the Kingdom of Naples by force of arms.

But before I make an end, I think it not useless to say a few small things again at the conclusion of the work. For I seem to see "barking mastiffs" <note>A metaphor for persistent critics</note> at these revelations, as if at the shadow of the moon, to whom perhaps a few more little bones must be thrown (as the previous ones were not enough), lest they beat the air with their barking in vain. I see likewise that laughter is drawn from the foolish; I see that sport is made by those who think themselves "know-it-alls." Perhaps they will contend that souls ought not to be tormented by fire for not having disregarded the healthy inspiration to enter a religious life? Or that in our time men are not found inspired by the divine spirit who enjoy conversations with Christ? But if they considered that sins worthy of pardon, rather than death, must be punished by the fire of Purgatory, they would not wonder that the just also pay penalties. Likewise, if one is not ignorant that the servant who knew the master’s will and did not fulfill it shall be beaten with many stripes (as Truth itself witnesses), why should he not suffer to pay the penalties immediately, even if he had been immune from all other faults? On the other hand, I cannot sufficiently wonder at the rude and tasteless cleverness of those who, while they believe Christ died for men, do not easily believe that He can speak to those same men. It must surely be observed that by a much stronger argument mortals cannot become sharers in the speeches of the Virgin Mother, the angels, and the blessed spirits of men, unless all lower things were governed by the superior.

<margin>Dionysius the Areopagite</margin>
As Dionysius the Areopagite also witnesses in his book *On the Celestial Hierarchy*, souls of a lower grade and nature, to whom the care of men is entrusted, are illuminated by superior minds, which in turn draw divine mysteries either from the highest minds or from God Himself. Men inspired by the divine spirit receive these same revelations, to be opened to the multitude of men when it is expedient. This is the most holy law of divinity: as we are taught by the same Dionysius in his book *On the Celestial Hierarchy*, that through the first things the following things may be carried up to the narrowest light. They are undoubtedly ignorant of divine literature, and of an insolent and stubborn disposition; for in those writings it is granted to see divine mysteries revealed sometimes not only through good men, but through wicked men and pseudo-prophets.

<margin>True things are sometimes predicted by pseudo-prophets.</margin>
What prevents one from having faith in this man who is powerful in both doctrine and so many virtues, and has already predicted many future things which have now happened? And he testified to this not in a sleepy manner, but affirming it strongly. Add that the philosophy of Aristotle does not cry out against these things, and Platonic philosophy supports them—though I have not accepted anything as a grave testimony except the authority of the Divine Scriptures. But it is not absurd to cite these external things occasionally, so that the arrows of the malevolent may return upon the authors with greater force than they came. But now we must return to ourselves: we for whom it is not so much to be mourned that we have lost such a man, as it is to give thanks to the King for whom all things live, that we had him and still have him. Indeed, having performed the duty of mortal life, and having long dwelled with the inhabitants of Kedar <note>A biblical reference to dwelling among the worldly or sorrowful</note>, whom he had drenched with no small light, he is now entering the inaccessible and infinite light of the heavenly fatherland and will enjoy without end the ineffable divinity, also bringing help to us day by day.

### Epitaph of Mirandola.

> Here lies Giovanni of Mirandola. The rest is known
> By the Tagus and the Ganges, and perhaps the Antipodes.

### A poem by Caecilius Cyprian, Bishop of Carthage, concerning the wood of the cross:

> There is a place which we believe to be the center of the whole world,
> The Jews call it Golgotha in their native name:
> Here I remember a tree, planted from sterile wood,
> Produced wholesome fruits from its strength:
> Yet it did not provide for those who placed themselves there as tillers;
> Strangers possessed the blessed fruits
> Of the tree: this species rises from a single trunk:
> And soon extends its arms into twin branches
> Just as the full, heavy sails of a yardarm stretch out.
> Or when the yokes are on the young oxen separated from the plow.
> The earth conceived what this tree bore, fallen from its first mature seed;
> Soon from here—wonderful to tell—
> On the third light, it had raised again a branch blessed with vital fruit,
> Formidable to the earth and to those above:
> But for twice twenty days that branch was strengthened,
> And it grew into the immense sky with its highest peak
> And touched it: and at last added its holy head to the deep:
> While yet it produced branches of a twelve-fold weight
> And, spreading, reached out into the whole world.
> That they might provide food and perennial life to all nations,
> And teach those who were able to die that death itself could die.
> And soon, when fifty days were completed,
> A draught of divine nectar from the highest summit...

<meta>This page continues from the previous discussion regarding Girolamo Savonarola’s sermon on the spiritual fate of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola. Having described the public reaction and Savonarola's visions, the text now presents an allegorical poem, often attributed to St. Cyprian, which serves as a poetic meditation on the "Tree of Life" and the path to salvation.</meta>

# THE LIFE

The breeze of the heavenly spirit carried it into the branches. 
From all sides, the heavy boughs dripped with sweet dew: 
Behold, beneath the shade of the branches' vast covering, 
there was a fountain: here, serene, with no accident disturbing 
the clear water in the depths: and the grasses all around 
poured out joyful colors from the various dews. 
Around this fountain, countless nations and peoples gathered. 
How many, from every kind, sex, age, and status— 
unmarried and married women together, widows and daughters-in-law, 
infants and boys, men, youths and elders. 
Here, where the branches bent low, leaning under many kinds of fruit, 
they strove to reach them with eager right hands: 
they rejoiced in the fruit soaked with heavenly nectar. 
Nor could they pluck these with longing palms 
before they wiped away the foul, muddy tracks of their former path, 
and washed their bodies in the holy fountain. 
Therefore, after wandering long upon the soft grass, 
the fruits hanging from the high tree sustain them. 
Then, the shells that had fallen from those branches 
and the sweet leaves dripping with much nectar

<column-break/>

they eat, desiring to take the true fruit. 
Therefore, when their mouths tasted the heavenly flavor, 
they changed their spirits and lost their greedy minds: 
Indeed, many, being renewed in their minds, restored 
their sick spirits; and things they once said were impossible, 
they endured, and received the fruit of their labor. 
Yet many, though they dared to touch holy minds, 
departed again, suddenly slipping backward, 
rolling once more in the same filth and mire. 
But many, bearing it with a good heart, receive it 
with their whole souls, and hide it deep within their being: 
Therefore, those who are able to approach the sacred springs— 
the seventh light <note>In Christian allegory, the "seventh light" often refers to the Sabbath or the final stage of spiritual completion and rest.</note> brings them to the longed-for waves. 
They bathe their fasting limbs in the clear waters. 
Thus at last they lay down the uncleanness of the mind 
and the stain of their former life; they bring back from death 
pure and bright souls, ready to travel to the threshold of heaven. 
From here is the path to the branches and sweet fruits of salvation; 
from there is the path to heaven through the branches of the tall tree. 
This is the tree of life <term>lignum vitae: literally "wood of life," a common biblical reference to the tree in the Garden of Eden and the New Jerusalem</term> for all who believe: Amen.

->THE END<- <note>original: "TELOS," a Greek word for the end, goal, or final purpose</note>

<vocab>heavenly, grasses, fountain, end/goal, tree of life, nectar, of salvation</vocab>

<meta>This page serves as the formal opening to Pico della Mirandola's *Heptaplus*, shifting from the biographical accounts of his life and Savonarola's visions (seen on the previous page) to Pico’s own intellectual project: a deeply philosophical and mystical commentary on the creation story in Genesis.</meta>

# THE HEPTAPLUS OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA
## ON THE SEVENFOLD EXPOSITION OF THE SIX DAYS OF GENESIS
### DEDICATED TO LORENZO DE' MEDICI.

---

#### P R E F A C E.

<margin>Moses on the preeminent doctrine</margin>
A rivalry with your own studies, Lorenzo de' Medici, moved me to review the secret volumes of Moses. During this past winter, I observed that whenever you were granted leisure from the affairs of the Republic <note>original: "a rep." (a republica); Lorenzo was the de facto ruler of Florence</note>, you devoted yourself to no other reading more readily than to this one. Moreover, a private reason of my own also invited me: for some time now, under your patronage and growing in your name, I have been working on another project where I have attempted not only to defend the Davidic hymns <note>The Psalms</note>—translated from the Seventy <note>original: "a LXX. uerfos"; the Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note> and sung continually in the Church—against all suspicion and slander, but also to illuminate them with the torches of interpretation. No study is found to be more useful, more fruitful, or more consistent (or, to speak more truly, more necessary) than the study of those books. It happened during these days that I was diligently occupied with those famous works of the six days in the "fabric of the world" <note>Genesis 1</note>. Great reasons suggest we should believe that the secrets of all nature are contained within them. For, setting aside the fact that our prophet <note>Moses</note>, full of God and with the heavenly spirit of the Master of all Truth dictating, received these things: have not the testimonies of our own people, his own people, and even the Gentiles <note>non-Jews/pagans</note> shown him to be most deeply versed in human wisdom and all the doctrines of literature?
<margin>The Book of Solomon</margin>
There exists among the Hebrews a book by that most wise man surnamed Solomon, titled *Wisdom*. It is not the work by Philo that is currently in circulation, but another composed in Jerusalem in what they call the "secret tongue." In this book, the man who is considered the interpreter of the nature of things confesses that he received all such discipline from the inner shrines of the Mosaic Law.
<margin>Luke, Philo</margin>
As for our own authors, Luke <note>Acts 7:22</note> and Philo are most weighty authorities stating that Moses was most learned in all the doctrine of the Egyptians. Furthermore, all the Greeks who were considered more "divine" used Egyptian teachers:
<margin>Pythagoras, Plato, Empedocles, Democritus, Hermippus, Numenius</margin>
Pythagoras, Plato, Empedocles, and Democritus. It is a well-known saying of the philosopher Numenius that Plato is nothing other than an "Attic Moses" <note>A Moses speaking Greek in the dialect of Athens</note>. Moreover, Hermippus the Pythagorean attests that Pythagoras transferred many things from the Mosaic Law into his own philosophy. But if Moses appears in his books to be unrefined and common, rather than a philosopher, theologian, or master of some great wisdom: let us recall that it was a famous custom of the ancient sages to write of divine things either not at all, or to write of them in a disguised manner <note>original: "dissimulanter"</note>.
<margin>The source of mysteries; why Pythagoras published neither his small works nor the Golden Verses. Lysis</margin>
Hence they were called "mysteries"—and they are not mysteries if they are not hidden. This was observed by the Indians, the Ethiopians (who are named for their nakedness), and the Egyptians. This is what those Sphinxes in front of the temples suggested. Pythagoras, taught by them, became a master of silence; he himself committed nothing to writing except for a very few things which he commended to his daughter Damo as he was dying. For the *Golden Verses* commonly circulated are not by Pythagoras, as is believed even by the more learned, but by Philolaus. The Pythagoreans thereafter guarded that law most religiously. For Lysis complains that it was violated by Hipparchus. Finally,
<margin>Porphyry</margin>
Porphyry is the authority that the disciples of Ammonius—Origen, Plotinus, and Herennius—swore an oath to this secrecy. Our Plato concealed his dogmas under the

<column-break/>

veil of winged riddles, fables, mathematical images, and the obscure signs of deep-seated meanings. He himself said in his letters that no one would openly understand his opinion on divine matters from what he had written, and he proved this to those who believed less. Therefore, if we think the reading of Moses is "trodden down" <note>trivial or commonplace</note> because it has nothing on the surface that is not ordinary, we would wrongly condemn all the ancient philosophers as unrefined and ignorant—the very men we venerate as masters of all wisdom. Indeed, we see this same practice observed in the Church.
<margin>Jesus Christ</margin>
Jesus Christ, the "image of the substance of God," did not write the Gospel but preached it. He preached to the crowds in parables, but privately to a few disciples, to whom it was given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, openly and without figures. Nor did he tell those few everything, because they were not capable of all things; there were many things they could not bear until the coming Spirit taught them all truth. If the disciples of the Lord, so few and chosen from so many thousands, could not bear many things, how could the whole Israelite crowd—sausage-makers, cooks, butchers, shepherds, servants, and maids, to all of whom the Law was given to be read—have borne the weight of the entire Mosaic or rather divine wisdom? Moses indeed, on the heights of the mountain—that mountain where the Lord also often spoke to his disciples—was illuminated by the light of the divine sun, and his whole face shone in a wondrous way.
<margin>Why Moses’ face was veiled. The Gospel was first written by Matthew.</margin>
But because the people, with their blinded and "nocturnal" eyes, could not bear the light, he spoke words to them with a veiled face. Let us return to our own. Matthew first wrote the Gospel, and as the prophet says, "hiding the words of God in his heart" so that he might not sin, he followed the history only of those things pertaining to Christ’s humanity, lest the memory of what was done be lost to oblivion. Thus, in the mystical vision of Ezekiel, we understand him through the figure of the "man." John, who above all others revealed the secrets of divinity in the three common Gospels, was forced to speak what he had long kept silent many years after the Lord’s cross, in order to abolish the heresy
<margin>The Ebionites</margin>
of the Ebionites <note>A Jewish-Christian sect that denied the divinity of Jesus</note>, who asserted that Christ was a man but not also God. He spoke of the eternal generation of the Son, but in few words and obscurely. He began: "In the beginning was the Word" <note>original: "In principio erat uerbum"</note>.
<margin>Paul</margin>
Paul denies "solid food" to the Corinthians because they still live by the laws of the flesh and not by the spirit; he speaks wisdom only among the "perfect."
<margin>Dionysius</margin>
The disciple of Paul, Dionysius the Areopagite, writes that it was a holy and established custom in the churches that the more secret dogmas should not be communicated through writing, but only by voice to those who had been rightly initiated. I have pursued these points at length because there are many who, judging by the "rough bark" of the words, despise and scorn the book of Moses as something common and trivial. To them, nothing is less credible than that he has something divine in reserve, rather than what he promises on the surface. But it is easily believed that he treated the nature and craftsmanship of the whole world, if anywhere in his work he buried treasures of all true philosophy, as if in a field. This was done especially in this part where he philosophizes most deeply, as if by profession, on the emanation of all things from God: on their degree, number, and the order of the parts of the world. For this reason, there was a decree of the ancient Hebrews, which
<margin>Jerome</margin>
Jerome also mentions, that no one should touch this account of the creation of the world unless they were of mature age. Perhaps I will seem to have done something worthwhile if, having lingered longer with more exact and laborious care (as far as my abilities allowed)...
