...our own weakness), I have searched with great zeal for the understanding of the Mosaic reading. Since I saw that many Latin and Greek authors had worked on its explanation—and furthermore, that there were nearly innumerable ancient and modern Chaldean and Hebrew interpreters—I did not even dare to think of writing or commenting on anything new regarding this matter. However, I remembered that the Mosaic law cautioned that no one should reap their field entirely and completely, but should leave an untouched portion for the poor and needy, who might take sheaves and handfuls from there to sustain themselves against hunger. When this came to mind, I began to survey with sharp eyes the widest fields of the prophet <note>referring to Moses</note>, to investigate whether the most learned interpreters—who were no less cultivators of the law than its explainers—had, according to the law's edict, left some part untouched for us, the weaker ones, to harvest. From this, I too might pluck even a few ears of grain to be placed upon the altars of the church as the first fruits of my labor, so that I would not be excluded from the privileges of the temple as if I were not a true Israelite or were entirely empty-handed.

<margin>The reason for this work after so many other interpreters.</margin>

The matter succeeded according to my wish—not because I could do anything they could not, but because they, out of respect for the law's precept, did not wish to block the path for the industry of those who came after. Furthermore, such is the vastness and fertility of that field that no equal number of grains can exist to match it; so that, although nearly infinite and most powerful efforts have exercised themselves in it with all their strength, we can still say that Gospel phrase:

<margin>Latin and Greek interpreters</margin>

*The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few.* <note>Matthew 9:37</note> Therefore, what the most holy men—Ambrose and Augustine, as well as Strabo, Bede, and Remigius, and from the more recent ones, Giles <note>Giles of Rome</note> and Albert <note>Albert the Great</note>—have written; and likewise what the Greeks—Philo, Origen, Basil, Theodoret, Apollinaris, Didymus, Diodorus, Severus, Eusebius, Josephus, Gennadius, and Chrysostom—have written, will be left entirely untouched by us. For it would be both rash and superfluous for a weak man to exercise himself in that part of the field where the most robust minds have long since exerted themselves. Likewise, regarding those things which either Jonathan, Onkelos, or Simeon <note>Rabbinic authorities and authors of the Targums (Chaldean translations)</note> handed down in Chaldean, or what the Hebrew authors wrote—

<margin>Chaldeans</margin>

whether the ancients, such as Eleazar, Aba, John, Neonias, Isaac, and Joseph; or

<margin>Hebrews. Seven new expositions.</margin>

the more recent, such as Gersonides, Saadia, both Abrahams <note>likely Ibn Ezra and Abraham bar Hiyya</note>, both Moseses <note>likely Maimonides and Nahmanides</note>, Solomon, and Menachem—we shall make no mention of them at present. Instead, we shall bring forward, in addition to all these, seven other expositions from our own findings and meditations. In these, our first care will be to overcome, if we can, three difficulties with which all those who have undertaken to explain this book seem to have had a great and difficult struggle.

<margin>The first difficulty.</margin>

The first difficulty is the risk that anything said by Moses might appear either insufficient or lacking in learning and wisdom. Some have freed themselves from this by claiming that Moses did not speak of everything, nor did he bring forth great and sublime things, because he was speaking to a "rude people" who were not fit for the understanding of all things. We, however, can believe that the unlearned listeners were satisfied if he drew a veil over the light of knowledge—which the wise might see into—surrounding it with thick words like a horn casing, lest the weaker eyes be blinded. He brought light, then, so that it might benefit healthy eyes, yet he brought it enclosed and veiled so that it might not harm the bleary-eyed. For he neither should, nor could, nor would have wanted to help the learned any less than the unlearned.

<margin>The second difficulty.</margin>

The second difficulty is that the same course of interpretation should be consistent with itself, fit together, and, as if by a single thread, the entire series should refer back to the same sense from which it first proceeded, as if remembering its purpose. Nor should we, if we introduce him talking about "Ideas" here, want him to deal with the elements or with man in the very next clause. Such a style of exposition is arbitrary and forced. Yet to avoid this in the explanation of this book seemed impossible to many, and certainly difficult and laborious to all. So great is the perplexity, the ambiguity, and the variety of the entire reading. See what a great labor it is—and how not easy to do—that which we have conceived in our mind (may we achieve it!): that we might interpret this whole creation of the world, not in just one, but in a sevenfold sense, always beginning a new work from the start in a continuous and unmixed order of exposition, using none of the resources of previous interpreters.

<margin>See the immensity of the labor.</margin>

<margin>The third difficulty.</margin>

<column-break/>

The third difficulty involves the danger of making the prophet <note>Moses</note> assert something foreign, monstrous, or alien to the nature of things as they are now perceived, or to the truth found by the better philosophers and accepted by our own thinkers. Rather, let us show the Divine Spirit speaking through the prophet. Why we have brought forward seven expositions, by what reasoning they were undertaken, what our plan was, and what necessity drove us to them—and indeed, what this "new thing" is that we are attempting to bring forth—we shall make clear in the following chapter. In that chapter, the person who is to write most perfectly on this matter (that is, on the creation of the world) in imitation of nature itself, by painting its "Idea," <note>The "Idea" here refers to the Platonic concept of a perfect archetype or blueprint.</note> will then attempt to prove by the facts in what follows that our prophet has not deviated from that archetype. Instead, he has perfected it in every detail, so that nothing

<margin>Moses is the correct "Idea" for writing about nature.</margin>

else should be proposed to everyone as such an "Idea" other than Moses himself, and we can all more easily admire his magnitude than estimate it according to its worth. 

However, these works of ours, whatever they may be—still the raw fruits of our youth—are owed to you, most illustrious Lorenzo <note>Lorenzo de' Medici</note>, either because they are mine (and I gave and vowed myself to you long ago), or because you yourself provided us with the leisure of this secular retreat in which they were born.

<margin>Angelo Poliziano.</margin>

This leisure is also seasoned by the frequent intervention, or rather the constant presence, of your close friend Angelo Poliziano <note>A famous humanist poet and scholar</note>. Just as his pleasant and fertile genius previously brought forth various flowers of literature, so now, I believe, it promises the solid and mature fruit of philosophy. It is also customary, when something festive or joyful happens to those we love or revere, not only to congratulate them with words but also to favor their happiness, so to speak, with some gift, and thus make the joy of our soul known to them. Therefore, this late-night work of ours comes to you opportunely at the time when your son Giovanni—at an age at which no one before was ever appointed to the highest order of Christians <note>the College of Cardinals</note> by the Supreme Pontiff Innocent VIII—has been so designated.

<margin>Innocent VIII</margin>

This was done both because of his own character, which promises all good things, and because of your merits and authority, which rightly and deservedly demand it for him. It remains only for us to hope that he shows himself worthy of this dignity. He will do so if he holds the same man as the exemplar of his life whom he has as his father and the author of his dignity—that is, if he follows you in prudence and in every virtue. Farewell.

### ANOTHER PREFACE TO THE WHOLE WORK.

<image-desc>An ornate historiated woodcut initial 'T' depicting a scholar in his study, sitting at a slanted desk and looking up toward a bird (the Holy Spirit) appearing from a cloud. Classical architectural elements and a window are visible in the background.</image-desc>

<margin>The constitution of the three worlds.</margin>

Antiquity fashioned three worlds. The highest of all is the "ultra-worldly" <note>supramundane</note>, which theologians call the Angelic and philosophers call the Intellectual; Plato says in the *Phaedrus* that no one has sung of this world worthily enough.

<margin>Plato</margin>

Next to this is the Celestial world. The last of all is this sublunary world <note>the world below the moon</note> which we inhabit. This is the world of darkness, while the first is the world of light; the heavens are tempered from both light and darkness. This world is marked by waters because of its flowing and unstable substance; the first world by fire because of the brightness of its light and its high position. The heavens, being of a middle nature, are therefore called by the Hebrews *aschamaim* <note>original: "asciamaim"; a transliteration of the Hebrew 'hashamayim' (the heavens)</note>, as if composed of *es* and *maim*—that is, from fire and water (as we have said). 

<margin>The Angelic, Celestial, and Sublunary Worlds</margin>

In this world, there is the alternation of life and death; in that world, perpetual life and stable operation; in the heavens, life and stability of operations, but an alternation of positions <note>referring to planetary orbits</note>. This world consists of the decaying substance of bodies; that world of the nature of the divine mind; the heavens are constituted of body, but incorruptible, and of mind, but bound to the body. The third world is moved by the second; the second is ruled by the first.

<margin>The series of motion.</margin>

There are, moreover, many other differences between them, which it is not our intention to explain here, where we are passing by these things rather than flooding over them. Yet I should not omit that these three worlds were most evidently figured by Moses in the construction of that admirable Tabernacle of his. For he divided the Tabernacle into three parts, each of which represents the individual worlds we have mentioned in the most expressive way. For the first part, protected by no roof or shade, was exposed to rains, snow, sun, heat, and cold; it is the most evident likeness of our sublunary world, inhabited not only by men—clean and unclean, sacred and profane—but also by all sorts of...

<margin>
Interpretation of the worlds.
</margin>
...creatures of every kind; and in it, because of the sacrifices and constant offerings, there was a perpetual cycle of life and death. The remaining two parts were both set apart and free on all sides from every foreign harm, just as both the celestial and super-celestial <note>The "super-celestial" refers to the realm of angels and divine intellects beyond the physical stars.</note> worlds are neither capable of injury nor subject to insult. Both were likewise honored with the name of holiness, yet in such a way that the one which was more secluded was called the **Holy of Holies**, while the other was graced only with the title of **Holy**. Similarly, although both the celestial and angelic worlds are each holy—since above the moon, after the fall of Lucifer, neither stain nor sin exists or can exist—the angelic world is nevertheless considered far holier and more divine than the celestial. But why do we pursue these more remote similarities? For if the last part of the tabernacle was common to men and beasts, and the second—which shone entirely with the splendor of gold—was illuminated by a candelabrum distinguished by seven lamps (which, as all Latin, Greek, and Hebrew interpreters say, signify the seven planets), and in the third part, the most sacred of all, were the winged **cherubim**, do they not place the three worlds before our eyes? This world which both beasts and men inhabit, the celestial world in which the planets glitter, and the super-celestial dwelling place of the angels.

<margin>
What the tearing of the veil through Christ’s death signifies.
</margin>
Furthermore, we are reminded from this of a deeper Gospel mystery. For since the way to the super-celestial world and the company of angels has been opened for us through the cross and blood of Christ, therefore, at His death, the veil of the temple was torn—the veil by which the **Holy of Holies** (which we said signifies the angelic world) was separated from the other parts. This served as a sign that an entrance now lies open for man to the kingdom of God and to God Himself—who flies above the cherubim—an entrance that had been closed from the beginning by the laws of justice on account of the sin of our first parent.

<margin>
Three causes of the harmony of the worlds as explained by the Pythagoreans.
</margin>
This is enough concerning the three worlds, in which this must be especially observed (and upon this almost our entire intention depends): that these three worlds are one world. This is not only because they are all related to one principle and to the same end, or because they are bound together by appropriate numbers and a certain harmonic kinship of nature and a regular series of ranks, but because whatever is in all the worlds at once is also contained in each individual one. Nor is there any one of them in which everything that exists in each is not present. This was the opinion, I believe, of Anaxagoras <note>A pre-Socratic Greek philosopher who famously taught that "in everything there is a portion of everything."</note>, if we think he was understood correctly, and it was later explained by the Pythagoreans and Platonists.

<margin>
A model of the proposed truth.
</margin>
Truly, the things that are in the lower world are also in the higher ones, but in a better form; likewise, the things in the higher worlds are seen in the lowest ones, but in a diminished condition and an "adulterated" nature, so to speak. Among us, **heat** is an elementary quality; in the heavens, it is a heating power; in the angelic minds, it is the *Idea* of heat. Let me say something more precise. Among us, **fire** is an element; the **Sun** is fire in heaven; in the ultra-mundane region, it is the seraphic fire of the intellect. But see how they differ: the elementary fire burns, the celestial fire gives life, and the super-celestial fire loves. There is **water** among us; there is water in the heavens, its mover and mistress, namely the Moon, the threshold of the heavens; there are waters even above the heaven, the cherubic minds. But see the disparity of condition in the same nature: elementary moisture overwhelms the heat of life; celestial moisture nourishes it; super-celestial moisture understands it.

<margin>
Ten spheres of the intelligible world.
Ten spheres of the celestial world.
Ten spheres of the elementary world.
</margin>
In the first world, God, the first unity, presides over nine orders of angels as if over so many spheres, and being Himself immovable, He moves all things toward Himself. In the middle world (that is, the celestial), the Empyrean heaven <note>The highest heaven, believed by medieval cosmologists to be the residence of God and the saved.</note> presides over nine celestial spheres like a leader over an army; though these revolve with a single unceasing motion, that heaven, imagining God, remains unmoved. There are also in the elementary world, after the first matter which is its foundation, nine spheres of corruptible forms. Specifically: three of bodies lacking life, which are the elements and their mixtures; then those between these, which are mixed but imperfect, such as the impressions made in the heights <note>Likely referring to meteorological phenomena like lightning or rainbows.</note>. Three of a vegetable nature, which is first divided into three kinds: herbs, shrubs, and trees. Three of the sensing soul, which is either imperfect (such as in the **Zoophytes** <note>Organisms like sea sponges or corals that appear to be between plants and animals.</note>) or perfect but within the limits of irrational imagination, or that which is highest in beasts and even capable of human training, which is like a middle ground between man and...

<column-break/>

<margin>
Evidence of the worlds is also found in the Sacred Scriptures.
</margin>
...beast, just as the **Zoophyte** is the middle ground between beast and plant. But enough of these things. Let us only add that the mutual containment of the worlds is indicated in the Sacred Scriptures as well. For it is written in the Psalms, "He who creates the heavens in understanding," and we read that the angels of God are "spirits" and His ministers a "flame of burning fire." For this reason, celestial names are often given to earthly things, and earthly names to celestial ones; sometimes they are figured by stars, sometimes by wheels and animals, sometimes by elements. Conversely, celestial names are often given to earthly things. This is because all these worlds, bound by the chains of concord, grant one another their names as they do their natures, through a mutual generosity. From this principle (if anyone has perhaps not yet noticed it) has flowed the entire discipline of allegorical interpretation. Nor could the ancient Fathers have appropriately represented some things by other figures unless they had been taught the hidden friendships and affinities, so to speak, of all nature. Otherwise, there would be no reason why they should have represented this thing by one image and that by another, rather than the reverse. But being knowledgeable of all things and moved by that Spirit who not only knew but made all these things, they most aptly figured the natures of one world through those things they knew corresponded to them in the other worlds. Therefore, the same knowledge is needed (unless the same Spirit is present) for those who wish to correctly interpret their figures and allegorical meanings.

<margin>
A fourth world is added to the others: Man, the <term>Microcosmos</term> <note>Greek original: miκroκosmos, meaning "small world."</note>.
</margin>
Moreover, besides the three worlds we have described, there is another fourth world in which all those things found in the others may also be found. This is man himself, who, as the Catholic doctors say, is for this reason designated by the name "every creature" in the Gospel. For while the Gospel is to be preached to men, not to beasts and angels, Christ nonetheless commands it to be preached to "every creature." It is a common saying in the schools that man is a "lesser world," in whom is seen a body mixed from the elements, a celestial spirit, the vegetable soul of plants, the senses of beasts, reason, an angelic mind, and the likeness of God.

<margin>
Scripture states that Moses treated all these worlds; this is the image of nature.
</margin>
Therefore, if we establish these four worlds, it is credible that Moses, about to speak sufficiently of the world, discussed all of them. And since a writer portrays nature—if he is as skilled in nature as we believe this man of ours to have been—it is credible that he would not have arranged the teaching about them differently than the Almighty God, the Craftsman, arranged them in themselves. Thus, this writing of Moses is a true and expressed image of the world, just as we also read that he was commanded on the mountain where he learned these things to "make all things according to the pattern" he had seen on the mountain. Therefore, the first thing, which is the greatest of all as we have shown—that the things in all the worlds are contained in each—meant that Moses, an emulator of nature, should never treat any one of those worlds without treating all of them together and equally under the same words and the same context.

<margin>
The root of the fourfold exposition.
</margin>
From this, a fourfold exposition of the entire Mosaic reading immediately arises: first, we explain whatever is written there concerning the angelic and invisible world, making no mention of the others. Second, we do the same for all things regarding the celestial world; then regarding this sublunary and corruptible world; and fourth, regarding the nature of man. For if the intelligible world, for example, is never discussed without the same words also describing the other worlds (just as that world contains all subsequent natures within itself), then we can interpret those words regarding all of them. Furthermore, just as the natures, although promiscuously contained within each other, have nonetheless been allotted distinct proper seats and certain peculiar laws, so also if the fourfold nature is discussed in the same series of letters in each part of the present work, it must be believed that the first part deals more specifically with the first nature, and so on in order for the rest.

<margin>
The root of the fifth exposition.
</margin>
From this, the necessity of a fifth exposition also arises. To this is added the reason why these things are distinct: because there is no multiplicity that is not one, they are bound by a certain "discordant concord" and tied together by manifold chains of connections.

<margin>
The root of the sixth exposition.
</margin>
Since it is likely that Moses deals with this in the entire work, it calls us, even if we are reluctant, to a sixth interpretation. In this, we shall show that there are fifteen modes by which we can understand one thing as related or joined to another; and since there are neither more nor fewer, so they...

...our own weakness) I have searched with zeal for the understanding of the Mosaic reading. Since I saw that many Latin and Greek authors had labored in its explanation, and moreover that the ancient Chaldean and Hebrew interpreters—as well as modern ones—were almost innumerable, I did not even dare to think of writing or commenting on anything new regarding this matter.

<margin>The reason for commenting after so many interpreters.</margin>
However, I remembered that the Mosaic law cautioned that no one should reap their field thoroughly and entirely, but should leave an untouched portion for the poor and the needy, so that they might take bundles and handfuls from there to satisfy their hunger. <note>Pico refers to the biblical law of "gleaning" found in Leviticus 19:9-10, where farmers were commanded to leave the edges of their fields for the poor.</note> When this came to mind, I began to survey the vast fields of the Prophet <note>Moses is frequently referred to by Pico simply as "the Prophet."</note> with keen eyes to investigate whether the most learned interpreters—who were no less cultivators of the law than its explainers—had, according to the edict of the law, left some part untouched for us, the weaker ones, to reap. From there, I too might gather even a few ears of grain to be placed upon the altars of the Church as the first fruits of the harvest, lest I be excluded from the privileges of the temple as if I were not a true Israelite or were entirely empty-handed. The matter succeeded according to my wish—not because I could indeed do anything that they could not, but because they, following the precept of the law, did not wish to block the path of those coming after them through their own industry. Furthermore, such is the vastness and fertility of this field that no number of grains could equal it. Thus, although nearly infinite and most powerful efforts have been exerted upon it with all their strength, we can still say that Gospel phrase: *The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few.* <note>Matthew 9:37.</note>

<margin>Latin interpreters. Greeks.</margin>
Therefore, what those most holy men—Ambrose and Augustine, as well as Strabo, Bede, and Remigius, and from the more recent ones, Giles and Albert—have written on this book, and likewise what among the Greeks Philo, Origen, Basil, Theodoret, Apollinarius, Didymus, Diodorus, Severus, Eusebius, Josephus, Gennadius, and Chrysostom <note>This list includes a wide range of early Christian Church Fathers, medieval scholastics, and Hellenistic Jewish writers like Philo and Josephus.</note> have written, shall be left entirely untouched by us. For it would be both rash and superfluous for a weak man to exert himself in that part of the field where the most robust minds have long since exerted themselves.

<margin>Chaldeans.</margin>
<margin>Hebrews. Seven new expositions.</margin>
Regarding those things which either Jonathan, Onkelos, or the ancient Simeon delivered in Chaldean <note>referring to the Targums, which are Aramaic translations and paraphrases of the Hebrew Bible</note>, or those which the Hebrews wrote—either the ancients like Eleazar, Abba, Joannes, Nehunia, Isaac, and Joseph, or the more recent ones like Gersonides, Saadia, both Abrahams, both Moseses, Solomon, and Menahem <note>This list includes major Jewish figures such as Gersonides (Levi ben Gershom), Saadia Gaon, Abraham ibn Ezra, Maimonides (Moses ben Maimon), Nahmanides (Moses ben Nahman), and Rashi (Solomon ben Isaac).</note>—we shall make no mention at present. Instead, we shall bring forward, beyond all these, seven other expositions of our own invention and meditation. In these, we shall first take care to overcome, if we can, three difficulties with which a great 

<margin>The first difficulty.</margin>
and arduous struggle seems to have existed for all those who undertook to explain this book. The first is to ensure that nothing said by Moses appears either insufficient or lacking in learning and wisdom. Some have freed themselves from this by saying that he did not speak of all things, nor bring forward grand and sublime matters, because he was speaking to an unrefined people who were not fit for the understanding of everything. We can believe that the unrefined listeners were satisfied if the light of knowledge—which the wise looked upon from within—was covered by more common words, as if by a horn lantern, so that duller eyes would not be dazzled. Thus, he brought the light to benefit healthy eyes, but brought it enclosed and veiled so as not to hurt those with weak vision. For he neither should have, nor could have, nor wanted to help the learned any less than the unlearned.

<margin>The second difficulty.</margin>
The second difficulty is that the course of the interpretation should be consistent with itself, fitting together, and that the entire series—as if guided by a single thread—should refer back to the same sense from which it originally proceeded, mindful of its purpose. It would not be right if we introduced him speaking of Ideas in one place, and in the very next clause we wanted him to deal with the elements, or with man. This would be an arbitrary and violent kind of exposition. Yet, to avoid this in the explanation of this book seemed impossible to many, and certainly difficult and laborious to all. So great is the perplexity, the ambiguity, and the variety of the entire reading.

<margin>See the immensity of the labor.</margin>
See how much labor and how difficult it is to achieve what we have conceived in our mind (may we succeed!): to interpret this whole creation of the world not by just one sense, but by a seven-fold sense, beginning a new work from the start each time in a continuous and unmixed order of exposition, using nothing from the riches of our predecessors.

<margin>The third difficulty.</margin>
The third 

<column-break/>

difficulty lies in this: that the Prophet should not bring forward anything foreign, monstrous, or alien to the nature of things as they are now seen, nor anything contrary to the truth which our own people have accepted as discovered by the better philosophers. Rather, let us show the Divine Spirit speaking through the Prophet. Now, why we have brought forward seven expositions, by what reasoning they were undertaken, what our plan is, and what necessity drove us to them—and what is entirely new about what we are attempting to bring forward—we shall make clear in the following chapter. In that chapter, sketching the "Idea" <note>Pico uses "Idea" in the Platonic sense: the perfect, archetypal pattern of a thing.</note> of one who is to write most perfectly on this matter (that is, the creation of the world) in imitation of nature itself, he will then attempt to prove in the following sections that our Prophet did not fall away from that archetype in any way. Rather, he is so perfect in every detail that nothing else should be proposed to everyone as such an Idea than Moses himself; and we can all more easily admire his greatness than estimate it according to its worth. These works of ours, whatever they may be—the still unrefined fruits of our youth—are owed to you, Lorenzo, most illustrious man, both because they are mine (and I have long since given and vowed myself to you) and because you yourself provided for us the leisure of this worldly retreat in which they were born.

<margin>Moses is the Idea of writing correctly about nature.</margin>
<margin>Angelo Poliziano.</margin>
This work is also seasoned by the frequent intervention or rather the constant presence of Angelo Poliziano, your close friend, whose pleasant and fertile genius, which previously brought forth various flowers of literature, now promises, I believe, the solid and mature fruit of philosophy. Additionally, it is customary when something festive or joyful happens to those we love or revere, not only to congratulate them with words but also to favor their happiness with some gift, so to speak, and to make our heart's joy known to them.

<margin>Innocent VIII.</margin>
Therefore, this study of ours comes to you opportunely at the time when your son Giovanni—at an age at which no one before him was ever appointed—has been destined by the Supreme Pontiff Innocent VIII for the highest Christian order and college <note>Pico is referring to Giovanni de' Medici being made a Cardinal at age 13 by Pope Innocent VIII. Giovanni later became Pope Leo X.</note>, both because of his own natural character, which promises all good things, and because your merits and authority rightly and deservedly demand it for him. It remains for us to hope that he shows himself worthy of this dignity. This he will do if he holds the one who was both his father and the author of his dignity as his exemplar for life: that is, as a model of prudence and of every virtue. Farewell.

### ANOTHER PREFACE TO THE WHOLE WORK.

<margin>The constitution of the three worlds.</margin>
Ancient times represented three worlds. The highest of all is the super-mundane, which theologians call the **Angelic** and philosophers call the **Intellectual**; of which 

<margin>Plato</margin>
Plato says in the *Phaedrus* that no one has praised it enough according to its worth. Next to this is the **Celestial**; the last of all is this **Sublunary** world which we inhabit. This one is full of darkness; that one is full of light; the heavens are tempered by both light and darkness.

<margin>Angelic World. Celestial. Sublunary.</margin>
This world is marked by a flowing and unstable substance, signified by water; that one by the brightness of light and the highness of its place, signified by fire; the heavens, being of a middle nature, are therefore called by the Hebrews *schamaim*, as if composed of *es* and *maim*—that is, of fire and water (as we have said). <note>original: "asciamaim quasi ex es & maim"</note>. In this world, there is the alternation of life and death; in that one, perpetual life and stable operation; in the heavens, there is life and stability of operations, but an alternation of positions. This world is made of the decaying substance of bodies; that one of the nature of the divine mind; the heavens are composed of body—but an incorruptible one—and of mind—but one bound to a body.

<margin>The series of motion.</margin>
The third world is moved by the second; the second is ruled by the first. Furthermore, there are many differences between them, which it is not our intention to explain here, where we prefer to skim over these matters rather than overflow with them.

<margin>The partition of Moses's tabernacle according to the likeness of the worlds.</margin>
I should not omit that these three worlds were most clearly figured by Moses in the construction of that admirable Tabernacle of his. For he divided the Tabernacle into three parts, each of which could in no way more expressively represent the individual worlds we have mentioned. For the first part, protected by no roof or shade, was open and exposed to rain, snow, sun, heat, and cold; and because it is a more evident image of our own—that is, the sublunary—world, not only did pure and impure, sacred and profane men inhabit it, but also animals of every sort...

<margin>Interpretation of the worlds.</margin>
...kinds of animals; and in this part, due to the sacrifices and constant offerings, there was a perpetual cycle of life and death. The remaining two parts were both covered and free from any external harm, just as both the celestial and super-celestial worlds are neither capable of suffering injury nor dishonor. Both were also honored with the name of "holiness," yet in such a way that the more secret part was called the "Holy of Holies," while the other was decorated only with the title "Holy." This is just as the celestial and angelic worlds are both holy—since above the moon, after the fall of Lucifer, there is not and cannot be any stain or sin—yet the angelic world is considered far holier and more divine than the celestial. But why do we pursue these more distant similarities? For if the last part of the tabernacle was common to men and beasts; and the second part, which shone entirely with the splendor of gold, was illuminated by a candelabra divided into seven lamps (which, as all Latin, Greek, and Hebrew interpreters say, signify the seven planets); and in the third part, the most sacred of all, there were winged cherubim—do these not place the three worlds before our eyes? This world which both beasts and men inhabit, the celestial world in which the planets gleam, and the super-celestial dwelling of the angels.

<margin>What the veiling signifies through Christ's death.</margin>
From this, we are also reminded of a deeper mystery of the Gospel. Since the way to the super-celestial world and the company of angels has been opened for us through the cross and blood of Christ, it was for this reason that, upon his death, the veil of the temple was torn. This veil had separated the Holy of Holies (by which we said the angelic world is signified) from the other parts. This was a sign that the entrance for man to the kingdom of God—to God himself, who "flies above the cherubim"—was now open, though it had been closed from the beginning by the laws of justice due to the sin of our first parent.

<margin>Three reasons the worlds are one, according to the opinion of Anaxagoras and explained by the Platonists.</margin>
This is enough regarding the three worlds. In these, the most important thing to observe—upon which almost our entire purpose depends—is that these three worlds are one world; not only because they are all referred to a single beginning and the same end, or because they are bound together by balanced numbers and a certain harmonious kinship of nature and an orderly series of steps, but because whatever is in all the worlds together is also contained in each individual one. Nor is there any one of them in which everything that exists in the others is not present. I believe this was the opinion of Anaxagoras <note>Anaxagoras (c. 500–428 BC) was a Pre-Socratic philosopher who famously taught that "everything is in everything."</note> (if we think he felt correctly), which was then explained by the Pythagoreans and Platonists.

<margin>Pattern of the proposed truth.</margin>
Truly, those things which are in the lower world are also in the higher ones, but of a better quality; likewise, those in the higher worlds are seen even in the lowest, but in a diminished condition and an "adulterated" nature, so to speak. Among us, heat is an elementary quality; in the heavens, it is a heating power; in the angelic minds, it is the Idea of heat. Let me speak more clearly. Among us, there is fire, which is an element; the Sun is fire in heaven; in the ultra-mundane region, fire is the seraphic intellect. <note>The Seraphim are the highest rank of angels, whose name is derived from the Hebrew word for "burning."</note> But see how they differ: the elementary burns, the celestial gives life, and the super-celestial loves. There is water among us; there is water in the heavens, which is the mover and mistress of our water, namely the Moon; there are also waters above the heaven, the cherubic minds. <note>The Cherubim are associated with "waters" or "fullness of knowledge" in this tradition.</note> But see the disparity of condition in the same nature: elemental moisture overwhelms the heat of life; celestial moisture nourishes it; super-celestial moisture understands it.

<margin>Ten spheres of the intelligible world.</margin>
<margin>Ten spheres of the celestial world.</margin>
<margin>Ten spheres of the elementary world.</margin>
In the first world, God, the primary Unity, presides over the nine orders of angels as if over so many spheres, and being himself immovable, he moves all toward himself. In the middle world, that is, the celestial, the Empyrean heaven <note>The Empyrean was considered the highest, most refined part of the heavens, filled with pure light or fire.</note> is rolled along with an ineffable motion; yet, mirroring God, it presides as a leader over the other nine celestial spheres, which remain immovable by comparison. There are also in the elementary world, after prime matter (which is its foundation), nine spheres of corruptible forms. Specifically, three of bodies devoid of life, which are the elements and mixtures; then between these, three of the middle kind, which are mixed but imperfect, such as the impressions made in the heights <note>Pico refers here to "meteors" or atmospheric phenomena.</note>.

<margin>Body, Nature, Soul.</margin>
Then there are three of a vegetable nature, which is first divided into three kinds: herbs, shrubs, and trees. Finally, there are three of the sensitive soul, which is either imperfect (such as that in <term>Zoophytes</term> <note>original: "Zoophitis." Creatures like sponges or corals that were thought to bridge the gap between plants and animals.</note>), or perfect but within the limits of irrational imagination, or (what is highest in beasts) even capable of human-like training, which is a middle point between man and beast, just as the Zoophyte is a middle point between beast and plant.

<margin>Evidence of the worlds also in Holy Scripture.</margin>
But enough of these things. Let us only add that the mutual containment of the worlds is also indicated in the Holy Scriptures: since it is written in the Psalms, "He who creates the heavens in understanding," and we read that the angels of God are spirits and his ministers a "flame of burning fire." Hence, divine things are often given celestial names, and often even earthly ones; they are figured now by stars, now by wheels and animals, now by elements. Hence also earthly things are often given celestial names. This is because all these worlds, bound by the chains of concord, grant to one another not only their natures but also their names, with mutual generosity. From this principle (if perhaps anyone has not yet noticed it) has flowed the entire discipline of allegorical sense. Nor could the ancient fathers have fittingly represented some things by other figures unless they had been taught the "hidden friendships" and affinities of all nature. Otherwise, there would be no reason why they should have represented this by one image rather than another. But being knowledgeable in all things and driven by that Spirit who not only knows all these things but made them, they figured the natures of one world most aptly through those things which they knew corresponded to them in the remaining worlds. Therefore, the same knowledge is needed (unless the same Spirit is present) for those who wish to correctly interpret their figures and allegorical senses.

<margin>A fourth world is added to the higher ones, that is, man, the <term>microcosm</term> <note>original: "μικρόκοσμος" (microkosmos).</note>.</margin>
However, besides the three we have described, there is another fourth world in which all those things found in the others may also be found. This is man himself, who, as the Catholic doctors say, is for this reason designated by the name "every creature" in the Gospel, when Christ commands that the Gospel be preached to "every creature." It is a common saying in the schools that man is a "lesser world," in whom are seen a body mixed from elements, a celestial spirit, the vegetable soul of plants, the sense of beasts, reason, the angelic mind, and the likeness of God.

<margin>He claims Moses treated all these worlds, and that this is a plural image of nature.</margin>
Therefore, if we establish these four worlds, it is believable that Moses, when he was to speak sufficiently about the world, discussed all of these. Since a writer depicts nature if he is skilled in nature (as we believe this man was, if anyone ever was), it is believable that he arranged his teaching about them in no other way than the omnipotent God the Creator arranged them in themselves. Thus, this scripture of Moses is a true, expressed image of the world; just as we read he was commanded on the mountain where he learned these things, that he should "make all things according to the pattern" he had seen on the mountain. Therefore, first and foremost—just as we have shown that what is in all worlds is contained in each—it was necessary that Moses, the emulator of nature, should never deal with any one of those worlds without dealing with all of them together at once under the same words and the same context.

<margin>The root of the fourfold exposition.</margin>
From this, a fourfold exposition of the entire Mosaic reading immediately arises. First, we explain whatever is written there concerning the angelic and invisible world, making no mention of the others. Second, we do the same for all things concerning the celestial world; then for this sublunary and corruptible world; and fourth, concerning the nature of man. For if the intelligible world is never discussed without containing within itself all the lower natures, then we must interpret the same words for all worlds. Again, just as natures, although mixed among themselves, have nevertheless been allotted distinct proper seats and certain peculiar laws, so also, if in each part of the present work we discuss the fourfold nature in the same series of letters, it must be believed that in the first part we deal more specifically with the first nature, and in the same order thereafter in the others.

<margin>The root of the fifth exposition.</margin>
From this also arises the necessity of a fifth exposition. To this is added that, by the same logic that these things are distinct, because there is no multiplicity that is not one, they are bound by a certain discordant concord and tied together by multiform chains of connections.

<margin>The root of the sixth exposition.</margin>
Since it is likely that Moses deals with this in the whole work, he calls us now, even against our will, to a sixth interpretation. In this, we will show that there are fifteen modes by which we can understand one thing as being related or joined to another; and since there are neither more nor fewer, we will...

He argues that Moses wrote the Genesis account to be interpreted on all these levels simultaneously, justifying his multi-layered "Heptaplus" commentary.</summary>

<margin>The root of the seventh exposition.</margin>
...all are sufficiently and clearly expressed by the prophet <note>referring to Moses</note>: so that Aristotle never wrote anything more clearly about the nature of things. Finally, just as the Sabbath—that is, rest—follows the six days of creation: it is fitting that we also briefly touch upon the orders of things proceeding from God: their explained union and difference, their covenants and relationships, in this seventh and "sabbatical" (so to speak) narration concerning the happiness of creatures and their return to God. This return happens for man—who was distanced from Him by the sin of our first parent—through the Mosaic and Christian law. We will refer to what Moses most clearly hid concerning these things in the present scripture: so that a most distinct prophecy of Christ’s coming, the progress of the Church, and the calling of the Gentiles may be read openly here. Truly, this book is—if ever there were such a thing—a <note>original: "liber septem signaculis obsignatus"</note> <term>book sealed with seven seals</term>, full of every doctrine and all mysteries. However, we will not imitate those who, having once attempted to explain this creation of the world, gathered here everything ever disputed among philosophers and theologians concerning God, angels, matter, heaven, and all of nature. 
<margin>Isaac the Persian and Samuel Ophinides.</margin>
In this, among the Hebrews, Isaac the Persian and Samuel Ophinides <note>Two medieval Jewish commentators whose works often blended astrology and philosophy with scripture</note> especially erred. Instead, we shall strive with all our strength to declare only what the Mosaic letter intends: what the context of the words either indicates or signifies. Nor, if we show that the "firmament" signifies, for instance, the eighth sphere, will we immediately begin a dispute about how it carries the other spheres: by how many signs it is distinguished, how many images, or whether it rotates in different directions by a simple motion, or rather two, or more truly three. Or if we say that the human soul is indicated by some mention of a "cube," we will not digress into everything

<column-break/>

written about the soul to clarify it. Rather, we will only note those things about each subject briefly and in passing, of which the author <note>Moses</note> seems to make express mention. I said briefly and in passing: because the purpose of this work is not that those who have not learned these things elsewhere should learn them here for the first time; but rather that they may recognize that the things they already knew to be true are present in the prophet’s words. Thus, understanding how he both included and concealed in a few words what they have read digested in immense volumes by theologians and philosophers, they may hear the Lawgiver speaking with a "revealed face" <note>An allusion to Moses removing his veil to speak directly, meaning the text's secret meaning is now clear</note>. 
<margin>These writings are entrusted to the learned, not to those unrefined in philosophy.</margin>
But if anyone, perhaps moved by a spirit of "holy rusticity," should not approve of these more deeply sought mysteries, but instead desires a simpler and more accommodating narration of the sacred text: I will bid him first remember Paul's precept, that neither he who eats should despise him who does not eat, nor he who does not eat judge him who eats. 
<margin>Paul</margin>
<margin>Augustine</margin>
Then I shall address him not with my own words, but with those of Augustine from his own exposition on Genesis, in this manner: "If you can, grasp these things; if you cannot yet, leave them to those more capable." 
<margin>The power of Scripture.</margin>
But you, as you make progress, will find that Scripture does not abandon your weakness, but walks slowly with you like a mother. For it speaks in such a way as to mock the proud with its height, terrify the attentive with its depth, feed the great with its truth, and nourish the small with its affability. But let us return to our task: and starting from this very corruptible world in which we dwell, let us provide as much as we can of what we promised. Otherwise, in great things, it is enough to have willed them: and as Pomerius <note>Julius Pomerius, a 5th-century Christian author</note> says, "the great effort toward great things is itself progress."
<margin>Pomerius</margin>

## The Mosaic words to be explained.
### These are the very words of the prophet which we have undertaken to explain.

<margin>The first day.</margin>
<image-desc>Large decorative woodcut initial 'I' depicting classical architecture with several figures, marking the beginning of the word 'IN'.</image-desc>
IN the beginning God created the heaven and the earth: but the earth was empty and void: and darkness was upon the face of the deep: and the spirit of the Lord moved over the waters: and God said let there be light and there was light: and God saw the light that it was good: and he divided the light from the darkness and he called the light day and the darkness night: and the evening and the morning were the first day. 
<margin>The second day.</margin>
And God said, let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters: and let it divide the waters from the waters: and God made the firmament and divided the waters which were under the firmament from those which were above the firmament: and it was so: And God called the firmament Heaven: and the evening and the morning were the second day. And God said, let the waters which are under the heaven be gathered together into one place and let the dry land appear: and it was so and God called the dry land Earth: and the gathering together of the waters he called Seas: and God saw that it was good: and he said let the earth bring forth green herbs, such as may seed and fruit trees yielding fruit after their kind, whose seed may be in itself upon the earth: and it was so, and the earth brought forth green herbs, such as give seed after their kind and the tree yielding fruit: and each having its own seed according to its species and God saw that it was good: and the evening and the morning were the third day. 
<margin>The third day.</margin>
And God said: Let there be lights in the firmament of heaven to divide the day and the night and let them be for signs and seasons and days and years to shine in the firmament of heaven: and to illuminate the earth: and it was so and God made two great lights, the greater light to rule the day: and the lesser light to rule the night and the stars and he set them in the firmament of heaven to shine upon the earth: and to rule over the day and night

<column-break/>

<margin>The fourth day.</margin>
and to divide the light and the darkness: and God saw that it was good: and the evening and the morning were the fourth day. God also said let the waters bring forth the creeping creature having life and the fowl over the earth under the firmament of heaven: And God created indeed great whales and every living and moving soul which the waters had brought forth in their kinds: and every fowl according to its kind: and God saw that it was good: and he blessed them saying. Increase and multiply and fill the waters of the sea: and let the birds be multiplied upon the earth: and the evening and the morning were the fifth day. 
<margin>The fifth day.</margin>
God also said let the earth bring forth the living soul in its kind: cattle and creeping things and beasts of the earth according to their species: and it was so: and God made the beasts of the earth according to their species: cattle and every creeping thing of the earth in its kind: and God saw that it was good and said. Let us make man to our image and likeness and let him have dominion over the fish of the Sea and the fowls of the air and the beasts of the whole earth and every creeping thing that moves on the earth: and God created man to his own image and likeness to the image of God he created him. Thus far we have undertaken to explain Moses. I have divided the entire exposition into seven books or treatises: rather to imitate Basil and Augustine, so that the reader’s attention may be refreshed. Furthermore, since there are seven expositions digested into seven books and each book is divided into seven chapters, everything corresponds to the seven days of creation. This was likewise done by us for a most fitting reason: so that just as the seventh day in Moses is the Sabbath and a day of rest: so our every exposition may always be directed in its seventh chapter toward Christ: who is both the end of the law and is our Sabbath, our rest, and our happiness.
<margin>The sixth day.</margin>

# FIRST EXPOSITION ON the elementary world.

## BOOK ONE, CHAPTER ONE.

<margin>He establishes the principle of natural things as matter through triple dimension and privation.</margin>
The Natural Philosophers <note>Referring primarily to the Peripatetics, or followers of Aristotle</note> who discourse on the nature of perishable things, generally establish the following regarding their principles: that there is a raw matter, devoid of forms, which is indeed suitable for receiving all forms but is by its own nature deprived of them all. Therefore, besides matter, they also make "privation" <note>the absence of a quality or form that should naturally be present</note> a principle of natural things. Averroes <note>A 12th-century Islamic philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were central to Renaissance study</note> added that matter is extended in triple dimension—in length, width, and depth—lest physical things be said to arise from a non-physical subject. Then they bring forward a changing "efficient cause" <note>the agent or force that brings something into being</note> by whose power the matter being handled—which exists only as a possibility—eventually becomes an actual thing. This is just as soft and undefined wax is transformed into various shapes by the movement and touch of the hand, according to the will of the person handling it. Moreover, because nature does nothing at random but for the sake of achieving some good, the "final cause" <note>the purpose or goal of a process</note> immediately introduces itself. The nearest goal of the acting cause is the "form," which it draws out from the lap of matter. The agent acts and moves matter with this specific plan: to lead it to the perfect state of form. Thus, "form" is the third principle established by Aristotle. However, this form cannot be drawn out from the heart of matter unless the matter is first influenced and prepared by suitable qualities. All the labor of the craftsman and the entire duration of the action is spent on these qualities, until the specific individual shape suddenly shines forth like the reward for the work. The Peripatetics call the craftsman himself a "cause" rather than a "principle." Yet the Platonists, always mindful of divine matters, remind us that although natural acting causes appear to us to be the only ones acting, forming, and changing bodies, they are not the primary causes of what is made. Instead, they are the instruments of a divine art which they obey and serve. Just as the hands of a builder—even if they assemble, arrange, and transform all the material of a house, the wood, stones, and mortar—are known to be merely an organ obeying and serving the art established in the architect's mind, so the divine art arranges and unfolds the house it once conceived, part by part, from unfeeling matter. From this, the Platonists add two more causes: the "organic" and the "exemplary" <note>the instrument used and the perfect model or idea being copied</note>. The Peripatetics do not deny this; indeed, they confirm it with that well-worn saying: "Every work of nature is a work of intelligence." These are the things commonly said about perishable things, all of which Moses embraced in the work of the first day so accurately and fittingly that the most esteemed philosophers have said nothing better.

<margin>The goal.</margin>
<margin>Form. The arrangements of matter.</margin>
<margin>Natural acting causes are the instruments of divine ones.</margin>
<margin>Cause.</margin>

<column-break/>

## CHAPTER TWO.

<margin>Earth is the material cause; heaven is the acting cause according to the Stoics.</margin>
In the beginning, therefore, Moses establishes two causes: the acting cause and the material cause—that which is actual and 그that which is potential. He calls the former "heaven" and the latter "earth." Our interpretation is first supported by the authority of the Stoics, who called the acting cause "heaven" and the material cause "earth," as Varro <note>A Roman scholar and writer</note> writes, not to mention the Greeks. Reason also supports this. For just as matter is the most lowly of all natures, so is the earth among all the elements; and as the Peripatetics prove, heaven and earth correspond in exactly the same proportion as the agent to the matter. Now, this earth—that is, matter—was "void and empty," as Jerome <note>translator of the Latin Vulgate Bible</note> translated it, or as the Septuagint <note>the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> has it, "invisible and uncomposed." All these terms suit raw and formless matter, which, being devoid of all forms, is rightly called "void and empty" and is entirely uncomposed and invisible. However, the Hebrew words *tou* and *bou* <note>original: "tou & bou"</note> <term>Tohu and Bohu</term> which are read in this passage are explained differently by many Hebrews. They interpret *Tohu* as a "brute thing," stunned and astonished. This is referred by them to the dark and deformed face of matter for this reason: because when we fix our attention on knowing it, it leaves us astonished. Because of this, Aristotle said it is known by "proportion" and Plato by "bastard reasoning" <note>a phrase from Plato's Timaeus describing how we perceive matter, which has no form of its own</note>. Many explain *Bou* from the power of the word as the "beginning" and "rudiment" of form. For if we translate word for word, *bou* <note>original: "bou"</note> is as if we said "in it is" or "something is in it." If we follow this, we will understand that besides the potential of the subject, there is an incipient form within it. Not only Albertus <note>Albert the Great, a medieval scientist and theologian</note> and many Peripatetics believed this, but even the ancient Hebrews, as we clearly gather from the records of the very ancient Simeon <note>likely referring to Rabbi Simeon bar Yochai, traditionally the author of the Zohar</note>. But in what way this "beginning" is to be understood, he declares by adding: "and darkness was over the face of the abyss." He calls the "abyss" the earth—that is, matter extended in the deepest depths by triple dimension. Over this is "darkness," which is "privation," a principle especially celebrated among the Peripatetics, and no name fits it better than darkness. Now, privation (by which it differs from mere negation, as the great Albertus most firmly maintains) is this very "beginning of form" of which we speak, a matter on which the same philosopher has lectured copiously and subtly. Furthermore, if the earth lies beneath the waters, then "water" in this place will signify the accidental qualities and affections of matter. These, by their flowing and manageable nature, bear the appearance of water; by these, so to speak, the moistened matter gives birth to the form which it brings into the light at the final moment of time. Over these waters, the "spirit of the Lord"—that is, the power of the efficient cause, the Lord's organ and instrument—is rightly said to be moved. It is not said to be moved over the "earth" because the agent does not touch...

<margin>Aristotle. Plato.</margin>
<margin>Albertus. The Ancient Simeon.</margin>

He uses Hebrew philology to explain that prime matter contains the seeds of form and that "darkness" refers to the philosophical concept of privation.</summary>

<meta>The previous page established Pico's framework for interpreting the creation of the world through Aristotelian physics, defining "matter" as a blank slate and "form" as the defining quality given by the Creator. He continues here by explaining how light emerges from this interaction.</meta>

->JOHN PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA<-

<margin>By joining evening and morning, one day was made.</margin>
The agent does not permeate the subject unless those intervening qualities are present; as the agent moves and acts upon them, light arises—that is, the beauty and appearance of "form" <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "form" is the essence or "blueprint" that makes a thing what it is.</note> which drives out and puts to flight the "darkness" we mentioned, which is "privation" <note>The absence of a form that ought to be there, like silence is the absence of sound.</note>. This occurs by the voice of God so commanding, because natural causes do nothing that the order of divine art has not first ordained. Then, from evening and morning, "one day" is made: because from the nature of potentiality <note>the capacity to become something</note> and the nature of the acting force, a third substance—which we call a "composite"—has sprung forth. There is now an obvious reason, according to this sense, why he said "one day" rather than "the first day," and why he rightly saw that the light was good.

<margin>What the nature of form is.</margin>
For the nature of form is nothing other than a thin image and a shadow-like resemblance of the "First Good" <note>God</note>. Thus far we have spoken generally about "corruptible substance" <note>physical matter that can decay or change</note>, which includes everything below the moon; there we saw both "heaven" and "earth"—that is, the nature that changes and the nature that is changed—and that same "earth," meaning matter, was empty of every specific type and void of every accidental form.

<margin>Epilogue.</margin>
And we saw the "darkness of privation" sitting upon that matter, which was extended into the three dimensions of the abyss. This darkness was not truly internal to it (for privation is not the essence of matter, as Aristotle proves), but rather occupied its outermost face.

<margin>A proposition against Aristotle.</margin>
We likewise saw the "Spirit of the Lord" being carried over the "waters"—that is, the fluid dispositions of matter—present as if to the earth. This spirit acted as the power of the "efficient cause" <note>the trigger or agent of change</note>, not as the principal cause itself,

<margin>Exposition of the Spirit of the Lord.</margin>
but as the "Spirit of the Lord"—that is, the instrument of divine art, just as our vital spirit is the instrument of the soul. Immediately, as that spirit handled those "waters" and persuaded the subject at the command of God the Craftsman, light arose: that is, the beauty and splendor of form.

---

### CHAPTER THREE.

<margin>According to Aristotle: What we understand by "waters" on the second day.</margin>
Now, since we rightly descend in order from general and common things to specific ones (as Aristotle proves), Moses is about to do the same. After he spoke of those things common to all elemental things, he divides the entire elemental substance into three parts on the second day. First, however, it must be understood that all "material forms" are designated by him here under the name of "waters"—a name that could not be more fitting. For in this sphere of things that can be generated and corrupted, matter stands like a seabed or a sea, where there is a perpetual and unending ebb and flow of waves: the coming and going of forms.

<margin>Solomon.</margin>
As Solomon says: "One generation passes away, and another generation arrives, but the earth stands forever" <note>original: "Generatio scilicet præterit... & generatio aduenit. terra autem stat in æternum." — Ecclesiastes 1:4</note>.

<margin>The Platonists, imitators of the Hebrews.</margin>
For among the Platonists—who are always imitators of Hebrew teaching—these forms are called "generations" rather than "forms," because they can more truly be said to be "becoming" than to truly "be." For this same reason, just as he previously used the name "waters" to call the qualities and accidental forms of matter, he here uses the same name for the material substances themselves—

<column-break/>

<margin>Alexander.</margin>
—but, as the Platonists take great pains to confirm, every "species" <note>the specific nature of a thing</note> that exists in matter should be referred more to the condition of an "accident" <note>a temporary quality</note> than to that of a true "substance." For those things rightfully claim the title of substance for themselves which stand by their own power, leaning upon themselves, and are true by their own nature, unmixed with foreign things and not at all diluted.

<margin>Heraclitus the Poet.</margin>
Heraclitus called the substance of sensible things "the sea," and among the poets who veil philosophy in the flight of fables, the same is found: when, after the "Saturnian unity" (that is, the union of the intellectual world which enfolds all things within itself), they divided the sensible world into three parts.

<margin>The kingdoms assigned to the three gods.</margin>
They assigned the celestial region to Jove, the subterranean to Pluto, and this middle region to Neptune—namely, the region stretching from the Moon to the earth, which we are now discussing. They called Neptune the "Lord of the Sea," and among the Platonists, he is understood to represent that power which presides over "generations" <note>the process of things being born and dying</note>. But let us return to Moses, who divides the "waters from the waters" by the "firmament" in the middle.

<margin>The first partition.</margin>
There is a triple partition of sublunary bodies <note>things located beneath the moon</note>. Some are above the middle region of the air; these are the highest things, namely a part of that same element and the purest fire, all of which is designated by the name "ether." There, the elements are pure, unmixed, and "legitimate."

<margin>The second partition.</margin>
Other things are below the very center of the air, where we are. Here, there is no pure element (for a pure element cannot be perceived by the senses), but all things consist of mixtures from the drossy and thicker part of the worldly body.

<margin>Third: Observe the triple element.</margin>
The intervening region of air is what is here called the "firmament," from which even the birds flying beneath it are introduced as being "under the firmament of heaven." This is the region in which those sublime "impressions" appear: rain, snow, lightning, thunder, comets, and the like. See how rightly this "firmament" distinguishes and separates the higher elements from the lower—as if "waters from waters"—not only by its location but by its natural property. Above it are pure elements; below it, things depart from elemental simplicity through perfect mixing. Within the region itself, things become mixed, but imperfectly and in a middle state, so that it is most truly said to be between the nature of mixtures and the nature of pure elements.

---

### CHAPTER FOUR.

But let us see what else Moses philosophizes. He says: "Let the waters which are under the heaven be gathered together into one place, and let the dry land appear."

<margin>How the earth, or the "dry land," is separated from the multitude of waters.</margin>
The "dry land" is matter, as we have already established. Matter does not "appear" or become visible unless it is clothed in the appearance of forms; but neither does it appear when clothed in the appearance of a simple element, because, as we have said and as the Philosophers prove, a simple element can neither be seen nor touched, nor can it fall under any sense at all. Therefore, if the earth, which was once invisible, is to come into view, it is necessary that the "waters under the heaven"—that is, under the middle region of the air—be gathered into "one place." This means they flow together into a common "sludge" of mixture, yet are prescribed by certain laws as if by shores, coalescing into a single form of mixture. This happens to the "lower waters," as we have shown, but not to the "upper" ones, where there is either no mixture at all or an imperfect one.

<margin>What the cause is for the earth immediately sprouting plants.</margin>
If the "vegetable soul" <note>the basic level of life that governs growth and nutrition</note> immediately follows the form of this mixture, what else should we expect from our philosopher than that, after that gathering of waters, he would immediately introduce the earth as being fertile with herbs, shrubs, and trees?

---

### CHAPTER FIVE.

Although it seemed that from here the order should proceed to animals (whose soul is most closely joined to the vegetable soul), nevertheless, as we are reminded by the topic of animals—in which every treatise on the corruptible world ends—Moses instead inserted some things concerning those objects which are in the firmament, and with which the firmament is adorned, just as the earth is adorned...

<summary>Pico explains the first few days of Genesis as an allegory for Aristotelian physics, where "waters" represent the fluid material forms of the sublunary world and the "firmament" acts as a boundary between pure elements and complex mixtures.</summary>

b ii
<meta>Ioannes Pico della Mirandola</meta>

<margin>What the firmament is. According to Ennius.</margin>
...with those metals, plants, and living creatures that are produced in it. These, however, are those "impressions" <note>Aristotle used the term "impressions" to describe meteorological phenomena like clouds or rain.</note> which occur on high, that is, in the middle region of the air. This region Moses called "heaven" and "firmament" above, but here he calls it the "firmament of heaven": so that we might know it is not that which is truly heaven, but that which lies beneath the heaven. For this reason, Ennius, in his play *Achilles*, called this part "the underlying part," because it is placed most closely beneath the heaven. Moreover, it is well known that these impressions are called "secondary stars" and "constellations" and "heavenly bodies" by the philosophers; there is no need to prove this with further evidence, nor should it seem too difficult for anyone if we explain the things said here about the stars in this light. <margin>The leader of the first cause.</margin> Since all the diversity of these things is traced back to two primary causes—heat and cold—we shall appropriately refer those things caused by heat to the sun, and those caused by cold to the moon. Nor do these things claim the name of the sun, moon, and other stars solely because they are the same in the lower heaven as those others are in their own more divine realm—or because they show a similar face to men, shining and gleaming alike—but because some of them follow one star in heaven as their prince and leader, and others follow another. Hence, they are also "signs" of those things: for they tend to portend to lower things the same outcomes as the stars by which they were excited. Proof of this is the fact that they follow the motion of the stars, by whose power and influence they consist of earthly matter—that is, a vaporous breath.

## CHAPTER SIX.

<margin>The opinion of the Pythagoreans.</margin>
The things that follow regarding the production of animals and of man are now manifest. For after plants come those mixed bodies that feel and move, although the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of the Greek philosopher Pythagoras.</note> also ascribe a "dull sense" to plants; we shall discuss this in our work on the *Concordance of the Long Bench* <note>Pico likely refers here to his projected but unfinished work harmonizing Plato and Aristotle.</note>. <margin>The Timaeus.</margin> These living creatures, however, which participate in motion and sense beyond all controversy, are distinguished here by Moses—and in Plato's *Timaeus*—as those that fly, those that live in the waters, and those that dwell on the land. The supreme and prince of them all is man: at whom the nature of the corruptible world, having progressed this far, comes to a halt and sounds the retreat.

## CHAPTER SEVEN.

<margin>Christ is our happiness.</margin>
Just as man is the absolute completion of all lower things, so Christ is the absolute completion of all men. Because (as the philosophers say) every perfection is derived from that which is most perfect in any given genus to the others of the same order, as if from a fountain, it is a doubt to no one that the perfection of all goodness is derived from the man Christ into all men. To Him alone, indeed, was the Spirit given "not by measure," so that we might all receive from His fullness. See how undoubtedly this prerogative is owed to Him, both God and man, which also fits Him by a peculiar and legitimate privilege insofar as He is man.

# THE SECOND EXPOSITION: ON THE CELESTIAL WORLD.

### PREFACE.

<margin>Let us rise to the celestial world.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'S' depicting a figure looking towards clouds and a landscape.</image-desc>
Let us rise from the elements to the heaven, from corruptible bodies to incorruptible ones, so that it may be clear to everyone that by the same words with which all the nature of the elemental world was shown to us, the most profound dogmas concerning the celestial beings were also encompassed by the prophet. <margin>Three reasons why Moses wrote figuratively.</margin> When we revolve this in our minds, there will be another reason ready for us besides those we mentioned in the general preface. Why, for example, when Moses was about to speak of the "agent cause" <note>the force that acts to create something</note> and of "matter," did he not call the former the "agent" and the latter "matter" in express words, but called them "heaven" and "earth"? And why did he call the arrangements of matter "waters" rather than "qualities" (as the philosophers do), and call the "form" "light" rather than "form"? Likewise, why did he name comets, lightning, and other such things "stars" and "heavenly bodies" rather than by their proper names, and so on for the rest? In the introductions, we brought forward both the ancient custom of writing great physical and divine matters in an occult and figurative way, and the unrefined state of the listeners who, since they could not bear the brilliance of the Mosaic teaching, needed him to speak with a "veiled face," lest those who were being taken in to be enlightened should be blinded by too much light. Now we have the opportunity for a third reason: namely, that if he had named "matter" and "form" and "qualities" and "the agent cause," those terms could serve the treatises on the corruptible world, but not the others. <margin>The wonderful artifice of Moses. The most absolute kind of writing.</margin> Therefore, it is a truly divine and not human industry, this unthought-of and wonderful artifice of Moses: to use words and arrange his discourse in such a way that the same words, the same context, and the same series of the entire scripture are aptly suited to represent the secrets of all worlds and of all nature. This is where the book of Moses surpasses all the learning, eloquence, and genius of the nations. This is that new and hitherto untouched thing which we have attempted to bring forward: namely, to prove to our people by the fact itself that this was done by Moses. This is the "Idea," this is the model of the most absolute writer; not only because this kind of writing (as we demonstrated above) portrays and emulates nature, but also because, just as among the angelic minds— <margin>Dionysius. Saint Thomas in Latin.</margin> according to the authority of Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian Neoplatonist.</note> and Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas, the great medieval theologian.</note>, the splendor of our theology—that mind is supreme which comprehends through its intelligence in a very few notions and forms those things which inferior minds comprehend through many and varied ones; so among writings, that one is supreme and holds the peak of all perfection which, in a very few words, encompasses all things just as individual and...

<summary>Pico defines the "firmament" as the middle atmosphere and argues that Christ is the ultimate perfection of humanity. He then begins his second interpretation of Genesis, explaining that Moses used figurative language so that his words could simultaneously describe the elemental, celestial, and angelic worlds.</summary>

<margin>
How the earth or dry land is separated from the multitude of waters.
