What the firmament is. Ennius.
</margin>
...those things which occur within it—metals, plants, and living creatures. These, however, are those "impressions" <note>In ancient physics, "impressions" or "meteors" referred to any atmospheric phenomena, including rain, wind, and comets.</note> which occur on high, that is, in the middle region of the air. Above this, he called it both "heaven" and "firmament," but here he calls it the "firmament of heaven": so that we may know it is not that which is truly heaven, but that which lies beneath heaven. For this reason, Ennius, in his *Achilles*, called this part "the underlying part," because it is placed nearest beneath the heaven. Moreover, it is too well known to require further proof that these secondary impressions are called "stars" and "constellations" by philosophers; nor should it seem too harsh for anyone if we interpret what is said here about the stars as referring to them.

<margin>
The two primary causes.
</margin>
Since all the diversity of these things is traced back to two primary causes—heat and cold—we shall appropriately assign those things which are hot by cause to the sun, and those which are cold to the moon. Nor do these things claim the name of the sun, the moon, and the other stars for that reason alone—namely, that they are the same in the lower sky as those others are in their own more divine sky, or because they show themselves to men with a similar appearance, shining and sparkling alike—but rather because some of them follow one star in the heavens as their prince and leader. Hence, they are also "signs" of those things: for they are accustomed to portend to lower things the qualities of the stars by which they were aroused. Proof of this is the fact that they follow the motion of the stars, by whose power and influence they consist of terrestrial matter—that is, of a vaporous breath.

### CHAPTER SIX

<margin>
The opinion of the Pythagoreans.
</margin>
What follows concerning the production of animals and man is now manifest. For after plants come those mixed bodies which feel and move, although the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of the Greek philosopher Pythagoras, known for their belief in the transmigration of souls and the interconnectedness of all life.</note> also ascribe a dull sense to plants; we shall discuss this in that "Concord" <note>A reference to Pico's planned (but largely unwritten) work *De Concordia*, which aimed to harmonize Plato and Aristotle.</note> which we are preparing with the labor of a long sitting. These living things, however, which participate in motion and sense beyond all controversy, are distinguished here by Moses (as in the *Timaeus* <note>Plato’s famous dialogue on the creation of the universe.</note>) into those that fly, those that dwell in the water, and those that are of the earth.

<margin>
Timaeus.
</margin>
The supreme of all and the prince is Man: at whom the nature of the perishable world, having progressed, halts its foot and sounds the retreat.

### CHAPTER SEVEN

<margin>
Christ our happiness.
</margin>
Just as man is the absolute consummation of all lower things, so Christ is the absolute consummation of all men. Because (as the philosophers say) from that which is most perfect in every genus, all perfection is derived to the others of the same order as if from a fountain: so no one doubts that from the man Christ, the perfection of all goodness is derived into all men. To him alone, surely, was the Spirit given not by measure, so that from his fullness we might all receive. See how undoubtedly this prerogative is owed to him as God and man, which also, insofar as he is man, belongs to him by a peculiar and lawful privilege.

## THE SECOND EXPOSITION: CONCERNING THE CELESTIAL WORLD

### PREFACE

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'S' featuring floral and leaf motifs within a square frame.</image-desc>

<margin>
Three reasons why Moses wrote figuratively.
</margin>
Let us rise from the elements to the heaven, from perishable bodies to incorruptible ones, so that it may be clear to everyone that by the very same words with which so many things of an elemental nature were shown to us, the highest dogmas concerning celestial things were likewise encompassed by the prophet. When we revolve this in our minds, there will be another reason ready for us besides those we mentioned in the prefaces. Why, for example, when Moses was about to speak of the "efficient cause" and "matter," did he not call them by those express words, but instead called them "heaven and earth"? And why did he call the arrangements of matter "waters" rather than "qualities" (as the philosophers say), and call the "form" "light" rather than "form"? Why did he likewise name comets and lightning and other things of that kind not by their proper names, but as "stars" and "constellations," and so on for the rest? In our introduction, we cited both the ancient custom of writing about great physical and divine matters in a hidden and figurative way, and the rudeness of the audience who, since they could not bear the splendor of Mosaic teaching, required him to speak with a veiled face, lest those who were being taken up to be enlightened should be blinded by too much light.

<margin>
The marvelous craft of Moses. The most absolute kind of writing.
</margin>
Now we have the occasion for a third reason: namely, that if he had named matter, form, qualities, and the efficient cause, those terms could indeed have served for treatises on the perishable world, but not for the others. Wherefore, it is a marvelous and unthought-of craft of Moses—truly by no human industry—to use those words and so arrange the discourse that the same words, the same context, and the same series of the entire scripture should aptly fit the secrets of all worlds and of all nature. This is that in which the book of Moses surpasses all the learning, eloquence, and genius of the nations; this is that new and as yet untouched thing which we have attempted to bring forward: namely, to prove to our people by the fact itself that this was done by Moses.

<margin>
Dionysius. Saint Thomas of the Latins.
</margin>
This is the idea, this is the model of the most absolute writer. This is not only because this kind of writing (as we demonstrated above) portrays and emulates nature, but because among the angelic minds—according to the author Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, an influential mystical theologian.</note> and Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas, the "Angelic Doctor."</note>, the splendor of our Latin theology—that mind is supreme which comprehends through its intelligence by the very fewest notions and forms those things which lower minds comprehend through various and manifold ones. Thus, among scriptures, that one is the highest and holds the peak of all perfection which, in the very fewest words, encompasses all things as if they were...

<margin>The tenth is the sphere or celestial globe, which theologians call the Empyrean <note>The Empyrean is the highest heaven in ancient and medieval cosmology, believed to be the dwelling place of God and the angels, consisting of pure light or fire.</note>, as do Strabo and Bede, along with Abraham and Isaac through the term Sapphire.</note></margin>
¶ ...it embraces [the subject] appropriately and profoundly. But why do we delay any longer the Prophet <note>Pico refers to Moses as "the Prophet," the traditional author of Genesis.</note> as he comes forward with his face revealed, to speak to us of celestial mysteries? Yet, before we hear him speaking, it will be useful to say a few words by way of preface concerning the tenth heaven, so that we may be more capable of understanding his words.

-> CHAPTER ONE. <-

Beyond the nine celestial orbs—that is, the seven planets and the eighth sphere which they call "unwandering" <note>The "unwandering" or fixed stars.</note>, and sometimes an [additional] orb which is grasped by reason rather than by sense, and is the first among moving bodies—it is believed that there is a tenth heaven, remaining fixed and quiet, which participates in no motion. Nor is this believed only by our more recent scholars, such as Strabo <note>Walafrid Strabo, a 9th-century Carolingian scholar.</note> and Bede <note>The Venerable Bede, the 7th-century English monk and historian.</note>, but also by many of the Hebrews, and furthermore by certain philosophers and mathematicians. From among these, it is enough to have cited two: Abraham the Spaniard <note>Abraham Ibe Ezra, a famous 12th-century Jewish astronomer and philosopher.</note>, a very great astrologer, and Isaac the philosopher, both of whom
<margin>They established [this] from Ezekiel. Note.</margin>
attest to this. Indeed, this Isaac understands the tenth orb to be designated by Ezekiel through the "Sapphire" <note>original: "Zaphirum", referring to the "throne of sapphire" in Ezekiel 1:26.</note> in the likeness of a throne, so that the color of the sapphire signifies the brightness of light, and the likeness of a throne signifies its immobility. He likewise understands the ten spheres to be figured by Zechariah through the golden lampstand distinguished by seven lamps, with a bowl <note>original: "lampadem", here referring to the central reservoir or oil-vessel.</note> above its head, and then two olive trees above the bowl. For since the seven lamps indicate the seven planets, and the bowl indicates the eighth circle shining with so many lights, he wishes the ninth and tenth spheres to be indicated by the two olive trees. This is because oil flows down from the olives to the bowl and the lamps for the nourishment of the light. Wherefore,
<margin>In what way light descends from the tenth to the final sphere.</margin>
by a similarity of reason, since the light of the heavens which we see emanates from and is preserved by those supreme heavens (for he who gives light also preserves it), those supreme ones are rightly compared to the olives, and these lower ones to the lamps and the bowl. But if two primary sources cannot be established for the same water, it is necessary that one of those two supreme spheres be the principle of all light. If this is referred to the one or the other, it must surely be the first—that is, the tenth—so that it is, as it were, the very unity <note>original: "vnitas", the source or Monad of light.</note> of lights; then the ninth receives light next in the whole essence of its substance. From there, it proceeds thirdly to the sun by full participation, and from the sun, now in the fourth and therefore the final step, it is divided among all the stars in parts. Therefore, let us establish above the nine heavens a tenth, which theologians call
<margin>The doubt of some.</margin>
the Empyrean. However, it has been doubted by some whether its nature is corporeal or rather incorporeal. For perhaps it is fitting by its unity that the analogy of its nature should correspond to the co-elemental number, and thus not be of the same genus. But whatever is decided about this question, let it remain unshaken: that the treasures of light are therein, and from there whatever light is possessed and seen in bodies is derived into the rest as if from a first fountain. Nor does it stand in the way if someone wishes to believe—more stubbornly than truly—that it is not of a truly 
<margin>Julian Caesar.</margin>
corporeal nature, since it is found in the theology of the Phoenicians, as Julian Caesar <note>The Emperor Julian, known as "the Apostate."</note> writes in his *Oration to the Sun*, that corporeal light emanates from an incorporeal nature. This [tenth heaven], therefore, stands before these nine heavens which follow it in sequence, like a leader to an army or a form to matter; and bearing the type of the Monad <note>original: "Monados", the Pythagorean term for the Number One or Unity.</note>, it completes the number ten.

-> CHAPTER TWO. <-

<margin>Interpretation</margin>
LET US COME to Moses, who, being about to speak of all these things, has deigned to give this one [the tenth heaven] a peculiar name as the first and principal heaven;

ii d

<column-break/>

<margin>The splendor of theology, and not without reason.</margin>
just as we are able to call the nine choruses of angels "Gods" because they participate in divinity. Hence that phrase: *God of Gods*.
<margin>The words of the Prophet.</margin>
Yet, when we say "God" absolutely, we do not mean any one of them, but we accept the indivisible Trinity presiding over them, just as the Empyrean heaven presides over the nine orbs subject to it. But he called the 
<margin>Heaven and earth.</margin>
last eight spheres "Earth"; and this was not done without cause, but because the extremes of this number claim the name of "earth" for themselves. These are the Moon and the Starry Heaven <note>The 8th sphere of fixed stars.</note>, both of which we are compelled to call "earth" by the authority of the ancients and furthermore by reason. For concerning the
<margin>Concerning the eighth sphere of the Pythagoreans.</margin>
eighth sphere, it was very frequent in the Academy <note>The Platonic Academy.</note> to give it the name of "earth." Likewise, Aristotle said the Moon was similar to the earth, following the Pythagoreans, who call it both a "celestial earth"
<margin>The opinion of the Academics and Aristotle.</margin>
and a "terrestrial heaven." But see what reason leads us to both: for if we seek the elements in the heavens, we establish the Moon as the lowest and most ignoble "Earth" of all the stars, just as the earth is of all the elements, very similar to it in the opacity of its substance and its spots. You [establish] Mercury as the changeable and transformable "Water"; therefore, in Lucan, it is called the arbiter of the waves. [You establish] Venus as "Air," life-giving with its temperate heat; [you establish]
<margin>Lucan. Commentary on the Starry [Heaven].</margin>
the Sun as "Fire" for the most manifest reason. Then, in inverse order, [you establish] the Mother [the 8th sphere] as Fire; Jupiter as "Air," related to Venus by nature; Saturn as "Water," the old man, namely of condemned coldness; it remains that we call the eighth sphere, the non-wandering one, "Earth," as the very order of computation demands. Rightly, therefore, he called this whole [system], which is enclosed on both sides by two "earths," and above which nothing is visible to us, "Earth." Then he adds: *And the earth was empty and void* <note>Genesis 1:2.</note>—empty, that is, of light not yet propagated from the first heaven to
<margin>Light is the receptacle of many virtues.</margin>
it, and empty of the remaining virtues of which light is the vehicle. Nor do we say this of ourselves, but the author himself declares it, adding of what thing it was empty: *and darkness was upon the face of the abyss*. He rightly calls the height of so many orbs and their wondrous depth the
<margin>What the Abyss is. Ephrem the Syrian.</margin>
"Abyss." But lest we should believe that there is nothing in the middle between the eighth sphere and the Empyrean seats—as many have believed, following only the evidence of the senses—he warned us of an intervening orb, which, because he figured it through "the waters," has been harmoniously called the "Crystalline Heaven" by more recent scholars. Upon this was borne—or, as the Hebrew truth has it and
<margin>Through the Crystalline [sphere], he understands the place between the eighth and the tenth, upon which the Spirit of the Lord, etc.</margin>
Ephrem the Syrian <note>A 4th-century Syriac theologian.</note> translated, "was brooding"—the Spirit of the Lord. That is, the spiritual Olympus, the seat of the spirits of the Lord, adhering most closely, was hovering over it with its life-giving light. And it was rightly done that that which is adjacent to the principle of light should drink in light with its whole body and its whole mass; yet it is invisible to us because it is not bounded by a more solid thickness. Therefore, the Empyrean, brooding upon that first [the 9th sphere], bestowed its light; which soon, after the darkness was shaken off at God's command, was derived into the remaining spheres which we say are designated by the "earth" and the "abyss." And *there was evening and morning, one day*, because through the reception of light and supernal influx, the lower heavens are federated with the first. In summary, then, on the first day, the eminence of the first heaven over the rest and the derivation of light from it to them is indicated; and through the names of "water" and "earth," many properties of the ninth orb and the others are shown.

## CHAPTER THREE.

<margin>
One day.
The summary of the firmament between the waters.
</margin>
Now, speaking more specifically about the moved spheres, he <note>Moses, whom Pico regards as the author of Genesis.</note> teaches that the "unwandering" sphere—which we call the <term>firmament</term><note>The word "firmament" comes from the Latin *firmamentum*, implying a solid support or sky that separates the waters above from the waters below.</note>—is in the middle between two waters. The reason for this statement is clear from what we have said: for both the ninth sphere and the planet Saturn, as we have explained, claim the name "waters" for themselves. Therefore, the firmament was placed by God in the midst of the waters. And "the waters which are under the heavens were gathered into one place," and it was done so that "the dry land"—that is, the earth—might appear, and all of this was provided for the safety of living things. Let us see what these things mean.

<margin>
From which comes the gathering of waters.
The Ocean.
Let the earth appear.
</margin>
The words of Moses: The waters that are under the heavens are the seven stars <note>The seven "planets" of ancient astronomy: Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, the Sun, Venus, Mercury, and the Moon.</note> which are under the firmament, which he called "heaven." The first of these is Saturn. These waters are gathered into one place for this reason: because all the power of the planets is collected in the one Sun. This is something all philosophers and all mathematicians confirm with one voice. And if this gathering of waters is called the "sea," then it is not absurd to say that this will be that <note>original: "oceanus"</note> Ocean which is called the "father of gods and men" by those who deemed the planets worthy of the name of gods. As for the "Earth," what else shall we call it <unclear>than</unclear> the Moon? It was called such by Aristotle and the Pythagoreans. When the Moon is overwhelmed by the waves of the aforementioned sea, it is neither useful to us nor visible; but it is suitable for the uses of animals and ourselves when, receding more and more from that sea, it comes into view. Then it is fertile, then it is fruitful, especially for those things which belong to <term>vegetative nature</term><note>In medieval science, the "vegetative soul" governed growth, nutrition, and reproduction.</note>, whose gifts are increase, nutrition, and generation. For the primary power of the Moon is in these things, as the Chaldeans said. And this is demonstrated most clearly here by Moses: for as soon as she appears, he makes her the parent of herbs, shrubs, and trees. See how he indicated to us the nature of the Moon and the Sun in very few words and through figures. But why is he silent about the rest, when we promised in our introduction that he would treat all things sufficiently and learnedly?

<margin>
Why there is no mention of the four planets.
</margin>
Why, I say, when he has made mention of the ninth and eighth spheres, of Saturn, and likewise of the Sun and Moon, is there not even a word about the four that remain: Venus, Mercury, Jupiter, and Mars? You might perhaps say this was done because an unrefined people knew only the Sun and Moon. But I have deprived myself of this refuge; I cannot turn there without blushing, for I have attested above that nothing was omitted by Moses that contributes to a perfect understanding of all the worlds.

<margin>
First solution.
Refutation.
</margin>
Another might say that by dealing with the Sun and Moon, he dealt with the rest: because these two hold the kingdom of heaven, and while the power of the others is particular, these two stars possess a universal influence. But this does not satisfy us; for by that same reasoning, he should have omitted Saturn, of whom we have nevertheless shown mention was made.

<margin>
Second solution.
Refutation.
</margin>
I believe a deeper mystery of the ancient Hebrew discipline lies hidden. Among its primary dogmas concerning heaven is this: that Jupiter and Mars are enclosed by the Sun, while Venus and Mercury are enclosed by the Moon. If we weigh the natures of these stars, the reason for this opinion is not obscure, <unclear>even though</unclear> they themselves offer no reason for their dogma.

<margin>
Third solution.
The affinity of the Sun with Jupiter and Mars.
</margin>
Jupiter is hot, Mars is hot, and the Sun is hot. But the heat of Mars is sharp and violent; that of Jupiter is beneficial. In the Sun, we see that sharp and violent quality of Mars and the beneficial property of Jupiter—that is, a nature mixed from these and tempered in the middle, so to speak. Jupiter is lucky, Mars is unlucky; the Sun is partly good and partly bad—good in its radiation, bad in its occult properties. Aries is the house of Mars, Cancer is the exaltation of Jupiter; the Sun, having attained its height in Cancer and its exaltation in Aries, shows a mani-

<column-break/>

<margin>
The affinity of the Moon with Venus and Mercury.
</margin>
fest kinship with both stars. Let us come to the Moon, which clearly participates in the "waters" of Mercury, and indicates how much affinity she has with Venus, especially from this: that she is so exalted in Taurus, the domicile of Venus, that she is judged nowhere more happy or more beneficial.

<margin>
Summary.
</margin>
Concerning the Empyrean heaven, the ninth orb, the firmament, the star of Saturn, and the Sun and Moon—which embrace the remaining things, reminding us of this embrace by his very silence—he has spoken sufficiently thus far.

## CHAPTER FOUR.

<margin>
Timaeus.
</margin>
It remained that after he had spoken of the nature of the stars, he should discuss their works and their office, declaring for what use they were founded and to what duty they were assigned by God. Know, however, that the Prophet <note>Moses</note> is still dealing with heaven as a luminous body, saying nothing yet of its intellect or its moving force; in this, even <note>original: "Timaeus"</note> Timaeus <note>The narrator of Plato's dialogue on the origin of the universe.</note> follows the same order: first fashioning the body, then applying a soul to the bodies once they are released. There are two operations of the celestial bodies manifest in the universe: motion and illumination.

<margin>
Motion:
Illumination.
</margin>
Motion is established as two-fold: one is the motion of the whole world, by which the heaven and the <term>aether</term><note>The "fifth element" that makes up the celestial bodies.</note> are revolved in a perfect circuit throughout the entire space of the universe in twenty-four hours. The other is the proper motion of the stars, which is manifold and varied; among these, the principal one is the motion of the Sun, which circles all the signs of the Zodiac in the space of twelve months. The former makes the "day," which is why it is called "diurnal"; the latter makes the "year." The motions of the remaining stars are completed in various intervals of time. Rightly and briefly, therefore, Moses reminded us of all these when he said the stars were placed in the firmament "for days, and years, and seasons." He added "for signs," which I pass over because it is sufficiently explained by other interpreters. He furthermore expressly indicated the remaining operation of the stars, which is illumination, when he said they were appointed "to shine in the heaven and illuminate the earth."

<margin>
What the celestial bodies influence in lower things.
Aristotle.
</margin>
Although the opinions of the ancients differ on what the celestial bodies influence in lower things, the words of Moses fit any of them aptly. For if they influence nothing other than light—which Aristotle seems to have intended, if we interpret his words religiously and not according to our own whim—nothing could be thought more consistent than the Mosaic sayings. If, besides light, they also influence heat, and nothing else besides, as

<margin>
Averroes.
Abraham.
</margin>
Averroes the Arab <note>Ibn Rushd, the 12th-century Islamic philosopher.</note> and Abraham the Jew <note>Abraham Ibn Ezra.</note> maintain, it was enough to have spoken of light, from which these same authors admit heat proceeds. Likewise, if many other and manifold virtues are sent down from heaven, as

<margin>
Avicenna.
The Babylonians.
</margin>
it seemed to Avicenna <note>The 11th-century Persian philosopher and physician.</note> and the Babylonians, the mention of light alone was not made rashly; for as Avicenna himself writes, it is light alone that carries all other virtues from heaven to us. To these ministries, therefore, the bodies of the Moon, the Sun, and the stars are distributed.

## CHAPTER FIVE.

<margin>
Signs of the eighth and ninth spheres.
</margin>
It remained for him to make mention of the signs that are visible in the Zodiac, and of those which, though invisible to us, are far more effective in the <term>crystalline heaven</term><note>The ninth sphere, believed to be composed of a clear, water-like substance.</note>. For nothing has been said of these so far. This, therefore, is the meaning of the "animals" which the waters produce and the earth produces: namely, those waters which are above the heavens, and the earth which is the firmament itself, as was proved above.

<margin>
Celestial signs noted by the Egyptians and Indians.
</margin>
For the signs which are seen in those two orbs alone [the 8th and 9th] are in the form of animals, such as those among us noted by the Egyptians and Indians, which were able...

They <note>Referring to the ancient Chaldeans and Egyptians mentioned on previous pages.</note> grasped these things more easily and correctly than our people, aided by the very flatness of the land and the serenity of the sky. Otherwise, the production of mortal animals that are here on earth pertains no more to these two elements—earth and water—than to the others, namely fire and air. And since he <note>Moses.</note> appropriately gave the name "waters" to the crystalline sphere, because the "animals" there are like fish; so again, in the firmament, which he calls "earth," he named the "beasts" and "cattle" <note>Pico is allegorically linking the stars and constellations to the animals mentioned in Genesis.</note>.

### CHAPTER SIX.

<margin>
Plotinus.
Timaeus.
</margin>
SO FAR we have spoken of the bodily nature of the heavens. Now, those same things are explained allegorically regarding the rational soul. He <note>Moses.</note> mentions "man," but certainly not that man who is fleeting and earthy and whom we see; but rather the one by whom, as Plotinus says, the visible man is ruled. That very thing is the rational soul: which, since Timaeus <note>A character in Plato's dialogue of the same name.</note> establishes it from the same elements and in the same mixing bowl from which he made the soul of the heavens, those things said about the human soul are not incongruously transferred to the soul of the heaven as well. Sacred scripture supports our exposition, in which all angelic and rational nature is designated by the name "man." This is most frequent in the prophets regarding good angels; and even regarding the evil demon (who differs from them in nothing by nature), it is written in the Gospel: "the enemy man <note>original: "inimicus homo"</note> has done this." God, therefore, added to the celestial machine a living and rational substance as a participant:

<margin>
It is necessary for the celestial bodies to obey and submit to their mover.
</margin>
The Intellect. And therefore, he wished for this, in his image and likeness, to preside over those living things of which we spoke a little while ago—that is, over all the starry signs and planets. These turn at its nod and obey its word so that there is no delay, no defiance—something that does not happen in the same way with the sluggish bodies of the elements. Nor will you easily find anything else in which the <term>Peripatetics</term><note>Followers of Aristotle's philosophy.</note> labor more than to prove that the celestial body does not struggle against its mover in the way our bodies struggle against us. Therefore, they do not experience weariness, difficulty, or fatigue from perpetual motion as we do. This is the "dominion" over the animals that Moses touched upon regarding the celestial name. Likewise, it is not without mystery that he created that man "male and female." For it is the prerogative

<margin>
Epilogue.
</margin>
of celestial souls that they perform both duties at once: both contemplating and ruling bodies; neither can the former be a noise to the latter, nor the latter an impediment to the former. This was used extensively by the ancients; we observe these two powers in the same substance even in the Orphic hymns: one of which contemplates, the other presides over the body, designated by the names "male" and "female." These things are handed down by the prophet regarding the celestial world: concerning the divine body, the number of spheres, their nature and properties, and their office. Finally, concerning its moving power, its rational substance, and its character.

<margin>
To what extent the heaven is to be honored by us.
</margin>

### CHAPTER SEVEN.

<margin>
Plato.
</margin>
THIS IS a noble creature, to be looked up to and celebrated by us. But even if we follow the Platonic opinion (to say nothing of the theologians), we have not forgotten that our souls were tempered by God the Maker in the same bowl and from the same elements as the celestial souls. Let us see to it that we do not wish to be the servants of those whose brothers nature intended us to be. Nor should we measure our condition by this weak body. For "man," as is written in the *Alcibiades* <note>A dialogue attributed to Plato.</note>, is not this fragile and earthy thing we see, but is the soul; it is the intellect which exceeds the entire circuit of heaven and the entire course of time. We must be careful, therefore, lest we—as many do—give more to the heaven and attribute more than is necessary, and así resist both the will of the Maker and the order of the universe. In doing so, we might displease the heaven itself, to which the counsels of God and the order of the world are most dear, while we are striving to please it.

<margin>
When Macrobius places the soul as a divine and greatest spiritual thing.
</margin>
The Chaldeans warn of this, saying: "Do not increase your fate." Jeremiah proclaims this: "Do not fear," he says, "the signs of heaven which the gentiles fear." Our prophet <note>Moses.</note> commands this elsewhere, warning that a man must be careful lest, looking up at the sun, moon, and stars, he worship those things which God created for the service <note>original: "ministerium"</note> of all nations. If anyone should not take this in the sense that those things serve us like ignoble or dead bodies, let us nevertheless understand it to mean that the author or mistress of our nature cannot be a substance whose most noble part is found to be viler than some part of us. For in a work, nothing can or should be more perfect than the things that are in the maker. Let us, therefore, fear, love, and venerate Him in whom, as Paul says, all things were created, whether visible or invisible. This is the "Beginning" <note>original: "principium"</note> in which God made the heaven and the earth; and this is Christ. For He himself, when asked who he was, being the best judge of himself, replied: "I am the Beginning, who speaks to you." Therefore, let us not reshape images of the stars in metals, but rather the image of Him—that is, the Word of God—in our souls. Let us seek neither from the heavens, nor from the body, nor from fortune (which they will not give), but from the Lord of heaven, the Lord of all good things to whom all power is given in heaven and on earth, both present goods (insofar as they are good) and the true happiness of eternal life.

<margin>
Chaldeans.
Jeremiah, Moses, Christ—the one to be worshiped from whom all good comes.
</margin>

<margin>
Paul.

## THE THIRD EXPOSITION: CONCERNING THE ANGELIC
### AND INVISIBLE WORLD. PROLOGUE TO THE THIRD BOOK.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'H' inside a square woodcut border featuring floral or foliate patterns.</image-desc>

<margin>
He desires wings in the manner of those above.
</margin>
Hitherto, we have disputed to the best of our ability, revealing the mysteries of Moses concerning the celestial world. But now, who will give me wings? "Like the wings of a dove, covered in silver and shimmering with the paleness of gold," and I will fly above the celestial region where there is true rest, true peace, true tranquility—peace, surely, which this visible and corporeal world cannot give. Open my eyes, you spirits from beyond the world, and I shall contemplate the miracles of your city, where God has stored up things for those who fear Him, which "eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man." Since many things have been said about this angelic and invisible nature by the ancient Hebrews, and many things likewise by Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian Neoplatonist who wrote "The Celestial Hierarchy."</note>...

He then begins the third part of his work, transitioning to an exploration of the angelic realm beyond the physical heavens.</summary>

# HEPTAPLVS

<margin>Dionysius. The ancient dogmas of the Hebrews are to be deferred.</margin>
It was my intention to explain the words of Moses according to the doctrine of both families <note>Pico refers to the "two families" of wisdom: the Christian tradition and the Hebrew/Kabbalistic tradition.</note>. But because the things said by the Hebrews are unusual among the Latins, they could not easily be understood by our people unless we started, as they say, "from the twin egg" <note>An idiom meaning to start from the very beginning or the very roots.</note> and described almost all the dogmas of the ancient Hebrew discipline. I thought this should be deferred until I have written more extensively about these things elsewhere and made their opinions known to our people. There, I will examine how much they agree with Egyptian monuments, Platonic philosophy, and Catholic truth. Where they agree with us, we will command the Hebrew to stand in the ancient traditions of his fathers; where they disagree, equipped with Catholic legions, we will make an impression <note>original: *impressionem*; here meaning a scholarly or theological attack/charge</note> upon them. Finally, whatever we find alien to the Gospel truth, we will refute to the best of our ability; whatever is holy and true, we will transfer from the Synagogue—as if from an unjust possessor—to us, the legitimate Israelites. <margin>Dionysius, Paul, Hierotheus.</margin> Meanwhile, following in the footsteps of Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, an early Christian theologian famous for his work on the celestial hierarchy.</note>, or rather of Paul and Hierotheus whom he followed, we will try—despite our weakness—to bring light into the darkness of the Law which the Spirit of God, the author of the Law, established as his hiding place.

---

<margin>Unity. Number.</margin>
### CHAPTER ONE.

Whatever exists after Unity is Number, perfected and completed by Unity. Unity alone, entirely simple and perfect in itself, does not go out of itself, but remains joined to itself in indivisible and solitary simplicity; for it is sufficient unto itself, needing nothing, and full of its own riches. Number, being a multitude by its own nature, becomes simple through the benefit of Unity—at least as much as it is capable of simplicity. However, the further a number is from Unity, the more it falls into a greater multitude, and the more dissimilarity of parts and composition there is within it. Yet, no number is so close to Unity that it is not still a multitude, having an "added" unity and being one not by nature, but by composition. <margin>A mathematical approach to divine things.</margin> Let us transfer these things to divine matters in the Pythagorean manner. God alone is the most simple and indivisible essence, because he is from no one else, and from him are all things. Whatever he has, he has from himself: by the same thing that he *is*, he also knows, wills, and is good and just. Nor can we understand anything by which he exists other than the very act of "Being" <note>original: *ipsum esse*</note> which he is. Other things are not "Being" itself, but exist *by* it. Therefore, an angel is not Unity itself; otherwise he would be God, or there would be many gods, which cannot even be conceived. For what can be "one" without Unity itself being one? It remains, then, that an angel is a "Number." If he is a number, he is a multitude made one. Every number is imperfect insofar as it is a multitude, but perfect insofar as it is one. Therefore, let us ascribe whatever is imperfect in an angel to his "angelic multitude" (which he has from being a number, i.e., a creature), and whatever is perfect to the "approaching unity" (which he has from being joined to God). <margin>A double imperfection accompanies the angel.</margin> We find a double imperfection in the angel: first, because he is not Being itself, but only an essence to which "to be" happens by participation; second, because he is not Understanding itself, but it comes to him to understand, even though he is by nature an intellect capable of intelligence. This second imperfection depends on the first, since that which does not exist of itself certainly cannot understand of itself. Both of these occur in the angel insofar as he is a "multitude." It remains that his completion and perfection come from the Unity approaching from above. God is that Unity, from whom being, life, and all perfection are derived for the angel. <margin>The empty earth.</margin> Just as there is a double imperfection—like a double multitude—so let us understand a double approach of Unity so that both may be perfected. The first is that where the essence is raw, unformed, and devoid of life and being; this is the "earth, void and empty" which God created. Nor should you believe, as 

<column-break/>

some have believed, that only the formation of essence pertains to the Creator, and not its creation. Together with the earth he created heaven—that is, the act of that essence, the Unity participating in the multitude, which is "Being" itself. Thus, the creation of heaven and earth is essentially the same, as they are a pair joined together, two natures meeting in the same bond. <margin>Xenophanes. The Saracens.</margin> Nor is it discordant with the ancients that we call "Being" <note>original: *ipsum esse*</note> (which is a participation in divinity) "heaven," since Xenophanes called the archetypal world a sphere, and the Saracens <note>Pico's term for Muslim philosophers and theologians.</note>—and even our own people—call God a circle.

### CHAPTER TWO.

By what we have said, the angel has now perfectly attained his nature and his intellectual property. However, he does not yet have that by which he may fulfill his duties of understanding and contemplating, unless he is first clothed by God with "intelligible forms" <note>term: <term>Intelligible forms</term> are the pure concepts or ideas provided by God that allow an intellect to actually think or perceive truth.</note>. <margin>Description of the abyss, which coincides with Lactantius's chaos.</margin> Therefore, there is still "darkness upon the face of the abyss." The "abyss" is the deep intellectual nature that penetrates and searches all things. Upon this is darkness, until it is illuminated by the rays of spiritual concepts through which it sees and contemplates everything. It is written "upon the face of the abyss," not "upon the abyss," because the same place holds both darkness and light. Light—that is, the intelligible forms—holds the "face," meaning the outer aspects of the angelic intellect, because they are accidental qualities and do not belong to the intellect's own essence. To show what comes between the driving away of darkness and the rising of light, he immediately adds: <margin>The Spirit of the Lord, i.e., of Love.</margin> "And the spirit of the Lord moved over the waters." What could the Spirit of the Lord be rather than the spirit of love? For we do not call the spirit of knowledge the "Spirit of the Lord" so properly, since knowledge sometimes leads away from God, but love always leads to him. Unless this spirit moves over that abyss, light will not be made. For just as the eye is not filled with light unless it is turned toward the sun, so the angel is not filled with spiritual light unless he is turned toward God. This movement of "turning" <note>original: *conversio*; a technical term in Neoplatonism for the soul or angel returning its gaze to its Creator.</note> is nothing else in the angelic nature than the movement of love. Therefore, the Spirit of the Lord was the spirit of love over the abyss—that is, over the angelic intellect (for love follows understanding)—and while the angel's mind is moved and stirred by it to turn toward God: <margin>Let there be light. One day. Averroes. Moses the Egyptian.</margin> God said "Let there be light," and light was made in the angel—the light of intelligible forms. and "there was evening and morning, one day." For as Averroes <note>A famous 12th-century Islamic philosopher from Spain.</note> proves, a greater unity is made from the intellect and the thing understood than from matter and form; and as Moses the Egyptian <note>Maimonides (Rabbi Moshe ben Maimon), the preeminent Jewish philosopher.</note> writes, this is found to be far more true in angels than in man. To leave those men aside...

<summary>Pico explains that angels are "Numbers" (composed of multitude and unity) rather than pure "Unity" (which is God alone). He interprets the "void earth" as the raw angelic essence and "light" as the divine knowledge that fills them when they turn toward God through love.</summary>

->GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA<-

They <note>Referring to the ancient Egyptians and Chaldeans mentioned in preceding text.</note> detected these things both more easily and more correctly than our people, aided by the very flatness of the ground and the serenity of the sky. Otherwise, the production of animals that are perishable here pertains no more to these two elements—earth and water—than to the remaining ones, namely fire and air. And since he <note>Moses</note> appropriately gave the name "water" to the crystalline sphere, he called the animals there "fish"; conversely, in the firmament, which he calls "earth," he named them "beasts of burden" and "wild animals."

## CHAPTER SIX.

<margin>Plotinus. Timaeus.</margin>
Thus far we have spoken of the corporeal nature of the heavens. Now, intending to declare the aforementioned things through the rational soul, he mentions "man" allegorically—not indeed that man who is perishable and earthly and whom we see, but the one by whom, as Plotinus says, "the man who is seen is ruled." That very one is the rational soul. Since Timaeus <note>A character in Plato’s dialogue of the same name who describes the creation of the world.</note> constitutes this soul from the same elements and in the same mixing-bowl as the soul of the world, those things said about the human soul are not incongruously transferred to the soul of the heaven as well. Sacred scripture supports our exposition, in which the entire angelic and rational nature is often designated by the name "man." This is very frequent in the prophets regarding good angels; and even regarding the evil demon—who differs nothing in nature from them—it is written in the Gospel: "An enemy man has done this." <note>Matthew 13:28. original: *inimicus homo hæc fecit*</note> 
<margin>It is necessary for celestial things to obey and submit to their mover.</margin>
Therefore, God added to the celestial machine a living and rational substance as a participant: the Intellect. And so, according to His own image and likeness, He willed this Intellect to preside over those living beings of which we spoke a little while ago—that is, all the stars, signs, and planets. These turn at its nod and obey its word so that there is no delay and no defiance. This does not happen equally to the brute bodies of the elements. Nor will you easily find anything else over which the Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle, known for walking while teaching.</note> sweat more than to prove that the celestial body in no way resists its mover, just as our bodies resist us. Therefore, they experience neither boredom, difficulty, nor fatigue from perpetual motion as we do; this is the "dominion" over the animals that Moses attributed to the celestial name. 
<margin>Epilogue.</margin>
It is likewise not without mystery that He created that man "male and female." For it is the prerogative of celestial souls that they perform both duties simultaneously: contemplating and ruling bodies. Neither should the former be a clamor against the latter, nor the latter an impediment to the former. This was most widely used by the ancients, as we observe even in the Orphic hymns, to designate these two powers in the same substance—one of which contemplates and the other presides over the body—by the names "male" and "female."

<column-break/>

These things are handed down by the prophet concerning the celestial world: concerning the divine body, the number of spheres, their nature and properties, and their office. Finally, they concern its moving force, its rational substance, and its character.

## CHAPTER SEVEN.

<margin>To what extent the heaven is to be honored by us.</margin>
This is a noble creature, to be looked up to and celebrated by us. 
<margin>Plato.</margin>
But if we have not forgotten that our tempered souls were made by God the Artificer in the same mixing-bowl and from the same elements as the celestial souls—to speak of the Platonic opinion, even if I remain silent on the theologians—let us see to it that we do not wish to be the servants of those whose "brothers" nature willed us to be. Let us not measure our condition by this weak body. 
<margin>Since Macrobius places the soul as more divine and especially spiritual.</margin>
For man is not, as written in the *Alcibiades* <note>A dialogue attributed to Plato.</note>, this fragile and earthly thing we see; rather, he is the soul—he is the intellect which exceeds the entire circuit of heaven and the entire course of time. We must be careful, therefore, lest we do what many do: by giving more to the heaven and attributing more to it than is necessary, we resist the will of the Artificer and the order of the universe. At the same time, we may displease the heaven itself, to which the counsels of God and the order of the world are most dear, even while we strive to please it. 
<margin>Chaldeans. Jeremiah, Moses, Christ—the one to be worshiped from whom all good comes.</margin>
The Chaldeans warn of this, saying: "Do not increase fate." Jeremiah proclaims this: "Do not fear," he says, "the signs of heaven which the heathens fear." <note>Jeremiah 10:2.</note> Our prophet commands this elsewhere, warning that man must be careful lest, looking up at the sun, moon, and stars, he worships those things which God created for the service of all nations. Even if one does not take this in the sense that those things serve us as if they were ignoble and dead bodies, let us nevertheless understand it to signify that the author or mistress of our nature cannot be a substance whose even "better" part is found to be more ignoble than some "lower" part within us. For in a work, nothing can or should be more perfect than the things that are in the Artificer. Let us, therefore, fear, love, and venerate Him. 
<margin>Paul.</margin>
In whom, as Paul says, all things were created, whether visible or invisible. This is the "Beginning" in which God made heaven and earth; and this is Christ. For He himself, when asked who He was, being the best judge of Himself, replied: "I am the Beginning, who speaks to you." <note>John 8:25 (Vulgate tradition).</note> Therefore, let us not reshape the images of stars in metals <note>A critique of astrological talismans/amulets.</note>, but rather the image of Him—that is, of the Word of God—in our souls. Let us seek neither from the heavens nor from fortune (which they will not give) but from the Lord of heaven, the Lord of all goods to whom all power is given in heaven and on earth, both present goods (insofar as they are good) and the true happiness of eternal life.

<margin>

Number.

Whatever exists after unity is a "number" <note>In Neoplatonic philosophy, "Unity" refers to God, while "Number" refers to anything created, which necessarily possesses multiplicity.</note>, perfected and completed by unity. Unity alone is altogether simple, perfected by itself, and does not go out of itself; rather, it is individual in its simplicity and remains solitary within itself. Because it is above itself, it lacks nothing and is full of its own riches. Number, being by its nature a multitude, becomes simple by the benefit of unity, as far as it is capable of simplicity. Therefore, the further it is from unity, the greater the multitude it falls into, and the more dissimilarity, parts, and composition it contains. Yet none is

Nor can we understand any thing by which He exists except the very "being" <note>original: "ipsum esse"</note> which He is. Other things are not "that very thing"—that is, being itself—but exist through it. Therefore, is an angel not "one unity" itself? But if it were, it would be God, which cannot even be conceived. For what would be "one" without unity itself? It follows that an angel is a "number." If it is a number, it is "one multitude" in another part of itself. Now, every number is imperfect insofar as it is a multitude, but perfect insofar as it is one. <margin>
The description of the abyss; it coincides with Lactantius's chaos.

Through what we have said, the angel has now perfectly obtained its nature and its intellectual property. <meta>This page continues Pico’s "Heptaplus," specifically the third exposition concerning the "Angelic World." GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA

...let this reason be sufficient for us: that the angelic species are joined to the angelic mind in an inseparable bond. Unlike the human intellect, where knowledge is wandering and transferred, in angels, these species are united by eternal connections.

### CHAPTER THREE.

WE HAVE seen the nature of the angel as a created being: how it is turned toward God by the spirit of love, and then illustrated and perfected by him through the light of intelligible reasons. Let us now see in what order the angelic hosts are distinguished among themselves.

<margin>The firmament in the midst of the waters.</margin>
We read that the firmament was placed in the midst of the waters. Here, three angelic hierarchies <note>Pico uses the term "hierarchia," following Dionysius the Areopagite, to describe the three-tiered structure of the celestial beings.</note> are shown to us: the first through the waters above the heavens, the last through those beneath the heavens, and the middle one, which divides them, is called the "firmament."

<margin>Waters above the heavens.</margin>
If we examine the nature and duties of these three hierarchies, nothing could harmonize more perfectly with the doctrine of Dionysius. The highest hierarchy, as he writes, is devoted solely to contemplation; it is rightly represented by the waters set above the heavens—that is, above all action concerning mundane, celestial, or earthly things—and they praise God unceasingly with a perennial sound. The middle order, being assigned to celestial duties, could not be more fittingly signified than by the firmament, that is, by the heavens.

<margin>Firmament.</margin>
<margin>Waters above the heavens.</margin>
The final hierarchy, although by nature it is above every body and above the physical heavens, nonetheless cares for those things which are beneath the heavens. Since it is divided into Principalities, Archangels, and Angels, the entire operation of these groups concerns only those things under the moon <note>The "sublunary" sphere, traditionally the realm of change and decay in ancient cosmology.</note>. The Principalities look after public affairs, kings, and princes (as we learn from Daniel); the Archangels look after mysteries and sacred ceremonies. The Angels attend to private matters, and individuals are assigned to individual men. Correct then is it that this sub-celestial host is represented by the waters beneath the heavens, for it presides over things that are fluid and falling, and is subject to that order which deals with celestial things.

### CHAPTER FOUR.

<margin>Paul.</margin>
BUT WHAT it means for the "waters beneath the heavens to be gathered into one place" might perhaps be doubtful, unless Paul declared it to us. In his writings, concerning these angels sent to perform the duties of this world, we read that they are "all ministering spirits, sent out to serve for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation" <note>Hebrews 1:14.</note>. From this, we can understand that these sub-celestial waters—that is, the angelic hosts—are gathered to one place for the sake of procuring the good and salvation of one thing: namely, man. For our sake, they are sent to us, appearing to us in various forms, places, and times, sometimes while we are at rest and sometimes while we are awake.

<margin>An objection that could be raised.</margin>
How this opinion is to be accepted we shall finally understand when we consider how it is true (as Moses says) that the waters were "gathered into one place." For that is not true in the sense that waters are never found in distinct and separate places; for the Indian Sea is separated from the Hyrcanian, the Hyrcanian from the Adriatic, the Adriatic from the Euxine <note>The Black Sea.</note>, and there are besides innumerable flows of rivers, springs, and lakes separated by a vast distance of places.

<margin>Solomon</margin>
But the waters are said to be gathered into one place because these particular and divided collections of waters, whether of the sea or rivers, all (as Solomon says) tend toward the primary sea and are united and meet in the one place of the Ocean. We must understand the angels who care for sublunary things in no other way.

<margin>Platonists.</margin>
For different angels preside over different physical things and other matters concerning man. Just as the Platonists believed, so too do our own thinkers believe that various spiritual substances have been set by God over the va-

<column-break/>

rious things of this corruptible world.

<margin>Augustine.</margin>
Wherefore Augustine also asserts that there is no visible thing among us which is not presided over by an angelic power, and that all bodies are constantly ruled by a rational spirit of life. Gregory later confirmed this same point.

<margin>Gregory, Origen, Damascene.</margin>
Similarly, Origen, in his commentaries on the Book of Numbers, says that the world has need of angels to preside over beasts and the natural growth of animals, and even of shrubs, plantations, and the increase of other things. Since Damascene <note>John of Damascus, an 8th-century monk and theologian.</note> also held this view, he believed that the angel who sinned was from among those of the lowest rank who preside over the terrestrial order. But just as all these things below man are referred back to man, so too all the care of the angels concerning these things primarily assists and serves him. By their labor and zeal, they care for human affairs and, helping our weakness, they ensure (as much as it is allowed) that we live our lives piously and happily. Therefore, Moses immediately added what that collection of waters intended: "that the earth may bring forth fruit, herbs, and plants and trees."

<margin>The earth of which Paul speaks in the Gospel.</margin>
But what is this earth, besides that of which it is written in the Gospel <note>Pico likely means the Parable of the Sower.</note> that one part brings forth a hundredfold fruit, another sixtyfold, and another thirtyfold? Surely it is the earth of our soul, concerning which Paul says these words: "For land that has drunk the rain that often falls on it, and produces a crop useful to those for whose sake it is cultivated, receives a blessing from God. But if it bears thorns and thistles, it is worthless and near to being cursed, and its end is to be burned" <note>Hebrews 6:7–8.</note>. Let us also take care that our earth yields fruit in its season: let it yield purgative virtues like herbs; let it yield knowledge and wisdom like greater shrubs; let it yield absolute and perfect virtue like the cedars of Lebanon <note>original: "libani cedros"</note>, so that its end may be a blessing and not a burning. And let us hear the Father saying: "Behold, the scent of my son is like the scent of a full field which the Lord has blessed."

<margin>Origen, Basil.</margin>
Nor should anyone wonder that "heaven and earth" signify one thing to us on the first day, and "firmament and dry land" signify another thing now. We have observed this in previous books, as Origen, Basil, and many others maintain that in Moses' account, the "heaven and earth" of the first day are one thing, and the "dry land and firmament" of the second day are another.

### CHAPTER FIVE.

<margin>Dionysian mysteries.</margin>
EVEN the celestial virtues favor this earth of ours. For the sun, the moon, and the stars are placed in the firmament to illuminate our earth. See how aptly these things agree with the Dionysian mysteries. We have spoken of the last hierarchy assigned to caring for things beneath the moon—that is, human affairs. Now we treat the middle hierarchy, to which the administration of celestial things is entrusted. Nor should we expect a similar treatment of the third; for nothing more needs to be said of it except what has been stated: that it is "above the heavens"—that is, above all movement of action and above the administration of all mundane things—devoted only to contemplation. At this point, let us not consider it forced or foreign to the sacred letters that he calls the sun and moon not the stars we see, but the angelic virtues that are the rulers of the sun and moon.

<margin>When there is a turning toward the inanimate, then the speech is called figurative.</margin>
For when Scripture says that a man becomes a "son of God" through grace, it does not mean this man whom we see as frail and falling, but the one who rules this very man whom we see. And in the history of the Kings, according to the Hebrew literature, we read Solomon praying with these words: "Hear, O Heaven," where he does not mean the physical sky, but calls upon God, the ruler and Lord of heaven and earth. Thus, when we hear of the sun and stars in this place, we should understand not the heavenly bodies, but the angelic presidents of the stars.

<summary>Pico explains the three-tiered hierarchy of angels (Contemplative, Celestial, and Terrestrial) by mapping them onto the biblical elements of the "waters above," the "firmament," and the "waters below." He argues that the physical cosmos is governed by angelic powers whose ultimate purpose is the salvation and spiritual productivity of the human soul.</summary>

He has been correlating the days of creation with the celestial hierarchies. This page concludes the third exposition and begins the fourth, which focuses on the nature of humanity.</meta>

-> APOLOGIA <-

<margin>Note.</margin>
...we should understand [an]gels <note>original: "angelos"; the word begins on the previous page</note>, who, since they are themselves invisible, also illuminate the invisible earth—namely, the substance of our soul. It was not stated by chance or in a common way that they are set there to illuminate. Rather, it is so appropriate and so consistent with what we have brought forward that, if from nowhere else, our interpretation is most certainly proven here. For since (as Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-century theologian whose "Celestial Hierarchy" defined the nine orders of angels for the Middle Ages and Renaissance</note> teaches) there are three angelic actions—purgation, illumination, and perfection—they are distributed such that the lowest order purges, the highest perfects, and this middle order, of which we now treat, illuminates. Therefore, the lower waters purge our earth, whence it comes to be seen as bright; once purged, the celestial waters illuminate it. Above these, the celestial ones perfect and fertilize it with a certain fiery and life-giving dew, often to such great happiness that the soul no longer germinates mere healing herbs, but the Savior himself, and a new virtue—even Christ, the fullness of all virtues—is formed within us.

### CHAPTER SIX.

<margin>Isaiah. Ezekiel. The Ancients. The Hebrews. The unity of the angelic legions.</margin>
NEXT FOLLOWS the production from the elements of a multitude of inhabitants: fish, birds, and beasts. Here, I would certainly have been held in great difficulty—as nowhere else in this whole work of ours—unless Isaiah were at hand for me, in whose writings we read of the winged Seraphim, and Ezekiel, in whose work (if we believe the Hebrews) both birds and beasts indicate to us spiritual substances. I would be lost unless the ancient Hebrews rushed to my aid, all of whom wish the angelic multitude to be suggested by Moses in this passage. Let us say, therefore, following in their footsteps, that the error of the philosophers is here refuted by the prophet. They believed that while there are indeed certain principal intellectual substances, they denied that each of them (as theologians say) presides over a subsequent numerous multitude, just as leaders preside over legions. Therefore, when we think of the nine angelic orders, let each order have its own leader

<column-break/>

<margin>Daniel.</margin>
assigned; let us imagine in our mind that leader and prince as a vast sphere, and then his following army as the inhabitants and ornament of that sphere—just as we think of fish in the water, birds in the air, beasts on the earth, and the stars in the eighth sphere. Then that saying of Daniel will be true: *ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him, and a thousand thousands ministered to him.* <note>original: "decies millia assistebant ei. & mille millia ministrabant ei." See Daniel 7:10.</note>

### CHAPTER SEVEN.

<margin>Jesus Christ, the firstborn of every creature. Dionysius. Paul.</margin>
FINALLY, he mentions man—not because man is an angel, but because he is the end and boundary of the angelic world. Just as in the treatment of corruptible nature <note>The first exposition of the Heptaplus, dealing with the elemental world.</note>, he also introduced man into that nature, not as a part but as the principle and head. Thus it happens that the treatment of man belongs to three worlds: to the one that is his own, and to each extreme—the incorporeal <note>the angelic world</note> and the elemental—of which he is the middle, being established as the end of the one and the beginning of the other. But I see a snare prepared for our interpretation: for it is added that man is to preside over the fish of the sea, the birds, and the beasts. For if those things signify the angelic nature to us, how will it be true (as is written) that man presides over them—man, whom philosophers know and the prophet testifies is "made a little lower than the angels"? May he be present with us and break the snare, he who also crushed Satan under our feet: Jesus Christ, the firstborn of every creature. He surely breaks the snare and unties and snaps every knot. For not only in him, in whom the whole divinity dwelt bodily, was human nature so sublimated that the man Christ, insofar as he is man (if we believe Dionysius), teaches, illuminates, and perfects the angels; having been made, as Paul says, so much better than the angels as he has inherited a more excellent name than they. But even all of us, to whom power is given to become the sons of God through the grace of which Christ is the giver, can be raised above angelic dignity.

# FOURTH EXPOSITION CONCERNING THE WORLD, THAT IS,
## THE HUMAN WORLD OR THE NATURE OF MAN,
### PROOEMIUM OF THE FOURTH BOOK.

<margin>The Delphic letter <term>Delphic letter</term> <note>Pico refers to the letter "E" inscribed at the Temple of Apollo in Delphi, which he links to the command "Know Thyself."</note> noted below in the margin of the book "On Being." Plato.</margin>
AFTER WE have shown that the prophet has sufficiently treated all parts of the world and every nature—celestial, angelic, and corruptible—it remains (if we are mindful of our promise) to interpret the entire reading again concerning man. This is to prove in reality that there is no discourse in this entire work which does not embrace hidden meanings and the highest truths concerning the nature of man, just as it did concerning the three worlds discussed above. Nor shall we have performed a less worthwhile service if we are diligent in explaining this fourth narration than we were in the previous ones. For how useful and how necessary the knowledge of oneself is to man (besides that Delphic letter) was so demonstrated by Plato in the first *Alcibiades* that he left nothing for successors to attempt to bring forward as new on this matter. And indeed, the pursuit of that man is wicked and rash who, while still ignorant of himself and still not knowing whether he can know anything, nevertheless so boldly affects the knowledge of things that are so far from him. Let us therefore return into ourselves, and see (as the prophet says) how many good things God has done for our soul. Lest, if perhaps the soul is less diligent in recognizing itself, it should hear the Father saying in the Song of Songs: *If you do not know yourself, O most beautiful of women, go forth and follow the tracks of your flocks.* <note>Song of Solomon 1:8.</note>

<margin>The triple punishment for ignorance of self: Above oneself. From oneself. Behind oneself.</margin>
You see what punishment for our ignorance awaits us. For we must depart from the Father—that departure which is followed by disinheritance, and what could be more unhappy than that? Likewise, we must go out, certainly out of ourselves. For the mind that does not see itself is not "at home" with itself. He who departs from himself is torn away from himself—and what could be more bitter? Third, we must go "after the tracks of our flocks," that is, after the tracks of the brutes which are within us (about which we shall say enough in this exposition). What could be more miserable, more despicable, or more contemptible than that?

<summary>Pico concludes his angelic interpretation by explaining how Christ elevates human nature above the angels and begins the fourth part of his work, emphasizing that self-knowledge is the essential foundation for all philosophy and spiritual safety.</summary>
<keywords>Angelic Hierarchy, Dionysius the Areopagite, Christology, Human Nature, Plato, Alcibiades, Self-Knowledge, Delphic Oracle, Allegory, Biblical Exegesis</keywords>
