<meta>This page transitions from the third exposition (the Angelic World) to the fourth exposition, which interprets the creation of the world as a metaphor for the creation and structure of Man, the "microcosm" or "lesser world."</meta>

# OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA

...let us follow those whom nature had appointed us to lead, even the beasts. Therefore, let us proceed not in the footsteps of brutes, but in the footsteps of Moses, and enter into our very selves—into the inner chambers of the soul—with the prophet himself opening the way for us. Thus, within ourselves, we may happily recognize both all the worlds and the Father and our true homeland.

### CHAPTER ONE.

<margin>
The rational soul.
Aristotle.
The Platonists.
Plotinus.
</margin>
Before we more accurately arrange our exposition according to the words and order of the prophet, we must first say something about the nature of man and briefly explain certain terms, so that the understanding of the entire meaning may then be clearer. Man consists of a body and a rational soul. The rational soul is called "heaven." For Aristotle calls heaven a living being moved by itself, and our soul (as the Platonists prove) is a substance that moves itself. Heaven is a circle, and the soul is likewise a circle; indeed, as Plotinus <note>Plotinus (c. 204–270 AD) was the founder of Neoplatonism, whose mystical philosophy deeply influenced Pico.</note> writes, heaven is a circle precisely because its soul is a circle. Heaven moves in a circuit; the rational soul, transferring itself from causes to effects and returning again from effects to causes, revolves in the circle of reasoning. If these points had to be explained individually to those who have not read them elsewhere, we would no longer be interpreters of Moses, but of Aristotle and Plato.

<margin>
The body.
The spirit.
</margin>
The body is called "earth," since earth alone is a heavy substance. For this reason, Moses says man was made from the soil, giving him his name <note>The Hebrew name "Adam" is related to "Adamah," meaning "ground" or "earth."</note>. However, between the earthly body and the celestial substance of the soul, there was a need for a middle link to join such distant natures together. Assigned to this duty is that thin and spiritual "little body" which both doctors and philosophers call the <term>spirit</term> <note>original: "spiritum"; in Renaissance medicine, "spirit" was a subtle vapor that carried life and sensation through the nerves.</note>.

<margin>
Aristotle.
</margin>
Aristotle writes that this spirit is of a more divine nature than the elements and corresponds in proportion to the heavens. Here, it is called "light." This name could not better suit the opinion of philosophers and doctors, whose common consensus is that this substance is extremely bright and delights in nothing more than being nourished and refreshed by light.

<margin>
Avicenna.
</margin>
Furthermore, just as every power of the heavens (as Avicenna <note>Avicenna (Ibn Sina) was a Persian polymath and one of the most significant physicians and philosophers of the Islamic Golden Age.</note> writes) is transferred to the earth by the vehicle of light, so every power of the soul—which we have called "heaven"—travels and is infused into this earthly body—which we have called "earth"—through the mediation of the luminous spirit: namely, the powers of life, motion, and sense. Let us now descend to the words of the prophet. We see first that heaven and earth are created: that is, the rational power and the earthly body, the two extremes of our substance. Finally, when light—the luminous spirit—is added, they are united. Thus, from "evening" and "morning"—that is, from the nocturnal nature of the body and the morning nature of the soul—one man is made. And since (as we have shown) every vital and sensory power descends to our "earth" through this light, it is with good reason that before the birth of light, the earth was "empty and void." Our "heaven" could not share its benefits of life and motion with the earth except through light as an intermediary messenger. Therefore, he immediately added the cause of this emptiness: namely, that "darkness was upon it" because the light had not yet risen.

<margin>
Man is established through the mediation of the spirit.
</margin>
### CHAPTER SECOND.

BUT IT remains to be asked what is meant by "and the spirit of the Lord moved over the waters." Here, an undifferentiated and universal teaching about the waters is delivered, which is more clearly distinguished on the following day when he teaches that some are above the heaven and others are below the heaven. If we desire the true meaning of all these things, let us consult nature itself, which our prophet (as we have often said) exactly portrays and represents. We have seen mention made 

<column-break/>

of the three parts of human substance: namely, the rational part, this mortal body, and the middle spirit. Two parts remain. For between the rational part by which we are men and everything that is corporeal in us (whether it be thick or thin and spiritual), there is a middle part—the sensory part—which we share with the brutes.

<margin>
The sensory soul.
</margin>
And since our communication with the angels is no less than our communication with the brutes, just as sense is below reason—

<margin>
Reason.
Intelligence.
John.
</margin>
whence comes our commerce with the animals—so above reason is "intelligence," through which we can say that word of John: "Our fellowship is with the angels." You see what is below and what is above our reason. If reason is called "heaven" (as we have proven), it is now manifest which "waters" in us are "above the heavens" and which are likewise "below the heavens." The name "waters" fits both the intellectual and sensory parts, though for different reasons: the former because it is most permeable to the rays of divine illuminations, the latter because it gapes for and delights in fleeting and flowing things. He warns us of this diversity when he places the latter "below the heaven," where all things are flowing and fleeting, and the former "above the heaven," where there is the administration of pure and perpetual intelligence. When, therefore, on the first day we read of the "spirit of the Lord" brooding over the waters, and the waters are divided into two parts, we should certainly not take this as being said of the waters below the heaven, for over these it is not the spirit of the Lord but rather the "heaven" that is carried. It remains that this was said of those waters which are "above the heaven."

<margin>
The divine intellect in participation.
</margin>
From this, a great doctrine concerning the soul is reported to us. For the intellect that is in us is illustrated by a greater and indeed divine intellect—whether it be God (as some wish) or a mind next to and related to man (as almost all the Greeks, the Arabs, and many of the Hebrews wish). The Jewish philosophers, as well as Albumasar <note>Abu Ma'shar, a famous Persian astrologer and philosopher.</note> and Al-Farabi <note>A renowned early Islamic philosopher who sought to reconcile Platonic and Aristotelian thought.</note> in the book he wrote on principles, expressly called this substance the "spirit of the Lord."

<margin>
Albumasar.
Al-Farabi.
</margin>
<margin>
Moses the Egyptian and Abubacher.
</margin>
Nor was it done without cause that he remembered this matter—that is, the moving of the spirit over the waters—before he had established man from soul and body by the link of light. This was done lest we might perhaps believe that this spirit is not present to our intellect except when it is joined to the body. This is what "Moses the Egyptian" <note>Moses Maimonides, the preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher.</note>, the Arab Abubacher <note>Abu Bakr ibn Tufayl, author of the philosophical novel *Hayy ibn Yaqdhan*.</note>, and certain others falsely believed.

### CHAPTER THREE.

<margin>
On which senses.
Aristotle in "On the Soul," Book 3, at length.
</margin>
IT REMAINS for us to explain what is meant when he says that the "waters which are under the heaven"—that is, the sensory powers which are under the rational part—are "gathered together into one place." This is very obvious to those not entirely uneducated in philosophy. For all sensitive powers flow to the <term>common sense</term> <note>original: "sensum... communem"; the internal faculty that integrates data from the five individual senses.</note> (as we call it from the thing itself). This, if we follow Aristotle, is in the heart, just as rivers flow together to the sea. Nor would we speak absurdly if we said that from that sea the five senses are spread out—which we see as hearing, sight, taste, touch, and smell—like five "Mediterranean seas" spread out and entering the continent of the body. This was clearly Plato's opinion in the *Theaetetus*.

<margin>
Plato.
</margin>
And since, from the perfection of the sensory powers (which we understand from this collection toward their source), there comes life, health, and nourishment for the body (which we call "earth"), he immediately introduces the earth as "green and blooming" after that gathering of the waters. For nature provided sense to all mortals for the life and health of the body...

<summary>Pico interprets the components of Man as the Microcosm, equating the rational soul to "Heaven," the body to "Earth," and the physiological spirit to "Light." He further maps the biblical "waters" to the human intellect (above) and the senses (below), which gather in the heart to sustain the body.</summary>
<keywords>Microcosm, rational soul, spiritus, common sense, Aristotle, Plato, Avicenna, Al-Farabi, Maimonides, sensory powers, allegory of Genesis</keywords>

--- Page 43 ---
<meta>This page continues the Fourth Exposition of the *Heptaplus*, in which Pico interprets the creation of the world as an allegory for the internal structure of the human being (the "microcosm"). He is currently explaining how the different elements of the Genesis narrative correspond to the faculties of the human soul and body.</meta>

->HEPTAPLUS<-

...must be cared for, so that through these [senses] they may know what is harmful and what is healthy for them. Once known, they may reject the harmful and desire the healthy through the appetite attached to the senses. Finally, through the joined motor power, they may flee evils and pursue what is useful. The eye sees the food; the nostrils smell it; the feet approach; the hands take it; and the palate tastes it. We say all these things so that we may recognize that the soul is aptly joined to the "establishment of the waters" <note>original: *stabilimento aquarum*</note> (that is, the sensitive powers) and to the "earth," which for a long time has signified for us the body’s abundant happiness.

### CHAPTER FOUR.

<margin>The opinion of the modern philosophers.</margin>
But indeed, since the rational nature is distinguished by many forces and powers, its naked substance has been discussed above. Now we must speak of its adornment and, so to speak, its royal furnishings. This is what [Moses] writes concerning the placing of the moon, the sun, and the stars in the firmament. Indeed, the younger philosophers <note>Pico likely refers to the "modern" Scholastic or Neoplatonic thinkers of his era.</note> might interpret the sun as the intellect in act and the moon as the intellect in potentiality. But since we have a great controversy with them on this matter, let us meanwhile explain it thus: that part of the soul which turns toward the "higher waters"—toward the Spirit of the Lord—is called the "sun" because it shines entirely. That part, however, which looks back at the "lower waters" (that is, the sensual powers), from which it contracts some stain of infection, should have the name of the "moon." The Greek Platonists, following the dogmas of their own teaching, called the sun <margin>The Platonists called them *Dianoian* and *doxan*.</margin> *Dianoia* <note>Greek: Διανοιαν; refers to discursive reason or thought.</note> and the moon *Doxa* <note>Greek: δοξαν; refers to opinion or belief based on appearance.</note>. Moreover, since we are wandering far from our homeland and living in the night and darkness of this present life, we mostly use that part of the soul which is deflected toward the senses—from which we "opine" more than we "know." But when the day of the future life dawns, we, being removed from the senses and turned toward divine things, will understand with that other higher part. Thus it is rightly said that this "sun" of ours rules the day, while the "moon" rules the night. Likewise, because once we have put off this dying garment [of the body], we shall behold with the single light of the sun that which, in this most miserable night of the body, we strive to see with many forces and powers rather than actually seeing it; for this reason, the day shines with a single sun. The night, by contrast, is composed of many stars: namely, the power of composing and dividing, reasoning, defining, and the rest, which the soul gathers and unites as auxiliary aids to the less powerful moon.

### CHAPTER FIVE.

Thus far we have spoken of the cognitive powers of the soul. Now he transfers himself to those whose work it is to desire: namely, the seats of anger and lust (that is, concupiscence). He designates these by the "beasts" and the irrational kind of living things, because these are <margin>The Chaldeans. Plato.</margin> common to us and the beasts, and—what is more unfortunate—they often drive us toward a brutal life. Hence that saying of the Chaldeans: "Beasts of the earth inhabit your vessel." <note>This refers to the *Chaldean Oracles*, a text Pico held in high regard as ancient wisdom.</note> And in Plato’s *Republic*, we learn that we have diverse kinds of brutes within our own home, so that the Pythagorean paradox is not difficult to believe (if understood correctly): that wicked men migrate into brutes. For brutes are so much within us and in our very vitals that we do not have to travel far to migrate into them. Hence the fables of Circe <note>The enchantress from Homer’s *Odyssey* who turned men into swine.</note>, and that line of Theocritus: "Whom the goddesses <note>Meaning Virtue and Wisdom.</note> have looked upon cannot be undermined by Circe’s cups." <margin>Both Theocritus and Maro [Virgil] mentioned this. The interior sense is called the "phantasia."</margin> But let us see what distinction among these brutes the Mosaic reading suggests to us. Some are produced from the waters that are under the sky; others from the earth. The waters, as we said, signify the sensual part which is "under the sky" because it is subject to reason and serves it closely. The earth is this very earthly and fragile body by which we are surrounded. Let us consider, therefore, whether among the affections by which we are moved, some belong more to the body, and others to the interior sense, which the philosophers call the *phantasia* <note>The "imagination" or the faculty that processes sensory images.</note>.

<column-break/>

Those [affections] which drive us either toward food or toward sex seem to me to pertain to the body. For these were given to us by God both for the protection of the body which we nourish, and for the procreation of children, in whom we may survive when we ourselves perish. We abuse these same things when we are enticed more than is proper by the lure of pleasure—through gluttony and through the hollow lust of the flesh—as Paul says, "acting in desires." <margin>Paul.</margin> In his words, it should be noted that he did not say "do not take care for the flesh," but "do not do so in desires." <note>Pico is referencing Romans 13:14: "But put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh, to gratify its desires."</note> This is because they must be used for necessity, not for pleasure, and much less should our happiness be placed in them. Let us therefore understand these affections as the "cattle and wild animals," which are called the offspring of the earth rather than of the waters. This is because they are both fulfilled and excited through the members of this thicker body, and were provided for us by God for its health—even if they become the destruction of those who wither from overindulgence or are dissolved by lust. To the "waters" (that is, the sense of imagination), let us refer those affections which are more spiritual and can be called the offspring of our thought rather than of the flesh. Of this kind are those that call us toward honors, toward anger, toward revenge, and other related affections. These are necessary and useful for those who use them moderately. For one must be angry, but within measure; and revenge is often a work of justice; and each person must protect their own dignity; nor should honors be refused when they are obtained through honest skills. I say this so that—since God created these "brutes" (which indicate the sensual appetites) and blessed them once created—we should not believe with the Manichaeans <margin>Manichaeans</margin> <note>A dualistic sect that believed the physical world and the body were created by an evil principle.</note> that they are evil by their own nature and were founded by an evil principle rather than by the good God. All those things are therefore good and necessary to man, but we make them evil by our own fault, exceeding into ambition, fury, outbursts of temper, and pride—things which that Best of Beings had established as the best of things.

### CHAPTER SIX.

See how perfectly those things that follow agree with what we have said: that man was made by God "in His image" so that he might rule over the fish, the birds, and the beasts which both the water and the earth had produced. Indeed, we were already discussing man above, but now for the first time we understand the "image of God" in him. From this comes his speech and his command over the brutes. For man was so instituted by nature that reason should dominate and bridle the senses, and that by its law, all fury and appetite—both of anger and lust—should be restrained. But because the image of God was defaced by the stain of sin, we have begun, miserable and unhappy, to serve our own "beasts." Like the Chaldean king <note>Nebuchadnezzar, who according to the Book of Daniel, lost his reason and lived like an animal in the wild.</note>, we dwell among them and fall prostrate upon the ground, greedy for earthly things, forgetful of our homeland, <margin>The Chaldean king.</margin> forgetful of our Father, forgetful of our kingdom, and of the privilege of our former dignity given to us. "Indeed, man, when he was in honor, did not understand; but was compared to the foolish cattle and became like unto them." <note>A quotation from Psalm 49:20.</note>

### CHAPTER SEVEN.

But just as all of us in the first Adam (who obeyed Satan more than God), whose children we are according to the flesh, are deformed and degenerate from men into brutes; so in the last Adam, Jesus Christ <margin>Jesus Christ. The last Adam.</margin> (who fulfilled the will of the Father and by His blood defeated spiritual wickednesses), whose children we all are according to the spirit, we are reformed through grace. We are regenerated from being men into the adoption of the sons of God—if only the "prince of darkness and of this world" finds nothing in us, just as he found nothing in Him.

<vocab>Adam, Jesus Christ, Plato, Chaldeans, Circe, Theocritus, Maro [Virgil], Manichaeans, reason, sense, phantasia [imagination], Dianoia [Thought], Doxa [Opinion]</vocab>

<summary>Pico interprets the sun and moon as the higher and lower functions of the soul (reason and opinion) and the "beasts" as the human appetites (anger and lust). He argues that while these appetites are naturally good and God-given for survival, sin causes humans to lose their rational "dominion" and live like animals.</summary>

<meta>This page begins the Fifth Exposition of the Heptaplus. In the previous four expositions, Pico examined the four worlds (angelic, celestial, elemental, and human) as they are reflected simultaneously within the Genesis narrative. Now, in Book Five, he shifts his focus to treat each world individually and sequentially, beginning with the angelic world as described in the first day of Creation.</meta>

->GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA’S FIFTH EXPOSITION ON ALL THE WORLDS SEPARATELY AND IN SUCCESSIVE ORDER. PREFACE TO THE FIFTH BOOK.<-

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'Q' featuring a circular illustration of a man, possibly a scholar or prophet, seated at a desk and pointing towards an open book while looking upwards as if receiving divine inspiration. The circle is set within a square frame with floral motifs.</image-desc>

<margin>The Homeric chain. The Platonic rings.</margin>
JUST AS Moses, as we have shown, discussed all the worlds—the intellectual, the celestial, the elemental, and the human—simultaneously in every part of his text, imitating nature, or rather the artist of nature, God (who enclosed all worlds within each single world), so too, following the example of that same nature which distributed proper seats, proper rights, and peculiar laws to each thing, our prophet [Moses] arranged his writing with a marvelous and perfect mastery of divine art. He did this so that, although he everywhere discussed all things under the same face and the same veil of words, he nevertheless assigned individual parts of his work to individual worlds in a successive order. To show this, we shall begin to interpret the first small part concerning the first world—that is, the angelic—and then the remaining parts concerning the others, sagaciously observing in the words of Moses that golden **Homeric chain** <note>A reference to the *catena aurea* or Great Chain of Being, a concept derived from the Iliad where a chain connects heaven and earth.</note> and the **Platonic rings** <note>In Plato's *Ion*, divine inspiration is compared to a magnet (the "Stone of Hercules") that transmits its power through a series of iron rings.</note> hung from the living power of the Maker as if from the true **stone of indomitable Hercules**.

---

### CHAPTER ONE.

<margin>The mind and the eye are the same according to reason, but differ in reality.</margin>
AS WE ARE about to speak of the angelic nature, which is pure intellect, let us first conceive in our minds that minds are like certain eyes. For what the eye is in bodily things, the mind itself is in the spiritual genus. Although the eye possesses something of light in the mixture of its innermost substance, it nevertheless requires external light to perform the duty of vision, in which it observes the colors and differences of things. Nor should it be said on that account that it is not sight by its own nature, even if it does not see except by the benefit of light. For even the ears (not to mention inanimate things) and all the other parts of the body are illuminated by light, yet they do not see. Therefore, that thing which has obtained the nature of seeing and is sight through the essence of its own reason is that which can see once light is received. Let us consider these same things in intellects: Intellects are the eyes; intelligible truth is the light. Since the intellect itself is intelligible, it has something of internal light by which it can see itself, but it cannot see the rest. Truly, it requires the forms and ideas of things, which act as certain rays of invisible light through which the intelligible truth is undoubtedly perceived. Nor should it be said—as we declared by the example of the eye—that they are not intelligent by nature, or that they obtained their intellectual property by accident under the same condition as our souls. From this error stems the opinion of those who think the name "intellect" is unworthy of God. For if we take the intellect as an eye which sees not from itself but by participation in light, then since God is light (for truth is light), and vision is the action by which the eye reaches the light, God does not need this operation, for He is light itself. He is as much further removed from ignorance of all things than the angels as the nature of light is further from darkness than

<margin>Angeli consist of act and potentiality.</margin>
the eye. But let us return to the angels. The eye—that is, the intellectual substance—is not entirely simple; otherwise, it would not permit the composition of the light that arrives. Hence the common saying that angels consist of **act and potentiality** <note>In Scholastic philosophy, "act" is the completion or perfection of a thing, while "potentiality" is the capacity to receive that perfection.</note>. How anxious is the dispute over what that act and that potentiality are, and what the reason for their composition is! Likewise, what **Averroes the Arab** <note>Averroes (Ibn Rushd) was a 12th-century Islamic philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were central to medieval and Renaissance thought.</note> 

<margin>Averroes the Arab.</margin>
intended when he said that both intellects—the one in act and the one in potentiality—exist in all intellects below God. But for our purposes in this place, the common opinion suffices, however it may be understood. Moses opens all these things we have said for us 

<column-break/>

on the first day. For he divides the substance of the angel into "heaven" and "earth"—namely, the nature of act and the nature of potentiality. Now, just as the same thing has different properties, so too it has different names. Therefore, this same act—taken as the power granting sight to the eye and as the consummation of potentiality—is called "heaven," because it stands in the same relation to potentiality as heaven does to earth. Again, because it is in need of light and cannot perform the proper duty of intelligence through itself, it is figured by "the waters": a body capable of light, yet by its own nature not shining at all. There is also another reason for the similarity: this act of potentiality, which he calls "earth," is as close to it as water is to the earth. But now let us engage with the words of the prophet: *God created heaven and earth*, the nature of act and the nature of potentiality, of which the angel consists; *and the earth* (that is, potentiality) *was empty and void*—empty of act and void of light, which it does not receive except through the mediation of the waters. And since opposites occur around the same thing, and it pertains to the same subject to host both light and darkness, he added: *and darkness was upon the face of the abyss.*

<margin>What the abyss is.</margin>
He did not say "upon the earth." For the **Abyss** is nothing other (unless we misuse the word) than the depth of the waters. *The spirit of the Lord was moved over these waters*—the spirit, 

<margin>The Apostle James.</margin>
surely, who is called the "Father of Lights" by the **Apostle James** <note>original: *Iacobo apostolo*; see James 1:17.</note>; from whom presently over those waters—that is, over the angelic minds—rises the light of intelligible forms. This was perhaps also 

<margin>The Saracens.</margin>
understood by the **Saracens** <note>Pico uses "Saracens" to refer to Islamic philosophers or theologians.</note> when they said that the angels were led forth by God from darkness into light and filled with eternal joy. For pleasure follows intelligence, and no pleasure is greater, none truer, and none more permanent.

### CHAPTER TWO.

CLOSEST to this world is the celestial world. Its primary property is that it is the gap between both worlds: the intelligible world, of which we just spoke, and this sensible world which we inhabit. We cannot more clearly indicate the essence of any middle nature than by expressing the extremes by which it is enclosed; for a middle nature is tempered from the extremes. Therefore, [Moses] opens to us the greatest knowledge 

<margin>Note.</margin>
concerning the condition of heaven when he says that the heaven is placed as a middle *between the waters and the waters*—that is, between the angelic and the corruptible substances—not so much by reason of location as by reason of essence. Now, we have already said that by "waters" are understood the forms which [pertain] to potentiality...

<summary>Pico begins the fifth book of the Heptaplus by explaining that Moses structured the Genesis narrative to describe the four worlds sequentially, starting here with the creation of the angelic world as a composite of act and potentiality. He uses the analogy of the eye and light to describe how angelic intellects receive divine truth, identifying the "heaven and earth" of the first day as the dual nature of angels.</summary>

HEPTAPLUS of GIOVANNI [PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA]

<margin>For it is clear above how the formal cause acts.</margin>
powers are present as if close to the earth, and they perfect the essence. Just as the earth of the angels is one thing and the earth of the elements another, because the power in each is different: so too the reason—that is, the form—of the waters is one thing in one place and another in the other. Between these truly lies the middle heaven: from one side divine life, from the other bodily form; from one side incorruptible substance, from the other visible substance; from one side the firmness of essence, from the other change of place; from there, whatever is unified, mixed, and dissimilar has been allotted by the disposing providence of the Creator.

## CHAPTER THREE.

<margin>The repression of the fury of the aged ocean.</margin>
After this, he briefly reminds us of the integrity, position, and order of the elements through the gathering of the waters into one place and the laws prescribed for the sea so that it does not overwhelm the earth. For there is nothing that indicates more clearly that there are laws implanted in the elements by an intelligent cause—by which they are ruled and held in their places—beyond the inclination of their bodily and brute nature, than these barriers of the waters. By these, the ocean is restrained, whose impulse would carry it across the entire circuit of the earth, just as the whole of fire rests upon the whole of the air; yet, as if warned by the rod of a schoolmaster <note>original: "pædagogi"</note>, it draws back its foot and does not advance further than our safety and the life of all living creatures requires. This cannot be referred to the necessity of matter (which rather inclines all elements equally toward a spherical shape), nor to a fortuitous collision of atoms—such as Epicurus dreams of, 
<margin>Epicurus believed that the world was fused together from atoms, or indivisible bodies. Strato.</margin>
who believed the world was fused together from indivisible bodies—nor to the "seminal force" of a mute nature (as Strato <note>Strato of Lampsacus, a Peripatetic philosopher known for a materialistic view of nature.</note> says), which is ignorant of any purpose, but only to the final cause: to direct toward which belongs solely to mind and intellectual providence. Therefore, it happened that Moses, when about to treat the order of the elements, mentioned only this fact, and the prophets so often bring it forward as a primary argument for divine power and wisdom. Hence in 
<margin>Proverbs.</margin>
Proverbs: "when he fortified the depths with a certain law and circle" <note>Proverbs 8:27</note>. Hence that: "who surrounded the sea with its boundary" <note>Job 38:8-11</note>, and in 
<margin>Jeremiah.</margin>
Jeremiah: "Will you not then fear me, says the Lord, who have placed the sand as a boundary for the sea?" <note>Jeremiah 5:22</note>. And: "You have set that boundary which they shall not pass, nor shall the waters cover the earth" <note>Psalm 104:9</note>. Since the whole constitution of the elements is ordered so that living things especially may be mixed in, immediately after the order of earth and water and the firmament, he added the command to the earth that it should sprout plants—a work which might rather have belonged to the discourse on the fifth day.

## CHAPTER FOUR.

<margin>Comparison.</margin>
After he discussed the celestial and elemental spheres, and therefore the whole integrity of the bodily universe, it remained to speak of the inhabitants and citizens (if I may call them that) of this worldly city along with the heavenly ones: concerning whom we must speak first as if regarding the senate and prefects of the city, and then also regarding the earthly ones as if regarding the common people and the populace. First, therefore, he mentions the heavenly beings: which God placed in the firmament so that they might be for signs and seasons, and might shine in the heavens and illuminate the earth. I mean the sun, the moon, and the stars. Here, most profound questions would have to be handled, each of which would require a full volume: In what way are these stars in the firmament? Are they like its nobler parts, as the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle.</note> believe? Or like animals in their spheres—fish in the water, beasts on the earth—as Eusebius, Medus, and Diodorus <note>Early Christian and Greek scholars.</note> hold?

<column-break/>

<margin>Basil. Apollinarius. Cyril. Aristotle. Theodoret.</margin>
Likewise, the subject would demand a place for a discussion with the astrologers <note>original: "genethliacis," those who cast birth charts.</note> concerning the science of divining by the stars and foreknowing future events. They confirm this from the fact that Moses said the stars were placed by God for "signs." This science is sharply criticized not only by our own [Christian] writers—such as Basil, who rightly called it a most busy vanity, and by Apollinarius, Cyril, and Diodorus—but it is also rejected by the good Peripatetics, and Aristotle despised it. What is more, Theodoret testifies that it was repudiated by Pythagoras, Plato, and all the Stoics. One might also think we should inquire here about the nature of the stars, their motion, their governance, the spots on the moon, and all sidereal science. Truly, if we descend to these things, though they are beautiful and worthy of knowledge, we might perhaps hear that line from Horace: "But now was not the place for these things" <note>Horace, *Ars Poetica* 19. Pico means he is staying on topic.</note>. Therefore, we defer these to the work destined for them, in which we have undertaken to treat and examine the whole of philosophy, reconciling Aristotle and Plato as far as our strength allows.

## CHAPTER FIVE.

<margin>What he is not going to treat.</margin>
Let us come, therefore, to Moses, who, after speaking of the heavenly things, mentions the earthly animals in a fitting order: those that inhabit the waters, the earth, or the air—if indeed birds can be said to inhabit the air. Let no one here expect or demand from us a disputation on how the bodies of animals are made from the elements, or what the "seminal reasons" <note>The *rationes seminales*, divine seeds of development within nature.</note> are that God has placed in the natures of things. Likewise, [do not ask] whether the life of brutes is drawn forth from the bosom of matter, or whether all life proceeds rather from a divine principle, as 
<margin>Plotinus.</margin>
Plotinus most constantly asserts. Our friend Marsilio Ficino will soon give Plotinus to be read in Latin for the public benefit, illuminated by even longer arguments. To this opinion, perhaps, the prophet [Moses] will seem to lend support in this place: for after he said, "Let the waters bring forth the creeping thing of a living soul," he added later, "God created every living soul." One might observe here not only that the waters bring forth at God's command, and then God also brings forth. But also that where it deals with God's work, it is written "God created the living soul," but where it speaks of the waters, it says not "soul" but "the creeping thing of a living soul" <note>original: "reptile animæ viuentis"</note>. It is as if the vehicle of the soul—that is, the mixture of the body—is credited to the waters, but the substance of the soul, which is the giver of life, motion, and sense, shines from without upon the already tempered body from God, that is, from a divine principle. But of these things elsewhere. Among the animals of the earth, Moses mentions three: 
<margin>Three general differences of brutes.</margin>
cattle, creeping things, and beasts, in which he suggests to us three general differences of irrational brutes, of which there are no more. For there are **beasts**, which possess a perfect imagination <note>original: "phantasia"</note> and occupy a middle place among irrational beings, yet they do not know how to be trained by man or become tame. There are **creeping things**, which have an imperfect imagination and are like a middle ground between brutes and plants. There are **cattle** (beasts of burden), which, although they lack reason, are nevertheless capable of human discipline in some way, and thus seem to participate in something of reason, having been allotted a middle condition between brutes and men.

<margin>A comparison commonly used for kings.</margin>
Thus far we have spoken of the three worlds: the supercelestial, the celestial, and the sublunary. Now we must treat of man, of whom it is written: "Let us make man in our image." He is not so much a fourth world as some new created thing,

It is a common custom, often practiced by kings and princes of the earth, that if they happen to build a magnificent and noble city, once the city is finished, they place their own image in its center to be seen and admired by all. We see that God, the Prince of all, did no differently; having constructed the entire machine of the world, He placed man—formed in His own image and likeness—in the center of it as the last of all His works. But it is a difficult question: why is it the unique privilege of man to possess the image of

God? the image of the Trinity is represented. What else can this 

<margin>
The Greek interpreters.

be? It can only be that the substance of man (as some Greek interpreters of the world also say) actually encompasses in itself the substances of all natures and the fullness of the entire universe. I say "actually" <note>original: "re ipsa"</note> because although angels and every intelligent creature contain all things within themselves in a certain way—since, being full of the forms and reasons of all things, they know all things—man is different. Just as God is the image of all not only because He understands all things, but because He unites and gathers within Himself the entire perfection of the substances of things, so too man (though in a different way, as we shall show, otherwise he would be God and not the image of God) calls together and unites all the natures of the entire world into the integrity of his own substance. We can say this of no other creature, whether angelic, celestial, or sensible. This is the difference between 

<margin>
The difference between God and man.
</margin>

God and man: God contains all things in Himself as the source <note>original: "principium"</note> of all, while man contains all things in himself as the middle <note>original: "medium"</note> of all. Thus it happens that in God all things are of a better quality than they are in themselves; in man, the lower things are of a more noble condition, while the superior things degenerate. Fire, water, air, and earth are present through the truest property of their nature in this coarse and earthy body of man which we 

<margin>
Aristotle.

Furthermore, there is in man the life of plants, performing all the functions for him that it does for them: nourishing, growing, and generating. There is the sense of the brute animals, both internal and external. There is a soul empowered by celestial reason. There is a participation in the angelic mind. 

<margin>
Hermes Trismegistus, not Mercury, is introduced here in the Asclepius.
</margin>

There is a truly divine possession of all these natures flowing together into one, so that one might feel like exclaiming that line of Hermes <note>original: "Mercurii"</note>: "O Asclepius, man is a great miracle." Human condition can glory in this name especially; for this reason, no created substance disdains 

<margin>
Paul.
</margin>

to serve him. The earth and the elements are at his hand and serve him; the heavens fight for him; the angelic minds procure his safety and good, if indeed it is true what Paul writes: that all are ministering spirits sent into service for those who are destined for the inheritance of salvation. Nor should it seem strange to anyone that he is loved by all things: for in him all things recognize something of their own, or rather, they recognize themselves and all that they possess.

<column-break/>

<margin>
Man is the bond and knot of earthly and heavenly things, as stated above: an "embrace and binding."
</margin>

Earthly things are enslaved to MAN; heavenly things favor man, because he is the bond and knot of both celestial and terrestrial things. Neither of these can fail to have peace with him, provided that he has peace with himself, for he sanctions the peace and treaties of these things within himself. But let us be careful, I pray, that being established in such great dignity, we do not fail to understand it. Rather, let us always have this before the eyes of our mind as a certain, explored, and indubitable truth: just as all things favor us when we keep the law given to us, so if we wander and fall away through sin and the transgression of the law, we shall find all things to be adverse, hostile, and inimical. For it is reasonable that, just as we do an injury not only to ourselves but to the universe which we encompass within us—and even to the author of the world, Almighty God—we should also experience all things in the world, and God first of all, as most powerful avengers and most heavy punishers of the injury received. Hence, let us fear what penalties and punishments await the transgressors of the divine law.

<margin>
An Oracle.
</margin>

These are they who (as the oracle said) *demones hoi phoitōsi peri chthona kai peri ponton akamatai demones tyumas plēgē theoio* <note>original Greek: "δαιμονες οἱ φοιτῶσι περὶ χθόνα καὶ περὶ πόντον ἀκαμάται δαιμονες τυυμὰς πληγῇ θεοῖο"</note>: that is, those who wander about the earth and the sea and are wretchedly subdued under the lash of God. Heaven strikes them; the earth strikes them; the unshakable justice of the entire worldly Republic pursues them. For they are guilty of violating the universe and of injuring the divine majesty, whose image they defile with the foulest stain of iniquity. This is perhaps why, among the prophets, when any command or prohibition is promulgated by God, heaven and earth are called as witnesses; because the transgression of the command also violates them, and having received a common insult, they too will receive the wicked for punishment while they serve God. And it surpasses all madness to be led to believe that in some city, a man placed and decorated with the highest honors could be allowed to offend the prince and the entire republic—which has deserved the best from him—with impunity, and not rather be given over immediately to be tortured and tormented by the lictors and the executioner, or be crushed with stones by the consensus of the whole people. And there are executioners; there are lictors in this 

<margin>
Wicked demons. Paul. Orpheus.
</margin>

Republic of God: the wicked demons assigned to the most vile ministry in punishment for ancient crime. Hence that saying of Paul: "I have delivered him to Satan for the destruction of the flesh." Hence also the naming of the "avenging demon" in Orpheus, if perhaps we trust our own writers less. But just as every creature hates and execrates the crimes of men, so his righteous life and conduct are pleasing to all. For all things, which are involved and joined to him in such a tight bond, cannot fail to be admitted into participation of both his good and his evil. Hence that Gospel saying: "If a sinner repents, all the angels exult with joy." Hence the clear reason for that mystery which was hidden for ages: that our nature, corrupted in the first Adam and defiled from its status, should be restored through the cross of Christ. Clearly, for our sake, the Son of God both becomes man and is fixed to the cross. For it was fitting that He who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature in whom all things were created, should be joined by an ineffable union to him who was made in the image of God—who is the bond of every creature, in whom all things are gathered together. Nor was it right, if the whole of nature was endangered along with man, that its loss should be neglected or repaired by any other than Him through whom the whole of nature had been established.

<summary>Pico explains that man is the "microcosm" or the central bond of the universe, containing the properties of all elements, plants, animals, and angels. Because man unites all creation, his virtue brings harmony to the world, while his sin turns all of nature into a hostile force of divine justice.</summary>

# SIXTH EXPOSITION: ON THE KINSHIP OF THE WORLDS WITH EACH OTHER AND OF ALL THINGS.

## PREFACE TO THE SIXTH BOOK.

<margin>
In creatures (how wonderful it is) are the traces of the trinity.
</margin>
GOD is a unity so distinguished by a triad that He does not depart from the simplicity of unity. There is a manifold trace of the divine trinity in the creature. We shall bring forward only this one point here—which I know has not yet been brought forward by anyone—that the unity we see in creatures is discovered to be divided in a threefold manner. First, there is that unity in things when each thing is "one" in itself and consists and coheres with itself. Second is that through which one creature is united to another, and through which, finally, all parts of the world are one world. The third and most principal of all is that by which the whole universe is one with its Maker, like an army with its leader. This threefold union is present in every single thing through its own one simple unity derived from that One which is the first one and triple at the same time and is one—I mean from the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

<margin>
Father.
Son.
Spirit.
The root of all ordered charity.
</margin>
For the power of the Father, producing all things, bestows His unity upon all; and the wisdom of the Son, rightly disposing all things, unites and joins all things to each other; and the love of the Spirit, turning all things back to God, joins the whole work of the Maker with the bond of <term>charity</term> <note>In this context, "charity" (caritas) refers to divine love or the force of attraction that holds the universe together.</note>. Just as God is more intimate to us, so is He more "one" to us than we are to ourselves; conversely, each thing is more closely joined to itself than to other parts of the world. Thus, having been taught the order of universal charity, if we wish to follow the divine law inscribed on the tablets of nature, we will love God Himself first above us and above all things; in the second place, ourselves; and in the third, our neighbor. Our Prophet <note>Pico refers to Moses, the traditional author of Genesis.</note> has already said enough about that unity by which each thing is one in itself when he examined the nature of all things individually. Regarding that unity by which we are united to God, it will be treated in the next discourse, where we shall debate concerning the summit of happiness. The remaining one is that by which diverse parts are joined together by a mutual treaty, which we must discuss at present.

---

## CHAPTER ONE.

<margin>
The diverse natures of things are constrained together.
</margin>
After we have seen the distinct natures of things and arranged them in separate stations, so to speak—lest we should believe for that reason that the one universe exists from all these only because individual things are contained by individuals (as we showed above) according to the condition of their nature—the Prophet also wished to indicate in his own context how many and what modes there were by which the natures of things might be joined together. These things call us not only to this inquisitive understanding, but by this they instruct and demonstrate by what path and reason we can be joined to those things which are better than we are. But as I thought—before I approached the exposition of the words—how many modes there either were or could be thought of by which certain things might obtain either an affinity or a bond with each other, and as I ran through all the dogmas of the philosophers in which I have labored since childhood, no more than fifteen kinds occurred to me. These I then saw, coming to Moses, indicated by him so clearly and so aptly that I believe no one could be better instructed about them anywhere else.

## CHAPTER TWO.

<margin>
By what modes something is said to be joined to another.
</margin>
Immediately, therefore, on the first day, he encompasses—I know not whether more briefly or more clearly—five modes by which something can be joined to another. For what is joined to another is either its essence, or it is a property of the essence, or it is in it as a form in a subject, or it touches it either like that which transforms what is being transformed, or like art touches the matter subject to it. Similarly, we read five things in Moses compared and connected to each other: heaven

<column-break/>

and earth, earth and emptiness, the abyss and darkness, the spirit of God and the waters, light and bodies.

<margin>
The five connections of Moses.
</margin>
Therefore, the first mode of conjunction is designated for us by the earth "without form and void," <note>original: "inanis & vacua"; Pico is quoting Genesis 1:2.</note> because the earth—that is, matter—is by its nature empty unless it is filled by forms from elsewhere. The second is indicated by the darkness over the face of the abyss. For the abyss by its own nature is neither luminous nor dark, but darkness follows its nature unless approaching light puts it to flight; just as the formlessness and emptiness of matter are followed by the darkness of <term>privation</term> <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "privation" is the absence of a quality (like light or form) that should naturally be present.</note> until arriving species expel them. The third is shown by the light that rose upon bodies. For light is in them as a form in a subject.

<margin>
Heaven as it is connected to the earth.
</margin>
The fourth is heaven and earth: because heaven does not inhere in the earth as a form or an accident exists in the thing it perfects, but it is joined to it as an <term>efficient cause</term> <note>An "efficient cause" is the primary source of change or rest; here, the heavens act upon the earth to cause change.</note> to a patient and a transforming cause to the body which is transformed. The example of the last is the spirit of the Lord, which is carried over the waters. For the craftsman—the wisdom of the Lord and the spiritual nature entirely separated from commerce with the body—is understood to be joined to bodies in no other way than art, which is in the mind of the architect, is joined to cement, wood, and stones. But consider again this reason of consequence: that the earth is empty of itself and has domestic darkness; then it is joined most closely to light through light, to heaven through heaven, and through heaven to spiritual substance. But let us see how these things behave in us. The earth is the earthly body, empty and void of life and sense; and over it are darkness, death, numbness, inefficacy, immobility, and lack of sensation. Light is the life which enlivens it, excites it, acts on it, moves it, and renders it endowed with sense. Heaven is the <term>soul</term> <note>original: "animus"; Pico often distinguishes the "animus" (rational soul/mind) from the "anima" (vital soul).</note>, the source of that light; and the spirit of God is the intellect of the divine light of His face. And regarding these things in this place, there is even more than is necessary...

### CHAPTER SEVEN. OF JOHN PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA.

...nature, which is the embrace and binding of the three worlds we have mentioned. It is a common custom used by the kings and princes of the earth that if, by chance, they have founded a magnificent and noble city, once the city is finished, they place their own image in the middle of it to be seen and admired by all. We see that God, the Prince of all things, did no differently; for when the entire machinery of the world had been constructed, He last of all placed man in the center of it, formed in His own image and likeness. But it is a difficult question why this privilege—of having the image of God—belongs specifically to man. For if we set aside the exploded insanity of Melito <margin>The error of Melito.</margin> <note>Melito of Sardis was a 2nd-century bishop who was later (perhaps unfairly) accused of "anthropomorphism," the belief that God possesses a physical human body.</note>, who depicted God with a human physical form, and return instead to the nature of the reason and the mind (which, like God, is intelligent, invisible, and incorporeal), we shall certainly prove from that that man is like God—especially in that part where the image of the Trinity is represented in the soul. Yet we must recognize <margin>In what part man is said to be like God.</margin> that these same qualities are greater and more powerful in the angels than in us, and are less mixed with a contrary nature; thus, they possess more similarity and kinship with the divine nature. 

However, we seek something peculiar to man: whence comes his own specific dignity and the image of the divine substance, which is found shared with no other creature. What else can this be but that the substance of man <margin>Greek interpreters.</margin> (as some Greek interpreters also suggest) encompasses in itself the substances of all natures and the fullness of the entire universe? I say "in itself" because although angels and every intelligent creature contain all things within themselves in a certain way—being full of the forms and reasons of all things—they know all things through these forms. But truly, just as God is the "image" not only because He understands all things, but because He unites and gathers in Himself the entire perfection of the true substances of things, so too does man gather and unite all the natures of the whole world into the integrity of his own substance (though he does so differently than God, as we shall show, otherwise he would be God and not God’s image). We cannot say this of any other creature, whether angelic, celestial, or sensible. There is, however, this difference between <margin>The difference between God and man.</margin> God and man: God contains all things in Himself as the *beginning* of all, while man contains all things in himself as the *middle* of all. The result is that in God, all things are of a better quality than they are in themselves; in man, the lower things are of a nobler condition, while the higher things are somewhat diminished. Fire, water, air, and earth are present through the truest property of their nature in this coarse and earthly body of man which we see. Besides these, there is another more divine spiritual body <margin>Aristotle.</margin> <note>Aristotle proposed a "fifth element" or aether, which Pico identifies here as a celestial spirit within the human body.</note> which corresponds in proportion to the heavens. There is, furthermore, in man the life of plants, performing for him the same functions as for them: nourishing, growing, and generating. There is the sense of the beasts, both internal and external. There is a soul powerful with celestial reason. There is a participation in the angelic mind. There is the truly divine possession of all these natures flowing together into one, so that we may rightfully exclaim that saying of Hermes: "A great miracle, O Asclepius, is man." <margin>Hermes. It is Trismegistus, not Mercury, who is introduced there to Asclepius.</margin> <note>Pico quotes the *Asclepius*, a famous Hermetic text. He notes that the speaker is Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary sage, rather than the god Mercury.</note> Human condition can glory in this name especially; for this reason, no created substance disdains to serve him. The earth and elements are at hand and serve him; the heavens fight for him; the angelic minds procure his safety and well-being—if indeed it is true what Paul writes, <margin>Paul.</margin> that "they are all ministering spirits, sent to serve for the sake of those who are destined to inherit salvation." <note>Hebrews 1:14.</note> Nor should it seem strange to anyone that he is loved by all, for in him all things recognize something of their own—indeed, they recognize themselves and all that is theirs.

<column-break/>

<margin>Man is the bond and knot of earthly and heavenly things, as mentioned above [regarding] embrace and binding.</margin> Earthly things are enslaved to man; heavenly things favor man, because he is the bond and the knot of both the heavenly and the earthly. It is impossible for both of these not to have peace with him, provided that he has peace with himself, for he sanctions the peace and treaties of both within himself. But let us beware, I pray, that being established in such great dignity, we do not fail to understand it. Let us always hold this before the eyes of our mind as a certain, explored, and indoubtable truth: just as all things favor us while we keep the law given to us, so if we fall away through sin and the transgression of the law, we shall find all things adverse, hostile, and inimical. For it is reasonable that, just as we do injury not only to ourselves but to the universe which we embrace within us—and indeed to the omnipotent God, the author of the world—we should also experience all things in the world (and God first of all) as most powerful avengers and most heavy punishers of the injury received. From this let us estimate what penalties and punishments await those who transgress the divine law. These are they of whom the oracle said: <margin>The Oracle.</margin> "Demons who wander around the earth and around the sea are tirelessly tamed under the lash of God" <note>original: $\delta\alpha\acute{\iota}\mu o\nu\epsilon\varsigma\ o\iota\ \phi o\iota\tilde{\omega}\sigma\iota\ \pi\epsilon\rho\grave{\iota}\ \chi\theta\acute{o}\nu\alpha\ \kappa\alpha\grave{\iota}\ \pi\epsilon\rho\grave{\iota}\ \pi\acute{o}\nu\tau\omicron\nu\ \alpha\kappa\alpha\mu\alpha\tau\omicron\iota\ \delta\alpha\mu\nu\alpha\nu\tau\alpha\iota\ \acute{\upsilon}\pi\omicron\ \mu\acute{\alpha}\sigma\tau\iota\gamma\iota\ \theta\epsilon\omicron\tilde{\iota}\omicron$ — This is likely a quote from the "Chaldean Oracles" or a similar Neo-Pythagorean source describing the punishment of fallen spirits.</note>; that is, those who travel about the land and sea and are hostilely subdued under the whip of God. The heavens thunder against them, the earth pursues them, and the unshakable justice of the whole worldly Republic strikes them down. For they are guilty of violating the universe and wounding the divine majesty, whose image they have defiled with the most foul stain of iniquity. This is perhaps why <margin>Hence even among the poets when the boundaries of nature are extended.</margin> among the prophets, when something is commanded or forbidden by God, heaven and earth are summoned as witnesses: because the transgression of the precept also violates them, and having received a common insult, they themselves will take part in punishing the wicked while they serve God. It exceeds all madness to believe that someone placed in a city and decorated with the highest honors should be allowed to offend the prince and the entire republic (which has deserved the best from him) with impunity; rather, he should be immediately given over to the lictors and the executioner to be tortured and racked, or overwhelmed with stones by the consensus of the whole people. And there are executioners and lictors in this Republic of God: the wicked demons <margin>Wicked demons.</margin> assigned to the vilest ministry as punishment for their ancient crime. Hence that saying of Paul: <margin>Paul.</margin> "I have handed him over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh." <note>1 Corinthians 5:5.</note> Hence also the name of the "Avenging Demon" <margin>Orpheus.</margin> found in Orpheus, if by chance we trust our own writers less. But just as every creature hates and execrates the crimes of man, so his righteous life and conduct are pleasing and acceptable to all. For all things, which are so tightly wound and joined to him, cannot fail to participate in both his good and his evil. Hence that Gospel saying: "If a sinner repents, all the angels exult with joy." Hence the clear reason for that mystery which was hidden for ages: that our nature, corrupted in the first Adam and defiled from its status, should be restored through the cross of Christ. Indeed, for our sake, the Son of God both becomes man and is fixed to the cross. For it was fitting that He who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature in whom all things were founded, should be joined by an ineffable union to him who was made in the image of God—who is the bond of every creature, in whom all things are concluded. Nor, if all nature was to be endangered along with man, was its loss to be neglected or repaired through any other than Him through whom all nature had been instituted.

# SIXTH EXPOSITION ON THE KINSHIP OF THE WORLDS WITH ONE ANOTHER AND OF ALL THINGS.

## PREFACE TO THE SIXTH BOOK.

<margin>In creatures (how wonderful!) is the footprint of the Trinity.</margin>
<margin>Father. Son. Spirit. The root of all ordered charity.</margin>
GOD is a unity distinguished by a triad in such a way that He does not depart from the simplicity of His unity. There is a manifold footprint of this divine Trinity within His creation. We have brought forward here this one point, which to my knowledge has not yet been proposed by anyone: that the unity we see in creatures is discovered to be divided into three types. First, there is that unity in things by which each thing is one with itself, and is consistent and coherent within itself. Second is that unity by which one creature is joined to another, and by which, ultimately, all parts of the world are one single world. The third and most fundamental of all is that by which the entire universe is one with its Maker, just as an army is one with its leader. This threefold union is present in each thing through its own simple unity, derived from that One who is both the first One and simultaneously Three and One: from the Father, I say, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. For the power of the Father, producing all things, bestows His unity upon all; the wisdom of the Son, rightly disposing all things, unites and couples all things to one another; and the love of the Spirit, turning all things back toward God, joins the entire work of the Maker in a bond of charity. Furthermore, just as God is more intimate to us—and thus more one with us—than we are to ourselves, so each thing is more closely joined to itself than to other parts of the world. Thus, having been taught the order of universal charity, if we wish to follow the divine law inscribed on the tablets of nature, we shall love God Himself first above us and above all things, second ourselves, and third our neighbor. Our Prophet <note>Pico refers to Moses, the traditional author of Genesis, as "the Prophet."</note> spoke enough of that unity by which each thing is one with itself when he examined the nature of all things individually. Concerning that unity by which we are joined to God, it will be treated in the next section, where we shall discuss the height of happiness. What remains is that unity by which diverse parts are coupled together in a mutual pact, which we must discuss at present.

---

### CHAPTER ONE.

<margin>The diverse nature of things is constrained together.</margin>
Therefore, after we have seen the distinct natures of things arranged in separate "stations," so to speak, we should not believe that a single universe is made from all of these simply because individuals are contained by individuals according to the condition of their nature (as we showed above). The Prophet also wished to indicate in his context how many and what kind of ways there were by which the natures of things were coupled together. These call us not only to a curious intellectual understanding, but through this, they instruct and demonstrate by what path and reason we can be joined to those things that are better than ourselves. As I considered—before approaching the explanation of the words—how many ways there were, or could be imagined, by which certain things might obtain either an affinity or a bond with one another, and as I ran through all the dogmas of the philosophers in which I have labored since childhood, I found no more than fifteen genera. Afterward, approaching Moses, I saw these so clearly and appropriately indicated by him that I believe no one could be better instructed about them anywhere else.

### CHAPTER TWO.

<margin>By what modes something is said to be coupled to another.</margin>
Immediately, therefore, on the first day, I know not whether more briefly or more clearly, he encompasses five modes by which something can be joined to another. For that which is joined to another is either its essence, or a property of its essence, or it exists within it like a form in a subject, or it touches it either as a transformer touches that which is transformed, or as art touches the matter subject to it. Similarly, we read in Moses five things compared and connected to one another, as it were: heaven

<column-break/>

and earth; earth and emptiness; the abyss and darkness; the spirit of God and the waters; light and bodies. <margin>The five connections of Moses.</margin> The first mode of conjunction is designated for us by the earth "empty and void," <note>In the Latin Vulgate, *inanis et vacua*.</note> because earth—that is, matter—is by its nature empty unless it is filled from elsewhere by forms. The second is indicated by the darkness over the face of the abyss. For the abyss, by its nature, is neither light nor dark, yet darkness follows its nature unless approaching light puts it to flight; just as the formlessness and emptiness of matter is followed by the darkness of privation <term>privation: the philosophical concept of the absence of a quality that ought to be present</term>, until arriving forms expel them. The third is shown by light arising in bodies. For light is in them as a form is in a subject. <margin>Heaven, as it is connected to earth.</margin> The fourth is heaven and earth: for heaven does not inhere in the earth as a form or an accident exists in the thing it perfects, but is joined to it as an efficient cause to a patient <term>patient: in philosophy, the entity that receives the action of an agent or cause</term>, and as a transforming cause to the body being transformed. The final example is the spirit of the Lord, which is carried over the waters. For the Artisan—the wisdom of the Lord and the spiritual nature, entirely separated from commerce with the body—is understood to be joined to bodies in no other way than art, which is in the mind of the architect, is joined to cement, wood, and stones. Furthermore, consider this logic of consequence: that the earth, being empty of itself, has domestic darkness; then, it is joined most closely to light through light, to heaven through heaven, and to spiritual substance through heaven. But let us see how these things behave within us. The earth is the earthly body, empty and void of life and sense; over it is darkness, which is death, torpor, inefficacy, immobility, and lack of sensation. Light is the life that vegetates, excites, acts upon, moves, and renders it endowed with sense. Heaven is the soul, the source of that light; and the spirit of God is the intellect, the light of the divine countenance. Concerning these things, I shall say even more in this place than may be necessary.

### CHAPTER THREE.

LET us examine what Moses intends in the following passages, and we shall see ten other modes suggested by him, through which we may understand a mutual alliance between certain things. For besides those modes we have already mentioned, there are again these others which we shall enumerate: because something is either a part of another or its effect. Likewise, if it is a part, it is either an indivisible part of its whole—in the same way that the sun, moon, and stars are in the firmament—or a separable part, such as the parts of water separated from the integrity of their element, into which they have flowed together. If it is an effect, it either buds forth from an intrinsic <term>seminal reason</term><note>Latin: *seminaria ratione*. A Stoic and Neoplatonic concept referring to the underlying formative principles or "seeds" within nature that direct the growth and development of living things.</note> just as plants sprout from the earth—yet remain fixed to their parent and bound by natural ties and ligaments—or it is composed and fashioned from its own principles, like a mixture of elements. In this way, the bodies of animals are made from water and earth. Or, the effect has an extrinsic cause, which can be divided in three ways: into the efficient cause, the exemplar, and the end. We have examples of these three from Moses: when God creates and brings man into being (the efficient), He creates him in His own image as if after a model (the exemplar), and the beasts are subject to man and exist for man’s sake (the end).

### CHAPTER FOUR.

<margin>The primary cause influences more than the secondary.</margin>
WE HAVE spoken of the part and the effect, and by the same reasoning, of the whole and the cause, for these relationships correspond to one another. But we have not yet fulfilled all the categories of kinship. For regarding the cause, there remains that species of affinity in which a secondary cause obeys and is joined to a primary one; just as when God produces something and the heavens also produce it—the heavens act first because they are the proximate cause, yet they act only at God's command, because the primary cause has a greater influence than the secondary. Similarly, there is a secondary end hanging from and annexed to a principal end, which Moses wisely signifies by saying the stars were placed to shine in the heavens and illuminate the earth. For the well-being of lower things is not the primary end of the celestial bodies; rather, they intend this first: 
<margin>Homer.</margin>
that they should shine for themselves; then, finally, that they might illuminate us. For this reason, we read in Homer that both the Dawn and the Sun rise to bring light first to the immortals and then to mortals. Besides all these, there is also the kinship of man to man and lion to lion; and yet a lion is neither a part nor an effect of another lion if it was not sired by it. The Prophet <note>Pico often refers to Moses as "the Prophet."</note> signifies this when he gathers and unites the fish, birds, and beasts of the earth together. There is a final mode of affinity, which is that of a middle nature toward the extremes. For man is suited to man and animal to animal because they participate in the same definition of essence, whether specific or general. But a "middle" is not of the same essence as the extremes; rather, it is tempered in some way from them, so that it differs from both while communicating with both. This was indicated to us by Moses when he places the firmament in the middle, dividing the waters above the heavens from the waters that are under the heavens; here he sufficiently reveals what the nature of a "middle" is, just as we have abundantly declared in the preface of the first book and the second chapter of the fifth.

### CHAPTER FIVE.

<margin>James, Iamblichus. From whom the true orators also, like M. Cato, the Greeks,</margin>
WE ARE also warned from this what we must do so that we may be united to better natures, in which the whole force and summit of our happiness is placed. For the first day teaches us that light first arose for the waters only after the night was driven away, when the Spirit of the Lord hovered over them. From this is signified that saying of James: *Every best*

<column-break/>

*gift is from above, from the Father of lights.*<note>Original Latin quote: *Omne optimum donum desuper esse a patre luminum.* (James 1:17).</note> And not to mention only our own writers, 
<margin>and others, took the beginning of their speaking from prayers to the Gods, which even the poets follow.</margin>
Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonic philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who emphasized the importance of theurgy and prayer in reaching the divine.</note> confirms this so strongly that he wishes human nature to promise itself nothing even mediocre unless it is aided by a greater, that is, a divine power. If this is true, and proved not only by our own but by philosophers as well, surely our whole study ought to be in this: that having turned toward higher things—which happens through sacred religion, through mysteries, through vows, through hymns, prayers, and supplications—we should seek there the strength for our weakness. Hence the Platonic and Pythagorean disputations, having begun from sacred prayers, end in the same; Porphyry, Theodorus, and all the Academics confirm with one voice that nothing is more useful, or rather more necessary, for man. We read that the Brahmins of India and the Magi of the Persians never attempted anything unless a prayer had first been sent forth. I bring forward these testimonies of the nations so that those who have been persuaded by an evil demon to believe the pagans rather than the Church might at least learn from those whom they trust that it is a thing neither laughable, nor useless, nor unworthy of a philosopher to take up the task—and indeed a great and constant one—of sacred 
<margin>Oracles.</margin>
prayers, mysteries, vows, and hymns to be sung continually to God. If this practice helps and befits any kind of men, it is especially useful and decorous for those who have given themselves to the study of letters and to quiet contemplation. For nothing is more necessary for them than that they should purify with integrity of life those divine things upon which they repeatedly fix their mental eyes, and that they should more liberally illuminate from above the light sought through the "rod of prayer," always mindful of their own 
<margin>The Apostle.</margin>
weakness, saying with the Apostle: *Our sufficiency is from God.*<note>Original Latin: *sufficientia nostra ex Deo est.* (2 Corinthians 3:5).</note>

### CHAPTER SIX.

LET US examine again what the arrangement of the waters and the earth teaches us. Let us learn from the earth that we will not produce the fruit we are pregnant with unless we repress and drive back the force of the flowing matter that invades us, and unless we cast out from our dwellings the whirlpools and torrents of pleasures that rush upon us like waters. Let us learn from the waters that they were not considered fit for procreating fish until they were collected into the single integrity of their whole element. For neither will we be able to bring forth any offspring worthy of our divinity into the light if we are torn apart and distracted toward diverse things—not unless we are carried with all our gathered strength toward a single intention. 
<margin>A deeper mystery.</margin>
A deeper mystery is also contained here: just as it is the happiness of drops of water to reach the ocean, where the fullness of waters is, so it is our happiness that the portion of intellectual light within us may one day be joined to that first Intellect of all and the primary Mind, where the fullness and the entire universality of intelligence resides.

### CHAPTER SEVEN.

BUT THAT greatest thing of all which the doctrine of the firmament signifies to us is this: we see that the lower waters cannot be enriched by any benefit of the higher waters unless the heavens intercede, which are placed as a middle between them. So I say, let us propose that the bond of extremes can only occur through that nature which, since it is the middle of the extremes, embraces both within itself. Therefore, it unites those extremes conveniently because it first united them within itself through the property of its own nature. We are warned here 
<margin>That men cannot be joined to God except—</margin>
of that great sacrament, which to the gentiles is foolishness and to the Hebrews...

H E P T A P L V S
c iii
<meta>Catchword: Io. Pic. (Ioannes Picus/John Pico)</meta>

<margin>If through Christ, God and man.</margin>
<margin>John. Paul. Christ.</margin>
What is a stumbling block to us is the power and wisdom of God: that it is impossible for man to be joined to God except through Him who, having joined man to God in His own person, became a true mediator. Only He can so connect men to God that, just as in Him the Son of God took on humanity, so through Him men might become sons of God. If what we say is true—that extremes do not meet except through a middle point—then that which is truly called "middle" is that which has already united the extremes in itself. Surely, if that inexpressible arrangement occurred in Christ alone, so that "the Word was made flesh," then Christ alone is also the one through whom "flesh" can ascend to "the Word." Nor is there (as John rightly wrote) any other name under heaven by which men must be saved. Let those who claim to believe in Christ take diligent note of this: yet they believe that a common religion, or the one into which each person was born, is sufficient for achieving happiness. Let them believe not me, nor these arguments, but believe John, Paul, and Christ himself, who said: <note>John 14:6 and 10:7-9</note> *I am the way. I am the gate:* and *he who does not enter through me is a thief and a robber.*
