# SEVENTH EXPOSITION ON HAPPINESS
## WHICH IS ETERNAL LIFE. PREFACE
### TO THE SEVENTH BOOK.

<image-desc>Large decorative initial 'S' containing a landscape scene with buildings and foliage.</image-desc> IF WE HAVE completed our explanation of the order and nature of the levels of the entire world in the sixth exposition—as if in six days—it remains for us in this seventh treatise (as if it were the Sabbath of our commentary) to treat of the Sabbath of the world and the rest of creatures. We shall discuss the happiness of those things we established in the preceding books, or (to put it more accurately) we shall listen to Moses as he speaks as a true prophet of all things to come. <margin>Twofold happiness.</margin> Now, happiness is (as the Theologians declare) of two kinds: one which we can achieve through nature, and another through grace. The former they call natural, the latter supernatural. Regarding the first, that is, natural happiness, Moses has said enough, because once the nature of things is known, we also know their natural happiness. <margin>The illusion of some.</margin> It remains, therefore, for him to teach us about the second kind, showing himself to be a prophet rather than just a teacher. For when Moses wrote, grace did not yet exist, but it was to come in the future. But because I seem to see certain <term>dilettantes</term><note>Latin: *sciolos*, meaning those who possess superficial or "smattering" knowledge.</note>—or should I rather call them good-for-nothings and scoundrels—who call themselves philosophers when they are nothing of the sort, immediately laughing at both grace and supernatural happiness as if these were empty names and old wives' tales, I wished to make a very brief dispute with them on this matter as the preface to this seventh book. In this way, we may clearly prove that the opinion of the theologians stands as a distinct and established truth. <margin>Definition of happiness.</margin> <margin>What the "desirable good" is according to Alexander.</margin> I define happiness in this way: the return of each thing to its own <term>principle</term><note>Latin: *principium*. In this context, it refers to the origin or source from which a thing began.</note>. For happiness is the highest good; the highest good is that which all things desire; and that which all things desire is the very same thing that is the source of all things, as <term>Alexander of Aphrodisias</term><note>A famous Greek commentator on Aristotle (c. 200 AD).</note> testifies in his commentaries on first philosophy, and as the Greek interpreters of Aristotle’s *Ethics* attest. <margin>He defines happiness as the return of each thing to its source.</margin> Therefore, the end of all things is the same as the source of all things: the one God, almighty and blessed, the best of all things that can either exist or be imagined. Here are those two primary names for Him among the <term>Pythagoreans</term><note>Followers of the philosopher Pythagoras, who emphasized numbers and harmony as the basis of reality.</note>: namely, the "One" and the "Good." <margin>The Pythagorean name for God.</margin> For He is named "One" because He is the source of all, just as unity is the source of every number; and He is called "Good" because He is the end of all, the rest of all, and absolute happiness. <margin>Whence it is said God is Alpha and Omega as will be said below.</margin> We can already see, if we are a little more skillful, the reason for this twofold happiness. For happiness is the possession and attainment of this first Good. Created things can attain this Good in two ways: either in themselves, or in Him. For this Good is both exalted above all things, dwelling in the depths of its own divinity, and is also found diffused through all things, here more perfectly, there more imperfectly, according to the condition of the things that participate in it. <margin>Poets.</margin> Hence (as the poets write): *Jupiter is whatever you see, and all things are full of Jove.* <note>Originally from Lucan's *Pharsalia* (9.580) and Virgil's *Eclogues* (3.60).</note> Therefore, since every single nature has God within it in some way—because it has as much of God as it has of goodness (and all things God made are good)—it follows that when a nature possesses its own form, perfect in all its parts, it has attained itself and thus also attains God within itself. And if the attainment of God is happiness, as we have proven, then it is in some way happy in itself. This is "natural happiness," which different things have received as a greater or lesser lot according to the diversity of their natures. <margin>What natural happiness is.</margin> <margin>In what way fire participates in God.</margin> Fire is a thing lacking a soul, yet it participates in God in many ways. First, it "is," and everything that exists participates in God, who is Being itself. Likewise, because fire is a specific form and an <term>act</term><note>Latin: *actus*. In Aristotelian philosophy, "actuality" as opposed to "potentiality."</note>, it is similar to God, who is the first form and the first act. And while fire produces fire, it imitates divine fertility; while it keeps itself within the boundaries of its own sphere, it imitates justice; and while it serves us, it imitates beneficence according to the small measure of its nature. When fire performs these things, having attained its own perfection, it is happy to the extent that it is capable of happiness. Plants are happier, for they possess life in addition; animals are even happier, for they are also granted knowledge. Thus, as they have more perfection, they also have more...

<summary>Pico concludes his discussion on Christ as the unique mediator and begins the final book of the Heptaplus, defining happiness as the return of all created things to God, their source. He distinguishes between natural happiness, found in the perfection of a creature's own nature, and supernatural happiness, which comes through grace.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico's Seventh Exposition, focusing on the distinction between "natural happiness"—attainable through human reason and philosophy—and "supernatural happiness," which requires divine grace. He argues that while philosophers identify happiness with the perfection of human nature, true fulfillment involves a "circular" return to God, the source of all being.</meta>

JOHN PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA

<margin>The condition of man is the best among all mortals.</margin>
...they find divinity within themselves. Man is in the best condition of all mortals; just as he excels others in his nature, so he excels them in natural happiness, being endowed with intelligence and freedom of choice—the principal gifts most conducive to happiness. The angelic mind is supreme among creatures, both in the nobility of its substance and in the attainment of its end, of which it is the greatest participant because it is both joined and closest to it. But as we said above, through this [natural] happiness, neither plants, nor beasts, nor man, nor even an angel reaches God—who is the highest good—in God Himself, but rather they reach Him within themselves. Therefore, the degree of happiness varies according to the capacity of their natures. For this reason,

<margin>The imperfection of natural happiness.</margin>
the philosophers, speaking only of this [natural] happiness, placed the happiness of every thing in the best operation of its own nature. Regarding the angels, whom they call "minds" and "intellects," even if they admitted that their highest perfection was to understand God, they nevertheless established that the knowledge of God they possess is no different from the knowledge by which they know themselves; thus, they understand as much of God as the nature of God is represented within their own substance. Regarding man, although various thinkers have held various views, they all kept themselves within the narrow bounds of human faculty: either placing human happiness in the search for truth itself (as the Academics <note>The followers of the later Platonic Academy, known for their skepticism regarding the possibility of absolute knowledge.</note> did), or rather in its attainment through the study of philosophy, as Al-Farabi <note>original: "Alpharabius"; a major medieval Islamic philosopher who integrated Aristotelian and Platonic thought.</note> said. Averroes, Avicenna, Abubacher, Alexander, and the Platonists

<margin>Al-Farabi. Averroes. Avicenna. Abubacher. Alexander.</margin>
seemed to grant something more, fixing our reason in the "intellect in act" <note>term: <term>intellect in act</term> (intellectus qui actu est); in medieval philosophy, this refers to the human mind when it is actually thinking and unified with universal truths.</note> or in some higher intellect related to us, as if in its own goal. But even these thinkers do not lead man back to his own beginning nor to the highest good. I neither reject nor despise these disputes and opinions if they profess to speak only of natural happiness. For it is certain that through it, neither man nor angels can be raised higher than what these men say. This is most strongly proven by this reasoning: if something striving by its own strength cannot rise above itself (otherwise it would be stronger than itself), then surely nothing striving by itself toward happiness will be able to attain anything greater or more perfect than its own nature. But let the philosophers tell me: if

<margin>Man cannot be joined to God by his own virtues. Theologians.</margin>
this is the only happiness in things, why do they themselves admit that among animals, only man is born for happiness? For why should other things besides man reach their own ends? We could say that the happiness of others is less than that of man, but how shall we defend the idea that they have none at all? Indeed, since all things below man never stray from the end established by nature, while man almost always goes astray, the human condition will seem the most unhappy of all unless he can boast of some other privilege. Let us therefore listen to the holy theologians reminding us of our dignity, and let us not, I pray, be cruel to our own souls and ungrateful toward God the Creator by rejecting the divine goods offered to us so freely by the most liberal Father. We said above that the summit of happiness is in the attainment of God, who is the highest good and the beginning of all things. However, this can happen in two ways: either we reach God in the creatures in which God shares Himself, or we reach God in God Himself. We have also shown, and will show again, that created things cannot reach this latter [supernatural] state by their own powers, but only the former. That [natural] state, if we observe closely, is a shadow of happiness rather than true happiness, just as the creature in which you reach God is not the highest goodness, but a thin shadow of the highest goodness—that is, the divine. Add to this that through that [natural] happiness, things are restored to themselves rather than to God; they have not achieved a return to their beginning, but only ensured they do not depart from themselves. But true and perfected happiness leads us back and draws us toward beholding the face of God, which is "all good" (as He Himself said), and toward a perfect union with that Beginning from which we emanated. Toward this,

<margin>Who are capable of supernatural happiness and in what way.</margin>
angels can indeed be lifted up, but they cannot climb to it [on their own]. For this reason, Lucifer sinned, saying: *I will ascend into heaven.* <note>Isaiah 14:13</note> Man cannot go toward this on his own, but he can be drawn. Hence Christ said of himself, who is happiness itself: *No one comes to me unless my Father has drawn him.* <note>John 6:44</note> Beasts and things below man can neither go nor be drawn toward it. Therefore, only man and the angel were made for that happiness which is true happiness. Vapor can climb on high, but only if attracted by a ray of the sun; a stone and every heavy substance can neither admit the ray throughout nor be lifted into the heights by it. This ray, this divine power, this influx, we call grace, because it makes both man and angel "gracious" [pleasing] to God. The philosophers have a clear example of this doctrine in physical bodies. For some bodies are moved in a straight line, others in a circle. Linear motion, by which elements are carried to their own proper places, represents the happiness through which things are stabilized in the perfection of their own nature. Circular motion, by which a body is revolved back to the same point from which it departed, is the most expressive image of true happiness, through which the creature returns to the same beginning from which it had proceeded. But see how everything fits on both sides. Only immortal and incorruptible bodies move in a circle. Only an immortal and eternal substance returns to God. To complete their motions, the elements need no other power than that implanted in them from birth, either the impulse of weight or lightness; in the same way, individual things are carried toward natural happiness by their own impulse and power. But celestial bodies, even if they are fit...

<summary>Pico distinguishes between "natural happiness," which is the perfection of one's own nature as described by ancient and Islamic philosophers, and "supernatural happiness," which is a circular return to God made possible only through Divine Grace. He uses the analogy of physics—linear versus circular motion—to illustrate how humans and angels are uniquely capable of being "drawn" back to their Creator.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico's argument that while natural bodies and human souls have an inherent capacity for motion and perfection, they cannot reach their ultimate end—God—without an external "Mover" or divine grace. He transitions from a philosophical defense of this need for grace to a biblical commentary on the early chapters of Genesis.</meta>

HEPTAPLVS.

<margin>The sum of true happiness. O how wisely, truly, clearly, and most Christianly spoken. Christ. Paul. The fall of the demon. The fate of infants who depart this life not yet initiated <note>The "uninitiated" refers to those not yet baptized into the Christian faith.</note>. Against those who think heresy arises from the fountains of philosophy.</margin>

*...are suited to circular motion, yet they are not sufficient in themselves to complete this movement; rather, they require a divine Mover to turn and revolve them. Indeed, those bodies are so adapted for perpetual circulation that they do not perform it themselves, but rather receive it. It is no different for us and for the angels. For we are such by nature that we cannot revolve and turn ourselves back, but we can be revolved by the moving power of grace and turned back toward God. Hence it is said, "those who are led by the spirit of God, these are the sons of God" <note>original: "qui aguntur spiritu dei hi filii dei sunt"; Romans 8:14</note>. He said "those who are led," not "those who lead." In this we differ from the heavens: the heavens are moved by the necessity of nature, while we are moved according to our freedom. For the moving spirit knocks constantly at your soul. If you do not listen, you are left to yourself, to your own sluggishness and your own misery and unhappiness. But if you admit the spirit, immediately full of God, you are carried back through the circle of religion to the Father and the Lord; you shall possess life in Him forever, in whom you were already life even before you were made. This is true happiness: that we be one spirit with God, that we possess God within God and not within ourselves, knowing "even as we are known" <note>original: "sicut & cogniti sumus"; 1 Corinthians 13:12</note>. For He did not know us through us, but through Himself. So too shall we know Him through Him, and not through ourselves. This is the whole reward, this is eternal life, this is the wisdom which the wise of this world did not know: that from all the imperfection of multiplicity we may be reduced into unity through an indissoluble bond with Him who is Unity itself. For this happiness Christ prayed to the Father in this way: "Father, grant that just as you and I are one, so these also may be one with us" <note>original: "Pater fac quemadmodum ego & tu unum sumus, ita & hi nobiscum unum sint"; referencing John 17:21</note>. This is what Paul hoped for when he said, "I shall know not in part, but as He is"; and since he hoped for this, did he not rightly say, "who shall separate me from the love of Christ?" <note>original: "quis me separabit a caritate Christi?"; Romans 8:35</note> and he desired "to be dissolved, that he might be one with Christ" <note>original: "cupiebat dissolui, ut cum Christo fieret unum"; Philippians 1:23</note>. From this state the demon fell, because he wished to ascend to it by his own power rather than be carried to it, and therefore he lost that which he would have possessed had he remained. From this root it is known what is the fate of infants who depart not yet initiated <note>baptized</note>: namely, they remain within themselves, neither stripped of their own natural goods nor enriched by divine ones. We, however, must fall into one side or the other: either the greatest misery or the greatest happiness. For he who is the cause of his own failure to receive the Mover not only makes himself immune to grace, but also vitiates <note>corrupts or spoils</note> his nature. It belongs to the integrity of nature to seek the recognized spirit, not to refuse it; and beyond doubt, a nature cannot be right which either rejects or despises the hope of a greater proposed good. Therefore, after Christ has been made known, if any do not "put on Christ," they are deprived not only of the first happiness <note>supernatural grace</note> but also of the second, which is their natural right; for to refuse grace can only belong to a corrupted and weakened nature. Furthermore, just as we who live under the Gospel receive Christ—the power and wisdom of God—into ourselves because we love and retain what has now been given to the human race, so also the fathers under the Old Law received Him, since they both believed in His future coming without doubt, hoped for it eagerly, and desired it ardently. But just as they received Him not as one already present but as one to come, so they did not experience the fruit of the indwelling spirit as present until after He arrived. After the ineffable sacrifice was performed on the altar of the cross, Christ descended to them, and being revolved by Him as their Mover in the moment of a whirlwind, they were carried to liberty and raised to the level of supreme happiness. Religion promotes, directs, and impels us toward this happiness, just as we use philosophy as a guide toward natural happiness. If nature is the first step toward grace, then surely philosophy is the beginning of religion; nor is there any philosophy that moves a man away from religion. Rightly, therefore, after we have philosophized about nature with Moses for six days, we shall speak on the seventh day about supernatural happiness, devoting ourselves to divine things.*

### CHAPTER ONE.

<margin>The angelic and human nature is capable of celestial happiness.</margin>

There is a twofold nature (as we have shown) capable of this supreme happiness: the angelic and the human. The former is called "heaven," the latter "earth," because angels inhabit heaven and we inhabit the earth. Of heaven there is nothing more to say, for Moses is about to write a law not for angels, but for men. Descending then to men, he says: *The earth was empty and void, and darkness was over the face of the abyss.* God does not create emptiness; He does not create darkness. But "the earth," he says, "was empty and darkness was." He does not say these were created, but that they existed. Why this was said will be clear once we understand what this emptiness and this darkness are. Human nature—which is called "earth" in comparison to the angels—right from the beginning, because it sinned immediately, was "empty and void" of original justice <term>originalis iustitia: the state of grace and harmony before the Fall</term>, and its "face," that is, its reason, was covered by the darkness of sin. God did not make these things; rather, they were made by the malice of man, who willfully deprived himself of those goods with which God

<column-break/>

had enriched him. Thus the state of corrupted nature is described by the prophet; he will demonstrate in what follows how it was thereafter restored to its former dignity and prepared for the highest happiness—first through Abraham, then through Moses, then through the prophets, and finally through His only-begotten Son. Truly, even at the time when the waters were covered with darkness—infected, that is, by the ancient filth of the mark of original sin—nonetheless "the spirit of the Lord cherished them." This is to be understood in two ways: first, that men were ruled by "the light of the divine countenance which is signed upon us" <note>referencing Psalm 4:6</note>, that is, by the light of natural intelligence; and second, that the human race was not destitute of the care of divine providence. Rather, the spirit of the Lord "cherished the waters"—that spirit which (as the Apostle says) "intercedes for us with unutterable groanings" <note>Romans 8:26</note>. Even then, that spirit was constantly considering how to purge those waters from the poisons with which the ancient serpent had infected them. And behold, He immediately commands the light to arise, and light was made: namely, that most wise Abraham, the first founder of the true religion. The first who...

OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA

...and would fulfill the law of nature, and meditate on the divine law: the first who would persuade men to the worship of the one God against idols and the nations. The first who attempted both to drive away the darkness of error and to declare war against the evil demons who are called "princes of darkness": wherefore he was deservedly named "light." Because the disciples of the Lord all did this, they were all called "the light of the world" by the Lord. This is the first light that shone upon the world, and distinguished between the religion of demons and the true God, as if between light and darkness.

## CHAPTER TWO

<margin>The Mosaic Law.</margin>
<margin>The song of David.</margin>
<margin>For the Jews first uncovered astronomical reasons, as Diodorus says. Jeremiah.</margin>
Following this was the Law, which is deservedly called the "firmament" right at its beginning, specifically announcing to us the works of God’s hands (as David sang: *and the firmament announces the works of his hands* <note>Psalm 19:1</note>). Therefore, the Law given through the angel to Moses was strengthened by the word of God; it distinguished the nations from the Israelites even more than the previous light did—that is, it separated those within piety from those without, just as the waters above the heavens were separated from the waters beneath the heaven. The Jews are called "waters above the heavens" because they alone (as Jeremiah says) do not fear the signs of heaven: which the nations fear, acknowledging not the stars or the sky, but the author and lord of the stars and heaven, whom they both recognize and worship. The nations, by the opposite reasoning, are "waters beneath the heaven" because they adore and worship both the demons who inhabit the misty air (the region just above the waters) and make the visible heaven, stars, and planets their gods and lords.

## CHAPTER THREE

It was to happen, however, that unless some greater power and mercy of God stood in the way, the waters which are beneath the heaven—that is, those serving idols—would invade and occupy the whole earth. This was how the infection of the whole world from the "first stain" <note>The original sin of Adam.</note> and the empire of Satan the avenger demanded his right over us, as we were guilty of ancient sin and nearly subject to such servitude. But the always beneficent and saving providence of God willed that one part of the earth, even if small, should remain free from the injury of the waters, as far as the laws of justice allowed. <margin>The preservation of Judea was promised to Abraham and the rest.</margin> This is called Judea, the land of promise, which was promised by God to Abraham and his posterity. All the prophets agree with this exposition of ours; in their writings, the onslaught of the nations against the Israelites is so often compared to the incursions of waters and the sea. Hence that phrase: *the rivers have lifted up their voice, and the wonderful surges of the sea* <note>Psalm 93:3-4</note>; and that other: *their waters sounded and were troubled* and *we will not fear while the earth is troubled, and the mountains are transferred into the heart of the sea* <note>Psalm 46:2-3</note>. And indeed, the nations surrounded Judea, which was enclosed within the boundaries of a small region, no differently than the ocean now surrounds this modest portion of the earth where we live. <margin>In Christian literature, the nations are designated by "waters."</margin> <margin>The Lord Jesus. Why water is mixed with wine in the mysteries.</margin> But in many places in Christian literature, the nations are most evidently designated by "waters." For it is written: *the waters which you saw are the nations* <note>Revelation 17:15</note>; and when the Lord Jesus made wine from water, which had run out in the Pharisee’s house, he figuratively signified (as our writers say) that the waters—that is, the nations—were to be called to that faith which would later fail among the Jews, where it had previously resided. Likewise, they hand down in the mysteries <note>The "mysteries" refers to the ritual of the Eucharist or Mass.</note> that water is mixed with wine for this reason: so that the waters—that is, the nations—may drink in and consume the blood of Christ through the faith of the cross. That part, therefore, was claimed from the yoke of the waters by God’s providence, so that if the rest of the earth, overwhelmed by the waves of spiritual wickedness, were to be useless and deserted, and not 

<column-break/>

fit for the fruits of true religion, this part at least would be. Having received the light brought forth on the first day, and helped toward abundance by the "dew of heaven" that was established—that is, the doctrine of the Law—it would meanwhile germinate like herbs, plants, and trees (representing judgments, ceremonies, and good morals) until the fullness of time had come. Then, it would germinate even that which Isaiah <margin>Isaiah.</margin> desired: the Savior most blessed.

## CHAPTER FOUR

<margin>The Messiah.</margin>
<margin>The number four is the fullness of numbers.</margin>
And behold, now is the fullness of time. For if the number four is the fullness of numbers, will not the fourth day be the fullness of days? See, therefore, what the fourth day brings us. On the second day, the heaven was made a firmament—that is, the Law—but it was without the sun, moon, and stars; it was capable of future light, but still dark and not yet illustrated by any notable brilliance. The fourth day arrives: on which the sun, lord of the firmament—that is, Christ, Lord of the Law—and the lunar Church, the partner and bride of Christ, and the apostolic teachers (who have instructed many unto justice) might shine in the firmament like stars for perpetual eternities, calling the world to eternal life. The sun does not dissolve the firmament but perfects it; and Christ did not come to dissolve the Law, but to fulfill it. <margin>Abraham most pious.</margin> <margin>Jesus Christ, the brightness of the Father's substance.</margin> Abraham, most pious, saw the light of the first day and saw the fourth day—which is the day of Christ—and rejoiced. He saw the ray of his light—that is, of true religion, which he had brought into the world—to be spread most widely throughout the whole world by the "sun of justice," through the "true light" illuminating all men. He saw Jesus Christ, the *brightness of the Father’s substance* <note>original: "splendorem paternae substantiae"; Hebrews 1:3</note>, shining upon those who sat in darkness and the shadow of death, and he saw the prince of darkness, the prince of this world, cast out and exterminated from the minds of men. These things he saw and exulted; he saw the fourth day and was glad. This is the day which the Lord has made; in which the Lord becomes man, in which God dwelt among us; let us exult and be glad in it. But I ask you to attend a little more diligently, Christian brothers, to how true and solid the reasoning of our exposition is. From this, the most powerful weapons will be supplied to you against the "stony heart of the Hebrews," taken from their own armories. We shall prove this first from the testimonies of the Jews: that the coming of Christ is signified to us through the works of the fourth day. Second, we will show that the Messiah is represented to us by nothing more fittingly than by the sun, and we will conclude most evidently from the chronology of the times that Christ is not yet to come in the future, but that Jesus of Nazareth, son of the Virgin, was the promised Messiah of the Hebrews. <margin>The dogma of the Hebrews.</margin> <margin>Moses Gerundinensis, a Hebrew doctor.</margin> <margin>Saint Jerome.</margin> <margin>A day of God is a thousand years.</margin> <margin>At what time Jesus appeared according to the Hebrew annals.</margin> It is among the decrees of the ancient Hebrew discipline that the six days of Genesis designate six thousand years of the world: so that those things which were to happen in the first millennium of the world would occur in the first day, the works of the second in the second, and so on, always preserving the same order of succession. Moses Gerundinensis <note>Better known as Nahmanides (1194–1270), a prominent medieval Jewish scholar and mystic.</note>, a theologian of the highest celebrity among the Hebrews, also attests to this opinion among the more recent writers. Saint Jerome also mentions it in his exposition of that psalm inscribed to Moses <note>Psalm 90:4: "For a thousand years in your sight are like a day that has just gone by."</note>; and this opinion seems to rest chiefly on the foundation that a thousand years are as a day. If this doctrine is true, the fourth day is a prophecy of those things which were to happen in the fourth millennium of the world. Come now, let us show, according to the Hebrew annals and the calculation of years which they themselves approve, that Jesus appeared in the fourth millennium of the world. They calculate 1,556 years from Adam to the flood...

# HEPTAPLVS BOOK II

...from the flood to Abraham, two hundred and ninety-two years; and so from Adam to Abraham, one thousand eight hundred and forty-eight years are gathered. Furthermore, from the birth of Isaac to the ruin of the second temple, which was after the death of Christ, they number approximately one thousand six hundred and sixty years (for I am not cutting to the quick <note>original: "neque... reſeco ad viuum" - a metaphor meaning he is using round numbers rather than precise calculations</note>). For they calculate four hundred and thirty years from Isaac to the departure from Egypt; from the departure to the temple that Solomon built, almost as many; from Solomon to the desolation of the temple by the Babylonians, four hundred and ten years; and from the restoration of the temple under Ezra to this captivity under Titus, four hundred and twenty years. Therefore, if you collect all these together, you will compute three thousand five hundred and eight years from the beginning of the world to Christ, according to the reckoning of the Hebrews themselves. Thus, Christ arrived in the very middle of the fourth millennium, and within that same millennium—as if within the boundaries of the fourth day—the light of the moon (that is, the Church) shone upon the whole world. An innumerable multitude of martyrs, apostles, and teachers, who all became famous within five hundred years after Christ’s death, illuminated both the obscurity of the "firmament" (that is, the Law) and the shadows of our night.

But the Hebrews will say: "Suppose Jesus did arrive during these times. You still do not have proof that Jesus was the Christ unless you show that it was believed by our ancestors that the Christ would come during those times." This is a fair point, and they demand what is just; we can easily provide what they rightly require. For there are manifest 
<margin>The oracles of Elijah.</margin>
and publicly known oracles of Elijah circulating among them, which, without any figure or veil, professedly state that the Messiah would come in the fourth millennium of the world. Lest these seem to be either fabricated by me or interpreted according to my whim, I will bring 
<margin>The Talmudists.</margin>
the testimony of the Talmudists themselves, with whom we have this controversy. They make mention of these oracles and, compelled by the truth itself, they confess that the time predicted by Elijah for the coming of the Messiah has already passed. These words 
<margin>In which part of the "Avodah Zarah" this is said.</margin>
are found in the section titled *Avodah Zarah* <note>original: "Anodazara" - a tractate of the Talmud concerning "Strange Worship" or idolatry</note> in the chapter *Libne*: "The school of Elijah taught: The world is to exist for six thousand years. Two thousand years of void; two thousand years of Torah; and two thousand years of the days of the Messiah. But because of our sins, which are many, there have passed of them what have passed." <note>Pico provides a Latin transliteration of the Hebrew text here: "Sene alaphim tohu..."</note> These are their words.

Come now, with these very words placed before everyone's eyes—since I can bring nothing counterfeit or arbitrary—let us discuss and examine the words of the oracle, and we shall immediately achieve our purpose. "The world," it says, "is six thousand years," which we might interpret to mean that after a circuit of six thousand years (as many of our own people have also believed), the consummation of the world will occur as a sort of Sabbath. Or if (as is more true) no one knows that day, let us take it in this sense: that there is no prophecy in the Law concerning any further time. But this does not pertain to the question at hand. Let us look at what follows: "Two thousand void, two thousand Law, then the Messiah." 
<margin>Hebrew interpreters.</margin>
He calls "void" (as all Hebrew interpreters say) the time before any law was given by God to men. But I see the Jew mocking and saying: "If there are two thousand years before the Law and two thousand of the Law, then the Messiah is to come not on the fourth day (that is, while the fourth millennium is passing), but rather on the fifth day, because it is after the fourth millennium." But the response is easy, supplied by the bold truth. For when it is said by Elijah "Two thousand void, two thousand Law," it should not be understood as if 

<column-break/>

the world was to be without law for a full span of two thousand years, and similarly that the Law was to endure for exactly two thousand years. Rather, it means that the time of the law of nature would reach into the second millennium, and the time of the Mosaic Law would reach into the fourth. But even before the second millennium is finished, there is the Law; and before the fourth passes away, there shall be the Messiah. I do not fashion or dream up this exposition for myself; 
<margin>Elijah. The Talmudists.</margin>
Elijah himself teaches it to me, and the Talmudists themselves teach it. This will soon be manifest to you, Jewish viper (unless you block your ears). 

Elijah says: "Two thousand void and two thousand Law." Let us see in what sense his statement about the "void" was true, and from that let us learn the method 
<margin>When the beginning of the Law should be reckoned.</margin>
for explaining what is said about the Law. We must take the beginning of the Law either from Moses or from Abraham. It cannot be taken from Moses, because there would have been a "void" of more than two thousand three hundred years, or thereabouts. For there were nearly that many years from Adam to Moses. Therefore, the beginning of the Law must be taken from Abraham, to whom the covenant of circumcision was given—the root and foundation of the whole ancient Law. However, from Adam to Abraham, if they consult their own histories, they find that a full space of two thousand years had not passed, but only one thousand eight hundred and forty-eight. Thus, it happened that the fullness of the Law succeeded the "void" not *after* the second millennium, but *within* its boundaries. 

By the same reasoning, the evangelical fullness ought to have succeeded the "void" of the Law not *after* the fourth millennium, but while the fourth was still passing. If they shamelessly and stubbornly persist in denying this, let them hear their own 
<margin>The Talmudists.</margin>
Talmudists, who most strongly support our view. For they themselves confess that even at the time they were writing, the time predicted by Elijah for the coming of the Messiah had already passed, and they attribute this to their own sins. If the words of Elijah were understood to mean that Christ was to come *after* the fourth millennium and not *within* the limits of that same fourth, the Talmudists could not and would not have said that the time of the Messiah promised by the prophets had already passed. For at the time when the Talmudic doctrine which we have cited was written, four thousand years had not yet passed since the beginning of the world. 

As we showed above, Jesus appeared after three thousand five hundred and eight years from the beginning of the world, according to the Hebrews. Moreover (as they themselves hand down), 
<margin>The Jerusalem Talmud. The Babylonian Talmud.</margin>
the Jerusalem Talmud was written in the three-hundredth year after Christ’s death, and the Babylonian Talmud a hundred years after the Jerusalem one. Therefore, both were composed within the boundaries of the fourth millennium, and yet they both confess and lament that the time spoken of by Elijah for the coming of Christ had already passed. 

Where will they turn now, or what hiding places will they seek, to utterly flee or ignore this sun of ours, which shines through the whole universe even against their will? The Talmudists confess (even if they do not believe the ancients) that the times predicted by the prophets for the coming of Christ have passed. They confess that the prophets believed he would come during those times in which we maintain Jesus arrived. Nor are their own teachers entirely wrong when they say the Messiah did not come because of their sins. For he did not come *to them*, who did not recognize him. Nor is he a Messiah—that is, a redeemer, an avenger of the worst captivity, a beneficent king, and the restorer of the land of promise (which is the heavenly Jerusalem)—except for those who have confessed him as Messiah. But if he came unto his own and his own received him not, those who were his own are his own no longer; instead, they come from the East and the West to rest in the bosom of Abraham, while the children of the kingdom are cast into the outer darkness. From this, their troublesome question is resolved: the Messiah was meant to be the salvation of the Hebrews, yet Christ brought them ruin and destruction...

->IOANNES PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA<-

<margin>What the advent of Christ brought to the human race.</margin>
Indeed, those are not truly Hebrews who not only fail to follow or worship the King and Lord promised to the Hebrews from the lineage of David, but who—with every kind of injury and insult—nail him to a cross as if he were a thief, a committer of sacrilege, or a profane man. If they were children of Abraham, they would abide by the institutions of Abraham; they would joyfully welcome the one whose "day" (that is, this fourth day <note>Pico identifies the "fourth day" of creation with the fourth millennium of world history, the era in which he believes Christ was born.</note>) Abraham foresaw and rejoiced in. The Messiah brought peace to men, but not to all. For the angels did not simply say, "and on earth peace to men," but added "to men of good will." <note>original: "hominibus bonæ voluntatis" — a reference to the Latin Vulgate translation of Luke 2:14.</note> Certainly, the same sun that illuminates clear eyes blinds and obscures those that are sick and weak. It is by right reason that the same thing which is healthful to the good is harmful to the wicked; and he who, being powerful and not ungrateful, blesses his friends, likewise strikes down and scatters his enemies with lightning. If things had gone poorly for the Jews because they *accepted* Christ, then he would not have been the Christ. But if things went poorly for them because they *crucified* him, then he was certainly the Christ: he who, even when nailed to the cross and appearing most defeated, triumphed over his conquerors with such slaughter and calamity for them. Why then, O blind ones, do you wait for the sun? The sun is present and shines, but it shines in the darkness, and your darkness does not comprehend it. The fourth day has passed, in which the sun rose. He did not dissolve the law but perfected it, just as the sun does not destroy the firmament but adorns, completes, and illustrates it. We have proved from the order of the fourth day and the time of his advent that the things said here must be understood as referring to Christ.

<margin>The sun as an image of Christ.</margin>
Let us prove the same from the similarity of the figure, because we can imagine Christ through no other thing more fittingly than through the sun. For "he placed his tabernacle in the sun," <note>A reference to Psalm 19:4.</note> and he came forth from the tribe of Judah, whose sign is the lion, a solar animal. And since 

<margin>Plato in the Republic.</margin>
Plato, in the *Republic*, calls the sun the visible son of God, why should we not understand ourselves to be the image of the invisible Son? If he is the "true light" illuminating every mind, he has his most expressive likeness in this sun, which is the imaginary light illuminating every body.

But why do we seek other proofs? Let us ask the sun itself, which, by failing through the opposition of the moon while Christ was suffering, clearly showed us the consensus of its own nature with his. <note>Pico refers to the solar eclipse reported during the Crucifixion.</note>

<margin>The day of the sun is the Lord's day.</margin>
Thus, by the best right—not to mention a more profound cause—we have called the day which the mathematicians call "Sunday" (the day of the sun) the "Lord’s Day," and we have devoted it entirely to his worship. By this we show there is no reason to worship the physical sun anymore (as the heathens once did) as if it were the king and lord of heaven, now that the invisible Sun—co-eternal and co-equal with the Father, through whom both heaven and earth were established—has illuminated men sitting in the shadow of death.

### CHAPTER FIVE.

BUT now let us examine whether the works of the days that follow correspond to those things which are known to have happened after the advent of Christ. Thus, we may finally receive this exposition of ours as true and stable when we recognize that all things testify to it and harmonize with it from every side.

<margin>The Gentiles are figured by the waters, the Israelites by the earth.</margin>
Let us see what happens after the fourth day. The waters bring forth fish and birds; the earth brings forth cattle and beasts of burden. Let us recall to mind what we said above was signified by the waters: those located under the heavens and gathered into one place; and likewise by the earth: that which was made free from their flood. We said that the Gentiles were figured by the waters and the Israelites by the earth, which we proved both by many testimonies of the prophets and by reasons of similarity. We saw, however, that before the rising of the sun, the sterile waters produced nothing that was good. The earth, 

<column-break/>

however, was indeed fertile, but only of meager fruit—namely, pot-herbs and grasses. After the sun, the waters bring forth two kinds of living creatures, birds and fish, with even greater fecundity than the earth. The earth, no longer content with trees and shrubs, also produces great cattle and beasts of burden.

<margin>Simeon.</margin>
Do you not see, even if I remain silent, the fulfillment of the word of the good Simeon: that our Sun would be "a light for the revelation of the Gentiles and the glory of your people Israel"? <note>Quoting the Nunc Dimittis, Luke 2:32.</note> Do we not have placed before our eyes—if we interpret it in no other way—the calling of the Gentiles and the transformation of the earthly Jerusalem and the shadowy synagogue into the true Church and the perpetual and heavenly city of God?

<margin>Indeed, with the sun intervening.</margin>
Before the rising of the sun, the waters produce nothing. The earth produces something, but it is thin and meager. This is because before the advent of Christ, there was no sign of life, no fruit of true religion among the Gentiles. Among the Israelites, there was indeed some hope of life; they knew the way of light in part and worshipped the true religion, but it was incipient and imperfect until he came who is "the way, the truth, and the life." 

<margin>Vegetative, sensitive, and rational things are generated, as Aristotle says.</margin>
And unless we recur to this mystery, let someone offer me a reason why Moses divided the adornment and offspring of the earth in such a way that it brought forth some things before the sun and others after the sun. Why also do the waters produce nothing before the sun, while the earth produces something? Why are two kinds of animals produced from the waters, and only one kind from the earth? Why is the bird, an animal of the air, ascribed to the waters? 

<margin>Abraham, most far-seeing.</margin>
For (to deal with the first point) it is not sufficient to say, as some have, that herbs and plants were brought forth from the earth before the creation of the sun so that they would not seem to be created by its power. For by that same reasoning, it would be much more necessary for the fish, the birds, and all the adornment of the elements to be made before the sun, lest they be believed to have been made by its power. 

<margin>Jesus Christ, more radiant than the aforementioned shadows.</margin>
Moses would therefore have left a suspicion: even if the light of the sun had not been necessary to produce plants (as they are more imperfect), it might have been necessary to produce animals, which are more perfect. For it follows that if the more perfect things had come into the light without the sun's help, those things which are less perfect could also have been made without it. 

<margin>Moses recounted everything skillfully.</margin>
However, the reasoning is not correctly applied: if the ignoble things (such as plants, the most despicable kind of living things) were made without the sun, it does not follow that the entire nature of animals could be produced without its work intervening. Therefore, the intention of the author is more truly investigated from the source we have stated. 

<margin>The Jews saw Moses concerning one and the other.</margin>
Similarly, if someone says the animals related to the waters are those that live in the waters, he will see that one kind should rather be referred to them, and two kinds to the earth, because the home of birds is the earth rather than the water. Without any controversy, if we consider the nature of the animal, a bird is either a terrestrial or an aerial animal; it is in no way aquatic. 

<margin>The teaching of the Hebrews.</margin>
But hear the highest reasons of all, drawing us even against our will to the mysteries of Christ and the Church. 

<margin>The highest reasons. Aristotle.</margin>
And certainly, if all things (as Aristotle says) harmonize with the truth, then all things must harmonize most of all with Christ, who is Truth itself. Not without cause and not for nothing did he say so often to the Hebrews, "Search the scriptures, for they are the ones that bear witness of me," and asserted that so many things were predicted concerning him. Indeed, all things in the Law, the Psalms, and the Prophets. 

<margin>Moses was given to the nation with divine gifts.</margin>
But we are often blind in the face of such great light, and we cannot consider the wonders of his law unless he reveals them to our eyes. 

<margin>The Lord’s day, the sent years.</margin>
Let us come, with him bringing us aid, to the revelation of the mysteries and figures. 

<margin>At what time the witness shall appear according to the annals of the Hebrews.</margin>
Two animals are produced from the waters, and one from the earth, because there was a greater fullness of believers from the Gentiles than from the Jews. The earth, though it produces fewer kinds, produces animals more perfect than those the waters produce: namely, cattle and four-footed beasts.

...all encompassing knowledge. For even if more from the Gentiles believed than from the Hebrews, the perfection nevertheless remains with those of the Hebrews, from whom came the apostles, the founders of the entire religion. Likewise, two different kinds and a double nature—of birds and fish—were brought forth from the water, but only one kind from the earth. This is because some from the Gentiles are transferred to Christ from the service of demons, while others are transferred from the law of nature. Every Hebrew is simply a Hebrew, because it was not permitted for him to live within the boundaries of nature; to him was given the peculiar law of God, which was not common to the other nations. For "He has not done so for every nation, and His judgments He has not revealed to them." <note>original: "non fecit taliter omni nationi & iudicia sua non manifestauit eis" — A quote from Psalm 147:20.</note> Therefore, the fish signify to us those who came to us from the cult of demons—not only because the waters (as we showed above) represent the impiety of the nations, but because it is often attested in the sacred scriptures that wicked demons are signified by these animals that live in the waters. 
<margin>Jonathan the Chaldean.</margin> 
Jonathan the Chaldean <note>referring to the Targum Jonathan, an ancient Aramaic translation and commentary on the Hebrew Bible.</note> signifies by the birds those who have been transferred from the institutions of nature to grace. The clear reason for this comes from those things we wrote abundantly in the preface of this book concerning natural and supernatural happiness. For we showed both that the heaven is the most expressive image of supernatural happiness, and that natural happiness is a kind of secondary and imaginary thing rather than true happiness. Therefore, those who attain this by using the laws of nature are most fittingly denoted by birds, the inhabitants not of the first and true heaven, but of the air—which by a certain secondary and imaginary reasoning also claims for itself the name of "heaven." Hence they are so frequently called "birds of heaven" and "fowls of heaven" in the divine scriptures. Notice, however, that it was done with profound counsel that the birds are referred to the water rather than the air. This is because those who lived according to nature were nonetheless counted among the "people of the nations" <note>the Gentiles</note>. Indeed, they both called themselves nations and lived among the nations—such as, perhaps, Socrates and most of the philosophers. For this reason, both kinds were referred to the waters in common. But it is easy to show how well this exposition agrees with the teachings of the Gospels and the Apostles.
<margin>
Paul.
The Gospel.
Christ.
</margin>
Since the apostles converted from the Hebrews were figured by Paul as "oxen" (terrestrial animals) and by our doctors in the Gospel—in which those selling are cast out of the temple—and Christ calls the Israelites "sheep." However, the Apostles, to whom the conversion of the nations was commanded, were called "fishermen" by the Lord. Their prince was Peter: who at Rome, the mistress of nations, was to be the fisherman and extractor of "whales" <note>original: "cætarum" — likely a misspelling of "cetorum," meaning sea monsters or whales, representing great worldly powers.</note> as if from the ocean. But Christ, who said he was not sent except to the sheep that were lost from the house of Israel, claimed for himself the name of "shepherd" rather than "fisherman."

### CHAPTER SIX.

<margin>
Why on the second day it was not said "that it was good."
</margin>
From this, the solution to the question that has long tormented the interpreters of this book <note>The Book of Genesis.</note> is manifest: Why was it not said on the second day, "and God saw that it was good"? For if we say what is usually said—that it was done because the work of the waters was not finished on that day, but on the third, when the waters under the heaven flowed together into one place—it will hardly seem a fully satisfying answer. For the proper work of the second day is not the arrangement of the waters, but the arrangement of the firmament, which was established in the middle place between the waters. On that day the firmament was made—when God said "let there be a firmament"—and the distinction of the waters—when He said "and let it divide the waters from the waters"—was quite complete. However, the collection of the waters called the "sea," the revealing of the land, and the production of plants, just as they have the character of an entirely different work, so too they were completed on another day (that is, the third day) to which they belonged. Therefore, a reason must be sought from a

<column-break/>

deeper mystery. The firmament (as we showed above) represents the Law. And the firmament was as unformed as it was simply imperfect until it was furnished with the sun, moon, and stars. In the same way, the Law was not indeed bad (as the <term>Manicheans</term><note>A dualist sect that believed the material world and the Old Testament God were evil; Pico is defending the Hebrew Law against this view.</note> say), but neither was it simply "good" (that is, perfect) until Christ came, who fulfilled the Law.
<margin>
The Manichean.
Christ fulfilled the Law.
</margin>
If the firmament had been "much," it would not have received the sun; if it had been "good," it would not have needed the sun. But the firmament was only good insofar as it was capable of receiving the sun and the other stars, just as the Law was good only insofar as it was a "schoolmaster" <note>original: "pedagogus"</note> for us in Christ. Moses permitted many things because of the hardness of the people’s hearts which the Gospel later does not permit. Moreover, that we cannot call the Law "evil" as
<margin>Manes.</margin>
Manes believed, yet we can call it "not good," is taught most clearly by the prophet; in his writings, God, speaking of the Hebrews, says: "I gave them precepts that were not good." <note>original: "dedi eis præcepta non bona" — Ezekiel 20:25.</note> He did not say "evil precepts," but "not good precepts"—that is, not perfect, not absolute, not consumed. This is confirmed by the
<margin>Ancient Hebrews.</margin>
ancient Hebrew doctors, who, interpreting that passage of Ecclesiastes, "Vanity of vanities and all is vanity," say: "Even the Law is vanity until the Messiah comes." And concerning these things, enough has been said.

### CHAPTER SEVEN.

<margin>
What the power of baptism effects.
</margin>
Since the supreme benefit of the Word made flesh was that through the sacrament of baptism—through which the power of Christ is poured into us—we might be reborn as children of God, born not of blood but of God. Finally, Moses indicates this to us when, after the rising of the sun and its demonstration to the world, and after the fertility of the waters and the earth, he makes man in the image of God—not an earthly man, but a heavenly one. For after the Gentiles and Jews were converted to Christ, this remained: that through the most holy washing, conforming themselves to the Lord's cross, they might be reformed into the image of God. For if baptism makes us children of God, and the Son is the image of the Father, was it not the power of the entire Trinity working in baptism that says:
<margin>Paul.</margin>
"Let us make man in our image"? <note>original: "Faciamus hominem ad imaginem nostram" — Genesis 1:26.</note> If, therefore, we are in the image of God, we are also children. If children, we are also heirs: heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ. But who are the children? It was written by Paul that we cry out "Abba, Father" in the Holy Spirit. Those, therefore, who live by the Spirit, these are the children of God; these are the brothers of Christ; these are destined for the eternal inheritance. This reward of both faith and a well-lived life they shall happily possess in the heavenly Jerusalem.

## EXPOSITION OF THE FIRST WORD, THAT IS, "IN THE BEGINNING."

<image-desc>Large historiated initial 'I' depicting a seated figure, likely a scholar or divine figure, within an architectural frame, with a landscape background.</image-desc>

What the first word of the Law, "In the beginning," means.

Now we have come to the end of the work, having run through the sevenfold exposition of the context of the universe. But I recognize that something still remains untouched and undiscussed by us, which it seemed should have been explained in the first place: that is, what the first word of the Law, which is "In the beginning," means. Not rashly or without cause did I wish to speak of this "beginning" at the end of the entire work. Nor am I about to dispute here concerning the Son of God, who is the "Beginning" through whom all things were made (for He is the Wisdom of the Father). Nor am I going to prove that the ancient Hebrews felt the same as our people on this point...

### OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA

<margin>
He promises that he will bring forth a dogma of such a kind that it is in accordance with the paradox of the ancient Jewish discipline. The complete knowledge of all arts, of all wisdom, both divine and human, is included in the five books of the Mosaic law.
</margin>

...we shall do there. But we intend, through another method of interpretation, to give readers a taste of the Mosaic depth. We shall not do this, however, until we have deliberated a little on a certain dogma which is truly a paradox of the older Jewish discipline. There is a firm opinion held by all the ancients, which they confirm with one voice as an indubitable truth: that the complete knowledge of all arts, of all wisdom—both divine and human—is included in the five books of the Law of Moses. They hold that this art is disguised and hidden within the very letters with which the words of the Law are woven together, in the manner we shall now declare.

Let us take, for example, the first small section of the Book of Genesis, namely from the beginning up to the place where it is written, *and God saw the light, that it was good.* <note>Genesis 1:4</note> That entire scripture is composed of one hundred and three elements <note>Pico uses "elements" to refer to individual letters of the alphabet.</note>, which, arranged in the way they are there, constitute the words we read, presenting nothing but what is common and trivial. This order of letters forms, as it were, the "bark" or outer layer of the text, while the "marrow" of the hidden mysteries lies concealed within. 

But if we take these same elements, broken down into separate letters, and properly reassemble them according to the rules they themselves hand down regarding what words can be formed from them, they say it will happen that—if we are capable of receiving this enclosed wisdom—the most secret dogmas regarding many things will shine forth to us. And if this were done throughout the entire Law, then finally, from this positioning and connection of elements, all the doctrine and secrets of all the liberal disciplines could be brought to light. 

I said, however, *if we are capable of receiving this enclosed wisdom.* For it can happen that while we are handling, dissolving, and recomposing certain words, many vocabularies and a manifold series of discourse may be produced which teach great things and signify great things; but unless someone has obtained instruction on that matter from elsewhere, they cannot help but despise those things as useless and accidental, not understanding what they signify. For we cannot *learn* dogmas and doctrines there for the first time, but we can only *recognize* them. 

As for myself, I do not offer these things as proven or attested, because I have neither put them to the test nor do I trust that I am able to do so. Yet, I neither deny nor despise them—partly because this opinion has great authors, and partly because concerning Moses, who was "faithful in all the house of God," <note>original: "Moses in tota domo dei fidelis." A reference to Hebrews 3:2.</note> even greater things can easily be believed. 

<margin>
Moses was faithful in all the house of God.
</margin>

However, I thought it would not be unwelcome to our people if I made public those riches of gems which I encountered—not indeed by entering those abysses, but by merely skimming the shore of this sea—gems which neither Hermes nor the Pactolus <note>A river in Lydia famous for its gold-bearing sands; Hermes is the Greek god associated with secret knowledge.</note> are said by the poets to bear. It pleased me to take a risk with the first word of the work, which among the Hebrews is *Bereshit* and among us is read as *In the beginning.* I wanted to see if I too, using the rules of the ancients, could bring to light something worthy of being known. 

Therefore, beyond my hope and beyond my expectation, I found—what I myself could hardly believe as I found it, and what others will not easily be able to believe—the entire account of the creation of the world and of all things opened and explained in that one single word. I say this is a marvelous, unheard-of, and incredible thing. But you will soon believe it if you pay attention, and the matter itself will prove me true. 

That word is written among the Hebrews in this manner:
-> ב ר א ש י ת <-
<note>Bereshit: Bet, Resh, Aleph, Shin, Yod, Tav.</note>

<margin>
That the entire account of the whole world is contained in the first word of the work.
</margin>

From this word, therefore, if we join the third letter to the first, it becomes the word אב (*Ab*), that is, **Father**. 

If we add the second letter to the first doubled, it becomes בבר (*Bebar*), that is, **in the son and through the son** (for the preposition *Beth* signifies both). 

If we read all the letters except the first, it becomes ראשית (*Reshit*), that is, **the beginning**. 

If we connect the fourth letter to the first and the last, it becomes שת (*Shabat*), that is, **rest and the end**. 

If we set the first three in the order they lie, it becomes ברא (*Bara*), that is, **He created**. 

If, omitting the first, we take the following three, it becomes ראש (*Rosh*), that is, **head**. 

If, omitting the first and second, we take the following two, it becomes 

<column-break/>

אש (*Esh*), that is, **fire**. 

If, having omitted the first three, we couple the fourth to the last, it becomes שית (*Shith*), that is, **foundation**. 

Again, if we join the second to the first, it becomes רב (*Rab*), that is, **great**. 

If after the third we place the fifth and then the fourth, it becomes איש (*Ish*), that is, **of man**. 

If we join the first two to the last two, it becomes ברית (*Berith*), that is, **by a covenant**. 

If we join the last to the first, and use the twelfth word—which is טוב (*Tob*), **good**, for the substitution of the letter *Tav* for *Tet* is very frequent among the Hebrews. 

<margin>
A faithful interpretation.
</margin>

Let us see, first, what these mean in English, and then what mysteries concerning the whole of nature are revealed through them to those not ignorant of philosophy. *Ab* signifies **Father**. *Bbar*, **in the son and through the son** (for the preposition *Beth* signifies both). *Reshit*, **the beginning**. *Shabbat*, **rest and the end**. *Bara*, **He created**. *Rosh*, **the head**. *Esh*, **fire**. *Seth* (or *Shith*), **foundation**. *Rab*, **of the great**. *Ish*, **man**. *Berit*, **by a covenant**. *Tob*, **good**. 

And if we weave the whole discourse in a following order, it will be of this kind: **The Father, in the son and through the son, created the beginning and the end (or rest), the head, the fire, and the foundation of the great man, by a good covenant.** 

<margin>
The Father, in the son and through the son, created the beginning and the end (or rest), the head, the fire, and the foundation of the great man, by a good covenant.
</margin>

This entire sentence leaps forth from the resolution and composition of that first word. How deep and how full of all doctrine its sense is cannot be clear to everyone. But so that some things may be immediately open—though not everything to everyone—that are signified to us by these voices: It is known to all Christians what it means for the Father to have created in the Son and through the Son. Likewise, what it means for the Son to be the beginning and the end of all things; for He is the **Alpha and Omega** (as John writes), and He called Himself the **Beginning**; and we have demonstrated that He is the end of all things, so that they may be restored to their source.

<margin>
John. Alpha & Omega. Beginning and end.
</margin>

The other parts are a little more obscure: namely, what they might mean by "the head," "the fire," and "the foundation of the great man"; what that "covenant" is, and for what reason it is called "good." For it is not immediately obvious to everyone to see here explained the entire account of the four worlds of which we have treated, as well as their kinship and happiness, about which we finally disputed. 

First, therefore, it must be noted that the world is called a **great man** by Moses. 

<margin>
The great world, which was called the fourth above, is Man.
</margin>

For if man is a "small world" <note>Microcosm.</note>, then surely the world is a "great man" <note>Macrocosm.</note>. Taking this opportunity, he most aptly figures the three worlds—the intellectual, the celestial, and the corruptible—through the three parts of man, simultaneously indicating by this figure not only that all worlds are contained within man, but also declaring briefly which part of man corresponds to which world. 

Let us consider, therefore, three parts in man: the highest, which is the **head**; then that which extends from the neck to the navel; and the third, which extends from the navel to the feet. For these are also separated and distinguished in the figure of man by a certain variety. But it is wonderful how beautifully and perfectly, by the most exact reasoning, they correspond in proportion to the three parts of the world. 

<margin>
Which part in man responds to which world. Knowledge. Motion. Generation. See the mystical investigation of the author.
</margin>

In the **head** is the brain, the source of **knowledge**. In the **breast** is the heart, the source of **motion, life, and heat**. In the lowest part are the **genital organs**, the principle of **generation**. 

In the same way, in the world: the highest part, which is the angelic or intellectual world, is the source of **knowledge**, because that nature was made for understanding. The middle part, which is the heaven, is the principle of **life, motion, and heat**, in which the sun rules like the heart in the breast. Below the moon is that which is known to everyone as the principle of **generation** and corruption. 

You see how aptly all these parts of the world and of man mutually agree. Now, Moses designated the first part by its proper name, the **head**. The second he called **fire**, both because the heaven is judged by many to be by this name, and because in us this portion is the principle of heat. The third he called the **foundation**, because through it (as is known to all)...

Moreover, he added that He created these things in a **good covenant**, because among them a covenant of peace and friendship was sanctioned by the law of God's wisdom, arising from a kinship of natures and mutual consent. This covenant is "good" for this reason: it is so directed and ordered toward God, who is Goodness itself, that just as the whole world is one within itself, so also it might ultimately be one with its Author. ## THE DEPRECATORY PRAYER OF GIOVANNI PICO
## DELLA MIRANDOLA TO GOD, 
## IN ELEGIAC VERSE.

> Gracious God, to be revered in highest majesty,
> Who truly holds one divinity in a threefold power,
> Whom, above the flaming walls of the high world,
> The blessed crowd of the angelic choir serves;
> Whose immense work, visible to our eyes,
> Your omnipotent right hand once created:
> You who twist the heavens, who guide the globe with a nod,
> From whose command the sent lightnings fall,
> Spare, I pray, the wretched; wash away our filth, I pray,
> Lest the just penalty of your fury drive us away.
> But if our debts were weighed on an even scale,
> And if the rule of your judgment were severe,
> Who could bear the horrendous whip of the living 
> Avenger, or withstand such heavy blows?
> The very Machine of the world <note>original: "Machina" — a common Renaissance term for the structure of the universe</note> would not remain against your angry hand,
> That Machine not intended to perish until the final day.
> What mind is not condemned by the origin of first sin? <note>Referring to Original Sin inherited from Adam.</note>
> Or what mind is not made guilty by its own crime?
> Or surely You are He whose nature is always to spare,
> And who holds justice and mercy in equal measure,
> You who repay rewards far greater than merits,
> Just as You repay lighter punishments for committed evils.
> For your clemency is greater than our sins,

<column-break/>

> And to give to the unworthy is a thing more worthy of God.
> Although they are worthy enough, if He deigns to love them—
> He who makes those worthy whom He did not find so.
> Therefore, I pray, look upon your people with a peaceful countenance,
> Whether you prefer them to be servants, or rather to be defendants;
> Defendants indeed, if you look at the crimes of our life,
> The work of a mind far too ungrateful,
> But if you should rather perceive your own gifts in us,
> Gifts ennobled by the most excellent benefits,
> We are the very ones whom nature once made your servants,
> And whom holy grace soon after made your children.
> But (alas!) the indulgence of such a great fate presses upon the wretched,
> Whom grace made children, but fault made defendants.
> Fault made them defendants, but let grace conquer the fault,
> So that your honor may increase through our crime:
> For otherwise your wisdom or power would flow,
> Able to reveal its own riches to the world;
> A greater glory of goodness exists in our errors,
> And that love shines to be loved above all things:
> Which was able to lead the Lord down from high heaven,
> And to lift the limbs of the highest God onto a cross,
> So that the blood and water from your side
> Might wash away the filth evilly contracted from our father's seed. <note>Refers to the blood and water flowing from the side of Christ at the Crucifixion (John 19:34).</note>
> Thus your love and mercy, most mild King,
> Provide the material to supply such great goods to evils.
> O love, O mercy, well-provided for our affairs!
> O goodness, made a servant of your servant!
> O love, O mercy, poorly known in our ages!
> O goodness, now nearly conquered by our evils!
> Grant, I pray, to this great love which always burns,
> That there be an equal ardor in our hearts;
> Grant us to set down the yoke, having shaken off 
> The empire of Satan, whom it shames us to have served for so many years.
> Grant, I pray, that the fires of a frantic mind be extinguished,
> And let your love live in our breast,
> So that when, having finished the duty of mortal life,
> The spirit shall be led before its Lord,
> Having obtained the happy lot of the promised kingdom,
> It may feel that You are not a Lord, but a Father.

### T  H  E    E  N  D.

## ROBERTO SALVIATI TO LORENZO
## DE' MEDICI, GREETINGS.

**C**<note>The decorative 'C' shows a serene landscape, perhaps symbolizing the "peace and friendship" mentioned in the text.</note> Having been born with such a temperament, most distinguished Lorenzo, and so instructed by nature that nothing is more important to me than to love, cherish, and venerate those who are either excellent in genius or singular in learning, I could not help but love your Pico della Mirandola above all others and admire a man surely most worthy of all admiration. Since he recently dedicated to you a book on the sevenfold explanation of the six days of Genesis <note>The *Heptaplus*</note> as the firstfruits of his studies—a work most excellent in the judgment not only of myself but of everyone—I wished to take care that it be published at my expense in a corrected edition. I have no doubt that I shall simultaneously satisfy both my love for him and the public usefulness for students. To this was added the hope that I would be doing something not ungrateful to you if those physical and divine mysteries which he shared with you were finally made common to all through me. Farewell.
->Giovanni Pico<-

# THE DEFENSE OF PICO'S QUESTIONS

# GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA TO LORENZO DE' MEDICI.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'A' framed in a rectangle. Inside the triangle of the letter 'A' is a smaller triangle with a bird (possibly a swan) perched on top. The phrase "THE SUN SHINES IN THE DARKNESS" <note>original Latin: "SOL IN TENEBRIS LUCET"</note> is split across the design: "IN TENE" on the left, "BRIS LUCE" on the right, and "SOL" at the bottom crossbar. I have dedicated our *Defense* to you, Lorenzo de' Medici, not because I saw it as a work truly worthy (I call God to witness) of such a great man, but because it is owed to you by that same right by which I realize all my efforts have long been yours. For you must be most fully persuaded that whatever I am, or am to become, is yours, Lorenzo, and shall remain so in the future. I say less than I wish, and these words are altogether too cold to sufficiently express what I feel—that is, with what love, what faith, and what respect I follow you, and have followed you for many years now. I am moved by the many kindnesses you have bestowed upon me, which clearly testify to your most loving spirit, as well as by your own excellences—not so much those of fortune as those of the mind—and those rare, indeed unique, virtues of yours which your own modesty prevents me from recounting at present. I return to the *Defense*, which I ask you to receive with a cheerful countenance; it is a small gift indeed, but a significant testimony of my faith and of my truly greatest respect for you at all times. If it should happen that you find time to look at it amidst the great affairs with which you are always most busily occupied, remember that this was a rushed work, rather than an elaborate one, and that the subject of the work had to be taken from the judgment of others rather than my own. I did not dedicate it to you so that you might recognize in me a brilliance of talent or learning that I do not possess, but so that you might know (for I shall say it again) that whatever I am, I am most devoted to your greatness.
