### THE DEFENSE OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA, COUNT OF CONCORDIA.

<image-desc>A circular emblem containing the coat of arms of Pope Innocent VIII (the Cybo family), featuring a shield with a chequered fess and a cross in the chief. The shield is supported by two figures (putti) at the base and is surrounded by a decorative wreath of flowers and foliage, all set within a square frame.</image-desc>

<margin>Innocent VIII, Supreme Pontiff.</margin>
<margin>Nine hundred questions proposed concerning divine and natural matters.</margin>
<margin>The trifles of detractors regarding five main points.</margin>
WHEN I RECENTLY CAME TO ROME to kiss the feet of the Supreme Pontiff Innocent VIII—to whom the name "Innocent" is most deservedly given due to the innocence of his life—I intended to follow my usual custom of always composing and treating something regarding literary matters. To perform a task worthy of the city of Rome, pleasing to a Christian prince, and useful to myself and to scholars, I proposed nine hundred questions concerning divine and natural matters. I intended to respond to these in a public assembly of the most learned men. Scarcely had they been made public when, among some who might have approved of my talent or learning, or at least my study of the fine arts, a manifold crowd of detractors arose. And although I saw that the distastes, the turned-up noses, the censures, and altogether the judgments of each individual were varied—as always happens when we attempt something new and not trivial—there were nevertheless five main points that these "shufflers" <note>original: "fummufflores" — likely a derogatory term for those who whisper or mutter criticisms</note> condemned in me. Some, for instance, criticized philosophy and literature altogether, even doing so to appear knowledgeable. They occasionally added that Adam was cast out of paradise because he wished to make himself equal to the gods through the knowledge of good and evil. They argued that those who wish to know more than is proper should be banished by a similar example from the court of Christ. Others did not so much disapprove of philosophy as of this very style of disputing and this practice of publicly debating literature; they barked that it was intended for the display of talent and the ostentation of learning rather than for the acquisition of erudition. Not-

<column-break/>

<margin>In what year of his life he had established the debate. Namely, not yet having reached twenty-four years of age.</margin>
<margin>Two impediments to writing.</margin>
-hing could stop some from calling me bold and rash, because at this age—not yet having reached my twenty-fourth year—I did not hesitate to propose a disputation on the highest points of philosophy, the sublime mysteries of Christian theology, and unknown disciplines, in the most celebrated city and in the most magnificent assembly of learned men. Many did not so much accuse me because I was in Rome, or because I was a youth, but because I was to dispute such a large number—that is, nine hundred questions—calumniating the act as superfluous, ambitious, and beyond my strength. Among those who professed a wisdom in the study of theology, there were some who, perhaps not content with lighter insults, proclaimed me not just bold, not just rash, not just boastful, but a magician, an impious man, and a new leader of heresy <term>heresiarch <gloss>a founder or leader of a heretical sect</gloss></term> in the Church of Christ. I was (I call God to witness) for a long time in doubt as to whether I should clear away these objections or pass them over in silence. Two things especially moved me to keep silent: First, that I, abhorring contention and quarrels, have always loved peace of mind and the tranquility of a most placid life, which my studies have provided me. Nor have I hated any task of writing more than that which is based on dispute and bitter altercation of any kind; for I have never considered it the mark of a good man or a philosopher to return an injury or an insult. The second reason was that I was content with the judgment of the Supreme Pontiff—whose memory I must always deservedly celebrate—and with the judgment of many from the most holy Apostolic Senate <note>The College of Cardinals</note>, whose kindness and most benevolent spirit toward me I can or should never forget. It seemed that I could easily ignore both the hatred and the insults of wicked men; and indeed, regarding the other charges, I was of the opinion that they were unworthy of a response. But regarding the one charge of the crime of heresy leveled against me, I feared that if I did this, I might seem to acknowledge the crime by not refuting it.
<margin>Rufinus. One should drive the name of heresy and the title of heretic far from oneself.</margin>
Moreover, Rufinus <note>Rufinus of Aquileia, a 4th-century monk and translator</note> writes most wisely that it is indeed glorious to patiently endure injuries after the example of Christ. But he who bears or ignores even a single mark of heresy is not a Christian.

<meta>This page continues the introduction to Pico della Mirandola’s *Apologia*. # THE DEFENSE OF THE QUESTIONS

<margin>Jerome</margin> ...Christian, and our Jerome <note>St. Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), a Church Father known for translating the Bible into Latin.</note> cries out with the greatest possible intensity of spirit and a most clear voice: "I do not wish anyone to be patient when under suspicion of heresy." Therefore, Jerome does not want me to remain silent; by his authority, he draws and compels an idle man to write. Consequently, if there are those who perhaps wish I would stay quiet, let them know they have a dispute not with me, but with Jerome, who does not wish me to be silent. Who can fail to listen to Jerome without committing a crime? Therefore, at his urging—or rather, his compulsion—I have set out to write even a brief defense, not to tear down or accuse anyone, but to legally excuse myself from the greatest crime of impiety which has been unjustly charged against me.

<margin>Paul. You indeed among Christians. To abolish the name of heretic, the burden of defense was taken up.</margin> I ask that my detractors endure this with the same spirit with which I have always endured their unfair offenses. Let them endure, I say, that I—who was born a Christian of Christian parents, who bear the standard of Jesus Christ on my forehead, and who would gladly die for the faith of Christ—might exclaim with a calm mind, as if with Paul <note>referring to the Apostle Paul</note> while they listen: "I am no more a non-Jew, nor an Ishmaelite, nor a heretic; but I worship Jesus, and I carry the cross of Jesus in my body; through whom the world is crucified to me, and I to the world." Finally, while I neither claim for myself nor take away from them titles of holiness, wisdom, or other such excellent honors, I ask that they do not take away this one thing, which I would even freely shed my blood to defend: namely, that I may call myself a Christian.

But if they grant this, I do not write to those from whom I have already obtained what our entire defense strives for. I write to others who believe or suspect that I am, or once was, a heretic. However, although our main purpose is to show that it is not I, but those who slander me as a heretic, who deviate from the orthodox and Catholic path, nevertheless, since I must write, we shall also say something about those things which were first objected against us, lest our detractors take advantage of my silence as if it were a confession of guilt.

In the first place, many found fault with my "philosophizing." To these people, I will say nothing at this point, because it is my plan to plead the cause of philosophy separately in a specific work; and altogether, if it is a disgrace to devote oneself to letters and to cultivate the good arts and disciplines, I would rather acknowledge this fault than beg for forgiveness. To those who detest this kind of disputation and this method of publicly debating about God, nature, and morals, I will not say much, since this crime—if it is a crime—is shared by me with great men, indeed with the most esteemed philosophers of almost every age. It was most certain to them that nothing was more useful for attaining the knowledge of truth they sought than to be very frequent in the exercise of debating.

<margin>He proposes the value of debating by comparing it to gymnastics.</margin> Just as the strengths of the body become firmer through gymnastics, so in this literary arena, as it were, the strengths of the mind turn out far stronger and more vigorous. I would not believe that either the poets meant anything else by the celebrated "arms of Pallas" <note>Pallas Athena, goddess of wisdom and war</note>, or the Hebrews when they say that "iron" is the symbol of the wise, other than to signify to us how honorable and utterly necessary this kind of contest is for acquiring wisdom. Perhaps this is why the Chaldeans <note>Ancient Mesopotamian sages/astrologers</note>, in the birth chart of one who is to be a philosopher, require that Mars look upon Mercury in a "trine aspect" <note>An astrological position of 120 degrees, considered harmonious and productive</note>; as if to say, if you remove these encounters and these "wars," all philosophy will become drowsy and sluggish. But as for these matters, as I said, I prefer to defend myself with the authority and judgments of great men rather than with arguments.

<margin>Defense against the charge of rashness.</margin> It seems a greater task to satisfy those who say I am unequal in age, talent, and learning to

<column-break/>

<margin>Horace.</margin> so great a province, and that I have not consulted my "shoulders" (according to Horace <note>A Roman poet who advised writers to choose subjects their "shoulders" can carry</note>) as to what they are able to bear or what they refuse. Truly, this is a difficult line of defense for me; for if I say I am equal to it, I seem modest <note>ironic usage: "I seem anything but modest"</note> and too full of myself; but if I confess I am unequal, I seem likely to suffer the mark of being rash and ill-advised. I have fallen into serious straits, as I cannot promise what I cannot do without fault, nor fail to perform it without fault.

<margin>Job. Timothy.</margin> And indeed, I could assert with Job that the "spirit is in all people," and perhaps hear with Timothy, "Let no one despise your youth" <note>1 Timothy 4:12</note>. But I will say more truly from my own conscience that there is nothing great or singular in me. I do not deny that I am perhaps studious and eager for the good arts, yet I neither claim nor arrogate the name of "learned" for myself. <margin>A most praised and approved saying of Hermolaus.</margin> For as my Hermolaus <note>Hermolaus Barbarus, a contemporary humanist scholar</note>—the delight of the Roman tongue and the splendor and glory of our age—once wrote: "He cannot help but be unlearned who believes himself to be learned." <margin>It is a profit to be defeated in literary battles.</margin> Wherefore, the reason I placed such a great burden on my shoulders was not because I was unaware of my own weakness, but because I knew that this kind of fight—that is, the literary one—is unique in that there is profit in being defeated. Thus, it happens that even the weakest person can and should, by right, not only not refuse these contests, but even seek them out. For whoever loses receives a benefit from the victor, not an injury; since through him, one returns home "richer"—that is, more learned—and better prepared for future fights. Encouraged by this hope, I, a weak soldier, did not fear to decide upon so grave a battle with the strongest and most vigorous of all. Whether this was done rashly or not could certainly be judged better by the outcome of the battle than by my age.

<margin>He refutes the objection regarding the multitude of questions.</margin> It remains for me to respond to those who are offended by the large number of proposed topics, as if this burden rested on *their* shoulders and not rather on mine alone, who had to endure whatever labor there was. It is truly indecent and overly fussy to wish to set a limit on another's industry; <margin>Cicero.</margin> and, as Cicero says, in a matter that is better the greater it is, to desire mediocrity. It was altogether necessary for me, in such grand attempts, either to succumb or to succeed. If I succeeded, I do not see why that which is laudable to perform in ten questions should be considered blameworthy to have performed in nine hundred. If I succumbed, they would have had reason to accuse me if they hate me, or to excuse me if they love me. Since in so serious and great a matter, it was more worthy of pardon than accusation that a young man of thin talent and meager learning should fail; for even according to the poet: "if strength fails, the daring will certainly be praised, and in great things, to have willed is enough" <note>original Latin: "in magnis voluisse sat est"</note>. <margin>Gorgias of Leontini. Like the Pythagoreans and Epicureans, so of the Thomists.</margin> If even in our age many have imitated Gorgias of Leontini <note>A Greek Sophist who claimed he could speak on any subject</note> by being accustomed to propose disputes not just on nine hundred, but on all questions of all arts, and not without praise—why should I not be allowed to dispute, without fault, on many, yet still certain and determined points? But they say this is "superfluous and ambitious." I contend, however, that this was done by me not superfluously, but necessarily; which they themselves must plainly admit if they consider my method of philosophizing. <margin>Which is called the family of the Scotists. Latin philosophers.</margin> For those who have devoted themselves to any one of the families of philosophers—namely, to Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> or Scotus <note>Duns Scotus</note>, who are now most in favor—can indeed make a trial of their learning in the discussion of a few questions. But I have so trained myself that, having sworn an oath to the words of no single master, I have poured myself through all the masters of philosophy, examined all their papers, and acknowledged all "families" <note>schools of thought</note>. Therefore, since I had to speak regarding all of them, lest I should seem bound to one while neglecting the rest as if I were a defender of a private dogma, even if I proposed only a few items from each, the points could not help but be very many which...

<summary>Pico della Mirandola defends his decision to propose 900 theses for debate, arguing that intellectual conflict is essential for wisdom and that his vast range of topics reflects his refusal to be bound to any single school of philosophy. He counters accusations of arrogance and heresy by citing religious and classical authorities like Jerome, Paul, and Horace, framing himself as a humble but dedicated seeker of truth.</summary>

# THE DEFENSE
[Signature: B2]

...at the same time, all things may be brought forward. Nor should anyone condemn me for being "carried as a guest wherever the storm may drive me." <note>original: "quocunq; ferat tepeftas deferar hofpes" — a quote from Horace, indicating Pico's intellectual flexibility.</note> For it was a practice observed by all the ancients to read every kind of writer and never pass over any commentaries they could study. This was especially true of Aristotle, who for that reason was called "the Reader" <note>original: "αναγνώστην"</note> by Plato. Certainly, it is the mark of a narrow mind to confine oneself within a single porch or Academy. <note>Refers to the Stoic "Porch" and Plato's "Academy."</note> One cannot have rightly chosen a path for oneself from among them all if one has not first become familiar with them all. Add to this that in every "family" of thought, there is something significant that is not held in common with the others. To begin with our own thinkers, to whom philosophy most recently arrived:

<margin>Scotus. Thomas. Giles. Albert. Henry. Averroes. Avempace. Alpharabi. Avicenna.</margin>
There is in John Duns Scotus <note>A major medieval Franciscan theologian known as the "Subtle Doctor."</note> something vigorous and discursive. In Thomas Aquinas, something solid and balanced. In Giles of Rome, something polished and precise; in Francis <note>likely Francis of Meyronnes</note>, something sharp and acute. In Albert the Great, something ancient, vast, and grand. In Henry of Ghent, it has always seemed to me, something sublime and venerable. Among the Arabs, there is in Averroes something firm and unshakable. In Avempace and Alpharabi, something heavy and meditative. In Avicenna, something divine and Platonic.

<margin>Greek Peripatetics. Simplicius. Themistius. Alexander. Theophrastus.</margin>
Among the Greeks, philosophy is, in general, especially bright and pure. In Simplicius, it is rich and abundant. In Themistius, elegant and concise. In Alexander of Aphrodisias, consistent and learned. In Theophrastus, weightily elaborated. In Ammonius, smooth and gracious. And if you turn to the Platonists, to review just a few:

<margin>Academics. Porphyry. Iamblichus. Plotinus. Proclus. Hermias. Damascius. Plato. Augustine.</margin>
In Porphyry, you will be delighted by the abundance of matter and a religion of many paths. In Iamblichus, you will venerate a more secret philosophy and the mysteries of the "barbarians." <note>In this context, "barbarians" refers to the ancient wisdom of non-Greeks, such as Egyptians or Chaldeans.</note> In Plotinus, there is nothing in particular to admire because he offers himself as admirable from every side; the sweating Platonists can scarcely understand him when he speaks divinely about divine things and, with a learned indirectness of speech, far above human capacity about human things. I pass over the more recent ones: Proclus, luxuriating in Asiatic fertility, and those who flowed from him—Hermias, Damascius, Olympiodorus, and many others—in all of whom that "divine" <note>original: "το θειον"</note> quality, the peculiar symbol of the Platonists, always shines. It is added that if there is any sect that attacks truer dogmas and mocks good causes with the slander of wit, it confirms the truth rather than weakening it; like a flame shaken by motion, it is fanned, not extinguished. Moved by this reason, I wished to bring into the open the opinions not of just one school (as some would prefer), but of every kind of doctrine. I did this so that by this comparison of many sects and this multifaceted discussion of philosophy, that "radiance of truth" of which Plato mentions in his letters might shine more clearly upon our minds, like the sun rising from on high. What would it have been if only the philosophy of the Latins—Albert, St. Thomas, Scotus, Giles, Francis, and Henry—were treated, while the philosophers of the Greeks and Arabs were omitted? For all wisdom flowed from the barbarians to the Greeks, and from the Greeks to us. Thus, our people have always been satisfied to stand upon foreign inventions and to cultivate the ideas of others in their way of philosophizing. What would it have been to have dealt with the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle.</note> regarding natural things, unless the Academy of the Platonists was also summoned? Their doctrine, even concerning divine matters, has always been held as the most sacred among all philosophies, according to Augustine; and it is now brought by me for the first time—may envy be absent from my words—after many centuries, into the public for the examination of debate.

<margin>Seneca.</margin>
What would it have been to have treated the opinions of as many others as there were, if, coming as guests to a banquet of the wise, we brought nothing of our own, produced and elaborated by our own wit? Surely it is ungenerous, as Seneca says, to be wise only from a commentary, as if the inventions of our ancestors

<column-break/>

<margin>Note what studies he has stirred up.</margin>
had closed off the path of our own industry, or as if the power of nature were exhausted in us, producing nothing from itself that might, if not demonstrate the truth, at least hint at it, even from afar. If a farmer hates sterility in his field, or a husband in his wife, surely the divine mind, joined and associated with the soul, will hate an unfruitful soul all the more, the more it desires a far nobler offspring from it. Therefore, not content with the common doctrines, I have added many things concerning the "Ancient Theology" of Hermes Trismegistus, <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure associated with a body of esoteric wisdom.</note> many things from the teachings of the Chaldeans and of Pythagoras, and many from the more secret mysteries of the Hebrews. We have also proposed for dispute many things discovered and meditated upon by us regarding natural and divine matters. We have proposed, first, the harmony <note><term>Harmony (Concordia)</term>: The philosophical attempt to prove that different systems, like those of Plato and Aristotle, fundamentally agree despite their surface differences.</note> of Plato and Aristotle, believed by many before this, but sufficiently proven by no one. Boethius, among the Latins, promised he would do this, but he is not found to have ever performed what he always wished to do. Simplicius, among the Greeks, professed the same; I wish he had fulfilled it as well as he promised. Augustine also writes in *The Academics* that there were many who tried to prove the same with their most subtle disputations: namely, that the philosophy of Plato and Aristotle is the same. Likewise, John the Grammarian <note>Also known as John Philoponus.</note> says that Plato differs from Aristotle only for those who do not understand Plato's words; yet he left this to be proven by posterity.

<margin>Augustine. John the Grammarian.</margin>
Furthermore, we have added many points in which we have asserted that the opinions of Scotus and Thomas, and many in which the opinions of Averroes and Avicenna, which are thought to be discordant, are in fact in agreement. In the second place, we have arranged the things we have thought out ourselves, both in Aristotelian and Platonic philosophy, and then seventy-two new physical and metaphysical dogmas. If anyone holds these, he will be able (unless I am mistaken) to resolve any proposed question about natural and divine things by a far different method than that which is taught in the schools and cultivated by the doctors of this age. Nor should anyone wonder that I, in my early years and tender age—during which some boast that it is barely permitted to read the commentaries of others—wish to bring forward a new philosophy, rather than simply praising it if it is defended or condemning it if it is rejected.

<margin>Note the new dogmas thought out. Note.</margin>
Finally, since these discoveries are ours and belong to our letters, those who will judge them should count not the years of the author, but rather the merits or demerits of the works themselves. There is also, besides those, another new method of philosophizing through numbers which we have brought forward. This is indeed an ancient method, observed by the earliest theologians—especially by Pythagoras, by Aglaophemus, by Philolaus, by Plato, and the earlier Platonists. But in this age, like other noble things through the neglect of posterity, it has become so obsolete that hardly any traces of it can be found.

<margin>A new method of philosophizing through numbers. Plato.</margin>
Plato writes in the *Epinomis* <note>OCR says Epimenide, but Pico refers to the pseudo-Platonic dialogue *Epinomis*.</note> that among all the liberal arts and contemplative sciences, the principal and most divine is the science of numbering. Seeking also why man is the wisest animal, he answers: because he knows how to count. Aristotle also mentions this opinion in his *Problems*. Albumasar writes that it was a saying of Avenzoar of Babylon <note>Likely referring to a source in Arabic astrological/philosophical tradition.</note> that he who knows how to count, knows everything.

<margin>Aristotle. Albumasar. Plato.</margin>
These things could in no way be true if by the art of numbering they understood that art in which merchants are now primarily most skilled. Plato himself testifies to this, warning us with an uplifted voice not to understand this "divine arithmetic" as the arithmetic of merchants. This arithmetic which he so extols—since I seem to myself to have explored it after many sleepless nights—I have publicly promised to answer seventy-four questions, considered primary among physical and divine matters, by means of numbers, to make a trial of this thing. We have also proposed theorems of magic...

# OF THE DISPUTATIONS
[Signature: d iii]
<meta>catchword: Io. Pic.</meta>

<margin>Double magic.</margin>
...propositions in which we signify that magic is two-fold. One consists entirely of the work and authority of demons—a thing, by my faith, to be cursed and regarded as a monster. The other, when well-examined, is nothing other than the absolute completion of natural philosophy. 

<margin>Worthy of blame is witchcraft <note>original: "γοητεία" (goeteia)</note>.</margin>
When the Greeks mention both, they do not deem the former worthy of the name of magic, calling it witchcraft <note>original: "goeteia"</note>. The latter they call by its own peculiar name, Magic <note>original: "mageia"</note>, as if it were a perfect and supreme science. 

<margin>What a Magus is according to Porphyry.</margin>
For, as Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher and student of Plotinus</note> says, in the language of the Persians, "Magus" means the same as what we call an interpreter and worshiper of divine things. 

<margin>The authority of Plato in the Alcibiades and Charmides regarding magic.</margin>
Indeed, the disparity and difference between these arts is great—or rather, the greatest. Not only does the Christian religion condemn and curse the former, but so do all laws and every well-ordered Commonwealth. All wise men and all nations devoted to the study of celestial and divine things approve and embrace the latter. The former is the most fraudulent of arts; the latter is a higher and holier philosophy. 

The former is fruitless and vain; the latter is firm, faithful, and solid. Whoever practiced the former always did so in secret, lest it bring ignominy and reproach upon the author. From the latter, the highest literary fame and glory have been sought since ancient times and almost always thereafter. 

<margin>Who the Magi were: Pythagoras, Empedocles, Democritus, Plato, Zamolxis, Abaris the Hyperborean, Zoroaster, Charondas.</margin>
No philosopher or man eager to learn the good arts was ever a student of the former. But to learn the latter, Pythagoras, Empedocles, Democritus, and Plato sailed abroad; they preached it upon their return and held it as paramount among their secret teachings. Just as the former is supported by no rational arguments, so it is supported by no certain authors. The latter, honored by the most illustrious "parents" as it were, has two primary authors: Zamolxis <note>A legendary social and religious reformer of the Getae</note>, whom Abaris the Hyperborean imitated, and Zoroaster—not perhaps the one commonly thought of, but that famous son of Oromasius. 

If we ask Plato what each kind of magic is, he will respond in the *Alcibiades* that the magic of Zoroaster is nothing other than the science of divine things, in which the kings of the Persians educated their sons, so that they might be taught to rule their own commonwealth according to the model of the commonwealth of the world. 

He will respond in the *Charmides* that the magic of Zamolxis is the medicine of the soul, through which temperance is brought to the soul, just as health is brought to the body through medicine. In their footsteps later followed Charondas, Damigeron, Apollonius, 

<margin>Damigeron, Apollonius, Hostanes, Dardanus, Homer, Eudoxus, Hermippus, al-Kindi, Roger, William, Anthony.</margin>
Hostanes, and Dardanus. Homer also followed, whom we shall one day prove in our *Poetic Theology* to have concealed this magic, like all other wisdom, under the disguises of his myths. 

Eudoxus and Hermippus followed, as did almost all who have scrutinized the Pythagorean and Platonic mysteries. 

Among more recent thinkers, I find three who have pursued it: the Arab al-Kindi, Roger Bacon, and William of Auvergne <note>Bishop of Paris and a notable medieval philosopher</note>. 

And in our own time, I have seen Antonio Cronico—who, although very busy with the handling of great affairs, possesses such sublimity and elegance of mind that he has touched upon this art most beautifully, just as he has all other liberal arts. 

Plotinus also mentions it where he demonstrates that the Magus is the servant of nature and not its master <note>original: "artificem"</note>. 

The wisest man approves and asserts this magic, while abhorring the other so much that when he was called to the rites of evil demons, he said it was more proper for them to come to him than for him to go to them—and rightly so. 

For just as the former makes man subject and enslaved to wicked powers, so the latter makes him their prince and lord. Finally, the former cannot claim for itself the name of either art or science. 

The latter is full of the highest mysteries and embraces the deepest contemplation of the most secret things, and ultimately, the knowledge of all nature. This magic, calling forth into the light—as if from hiding places—the virtues sown in the world by the grace of God, does not so much 

<column-break/>

perform miracles as it sedulously serves nature as she performs them. Having scrutinized more deeply that universal harmony <note>term: <term>sympathia</term> — the Greek concept of "sympathy" or "universal consensus," where all parts of the cosmos are interconnected</note> which the Greeks more expressively call *sympathia*, and having a clear understanding of the mutual knowledge of natures, this magic brings forth into the public eye the miracles hidden in the recesses of the world, in the lap of nature, and in the storehouses and secrets of God, as if it were the artisan herself. Just as the farmer marries elms to vines, so the Magus marries earth to heaven—that is, he marries lower things to the gifts and virtues of the higher. Thus, as the former magic appears as monstrous and harmful, the latter appears divine and salutary. 

<margin>What leads to the contemplation of God.</margin>
This is chiefly because the former, by enslaving man to the enemies of God, calls him away from God; the latter excites in him that admiration for the works of God, which is followed by ready charity, faith, and the most certain hope. 

For nothing promotes religion and the worship of God more than the persistent contemplation of the wonders of God. When we have well-explored these wonders through this natural magic of which we speak, we will be more ardently animated to the worship and love of the Creator, and we will be compelled to sing: 

> The heavens are full, the whole earth is full of the majesty of your glory. 

And this is enough regarding magic, of which we have said these things because there are many who—just as dogs always bark at strangers—often condemn and hate what they do not understand. 

<margin>Confirmations of the most holy and Catholic faith brought by him, etc.</margin>
I come now to those things which I have brought forward, excavated from the ancient mysteries of the Hebrews, to confirm the most holy and Catholic faith. 

Lest these things perhaps be thought of as fictitious trifles or the fables of charlatans by those to whom they are unknown: 

<margin>Cabala, that is, "reception."</margin>
I want all to understand what and of what sort they are, from where they are sought, by which and how illustrious authors they are confirmed, how recondite and divine they are, and how necessary they are for our people to defend religion against the persistent slanders of the Hebrews. 

<margin>Esdras, Hilary, Origen. The public law given.</margin>
Not only the famous doctors of the Hebrews write this, but among our own, Esdras, Hilary, and Origen write that Moses received on the mountain from God not only the Law, which he left to posterity written in five books, but also a more secret and true explanation of the Law. 

<margin>The interpretation of the Law to be revealed to a few.</margin>
Moreover, he was commanded by God to make the Law public to the people, but he was neither to commit the interpretation of the Law to writing nor to make it common. Instead, he himself was to reveal it only to Joshua, and then he to others of the chief priests succeeding him in turn, under a great religious obligation of silence. And rightly so. 

For it was enough for the common people to recognize through the simple history now the power of God, now His wrath against the wicked, His mercy toward the good, and His justice toward all; and to be instructed through divine and salutary precepts for living well and happily and for the worship of true religion. 

But to make public to the common people the more secret mysteries and the secrets of the highest divinity, which lie hidden under the rough shell of the Law and the crude pretext of words—what else would that be than to give what is holy to dogs and to scatter pearls among swine? Therefore, to keep these things hidden from the crowd and to communicate them to the "perfect"—among whom alone Paul says he speaks wisdom—was a matter not of human counsel but of divine command. 

The ancient philosophers also observed this custom most religiously. 

<margin>This same thing regarding Pythagoras in the *Heptaplus*.</margin>
Pythagoras wrote nothing except a few small things, which he commended to his daughter Dama as he was dying. 

The sphinxes carved on the temples of the Egyptians warned this: that mystic dogmas should be kept inviolate from the profane multitude by the knots of riddles. 

<margin>Plato.</margin>
Plato, writing certain things to Dion concerning supreme substances, said: "I must speak in riddles, so that if the letter should happen to fall into the hands of others, what we write to you may not be understood by them." 

<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
Aristotle used to say that his books on First Philosophy <note>the *Metaphysics*</note>, in which he treats of divine things, were "both published and not published." 

<margin>Origen.</margin>
What more? Origen asserts that Jesus Christ, the Teacher of Life, revealed many things to his disciples which they did not wish to make common, lest they... 

<summary>Pico distinguishes between demonic witchcraft and "natural magic," which he views as the pinnacle of natural philosophy. He then introduces the Cabala as a secret oral tradition given to Moses, arguing that profound truths must be protected from the uninitiated.</summary>

# APOLOGIA

**Column 1:**

<margin>
Dionysius.
</margin>

...they refused to write down everything. This is strongly confirmed by Dionysius the Areopagite <note>A 5th-century Christian theologian and mystic, believed in Pico’s time to be the direct disciple of St. Paul mentioned in the Book of Acts.</note>, who says that the more secret mysteries were transferred from the souls of the authors of our religion to other souls <gloss>that is, from spirit to spirit, without letters, through the intervening spoken word.</gloss> In this very same way, when that true interpretation of the Law, divinely handed to Moses, was revealed by God’s command, it was called the **Cabala** <note>original: "Cabala"; from the Hebrew "Qabbalah," meaning "reception" or "tradition."</note>: which means the same thing among the Hebrews as "reception" does among us. It is called this, of course, because that doctrine was received from one person to another—not through written records, but through a continuous succession of revelations, as if by a hereditary right. However, after the Hebrews were restored from the Babylonian captivity by Cyrus, and the Temple was rebuilt under Zerubbabel, they turned their minds to restoring the Law.

<margin>
What Cabala is: the first reception.
</margin>

<margin>
What Ezra the priest did.
</margin>

Ezra, then the leader of the Church, after amending the book of Moses, realized that because of the exiles, slaughters, flights, and the captivity of the Israelite people, the ancestral custom of handing down the doctrine by hand could not be preserved. He saw that the secrets of heavenly doctrine, divinely granted to them, would perish, for their memory could not last long without the aid of written commentaries. He decreed that the remaining wise men be assembled, and that each should bring forward what they held in their memory regarding the mysteries of the Law. With the help of scribes, these were compiled into 

<margin>
Seventy volumes, and as many wise men. The words of Ezra.
</margin>

seventy volumes: for there were about that many wise men in the Sanhedrin <note>The supreme judicial and ecclesiastical council of ancient Israel.</note>. If they do not believe me on this matter, let them hear Ezra himself speaking thus: "After forty days had passed, the Most High spoke, saying: 'Publish the first things you wrote so that the worthy and unworthy may read them. But you shall keep the last seventy books to hand them over to the wise among your people. For in these is the vein of understanding, the fountain of wisdom, and the river of knowledge.' And so I did." These are Ezra's words, verbatim. These are the books of the science of **Cabala**, in which Ezra rightly proclaimed with a clear voice that there is a "vein of understanding"—that is, an ineffable theology of the substantial deity from above; a "fountain of wisdom"—that is, an exact **metaphysics** <term>metaphysics: the study of things beyond the physical world, like angels and divine forms</term> regarding the intelligible and angelic forms; and a "river of knowledge"—that is, a most firm philosophy concerning natural things.

<margin>
Mirandola was compelled by Sixtus to publish certain questions.
</margin>

Pope Sixtus IV—the Supreme Pontiff who immediately preceded Innocent VIII, under whom we happily live—took the greatest care and zeal to ensure these books were translated into Latin for the public benefit of our faith. By the time he died, three of them had reached the Latins. Among the Hebrews today, these books are held in such religious awe that no one under forty years old is allowed to touch them. When I had acquired these books at no small expense and read them through with the utmost diligence and tireless labor, I saw in them (God is my witness) a religion not so much Mosaic as Christian. There I found the mystery of the Trinity; there the incarnation of the Word; there the divinity of the Messiah; there original sin and its expiation through Christ; the heavenly Jerusalem; the fall of the demons; the orders of angels; purgatories; and the punishments of hell. I read the same things we read daily in Paul and Dionysius, Jerome and Augustine. Indeed, in matters pertaining to philosophy, you would hear Pythagoras and Plato, whose decrees are so akin to the Christian faith that 

<margin>
Augustine.
</margin>

our Augustine gives immense thanks to God that the books of the Platonists came into his hands. In short, there is almost no controversy between us and the Hebrews regarding which they cannot be so refuted and convinced by the books of the Cabalists that not even a corner remains for them to 

<column-break/>

**Column 2:**

hide. I have a most weighty witness to this: Antonius Chronicus <note>Antonio Vinciguerra, a Venetian diplomat and scholar.</note>, a most learned man, who with his own ears (when I was with him at a banquet) heard Dattilus the Hebrew <note>Dattilo, a Jewish scholar from whom Pico learned Cabala.</note>, a master of this science, agree completely <note>original: "pedibus manibusque descendere," literally "to go down with hands and feet," an idiom for total agreement.</note> with the Christian view of the Trinity. And to review the remaining heads of my disputation: I have also brought forth our opinion on interpreting 

<margin>
Orpheus. Zoroaster. Who were anciently held as the wisest. Iamblichus. Note.
</margin>

the songs of Orpheus and Zoroaster. Orpheus is read almost in full among the Greeks; Zoroaster is fragmentary among them, but more complete among the Chaldeans. Both are believed to be the fathers and authors of ancient wisdom. To say nothing of Zoroaster, whose mention is frequent and always with the highest veneration among the Platonists: Iamblichus of Chalcis <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher.</note> writes that Pythagoras took Orphic theology as a model upon which to mold and form his own philosophy. Indeed, they say the sayings of Pythagoras are called "sacred" only because they flowed from the institutions of Orpheus. From there came the secret doctrine of numbers and whatever was great and sublime in Greek philosophy, flowing as if from a primary source. But as was the custom of ancient theologians, Orpheus so wove the mysteries of his dogmas into the wrappings of fables and disguised them with a poetic veil, that if anyone reads his hymns, they would believe nothing lies beneath except trifles and the purest nonsense. I wanted to say this so it might be known what labor and difficulty it was for me to drag the hidden senses of secret philosophy out of the intentional riddles <note>original: "scyrpis," referring to knotted reeds or difficult enigmas.</note> and the hiding places of fables—especially in a matter so grave, so hidden, and so unexplored, without the help and diligence of other interpreters. And yet, my "dogs" <note>A common metaphor for aggressive critics.</note> barked that I had accumulated some tiny and light things just for a show of numbers—as if all these questions are not the most ambiguous and controversial, over which the principal academies duel; as if I have not brought many things, even to these very people who pluck at me and believe themselves the "princes of philosophers," that are completely unknown and unattempted. Indeed, I am so far from that fault that I have taken care to compress the disputation into as few heads as possible; if I had wished to divide and slice it into its parts as others are accustomed to do, it would surely have grown to an innumerable number. To say nothing of the others, who does not know that one single dogma out of the nine hundred—namely, the reconciliation of the philosophy of Plato and Aristotle—I could have expanded into six hundred, if not more, chapters, by enumerating individually all the points where others think they disagree and I believe they agree? But why do I linger on these things any longer, and not rather come to the reason for which this entire work was undertaken: to prove, as clearly as light and beyond all controversy, that not only am I not impious, but those men are impious and heretical who do not blush to say I am or once was a heretic. I shall do this not with insults and outrages, but by the facts and reasons themselves, bringing into the light what I have said, what I have written, and what I have felt. Likewise, let what they have said and felt be seen. Then other learned and distinguished men in our and foreign academies will examine these things, and 

<margin>
The Holy See. Innocent.
</margin>

the Holy See and Innocent VIII, who sits upon it, shall judge. To neglect or violate his judgment is a sin and a crime. He is the supreme judge on earth, representing Him who is the judge of the living and the dead. # FIRST QUESTION REGARDING
## THE DESCENT OF CHRIST
### INTO HELL.

<margin>How he intends to proceed in declaring the conclusion.</margin>
The first conclusion from those I proposed in my debate—which these men have condemned—was this: **Christ did not descend to Hell truly and as a real presence (as Thomas <note>Saint Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the dominant authority in medieval theology.</note> and the common path maintain), but only in terms of his effect.** Regarding this conclusion, I first wish to clarify my meaning and what my mind and opinion are concerning the *mode* of Christ's descent. It was my intention to show that this view is not only Catholic and believed and approved by many Catholic doctors, but also far more probable than its opposite. Second, I will clarify how this proposition, according to the literal force of the words and the meaning used by learned men, is in no way heretical nor should it be judged as "smacking of heresy." Third, I will clarify that they themselves err in the faith if they persist in the opinion that I cannot defend my conclusion from heresy, even in the sense permitted by the force of the words. Fourth and last, I will show beyond all doubt that they cannot excuse themselves from the fact that their condemnation of it was done without proper consideration.

<margin>The descent of Christ was given to us by Philip.</margin>
Before I explain the manner in which I hold that Christ descended to Hell, I wish to state this: although I hold that we are required to believe explicitly and in particular that Christ descended to Hell as an article of faith—handed down and promulgated to us by Philip <note>Traditional medieval belief held that each of the Twelve Apostles contributed one line to the "Apostles' Creed." Philip was credited with the line "He descended into Hell."</note>—it does not seem that every faithful person is required to believe in a *specific mode* of that descent. Rather, it seems sufficient for a Christian to believe that Christ descended to Hell not according to his body, nor according to body and soul together, but according to his soul alone; and that he should believe this descent of the soul happened in a way that was possible, fitting, expedient, and opportune. This is because a specific mode of that descent is not explicitly stated, nor does it seem to be proven by Holy Scripture, nor by any determination of the universal Church, nor by special revelation from God or the faithful report of the Apostles. In fact, what is more,

<margin>Scotus.</margin>
<margin>Francis de Mayronis.</margin>
Scotus <note>Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a major Scholastic philosopher who often disagreed with Thomas Aquinas.</note>, who was no stranger to the Holy Scriptures, says that it is not even held from Holy Scripture that Christ descended into Hell, as Francis de Mayronis <note>A 14th-century follower of Scotus.</note> reports in his fourth book of *Sentences*. How much less, then, can we say that a certain and determined *mode* of Christ's descent is held from Scripture? Thus, there has been no lack of doctors (whose condemnation I have never read, even regarding this article) to whom it seemed probable—and defensible within the truth of the article—that the soul of Christ was not *presentially* in Hell. They argue that all the authorities which Francis and other theologians cite can be interpreted as a descent by "effect" just as well as by "real presence." This follows

<margin>Thomas.</margin>

the way of interpreting Scripture followed by the very same doctors who hold the opposite. For we read in Ecclesiasticus 24: "I will penetrate all the lower parts of the earth." <note>original: "Penetrabo omnes inferiores partes terræ." This refers to the Latin Vulgate version of Sirach 24:45.</note> Explaining this in the third part of his *Summa*, Thomas [Aquinas] says it must be understood "by effect." Therefore, by the same token, someone might say that the authorities stating that He "penetrated" into Limbo or the "Bosom of Abraham" <note>The "Bosom of Abraham" was the place where the souls of the righteous stayed before Christ opened the gates of Heaven.</note> can be explained the same way. For to "penetrate" is the same as to enter "thoroughly" and "within." This is even stronger than "to descend." Therefore, if He is said to have not only entered but to have thoroughly entered the lower parts of the earth—not because He was really present there, but only because He was there through His effect—then He could also be said to have been in the Bosom of Abraham and to have entered the Bosom of Abraham by effect alone, and not by real presence. Now, I do not say these things because I ever believed that Christ, being present elsewhere, is said to have been in Hell *only* because He worked something there (like a King staying in his palace is said to be in another part of the province where he effectively accomplishes something by his authority and command). That was never my opinion, as will soon be clear in the declaration of my views. On the contrary, I firmly hold and have held, and have always said both publicly and privately, that if the soul of Christ was anywhere during those three days, it was in Hell, and it was truly present there.

<margin>Augustine.</margin>
But I wanted to say these things for a fuller examination of this matter, so that we might see the truth of that saying of Augustine in his *Book of Heresies*: that nothing is more difficult than defining what is or is not heretical. For this reason, he says it happened that when two very famous writers, Epiphanius and Philastrius, wrote about heresies, they disagreed greatly in counting them—for no other reason than that what seemed heretical to one did not seem so to the other. But now I come to reveal my opinion on the mode of Christ’s descent and to perfectly declare my conclusion. First, I will state its meaning in summary. Second, I will explain and prove it more broadly.

<margin>Note. Twofold opinion on separated substances.</margin>
The summary sense of my conclusion is this: Because Christ descended to Hell according to his soul alone, and since it seems that a soul—just like any "separated substance" <note>term: separated substance <gloss>An incorporeal being, such as an angel or a human soul after death, that exists without being joined to a physical body.</gloss></note>—cannot be located or moved locally except by reason of its "operation" <note>In Scholastic philosophy, "operation" refers to the action or work a being performs.</note>. Therefore, I say that to have descended to Hell, or to have been in Hell locally, does not seem to have applied to Christ except by reason of His operation; so that although the soul of Christ was truly present in Hell, His substance was not the reason for that presence, but only His operation. To understand these words more fully, one must note that there is a twofold opinion among those who posit that separated substances are in a place only through a "transient operation." Some say that a place is in no way owed to an incorporeal substance by reason of its substance, just as it is never truly "white" or "black." Thus, according to them, one can reasonably say that it is "not in a place" and "nowhere," just as it is truly said to be neither hot nor cold. They say the authorities of Scripture which seem to give angels a place (saying they are in Heaven or sent to this place or that) are to be understood like this: not that they are *here* or *there* (since they are not properly in a place), but that they *act* here or there, or begin to act where they did not act before.

<margin>The first: Gregory of Nyssa.</margin>
These people rely heavily on the words of Gregory of Nyssa, who says that since we ought to say "the spirit operates here," we say "it is here" only by an abuse of language. And so this opinion maintains that the substance of an angel or a separated soul can never be said...
<meta>catchword: to be [stā]</meta>

<summary>Pico begins his defense of his first condemned thesis: that Christ's descent into Hell was "by effect" rather than "real presence." He argues that since souls (separated substances) do not occupy physical space, their "presence" in a location is defined by where they act or operate.</summary>

# APOLOGIA
<note>original: "MARIAPOLITOGIA" — likely an OCR error for "APOLOGIA."</note>

<margin>
See the false opinion.
</margin>

...present in this or that place except in a negative sense—that is, by not being distant from it. But if it is ever said to be or to have been somewhere, it is the same as saying it is working or has worked somewhere. They add that this way of speaking is borrowed from physical objects; because we see that bodies cannot act unless they are present (at least according to common opinion), we believe the same of incorporeal beings. We conclude that wherever they work and wherever their operation is found, their substance must also be locally present. Finally, they conclude that it is a dullness of mind <note>original: "ruditas est ingenii"</note> and a failure of the imagination to be unable to understand that something can be a "being" <note>original: "ens"</note> and yet not be in a place. They argue it is a frivolous claim to say that "being" presupposes "working," because that proposition is only true in the sense that a non-existent thing cannot work. Indeed, an agent must be in a state of actuality, following the rule that some moving species will always be perceived. But it is not true in the sense that working in a place presupposes being in that place, since it remains possible for the worker to be of such a nature that local presence or distance is no more owed to it than whiteness or blackness is. Therefore, those who hold this opinion would say that the soul of Christ, when separated from his body, was in its substance neither in hell nor outside of hell, but was truly nowhere. However, it is said to have been in hell because it operated in hell; and it is said to have been most principally in that part of hell where it most principally operated. Although many doctors hold this opinion about the way of being present in a place, I do not hold it, nor did I follow it in my conclusion; rather, I held the one I shall immediately subjoin.

<margin>
The second opinion which the author held.
</margin>

There is, therefore, another opinion which says that a separated substance <note>A "separated substance" refers to a spiritual being not joined to a body, such as an angel or a human soul after death.</note>—such as an angel or a soul not united to a body—is indeed truly in a place. It is just as truly "definitively" <term>Definitively present: Being in a place by occupying its boundaries, rather than filling it like a liquid or a solid.</term> present in a local sense as a physical thing is "commensuratively" <term>Commensuratively present: Occupying space in a way that can be measured, where the object’s size matches the space it fills.</term> present. In this regard, this path agrees with the common view held by Scotus <note>John Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a hugely influential Franciscan theologian.</note> and all the Scotists. But they differ in this: the Scotists say that the definition and limitation of the essence—the internal determination of its substance—is the reason why a separated substance is in a place.

<margin>
Clarification of the opinion.
</margin>

However, this opinion which I followed in my conclusion says that, although a physical substance is in a place commensuratively, the reason it is in that place is not its "substance-ness" but its "quantity" (which is external and foreign to the definition of its substance). Likewise, although an incorporeal substance is truly and definitively in a place and locally present, the reason for its being in that place is not its substance, but its operation <note>The "operation" refers to the spiritual action or power the soul exerts on its surroundings.</note> passing from itself to the outside. I judge that this opinion should be understood in this way, and so understood, I judge it not only to be non-heretical, but even more probable than its opposite. Even if the finitude or limitation of a separated nature is the reason why it is not everywhere—or the reason why it is in one place and not simultaneously in another—it is not the reason for the separated substance's existence in that place in a simple sense. Rather, its effect or operation is the reason (taking "operation" to mean every relationship to a body or place, whether acting or being acted upon). This is distinct from the relationship of being locally present. I mean this as a matter of fact, without denying other possible ways a separated soul might descend or be located (as I say in the following conclusion), though such ways are unknown to us.

<margin>
He shows the necessity of his opinion.
</margin>

Having followed this opinion in my conclusion, I say that Christ was in hell only by his effect. Since he was not there except according to his soul, one must say (according to this opinion) that just as it does not belong to a physical substance to be somewhere commensuratively except

<column-break/>

by its quantity, so it did not belong to that soul to be in hell (where it is believed to have been) except by its effect and operation. But just as the reason for the presence of the souls of the Holy Fathers <note>The "Holy Fathers" refers to the Old Testament righteous who were waiting in the "Limbo of the Patriarchs" for Christ to rescue them.</note> was their relationship to that place—a state of being acted upon, such as their detention and binding to that place until the door was opened and they were drawn out by the Redeemer—so the reason for the presence of Christ’s soul was the operation he performed there. I will manifest below that this was my meaning and that the words of my conclusion intended this; there, I will clarify the conclusion itself and show that, according to the literal force and power of the words, it must not be judged heretical.

<margin>
Note.
</margin>

As to which opinion is truer regarding the way separated substances are in a place—that of the Scotists or that of those I have followed—I do not determine. I only say this: my opinion has been believed and held as most true by so many great masters and Catholic doctors, celebrated for their learning and holiness, that those who dare to judge the opinion of such proven doctors as heretical or "smacking of heresy" should be judged far more reckless than I, who prefer the authority of those ancient theologians over the rulings of the juniors. For this opinion which I follow is held assertively not only by Durandus, <note>Durandus of Saint-Pourçain (c. 1275–1334), a Dominican philosopher known for his independent mind.</note> but also by Bernard of Gannaco in his rebuttals to Henry's second *Quodlibet*.

# OF THE QUESTIONS

To claim that a separated substance <note>A "separated substance" refers to a being without a physical body, such as an angel or a human soul after death.</note> is not in a place except through an "operation" <note>In this context, "operation" refers to an action or effect produced by the spirit upon a physical object.</note> consisting of external local motion or real alteration is considered an error. That this is the meaning of the article is clear from Article 77, which states, as if by way of explanation, that if there were a separated substance that did not move any body in this world, it would not be contained within the universe; this is marked as an error. Observe that just as the article cited by my opponent claims it is an error to say an angel is in a place only through operation, so too this article says it is an error to say a separated substance is not included in this universe except through the movement of a body. Thus, "operation" in Article 204 seems to mean the same thing as "motion" in Article 77. However, the position I hold does not claim that an angel is in a place *only* through operation in that specific sense, as will be clear in the response to the third point.

<margin>Second point: Godfrey of Fontaines. Note.</margin>
Furthermore, the solemn doctor Godfrey of Fontaines says that these articles require significant correction, because some are false and others contradict one another. Indeed, in this matter, it is necessary either that the article be interpreted in the manner just proposed, or that there be a manifest contradiction within the articles themselves; I prove it thus: Article 218 says that if it is understood that an angel's substance is not the reason for its being in a place, then it is true to say that, according to its substance, it is nowhere.

<margin>Henry.</margin>
And Henry <note>Henry of Ghent (c. 1217–1293), a major scholastic philosopher.</note> testifies in his *Quodlibet* II, question 9, that all the masters of theology, when gathered together, unanimously agreed on this: that the substance of an angel is not the reason for that angel being in a place. He mentions that he was among those masters who made this determination. Henry further adds in the same place that, by similar reasoning, it is undoubtedly true that if an angel does not apply its power—namely, through its intellect and will—to a place by acting upon it, then its power (intellect and will) is simply not the reason for its being in that place. This is because its power is no less abstract than its substance. Therefore, it follows that we must either admit that the reason for its being in a place is something acting upon a body (whatever that may be, which is the position I follow), or there will be a manifest contradiction in the articles. Hence, Henry confesses in the same passage that he cannot understand how a separated substance can be in a place unless it does something or is acted upon by the place or by a thing existing in that place.

<margin>Third point: Giles. Note.</margin>
Giles <note>Giles of Rome (c. 1243–1316), a prominent theologian and student of Thomas Aquinas.</note> and many others say that these articles are of no concern, because they were created without summoning all the doctors of Paris, but rather at the request of certain chapters. Regardless of that, I wish to say two things: First, our proposition—Article 218—does no less to support us than Article 204 does to oppose us. Second, it is certain that even the Parisians themselves admit that those articles do not bind all the faithful; nor are we held to believe them except insofar as they rely on Holy Scripture or the determinations of the universal Church.

<margin>The saying of the English.</margin>
Thus, the English are fond of saying that those articles "do not cross the sea" <note>A common medieval academic joke: the condemnations issued by the Bishop of Paris had no legal or theological authority outside of his specific jurisdiction (Paris).</note>; and so we, if one may joke in such a serious matter, can say they "do not cross the Alps." Therefore, even if my conclusion were against an article, those who condemned me should remember that they were entirely in error by condemning me, for they claimed my conclusion was against the Apostles' Creed, when they should have said it was against the "Parisian Creed"—though even that is false, as we have already shown.

<margin>Declaration of the articles.</margin>
It seems to me that the true understanding of those articles is this: In Article 204, if it speaks of operation in the common sense mentioned above, the intent is that even if all

<column-break/>

operation were set aside, the finiteness or limitation of a separated nature would still be the reason why it is not everywhere, or the reason why, if it is in one place, it is not simultaneously in another entire place—and this in both cases by its nature. In Article 228, I believe the intent is that the substance, or the finiteness of the substance, is not the reason for an angel being simply in a place. By explaining them this way, there is no contradiction in the articles; and articles understood in this way are not only not against my position, but they confirm it entirely from both sides, as is clear from the declaration of the position stated above.

<margin>Solution of the second argument according to many.</margin>
Regarding the second point, many respond by granting that it is possible for an incorporeal substance to exist without an operation passing to the outside. Given this, the argument seems to suggest that one of three "inconveniences" <note>In medieval logic, an "inconvenience" refers to a logically problematic or absurd conclusion.</note> would follow.

<margin>"Part" is understood in two ways.</margin>
The first is that since it is a part of the universe, it would be "inconvenient" for it not to be *in* the universe. To this, they would say that the one arguing is using the word "part" equivocally. For if by "part of the universe" one understands something that has a determined location in the universe, then they will say that when an angel is not operating, it cannot be called a part of the universe. But if one understands "part of the beings"—that is, one of the entities and natures of the universe—then they grant it is a part of the universe, and indeed one of the noblest. But it does not seem to follow from this that it must have a location or a definition relative to a place.

<margin>"To be everywhere" is understood in two ways.</margin>
The second "inconvenience" is that it cannot be said to be everywhere, as this is proper to God alone. To this, it is said that "to be everywhere" in the way theologians say God is everywhere—namely, by essence, power, and presence—is proper to God and can belong to no created nature. However, whether "to be everywhere" (meaning being here or there indifferently, or truly being according to a substance that is not distant from any place) is repugnant to a creature, you may hear Henry in his *Quodlibet* VII, question 9, saying the following:

<margin>Henry: Twofold limitation.</margin>
In a creature, a twofold limitation can be understood. One is in nature and essence, by which it is finite and contained within certain bounds; in this way, God alone is unlimited and infinite in nature. Another limitation of nature can be understood: a limitation to a location, by which it is so finite and contained within certain limits that it must be somewhere, and not "nowhere" or "everywhere." It must be "here" such that it is not "there," or even if not determinately "here" or "there," it must be under the determination of being "either here, or there, or somewhere." This limitation belongs to the category of "Where." I see clearly how every creature differs from God by this first limitation. However, as for how it is necessary for every creature to differ and be distant from Him by the second limitation—because He is everywhere, while every creature is necessarily somewhere but not everywhere—I say that I am entirely ignorant of this. These are Henry’s literal words, from which we can see clearly enough that Henry could not understand how the point they bring up as an "inconvenience" is actually inconvenient.

The third "inconvenience" is that unless it is granted to be somewhere, it must be granted to be nowhere. To this, hear Blessed Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the most influential medieval theologian.</note> responding in his commentary on the first book of the *Sentences*, distinction 37, as follows:

<margin>Saint Thomas.</margin>
"I must say," he writes, "that I do not consider it inconvenient that an angel can exist without a place and not be in a place when it has no operation regarding a place; nor is it inconvenient for it then to be said to be 'nowhere' or in no place. But nevertheless, this is not imaginable, because the imagination does not transcend the physical continuum." These are the literal words of Thomas.

<margin>"Operation" is understood in two ways.</margin>
To the third point, I say that the argument proceeds from an incomplete understanding of our position. For our position does not understand "operation" (by which an incorporeal thing is located) to mean only an operation that is an external local motion or a real alteration, as even...

-># APOLOGY<-

<margin>St. Thomas [Aquinas]</margin>
We touched upon this in the response to the first point in the exposition of the Parisian article. But "operation" <note>original: "operationem"; here meaning the action or influence a spirit exerts on a physical body.</note> is taken broadly for every motion, influence, or relationship signified by the mode of a transitory operation passing into a body from an angel, or vice versa. That this is the correct understanding of the position is clear from the words of Thomas in the *First Book of Sentences*, distinction 37, question 1, article 1, where he seems to follow this opinion, saying: "It remains, therefore, that an angel cannot be defined and determined to a place except through action or operation. I speak of operation commonly, insofar as the angel relates to the body contained in the place in the manner of a presider or minister, or in some way as an agent or patient." These are Thomas’s words verbatim. From these words, the response to the argument is clear; for although angels do not have an operation toward the empyrean heaven <note>The highest, most spiritual part of the heavens in medieval cosmology.</note> that consists of local motion or real physical change, they nevertheless have something that functions like a transitory operation, such as their "presiding" or something similar. Regarding the fourth point, upon which that Master General so heavily relied, what needs to be said is clear enough from the words of Henry [of Ghent] cited above in the solution to the second point; nevertheless, let us hear

<margin>St. Thomas [Aquinas]</margin>
what Saint Thomas says about that reasoning. Some say that an angel is not in a place "circumscriptively" <note>Filling a space based on physical dimensions, like water in a glass.</note> but "definitively," because it is determined to a certain place such that it is in this place and not another, since its essence is finite. For they say that because an angel is a created being, it must be understood as being limited to a specific location. But this is a

<margin>The word "End" is taken in two ways.</margin>
very crude proof, because it proceeds from an equivocation of the word "end" <note>original: "finis"; meaning both a "limit" in space and a "definition" in logic.</note>. For when the essence of an angel is called "finite," the "end" is taken as the limit of essence and power—just as a definition is called a "term"—and not as the limit of physical dimension. A "place," however, is called finite according to the three dimensions of quantity. An "end" in these two different senses has no shared measurement or proportion. Therefore, it is not necessary that what is finite in essence must be limited by the boundaries of a physical place. These are Thomas’s words to the letter. From which it follows that, if Thomas is not lying, that Master is "crude" indeed, for he called his own crude proof a "demonstration." Regarding the other argument about the point,

<margin>What a point is.</margin>
I say that it is even cruder than the first argument. For a "point" is a thing belonging to the category of quantity, having a position by its very nature. An incorporeal thing, however, is entirely removed from position; and truly, it is a great crudeness of mind to imagine that the "indivisibility" of a spirit is the same as the "indivisibility" of a point.

<margin>Arguments against the opponent. Point. Unity.</margin>
To make this even clearer to that Master, let him tell me, I pray: if there were a "separate Unity" <note>A pure mathematical "one" existing outside of physical objects.</note>, would it have a determined position? Certainly it is clear that it would not, since a "unity" is distinguished from a "point" precisely because a point has position, while a unity does not. But it is manifest that an angel, and indeed any incorporeal substance, is even more abstract than any quantity, whether continuous [like a line] or discrete [like a number]. For Metaphysics, as is clear to everyone, deals with things more abstract than Arithmetic (which is one of the mathematical sciences). Therefore, it can be said even less of an angel that it has a "position." If this Master cannot imagine the abstraction of an angel, let him at least consider the abstraction of a Unity. Let him hear what should be said of him according to

<margin>Henry [of Ghent].</margin>
Henry. For he, speaking of this matter in the place cited above, says: "Those who cannot understand an angel according to the nature of its substance as a Unity, without the notion of a point, are those of whom the Commentator <note>Averroes, the famous 12th-century commentator on Aristotle.</note> speaks in the second book of the *Metaphysics*: those in whom the imaginative power dominates the reasoning power." And therefore, as he says, we see that such people do not believe demonstrations unless their imagination accompanies them. They think of everything as something having a position in space, like a point. Such people are "melancholic," and though they make the best mathematicians, they are naturally inept at science.

<column-break/>

These are Henry's words verbatim. From which it follows that, according to Henry, this Master is ill-disposed to the study of natural philosophy, worse for the study of metaphysics, and worst of all for the study of theology, which deals with the most abstract things of all. There remains for him, therefore, only an aptitude for mathematics; and since he has not practiced in that field, let him judge for himself what judgment should be made of him. Now that the arguments commonly brought against the foundations of my position have been resolved—the position I followed in my conclusion regarding the manner of Christ’s descent—I wish also to bring forth

<margin>Albert the Great.</margin>
the words of our Albert [the Great], no less great in learning than in name, which I remember reading in his *Physics*. In the first treatise of the fourth book, after explaining Aristotle's point that the ancients were deceived in believing that just as "that which is not is nowhere," so "nothing is a being unless it is in a place," he digresses. Then, upon that passage, he says: "There are also many of the moderns who concede the conclusion of this reasoning, even though they know the logic is invalid. For we know from logic that one cannot prove a point by simply destroying the premise. Therefore, although it is true that 'that which is not, is nowhere,' it does not follow from this that 'that which is, is somewhere [in a place].'" And even though this does not follow logically, there are many who say that everything that exists is in some place, using this reasoning: "Everything that exists is a particular thing. A particular thing is 'here and now,' and what is 'here and now' is in a place. Therefore, everything that exists is in a place." Furthermore, they say everything that has a "defined essence" is constrained within its own limits, and what has a defined essence is defined in a place. They distinguish this using [St.] John

<margin>John Damascene. Being in a place in two ways.</margin>
Damascene, who says that "being in a place" can be said in two ways. First, something is in a place "circumscriptively," where a beginning, middle, and end can be assigned to it in space—and in this way, they say bodies are in a place. Second, something is in a place "definitively," whose essence is so finitely enclosed in one place that nothing of it is found outside that place—and in this way, they say indivisible things, like intelligences [angels] and souls, are in a place. But we do not believe these things. For even the highest

<margin>Explanation of the words of the conclusion regarding the force of the speech.</margin>
heaven is not defined or circumscribed by a place, because everything in a place is enclosed and contained by that place, and an "intelligence" by its very nature is not in a place nor in any spatial dimension. These are Albert’s words to the letter. He does not approve of that common distinction between being in a place "definitively" and "circumscriptively"—a distinction which some Masters thought it a sacrilege to deny. Now, finally, it remains for me to show how the words of my conclusion are to be understood, and to declare that, according to the proper force of the language, the conclusion is Catholic <note>Meaning "orthdox" or "theologically sound."</note>. The conclusion says: "Christ did not truly and according to a real presence—as Thomas and the common way hold—descend to the underworld, but only in terms of his effect." Here it must be noted that the word "and" in "and according to a real presence" is used to link the ideas, and the word "as" in "as Thomas holds" is used to specify and define, as I will soon explain. From this, it is clear that the aforementioned conclusion is a "negative cumulative proposition" <note>A logical term for a statement that denies several things joined together.</note>. Its sense is:
