-># OF THE QUESTIONS<-

It is not the case that Christ truly and according to a real presence—in the way that Thomas posits—descended to hell, etc. And that conjunctive statement <note>A statement combining two conditions with "and."</note> is equivalent to an affirmative disjunctive statement <note>A statement offering an "either/or" choice.</note> of contradictory parts: namely, this one: Christ did not truly descend to hell, or he did not descend to hell according to a real presence, etc. From this, it follows that by inferring from the said conclusion that "Christ did not truly descend to hell," one is arguing from the whole affirmative disjunction to one of its parts specifically. However, such an argument fails because of the "consequent" <note>A logical fallacy where one assumes that because the whole is true, a specific part must be true in a particular way.</note>. For an affirmative disjunction is the result of its parts. It follows further that by reason of the falsity of the aforementioned part, the whole aforementioned disjunction should not be falsified. Thus, in a similar case, this proposition is true: "Socrates is a man." And this one is false: "Socrates is a man and God is not God." To argue from this that "therefore Socrates is not a man" is surely childish. Similarly, from this negative conjunction—"Christ did not truly and according to a real presence, as Thomas posits, descend," etc.—to argue "therefore Christ did not truly descend" is childish; it is the mark of a man who utterly lacks knowledge of logic, philosophy, and even theology. For I do not only intend for that proposition to be true in my conclusion—"Christ did not truly descend to hell"—but not even this one: "Christ, or the soul of Christ, was not presentially in hell, both through a real and true presence or substance." Rather, I only intend that he was not there by a real presence *in the way* that Thomas and the common path <note>The "common path" (communis via) refers to the standard theological consensus of the era.</note> posit. Therefore, I said that <term>the word 'as'</term><note>original: "ly vt"; 'ly' was a technical term used by medieval logicians to indicate they were discussing a specific word as a term.</note> is held specifically and determinatively regarding the "real presence." Therefore, this does not hold: "He was not really present there in the way such a Doctor says; therefore, he was not really present there."

<margin>Scotus. St. Bonaventure. Nominalists. St. Thomas. The Common Path.</margin>
The common path, however—that is, the path of Scotus, Bonaventure, all the Scotists, and almost all the Nominalists <note>Major schools of medieval thought named after Duns Scotus, St. Bonaventure, and those who believed universal concepts are just names (Nominalists).</note>—holds that he was present there in such a way that his substance was the reason for his presence and locatability. Because it seems to me that Thomas also follows this opinion in this matter, I therefore said, "as Thomas and the common path posit."

<margin>University of Paris.</margin>
I call the "common path" of theologians that which is commonly held now in Paris, where the study of theology chiefly flourishes. For there, almost everyone proceeds in this matter concerning the presence of the soul in a place alongside the Scotists and Nominalists. And I, for this reason alone—namely, out of reverence for the University of Paris—did not wish to propose this conclusion of mine except as "probable," even though I saw that according to many of the most proven doctors, it could even be proposed "assertively" <note>An "assertive" statement is one made as a definitive fact; a "probable" one is presented as a strong possibility for debate.</note>. Moreover, it is clear that the word "as" can be held determinatively in common speech. For if someone says "the attributes are not distinguished, as Scotus says," that proposition would have a double proper sense among everyone. One would be by taking the word "as" relatively, and it would be equivalent to saying that "the attributes are not distinguished,"

<margin>Scotus. Thomists.</margin>
which—namely, that the attributes are not distinguished—is what Scotus says. And the proposition would be false even according to the Thomists <note>Followers of Thomas Aquinas.</note>, because even they concede that the attributes are in some way distinguished. The other sense would be by taking the word "as" determinatively and specifically, and it would be equivalent to saying "the attributes are not distinguished in that mode of distinction in which Scotus says they are distinguished," and then among the Thomists the proposition would be true. And it is the same in any proposition where, after an opinion is recited, the authority of someone is placed, joined by this word "as." If, therefore, this manner of speaking—both proper and most common among all theologians—is conceded, it must also be

<column-break/>

conceded that in our proposition, in which it is said "Christ did not descend as Thomas says," the word "as" can just as well be held relatively—so the sense would be "Christ did not descend," which descent Thomas says occurred—as it can be held specifically and as an equivalent to this: "although Christ descended presentially, it was not, however, in that presential manner which the common path says," and that is the sense I intend.

<margin>Objection.</margin>
But perhaps someone would say: "You still do not escape, because you then add, 'but only as to effect'; therefore, you do not only exclude real presence in the way the common path posits it, but you simply exclude all real presence, since you say 'only as to effect.'" Thus, these people will say that the proposition is not merely a negative conjunction as you say—denying, for instance, presence in the manner of Thomas, etc.—but also an affirmative one, saying affirmatively that Christ was in hell

<margin>Solution.</margin>
only as to effect. But this objection is crude. For this word "but" <note>original: "sed"</note> is an adversative word, and by its power, the following words import an affirmative truth opposite to the statement that the upper part of the conclusion denies. If, therefore, as has been proven in the upper part, only the presence of the soul *through substance* is denied—not as to *what* it is, but as to the *how*—that is, it is not denied that the substance was present, but that the substance was the *reason* for the presence. So too in this last part, where it posits affirmatively and precisely that he was in hell through "effect," it must be understood not as to the thing located, but as to the reason for locating. To be brief, the sense that can be clear even to the unlearned is this: since the finitude of the substance was not the reason for his presence, the effect alone was such a reason.

<margin>Epilogue of the Conclusion.</margin>
Gathering this together briefly, I say that Christ truly descended to hell, and that he was in hell through a real presence. But I say that he was not there "truly and presentially" in the way that Thomas and the common path say, because his substance was not the reason for his being in that place (as they posit), but rather his operation. And how probable this opinion is, and how it is believed by many Catholic and most excellent doctors, has already been made clear enough above; we have also sufficiently explained that by the virtue of the speech itself, it should be judged true and not heretical.

<margin>Arius.</margin>
For we know that this is true: "Christ did not, as God and man in the way Arius posits, satisfy for us," because although it is true that he satisfied as God and man, it is nevertheless false that he existed as God and man in the way Arius posits <note>Arius was a 4th-century priest whose "heresy" involved denying the full divinity of Christ. Pico is using him as a grammatical example: you can agree with the words "God and man" while disagreeing with the heretical definition behind them.</note>. Likewise, although it is true that Christ was truly and presentially in hell, it is nevertheless probable and believed by many that he was not there truly and presentially in the way Thomas and the common path say, in the manner explained above. But one scruple seems to remain: that this was not my intention when I proposed the conclusion.

<margin>Objection.</margin>
Because if Thomas, in the *First Book of Sentences*, also holds this path himself—that operation is the reason for an angel being in a place—it seems that the conclusion is also true according to Thomas. Therefore, when I say "not as Thomas posits," it seems I was opining something different about that descent than what I have said.

<margin>Solution.</margin>
They would not have this scruple if they had considered my conclusions well. For I am of this opinion: that Thomas felt differently in this matter concerning the way separate things exist in a place, and

<margin>That Thomas thought differently regarding this question. Scotists.</margin>
he did not follow the same opinion everywhere. Therefore, although in the *First Book of Sentences* he seems to hold this path that I follow in my conclusion, nevertheless elsewhere—as in the *Fourth Book of Sentences* and especially in the third part of the *Summa*, where he treats this descent and from which [writings]...

<summary>Pico defends his thesis on Christ's descent into hell by using logic to show that denying the *manner* of a presence (as Thomas Aquinas describes it) is not the same as denying the presence itself. He argues that Christ was present through his "operation" (action) rather than his "substance" occupying a physical space, noting that Aquinas himself was inconsistent on this topic across his various works.</summary>

...his opinion must be judged, and it seems to agree with the opinion of the **Scotists** <note>Followers of Duns Scotus, a major medieval philosopher and rival to the Thomist school.</note>. It follows that he was there by essence in such a way that his essence was for him the **reason for being localizable** <note>original: "ratio locabilitatis"; the underlying principle that allows a spiritual being to be in a physical place</note> and not solely his effect or operation. For **Thomas** <note>St. Thomas Aquinas</note> says there that the soul of Christ was present by his **effect** <note>Through the power or result of his presence</note> in other parts of hell, but by **essence** in **limbo** <note>The "Limbo of the Patriarchs," where the righteous of the Old Testament waited for Christ.</note>, etc. From this statement, I argue as follows: Wherever something is present through that which is its reason for being localizable, it is there through its substance and real presence. Therefore, if "effect" was the reason for the localizability of Christ's soul, then wherever he was present by effect, he was there by the real presence of his substance. But according to Thomas, he was in some places by effect where he was not present by his real substance. Therefore, according to Thomas, effect was not his reason for being localizable. This is what moved me to probably believe that Thomas, on this point, 

<margin>
Disagreement among the Thomists.
</margin>

walks with the Scotists. But whatever the case may be regarding the opinion of Thomas, it is irrelevant to the matter at hand: because to err regarding the opinion of Thomas is not to err in faith. Indeed, there is often a manifold opinion among the **Thomists** <note>Followers of Thomas Aquinas</note> concerning his actual opinion. It suffices that this is evidently clear: when I proposed the conclusion, I believed this was the opinion of Thomas, and I am not now twisting the proposition into a sense different from the one I held then. That I 

<margin>

It is well known, however, that Scotus expressly says that even if all operation were excluded, a place is still owed to incorporeal substances. Therefore, it was necessary for me to believe that Thomas held this same view. And so, although I firmly held that Christ was truly and presentially in hell—and in this I agreed with Thomas and all Catholics—nevertheless, because I thought Thomas believed his substance was the reason for his localizability and not his operation, I said in my conclusion "not in the way that Thomas and the common way posits." marvelous to anyone that Thomas follows one opinion in one place and another in another. Likewise, in *Sentences* II, he follows the Commentator's opinion on the matter of the heavens, which he later rejects in his commentary on *The Heavens*, Book II, and in his *Summa*. Likewise, in *Sentences* IV and in his *Questions on Boethius's De Trinitate*, he holds the Commentator's path regarding "indeterminate dimensions," yet in his own later booklet (as it is believed) and in many other places, he does not hold it. Likewise, in *Sentences* I, he says that the same action understands the "intelligible thing" and the "act of understanding" itself. But in the First Part of the *Summa* and in *Sentences* III, he holds that a "reflexive action" <note>Thinking about one's own thinking</note> differs from a "direct action." Likewise, in his writings, he holds that the soul of Christ, insofar as it is joinable to a body, was like the soul of a **traveler** <note>original: "viator"; a person still living their earthly life and not yet seeing God directly.</note>; but insofar as it is joinable to the Word, it was like the soul of a **comprehensor** <note>original: "comprehensoris"; one who has achieved the "beatific vision" or direct sight of God in heaven.</note>. However, in the *Summa*, he holds that the soul of Christ was totally and in all respects like that of a comprehensor, and that the fact that it did not transfer the gift of clarity and impassibility <note>The inability to suffer or be harmed</note> into the body was due to a divine dispensation. Likewise, he feels one way about the knowledge of Christ in his writings and another way in the *Summa*, and so it is with many other things where one can see that he followed different opinions in different places. Therefore, if these men insist that the opinion about "mode of being in a place through operation" also belongs to Thomas, they will have nothing more against 

<column-break/>

And the contradictory of this statement—"by 'the common way' in theological matters we can appropriately understand the way that is commonly held in that University in which, at the time of the speaker, the study of theology most flourishes"—is not a matter of faith. And the contradictory of this statement—"at this time the study of theology flourishes more at the **University of Paris** than elsewhere"—is not a matter of faith. And the contradictory of this statement—"at the University of Paris it is now commonly held that the limitation of nature is the reason for the localizability of a separated substance"—is not a matter of faith. And the contradictory of this statement—"Scotus and the majority of the **Nominalists** <note>A school of philosophy that argued universal concepts are just names, not real things.</note> hold the aforementioned opinion, and Thomas seems to hold it in the third part of the *Summa* where he deals with the descent of Christ"—is not a matter of faith. Then it follows: if the contradictories of these statements are not matters of faith, it follows that to posit, believe, and dispute these statements is not heretical in itself or against the faith; nor can the person who posits, holds, and disputes them, either separately or together, be accused of heresy. But from these statements, when posited together and collectively, follows the position of my conclusion exactly as it stands. Therefore, one who posits my conclusion exactly as it stands cannot be accused of heresy. Proof...

# ON THE QUESTIONS

[conclusions] <note>The text begins mid-word: "conclusiones."</note> of all the aforementioned points are held from what has been written above. For concerning the first point mentioned, it is clear that it is not only not heretical, but is even believed and approved by many Catholic doctors <note>Teachers/theologians of the Church</note> for reasons opposing its contrary. In the second point, all logicians and all theologians who have ever known logic agree. So it is with all the others, concerning which, even if someone might doubt whether they are true or false, no one is so crude, so lacking in all learning, so ignorant of the faith and of those things which pertain to the faith, that they would say those things cannot be believed without heresy, and thus that their contradictions are "of the faith" <note>A technical term meaning a mandatory dogma of the Church.</note>. Then, let it be argued further as follows: Anyone who believes that this conclusion—"Christ, etc."—cannot have a Catholic sense according to the force of the words and according to proper and non-derived usage, believes the contradiction of one or some of the seven aforementioned points to be "of the faith." But those who hold something to be "of the faith" which is *not* "of the faith" have a wrong understanding of the faith, because it is against the word of the Lord in **Deuteronomy 4**: *You shall not add to the word that I speak to you, nor shall you take away from it.* Therefore, those who have a wrong understanding of my conclusion (as stated above) have a wrong understanding of the faith.

<margin>An Exclamation</margin>
I see, O Supreme Pontiff; see, O most august senators of the apostolic order; see, O entire Rome, indeed Italy, indeed the Church of Christians, how they are refuted in this first proposition! In this one, they were lightning-striking me the most, and in this one, many seemed to have some handle not so much for accusing me as for excusing their own condemnation of me. Regarding the other conclusions, it will be clearer than light that they could not have had even the smallest occasion for condemning them as heresy. And now, concerning this first one in which they were strongest, it has been seen what its nature is, and whether it was condemned by them rightly or wrongly—especially since the sense I intended through it has now been explained to them, and applied to the words of the conclusion without any abuse or distortion of terms or speech. And

<margin>
Finally he defends the conclusion by the authority of Durandus in abundance.
Words of Durandus.
</margin>
although this suffices for the defense of my conclusion, yet for a fuller discussion of this matter, I say that even interpreting the conclusion in the way they interpreted it—namely, that Christ was in hell effectively only and not by presence—it might still perhaps seem to some that it was determined presumptuously by them that the conclusion was simply heretical. For it is a fact that **Durandus** <note>Durandus of Saint-Pourçain (c. 1275–1334), a Dominican theologian known for his independent and often controversial "Nominalist" views.</note>, a greatest theologian of the Order of Preachers who perhaps exceeds these masters of learning no less than I am exceeded by them, held that opinion to be probable and well-defensible along with the truth of the Article of Faith. For thus it is written in the *Third Book of the Sentences*: "Regarding the third point, we proceed as follows: and it seems that Christ, according to the soul, did not descend into hell, because the same finite thing cannot be in different places at the same time. But the soul of Christ, since it was a finite creature, was in paradise with the soul of the thief immediately after death, to whom it was said in **Luke 23**: *Today you will be with me in paradise.* Therefore, at least then, it could not be in hell. Also, those things which Christ did and suffered in the assumed nature were ordained for human salvation. But it would not have benefited this salvation for Christ to descend to the underworld, because through the passion which he sustained in this world, he liberated us from all fault and punishment; therefore it seems that Christ did not descend to the underworld. To the contrary is what is said in the **Creed**: *He descended into hell.* And the Apostle says in **Ephesians 4**: *But that he ascended, what is it but because he also descended into the lower parts of the earth?* (Gloss: i.e., to the underworld). I respond that since the Article is

<column-break/>

that Christ descended to the underworld, and it cannot be understood by reason of his divinity (according to which he is everywhere) nor by reason of his body (according to which he was in the tomb), it remains that it be understood by reason of the soul of the human nature. Two things must be seen: first, by what mode the soul of Christ descended to hell; second, to which hell he descended. As for the first,

<margin>
How angels move to a place.
</margin>
it should be known that since a separated soul is not a body nor a power in a body, it cannot be said that the soul of Christ descended to the underworld by that kind of motion or descent by which bodies move. It is not clearly evident that it moved by that kind of motion by which angels move. For angels are said to move from place to place insofar as they operate successively in different places. A separated soul is not said to have any operation regarding a place or regarding a body existing in a place because, since by its nature it is determined to a specific body, it cannot move or act upon another except through its own body; but it lacks that while it is separated. Therefore, the soul cannot be moved from place to place by reason of an operation it has regarding a place or a body existing in a place. Nevertheless, notwithstanding this,

<margin>
The descent of separated souls to hell is understood in two ways; a double assignment.
Note the double effect.
</margin>
a separated soul can be said to have descended to hell in two ways. One way is according to **assignment** <note>original: "deputationem"; being legally or divinely assigned to a place</note>, and thus the souls of the damned are simply said to descend to hell, because they are simply assigned so that, having resumed their bodies, they may be in hell, which is why they are said to be there—these are simply assigned. However, the souls of the holy fathers are said to be in **Limbo** <note>The "Limbo of the Patriarchs," the dwelling of the righteous who died before Christ's redemption.</note> or to have descended to Limbo because of an assignment that is not simple but conditional: because, having resumed their bodies, they would remain there unless they were liberated by the Redeemer. But in this way, the soul of Christ is not said to have descended to hell (namely, because of assignment), because every such assignment is because of a contracted or committed fault, which was not in Christ. In another way, a separated soul can be said to descend to hell according to **effect**, and in this way the soul of Christ can be said to descend to hell because of a double effect which he had in those who were in hell. One effect was the offering of the **Divine Vision** <note>The "Beatific Vision," or direct perception of God, which constitutes the happiness of Heaven.</note> which they lacked, toward which the passion of Christ acted by way of merit. And because the whole merit depends principally on the act of the soul, therefore this effect is attributed to him as to the principal source of meriting. Also, by appropriation: just as Christ was blessed according to the soul, so according to it, he is attributed as having been the cause of blessedness in others. For it is fitting that a being in potentiality be reduced to act by that which is in act <note>A core principle of Aristotelian logic: something can only become "actual" (in act) if acted upon by something already "actual."</note>. The other effect was according to

<margin>
Whence something is said to be led from potentiality to act through a mediated act.
Dionysius.
First reason.
Second.
</margin>
certain people toward whom the soul of Christ acted directly by way of an agent—namely, to illuminate the souls of the fathers who were in Limbo concerning the mysteries which fall under revelation. For according to **Dionysius** <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-century Christian Neoplatonist.</note> in the seventh chapter of the *Celestial Hierarchy*: Christ, according to the soul, has the task of teaching the angels. And by reason of this double effect, the soul of Christ can be said to have descended to hell. This is confirmed by a triple reason. The first is because moving or descending belongs to a separated soul not by the mode of motion of bodies, but by the mode in which moving belongs to a spiritual substance. But for other spiritual substances—namely, God and the angel—moving from place to place does not belong to them through a motion that is subjectively within themselves, but through the effect they have in other things. Therefore, in a similar way it belongs to a separated soul, and it belonged to the soul of Christ. The second reason is this: Christ is said to have descended to hell in order to illuminate the souls of the holy fathers to see God...

<summary>Pico defends his thesis on Christ's descent into Hell by appealing to the Pope and citing the theologian Durandus. He argues that a soul's "descent" is not physical movement, but an exercise of power and the granting of the Divine Vision to the righteous in Limbo.</summary>

<meta>Pico continues his defense by citing the theologian Durandus of Saint-Pourçain to argue that his own views on Christ's descent into Hell are within the bounds of acceptable theological debate. He is addressing the specific charge that his "conclusions" are heretical by showing that even famous, respected Church doctors held similar nuanced views.</meta>

# A P O L O G Y

<margin>Third [argument].</margin>
At the very same instant in which Christ died, the holy fathers <note>The patriarchs and prophets of the Old Testament waiting in Limbo.</note> saw God; however, at that same instant, the soul of Christ could not have been in Hell through physical movement. Therefore, He did not descend there by a movement that occurred within Himself, but rather through the effect He had upon others. Similarly, just as the soul of Christ is said to have been in Hell with the souls of the holy fathers during those three days, so too in that three-day period (or part of it) it is said in **Luke 23**: *Today you shall be with me in paradise.* But this cannot be understood as a location reached through physical movement. According to those who posit that a spirit is moved from place to place *definitively* <note>A technical term meaning being in a place without occupying physical space.</note>, the same spirit cannot be in multiple places at once, nor can it be moved by multiple movements tending toward multiple places simultaneously. Therefore, it must be understood according to its effect.

<margin>Paradise is spoken of in two ways.</margin>
If anyone should say that "Paradise" is spoken of in two ways: one way as a physical place, namely the empyrean heaven <note>The highest part of heaven, believed by medieval scholars to be made of pure light or fire.</note>, and in this sense the soul of Christ was not in Paradise until after the Ascension. In the other way, "Paradise" refers to the vision of the divine essence <note>The "Beatific Vision," or seeing God face-to-face.</note>. In this sense, the soul of Christ was in Paradise from the instant of His conception, and the soul of the thief was there on the very day of the Passion. In this way, it is not contradictory for the soul of Christ to have been in Paradise (meaning He saw God) while simultaneously being locally in Hell. 

<margin>Hell is spoken of in two ways.</margin>
If this is said, it does not hold up, because just as "Paradise" is spoken of in two ways, so is "Hell." In one way, "Hell" is the place corresponding to the space beneath the earth. In the other way, it is the lack of the divine vision. Therefore, just as the soul of the thief is said to have been with Christ in Paradise only <gloss>because</gloss> by the merit of Christ’s passion the thief's soul saw God, so Christ’s soul is said to have been with the souls of the chosen fathers in Hell only because their souls—which lacked the divine vision and were thus said to be in "Hell"—were purged of this lack by the merit of His passion. Both, therefore, must be understood equally regarding their *effect*, not regarding a physical location or local movement within the soul itself. Whoever says this has spoken with probability, even if it seems to preserve the article of faith and the words of Scripture. However, because divine power is not fully grasped by human reason, one must not stubbornly assert that the soul of Christ could not have descended into Hell by some other means unknown to us. 

To the first argument, it must be said that the same finite thing cannot be in multiple places at once *definitively* or *circumscriptively* <note>Occupying space so that it is "measured" by its boundaries.</note>. The soul of Christ is not claimed to have been in Paradise and Hell at the same time in that manner. But according to *effect*, nothing prevents a finite thing from being in multiple places when those effects are compatible and subject to the power of the same agent. Thus, Christ’s soul is said to have been in Paradise and Hell simultaneously because, by His merit, the thief's soul saw God (which is to be in Paradise), and the fathers’ souls (which lacked the vision and were thus in "Hell") were freed from this lack. Indeed, according to one and the same effect—namely the liberation of the fathers—the soul of Christ could be said to be in Paradise and Hell at once, considering the starting point and the ending point of that effect. By reason of the lack of divine vision from which they were freed, His soul was in Hell; by reason of the vision to which they were admitted, His soul was in Paradise. 

To the second argument, it must be said that by the very fact that we are freed from guilt and punishment through Christ's passion, Christ is said to have descended into Hell, because by the merit of His passion some were taken from the punishments of Hell. For that "descent" is not measured by a local movement existing in the soul,

<column-break/>

but according to the effect He had on those to be saved. These are the words of Durandus <note>Durandus of Saint-Pourçain (c. 1275–1334), a famous Dominican philosopher known as "The Resolute Doctor."</note> verbatim. Since he is never found to have retracted such an opinion, if it were simply heretical and contrary to what has been determined by the Church, it would follow that Durandus died a heretic.

<margin>An Exclamation</margin>
O distinguished Order of Preachers <note>The Dominicans.</note> and greatest splendor of our religion! Can you endure that your doctor—perhaps the first after Thomas [Aquinas], or certainly among the first—whose books are held, read, and honored daily in your schools, cloisters, and libraries, is now pronounced a heretic? You must plead the cause of your doctor; I have pleaded mine. Nay, O Church, you must plead your own cause, you who have permitted Durandus to be read publicly for so many years and permit it still! Either you never recognized his "abominable heresy" (according to these masters) through ignorance, or you recognized it and did not condemn it through negligence and contempt for divine matters. 

If they say there was no need for a new condemnation because this opinion is among those already condemned: first, it follows from what I said above that Durandus died a heretic. Second, it follows that Capreolus, Durandellus <note>Jean Capreolus and Nicolaus de Durando, major commentators on Aquinas and Durandus.</note>, and many other doctors who recount Durandus’s opinion without accusing it of heresy were ignorant and unrefined in the faith, unable to distinguish a heretic from a non-heretic. Third, let these fathers tell me where they have read a condemnation of this opinion. As for me, I confess I do not remember ever reading it anywhere. They certainly cannot bring forward any determination from the Councils against Durandus. Not only has this opinion never been condemned in Councils, but it was never even mentioned in any of them. 

Likewise, I do not know how they can allege the words of Holy Scripture against him, unless Scotus <note>John Duns Scotus, the "Subtle Doctor."</note> is lying when he says (on the testimony of Franciscus <note>Francis of Meyronnes, a student of Scotus.</note>) that no express mention is found in Gospel teaching even regarding the descent of Christ itself, much less the *mode* of the descent. And through what we established at the beginning of the Question, it is clear how Durandus would perhaps use interpretations to explain the scriptural authorities that seem to be against him. 

Perhaps they could bring forward many authorities from the Saints <note>The Church Fathers.</note> who say that Christ's soul was in Hell for three days just as His body was in the tomb, and similar things. Whatever Durandus’s "fantasy" might be—that is, the way he would explain the aforementioned authorities—perhaps by saying 

<margin>Note: Durandus's opinion is against Augustine, Jerome, and Gregory.</margin>
that this is said of the soul and not the whole composite person <note>The union of body and soul.</note>, because He worked primarily through the soul—whatever, I say, he might say, I do not hold his opinion nor have I ever held it. I say this and firmly assert: that this consequence does not hold: "This opinion is against the words of Augustine, or Jerome, or Gregory, and the other doctors of the Church; therefore it is heretical." The truth of this statement is believed by all good and subtle theologians, and I will evidently prove it. 

For although the writings of the holy doctors outside the biblical canon are to be handed down, read, and received with due reverence, their words are not of such firm and immovable authority that one is forbidden to contradict them or doubt them, unless they are otherwise proven evidently and expressly by Holy Scripture, or determined by the Church (authorizing them) to contain firm and indubitable truth. Therefore, an opinion cannot be clearly convicted as heretical precisely through the words of the Saints outside the biblical canon. For where there is no infallible truth, there is no certain and indubitable faith. Since certain faith relies on infallible truth, indeed, regarding such matters, there is no infallible assent nor adherence...

<meta>catchword: Reason [Ratio]</meta>

<summary>Pico defends himself by citing Durandus of Saint-Pourçain's view that Christ's descent into Hell was an "effect" rather than a physical movement, arguing that if this view were heresy, many respected Church doctors and the Church itself would be complicit. He concludes by asserting that contradicting the Church Fathers (like Augustine or Jerome) is not automatically heresy unless the point is settled by Scripture or a Church Council.</summary>

--- Page 73 ---
<meta>Pico continues his argument regarding the fallibility of human authorities in contrast to the absolute certainty of Divine Scripture. Having previously discussed the nature of Christ's descent, he now shifts to a broader epistemological point: that while the Bible is infallible, the writings of even the greatest Church Doctors are subject to error and disagreement.</meta>

### OF THE QUESTIONS

<column-break/>

<margin>Augustine.</margin>
...become firm. For where certain truth and indubitable faith are not present, men always assent with doubt and with the fear of falsehood. As Augustine says in his *Letter to Jerome* and in the eleventh and sixteenth books of *Against Faustus*: <note>original: "si scriptura non continet infallibilem veritatem... tota suspecta habetur"</note> if the Scripture does not contain infallible truth, and if it is found to be false in any part of itself, there remains no certain faith by which it may be firmly believed; and because of the falsehood found in one part, the whole is held suspect, and thus faith would totter. For as Augustine says in the seventh chapter of *On Christian Doctrine*: <note>original: "titubat fides si sacrarum scripturarum vacillat auctoritas"</note> faith totters if the authority of the sacred scriptures wavers. 

However, concerning the fact that there is no infallible truth in the sayings of the saints outside the canon of the Bible, three proofs occur to me. 

<margin>The first proof that there is no infallible truth in the sayings of the saints outside the biblical canon.</margin>
The first proof is that the Doctors themselves doubt their own sayings, wondering whether they have erred or not. Hence Augustine, in the first book of *On the Trinity*, chapter one, says: "Let it not trouble me to seek where I hesitate, nor will it shame me to correct myself where I err." And in chapter two: "Accordingly, let whoever reads this, where he hesitates along with me, let him seek; where he recognizes his error, let him return to me; where he recognizes mine, let him call me back." Hence also Augustine’s *Book of Retractations*, in which he condemns and retracts many things from his earlier sayings. For this reason, in the second book of *On the Trinity*, he says: "I would rather be corrected by anyone than be praised by someone who is either erring or flattering. For the erring praiser confirms the error, while the flatterer entices one into error. Let the righteous man correct me in mercy and rebuke me; but let not the oil of the sinner fatten my head." 

<margin>Guido the Carmelite.</margin>
And as <term>Guido the Carmelite</term> <note>Guido Terreni (c. 1270–1342), a philosopher and theologian who wrote on heresy.</note> says in his *Book on Heresies*: although Augustine speaks humbly in these sayings, he nevertheless speaks truthfully. Hence Augustine himself says to Vincent: "I cannot and should not deny that, just as in the works of my predecessors, so too in my own many small works there are many things that can be rebuked by a just judgment and without any rashness." And in the book *On True Religion* he says: "Whatever error shall be found in my books is to be attributed to me alone; but whatever is true or well-explained, let that be attributed to God, the one rewarder and giver of all things." Therefore, the sayings of the eminent and divine Doctor Augustine may not always contain indubitable truth in all matters, since he himself doubts whether he has erred or not. And what has been said of Augustine should be understood similarly of the other Doctors.

<margin>Second [proof].</margin>
The second proof is taken from the discord that exists among the authors themselves. For discord among writers is a testimony of falsehood, since it is necessary that at least one of the disagreeing parties says what is false, because one side of a contradiction is necessarily false. Therefore, Augustine, in the sixteenth book of *The City of God*, proves the truth of the Holy Scripture from the mutual concord of its writers, in which all agree and 

<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
none disagrees with another, which bears witness to the indubitable and infallible truth of the sacred scriptures. For, as <term>the Philosopher</term> <note>A standard medieval reference to Aristotle.</note> says in the first book of the *Ethics*, "all things harmonize with the truth," which does not happen in other writings. For how great the discord is in the sayings of the saints outside the canonical scriptures, no one remains ignorant unless they have not read their books. 

Augustine disagrees with the other holy Doctors concerning the understanding of the <term>Six Days of Work</term> <note>The six days of creation in Genesis.</note>. For others posit that God performed those works of the six days according to a succession of time; Augustine disagrees with them, positing that all things were made simultaneously, according to the verse: *He who lives forever created all things at once.* Hence, moved by this, Augustine numbers those six days not according to a succession of time, but according to the distinction of the angelic knowledge of things, both in their own kind and in the Word. And yet neither these nor those are called heretics, even though it is certain that one 

<column-break/>

of the opinions is false, and consequently their sayings do not rest upon infallible truth. 

Similarly, Jerome and Augustine disagree, because <margin>Dissensions between Jerome and Augustine.</margin> Augustine makes David the author of all the Psalms, which Jerome denies. They similarly disagree over the rebuke of Peter by Paul, whether it concerned a mortal or venial sin on Peter's part. They also disagree on the cessation of the legal ceremonies <note>The Jewish laws of the Old Testament.</note>, such that by contradicting each other, one necessarily speaks falsely; yet because of this, neither of them is considered a heretic. 

Similarly, <margin>Bede agrees with Jerome on this question.</margin> Bede, commenting on the first book of Kings, says that Samuel was a true priest, which Augustine expressly denies in his *Book of Questions on the New and Old Testament*, saying that Samuel was not a priest since he was not of the sons of Aaron. And Jerome, in the first book *Against Jovinian*, says: "At the same time it should be known that Samuel was a Levite, not a priest nor a high priest; therefore he is not named among the priests, but among those who call upon the name of the Lord." 

The sayings of these men, therefore, <margin>Aristotle.</margin> do not rest upon infallible truth since they contradict one another, one part of which is necessarily false, as is clear from the Philosopher in the fourth book of the *Metaphysics*. Indeed, Augustine himself seems to oppose his own opinion on this matter; for in the *Book of Questions on the New and Old Testament*, question 46, he says (as we have mentioned) that Samuel was not a priest, and yet in the twelfth book *Against Faustus*, chapter 35, he says: "the priesthood was changed into Samuel, Eli having been rejected, and the kingdom was changed into David, Saul having been rejected," where Augustine clearly says the priesthood was transferred to Samuel, so that Samuel was truly a priest just as David was truly a king. 

Regarding this same Samuel, as to whether he was raised from the dead, Augustine seems to disagree with himself. For in the *Questions on the New and Old Testament*, question 27, he holds that Samuel was not truly raised by the <term>pythoness</term> <note>The Witch of Endor.</note>, but that a demon appeared to Saul in the likeness of Samuel. Yet in the book *On the Care to be Taken for the Dead*, he posits that the soul of Samuel was truly summoned by a demon through magic and spoke to Saul. 

Jerome also, in that question of whether Samuel was in Jerusalem, seems in a certain letter of his (the title of which I do not recall) to be contrary to himself; he also holds an opinion contrary to Augustine regarding the seventy interpreters <note>The translators of the Septuagint Greek Bible.</note>. Likewise, Gregory and Dionysius disagree <margin>The discord of Gregory and Dionysius the Areopagite.</margin> regarding the orders of angels. And Jerome alone opposes all others regarding the promotion of a <term>bigamist</term> <note>In this context, a "bigamist" was a man who had been married twice, such as a widower who remarried, which was a point of legal debate regarding eligibility for the priesthood.</note>; for he holds and writes in his *Letter to Oceanus* that a bigamist before baptism can be promoted after baptism, provided he does not know more wives after baptism. The others contradict him, saying that a bigamist, whether before or after baptism, cannot be promoted; and in this, the latter are judged to have spoken better, as Augustine writes in *On the Good of Marriage* and Ambrose in *On Duties*. 

Likewise, Jerome, writing to Marcella on five questions, says that the saints found alive at the end of the world will not die but will be taken up alive; Augustine, however, in *The City of God*, affirms that all will die then. Likewise, Jerome, commenting on Matthew, says that the verse of the Psalm, *their sound has gone out into all the earth*, and that saying of Christ, *this gospel shall be preached in all the world*, was completed through the apostles; Augustine, however, in his *Letter to Exitius* (with whom Origen agrees on Matthew), holds that this has not yet been completed. Likewise, Jerome, on the *Epistle to Titus*, holds that angels existed for many ages before the visible world and served God, which Ambrose also holds in the *Hexameron*; Augustine, however, in *On Genesis*, holds that they were created simultaneously with the empyrean heaven.

->Io. Pic.<- <note>Ioannes Picus (Giovanni Pico della Mirandola).</note>

<meta>Pico continues his defense by demonstrating that the revered Doctors of the Church—such as Augustine and Jerome—frequently disagreed with one another on significant theological points. This serves his broader argument that while the Bible is infallible, the opinions of individual theologians (including those he is currently defending, like Durandus) are subject to debate and correction without necessarily being heretical.</meta>

-> # APOLOGIA <-

-> ### ii o ### <-

<meta>Catchword: ob-</meta>

<margin>Jerome and Augustine with Damascene and Origen: The words of the creature.</margin>
Likewise, Jerome, in his prologue to the Book of Wisdom, maintains that the book is by Philo and is not to be counted among the sacred scriptures. Augustine, however, in the third book of his *Retractations*, shows that he once held it was published by Jesus Sirach <note>A Jewish scribe also known as Ben Sira, the traditional author of Ecclesiasticus.</note>, though he retracts that there; and while he does not explicitly state who published it, he nevertheless enumerates it among the sacred books in his work *On Christian Doctrine*. Similarly, Jerome, in his book *Hebrew Questions*, says that God created Paradise before He made heaven and earth, based on the passage stating God had planted Paradise "from the beginning." Augustine, however, in his literal commentary on *Genesis*, interprets "from the beginning" to mean the third day. Furthermore, Augustine, in his book *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, asserts that Peter's entire denial took place in the courtyard of Annas, and that the things said thereafter about Jesus being sent to Caiaphas were stated as a recapitulation. Jerome, however, in his commentary on *Matthew*, seems to hold that Peter denied Christ in the courtyard of Caiaphas—an opinion with which Bede seems to agree in his commentary on *Luke*. Again, Jerome, commenting on the passage in Habakkuk "Your eyes are pure," denies that individual angels are placed in charge of individual physical creatures; yet Augustine, in his *Eighty-Three Different Questions*, holds that they are. Origen and Damascene <note>John of Damascus, an influential 8th-century theologian.</note> agree with Augustine. Jerome, commenting on the passage in Jonah "Pick me up and throw me into the sea," says that it is permissible to perish by one's own hand when chastity is at risk; Augustine, however, in the book *The City of God*, affirms the contrary. Finally, many such instances are found where the holy Doctors have written opposing views <term>salva fide</term> <note>original: "salva fide"; meaning "while keeping the faith intact" or without violating core dogma.</note>. But I cannot recount all of them, especially in such haste; for this work could not be labored over by me with more exact diligence because I wished to immediately counter the spreading disease of unjust infamy. I shall write elsewhere on this matter with greater leisure and care, and perhaps I shall add more and better points.

<margin>Jerome's [words]</margin>
I will, however, add what now occurs to me from Jerome's letter to Augustine, where he says: "Do not wonder if, in your books, and especially in your explanations of the Scriptures (which are most obscure), some things seem to deviate from a straight line. I say this not because I judge some things in your works to be blameworthy—for I have never devoted effort to reading them, nor is there a supply of copies of them among us, except for your books of *Soliloquies* and certain commentaries on the *Psalms*. If I wished to examine these, I would not say it as from myself, for I am nothing, but I would show from the interpretations of the ancient Greeks that these things deviate." Thus he spoke. Therefore, just as they did toward one another, so we too may disagree with them in many things, <term>salva fide</term>, while preserving the truth of Scripture and the determinations of the Holy Church.

<margin>The third proof</margin>
The third proof is taken from the special prerogative of Sacred Scripture and the decrees of the Universal Church, to which alone we grant the excellence of infallible truth. Hence Augustine, in a letter to Jerome,

<margin>Augustine.</margin>
speaks thus: "For I confess to your charity that I have learned to yield this fear and honor only to those books of Scripture which are now called 'canonical,' <note>The "canon" refers to the official list of books recognized as the inspired Word of God.</note> so that I most firmly believe that none of their authors erred in writing. Or, if I encounter anything in those writings that seems contrary to the truth, I shall not hesitate to believe nothing else than that the manuscript is flawed, or the translator did not grasp the meaning, or I have understood it not at all. But I read the writings of others in such a way that, no matter how much they excel in holiness and learning, I do not consider a thing true simply because they thought so, but because they were able to persuade me, either through other passages of Sacred Scripture or by probable (that is, evident) reason, that it does not shrink from the truth. Nor do I think, my brother, that you wish your books to be read as though they were those of the prophets and apostles, about whose writings it is a sacrilege to doubt that they are free from all error. May such a thing be far from your pious humility and your true

<margin>Augustine.</margin>
thought regarding yourself." And Augustine himself, in the third book of *On the Trinity*, says: "Indeed, since in all my writings I desire not only a pious reader but also a free corrector."

<column-break/>

"Nevertheless, just as I want my reader to be devoted to me, so I do not want my corrector to be devoted to me; and I say to them, as I say to those others, that they should not be enslaved to any of my writings as if they were canonical scriptures. But in those [the scriptures], believe without hesitation even what you did not previously believe when you find it; in these writings of mine, however, do not firmly hold what you did not have as certain unless you have understood it to be certain." Thus he says to him: "Do not correct my writings based on your own opinion or out of contention, but from divine reading or unshakable reason." And

<margin>Augustine.</margin>
Augustine, in his letter or book to Vincent: "Therefore, brother, do not collect or bring false charges against the writings of lesser bishops—such as Hilary, Cyprian, or Agrippinus—against so many, so clear, and so indubitable divine testimonies. For this kind of literature must be distinguished from the authority of the canons. They are not read as if testimony were brought from them such that one is not permitted to think otherwise." And

<margin>Augustine.</margin>
in his letter to Fortunatus, the same Augustine says: "Neither ought we to hold the disputations of any persons, however catholic and praised they may be, as we do the canonical scriptures; so that it is not permitted to us, while preserving the honor due to those men, to disapprove of and reject something in their writings." And in the book *On Unique Baptism*: "Who does not know that the holy canonical Scripture of the Old and New Testaments is contained within its own certain limits, and that it is so preferred to all later letters of bishops (so that it is impossible to doubt it) whether whatever is established to be written in it is true or right? However, the letters of bishops which were written or are being written after the canon was confirmed may be corrected—if perhaps something in them has deviated from the truth—both by the speech of someone perhaps wiser, and by the more pleasing authority and more learned prudence of other bishops, and by councils." Infinite examples of this kind could be brought forward. From these it would be clear that the sayings of the saints do not rest upon infallible truth precisely as they are the sayings of the saints. Whence you will often find modern doctors departing from the sayings of the saints. For

<margin>Robert Holcot, Ockham, Scotus</margin>
Robert Holcot says that the holy man Anselm was deceived in many things because of his ignorance of logic; and Ockham does not agree with Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a highly revered mystical theologian.</note> concerning the hierarchy of acts. And [Duns] Scotus, in his third book of the *Sentences*, nearly destroys the whole process of Anselm in the book *Why God Became Man* <note>original: "Cur Deus homo"</note>; and so you will frequently find the same regarding other

<margin>He concludes that Durandus has erred.</margin>
doctors. I wanted to bring these things forward here not so much on account of the opinion of Durandus—which I neither hold nor have ever held—but on account of what will soon be treated at the beginning of the second question. From all these things, I conclude that since no express determination of either Holy Scripture or the Universal Church is found against the opinion of Durandus, it is presumptuous to call it simply heretical.

<margin>Objection.</margin>
If, however, such a determination is found, Durandus must bear this mark of heresy patiently. But someone will say: "Granted that your meaning, which you claimed to intend by that proposition, is catholic; and granted that the force of the words also permits it; can your proposition not also produce that meaning of Durandus which you yourself detest? And therefore, did you not err by putting forward a conclusion that could cause scandal

<margin>First response.</margin>
in the minds of the faithful?" To this I say first: that there is one reasoning for things proposed for the sake of dispute, and another for things handed down in writing as doctrine to be read. For when something is proposed to be disputed, the proposition is put forward as brief, concise, and inexplicit in itself, involving multiple difficulties of both words and meanings to be dissolved in the encounter of the dispute itself. Otherwise, if everything were explained there, no room for dispute would be left; therefore, an ambiguous...

-> # OF THE QUESTIONS <-

<columns>2</columns>

<margin>Second point.</margin>
A person putting forward an ambiguous or equivocal proposition to be disputed is excused because it is expected that he will distinguish and declare his meaning during the dispute itself. However, those who commit something to writing for the purpose of teaching do by writing what is done here by disputing. Therefore, in writing, everything ought to be clear, lucid, and settled. Second, let those most severe censors consider that it is not only difficult but nearly impossible to so weigh and examine the words of every proposition one puts forward that no ambiguity of sense could exist, and no erroneous opinion could be drawn from it. Indeed, I certainly do not wish to claim for my propositions a quality that many Gospel and Apostolic propositions do not possess. For many are found among them that have multiple interpretations and can be turned toward an erroneous sense; indeed, some even seem to sound like heresy at first glance. From this source, all heresies have sprouted: namely, 

<margin>Note on the heresy of heretics and from where they sprouted.</margin>
that some did not look into the depth of the meaning as much as they attended to what the "bark" <note>The outer surface or literal phrasing.</note> of the words of the Gospels sounded like. Hence Arius <note>A 4th-century priest whose teachings on the nature of the Trinity were ruled heretical at the Council of Nicaea.</note>, hearing "the Father is greater than I" <note>original: "pater maior me est"</note>, believed the Father to be greater than the Son and said the Son was a creature. Hence Helvidius <note>An 4th-century writer who opposed the doctrine of Mary's perpetual virginity.</note>, hearing that Joseph did not know Mary "until she brought forth her firstborn" <note>original: "donec peperit primogenitum suum"</note>, attending more to the grammatical force of that word "until" <note>original: "donec"</note> than to the truth of the Gospel sense regarding the perpetual virginity of Mary, expressed doubt. Hence Marcion <note>A 2nd-century heretic who rejected the Old Testament God.</note>, reading that of Paul, "The law entered that sin might abound" <note>original: "Lex autem subintrauit vt abundaret delictum"</note>, believed the law of Moses to be evil and from an evil principle, following the Manicheans. And Basilides <note>An early Gnostic teacher.</note>, reading "I once lived without the law" <note>original: "ego aliquando sine lege viuebam"</note>, believed that the soul of Paul had once lived in another body. Hence Eunomius <note>A radical Arian leader.</note>, hearing Christ responding to the Jews who accused Him of calling Himself the Son of God, that it was written "I said, you are gods and all of you are sons of the Most High" <note>original: "ego dixi dii estis & filii excelsi omnes"</note>, attended more to the thing said and the literal response than to the intention and purpose of the respondent; he believed Christ was called the Son of God in the same way that any holy person is called a son of God. Similarly, the proposition "That day even the Son does not know" <note>original: "illam diem neque filius nouit"</note> was the occasion for many to believe the Father understands more than the Son; for if we interpret it according to the common sense of the words, it seems to present that meaning, even though the truth of the latent sense is otherwise. I could bring forward infinite similar propositions from the canon of the Scriptures; and therefore,

<margin>Hilary.</margin>
Hilary <note>Hilary of Poitiers, a 4th-century bishop and theologian.</note> rightly said that the understanding of what is said must be taken from the causes of the speaking, because the subject matter is not subject to the speech, but the speech to the subject matter.

<margin>Gloss.</margin>
And the Gloss <note>Standard medieval biblical commentary.</note> upon that text says: we ought not always to understand words as they seem to sound at first glance, especially where they are ambiguous, but we ought to recur to the intention of the speaker.

<margin>Gregory.</margin>
And Gregory says that often, while the propriety of the words is attended to, the sense of truth is lost. And Gregory, in the twenty-sixth book of the *Moralia*, says: one ought not to consider the words, but the will and intention; for the intention ought not to serve the words, but

<margin>Jerome.</margin>
the words the intention. And Jerome, on the *Epistle to the Galatians*, testifies that the Gospel is not in the words of the Scriptures but in the sense; not on the surface, but in the marrow <note>original: "in medulla"</note>; not in the leaves of the speeches, but in the root of the reason.

<margin>Ockham.</margin>
Therefore, Ockham <note>William of Ockham, a 14th-century Franciscan philosopher.</note> in his *Dialogue* falsifies this common proposition: "words are to be taken not from the opinions of individuals but from common usage," especially in the second part. For he says that in ambiguous and multifaceted words, one should not recur to common understanding, but rather to the intention of the speakers. And so, when there is ambiguity in the teaching of someone speaking or writing, one must similarly recur to the intention of the speaker, so that he may explain himself and express 

<column-break/>

<margin>Epilogue.</margin>
the true sense which the force of the words allows. Nor is he to be reproved unless it could be proven that such a sense was contrary to his other true sayings or was irrelevant to his purpose. And the same Doctor <note>Referring to Ockham.</note> says that even in simple speech, one must recur to the intention of the speaker; and one must stand by his interpretation unless it is certain, or probably or strongly presumed, that he used such an ambiguous way of speaking to deceive or for some other evil end. From all of which I conclude that I did not err, I who, with a protestation, probably put forward a multifaceted proposition to be declared during a dispute—a proposition which, moreover, can make no sense that some doctor, either not reproved or not yet declared as such by the Church, has not held. Rather, those have erred who judged a proposition having a Catholic sense allowed by the force of the words—and which was already declared to them in that Catholic sense by the proposer—to be simply heretical. Even if they had done this before my sense was declared, they might perhaps have erred more excusably; however, because if they are truly learned, they could have known for themselves that the proposition had a double sense, and attending to this, they should not have simply 

<margin>Augustine.</margin>
damned it, but rather interpreted it in a good sense. For Augustine, in his book *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, explaining that passage of Matthew, "Judge not, and you shall not be judged," says: in this place, I think nothing else is commanded but that we interpret those deeds, which are doubtful as to the spirit in which they are done, in the better part. For regarding neutral deeds, which can be done with a good or bad spirit, it is rash to judge, and especially to condemn. Therefore, let us understand what Augustine says about things that are *done* as being said equally about things that are *said*; and so, applying Augustine's sentence to speculative matters, let us conclude that in those sayings which can have a good and bad sense, it is rash to judge, and especially to condemn.

### SECOND QUESTION: ON THE
### PUNISHMENT OF MORTAL SIN

The second conclusion which they condemned is this: **A punishment of infinite duration is not owed to a mortal sin of finite time, but only a finite punishment.**

<image-desc>A rectangular decorative woodcut initial 'T' showing a bearded scholar or saint in robes seated at a desk, gesturing with his right hand.</image-desc>
Because when I placed the conclusion in my little book, these words were prefixed: "Unless there were the sayings of the Saints which, in the manifest surface of their speech, seem to say the opposite of firmly asserting the below-written conclusions, I nevertheless assert them to be probable and able to be reasonably defended." The first of these is this: "Mortal sin is in itself a finite evil." The second is this: "To a mortal sin of finite time, etc." A certain Master, holding a disputation regarding this conclusion of mine, said: "What other testimony do we seek that your conclusion is heretical, since you yourself manifestly say it is against the sayings of the Saints? For the consequence holds: 'it is against the sayings of the Saints, therefore it is heretical.'" I showed him then, as I will also show below, how my conclusion was in no way repugnant to the opinions of the Saints, and how their words were to be understood. But even if it had been so...

Because the conclusion would be contradicted by the saints—however much its logic might hold—and since it would be unworthy of a "learned theologian" (as he boasts himself to be), the truth can be clear to anyone from what was said above in the first conclusion. I know what I might say here about that master. He is the one who so often sent letters back home about me, promising a trophy and a triumph, as if he had already defeated me. But I wish to plead my case with the reasons set down from the beginning, not with insults. I come now to the conclusion. And because these masters have judged both the conclusion itself and the answers I gave them when they questioned me on it to be false, erroneous, and heretical, I wish first to declare that the conclusion itself is Catholic <note>In this context, "Catholic" means orthodox or in accordance with universal Church teaching.</note> and in harmony with the sayings of almost all the doctors. I call it "my" conclusion because if you take it in a sense other than the one I intend, it is no longer the conclusion I proposed. For a proposition is manifold. Next, I wish to declare that my responses are also of such a kind, explaining my meanings for both the conclusion and the responses, provided that the force of the words allows it.

<margin>
First, note two things in sin: namely, turning toward and turning away.
</margin>
For the declaration of this conclusion, five things must be noted. First, it should be noted that in sin, two things can be considered: the *turning toward* <note>original: "conversio"</note> a created good, and the *turning away* <note>original: "aversio"</note> from the unchangeable and uncreated Good [God]. In the first way, sin is a finite evil, even according to all the doctors. In the second way, sin is an infinite evil according to the common path of thought. And because the "turning toward" a created good—which the sinner misuses by sinning—is part of the intrinsic nature of the sin itself, it is therefore said that sin is intrinsically a finite evil. However, the "turning away" from the uncreated Good makes it extrinsically infinite; it is called an infinite evil only insofar as it is a turning away from an infinite Good, and therefore it remains only an extrinsically and objectively infinite evil.

<margin>
Second, note what is meant by "time."
</margin>
Second, note that by "time" we can understand only the "time of the way" <note>The "way" (via) refers to the duration of a human's earthly life.</note>; and in this way, it is certain that neither sin nor anything else pertaining to man can be infinite according to time, since the "time of the way" for any traveler is not only finite in duration but even brief. In another way, we can understand by "time" both the time of the way and the time of the end <note>The "end" (terminus) refers to the eternal state after death.</note>; and it is in this way that it is taken in the conclusion. Thus, something in man can indeed last for an infinite time.

<margin>
Third, sin is taken in two ways.
</margin>
Third, note that mortal sin can be understood in two ways. In one way, as the prohibited act or the omission of an act commanded by God. In another way, as the *guilt* <note>original: "reatus," referring to the legal debt or state of being liable for punishment</note> left behind from the aforementioned prohibited act or omission. Indeed, in many places in Holy Scripture, this guilt is called "sin." By such "sin," a person is called a sinner even when the act of the sin (in the first sense) has ceased or passed away. From this third point, it is clear that it is reasonable to say that although the actual act of sin for which a man is damned eventually ends, the sin does not end in terms of its *guilt*. Indeed, if the guilt were to end, eternal punishment would not be owed to him. Thus, the sin to which infinite punishment is owed is "infinite according to time" in regards to its guilt.

<margin>
Fourth, "to be owed" is taken in two ways.
</margin>
Fourth, it must be noted that "to be owed" <note>original: "deberi"</note> is taken in two ways, or rather, it can be understood in two ways that a certain punishment is owed to a sin. In one way, that is said to be "owed" to someone which will eventually be rendered to them. In this sense, it is said reasonably and Catholically that for a sin of finite time—in regards to its intrinsic entity and guilt—an infinite punishment according to time is not owed. It is in this sense that the present conclusion is understood: namely, that 

<column-break/>

to a sin of finite time, [punishment] is not owed, etc. For every sin to which [punishment] is owed in this way—that is, for which an infinite punishment will eventually be rendered—is "infinite" in the aforementioned way. Nor is anyone ever damned unless the sin for which they are damned is, in that way, infinite according to time. Moreover, the conclusion has another Catholic sense, namely: that it is never "owed" in such a way that an infinite punishment in time will be rendered to someone unless that person is finally impenitent and, without end, neglects to repent for that sin which he committed or omitted in life. Thus, for a temporal sin, infinite punishment is owed in the aforementioned way only if the sinner does not return to justice.

<margin>
Scotus.
<note>Unclear: regarding involuntary punishment and innocence.</note>
Augustine.
</margin>
For just as repentance finishes a sin in regards to its rejection by God—according to the text: "at whatever hour the sinner shall groan [in repentance]," etc.—so too does impenitence regarding a sin perpetuate it in guilt and rejection unto infinite punishment. And thus, infinite punishment is never owed to anyone in that first sense unless they have a sin that is infinite according to time.

<margin>
Note on vengeance.
</margin>
For the "vengeance" which God seeks from the sinner is that the sinner should return voluntarily to due obedience, grieving for his contempt; otherwise, he will be tormented as long as he chooses to remain in that state. In another way, "to be owed" can be understood as that which someone is worthy of by merit or demerit, and which will be rendered to him if he dies in that state. In this sense, for a mortal sin of finite time, infinite punishment *is* owed, because whoever sins mortally in the space of a single hour is worthy of infinite punishment. And that punishment will be rendered to him if he finally dies in that state, even assuming he has no other sin that is infinite according to time. This distinction of the word "owed" is in frequent use among theologians. Hence, according to this distinction, the Doctors say that eternal life is not "owed" to a person known by God to be lost <note>original: "praescito," one foreknown to be damned</note> for a meritorious act he performs while in a state of grace—if "owed" is taken in the first sense—because it will never actually be rendered to him. Similarly, it is said that eternal punishment is not "owed" to a person predestined for heaven while he is in a state of mortal sin, because it will never be rendered to him, since that sin will be finished and he will not die in it, but in grace.

<margin>
Epilogue.
</margin>
From the points above, it is clear that my conclusion has a Catholic sense even according to the common way of speaking used by Catholic doctors. It should not have been condemned as heretical, false, and erroneous, since its opposite is rather what is false and erroneous.

<margin>
Note.
</margin>
It was a sign of the greatest ignorance <note>original: "ruditatis," or lack of education</note> to believe that from the aforementioned conclusion I intended to deny the eternal punishment of the damned. On the contrary, from my conclusion one finds an investigation into the *cause* for which the damned are punished forever. I said the cause is the perpetuation of guilt in the soul of the sinner through his final impenitence and the perpetual omission of grieving for his sin. This opinion not only seems not to be heretical, but so Catholic that no one, if he is Catholic and practiced in holy letters, can rightly and reasonably deny it.

<margin>
He declares the conclusion is not heretical based on the meaning of the terms.
Master of the Sentences.
</margin>
That the proposition carries this sense by the very force of its terms is clear. For the proposition says: "To a mortal sin of finite time, infinite punishment according to time is not owed." In this proposition, I take "to be owed" for that which will eventually be paid out—a usage most common among the Doctors, as shown above. And I take "sin" for the offense and the guilt; which usage is not only not improper or abusive, but frequent in Holy Scripture. For after the Master of the Sentences <note>Peter Lombard, the author of the standard medieval theology textbook.</note> asks in his second book whether, after the act of sinning passes, the sin remains in the one who sinned until he repents, he answers thus: "It must not be ignored that sins are in someone and pass away in two ways: namely, in act and in guilt."
