<margin>Thomas Aquinas</margin>
Furthermore, that the term "liability" <note>original: "reatus"</note> is also sometimes expressly called "sin," Thomas says in the same place: "Liability, acting as a mediator between the fault and the punishment, takes the name of both extremes." But is not sin also taken to mean "liability" in this passage: "It is therefore a holy and wholesome thought to pray for the dead, that they may be loosed from sins" <note>2 Maccabees 12:46</note>? For those dead for whom we must pray to be loosed from sins are not in a state of sin if we take "sin" to mean "mortal fault" <note>original: "culpa mortali"</note>. Nor are they loosed from such sin after death, but only from sin understood as "punishment" or "liability for punishment." In this same way, "sin" is also understood in the passage: "Redeem your sins with alms" <note>Daniel 4:24</note>; and so it is in many other passages of Scripture. If, therefore, both the sense of the proposition is Catholic and the use of the terms in the proposition is Catholic and highly approved, why was there any reason for them to condemn this conclusion of mine as heretical?

<margin>Responses which the author had given. First.</margin>
I come now to my responses. First, I said that if someone perseveres only for a finite time in mortal sin, that person will not be punished except for a finite time. This statement is verified in three ways. First, when we take "mortal sin" to mean "liability" <note>reatus</note> and not the act of commission or omission, as was said in the declaration of the conclusion.

<margin>Second.</margin>
Second, it should be noted that the term "mortal sin," according to the rigor of logic, is taken in a general sense <note>original: "confuse"</note> rather than a specific one.

<margin>Third.</margin>
Third, because it is true that if someone who sinned persevered only for a finite time in a specific sin—for instance, in the omission of repenting for their sin—such that they eventually repented of it, that person will not be punished for it except for a finite time. And that I intended these Catholic meanings, and none inconsistent with the faith, is clear from what I added in the response when I said: "It stands with the truth of the conclusion that anyone dying in mortal sin will be punished forever." However, when it was further asked of me whether someone who sins only for a finite time with one mortal sin and dies unrepentant is punished forever, I answered yes. But I said that such a person will not be punished for that act alone. This was a true response to the question asked, even though it is also true that if they had sinned only by that act, they would be punished eternally.

<margin>Question. Response.</margin>
But because the question posits that this person dies unrepentant, they would also be punished for that very impenitence—indeed, for infinite omissions of repenting and for infinite other evil acts, total or partial, in which the damned soul consists. For just as the damned soul continuously wills evil, so it continuously sins and earns demerit. It is not, to be sure, a different essential punishment—at least not one that is not the fault itself—but the same punishment multiplied. Thus, the soul is punished for those evil acts in which it continues. Because, however, this seems to be

<margin>Note.</margin>
contrary to the common way of speaking used by the Saints—though not contrary to the actual matter and sense of their words—I stated both in writing and in speech that I do not "assert" this opinion (meaning, in this specific way of speaking) out of reverence for the Saints. Rather, I said it could be defended as probable. Finally, beyond the points mentioned above, I added: anyone dying in mortal sin is punished forever because of the liability of that sin. This is because by dying in that state of liability, they are placed in a condition where they are necessitated to sin forever—at least by the perpetual sin of omitting to repent and prepare for grace. Those masters, however, said that these responses of mine were not satisfactory to their arguments and inquiries. Indeed, they claimed I added error upon error through such a response, for which reason they declared both the responses and the declarations to be false, erroneous, and

<column-break/>

heretical. But who cannot see that in this most reprehensible condemnation of theirs, it is they who add error upon error, and not I—unless it be someone who hates Catholic truths along with them, or does not understand them. Briefly recapitulating:

<margin>Recapitulation.</margin>
What I intend in this conclusion is this: it is indeed true that a mortal sin of a finite time is worthy of eternal punishment; it is owed to it, and sometimes eternal punishment is paid out if the sin was not forgiven before death. Nevertheless, if mortal sin is finite in terms of time—not only regarding the intrinsic positive entity of the act forbidden by God (or the privative omission of an act commanded by God), but also regarding its imputation, its rejection, and also the liability and stain which in many places of Scripture and in the common speech of the Doctors is often called "sin"—then it is of the nature of sin to be punished eternally. Because if the said imputation or stain does not remain, eternal punishment will never be owed, nor will it ever be paid out. I am speaking of such a sin, I say, which is finite in all the aforementioned ways—a finitude achieved through repentance, at least for actual mortal sin. I say that eternal punishment is not "owed" to it, understanding "owed" as something that will one day be rendered or paid out. On the contrary, to whomever eternal punishment is rendered for mortal sin, they were in that sin without end in the manner described above. And this is what Gregory intends to

<margin>Gregory</margin>
say: that the sinner is punished with eternal punishment because he "sinned in his own eternity," <note>A famous argument by Pope Gregory the Great: the sinner would have sinned forever if they had lived forever, so God punishes them forever.</note> that is, without end. And thus we say that every person who is damned dies in the sin for which they are damned. Thomas [Aquinas] also agrees in the fourth book of the *Sentences*, saying

<margin>Thomas</margin>
that the punishment of the damned lasts forever for this reason: because the fault lasts forever. Therefore, I say that in every person who is damned, there is one sin of infinite duration, speaking of the time of the journey [life] as well as the end [afterlife]: namely, the omission of repenting, which in the damned never has an end. Thus it is clear that the infinity of the duration of this sin—the infinity, I say, of the liability of imputation, or the stain and impenitence, or the omission of repenting for it—is the cause why eternal punishment is owed and sometimes paid. And this is enough regarding that conclusion.

<meta>Pico is continuing his defense of his theological theses. On the previous page, he discussed the nature of sin and punishment. Now, he moves to a highly contentious issue: the adoration of images and the Cross, specifically addressing the views of Thomas Aquinas versus other scholastic theologians like Durandus and Henry of Ghent.</meta>

->A P O L O G Y<-

<margin>Thomas Aquinas.</margin>
I provide this in the conclusion. Thomas says, therefore, that because—as the Philosopher <note>The "Philosopher" refers to Aristotle, the primary authority on logic and nature for medieval scholars.</note> says in his book *On Memory and Reminiscence*—there is a twofold movement of the soul toward an image: one toward the image itself as a certain physical thing, and another way toward the image insofar as it is an image of something else. Between these two movements there is a difference, because the first movement, by which someone is moved toward an image as a physical object, is distinct from the movement toward the reality of which that thing is an image. However, the second movement, which is toward the image insofar as it is an image, is one and the same as that movement which is toward the reality itself. Therefore, he concludes that although the image of Christ, as a physical thing in itself, is not owed adoration, nevertheless, insofar as it is an image, it is owed the same reverence that is owed to Christ himself, which is divine worship <note>original: "latria," the Greek-derived term for the highest form of worship reserved for God alone.</note>. This is Thomas’s method, which to other doctors rightly seems strange and dangerous. For the image itself, even as an image, is distinct from the thing imagined; for in this way it is related to the thing imagined as to something distinct from itself. Therefore, even if it were to serve as the end point for divine worship in this way, it seems to follow that something other than God will be worshipped with divine worship, which is absurd.

<margin>Against the response of Capreolus.</margin>
Nor can it be said, as Capreolus <note>Jean Capreolus (c. 1380–1444), known as the "Prince of Thomists," who defended Aquinas’s works.</note> says when trying to save Thomas’s statement, that the image itself is not worshipped separately, but that the image and the thing imagined are one total object of adoration. For either one part of this "total object" is the image itself—which is a created, relative being—or it is not. If it is not, then it should not be said that one total object is made from those two, because from such a statement it follows that each of them is a partial object, even if one of them is more principal. If it is so, it follows that some created thing of the category of "relation" will, at least partially, serve as the end point of divine worship.

<margin>Against the foundation of this opinion.</margin>
To say such a thing certainly seems "poorly Catholic," <note>An idiom meaning "heterodox" or "verging on heresy."</note> all the more so because not only can this not be said of a created thing, but even the Persons in the Divine Trinity, by reason of their relative properties, are not the formal end point of adoration <note>A dense theological point: we worship the Persons of the Trinity because of their shared Divine Essence, not merely because of the relations (Father, Son, Spirit) between them.</note>. Furthermore, Thomas’s foundation seems to have little force. For when the Philosopher says that the movement of the soul toward the image and the thing imagined is the same, he does not mean it in the sense that the soul declares the image, insofar as it is an image, to be the same as the original, and thus whatever is owed to one is also owed to the other. Rather, the Philosopher only intends this: that the act of remembering, by which the soul is moved through memory toward the image as an image, also terminates at the thing imagined. There is also another true sense of this: because if I have a definitive concept of one relative thing, I also understand the other. But that every movement of the soul—and especially of the *will*—should be the same toward the image and the thing imagined, the Philosopher in no way intends. This is clear by a similar case, even according to the way of speaking that Thomas himself often uses. For he often says that the movement of the will is the same when the will is carried toward an "end" <note>the goal</note> and toward the "means to that end" when it wills them for the sake of the end. And yet it is certain, even according to him, that this movement, as it reaches the end, is "enjoyment" <note>original: "fruitio"</note>, but as it reaches the means to the end, it is "use" <note>original: "usus"</note> and not enjoyment. Therefore, it seems to other doctors that it should in no way be said that we adore the image of Christ, even as an image, with divine worship, because as such it is a created, relative thing. For this reason, Durandus <note>Durandus of Saint-Pourçain (c. 1275–1334), a philosopher known for disagreeing with Aquinas.</note> says that this proposition—"the cross of Christ is worshipped with divine worship"—is false in its proper sense, but has a true improper sense. And it is this: Christ, as remembered through the cross, or as present in the cross just as a thing imagined is present in its image, is adored with the same adoration as if he were present in himself. And according to this sense, I also concede this proposition: "The Cross is adored with divine worship." This is therefore what Durandus says: that it is adored through remembrance—

<margin>Opinion of other doctors.</margin>
<margin>Opinion of Durandus.</margin>
<margin>Opinion of Robert Holcot and Henry.</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>And John de Guerra and Peter of Aquila. What Henry and John de Guerra add.</margin>
—and Robert Holcot <note>English Dominican theologian (d. 1349).</note> intends the same meaning when he says that the more proper way of speaking is to say, "we adore *before* the cross" rather than to say "we adore the cross." Finally, Henry <note>Henry of Ghent (c. 1217–1293).</note> and John de Guerra intend the same meaning when they say that it is adored "accidentally"; and Peter of Aquila says the same. Truly, that which Henry and John de Guerra add—who speak more completely on this matter—is this: they say that the honor which is owed "of itself" <note>original: "per se"</note> to the thing imagined and remembered is owed to the image "accidentally" <note>original: "per accidens," meaning indirectly or by association</note> or through remembrance. Now, it is certain that there is nothing to which divine worship is owed "of itself" except the God who is Three and One, and Christ on account of the unity of his person; for there can be no "image" of God <note>in his pure essence</note>. It remains that if there is any image to which divine worship is owed accidentally and through remembrance, it would be the image of Christ. But because such an image primarily represents the humanity of Christ to us, and secondarily his divinity, it seems that primarily there is owed to it, accidentally, such honor as is owed "of itself" to the humanity of Christ. But the humanity of Christ, taken by itself, is only worshipped with *hyperdulia* <note>A level of veneration higher than that for saints (dulia) but lower than that for God (latria).</note>. Therefore, to such an image, primarily and accidentally, only the adoration of *hyperdulia* will be owed. Secondarily and accidentally, however, even the adoration of divine worship will be owed in the way that has been described: because the image itself also secondarily represents and reminds us of the divinity of Christ himself. In this, Francis of Meyronnes and all the Scotists <note>Followers of John Duns Scotus.</note> agree with Henry, saying that divine worship is not owed to the humanity of Christ <note>as distinct from his divine nature</note>. Thomas, however, because he seems to hold the opposite regarding the adoration of Christ's humanity, would perhaps also dissent from Henry in this case. And truly, the opinion of Thomas, as Francis says in his third book, is somewhat dangerous, and in this matter of adoration his path does not seem to me to be very safe. For he went so far as to say, in his commentary on the *Sentences*, that the Cross of Christ on which he hung—even as an inanimate thing—should be owed a reason for worship. And yet we know, according to all theology, that that which cannot be a subject for the reception of holiness or virtue cannot be the end point of any adoration. Even John Capreolus, the defender of Thomas, himself confesses that this statement of Thomas cannot be defended; nor does he have any other way of saving Thomas except by saying that Thomas himself seems to have felt differently later in his *Summa*.

<margin>Francis’s agreement with Henry and the Scotists.</margin>

From these things, therefore, it can be clear how Catholic my conclusion is, and how much more rational it is than its opposite, and more in harmony with the common path of the theologians. Briefly recapitulating its sense, I say that this proposition—"the cross of Christ is adored"—can have two senses. One is proper: namely, that the cross of Christ—whether as a physical thing, as an image, as a partial object, or as a total object—is adored as the final point of adoration. This is the sense that Thomas intends and which I deny. The other is the improper sense of said proposition: "The cross of Christ is adored," meaning "Christ is adored *in it* as in his memorial," as if he were present in himself. And I concede this sense, and with the Church I pray, saying:

<margin>...and is condemned by Francis and the Scotists against Thomas, and cannot be defended by Capreolus.</margin>

> Hail, O Cross, our only hope.

And with the Church:

> We adore [thee], O Lord.

<margin>Recapitulation of the meaning of the conclusion.</margin>

Many things can now be clear from what has been said. First, it is clear what I meant when I said elsewhere that, following the opinion of Henry and John de Guerra, *hyperdulia* is owed to the image of the crucifix; this was to be understood by reason of that which is primarily brought to our memory, which is the humanity of Christ. I said this "truncatedly" <note>briefly or incompletely</note> because I was referring to those authors whom I considered these Masters <note>his inquisitors</note>—being veterans—to have already read and re-read ten times over. Second, it is clear that they falsely said I deny all—

<margin>Many things are deduced. First.</margin>

->OF THE QUESTIONS<-

<margin>Second point.</margin> Regarding Thomas’s method: even if I had not specified it, but the proposition simply stood as "neither the cross nor any image is to be adored with divine worship" <note>original: "latria," the highest form of worship reserved for God alone</note>, still, by the force of the words, that proposition would not deny every mode of divine worship. For it is clear according to good logic that the negation or distribution of a term with multiple meanings does not deny or distribute it for every possible meaning. Otherwise, the proposition "every dog is a star" would have to be simply granted or simply denied. Just as one does not say collectively that every heavenly dog <note>the star Sirius</note>, every sea dog <note>a shark or seal</note>, and every barking dog is a star—even if it is said of all of them individually—so too in the negative statement "the cross is not adored with the worship of latria." In this case, the word "adored" is equivocal; it can mean adoration directed toward a thing as an ultimate end, or adoration directed toward a thing as a reminder. Thus, every mode of adoration is not denied collectively. <margin>Third point.</margin> Thirdly, it is clear that this proposition could be stated absolutely and without distinction. "The Cross is not to be adored with divine worship" is true in its proper sense, or at least more probable than its opposite. The literal rigor of the speech is more to be considered than an improper sense in which it might be false. Just as a term with multiple related meanings <note>an "analogical term"</note> stands for its most famous meaning when placed by itself, so too a statement having both a proper and an improper sense should be taken in its proper sense if it is spoken without specification. Therefore, as I said, I could have put it forward without distinction, intending to declare the sense in which I understood it during the debate. <margin>Note.</margin> From this I infer that although it is perhaps better to do as I did—to specify the sense in which a multi-layered proposition is used—there is a greater fault in condemning, without distinction, a proposition that is true in its proper sense just because it is false in an improper sense. I wanted to note this here not only for this specific conclusion (in which I specifically deny Thomas's method), but also because of many other conclusions which, although they have a Catholic meaning that I always promised to declare (as I am doing now), were nevertheless condemned simply and without distinction. Truly, whatever the case may be regarding my conclusion, they cannot excuse their condemnation from error. I declare this clearly: this was formally their determination because they deny every mode of divine worship toward the cross, following the path of Catholic doctors and the prayer that the universal Church makes to the cross. Therefore, they say the aforementioned conclusion is "scandalous and offensive to pious ears" <note>a technical grade of ecclesiastical censure for ideas that are not necessarily heretical but are dangerous to the faith of simple people</note> and against the custom of the universal Church. This was precisely their judgment. First, let them tell me where it appears to them that I deny every mode of divine worship toward the cross according to the path of Catholic doctors. They certainly do not have this from my conclusion, in which I expressly and specifically say I deny "Thomas's method"—unless perhaps (which I cannot believe) they think no other doctor exists, and that Thomas’s way is the only way. Furthermore, they could not have gathered from my response that I deny every mode of divine worship according to the path of Catholic doctors, since I expressly say in my response that I concede the method granted by John de Guerra, who was <margin>Teacher of Scotus.</margin> the teacher of Scotus, and by the solemn doctor Henry of Ghent. Unless, perhaps, they wish to say that both Henry and John are not Catholics—which necessarily follows from their statements. For since I told them I follow Henry and John, and they

<column-break/>

then say that I do not follow Catholic doctors, who would not infer from this that the doctors I said I follow are not Catholic? But who could bear this? Who could suffer with a calm mind that Henry and John—such illustrious and excellent doctors of the Church, lights of the faith, and bulwarks of defense—should be rejected as non-Catholics, and consequently as Heretics and infidels? I cannot help but be annoyed sometimes, but I will restrain myself. Let us, however, attend to the second error. They say the conclusion is "scandalous and offensive to pious ears and against the custom of the universal church." Oh, most damned judgment! Let them see that they cannot escape the snare. For either my conclusion denies nothing except Thomas's method (in the way explained above), and then it is clear my conclusion is not against the custom of the church, as has been most extensively declared; or, as they wish, it denies every mode of adoration and denies that images are to be adored in the custom of the church. In that case, the conclusion is not merely "scandalous" or "offensive to pious ears," but simply heretical. For according to <margin>Damascene.</margin> Damascene <note>John of Damascus, an 8th-century theologian who defended the use of icons</note>, the honor shown to an image according to the rite of the Church reaches the prototype. He who does not observe the custom of the church in adoring images does not adore the one imagined and represented (which is God) with divine worship. Therefore, whoever judges a conclusion that denies this as "scandalous" and not "simply heretical" must himself be called simply a heretic.

# QUESTION FOUR: WHETHER AN IRRATIONAL NATURE CAN BE ASSUMED BY GOD.

### The fourth conclusion condemned by them is this: "Contrary to the common opinion of theologians saying that God can assume any nature into a divine person, I concede this only regarding rational nature."

---

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'N' depicting a figure sitting in a landscape with trees and a building in the background.</image-desc>

I DO NOT agree. By this conclusion, I do not intend to deny that God *could* assume <note>term: "suppositare" - to take a nature (like humanity) and make it subsist in a divine Person (suppositum), as in the Incarnation</note> any nature. Rather, I only intend to deny a particular and explicit assent to this assertion: "God can assume any nature." Between these two intentions there is a great difference. For even if this were among the things possible according to the absolute power of God, nevertheless, a proposition which, by the force of the words, only denies a positive explicit assent in this particular case, does not detract from the omnipotence of God, nor does it savor of heresy. The reason is that not every faithful believer is bound to assent explicitly and in particular to everything possible according to the absolute omnipotence of God, or to profess these things explicitly and in particular. Instead, it is sufficient to believe such things in general and implicitly, and to stubbornly disbelieve nothing. Therefore, not without mystery, I did not phrase the conclusion in these terms: "God cannot assume any nature," but in these: "I do not assent to the opinion saying that God can assume any nature." From this conclusion, by the force of its words, it cannot be inferred that God cannot do this; nor can it be said that I asserted this in the conclusion. Not in the first part, which is negative, nor in the second part, from which it only follows that a concessive act is held only regarding rational nature distinctly and in particular. I deny, therefore, a particular assent...

<meta>Pico continues his critique of Thomas Aquinas's position on the adoration of the Cross. Having established that his view aligns with other respected theologians, he now dissects the logical and philosophical failings of the Thomist argument, contrasting it with the "safer" opinions of Durandus, Henry of Ghent, and others.</meta>

->A P O L O G I A<-

<margin>Thomas.</margin>
...I provide in the conclusion. Thomas says, therefore, that because (as the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> says in his book *On Memory and Reminiscence*) there is a twofold movement of the soul toward an image: one toward the image itself according to what it is as a physical thing; another toward the image insofar as it is an image of something else. Between these two movements there is a difference, because the first movement—by which something is moved toward the image as a physical thing—is distinct from the movement toward the thing of which it is an image. However, the second movement—which is toward the image insofar as it is an image—is one and the same as the movement toward the actual thing. Therefore, he concludes that although the image of Christ, as a thing in itself, is not owed adoration, nevertheless, as an image, it is owed the same reverence owed to Christ himself, which is the <term>latria</term> <note>the highest form of worship, reserved for God alone</note> of adoration. This is the method of Thomas, which to other doctors rightly seems strange and dangerous. For the image itself, even as an image, is distinct from the thing imagined; as such, it refers to the thing imagined as something distinct from itself. Therefore, if as such it terminates the adoration of <term>latria</term>, it seems to follow that something other than God will be adored with <term>latria</term>, which is absurd.

<margin>Against the response of Capreolus.</margin>
Nor can it be said, as Capreolus says (wishing to save Thomas’s statement), that the image itself is not adored separately, but that the image and the thing imagined are one total object of adoration. For either one part of this "total object" is the image itself—which is a created relative being—or it is not. If it is not, then one should not say that those two things become one total object, because from such a statement it follows that each of them is a partial object, even if one of them is more principal. If it is so, it follows that some created thing of the category of "relation" will, at least partially, terminate the adoration of <term>latria</term>.

<margin>Against the foundation of the opinion.</margin>
Which certainly seems poorly Catholic to say, all the more so because not only can this not be said of a created thing, but even the Persons in the Godhead <note>The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit</note>, by reason of their relative properties, are not the formal terminus of adoration. Furthermore, Thomas’s foundation seems poorly effective. For when the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> says that the movement of the soul toward the image and the thing imagined is the same, he does not mean that the soul declares the image (as an image) to be the same as the original <note>original: "exemplari"</note> and thus whatever is owed to one is also owed to the other. Rather, the Philosopher only intends that the recollective movement—by which the soul is moved responsively toward the image—is also terminated at the thing imagined. It also has another true sense, which is: if I have a definitive concept of one relative thing, I also understand the other. But that every movement of the soul (and especially of the will) is the same toward the image and the thing imagined—the Philosopher intends this in no way. This is clear by a similar example, even according to the way of speaking used by Thomas himself. For he often says that the movement of the will is the same when the will is carried toward an end and toward those things which lead to the end (when it wills them for the sake of the end). And yet it is certain, even according to him, that the movement insofar as it reaches the end is <term>fruitio</term> <note>delight or enjoyment of the ultimate goal</note>, but insofar as it reaches the things leading to the end, it is <term>usus</term> <note>use of a means</note> and not <term>fruitio</term>.

<margin>Opinion of other doctors.</margin>
It seems, therefore, to other doctors that it should in no way be said that the image of Christ—even as it is an image not united to the divinity, and (what is more) is as such a relative entity—[should receive such worship].

<margin>Opinion of Durandus.</margin>
For this reason, Durandus says that this proposition, "the cross of Christ is adored with latria," is false in its proper sense, though it has an improper sense that is true. It is this: Christ, as remembered through the cross, or as present in the cross (just as the thing imagined is present in its image), is adored with the same adoration as if he were present in himself. And according to this sense, I also grant this proposition: "The Cross is adored with the adoration of <term>latria</term>." This is, therefore, what Durandus says: that it is adored as a reminder—

<margin>Opinion of Robert Holcot and Henry.</margin>
O

<column-break/>

<margin>and John de Guerra and Peter of Aquila.</margin>
—as a reminder; and Robert Holcot intends the same sentiment when he says that the more proper way of speaking is to say "we adore before the cross" rather than to say "we adore the cross." Finally, Henry <note>Henry of Ghent</note> and John de Guerra intend the same sentiment when they say that it is adored "by accident" <note>incidentally or indirectly</note>, and Peter of Aquila says the same.

<margin>What Henry and John de Guerra add.</margin>
However, that which Henry and John de Guerra (who speak more fully on this matter) add is this: they say that to an image, "by accident" or as a reminder, that honor is owed which is owed "of itself" <note>essentially</note> to the thing imagined and remembered. Now, it is certain that there is nothing to which <term>latria</term> is owed of itself except the triune and one God and Christ <term>because of</term> <note>original: "ꝓpter," shorthand for "propter"</note> the unity of his person <note>original: "suppositi"</note>; but an image of God cannot exist. It remains that if there is any image to which <term>latria</term> is owed "by accident" and as a reminder, it must be the image of Christ. Truly, because such an image principally represents to us the humanity of Christ, and secondarily his divinity, it seems that primarily "by accident" such honor is owed to it as is owed "of itself" to the humanity of Christ. Now, the humanity of Christ, taken by itself, is only adored with <term>hyperdulia</term> <note>original: "yperdulia," a level of veneration above saints but below God</note>; therefore, to such an image, primarily and "by accident," only the adoration of <term>hyperdulia</term> will be owed. Secondarily, however, and "by accident," the adoration of even <term>latria</term> will be owed in the manner already stated: because the image itself also secondarily represents and reminds us of the divinity of Christ himself.

<margin>Francis’s agreement with Henry and the Scotists.</margin>
And in this, Francis of Meyronnes and all the Scotists <note>followers of Duns Scotus</note> agree with Henry, saying that <term>latria</term> is not owed to the humanity of Christ. Because Thomas seems to hold the opposite regarding the adoration of Christ's humanity, he might perhaps also dissent from Henry in this case. And truly, Thomas’s opinion (as Francis says in his third book) is in some way dangerous, and in this matter of adoration his path does not seem to me to be very safe. Indeed, he proceeded so far as to say in the third book of his *Sentences* that the cross of Christ upon which he hung, even as an inanimate thing, was owed some adoration.

<margin>Thomas is condemned by Francis and cannot be defended by Capreolus.</margin>
And yet we know, according to all theology, that that which cannot be a subject capable of holiness or virtue cannot be the terminus of any adoration; and that John Capreolus, the defender of Thomas, himself confesses that this statement of Thomas cannot be defended. Nor does he have any other way of saving Thomas except by saying that Thomas himself seems later to have felt otherwise in his *Summa*.

<margin>Recap of the meaning of the conclusion.</margin>
From these things, therefore, it can be clear how Catholic my conclusion is, how much more rational it is than its opposite, and how much more in harmony with the common path of theologians. Recapping its meaning briefly, I say that this proposition "the cross of Christ is adored" can have two meanings. One is the proper sense, namely, that the cross of Christ—whether as a thing, or as an image, or as a partial or total object—is adored as the terminus of adoration. And this is the sense Thomas intends, and which I deny. The other is the improper sense of said proposition, which is: "the cross of Christ is adored," meaning Christ is adored in it as in his reminder, just as if he were present in himself. And this sense I grant, and with the Church I pray, saying:
> Hail, O Cross, our only hope. <note>original: "O crux aue spes vnica," from the hymn Vexilla Regis</note>
And with the Church: "We adore you, O Lord." <note>original: "ecclesia adoramus domine"</note>

<margin>Many things are deduced. First.</margin>
From what has been said, many things can now be clear. First, it is clear what I meant when I said elsewhere that, following the opinion of Henry and John de Guerra, <term>hyperdulia</term> is owed to the image of the Crucified. This was to be understood by reason of that which is primarily brought to our memory, which is the humanity of Christ. I said this truncatedly because I was referring to those authors, whom I considered to be veterans and already read and re-read ten times over by these masters <note>his censors</note>. Secondly, it is clear that they spoke falsely when they said I deny all [veneration]...

# OF THE QUESTIONS
23

<margin>Second.</margin>
Regarding the method of Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note>: even if I had not spoken as I did, but the proposition simply stood as "neither the cross nor any image is to be adored with <term>latria</term> <note>the highest form of worship, reserved for God alone</note>," still, by the force of the words, that proposition would not deny every possible mode of the adoration of <term>latria</term>. For it is clear according to sound logic that the negation or distribution of a "multiple term" <note>a word with multiple meanings or applications</note> does not deny or distribute it for every single instance of every possible meaning. Otherwise, the proposition "every dog is a star" would have to be simply granted or simply denied. Just as one does not say conjunctively that every celestial dog <note>the constellation Sirius</note>, every sea dog <note>a shark or seal</note>, and every barking dog is a star—even though this might be said of each one individually—likewise in this negative statement "the cross is not adored with the adoration of <term>latria</term>," where the word "adored" is equivocal <note>has more than one meaning</note> between adoration "by way of the end" and adoration "by way of a reminder," every mode of adoration is not denied conjunctively.

<margin>Third.</margin>
Third, it is clear that this proposition could be stated even thus, absolutely and without distinction: "The Cross is not to be adored with the adoration of <term>latria</term>," because in its proper sense it is true—or at least more probable than its opposite—and the proper sense is to be more regarded in the rigor of speech than the improper sense in which it is false. For just as an analogical term standing by itself represents its most famous meaning, so a statement having both a proper and an improper sense, if spoken without specification, is to be understood according to the proper sense rather than the improper. Therefore, as I said, I could have stated it even without distinction, intending to declare the sense in which I understood it during the debate.

<margin>Note.</margin>
From this I infer that although in a multiple proposition it is perhaps better to do as I did—that is, to determine the sense in which it is placed rather than to state it indistinctly—there is a greater defect in condemning a proposition that is true in its proper sense simply because it is false in an improper sense, than there is in stating that proposition indistinctly because of the truth of its proper sense. I wanted to note this here not only for this specific conclusion in which I determinately deny the method of Thomas, but for many other conclusions which, although they have a Catholic sense (which I always promised to declare, as I do now), were nonetheless condemned simply and indistinctly. Truly, whatever may be the case with my conclusion, they cannot excuse their condemnation from error. For I clearly declare that this was formally their determination: because he denies every mode of the adoration of <term>latria</term> toward the cross, according to the way of Catholic doctors and the prayer which the universal Church makes to the cross, therefore we say the aforementioned conclusion is "scandalous, offensive to pious ears, and against the custom of the universal Church." This was precisely their judgment. First, let them tell me where it seems to them that I deny every mode of adoration of <term>latria</term> toward the cross according to the way of Catholic doctors. They certainly do not have this from the conclusion, in which I expressly and specifically say I deny the "method of Thomas"—unless perhaps (which I cannot believe) they thought the method of Thomas was the *only* method because they had seen no other doctor. Likewise, they could not have gathered from my response that I deny every mode of adoration according to the way of Catholic doctors. For I expressly say in my response that I concede that mode

<margin>Scotus's teacher.</margin>
which Johannes de Guerra <note>John of Guerra, a Franciscan theologian</note> (who was the teacher of Scotus) and the solemn doctor Henry of Ghent <note>a highly influential 13th-century philosopher</note> concede. Unless, perhaps, they wish to say that both Henry and Johannes are not Catholics—which necessarily follows from their statements. For when I told them that I follow Henry and Johannes, and they

<column-break/>

then say that I do not follow Catholic doctors, who would not infer from this that those whom I said I followed are not Catholic doctors? Who could bear this? Who could patiently endure that Henry and Johannes—such illustrious and excellent doctors, lights of the Church, bulwarks of the faith—should be rejected as non-Catholics and consequently as heretics and infidels? I cannot help but be indignant sometimes; but yet I will restrain myself. Let us attend, however, to the second error. They say that the conclusion is "scandalous and offensive to pious ears and against the custom of the universal Church." Oh, most damned judgment! Let them see that they cannot escape the snares. For either my conclusion denies nothing but the "method of Thomas" in the manner explained above—and then it is clear my conclusion is not against the custom of the Church, as has been most extensively declared—or, as they wish, it denies every mode of adoration and denies that images are to be adored in the custom of the Church. If that were the case, then the conclusion would not be "scandalous" or "offensive to pious ears," but simply heretical. For

<margin>Damascene.</margin>
according to Damascene <note>John of Damascus, an 8th-century defender of icons</note>, the honor shown to an image according to the rite of the Church reaches the prototype <note>the original being represented</note>. He who does not observe the custom of the Church in adoring images does not adore the one imagined and represented (who is God) with <term>latria</term>. Therefore, he who judges a conclusion that denies this as "scandalous" and not "simply heretical" is himself to be called simply a heretic.

### FOURTH QUESTION: WHETHER AN IRRATIONAL
### NATURE CAN BE ASSUMED BY GOD.

->The fourth conclusion condemned by them is this: 
against the common opinion of theologians who say
that God can assume <note>original: "suppositare"</note> any nature,
but I concede this only regarding a rational nature.<-

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap initial N showing a figure in a landscape with buildings and a high tower or steeple.</image-desc>
**I** DO NOT ASSENT. By this conclusion I do not intend to deny that God *could* assume <note>the term "suppositare" refers to God the Son taking on a nature, as he took on human nature in the Incarnation</note> any nature. Rather, I only intend to deny a particular and explicit assent to this assertion: "God can assume any nature." Between these two intentions there is a great difference. For even if this were among the things possible according to the absolute power of God, nevertheless, a proposition which, by the force of the words, only denies a positive explicit assent in particular to that saying, does not detract from the omnipotence of God, nor does it savor of any heresy. And the reason is because not every believer is bound to assent explicitly and in particular to all things possible according to God's absolute power, or to profess these explicitly and in particular. It suffices to believe some such things in general and implicitly, and to stubbornly disbelieve nothing. Therefore, not without mystery <note>deliberate purpose</note>, I did not place the conclusion in these terms: "God *cannot* assume any nature," but in these: "I do not assent to the opinion saying that God can assume any nature." From which conclusion, by the force of the words, it cannot be inferred that God cannot do this, nor can it be said that this is asserted by me in the conclusion. For it is not in the first part, which is negative, nor in the second, from which it only follows that a concessive act is held regarding a rational nature specifically and in particular. I deny, therefore, a particular assent...

<meta>Catchword: particular-</meta>

<summary>Pico argues that his views on the adoration of the Cross are logically sound and backed by respected theologians like Henry of Ghent, accusing his critics of inconsistency. He then begins to defend his refusal to explicitly state that God can assume an irrational nature (like a stone or animal), distinguishing between God's absolute power and what a believer is required to explicitly affirm.</summary>

<meta>The previous page discussed the adoration of the Cross and the logical nuances of theological propositions. Here, Pico transitions to the fourth conclusion of his "Apologia," debating whether God's omnipotence implies He can assume any nature (like that of a rock or animal) or only a rational nature (humanity).</meta>

# APOLOGIA

The matter and the explanation of this assertion in my view: that "God can assume any nature into a Divine Person <note>original: "suppositare," a technical term meaning to give a nature its existence within a Divine Hypostasis or Person</note>" is something I can reasonably deny. This is partly because even if the opposite were true, it remains unknown to us in particular detail, and it does not seem that I am explicitly bound to believe it. It is also because it is not easy to falsify or disprove the assertion that "God cannot [assume any nature]," without it being a derogation of His omnipotence. This is strongly confirmed by the authority of the 

<margin>Henry of Ghent</margin>
solemn doctor, Henry of Ghent <note>A famous 13th-century theologian at the University of Paris</note>. Although he originally held the opposite opinion—namely, that any nature could be assumed—he

<margin>Words of Henry</margin>
later leaned toward the view that only a rational nature can be assumed. 

<margin>The first position which Henry recites</margin>
For Henry writes that regarding the possibility of a nature being assumed, there is no doubt whether God has the power to assume any nature that is "assumable"; therefore, the whole difficulty of this 

<margin>Argument against this position</margin>
question revolves around the "possibility" of the nature itself being capable of such an assumption. On this, he says there are two solemn positions. He describes the 

<margin>God has being in creatures in two ways</margin>
first position, which is more common and more solemn—and which he admits he once used to agree with—as holding that any nature subsisting in creatures can be assumed. Those who hold this believe that a nature can be "elevated" <note>raised to a higher mode of being</note> even if the corresponding power <note>the capacity for intellect or will</note> is not elevatable. To me, this does not seem capable of being reasonably held. To understand this, one must note that God has being in creatures in two ways. One way is natural and in a manner congruent to nature; the other is voluntary and in a manner that transcends the limits of nature. In the first way, He has being through "indwelling" <note>original: "illapsum," the natural presence of God sustaining all things</note> in every nature and creature. In the second way, He has being only in the assumed nature through "interpenetration" <note>original: "circuincessionem," often known by the Greek term "perichoresis," referring here to the intimate union in Christ</note>. And although through "indwelling" God is intimate to every creature—more intimate than the creature is to itself or the form is to the matter—nevertheless, through "interpenetration," He becomes most intimate to the assumed nature, and more intimate than He is in any nature through "indwelling" alone. Indeed, through the intimacy of interpenetration with the assumed nature, the One assuming <note>the Word/God</note> is united ineffably and incomprehensibly to the nature assumed. This makes it necessary for the assumed nature to lose its own "being of subsistence" <note>its independent existence as a separate person</note> if it had it before the assumption; or, if it never had it, to enter into the "being of subsistence" of the nature into which it is assumed, so that there is one "suppositum" <note>one Person</note> subsisting in a dual nature. For both of those natures in their union retain their own proper "being of essence." Through "indwelling," however, God is intimated to every creature naturally and in a manner congruent to nature for two purposes: first, for the primary act of nature, which is to stabilize its being so that it persists; and second, for the secondary act of nature, which is to produce its operation so that it acts. For without that indwelling, the creature cannot persist in being, nor can it draw forth its own operation. Because through indwelling, God preserves the creature in being and, by cooperating, provides all its 

<margin>Intimacy through indwelling</margin>
actions or operations, as Gregory says 

<margin>Gregory</margin>
in the 16th book of his *Moralia*, commenting on Job 23: "He is alone..."

<margin>Being Absolutely and Principally</margin>
> Are there not angels and men, heaven and earth? Indeed there are. 
> But it is one thing to be "absolutely" and another to be "principally." 
> For these things exist, but they do not exist "principally" because they do not subsist in themselves since the time they were created. For all things were made from nothing, and their essence would turn back to nothing unless the hand of the Ruler held it.
Behold the first of the points mentioned. And it follows concerning the second: "They would neither be able to subsist nor to move by themselves. They subsist only insofar as they have received the command to be; they move only insofar as they are disposed by a hidden instinct. The earth dries up, the sea is shaken, the air catches fire, the sky grows dark, men are inflamed, angelic virtues are moved. Are these things not driven by their own instincts, and even more by divine impulses?" 

<margin>Through interpenetration</margin>
But through "interpenetration," God is intimated only to the nature which He voluntarily assumes, and in a supernatural way.

<column-break/>

<margin>To whom God is intimated</margin>
And this is likewise for two purposes: to elevate the nature to the "primary act," which is the being of subsistence of the divine Person; and to elevate its power to the "secondary act," which is the beneficial operation of understanding and willing. For without the said interpenetration, a nature could not be elevated into the being of divine subsistence, nor perceive the difference of operations—namely, by seeing and loving the divine essence in a manner congruent to a creature. But through interpenetration, God raises the assumed nature to the divine being of subsistence and promotes it to divine operation, as 

<margin>Damascene</margin>
Damascene <note>John of Damascus, an 8th-century Church Father</note> says in book 3, chapter 18:
> The flesh of the Lord is said to be deified... not according to a change of nature, but according to the dispensation of the union, according to which the flesh is united indivisibly to God the Word by that mutual interpenetration of natures; and thus the divine flesh is enriched with divine actions because of its most pure union with the Word.

<margin>Henry's argument</margin>
He uses "flesh" there to stand for the whole human nature. From these points, I argue as follows: just as God is in every creature through natural indwelling for the two aforementioned actions, so He is in the assumed nature in a way that transcends the limits of nature. As is now clear from the words of Damascene, the similarity cannot be denied in some respect: for just as "indwelling" is meant to work those two things in the one in whom God dwells, so "interpenetration" is meant by its very nature always to work those two. But no non-rational creature is capable—nor can it be capable—of the "indwelling" of God for the purpose of receiving in itself, in a manner congruent to nature, the first divine operation mentioned, unless it is also capable of the second operation. For no creature can exist as a substance if it cannot also perform some operation through a power. 

<margin>Aristotle</margin>
Because according to the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> at the end of the 4th book of *Meteorologica*, all things are defined by their function; they exist for the sake of their operations. They "are" as long as they can perform their proper operations; and when they cease to be able to perform their proper operations, 

<margin>Damascene</margin>
they simultaneously cease to be. For as Damascene says in the same place, chapter 17:
> An intellect that is foolish and deprived of knowledge will not exist at all; for if it is inoperable and immovable, it is entirely non-existent.
By this, he clearly suggests that if it could not be elevated in terms of intellect, the substance of the intellect itself would not be assumable, nor would the man himself; for he would not be a "man" as he explains in the same place. Since a man is a "rational intellectual [being]," how then was God made man if He had assumed inanimate flesh or a soul without an intellect? That would not be a man. Therefore, likewise, no nature of a creature is capable—or could be capable—of the interpenetration of God for the purpose of receiving the first divine operation mentioned (above the limits of nature), unless it is also capable of the second operation. But the second is only possible 

<margin>Augustine</margin>
through the powers of intellect and will. Therefore, etc. For this reason, although the argument of Augustine touched upon in the first reason does not hold in its logical "form," it does not fail in any "matter" <note>A distinction in logic: "form" is the structure of the syllogism, "matter" is the specific subject being discussed</note>. It follows that if this nature (say, of a man) is elevatable according to its essence, it must necessarily be elevatable according to its power; and if not according to its power, then not according to its essence. Just as a man is immortal—and if not every man, then not as it follows—if a brave soul is immortal, then a non-brave one is too, because the reason for immortality or mortality is the same in all. And therefore, such an argument holds well by reason of the "matter," even if it were to hold by the "form" of the argument, which in truth holds by virtue of the form when looking at the common reason that applies to a nature. For instance, the immortality of the soul is the same in every soul. Let us look, then, at the possibility and impossibility of this assumption. Regarding God's side, as we said, there is no doubt. But because it is unknown to us from the side of the creature receiving it, for that reason, the understanding of the truth in this matter is difficult for us.

<summary>Pico argues that God's power to assume a nature into a divine union is logically restricted to rational natures (those with intellect and will), as a nature defined by its function cannot be elevated in its essence if it cannot also be elevated in its operation.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the defense of Pico's fourth conclusion from the Apologia, specifically detailing a second, "less solemn" but perhaps "truer" position held by Henry of Ghent regarding which natures God can assume.</meta>

### OF THE QUESTIONS

<margin>Another position recited by Henry</margin>
On this question: Therefore, here is another position different from the aforementioned, and although it is less solemn <note>meaning less commonly accepted in the schools of the time</note>, it is nevertheless more applicable to the truth. Though it may not seem as true due to its lack of familiarity, it is perhaps more true to say that no nature is susceptible to being assumed in the said manner through mutual indwelling <note>original: "circumincessionem," a theological term for the mutual indwelling of the divine and human</note> unless it is an intellectual nature—this pleases me more. 

Holding this opinion for the present, I say in response to the first opposing argument that the incorporeal soul of a rational being or an angel—and in man, the nature of the body insofar as it is ordered toward the soul as a thing to be perfected is ordered toward its perfection—is where the soul operates its intellectual activity more effectively when removed from every accidental disposition that might hinder it than when it is separated. Thus, the whole composite of body and soul, with its intellect, is the "susceptible" thing; the body is assumed through the mediation of the substance of the soul and in order to that substance, insofar as the soul is the intellectual power. So, in no way can that in which there is no intellectual power be susceptible to being assumed. 

By "intellectual power," I include everything in which the "essence of the image" <note>the *ratio imaginis* or the "Image of God" in man</note> principally consists within the substance of the soul. Thus, nothing is susceptible to assumption except by reason of the image of God which is in it, whether by mutual indwelling or according to substance and power (the latter being the case in Christ alone), or according to power alone (as in all those where the image of God is, as it were, impressed by its prototype, just as a coin receives the figure from which its image was pressed). Hence, 

<margin>Damascene</margin>
John of Damascus <note>An 8th-century Church Father</note> says in the aforementioned chapter that "according to the image," God the Word became a willing man in a willing thing; man is the image of God according to the intellect. What is "according to the image" if not the intellect? Therefore, leaving behind what is worse, He assumed what is better. It is as if he were saying: This is by no means possible to happen except by reason of the order which the nature has toward the intellect. He speaks against those who held that the human body was assumed in Christ without a rational soul. 

He also includes under the "intellect" the substance of the soul, showing that its force and power are involved in the assumption, adding: "For the intellect is in the middle between God and the flesh; the inhabitant of this is the image of God. Therefore, intellect is mixed with intellect, and the intellect mediates between the purity of God and the density of the flesh." I understand this "mixture" to mean the union through the mutual indwelling of the divine intellect with the human intellect, which—existing as three powers (namely, memory, intelligence, and will)—is united to the being of the soul. It is united through a certain mutual indwelling to the Trinity of Persons in the unity of the divine nature. 

<margin>Note the powers.</margin>
Thus, the direct and proximate cause or reason why something is "assumable" by God is the "reason of the image of God," which exists only in an intellectual substance. Because of this, only an intellectual substance is susceptible to being assumed. According to this, in the glorious assumption through mutual indwelling, the divine nature enters the assumed nature. This is like a seal: if the seal itself were reapplied to the wax in which its figure was already impressed, it would enter into all its corners in a way that it could not be applied to something in which the figure had not been previously impressed. In other creatures, there is only a "trace" <note>original: "vestigium," a footprint or faint sign</note> of God, which is found in every non-intellectual creature. Thus, no non-intellectual nature can be assumed except through the mediation of an intellectual one. 

To the second point—that an assumption to God could occur because the "efficient and substantial cause" is found in the assumed nature—I say this is true as a "co-cause." For if that were not the case, nothing could be assumed by God, just as one creature cannot be assumed by another. But this is not the *whole* cause, even if it is the cause on the part of the one assuming; though it allows the assumption to happen, it is not 

<column-break/>

on the part of the thing to be assumed. On that side, the entire cause of "assumability" is that the nature is an "image." By this alone is it capable of mutual indwelling with God and capable of being raised to that union in the divine essence in the unity of a Person. Therefore, there can be no final cause for why God should assume any nature other than an intellectual one; for the assumption of a nature is ultimately for its promotion and perfection in its elevation, which only an intellectual nature can receive. 

These are the words of Henry, almost word for word. It was therefore not rightly determined that my conclusion "savors of heresy" <note>A technical term in the Inquisition for a statement that sounds like heresy even if not explicitly condemned</note>, for my conclusion only denies a positive assent to those who contradict Henry. I have never read of a condemnation of Henry's opinion, 

<margin>Authors who agree with Henry. Two reasons against Henry.</margin>
nor do I believe those [my accusers] have ever read one. I know this: that neither Scotus, nor Godfrey, nor John of Guerra, nor Durandus, nor Thomas the Englishman, nor Robert of Colletorto, nor Bernard of Gannat—all of whom I have seen reciting Henry’s opinion—ever judged it to be heretical or to "savor of heresy." 

Lest they seem to have done this without reason, I wish to briefly set forth the way Henry seems to defend his position. There are two main reasons against Henry. The **first reason** is that in God is every "reason for providing substance," because He is the fullness of all being; therefore, it seems He can provide subsistence and personhood <note>original: "suppositare," to make a nature exist as a person</note> to any nature whatsoever. The **second reason** is that during the three days [He was dead], God provided personhood to the body that was in the tomb, which was not then rational; and just as He did so for those three days, He could have done so for as long a time as He wished. These are the two primary foundations of the opposing opinion, and Henry brings these very points up against himself. 

<margin>Solution to the first.</margin>
To the first reason, as we have seen, he responds that it is true that the fullness of all being is in God and every reason for providing subsistence and personhood is most fully found in Him. But this is not the *total* cause of a nature’s "assumability"; it is a "co-cause." Without it, the one assuming could not assume. But beyond this, something is required in the *thing being assumed* by which it is made "assumable." This is the "reason of the image" and, ultimately, a supernatural aptitude for elevation to a blessed operation <note>the Beatific Vision</note>. Since this is found only in intellectual nature, it seems reasonable that it alone is assumable. 

It seems rational that a nature which cannot be raised to the "second act" <note>actual operation or function</note> cannot be raised to the "first act" <note>the state of being/subsistence</note>. From this response, Henry seems to want to preserve the idea that nothing is taken away from God’s omnipotence. For while some conclude that because God has this power He *can* so provide subsistence, Henry grants all that power to God. He does not deny that God has the power on His part; he says it is because the irrational nature itself is not "assumable"—not because of a defect in divine omnipotence, but rather because of the excellence of the divine nature and the 

<margin>Multiple solutions to the second. The first.</margin>
deformed deficiency of the irrational nature. To the second reason, it seems many things can be said. First is the response of Henry, who says that God assumed the nature of that body [in the tomb] insofar as it was ordered toward the intellectual soul. By reason of that ordering, the body itself can be called "intellectual" in a ministerial and preparatory sense. To respond more completely, it must be said that when it is said that "nothing but an intellectual nature can be assumed by God," it means that nothing else can be assumed *primarily* as the total and equal object of assumption. The body in the three days was not assumed in that way, but only as a part of the rational nature which was the total...

<summary>Pico defends his theological claim by citing Henry of Ghent, arguing that only intellectual natures (like humans or angels) can be assumed by God because they alone bear His "image." He refutes charges of heresy by listing respected theologians who debated this view without condemnation and addresses the problem of Christ's body in the tomb.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico’s defense against the theologians who condemned his conclusions. Specifically, it concludes his argument regarding whether God can take on the form of an irrational creature (like an animal) and begins his defense of his controversial claim that Magic and Cabala are the best sciences for proving the divinity of Christ.</meta>

# DEFENSE

<margin>Second point.</margin> And first, regarding what was assumed: someone might perhaps say that the body of Christ was not properly <term>suppositated</term> <note>meaning: "given personal existence by the Divine Word." In theology, a "supposit" is the individual subject or person that "owns" a nature.</note> during the three days <note>the *triduum*, the period between Christ's death and resurrection</note>, because a body alone is not a nature capable of being its own person. Consequently, one might argue without being unreasonable that ending the dependence of such a body’s nature is not the same as "suppositating" it. Otherwise, anything that ends the dependence or supports a part would be said to "suppositate" it, which is not what we say. Thus, although the Word during those three days ended that dependence of the body—which the entire humanity would have ended, and by virtue of which the body in those three days shared with Christ its "property" of lying in the tomb—it did not, strictly speaking, "suppositate" the body in the same way it would "suppositate" a full human nature.

The clearest sign of this is that the nature of that body did not share with Christ the specific name "body" during those three days, in the same way that human nature had shared and still shares the specific name "man" with Him in a concrete way. Thus, the response is clear regarding the objections raised against the opinion of Henry <note>Henry of Ghent, a 13th-century theologian</note>, who seems to say this about other irrational natures: that the Word could not assume them through <term>circumincession</term> <note>original: "circumincessionem," meaning mutual indwelling</note> or "suppositate" them, especially considering the final cause <note>the ultimate purpose</note>. For Henry himself says: "No purpose could exist for the assumption of any nature other than an intellectual one," because assumption only happens for the advancement of the nature assumed—an advancement which only an intellectual nature can receive. 

<margin>Augustine.</margin> Hence, Augustine says in his commentary on John: "The Word willed to be born of man, so that you might be born safely of God." <note>original: "verbum voluit nasci ex homine: vt tu securus nascereris ex deo"</note> From this it seems that God would be born in vain from any other nature that cannot be born of God through grace. From these points, it should be clear that it is not irrational for me to lack an explicit act of contradicting this opinion in detail. 

And because these masters <note>the investigating theologians</note> especially insisted that such conclusions should not even be debated because of the "scandal" <note>public offense or stumbling block to faith</note> they cause, I want to say this about the conclusion: even if the opposite view is "truer" and follows the common path, if it were publicly debated, it would be far more scandalous to common people and offensive to "pious ears." For who among the uneducated and simple would not be offended to hear someone say it is possible that these propositions are true: **"God is a donkey"** or **"God is a piece of wood"**? <note>original: "Deus est asinus deus est lignum"</note> Or what about those claims which many who follow the aforementioned common opinion concede: **"God can be damned to hell"** or **"God could be tortured by the devil in hell"** or **"The Devil can be God"**? <note>original: "Deus potest esse damnatus ad infernum... Diabolus potest esse Deus"</note> While these might cause no scandal among many learned men when speaking of God's "absolute power," common and simple people would certainly be much more offended by them than by hearing that a donkey *cannot* be united to the divine nature in a unity of person. Yet these "fathers" have said that my conclusion, by the literal force of its words, derogates from divine omnipotence and therefore "tastes of heresy"—though I do not know what logic or indeed what theology they are relying on.

For let them say, I pray, whether he who says he does not assent to a proposition is saying the opposite? By the rigor of speech, does this consequence hold: "I do not assent (or I hold no belief) to this conclusion: 'The Pope is sitting,' therefore I believe the conclusion: 'The Pope is not sitting'"? Would not the first part be true of a sleeping man, or someone who had no mental act at all, while the second part could be false? Furthermore, if the present conclusion derogated from divine omnipotence according to true theology, it would not merely "taste of heresy" but should be judged as outright heretical. Indeed, even a sleeping Catholic or a small child who lacks the use of reason—and who does not hold assent to the proposition: **"God can 

<column-break/>

suppositate any created nature"**—would be a heretic, or at least would err in faith, which no one would say. 

From this, it is clear that their condemnation of these points is not correct. For their formal determination was made after considering the response of the one proposing it <note>Pico himself</note> and the opinion and motives and reasons of Henry, upon whose opinion the one posing the conclusion relies. They said: "It seems to us that the aforementioned conclusion, by the force of its words, derogates from divine omnipotence and therefore tastes of heresy." 

First, they were deceived because when I said I followed Henry in "this," they did not understand that by the pronoun "this" I was denoting the conclusion itself which they asked to be explained. Therefore, in "this"—that is, in the conclusion itself, in not assenting to the idea that "God can [suppositate] any nature etc."—I said I followed Henry. I did not mean to denote the full opinion that says "God *cannot* suppositate any nature." But they perhaps believed there was no difference between one statement and the other. However, if they are learned theologians, they ought to know the difference between explicitly *not believing* something is possible by the power of God, and explicitly *disbelieving* it. 

<margin>Why Henry is called the Solemn Doctor.</margin> Second, they ought to remember that from their statements it follows that Henry—who, because of the excellence of his teaching, is called the "Solemn Doctor"—died a heretic. For, as seen above, in his old age he inclined toward this opinion and remained in it: that not every nature can be suppositated by God. 

Third, just as in the condemnation of the previous conclusion, so in this one: however it may be with the conclusion, they are entirely in error. Because if it is true, as they say, that the conclusion is against the omnipotence of God, then the conclusion is simply heretical, and not merely "tasting of heresy" as they claim. 

Fourth and finally, they erred because even if Henry’s opinion were entirely heretical, the conclusion "by the virtue of the words" <note>literally interpreted</note> would not be heretical. For by the force of its language, it does not imply that opinion, as has been very extensively declared; and yet they specifically condemned it "by the virtue of the words."

### FIFTH QUESTION: ON NATURAL MAGIC AND THE KABBALAH OF THE HEBREWS.

The fourth conclusion condemned by them was this:
> There is no science that makes us more certain
> of the divinity of Christ than magic and kabbalah.

<image-desc>Woodcut decorative initial 'H' depicting a male figure standing in an interior space with a tiled floor and a large window looking out onto a landscape with buildings.</image-desc>
IN EXPLAINING this conclusion, I said that among the sciences—those which are sciences in such a way that they do not rely on revelation, neither in their method, nor in their principles, nor in their conclusions—there is none that makes us more certain (in the way that humanly discovered sciences can provide certainty) than that Magic about which conclusions are placed there (which is a part of natural science) and that part of Kabbalah which is a science and not revealed theology. 

These masters said that my explanation was not relevant to the words of the aforementioned conclusion, and that the conclusion, by the force of its words, was false, erroneous, and heretical. In their condemnation, I ask, let us see how many things are to be condemned, point by point. First, let them tell me: how could my explanation be *more* relevant to the words of my conclusion? For what is in that explanation other than an explicit declaration of the force of every single term in...
