<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s defense of his "Orphic" and "Magical" conclusions. Having defined his terms on the previous page, he now addresses the logical and theological validity of his claim that Magic and Cabala are the most effective human sciences for proving Christ’s divinity.</meta>

### OF THE QUESTIONS

placed in the conclusion. For there, I first explained what I mean by "science" when I say "no science," and what I mean by "to certify," what by "magic," and what by "cabala" <note>Kabbalah, the Jewish mystical tradition which Pico sought to synchronize with Christianity</note>. I do not see what further remains to be declared.

<margin>Second.</margin>
Second, I wish to show that according to the **literal sense of the words**, this conclusion is not only not false or heretical, but indeed its opposite is false—and according to my critics' own logic, totally heretical. For the stated conclusion is a negative one, which is explained disjunctively through three categorical statements as follows: "No science not revealed, etc., other than magic and cabala, certifies the divinity of Christ"; or "Magic and cabala do not certify, etc."; or "Magic and cabala certify us more regarding the deity of Christ than any other non-revealed science." This disjunctive statement is true and Catholic because at least one part of it is true. Thus it is now clear that according to the literal sense it is not false. But it is also clear that its opposite, according to them, would be heretical. For the opposite of "no non-revealed science... certifies more" is this: "Some non-revealed science certifies the deity of Christ more than magic and cabala," from which it follows by the literal sense that magic and cabala *do* certify the divinity of Christ—a claim they themselves regard as heretical. Thus it is clear that while they wish to condemn this negative statement according to its literal sense, they are forced by their own judgment to hold this affirmative statement as Catholic: "Magic and cabala certify us of the divinity of Christ." However, how true the conclusion is in itself can certainly be declared most evidently. For although there is no science invented by humans that can certify us of the divinity of Christ (since, as we said in the preceding conclusion, we only have certification of His divinity from the manner in which He performed His miracles, and we only know those miracles were done by Him and done in such a way from the testimony of Scripture), nevertheless, if human sciences can help us at all in this—just as they help in the knowledge of many supernatural truths—there is no science that can help us more than magic and cabala.

<margin>How many and what things are required to know the divinity of God.</margin>
For this purpose, so that the miracles of Christ may testify to His divinity for us, it is necessary to know first that they could not have been done by natural power, but only by the power of God. Second, it is necessary to know that Christ held that power from Himself and not from elsewhere. In the first point, no human science can help us more than that which knows the powers and activities of natural agents and their applications and proportions to one another and to their natural subjects; and what they can do by their own power and what they cannot. Among human sciences, this is best known by that science which I call **natural magic**, about which conclusions have been set down; and that part of **cabala** which concerns the powers of the celestial bodies. Because through these it is known that the works Christ performed cannot be done through natural powers, I placed that proposition among the magical conclusions: "The miracles of Christ could not have been performed through magic," as a conclusion whose truth can be obtained from that science. Thus it is clear that the judgment of those masters was not well-mastered, especially since they condemn the literal sense of a statement which, even if its meaning were not Catholic as we explained, still should not be condemned in itself; because by the literal sense it does not—

<column-break/>

<margin>To these things, it is said that if there is any human science invented by hand and not (like theology) revealed by God which leads us to understand the divinity of God, it is especially magic and cabala, wherefore let the explanation be clear. *Magi* [magicians], i.e., *mali* [evil ones]; *magi*, i.e., *magni* [great ones]. William of Paris. The ambiguity of "magic."</margin>

—infer that meaning, since it is a negative proposition explained disjunctively through three categories as said above. And for a fuller declaration of this conclusion: first, it must be known that, as I said above, through this conclusion I do not intend to compare magic and cabala to revealed sciences <note>i.e., Theology</note>. For I do not take "science" in the general sense in the conclusion, but for a science which rests neither on revelation in its method of proceeding, nor in its principles, nor in its conclusions. Nor do I speak in the present conclusion about the certainty of science held from revelation in the aforesaid manner, but about the certainty of a science found or acquired through demonstration—not **a priori** <note>reasoning from causes to effects</note> but **a posteriori** <note>reasoning from observed effects back to their causes</note> through effects. Therefore, I intend to say that if any science discovered by humans and not revealed certifies the divinity of Christ through His miracles, this is best done by the science through which the powers and activities of natural agents are known, along with their applications to each other and to their natural subjects, and through which it is known what natural agents can do by their own power and what they cannot. For once this is known, and then seeing the works of Christ exceed the degree and limit of those things which can be done by natural agents, we conclude necessarily that they were done by divine power—which we could not know if that were unknown. For to those ignorant of the limits of the power and strength of natural things, it remains possible to doubt whether those same works which Christ did could be done through natural means. Since, therefore, that part of cabala which concerns the powers of celestial bodies, and that part of natural science which I now call **natural magic**, best knows such things—and many Catholic doctors have named it so, however others may wish to name it—I said, not heretically, not superstitiously, but scientifically, most truly, and Catholically, that we are helped in knowing the divinity of Christ by such magic and cabala. Of this natural magic, even the supreme theologian **William, Bishop of Paris** <note>William of Auvergne (c. 1180–1249), a prominent philosopher and theologian</note>, a contemporary of Robert of Lincoln <note>Robert Grosseteste</note>, makes mention. He says that the forbidden *magi* are called such as if they were *mali* [evil men], because they do evil things. But natural *magi* are called such as if they were *magni* [great men], because they do great things. And because those [critics] could not tolerate this name "magic" and shouted throughout the city that I approved of **necromancy** <note>communication with the dead or demons</note> which the whole Church condemns, I say again and again that this name "magic" is an equivocal term for that which is called necromancy (which is done through pacts and treaties with demons) and for the practical part of natural science. The latter teaches nothing other than how to perform wonderful works by mediating natural powers through their application to each other and to their natural subjects. And this the Church has never condemned, nor can it condemn; rather, many ecclesiastical and Catholic doctors have approved and followed it.

<margin>Where both types of magic are practiced. In Egypt, in Ethiopia, and India.</margin>
Concerning this, as I said, William of Paris treats it in his *On the Universe, Corporal and Spiritual*, and he says that the forbidden magic flourished most in Egypt, because the worship of demons thrived there. However, this natural magic flourished in Ethiopia and India, because there is the greatest abundance of herbs and other natural things having efficacy in this natural magic. And elsewhere in his book *On Laws*, he mentions the same science, asserting it to be a part of natural science. A Catholic and most holy man is not ashamed of this natural magic—

On the previous page, he began justifying his conclusions by defining "science" and "certitude." Here, he moves into a linguistic and historical defense of "Natural Magic" to distinguish it from the forbidden arts.</meta>

### APOLOGY

<margin>
*Albertus Magnus.*
*He confesses that he has attained [this knowledge].*
</margin>
Albertus Magnus <note>A 13th-century Dominican friar and philosopher known as "Doctor Universalis" for his vast knowledge of the natural sciences</note> said that he had followed and discovered many things through experiences in this field. And what more needs to be said? Let these masters tell me whether this which I call "natural magic" is a prohibited thing or contains anything against the faith; they cannot say this even if they wished to.

<margin>
*Second objection.*
</margin>
But they will say: "We rebuke you for this—that you call it 'magic.' By using a word with multiple meanings, you create a scandal in the minds of the faithful. Furthermore, we hold from our doctors <note>The authoritative teachers of the Church</note> that all magic is forbidden. If all is forbidden, it follows that none is allowed; yet you say that some is not forbidden. Therefore, your opinion contradicts the doctors of the Church."

<margin>
*Response.*
</margin>
The ignorance of those speaking thus is truly remarkable. For first, the assignment of names is not being done by us now, but we use names and their meanings according to the custom of the ancients. If they chose to call this branch of natural science "magic," why do you want me to change the names? Should what they called "magic" be called "geometry" or "arithmetic" by me? I am not the first nor the latest to call this science magic; many holy and learned men did so before me. Let them be brought to court, let them be condemned, if it is a damnable thing to call this science by this name. Nevertheless, this assignment of the name was correctly established.

<margin>
*To which nation the word "Magi" properly belongs.*
*The word "Magus" means "wise" in Persian, like "philosophers."*
</margin>
If we consider Paul <note>The Apostle Paul</note> correctly, we can easily understand. For this word, "magus," is neither Latin nor Greek, but Persian. In the Persian language, it means the same thing that "wise man" <note>original: "sapiens"</note> does among us. Among the Persians, these wise men are the same as those called "philosophers" among the Greeks—a term first used by Pythagoras, though they were previously called wise men.

<margin>
*Look here to see the name given to the wise.*
</margin>
For among different nations, their wise men were called by various names: the **Druids** among the Gauls; the **Prophets** or **Sanhedrin** <note>original: "fenedrim"</note>, or **Pharisees**, or **Cabalists** among the Hebrews; the **Gymnosophists** <note>literally "naked wise men," referring to Indian ascetics</note> among the Indians; **Priests** among the Egyptians; **Philosophers** among the Greeks; **Magi** among the Persians; and so with others. Just as royal dignity has specific names among different nations, such as the King of the Egyptians who was first called **Ptolemy** and later **Pharaoh**; the **Artaxerxes** of the Persians; the **Caesar** of the Romans; the **Prestan** of the Indians <note>likely referring to the legendary Prester John</note>—which is what he is now called by our common people by the corrupted word "Prester John"—and so with others.

<margin>
*Magic, that is, wisdom.*
</margin>
If, therefore, magic is the same as wisdom, they rightly wished to call this practical branch of natural science—which presupposes an exact and absolute knowledge of all natural things, like the peak and summit of all philosophy—by the specific and appropriate name of **Magic**, that is, **Wisdom**. This is just as we call Rome "The City," Virgil "The Poet," or Aristotle "The Philosopher." If we were to abhor this name of "Magi" so much, we would certainly not listen patiently to the Gospel saying: "That Magi came from the East to adore Christ." Those Magi were not necromancers <note>sorcerers who communicate with the dead</note> or in league with demons; for they came to adore the enemy of demons—indeed, their Lord—who was to triumph over them. Rather, they were wise men learned in the science of celestial and earthly things, who worshipped and venerated the very Wisdom of the Father made visible in a human body. Jerome <note>St. Jerome, the 4th-century translator of the Vulgate Bible</note> makes this distinction very clearly in his letter to Paulinus, where, mentioning Apollonius of Tyana, he says: "Apollonius of Tyana, whether a Magus as the common people say, or a philosopher as the Pythagoreans say." In these words, he expressly signifies

<column-break/>

<margin>
*Note.*
</margin>
Jerome's point is that what is true philosophy is sometimes believed by the common people to be that which they call magic. Therefore, I should not be rebuked for having called this natural wisdom "magic," following the proper and customary way of speaking used not only by the doctors of the church but even by the Gospel itself. Nor have I caused scandal to the faithful by the ambiguity of the word, because in my conclusions I did not use this name indistinctly or equivocally. Instead, to remove every occasion for any sinister opinion, I distinguished **lawful magic** from **unlawful**, and **natural** from **superstitious**. I declared what this natural magic is and what it can and cannot do, so that even the simple and unlearned could not suspect anything impious or erroneous in the faith regarding my conclusions. In those conclusions, utterly rejecting and detesting prohibited magic, I placed this first conclusion precisely in these words:

"All magic which is in use among moderns, and which the Church rightly exterminates, has no firmness, no truth, no foundation, because it depends on the hand of the enemies of the first truth—those powers of darkness which pour the darkness of falsehood over ill-disposed intellects."

And after that conclusion, I placed a second which says that **natural magic is lawful and not prohibited**. I protest that I shall speak only of these things. Once this is done, what further suspicion can remain? Or what scandal can be caused by the ambiguity of this name "magic"? By distinguishing it thus and approving the natural while reproaching the superstitious and diabolical, it can serve the simple for edification rather than scandal.

<margin>
*Note.*
</margin>
Indeed, I have seen many who, hearing that the Magi came to adore Christ and believing the name "Magi" signified nothing other than necromancers, took this as an argument that magic is not prohibited nor against the faith of Christ, since practitioners of magic were the first to adore Christ. It is useful, therefore, to have taught the faithful so that when they hear "Magus," they do not always understand it to mean a worshiper of demons. And when they hear that among the Persians the Magi were held in the highest honor and reverence for their learning and wisdom, let them know that those were philosophers, not necromancers. For all nations have always cast out, persecuted, and detested necromancers as deadly and harmful—even pestilential—to the people.

<margin>
*For this has been conjectured everywhere about Albertus.*
</margin>
Similarly, when they read that Albertus <note>Albertus Magnus</note> spent much time among the experiments of magic, let them understand this as natural magic, not the prohibited kind. This prevents them from surrendering themselves to forbidden acts by following the example of such a great man, presuming that what was permitted to him is also permitted to them. Our "magical" conclusions therefore remove scandals from the minds of the faithful; they do not generate them. If they ever read in the doctors that "all magic is prohibited," they will immediately understand from the reasons for the prohibition that those doctors speak only of the magic that has commerce with demons, and that they intend nothing regarding natural magic.

<margin>
*Hilary.*
</margin>
Moreover, as Hilary <note>St. Hilary of Poitiers, a 4th-century theologian</note> says: "The understanding of what is said must be derived from the reasons for saying it." If they wish to return to the force of the words, they can know from logic <note>original: "dialectica"</note> that the negation or distribution of a term with multiple meanings does not negate or distribute it for every possible meaning combined. Therefore, since this term "magic" is equivocal <note>has multiple meanings</note>—applying to both the superstitious and the natural—a distribution added to it does not distribute it for every...

<margin>The number 14</margin>

Regarding doctors, astrologers, and philosophers—especially the Platonists and Pythagoreans—I assert nothing, but speak only of our own Church teachers. The question at hand is whether believing that there are properties in numbers and certain natural virtues in some way conflicts with the truth of the Catholic faith. Since we see these things observed by Catholic authors—perhaps even to the point of curiosity—there is no further reason to doubt that such an opinion should not be rejected as heretical. Therefore, when I speak in my conclusions about figures and numbers, I do not speak regarding their superstitious use through pacts and agreements with demons; for I have rejected all such things in my first conclusion. Similarly, regarding the idea that names have some 

<column-break/>

natural activity, this is known to everyone. Indeed, they do not have this natural activity merely as signs chosen by human whim <note>original: "ad placitum"</note>, but as they are in themselves certain natural things. <margin>Stoics, Peripatetics, Plato, Origen</margin>
names, an idea the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle.</note> oppose; yet Plato in the *Cratylus* agrees regarding those names that are correctly imposed. I intended to say only this when I compared meaningful names to meaningless ones, and Hebrew names to others in their efficacy in natural magic, etc. I wish to speak more broadly about this "Cabala," although we have already said much in the first part of our Apology; but those things will perhaps be no better understood by these masters than "barbarous" tongues are understood by the learned. Who, I ask, could hold back laughter at this? It must be known, therefore, that it is the opinion not only of Rabbi Eleazar, Rabbi Moses of Egypt <note>Maimonides.</note>, Rabbi Simeon ben Lakish, Rabbi Ishmael, Rabbi Judah, and Rabbi Nachman, and many others among the wise of the Hebrews, but also of our own

Finally, they say that Moses received a double law on the mountain: the literal and the spiritual. 
<margin>Literal law; spiritual law</margin>

<margin>The science of reception; Cabala means reception. Whence Cabala is derived and why it is so named</margin>
reception of one from another, the science itself was called the "Science of Cabala," which is the same as the "Science of Reception"—for "Cabala" means the same thing among the Hebrews as "reception" does among us. Later, these mysteries were committed to writing for reasons and at a time I will state below, and those books were called the Books of Cabala. In these books, many things—indeed, almost everything—are found to be in harmony with our faith. For they were both handed down from the mouth of God and written by Jews before Christ, at a time when they could be moved by no passion to defile or corrupt the truth itself. From these books and the authors of this science, I have set forth many conclusions for the confirmation of our faith against the Jews; which, since these masters perhaps not considering them well, [suspected]...

Two denarii <note>Roman silver coins; Pico is likely referencing the Good Samaritan's payment</note> also signify a certain sect by their property in the twelve tribes of Israel, in the twelve apostles, and in the twelve stones of the heavenly Jerusalem. They also believe—not without cause or by chance—that the number ten coincides with the commandments of the Law, the ten strings of the psaltery, and among the Hebrews (as found in the Midrash <note>A genre of rabbinic literature that interprets and elaborates on biblical texts</note>), the ten singers of the psalms <margin>Singers of the psalms</margin> who are Adam, Abraham, Melchizedek, Moses, Asaph, David, Solomon, and the three sons of Korah. Although they are enumerated differently by our people, they correspond to the ten instruments <margin>10 instruments.</margin> (that is, the ten instruments or ten modes of music) by which the psalms are sung, named among the Hebrews as:
<gloss>Nitsach, Mizmor, Shir, Tephila, Beracha, Halel, Hodaya, Ashrei, Alleluia <note>These are transliterations of Hebrew musical and liturgical terms: Victory, Psalm, Song, Prayer, Blessing, Praise, Thanksgiving, Happy/Blessed, and Hallelujah.</note>. I have observed they should be distinguished thus: through the first, odes are sung. The second is the instrument itself. Through the third, psalms. Through the fourth, canticles. Through the fifth, prayers. Through the sixth, blessings. Through the seventh, praises. Through the eighth, thanksgivings. Through the ninth, the happiness of someone. Through the last, the praises of God alone. You may add *Maskil* <note>original: "meſchil"; a Hebrew term for a contemplative or didactic poem</note>, by which contemplations are sung, and *Alleluia* will be like the *Ein Sof* <note>original: "eiſoph"; the Infinite or Boundless in Cabalistic thought</note>, not being placed in the count with the others. They also add the ten days during which the Spirit descended after the ascension of Christ, the ten curtains in the Temple, and countless similar things, always saying that nothing happens by chance, but God disposed all things by His wisdom "in weight, measure, and number" <note>A common medieval citation of Wisdom 11:20</note>.</gloss>

When the question is asked whether believing there are properties in numbers and certain natural virtues in any way contradicts the truth of the Catholic faith: since we see these things observed by Catholic authors, perhaps even to the point of curiosity, there is no further reason to doubt that such an opinion should not be rejected as heretical. Here, therefore, commenting on that passage of Paul in Romans 3: "What then is the Jew's advantage? Or what is the benefit of circumcision? <margin>The letters of God. The utterances of God.</margin>
From this saying of Origen, you see that besides the literal Law, something else was handed down to the Jews which Paul here calls the "utterances of God." For no one denies that the letters, that is, the literal Law, were handed down to them, but this is not credited to them as a prerogative; for the letter by itself kills, and unless the vivifying spirit is present, it is entirely a dead thing in itself. But besides these letters, the utterances of God were handed down to them: in which they rightly glory, and which are nothing other than what is called among the Hebrews the Cabala <note>term: Cabala; from the Hebrew 'Qabbalah', meaning 'reception' or 'tradition'</note>, that is, the true sense of the Law received from the mouth of God. Whence among the Hebrews it is sometimes called 
<margin>Cabala, that is, the true sense of the Law received from the mouth of God.</margin> 
the "Law born from the mouth," <note>original: "lex de ore nata"</note> which, because of that successive reception, was thereafter called Cabala. And that Moses then communicated this science, already received from God, only to the seventy elders, is openly testified by Hilary, who, in his exposition of Psalm 2 ("Why do the nations rage," etc.), writes: "It had already been established by Moses that there should be seventy doctors in every synagogue. For although Moses had preserved the words of the Old Testament in letters, he had nevertheless intimately disclosed certain more secret mysteries from the hidden depths of the Law to the seventy elders who would thereafter remain as doctors." The Lord also remembers this doctrine in the Gospels, saying: "The scribes and Pharisees sit on Moses' seat. Therefore, do all things whatsoever they tell you, and observe them; but do not do according to their deeds." <note>Matthew 23:2-3</note> Their doctrine, however, remained for posterity. These are Hilary's words verbatim. Behold, Hilary expressly testifies that there was another, more secret doctrine besides the written Law, which Moses disclosed to those seventy wise men. That this more secret and truer exposition of the mysteries of the Law was not published to everyone everywhere, but was revealed specifically by God only to Moses, and by him only to the other seventy wise men, is also testified by Origen in the previously cited place, saying of Moses and the prophecies: "These things are to be understood as being said to those to whom the utterances of God were entrusted." He adds: "And if there was anyone among them a wise and understanding listener and a wonderful counselor..." These are Origen's words. By these "wonderful counselors," they understand those whom the Hebrews call the Sanhedrin <note>original: "senedrim"; the supreme council and tribunal of the ancient Jewish nation</note>, that is, those seventy elders whom Moses chose by the command of the Lord. For until the time of Ezra, nothing was written concerning this doctrine; rather, as I said, it was handed down only through successive reception, whence it took the name "Cabalistic." But after they were restored from the Babylonian captivity through Cyrus, and the temple was restored under Zerubbabel, then Ezra, who was the leader of the synagogue, after he repaired the written Law of Moses and corrected the Old Testament, 
<margin>

desired also that those secret utterances of God, which until that time had not been written, should be written down. This was because, due to the captivity of the nation, they could not maintain that order of handing down the doctrine by hand <note>meaning: by oral tradition from person to person</note>, and it was rightly to be feared that because of their dispersion, if the teachings were not found in writing, they might eventually perish. Ezra therefore decreed that they should be written, employing special notaries for this purpose. And because there were seventy elders or counselors among whom this doctrine resided, he ordered that all those secrets be redacted into seventy principal volumes, which nevertheless were even then only to be communicated to the wise. This is what is read in Ezra in these words: "After forty days had passed, the Most High spoke, saying: 'The first things that you wrote, place in the open; let the worthy and unworthy read them. And so I did." <note>2 Esdras 14:45–48</note> These are Ezra's words verbatim. Broad and extensive mention of that council in which these books were written is found among the Hebrews in the book called *Seder Olam* <note>term: Seder Olam; 'The Order of the World', a 2nd-century Hebrew language chronology</note>, that is, the "Book of Ages," where it is recorded who sat in the council, and finally the acts and order of the entire council. From all this, it can be clearly seen that it is not a fiction of mine that Moses received a true exposition of the Law from God, and that it was thereafter revealed by succession from Moses to the seventy elders, and from them to their other successors. From this it took its name, being called Cabalistic; and in the time of Ezra, it was redacted into many books which are called the books of the Cabala—books which I acquired for myself at great expense. For the Hebrews do not wish to share them with us Latins. Since I have read through them diligently, finding there many things—indeed, almost everything—consonant with our faith, it seemed to me that Christians could have the means to pierce the Jews with their own weapons, since the authority of the Cabalists, whom they hold in great honor and reverence, cannot be denied by them.

Furthermore, it should be known that this exposition of the Bible corresponds to the mode of interpreting the Bible which among us is called "anagogical." <note>term: Anagogical; an interpretation that finds a spiritual or mystical meaning in the text, usually pointing toward heaven or the divine</note> Just as there is a fourfold mode of interpreting the Bible among us—literal, mystical or allegorical, tropological, and anagogical—so it is also among the Hebrews. The literal is called *Peshat* <note>original: "Pesat"</note> among them; this is the mode held by Rabbi Solomon <note>Rabbi Shlomo Itzhaki, known as Rashi</note>, Kimchi <note>original: "Chemoy"; likely David Kimchi</note>, and similar ones. The allegorical is called *Midrash*; whence you will often hear among them *Midrash Ruth*, *Midrash Tehillim* (on the Psalms), *Midrash Kohelet* (on Ecclesiastes); that is, the exposition through Midrash, or the mystical exposition upon Ruth, upon the Psalms, upon Ecclesiastes, and so for others; and this mode is followed mostly by the Talmudic doctors. The tropological <note>term: Tropological; an interpretation that finds a moral or ethical meaning</note> is called *Sekhel* <note>original: "Sechel"</note>; this is followed by Abraham Ibn Ezra <note>original: "Abraam abnazara"</note> where he does not explain literally, and Levi ben Gershon <note>original: "leuibengerfon"</note>, and many others, and before all, Rabbi Moses the Egyptian <note>Maimonides</note>. The anagogical is called Cabala; and this is because that exposition which is said to have been handed down to Moses by the mouth of God and received by succession in the manner aforesaid, almost always follows the anagogical sense, which is also the most sublime and divine among all...

...leading us from earthly things to heavenly things; from things sensed to things understood; from temporal things to eternal things; from the lowest to the highest; from human things to divine; from physical things to spiritual

Let a single example now

Thus it will be known to be the case with all other matters, if the proofs of my Cabalistic 
conclusions were seen: namely, that there is almost no article of faith in which the Jews are not compelled to agree with us through the authority of the Cabalists. But 
<margin>Objection. Response.</margin>

<margin>Origen.</margin>

<margin>Paul the Apostle.</margin>
to be this Cabalistic tradition, Paul speaks in this manner: "For what if some of them did not believe? Shall their unbelief make the faith of God without effect? God forbid! Therefore, it is no wonder if you never hear the authors of the Cabala cited by them by name. Truly, when we see our doctors

And Jerome himself even calls them "masters," saying: "This is the opinion of the masters." <margin>Philosophers, Cabalists, Talmudists.</margin>
into three sects: the Philosophers, the Cabalists, and the Talmudists. That the Talmudists were cited by our ancient doctors is not to be believed: partly because Clement and many others who cite the Hebrews lived before the composition of the Talmud itself (which was more than 100 years after Christ's death); and partly because the Talmudic doctrine was fabricated by the Hebrews entirely against 
us, while they were already fighting against Christians. Therefore, our ancestors would not have conferred such honor upon that doctrine as to think something said by them was particularly firm when corroborated by the testimony of the Jews. Likewise, it is certain they do not cite the Philosophers, because those who began to explain the Bible according to Philosophy began only recently. 
For the first was <margin>R. Moses the Egyptian [Maimonides], the first expositor of the Bible. Note the time of Averroes. It remains, therefore, that this doctrine of the Hebrews—to which Catholic doctors, by Jerome’s testimony, grant so much weight and which they occasionally approve—is that which our own doctors admit and believe was revealed by God to Moses, and by Moses through succession to other wise men. It is this which, from this mode of 
transmission, is called Cabala, which I also often see designated by our authors in this way, by saying: "as the ancient tradition says." This is the first and true Cabala, of which I believe I was the first among the Latins to have made explicit mention; and it is that which I use in my conclusions, which, since I set them forth expressly against the Hebrews for the confirmation of our faith, I do not know how those 
masters could have held them suspect in the faith. Truly, because this mode of transmitting by succession which is called "Cabalistic" seems to suit every secret and mystical thing, hence the Hebrews usurp it, so that they call every science held among them as secret and hidden "Cabala," and every knowable thing obtained from elsewhere by an occult path is said to be held "by way of Cabala." In general, however, they honor 
<margin>Usurpation by the Hebrews. The Art of Ramon.</margin>
two sciences by this name: one which is called <term>חכמת הצירוף</term> <note>original Hebrew: "Hokmat ha-Tzeruf"</note>, that is, the "Art of Combination." It is a certain way of proceeding in the sciences and is something similar to what is called among our people the "Art of Ramon" <note>The combinatorial logical system of Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1316)</note>, though perhaps they proceed in different ways. The other is concerning the virtues of superior things which are above the moon, and is the highest part of natural magic. Both of these are also called Cabala among the Hebrews for the reason already stated, and we have also made mention of both of these occasionally in our 
conclusions.

# OF THE QUESTIONS

<margin>This name is usurped by the impious.</margin>
in our conclusions. For that "combinatory art" is what I call in my conclusions "alphabetical revolution" <note>original: "alphabeticariam reuolutionem" — a method of rearranging Hebrew letters to find hidden meanings</note>. And there is that other art concerning the powers of higher things, which can be understood in one way as a part of natural magic, and in another way as a thing distinct from it. It is this latter art of which I speak in the present conclusion, saying that it helps us in knowing the divinity of Christ in the manner already declared. And although the name "Cabala" may not fit these two sciences by their primary and proper definition, it could nevertheless be applied to them figuratively. Truly, just as once only wise men were called "magi," but later necromancers and diabolical men—falsely claiming the name of a wise man for themselves—called themselves "magi"; so also among the Hebrews, certain men, polluting divine things with false and vain superstitions (indeed, in truth, differing almost nothing from necromancers), said that they possessed secrets about names and powers with which they could bind demons, perform miracles, and claimed that Christ performed miracles by no other way. These men falsely claimed the name of "Cabalists" for themselves, saying their art was that true Cabala which God revealed to Moses—just as necromancers say they received their incantations and brutish acts from Solomon, Adam, Enoch, and similar figures.

<margin>From whence the accusation against Christ regarding miracles came.</margin>
However, not only did I not approve or follow this falsely-named Cabala in my conclusions, but I expressly rejected it, setting down a specific conclusion directly against it, which states that the miracles of Christ could not have been done by way of the Cabala. Let these things suffice for the present conclusion, which would require a special book if we wished to declare exactly what natural magic and Cabala are. Here it is enough to have shown that nothing is contained in them which is repugnant to the Catholic and orthodox faith.

# SIXTH QUESTION ON THE
## SACRAMENT OF THE
### EUCHARIST.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'U' featuring an architectural scene with buildings and a landscape background.</image-desc>
UPHOLDING the common path concerning the possibility of "supposition" <note>In Scholastic logic, "supposition" or "assumption" refers to how a person (the "suppositum") can take on a nature, such as the Word taking on human nature</note> in respect to any creature, I say that—without the conversion of the substance of bread into the body of Christ or the annihilation of "bread-ness"—it is possible for the body of Christ to be present in another way, according to the truth of the sacrament. This is stated as a matter of *possibility*, not as the *actual state of affairs*. By this conclusion, I do not intend to say that the bread is not converted into the body of Christ, or that the body of Christ is not in fact in the sacrament as instituted by Christ, or that the actual truth of that sacrament is merely the presence of Christ's body alongside the bread assumed or "supposited" by the Word <note>Pico is treading carefully; he affirms the Church's doctrine of Transubstantiation (bread changing into Christ) but argues that God *could* have chosen a different method, like "impanation" (God becoming bread)</note>. For I expressly reject those claims regarding the facts in the conclusion itself, where I say it is "stated as a possibility, not as the fact." By "possibility," I wish to refer not only to the preceding statement about the assumption of bread by Christ, but also to the truth of the sacrament of the Eucharist and to the sacrament itself—indeed, even to the presence of the body of Christ together with the bread through assumption. Thus, perhaps it would not be necessary that, by virtue of this assumption of bread by the incarnate Word, the bread would be the body of Christ which he already assumed from the Virgin. Nevertheless, it is possible that he would be on the altar together with the bread if it were assumed by Christ. I speak, therefore, in the pre-

<column-break/>

-sent conclusion about a *possible* sacrament, its *possible* truth, and the *possible* presence of the body of Christ together with this "assumable" bread. Therefore, I am amazed that the present conclusion has been condemned as erroneous on the grounds that the aforementioned things are false regarding the sacrament of the Eucharist as it is now instituted (which they claim I am speaking of), when I expressly profess in the conclusion to be speaking of a *possible* sacrament and its *possible* truth. Let them, therefore, consider the words of the conclusion more attentively before they condemn a conclusion that so expressly refutes the sense they are condemning. Indeed, I say confidently that their determination can hardly be defended from error; for if the conclusion intended to uphold the truth of the sacrament according to Christ's institution as the Church holds it (as they say), then it would not only be erroneous but simply heretical. However, if the meaning of the conclusion is the one explained by me, it is not only not erroneous in faith, but rather it is erroneous to say the opposite. For there are many things which, as statements of fact, are heretical, but whose opposite as a statement of possibility would be heretical. For example, to say "the Father is incarnate" as a fact is heretical; but to say "the Father *could* be incarnate" is not only not heretical, but to say the opposite is heretical. And let these things suffice for the declaration and defense of the conclusion. But for the sake of scholastic exercise, leaving my conclusion aside, let us see if it is true that the body of Christ could be on the altar by another mode than the conversion of bread into it—namely, by the "subsistence" of bread-ness in the divine person <note>original: "diuino ſuppoſito"</note> together with the assumed humanity, so that there would be one person in three natures: divinity, humanity, and bread-ness. In this case, by reason of that person, any nature taken concretely could be predicated of the other, through the "communication of properties" <note>term: "communicatio idiomatum" — the theological principle where attributes of one nature (human or divine) are assigned to the person of Christ</note>: "God is bread and man," and vice versa. And "Christ the man is on the altar" just as "Christ the bread is on the altar," and so on. This would be sacramentally, or by virtue of the sacrament, if power for this were given divinely to the sacramental word. Nor should we concern ourselves with whether the phrase "This is my body" would suffice for this with the aforementioned power, or if something else would be required.

<margin>Damascenus: First argument for the affirmative side.</margin>
And first, for the affirmative side, it is argued that this should be held because John of Damascus <note>An 8th-century Syrian monk and Church Father</note> seems to hold this as a fact—namely, that this sacrament exists through "assumption." For he says: "And now, asked how the bread becomes the body of Christ and the wine and water the blood of Christ, I say to you also: the Holy Spirit comes upon them and performs this which is beyond reason and understanding. The bread and wine are assumed..." and further on in the same place: "Just as in baptism, because it is the custom for men to be washed with water and anointed with oil, God joined water and the grace of the Holy Spirit and made it the bath of regeneration; so, because it is the custom for men to eat bread and drink wine, God joined them to the deity and made them his body and blood." And further in the same chapter, speaking of this sacrament of the altar: "Isaiah saw a coal; but a coal is not simple wood, but wood united to fire. So also the bread of communion is not simple bread, but united to the deity."

<margin>Dionysius.</margin>
Moreover, Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a highly influential mystical theologian</note> in the third chapter of *The Ecclesiastical Hierarchy* calls this sacrament an "assumption." Therefore, what these doctors seem to say regarding the fact can be held much more strongly regarding the possibility.

<margin>Second argument: From Augustine.</margin>
Secondly, it is argued because, according to Augustine in his letter to Volusianus: "In miraculous things, the whole reason for the deed is the power of the Doer." Thus, to restrict this wonderful sacrament to a determined mode of defense which is not found expressed in the canon of Scripture or the determination of the Church is to limit the divine...

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s defense of his controversial theological propositions. Having previously discussed the "Cabala," he now addresses the technical nuances of the Eucharist, specifically defending the logical possibility that the substance of bread could remain alongside the Body of Christ through a "union" similar to the Incarnation, provided it is held as a possibility and not a definitive dogma of the Church.</meta>

-># APOLOGY<-

to restrict [divine] power to the capacity of our own understanding. This is dangerous, and goes against Saint Augustine, who says in the same place: <note>Augustine, Letter 137.</note> "If a reason is sought, it will not be wonderful; if an example is provided, it will not be unique." <note>original: "Si ratio quæritur non erit mirabile si exemplum ponitur non erit singulare."</note> Let us grant that God can do something that we must admit we cannot investigate.

<margin>Third [Argument].</margin>
Thirdly, it is argued: that anything whose opposite is not clearly established from the sayings of the Saints—even as a matter of fact—can even more strongly be held as a matter of possibility. But the opposite of this—namely, that in fact the "bread-ness" <term>paneitas: a scholastic term for the essential substance or "bread-ness" of the bread</term> remains on the altar, sustained by the divine <term>suppositum: the individual person or "subject" that holds a nature; in this case, the Person of the Word</term>—is not clearly established from the sayings of the Saints; therefore, etc. 

<margin>Gregory.</margin>
This is proven because that statement of Gregory in his Easter homily, saying that "the appearance and likeness of those things are the names of the things that were before" (that is, bread and wine), is explained by those holding this opinion as meaning they were "only" those things before. Now, however, they are not "only" those things, because the body of Christ is hidden there. 

<margin>Ambrose.</margin>
Likewise, there is the statement of Ambrose that the power of God, which creates creatures out of nothing, here "changes the creatures." Others, who say that the bread and wine do not remain after the consecration but are converted, explain this by saying the bread does not remain *as it was* bread—even though the same "bread-ness" is there—because of the different *suppositum* [the divine subject]. For this word "bread" signifies a subject in the nature of bread-ness, and this does not remain. 

However, there is a great difference between saying that the bread-ness remains sustained (hypostatized) in the divine subject, and saying that the bread-ness remains in its own proper subject. In this second way, there would be no <term>communication of idioms: the theological principle where properties of one nature (like humanity) are attributed to the person (Christ) who also possesses another nature (divinity)</term>, which does occur in the first way. I believe these authorities are entirely against those who claim this happens as a matter of fact and actuality, but not against it being a mere possibility.

<margin>Fourth [Argument].</margin>
Fourthly, it is argued thus: This opinion is approved as a matter of fact in the confession of Berengarius, <note>Berengarius of Tours (d. 1088) was a theologian who famously argued that the bread remains bread; he was forced to recant using this specific, very physical language.</note> which was approved by Pope Nicholas in Rome before 113 bishops. Therefore, it can much more strongly be held as a matter of possibility. 

<margin>Berengarius.</margin>
The premise is deduced thus: because Berengarius confesses that after the consecration, not only the sacrament but also the true body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ are on the altar, and are "sensually—not only sacramentally, but in truth—handled by the hands of priests, broken, and ground by the teeth of the faithful." <note>original: "sensualiter non solum sacramentaliter sed in veritate manibus sacerdotum tractari frangi & fidelium dentibus atteri."</note> These words do not seem capable of being taken in a clear and ready sense—the kind of sense the words of a so-solemnly approved confession ought to have—except by the sustaining of the bread-ness in the subject of God along with the body of Christ in the manner aforementioned. In this way, the same body of Christ becomes both "man" and "bread"; and thus it becomes whole insofar as it is the body of a man, and is ground insofar as it is bread—just as Christ died and lived on the cross: he died as a man, but lived as God. 

That some have accepted the words of the aforementioned confession in this way is evident from the "Master of the Sentences" <note>Peter Lombard, whose "Sentences" was the standard theology textbook of the Middle Ages.</note> in Book 4, Distinction 7. 

<margin>Master of the Sentences.</margin>
His words are these: "Others hand down that the body of Christ is essentially broken and divided, and yet exists whole and incorruptible; they assert that they gather this from the confession of Berengarius, who confessed before Pope Nicholas and many bishops that the bread and wine which are placed on the altar after consecration are not only a sacrament, but also the true body and blood of Christ, and are sensually—not only in the sacrament, but also in truth—handled and broken by the hands of priests, and ground by the teeth of the faithful." 

Behold! The confession of Berengarius, examined and tested by the Church, contains the claim that the body of Christ—not in sacrament only, but in truth—is ground by the teeth of the faithful. This, if taken plainly, would have truth through the "communication of idioms": for it is ground by the teeth according to its bread-ness, yet remains whole according to its humanity. 

But if someone wishes to explain the said confession by saying

<column-break/>

that "truly and not in sacrament only" refers only to the immediate verb—that is, "handled by the hands of the priests"—and the following words refer to the "species" <note>The outward appearances (smell, taste, texture) of the bread.</note> or the external sacrament, under which (being broken and ground) the body of Christ is received whole: then it seems the words of the confession are not being taken plainly as they lie and as they sound on the surface. Yet the words of a confession thus examined ought to be taken without violent interpretation or distortion, according to the sense they openly present.

But it is argued to the contrary on the opposite side: because this opinion regarding the remaining of the substance of bread on the altar has been condemned by the Church, it must therefore be avoided as heretical.

<margin>The first opposition. The first response.</margin>
According to those who hold this opinion, the first response to this is: it was condemned as a matter of "how it is" (*de sic esse*), not as a matter of possibility. 

<margin>Second [response].</margin>
Secondly: the condemned opinion differs from this one, which posits that the bread-ness remains sustained by the Word-Man. For that [condemned] opinion posits multiple subjects <note>supposita</note> after the consecration—the man Christ and the bread. This [Pico's] opinion posits one single subject in three natures—just as in the Trinity there is one nature in three subjects. 

<margin>Differences between this opinion and the condemned opinion.</margin>
That [condemned] opinion posits that the substance of bread remains after the consecration; this one, however, does not posit it in the manner of a substance, but in the manner of an "accident" <note>In scholastic logic, an "accident" is a quality that exists in something else (a substance), rather than existing on its own.</note>, similar to how it is with the assumed humanity [in the Incarnation]. That opinion posits that bread and wine remain; this one, however, does not, but rather "another bread," even though it is the same bread-ness. From that [condemned] opinion, it follows that the body of Christ cannot truly be on the altar under the sacrament, since the bread is changed in nothing. From this one, however, that does not follow, since it posits that the bread is changed, even in its bread-ness, as to its way of being. From that opinion, it cannot be verified that "the bread is the body of Christ," since they are two different subjects. From this one, it is verified because of the unity of the subject, which is one in two natures. From that opinion, it follows that whatever is in this sacrament is not to be adored with *latria* <note>The highest form of worship, reserved for God alone.</note>, since there are two subjects—Christ and Bread. This opinion, however, posits that whatever is under the sacrament is adored with a single adoration because of the unity of the subject.

<margin>Second [Argument].</margin>
Secondly, it is argued that there is no way it can be saved that the body of Christ could be on the altar through that method. For when it is asked whether the body of Christ can be on the altar, etc., it is not understood as the "body" that Christ *is* (taking "body" as a genus or category), but it is understood as the "body" that is a *part* [of him], which is not predicated of the man directly. Such a body, which is a part, does not communicate its properties to a co-assumed nature, nor to the subject, nor vice versa. For although God is man and vice versa, God is not the "head of Christ" and vice versa. And although Christ as man is everywhere by reason of his person <note>suppositum</note>, the head of Christ as man is not everywhere, because the parts of the assumed nature do not communicate their properties to the person, nor are they predicated of it, or vice versa. Therefore, even if bread-ness were assumed by the Word along with "body-ness," it still would not be said that "the body of Christ is bread," or that "because the bread is on the altar, the body of Christ is on the altar." It could, however, be said and verified that "the bread is the body" that Christ is, according to how "body" is taken as a genus. 

That it is not understood in any other way in this question and in the sacrament is apparent: first, because the "body" as a genus which is said directly of Christ is not called "the body of Christ," just as the "animal" or "man" that Christ is, is not called "the animal of Christ" or "the man of Christ." Secondly, because the form of the words in which this sacrament was instituted is this: "This is my body." It is certain that the truth of those words is not preserved regarding "body" as a genus. For the "animal" that is predicated of me directly is not "my animal," but the "animal that I am." Thirdly, because if it had been consecrated during the three days of Christ's death, there would have been on the altar not "body" as a genus, but "body" as a part only. 

<summary>Pico defends the logical possibility of the bread's substance remaining in the Eucharist alongside Christ's body by comparing it to the Incarnation. He analyzes historical texts and the "Confession of Berengarius" to argue that this view, while not the Church's official "fact," is a valid intellectual possibility.</summary>

## QUESTIONS 29

...for it is a living body: which at that time was not, therefore the body of Christ, as is asked here and as is dealt with in the sacrament, is only a part—which is not predicated of the bread, or of God, or of man. For it does not share the <term>idiomata: the specific properties or characteristics of a nature</term> of the other natures. Therefore, it would not be true to say that the body of Christ was on the altar in the aforementioned way by reason of the bread or the <term>suppositum: the individual person or "subject" that holds a nature; here, the Divine Person of the Word</term>.

<margin>Third [Argument].</margin>
Moreover, given that by reason of the said <term>substentificatio: the act of a Person (suppositum) sustaining a nature</term> within one person, the bread were the body: yet, it does not follow that where the bread is on the altar, there the body of Christ is; rather, the bread on the altar would be the body of Christ in heaven. This is just as in the <term>triduum: the three days between Christ's death and resurrection</term>, the soul and body were sustained in the person [of the Word]; yet because of this, the soul was not in the tomb with the body, nor was the body in hell with the soul.

<margin>Fourth.</margin>
Moreover, if there were this "sustenance," it would have to end at that which we say the conversion of the bread ends at—which is the body of Christ. But the sustenance of a foreign nature cannot end there; for this is proper to the uncreated person alone according to the common path. Therefore, a sustenance of "bread-ness" <note>original: "paneitatis"</note> cannot occur in the person of another nature in this sacrament.

<margin>Fifth.</margin>
Likewise, it is argued thus: because according to the aforementioned mode of the sustenance of "bread-ness" in the Word together with the body of Christ long ago assumed, the body would not *begin* to be on the altar; instead, something would newly begin to be the body of Christ. If, however, it does not begin—since it was not there before—it follows that it will not be on the altar.

<margin>Sixth.</margin>
Likewise, it is argued that although the person of the Word could assume a "bread-ness" which, in assuming, He would create (just as we hold regarding the humanity of Christ), yet He cannot assume a "bread-ness" existing in its own person [suppositum]: because this is to destroy the "bread-ness," not to assume it.

<margin>Seventh.</margin>
Moreover, it seems that power cannot be conferred on the Word regarding the union of "bread-ness" to the Word, because the assumption of "bread-ness" into the person of the Word is of greater difficulty than creation. This is because the Divine Being is further removed from the nature of "bread-ness" (to which it is said to be communicated in the assumption) than being is from non-being. And yet, power cannot be communicated to a creature to operate or cooperate in creation; therefore, neither can it be for assumption.

<margin>Thomas. Eighth. Ninth.</margin>
This is confirmed by the authority of Saint Thomas [Aquinas] in the third part [of the Summa], who says that a creature cannot cooperate toward the union. Moreover, if that were granted, after receiving the sacrament, the priest would not be fasting, and there would be not only spiritual food there, but also bodily food—which is against the dignity of the sacrament. Item: Christ would be "letting go" of something after He had assumed it into the unity of His person, because He would assume "bread-ness" which He would then let go of once the bread was converted into limbs.

<margin>Response. To the second [argument] on the opposite side.</margin>
To these things, it might perhaps be said first, by upholding this statement: that without the conversion of bread into the body of Christ, it can happen that the body of Christ comes to be on the altar in the aforementioned way through the sustenance of "bread-ness" in the Word together with the humanity long ago assumed. Regarding the "body" as a <term>genus: a general category or classification</term>, it is not a part, and so it is regarding the body which is Christ; it is derived from "corporeity" which is a nature, and it is predicable "in the nominative." And when it is argued regarding the "body as genus," that is, that which is God: just as when it is said "by the Word of the Lord" (that is, by the Word who is the God of heaven) "the heavens were established," <note>Psalm 33:6</note> so we say the substance of matter remains through the whole natural <term>transmutation: change or transformation</term>, namely the substance which is matter. Just as it is also said by our adversaries that the substance of the bread is converted into the body of Christ—certainly the substance which is bread, not that which is a *part* of bread.

<margin>Damascene.</margin>
So also Damascene <note>John of Damascus, 8th-century theologian</note> in Book III, Chapter 17, accepts the "flesh of Christ" (that is, the flesh which is Christ) as a genus, saying that the flesh of the Lord is said to be deified and con-

<column-break/>

-substantial with God. And when it is argued that the form of the words would not be fitting...

<margin>Response to the third.</margin>
..."This is my body" [meaning] "the body is a part of me"—it will be said that perhaps it would not happen through such a form of words. Perhaps a sacramental power would be divinely given to any word whatsoever; and perhaps every power that God could give, He could give to any word. God could give it to this word: "This is my body," or even to a non-significant word by His absolute power, because the power of God is not bound to the meaning of words. And when it is argued that granted that bread is the body and vice versa, it still does not follow that where the bread is on the altar [the body is], it will be said that indeed it *does* follow. For whatever is said of the predicate is also said of the subject. For instance, because God is man and God is everywhere, it follows that the man Christ is everywhere just as God is; and that God is enclosed in the cradle and is the Son of the Virgin, and seeks the breast just like the man Christ. Thus it follows if Christ-man is bread and vice versa: that if the bread is on the altar, therefore Christ-man is also there, not only by that reason by which He is everywhere as God, but because the bread is on the altar. For the assumed natures share their properties [idiomata] on the part of the subject, especially because in the subject it is held as the <term>suppositum: the person</term>. It is said "on the part of the subject" because on the part of the predicate they perhaps do not necessarily share properties, because there it is held as the nature. Therefore, perhaps it is not necessary that Christ be "man" everywhere, though He is God everywhere, even if on the part of the subject the "man Christ" is everywhere. Nor is the argument brought forward about the soul and body in the *triduum* valid, because they were not so united in the person that they were predicated of the person or of each other when they were united as parts of one nature; and therefore it is not necessary for them to share properties among themselves like those natures which are spoken of in relation to each other. It is certain, however, that if it does not follow by necessity, it follows at least by possibility.

<margin>Response to the fourth.</margin>
Regarding what is said—that if there is a sustenance of bread-ness, it must end at that which we say the conversion ends at (the body)—it is answered that this has no necessity. But we can say the sustenance happens in the person [suppositum] simply, even if those positing conversion say it ends at the "body as a part." It could also perhaps be said, as will be discussed below, that the sustenance can end at the "body" not as human, but as united. For if the Divine Person has another nature to sustain in itself insofar as He draws it into His own being, to whomever He communicates His infinite being, He could communicate that He sustains another nature united to Himself in that same being; and regarding this, see below.

<margin>Response to the fifth.</margin>
When indeed it is objected that according to this mode the body of Christ (or "Christ the body") would not *begin* to be, it would be said that: just as if bread-ness were to come to Christ (who was already man), Christ-man would begin to be bread; so He will begin, by accident, to be on the altar in a new way because it happens to the bread. Namely, Christ-man will begin to be on the altar visibly, and as the food of the faithful by reason of the assumed bread-ness—just as Christ-God began to be in the lap or womb of His mother in a new way by reason of the assumed humanity.

<margin>Response to the sixth.</margin>
To that which is said about the assumption of a bread-ness pre-existing in its own person: it is answered that God can assume every assumable nature pre-existing in its own person and, in the act of assuming, deprive it of its own personhood and draw it to His own being. For it is established that the Word could let go of the human nature, which would immediately have its own sustenance and the status of a person—even though it does not have this while united to the Word—and it would be, as to its essence, the same humanity that was previously united. <meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s defense of his thesis on the Eucharist. He is responding to objections regarding the "Third Opinion"—the theory that the bread might remain substantially present alongside Christ's body. <header>APOLOGIA</header>

In a similar way, he could assume a humanity that previously existed in its own <term>suppositum: the individual person or "subject" that holds a nature</term> in the manner already described; it would be the same nature, now assumed, which was previously not assumed. When it is argued that power cannot be conferred to the Word for this purpose, perhaps it can and perhaps it cannot. If an inherent power cannot be given because such power would be a created thing, perhaps an "assistant" power can be given, because such a power would be uncreated <note>Pico is distinguishing between a power that lives "inside" the sacrament (inherent/created) and God's own direct power acting "alongside" it (assistant/uncreated).</note>. In this way, the "assumption of breadness" <note>original: "assumptio paneitatis"; the act of the Divine Word taking on the nature of bread</note> would occur sacramentally by the power of the Word, just as great men believe power is conferred upon the sacraments of the New Law. Perhaps, if inherent power can be conferred to the sacramental word to convert the whole into the whole—especially into something already existing without increasing it—it could also be conferred for the aforementioned effect. For it might seem to some that the latter is just as difficult as the former.

<margin>Reason for the seventh [argument].</margin>

Regarding what is said about breaking the fast, one would respond that the rule about not breaking the "natural fast" <note>The "natural fast" required total abstinence from food and drink before receiving the Eucharist.</note> follows the commonly held view: namely, that the substance of the bread does not remain. If we propose that the substance *does* remain, we would say something else. Or perhaps it will be said that a priest is not called "fasting" after taking the sacrament simply because the substance of the bread is absent; for no matter how much the substance of the bread is gone, if a Jew or a Christian were to consume the sacramental species as physical food and with the intention of eating, they would break the fast. But because the priest does not consume it as physical food, but as a sacrament, the fast is not broken. It would be similar here: if the substance of the bread remained, it would still not break the natural fast, provided it was not consumed as physical food.

<margin>Reasons for the eighth.</margin>

As for the saying that "Christ does not let go of what he once assumed," this is said by presupposing that he is held to have assumed only human nature—as in fact he only assumed that. However, he could assume another nature and then let it go. It can also be said that if "breadness" were assumed by the Word, it would never be let go by the Word of its own accord or on its part; rather, "by accident," due to the condition of the assumed nature with its natural defects, he would let it go because of the corruption of the assumed nature—just as he let go of the humanity <note>i.e., the union of soul and body was severed at death</note> during the three days <note>The "triduum," the period between Christ's death and resurrection.</note>.

<margin>Reasons for the ninth.</margin>

But let us inquire again by way of debate whether the body, which is a part of Christ's being, can be saved on the altar truly without the conversion of the bread into it. It seems it can. Just as color is sustained in a substance as its subject by means of another <term>accidens: an attribute or quality that is not essential to a thing's nature</term>—for example, a surface—it is not that the surface is the "subject" of the color (for one accident is not the subject of another, as the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> says "quality is not quality"), but rather because color does not exist in a subject except in relation to the surface. In this same way, "breadness" can be sustained in the Word by means of the body. Not that the body is the immediate sustainer and "sustenance-maker" of the assumed breadness, with the Word being primary, but because "breadness" does not have its sustenance in the person of the Word except in relation to the body of Christ as a part. God can place this order between "assumable" natures, even if they do not have that order in their own nature, just as he can take away the natural order from things they have between themselves—as he did with heat and the act of heating in the furnace of the Chaldeans <note>A reference to the Biblical story of the three youths in the fiery furnace, where the fire existed but did not burn them.</note> and in many other cases.

<margin>Argument for the affirmative side.</margin>

Therefore, just as color—because it exists in a substance in relation to the surface—is spoken of in the concrete by way of an accidental quality (saying "the surface is colored"), so "breadness," which is a substance, will be spoken of in relation to the body of Christ taken in the concrete. This is done by way of a "substantial quality" or by way of "whatness" <note>original: "per modum quid"</note>, by saying "the Son of God is bread" and vice versa—just as humanity is spoken of regarding the <term>suppositum: the Divine Person</term>

<column-break/>

in its "whatness" by saying "the Son of God is man" and vice versa. Therefore, because God is man and vice versa, they share their <term>idiomata: the specific properties or characteristics of a nature</term>; where there is God, there is man. And similarly regarding the surface and the white thing, so too regarding the bread and the body. For if the bread is on the altar, the body of Christ is on the altar. 

<margin>The dogma of the ancient theologians.</margin>

Perhaps it should be said differently: that assumed natures have the "mode of an accident," as the ancient theologians used to say, insofar as they come to a person who already exists in actuality and do not "constitute" that person, but rather are themselves "constituted in being" through that person. Just as in accidents one is found to be the subject of another (though not the ultimate one), as we say the power of the soul is the subject of the virtues and habits that are sustained by the soul, and similarly the surface is in some way called the subject in respect to color; so, although one assumed nature cannot of itself and primarily sustain another nature, nevertheless, insofar as it is united to the Word and sustained in it, it can sustain another nature in itself. It can have the mode of a "quasi-subject" in respect to that other nature, and that other nature can have the "mode of an accident" in respect to it—solely in that one is sustained in the other as it is united to the Word and sustained by it. For if the person (the Word) only provides sustenance to an assumed nature by reason of its infinite being (to which it draws the nature united and associated with it), then to whatever nature it communicates its infinite being, it also communicates the power to sustain another nature united to itself.

In this way, also, a substance—insofar as it draws an accident to its own being (because an accident is not a "being" except because it belongs to a "being")—gives to it the ability to sustain another accident that comes to it, just as an act comes to a potentiality, within itself and in its own being. 

<margin>How an accident is a being.</margin>

Therefore, the body (accepted as a part) as united to and sustained by the Word in its own being—which is the being of the Word communicated to it—can provide sustenance within itself to the "assumable" nature of the bread, which takes on the mode of an accident. For it is presupposed that just as God gives to accidents the mode of a substance <note>In the traditional view of the Eucharist, the appearances (accidents) of bread and wine exist without a subject/substance.</note>, so he can give to "breadness" the mode of an accident by sustaining it in something else that acts as a subject toward it. It makes no difference in this regard whether that thing is "perfect in its species" or not; for sometimes the subject of an accident is imperfect in its species, such as a head or a hand. Just as God produces some creatures immediately and others through intermediaries, and just as he terminates some creatures in himself as their end through others; so also the Word can terminate some creature in himself as the sustaining person through the mediation of another. And just as the creatures through which God produces things are called "producers," and creatures through which he terminates things in himself as their end are called "ends" or "sub-ends," so the creature through which the Word sustains another in himself will be said to "provide sustenance." 

Therefore, by reason of such sustenance in the body of Christ as a "quasi-subject" and immediate sustainer, it will be said in the concrete: "the bread is the body" and vice versa, just as "the Son of God is man" and vice versa. They will share their properties in the manner mentioned above, like the surface and the colored thing. For "bread" stands for that which sustains "breadness," just as "white" stands for that which sustains "whiteness." For as the Philosopher says in the first book of the *Topics*, "white" is a body having such a color; and as Damascene says in Book III, Chapter 11, "God" is he who has the divine nature, and "man" is he who has the human nature, and so on for the rest. And just as it makes no difference to something being "white" whether that in which the whiteness is sustained is perfect in its species or not, so it makes no difference to something being called "bread" whether that which is the "quasi-subject" in which the "breadness" is immediately sustained is perfect in its species or...

<margin>Aristotle. [John] Damascene.</margin>

He defends this "Third Opinion" by explaining that fasting is an intentional sacramental act rather than a physical one, and that God can alter the natural order of subjects and attributes.</summary>
