<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s complex theological inquiry into the "Third Opinion" regarding the Eucharist. In the previous pages, he explored the possibility of the Divine Word "assuming" the nature of bread (impannation) rather than the bread being destroyed or converted into flesh. Here, he examines the philosophical mechanics of how one nature can support another and addresses arguments that claim this "assumption" model is more logical than the traditional "conversion" (transubstantiation) model.</meta>

### QUESTIONS

<margin>Objection.</margin> ...is perfect, or a nature, or a part of nature. On the contrary, because an assumed nature, or a part of an assumed nature, does not have the character of a <term>suppositum: the individual "subject" or "person" that exists in itself</term>; nor does it have the "being of subsistence" in itself. For although the "being of the Word" is communicated to it, nevertheless, insofar as it belongs to that nature, it is not the "being of subsistence," but rather the "being of existence" in another. Therefore, an assumed nature, in the state of being united, cannot sustain another nature within itself, nor can it draw it to a <term>suppositum</term> since it does not possess the character of a <term>suppositum</term> itself.

<margin>Solution.</margin> But if this conclusion holds, would it not also conclude that a surface cannot support color within itself? For the "being" which belongs to subsistence in respect to a substance—when communicated to an <term>accident: a non-essential quality like color or smell</term>—becomes the "being of existence." Thus, a surface could not be the subject of color because the surface itself is an accident. Must we then say that the "being of the Word," as it belongs to the assumed humanity in relation to the Word, is the "being of existence," but as it belongs to that same humanity in relation to <term>breadness: the essential nature of bread</term>, it is the "being of subsistence"? However, as it belongs to the nature assumed last, it is simply the "being of existence," just as might be said of a surface.

<margin>Objection.</margin> But against the previous points, it is argued as follows: a nature is united immediately to a <term>suppositum</term>. Therefore, it is not possible for "breadness" to be united to the <term>suppositum</term> of the Word through the mediation of another nature, since nothing can fall as a medium between a nature and its <term>suppositum</term>.

<margin>Solution.</margin> But perhaps a nature is united immediately to its *own* <term>suppositum</term>; however, regarding an external <term>suppositum</term>, in respect to which it has the mode of an accident, this is not necessary. Instead, one nature can be united to a <term>suppositum</term> through the mediation of another in the manner described above.

<margin>Objection.</margin> On the contrary, if the analogy of the surface holds, it would follow that just as a surface separated from its substance is the subject of color and is "colored," so too, if the body were separated from the <term>suppositum</term> of the Word, it could itself be a sort of subject for "breadness," and would still be called "bread"—which is absurd.

<margin>Solution by Hilary.</margin> This will not happen if we say, as <note>St. Hilary of Poitiers (c. 310–367 AD), a Bishop and Doctor of the Church who wrote extensively on the Trinity.</note> Hilary says, that a "being" and a "mode of being" of a substance can be conferred upon a surface separated from its substance (by reason of which it was the subject for accidents); but the infinite "being" of the Word’s <term>suppositum</term> cannot be conferred upon a separated humanity in the same way, by reason of which it could sustain another substantial nature.

<margin>Objection.</margin> And note that in all these inquiries, it has always been presupposed that to provide a <term>suppositum</term> for an external nature is a property unique to an infinite "being."

<margin>Solution.</margin> But it is still argued against this: the Word assumed flesh through the medium of the soul, yet because of this, the soul is not said of the flesh, nor vice versa. Therefore, granted that the Word assumed "breadness" through the medium of the body, one would not be predicated of the other for that reason. But perhaps it is not similar; for the Word is said to have assumed flesh through the medium of the soul as if the soul were the medium regarding the "being of nature." Likewise, it is through the medium of the soul regarding the "act of assumption." But he did not assume the flesh through the soul as if the soul were first supported [by the Word] and then the soul supported the flesh (as is said of humanity and breadness); rather, it is because he only assumed flesh in relation to the human nature, of which the flesh is a part through the soul united to it.

<margin>Argument for the false side. First.</margin> Again, it is argued in favor of the "false side" <note>The "false side" refers to the position Pico is currently exploring for the sake of argument, which challenges the orthodox view of transubstantiation.</note> that it would be more fitting to posit that, in fact, the body of Christ is in the altar through the "hypostatization" <note>original: "hypostatizationem"; the union of two natures in one person/subject.</note> of breadness in the <term>suppositum</term> of Christ the God, rather than through "conversion" <note>Transubstantiation: the total change of the bread's substance into the body of Christ.</note>. For if that model is considered unsuitable, it is because it is against the determinations of the Church; but it is proven that this is not so. For if this position seemed to be against the Church's determinations in anything, it would most seen in two points: namely, that the bread remains, and that the accidents are there without a subject. But this position says neither. For it concedes that the bread does *not* remain, because the <term>suppositum</term> of the bread does not remain; and it can also say that the accidents are there without a subject. For an accident depends on a substance only in regard

<column-break/>

<margin>The dependence of an accident on substance.</margin> to existence—at least according to the common way, and not according to its essence. Therefore, although the "essence" of the bread remains, since the "subsistence" of the bread (through which the accidents subsisted) ceases to be there, it follows that the accidents subsist by themselves—unless we posit that they migrate from subject to subject.

<margin>Second.</margin> Second, it is argued that this position is more fitting because more difficulties are resolved by it. Only the difficulty regarding the union remains here. However, special articles of faith should not be multiplied unless faith compels it. Since "assumption" is a special article, one ought not to multiply miracles and things to be believed beyond our reason without evident and compelling necessity. <note>Pico invokes a principle of parsimony, similar to Occam's Razor: why invent a new miracle (the total conversion of substance) if an existing one (the act of Divine Assumption) can explain the Eucharist?</note>

<margin>Third.</margin> Third, because through this method, appearances are better preserved. For in this sacrament, there appears to be bread and wine, which "assumption" preserves but "conversion" does not. For we see someone nourished by the hosts just as by true bread, and we see the hosts rot—and finally, all things happen to them which happen to the substance of bread. Therefore, if all these things can be preserved while the body of Christ is truly on the altar, and that bread which (as <note>Berengarius of Tours (c. 999–1088), a theologian who sparked controversy by arguing for a more symbolic or spiritual presence in the Eucharist.</note> Berengarius says) is ground by the teeth of the faithful is the true body of Christ, it is better to adhere to this way than to the way of "conversion," through which these things are not preserved without the multiplication of miracles.

<margin>Fourth. Paul. Fifth.</margin> Fourth, because <note>The Apostle Paul.</note> Paul says in 1 Corinthians 10: "The bread which we break, is it not the participation of the body of the Lord?" Fifth, because Christ is there sacramentally where he is directly by the power of the sacrament; but Christ would be on the altar more directly through "assumption" than through "conversion." For the form of this sacrament, which works by signifying, works more directly on that which it more properly signifies; and this is the union through "assumption" by which the <term>idiomata: the properties of both natures (divine and bread)</term> are communicated, so that "this" is "that," which is what the formal words sound like: *This is my body*. It is not, however, a union of "conversion," because through that, the bread is not Christ, nor vice versa; rather, the bread "becomes" Christ or is "converted" into Christ.

<margin>Sixth.</margin> Sixth, because that method of "conversion" is intricate and has many difficulties; this one, however, is clear and straightforward. For we already believe in "assumption" through another article [of faith]. Whatever things are identical in a limited <term>suppositum</term>, wherever one is, the other is also—just as wherever there is a strong music, there is its whiteness <note>A scholastic example: if a man is both a musician and white, where the musician is, the white man is.</note>. I say "limited" because if one were limited and the other unlimited, where the limited was, the unlimited would be, but not vice versa. But if bread were assumed, the human body of Christ and the body of the bread would be one in <term>suppositum</term>, and both would be limited. Therefore, since the assumed bread would be on the altar, the body of Christ would consequently be there. Likewise, the medium is closer than the extreme. But if Christ were to assume bread or "breadness," he would do this through the medium of his corporeality—as it is the less worthy part of the assumption. Therefore, since the assuming <term>suppositum</term> of Christ would be on the altar with the assumed bread, much more so would the body of Christ be there, as it would be the medium of the assumption.

<margin>Last.</margin> Lastly, it seems that the authorities of the Saints regarding "conversion" can nonetheless be preserved while holding to "assumption." Since "being" differs from "essence," one can be assumed without the other being assumed. Hence, the Word is not incarnate in "breadness" in the same way [as in humanity], because in that [human] assumption, the essence was anticipated/assumed before it had being. Hence, it never had any "being" other than the divine "being" communicated to it. For this reason, it was an assumption without any conversion of the thing assumed into the one assuming, and vice versa. Hence the Church says: "not by the conversion of the divinity into flesh," nor (consequently) vice versa, "but by the assumption of humanity into God."

<summary>Pico compares the "Assumption" model of the Eucharist to the "Conversion" model, arguing that viewing the bread as being "taken up" into Christ's divine personhood better explains physical realities like nourishment and decay without needing extra miracles. He utilizes scholastic logic and analogies involving surfaces and accidents to explore how the Divine Word could support the nature of bread.</summary>
<keywords>Eucharist, transubstantiation, assumption, breadness, suppositum, accidents, Hilary of Poitiers, Berengarius, St. Paul, scholasticism, hypostasis</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the "Third Opinion" of the Eucharist, specifically comparing the concepts of "Assumption" (the Divine Word taking on the nature of bread) versus the traditional "Conversion" (Transubstantiation). Pico is here presenting the arguments of the theologian Durandus of Saint-Pourçain and contrasting them with the views of St. Thomas Aquinas.</meta>

### APOLOGIA

The pre-existing thing possesses being and essence, and the assumption to the humanity of the <term>suppositum: the individual person or subject</term> consumes its own subsistence; this mystery is perfected not through annihilation, but through the "taking up" of the substantial essence. Thus, all authorities speaking of <term>transubstantiation: the change of the bread's substance into the body of Christ</term> and conversion can be referred to "being" and not to "essence." And the authorities saying that after the consecration the bread does not remain but "was," is true according to being: because it remains only according to essence. From these things, it seems that the body of Christ can be just as truly and sacramentally on the altar without a "conversion"—through the assumption of <term>breadness: the essential nature of bread</term>—as is now commonly proposed through "conversion." Indeed, a clear distinction between these
<margin>Assumption</margin>
three terms—assumption, conversion, and annihilation—cannot be understood without presupposing the mode of this opinion. We say that a thing is "assumed" when something that previously lacked its own <term>suppositable: capable of existing as an independent subject</term> being is taken up into a new being of a <term>suppositum</term>. That thing is "annihilated"
<margin>Annihilation</margin>
which simply ceases to be, such that its reproduction would be a [new] creation; it is entirely irrelevant to this whether something succeeds it or nothing succeeds it, because this is entirely external to the thing which ceases to be. That thing,
<margin>Conversion.</margin>
however, is "converted" which, remaining according to essence but having lost the proper being of its <term>suppositum</term>, passes into the being of another <term>suppositum</term> and truly becomes that person. This is the true logic
<margin>Logic of conversion.</margin>
of conversion, in which two things are understood in the thing converted: first, that it remains through its essence (and by this it differs from what is annihilated); and second, that it becomes another thing by reason of the <term>suppositum</term> (by which it differs from what is not converted). While it becomes another thing by reason of its own <term>suppositum</term>, it sets aside [its former self], and by this it differs from what is "assumed." However, by holding the common mode of conversion, the bread is not converted but annihilated; and those who wish to save the idea that a conversion occurs (so that it is not an annihilation) seem to satisfy the requirement more by words than by reality. Whence many following that path have conceded that it is an annihilation, etc. On the opposite side, for the true part, 
<margin>The first argument of Durandus for the [other] side.</margin>
it is argued that the opinion positing that the sacrament of the Eucharist is in fact performed through the "assumption" of breadness is inconvenient and irrational. First, Durandus argues thus: that it is ridiculous <note>original: "ridiculum est"</note> that every day one nature—indeed many—should be assumed by the divine <term>suppositum</term> and every day be laid down. This would be the case if the substance of bread in this sacrament were assumed anew; for there would be as many assumptions as there are consecrations, and as many depositions as there were sacramentals. But perhaps this "ridiculousness" does not 
<margin>Second.</margin>
demonstrate the falsehood of the premise. Second, it is argued because it seems impossible that such an assumption could be made through some "created medium" as the aforementioned opinion posits. For that medium either behaves as the efficient cause of such an assumption or as the terminating cause; but nothing created can relate to the assumption in either of these ways, therefore, etc. The minor premise is proved: that nothing created can be the efficient cause of such an assumption is clear because such an assumption occurs when a thing loses its own natural mode of being and puts on a foreign one. This does not seem possible for anyone except the Author of Nature, who alone instituted the natures of things; thus he alone seems able to change them.
<margin>Response.</margin>
This argument of Durandus perhaps shows that the created thing cannot be the principal efficient cause. By the same logic, it seems that nothing created can terminate such an assumption, because it cannot be attributed to any nature that which is above nature and the whole course of nature—namely, <term>to substentificate: to provide the underlying existence for</term> another nature which is born to subsist in itself. Perhaps this erroneous opinion mentioned above would believe it could avoid this through certain things said previously. For a falsehood is not always easily convicted of its own falsity through 

<column-break/>

evident reasons: so weak is the light of our intellect, as it is the very lowest in the hierarchy of intellectual natures. Furthermore, Durandus argues as follows: whatever may be the case regarding the position of such an assumption, it is altogether inconvenient that it should happen by means of a "body-part" <note>This refers to the idea that the bread is united specifically to Christ's body rather than his whole person.</note>. For a body—when taken as a part of human nature, assuming only one "form" in man—cannot name matter alone, but must necessarily name the composite of matter and the form that gives "corporeal being." It is necessary that the "human body" refers to the reality of the whole and not just a part, even if by logic it can name a 
<margin>Third. In saying man is from body and soul, it is said according to the logic of a composite; but from body etc., that is reality. Response.</margin>
part, because the soul gives all the perfections which the lower forms give. And therefore, if one considers the composite of matter and the form which is the soul insofar as it gives corporeal being only, and compares it to the same composite insofar as through the soul it has not only corporeal being but sense, life, and reason, then "body" in the first way is taken as a part, and in the second way as the whole. But since this difference is only logical, it does not serve the purpose of those who say a real assumption of bread occurs by means of the "body-part." For a logical difference contributes nothing to the difference of a real assumption. Whatever may be the case regarding the efficacy of this argument against those who posit only one form [in a human], it is clear that it does not proceed against those who do not hold to one form. Likewise, he argues thus: this position fails in
<margin>Fourth.</margin>
this, that it posits that through such an assumption the body of Christ (taken from the Virgin) becomes present in this sacrament through the <term>communication of idioms: the theological principle where properties of Christ's human and divine natures are shared</term>, because one is predicated of the other. For by the same logic that the body of Christ would be in the sacrament of the altar through the assumption of the substance of bread, the blood would be in this sacrament through the assumption of the substance of wine. But this is not true, as will be proved, therefore, etc. The premise is proved because if the blood of Christ were in this sacrament through the assumption of the substance of wine (just as it is posited for the body of Christ through the assumption of the substance of bread), then it would be necessary that, just as the bread is assumed by means of the body which belongs to the unity of the assuming <term>suppositum</term>, so the wine would be assumed by means of the blood belonging to the unity of the assuming <term>suppositum</term>. Now, it is established that the blood of Christ does not belong to the identity of the <term>suppositum</term> of Christ, since blood is not yet under the "human form," but is a humor on the way to conversion so that it may come under the human form. Therefore, it cannot be assumed by the <term>suppositum</term> of Christ by means of the blood—unless perhaps it were said that in every performance of this sacrament there was an assumption of Christ’s blood immediately, and through that blood the assumption of wine. Thus, every day there would be an assumption of a new nature, namely blood, without any order to the nature of the bread assumed (which others deny), and through this, there would be the assumption of wine. But in this, perhaps many would not only reject Durandus’s logic but would rebuke him no less than the aforementioned opinion—namely, regarding 
<margin>Response.</margin>
the non-assumption and non-<term>hypostatic union: the union of divine and human natures in one person</term> of the blood of Christ shed on the cross and presented in the sacrament to the <term>suppositum</term> of the Son. For it seems that according to this, that blood would not have been a sufficient price for the redemption of the human race, since it would not have been united to the hypostatic divinity. Whence Saint 
<margin>St. Thomas.</margin>
Thomas, in the sixth *Quodlibet*, question six, says: "The blood of Christ shed in the Passion sanctified the human race according to that [passage] at the end of Hebrews: 'Jesus, that he might sanctify the people through his own blood, suffered outside the gate.'" Christ's humanity also had its saving power from the power of the Word united to it, as 
<margin>Damascene.</margin>
Damascene says in his third book. Whence it is manifest that the blood shed in the Passion, which was the greatest source of salvation, was united to the divinity...

<meta>This page continues the technical debate regarding the "Third Opinion" of the Eucharist. Having defined "Assumption" (the Word taking on the nature of bread) in the previous page, Pico now presents the counter-arguments of major Scholastic theologians like Durandus of Saint-Pourçain and Peter of la Palu to test the validity of this theory against traditional Transubstantiation.</meta>

# QUESTIONS 31

<margin>Another argument of Durandus.</margin>
...and therefore it was necessary that in the resurrection it should be joined to the other parts of the humanity, etc. Thus he says. Durandus follows with an argument against the aforementioned position, because the body of Christ is on the altar—or in the sacrament of the altar—through the true existence of its nature, and not merely because of the <term>communication of idioms: the theological principle where properties of one nature (divine or human) are attributed to the single person of Christ</term>, as this opinion suggests. This is evident because a reference always points to the same numerical thing that preceded it. But Christ, in instituting this sacrament, spoke these words in Luke 22: "This is my body which is given for you," etc. And "This cup is the new testament in my blood which is shed for you." Therefore, it is that same numerical body which was afterward given to the apostles in the sacrament to be eaten. But the body that was given to be crucified was not of the nature of bread, but was a body pertaining to the nature of humanity. Therefore, the body given to the apostles in the sacrament of the altar was truly of the nature of humanity; and by the same reasoning, in our sacrament, the body of Christ is that which pertains to his humanity, and it is not there solely through the communication of idioms resulting from the "assumption" of <term>breadness: the essential substance or "nature" of being bread</term>.

<margin>Removal of an Objection.</margin>
If someone were to say that the relative term refers to the same <term>suppositum: the individual person or subject</term> and not the same nature—and thus it could be truly said, pointing to the assumed bread, "this is my body which will be given for you" because it is the same subject possessing both the assumed bread-nature and the later-given body-nature, and thus the same subject was first pointed to and then given, albeit according to different natures—this does not hold. For when it is said "this is my body," the word "body" cannot be taken there for the subject possessing a "body-nature," but rather for the nature possessed, as indicated by the possessive pronoun "my" to which it is added when one says "this is the body that I have."

<margin>Response: Another argument of Durandus.</margin>
But perhaps this argument would have greater weight among grammarians than among theologians. He further argues that the said "assumption" of the bread does not suffice for the body of Christ to be on the altar either in reality or according to the communication of idioms. It is not there in reality because the assumption of two natures by one subject does not suffice for one nature to be wherever the other is. For if the subject of the Son had from the beginning assumed the humanity of Peter in Rome and that of Paul in Judea, it would not follow that wherever Peter was, Paul would be, and vice-versa—except regarding the subject, which is predicated of both and of which both are predicated concretely. Similarly, granted that the subject of the Son assumed both humanity and bread-nature, it does not follow that wherever the nature of bread is, the nature of humanity must be. Nor could it be said by reason of the subject that the bread is the body of Christ through the communication of idioms, because according to that opinion, the name of the subject does not receive the predication of the assumed bread nor the parts of the body. For according to these thinkers, it is not true to say that the Son of God is bread, or a body which is a part; therefore, by reason of a common subject, one cannot be predicated of the other so as to say one *is* the other, or one is *where* the other is. Nor is it like the tooth of an Ethiopian and his whiteness <note>A common Scholastic logic puzzle: is an Ethiopian "white" because his teeth are white?</note> because "white" is said of the tooth and the tooth is said to be white, and where one is, the other is, because they are one in the subject—and consequently indistinct in subject and place. This cannot be said of the human body and the assumed bread-nature. Whatever the case with this argument, this much is true: while it does not follow by necessity, it follows as a possibility, etc.

<margin>Response.</margin>
<margin>First argument of Peter of la Palu.</margin>
Peter of la Palu <note>A 14th-century Dominican theologian and contemporary of Durandus.</note> argues thus: either He would assume the substance of the bread with its <term>accidents: outward physical properties like color, weight, and taste</term> or without them. Not without them, because that is impossible; for that which cannot be made or sustained on its own by any 

<column-break/>

power—such as a "relation" or something of that sort—is not "assumable" on its own. Moreover, a physical substance cannot exist without quantity, because quantity (or shape) is its own limit and proper characteristic—though many would deny this. If, however, He assumes it *with* the accidents, then He would not be in the altar sacramentally, but locally <note>Meaning he would occupy physical space like a normal object rather than being present in the mysterious "sacramental" way.</note> through quantity along with the substance assumed on the altar; nor would He be moved from there, just as He was locally in the womb through quantity with the humanity assumed there. And perhaps this concludes that He is not there in the sacramental way described by the Thomists <note>Followers of St. Thomas Aquinas.</note> who argue for "conversion" (Transubstantiation). They say He is not there by His own quantity but by the quantity of the bread; but if He assumes the bread, it would then seem He is there by a quantity that is His own. However, the Thomist method is not held by everyone.

<margin>Response.</margin>
<margin>Second.</margin>
Secondly, Peter argues that this cannot be understood regarding "body" as a general category (genus), but only regarding "body" as a part. For a general category is not predicated possessively of its subordinates in the same way a part is of a whole. For instance, I say "my humanity" and "my hand," but I do not say "my animal" or "my human" of myself. This is also apparent in the consecration of the blood, where it is said, "this is the cup of my blood." "Blood" is not an ambiguous term for a general category and a father as "body" is, but is taken only for a part. Even if we granted that the "body which is Christ" were on the altar by force of the sacrament through "assumption," the "body of Christ which is a part" would still not be there, except through natural concomitance. This is because "assumption" would not create a union of natures, but only a union in the person. Thus, through that assumption, the bread would become the "body which is Christ," but not the "body of Christ"—just as currently the divinity is not the humanity. Enough has been said on this above (see the section on "body as a part" and "body as a genus").

<margin>Response.</margin>
<margin>Third.</margin>
Thirdly, he argues: just as the assumed body of the man [Christ] was not permitted to corrupt or rot, neither in substance nor in quantity, so too the bread should not corrupt if it were assumed. Perhaps, however, this comparison does not hold by necessity.

<margin>Response. Response to the first argument for the opposing side.</margin>
Regarding the arguments for the opposing side: as for the authority of Damascene <note>St. John of Damascus, an 8th-century Father of the Church.</note>, it is said that just as it is clear that the water of baptism is not "assumed" into the unity of the divine subject—nor is the grace of the Holy Spirit united to it so as to make one subject—similarly, bread and wine are not "assumed" into the divine subject, nor is the divinity joined to them in a unity of subject. Rather, just as water is assumed there as the *permanent* matter of the sacrament, so bread and wine are the *transitory* matter. This is because the matter of the sacrament is "converted" into the Body of Christ; consequently, it is said to be united to the divinity in some way—not through "assumption" while the nature of bread or wine remains, but through transubstantiation into the humanity previously assumed. This is clear from the following words [of Damascene] where it is said: "Just as naturally, through eating, bread and wine and water (through drinking) are transformed into the body and blood of the one eating and drinking, and do not become something other than what was there before; so also the bread, wine, and water of the offering, through the change and arrival of the Holy Spirit, pass supernaturally into the body and blood of the Lord, and therefore they are not two things, but one and the same." From these words, it appears that Damascene’s intention is not that the substance of the bread and wine remain and are "assumed" by the divine subject, but that they "pass into" the body and blood of Christ and are thus united to the divinity.

<margin>Objection.</margin>
Those people persist, asking: how can that which is "annihilated" be united? That is, that which truly ceases to be in itself. They persist with that analogy of the "glowing coal," in which it is said that just as a coal is not simple wood but is wood united to fire, so the bread of communion is not simple bread but is united to the divinity.

<margin>Solution.</margin>
And he says that the coal and the fire are not identical in their subject; rather, one, through its corruption, passes into the other...

Pico cites Durandus and Peter of la Palu to argue that Christ's presence must be based on his human nature, not a temporary union with the substance of bread.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes Question 6 regarding the nature of the Eucharist and begins Question 7 concerning the salvation of the early Christian theologian Origen. The previous page discussed the philosophical distinctions between "assumption" (the Word taking on the nature of bread) and "transubstantiation" (the bread becoming the body of Christ), focusing on whether Christ's body is present through its own nature or merely through a theological link. Pico continues here by citing John of Damascus and Thomas Aquinas to refine his position.</meta>

# DEFENSE

<margin>Objection.</margin>
Thus, the bread of communion is not one in <term>underlying personhood: the "suppositum," or the individual substance that acts as the subject of properties</term> with the divinity, but through its own departure, it passes into the body of Christ which is united to the divinity. But against this, it is argued that the bread of communion would then be like fire into which a piece of coal has passed through its own corruption, rather than being like the coal itself, in which the nature of fire is found alongside the preservation of the nature of the wood. Therefore, the response—and perhaps it would be better 
<margin>Response.</margin>
if <note>John of</note> Damascus had not used that analogy—is that when 
<margin>Damascenus</margin>
the same Damascus says that God "joined the divinity to the bread," it must be said that this was not through an <term>assumption: a theological term for when the Divine Word takes on a nature, as in the Incarnation</term>, but rather just as food is joined to the one who eats it because it is converted into them. However, between this conversion and that one, let that 
<margin>St. Thomas.</margin>
analogy be accepted insofar as it can apply. St. Thomas <note>Aquinas</note>, in the fourth book of his <italic>Commentary on the Sentences</italic>, says that the word of Damascus is to be understood regarding the <term>species: the outward appearances (color, taste, texture) of bread and wine that remain after the substance changes</term> by which the body of Christ—united to the divinity in an ineffable way—is joined. Thus he says; and because this mode is ineffable <note>original: "ineffabilis," meaning beyond words or description</note>, one ought not to inquire further about it. In the third part of the <italic>Summa Theologiae</italic>, question 75, he says God "joined his divinity"—that is, his divine power—to the bread and wine, not so that they remain in this sacrament, but so that from them He might make His body and blood. Regarding the authority of the Apostle <note>St. Paul</note>, it is said that his speech is figurative both on the part of the subject and the predicate. For "bread," as the subject, stands for the sensible sacrament—namely, the species of bread. The "Body of Christ" is also taken figuratively. Hence, according to the gloss <note>a standard medieval biblical commentary</note> on that passage, 
<margin>Gloss on the apostolic authority.</margin>
it is not to be understood that the substance of the bread or the appearance of the bread is truly and actually Christ or the body of Christ; nor is the body of Christ directly predicated of the substance or appearance of the bread. Rather, the sense is: the bread which we break in the sacrament—that is, the participation in the bread broken on the altar—is the participation in the divine body; that is, it makes us be one with Christ. Let those masters who condemn my view remember: if the words of Damascus and Paul in this matter were taken as they seem to sound at first glance and superficially, they could create a sense in many that is erroneous in faith. 
<margin>First solution to the other point.</margin>
When it is said that fewer difficulties follow from this position of "assumption," it must be said that in matters of faith, one should not always choose that which leads to fewer difficulties, but rather that which is more in harmony with apostolic traditions and ecclesiastical dogma, even if more difficulties arise. For it is necessary to <note>original: "intellectum captiuare," based on 2 Cor 10:5</note> "take the intellect captive" in service of the faith and to commit oneself with obedient humility to the traditions of the fathers, as even Plato says well and most religiously in the <italic>Timaeus</italic>. Likewise, someone might say that although that "assumption" would better preserve appearances to the senses, "conversion" <note>transubstantiation</note> better preserves appearances to the intellect—that is, the words of the Gospel, which it is better to preserve because they cannot lie, whereas 
<margin>Plato.</margin>
<margin>Second.</margin>
<margin>Objection.</margin>
senses can be deceived. But it is still argued for the opposite side: that if this does not happen through assumption so that it is included in the Article of the Incarnation, then since the same belief would be required, there ought to be a special article in the Creed about this conversion, which nonetheless is not there. 
<margin>Response: Peter of la Palu, St. Thomas.</margin>
Some say, such as Peter of la Palu, that the article on the Eucharist is perhaps specifically under that phrase "the communion of saints," etc. St. Thomas says in the <italic>Secunda Secundae</italic> that in the sacrament of the Eucharist two things can be considered: one, that it is a sacrament, and this has the same rationale as other effects of sanctifying grace. The other is that the body of Christ is miraculously contained there; and thus it is included under the article on omnipotence, like all other miracles attributed to almighty power. In the third book

<column-break/>

<margin>Gloss on the confession.</margin>
<margin>Berengarius.</margin>
<margin>Peter of la Palu.</margin>
<margin>To another.</margin>
<margin>To the last.</margin>
of the <italic>Sentences</italic>, he says that faith regarding the body of Christ and all such sacraments and <term>keys: the authority of the Church to forgive sins</term> and all such things is included in the article concerning the effect of grace, which is "the holy Catholic Church," etc. Regarding the <term>Confession of Berengarius: a famous recantation by a theologian who had questioned the physical presence of Christ in the Eucharist</term>, it must be said (as the gloss says there) that unless you understand the words of Berengarius healthily, you will fall into a greater error than he himself held. Therefore, Peter of la Palu says that when it is said "the body of Christ is broken," it must be explained: that is, it remains under the species which are broken as long as it remains in any part whatsoever. Peter adds these words: "So I say that God *could* assume bread and wine just as He could convert them, and He could institute words at the pronunciation of which 'assumption' would follow, just as 'conversion' now follows the pronunciation of these words; however, He did not give this power to these words, nor could the sense of the moderns be preserved if assumption happened and not conversion." These words are most effective for the truth of my conclusion, which is entirely about what is *possible*, not what *is*, etc. Regarding the point that "whenever two things are identical in their underlying personhood, wherever one is, the other is," it is said that this logic holds only for things that are in a place <term>accidentally: by circumstance rather than by their own nature</term>. It is otherwise for things that are in a place <term>by their own nature: "per se"</term>. When it is said that "this bread is the body of Christ" or "the body of Christ is bread," these cannot be verified unless the bread remains; it must be explained as: "where the bread was, there the body of Christ is made." And let it suffice to have disputed this question, from all of which I hold those things which are in harmony with the declaration of my conclusion explained above. Those things which are dissonant, I judge should be rejected and reproved.

### SEVENTH QUESTION
#### ON THE SALVATION OF ORIGEN.

-> **It is more reasonable to believe that Origen is saved than to believe he is damned.** <-

<margin>The process for Origen's salvation is made in seven articles. He defends that Origen is not damned in seven articles.</margin>
<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'D' with foliage and floral patterns inside a square frame.</image-desc>
THESE masters have said that this conclusion is rash, reprehensible, and "savoring of heresy," and against the determination of the universal Church. But I, to speak of them more modestly, wish to show that their judgment is not correct: and that this conclusion is not against the determination of the Church; and what is more, even if whatever they bring against me were true, it still cannot be said that this conclusion is heretical or "savors of heresy." For a fuller declaration of this matter, there will be seven articles. In the first, it will be seen whether <term>Origen: a highly influential but controversial early Christian scholar (c. 184–253 AD)</term> ever wrote and believed any heretical opinion regarding matters of faith. In the second, given that he wrote such things, whether he wrote them dogmatically, or with personal adherence, or merely as an inquiry. In the third, given that he adhered to them, whether he did so in such a way that he sinned mortally in writing them and can be called a heretic. In the fourth, given that he wrote and wrote in such a way that he erred, whether he ever repented for such things. In the fifth, given that neither his repentance nor his lack of repentance is certain, whether it is more reasonable to believe him damned or saved. In the sixth, what should be judged from the dictates of the decrees...

<summary>Pico concludes his defense of the "Third Opinion" of the Eucharist by arguing that while his view on the "assumption" of bread is not the Church's actual practice, it remains a logical possibility. <meta>This page transitions from the discussion of the Eucharist into "Question 7," which concerns the theological status of the early Christian scholar Origen (c. 184 – c. 253 AD). The author, Pico della Mirandola, is beginning a defense of Origen, arguing that many of the heresies attributed to him were actually inserted into his texts by others.</meta>

# OF THE QUESTIONS

<margin>Regarding the first article. Augustine, Rufinus, and Jerome’s contention.</margin>
...had mentioned concerning Origen. In the seventh question, we consider to what degree the determination of the Church obliges our belief in this matter. Regarding the subject of the first article, there was a bitter contention between <term>Rufinus: Tyrannius Rufinus (c. 345–411), a monk and translator who defended Origen</term> and <term>Jerome: St. Jerome (c. 347–420), the translator of the Vulgate Bible, who became a fierce critic of Origen</term>. To these two men—as stated by <note>St.</note> Augustine, who deplored the discord that arose between them—God had granted that, as the closest and most intimate companions, they might "lick together the honey of the Holy Scriptures" <note>original: "mella scripturarum sanctarum pariter lamberent"</note>. Rufinus is of the opinion that the heretical dogmas found in Origen's books were falsely inserted by heretics who corrupted his works, and that these ideas did not reflect Origen’s own mind. Jerome feels the opposite. But let us see what probability each opinion holds, and it will perhaps appear that—without harm to the faith and with full satisfaction of all those things which we are bound to believe by the necessity of salvation—one can still freely and probably believe that those principal heresies (by which Origen's sin and subsequent condemnation are proved) were not from Origen’s mind, but were falsely imposed upon him by treacherous heretics corrupting his books. 

<margin>Pamphilus the martyr.</margin>
Indeed, on this side, there is first the authority of <term>Pamphilus the martyr: a 3rd-century scholar and friend of Eusebius who wrote a defense of Origen while in prison</term>, whose book is circulated in defense of Origen. In this work, the most glorious martyr shows, from Origen’s own words and from his books recited there, that Origen thought in a Catholic manner regarding those points upon which he is accused of being a heretic. 

<margin>Jerome's testimonies indicating Origen’s heretical views.</margin>
Jerome, however, denying that this book is by Pamphilus, speaks as follows in his responsive "Apology to Oceanus and Pammachius": "If you say his books were violated by Origen’s enemies to bring him into infamy, why may I not say that a volume was composed by his friends and followers under the name of Pamphilus, to claim him from infamy by the testimony of a martyr?" From these words, it seems sufficiently noted that Jerome proposes both as probable: just as Rufinus cannot prove that those books were not corrupted, so Jerome himself cannot prove that the book in question belongs to Pamphilus. Further down, Jerome adds that the very name "Apology" shows an excuse, for "nothing is defended unless it is under accusation." 

But someone might perhaps say: since Jerome himself titles this very treatise in which he writes these things an "Apology"—in which he defends himself, saying he followed Origen’s learning but not his dogma—he likewise shows himself guilty of a crime, since "nothing is defended unless it is under accusation." Thus, no one could be justly excused if an excuse always presupposes a just accusation. 

But let us see what conjectures move Jerome to believe the book is not by Pamphilus. The first thing that moves Jerome is that the same things are read in the first book of <term>Eusebius: Eusebius of Caesarea, a 4th-century historian</term>, out of the six books he wrote in favor of Origen. The second is that Eusebius himself, writing the *Life of Pamphilus*, said that Pamphilus wrote nothing of his own work. For Jerome says this in the first book *Against Rufinus*, addressed to Pammachius and Marcella: "Eusebius, Bishop of Caesarea, once the standard-bearer of the <term>Arian faction: followers of Arius who believed Jesus was a created being, not co-equal with God the Father</term>, wrote six books for Origen—a very extensive and laboured work—and with many testimonies he approved Origen to be a Catholic according to himself (that is, an Arian according to us). You translate the first of these books under the name of the martyr." And further: "If this book is by Pamphilus, which of the six will be the first by Eusebius?" And further: "Likewise, Eusebius, the lover, herald, and companion of Pamphilus, wrote three most elegant books containing the *Life of Pamphilus*, in the third of which he says of Pamphilus: 'And he himself indeed wrote nothing at all of his own work, except letters which he perhaps sent to friends.'" To such an extent did the defender of Origen and praiser of Pamphilus humble himself in humanity, saying Pamphilus composed nothing at all, not even any of his own speech; and he said this after Pamphilus had already been crowned with martyrdom, so that you might have no

<column-break/>

refuge in saying Pamphilus wrote this after Eusebius published his books. And further: "What will the letters of Bishop Theophilus do? What will those of Pope Anastasius do, who pursue the heretic throughout the whole world? When your book, put out under the name of Pamphilus, fights against their letters." And in the second book, Jerome writes: "When nearly ten years ago my friend Dexter, who served as Praetorian Prefect, asked me to weave an index of the authors of our religion for him, I placed this book among other treatises as edited by Pamphilus, thinking it was as had been spread abroad by you and your disciples. But since Eusebius himself says Pamphilus wrote nothing except letters, etc. And the first book of the six volumes of Eusebius contains the same things and in the same words which were forged by you under the name of Pamphilus, it is clear that you wished to disseminate this book so that you might bring forward heresy under the person of a martyr. Since even in the one you feign to be by Pamphilus, you have perverted many things, and it is one way in Greek and another in Latin." 

Moreover, in the responsive "Apology to Oceanus and Pammachius," in which he shows he followed the learning of Origen and not the dogma, he says this, speaking of the same book of Pamphilus: "It seems to have been a little work of either <term>Didymus: Didymus the Blind, a 4th-century Alexandrian theologian</term> or anyone else. Even if we concede for the sake of argument that it is by Pamphilus, he was not yet a martyr; for he wrote it before he underwent martyrdom. And how, you will ask, was he worthy of martyrdom? Perhaps so that he might erase his error through martyrdom." These are Jerome's words, verbatim, in various places as they are cited concerning this book of Pamphilus.

<margin>Rufinus’s opinion against Jerome.</margin>
Rufinus, however, proving the book to be by Pamphilus the martyr and written for Origen's defense, says in his second book of invective against Jerome that it is easy to say of any work that it does not belong to the author to whom it is ascribed. He then says: "But let us suppose that this booklet is not the martyr's, but of any single person of the Church; did whoever that writer is use his own words, so that it seems one must yield to the merits of the author? He places examples from Origen's own volumes. And he shows what he thinks of individual points not with his own defensive words, but with the words of the one who is accused. Therefore, the question of the author is superfluous where the defense is such that it needs no advocate." These are Rufinus's words. 

<margin>Jerome's sayings are refuted by Pico.</margin>
To those things which Jerome says, someone might perhaps respond thus on behalf of Rufinus: First, when he says Eusebius wrote six books in which he proves Origen was an Arian, and that the first of these was translated by Rufinus under the name of Pamphilus—how can it stand that the book of Pamphilus is the first of Eusebius, when entirely different and conflicting things are intended in those books? For Eusebius, according to you, O Jerome, tries in his books to prove Origen was an Arian. But in the book of Pamphilus, nothing else is attempted but to prove that Origen was *not* an Arian, and that whatever things are found in his books confirming the heresy of Arius were inserted by the Arians themselves (such as Eusebius was, and many others). Therefore, it is necessary that this book be entirely different from that one which pleads a completely different, indeed contrary, cause. 

Nor is it enough if someone says those things which pertained to the Arian heresy were changed from the book of Eusebius. For even regarding what pertains to other heresies, Jerome cannot say that Eusebius showed Origen's books were corrupted in those points. Because Jerome himself, in the second book *Against Rufinus*, says that besides what pertains to the Son and the Holy Spirit, in other dogmas Eusebius and Didymus most openly concede to the sect of Origen. For this reason, it cannot well be understood how the same things read in the book of Pamphilus could be read in the first book of Eusebius, unless perhaps some common things concerning Origen and the point of this conclusion...

<margin>Objection.</margin> Thus, the bread of communion is not one in person with the divinity, but through its own ceasing <note>ceasing to be bread</note> it passes into the body of Christ which is united to the divinity. But to the contrary: because then the bread of communion would be likened to fire into which, clearly, a coal passes through its own corruption <note>the coal being consumed to become fire</note>, and not to the coal itself, in which the nature of wood is preserved at the same time as the nature of fire is found within it.

<margin>Response.</margin> Regarding the response—and perhaps this would be the case—it is that the similarity does not hold in all respects, and perhaps it would have been better 

<margin>Damascene.</margin> if <term>Damascene: John Damascene (c. 675–749), an influential Syrian monk and theologian</term> had not proposed that similarity. And when the same Damascene says that God joined the divinity to the bread, it must be said that this is not through "assumption" <note>the idea that the Word "took on" bread as a nature, similar to taking on human flesh</note>, although it is just as food is joined to the one who eats it because it is converted into him. Let that similarity which can apply there be accepted between this conversion and that one. 

<margin>St. Thomas.</margin> <term>St. Thomas: Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the preeminent Scholastic philosopher</term> in the fourth book <note>of his commentary on the Sentences</note>, 11th distinction, 1st question, says that Damascene’s word is to be understood regarding the "species" <note>the outward appearances of bread and wine</note> through which the body of Christ, united to the divinity in an ineffable way, is joined—thus says he—and since this manner is ineffable, one ought not to seek further concerning it. In the third part of the *Summa*, question 75, he says God joined his divinity (that is, divine power) to the bread and wine: not so that they remain in this sacrament, but so that they might make from them his body and blood. Regarding the authority of the Apostle <note>St. Paul</note>, it is said that this expression is figurative, both on the part of the subject and the predicate. For "bread" on the part of the subject stands for the sensible sacrament, namely, the species of bread. The "body of Christ" is also taken figuratively. 

<margin>Gloss on the authority of the Apostle.</margin> Whence according to the <term>Gloss: the Glossa Ordinaria, the standard medieval Bible commentary</term>, by that expression it is not given to be understood that the substance of the bread or the species of bread is truly and really Christ or the body of Christ: nor that the body of Christ is predicated directly of the substance of bread or the species of bread: but the sense is: the bread which we break in the sacrament (that is, the participation in the bread broken on the altar) is the participation of the divine body—that is, it makes us to be one with Christ. Those masters who condemned my views should remember: that if the words of Damascene and Paul in this matter were taken as they seem to sound at first glance and superficially, they could create a sense erroneous in faith for many. 

<margin>First solution to the other point.</margin> Furthermore, when it is said that for this position concerning "assumption," fewer difficulties follow, it must be said that in those matters which belong to faith, that which leads to fewer difficulties is not always to be chosen, but rather that which is more in harmony with apostolic traditions and ecclesiastical dogma, even if more difficulties occur. For it is necessary to "captivate the intellect in obedience to faith" <note>original: "intellectum captiuare in obsequium fidei"</note> and to commit to the traditions of the fathers with obedience or humility, as <term>Plato: the Greek philosopher</term> also says very well and most religiously in the *Timaeus*. 

<margin>Plato.</margin> Likewise, someone will say that although that "assumption" would better preserve the appearance to the senses, "conversion" <note>transubstantiation</note> better preserves the appearance to the intellect—that is, the words of the Gospel, which it is better to preserve because they cannot lie, whereas the senses 

<margin>Second [solution].</margin> can be deceived. But it is still argued to the contrary on behalf of 

<margin>Instance.</margin> the opposite side. Because if this does not happen through assumption (in such a way that it would be included in the article of the Incarnation, for it would be the same belief), it would be necessary for there to be a special article concerning this conversion, which nevertheless is not in the Creed. 

<margin>Response of Peter of Palude and St. Thomas.</margin> Some say, such as <term>Peter of Palude: a 14th-century Dominican theologian and Patriarch of Jerusalem</term>, that the article concerning the Eucharist is perhaps specifically under that phrase "the communion of saints," etc. Saint Thomas in the *Secunda Secundae* <note>the second part of the second part of the Summa Theologiae</note> says that in the sacrament of the Eucharist two things can be considered: one, that it is a sacrament, and this has the same rationale as other effects of sanctifying grace. The other is that the body of Christ is miraculously contained there: and thus it is included under the article on omnipotence, just as all other miracles which are attributed to omnipotence are. However, in the third [book]...

<column-break/>

...of the *Sentences*, he says that faith regarding the body of Christ and all the sacraments and keys and all such things 

<margin>Gloss on the confession.</margin> is included in the article which concerns the effect of grace, which is "the holy catholic church," etc. Regarding the confession of Berengar, it must be said, as the Gloss says there: that unless you understand the words of <term>Berengar: Berengar of Tours (d. 1088), who famously disputed the nature of the Real Presence</term> soundly, you will fall into a greater error 

<margin>Berengar and Peter of Palude.</margin> than he himself held. Peter of Palude says, therefore, that when it is said "the body of Christ is broken," it is to be explained as: that is, it remains under the species which are broken as long as it remains in however small a part. Furthermore, Peter adds these words: "Thus I say that God could assume bread and wine just as he could convert them, and that he could institute words upon the speaking of which 'assumption' would follow, just as now upon the speaking of these [words] 'conversion' follows; however, he did not give this power to those words, nor could the sense of the moderns be preserved if assumption took place and not conversion"—thus says he. These words are most effective for the truth of my conclusion, which is entirely about what is *possible*, not about what *is*, etc. To the point that whenever there are two things identical in their underlying subject/person 

<margin>To the other point. To the last point.</margin> and limited, wherever one is, the other is. It is said that the reasoning holds only in those things which are in a place "by accident" <note>incidentally</note>. It is otherwise, however, for those things which are in a place "by themselves" <note>essentially</note>. When it is said "this, namely the bread, is the body of Christ" and "the body of Christ is the bread," which cannot be verified unless the bread remains, it must be said that it should be explained as: "that is, where the bread was, there the body of Christ is." And let it have been sufficient to have disputed this question; from all of these things, I hold those which are in harmony with the declaration of my conclusion explained above. Those things which are dissonant, I judge should be cast aside and rejected.

## SEVENTH QUESTION
### CONCERNING THE SALVATION OF ORIGEN.

->It is more reasonable to believe that Origen is<-
->saved than to believe that he is damned.<-

<margin>The salvation of Origen is proceeded through seven articles. He defends in seven articles that Origen is not damned.</margin> THESE masters <note>Pico's critics at the University of Paris and the Roman Curia</note> have said that this conclusion is rash and reprehensible and savoring of heresy, and against the determination of the universal church. I, however, to speak more modestly of them, wish to show that their judgment is not right: and that this conclusion is not against the determination of the church: and what is more, even if whatever they bring against me were true, it still cannot be said that this conclusion is heretical or savors of heresy. There will be, for a fuller declaration of this matter, seven articles. In the first, it will be seen whether <term>Origen: a foundational but controversial early Christian scholar (c. 184–253)</term> ever wrote and believed any heretical opinion concerning matters of faith; in the second, granted that he did write [them], whether he wrote dogmatically, or as an adherent, or merely as an inquirer. In the third, granted that he [wrote] as an adherent, whether he adhered in such a way that by writing those things he sinned mortally and can be called a heretic. In the fourth, granted that he wrote and wrote in such a way that by writing he erred, whether he ever repented for such things. In the fifth, granted that it is not established whether he repented or did not repent, whether it is more reasonable to believe him to be damned or saved. In the sixth, what is to be judged from the sayings of the decrees [where] the church determined...

# ON QUESTIONS

<margin>On the first article. Augustine, Rufinus, and Jerome. The conflict.</margin>
...born from Origen. In the seventh part, we determine how much the decision of the Church obligates our belief in this matter. Regarding the subject of the first article, there was a bitter conflict between <term>Rufinus: Tyrannius Rufinus (c. 345–410 AD), a monk and translator who was once a close friend of Jerome</term> and <term>Jerome: Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the famous biblical scholar and translator of the Vulgate</term>. As <term>Augustine: St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD)</term>—who deplored the disagreement that arose between them—says: God had granted that, as the closest and most intimate of friends, they might together lick the honey of the Holy Scriptures. Rufinus is of the opinion that the heretical ideas found in the books of Origen were falsely inserted by heretics who corrupted his books, and that these ideas were not from Origen’s own mind. Jerome thinks the opposite. But let us see what probability each opinion holds. It will perhaps appear that, while keeping the faith and fully satisfying all those things which we are bound to believe for the necessity of salvation, it can still be freely and probably believed that those principal heresies—by which Origen’s sin is proved and his subsequent condemnation followed—were not from Origen’s mind, but were falsely attributed to him by treacherous heretics who corrupted his books.

<margin>Pamphilus the martyr.</margin>
First, there is for this side the authority of <term>Pamphilus the martyr: A scholar and friend of Eusebius who was imprisoned and executed for his faith in 310 AD</term>, whose book is circulated in defense of Origen. In this work, the most glorious martyr shows, from the words of Origen himself and from his books cited there, that Origen held orthodox Catholic views on the very points for which he is accused of being a heretic. Jerome, however, denying that this book is by Pamphilus, says the following in his responsive apology to <note>original: "apologia sua ad Oceanum & Pammachium reſponſiua"</note> Oceanus and Pammachius:

<margin>Jerome's testimonies indicating Origen's heresy.</margin>
“If you say his books were violated by Origen’s enemies to bring him into infamy, why should I not be allowed to say that a volume was composed by his friends and followers under the name of Pamphilus, which would vindicate him from infamy by the testimony of a martyr?” From these words, it seems it can be noted that Jerome considers both possibilities probable, implying that just as Rufinus cannot prove those books were not corrupted, neither can Jerome prove that the book in question belongs to Pamphilus. Further down, Jerome adds: “The very name ‘apology’ <note>A formal defense</note> shows an excuse is being made. For nothing is defended except that which is under accusation.” But someone might perhaps ask: since Jerome himself labels this very treatise in which he writes these things as an "Apology"—in which he defends himself, saying he followed Origen’s learning but not his dogma—does he not likewise show himself to be guilty of a crime, since nothing is defended unless it is under accusation? Thus, no one could be justly excused if an excuse always presupposes a nearby accusation. But let us see then by what conjectures Jerome is moved to believe the book is not by Pamphilus. The first thing that moves Jerome is that the same things are read in the first book of <term>Eusebius: Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD), the "Father of Church History"</term>, out of those six books he wrote in favor of Origen. The second is that Eusebius himself, writing the *Life of Pamphilus*, said that Pamphilus wrote no work of his own. For thus says Jerome in his first book against Rufinus, addressed to Pammachius and Marcella: “Eusebius, Bishop of Caesarea, formerly a standard-bearer of the <term>Arian faction: A heretical movement that denied the full divinity of Christ</term>, wrote six books for Origen—a very long and elaborate work—and by many testimonies he approved Origen to be Catholic according to him (that is, Arian according to us). You translate the first of these books under the name of a martyr.” And further down: “If that book is by Pamphilus, which of the six books will be the first by Eusebius?” And further: “Likewise Eusebius—the lover, herald, and companion of Pamphilus—wrote three most elegant books containing the *Life of Pamphilus*, in the third of which he says of Pamphilus: ‘He himself wrote nothing of his own work at all, except perhaps letters which he sent to friends.’” To such an extent did the defender of Origen and praiser of Pamphilus humble himself in his kindness as to say that Pamphilus produced nothing at all, not even any of his own speech; and he said this after Pamphilus had already been crowned with martyrdom, so that you would have no

<column-break/>

refuge <note>A way to escape the argument</note> to say that Pamphilus wrote this after the books published by Eusebius. And further down: “What will the letters of <term>Bishop Theophilus: Theophilus of Alexandria, a fierce opponent of Origenism</term> do? What will those of <term>Pope Anastasius: Pope from 399–401 AD who condemned Origen's works</term> do, who pursue the heretic throughout the whole world? Since your book, issued under the name of Pamphilus, fights against their letters.” And in the second book Jerome writes thus: “Nearly ten years ago, my friend <term>Dexter: Flavius Lucius Dexter, a high official and historian</term>, who administered the Praetorian Prefecture, asked me to weave for him an index of the authors of our religion. Among the other writers, I placed this book as published by Pamphilus, thinking it was so, as it had been made known by you and your disciples. But since Eusebius himself says Pamphilus wrote nothing except letters, etc., and the first book of Eusebius’s six volumes contains the same things in the very same words which were forged by you under the name of Pamphilus, it is clear that you wished to disseminate this book so that you might promote heresy under the person of a martyr. Since even in the very book you pretend is by Pamphilus, you pervert many things, and it is one way in the Greek and another in the Latin.” Moreover, in his responsive apology to Oceanus and Pammachius, in which he shows that he followed the teaching of Origen and not his dogma, he speaks thus of the same book of Pamphilus: “It seems to have been a small work of either <term>Didymus: Didymus the Blind (c. 313–398 AD), a scholar of Alexandria</term> or someone else. Even if we should grant for the sake of argument that it is by Pamphilus, he was not yet a martyr; for he wrote it before he underwent martyrdom. And in what way, you will ask, was he worthy of martyrdom? Specifically, so that by martyrdom he might wipe away his error.” These are Jerome’s words, quoted verbatim from various places regarding that book of Pamphilus.

<margin>Rufinus's opinion against Jerome.</margin>
Rufinus, however, proving the book to be by Pamphilus the martyr and intended for Origen’s defense, says the following in his second book of invective against Jerome, after stating that it could easily be said of any work that it does not belong to the author to whom it is ascribed: “But let us suppose that this booklet is not by the martyr, but by any one person from the Church. Did the writer, whoever he was, use his own words so that we should defer to the merits of the author? He places examples from the volumes of Origen themselves. And he shows what Origen thinks on individual points, not by his own defensive words, but by the words of the man who is being accused. Therefore, the question of the author is superfluous where the defense is such that it does not need a proponent <note>Because the evidence speaks for itself</note>.” Thus says Rufinus.

<margin>Jerome's sayings are refuted by Pico.</margin>
To those things which Jerome says, someone might perhaps respond on behalf of Rufinus as follows: First, when Jerome says Eusebius wrote six books in which he proves Origen was an Arian, and that the first of these was translated by Rufinus under the name of Pamphilus—how can it stand that the book of Pamphilus is the first book of Eusebius, when entirely different and conflicting things are intended in those books? For Eusebius, according to you, O Jerome, tries in his books to prove that Origen was an Arian. But in the book of Pamphilus, nothing else is attempted but to prove that Origen was *not* an Arian, and that whatever things are found in his books confirming the Arian heresy were inserted by the Arians themselves (of whom Eusebius was one, among many others). Therefore, this book must be entirely different from that one, as it argues a completely different—indeed, a contrary—case. Nor is it sufficient if someone should say that the parts pertaining to the Arian heresy were changed from Eusebius’s book. For even regarding what pertains to other heresies, Jerome cannot say that Eusebius showed Origen’s books were corrupted in those matters. Because Jerome himself, in his second book against Rufinus, says that except for what pertains to the Son and the Holy Spirit, in other dogmas Eusebius and Didymus most openly yield to Origen’s sect. Therefore, it cannot be well understood how the same things read in Pamphilus’s book could be read in the first book of Eusebius, unless perhaps some common points about Origen and the point of this conclusion...

apology on behalf of **Origen** cannot perhaps rightly be called a "proper work"
since **Pamphilus** does not dogmatize <note>original: "dogmatizet," meaning to establish formal church doctrine</note> there; indeed, no question
of a universal matter is treated there, but rather it deals briefly
with a particular man—that is, with **Origen**. Whether
his books were corrupted or not is not to "found" a proper
work, nor is it to elevate oneself out of humility by
avoiding the name of "dogmatist" or "author."
Third, it is possible that this book
did not come to the notice of **Eusebius**: both because of the smallness of the book,
and because of the author’s humility (which [Jerome] himself mentions) as one
who wrote nothing great and who hid those slight and
minute things he did write, rather than showing them off. Fourth, **Rufinus** will say
it is also possible that **Eusebius**, as a defender of the <term>Arian treachery: the Arian heresy, which claimed Jesus was a created being and not co-eternal with God</term>,
not only wished to hide the book of the martyr [Pamphilus] which
deprived his own sect of **Origen’s** testimony, but
also acted through this indirect testimony so that
posterity would believe it was not by **Pamphilus**. Therefore, when **Jerome**, as
if to corroborate his reasoning, says that the "defender of **Ori-**
**gen**" [Eusebius] says **Pamphilus** wrote nothing etc., it is
rather against him than for him. For since **Eusebius** defended
**Origen** not as a Catholic but as an **Arian**,
he could rightly be suspect in this matter, as I have said. But why
must we labor over these things? Or how can
**Jerome** prove at all from **Eusebius’s** testimony that the
Apology on behalf of **Origen** is not by **Pamphilus**, when **Euse-**
**bius** himself, in the sixth book of his *Ecclesiastical History*, says that the
Apology for **Origen** was written by the holy
**Pamphilus** the martyr? When, however, **Jerome** adds: "What will the letters
of Bishop **Theophilus** do? What of **Pope Anastasius**, etc.?"
**Rufinus** would perhaps say that the book of **Pamphilus** does not fight against
their primary intention. For it was their purpose
to root out from the world those most wicked and poisonous heresies and dogmas,
whosoever they were, because this pertained to the faith,
to the confirmation of religion, and the stability
of the church. Whether those ideas were **Origen’s**, as was believed by
many, or were not, those most religious
pontiffs would have cared very little. On the contrary, it would perhaps have been
desirable and most acceptable to them if it could have been proven by certain
and valid arguments that those heretical opinions were not
believed by **Origen**; for this would be in favor of the faith, not
against the faith—against the heretics, and not for the heretics
who relied not a little on the testimony of such a great man
(so highly praised by Catholics) and defended their error
by his authority. Therefore, **Pamphilus’s**
book would fight against those letters only if the heresies which they
accused were excused in it. But not if its whole effort
is to deprive the supporters of those [heresies] of such a good patron,
whom those letters pursue. It is
certain that they pursue him only as a <term>heresiarch: a founder or leader of a heretical sect</term>
of those believed opinions. Regarding those things which [Jerome] brings forward in the second

<column-break/>

book, one might perhaps respond thus: First, when
he says that he himself at one time believed and thus wrote that
it was the book of **Pamphilus**, before he had read in **Eusebius** that
**Pamphilus** wrote nothing, and so on. From this statement of his,
**Rufinus** would perhaps argue against him thus: "If, having read
it, O **Jerome**, you at one time both believed and wrote that the book
was by **Pamphilus**: tell me, I pray, what lies
did you read in it, or what heresies or favors to heresy did you recognize?
Or was it rather truths, or things like the truth, that
did no harm to the Catholic faith? If they were false and heretical, how could you
be led to believe the author of the book was a Catholic martyr,
concerning whose testimony and words no one could suspect anything
sinister without it being a crime? But if they were both Catholic and
worthy of a Christian martyr, why do you now condemn them and call them
forgeries, and say they were disseminated to introduce heresies?
In short, why do you now judge them unworthy of a martyr, when you
once judged them worthy of a martyr? Since they are the same things that you
read now and which you read then—as if we were to set aside the author's
title itself and consider the things said there in defense of **Ori-**
**gen** on their own merits. If they are bad, why then did you judge them to be of
a holy martyr? If they are good, why even
now, whosever they are, are they not accepted as good?"
Furthermore: "How can you, O **Jerome**, say that I disseminated
the book to introduce heresies, when in that
book nothing else is done (as was also said above) except to ensure
that the heretics cannot strengthen themselves by **Origen’s** testimony?
This serves to uproot heresy, not to disseminate it."
Furthermore, this book is found not only in Latin but in Greek.
I, **Rufinus**, made the Latin version by translating from the Greek.
Who published the Greek if not **Pamphilus**? Certainly not
I, **Rufinus**, according to you who accuse me of ignorance
of Greek literature—how could I have written a book so eloquently in Greek that
it equaled the style of **Eusebius**? If another author is
proposed, **Jerome** responds that it is by **Didymus** <note>Didymus the Blind (c. 313–398 AD), a prolific theologian who was Jerome's own teacher</note> or someone
else. **Rufinus** will insist: "Whoever that other person is, it is no longer
I, **Rufinus**, but another who will be held guilty of this crime. And
if **Didymus** is a liar according to you, then the deceiver is **Dy-**
**dimus**, your own teacher, O **Jerome**, whom you called both a
'seeing prophet' and the 'eye of the bride' from the *Song of
Songs* and an 'Apostolic man' in your own books. He, I say, is the liar
who published the Greek version and falsely ascribed it to **Pamphilus**;
it is not I, who found it in Greek under the title of **Pamphilus** and, under the
same author's title, shared it with the Latins by translating it.
Nor should it be a wonder to you that I believed **Didymus** in this matter,
since you believed him in the explanation of the Scriptures."
As for [Jerome's] claim that it is one way in Latin and another in Greek: **Rufinus**
would say, "Why do you not bring forward the passages, O **Jerome**, that were badly
translated? Is it so that I cannot clear myself of the fault?
Just as when **Augustine** wrote to you that certain things from your translation
from the Hebrew were condemned, and yet he did not list the passages.
You say that was done so that you could not defend yourself
and prove the truth of your translation. Therefore, what you said
of **Augustine**, O **Jerome**, allow it to be permitted to me to
suspect of you as well." These things are said concerning the disagreement between **Jerome**
and **Rufinus** over the book of **Pamphilus**; in which I, as in all
other things, place the judgment of **Jerome** above the judgment of **Rufinus**.
