### OF QUESTIONS

<columns>
1

...doctrine might be set forth as if truly apostolic: in some places the dogma of **Eunomius** <note>Eunomius of Cyzicus (died c. 393 AD), a leader of the "Anomoean" radicals who argued that the Son was unlike the Father</note> is inserted such that no one other than **Eunomius** himself would be believed to be arguing, saying that the Son of God was <term>created from nothing</term> <note>This phrase "ex nihilo" was a hallmark of Arianism, contradicting the orthodox view that the Son is "begotten, not made."</note>. Likewise, in the writings of **Clement of Alexandria**, a priest and a Catholic man, it is found written that the Son of God was created; and in the four books of **Dionysius**, bishop of the city of Alexandria, where he argues against **Sabellius** <note>Sabellius (3rd century) taught that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit were merely different "modes" or masks of one person</note>, there is a confirmation of the **Arian** dogma. And why is it necessary to bring up apostolic men, when we know that the very Gospels and the words of the apostles themselves have often been depraved by heretics? This is especially clear to anyone from the book of **Tertullian** against **Marcion** <note>Marcion of Sinope (c. 85–160 AD) edited the Gospel of Luke and Paul's letters to remove Jewish influences, which Tertullian famously critiqued</note>. 

Therefore, since this happened to their books, why could it not also have happened to the books of **Origen**? And why, in an entirely similar case, is a similar excuse not accepted in all respects? This excuse seems even more acceptable regarding the books of **Origen** because he himself, while still living, complained about this in his letters (as will be shown below): namely, that his books were being corrupted and depraved by heretics. 

But if **Jerome** considers this to be impossible, asserting that if this were so, then whatever is found in the books of anyone could be said by others to be corrupted, and that it is difficult for all copies to be spoiled—I do not know how he himself will be able to respond to the **Eunomians** when they prove their dogma by the testimony of **Clement**, the disciple of the apostles, in whose works it is found expressly written that the Son of God was created. For if he should resort to the claim that the books of **Clement** were corrupted by those heretics, they will argue using **Jerome’s** own words that this is impossible, saying the same thing: namely, that whatever is found in the books of anyone can be said by others to be corrupted, and that it is impossible for all copies to be corrupted. 

Therefore, perhaps care must be taken lest, while we wish to make **Origen** an absolute heretic, we make the apostles and the disciples of the apostles into heretics as well. For I see no reason why, since no less detestable and execrable heresies and no less impious dogmas are found in their books than in the books of **Origen**, they should not be either similarly accused or similarly excused. 

**Jerome**, however, responds to the corruption of the books of **Clement** and others with these words: "And how," you will ask, "are there several faulty things in their books? If I answer that I do not know the causes of the faults, I will not immediately judge them to be heretics. For it is possible that they simply erred, or wrote in another sense, or their writings were gradually corrupted by unskilled scribes; or they spoke some things innocently and with less caution, which could not avoid the <term>calumny</term> <note>original: "calumniam," meaning a false and malicious accusation</note> of perverse men." 

To this response of **Jerome**, **Rufinus** might perhaps respond thus: that you do not wish to immediately judge those men to be heretics just because there are some faulty things in their books, even if you do not know the causes of the faults. Why then, having seen some faulty things in a book of **Origen**—in which you also read **Origen** contradicting himself elsewhere—do you immediately judge him a heretic? What is the cause of this great inconsistency, especially since you yourself have known, written, and preached that there was in **Origen** such nobility of mind, such zeal for the faith, and such great study of the Scriptures? Thus, you might not undeservedly suspect that the fault was in the manuscripts from whatever source, rather than in his mind. 

Furthermore, just as it was possible according to you that those others either simply erred or wrote in another sense or spoke innocently and less cautiously—why was it not similarly possible that **Origen** either simply erred or wrote in another 
<margin>Didymus</margin> 
sense (as **Didymus** <note>Didymus the Blind (c. 313–398 AD), a loyal follower of Origen's thought in Alexandria</note> contends) or spoke some things innocently and less cautiously which cannot avoid the calumny of perverse men? And just as you say their writings could have been corrupted by 

<column-break/>

unskilled scribes, why could the writings of **Origen** not have been similarly corrupted either by unskilled scribes or by treacherous heretics? The cause for inconsistency does not appear at all. 

**Rufinus** also reports 
<margin>Rufinus’s examples</margin> 
that the book of **Hilary the Confessor** <note>Saint Hilary of Poitiers (c. 310–367 AD), a staunch defender of the Trinity</note> was falsified by heretics after the **Synod of Ariminum**; and for this reason, when a question was raised against him in a council of bishops, he ordered the book to be brought from his house, which (unknown to him) was being held in his cabinets as a heretical work. He says that when it was brought forth and judged heretical by everyone, **Hilary**, the author of the book, left the council having been excommunicated. 

**Jerome** says this is false and a fiction made to slander **Hilary**, 
<margin>Jerome</margin> 
bringing forward nothing else; but whether it was true or not cannot be well known, nor does it pertain much to the defense of **Origen**. What is true is that **Rufinus**, about to recite this concerning **Hilary**, prefixes these words: "And lest anything be lacking for open belief, I will recount things that are still within our memory, so that the truth of the testimony may be hidden from no one." Therefore, it was either true, or it was a great impudence on the part of **Rufinus** to weave an open lie and a new fable regarding a matter of such recent memory. But whether it be true or false, it does not seem to have been invented or recited to slander **Hilary**, because it slanders those who had depraved **Hilary’s** book rather than **Hilary** himself, whom he attests was innocent of heresy, unjustly excommunicated, and craftily deceived. 

After this, **Rufinus** recites that a book of **Tertullian** titled *On the Trinity* was being read under the name of **Cyprian the Martyr** <note>Cyprian (died 258 AD), the influential Bishop of Carthage</note> in Constantinople by heretics of the **Macedonian** party <note>Followers of Macedonius I, who denied the full divinity of the Holy Spirit</note>. **Jerome** says that the book is not by **Tertullian**, nor is it said to be by **Cyprian**, but by **Novatian**. Neither of them brings forward anything else for themselves, except that **Jerome** says the author's eloquence demonstrates the property of his style. Although it is often possible to detect a similar face and tenor of style in many men. But these things are nothing to **Origen**. 

**Rufinus** himself, however, shows 
<margin>Note</margin> 
that the same thing happened to **Jerome** which he reports happened to the books of **Origen**. For he relates that when ecclesiastical letters to be dictated had been handed to him by **Damasus**, bishop of the city of Rome, the **Apollinarists** <note>Followers of Apollinaris of Laodicea, who taught that Christ had a human body but a divine mind</note> took a book of **Athanasius** <note>Saint Athanasius (c. 296–373 AD), the chief defender of Trinitarian orthodoxy</note> (where "the Lord’s man" was written) to read. They corrupted it so that they wrote back into the book that which they had erased, namely, so that it would be thought not to have been falsified by them, but added by **Jerome**. 

And take note that **Jerome**, responding to **Rufinus** on this part, when he says "my own little story is being thrust at me," nevertheless does not deny that it was true, but at the end says this: "It is possible, **Rufinus**, that even if you heard the truth from me, another who is ignorant of this matter might say it was composed and invented by you." 

The third thing that makes it probable that the books of **Origen** were corrupted is that he himself complained of this while living. For there exists in the fourth book of **Origen** a letter of his to certain dear friends of his in Alexandria, 
<margin>He complains in a letter. Note Origen’s words.</margin> 
in which he complains in these words: "But it seems to me nothing marvelous if my doctrine is adulterated by enemies; and is corrupted by such adultery as that by which the epistle of the **Apostle Paul** was corrupted. For some persons composed a false epistle under the name of **Paul**, so that they might trouble the **Thessalonians** as if the day of the Lord were at hand, and might seduce them. Because of this epistle, therefore, in the second epistle which he wrote to the **Thessalonians**, he said these things: 'But we beseech you, brethren, by the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ and our gathering together unto him, that you be not quickly shaken in your mind, nor be terrified, neither by spirit, nor by word, nor by epistle as if sent by us, as if the day of the Lord were at hand; let no man seduce you in any way.' Therefore I see certain such things happening to us. For a certain author of a heresy, when a discussion was held in the presence of many..."

<meta>This page continues the defense of Origen, arguing that his works were systematically corrupted by heretics. The author (Rufinus) is providing specific evidence—including a letter from Origen himself—to show that controversial "heretical" passages were added by others to tarnish Origen’s reputation.</meta>

# A P O L O G I A
-> ii 3 <-

...our debate had taken place, he took the writings from those who had transcribed the manuscript, added what he wanted, took away what he wanted, and changed things as it seemed fit to him. Now he carries it around under my name, insulting me and showing off the things he himself wrote. My brothers in Palestine, being indignant at this, sent a man to me in Athens to receive the actual authentic copies from me. These had not even been re-read or reviewed by me before; they lay so neglected that they could hardly be found. Nevertheless, I sent them, and I speak with God as my witness: when I confronted the man who had corrupted the book and asked why he had done this, he replied as if to satisfy me, saying, "I wanted to further adorn the debate and purify it." Look at what kind of "purification" he used to "cleanse" our debate! It is surely the same kind of "purification" with which **Marcion** <note>Marcion of Sinope (c. 85–160 AD) famously edited the New Testament to remove what he considered "Jewish" corruptions.</note> "purified" the Gospels or the Apostle, or that which his successor **Apelles** <note>A disciple of Marcion who further modified Marcionite teachings.</note> used after him. For just as they subverted the truth of the Scriptures, so this man, having removed what was truly said, inserted false things to incriminate us. These words are read verbatim in the letter of **Origen**. If heretics did not hesitate to corrupt his books while he was still alive, how much more must we believe they dared to do so after his death? He also complains about a certain other heretic in Ephesus who brought together many false things as if they were Origen's own, and there is even another letter of his containing a complaint about the falsification of his books. 

The fourth point, which gives the greatest credibility to this matter—namely, that those heretical ideas are not Origen's but were inserted by heretics—is that Origen is found elsewhere determining those same points in a pious and <term>Catholic</term> <note>In this context, "Catholic" refers to the "universal" or "orthodox" consensus of the early Church.</note> manner. From this it follows that if those heretical views were truly Origen's, he would be contradicting himself. One can see very many places where he acts piously regarding these things in the *Apology of Pamphilus*. This is why **Rufinus** says there is no need to worry about the name of that book's author, since the defense is valid in itself, regardless of who wrote it, because it provides proof of Origen’s Catholic and orthodox dogma through his own words and sayings. This also seems to answer a certain saying of **Jerome** against **Rufinus**. For when Rufinus piously and catholically said the same—that Origen had elsewhere determined these matters—Jerome said against him: "Where is that confidence with which, with puffed-out cheeks, you so frequently proclaimed that you had corrected the things you read in Origen’s other books in the books of the <term>Peri Archon</term> <note>Greek: *Peri Archon*, Latin: *De Principiis* ("On First Principles"), Origen's most controversial and influential theological work.</note>, and that you had restored his own words to his own works? From such a forest of books, you cannot produce a single sprout or twig." Rufinus might perhaps respond that he did not need to produce twigs from that forest because **Pamphilus** had already produced many whole trees from it. Indeed, Pamphilus cites those passages most copiously, and with that already presupposed, Rufinus argues in his own booklet (which he added to Pamphilus's book) to show how it came to pass that contradictions are found in Origen's books, assigning the cause to falsification by heretics.

<margin>Which principal heresies are attributed to Origen.</margin>
The fifth point, which also does much to assert that those heresies are not from the mind of Origen, is that from the testimony of many to whom we are rightly bound to give faith, we hold that Origen felt catholically on the principal opinions in which he is said to have erred. 
<margin>And there are two principal ones, and four others.</margin>
For there are two principal heresies charged against Origen. 
<margin>Defense of the first heresy.</margin>
The first concerns the **Trinity**: namely, that he felt wrongly about the Son and worse about the Holy Spirit. The second concerns the **salvation of the devil**: namely, that his punishment and the infernal suffering would not be eternal, but that he would eventually be liberated. From this second point, many others ascribed to him seem to depend. For instance, 
<margin>Didymus. Athanasius.</margin>
that for the sake of saving these demons, Christ would have to be crucified again in a higher element; and 

<column-break/>

that all things must be restored into one; and that the devil can repent; and that the punishment of the damned is not eternal. Regarding these two heresies, there seem to be evident arguments that they were not part of Origen’s mind. For concerning the Trinity, not only does **Didymus** <note>Didymus the Blind (c. 313–398 AD), a famous theologian in Alexandria who was a great admirer of Origen.</note>—in whose teaching Jerome so greatly glories—say that Origen felt catholically, and proved this in his own published commentaries on the *Peri Archon*; but also **Athanasius** <note>St. Athanasius the Great (c. 296–373 AD), the staunch defender of the Trinity against Arianism at the Council of Nicaea.</note>, the defender of the Council of Nicaea, in his own books against the **Arians**, called this man a witness to his faith with a clear voice. We even read that **Methodius** repented of having condemned Origen, saying that he 
<margin>Sayings of Origen by which he is judged not a heretic but a most Christian man.</margin>
was finally found to believe nothing wrongly concerning the Holy Trinity. Indeed, we have Origen’s own sayings about the Trinity that differ in no way from the Catholic faith. For concerning that passage of Paul to the Romans, *and the Spirit helps our infirmity* <note>Romans 8:26</note>, he expressly holds that the Holy Spirit is not a creature. And on the passage, *He who did not spare his own Son but delivered him up for us all, how has he not also with him given us all things?* <note>Romans 8:32</note> Origen, explaining this, says: "For there is nothing in either visible or invisible creation that can be equaled to the Son, for in no way can a creature be compared to its Creator; and if the Creator himself was given to us, how will every creature not be given to us with him?" And further on, regarding Paul’s words, *who is over all things, God blessed forever* <note>Romans 9:5</note>, Origen says: "That Christ is one thing according to the flesh and another according to the Spirit, he already designated in the earlier parts of this same epistle where he says, *who was made of the seed of David according to the flesh, who was destined the Son of God in power according to the Spirit of sanctification* <note>Romans 1:3-4</note>. And how he is the Son of God according to the Spirit and the son of David according to the flesh, we have explained more fully there to the best of our ability. Therefore, the one whom he called the Son of God there according to the Spirit, here, as the doctrine proceeds in order for the advancing listeners, he pronounces to be God himself who is over all things. I wonder how some, reading what the same Apostle said in other places—*There is one God the Father from whom are all things, and one Lord Jesus Christ through whom are all things* <note>1 Corinthians 8:6</note>—deny that the Son of God should be confessed as God, lest they seem to confess and speak of two gods. What will they do with this passage of the Apostle in which Christ, through whom are all things, is openly described as being God over all things? But those who feel this way do not notice that just as he said the Lord Jesus Christ is the one Lord in such a way that God the Father is not thereby denied to be Lord, so also he did not say God the Father is one God in such a way that the Son is not believed to be God. For the Scripture is true which says: *Know that the Lord himself is God.*" <note>Psalm 100:3</note>

"But each is the one God because there is no other beginning of divinity for the Son than the Father, but as Wisdom says, the Son is the most pure emanation of that one paternal fountain. Therefore, Christ is God over all things—all those things, without doubt, which we spoke of a little earlier: over principalities, and powers, and virtues, and every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the future. He who is over all things has no one over himself, for he is not after the Father, but from the Father. This same thing must also be understood concerning the Holy Spirit from the Wisdom of God, where it is said: *The Spirit of the Lord has filled the world,* and *that which contains all things has knowledge of the voice.* If, therefore, the Son of God is said to be over all things and the Holy Spirit is remembered to contain all things, and God the Father is he from whom all things are, then the nature of the Trinity and the one substance which is over all things is evidently shown." These are Origen's words verbatim; and elsewhere, regarding that passage of Paul, *But how shall they preach...*

<meta>This page continues the defense of the Early Christian scholar Origen (c. 184–253 AD). Having previously argued that Origen's works were tampered with by later heretics, the author now addresses specific accusations: his views on the Trinity, the eventual salvation of the devil, and the pre-existence of human souls.</meta>

# OF THE QUESTIONS

<columns>
<margin>
Defense of the second heresy by Origen himself.
</margin>
...they will [not] preach unless they are sent. For he says: "There are some who indeed announce and preach concerning the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, but not sincerely or completely, as is the case with all heretics. They announce the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, but they do not announce them well or faithfully. For they either wrongly separate the Son from the Father—saying the Father is of one nature and the Son of another—or they wrongly confuse them, making God a composition of three parts or merely a triple name. Those, however, who announce good things correctly will give to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit their own distinct properties, yet they will confess that there is no diversity in substance or nature." These are the words of Origen. What could be more Catholic or more clearly expressed than these words? Therefore, if anything is found written otherwise in Origen's books, it is necessary to conclude it is not Origen's, but the work of heretics who wished to have Origen as a patron of their error through the corruption of his books. Regarding the second heresy <note>The "second heresy" mentioned here refers to the doctrine of "Apocatastasis," the belief that all beings, including the devil, might eventually be reconciled to God.</note>, there exists such evident testimony that in my judgment it can hardly be denied. For in a letter of his own—and according to the translation by **Jerome** <note>St. Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), known for the Vulgate Bible, was initially a fan of Origen but later became a fierce critic.</note>, who expressly mentions that letter—Origen himself denies that the devil can ever be saved, saying that no one but a madman could say such a thing.

<margin>
Origen's dialogue testifies to the truth.
</margin>
Furthermore, there exists a dialogue between Origen and **Candidus** <note>A follower of Valentinus, an early Gnostic teacher.</note>, a follower of the Valentinian dogma. When Candidus raised this same error as an objection, Origen refuted it and denied that he held this view. Regarding the passage where Paul asks if they stumbled so as to fall, Origen, looking at this "fall," refers to what Christ said: "I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven." He denies that Israel has fallen [permanently], for their conversion will happen at the end of the age, when the fullness of the nations has come in, and all Israel shall be saved. But for that one who is said to have fallen from heaven, there will be no conversion, even at the end of the age. These are Origen's words. Moreover, the heresy attributed to him—that the Spirit does not understand the Son, and the Son does not understand the Father—is falsely attributed. This is clear from what he says regarding Paul's words: *O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God!* <note>original: "O altitudo diuitiarum sapientiæ & scientiæ dei." from Romans 11:33.</note> For he says that he calls this depth of God "unsearchable" for every *creature*; but he could not say this regarding the Son and the Holy Spirit, because the Son says to the Father in the Gospel: "Father, all mine are yours, and yours are mine," and Paul himself pronounces concerning the Holy Spirit, saying: "No man knows the things of a man except the spirit of the man which is in him; even so, the things of God no one knows but the Spirit of God." Therefore, when Paul says, "Who has known the mind of the Lord," he is speaking of creatures, but he excepts the nature of the Trinity. These are Origen's words.

<margin>
A defense offered for the heresy regarding the creation of souls.
</margin>
There remains one heresy attributed to Origen: namely, the opinion that souls were created from eternity and fell from heaven into bodies. Regarding the soul, Origen himself writes in his commentaries on Paul's letter to Titus that he can determine nothing from Church dogma except that all souls are of the same species, that they possess free will, that they are rational and immortal, that they were created by God, and that they will face punishment for evil and rewards for good. He says he affirms only these things concerning the soul.

<margin>
What Rufinus felt overall regarding the soul.
</margin>
For these points, evident testimonies are found in the Scriptures. In other questions about the soul, however, he says what seems more probable to him, proceeding by inquiry rather than by definitive statement, because nothing definitive is held regarding them in Church dogma. However, it is widely agreed that Origen's preferred view was that souls existed in heaven before bodies. **Rufinus** <note>Tyrannius Rufinus (c. 344–411 AD), a monk and translator who was Origen's greatest defender in the Latin West.</note>, in his apology to **Anastasius of Rome** <note>Pope Anastasius I (reigned 399–401 AD).</note>, after he

<column-break/>

recounted three opinions regarding the soul, says at the end: "Truly, having read each of these, I say with God as my witness that up to the present, I hold nothing certain or defined regarding this question; I leave it to God to know what is true, and to whomever He deigns to reveal it. However, I do not deny that I have read these various views, and I confess I am still ignorant." Beyond this, the Church clearly teaches that God is the creator of both souls and bodies. Even in the book by **Pamphilus** <note>Pamphilus of Caesarea (d. 309 AD), a martyr and scholar who wrote an influential "Apology for Origen."</note>, it is not denied that Origen held that opinion [of pre-existence], but his defense is written thus: "Since there is diversity among churchmen, and some feel one way about the soul and others another, why should this man be accused more than the rest?" Then, after these words, the opinions about the soul that existed then are recited—including the one now held by Catholics. When it is shown that manifest proofs for these cannot be produced from the Holy Scriptures, and that great difficulties befall the authors of those views, it is concluded: "What we wish to show from all this is that, just as no one rightly calls those heretics who think any one of the opinions we explained above is true (because nothing certain or manifest is said of them in Divine Scripture, nor is it thought to be contained in Church preaching), so it is not just to blame this man for discussing what seemed more likely to him."

<margin>
First proposition.
</margin>
From all the above, I infer two propositions. The first is that if Origen thought in a Catholic manner regarding both the Trinity and the salvation of demons—as seems proven by the testimonies—we cannot prove his condemnation based on an erroneous opinion about the soul. For Origen was not bound to believe everything explicitly about the soul in his time that we are bound to believe now, because those things were neither manifest in Scripture nor determined by the Church as they were later.

<margin>
200 years from Origen to Augustine. Augustine was always doubtful about the creation of the soul.
</margin>
Indeed, not only in the time of Origen, but even in the time of **Augustine** <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), the most influential theologian of the Western Church.</note>—who lived 200 years after Origen—nothing had yet been determined by Catholics (that is, by the universal Church) concerning the soul. For Augustine himself was doubtful in his opinion on the soul, as is clear from his letter to Jerome: namely, whether individual souls are created for individual people (as orthodox tradition now holds). From that opinion, it seemed to Augustine to follow that God would be unjust. Or [he wondered] whether they were propagated from that one soul made in Adam by God, just as body comes from body—a view called **traducianism**. Do not believe that Augustine doubted this only in his youth; for even in the first book of his *Retractions* <note>A late work where Augustine reviewed and corrected his earlier writings.</note>, which was among his last, he doubts this question. He writes: "Regarding its origin [the soul] in the body—whether it comes from that one who was first created when man became a living soul, or whether individual souls are made for individuals—I did not know then, and I still do not know." These are Augustine's words, verbatim. From this, it is clearly evident that Origen can in no way be called a heretic for the aforementioned erroneous opinion about the soul.

<margin>
Second proposition. St. Thomas.
</margin>
The second proposition I state is this: if it is true what **Thomas [Aquinas]** <note>The great medieval scholastic philosopher and theologian (1225–1274 AD).</note> says in his *Quodlibets* (as will appear more broadly in the 7th article of the defense of Origen), it is good theology that we are not bound by the necessity of salvation to believe not only the doctors of the Church—such as Jerome, Augustine, and the like—but not even the Church itself, except in those things which pertain to the substance of the faith. And if we add that these things [the origin of souls] pertain nothing to the substance of the faith...

<summary>This page argues that Origen's controversial views should not be considered heretical because, at the time he wrote, the Church had not yet officially defined its doctrines on the origin of the soul. The author uses the later uncertainty of St. Augustine and the theological principles of Thomas Aquinas to defend Origen's right to philosophical inquiry.</summary>
<keywords>Origen, St. Augustine, Rufinus, Jerome, pre-existence of souls, Trinity, salvation of the devil, heresy, Church dogma, Thomas Aquinas</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the defense of Origen, moving from the specific contents of his disputed writings to a broader argument regarding his intent and the nature of heresy. The author compares Origen to other Church Fathers to show that intellectual error is not the same as being a heretic.</meta>

-># A P O L O G Y<-

<columns>
...pertain to whether Origen was the author of those heresies, or someone else, so long as we admit that those heresies are indeed heresies—that is, impious dogmas. It seems to follow that a faithful and true Christian is not bound, for the necessity of salvation, to believe **Jerome** <note>St. Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the primary critic of Origen's orthodoxy.</note> in this matter (even if the Church leans more toward him) rather than **Athanasius**, **Didymus**, **Methodius**, or **Rufinus**. Rufinus’s faith was proven by imprisonment and exile in the holy Church of Alexandria during the time of the persecution by heretics. Indeed, one should believe Origen’s own words, especially since we do not approve of Jerome in many other matters that pertain even more to the substance of the faith. 
<margin>Jerome is not always to be believed, for he is often condemned for the vice of mockery.</margin>
For instance, in the matter of ceremonial laws, it is pious not to believe Jerome where he calls the commentaries of **Ambrose** <note>St. Ambrose (c. 340–397 AD), Bishop of Milan and a contemporary of Jerome.</note> "trifles" and calls Ambrose himself first a "raven" and then a "jackdaw." Also, where he condemns Ambrose’s book on the Holy Spirit, saying he had seen good Greek sources but "not good Latin" ones; and where he accuses **Basil the Great** of pride; and where he says in his letters to **Augustine** that he had read certain heretical things in Augustine's works. Thus, perhaps in this case as well—where Jerome prefers to think the works showing Origen as a Catholic are forgeries while those proving him a heretic are genuine—it is neither impious nor harmful to the faith to disagree with him. To defend Origen actually seems to confirm the faith and take away ammunition from heretics, as is written in the book of **Pamphilus** <note>Pamphilus of Caesarea (d. 309 AD), an early martyr who wrote an "Apology for Origen."</note>: they ought to consider what great material for mockery they provide to heretics when they see the men they consider champions and defenders of Christian doctrine being refuted by their own side. They rejoice in this "civil war," seeing an enemy attacked from within whom they could not defeat from without. There were also teachers of the Church later than Jerome who held the opinion that those heresies were not in Origen’s mind but were falsely attributed to him by heretics. Thus **Aymo** <note>Likely Haymo of Auxerre (9th century), a Benedictine monk and commentator.</note>, one of the noble and ancient 
<margin>The words of Aymo in testimony of Origen.</margin>
teachers of the Church, says in his book *On the Memory of Christian Affairs*: "I would surely say of Origen, a man so illustrious, of such abstinent and chaste life, of such excellent doctrine and pure, lucid speech (saving the faith of the Fathers), that he did not write these things at all. Instead, they were malignantly forged by heretics to darken his excellent name and titled with his name." These are his words exactly. These things have been said regarding the first article: examining and inquiring whether those two opinions of Origen were heretical or not. In this matter, as in all others, I always place the judgment of the Church above the judgment and reasons of all others. Regarding the second article, it seems more reasonable 
<margin>Regarding the second article, beginning from the 7th proposition.</margin>
that Origen should be excused because, if he wrote anything not accepted by Catholics, he did not proceed in those writings in a "dogmatic" <note>In this context, "dogmatic" means making a final, authoritative declaration of truth.</note> or assertive way, but always in a "dubitative" and "inquisitive" manner (as one asking questions). Just as there are many things in **Augustine’s** books on Genesis that are not accepted, we excuse them because, as he says in his book of *Retractions*, there are more things "sought" in that book than "found." So too, there may be many things in Origen's books 
<margin>What is properly called heresy. Note. The words of Origen.</margin>
to be rejected and condemned; but because he spoke not by determining but by inquiring, he should not be called a heretic. For a "heresy" is properly called a dogma asserted against the express truth of Scripture or the determination of the Church. That Origen always spoke in this way is clear from many places. After a disputation on the soul, he says: "Let these not be dogmas according to our opinion, but only things sought out and put forward

<column-break/>

lest the subject seem entirely unaddressed." Elsewhere, speaking of the resurrection, he says: "If these things are not contrary to the faith..." and below: "a triple suspicion <note>Here, "suspicion" means a hypothesis or speculative idea.</note> is suggested to us regarding the end, of which the reader may inquire which is true and better." He then adds three opinions on the resurrection. In the preface to his books *On Genesis*, he says: "If something deep occurs regarding this, it should be spoken of, but not affirmatively." And below: "Regarding great things that are above us, we are not ignorant of our own ignorance." In his commentary on the *Epistle to the Romans*, he says: "Let these things be said by us on the condition that if anyone says something better and more reasonable, their words should be held rather than ours." And in Book IV: "These things are brought forth as best we could in such arduous and difficult matters; if someone considers the zeal of our mind, he may embrace them; but if he notes the weakness of our perception, we ask for pardon and gladly yield to anyone who can discuss or explain these things better." And elsewhere: "Let the reader prove which of these is more in line with the Apostolic sense and hold to that." And in Book V: "These things have occurred to us for the present; if anyone perceives something better, let him not be reluctant to look to those and set these aside." Why say more? Let the book *Periarchon* <note>original: "periarchon"; This is the Greek title for Origen's most famous and controversial work, "On First Principles."</note> be read; we will see him proceed in this order: first, he sets down those things which seemed to him expressly determined in Scripture, and in those he does not wander from the Church. Other things he says are doubtful, and he wishes to inquire into them, asserting that only that truth should be received which in no way opposes Apostolic and ecclesiastical dogmas. Regarding the third article, which is a confirmation of the second, I offer this proposition: if 
<margin>Regarding the third article, a proposition at the beginning. A proposition to be noted. A corollary.</margin>
there is someone holding an erroneous opinion about matters of faith not yet determined by the Church, provided there is no stain in his will but rather a firm purpose to always believe what is in harmony with Scripture and the Church, that person neither sins mortally nor should be properly called a heretic. From this proposition, it follows as a corollary that it is possible for holding an opinion at one time to be a mortal sin, while it would not be so at another time. This is because one can believe something without "pertinacity" (stubbornness) at one time, which at another time—such as after a determination by the Church or a 
<margin>What makes a heretic. Augustine.</margin>
clarification of Holy Scripture—one could not believe without pertinacity. The opinion of all teachers testifies to the opposite of what was believed, saying that it is not precisely an error of the intellect that makes a man a heretic, but 
<margin>Confirmation of those who were heretics and later canonized.</margin>
there must also be malice and perversity in the will. Therefore Augustine used to say: "I can err, but I cannot be a heretic" <note>original: "errare possum hæreticus efse nō possum"</note>. This is confirmed by the determination of the universal Church, which has canonized many who nevertheless persevered until death in erroneous opinions regarding the faith, which were afterwards rejected by the Church as heretical. It is nowhere read that they retracted these opinions. Such 
<margin>Papias. Victorinus. Irenaeus. Cyprian.</margin>
were **Papias**, Bishop of Hierapolis; **Victorinus** of Pettau; **Irenaeus** of Lyons; **Blessed Cyprian**; and many others whom we know erred in faith and whose opinions were condemned as heretical. Yet they are held in the canon of the saints. From this, it follows that we must necessarily say either that they did not die in mortal sin despite dying with those erroneous opinions, or that the Church erred in their canonization. If someone says—as one of those who attacked me said—that perhaps they were not truly canonized, then it is they, not I, who think against the determination of the universal Church. From this proposition, I infer regarding Origen that even if it is granted that Origen held many and numerous...
</columns>

<summary>This page argues that Origen should not be labeled a heretic because his controversial ideas were presented as philosophical inquiries rather than rigid dogmas. The author highlights that many canonized saints, such as Cyprian and Irenaeus, held errors that were later condemned, yet they remain saints because they lacked the "perverse will" required for true heresy.</summary>

--- Page 109 ---
<meta>This page continues the logical defense of Origen, shifting from the authenticity of his texts to the theological definition of heresy. The author argues that for a person to be a "heretic" in a way that leads to damnation, there must be a "malice of the will" rather than a mere "error of the intellect." This distinction is used to compare Origen's situation to other respected Church figures like Cyprian and Papias.</meta>

-># OF QUESTIONS<-

<columns>
...had erroneous opinions regarding the faith, specifically if there was no stain in his will in any way, it cannot be an argument that his soul is damned. To argue thus: either a great error—however large—about any matters of faith in a person's intellect does not hinder their salvation as long as there is no stain in the will; or an error—however small—about any matter does hinder it; or some errors do and some do not. If a great error does not hinder it, even in the most fundamental matters, provided his will was well-disposed and in no way stained, then nothing hindered his salvation. Thus, for those who wish to prove his damnation, it is not enough to show his errors and his perseverance in them. Rather, they must show perseverance joined with <term>pertinacity</term> <note>original: "pertinacia"; in canon law, this refers to a stubborn, willful adherence to error even after being corrected.</note> or negligence or some other malice of the will. 

If even a small error is sufficient to damn, then the error regarding the re-baptism of heretics should have hindered the salvation of **Cyprian** <note>St. Cyprian of Carthage (c. 210–258 AD), who famously disagreed with the Pope over whether those baptized by heretics needed to be re-baptized.</note>. 
<margin>The Chiliast heretics.</margin> 
Likewise, the heresy of those called **Chiliasts** <note>Also known as Millenarians; those who believe in a literal 1,000-year earthly reign of Christ.</note> should have hindered the salvation of **Papias**, who was the author of that heresy 
<margin>An objection.</margin> 
and died with it. If so, then they were wrongly canonized by the Church. If some errors hinder salvation and others do not, those who say so must state which errors hinder and which do not. Where is such a distinction ever found made by the Church? For example, where is it said that having an error in things pertaining to such-and-such an article—even if it is strictly a weakness and defect of the intellect and not any perversity, negligence, pertinacity, or any other malice in the will—is a mortal sin? Or that having an error in such-and-such a matter is not a mortal sin unless there is a defect in the will? If such a distinction is found neither from the Church nor from the doctors, nor appears able to be made reasonably, then the claim of certain people appears invalid when they say there is one rule for Cyprian, Papias, and their like, and another for **Origen** because Origen erred in fundamental principles. For however great an error may be, provided it is only an error in the intellect and there is no malice in the will, it does not seem that such an erring person sins mortally. 
<margin>The first reason for the objection. The second.</margin> 
Therefore, since we do not read that there was such malice in Origen's will—even granted that he erred in the most fundamental mysteries of the faith with a most grave error, rightly condemned by the Church—it cannot be proven that he himself is damned in his soul. 

Now, if someone says there are many degrees of propositions to be believed, and that even if there is no pertinacity, it is a sign of pertinacity to assert things whose opposites one is bound to hold by explicit faith; and that an error is not only mortally culpable because of pertinacity but also sometimes because of negligence in seeking the truth (which is not pertinacity, at least properly speaking), it seems a reasonable response can be given. First, that Origen cannot be blamed for negligence in seeking the truth in this matter because, as **Jerome** <note>St. Jerome, though often a critic, acknowledged Origen's incredible work ethic.</note> rightly says, he "sweated over the scriptures day and night." Second, Origen erred in nothing that he was then bound to believe so explicitly that he could be called a heretic for asserting the opposite—not as dogma, but as it seemed more probable to him. I prove this evidently from a certain saying of Jerome himself, cited above. For when Jerome says that even if certain faulty things are found in **Clement** <note>Clement of Alexandria (c. 150–215 AD), another early Christian teacher.</note> (the disciple of the Apostles) and others like him, he would not immediately judge them as heretics. He then 

<column-break/>

<margin>Note the causes for which someone is called a heretic.</margin> 
adds a fourfold cause. First, that the books could be corrupted. Second, that they wrote with a different meaning. Third, that they simply erred. Fourth, that they spoke less cautiously. In these words, we should notice that even if the book of Clement—in which he says the Son of God is a creature—is not corrupted, and even if the author intended no other meaning, Clement is still not immediately to be judged a heretic, because he could have simply erred. What is it to "simply err" except to err from a defect of intellect and an erroneous judgment of reason, and not from malice or perversity of the will? If one can "simply err" in that heresy stating that the Son is a creature (which is the greatest error and even the one charged against Origen) because no other determination of the Church or certain verification through a greater elucidation of the scriptures existed yet, then if Clement was not bound under penalty of mortal sin to believe otherwise by explicit faith, what can we say Origen was obligated to believe explicitly regarding those things in which he is said to have erred? 

It must be noted, however, that because heresy can exist both in words spoken badly and inordinately (as **Augustine** says) and in the meaning, Jerome gives a way of excusing one who has erred in either or both through a defect of intellect alone and not of will. He says they "spoke less cautiously" (if the heresy appears in the words) or "simply erred" (if the heretical meaning was produced by a simple and upright will but a weak and erring intellect). These words of Jerome are to be well noted and weighed, for in them a useful and healthy doctrine concerning heretical pertinacity is rightly founded. 
<margin>Regarding the fourth article, proving Origen repented. An apocryphal book.</margin> 
Concerning the fourth article, some who say Origen repented cite "The Lament of Origen," but that book is considered apocryphal <note>meaning of doubtful authenticity or not part of the accepted canon.</note> as held in the <term>Decretals</term> <note>The collected laws of the Church; specifically refers to the Decretum Gratiani, distinction 15.</note>. I, however, cite the testimony of Jerome himself, which cannot be held as apocryphal, who expressly testifies that Origen repented of his errors. I do not bring this up because it is reasonably necessary for believing in Origen's salvation (as will appear in the next article), but because these masters never cease crying out: "I show you Origen erred; you show me he repented! You will never show this; you will never find it written that Origen repented of what he wrote." 

Let these reverend fathers therefore hear Jerome himself, by whose authority they strike down Origen, in his *Apology to Pammachius and Oceanus*, in which he shows he followed Origen's learning but not his dogma. After reciting Origen's errors, he adds these words: "Origen himself, in the letter he wrote to **Fabian**, Bishop of the city of Rome, does penance for why he wrote such things, and 
<margin>Ambrose.</margin> 
refers the causes of his rashness to **Ambrose** <note>This refers to Origen’s patron, Ambrose of Alexandria, who paid for Origen's secretaries and published his works, sometimes before they were polished.</note>, saying that he brought into public things that were edited in secret." These are Jerome’s words, verbatim. What could be clearer? What more express? How or with what face can they now say it is nowhere found that Origen repented? 
<margin>Note the wit.</margin> 
I will also mention what happened to me these days with two of those who were condemning this conclusion in a similar discussion. For when I, in defending Origen against pertinacity, told someone insisting that the Church had determined Origen was damned in his soul for pertinacity, that I held from Greek histories that Origen’s dogmas were condemned many years after his death, I referred him—if he did not have the books at home—to the **Bishop of Trogir** <note>A city in modern-day Croatia.</note>, a man no less outstanding in learning and character than in his dignity, with whom I had seen a Greek book in which many things concerning the councils were collected. That good father said...

He provides historical evidence from Jerome that Origen actually expressed regret for his more controversial writings, blaming their premature publication on his patron.</summary>

-># APOLOGIA<-

<columns>
...“Then,” he said, “why do you send me back to the Greeks when you know I am completely ignorant of Greek letters? Let us seek Latin ones.” “Do we not have the *Bundle of Times* <note>original: "fasciculum temporū"; the *Fasciculus Temporum*, a popular 15th-century world chronicle by Werner Rolevinck.</note> which treats these matters most elegantly? Let that bundle be brought,” I said, though I added: “If you prepare a fire for me as a heretic, as if this bundle were the kindling placed beneath me, I will immediately cast both you and your bundle to the devil <note>original: "in malā crucem"; literally "to the bad cross," a common Roman idiom for a curse or "go to hell."</note>, for there is no faith to be had in it.” He flared up as if I had blasphemed the Trinity. “Don't get angry with me,” I said, “let the bundle be brought, and do not wish to strike me down as if with unbound rods <note>original: "solutis fascibus"; a play on the word "fascis" (bundle/authority) and the "Fasciculus" book title.</note>.” It was brought, and in it we read these things regarding Origen: “Origen, an outstanding teacher and of incomparable holiness of life, most famous in the church of God...” and a few things later at the end it says: “A great labyrinth is woven by various people concerning Samson, Solomon, Trajan, and this Origen—namely, whether they are saved or not. Because these things are unknown without peril, and the Church has not certified anything about them, they must be committed entirely to the Lord.” This is a good bundle! When he had read this and heard that the Church was not certain about Origen's damnation, it is a wonder how pale he turned; and while the authority of the most proven men could do nothing with him, this little bundle was able to change his opinion immediately.

<margin>Note another story.</margin>
On the following day, someone else addressed me more sharply, carrying a quite large book in his hand. “How,” he asked, “or by what way at all do you dare to defend Origen from the punishment of eternal fire? Behold, I will show you a testimony you cannot contradict, which says Origen cannot be defended.” “Produce your witnesses, venerable man,” I said, “if you have them.” Then he said, “Here is a certain great witness,” and he added a name—but I do not wish to mention the name. “These are his sermons and preachings.” Then I said, “What sermons are you bringing me? What trifles!” “Trifles?” he responded, now glowing with rage. “Trifles, I say, in which—even regarding this matter if he has a sermon on it (for far be it from me to ever read that family of works)—unless some most express error is found. Now I want to break Origen's head with you on Ixion’s wheel <note>A mythological reference to eternal punishment; Ixion was bound to a perpetually turning fiery wheel.</note>.” Impatient and seething with bile, he opens the book and begins to read, raging in a very loud voice. “Wednesday, sermon eleven, on the Origenists.” Then, in his persecution of what was written, he exclaimed at every single word: “Is this not an error?” And behold, while he was shouting thus to the envy of Stentor <note>A Greek herald in the Iliad known for a voice as loud as fifty men.</note>, he read these things written in the book: “Finally, **Jerome** <note>original: "Hieronymus"; Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the translator of the Vulgate Bible.</note> confesses that he read six thousand of Origen's books.” Having immediately read this, he cries out again: “Is this not an error?” “Here indeed is an error,” I said, “and a great one! Here is an open lie, here is expressed falsehood!” And to restrain the man immediately, I ordered the letters of Jerome to be brought. Running straight to the second book of his invective against **Rufinus** <note>Tyrannius Rufinus (c. 344–411 AD), a friend turned rival of Jerome who defended and translated Origen.</note>, I showed him Jerome responding to Rufinus—who was claiming that Pope Epiphanius boasted of having read six thousand of Origen's books—with these words: “Regarding the six thousand books which you invent were read by him: who believes either that you are telling the truth or that he could have lied? For if Origen had written six thousand books, it might have been possible for a learned man, instructed in sacred letters from infancy, to have read the works of others out of curiosity and knowledge. But since he did not write them, how could he have read them? Count the index of his books which are contained in the third volume of **Eusebius** <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD), the first great historian of the Church.</note>, in which he wrote the *Life of Pamphilus*, and I do not say six thousand, but you will not even find a third of that number.” These are the words of Jerome to the letter.

<margin>Epilogue.</margin>
He blushed, and my case was saved. But let us now return to the point, concluding that either with Rufinus and others whom we cited above in the first article, we must concede that Origen never sinned; or if we contend entirely with Jerome that he himself sinned, let us know that we must also concede

<column-break/>

with Jerome that Origen repented of his sin in a personal pamphlet given to the Bishop of Rome. I, however, after I diligently weighed and examined within myself those things which are said especially by Eusebius, Rufinus, and Jerome concerning Origen, conjecture that Origen, laboring long in the investigation of the Scriptures, was uncertain about many arduous and principal questions of theology. It did not seem to him that he could assert anything with certainty and without doubt from the testimony of the Scriptures. Because of this, regarding many mysteries of the faith, he perhaps said many things by way of inquiry and dispute in the earlier years of his life which the Catholic faith would not receive. Therefore, Origen—who, as he himself says, was not ignorant of his own ignorance and clearly recognized that he had not yet attained the truth of those questions—never wanted what he preached in the churches to be taken down by notaries for public release before his sixtieth year, as Eusebius reports.

<margin>Eusebius.</margin>
Let us notice, therefore, what Eusebius writes in the twenty-sixth chapter of the sixth book of his *Ecclesiastical History*: that in the third year of the reign of Emperor Philip, and under Pope Fabian, when he was already sixty years old, Origen began to commit his sayings to public writing. And let us notice what he says earlier in the seventeenth chapter: that under Pope Urban, who was succeeded by Pontian—already before the time of Fabian—Origen began writing commentaries on the Holy Scriptures at the urging of **Ambrose** <note>Not St. Ambrose of Milan, but a wealthy friend and patron of Origen who provided him with secretaries.</note>, who compelled him with great force of prayers and entreaties. Eusebius says that Ambrose seemed most worthy for this duty to be bestowed upon him, and to whom whatever was secret and hidden in the sacred letters should be opened. From these two passages of Eusebius, in which a kind of contradiction appears, it is evidently gathered: that at the urging of Ambrose, he dictated certain things in his earlier years before he had yet discovered the truth, to be communicated only to Ambrose privately, and not to be published for the general public, as he did not yet know if they were safe and consonant with Apostolic truth. Ambrose, however, brought those secretly produced things into the public light. Then, once the Catholic truth was discovered by Origen (now a sexagenarian), he began to write boldly and publicly in a Catholic manner. He was vehemently grieved that those things he had written for the private use of Ambrose had now been published by him. 

<margin>Jerome.</margin>
To clear himself of this, as I conjecture from the words of Jerome and Eusebius, he provided a testimony of his Catholic faith by writing the whole sequence of events to **Fabian**, the Bishop of Rome <note>Pope Fabian (reigned 236–250 AD).</note>, narrating that those things previously found written by him were not written to be published, for he himself was doubtful whether they were Catholic or not. But Ambrose had published them. For this is what Jerome says: Origen himself, in the letter which he writes to Fabian, Bishop of the city of Rome, does penance for why he wrote such things, and refers the causes of his rashness to Ambrose, who brought into the public those things produced in secret. Eusebius, however, narrating what he wrote after his sixtieth year—after he counted the *Book Against Celsus*, twenty-five books of *Commentaries on Matthew*, and twenty on the Prophets—adds: “He wrote also to Fabian, Bishop of the city of Rome, and to many other leaders of the churches concerning his Catholic faith.” These are his words. Let it be true, then, that before his sixtieth year Origen was doubtful about many mysteries of the faith. And let it be true that he secretly communicated many things in writing to Ambrose, which he then thought not by firmly adhering to them, but by inquiring with doubt—things now not to be received by Catholics. And thus let Jerome speak the truth: that those things found in many of Origen's books which are not Catholic are indeed Origen’s, because they were truly dictated by him, though not as things believed, but as things sought after.

...rather than discovered; and consequently, those things in which Catholic truth was later found should not be blamefully ascribed to Origen, since many of those points were invented by heretics, according to Rufinus <note>Tyrannius Rufinus (c. 345–410 AD), a monk and translator who famously defended Origen and argued that heretics had tampered with Origen's original texts.</note>. We can also accept this as true because Origen himself complained of this very thing while he was still alive. Let it therefore be true—following Eusebius in his *Ecclesiastical History*, which was approved as true by Jerome—that Origen is not to be held responsible for his works (that is, those in which he speaks definitively and with firm adherence) except for those he wrote after his sixtieth year. And let it also be true, according to Jerome, that he repented of his earlier writings which were rashly published by Ambrose <note>St. Ambrose of Alexandria, Origen's wealthy patron who provided the stenographers for his prolific output.</note>, and consequently, that he died a Catholic. Thus,

<margin>Concerning the fifth article. The fifth proposition.</margin>

not only according to Rufinus, Pamphilus, and Eusebius, but even according to Jerome, it is more reasonable to believe that he is saved than to believe that he is damned. For the fifth article, I state this proposition: however gravely someone may sin mortally in life, and even if it is certain that they did sin mortally, unless their final impenitence is certain, it is rash to truly assert that they are damned. The truth of this proposition is evident from the common opinion of all the Doctors <note>The "Doctors of the Church," the authoritative theologians of the medieval and early modern period.</note> who agree on said proposition. From this proposition, I infer two

<margin>First corollary proposition</margin>

corollary propositions. The first is this: it is not simply because someone has sinned mortally in life and we are not certain that they repented that we must firmly judge them to be in hell. This is evident because the existence of a mortal sin alone does not constitute the entire condition from which eternal damnation follows. Rather, beyond the sin, one must also posit and be certain of final impenitence. And I,

<margin>Henry of Hesse.</margin>

who deny that it must be firmly believed that he is in hell, do not have to prove his repentance to you. Instead, you, who assert that he is damned, must provide certainty of his impenitence. In support of this, much is contributed by the saying of Henry of Hesse <note>Henry of Langenstein (1325–1397), a prominent German theologian and rector of the University of Vienna.</note>, who, in his exposition on the fourth chapter of the book of Genesis, says these formal words: "If the argument of certain people were effective—by which they persuade others that someone is damned, as they do concerning Solomon, because Scripture records his sin and makes no mention of his righteousness or repentance—then the first man [Adam] would be convicted of being damned for his sin just like the first angel [Lucifer]." For nowhere is mention made of Adam’s repentance, only of his sin. Similarly, in Judges 8, we read of the sin of Gideon and not of his repentance; and yet his salvation is well believed by the Doctors. You can also say that by this same argument, certain people were deceived and erroneously said that Moses was damned, because his sin was read of at the "waters of contradiction" <note>original: "aquis cõtradictionis"; the waters of Meribah, where Moses struck the rock in anger (Numbers 20).</note> and nothing was explicitly recorded of his repentance; and yet God said, "Joshua, Moses my servant is dead." The second

<margin>Second corollary proposition.</margin>

corollary proposition is this: no one can be certain that someone is damned to hell unless they have this through a special revelation from God, or from those to whom it is believed God has revealed it. The truth of this is evident from the preceding propositions, because no one can be certain of final repentance or impenitence except He who knows the secrets of the heart and those to whom He has wished to reveal them. Since no one is as certain of another's state as they are of their own—because "no one knows the things of a man except the spirit of the man which is in him," as is said in 2 Corinthians—and a man cannot even be certain of himself "whether he be worthy of hatred or love," as is said in Ecclesiastes 9, how much more can he not be certain of another unless he has a special revelation regarding it? From this main proposition and its corollaries, I infer for the purpose of my conclusion that even granted

<column-break/>

that Origen sinned mortally by erring in those errors, since we are uncertain of his final impenitence or repentance, it is an entirely rash judgment to assert that he is damned, and it must be rejected. Therefore, since we can be certain neither of his salvation nor of his damnation, it is nonetheless pious and very reasonable to believe, as I have said, that God saved a man of such and so great knowledge. Concerning him, Jerome says in his preface to the *Song of Songs*:

<margin>Jerome's words.</margin>

"While he surpassed all others in other things, in this he surpassed himself," and of him it may be verified: "The king has brought me into his chamber." Elsewhere, wishing to partially imitate Origen, whom Jerome says no one but the unskilled denies to be the

<margin>Origen. Justly called Adamantius.</margin>

master of the churches after the apostles; and elsewhere: "Origen sweated with such labor over the Scriptures that he justly received the name *Adamantius*" <note>Greek for "man of diamond" or "unbreakable," referring to Origen's tireless work ethic.</note>. After certain remarks, Jerome adds this: "Who can ever read as much as he wrote? And for this sweat, what reward did he receive? He is condemned by Bishop Demetrius; with the exception of the priests of Palestine, Arabia, Phoenicia, and Achaia, the city of Rome itself consents to his condemnation. It gathers a senate against him, not because of the novelty of his dogmas, not because of heresy (as rabid dogs now falsely pretend against him), but because they could not bear the glory of his eloquence and knowledge. Why I have written this, and dictated it quickly but not cautiously by the flicker of a poor lamp, you can understand if you consider the likes of Epicurus and Aristippus" <note>Hedonistic Greek philosophers often used as foils for Christian asceticism and intellectual labor.</note>. These are Jerome's words, verbatim. I ask the diligent reader to attend to these words one by one with their intellect, and through them understand for yourself the things I do not express. In the preface to the *Hebrew Questions*, speaking of the same Origen, Jerome says: "This one thing I say: I wish that along with the envy of his name, I also possessed his knowledge of the Scriptures," counting as nothing the "images and shadows of ghosts whose nature is to terrify children and chatter in dark corners."

<margin>Note.</margin>

I pass over what the same Jerome proclaims: that he trampled upon avarice; that he "castrated himself out of zeal for God, though not according to knowledge" <note>A reference to the famous story that Origen took Matthew 19:12 literally and emasculated himself to avoid temptation while teaching women.</note>; that he sweated days and nights in the explanation of Scripture—"those who clarify it shall have eternal life," as the Wise Man says; and as is written to Vigilantius, he explained the obscurities of the prophets and revealed the greatest mysteries of both the New and Old Testaments. I pass over the fact that he was not only the son of a martyr, but he himself was but a little way from the merit of martyrdom. For Eusebius says that even as a small boy he burned with such ardor for attaining martyrdom that he would voluntarily throw himself into dangers; and

<margin>Origen was desirous of attaining martyrdom.</margin>

later, in the time of the Decian persecution <note>The Roman persecution of Christians under Emperor Decius (c. 250 AD).</note>, he endured new crosses, new kinds of punishments, and tortures unheard of in all ages, so that—Eusebius says—he was vexed by "a thousand deaths," so that even the one death he longed for might not happen to him, the persecutor acting with the greatest zeal to ensure that neither death was granted nor the punishment ceased. See how little he lacked of the praise of martyrdom, which many of his disciples attained with him as their leader and encourager! I say again, he was surely but a little way from the praise of martyrdom; indeed, he earned an almost equal merit. For Augustine also says in his book *On the Good of Marriage*:

<margin>Augustine.</margin>

"The merit of martyrdom is not unequal in John [the Evangelist] who did not suffer [death], and in Peter who did suffer." Note these words of Augustine well. Thus, just as John—though he did not die by the sword—was nevertheless ready to endure martyrdom when he was cast into the cauldron of boiling oil, so too was Origen. Although he did not undergo death by martyrdom, he was nonetheless ready; indeed, he was most eager to undergo it, and he suffered so many tortures (as Eusebius says) that he underwent a thousand deaths for the sake of one. And this is what Bernard says in a sermon...

John the Evangelist suffered the martyrdom of will alone, of whom it was said (and to his brother): "You shall drink of my cup" <note>Matthew 20:23. Since John did not die a violent death, theologians argued he "drank the cup" through his willingness to suffer.</note>. So too of Origen, let us piously believe that the blood of martyrdom—poured out by him not so much outwardly upon the earth as inwardly over his heavenly soul, burning with zeal for God and charity—washed away every stain of heresy. Let us say with David <note>The traditional author of the Psalms.</note>: Blessed is Origen, who, though he once walked in the counsel of the erring, yet did not stand in the way of sinners through impenitence, and never sat in the seat of pestilence through obstinacy <note>A paraphrase of Psalm 1:1. The author argues Origen wasn't "stubborn" (pertinax) in error, which is the legal requirement for heresy.</note>; but his will was in the law of the Lord, and on His law he meditated day and night. Blessed is Origen, whose iniquities were forgiven through baptism and whose sins were covered through penance, and to whom the Lord did not impute sin on account of his martyrdom. Finally, such a great man—even if he occasionally erred in the mysteries of the faith out of a defect of intellect rather than any malice of will—let us believe that he was not abandoned by the Lord at his end. Let us believe instead that he was visited by God’s most clement mercy and illuminated regarding the secrets of the faith (if he erred in any), being recalled from an erroneous path to the way of salvation. This is what I meant in my brief response when I said elsewhere: since he is not found to have been obstinate, it is likely to believe that God saved him—that is, by visiting him with the visitation I mentioned, mercifully placing him in a state worthy of salvation, and illuminating him regarding the secrets of the faith in which he erred, calling him to a saving repentance for them. Whether this happened or not, no one can know with certainty unless it has been revealed from above. But that it happened this way, rather than not, seems more consistent and more reasonable to one considering the acts and life of Origen. For in doubtful matters, one should always reasonably adhere to the more favorable side. Let these things be said so that they might carry weight even if Origen’s penance were not established; however, we have most clearly shown above, from the testimony of the most blessed Jerome, that his penance is indeed established. Regarding the sixth article, I say that it does not seem believable that the Church ever determined that Origen's soul was damned to the underworld. I prove the truth of this proposition with two reasons. The first reason is this: concerning a matter where one side or the other cannot be determined with certainty except rashly, one should not believe a determination was made by the Church. But regarding this question—whether Origen is saved or damned—neither side can be determined except rashly (at least without a special revelation from God). Therefore, since such a revelation is not established, it should not be believed that a determination was made by the Church. The major premise is well-known; and to believe the opposite would be an insult to the Church—namely, to believe that it could judge something unadvisedly or rashly. because it does not pertain to the Church to damn or save the souls of men; that belongs only to Him who is the judge of the living and the dead. Therefore, if one reads in the Decretals "We damn Origen," it is ridiculous to interpret it as "We damn his soul with the damnation of hell." This is also evident from the way of speaking used by Gelasius himself, who says his other works "must be rejected along with their author." This word "reject" <note>original: "renuere"</note> can in no way signify what they intend; the Pope intends nothing else except that his works are not accepted as authoritative in the Church, nor is he himself received as an approved doctor whose sayings are to be believed. Even if the Pope had not only said "we reject" but also "we damn," it would not help their case. We are accustomed to speaking this way even now: "In this point, Scotus damns Thomas" or "Herveus damns Scotus" <note>References to famous medieval theologians (Duns Scotus, Thomas Aquinas, Herveus Natalis) who disagreed with each other's theories.</note>, and in all such speech we must understand the damnation of the doctrine, not the soul, according to the customary and proper mode of speaking.

I ask them: if this consequence is made—"Origen himself is damned, therefore his writings are damned"—how is the word <term>damned</term> <note>original: "ly damnatus"</note> used in the first part? If it means "not approved in his doctrine" and "not accepted as a teacher," then I have proven my point. But if it is understood as being damned in his soul to hell, then the logic fails. The damnation of a soul is entirely irrelevant to the damnation of a doctrine, because the former looks to the malice of the will, while the latter looks to a defect of the intellect. <meta>This page continues the defense of Origen, arguing that a person can be considered a holy figure in "Paradise" even if some of their writings are later rejected by the Church as erroneous.</meta>

-> OF THE QUESTIONS <-

He is in paradise, therefore his sayings are Catholic. For Papias is in paradise, as are Irenaeus, Victorinus, Cyprian, and many others whose sayings are nevertheless rejected as heretical in many matters which they are never read to have revoked. <margin>Confirmation.</margin> I confirm this from that saying to which the gloss on heretics refers in the chapter *Fraternitas* <note>A reference to Canon Law, specifically the Decretals of Gregory IX regarding the treatment of heretics.</note>, where it is said: if Celestine and Pelagius <note>Pelagius was the famous opponent of Augustine; Celestine here likely refers to one of his followers, Caelestius.</note> were condemned in the Synod of Ephesus, how could those chapters be received if their authors are condemned? It is certain, however, that in that synod Celestine and Pelagius were not condemned in themselves—that is, in their souls—but in their doctrine. This is both because, as stated above, the Church is neither accustomed nor able to condemn men [after death], and because we must understand the sentences according to what was first questioned and disputed. But in that synod, as is clear from the acts of the council, there was no question of whether the souls of Celestine and Pelagius were in paradise or hell, but whether their sayings and dogmas were Catholic or not Catholic. Therefore, we must understand the sentences as pertaining to the truth of their dogmas and the approval or rejection of the authors only insofar as they were dogmatizing in that way.

<margin>Third.</margin> Thirdly, it is foolish to say that the Church has determined Origen's soul to be damned, because the Church is not accustomed to damn people—that is, to decree by sentence that they are in hell—in the same way it is accustomed to canonize some. The reason why it is accustomed to the latter and not the former is that to decree that someone is saved, we must be certain that they died in a state of grace. Signs of this, though not absolutely certain, can be had not from what they did in life (for those are not sufficient, since as long as one is "on the way" <note>original: "in via" — a theological term for being alive and capable of change</note> there is always room for merit or demerit and for changing from one purpose to another), but we have signs after death, such as miracles or something similar. However, it is not easy to find such a sign by which we might be convinced of someone's damnation after death; indeed, without doubt, no other sign can be had except a special revelation regarding this. If such a revelation were to happen or had happened, then just as the Church testifies to miracles when it canonizes someone, it would also mention the special revelation if it were to damn someone, so as not to seem to have decreed such a thing rashly or ill-advisedly. Yet the Church never narrates such a thing concerning Origen. We must therefore understand Origen to be "damned" by the Church in the way he appears deserving of damnation based on what is narrated and testified about him. But nothing else is narrated about him except that he erred in the mysteries of faith; and from this error, an absolute damnation of Origen in himself does not follow, but only in his writings and doctrine, as is clear from the preceding points. Thus we should judge him damned by the Church and not otherwise. Furthermore, we know he was not stubborn <note>original: "pertinacem" — pertinacity or stubbornness was a legal requirement for a formal charge of heresy.</note> against the Church's determination in those opinions, because the councils in which those opinions were condemned took place long after Origen's death, as is clear from Greek and Latin histories. And we can in no way know if he was unrepentant of them; rather, we have proved above through Jerome that either he did not write them, or if he did, he repented.

<margin>Regarding the seventh article of St. Thomas.</margin> Regarding the seventh article, I say this proposition: that according to the doctrine of St. Thomas, not every member of the faithful is bound by the necessity of faith to believe that someone is in hell just because the Church has judged and sentenced them to be in hell. <margin>The necessity of pious faith.</margin> The truth of the proposition is deduced thus: as much faith is to be given to the Church in the damnation of someone as is given in the canonization of saints. But Thomas says in the last article of the *Quodlibetal Questions* IX that we are not bound by the necessity of faith to believe that saints canonized by the Church are in glory, but only by the "piety of faith" <note>original: "pietate fidei" — a belief held out of respect for the Church's judgment but not strictly required for salvation.</note>. Therefore, we are not necessarily bound to believe that those damned by the Church are in hell, but it is only to be believed piously. Thomas’s foundation is that we are only bound by the necessity of salvation to believe the Church in those things which pertain to the substance of faith. In those matters, the coming Spirit teaches her all truth. But whether the soul of this or that person is in hell or paradise pertains nothing to the substance of faith, except insofar as the honor we show to saints is a profession of faith by which we believe in the glory of the saints. Therefore, although we are not bound to this by necessity of salvation, it is nevertheless to be piously believed. From this proposition, I infer for the purpose of my conclusion that even if the Church had determined Origen was damned, we are still not bound by the necessity of Catholic faith to agree that it is so. From this it is clear that even if it were true what they bring against me—namely, that the Church had determined the opposite of my conclusion—it would still have been poorly judged by them that my conclusion "savored of heresy." Let these masters see, therefore, that it has not been rightly determined by them against my conclusion, even if the things they bring against me were true. Let them beware lest they institute new things to be believed by the faithful on their own authority and determine them to be "of the faith." Let them hear that prohibition of the Lord in the fourth chapter of Deuteronomy: *You shall not add to the word that I speak to you* <note>Deuteronomy 4:2.</note>. This saying condemns not only those who by their own authority add new beliefs to previous ones, but also those who reject Catholic truth as heretical.
