### QUESTION EIGHT: ON THE FREEDOM OF BELIEF.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'S' depicting a scholar or religious figure seated at a desk, surrounded by books and writing or studying in a library setting.</image-desc>
<margin>Proof of the conclusion for its first part.</margin>
Just as no one opines in a certain way precisely because they *will* to opine so, likewise no one believes a thing to be true precisely because they *will* to believe so. From this conclusion, I infer this corollary: It is not in a human's free power to believe an article of faith is true whenever it pleases them, and to believe it is not true whenever it pleases them. These masters have judged that this proposition with its corollary is erroneous and "savors of heresy." I, however, consider the principal conclusion to be not only Catholic but most true, and far truer than its opposite. And I say the same of the corollary when understood correctly; its sense, if taken according to my mind, is not to be taken otherwise than as follows from the principal conclusion of which it is the corollary. <margin>Aristotle.</margin> That the conclusion is not only Catholic but also most true is clear for its first part—which is that no one opines something to be so precisely because they will it—from Aristotle in the second book of *On the Soul* <note>original: "de anima"</note>, text comment 253, where Aristotle places a difference between imagination and opinion. This sentiment of Aristotle’s has not only not been rejected but has been unanimously approved by all our theologians. <margin>Proof for the second part.</margin> <margin>Augustine.</margin> The second part of the conclusion—which is that no one believes something to be precisely true because they will to believe it is true—is found in many places in Augustine, who often says that no one can believe by free choice (that is, by a mere command of the will without the persuasion of reason or a motive). My whole conclusion, which summarily holds this opinion—that when some doubtful proposition is proposed, the mere apprehension of the terms and the mere command of the will are not enough for someone to believe or disbelieve it—is held by <margin>Pierre d'Ailly.</margin> Pierre d'Ailly, Henry of Ghent, and Henry of Hesse. And when I was in Paris, almost the entire University of Paris held this, and many Catholic doctors hold it as so true that they regard their...

<margin>
Doctors by whom this conclusion is proved.
Declaration of the corollary proposition.
</margin>

...they hold the opposite to be impossible; indeed, I have not yet read any doctor who contradicts this opinion. However, the corollary proposition <note>A "corollary" is a secondary statement that follows naturally from one already proved.</note> should not be understood or accepted in any way other than with the restriction or determination placed in the preceding statement: namely, that it is not in the free power of the will to believe an article of faith to be true whenever it pleases, and to believe it to be false when it pleases. Thus, it is not precisely because it pleases the will that the intellect believes; such an understanding of one proposition through another linked to it is not unusual. Indeed, in Holy Scripture, the meaning of the letter is often taken from what precedes or follows it, which is exactly what should be done in our case because this statement "it is not in our power," etc.

<margin>
Something is said to be in free choice or the free power of the will in two ways.
First.
Second.
</margin>

I do not set this down as a statement in itself or as a separate conclusion, but as a corollary following from the preceding one. If it does not please them to accept the meaning of the present corollary from its principal statement to which it is annexed and linked, let them observe that something is said to be in "liberty" or in the "free power of the will" in two ways. In one way, because once an apprehension <note>The simple act of the mind grasping a concept without yet judging it true or false.</note> is placed in the intellect, no other act of the intellect is required, and it is within the imperative power of the will to perform that act. In this sense, it is denied in this conclusion that the act of believing is in the free power of man; nor is it necessary for every act of command, whether meritorious or demeritorious, to be in man's power in such a way for the purpose of believing. For to believe, the mere apprehension of the terms of an article of faith is not enough; rather, persuasion or some other probable reason is required, as has been alleged from Augustine. In the other way, something is said to be in the free power of the will because, once all other things required for that act are present, the will is able to bring that act into being or not, and the will is not necessitated to this act even when all other conditions are met. This is the way the act of believing an article of faith is in the free power of the will, and this is the meaning of the corollary proposition. From these statements, anyone with an intellect can recognize that those masters did not do well to say absolutely that the position is "erroneous and tastes of heresy." That the opinion of those doctors whom I follow—who say that the mere apprehension of terms along with the mere command of the will is not enough to cause the assent of faith—is probable and reasonable, can be seen not only by the authority of Augustine (who affirms this in many places, as I have said), but also by most effective reasons.

<margin>
Augustine.
He argues first.
</margin>

And first, it is argued thus: It is not in the free power of a man to form an opinion this way or that way whenever he wants; therefore, it is not in the free power of a man to believe this way or that way whenever he wants. The consequence is clear. Because if something is not present where it would most likely be expected to be present, then it is not present at all. <note>original: "a fortiori" logic—if the easier task (forming an opinion) is impossible, the harder task (firm belief) must also be.</note>

<margin>
Aristotle.
</margin>

But it is less to adhere to something while fearing the opposite might be true <note>A definition of "opinion."</note> than to adhere to it without such fear <note>A definition of "faith" or "certainty."</note>. Therefore, the premise is expressly stated by Aristotle in the second book of *On the Soul* <note>original: "ii. de anima"</note>, in the text of comment 153. This is clear through experience: for anyone experiences in themselves that when a doubtful proposition is offered, if it is truly doubtful, they are not inclined toward either side by assent until some new appearance comes upon them—either through syllogistic reason, or through intuitive knowledge, or by the testimony of many, or by the authority of the speaker, or something similar.

<margin>
Second.
</margin>

Second, it is argued thus: It is not in the free power of a man to make something appear true to his intellect or to make it appear not true; therefore, it is not in the power of a man to believe something to be true or not true. The consequence holds because it is a contradiction for someone to believe something and assent to it if it does not appear true to him. The premise is proved because for this or that to "appear" such to the intellect is for this or that to be "represented" to the intellect in such a way, and this cannot depend on the command of the will because

<column-break/>

<margin>
Confirmation.
</margin>

this precedes the act of the will. This is confirmed because something "appearing" as such to the intellect occurs because the object representing itself is such, and the evidence (or whatever it is that makes it credible or not credible) is such, and the intellect is such. But making the object be such, or the intellect be such, is not within the choice of the will; therefore, a thing appearing this way or that way to the intellect is not under the command of the will.

<margin>
Third.
</margin>

Third, it is argued thus: Whenever there is a power that is purely neutral and indifferent toward two opposite "second acts" <note>In scholastic philosophy, a "first act" is the capacity or habit, while a "second act" is the actual exercise of that capacity.</note>, it cannot move into one of them unless it is first determined by something that acts as a "first act," or stands in the place of a first act regarding one of those second acts. But the intellect is a power that is purely neutral and indifferent toward the specification of any of its second acts; therefore, it can be determined to no such specification unless something else arrives which is either a first act or stands in its place. Then, under this reasoning, I assume this consequence: a mere act of the will cannot function as a "first act" regarding the specification of the acts of the intellect; therefore, by the command of the will alone, the intellect cannot be determined to such a specification. The consequence is noted from the previously assumed reason, and the premise is clear from the common opinion of all doctors consenting in this: that although the act of the intellect depends on the will regarding its *exercise* <note>The decision to think about a topic.</note>, it does not depend on it regarding its *specification* <note>The content or truth-value of the thought.</note>. Having accepted these points, I argue for the proposition: the act which is "assenting" and the act which is "dissenting" are acts having opposite specific reasons; therefore, the intellect cannot be determined to assent or non-assent by the command of the will. Therefore, when someone believes through the intellect that an article of faith is true, or does not believe it, it is not precisely because he wants or does not want to believe, but from something else determining the intellect, which of itself is neutral toward the specification of such an act.

<margin>
Fourth.
Eight reasons why we should believe the Gospel are assigned by our theologians.
</margin>

Fourth, it is argued thus: a person is not determined to believe something precisely by an act of the will if, when asked why he believed it, he does not assign the act of the will as the reason. But when someone is asked why he believes the Christian faith rather than the faith of the Muslims <note>original: "maumethensium" (followers of Muhammad).</note>, he will not assign precisely an act of the will. Therefore, he was not inclined to believe by a precise act of the will. That a mere act of the will is not assigned is clear from experience and from the sayings of our theologians, by whom those eight reasons are commonly alleged for why we should believe the Gospel: 1. prophetic pronunciation; 2. the harmony of the Scriptures; 3. the authority of the writers; 4. the reasonableness of the contents; 5. the unreasonableness of the contents [of individual errors]; 6. the unreasonableness of each individual error; 7. the stability of the Church; 8. the clarity of miracles.

<margin>
Albert.
</margin>

Fifth, it is argued thus: Whenever two people are determined to believe opposites, and each is determined precisely because he *wants* to be so determined—indifferent to any judgment or persuasion of reason—it cannot be said that one is moved more reasonably than the other. But given two people, one of whom wants to believe "A" is true and the other does not, we can say that this one or that one wills more reasonably or more irrationally. Therefore, they are not determined to will this way or that precisely because they want to. The major premise of this reason is noted because, as Albertus Magnus says in the third book of *On the Soul*, when the will acts precisely because it *wants* to act so, it resembles a tyrant; in its action, the reason for the act is not sought, because its acting is not according to reason but according to whim. The minor premise is manifest, for daily we say that the Muslims or the Jews act irrationally in this...

-> ### OF QUESTIONS 38 <-

acting on what they do not believe, and that we act reasonably because we believe. If the precise reason why I believed and another did not was simply that I willed it and he did not, then both would be a tyrannical act of the will. In neither would there appear a greater or lesser degree of reasonableness; rather, in neither would there be reason at all, but merely the power and tyrannical command of the will. From what has been said in this argument, the meaning of the brief words I spoke in my response regarding the "tyrannical act of the will" will be clear to these masters of the intellect. Many other arguments could be brought forward for this opinion. However, it is not my purpose here to treat these matters or to discuss the proposed questions at length, but only to show that the determination of my conclusions is not heretical. And although these points suffice for the defense of my conclusion, I wish to say this as well: there was also a certain doctor whose condemnation on this article—to confess for my part—I have never yet read, who held simply that the act of believing was not free. This was held assertively by Robert Holcot, <margin>Praise of Robert Holcot.</margin> a most subtle doctor of the Order of Preachers <note>The Dominicans</note>, in his first book on the *Sentences*. And when it is argued that it would follow that the act of believing or not believing would not be meritorious or demeritorious, he says this objection is worthless and frivolous. He argues that an act is not meritorious because it is free, but because it conforms to some law promising a reward for that act to the one performing it or to another. Consequently, he says the act of believing is not meritorious because it is free, but because it conforms to divine law, which promises such a reward—namely, eternal life—to anyone who believes. He adds that God could change this law and decree that whoever happens to fall over a cornerstone tomorrow by accident would be saved; then that fall would be meritorious of eternal life. This is because our acts are not meritorious because they are free, but because they are accepted by God for eternal life. God can accept natural acts just as He can voluntary acts; thus He is seen to have accepted the death of the Holy Innocents <note>The children killed by Herod in the Gospel of Matthew</note> for eternal life, in whom there was no use of free choice. Nor does God act unreasonably in doing so, because His will is a sufficient reason for all things that He decrees or ordains. Therefore, Holcot concludes that if we take "to believe" to mean adhering with firm assent to those things whose truth is not evident to us <margin>To believe is said in two ways.</margin> except by the testimony of others—according to the way Augustine defines it in his homily on John, saying "What is faith if not to believe what you do not see?"—then such an act of believing is not in the free power of man. If, however, "to believe" is taken to mean assenting to whatever is revealed by God and testified by miracles, and willing to live and work according to them, then because this "believing" includes both the act of the intellect and the will, he grants that it is free. <margin>Augustine.</margin> Following this mode, Augustine, defining it in his homily on John, says "to believe in God is to love by believing, to go into Him by believing, to adhere to Him by believing, and to be incorporated into His members." It is of this kind of belief that it is said: "Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness." Of the first kind, however, it is said "the demons believe and tremble." The first <insert>type of believing in the second definition</insert> is meritorious; the second <insert>type in the first definition</insert> is not. And when it is said that faith is only in those who are willing, Holcot says that <margin>Holcot.</margin> this must be understood as "formed faith" <note>Faith animated by love (charity)</note> according to this second mode, which is faith operating through love, but not concerning faith accepted in the first mode; for he maintains that a person can be compelled to believe by the necessity of seeing miracles. I do not believe this opinion to be true. Yet, after his inquiry, the same doctor, re-examining several of his opinions, says that although the will is necessitated 

<column-break/>

to believe when evidence stands in the way of reason, yet because he was himself the cause of such necessity, it is therefore imputed to him as a sin. He says he was the cause because he neglected to consider and persevere diligently and to discuss those things which created the false evidence for him. If he had done so, it would not have appeared that way to the intellect, but otherwise. Therefore, he concludes that when someone believes wrongly or disbelieves, his primary sin is one of negligence. This is the opinion of Robert Holcot on the freedom of belief, which never appeared good or probable to me. Let these fathers consider whether they should anathematize <note>Formally curse or excommunicate</note> this doctor along with Durandus, Henry, and the other heretics from the Church.

### NINTIETH QUESTION ON ACCIDENTS 
### IN THE SACRAMENT.

-> Whoever says that an accident cannot exist unless it <-
-> exists within a subject could still hold to the <-
-> sacrament of the Eucharist even while holding that <-
-> the substance of bread does not remain. <-

<margin>Note</margin>
These masters did not say that this conclusion was heretical or "smacked of heresy," but only that it was erroneous. If they had brought forward any reasons for this opinion of theirs, I could either believe them or answer them; but they have not brought forward any reasons that I have seen, either in the condemnation of this or of other conclusions. For the declaration of the conclusion, I say that by this conclusion I do not intend to say categorically and absolutely that an "accident" <note><term>Accident</term>: A philosophical term for properties like color, smell, or shape that usually need a "substance" (like bread) to exist in.</note> cannot be without a subject, or that in fact it is in a subject; indeed, I firmly hold with the Church that the sacramental accidents are in fact without a subject. But I say that he who would say that accidents cannot be without a subject, and who held with Thomas <margin>Thomas.</margin> <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> the real distinction of the "existence" of the bread from its "essence," could say that it is not repugnant to divine omnipotence to preserve the *existence* of the bread without its *essence*, just as God preserves both substantial and accidental acts without His power. Consequently, in that "being" of the bread, the accidents could be supported even though the *substance* of the bread does not remain. The body of Christ could have a real presence in relation to these accidents just as it now does to the accidents which are supported by no subject. And whatever the case may be regarding the fact of the Eucharist as instituted by Christ and believed by the Church—in which it is harmoniously held that nothing of the bread remains, so much so that its reproduction would be a creation—nevertheless, holding the aforementioned opinion of Thomas concerning the real distinction between essence and existence, and taking the sacrament of the Eucharist in an extended sense to what is or *can be* (as it is taken in my conclusion, which is a "modal" <margin>Note</margin> proposition), it is not erroneous. Indeed, it is erroneous to say that there could not be some sacred form of the Eucharist in which the accidents were in a subject. Nor do I know by what logic these masters saw fit to condemn a "possible" proposition because of the falsity of a "factual" one made of the same terms. I wonder that they do not know the "fallacy of the consequent": arguing from a specific case to a general one while destroying the general, as if someone were to say, "No man is in the house, therefore no man *can* be in the house." For they argue similarly in the condemnation of this proposition: "In no sacrament of the Eucharist which actually exists or was actually instituted by Christ are the accidents in a subject; therefore, in no sacrament which is or *can be* or *could be* instituted by Christ can accidents exist without a subject."

# DEFENSE V O

From what has been said, it is clear how wrongly the present conclusion regarding possibility was condemned as erroneous by those fathers who ought to remember that there have even been among Catholic doctors those <margin>The opinion of certain theologians which Peter of la Palud recounts.</margin> who held that, in fact, the accidents <note>the outward, sensible qualities of a thing, like color or taste</note> in the sacrament of the altar <note>the Eucharist</note> subsist within the existence and subsistence of that which remains. For there is one path of theologians—as Peter of la Palud <note>original: "Petrus de palude," a prominent 14th-century Dominican theologian and Bishop</note> reports in his fourth book on the *Sentences*—who say that just as a quality remains here naturally because its immediate subject (which is quantity) remains, even though its remote subject (which is the substance) is removed, and thus the quality itself does not subsist on its own but inheres in the quantity; so also quantity is indeed deprived of its remote subject (which is the substantial essence), but it retains its own proper and proximate subject, which is "substantial being" <note>original: "esse sube" [substantiale]</note>. By means of this "being," it exists in the substance, because it is possible for this "being" to remain even if the essence does not remain. Indeed, they say it is necessary for it to remain, considering the way in which "being" is defined here.

And they say it is clear that this is possible: for although essence is prior to "being" (which would suggest "being" could be separated from the essence more easily), if we consider it from another side, essence relates to "being" as potentiality relates to act, or as matter relates to form. Since an act depends less on potentiality than vice versa, it seems more feasible for "being" to exist without essence than the other way around. But God, in the incarnation of the Word, created the essence of humanity without its own independent "being" (as is said by many doctors); therefore, He can much more easily make the "substantial being" of the bread exist here without its essence. Just as in the Incarnation the essence is assumed and remains while its own "being" does not, so here in the conversion <note>Transubstantiation</note> the essence can be changed and not remain, while the "being" is not changed and remains.

Secondly, they show that this is not only possible but necessary, because nothing created can be converted into the uncreated; but one created thing can be converted into another when they share in matter and genus. Otherwise, it would not happen—just as an accident is not converted into a substance, nor into an accident of a different category according to common opinion. Now, the essence of the bread shares in matter and genus with the essence of the body of Christ; thus, one can be converted into the other even by nature if the body were mortal. But the "being" of the bread does not share in matter or genus with the substantial "being" of Christ’s body, since the latter is uncreated and divine, belonging to the Divine Person <note>original: "suppositi diuini"</note>, as there is only one act of substantial existence in Christ. Therefore, it is impossible for the "being" of the bread to be converted, and it is necessary for it to remain.

<margin>The author’s opinion.</margin> I am of the opinion that it is not necessary for it to remain: both because if it cannot be converted, it can nevertheless be annihilated or corrupted by yielding into the potentiality of matter. Thus, just as humanity could be assumed without its "being" being assumed (remaining instead in the potentiality of matter), so also the essence can be converted without the "being" being converted (having been reduced to potentiality)—though, to tell the truth, these "reductions" are easier to say than to understand. Likewise, although the "being" of the bread cannot be converted into uncreated "being," it can nevertheless be converted into a created essence; for things that share in matter are mutually transmutable, even if they share only in "remote" matter rather than "proximate" matter (just as an element can be converted into a living thing and vice versa). The "being" of the bread and the essence of Christ’s body share in "prime matter," which is the remote potentiality of both, even if they do not share in proximate matter—since matter is pure potentiality, while essence is potentiality with act. Indeed, if that previous reasoning were valid, it would conclude that of all the food Christ ate before His passion, only the essence was converted into Him and not the "being," but that it remained or was otherwise corrupted through conversion, because the substantial "being" of Christ was uncreated before the resurrection just as after. Likewise, some say that just as water (which by "ordained power" <note>God's established laws of nature</note> cannot be converted into the blood

<column-break/>

of Christ) is first converted into wine and afterward the whole is converted into blood; so if "being," by "absolute power" <note>God's total, limitless power</note>, cannot be converted into something of Christ, it is first converted by nature into its own essence, passing into it like a form that yields to the potentiality of matter, and afterward that whole essence is converted into the [other] essence. Thus, it is not necessary for the "being" to remain. However, just as it seems erroneous to me to say that it is *necessary* for the "being" to remain, it is no less erroneous to say that it *cannot* remain.

### TENTH QUESTION CONCERNING THE WORDS OF CONSECRATION.

->Those words "This is [my] body," which are spoken in the consecration, are held materially and not significantly.<-

<margin>To be noted.</margin>
These masters said that this conclusion is scandalous and against the common opinion of the holy doctors, and that the opinion of the glossator <note>the author of the standard legal/theological commentary</note> on this point is not to be held. I, however, say that their determination is scandalous and against the common opinion of many doctors, and that the glossator’s opinion ought to be held rather than theirs. That this is so is clearly evident once the meaning of the conclusion is understood.

First, it must be noted that I do not intend for these words to have been accepted "materially" <note>referring to the words as a quote or objects of speech</note> when they were uttered by Christ, but only when they are uttered by the Gospel priest who is consecrating. Therefore, I said in the conclusion: "the words which are spoken in the consecration," that is, those which are now uttered by those consecrating. It is certain that the priest, in consecrating, recites the aforementioned words of Christ, so that the prayer uttered by such a priest stands for the prayer of Christ taken "significantly" <note>meaning the words refer to their actual definition</note>. Such an opinion is not only not erroneous or scandalous, but rather the opposite view of the aforementioned masters seems to be contrary to the form of consecration in which the priest speaks those words "recitatively."

For the priest, in consecrating, recites that Christ said to the apostles: "Take and eat," etc. Now, the priest who is consecrating is neither speaking to the apostles, nor is he saying "take" to them, except recitatively. For he alone receives the sacrament; nor does he say "take and eat" to those standing by. Similarly, when he says "This is my body," that which is recited by the priest is that prayer "This is my body" taken materially as a stand-in for a similar prayer composed of similar sounds uttered significantly by Christ. This is also clear through those words spoken before or after the consecration of the blood: namely, "which shall be shed for you and for many," etc. For these would be false if they were taken significantly, because the blood of Christ will not be shed in that manner anymore; therefore, those words are taken only recitatively. What is recited but a voice uttered by another, for which the voice of the reciter himself stands? And therefore, this voice, being a recitation of another’s voice, is to be taken materially. Furthermore, if these words were taken significantly and not recitatively, they would denote that the blood of Christ is shed for others and not for the one consecrating, since he says "which is shed for *you* and for many." It ought rather to be said, "which is shed for *us*," etc. I do not say this because I believe the opposite opinion cannot be defended, but so that it may be clear that my conclusion is not only Catholic but even more probable than its opposite. From this, it is clear that the present conclusion is not scandalous but probable, and the opinion of the solemn glossator (regarding the *De Consecratione*, distinction 2, chapter "Timore") is not to be rejected but approved, just as it has never been rejected by the Church up to these times.

<summary>The author argues that the "act of being" (esse) of the bread can theoretically remain after the essence is changed during the Eucharist. He further defends his view that a priest recites the words of consecration as a historical quote (materially) rather than speaking them as a direct, personal statement (significantly).</summary>

## The miracles of Christ are the most certain argument of his divinity, not by reason of the thing performed, but by reason of the manner of performing it.

<image-desc>A decorative drop cap 'Q' containing a scene with a seated figure, possibly a scholar or religious figure, within a classical architectural setting.</image-desc>
In explaining this conclusion,
I said that because there is 
a firm consensus among theologians
that the miracles which Christ
performed could be done by a 
mere human through the power of God.
For Christ says in John 14:
"Truly I say to you, he who believes
in me will do the works I do,
and greater than these will he do." <note>original: "Amen dico vobis qui credit in me opera quę ego facio ipse faciet & maiora horum faciet."</note> 
Therefore, it is also unanimously concluded by these same theologians that the basis from which we can conclude Christ was God is not the deed itself, but the manner of doing it. For he acted in the same way as those who act by their own power and not by power received from elsewhere—which is proper to God alone: to act independently and not by another’s power. This manner of acting cannot be communicated to a creature. Because Christ performed many things in such a way—not by praying or asking, but by ordering and commanding as one having authority—it is clear that he worked as one who is himself God, and not merely as a man existing in the power of God. After seeing this explanation of mine, they said the conclusion could be drawn toward a bad meaning because it is contained among "magical" matters. Given that my explanation is true, I marvel at their judgment so much that I cannot marvel more. First, let them tell me whether my words, to anyone interpreting them correctly and according to the usual way of speaking, could have any meaning other than the one I stated. For what could be clearer or more expressive than these words: "The miracles of Christ are the most certain argument of his divinity, not by reason of the thing performed, but by reason of the manner of performing it." Second, let them tell me whether this is the sentence of a just judge: "This conclusion, though it is true and Catholic, is nevertheless to be condemned because it can be drawn toward a bad meaning." If so, then the statement "Christ cast out demons" must be condemned because the Jews drew it toward a bad meaning, saying that he cast out those demons by Beelzebub, the prince of demons. And this must be condemned: "The Father is greater than I," because Arius <note>a 4th-century priest whose teachings—Arianism—denied that Jesus was of the same substance as God the Father</note> imagined from it an inequality of the Son to the Father. And this must be condemned: "He knew her not until she brought forth her firstborn son," because Helvidius <note>a 4th-century writer who argued that Mary had other children after Jesus</note> formed a heresy from it against the perpetual virginity of Mary. And this must be condemned: "Of that day the Son does not know," because from it some wish the Father to know more than the Son knows. Why say more? Almost all Evangelical propositions would have to be condemned, because they could be drawn toward a bad meaning by heretics. When my proposition is set down in the same terms in which it is placed by many Catholic doctors, must we therefore condemn it even though it is true, simply because some might draw it to a bad meaning? Truly, if any interpret it poorly, it is their sense that is to be condemned, not mine, which is holy and Catholic. Third, let them tell me what this bad meaning is that could be made; let them say it if they know. Surely it is not even possible to say or think a bad meaning from that proposition, even if one wished to. For if there were one, it would perhaps be that someone might suspect I wished to say that the same miracles Christ performed—in terms of the deed done—

<column-break/>

could be performed through magic. But this cannot be suspected of my conclusion, because immediately before it, I placed another conclusion: that the miracles of Christ could not be performed by way of magic or the Cabala <note term="Cabala">A form of Jewish mysticism. The author is defending himself against charges that his interest in these esoteric traditions was heretical or "magical."</note>. I do not see any other bad meaning that could be found or devised; let them say it themselves if they can. Fourth, let them tell me what kind of logical consequence this is, and whether it holds in matter or form: "It is among the magical [conclusions], therefore it is to be condemned." Truly, this is a similar form of arguing to that which they used when they were trying to condemn the magical conclusions from the start; for they argued thus: "These conclusions are intricate and not understood by us, therefore they are to be condemned." O wondrous and unheard-of form of refutation! Now let those be silent who say judgment cannot be passed on unknown things, since it has now been decreed that those things are most especially to be condemned which are most especially unknown. But let us return to the point. They say: "It is among the magical ones, therefore it is to be condemned." Let them tell me whether magical conclusions are good or bad. If bad, they have still judged poorly. For Christ suggested in the parable of the tares <note>original: "zizaniis," referring to the weeds sown among wheat</note> not only that the wheat should not be rejected because of the mixed-in tares, but rather, to save the wheat, he suggested that the tares should not be rooted out before the harvest. If they are good, why should they have condemned a good conclusion placed among other good things, if they themselves are good men?

<image-desc>A decorative drop cap 'Q' showing two figures in discussion or study.</image-desc>

And so that they may understand my mind more clearly, I will briefly explain the foundation of both the

It is therefore to be noted that just as "reason" refers to the discursive knowledge proper to humans—which reason would indeed be improperly said to be in God—so similarly Dionysius says that "intellecting" <note>the act of understanding</note> is the knowledge appropriated to an angel, caused by the angel and the angelic intellect, informing it and changing it in such a way. He says such "intellecting" is not in God. Nor, by taking "intellecting" in this way, can the conclusion be drawn to a bad meaning; for Dionysius does not therefore deny that there is knowledge of all things in God. But this [God's knowledge] is further removed from "intellection" properly taken in the aforesaid manner than a human is from an angel. However, when it is said "God understands," one takes "understands" generally for all knowledge. Briefly, let them know this: that by this conclusion I do not intend to deny the most perfect knowledge of all things to God, just as I do not deny any simple perfection; indeed, I do not even intend to deny that God "understands" if "understanding" is taken in the common sense.

A P O L O G I A

...from what has been said, it is clear how poorly the previous conclusion regarding what is possible was condemned as erroneous by those fathers who ought to remember that there have even been Catholic doctors <note>The term "doctors" here refers to "Doctors of the Church" or high-level academic theologians.</note> who held that, in fact, the **accidents** <term>Accidents: In Aristotelian philosophy, these are the sensory qualities of a thing (like the color, smell, or taste of bread) that do not belong to its essential nature.</term> in the sacrament of the altar are subjected in the existence of the remaining substance. For there is one path of theologians, as 
<margin>The opinion of certain theologians which Peter of Palude recounts.</margin>
Peter of Palude <note>Petrus de Palude (c. 1275–1342) was a prominent Dominican theologian and Archbishop.</note> relates in book four, distinction twelve, question three, who say that just as a quality remains here naturally because its immediate subject (which is **quantity**) remains, even if its remote subject (which is **substance**) is removed—and thus the quality itself does not subsist on its own but inheres in the quantity—so too the quality lacks its remote subject (the essence of the substance), but it possesses its own proper and proximate subject, which is the **being** <term>The author distinguishes between "essentia" (what a thing is) and "esse" (the act of existing).</term> of the substance. Through this "being," it exists in the substance, because it is possible for that "being" to remain even if the essence does not remain. Indeed, they say it is necessary for it to remain, considering the way in which it ceases to be here. They say it is clear that this is possible because, although essence is prior to being (since the prior can be separated from the posterior), and essence could more easily be separated from being than the reverse, yet considering from another side that essence relates to being as **potency** relates to **act**, and as matter to form—and since the act depends less on the potency than vice versa—it seems more doable for being to exist without essence than vice versa. But God, in the incarnation of the Word, made the essence of humanity exist without its own personal being (as is said by many doctors); therefore, He can much more easily make the being of the substance of bread exist here without the essence. Thus, just as there the essence is assumed and remains while its own being does not, so here the essence can be converted and not remain, while the being is not converted and will remain. Secondly, they show that not only is this possible, but necessary, because nothing created can be converted into the uncreated; but one created thing can be converted into another when they share in matter and genus. Otherwise, it would not be possible, just as an accident is not converted into a substance, nor into an accident of another category, according to common opinion. Now, the essence of the bread agrees with the essence of the body of Christ in matter and genus; whence one can be converted into the other even by nature (if the body were mortal). But the **being** of the bread does not share in matter or genus with the substantial **being** of the body of Christ, since that being is uncreated and divine, belonging to the divine person. Since in Christ there is only one being of actual substantial existence, it is therefore impossible for the being of the bread to be converted, and it is necessary for it to remain.

<margin>The author's opinion.</margin>
I am of the opinion that it is not necessary for it to remain: both because if it cannot be converted, it can nonetheless be annihilated, or it can be corrupted by yielding into the potentiality of matter. Thus, just as humanity could be assumed without its own being being assumed (instead remaining in the potentiality of matter), so too can the essence be converted without the being being converted (instead being reduced into the potentiality of the essence), though to tell the truth, these "reductions" are easier to say than to understand. Likewise, although the being of the bread cannot be converted into uncreated being, it can nevertheless be converted into a created essence, because things that share in matter are mutually transmutable—granted they may not share in "proximate" matter, but only in "remote" matter, just as an element can be converted into a living being and vice versa. Now, the being of the bread and the essence of Christ's body agree in **prime matter** <term>Prime Matter: The most basic, formless reality that underlies all physical things.</term>, which is the remote potentiality of both, even if they do not agree in proximate matter (since matter is pure potency, while essence is potency with act). Indeed, if that reasoning were valid, it would conclude that of all the food Christ ate before his passion, only the essence was converted into him and not the being, but the being remained or was otherwise corrupted through conversion, because the substantial being of Christ was uncreated before the resurrection just as after. Likewise, some say that just as water (which by **ordered power** <term>Ordered power: God's power acting through the established laws of nature and the Church.</term> cannot be converted into the blood

<column-break/>

of Christ) is first converted into wine and afterwards the whole is converted into blood, so if the being cannot by **absolute power** <term>Absolute power: God's raw ability to do anything that is not a logical contradiction, regardless of the laws of nature.</term> be converted into something of Christ, it is first by nature converted into its own essence, passing into it like a form that yields into the potentiality of matter; and after that, the whole essence is converted into the essence [of Christ], and thus it is not necessary for the being to remain. But just as it seems erroneous to me to say that it is *necessary* for the being to remain, it is no less erroneous to say that it *cannot* remain.

## TENTH QUESTION REGARDING THE WORDS OF CONSECRATION.

->Those words "This is my body," which are spoken in the consecration, are held materially and not significatively.<-

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial D depicting a floral or foliate design.</image-desc>
These masters said that this conclusion is scandalous and contrary to the common opinion of the holy doctors, and that the opinion of the **Glossator** <note>The "Glossator" refers to the author of the *Glossa Ordinaria*, the standard medieval commentary on Canon Law or the Bible.</note> is not held in this matter. I, however, say that their determination is scandalous and contrary to the common opinion of many doctors, and that the opinion of the Glossator is to be held rather than theirs. That this is so will be clearly evident once the meaning of the conclusion is understood.

<margin>Note this.</margin>
It must first be noted, therefore, that I do not intend for these words to have been taken **materially** <term>Materially: Using words as a quote or as sounds themselves, rather than the speaker using them to make a personal statement.</term> when they were uttered by Christ, but only when they are uttered by a priest of the Gospel while consecrating. And therefore I said in the conclusion: "the words which are spoken in the consecration"—that is, those which are now uttered by those consecrating. For it is certain that the priest in consecrating recites the aforementioned words of Christ, so that the prayer uttered by such a priest stands for the prayer of Christ taken **significatively** <term>Significatively: Using words to actually mean what they say in the present moment (e.g., the priest literally claiming the bread is his own body).</term>. Such an opinion is not only not erroneous or scandalous, but rather the opinion opposed to this sense seems to be contrary to the form of consecration in which the priest speaks those words **recitatively** <note>original: "recitative"</note>. For the consecrating priest recites that Christ said, etc., [speaking] only recitatively: "Take and eat," etc. The consecrating priest neither speaks to the apostles nor says to them "Take," etc., except recitatively. For he alone receives the sacrament; nor does he say "Take and eat" etc., by speaking to those standing by. Similarly, when he says "This is my body," that which is recited by the priest is that prayer "This is my body" taken **materially** as standing for a similar prayer composed of similar words uttered significatively by Christ. This is also evident through those words which are said before or after the consecration of the blood: namely, "which will be shed for you and for many," etc. For these would be false if they were taken significatively, because the blood of Christ will not be shed again; therefore those words are taken only recitatively. Now, what is recited but a voice uttered by another, for which the voice of the one reciting stands? And for that reason, this voice, being a recitation of another's voice, must be taken materially. Also, if it were taken not recitatively but significatively, those words would denote that the blood of Christ is shed for others and *not* for the one consecrating. For he says: "which will be shed for *you* and for many." It ought rather to be said, "which [is shed] for *us*," etc. I do not say these things because I believe the opposite opinion cannot also be defended, but so that it may be clear that my conclusion is not only Catholic, but even more probable than its opposite. From which it is clear that the present conclusion is not scandalous but probable, and the opinion of the solemn Glossator regarding Consecration (distinction 2, chapter "Timorem") is not to be rejected in this matter but approved, just as it has never been rejected by the Church up to these times.

He also argues that a priest recites the words of consecration as a quote from Christ rather than speaking them as his own personal claim.</summary>

->OF THE QUESTIONS<-

# ELEVENTH QUESTION
# CONCERNING THE MIRACLES OF CHRIST.

**The miracles of Christ are a most certain argument for his divinity, not by reason of the thing performed, but by reason of the manner of performing.**

<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'Q' depicting a seated figure in clerical or scholarly robes working at a desk, enclosed within a circular frame and surrounded by foliate decoration.</image-desc>
In explaining this conclusion, I stated that there is a firm consensus among theologians that the miracles Christ performed could have been done by a mere human through the power of God. For Christ says in John 14: <note>John 14:12</note> "Truly, I say to you, he who believes in me will do the works that I do, and greater works than these will he do." <note>original: "Amen dico vobis qui credit in me opera quæ ego facio ipse faciet & maiora horum faciet"</note> Therefore, it is also unanimously concluded by those same theologians that the basis upon which we can conclude Christ was God is not the deed itself, but the *manner* of doing it. He acted as those act who work by their own power and not by power received from elsewhere—which is proper to God alone, to act independently and not by another’s strength. This mode of acting cannot be communicated to a creature. In this way, Christ did many things without praying—that is, without asking—but by commanding and ordering as one having authority. It is clear that he worked as God himself, and not merely as a man existing in the power of God. 

After seeing this explanation of mine, they <note>Referring to the papal commission investigating his work.</note> said the conclusion could be drawn toward a "bad sense" because it is contained among "magical" matters, even granting that the explanation itself is true. I am so astonished by this judgment of theirs that I could not be more amazed. First, let them tell me whether my words, if interpreted by anyone correctly and according to the common use of speech, could have any other meaning than the one I stated? What could be clearer or more expressive than these words: *The miracles of Christ are a most certain argument for his divinity, not by reason of the thing performed, but by reason of the manner of performing*? Second, let them tell me whether this is the sentence of a just judge: that a conclusion, though true and Catholic, must be condemned because it *could* be drawn toward a bad sense? If so, then the statement "Christ cast out demons" must be condemned, because the Jews drew it toward a bad sense by saying he cast out demons by Beelzebub, the prince of demons. And that statement "The Father is greater than I" <note>John 14:28</note> must be condemned because Arius <note>Arius (c. 250–336) was a priest whose teachings—denying that Jesus was of the same substance as God the Father—led to the Arian controversy.</note> used it to imagine an inequality between the Son and the Father. And the statement "He did not know her until she brought forth her firstborn son" <note>Matthew 1:25</note> must be condemned because Helvidius <note>A 4th-century writer who argued against the perpetual virginity of Mary.</note> based his heresy against the perpetual virginity of Mary upon it. And the statement "That day even the Son does not know" <note>Mark 13:32</note> must be condemned because some want to use it to claim the Father knows more than the Son knows. 

Why say more? Almost every Gospel proposition would have to be condemned, because they could be drawn toward a bad sense by heretics. Why, then, should we condemn my proposition, which is set down in the same terms used by many Catholic doctors, simply because some might pull it toward a bad sense, even though it is true? Surely, if any interpret it poorly, it is their sense that is more deserving of condemnation, not mine, which is holy and Catholic. Third, let them tell me what this "bad sense" could even be; let them say if they know. Certainly, it is impossible for anyone even to think of a bad sense from that proposition. If there were one, perhaps it would be that someone might suspect I meant to say that the miracles Christ did could be done through magic as far as the deed itself is concerned. But this cannot be suspected of my conclusion, because immediately before it, I placed another conclusion: *that the miracles of Christ could not be performed by way of magic or Kabbalah.* <term>Kabbalah: A tradition of Jewish mysticism. The author was famously interested in combining Christian theology with Kabbalistic and Hermetic ideas.</term> I see no other bad sense that could be found or devised; let them say so if they can. Fourth, let them tell me what kind of counter-argument this is: "It was among the magical ones, therefore it must be condemned." Truly, the form of their argument is like this: "These conclusions are intricate and not understood by us, therefore they must be condemned." O wondrous and unheard-of form of rebuttal! Let those who say judgment cannot be passed on the unknown be silent, since it has now been decreed that those things which are most unknown are most of all to be condemned. 

But let us return to the point. They say, "It is among the magical ones, therefore it is condemned." Let them tell me whether magical conclusions are good or bad. If they are bad, then they have still judged poorly. For Christ suggested in the parable of the weeds <note>Matthew 13:24-30; the "parable of the zizania."</note> that not only should the wheat not be rejected because of the mixed-in weeds, but indeed, to save the wheat, he suggested the weeds should not be uprooted before the harvest. If the conclusions are good, why should they have condemned a good conclusion placed among other good ones, if they themselves are good men?

# TWELFTH QUESTION
# WHETHER GOD UNDERSTANDS.

**It is more improperly said of God that he is "intelligent" or "intellect" than of an angel that it is a "rational soul."**

<margin>
For just as man is called rational, so an angel is called intelligence.
</margin>
<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'Q' depicting a seated figure reading or gesturing, set within a circular frame with decorative corner elements.</image-desc>
In explaining this conclusion, I said that it relied on the way Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a highly influential 5th-6th century Christian philosopher who emphasized that God is beyond all human descriptions and categories (apophatic theology).</note> speaks, who often says of God that He is neither intellect nor an object of the intellect. Similarly, I said my words were to be taken in the same way the words of Dionysius were taken. They said the conclusion was false and could be transferred to a heretical sense, and that my explanation did not satisfy them. I am not a little amazed by their determination. I wonder, if they are wise men, how they can say a conclusion is false which is not mine, but the conclusion of Dionysius himself. To make my mind understood more clearly, I will briefly explain the foundation of the conclusion and of Dionysius's own speech. 

It should be noted that just as "reason" denotes the discursive knowledge <term>Discursive knowledge: Step-by-step logical reasoning, which was considered a lower, human form of knowing compared to the direct intuition of angels.</term> proper to humans—which "reason" would be improperly said to be in God—so Dionysius similarly says that "to understand" is the knowledge appropriate to an angel, caused by the angel and the angelic intellect, informing and changing the intellect in such a way. He says that this kind of "understanding" is not in God. Taking "to understand" in this way, the conclusion cannot be drawn to a bad sense, because Dionysius does not deny that God has knowledge of all things. But God's knowledge is further from "understanding" (taken in the angelic sense) than a human is from an angel. When it is said "God understands," it takes "to understand" generally for all knowledge. Briefly, let them know this: by this conclusion, I do not intend to deny that God has the most perfect knowledge of all things, just as I do not deny any perfection whatsoever; indeed, I do not intend to deny that God "understands" if "understanding" is taken in the common sense.

<margin>Objection.</margin>
But I deny that "understanding" which, according to Dionysius's way of speaking, refers to the knowledge appropriate to an angel, just as...

->APOLOGIA<-

...and reason implies a type of knowledge appropriated to man, just as reason is also said to be in God, though only in an improper <note>Here meaning metaphorical or non-literal.</note> sense. For they say that you claim it is more "improper" to say God is an "intellect" than to say an angel is a "rational soul." They argue this is false because no one would ever say an angel is a "soul," while it is very frequently said that God is an "intellect"; therefore, they claim my phrasing is the more improper one. I marvel at the learning and extensive reading of these fathers in sacred matters, who say <margin>Augustine.</margin> that it is never said of an angel, either properly or improperly, that it is "rational." But let them read Augustine in his book *On Music*, in his book *On True Religion*, in his *Acts Against Fortunatus*, and in his book *On Catechizing the Unlearned*. For in all these places, I remember that angels were called by the name of "souls" by Augustine—and yet I have not seen everything, nor can I remember every single place where <margin>Note.</margin> I may have read in the sacred doctors that angels were called by this name. Indeed, there is nothing that is not worthy of great attention when it is read. However, when I said that it is more "improperly" said of God that He is "intellect," I intended nothing other than that angelic knowledge (which appropriates the "intellectual" knowledge of God to itself) is further removed from the infinite knowledge of God (which knows all things through His essence) than it is from the "reasoning" knowledge appropriated to the rational soul or to man. If, however, it is inferred from this present conclusion that God is "improperly" said to understand—just as a comparative term implies a positive one—let that consequence be accepted only in this sense: God is not called an "intellect" according to the strict or "appropriated" definition of this word "to understand," etc., but according to the common, less strict way, as was clear from the manner of speaking used by Dionysius <note>Referring to Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, an influential Christian mystic and philosopher.</note>.

## QUESTION XIII. ON THE HIDDEN INTELLIGENCE OF THE soul.
### The soul understands nothing actually and distinctly except itself.

<margin>Augustine. Henry.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative initial letter H depicting a scholar or monk seated at a desk with books and writing instruments.</image-desc>
In declaring this, I said that I was speaking of that "hidden understanding" <note>original: "intelligere abdito"</note> which Augustine mentioned in his book *On the Trinity*, and Henry <note>Henry of Ghent, a 13th-century theologian.</note> in his *Quodlibets*. These masters said that my conclusion did not match the meaning of the doctors I was citing in my response; I do not know how they can say this if they have actually seen those doctors. And because this matter of "hidden understanding" is subtle and profound, I do not wish to explain it more extensively here. Since they do not condemn the conclusion on other grounds, I wish to say only two things. First, that I do not intend to universally deny that the soul, in whatever state, has any distinct cognition of things other than itself; for I concede that the soul of Christ understands other things actually and distinctly, and likewise the souls of the blessed through revelations or infused "species" <note>In medieval philosophy, "species" are the mental forms or images through which we perceive objects.</note>. Second, I say that I am speaking of that "hidden understanding" which occurs without a "phantasm" <note>A mental image derived from the senses.</note> or the assistance of the senses or the imagination—and not just any such understanding, but a "direct and permanent" hidden understanding. Regarding this, I placed a conclusion next to this one stating: "the soul always understands itself, and by understanding itself, it in some way understands all beings." And so, in all my conclusions, there is always a certain hidden "concatenation" <note>A logical chain or linking together.</note> which perhaps they do not notice. But returning to the point, I say that the soul through such

<column-break/>

direct and permanent hidden understanding understands nothing actually and distinctly except itself. From this it is clear that the present conclusion, understood in this way, should not have been condemned without distinction as erroneous, even if in some sense it were not true. For in that way, many propositions of both philosophers and theologians, and even of Holy Scripture, would be condemned. Such is that passage from Habakkuk <margin>Habakkuk. Matthew.</margin> <note>original: "Abachuh"</note> in the first chapter: "Your eyes are pure, that you may not see evil, and you cannot look at iniquity." <note>Habakkuk 1:13</note> And similarly that passage in Matthew 25 <margin>Matthew 25.</margin> concerning the foolish virgins: "I do not know you." <note>Matthew 25:12</note> For although the vision of God or His knowledge is unique and most simple, and although the stated propositions seem to universally deny such vision or knowledge even of God with respect to evil (because of the negation placed before the verb "to see" or "to know"), they are nevertheless explained by the doctors specifically as referring to God’s "approving" vision or knowledge, and the negation in them is not taken to deny every mode of God's vision or knowledge. Because it <margin>Psalm.</margin> is also true what the Psalmist says: "My sins are not hidden from you." <note>Psalm 69:5</note> If, therefore, many such statements are distinguished by expositors and doctors and drawn toward a true meaning rather than being condemned, I do not know what this [thesis of mine] has done to deserve being so simply condemned, even after it had been explained and declared to the judges in the manner mentioned above. Let these things be dictated by me now with a "hurrying pen" <note>original: "properanti stilo"</note>; I will write at another time with greater leisure and care so that as there are more things, they may perhaps be better. This work itself, such as it is, was "labored over for twenty nights" <note>original: "viginti... noctibus elucubratum"</note>; in publishing it, speed was more desirable to me than diligence. For it was necessary to have something for my friends to throw like a "morsel to Cerberus" <note>In mythology, Cerberus is the three-headed dog guarding the underworld; a "sop to Cerberus" is a bribe or distraction given to a troublesome person.</note> at my barking enemies, and thus to immediately confront the disease of unjust infamy that was coming upon me. Whatever we have written and will write in the <margin>Note.</margin> future is said with this perpetual preface: that only that shall be held as certain and holy which the Supreme Pontiff and all those whose judgment he approves shall decree to be certain and holy. And would that he had already decreed something concerning these opinions of ours which have been called into doubt, according to his wisdom and authority! It would not then have been rash for me to take up this work to defend what he had condemned, nor superfluous to defend what he had approved. While, therefore, we cannot yet use the sentence of so great a judge, let us write these things so that my detractors do not have anything "sinister" they can say about the questions I proposed for dispute, nor the unlearned and simple have anything they might suspect. For it can happen that when someone less educated touches upon them, he reads this proposition: "Christ did not descend to hell truly and as to a real presence as the common way posits," and being offended by that word "not truly," he might believe the sense of the proposition is that the article of faith concerning the descent of Christ is not true. Likewise, when he reads: "infinite punishment is not owed to a mortal sin of a finite time," he might doubt me in that heresy that holds the punishment of hell is not eternal. And when he understands that I think well of the "salvation of Origen," <note>Origen was a 3rd-century theologian whose orthodoxy was debated for centuries; Pico argued he might have been saved.</note> he might suspect that I love not so much the life, morals, teaching, and penance of Origen as the dogmas of Origen that were believed [to be heretical]. It is the same with many other propositions which perhaps have on their "first front" <note>At first glance.</note> something that offends "holy rusticity"—that is, ears that are as pious as they are unlearned. For that reason, just as we have written these things to be read so that no one thinks ill of us or of the orthodox dogma of our holy religion, so I would not want these "raw" and unexplained propositions (so to speak) to be read by our people unless they have first reached these [explanations]; for they might conjecture many things from them that are as foreign to the Catholic faith as they are to our own mind—especially the more dull-witted and those [ignorant] of doctrines...

# OF THE QUESTIONS

<margin>Note.</margin>
...of more remote things are rude and unaccustomed. I therefore pray, beseech, and entreat friends and enemies: the pious and the impious: the learned and the unlearned, by the mercy <note>original: "per viscera," literally "by the bowels," a common biblical idiom for deep compassion</note> of Jesus Christ our Lord: by the wondrous mystery of His descent into the underworld: by the eternal fire of the damned which is not extinguished—a fire especially owed to heretics and the enemies of the most holy Roman Church: by the sacrament of the true and mystical body and blood: by the omnipotence of God: by the reverence that must be shown to the images of His Son and his co-heirs: let them read what we now write without malice and without envy. Let them not read the earlier parts—that is, the propositions themselves—unexplained and uninterpreted. For when we proposed them among the learned to be debated, we did not publish them to be read everywhere by everyone.
<margin>Averroes Alexander.</margin>
For even in those propositions, there are many of the impious dogmas of the ancient philosophers, Averroes and Alexander <note>Averroes (Ibn Rushd) and Alexander of Aphrodisias were famous commentators on Aristotle whose views, particularly regarding the mortality of the individual soul, were often seen as heretical.</note> and many

<column-break/>

others. Even if we have always professed, asserted, and preached these publicly and privately to be no less alien to true and right philosophy than they are to the Faith, we nevertheless undertook to dispute them as a scholastic exercise, following the custom of the Academies <note>Refers to the "Academic" style of debate where one argues for various positions to find the truth, without necessarily believing them personally.</note> in a private gathering among a few learned men. Truly, anyone who reads the booklet of propositions to be debated will see from my own stated opinion—which I distinguish from the opinions of others—that I did not propose them as my own or as true opinions, but as views believed by those philosophers. Thus, one might suspect that even if they are called the dogmas and intentions of others, they might still seem to me to be true and probable. Therefore, let him who hates me not read them because they are ours. Let those who love me not read them for this reason: because from those things which are mine, they might think many things which are not truly ours.

These bishops and professors reported to the same predecessor that certain conclusions seemed to them suspect and, as they claimed, "smacking of heresy." Nevertheless, you had published those conclusions only for the sake of scholastic debate and under the correction of the Apostolic See; and you finally professed that you would hold them to be such as they were

<column-break/>

# JOHN PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA ON BEING AND THE ONE TO ANGELO POLIZIANO.

## PREFACE.

<margin>The very sharp intellect of Lorenzo.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative initial 'N' containing a small illustration of a scholar or monk seated in a landscape.</image-desc>
You were telling me in recent days what Lorenzo de' Medici <note>Lorenzo "the Magnificent" de' Medici, the de facto ruler of Florence and a great patron of the arts and philosophy.</note> had discussed with you regarding Being and the One, when he disputed against Aristotle—whose *Ethics* you are publicly lecturing on this year—relying on the arguments of the Platonists. <margin>The harmony of Aristotle and Plato. He dedicates this work to Angelo Poliziano.</margin>
I said what came to mind then, confirming what you had replied to Lorenzo during the dispute rather than bringing forth anything new. This was when, by chance, Domenico Benivieni <note>A Florentine theologian and close friend of both Pico and Savonarola.</note> had also joined us, a man most dear to us both for his learning and integrity. <margin>Manilius.</margin>

### Chapter One: It has been asserted by the Platonists that the One precedes Being.

<margin>The One, Being, the True, the Good.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative initial 'A' featuring a male figure standing within the crossbar of the letter.</image-desc>
Aristotle says in many places that these things correspond to each other and are of equal scope: namely, the One and Being; likewise the True and the Good. But more on these later. The Academy <note>Referring to the Neoplatonists, the followers of Plato's later tradition.</note> resists this, for it pleases them that the One is prior to Being; and when they say "prior," they want it to be understood as simpler and more universal. For this reason, they say that God (whose simplicity is supreme) is indeed the One, but is not Being. Likewise, they claim that the first raw matter—that which is formless—is included within the boundaries of the One, even though it is (as they wish) outside the limits of Being. Then they bring forward the point that 

<column-break/>

it is not the same thing which is opposed to the One as that which is opposed to Being: for nothing is opposed to Being, but "multitude" is opposed to the One. Therefore, by the same law by which opposites are judged, these two—Being and the One—are not considered to be interchangeable nor to correspond to one another.

### Chapter Two: That Plato nowhere suggested the One is superior to Being, but rather that they are equal.

<image-desc>Decorative initial 'H' with a small human figure appearing inside the upper half of the letter.</image-desc>
They rely on these arguments; before we dissolve them, it will not be out of place to bring into the open what is found expressed by Plato on this question. I find Plato disputing about Being and the One in two places: namely, in the *Parmenides* and the *Sophist*. The Academics contend that in both places, the One is placed by Plato above Being. I, however, will say first regarding the *Parmenides* that nothing is affirmed in that entire dialogue; and even if it were affirmed to the highest degree, nothing is found clearly enough from which Plato...
