# BOOK ONE.

...unless we certainly ascribe a dogma <note>a settled opinion or tenet</note> of this kind to it, the book is surely not to be counted among the dogmatic ones; for it is entirely nothing other than a certain <term>dialectical exercise</term> <note>original: "dialectica exercitatio"; Pico argues that Plato's "Parmenides" was meant as a logical workout rather than a statement of divine truth</note>. So far are the very words of the dialogue from contradicting our opinion that no interpretations exist that are more arbitrary and violent than those brought forward by men who wished to interpret Plato’s *Parmenides* in another sense. But let us set aside all interpreters. Let us look at the series of the dialogue itself: how it begins, where it tends, what it promises, and what it carries out. Furthermore, it holds itself thus: when Socrates had turned toward the <term>Ideas</term> <note>Plato's theory of perfect forms</note> from that dispute over whether all things are one or whether the things that exist are many, and when he had asked much about these from Parmenides, Parmenides responds that he is pleased by that impulse and the inclination of his mind toward defining the most exalted things. "However," he says, "collect yourself and, while you are young, exercise yourself more diligently in that faculty which seems useless to many and is called <term>idle talk</term> <note>original: "nugacitas siue garrulitas"</note> or wordiness by them; otherwise, truth will flee you." Moreover, it is admitted by all—and the following things make it manifest—that by these words he signifies <term>dialectics</term> <note>the art of investigating the truth of opinions; logic</note>. After these things, when Socrates asks Parmenides in this way:
<margin>The words of Parmenides.</margin> "What is the mode of this exercise,
<margin>The utility of logic.</margin> Parmenides?" he responds first that it is the one he had heard from Zeno; then, teaching more particularly about this matter, he warns that he should look around with sharp-sighted skill not only at what follows if a certain thing *is*, but also what follows if it *is not*. Then he should see what follows for that thing which we suppose to be or not to be, both in respect to itself and in respect to others; and likewise, how others relate to themselves and to it. And when he said more to this effect, then Socrates said: "You bring a difficult task, and I do not entirely understand you. But why do you yourself not propose something and treat it in that way which you approve, so that my understanding of this matter may become clearer?"
<margin>From this we gather it is unseemly for an old man to discuss and debate.</margin> Parmenides responds that this is laborious for him as an old man. Finally, Zeno says that this should be done by Parmenides when he is in a gathering of a few people; otherwise, he says, it is hardly becoming for such things to be treated in a crowd of many by an old man, since few know that such treatment and wandering <note>original: "euagationem"; a technical term for the exhaustive logical paths taken in the dialogue</note> are necessary for attaining the truth. These words of Zeno itself give full credit to what we have said: that what Parmenides is about to treat is of such a kind (if we believe Zeno) that it should not be treated openly in a gathering of many by an old man. But if, as those others wish, he is dealing with divine orders and the first principle of all things, what treatment could be more fitting for an old man or less to be blushed at? But it is beyond all controversy—unless we wish to deceive ourselves—that the business Parmenides was about to engage in was dialectical, and Socrates had asked for something else from him. Moreover, Zeno had judged that to be the duty of a youth rather than an old man. Even if we do not believe these testimonies, let us run through the dialogue itself. We will see that nowhere is anything affirmed. But everywhere it is only asked: "If this is so, what follows?" and "What follows if it is not?" On this basis, the <term>Academics</term> <note>philosophers of the later Platonic school who embraced skepticism</note> snatched the opportunity for their opinion about Being and the One: because in the first position he exercises himself with this problem to see, if all things are one, what might follow. And he responds that it will happen that the "one" which we suppose to exist would be indivisible, would be infinite, would be nowhere; and while he enumerates many things of that kind, he asserts this among the rest: it would happen that the "one" would not be <term>Being</term> <note>original: "ens"</note>. But pay attention: even if this were not a dialectical exercise, but a dogma being handed down about Being and the One, how much these things would then differ! Namely, to assert that the "one" is above Being, and to assert that it would happen that if all things are "one," that "one" would not be Being. And enough about Parmenides. For indeed, in the *Sophist*, he speaks rather in this sense: that

<column-break/>

the One and Being are equal, rather than the One being superior to Being.
<margin>On Being and the One.</margin> For where he might explain that [the One is superior], I do not find. He signifies the former in many ways, as through these words: "For considering it thus, you confess it is necessary that he who says 'something' says 'some one thing'"; and soon after, "He, however, who does not say 'something,' it is necessary that he says 'not even one thing,' that is, nothing." These are his words. Therefore, for him, "not one" and "nothing" are equal—indeed, the same—and likewise "one" and "something" are equal. After these things, he likewise proves that it cannot be said that "non-being" is "one." And thus he concludes: Being does not happen to non-being; therefore, the One does not happen to non-being. He speaks, however, of the "one" which he had said above was equal to that which is "something." Therefore, he seems to take it as granted that the One is Being. But let it be; let us grant that Plato affirmed this, which he certainly nowhere affirmed. Come, let us examine in what sense it could truly be said, first laying the foundations of the Aristotelian opinion itself in this manner.

### Chapter Three: By the testimony of Parmenides, Dionysius, and Simplicius, it is proved that Being and the One are equal to one another.

<margin>The double mode of Being.</margin> **I** say this: "Being," about which it is doubted whether it is equal to the One, can be taken in a double way. The first is when we say "Being," we understand all that which is outside of nothing. This is the way Aristotle used it when he made Being equal to the One. Nor did he use the word thus without reason; for as it is truly said: we ought to think like the few, but speak like the many. For we think and hold opinions for ourselves; we speak to others—that is, to the multitude—and therefore we speak so that we may be understood. But the common people and everyone from the middle ground take "Being" in such a way that everything is called "Being" which does not lack "to be" and which cannot truly be called "nothing." But even those who are held to be the wisest among these very people who think otherwise, we find to have used this word in this way. For Parmenides the Pytha-
<margin>Parmenides the Pythagorean. Simplicius.</margin> gorean said that the "One" is that which is; he understood God. If we believe Simplicius and many others who wish to defend Parmenides against those who slander him—as if he had said all things are one—they respond with one voice that it was never believed by Parmenides that there is no division, multitude, or plurality in things. He himself openly confesses this elsewhere in his poems; but when he said "that which is, is one," it was judged by him that the name of "Being" truly suits that thing which truly is, and that which truly is, is only "one"—which one is God. Wherefore, if we believe Parmenides and his defenders (even the Platonists), the One cannot be above Being unless it is above God; and so far is Parmenides from denying that God is Being, that he concedes the true name of "Being" to God alone. And thus the solution to the first argument of the Platonists occurs to us in passing. But also
<margin>Dionysius the Areopagite.</margin> Dionysius the Areopagite <note>a Christian theologian and philosopher of the late 5th to early 6th century</note>—whom those who dispute against us make a supporter of their opinion—will not deny that it was truly said by God to Moses, "I am who I am," which we read in Greek as: *ego eimi ho on* <note>original: "εγω εἰμι ὁ ὤν"</note>, that is, "I am Being." Indeed, since they themselves say that "nothing" or "non-being" is opposed to Being just as "multitude" is opposed to the "One," they will necessarily concede that that which is not Being is nothing or non-being. Just as that which is not "one" is "many" or "multitude." Wherefore, if they keep the same law of speech, they must confess either that God is nothing (which the ears themselves dread) or that He is Being. In this way, when "Being" is accepted, we establish that first axiom and universal pronouncement: that concerning any thing, it is necessarily said to either be or not to be; but of nothing can both be said or thought at the same time. Since, therefore, outside of all things there is nothing except Nothing itself, if "Being" accepted in this way is only...

--- Page 124 ---
<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's systematic reconciliation of Plato and Aristotle. Having previously argued that "the One" and "Being" are coextensive (meaning they cover the same scope), he now addresses the Neoplatonic claim that God is "above Being." Pico uses Scholastic linguistic distinctions to show that this is a matter of terminology rather than a fundamental disagreement between the two great philosophers.</meta>

# EXPOSITIONS ON BEING AND THE ONE

...it must undoubtedly encompass all things without excluding itself. For this reason, the **One** cannot encompass more things than **Being**, unless it encompasses nothingness—which Plato denies in the *Sophist*. When he says that "non-being" or "nothing" cannot be called "one," it follows that it does not encompass fewer things (as they claim); therefore, **Being** and the **One** are equal.

-> Chapter four, in which it is declared how something can be said to be superior to Being. <-

<margin>What an abstract and concrete name are.</margin>
We have explained one of these ways in which we said **Being** could be understood; they use this way when they most truly affirm (as they are rightly able to do) that nothing is more common than "Being." It remains for us to explain the other way, according to which it will nonetheless be manifest and truly said that there is something situated above the excellence of **Being**. Among names, some are <term>concrete</term> <note>refers to a thing that possesses a quality (e.g., "a white thing")</note> and others are <term>abstract</term> <note>refers to the quality itself in its pure form (e.g., "whiteness")</note>. Concrete names are "hot," "shining," "white," "man." Abstract names are "heat," "light," "whiteness," "humanity." Moreover, the power and difference between them is this: that which is called "abstract" signifies that which is such *of itself* and not from another. The "concrete," on the other hand, signifies that which is not such of itself, but is so by the benefit of another. Thus, a "shining thing" shines by "light." A "white thing" is white by "whiteness," and a "man" is a man by "humanity." Since, in truth, nothing participates in itself, nor can the same condition belong to the same thing both *of itself* and by the *participation* of another, it follows that what is called "abstract" 

<margin>The rule of denomination. That things are denied to belong to something in two ways.</margin>
cannot be named after the "concrete." For this reason, it is not properly said that "whiteness is white" or "blackness is black"; indeed, anyone who would utter such things would be ridiculous. This is not because whiteness is black or heat is cold, but because whiteness is so far from blackness, and heat so far from coldness, that whatever things are "white" are white by that whiteness, and whatever things are "hot" are hot by participation in this heat. Therefore, we deny that certain things belong to a certain subject either because that subject does not have them (as when we say "black is not white") or because it possesses them in a more excellent manner and a more perfect way than we signify by such a manner of speaking. For example, when we deny that "whiteness is white," it is not because it is black, but because it is not only not black because it is white (which is the same as saying it has whiteness), but because it is whiteness itself. 

<margin>Being is concrete; 'To Be' is abstract.</margin>
Let us come to our subject: **Being** <note>original: "ens"</note> has the appearance of a concrete name. For "Being" is the same as saying "that which is." The abstract form of this word appears to be "To Be" <note>original: "esse," referring to the pure act of existence</note>, so that "Being" is said of that which participates in "To Be" itself. Just as "shining" is said of that which participates in light, and "seeing" of that in which "to see" itself resides. 

<margin>How God is said not to be "a being" but above all being, as Dionysius and Damascene wished.</margin>
If we look to this exact signification of **Being**, we shall deny that "To Be" itself is "a being"—not only because it is not a thing and is nothing, but because it is from God, so that He is "To Be" itself, which is of itself and from itself, and by whose participation all things exist. Just as we would not only deny that something is "hot" because it lacks heat, but also because it is "Heat itself." Such a one is God, who is the fullness of all "To Be," who alone is of Himself, and from whom alone—with no intervening medium—all things proceeded into existence. By this reasoning, therefore, we shall truly say that God is not "a being" <note>ens</note>, but "above Being" <note>super ens</note>, and that there is something superior to Being—namely, God Himself. Since the name of "the One" is given to Him, it follows that we confess the "One" to be above "Being." However, we then call God "One" not so much stating *what* He is as *how* He is all things that He is, and how other things are from Him. For <term>Dionysius</term> <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a highly influential Christian mystic/philosopher</note> says God is called "One" because He is all things uniquely; again, He is called "One" because He is the principle of all things that exist, just as **Unity** is the principle of all numbers. Wherefore, if (as the Academicians wish) Plato affirms in the first position of the *Parmenides* that the One is superior to Being, that One will be nothing other than God. They themselves admit this by common consent, asserting that the first principle of all things is treated there by Plato. But someone will say that at least in this 

<column-break/>

part Aristotle will be at odds with Plato. For Aristotle never accepts "Being" in such a way that it is beneath "the One" and does not include God, which Plato does. Those who say this have not read Aristotle, for he himself does this, and far more clearly than Plato. For in the sixth book of the *First Philosophy* <note>Aristotle's *Metaphysics*</note>, he says that "Being" is divided into "Being per se" <note>being in itself</note> and "Being per accidens" <note>being by chance/attribute</note>. Since "Being per se" is divided into ten genera <note>the Categories</note>, 

<margin>As in "On Being and Essence," also on the nature of genus. Thomas explained this.</margin>
there is no doubt among good interpreters that God is not contained under this "Being," for He is neither "Being per accidens" nor is He contained under any of the ten genera into which "Being per se" is divided. Likewise, that division is common among the Peripatetics <note>Aristotelians</note> by which "Being" is said to be divided into substance and accident; when it is so, we accept "Being" in such a way that God is above Being and is not under Being, just as **Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> teaches in the first book of his commentaries on the *Sentences* <note>a standard medieval theological textbook by Peter Lombard</note>. I will add this also: that certain Platonists boast unjustly, as if they held a mystery unknown to Aristotle when they say that there are two proper names for God, namely "the One" and "the Good," and thus the Good and the One are before Being. Just as we have shown that it is not hidden from the Peripatetics how God can be understood as "above Being," we can also show that Aristotle gave these two names, the "Good" and the "One," to God in the first place. For in the twelfth book of the *First Philosophy*, after he disputed concerning the whole of Being and the separate intellects, he asks finally (as if having turned toward investigating the properties of God alone after all other things) whether, besides the "Good" which is in the universe of beings like an army, there is some "Separate Good" like the leader of this army. And he determines that this is so: that God is the Good. Consequently, in the same chapter, he proves the **Unity** of God, citing—after powerful arguments—that verse of **Homer**: *“Let there be one ruler, one king.”* <note>original Greek: εἷς κοίρανος ἔστω, εἷς βασιλεύς</note> Where then is Aristotle false? Where is he discordant with Plato? Where is he profane? Where does he think of God less honorably than is fitting?

-> Chapter five, in which he declares for what reason the Peripatetics ascribe many things to God which the Platonists deny of Him, and teaches by what pact we ascend through four stages to the darkness in which God dwells. <-

<margin>A twofold imperfection in things. Sensory knowledge. An example of that which is not perfect in its own kind.</margin>
Let us now resolve the arguments of the Platonists by which they contend that the One is superior to Being—not only in the way we agree with, but absolutely against Aristotle. Although the first argument (by which it was said God is the One but not a Being) has been sufficiently resolved from the previous points, it would still be worth the effort to digress further to show why many things are truly affirmed and truly denied of God, not only by different people (such as Platonists and Peripatetics) but often by the same author. God is all things, and He is all things most eminently and most perfectly. This would not be so unless He enclosed within Himself the perfections of all things in such a way as to reject from Himself whatever pertains to imperfection in things. Moreover, we can define whatever has the character of the imperfect in these existing things under two headings. One is when something is in a thing that is less perfect *within the genus* of that thing. The other is when it is perfect in its own genus, but is therefore not *simply* perfect because it possesses the perfection of only one genus, and there are many genera outside it, honored with their own perfections, which are not included in it. An example of the first is **sensory knowledge**; it is imperfect not only because it is only knowledge and not appetite, but because it is also an imperfect *kind* of knowledge. This is both because it requires a brute and corporeal organ, and because it only reaches the surfaces of things and does not penetrate to the innermost part (that is, to the substance). Likewise, **human knowledge**, which is called "rational," is imperfect...

<summary>Pico explains that "Being" can be seen as a concrete participation in existence, whereas God is the pure "Act of Being" (Esse) and thus "above Being." He argues that Aristotle and Plato are in complete agreement on the transcendence and unity of God when terms are properly defined.</summary>

# BOOK ONE

<margin>Human intellectual knowledge. Life in every kind of body.</margin>
...is [imperfect] knowledge: because it is wandering, uncertain, changeable, and laborious. Add to this the intellectual knowledge of divine matters—those which theologians call <term>angels</term> <note>Pico identifies the philosophical "intelligences" with the biblical "angels."</note>—and even that is imperfect knowledge. This is at least because it seeks outside itself what it does not fully possess within: namely, the light of truth which it needs and by which it is perfected. Now, consider life. That life which is in plants, or rather, which is in every body, is not only imperfect because it is merely "life" and not "knowledge," but because it is not pure life; instead, it is a kind of "living-force" derived from the soul into the body, always flowing and always mixed with death.

<margin>Note. The life of angels. How human knowledge is imperfect. How angelic knowledge is imperfect. When we begin to die rather than live.</margin>
In short, it should be called death rather than life. For we begin—in case you did not know—to die at the very moment we begin to live, and death is extended along with life. We only first cease to die when we are released from "this body of death" <note>A reference to St. Paul in Romans 7:24: "Who will rescue me from this body of death?"</note> through the death of the flesh. But even the life of angels is not perfect; unless a perpetually life-giving ray of divine light cherished it, it would all slip away into nothingness. The same reasoning applies to everything else. Therefore, when you conceive of God as "knowing" or God as "living," you must first take care that the life and knowledge ascribed to Him be understood as free from all these defects. But this is not enough. There remains another imperfection, for which this is an example: Conceive of a most perfect life—one that is entirely life and pure life, having nothing mortal and nothing of death mixed in, needing nothing outside itself to remain stable and permanent. Conceive also of a knowledge by which all things are known simultaneously and most perfectly. Add to this that the "knower" knows all these things in himself, so that he does not seek truth outside himself to know it, but is himself that very Truth. Yet, even if both of these were most perfect in their kind (such that they could not exist outside of God), if they are accepted as distinct from one another, they are unworthy of God. For God is all-encompassing and infinite perfection; but He is not all-encompassing and infinite simply because He contains all particular and infinite perfections within Himself. For if that were so, He would neither be "most simple" <note>In Scholastic theology, "simplicity" means God is not composed of parts (like "life" + "knowledge"). God is a single, unified essence.</note>, nor would the things within Him be infinite; rather, He would be one infinite thing composed of many parts that are infinite in number but limited in their specific perfection—which is a profane thing to say or think about God.

<margin>God is understood by abstracting everything that is imperfect from Him. How God is "Being Itself" according to Augustine.</margin>
But truly, if life—which is indeed the most perfect life—is *only* life and not knowledge; and likewise, if you apply "will" but it is *only* will and not life or knowledge; and if other similar attributes are placed in God, it will clearly follow that the divine life is of a limited perfection. This is because it would have the perfection belonging to life but not that belonging to knowledge or desire. Let us, therefore, take away from "life" not only that which makes it an *imperfect* life, but also that which makes it *only* life; and do the same for knowledge and the other names by which we call God. Then, what remains from all of them will necessarily be that which we wish to understand as God: namely, the One, most perfect, infinite, and most simple. And since life is a kind of "being," and wisdom is likewise a kind of "being," and justice is the same—certainly, if you remove the condition of particularity and boundaries from these, what remains will not be "this" or "that" being, but **Being Itself** <note>original: "ipsum ens"</note>; simple being, universal being—not universal in the sense of a logical category, but in the sense of perfection. Similarly, wisdom is a kind of "good" because it is "this" good (wisdom) and not "that" good (justice). Take away, as Augustine says, "this" and take away "that"—meaning, take away this particular limitation by which wisdom is a good that is specifically wisdom and not the good that is justice (and likewise that justice has the goodness of justice but not that of wisdom). Then, as if in a <term>riddle</term> <note>original: "enigma." Referring to 1 Corinthians 13:12: "For now we see through a glass, darkly [in an enigma]..."</note>,

<column-break/>

<margin>To see the face of God in a riddle. How God is "The One Itself."</margin>
you will see the face of God: that is, every good, Goodness itself, simply Good, the Good of every good. Just as life is a kind of being, so it is a kind of "one"; for it is one perfection, and wisdom is likewise one perfection. Cast away the particularity, and there remains not "this" or "that" one, but **The One Itself** <note>original: "ipsum vnum"</note> and simply The One. Therefore, since God is He who (as we said from the beginning) is "all things" once all imperfection has been removed: surely, when you have cast off from all things both the imperfection belonging to their class and the particularity of their kind, that which remains is God. God, therefore, is Being itself, the One itself, the Good itself, and similarly Truth itself. We have now advanced two steps, ascending toward the "darkness" where God dwells, purging from the divine names every stain arising from the imperfection of the things they signify.

<margin>God is above everything that can be said or conceived by us. Psalm.</margin>
There still remain two steps: one of which argues the deficiency of names, and the other accuses the weakness of our understanding. These names—"being," "truth," "one," "good"—speak of something concrete and, as it were, "participated" <note>In Platonic thought, things "participate" in a quality (like beauty) but are not the Quality itself. Pico argues God is so transcendent He is even above these abstract concepts.</note>. Therefore, we say again that God is **above being**, **above truth**, **above the one**, and **above the good**. For His "being" is Existence itself, Truth itself, Unity itself, and Goodness itself. Yet, we are still in the light; but "God made darkness His hiding place" <note>Psalm 18:11.</note>. Therefore, we have not yet reached God as long as we still understand and comprehend what we say about Him. For we are said to be in the light, and we speak and think things that are smaller than God to the extent that our understanding is smaller than His infinite divinity. Descending, therefore, to the fourth step, let us enter the "light of ignorance"; and, blinded by the darkness of divine splendor, let us cry out with the prophet: "I have fainted in your courts, O Lord." Saying this one last thing about God: that He exists intelligibly and ineffably above everything most perfect that we can either speak of or conceive. Thus, we place God most eminently above even that unity, goodness, and truth which we had conceived, and above Being itself.

<margin>Dionysius.</margin>
Looking toward this, <term>Dionysius the Areopagite</term> <note>A 5th-century Christian Neoplatonist whose "Mystical Theology" argued that God is best known through negation (saying what He is NOT).</note>, after everything he had written in *Symbolic Theology*, in *Theological Institutes*, and what he wrote concerning the *Divine Names* and *Mystical Theology*, finally at the end of that same book—as one who was already in the "darkness" and speaking of God as holily as possible—exclaimed, after some other points pertaining to the same matter:

<margin>God is known more through negation. The first step.</margin>
"He is neither truth, nor kingdom, nor wisdom, nor the one, nor unity, nor deity, nor goodness; nor is He 'spirit' as far as we can know; neither is there a name for Him as 'Son' or 'Father,' nor anything else of those things known to us or anyone else in the world. He is none of the things that are not, nor any of the things that are; nor do the things that are know Him as He is, nor does He know the things that are as they are. There is no discourse of Him, nor name, nor knowledge; He is neither darkness nor light, neither error nor truth; nor is there any 'position' <note>Positive affirmation.</note> or 'removal' <note>Negation.</note> of Him at all."

<margin>Against the Epicureans and Egyptians. Varro and others. The fifteenth decade of the harmony of Plato and Aristotle.</margin>
These are the words of that divine man, verbatim. Let us recall what we have said, and we will see that in the first step we learn that God is not a body (as the **Epicureans** <note>Ancient philosophers who believed the world was made of atoms and that gods, if they existed, were material.</note> thought) nor the "form of a body"—as those want who assert that God is the "soul of heaven" or the "soul of the universe." The **Egyptians** (as Plutarch writes) held this view, as did **Varro**, the Roman theologian. This gave both groups a great basis for idolatry, as we shall declare elsewhere. But there are even some among the **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle.</note> so dull-witted that they confirm this to be the true opinion of Aristotle. See how far these men fall short of a true knowledge of God! They rest in their prison as if in a sanctuary, believing they have reached the heights of God when they are still lying on the ground...

<summary>Pico outlines a four-step "ascent" to God, moving from human life/knowledge to the realization that God is simple "Being Itself," and finally to a mystical "divine darkness" where God is above all names, as taught by Dionysius the Areopagite.</summary>

-># EXPOSITIONS ON BEING AND THE ONE<-

...did not yet move him: for in that way, God would be neither perfect life, nor perfect being, nor would he even be perfect intellect. However, we have extensively attacked this profane opinion in the fifth decade of our *Harmony* <note>original: "concordiæ"; Pico refers to his major unfinished project, the *Concordia Platonis Aristotelisque*, intended to prove the agreement between the two philosophers.</note>. We learn in the **second grade**: something that fewer people correctly grasp, and in which we can err more easily if we deviate even slightly from true understanding: namely, that God is neither life, nor intellect, nor the intelligible, but something better and more excellent than all these. For all these names signify a particular perfection, none of which exists in God.

<margin>Second grade.</margin>

<margin>Dionysius & Platonic peripatetics.</margin>
Regarding this, both Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-century Christian Neoplatonist whose "negative theology" argued that God is best known by denying all human attributes to Him.</note> and later the Platonics deny these things are in God. But since God himself, by his own unique perfection—which is his infinity, his godhead, which is himself—unites and gathers the whole perfection of these things (which in them is manifold and divided) within himself, He does so not as one made from many, but as the One who exists before those many. Therefore, certain others, especially the Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle, named for the "peripatos" or covered walkway where they held their discussions.</note>—whom the Parisian theologians <note>The Scholastic theologians of the University of Paris, known for their rigorous use of Aristotelian logic.</note> imitate in almost everything as far as they are allowed—concede that all these things are in God. In saying and believing this, we not only speak and believe correctly, but we do so in harmony with those who deny them, provided that we always keep before our eyes that saying of Aurelius Augustine: that the wisdom of God is no more wisdom than it is justice, and the justice of God is no more justice than it is wisdom. Likewise, life is not more in Him as life than as cognition, nor is cognition more cognition than life. For all these are one in God, not through confusion or mixing, or as if through the mutual penetration of distinct things, but through a simple, supreme, ineffable, and foundational unity. In this unity, every act, every form, and every perfection is enclosed excellently—as if in the first and most eminent leader or in the innermost treasures of divine infinity—above all things and outside all things. Yet, it is not only the beginning of all things but is more "one" with all things than they are with themselves. Truly, words fail, and it is entirely less than what is conceived. But see, my dear Angelo <note>Pico is addressing his friend, the renowned poet and scholar Angelo Poliziano.</note>, what madness holds us.

<margin>Mirror of Parisian theology.</margin>

<margin>Augustine.</margin>

<margin>To love God is the reason for knowing Him. Note.</margin>
While we are in the body, we are able to love God more than we can either speak of or know Him. By loving Him, we benefit ourselves more, we labor less, and we obey Him more. It is better, however, to possess Him by loving Him than to never find what we seek through constant inquiry and cognition—for He would be gazed upon in vain through knowledge if He were not also loved. But let us return to our subject. It is now clearly evident to you how God may be called Mind, Intellect, Life, and Wisdom at one time, yet at another time be placed above all these. Both views are proven to be true and consistent. Nor does Plato disagree with Aristotle for this reason: that in the book of the *Republic*, he places God—whom he calls the Idea of the Good—above intellect and the intelligibles, giving to the former the power to understand and to the latter the power to be understood. Yet here, Aristotle often calls God both intellect, the one who understands, and the intelligible. For even Dionysius the Areopagite agrees with Aristotle that God is not ignorant of himself and other things. Therefore, if He understands Himself, He is both intellect and intelligible; for he who knows himself must necessarily know and be known. And yet, if we take these as "particular" perfections, as I said—or if by "intellect" we mean a nature that tends toward an intelligible object as if toward something outside itself—Aristotle would most firmly deny that God is intellect and intelligible, just as the Platonists do. In the **third grade**, as we approach the darkness, something more has shone upon us: so that we do not merely refrain from imagining God as some imperfect or defective being in our impious

<margin>Plato.</margin>

<margin>Aristotle. Dionysius.</margin>

<margin>From where that comes: <term>Know thyself</term> <note>original Greek: "γνωθι σεαυτόν" (gnothi seauton); the famous Delphic maxim.</note>.</margin>

<margin>Third grade.</margin>

<column-break/>

thought—as would be the case if He were called a body, or the soul of a body, or a creature composed of them—nor should we make Him like some particular genus, however perfect (as the "wise" do when they make him human-like), by calling Him "life" or "mind" or "reason." Instead, we should recognize that He is better even than what universal names indicate—those which encompass everything—namely, "True Being" and "the One." In the consideration of these things, there is nothing like what exists in God. We knew that He exists above every nature that can be formed or conceived by us. Then, we first knew Him in some way when we were entirely ignorant of Him. From this, it can be gathered that God is not only—as Anselm says—"that than which nothing greater can be conceived," but He is that which is infinitely greater than everything that can even be thought. Thus, the prophet David spoke truly according to the Hebrew text: "To You, silence is praise." <note>Psalm 65:2. Pico notes that the Hebrew original differs from the standard Latin Vulgate translation of "A hymn, O God, becometh thee."</note> We have said these things to solve the first argument; from this, a great window is opened for the legitimate understanding of Dionysius’s books titled *On Mystical Theology* and *On the Divine Names*. In these, one must be careful neither to make his writings out to be less than they are (for they are very great), nor, while we think little of all we understand, to stumble upon dreams and inextricable fictions.

### Chapter Six: In which he solves the second argument of the Platonists concerning Prime Matter.

<margin>This is matter which is called "hyle" by another name, about which I wrote in the *Heptaplus* <note>Pico's work on the seven days of creation.</note>.</margin>
As for what they object regarding **prime matter**, it is frivolous. For to the extent that matter is "being," it is to that extent "one." Indeed, if they wish to follow Plato’s words to the letter, they must grant that matter has the same logic of the "One" as it does of "Being." For Plato does not want it to be absolutely nothing; otherwise, how would it be the "receptacle of forms," the "nurse," a "certain nature," and the other things he confirms it to be in the *Timaeus*? It is therefore not nothing—that is, it is not entirely devoid of being, if we believe Plato. Yet, in the *Philebus*, he calls this same thing not only "multiplicity" (which, as they wish, is opposed to the One, just as nothing is opposed to being) but "the infinite." Multiplicity, however, if it is finite, does not entirely escape the logic of the One, because insofar as it is finite, it is one. But an infinite multiplicity lacks the nature of the One just as it lacks a limit. Therefore, according to Plato, prime matter is "being" more than it is "one." Those who argue against this, in order to prove the "One" is superior to "Being," used to say that matter is not "being" and yet is "one." Likewise, the Platonist Iamblichus, in the book he wrote on the Pythagorean sect, calls prime matter "duality," because first duality is multiplicity and the root of all other multiplicities. Therefore, according to him—who is so great among the Platonists that he is called "divine"—prime matter is not only not "one," but it is multiplicity itself, the root of all the multiplicity that exists in things. We have said these things by throwing their own objections back at them. Furthermore, that matter is not entirely devoid of unity, just as it is not devoid of being. However, it receives its exact unity from the same source from which it receives its being: namely, from Form. Beyond this, there is debate about whether its unity is affirmative or negative—all of which is well known to those who have taken even a single "little walk" <note>original: "deambulationiunculam"; Pico uses a playful diminutive to mock those who have only a superficial knowledge of Aristotle's philosophy.</note> with Aristotle.

<margin>Since multiplicity arose from units.</margin>

<margin>Iamblichus.</margin>

### Chapter Seven: In which he solves the third argument of the Platonists concerning multiplicity; and shows that those who say the One is more common than Being must concede something which Plato denies.

<margin>Solution of the third reason.</margin>
Moreover, they are greatly mistaken in the third reason. For multiplicity is not opposed to the One in the same way that non-being is opposed to Being. These latter have a contradictory opposition; the former have either a privative or a contrary opposition.

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s argument regarding the relationship between "the One" and "Being." He is specifically addressing the Platonic view that "the One" is superior to "Being," a point of contention he seeks to resolve by harmonizing it with Aristotelian metaphysics.</meta>

# BOOK ONE
43

...about which matter Aristotle <note>The Greek philosopher (384–322 BC) whose work forms the basis of Western logic and science.</note> disputes at length in the tenth book of *First Philosophy* <note>original: "primæ philoſophiæ"; this refers to Aristotle's *Metaphysics*.</note>. But let those who are called Platonists see what ruins they fall into when they say that the **One** is superior to **Being** <term>Ens (Being): The quality of existence; Vnum (the One): The quality of unity or being undivided.</term>. It is certain that whenever two categories are related such that one is more common than the other, it is possible for something to escape the reach of the lower category without escaping the higher one. This is exactly why the higher is called "more common." A ready example is that "animal" is more common than "man": it can happen that something is "not man" while still being "animal." By the same logic, if the **One** were more common than **Being**, it would be possible for something to be "non-being" (or nothing) while still being "one"; and thus "one" would be predicated of "non-being"—a concept which Plato expressly refutes in the *Sophist* <note>A dialogue by Plato exploring the nature of being, non-being, and the philosopher's definitions.</note>.

### Chapter eight, in which it is declared how these four—namely Being, the One, the True, and the Good—are in all things that exist after God.

<margin>Followers of Avicenna. They established six terms. Avicenna, who bit at the opposing Averroes.</margin>
The truest opinion, therefore, is that there are four things which encompass all: **Being**, the **One**, the **True**, and the **Good**. This holds if they are understood such that their negations are "nothing," "divided," "false," and "evil." To these four, two others were added: **Something** and **Thing**, by those later thinkers who followed Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath and influential philosopher.</note>. Avicenna modified the philosophy of Aristotle in many places, which led to great battles between him and Averroes <note>Ibn Rushd (1126–1198), an Andalusian philosopher known as "The Commentator" on Aristotle.</note>; but as far as this matter is concerned, the disagreement is small. For these thinkers divide what is understood as "the One" into "the One" and "Something"—a view not foreign to Plato, who in the *Sophist* counts "**Something**" among these most common terms. They also divide what is contained under "Being" into "**Being**" and "**Thing**." But we shall discuss these elsewhere. Let us proceed as we began: these four exist one way in God, and another way in those things that come after God, since God has these by his own nature, while other things have them from him. Let us first see how they exist in created things. All things that exist after God have from him an **efficient**, an **exemplary**, and a **final** cause <note>Efficient cause: the source of change/creation; Exemplary cause: the model or "Idea"; Final cause: the purpose or goal.</note>; for from him, through him, and toward him are all things. If, therefore, we consider things as they are established by God as the **efficient cause**, they are called **beings** because they participate in that efficiency. If we consider them according to their **exemplar** (which we call the **Idea**) <margin>Being, the One, the True, the Good, Something, Thing; the last two were added by those following Avicenna.</margin> according to which God founded them, they are called **true**. For an image of Hercules is called a "true" image if it conforms to the real Hercules. If we consider them as they tend toward him as their **final** <margin>The order of these four.</margin> end, they are called **good**. If, however, each thing is taken absolutely in itself, it is named **one**. The order is such that each thing is first conceived under the rationale of **Being**, since the agent creator first makes the thing exist before it is "something" in itself—otherwise, the whole of what it is would not come from the agent. Thus, there is nothing after God that we can understand without understanding it as "being from another," "finite being," or "participated being." **The One** follows **Being**. The third is **Truth**, because after a thing exists in itself, it must be seen whether it is such as the exemplar to which it was formed. If it is found similar to that, it follows that it turns toward it through **Goodness**, as if toward its kin and relative. Who cannot see that these four have an equal reach? Grant that something exists, and it is certainly "one." For he who does not say "one," <margin>Plato.</margin> says "nothing," as Plato says in the *Sophist*. For a thing is whatever it is, undivided in itself and divided from others which are not itself. When we say this, we understand "the One"—or to use Plato's words, it is "the same as itself and other than others," which <margin>The "True" is converted with the others in reality. Augustine.</margin> he confirms in the same dialogue to be true of every single thing. It is also necessarily **True**. For if it is a man, then he is a "true man." It is the same to say "this is not true gold" as it is to say "this is not gold." For when you say "it is not true gold," you mean it looks like gold and is something similar to gold, but

<column-break/>

it is not gold. Therefore, Aurelius Augustine <note>St. Augustine (354–430 AD), influential Christian theologian.</note>, defining in his *Soliloquies* what is **True**, says: "The True is that which is" <note>original: "verum eſt id quod eſt"</note>. This should not be taken to mean that "Being" and "True" are the same thing. For although they are the same in reality, they differ in reason and definition; therefore, one should not be defined by the other. Rather, Augustine wanted to express that a thing is called "true" when it is that which it is called and said to be; just as gold is "true gold" when it is gold and nothing other than gold. This is what he meant by "the True is that which is." Some people, not noticing this, <margin>The **Good** is converted with **Being**. Disputing against Olympiodorus.</margin> calumniate the definition. Similarly, a thing is also **Good**, because whatever is, insofar as it is, is good. In my opinion, Olympiodorus <note>A 6th-century Neoplatonist philosopher and commentator.</note> is far in error, believing he can prove that "the Good" and "Being" are different because we desire "to be well" (*bene esse*) rather than "simply to be" (*esse simpliciter*). He argues that if we are in a bad state, we might desire not to be. But setting aside whether those in a wretched state can, by a right and natural desire, wish not to exist—he fails to notice that just as "being" is manifold, so also "goodness" is manifold. First, there is the **natural being** of things, such as for a man to be a man, a lion to be a lion, or a stone to be a stone; "natural goodness" follows this being inseparably. There are other forms of being which can be called **adventitious** <note>original: "aduētitia"; qualities that are added to a thing rather than being part of its essential nature.</note>, such as for a man to be wise, or handsome, or healthy. Just as wisdom and beauty are "beings" distinct from humanity, so they are distinct "goods." For the goodness by which a man is a man is one thing, and the goodness by which he is not just a man, but a wise man, is another. Just as these are different kinds of being, they are called by different names. <margin>As there are diverse ways of being, so there are diverse ways of being good.</margin> Therefore, just as all things seek the **Good**, so all things seek **Being**. First, they seek that goodness which follows natural being, because this is the foundation of all subsequent goodnesses, which are added to it such that they cannot stand without it. For how can one be happy if one does not exist at all? Indeed, that goodness which they obtain when they first exist is not sufficient for them; they desire to attain the remaining goods which complete and adorn that first one. Just as we truly say that they seek other goodnesses beyond the first, so we can truly say they desire other forms of "being" beyond the first; for to "be happy" is a different "being" than to "be a man." And if someone grants that a person might not want to exist if they are not happy, it does not follow <margin>The error of Olympiodorus.</margin> (as Olympiodorus thinks) that "the Good" and "Being" are different things. Rather, it means that "being a man" is one thing and "happiness" is another; likewise, the goodness of a man is one thing and the goodness of happiness is another. A man does not want the first (being a man) unless he also has the second (happiness). I set aside whether something is called "good simply" and "being simply" for the same reason. This is not the place for all those disputes. We were saying truly, therefore, that everything that exists is good insofar as it exists; for "God saw all the things he had made, and they were very good." <note>A reference to Genesis 1:31.</note> Why shouldn't they be? They are from a Good Architect, who imprints his likeness on all things that are from him. In the **Entity** of things, therefore, we can admire the power of God the Creator; in their **Truth**, we can venerate the wisdom of the Artisan; in their **Goodness**, we can proclaim the generosity of the Lover; in their **Unity**, we can embrace the unique simplicity (so to speak) of the Founder. This Unity joins each thing to itself, then all things to each other, and finally calls all things to the love of God. Let us also examine their opposites to see if they have an equal reach. **Falsehood** and **Nothing** sound the same as what we said above. If we say **Evil** and **Nothing** differ, the Philosophers and Theologians alike will object. Therefore, to do evil <margin>**Evil** and **Nothing** are converted. Against the error of the Manichaeans.</margin> is to do nothing; and it is usually said that evil has no **efficient cause**, but only a **deficient** one. By this, the insanity of those who established two principles—one of good and one of evil—is refuted <note>Pico is referring to the Manichaeans, a dualistic religious movement that believed in a cosmic struggle between a Good God and an Evil God.</note>, as if there were some efficient principle of evil. But to divide a thing is the same as to destroy it; nor can we desire the destruction of a thing...

Io. Pic. i <note>Signature of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola.</note>

<summary>Pico explains that Being, the One, the True, and the Good are universal attributes (transcendentals) that apply to all created things, reflecting God's power, wisdom, love, and simplicity. He refutes the idea that "the One" is superior to "Being" and argues against dualistic views of evil, defining evil as a lack of being or "nothing."</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's argument from the previous page, where he established that Being, the One, the True, and the Good are co-extensive. He now transitions from the metaphysical relationship of parts and wholes to a theological and moral application of these four transcendental terms.</meta>

**OF BEING AND THE ONE**
i

<margin>
Nothing divided can be converted.
Aristotle.
</margin>
...to take away its own natural unity: so that nothing less than that remains in its integrity. For the whole is not merely its parts, but that "one" which results from the parts, as Aristotle <note>The Greek philosopher (384–322 BC).</note> teaches in the eighth book of *First Philosophy* <note>original: "primæ philosophiæ"; this refers to Aristotle's *Metaphysics*.</note>. Therefore, if you divide a whole into parts, the parts indeed remain, but the whole itself which is divided does not remain; it ceases to be in "act" and exists only in "potential," just like the parts. Those parts, which were previously potential, then begin to be in "act"; for previously, when they were in the whole, they did not have their own proper unity in act, which they then obtain for the first time when, separated from the whole, they subsist by themselves.

### Chapter 9, in which he declares how those four are in God.

<margin>
Three conditions of the Good according to Plato.
</margin>
Let us examine again how these things are in God, in whom they do not exist in respect to a cause—for He has none; He himself is the cause of all and is from no one. They can be considered in God by a double reasoning: either insofar as He is the cause of others (a distinction which does not apply to created things as far as the present business is concerned, since God can be such that He is not a cause), or in His own nature. Other things cannot be such that they are not from Him; therefore, we first conceive of God such that He is the universality of all action: the fullness of Being itself, which is followed by such an understanding that He is **One**, so that even the opposite cannot be conceived. See how much they wander who imagine multiple first principles or multiple gods! Immediately, it is also most **True**: for what can He have that appears to be and is not, He who is Being itself? It follows certainly that He is Truth itself; but He will also be **Goodness** itself. For there are three conditions of the Good, as Plato writes in the *Philebus* <note>A late Platonic dialogue concerning pleasure and the good life.</note>: that it be perfect, sufficient, and desirable. Moreover, that which we conceive as such will be perfect, because nothing will be lacking to Him who is all things; He will be sufficient, because to those possessing Him nothing will be lacking; and in Him, finding all things, He will be desirable, because from Him and in Him are all things which can be desired for any reason. God is therefore the fullest **Entity**, individual **Unity**, most solid **Truth**, and most blessed **Goodness**. This, if I am not mistaken, is that <term>τετρακτυς</term> <note>original: "tetraktys"; the Quaternary or number four, which the Pythagoreans considered the root of all nature.</note>, the quaternary by which Pythagoras swore and which he called the "principle of ever-flowing nature." For we have demonstrated that these things, which are the one God, are the principle of the being of all things. But we also swear by those things which are holy, firm, and divine; what is firmer, holier, or more divine than these? But if we assign these four names to God as He is the cause of things, the whole order is inverted. First, He will be **One**, because He is understood in Himself before He is understood as a cause. Second, He will be **Good**. Third, **True**. Fourth, **Being**. For since the cause which is called the "final" <note>The purpose or goal for which something is done.</note> is prior to that which is "exemplary" <note>The blueprint or pattern (Ideal cause).</note>, and the exemplary is prior to the "efficient" <note>The force that brings something into being.</note>: for first we desire this—to be protected from the injury of storms—then we conceive the idea of a house in the mind, and finally we form it in matter by making it outwardly. Therefore, if (as we defined in the previous chapter) the **Good** pertains to the final cause, the **True** to the exemplary, and **Being** to the efficient, then God, as He is the cause, will first have the character of the Good, then the True, and finally Being. We touch upon all these things briefly here, though they otherwise involve many great questions.

<margin>
Tetraktys,
The Quaternary
Pythagoras
</margin>

<margin>
By what way these terms belong to God through those four causes.
</margin>

### Chapter 10, in which he turns the whole dispute toward the institution of life and the amendment of morals.

<margin>
Note.
And this chapter contains both contemplation and action together most wisely.
</margin>
But let us not dispute for the sake of others rather than ourselves; we must take care lest, while searching out the highest things, we live in a lowly state—that is, a state unworthy of these conditions which have been given to us from heaven so that we might even investigate the reasons of celestial things. But we must constantly meditate on this: that this mind of ours, even though it is from a mortal seed, cannot exist or be happy anywhere except in the

<column-break/>

<margin>
The goodness of God created the world.
Plato's inquiry.
</margin>
possession of divine things. And the more it approaches happiness here as a wandering stranger, the more it raises itself and approaches divine things, having left behind the care for earthly ones. This present dispute seems to admonish us above all that if we wish to be blessed, we should imitate the most blessed God of all, possessing unity, truth, and goodness within ourselves. Ambition disturbs the peace of **Unity**, and snatches the soul, which should cling to itself, outside of itself; it drags and tears it apart as if it were broken into diverse pieces. Who will not lose the splendor and light of **Truth** in the filth and darkness of pleasures? A most thieving greed—that is, avarice—steals **Goodness** from us. For it is peculiar to goodness to communicate to others the goods which you possess; wherefore, when Plato asked why God founded the world, responding to himself, he said: "He was good." These are those three: the pride of life, the lust of the flesh, and the lust of the eyes <note>A reference to 1 John 2:16.</note>, which, as John writes, are of the world and are not of the Father, who is Unity itself, Truth itself, and Goodness itself. Let us flee from here, therefore—that is, from the world, which is placed in malice—and let us fly to the Father where there is unifying peace, where there is the truest light, where there is the best pleasure. But who will give us wings so that we may fly there? The love of those things which are above. Who will take them away? The lust for things which are upon the earth; if we follow these, we suffer the loss of unity, truth, and goodness. For we are not **One** if we do not bind together the downward-leaning sense and the reason that looks toward heavenly things by a covenant of virtue; instead, there are two princes in us, as it were, reigning across an interval, while now we follow God through the law of the mind, and now Baal <note>A biblical term for a false god, used here to represent fleshly desires.</note> through the law of the flesh, and our kingdom, divided against itself, is desolated with a whip. But if we are "one" in such a way that reason, enslaved to sense, is commanded only by the law of the members, this unity will be false because we will not be **True**. For we will be said and appear to be men—that is, animals living by reason—and yet we will be brutes, for whom sensual appetite is the law. We will perform a trick before those who see us and among whom we dwell. The image will not correspond to its exemplar; for we are in the likeness of God, but God is spirit. We are no longer spiritual (to use Paul’s words) but animal. However, when through **Truth** we do not depart from the exemplar, it will remain for us to be joined to Him at last by tending toward Him through **Goodness**. But if these three—the True and the Good being perpetually annexed to the One—follow Being, it remains that when we are not those things, we also are not at all; even if we seem to be, and although we are believed to live, we nevertheless die continually rather than live.

<margin>
All things must be meditated upon with much salt: ambition, pleasure, avarice.
</margin>

# FIRST OBJECTIONS OF ANTONIUS FAVENTINUS <note>Antonio Cittadini da Faenza (d. 1518), a philosopher and critic of Pico.</note> AGAINST THE LITTLE BOOK ON BEING AND THE ONE.

---

[Decorative drop cap initial S]
<margin>
First objection.
</margin>
If any little book deserves to be inscribed "On Being and the One," it is necessary that it explain the nature and property of each. However, in this little work which recently came into my hands, and which is titled *On Being and the One*, some things are treated that are almost foreign to the title and inscription. For the principal purpose of the author is to dispute whether, according to Plato, Being and the One mutually follow each other, or whether (as the Academics think) the One is more common than Being. But this is not to treat of "Being and the One" but of the "mutual conversion of Being and the One"; nor even absolutely, but only according to Plato. For if any philosopher were to discuss only the question of whether the soul is immortal, he would not therefore be disputing "on the soul," but a treatise would be held on the "immortality of the soul" alone. Furthermore, the author of the work says that the Academics think God, according to Plato, truly...

The text then transitions to a critique by Antonius Faventinus, who argues Pico's title is too broad for his specific focus on Platonic conversion.</summary>

--- Page 129 ---
<meta>This page continues the technical debate regarding whether God can be properly called "Being" (ens) or if He transcends being as "the One." Pico is engaging with criticisms of his work *De ente et uno* (Of Being and the One), specifically addressing arguments that draw upon Platonist and Aristotelian traditions.</meta>

**BOOK ONE**

<margin>Second.</margin>
...and that He is not properly Being; a claim that truly astonishes me. For if the author means to include all Academics or Platonists—as his phrasing seems to indicate—he may be speaking untruthfully, as he would otherwise not pronounce so absolutely that this is what the Academics believe.
<margin>Themistius</margin>
Themistius <note>A 4th-century Greek philosopher and commentator on Aristotle.</note>, for instance, a philosopher of no small standing among the Platonists, testifies that according to Plato’s view, the Idea, which is the principle of all things, is truly and properly Being and the One. Indeed, most—if not all—Platonists do not consider the Idea to be one thing and God the Creator to be another. He goes on to say:
<margin>Third.</margin>
If it can be defended in any way according to Plato that "the One" is more universal than "Being," it must be judged thus: he says that words which, in a somewhat unrefined Latin term, are called "concretions" <note>original: "concretionem"; in medieval logic, this refers to a concrete noun like "white" as opposed to an abstract noun like "whiteness."</note>—such as "brightly white," or "being"—signify something external by whose presence the things receive their names. For whiteness is one thing, and a white thing is another; a human is one thing, and humanity is another. Therefore, that shall be called "being" in which "to be" is one thing, and that which subsists is another. God, therefore, who is "to be" itself, could not be considered "being," but rather "the One," from whom all things are contained and enclosed. But does such a defense not lack internal consistency? For by the same reasoning that "white," "human," and "being" signify something external, it must follow that "the One," "the Blessed," "God," and many similar terms also signify something external. Thus God—who is Unity, Beatitude, and Divinity all at once—could not be called "one," nor "blessed," nor "God" at all. How then can he be "the One" if he is not "Being"?
<margin>Confirmation. Fourth.</margin>
Furthermore, "being" is so called because it *is*. Just as it is impossible for one who sits not to be "sitting," it is impossible for He who truly and properly *is* not to be "Being." For He says, "I am who I am" <note>A reference to God's revelation to Moses in Exodus 3:14.</note>. It may seem even more remarkable that the critic tries to defend the idea that God is not Being not only according to Plato, but even attempts to drag Aristotle himself into the same opinion.
<margin>St. Thomas. Aristotle.</margin>
For in the fifth book of the *Metaphysics*, Aristotle divides "being" into "being through itself" (per se) and "being by accident" (per accidens). Being *per se* is divided into the ten categories <note>original: "praedicamenta"; the ten fundamental ways of being defined by Aristotle (substance, quantity, quality, etc.).</note>. But the critic claims God cannot be placed in any genus, just as he believes Blessed Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential Dominican theologian.</note> has demonstrated. Therefore, if God is not being *per se* (because He is not in a category) nor being by accident (as is obvious), then according to Aristotle, He will not be Being at all. Furthermore, "being" is separated into substance and accident according to the most common division; but God is neither an accident nor a substance, for he says God exceeds the limits of every genus. But truly, I do not see by what reasoning the author of this work ascribes a Platonic opinion to our Aristotle—if indeed it is even Plato's opinion. For the division of "being" into *per se* and *per accidens* is a division of "complex being," as Blessed Thomas—to whom the author grants much authority—subtly writes in that place.
<margin>Confirmation</margin>
The same is clear from examples: for "being by accident," according to Aristotle, is threefold: either an accident is predicated of a subject, or a subject of an accident, or an accident of an accident. All of these pertain to a combination. In the same way, those things are called "beings through themselves" (per se) in which something is predicated that belongs to substance, or quantity, or another genus, provided that what is predicated belongs to the subject through itself—such as "white" to Socrates, though not to "man"; or "animal" to "horse." This encompasses a division made through affirmation and negation. For "substance" is that which rests on nothing else but exists through itself; "accident" is that which exists in another as if in a subject. Between these, there is no middle ground, as Blessed Thomas believes; for indeed, no middle ground can be imagined between "having a subject" and "not having a subject." Therefore, "substance," which is the opposite of "accident," will not be a genus if God is contained in no genus. Furthermore, it is not an undisputed opinion of Aristotle that God is contained in no genus *per se*; for there are some followers of Aristotle who believe that God is placed in a category through himself; and

<column-break/>

<margin>Boethius. Augustine. Fifth.</margin>
I indeed believe that the distinguished philosopher Boethius <note>Roman statesman and philosopher (c. 477–524 AD).</note> held this view; and I would show, if necessary, that this can be aptly gathered from the words of Boethius and even Augustine. Again, the critic says that "the divided" is the negation of "the one." He proves this by the fact that a thing is destroyed when it is torn apart and divided. But how can "the divided" be opposed to "the one" as a negation? For a contradiction exists between affirmation and negation; yet a chimera <note>A mythological creature used in logic to represent something non-existent or impossible.</note> is neither one nor divided. Nor is the statement "the diameter of a square is commensurable with its side" <note>A classic example of a mathematical impossibility.</note> either one or divided. He also thinks that "the false" is the negation of "the true"—which might be defended in some way.
<margin>Sixth. Blessed Thomas.</margin>
However, it is a contrary rather than a negation, as Blessed Thomas shows. For a chimera is not true or false unless we utterly abuse the word. For the "true" is that which *is*; that is, as he explains it, that which is what it seems and is said to be. The "false" will therefore be that which is *not* what it seems and is said to be—like a counterfeit coin. Thus, nothing happens to be false unless it seems to be something else that it is not. But between that which seems to be what it is, and that which is not what it seems, there is no contradiction. Therefore, the true and the false are not opposed by the opposition of affirmation and negation.
<margin>Seventh. Aristotle. Confirmation</margin>
He also thinks "evil" is the negation of "good." But Aristotle affirms in the *Categories* that "good" and "evil" are genera of contraries. Now, that which is a negation cannot be a genus. Furthermore, "good" by its very nature is that which is to be sought; "evil" is that which is to be fled. Seeking and fleeing are contraries to each other, just as gathering and separating are. Therefore, good and evil will be contraries—which Boethius also asserts in his commentary on the *Categories*, whatever others may have said about it.

->Response to the first objections.<-

### GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA TO ANTONIO FAVENTINO, GREETINGS.

<image-desc>A woodcut ornamental initial 'Q' containing a circular illustration of a landscape with buildings and a prominent tree under a sky with clouds.</image-desc>I have read your questions against the little book I recently published, *Of Being and the One*, with as much pleasure as the affection and freedom of mind with which you wrote them. I owe you a great deal for this service. If we were to bestow such honesty more freely upon our friends, or demand it more willingly from them, we would certainly be far more learned and better people than we are. But a deadly persuasion has seized the minds of men: we think that we do not please those who are not pleased by our errors. We interpret the free judgment of friends as hatred or ill-temper, while we interpret flattery as love and goodness of nature.
<margin>All praise is harmful; criticism is useful.</margin>
Thus it happens that while we prefer to be praised even when undeserving, rather than be corrected when we deserve it, we are always mocked and never deserve praise. See how much we err! For almost all praise is always useless, and often harmful. If it is true, what utility does it bring? If it is false, it surely makes us who are praised insane, and those who praise us ridiculous. Criticism is certainly always useful: if it is just, it rouses us to knowledge; if less than just, it rouses us to the defense of the truth. Finally, what else is being corrected than becoming better through another's labor? Or what else is it for a friend's file to polish a book, than for you to benefit from his sleepless nights while you sleep? I cannot, therefore—as I was saying—help but owe you a great deal, you who have freely indicated to me what you thought of those things in my book that pleased you less. I recognized in your writings, besides your benevolence, also that quality of yours which I have long...
