<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s defense of his work "Of Being and the One." He is responding to criticisms regarding the book's title and his interpretation of how Platonist and Aristotelian philosophers define the relationship between God, "Being" (the state of existing), and "the One" (the state of absolute unity).</meta>

### OF BEING AND THE ONE

...noting the cleverness of your talent: I began at once—not as a father, but as a judge—to examine whatever you had noted, especially since those points had already come under my own suspicion of being false based on your testimony. But as I thought about it, several points occurred to me by which those ideas might be defended and cleared of fault. I wanted to write these to you freely, lest I fail to embrace the very virtue of liberty that I praise in you; so that even if I do not imitate your judgment in criticizing these points, I might at least imitate your freedom in defending them. You say the book is not correctly titled *Of Being and the One* since you do not treat all the natures and properties of being and the one, but only the interchangeability of the one and being. To me, Antonio, it usually seems that two "vestibules" are set before books:

<margin>
Solution to the first objection.
</margin>

the Title and the Preface. The Title is a short Preface; the Preface is a Title expanded and explained. The Title promises

<margin>
What the Title and Preface are.
</margin>

a treatise on being and the one, but the preface explains what specific aspects of being and the one are to be treated. If this were done in the title, we should fear the title of the book becoming a book itself. This could be defended by the precedent of a thousand authors whose chosen titles for their books would suffer the same accusation. But this question is not so weighty that either you or I should be occupied with it any longer. Furthermore, you marvel that I said the Platonists believe God is not properly "being." Do not marvel at me, but at

<margin>
Second solution.
Syrianus.
Proclus.
Plotinus.
</margin>

those whom I, along with you, do not approve of in the assertion of this dogma. However, that they felt this way—which seems almost incredible to you—and left it in writing for posterity is very well known to all who have read the Platonists. Syrianus, Proclus, Plotinus <note>Key Neoplatonist philosophers who argued that the ultimate principle (the One) is beyond "Being."</note>, and all the surviving interpreters of Plato confirm this with one voice. But, you say, Themistius <note>A 4th-century commentator on Aristotle and Plato.</note>, who is not ignoble among the Platonists, asserts that according to Plato's opinion, the "Idea" is truly and properly "being" and "the one." Moreover, all or most Platonists think the "Idea" is nothing other than God the Creator of things. Therefore, if the Idea is properly called "being," God himself will also be properly called "being." You argue this quite cleverly, but see if you do so with enough expertise. For those men—namely Proclus and Plotinus—confess that the Idea *is* and is *called* "being," but they contend that God is above the Ideas, just as he is above all beings. For Plotinus placed all the Ideas in that Mind which is closest to God, which he calls the "first being," the "first intelligible," and the "first life," so that God is not the "womb" of the Ideas, but their source; not their receptacle, but their principle. Proclus makes not just one way, but many intermediate orders of minds between God and the Ideas, and emulating their fullness, he called them "the Living Thing itself" in his commentary on Plato's *Timaeus*. I pass over Syrianus, Amelius, Iamblichus, and many others who feel the same. These are the rudiments and, as it were, the nursery of that doctrine which is considered Platonist. Even if someone granted you that the Idea and God are the same in reality, you would not deny they are different in "reason" <note>A scholastic distinction: two things might be the same physical object but different concepts.</note>. This diversity is quite enough so that God, insofar as he is the pattern for man, horse, and lion, can truly be called "being"; but insofar as he looks at nothing outside himself and has no relation to created things, but remains solitary in the recesses of his divinity, he exceeds every naming of "being." As Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian mystic who influenced medieval theology by saying God is "beyond being."</note> says, he has neither a name nor a conceptual definition. Therefore, it is most manifest that among the leaders of the Academy, God cannot properly be called "being." Even if one grants that the Idea and God are the same in reality, it does not immediately follow that if the Idea is "being," God must also properly be called "being." Let us pass to other matters, among which this displeases you most: that I said there is a certain way of speaking which, if we follow it, we can truly say "the One" is higher than "being." Since we can give God the name of "the One," but not "being," because "being" has the form of a "concrete noun" <note>term: concrete noun (nomen concretum) — in medieval logic, a noun that implies a subject participating in a quality (like "a white thing" participating in "whiteness").</note> (for so we can speak in Latin). It signifies that which participates in existence from another, which cannot be said of God, who is existence itself. You say that by the same reasoning, he could not be called

<margin>
Opinion of Plotinus on Ideas.
Opinion of Proclus on Ideas.
St. Thomas, Part 1, sufficiently on Ideas.
Another solution: Dionysius.
Third solution.
</margin>

<column-break/>

"one," because "one" is also a concrete noun just like "being." I saw this question when I was writing and I resolved it. For as soon as I proved that "being" cannot be predicated of God because it signifies what is not of itself but by participation in another, I added that since the name of "the One" is given to God as a consequence, we must confess that "the One" is above "being." Immediately after this, meeting your objection, I added: "But we then call God 'One,' not so much stating *what* he is as *how* he is all the things that he is," for in whatever

<margin>
Dionysius.
</margin>

way all things are from him, they are "one." Dionysius says God is called "One" because he is all things uniquely; again, he is called "One" because he is the principle of all things that exist, just as Unity is the principle of all numbers. These are my words there, verbatim. If, therefore, when we call God "One," we wish to state *what* he is, I confess that for the same reason he cannot be called "one" just as he cannot be called "being," because both are concrete nouns. Indeed, I was the first to openly assert this to you in the same book with these words: "These names—Being, True, One, Good—state something concrete and, as it were, participated. Therefore, we say again that God is above Being, above the True, above the One, and above the Good, because he is Existence itself, Truth itself, Unity itself, and Goodness itself." Those were my words there. It did not escape me when I was writing that "being" and "one" are equally concrete, and by reason of that concreteness, either neither or both are equally to be removed from God. But, as I had advised above: when we say God is "one" but not "being," we are not signifying what God is, but how he is what he is—namely, because he is all things most principally and most simply. This "mode" can in no way be indicated or figured by the name of "being," but it can be by the type and naming of "unity." For, as Aristotle writes, beings are related to each other just like numbers; and of numbers, Unity is both the most principal and the most simple. You add that you marvel that I wish to defend

<margin>
Aristotle.
Fourth solution.
</margin>

that God is not "being" not only according to Plato, but also according to Aristotle. But if you have run through the book more attentively, my primary aim in this whole work is to show that God both is and is properly called "being"—not only from Aristotle's dogma but also consistently from Plato's—

<margin>
Aristotle.
Plato.
Dionysius.
</margin>

and that "the One" is not higher than "being." However, lest those who said God is not "being" but "above being" should seem entirely insane—among whom, if neither Plato nor Aristotle is counted, certainly Dionysius the Areopagite is, who is greater than both—I have tried to prove that there is a certain way of speaking which, if we follow it, will not be far from the truth to say God is greater than the naming of "being." You cannot deny that this way of speaking is sometimes used even by the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle.</note> (though you shrink from it), unless you deny the authority of those to whom, in your own opinion, the first place in that school is owed. For who does not know that the division of "being" into "substance" and "accident" is frequent among the Aristotelians? When "being" is divided this way, it is the opinion of your Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas.</note> that God is not "being" but "above being." Regarding him, you used to say: "Take away Thomas, and Aristotle becomes mute." The words of Thomas are roughly these: "God is not an accident, nor can he properly be called a substance," both because substance

<margin>
To Thomas, immortal glory and praise.
</margin>

is called "substance" because it "stands under" <note>The literal meaning of the Latin *substantia*.</note> something, and because substance indicates a "quiddity" (an essence) which is different from its "being" (existence). Therefore, that division of "being" into substance and accident is a division of *created* being. Thus speaks Thomas. Furthermore, when Aristotle says that the First Philosopher treats "being" insofar as it is "being" and the causes and principles of "being," there are many among the Peripatetics who want God not to be placed among "beings" there by Aristotle, but among the "causes of being." However, it can also be said properly by another way of speaking that God is "being"...

### OBJECTIONS: BOOK TWO

<margin>Solution of the confirmation. Boethius. Solution 5.</margin>
...I did not deny, but rather asserted and confirmed with many reasons in the third chapter of that same work. However, I do not know why you—always an imitator of illustrious authors—now desert the most famous <term>Peripatetics<note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy, who often focused on the classification of things into categories.</note></term> for those who place God within a <term>genus<note>A general category or class in logic. Pico argues God is beyond all categories.</note></term>. I have no doubt that Boethius would in no way wish to be numbered among them. Finally, you contend that the "divided" is not the negation of the "one," nor "falsehood" the negation of "truth," nor "evil" the negation of "good." Indeed, regarding these oppositions, I know there is no easy controversy among great authors; for that reason, I ended the book in which these were briefly treated with this closing statement: "We touch upon all these things here briefly; otherwise, they are the seeds of many great questions."

But as for your objections—that the opinion I followed is less probable or true—they do not move me to doubt in the least. You say a <term>Chimaera<note>original: "chimera"; a mythical hybrid creature often used in philosophy to represent a concept that is logically impossible or non-existent.</note></term> is neither one nor divided. I, however, say that the Chimaera we conceive in the mind does not exist precisely because the parts we understand it to consist of are, in the nature of things, divided and not united. And just as that thing does not exist whose parts—from which it would be constituted if they existed—are divided, so that thing not only does not exist but is impossible, whose parts are neither united nor can be united by the force of nature. Therefore, we say a Chimaera does not exist, and we believe it cannot possibly come to be, for no other reason than this: it is not believable that the brute parts from which we fashion it will ever come together into a single animal composition.

Again, you insist that because the <term>diameter<note>Referring to the mathematical proof that the diagonal (diameter) of a square is incommensurable with its side.</note></term> is not <term>commensurable<note>Having a common measure; here referring to the fact that the ratio is an irrational number.</note></term>, it is neither one nor divided. You are mistaken, in my opinion. For by the same reasoning that it is "false" [that they are commensurable], it is necessarily "divided" within itself. For a thing is detected to be false precisely to the extent that it fights with itself and includes a contradiction. What else is it to include a contradiction than to be divided within itself? Therefore, every truth is "one" because it is consistent and harmonious with itself; every falsehood is "divided" because it fights with itself and does not cohere.

<margin>Solution 6.</margin>
Many have believed that falsehood is the negation of truth, a fact that is not hidden from you. Nor do the arguments you bring forward stand in the way. For as I said, we call that "false" which is not what it appears to be: as "false gold" is what appears to be gold but is not gold. Although false gold is not only "not gold" but is also "something other than gold," it nevertheless happens to it, insofar as it is false, to be something else besides gold; but it is false because it is *not* the gold it appears to be. Therefore, gold is false when it does not match the <term>Idea<note>In the Platonic sense, the perfect mental archetype or form of a thing.</note></term> of gold; but because it matches the Idea of brass or silver, it is not "absolutely false," but only "false gold"—just as it is not "absolutely non-being," because although it is not gold, it is something else, like brass, lead, or silver. But that which corresponds to no Idea is "absolutely and totally false," just as it is also

<margin>What absolute falsehood is. Solution 7. Albert. Thomas.</margin>
"absolutely non-being," such as that which we call a Chimaera. See, then, how they proceed with an equal pace: non-being, the divided, and the false; and how a Chimaera may rightly be called both "false" and every falsehood "divided."

Truly, "evil" does not oppose "good" by a contrary opposition, as you think; so teaches <term>Albert<note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a major medieval philosopher and teacher of Thomas Aquinas.</note></term> in explaining Aristotle’s *Categories*, and your <term>Thomas<note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the preeminent Scholastic theologian.</note></term> most extensively in the first question *On Evil*. I believe all these things have long been well known to you.

How much I love you and have always honored you, most excellent man, you yourself are a witness; you can easily recall, if you wish, my diligent and special devotion toward you. But let us come to our business. You say that your little book *Of Being and the One* could be correctly titled so, because even if the title of the work is brief, and although it promises a treatise on being and the one, the preface—which is a fuller title—explains what kind of treatise it promises: namely, the mutual interchangeability of being and the one.

<margin>First objection.</margin>
But see, I pray, whether this defense of yours is sufficient. By the same reasoning, if a book were published in which only the immortality of the soul was asserted by the author, it could rightly be titled *Of the Soul*. For the author, entering the discussion, might soon propose the question asking whether the soul is immortal or not. Indeed, this whole objection was explained in my previous letter, but in my judgment, you answered nothing. Furthermore, if a question should arise concerning the speed of motions—whether it follows arithmetic or geometric proportion—and at the beginning of the work the author promises to take many things from geometry, could the book be titled *Of Geometry*, even though it is concerned with motions? But let us omit these things as trivial.

<margin>Second objection.</margin>
In another short book, I wrote on this opinion: No one, I say, has said that the Platonists feel otherwise unless all or most of them feel so. If indeed <term>Themistius<note>A 4th-century philosopher and commentator on Aristotle.</note></term>, not ignoble among the Platonists, affirms according to Plato's opinion that the "Idea," which is the principle of things, is "truly and properly being," then it should not have been pronounced absolutely that "the Platonists, following Plato, judge that God is not truly and properly being." For the Idea *is* God. You, however, answer that the Idea is one thing and God is another. Even if it were granted that the Idea is God, it would not necessarily follow that God is "properly and truly being"; for although God and the Idea are not different in reality, they differ in "reason" (concept).

But I would not wish to dispute in this place whether the Platonists think God is one thing and the Idea another, since that question is far removed from our purpose—even though many authors, Greek and Latin alike, place Plato's Ideas in God. I seem to have done enough to imitate Plato by showing that a certain Platonist, and by no means an ignoble one, asserts according to Plato that the Idea (and therefore God) is "truly and properly being." Nor does the "difference in reason" to which you flee do anything in this matter. For "Idea" is a relative term, but God is an absolute thing. If, therefore, God is "truly and properly being" in that part where He refers outward [as an Idea], how much more should He be considered "being" by that reason by which He is God and consists in His own nature? For why is the Idea, by the reason that it is an Idea, "truly and properly being"? No reason, I say, can be assigned unless one says it is "truly and properly being" because it truly and properly *is*. Therefore, God, by the reason that He is God, will be "truly and properly being" more so. <note>original: "ego sum qui sum"</note> "I am who I am" [Exodus 3:14]. Furthermore, it was objected in this way: if the Platonists can be rightly defended because they say God is not truly and properly "being," but "the One," because...

# ON BEING AND THE ONE

The name of "Being" is a <term>concrete name<note>In Scholastic logic, a "concrete" name (like 'human') refers to a subject possessing a quality, whereas an "abstract" name (like 'humanity') refers to the quality itself. Pico is arguing about whether these terms imply a composite nature that shouldn't apply to God's absolute simplicity.</note></term> because it signifies something different from that which *is*. However, if one argues that God is "the One" because He is uniquely all things, one could just as easily conclude that God is not "the One," for "One" is also a concrete name. Indeed, He would be neither "Blessed" nor "God," as both these words are concrete. You respond that you do not call God "the One" as if the name "One" points to the substance of God, but rather to explain how He is that which He is. But I ask: to what end? This does not yet solve the objection. You say God is not Being but is the One, because the name of Being is concrete. If, therefore, "the One" is also concrete, must we not conclude by the same logic that God is not the One? Nor would He be God, which is a name pertaining to His substance, just as "Being" does. Furthermore, if He is "the One" because He is uniquely that which He is, why should He not also be called "Being"? For to be "One" is to be all things: namely Wisdom, Goodness, and Power. He is not called "One" because He is merely a single thing. By that same logic, He can be called "Being" even if He is not the only being; for He is Being in the highest degree. Furthermore, the reason has not yet been resolved which says: God is truly and properly Being, for He said, "I am who I am" <note>original: "ego sum qui sum"; a reference to Exodus 3:14.</note>. Again, I was surprised that you defended the idea, following Aristotle, that God is sometimes not considered under the name of "Being" because He is neither being *through itself* nor *by accident*, nor substance nor accident. For I have shown that God is neither being through itself nor by accident, nor can any middle ground be imagined between substance and accident. You, however, give no answer to the first objection. Against the second, you allege only one interpreter of Aristotle, namely the Blessed Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas.</note>, who says God is not properly a substance because He "stands under" <note>A literal translation of the Latin *sub-stare*, the root of "substance."</note> no accidents, nor is the essence of God anything other than God Himself. But look, most excellent man, does not Thomas bear witness against you? For if the division of Being into substance and accident is, according to Blessed Thomas, a division of *created* being (as you report), how can it be ignored that there is something that is *uncreated* Being, which is God? By what logic then can you maintain, according to Thomas’s interpretation, that Aristotle thought God is not properly and truly Being? Although Blessed Thomas in a certain place seems to deny that God is properly a substance—imitating the Master of the Sentences <note>Peter Lombard, the author of the standard medieval theology textbook.</note>—on the grounds that He stands under no accident, it is not therefore false what I wrote in the previous letter: that there is no middle ground between substance and accident. This, Thomas proves in many places with powerful arguments, and you have not resolved a single one of the points written to you. If, therefore, he sometimes denies that God is a substance, the very words you bring forward clearly reveal the man's mind: for "Substance" can be said in many ways, as he explains more widely in the first part. For sometimes a substance is properly so called because it "stands under" accidents, in which sense he denies God is a substance—nor is that denied simply and absolutely, but he says He is not "properly" a substance because He stands under no accident. Yet "Substance" is sometimes said to be that which exists through itself and needs no subject; in this way, Blessed Thomas sometimes—indeed frequently—uses the name of substance. In this sense, no middle ground can be imagined between substance and accident, for it is a division of both by affirmation and negation. As for the fact that I affirmed, led by no necessity but of my own accord from the opinion of Boethius and Augustine, that God is placed in a <term>category<note>In logic, a "predicament" or category is a class of things. Pico is debating whether God can be categorized or if He transcends all classes.</note></term> through Himself, I did not say that because I do not value, revere, or approve of Blessed Thomas. I said it because the authority of Thomas alone is not enough to show that either Aristotle or the Aristotelians thought God is by no means placed in a category. Nor have I for that reason deserted the best authors 

<column-break/>

for the wicked and the common; on the contrary, I follow and approve of the best. Do you make Blessed Thomas equal or superior to Boethius or Augustine? I myself have read them all in the past and read them daily; nor do I think anyone is of a lively mind who is either ignorant of or neglects those things devised by our British thinkers—I mean Suisset <note>Richard Swineshead, known as "the Calculator," a 14th-century mathematician and philosopher at Oxford famous for his logical subtlety.</note> and his like. I do not indeed approve of and admire everything written by them, but certainly not a few things show the greatest human subtlety and the sharpest reasons in physical matters, which Aristotle himself, if he rose from the dead, would admire and extol in a wondrous way—approving at least of their subtlety in most cases, if not their truth. You defend, furthermore, that the negation of the "One" is the "Divided." For a Chimera, you say, is "divided" because the parts from which it would consist, if it existed, are divided from each other and cannot be united. You think a "commensurable diameter" is "divided" because it is divided from itself and is dissonant. These are the words you use: "For a thing is detected to be false to the extent that it fights with itself and includes a contradiction." But what else is it to include a contradiction than to be divided within itself? Therefore, every true thing is "one" because it is consistent and harmonious with itself; every false thing is "divided" because it fights with itself and is not coherent with itself. But see how you can sustain your position. For if a thing is "one" because it is harmonious with itself and undivided from itself, then falsehood itself and the impossible will be "one" and "true." I would not say that this false thing or that which is—like a Chimera or a flying stag—is "one," but I mean the nature of the false and the impossible itself, which I will prove to be one and true. A Chimera, according to your dogma, is divided because its parts are always divided from each other, and also because it is divided from itself; for a Chimera is not a Chimera. By the same logic, a "commensurable diameter" is divided; for it cannot be understood otherwise than as something dissonant from itself and fighting with itself. But if you look at "the False" itself separately, the false is false, and the impossible is impossible. Neither, therefore, fights with itself; neither is dissonant from itself. For the same reason, the dead do not fight with themselves; for they are dead who are already dead. Therefore, any of these is "one" and "true" if a thing is "one" because it is undivided from itself. Furthermore, how is it true that everything false "includes a contradiction"? Are there not many false things which, by the power of nature or of man, could be true? You also try to defend the definition of Truth again posed by you, saying that the "True" is that which seems to be what it is, and the "False" is what seems to be what it is not. Now you think it follows that the False is not the negation of the True. But to my argument—if you will pardon me—you have so far said nothing. The argument is this: If the True is what seems to be what it is, and the False is what seems to be what it is not, since there is no contradiction between "seeming to be what it is" and "seeming to be what it is not," the False will not be the negation of the True. For if neither man nor God existed in the nature of things, Socrates would not exist; thus he would not "seem to be what he is," nor "what he is not." He would therefore be neither true nor false; but he would be non-being. Therefore, "non-being" and "false" sometimes disagree. Even Blessed Thomas, whom you do not contradict, pronounces that truth and falsehood are contraries to each other if they are referred to the mind—upon which, in your opinion, the ratio of truth and falsehood depends. "True and false estimations," he says, "are contraries to each other," just as Aristotle says. Finally, you deny that good and evil are in turn...

He argues that if God is called "the One" because the term "Being" is too concrete, then "the One" must also be rejected for the same reason, and defends the use of earlier authorities like Augustine and Boethius alongside Aquinas.</summary>

For I spoke thus: "no negation, especially one that encompasses those things which do not exist, can be a <term>genus<note>A 'genus' is a general category in logic. Farewell, and be mindful of us. From Ferrara, the 11th day before the Kalends of June, 1491 <note>May 22, 1491.</note>.

### GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA TO
### ANTONIO OF FAENZA, GREETINGS.

<image-desc>Decorative initial V within a square frame, depicting a seated scholar at a lectern reading or writing in an interior setting.</image-desc>
<margin>He briefly corrects Antonio. He reviews those points about which Antonio doubts again.</margin>Just as my prior letter was far too brief or certainly more obscure in solving your questions regarding that little book I recently published, *On Being and the One*, you now repeat those same questions and doubt the same things. Indeed, I will not deny that in my first letter certain things were omitted to which no answer was given, lest I waste words on trivial matters; some things I treated briefly, as one who believed matters should be pointed out to a fellow philosopher rather than fully explained. Now, since you demand this of me, we shall pursue even the smallest details. Through each head of your questions, I will command you to remember what we wrote before, and I will rouse you, where necessary, to a deeper understanding of them. Furthermore, since you have touched neither the Platonic commentaries nor the Greek <term>Peripatetics<note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy.</note></term> until now (due to your ignorance of the Greek language), I shall lead you through the lines and decrees of the Latins—especially Thomas, who is more familiar to you—so that you may perceive the meanings of those Platonists discussed in my book. The first thing that affects you is this: by what logic do the Platonists place God above Being? For if God

<column-break/>

truly *is*, you say, then surely He truly and properly *is* "Being," and is called so; just as someone sitting is truly said to be "sitting" because he sits. You add: insofar as He is an <term>Idea<note>In Platonism, 'Ideas' or 'Forms' are the perfect, eternal patterns of all things.</note></term>, He is Being; much more so, insofar as He is God, will He exist so as to be called Being. Even if not all Platonists concede that the Idea and God are the same, you say it is enough to oppose me if even Themistius alone did not say what I have ascribed to the Platonists in common. You also cannot understand how I say God is called "the One," since by this we signify not *what* He is, but the *way* in which He is what He is. For if He is "the One," you ask, because He is all things uniquely, why should He not also be called "Being," since to be the One is to be all things that exist?
<margin>How essence and existence are held according to Thomas.</margin>He is not called "the One" as if He were only one thing. Therefore, He could equally be called Being, even if He were not the only being. These are the first things from which you cannot extricate yourself; but in a few words, and just as I promised—even from those things known to you—I shall remove every scrap of doubt. You know that in Thomas, the **essence** of a thing is one thing, and its **existence** is another. The existence of a thing is that by which the thing *is* (that is, it exists); the essence is that by which a thing attains a certain species, such as that of a horse, a stone, or a shrub. Therefore, what is called "essence" is also called <term>quiddity<note>Literally 'whatness'; the defining nature of a thing.</note></term> by more recent scholars, because from the notion of essence we know "what" the thing is. Since, therefore, as Aristotle teaches in the second book of the *Posterior Analytics*, <margin>Aristotle. Another aforementioned point.</margin> the question we ask when we inquire "whether a rose exists" is one thing, and it is another when we want to know "what a rose is." The first question pertains to **existence**. The second pertains to **essence**, or (to use the words of the moderns) to **quiddity**. Again, remember that according to the opinion of Thomas, all things short of God that exist in act are composed of **essence** and **existence** (for so he calls *esse*). God Himself is neither composed of essence and existence, nor is He "an essence"; rather, He is pure existence itself, from which every other existence of created things is subsequently derived, <margin>The third point from Thomas.</margin> being communicated to created essences. Add to this that by the word "Being" (*ens*), essence is usually indicated; but by the word "is" (*est*), existence is indicated, not essence. This same Thomas teaches you this in the first question *On Evil*, where he says: when we say this or that is a "Being," we respond to the question asking "what" the thing is (which, as we said, pertains to the essence); but when we say "it is" or "it is not," we satisfy one asking "whether" the thing is (which pertains to existence). Now the entire opinion of the Platonists and the solution to your objection <margin>Solution of the argument from the opinion of Thomas.</margin> is open. For if God is **existence** itself, but not "a being" in the sense of an **essence**, then just as we truly say God *is*, so we truly deny that God is "a Being" (*ens*). I cannot help but wonder that, even if you have not read the Platonists, you—who are frequent in reading Thomas—insist so much on this argument: "God is, therefore He is Being." For Thomas himself says, word for word, that these do not mutually follow—to exist (*esse*) and to be a Being (*ens*)—but pertain to entirely different and unrelated questions. Indeed, what need is there for Thomas's authority here? Who but a fool doubts "whether" God is? Yet who but a fool presumes to know even in the smallest part "what" God is? Since, therefore, <margin>Note. Poliziano, Simonides the poet.</margin> knowing "whether" God is and knowing "what" God is are most different things, the statement by which it is said "God is" will also be most different from that by which it is said "God is Being." For the former asserts that God exists (than which nothing is more certain), while the latter dares to pronounce what God is in some part (concerning which nothing is more uncertain). Wherefore, our most learned Poliziano answered you most correctly when you asked during a dispute "what" God was; he replied, following the opinion of the poet Simonides, that he did not know what He was. But far from this purpose is the example...

<meta>This page continues Giovanni Pico della Mirandola's response to Antonio Cittadini regarding the metaphysical hierarchy of "the One" and "Being." # ON BEING AND THE ONE

<margin>Solution to the confirmation.</margin>
Regarding what you assert about the one who is sitting: "being a sitter" and "to sit" do not differ in the same way as "to be" <note>original: *esse*</note> and "being" <note>original: *ens*</note>.

<margin>He shows that the example is not valid.</margin>
For I shall answer the same question when I say "Socrates sits" as when I say "he is a sitter"—namely, to whatever question asks me about Socrates' posture. Just as when we say "Socrates is white" and "Socrates is whitening," the same question is satisfied: namely, the one asking what kind of thing Socrates is. But the relationship is not the same between "being" <note>The noun form of 'to be,' referring to a thing that exists.</note> and "is" <note>The verb form, indicating existence itself.</note>. To repeat the same point once more: the former reveals to the questioner *what* the thing is, while the latter reveals *if* the thing is. From this it is also clear: if God is called "being" as an "Idea," it does not follow that He bears the name of "being" insofar as He is conceived as absolute in Himself. For just as He takes on the role of an "Idea," so He takes on the role of an "essence"; but in truth, He is greater than the name of "being," understood as being above all essence and any relationship to created things. For the fact that He is not called "being" is not due to a deficiency, as you believe, but due to His eminence <note>Pico argues that God is "above being" because He is so superior that human categories of "existence" are too small for Him.</note>.

<margin>Solution to another argument.</margin>
<margin>The Platonists.</margin>
Wherefore, the Platonists also declare Him to be "above being" rather than "non-being." I truly do not know why you so stubbornly count Themistius <note>A 4th-century philosopher and statesman known for his commentaries on Aristotle.</note> among their ranks. If you ask the ancients, they will all answer that Themistius is a Peripatetic <note>A follower of Aristotle.</note>, not a Platonist. If you ask the man himself, I think he would call himself a paraphraser and follower of Aristotle, not Plato. But perhaps (forgive me for joking) you drag him into the Academy <note>Plato’s school in Athens.</note> against his will so that you do not appear entirely ignorant of Platonic and Greek matters, having at least read Themistius thanks to our friend Hermolaus <note>Hermolaus Barbarus (1454–1493), a famous humanist who translated Themistius into Latin.</note> who made him available in Latin. But even if Themistius were a Platonist—and even if he were entirely correct—we have clarified abundantly in both this and the previous letter that nothing he says contradicts our view, since the Platonists will say some things about God insofar as He is God, and other things insofar as He is an Idea.

<margin>That Themistius is not a Platonist, but a Peripatetic with Hermolaus.</margin>
<margin>Solution to another argument.</margin>
Let us come to why God is called "The One," even though He is not called "being." Recall what we wrote to you in our first letters. When the Platonists call God "The One," they are not stating *what* He is, but *how* He is that which He is—though you do not yet understand this sufficiently. I will speak more clearly. If you ask a man of the Academy what God is, he will answer not only that he cannot tell you what He is, but that you have no right even to ask. Indeed, he would say such a question about Him is unworthy. For He who is above all essence and above all that can be understood, can only be asserted by the philosopher to be most similar to "Unity." For just as Unity is the principle of all numbers, so is He the principle of all things that exist. Just as Unity, in its indivisible simplicity, encompasses all numbers—both even and odd—while being itself neither even nor odd, so He, in His impartible infinity, encloses and contains all things. Do you see what is meant? That by the name "The One," it is not indicated *what* God is, but *how* He is that which He is. Finally, if we say "God is like Unity," which is what we mean when we give Him the title of "The One," we shall certainly be speaking the truth. If we say to our listeners "God is like a being," we shall surely make them laugh. But why say more to you on such obvious points? For He says these things are enough, or I do not know what words could ever be enough.

<margin>Why God is under no genus.</margin>
It is also gathered from this why God is under no genus <note>A 'genus' is a logical category, like 'animal' or 'plant.'</note>. For the genera of things are essences; but God is neither an essence nor does He possess an essence. Therefore, since "being" is sometimes understood by the Peripatetics to encompass only the ten categories <note>Aristotle’s ten 'Categories' or ways of being (substance, quality, quantity, etc.).</note>, it is manifest that God is not contained under the name of "being" as it is sometimes used by the followers of Aristotle. But you insist that Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas.</note> and others of that same school often use "substance" and "being" in such a way that God is called both a substance and a being. As if I were ignorant of this—which everyone knows!—or as if it were not enough for me that they occasionally do otherwise; for they do not always use these words in that way, but only sometimes.

<column-break/>

<margin>Solution to another objection, namely the third main one.</margin>
Let us move on to those things you object regarding the opposition of "The One" and "the divided." In the same way, I think, you test me with childish quibbles, as if playing a game. For you say, "if the divided is false, then surely the false is not divided." For "false" is not divided from itself, because "false" is "false." Likewise, you say that the dead do not fight among themselves, for they are dead who are already dead. Furthermore, you say it is "Antonian" <note>A reference to Antonio's own logic or perhaps a rhetorical jab.</note> to say that things which are false fight with themselves. If this "fight" must happen with fists or weapons, I admit that even the dead do not fight among themselves, nor are they false. But just as "false" is "false," so "to be false" is not "false," but true; therefore it is not divided, but one. You add that it is

<margin>Solution to another.</margin>
falsely stated by me that "the false" is enclosed in contradiction. For there are many things that are false which could be true by the power of nature or of man. But consider this: everything that is false, for as long as it is false, is enclosed in contradiction. Just as some things are so false that they could become true, while others are so false that they can never be true, so some things are so contradictory and in conflict with themselves that they can never return to friendship and concord. Others hate each other in such a way that they can, nevertheless, return to favor.

<margin>Example</margin>
An example will make this manifest: "A man is a lion" is always false because it always contains a contradiction; and just as it can never be brought to union, so it can never be brought to truth. But "that I am sitting" is neither true nor false <note>It is a 'contingent' statement—it depends on whether Pico is actually sitting.</note>. If, however, you add "that I am sitting while I am standing," you immediately bring in falsehood, and thus you bring in contradiction. For "that I am sitting while I am standing" includes a contradiction; and as soon as it ceases to be false—as when I begin to sit—it immediately returns from division to unity. Furthermore, the things you object regarding the opposition of the false and the true have already been resolved in my previous letter.

<margin>Solution to another.</margin>
For you say: "If the true is that which is seen to be what it is, and the false is that which is seen to be what it is not, since there is no contradiction between 'seeming to be what it is' and 'seeming to be what it is not,' the false will not be the negation of the true." But I do not define the nature of the false as consisting in something "seeming to be what it is not." Rather, I maintain that its nature consists in this: that it *is not* that which it is said to be. For "false gold" is false because it is not gold; and as far as the definition of falsehood is concerned, it is accidental whether it *seems* to be or *is* something other than gold.

<margin>Solution to another.</margin>
<margin>Note.</margin>
As for your claim that I have not resolved your argument by which you prove that Good and Evil are contraries, I will speak frankly. I did not think a solution was needed where there was no knot. Your argument is of this kind: "Good is to be desired, and evil is to be avoided. Desiring and avoiding are contrary motions. Therefore, Good and Evil are contraries." To me, your reasoning seems so effective and of such great force that it proves to be contraries not only Good and Evil (about which someone might perhaps doubt), but even "Being" and "Non-being," which everyone knows are contradictories.

<margin>Solution to another.</margin>
For we shall conclude thus: "Being is to be desired, non-being is to be avoided; desiring and avoiding are contrary motions; therefore being and non-being are contraries." Either, then, grant me that being and non-being are contraries, or I shall not grant you that good and evil are contraries. But you will say another reason must be resolved. For "non-being" is not a genus; how then is evil "nothing," when Aristotle says in the *Categories* <note>original: *prædicamentis*</note> that good and evil are the "genera of contraries"? Everyone is full of

<margin>Solution to another.</margin>
<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
the interpretations of Aristotle regarding the solution to this question, to whom I referred you in my previous letter, lest I entangle us both in unnecessary labor. Therefore, I will omit the fact that it did not displease Simplicius <note>A 6th-century commentator on Aristotle.</note> that Aristotle spoke there according to the custom of the Pythagoreans, who establish two orders of things...

If you pay attention, you will see why he wishes this to be so: it is because evil itself is entirely ignorant of the properties of a contrary. For he concedes that these things can, in some way, obtain the name of "contrary" only insofar as they do not possess the full character of evil, but retain something of goodness which they have not yet lost. Therefore, they are in some way contraries only insofar as they are not entirely evil. But if I were to set before you death or blindness, and I were to ask whether these are "true evils" according to the judgment of Thomas, and again whether they oppose each other with that "hope of contrariety" you speak of, I do not see at all what you would answer. For if these are evils—and in that very place from which you bring Thomas’s testimony for your side—he contends with great assertion that these things can in no way be contraries, which is the very "hope of contrariety" you bring into the open. With what mind, then, do you affirm that according to Thomas, good resists evil by some contrary opposition? Certainly, you ought to have considered this: that what is conceded regarding certain imperfect evils (because of the mixture of goodness they still retain) must not be transferred to the unmixed and absolute nature of evil itself.

# EXPOSITIONS ON BEING AND THE ONE
<meta>catchword: sol- [solutions]</meta>

## ANTONIO OF FAENZA SENDS GREETINGS TO
## GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA.

<margin>
I have not forgotten, dear colleague <note>original: *compater*</note>, do not doubt it. I remember everything quite clearly; you will see plainly that it is no great loss if those very light matters we discussed together in person should fall away. For these are all the things with which you occupy yourself and with which you keep me, a man not without business, occupied. But lest you believe I am imitating Nicoletto <note>Nicoletto Vernia (c. 1420–1499), a philosopher at Padua who famously clashed with Pico and sometimes ignored his letters</note>, who thought it beneath him to answer you when you wrote against him, I shall briefly note the solutions to your doubts. "God is": I said it is truly said that God is. I would define Him, according to the opinion of Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian Neoplatonist who argued God is "beyond being"</note>, as being greater than every name, even this name "God," as he did in his book *On Mystical Theology*. You have not yet moved Dionysius from his place by your writings; nor is it a wonder, for he stands far stronger than you, even though you might despise his authority when I use it against you. I likewise said that it is sometimes conceded by those who deny God is "being" that God is "one." I have declared the reasoning for their opinion both in these commentaries of ours *On Being and the One* and in two letters to you. But you might say: I said in my last letter that there is no one who does not know that among Thomas and other Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle</note>, "being" and "essence" are often accepted such that both are said of God. But it is enough for me that they sometimes use "being" and "essence" in such a way that they cannot be said of God—this is what you must disprove. Nor will you ever bring more to this matter than is necessary. Furthermore, in your booklet, there is a crude objection: for the Platonists, when they say this, do not mean that essence and being are in God, but rather that they do not differ in Him. But "being" <note>original: *esse*</note> holds that place in God which "essence" holds in other things, so that for Him, essence is nothing other than being itself. Again, you might say: read the earlier letters and you will see. For your argument is rather tasteless <note>original: *insulsum*</note>, since it is one thing for a thing "to be" (that is, to exist) and another to be "being" <note>original: *ens*</note>, as "being" is an essential predicate. Let it be true; you must confess it to be true, unless you then abandon the words of Thomas. These are the things which, if you had seen them before, perhaps you would not have erred. It is demonstrated. Thomas. I marvel that you always insist on the same things; has it not been said a thousand times already that "being" can be taken so that it is said of Him—namely, when it signifies "that which is"—but then again it can be taken so that it is not said of Him—namely, when it signifies "essence," which is different from existence? "Something" and "being": See how much you are deceived; according to Thomas, evil is not such that we can answer "something" or "being" to one asking what God is, and yet to one asking "what is sin?" we can answer that it is "evil." Furthermore, you will dare to say: "Being," when it is interchangeable with "good" in Thomas, is not taken in the same way as when it is denied of God? You are joking against yourself, for this is the very thing I say, and whether you do not wish to or are unable to understand what has been drummed in a hundred times: in the first way, God is not "being," although in the second way (namely, through "being") the question "is He being?" may be answered. For I was saying that not in every way, but in some way, even according to Thomas, God cannot be called "being." However, it is permitted to argue thus, colleague: God in the first way is not "being," therefore in some way He is not "being." "Narrowed": These "narrowed" and "not narrowed" terms are yours, not Thomas's. Ridiculous: That which is not asked ridiculously is not solved ridiculously, although many things are asked [so]...
</margin>

<image-desc>A circular woodcut emblem. In the center is a radiant sun with a human face. A circular band contains the Latin text "DEVS EST VNVS" (God is One) and other philosophical axioms. The emblem is placed to the left of the main text block.</image-desc>

Conclusions once conceded by word, unless perhaps you have forgotten, were:
"God is"; "God is one"; "God is not God." This last includes a contradiction: that the first being is not, and that gold is [God]. Against these I formed several objections and gave them in writing; I was expecting you to finally respond to these objections after you were silent for four months, perhaps entangled in greater business. But you respond only to the first ones, which I had previously formed against the solutions of certain arguments. You say, however, in this first way: "I shall show you through the decrees of the Latins, and especially of Blessed Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note>, that although God truly and properly *is*, He is nonetheless not properly *being* <note>original: *ens*</note>." For God, according to Thomas, is not among those things in which there is essence. Likewise, according to the same Thomas: the word "being" usually signifies "essence" and answers the question "What is it?" <note>original: *quid est*</note>; but the word "is" <note>original: *est*</note> is usually returned to the question "Does it exist?" <note>original: *an est*</note>. Wherefore you conclude, according to Thomas, that God is not "being" if He neither "is" [in that sense] nor has essence, but merely exists.

But tell me, I ask, where in Thomas did you learn that God is not essence? Since all of Thomas cries out against this opinion! For in the first part [of the *Summa*], in the *Summa contra Gentiles*, in the *Disputed Questions*, in the booklet *On Being and Essence*, in the commentaries on Aristotle—in all places, finally, where the matter requires it—he both holds and proves that God is essence. Nor is there a need to cite the man’s words in so clear a matter; if you deny it, I shall recount more than is necessary. Furthermore, in your own booklet *On Being and the One*, unless it has slipped your mind, you previously said: "Therefore, according to the Platonists, God is not 'being' because God’s being is not different from His essence." How then, now following them and defending them, do you deny that God is essence?

Likewise, tell me: from what passage of Saint Thomas did you perceive that the word "being" usually signifies essence and not also "to be" <note>existence</note>? Since in the fourth book of the *Metaphysics* and the first question of *On Truth*, and elsewhere, he says that it is called "being" <note>*ens*</note> because it *is* <note>*est*</note>, but a "thing" <note>*res*</note> because it is essence or has essence. Likewise, tell me where in Thomas you could have known that it is reasonably answered to the question "What is it?" if one says "it is being"? For it is tasteless to ask "What is it?" unless it is known that the thing *is*, as Aristotle in the second book of the *Posterior Analytics* and Thomas openly testify. By "to be," I mean the way substances and accidents "are," in which both are essence; not the way privations and negations "are," in which Thomas seems to deny that what is usually answered to the question "What is it?" can be found, whether that be true or false—which he omits for the present. 

The words of Thomas in the first question of *On Evil*—which, if I am not mistaken, provided you the occasion for error, and which you also seem to hint at—are these: "Being is said in two ways: in one way, according to which it signifies the nature of the ten categories, and thus neither evil nor any other privation is being, nor is it 'something'; in another way, according to which it answers the question 'Does it exist?' <note>*an est*</note>, and thus evil exists, just as blindness exists. Yet evil is not 'something,' because 'to be something' signifies not only what is answered to the question 'Does it exist?', but also what is answered to the question 'What is it?'" 

But repeat, I pray, more diligently the words of so great a philosopher; for they bear judgment against you, as is shown thus: Thomas plainly says "being" and "something" are said in two ways. In one way, that which has the nature of some category; in the other way, that which answers the question "Does it exist?" Now, "God" is the answer to the question "Does God exist?", and the response is not a lie; therefore, God is "being." If we must proceed further, let us say this, departing in nothing from Thomas: since it is rightly answered to the question "Does it exist?" that "it is being," then that which is the answer to whether a thing truly and properly *is* must truly and properly be "being." For just as the fact that God simply *is* relates to that which truly and properly is, so to one asking whether He truly and properly is, "God" is reasonably answered; therefore, God is truly and properly "being." 

Furthermore, Thomas calls "something" and "being" according to the first way that which answers the question "What is it?" To one asking "What is it that preserves and moves the world, and that raises the dead?", "God" is reasonably answered. Therefore, in both the first and second ways, God is "being" and "something." Furthermore, will you dare, according to Thomas, to deny that God is "good" or "one"? Since, therefore, "good" and "being" and "one" are mutually interchangeable, how, according to Thomas, can it be said or imagined that God is not "being"? 

You, however, seem to argue from these words, if I am not mistaken, in this way: "Being" in one way means that which signifies the nature of the ten categories; but God is in no category, as Thomas himself testifies; therefore, God is neither "being" nor "essence." But you ought to have noticed (suffer me to joke) that if the reasoning is effective that God is not "being" in the first way—for although He is in no category, nothing prevents Him from truly and properly existing in the nature of things—and if it is truthfully answered to the question "Does He exist?", how could you not know that He is "being" in the other way? Furthermore, the reasoning has no strength. For the sense of Thomas’s words is of this kind: "Being" in one way means that which signifies the nature of the ten categories; that is, what signifies substance and accident and all positive things contained in the ten categories—either through themselves (as species and genera) or as certain principles, whether narrowed or not (like primary matter and fortune in the category of substance, and God, and altogether substantial differences). In this way, certainly, negations and privations cannot belong to a category. 

In another way, "being" is said of that which can be answered to the question "Does it exist?", whether it be a true and positive being or not. Whence, adding an example, he says: "and thus evil is," just as "blindness is"; that is, "and thus evil is being," just as "blindness is being." For in Thomas, there is no difference in the words whether one says "is" or "is being." As for what he subjoins—"because to be something signifies not only..."—it does not tend toward the meaning that to one asking "What is the moon?"...

He critiques Pico's claim that God exists without having an essence, citing numerous works of Aquinas to prove God's status as the ultimate Being.</summary>

So he says: These same things apply to those who, in the first question concerning evil, [discuss] "God" and "Lord" and it is denied how it is "being." But if we show it is not true, then the reasoning is solved. But from **Thomas**: Yet you yourself, in explaining the words of **Thomas** above, fell into our opinion when you said God is called "being" insofar as "being" answers the question "whether he is" <note>original: *an est*</note>, but not insofar as it signifies the essence of things. Do not ascribe false things to **Thomas**, for I do not imitate you, dear colleague <note>original: *compater*</note>, you who say that from **Thomas's** opinion good and evil are properly and truly contraries, and that this is even confirmed by the authority of **Simplicius** <note>Simplicius of Cilicia (c. 490–560 AD), a Neoplatonist commentator on Aristotle</note>. When I showed there was not a single word of this in **Simplicius**, you replied that you had gathered that this was said by **Simplicius**. But the book is in our hands, dear colleague. **Simplicius** does not say that; therefore, you gathered it incorrectly. For it has now been shown.
It has also been demonstrated that you have not demonstrated well. For previously, "God" and "Idea" are the same, nor is the "being" of the Idea different from the "being" of God; but because the definitions are different, one is pronounced concerning God as He is God, and another as He is the Idea.
<margin>Composition</margin> This composition is according to reason, not according to the thing itself. 
<margin>Subtle</margin> **The Subtle [Doctor]** <note>A reference to Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), known as the *Doctor Subtilis*</note>. So subtle indeed that you could not understand it even after it was repeated, as will soon be clear from the trouble you cause us.
It is not possible to speak with you unless [terms] are predefined; but you should know that this kind of speaking is often used by famous authors, even sacred ones, such as that [phrase] "according to the likeness of Melchizedek" <note>A biblical reference to Christ being a priest according to the "order" or "likeness" of Melchizedek (Hebrews 7:15)</note>.
Furthermore, if "The One" which the Platonists pronounce regarding God is not denominative but substantive, this is because you are entirely ignorant of Platonic matters and cannot understand the Greek language. See, therefore, how subtle this reasoning of naming is.
Furthermore, it is clear from here how "matter" is called "one" in one way, and "God" in another.
Platonists: how can you say I follow the reasoning of the Platonists rather than **Dionysius**, when I do not hold God as "uniquely" <note>original: *vnice*</note> [all things] either among the Platonists or in **Dionysius**? Therefore, I could [say] all these things even if God were not. And gold would be gold.

<column-break/>

...or thunder, it would be answered reasonably: if it is said "it is a being" or "something," as you seem to have thought, for such a solution is ridiculous. But this kind of "to be" signifies "something," especially according to the first mode: that which can reasonably be answered to the question "what is it?" For example, it signifies that it is a substance, or an accident, or an animal, or a color, or something of this sort, which can rightly be answered to one asking "what is it?" Blindness, however, and evil are none of these things. That **Blessed Thomas** would not wish to interpret the first part of the division with that mind, he himself explains in the first part, question 48, article two, where it is asked whether evil is in things. For responding to the second argument, he says: "As it is said in the sixth [book of] Metaphysics, Being <note>original: *ens*</note> is said in two ways: In one way, according to which it signifies the entity of a thing as it is divided through the ten predicaments <note>The ten Categories of Aristotle</note>, and thus it is convertible with 'thing'; and in this way, no privation <note>A 'privation' is the absence of a quality that should be present, like blindness is the absence of sight</note> is a being, and thus neither is evil. In the other way, 'being' is said that signifies the truth of a proposition which consists in composition, the sign of which is this word 'is': and this is the 'being' that answers the question 'whether it is' <note>original: *an est*</note>, and thus we say blindness is in the eye, or any other privation: and in this way even evil is called a being." These are the words of **Thomas**. Do you not see, therefore, how he pronounces that the first part of the division is convertible with "thing"? Yet he does not deny that God is a "thing" and whatever is good; for by that argument and the first question on evil, he confesses that every good is a thing.
If these things are true, the reasoning I spoke against the Platonists is not yet solved: "being" <note>original: *ens*</note> is so called because it "is," just as "a seater" <note>original: *sedens*</note> is so called because he "sits." God, however, not only "is," but also "is" properly and truly; therefore, He is truly and properly "being." For you wished to solve the argument not from the Platonists but from **Thomas**, ascribing to **Thomas** things that no one who has read him would fail to know are entirely foreign to the man's opinion. 
Hence, the other reasoning I gave is not solved: if God is "being" in that part where He is an "Idea," much more is He "being" in that part where He is God; for this is something absolute, while that is relative. For it is not true what you just replied—that God is "Essence" in that part where He is an Idea, but not in that part where He is God—for it has already been shown that He is both "being" and "essence."
Furthermore, if God is "being" and "essence" in that part where He is an Idea, it is necessary that there be composition in God, which is easily proven in this way: for you previously said that according to the Platonists, God is not "being" because the "being" of God is not different from God. If, therefore, the Idea is "being," this will be because the "being" of the Idea is different from the Idea; but the "being" of the Idea cannot be located or imagined outside of God if God is the Idea (as was given); therefore, it is necessary that there be composition in God.
You say, furthermore, that God is called "The One" by the Platonists because He is similar to unity; which, although it contains all numbers in power (namely even and odd), is itself neither even nor odd. A "subtle" <note>Sarcastic reference to the "Subtle Doctor"</note> way of naming, indeed! Which, besides the fact that God cannot be similar to things—as **Cicero** and **Thomas** say, for the exemplar of the world is not similar to the world, nor is a man similar to a painting—cannot stand for another reason. For that which borrows a name from another due to similarity or analogy is usually called by the proper name of the same thing: we call a statue a "man," not "human," even if we do not imitate the man; there is also a difference in the propositions of "place": or we call a "maximal proposition" <note>A self-evident principle in logic</note> a "place" from the analogy of a natural place, but not "local." Therefore, if God obtained the name from unity due to similarity, He should not be called "One," but rather "Unity."
Furthermore, if every concrete name signifies one thing [the subject] and another [the form], why do the Platonists call God "Likeness" rather than "Like"? Furthermore, if matter is "one" according to the Platonists, as you write, and the unity of matter is not one thing and matter another—which I do not think you deny—by what reason can "one" be defended? For it is not similar to unity; otherwise, it would also be similar to God.
Furthermore, you also said before that God is "one" because He is "uniquely" all things. But now you seem to approve the reasoning of the Platonists rather than **Dionysius**, perhaps having cast off the former; if you still hold it, it remains for you to answer the arguments that have been written. For the root upon which you lean to solve my objections—namely, that God is neither "being" nor "essence"—is not true, as I have now nearly declared.
But let us now come to the definition of "Truth" demanded by you. You said in the earlier booklet that "Truth" is defined by **Augustine** thus: "Truth is that which is." And lest the definition of truth and being seem the same, you say it ought to be added in this way: "Truth is that which is that which it is said to be." I, therefore, opposed the definition in this way: "to be that which it is said to be" seems to signify nothing else than "to be that which it is called." But for a thing to be called by this name or that is for it to "seem" to be this or that; wherefore it finally seemed to be concluded in this way: "to be that which it is said to be" is nothing else than "to be what it seems to be." Since, therefore, there is no contradiction in "seeming to be what is" and "seeming to be what is not," I proved that "falsehood" was not the negation of "truth," if the definition held. 
Since you have now explained your definition more clearly, there will be many things that seem more numerous to disprove your formal definition. For you say "Truth is that which it is said to be." This is: "Truth is that which is that which itself is." For example, gold is "true gold" because it is gold. But against this: if God did not exist and gold were to exist, gold would be that which itself is, and it would be "true," yet it would not be [real], since it would match no Idea—for you later say that things are "true" because they match and respond to Ideas. If the true definition of man is "rational animal" <note>original: *animal rationale*</note>, it is a contradiction to think that if God did not exist and man were a "rational animal," man would not be man. Nor can that be answered which was said elsewhere: namely, that it involves a contradiction for God not to exist and gold to exist. For it can be imagined that gold exists and yet God does not exist, nor any first cause. Nor do they openly confess this: for they think there are infinite worlds, or that the heavens are multiplied unto infinity, or many similar things; they do not therefore deny that gold exists which is seen with the eyes and handled with the hands.
Furthermore, even if it were gold, it would not be "true." Therefore, the formal definition of truth is not "to be that which itself is." Just as the definition of a man would not be formal if I said: "If God did not exist and man were a rational animal, man would not therefore be a man." For nothing can be deprived of its own definition, nor can a definition fit anyone to whom the defined name cannot be applied. Furthermore, you cannot deny that gold is "gold" by nature before it matches God...

<margin>
**Dionysius**: As you boast with a loud voice that you have ever read [him], yet know that it is the same among the Platonists that the type of God is "Unity," and in **Dionysius** that God is "uniquely" all things.
The root upon which you lean: see how firm that root is, which you can neither overcome with any strength nor tear up with hard iron. 
I therefore: To all these things it was determined in the previous letters.
This is true: You love gold too much, dear colleague, to attribute so much to it that you believe it can exist even if God does not.
Worlds they think: Those who say these things, and say that gold exists, say conflicting things and are ignorant of their own voice.
If God did not exist: And gold were gold: and gold were not gold—impossible. For the impossible gives birth to the impossible.
</margin>

<summary>Antonio of Faenza defends his metaphysical positions against Pico della Mirandola, arguing that God can be properly termed "Being" and "Essence" according to Thomas Aquinas, while critiquing Pico's definitions of "Truth" and "The One." The text explores the logical consequences of defining things (like gold) independently of God as the First Cause.</summary>
