<meta>This page continues the philosophical dispute between Antonio of Faenza and Giovanni Pico della Mirandola regarding the nature of being (ens) and truth (verum). Antonio is responding to Pico’s arguments about whether truth and being are identical and how falsehood relates to the "One."</meta>

# ON BEING AND THE ONE

<margin>
**Absolute.** For it is not an accidental relation distinct from gold, but a substantial one, regarding which see **Henry of Ghent** <note>Henry of Ghent (c. 1217–1293) was an influential Scholastic philosopher who argued for the "intentional" distinction between essence and existence.</note> except for the matter of dignity.
</margin>

<margin>
**We said the same.** Everything that is, is this: that which it is; wherefore every being <note>original: *ens*</note> is true, and every true thing is a being. But the reasoning <note>original: *ratio*</note> for one is different from the other.
</margin>

<margin>
**Blindness, however.** It is one thing for blindness to be true, and another for it to be true that blindness is blindness; wherefore you labor in many words in vain to show that blindness is not true.
</margin>

...of **ideas**: for the absolute is prior to the relation. Gold, therefore, even if it be gold, nevertheless cannot "be" unless a certain likeness <note>A reference to the Platonic "exemplar" or form</note> is added beyond the nature of the gold, by which it corresponds to its exemplar; whether the likeness be one thing and the gold another or not is a question that belongs elsewhere. Furthermore, you seem to posit a definition of **being** in this way: "being is that which is." Otherwise, you would not say the definition of **Augustine** <note>St. Augustine defined truth as "that which is."</note> must be completed in this way: "The true is that which is itself," lest, if we said only "that which is," the definition of the true and of being appear to be the same. 

If, therefore, the definition of being is "that which is," by that same reasoning by which being is "that which is," it is also itself and being. Therefore, by the same reasoning that something is a being, it must also be true—which is utterly false. Furthermore, if the true is "that which is itself," then **blindness** will be true, and **death**, and **falsehood**, and **non-being** entirely. For blindness is blindness, death is death, falsehood is falsehood, and non-being is non-being; any of these would be true without any intellect thinking of them at all.

But if any of these is true, it must be **one**. But I know you will soon say: "Did I not concede that any of these is 'to be' and therefore 'true' in these words I wrote to you: 'just as falsehood is false, so it is true that falsehood is false; it is not false, but true, and for that reason not divided, but one'?" But against this is the fact that every **one** is **good**, and in the same way, true. **Blindness**, however, is not only bad, but according to what you write, it is entirely bad and tastes of nothing good. Similarly with **death**. For you seem to call the nature of blindness and death an "absolute bad nature" unmixed with good; therefore none of these is true, nor "one," especially when the soul is not thinking. 

Furthermore, the true is that which squares with an **idea**; but blindness and death have no idea. Furthermore, if God did not exist, nor anything else capable of intelligence, nonetheless non-being is non-being, and nothing is nothing; for it is either something or nothing. It is certainly not "something," as is established; therefore it is "nothing" and "non-being." It would be then what it is now, and would be so then. If, therefore, the true is that which is what it is, then non-being and nothing would be true—which cannot happen, for it would square with no idea. Therefore, the formal definition of the true is not "to be that which it is itself." 

Furthermore, you try to defend what you previously said: that any falsehood contains a **contradiction**. You say every falsehood contains a contradiction as long as it is false. You also add these words: "But for me to sit is neither true nor false. If, however, you add that I sit while I am standing, you immediately bring in contradiction just as you do falsehood; for 'me sitting while I stand' contains a contradiction. And as soon as it ceases to be false—as when I begin to sit—it immediately returns from division to unity." But see, I ask, if you agree with yourself. For you think the true and the false are opposed, not as contraries, but as affirmation and negation. How then can a middle ground be found, unless there be a middle between affirmation and negation? Furthermore, every proposition is either true or false, unless you deny the first principle: that in any contradiction, one part is true and the other is false.

<margin>
**True.** For "me sitting" is always either true or false, because I am always either sitting or not sitting. And what is said—that "me sitting" is neither true nor false—means that this proposition does not determine truth or falsehood by itself, which is what **necessary** <term>Necessary propositions: statements that must be true by their nature, like 2+2=4</term> propositions do. But since it can be true (when I sit) and false (when I do not), it is indeterminate by itself toward either. But doubtlessly, **dear colleague**, you abound in paper and leisure, since you descend to things known even to boys.
</margin>

<margin>
**But true.** Good and bad are in things; false and true are in the soul. Therefore a true proposition can signify a bad thing, even though the proposition itself, insofar as it is true, is good; and the thing itself, insofar as it is bad, is false. It is one thing to say, "It is true that Judas sins," and another to say, "The sin of Judas is true."
</margin>

<margin>
**Moreover every.** Every falsehood is "divided," as we said in the previous book, but not every falsehood is equally false; therefore not every falsehood is equally "divided," as we said to you in the letters. For those things which are necessarily false and always false are not "equally" false to those which are not necessarily or always false. Wherefore, these and those do not have the same character of division. See if there is anything in these that I should have feared to say or that you can refute.
</margin>

How then is "you sitting" neither true nor false? Indeed, I do not see by what reason you can maintain this unless you remove all philosophy and every concept of contraries. Furthermore, if every falsehood contains a contradiction as long as it is false, then "God does not exist" (which is false) will contain a contradiction as long as God exists in the nature of things. If, therefore, God did not exist, then "God does not exist" would be neither false nor a contradiction. If, then, the false is the negation of the true as you posit, it will be **true** that God does not exist if God were not to exist. But every true thing is good, as you grant; therefore, if God did not exist, it would be **good** that God does not exist—which seems absurd. For it would be neither simply good nor good for anyone, but entirely non-being. 

Furthermore, in your previous letter, you said every falsehood is "divided" from itself because it contains a contradiction. If, therefore, not every falsehood simply and absolutely contains a contradiction, but only as long as it is false is it "divided." For if the reason for being and the cause do not apply to it, then surely that which follows from the reason does not apply either. And if neither "one" nor the other applies simply, then not every falsehood is simply "divided"—which cannot be granted. For every falsehood is simply and absolutely "being/non-being" <note>An ontological contradiction</note>. For both are converted; therefore, by the same reasoning, it is simply "divided," if being divided and non-being go together. 

Furthermore, every true thing is simply **one**; therefore every false thing is simply **divided**. For one is the negation of the other. Furthermore, if I show that every falsehood is divided in the absolute sense, what reason was there for you not to dare to state simply and absolutely that every falsehood is divided, but only then when there is opposition? 

We demonstrate the division of the false in this way: "Socrates sits" is false; but "Socrates sits" is not "Socrates sits," therefore it is divided from itself. For if "Socrates sits" is "Socrates sits," and "Socrates sitting" is "Socrates sitting" (for both are linked), then if "Socrates sitting" is Socrates, it follows by simple conversion that "Socrates is Socrates, sitting is sitting," therefore he sits—which is false. By the same reasoning, I will prove that a **Chimera** <note>A mythological creature used in philosophy to represent an impossible or non-existent entity.</note> is not a Chimera, nor is "to be a Chimera" "to be a Chimera." For if a Chimera is a Chimera, it is an animal. For we understand a Chimera to be an animal composed of a goat and a lion, or something of that sort. If it is an animal, it can live and die—which we do not agree upon, we who posit that a Chimera can by no means be produced by nature, just as a **golden mountain** cannot be generated. 

Furthermore, if a Chimera is an animal, some animal is a Chimera; but no animal is a Chimera. For every animal "is" and "lives" and is simply a being and something; for that which is not, is not an animal except equivocally. Therefore, a Chimera is not a Chimera by the same reasoning, nor is "to be a Chimera" "to be a Chimera." For if "to be generated" is "to be moved," then generation is motion. Therefore, if generation is not motion, then "to be generated" is not "to be moved." By similar reasoning, if "to be a Chimera" is "to be a Chimera," then a Chimera is a Chimera. For both are linked. But a Chimera is not a Chimera, as has been proved; therefore "to be a Chimera" is not "to be a Chimera." 

Furthermore, no Chimera is a Chimera, therefore it is **true** that "no Chimera is a Chimera"; therefore it is **false** that "some Chimera is a Chimera." By the same reasoning, it will be shown that a **vacuum** is not a vacuum since it does not exist, nor is blindness blindness if nothing is blind. Yet always, non-being is non-being; for it to not be non-being is both true and necessary, just as for a Chimera not to be is both true and necessary. Why then was it necessary to fear being refuted if you had stated simply and absolutely that every falsehood is divided in itself? Therefore, there was no need to flee to "contradiction." Next, you frankly confess that my argument—by which I proved good and evil are contraries to each other—was not solved; but you say it was not solved because there was no "knot" in it. By Hercules, what a clever excuse! But it is a wonder: if there was no knot, how could you have untied the knot?

<summary>Antonio of Faenza critiques Pico della Mirandola's definitions of Truth and Being, arguing that if truth is merely "being what it is," then non-existent or evil things like Chimeras and blindness would be "true." He uses rigorous logic to show that falsehood must be "divided" from itself rather than merely being a temporary contradiction.</summary>
<keywords>Being, Truth, Falsehood, Contradiction, One, Good and Evil, Chimera, Socrates, Henry of Ghent, Scholastic logic, Ontology</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the heated philosophical debate between Antonio of Faenza and Giovanni Pico della Mirandola. Antonio is defending his earlier arguments concerning the nature of Good and Evil, specifically whether they should be categorized as "contraries" (like black and white) or as "privations" (the simple absence of a quality, like blindness is the absence of sight). Antonio relies heavily on the Latin Scholastic tradition, while Pico favors the Greek commentators and a more metaphysical approach.</meta>

# OBJECTIONS: SECOND BOOK

k

...you were able: the words of my argument, which were written to you in my first letters, are as follows: the **good**, by the very reasoning that it is good, is something to be sought <note>original: *expetendum*</note>, while **evil** is something to be fled <note>original: *fugiendum*</note>. To seek and to flee are opposites, just as gathering and scattering are. Therefore, good and evil will be opposites to each other; this is something **Boethius** <note>An influential 6th-century philosopher whose translations of Aristotle formed the basis of medieval logic.</note> also asserted in his commentary on the *Categories* <note>Aristotle's *Categories* (Praedicamentis) is a foundational text on how we classify things in the world.</note>. 

But you respond in this way: "to be" is to be sought, and "not to be" is to be fled; yet it does not follow that they are contraries. But I ask you, does your argument not seem similar to mine? You might say it this way: "to be," by the very nature of being, is to be sought—that is, the specific nature of being is something desirable—and "not to be," by its own nature, is something to be fled. Therefore, they are contraries. You would conclude the argument beautifully. For in this form we have demonstrated that hot and cold, or white and black, are contraries. For the nature <note>original: *ratio*</note> of heat is to separate different things, while the nature of cold is to bring them together; likewise, the nature of white is to disperse the vision, while black draws it together. 

When you responded to my argument in person, you said that the specific nature of the good is not "that which is to be sought." Yet this is conceded by all philosophers, especially the Latins; even **Aristotle**, in the first book of the *Ethics*, says they have rightly defined the good by saying it is "that which all things desire." <note>A famous opening line from Aristotle's *Nicomachean Ethics*.</note> This seemed a wonder to those listening. When the definition of the good was asked of you, you said something is good because "it is ordered toward God." But I immediately replied: "Therefore, God is not good." It was said then that God is not "good" but is "Goodness itself." I added: therefore, there is something in the middle between good and evil. For if God is not "good" (in the categorical sense), He is also certainly not "evil." How then can it be defended that evil is merely the negation of the good, if a "middle ground" is conceded? 

Furthermore, if evil is the negation of the good, then "evil" and "not-good" are the same thing. For a single thing has only one negation. It follows then: if it is "not-good," it is therefore "evil." Thus, from a negation, an affirmation can be gathered. Furthermore, it does not follow: for if evil is either a privation or a "something" according to Aristotle—if it is a "deprived subject," it is something, and therefore a "good" (as a being); if it is a privation, it is in a subject, and therefore it exists. But whatever is a "being" <note>original: *ens*</note> is in some way also "good"; therefore, it is not "not-good." 

Furthermore, you deny it is true what Aristotle says in the *Categories*, namely that good and evil are the "genera of contraries." Yet neither Boethius nor the Latin commentators dare to deny this. You, however, having cast aside the Latin interpreters, flee only to **Simplicius** <note>A 6th-century Greek philosopher and one of the last great Neoplatonists.</note>, who says that good and evil are the genera of contraries for this reason: that of any two contraries, one is always "better" and the other is "worse." **Saint Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the preeminent Scholastic theologian.</note> also reports this from Simplicius. But if one may oppose Simplicius: there is the fact that Aristotle says in the same place that not only is good the contrary of evil, but sometimes an evil is the contrary of another evil. If Aristotle calls "good" that which is "better" and "evil" that which is "worse," then the good will always be the contrary to the evil. Furthermore, if the good and evil that Aristotle says are "genera of contraries" are actually "better" and "worse," then good and evil would be placed in the category of *relatives* (since "better" and "worse" are relative terms). Aristotle, however, says good and evil are not *in* a genus, but are themselves *genera*.

Finally, you wonder that I affirm good and evil to be contraries even according to the opinion of Thomas; and what is more, you say I am wandering from the truth because you claim I falsely allege Simplicius, and that I falsely said Saint Thomas proves by Simplicius's testimony that good and evil are contraries. But take care that you are not the one in error, you who have poorly weighed my mind and words. The words written to you in the second letter are read in this sequence: "I say therefore again, and I approve, that good and evil are contraries to each other; not indeed in the way that white and black or hot and cold are (which are both positive qualities), but in the way that healthy and sick, strong and weak, rare and dense, beautiful and ugly, and many similar things are." 

Nor does Saint Thomas deny this; indeed, that most eminent man, in the first question of *On Evil* <note>original: *De Malo*, one of Aquinas's major works discussing the nature of sin and privation.</note>, shows how good and evil—even if they oppose each other as "privation" and "possession"—are nevertheless usually counted among the contraries. He confirms this by the authority of Simplicius. Remember, therefore, that Aristotle in the *Categories* assigns four types of opposition. Also remember that Aristotle separates these types of genera from each other. Again, note that "healthy" and "sick" are numbered by him among the contraries. Therefore, by this reasoning—by which Aristotle separates contraries from other types of opposition—I affirmed that good and evil are contraries, and I confess it again. 

And this is also what the divine Thomas said in the first question of *On Evil*: that good and evil are contraries, just like "healthy" and "sick," but not like "sight" and "blindness." You, however, say: "I will show you how evil is entirely ignorant of the properties of a contrary." For although a certain evil might seem contrary to a certain good, as "sick" to "healthy," because it leaves behind some of the good, I will nevertheless offer a certain evil that can in no way be opposed by this reasoning: for instance, **death** and **blindness**. 

But indeed, I do not know if you are pretending. For if you had read the words of Thomas more accurately, it could be clearly understood how neither blindness nor death nor any other evil can totally remove the good. Blindness indeed removes sight, and it removes it totally; but it does not remove life nor the body. Death indeed removes life entirely, but it removes neither the body nor "prime matter" <note>The most basic, formless reality that underlies all physical things.</note>. What deceived you, then, is this: blindness is surely the privation of sight, and death the privation of life, but one should not therefore believe that it is a *perfect* privation of the good. Does Thomas not openly confess and say there that evil is contrary to the good just as "sick" is to "healthy," and not as "blindness" is to "sight"? Therefore, blindness, insofar as it is evil, leaves behind some good upon which it rests; but insofar as it is "blindness," it permits no sight to be present. 

As for what Saint Thomas says—that good and evil are opposed like "possession" and "privation"—this is most true. For in that place, Saint Thomas properly calls those things "possessions" <note>original: *habitus*</note> and "privations" which are not only perfect possessions and perfect privations (which are the only things Aristotle calls by those names in the *Categories*), but he pronounces more broadly that all things—whether the privation be total or only "half-full"—are opposed as possession and privation. What did I say, then? That this is confirmed by the authority of Simplicius. It is like this: Saint Thomas says that Simplicius, in his commentary on the *Categories*, says those things are properly called "contraries" of which each one is "something else." Aristotle, however, numbers "healthy" and "sick" among the contraries, but not "blind" and "seeing." Simplicius, therefore, who interprets Aristotle, must necessarily feel the same. 

Furthermore, where Thomas in the question *On Evil* says that evil is not contrary to the good by way of a "contrary" <note>This refers to a technical distinction between a "positive" opposite and a "privative" opposite.</note>... whether a privation which is nothing is a "half-full" privation... likewise we say blindness has the perfect reasoning of evil... for who does not know this? But because it takes away that whole good of which it is called the privation (that is, sight), which a simple eye-inflammation <note>original: *ophthalmia*</note> does not do, Thomas in no way wants them to be called contraries. Since it has the true reasoning of evil, surely he who says that evil (according to Thomas's opinion) is [not a contrary] errs; just as that fellow of mine erred who said Simplicius says things which he does not say.

-> Giovanni Pico <-

<column-break/>

But it is a wonder. You ought to have said how you have now solved this, for it is no wonder not to solve that which has no "knot" <note>A "knot" (*nodus*) is a common scholastic metaphor for a difficult logical problem.</note>. In this, therefore, you should wonder at me: what did I solve in which there was no knot? 

"Similar to be"... why not similar? Since just as those arguments have no strength, so neither do these. For if the good, by the reasoning that it is good, is to be sought, and evil is to be fled, and if "fleeing" and "seeking" are contraries—how do you prove from this that good and evil are contraries? This is what you must prove, yet toward proving it you have never before spoken a word, nor do you do so now. Rightly, therefore, I said there was no knot in your argument, because that which you must prove, you not only do not prove validly, but you do not prove it at all, nor do you even attempt to prove it. 

"You, however"... are you, who are accustomed to be a follower of Boethius and a mocker of the "barbarians" <note>Pico uses "barbarians" to refer to the non-humanist Scholastic philosophers of the Middle Ages.</note>, now rebuking those who follow the Greek interpreters after setting aside the Latins? But even your Thomas is not only a Latin, but the foremost among the Latins, and he not only reports Simplicius’s exposition but also approves of it. You, however, not only do not agree with Simplicius or Thomas, but you say the Latin interpreters "do not dare to deny it." You are a strange man. 

"You wonder"... who would not wonder? I wondered then, when I had not yet seen through your sharp wit; now I do not wonder at many such things. 

"I allege falsely"... and you confess below that you alleged falsely, but you say this is of no importance. How then does my mind escape you? I confess that it escaped me that it is of "no importance" to ascribe to Simplicius things he does not say. For I would believe that he who said "Simplicius says this" (when Simplicius would never say it) is the one in error. 

"For if"... why, in order to explain yourself, must you pervert the whole of Thomas and invent for yourself I-know-not-what "half-full privations," and deny that Thomas there properly accepts "privation" and "possession" when he says evil is privatively opposed to the good? Does he not prove in the whole question that evil is "nothing," and gather from this that evil is a privation, not a contrary? Because it takes away every good, these are therefore the evils which... no less to be a contrary...

<meta>This page continues the sophisticated metaphysical debate between Antonio of Faenza and Giovanni Pico della Mirandola. The previous page established the definitions of "good" and "evil" as contraries. Here, the author challenges his opponent’s view that evil is a total negation of being, using the logical example of a "chimera" to prove that anything conceivable must possess some degree of goodness or being.</meta>

# EXPOSITIONS ON BEING AND THE ONE

<margin>Whether true, why then do you not frankly admit that you have erred? For it is no wonder you are a man.</margin>
<margin>Or a chimera: In that chimera of yours, you imagine many chimeras.</margin>
<margin>To be created: If a chimera can be created by God, this power is not in the chimera but in God.</margin>
<margin>Furthermore, the Chimera: The notion I form for myself of a Chimera, insofar as it is something, is good; but the chimera itself, insofar as it is nothing, is likewise not good.</margin>
<margin>Aristotle, 4th Book of Metaphysics. Good and evil according to you are contraries, and each of the contraries is something positive; therefore, what is good is something positive and what is evil is something positive. And according to you, non-being is good; therefore, according to you, non-being is something positive. And "something" and "being" are interchangeable; therefore, according to you, non-being is positive being. See where your chimera has led us.</margin>
<margin>Furthermore, evil is: But according to you it is a contrary, not a privation.</margin>
<margin>Augustine says: He did not say evil is good, but that it is *in* the good.</margin>
<margin>Furthermore, if evil: Insofar as it is a privation, it is a privation of being. Formally, it is a negation.</margin>
<margin>Show [me]. Reread your earlier letters, and you will see this was shown to you in them, perhaps more than you might desire.</margin>

...let him provide the reason: why Aristotle did not count all privations among the contraries. He cannot explain the cause unless it is the one already stated. Blessed **Thomas [Aquinas]** <note>The most influential medieval theologian, known for synthesizing Aristotelian philosophy with Christianity.</note> is right, who says that **Simplicius** <note>A 6th-century Greek commentator on Aristotle whose works were essential for Renaissance philosophers.</note> says those things are properly called contraries when each is a distinct "other." Since he explains the cause why health and sickness are numbered among contraries, but not blindness and sight, he must necessarily conclude this from Simplicius. He who explains Aristotle—whether this be true or false—it is a matter of no importance to wander through.

But because in your last letters you seem to call "evil" that which you think is the negation of "good"—an evil that is entirely evil—and in the same way you ask about the "false" as divided from the "true" and the "one," I want to ask you: Do you think a **chimera** <note>A mythological creature composed of different animals, often used by logicians to represent an imaginary or "impossible" object.</note> is entirely non-being? If you deny it, you must necessarily contradict yourself, for you said before that a chimera is entirely non-being and false. But if you grant that it is entirely non-being, I will proceed this way: "non-being" and "entirely evil" are equal. Now, a chimera is entirely non-being; therefore, it is also entirely evil. But this cannot be. For a chimera does not contain a contradiction; therefore, it can be created by God. But that which can be, exists; and to exist is a good. Therefore, what can be created can be good. But the potential for good is itself good. Therefore, the chimera is not entirely evil.

Furthermore, a chimera can be understood both by God and by us; it can therefore exist in our mind and soul. Thus, it can exist in some way. But whatever can exist in some way participates in goodness in some way. Therefore, the chimera is not entirely evil. Furthermore, nothing can be evil unless it is to be fled from; yet nothing can be fled from or avoided unless it is known, either by the one who flees or by God, who implanted the natural instinct for flight. It is necessary, therefore, for all evil to be knowable in some way. But knowledge is a certain good; therefore, to be knowable is also a good, for the potential for a good is a certain good.

Furthermore, Aristotle says in the fourth book of the *Metaphysics* that negations and privations are in some way "beings"; indeed, he even says that non-being itself is in some way "being," the sign of which is that we say "non-being *is* non-being." But whatever is in any way a "being" is in some way "good." Therefore, the chimera, regarding which it is true to predicate the term "non-being," is in some way being and good.

Furthermore, evil is the **privation** <note>term: privation (a lack or absence of a quality that should normally be present, like blindness is the privation of sight)</note> of good. But every privation is a negation of a form in a subject naturally suited to have that form and habit. Therefore, nothing can be evil that is not capable of good; but capacity and aptitude for good is good. Therefore, evil cannot be entirely evil; whence **Augustine** says that evil is always *in* the good.

Furthermore, if evil is the privation of good as you say, how can it be the negation of good? For the opposition of privation and habit is one thing, while the opposition of affirmation and negation is another. Furthermore, it is your part to show that the argument you made earlier was valid, by which you tried to prove from Aristotle and Thomas that God is not a "being." For I have weakened both points, nor is it enough to say: "I know that sometimes the Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle's school of philosophy.</note> call God a being; but I also know that with them, God is sometimes not included under the name of being." Show me, I ask, in what place either Aristotle or the Aristotelians do not consider God under the name of "being."

<margin>Otherwise, pay attention: I will soon explain that when you conceive of "God" through this word, in so far as it is signified by the name, this word does not have the nature of a predicate but of a subject. For it is that about which it is asked what can or should be announced about it, not that which is announced about another. Therefore, this was neither unknown to **Simonides** <note>A Greek poet who, when asked by a tyrant "What is God?", repeatedly asked for more time to think, eventually concluding that the more he thought, the more obscure God became.</note> nor was his counsel to the tyrant about this. Likewise, when you ask if "God" cannot be called "God," whether he is something other than God, I ask you what you conceive through this word "God" that you announce about God. If you conceive nothing, you do not err, because you say nothing. If you conceive something, say that God is something other than what you conceive and what you explain through this word "God," because he is above all that can be conceived by us. That God is not. Have mercy, then, on your ancestor, whom you do not want to benefit at all, even if God benefits him. It cannot be that something exists and "Being" itself does not exist; therefore, it cannot be that gold exists if God does not exist. Furthermore, if God is not, then there is infinity; if there is infinity, there is nothing, because if there is infinity, there is no limit; but if there is infinity, there is no infinity, because it is infinite.</margin>

Otherwise, if you have time, explain how you defend that God exists and is One, yet God is not God. For if the word is understood, it is necessary for some description to be formed by the mind; which being given, it follows immediately that "God is God." For the poet Simonides would not have asked the tyrant for time to respond to the question "What is God?" unless he had conceived in his mind the interpretation and sign of the word; for in every question, the first thing is the meaning of the word.

Furthermore, if God is one, God is another "one," which can be nothing but God. Likewise, if God exists and is not God, he is something other than God. Therefore, it is necessary for him to be other than himself. Furthermore, if God is not God because the name of God is a "concrete" term signifying one thing and another should not be conceded to be God, then God is one, for there is nothing in the nature of things that is God by participating in deity. Finally, you will show how you either prove or defend that it is a contradiction for God not to exist and for gold to exist. A dispute of this kind will be pleasing to me, nor should it be troublesome to you; for **dispute is the sieve of truth**, the sweetest food for the soul, having nothing unpleasant. Farewell.

---

### Fourth Objections.

Not therefore was it said that God is not a "being" because existing in God stands for his essence, but because "to be" is not different from "essence"—which is a very different thing. Otherwise, the very existence of a stone, which stands for its essence, would be neither being nor good; for the existence of a stone is not its essence, but is itself for itself, and its own existence, and its own essence. Or regarding negations and privations, it cannot be asked "what they are"; since they exist, it is not enough to form a question to know that the thing asked about exists, but it is necessary to know more: both that it exists and that it is "something." To one asking "what is it?", it is answered ridiculously and irrationally: "being" or "something," whether "being" is taken in the first way or the second. For if it is asked what "sin" is, it is a question of the word rather than the thing.

If something is a "being," then according to your position it is a being because its "to be" is a different thing from its essence. You say humanity is one thing, a man another; white is one thing, whiteness another, and a white thing another still. Therefore, if an **Idea** <note>Platonic Ideas or Forms: the eternal, perfect patterns of all things.</note> is a being, it will be a being because the "to be" of the Idea is different from the Idea itself. But the Idea is God; therefore, the "to be" of the Idea is different from God. Thus, there is in God a "real composition" and not just a "composition of reason" <note>This refers to the debate on Divine Simplicity: is God a single, simple substance, or is He "composed" of different attributes?</note>.

According to the definition of denominations, "one" is derived from "unity." But God, according to your position, is called "one" from the likeness of unity; therefore, the predication does not pertain to the substance of God by which the Platonists say "God is one." Furthermore, when we say "God is one," you think not "what he is" but "how he is" is signified; but "how" belongs to the category of **accidents** <note>In Aristotelian logic, an 'accident' is a property that isn't essential to a thing's nature.</note>. Therefore, the word "one" in God is not substantive, nor does it pertain to the matter.

It does not matter whether I have not learned the Platonic sect or am ignorant of the Greek language; for that is not enough to protect the discipline of the Academics. If God does not exist, and gold were to exist; you say gold would exist—gold would both exist and not be gold; therefore, it would be gold. If the definition of truth stands, it will be true that you fit no Idea. If Socrates sitting is neither true nor false because it is not necessary, then defend that affirmation is not true in everything nor negation, for in everything neither one nor the other has a necessary truth.

If good and evil are in things, but truth and falsehood are in the soul, where is your opposition of affirmation and negation? For negation posits nothing. How also is a chimera in things and the soul, if it is entirely non-being and false? Since you think non-being and evil are interchangeable. If for blindness to be blindness is true, and one does not see that for blindness to be true is the same, then he suppresses himself just as other things that contain a contradiction; if nothing exists, gold does not exist. I believe these things are enough for you, a man however ingenious.

It concludes with the "Fourth Objections," which challenge the relationship between God's essence and his existence.</summary>

# OBJECTIONS, BOOK TWO

...they are; for by the positing of blindness alone, it posits itself. This is because the "being" of blindness is the same as blindness itself. By the same reasoning, the removal of it takes it away. For the same reason: Socrates and "Socrates being Socrates" are the same thing, and both are brought into being by the same act of generation. Even God himself and "God being God" are the same; for both are eternal and the primary truth. If everything false is simply divided—as you do not deny has been proven—then it should not have been said that something false is divided only under this condition: namely, as long as it is false. For if every human is simply and absolutely capable of laughter <note>original: "risibilis"; in scholastic logic, the "ability to laugh" was considered a unique property that defined the human species</note>, there is no need to add a condition to restrict it by saying: "every human is capable of laughter as long as he is a human." Nor should a restriction have been added because not all false things are equally divided, or equally false. For not all beings are equally good, yet all things are absolutely good. How one concludes that good and evil are contraries will be easily established if the following and fleeing <note>The psychological acts of "pursuing" the good and "fleeing" the evil</note> are contraries—provided the logic of mutual contraries has been sufficiently understood by you.

Why do you marvel if I say that the Latins do not deny Aristotle? Simplicius <note>A 6th-century commentator on Aristotle</note> denies it, but Boethius <note>The 6th-century philosopher who bridged classical thought and the Middle Ages</note> does not. Should I, for that reason, either fail to imitate Boethius or extol the "barbarians" <note>A common humanist term for medieval Scholastic philosophers</note>? Do you call me a "wonder" of a man? Truly, I should call *you* wonderful: you think that while I imitate Boethius, I am spurning him and following the barbarians just because I have set Simplicius aside for a moment. If good and evil are contraries, you wish to prove that a "Chimera" <note>A mythical beast often used in logic to represent a concept that can be thought of but cannot exist in reality</note> is something that exists in the nature of things. But if the reason why I called good and evil contraries were understood—which you either do not yet wish to, or cannot, understand—you would have proven nothing regarding the Chimera. 

You marvel greatly that certain privations <note>A "privation" is the absence of a quality that should normally be present, like blindness in an eye</note> are called "Half-full" <note>original: "Semiplenas"</note> by me, and you try to prove they do not exist in this way: "Evil is nothing; therefore, it is not a half-full privation." But I, following your own argument, shall say: "Sickness is evil; therefore it is nothing, and therefore it is not a half-full privation." Yet sickness is a certain kind of privation; therefore, it is not a half-full privation of health or of any particular good, but rather a full and perfect one. But that cannot happen imperfectly; therefore, privations are "half-full"—such as sickness, rarity, ugliness, or blindness. These are "perfect" as absences of a good, but "imperfect" in themselves; for the good that exists in the one who sees is not entirely taken away <note>The author argues that as long as the subject exists, some "good" (being) remains, so the privation isn't a total void</note>.

If it is true, as you write, that every evil leaves behind some element of good, then the Chimera—which is entirely non-being and evil—must also retain something of the good. If it truly preserves something of the good, then it is not entirely evil, nor entirely non-being. Even though the power by which it can be created and exist is in God, and the notion by which it can be understood is in the mind, this does not prevent the Chimera from being "potentially good" and "being." For the power of God and the power of the Chimera are two different things. Nor do we deny that the Antichrist is "potentially good," whose power to exist is partly in matter and partly in the heavens and in man. Furthermore, how could the Chimera—if all thought and the power of God were excluded for a moment—be entirely non-being and evil? For in order to be "non-being," it certainly cannot be "evil." For evil is a privation that resides in a subject, and that subject must necessarily participate in goodness; otherwise, it could not be a subject at all. That which is entirely nothing cannot be a subject for anything.

You have not yet disproven what I said, and you confirm it by the authority of Simplicius, except you claim Simplicius does not say it. But there was no need to boast about that. For I did not say that Aristotle felt that every single being exists either through itself or by accident, nor did I falsely ascribe anything to the Blessed Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas</note> because of it.

Although every privation is a certain kind of negation, it is not yet established that there is not another

<column-break/>

opposition between affirmation and negation, and another between privation and habit <note>In logic, "habit" refers to the presence of a quality, while "privation" is its absence</note>. Therefore, if evil is the privation of good, it does not necessarily follow that "evil" and "not-good" are interchangeable terms.

I do not think your defense—by which you wish to protect the idea that "God is not God"—is consistent with the truth or with the Blessed Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian Neoplatonist</note>. Nor did the Blessed Dionysius ever deny that God is God. Rather, interpret him as the Blessed Thomas does: he does not think affirmations about God are "unbound" <note>original: "incompactas"</note> for any other reason. You say that the name of God, if it has a description, has the quality of a subject but not of a predicate. But even if this is granted, the argument stands: Let "a" be the definition of the name, and let it be said in this way: "God is a." For the definition of anything is predicated of that which it defines. Therefore, by a simple conversion, "a is God." Therefore, "God is God." 

Likewise, you say when it is asked whether God is something other than God or not, one must know what is conceived by the name of God. You say that whatever else is given, I will say it is God; for He is above all that can be conceived. But does not a solution of this kind contradict itself? For if you confess a proposition of this kind—which is "God is above that which can be conceived"—are you not openly affirming something about God? Let the definition of the name then be that phrase: "that which is above what can be conceived," and the argument will hold. Furthermore, it follows that "God is above all that can be conceived; therefore God cannot be conceived." Otherwise, the same thing would be above itself. Therefore, He could neither be loved nor worshiped. 

Finally, you seem to think the power of gold is so great that, whether we wish it or not, it necessarily drags God along with it in this way: "Gold is. Therefore, Being itself is. Therefore, God is." Likewise: "God is. Therefore, the Infinite is. The Infinite is. Therefore, it is nothing." You say that if a being is infinite, it is not finite. It is as if you were arguing: "It is not finite; therefore it is nothing." Then: "It is infinite; therefore it is not infinite," for you say the infinite destroys itself. 

I truly think that if someone had written such arguments to Nicoletto <note>Nicoletto Vernia (d. 1499), a famous philosopher at the University of Padua</note>, he would have replied nothing. Nor will I oppose anything against them, lest in a matter that seems clearer than light to me, I appear to doubt. But if you prove your position with those same arguments, I truly fear you may lose your gold.

Respond to these objections if you wish, my best friend <note>original: "compater optime," literally "best fellow-father" or "godfather," used here as an intimate address between colleagues</note>, so that we may now bring an end to this disputation; for we have played enough. Moreover, I would not want you to think I turned to these matters out of hatred or ill will. I know you remember that before I wrote anything to you, I asked if you were willing. Truly, God is my witness, I both love and venerate my colleague Mirandola <note>Referring to his uncle, the famous Giovanni Pico della Mirandola</note>; if you should ever wish to put it to the test, you will know I have told no lie.

### GIOVANNI FRANCESCO PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA TO ANTONIO OF FAENZA, DISTINGUISHED PHILOSOPHER.

<meta>This page continues Giovanni Francesco Pico della Mirandola’s introductory defense of his late uncle’s work. Having previously discussed the nature of privation and the logical identity of God, he now recounts his journey to Florence to recover his uncle’s manuscripts and explains his decision to publish the "De Ente et Uno" (Of Being and the One) alongside Antonio’s criticisms and his own defensive responses.</meta>

# OF BEING AND THE ONE

faith—once all errors had been eliminated and heresies repelled—might be fortified with the strongest towers against opposing enemies. Yet I was not so disheartened in spirit that I did not labor with all my strength to ensure that all the sleepless nights and the initial scholarly works that had flowed from that man <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), the author’s uncle</note>—who was admired everywhere in the world of letters—did not utterly perish. Therefore, looking out for myself and for our people, I hastened to Florence by the fastest routes I could. I took pains, by whatever means I was able, to ensure that whatever had been noted down by him—even if unpolished and unrefined—should be committed to our power. Our efforts were not entirely in vain; for even if the ledgers <note>original: "tabulae"; referring to organized accounts or records</note> were not yet opened, nor the heir known, the chests were nevertheless opened so that we could inspect and turn over all his commentaries. In those scattered paper volumes, we saw the man's incredible zeal: a reading of every kind, and concepts admirable beyond the grasp of the human mind. Truly, however, in the arrangement of his writings, there was a lack of care not to be praised: everything was cast down and scattered here and there—but more on this another time. While we were unrolling these with diligent care, his little work *Of Being and the One*—issued nearly four years before his death—fell into my hands, along with three letters written by you to him on the subject and his responses to them. Because of the novelty of the matter, I did not just read them, but drank them in—or rather, as they say, devoured them. (For I had known by rumor that this had happened, but I did not have sufficient evidence of what weight had been brought to bear.) I began to think and debate with myself whether I ought to give that work to the printers for publication along with the other works I had collected, making no mention of your objections; or whether it would be more advisable if it went out in public attacked on one side by obstacles and fortified on the other by defenses. After a long discussion of the matter, the latter opinion finally settled in my mind. Indeed, it would seem to bring a mark of infamy to learned men if he should not only fear his accusers, but also not dare to summon them to judgment correctly—as if he were little confident in his conscience. Equally, it seemed appropriate that he go accompanied by responses, as if to defend the cause of innocence with witnesses. I did not doubt that our counsel would be praised by upright men, since I would have had to suffer either that my deceased uncle—a man certainly most deserving of me—be defrauded in some part of his celebrated learning by not publishing such a booklet, or that, by him proceeding alone, an occasion for criminal accusation be left to the most wicked detractors, because the letters which had been composed on both sides—both in objecting and repelling—had not been summoned into the forum. But when some letters of our Christoforo Faxoli, both citizen and physician, were presented to us, in which it was indicated that you had forged a fourth letter on that business which lacked a response (as you said), the matter was recalled into doubt. Once again made of a wavering opinion, I thought my judgment—already freed—must be weighed more exactly, since a final accuser was urging the cause and there was no one to act as patron <note>a legal metaphor for a defense attorney</note>. Then a certain tickling desire to undertake the defense entered my mind, yet it was not immediately clear where I should turn to maintain my silence. On one hand, I was moved by the man’s modesty and his kindness toward all, as well as the skill and sharpness of his genius in untying and dissolving even difficult knots and inexplicable riddles <note>original: "scyrpis"; a term for complex puzzles</note> on the spot; thus I judged that your final letter had not been safely delivered. I thought it would have been easy for him to have written back: if your letters were delivered to such a faithful messenger, they must have perished on the journey either by the negligence of the couriers (as often happens) or by some other accident. Finally, it occurred to me in the explanations

<column-break/>

of your prior questions that he had complained that you often repeated the same things and often doubted the same points. Because of this, I immediately ran through the headings of your entire controversy to see if anything could be found in the first responses by which I might show that the fourth letter had been satisfied in part before it was even written. The matter succeeded according to my wish, and I found such great things pertaining to the purpose that, if not in words, I responded as much as possible to the objections of the last letter—so much so that you can recognize the knots of those very questions to be opened in great part from his prior solutions. We added many things sought as testimony even from great authors, all of which I would wish you to believe I have done for no other reason than to meet the judgments of those who are ignorant and unaccustomed to philosophy, and of the malevolent. For if the rumor had reached them that you had given a fourth letter to my uncle on that controversy to which he had not responded, they would have immediately brought a verdict (as is the custom for babblers and the envious) that Pico had not cared to write back for some other unjust reason. Otherwise, my dear Antonio, I would have most willingly omitted the work undertaken from the beginning. First, so that I would not seem to be initiated into controversies—from which I am shrinking, even if I were acting in a most just cause; and second, so that I might not deviate from the true path of philosophy. This path I began to travel—after horses and arms (though I had smelled certain little flowers of literature from boyhood) and after dealings with great leaders—under the guidance of my uncle Giovanni Pico and our Giovanni Mainardo. This is because the knowledge of nature is not ordained for sweating in literary agonies, but for recognizing the Creator of nature itself; and philosophical commentaries should always, of their own accord, invite us to track down the innermost meanings of the divine words. This is the end of all studies; by these, the way to heaven is revealed to us—if, however, we have not cultivated them for the sake of catching our own glory, but so that we may be able to both know our God more easily and love Him more fervently. Thus, we may more promptly pursue what He commanded to be done, and flee what He taught to be avoided. Behold, the cause of this burden I have undertaken and the business with you is explained; it is most just, as it seems, and therefore to be endured by you with an even mind. Moreover, I could perhaps even think that I might use these works as intermediaries in the benevolence already auspiciously contracted with you at Ferrara, which is to be confirmed. For when I arrived there in recent days, you deigned to visit me with your typical humanity. And while talking about literature, the death of my uncle, and his many unfinished works, once you perceived my intention of responding to you and solving your arguments, you showed yourself so far from being offended that you even praised what I was going to do. But now, approaching the business itself, let us first apply our hands to dissolving the first objection.
<margin>First objection.</margin>
It is of this kind: "It was not said that God is not a being <note>original: "ens"</note> because 'to be' <note>original: "esse"; the act of existence</note> in God is before essence; rather, because 'to be' is not different from essence. This is a far different thing; otherwise, the very 'to be' of a stone, which is its essence, would be neither a being nor good. For 'to be' is not the essence of a stone, but 'to be' itself is both its existence and its essence." To this we shall respond most easily. But first, I will bid you to remember those things which were written by him for the sake of this matter, lest he seem to have uttered conflicting words.
<margin>A certain preface. Amelius. Iamblichus. Syrianus.</margin>
Indeed, in that commentary *Of Being and the One* (which even the rasp of your objections mentioned), he not only approved of Amelius, Iamblichus, Syrianus, and many Platonists who said that God is not a "being," but in the whole treatise he principally drove at this: to show, not only from the dogma of Aristotle but also from that of Plato, that God both is and is properly called "being." # OBJECTIONS: BOOK TWO

<margin>Dionysius, Thomas, the Solution.</margin> He showed that the reason for this expression was such that, for one who followed it, it was not inconsistent with the truth to say that God is greater than the name of "being." And for this reason, he did so in order that both the authority of Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-century theologian who argued God is "beyond being."</note> and the reasoning of Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the preeminent Catholic philosopher.</note> might be respected, lest those most learned and holy men who said that God is not "being" but "above being" <note>original: "Deum non esse ens, sed super ens"</note> should seem altogether insane. The former repeated this opinion a thousand times; the latter employed it occasionally. <margin>On the Objection</margin> But let us return to our own concerns. When it is said in this manner that God is not "being," we assert that it is uttered for this reason: because in God, "to be" stands for His essence. You object to this, asserting it is not for that reason but for another—namely, because "to be" is simply not different from essence. You think these two things are entirely different, but I contend that one is the opening and clarification of the other. For when it is said that God is not "being" because in Him "to be" is not separated from essence, nothing else is meant but that "to be" in God is his very essence. Nor do we judge, through this phrase—namely, that in God "to be" is not different from His essence—that there is an essence in God in the same way it is perceived clearly in the words of the one against whom you argued. For my uncle <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola</note> refuted your objection, which concerned this very matter, saying: "For the Platonists, when they say this, do not mean that essence and being exist separately in God, but that in Him they do not differ." Rather, "to be" in God holds the place that essence holds in other things, so that for Him, essence is nothing other than "to be" itself. However, you might find it entirely inconsistent to believe that the very "being" of a stone cannot be called "being" or "good"; you will perhaps change <margin>Thomas.</margin> your opinion if you consider what is said by Thomas Aquinas—who was summoned by you as a sort of judge of this controversy—in the first part of the *Summa*, question 45, article 4. There you will openly recognize that the "to be" <note>original: "esse"; the act of existing</note> which falls into the composition of an essence should be called neither a "being" <term>ens|The Latin term for a thing that exists; a 'being'</term> nor a "created thing," since he pronounces that all non-subsistent forms, accidents, and other things of that kind can be called "co-existents" and "co-created" rather than "created" and "beings." For this reason, his followers, especially Capreolus <note>Jean Capreolus (c. 1380–1444), known as the 'Prince of Thomists.'</note> when the question of the distinction between "being" and "essence" arises, hold that the "to be" of created things is received neither in the number of true beings nor of creatures. Since it does not take the name of "being," it undoubtedly does not take the name of "good," since being and good follow one another and are reciprocal in scope. <margin>Second Objection.</margin> In the second place, you argue in this manner: if, in the case of negations and privations <note>A "privation" is the absence of a quality that should be present, like blindness is the privation of sight.</note>, one cannot ask "what they are" when they exist, then it is not enough for forming the question "what is it?" to know that the thing being asked about exists; rather, one must know both that it "is" and that it is "something." Therefore, to one asking "what is it?", the answer "being" or "something" is given ridiculously and irrationally, whether "being" is taken in the first or second sense. But if it is asked what "sin" is, it is a question of the <margin>Its solution</margin> word rather than the thing. To this objection we reply: he never said that in privations and negations one could not ask what they were. Rather, he said that it could not be answered "what" they were in the way Thomas meant, whom he cited in previous letters when you were doubting whether this was true or false. He said you must confess it is true unless you abandon your Thomas; and <margin>Giles.</margin> we also find this asserted by Giles of Rome <note>Egidius Romano (c. 1243–1316), a student of Aquinas.</note> in the second book of his commentaries on the *Sentences*. For it is enough to form the question "what is it?" to know that the thing being asked about exists. Nor is it necessary for one who is about to investigate what a thing is to know the thing "is" or is "something" in the first sense, but only in the second—that is, that it exists. But if you were to contend that you understood the question to be one that can be formed and to which a right and affirmative answer can be given—firstly, if you think that question cannot be rightly formed unless the thing being asked about is such that an answer can be returned through it, I do not agree with you.

<column-break/>

For it is the opinion of Aristotle that one can ask whether a centaur <note>A mythical creature, half-man and half-horse, often used in logic puzzles to discuss things that don't exist in reality.</note> exists or not, yet such a centaur does not exist in a way that the question "is it?" can be answered by it, since it is a mere fable and a total fiction. Likewise, I disagree if you believe that the questioner must know this same thing; for he who rightly inquires what a thing is does not need to know more (as we have shown) than that it exists. Therefore, to one who knows a thing is "something," it is not ridiculously answered that it is "something" to a person who is ignorant and asking about it. And because we are not accustomed to teaching those asking "what a thing is" that it is either "being" or "something" so that we might answer completely, it happens that: having discovered that it is something, they would still search for what kind of "being" it might be. Thus, we satisfy not only their express request but also their desire for investigation when we dissolve their conceived but unuttered questions by anticipating them with our responses. However, those words—that if it is asked "what is sin," it is a question of the name rather than the thing—which were used in the objection made against you, seem to have brought laughter rather than much weight. For you had previously argued from the opinions of Thomas: namely, that "being" in the first sense is called that which answers the question "what is it?"; and to one asking what it was that preserved and moved the world, "God" was reasonably answered. From these points, you gathered <margin>Showing the error.</margin> that God is "being" and "something" in the first sense. He replied: "See how greatly you are deceived; evil, according to Thomas, is not such that we can answer 'something' or 'being' to one asking what it is; and yet to one asking what 'sin' is, we can answer that it is an 'evil.' Therefore, this response of yours—namely, that if 'sin' is asked about, it is a question of the word rather than the thing—does not help you at all." For the question of the name is not too different (though the reasoning differs here and there) from "what is it that governs the world?" as "what is sin?", since the one who governs the world—namely, God—does not have a "quiddity" <term>quidditas|The 'what-ness' or essence of a thing that defines it.</term> as the more recent thinkers say. This is confirmed most clearly by all except those who place Him in a category. And as the most holy <margin>Dionysius.</margin> Dionysius says, the prince of our theology after the apostles: "He has neither a name nor a definition." Moreover, this response of yours does not harmonize with those things you said before, when <margin>Third objection.</margin> you previously said that "evil" itself is not "nothing" but something "positive"; yet now you confess that a question is formed only of its name. You object thirdly with these words: "If something is 'being,' it is 'being' according to your position because its 'to be' is something different from its essence in reality. You say humanity is one thing, a man another; whiteness one thing, a white object another. Therefore, if an Idea is 'being,' it will be 'being' because the 'to be' of the Idea is something other than the Idea. But the Idea is God; therefore, the 'to be' of the Idea is something other than God. There is, therefore, in God a composition according to the thing, not only according to <margin>Its solution.</margin> reason." To these we say an answer has already been given. For when you argued in the third letter with almost the same means you use now, he replied that the composition of "being" and "essence" in divine matters is "according to reason," not "according to the thing." Therefore, we deny that the first proposition of this hypothetical syllogism <term>syllogismus|A logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two premises.</term> you bring forward is true. For even if in created things essence differs from "to be" in reality, it does not necessarily follow that whatever can be called "being" must be composed of essence and "to be" (or existence) as if from parts. Therefore, the "to be" and "existence" of an Idea—which is the pattern of created <margin>Use of the Peripatetics. Seneca</margin> things—do not belong to it as distinct in reality. But this composition is made by us: when we weigh that Idea as the exemplary cause of the essence and "being" (or existence) found in created things. We likewise apply this composition and distinction even to the simplest things, and we call it "according to reason" since our intellect has manufactured it. <meta>This page continues the defense of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola’s philosophical work "On Being and the One." The previous page discussed how God is "above being" by harmonizing the views of Thomas Aquinas and Dionysius the Areopagite. ### ON BEING AND THE ONE

As Posidonius recorded in his letters to Seneca, we can say that according to the logic of essence and existence, an "idea" is composed in this manner and call it "being" <note>original: "ens"</note>. For example, when we consider the "exemplar" <note>An "exemplar" is a divine blueprint or perfect pattern of a created thing.</note> of creatures, they are composed of a distinct "being" and "essence." However, we do not apply this composition to God when we contemplate Him not merely as the pattern for others, but as He is in the innermost depths of His divinity, enjoying His own self.

<margin>Fourth objection.</margin>
The fourth objection is this: the word "one" is derived from the concept of "unity." According to your position, God is called "one" based on a likeness to unity; therefore, the declaration made by the Platonists that "God is One" does not actually describe God's substance. Furthermore, when we say "God is one," you think we are signifying *how* He is <note>original: "quo modo sit"</note>, not *what* He is. But a "mode" belongs to the category of accidents <note>In traditional logic, an "accident" is a property that isn't essential to a thing’s nature (like being tall), whereas "substance" is what the thing is.</note>; therefore, the term "one" as applied to God is not substantive. Either I have not learned the Platonic sect, or I am ignorant of the Greek language, for this is not enough to defend the Academic <note>The "Academics" were followers of the Platonic school.</note> discipline.

<margin>Its solution</margin>
But the response is easy. When the Platonists stated that the "One" predicated of God is substantive and not merely a descriptive label, it was correctly asserted. Again, when it is affirmed that He is called "one" because He is like unity, this is not inconsistent. It cannot be argued that the term is not substantive simply because of that; for even if a name 

<margin>Thomas,</margin>
is adapted to something because of a specific property or likeness, it does not necessarily follow that the name is not substantive—provided that it is accepted as a substantive name that signifies something existing by itself <note>original: "per se stantis"</note>, rather than as an attached attribute. It is clear that the "one" predicated of God is understood not as an inherent accident but as a self-standing reality, so clear that it needs no proof. You have, therefore, a property from which the name is derived, but that does not take away from its substantive nature. For your Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note>—or rather, ours—reports in both the *Prima Pars* <note>The first part of Aquinas's *Summa Theologiae*.</note> and other places that the thing a name is meant to signify differs from the reason the name was first imposed. 

<margin>John Scotus.</margin>
For example, the name "stone" <note>original: "lapis"</note> is applied to signify that specific substance, but it is said to be named from a related property—namely, that which "hurts the foot" <note>A traditional (though linguistically incorrect) medieval etymology: lapis = laedit pedem.</note>. Thus, in another place, he teaches that grammarians use a name to denote a "substance with quality," which John Scotus <note>John Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a hugely influential Franciscan philosopher.</note> also affirms in the first book of his commentaries on the *Sentences*. Therefore, my dear Antonio, when we declare that God is "one," we are declaring it truly and as a substantive name, because we both conceive and predicate it as a self-standing reality. Again, when we say it is applied from the likeness of unity and its properties, we come as close to the truth as is allowed to us. We are using a fitting term to indicate how far that ineffable Deity is above all created things; just as unity is the principle <note>The "principle" here means the foundational source or starting point.</note> of all numbers, so God is the principle of all things that exist. From these words, you will also gather the solution to your other argument about "mode," which you claim can only belong to the category of accidents. In the statement "God is one," it is possible to signify *how* God is one, and nonetheless, the word "one" remains substantive in God, if you consider both the source from which the name is taken and the thing it is attributed to denote. You can also recognize the solution to your doubt quite briefly from the words 

<margin>A brief solution from the words of the uncle.</margin>
of my uncle <note>The "uncle" is Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494).</note> when he says: "How can you say I follow the logic of the Platonists rather than Dionysius? For you have never read either Dionysius or the Platonists, even though you boast of it loudly." Know that among the Platonists, the "Type" of God is Unity, while in Dionysius, God is "all things uniquely." 

<column-break/>

No one could rightly desire a more direct solution. For when it is said that the "Type" of God is unity, it refers to the likeness and the mode; but when it is said that God is "all things uniquely," it must be referred to His substance. Yet it has been asserted that these are entirely the same thing. Furthermore, in the Greek language, which he knew well, the abstract and the concrete can sometimes be signified by the same word.

<margin>Solution to the fifth objection.</margin>
To provide a solution to your fifth doubt, many words are not needed. He says: "If God did not exist and gold existed, gold would exist and gold would not exist." You add these words: "Therefore gold would be such that, if the definition of truth stands, it would be a truth corresponding to no Idea." <note>An "Idea" here refers to the Platonic Forms—the eternal blueprints of things in the divine mind.</note> Please add also these few words which he said follow from his own statement, and you will recognize how it would be a truth corresponding to no Idea. What do I mean? Simply that the impossible gives birth to the impossible <note>A rule in formal logic: from an impossible premise, any conclusion can follow.</note>. It is no wonder if you make whatever you wish follow from your impossible proposition. For if God did not exist and gold did exist, it would be a truth corresponding to no Idea, since from the impossible the impossible is born. In this, not only the logicians but also the theologians 

<margin>John of Baconthorpe.</margin>
give their support. For if you ask John of Baconthorpe <note>A 14th-century English Carmelite theologian known as the "Prince of Averroists."</note>, the Carmelite, whether it could happen that gold exists and God does not, he will respond to you in the first book of the *Sentences* that no thing whatsoever can be understood unless God is understood first. Since God is involved in the understanding of all things, you can conclude for yourself whether it can be pronounced—beyond all controversy, even among novice logicians—that it is impossible for gold to exist and God not to exist. But 

<margin>Cardinal of Cambrai.</margin>
we will speak of this again at the end of the work. If you later consult the Cardinal of Cambrai <note>Pierre d'Ailly (1351–1420), a famous theologian and philosopher.</note>, you will hear a man practiced in every philosophy saying in his first commentary on the *Sentences* that a contradiction follows from any impossible premise. In the sixth place, you said that if 

<margin>Sixth objection.</margin>
it were neither true nor false that Socrates is sitting (which he had asserted because it was not necessary), you could defend the idea that a negation or affirmation is not true in every case, since in some cases neither one nor the other has a necessary truth. Solving this objection, 

<margin>Its solution</margin>
we respond that the statement "Socrates sits," as far as it is concerned, does not necessarily determine its own truth or falsehood. But it does not follow from this that the affirmation or negation is not true for any given thing. However, if you understand it in the way he teaches, you could also deny that in every case an affirmation or negation is true in such a way that one side is *necessarily* true. For he says "That I sit is always either true or false, because I am always either sitting or not sitting." When it is said "That I sit is neither true nor false," this means that the proposition does not determine its own truth or falsehood from itself, which is what necessary propositions do. But since it can be true (when I sit) and false (when I do 

<margin>Seventh objection</margin>
not sit), it is indeterminate in itself toward either possibility. Furthermore, against some of his words regarding good and evil, truth and falsehood (which he had said were in things and in the soul), you insist in this way: "If good and evil are in things, and truth and falsehood are in the soul, where is your opposition of affirmation and negation? For a negation poses nothing; how then is a 'chimera' <note>A mythological beast used in logic to represent a "non-being" or something that cannot exist.</note> in things and in the soul if it is entirely non-being and false, since you think 'non-being' and 'evil' are interchangeable?" But I pray you pay attention and notice that evil and good are pronounced to be in things for the same reason that truth and falsehood are considered regarding the soul. For truth and falsehood are not in things, as Aristotle writes in the sixth book of the 

<margin>Its solution: Aristotle.</margin>
*First Philosophy* <note>Aristotle’s *Metaphysics*.</note>, but in the mind. Yet it does not necessarily follow from this that a thing which is entirely evil is a true thing...
