<meta>This page continues the defense of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola’s "On Being and the One." The previous page addressed the fourth objection concerning whether "One" describes God's substance or merely a mode of being. This page moves into the eighth, ninth, and tenth objections, focusing on logical distinctions between things (like blindness) and the truths we state about them, as well as the nature of "Good" and "Evil" in relation to existence.</meta>

### OBJECTIONS. SECOND BOOK

...also that false point which Aristotle mentions in that place is included: nor does it follow that if good and evil exist in things, they cannot be opposed by contradiction. This is because the evil that is declared to be in things is not said to be "in things" so that it may be understood as being a particular "thing" itself, but because it is observed and considered regarding the things themselves—that is, insofar as it deprives things of their perfections. <note>In Scholastic philosophy, "evil" was often defined not as a positive "thing" but as a "privation" (the absence of a good that ought to be there, like darkness is the absence of light).</note> It acts to make them "not good." A chimera <note>A mythical creature composed of parts from different animals, used in logic to represent an impossible or non-existent concept.</note>, however, is not in things because it is entirely non-being; yet, if it were possible for nature to make it a thing, it would be both a thing and good. It is "false" only insofar as it does not exist at all and does not match any divine Idea. Nor do we claim that the chimera itself is in the soul, but rather the *notion* of the chimera: which, as a certain thing [a thought], is good and true; but it is false insofar as it represents a chimera, since the chimera itself is both nothing and evil.

<margin>Eighth objection.</margin>
After this, you believed you could prove that blindness is "true," which he had denied—even though he would neither have rejected nor conceded that "blindness being blindness" is a truth. But he would have said these are very different things. This is how you argued: "If it is true that blindness is blindness, who does not see that blindness is true?" For these are the same: if blindness alone is posited, then "blindness being blindness" is posited; and if it is taken away, the statement is taken away. By the same reasoning, you argue that Socrates and "Socrates being Socrates" are the same thing, and both are generated by the same process; and by itself, God and "God being God" are the same, for both are eternal and the First Truth.

<margin>Its solution</margin>
<margin>Gregory of Rimini</margin>
<margin>The Cardinal of Cambrai</margin>
But I, my dear Antonio, contend the opposite and deny that the things you claim are the same are indeed so. For when one of the things you bring forward is posited, the other is not necessarily posited. If blindness alone is posited, with no intellect considering it, blindness will indeed exist, yet "blindness being blindness" <note>The author is distinguishing between the *fact* (the state of being blind) and the *propositional truth* (the mental statement that blindness is blindness), which requires a mind to think it.</note> will not exist. For this reason, the argument concerning God and the generation of Socrates is also resolved. For Socrates is generated by himself, not the fact that "Socrates is Socrates," since complex propositions are not "generated" in the same way. Even if I were to grant you that they are the same, we say it still does not follow as you concluded because of the different way of signifying: namely, complexly and incomplexly. <term>Complex vs. Incomplex</term> <note>In logic, an "incomplex" term is a single word like "blindness." A "complex" term is a whole statement or proposition like "blindness is blindness."</note> This argument would be of no value: "blindness and 'blindness being blindness' are the same; but this statement is true, therefore blindness itself is true." By that same logic, it would follow that "this is a complex proposition, therefore blindness is a complex proposition," which is absurd. Since "blindness" is a simple name, not a complex or a specific announcement, it is one thing for blindness to be "true" and another for the statement "blindness is blindness" to be true. And although these points suffice for my uncle’s defense, do not think there is a lack of other ways to defend him. To give you a more complete response, know that according to the opinion of Gregory of Rimini <note>A 14th-century theologian known for his strict readings of Augustine and his work on logic.</note>, I could have said that even if "blindness being blindness" were posited by blindness alone, it does not necessarily follow that they are the same. He denies this consequence, along with many others like it: "Setting aside everything else other than God, God is; therefore God is 'God being God'." The Cardinal of Cambrai <note>Pierre d'Ailly (1351–1420), a famous philosopher and ecclesiastical leader who wrote on the "Sentences" of Peter Lombard.</note> also denies all statements in which something is announced about an infinitive phrase used significatively, asserting them to be both false and incongruous, as can be seen in his first book on the *Sentences*.

<margin>Ninth objection.</margin>
<margin>Its solution</margin>
Next, you complain that the "false" should not have been declared "divided" with this condition: namely, "so long as it is false." You explain it in these words: "If every false thing is simply divided—which you do not deny has been proven—it should not have been said that a certain false thing is divided only with this condition: 'so long as it is false'." For if every man is simply and absolutely "risible" <term>Risible</term> <note>From the Latin "risibilis," meaning "capable of laughing." In logic, this was the standard example of a "proper accident"—something that is not the definition of a human, but belongs uniquely and always to all humans.</note>, there is no need to add a condition to restrict it by saying "every man is risible so long as he is a man." Nor should a restriction have been added because not all false things are equally divided or false; for not all beings are equally "good," yet all things are absolutely good. But consider his words carefully; by them, you can cast away every scrap of doubt. He says every false thing is "divided," yet not every false thing is equally false, because things are not equally divided when they are not equally false; they are "false" through and by necessity. Therefore, Antonio, that phrase "as long as" was correctly added, because those things which are false are not *always* and *necessarily* false, since they can become true and "united" either by the work of nature or an artisan—as you yourself said in your second set of objections. However, as long as they are divided, they are only false; but those things which can never return to "friendship" [unity] are always truly false, as is seen abundantly in the response to the second objection. Nor do your analogies about "beings" and "risibility" help you much. For beings are also always and absolutely good. Although some may not be equally good and some participate more in the nature of goodness than others, they are nevertheless always and necessarily good: for insofar as they are beings, they are good, and they cannot become non-beings and non-good unless they are reduced to nothing. But in the case of the "false" and the "divided" which consists in a complex statement, it can become "not-divided" and "true"; therefore the analogy does not fit. For although not all false things are equally divided, they are nonetheless false insofar as they are not united and not true. Furthermore, this objection should have troubled us very little; for who would doubt that a man (who is absolutely and always risible) can be declared to be risible under the condition "so long as he is a man"? Would learned men disapprove of the phrase "a man is risible so long as he is a man"?

<margin>Solution to the tenth objection.</margin>
<margin>Aristotle</margin>
The tenth head of your objections brings nothing else against him except that what you said could have been easily established if the logic of "contrary motions" had been sufficiently understood by him. But he—unless his memory fails—complained that you did not prove what you claimed followed so many times: namely, that from the contrariety of "pursuing" and "fleeing," the contrariety of "good" and "evil" is inferred. For he asks: by what reasoning is good to be sought and evil to be fled? And since "fleeing" and "seeking" are contraries, how do you prove from this that good and evil are contraries? This is what you must prove; yet to prove this, you have never said a single word, nor do you do so now. He denies the form of your argument, perhaps because "seeking" and "fleeing" are not properly "contrary motions" from which contrary terms can be inferred. Even Aristotle assigns a certain contrariety of changes in the sixth book of his *Physics*, where the terms are not "contraries" but "contradictories": namely, "being" <note>original: "ens"</note> and "non-being" <note>original: "non ens"</note>, since generation proceeds from non-being to being, while corruption falls from being into non-being. You, however, have treated this contrariety of good and evil again without bringing any other proof or reason. Do not doubt that he has carefully looked into the logic of contrary motions "from his very fingernails" <note>A Latin idiom meaning "from earliest childhood" or "thoroughly."</note>. Indeed, he has frequently not only repelled your arguments against him regarding this contrariety but has also turned them against you. In his second letter, he deduced that your proof implies not only that good and evil are contraries, but that contradictories are contraries. Secondly, he turned your weapons back on you in this way: "According to you, good and evil are contraries, and each of two contraries is something positive; and according to you, 'non-being' is [the same as] evil; therefore, according to you, non-being is something positive. And since 'something' and 'being' are convertible terms, then according to you, non-being is something positive [which is a contradiction]."

# OBJECTION. BOOK TWO

<margin>
Privation can be considered in two ways. Dionysius.
</margin>
...I believe he has turned his attention toward privation (if, in fact, your final objections were seen by him). He had said to you: "Evil is; therefore, nothing is not a semi-full <note>original: "semiplena" - meaning a partial or incomplete absence of a quality.</note> privation." You, however, pursue this argument for them in this manner: "Sickness is evil, therefore it is nothing; it is therefore not a semi-full privation. But sickness is a certain kind of privation; therefore, it is not a semi-full privation of health or of any good, but rather a good and perfect thing, which is impossible." Therefore, you argue that imperfect privations are semi-full, such as sickness, rarity, ugliness, or the blindness of sight—the first being a perfect privation of a good, the latter being imperfect. These are your words exactly. But I, my dear Antonio, would say freely that these words of yours either achieve nothing against him—which you will see more clearly as I review them one by one—or they miss the mark. You say first, from his own words: "Evil is nothing, therefore it is not a semi-full privation." You are on the right track. Again: "Sickness is evil, therefore it is nothing; therefore it is not a semi-full privation." Up to this point, you also proceed correctly, because sickness, insofar as it is evil, is to that extent "nothing." Then you say: "But sickness is a certain privation, therefore not health, etc." all the way to the end, by which words, with your leave, a falsehood is asserted in my judgment, as we shall attempt to show. Blindness is not only a perfect privation of sight, as you say, but it can also be called a perfect privation of a *good*, because it takes away all of that good which it is naturally meant to take away—namely, sight. This is not what <term>ophthalmia</term><note>An inflammation of the eye; here used as an example of a partial loss of health compared to total blindness.</note> does, even though it also destroys the good it is naturally meant to take away; yet of that which it is not apt to destroy, it can in no way be called a privation, whether you call it semi-full or full. For privation is considered either absolutely—that is, as it regards a <term>habit</term><note>In scholastic philosophy, a "habit" (habitus) is a positive quality or state of being, like health or sight, which a "privation" removes.</note> in general—or as it is restricted to a certain and limited kind of being, such as health of the whole body, the eye, beauty, and other things of that sort. Taken in the first way, it does not deprive a person of any particular habit, because a total privation, as Dionysius says in the book *On Divine Names*, fails entirely in its powers. Taken in the second way—which Dionysius calls "singular" privation to distinguish it from the "universal"—it deprives one of that specific habit which it regards. And in this way, this kind of privation is "full" in relation to what it is naturally meant to harm, and not a "semi-full" privation of something else. For who would dare to say that blindness is a "semi-full" privation of a human being, or of some other good that might be in a human? Therefore, absolute privation regards a habit absolutely, and a specific and particular privation regards its own specific and particular habit, and does not exceed its limits. For this reason, sickness is a full privation, not a semi-full one, whether you ascribe it to the whole body or to a particular limb. For a fever is a perfect privation of that temperature which it is naturally meant to corrupt. Ophthalmia too, even if it does not remove the total good that is in the eye, is nevertheless a perfect and proper privation of *some* good, because it destroys all of that good which it is naturally meant to destroy, even when it does not take away sight, provided that the ophthalmia does nothing else. Ugliness also, because 
<margin>
The destruction of Antonio's reasoning through examples.
</margin>
it removes all that good which it is able to remove—namely, the perfect composition of parts which is called beauty—is a perfect privation, and so it is in other cases. Consider this also, which we say in abundance: blindness, insofar as it is blindness, is an evil; insofar as it is evil, it is nothing; and insofar as it is nothing, it is not a "semi-full" privation, because if it were semi-full, it would leave behind something positive, which evil does not do. Furthermore, no privation in itself actually deprives one of *every* good; therefore, all privations would be "semi-full" privations, which goes against your own argument, since you contend that some are full and some are semi-full. The connection is excellent and necessary, and what we have assumed we prove by this argument: no good would ever be found if a total and universal privation were discovered in the nature of things,

<column-break/>

as we hinted a little earlier from the words of Dionysius. For evil deprives a particular good, since evil exists *in* the good, and a universal evil would destroy universal good—if, however, such a thing could be found, which is impossible. And thus you may conclude that one finds not "semi-full," but always "full" privations of their own proper habits. 
<margin>
Solution to the fourteenth objection.
</margin>
To the fourteenth objection, which contains several questions, I respond one by one. First, that not every evil leaves behind something of the good, unless you understand it to be in some subject <note>The "subject" is the physical thing (like a body) that the evil or privation exists within.</note> which the evil itself does not affect, or you take that subject whose habit is destroyed by the evil itself. Nor do I claim that opposite habit which you nevertheless impose upon him and catch at as a hypothesis. For he abundantly testified that an evil is found which entirely removes every good it is naturally meant to take away, since he moved you on this point in the response of the second letter, writing in this manner: "You certainly ought to have considered this: that what is conceded regarding certain imperfect evils, because of that mixture of goodness which they still retain, must not be transferred to the unmixed and absolute nature of evil itself." And so that you may perceive the truth more clearly, I will not be loath to explain the distinction: evil can be considered in two ways. First, absolutely and under the proper definition of evil—that is, insofar as it is nothing. Second, insofar as it is the privation of some good—that is, a particular evil. And evil accepted in this second way leaves behind only the *subject* of the good; 
<margin>
Evil can be understood in two ways.
</margin>
it does not do what the other evil does, which is entirely non-being and nothing, such as we say a <term>Chimera</term> <note>A mythological beast (lion/goat/snake). In logic, it represents an impossible object that can be described but cannot exist in reality.</note> is, since it does not regard any subject or habit. And for this reason, it is called "entirely evil" by him, and an "absolute and unmixed nature of evil." This, I say, is what he means; 
<margin>
Dionysius.
</margin>
to use the words of Dionysius in the book *On Divine Names*, because it lacks a subject, it is "in no way, nowhere, and is a non-existent nothing." A Chimera, indeed, although it might be called "good in potential" because of the power of producing it which exists in God, nevertheless can be called neither a "being" nor "good." For if this connection—namely, "something is good in potential, therefore it is good"—were valid, I think it would bring the author of that blow to admit that all things which ought to be created by God, but are not yet made by the force of nature, and even those things which have been destroyed, would both be "something" and "not something." For if, according to him, they were both beings and good by the power of the Creator, then they would necessarily be "something," since "something" and "good" are interchangeable and cover the exact same range. But that they could not be "something," I will argue thus: from nothing, nothing can be made. Before a Chimera is created, according to you, it cannot "be" unless it is created; it is therefore created from nothing. Therefore, before it was created from nothing, it was not "something." Thus, because of the power of goodness which is in the Creator, a thing cannot be called "absolutely good" [before it exists]; otherwise, to use the language of our logicians, a "fallacy of the relative to the absolute" <note>original: "fallacia secundum quid ad simpliciter" - a logical error where one assumes that what is true in a specific case is true in all cases.</note> would be committed. I deliberately set aside those things which they assert against that opinion concerning—if I may speak thus—eternal quiddities and objective potential, even if your opinion could perhaps be weakened by those very same reasons. For our desire is satisfied if we have proved that a Chimera cannot be called "good." Add to this that, imitating <term>Averroes</term> <note>Ibn Rushd (1126–1198), the great Andalusian Muslim philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were central to Western university life.</note>

in this part, we can say that "being in potential" is not "being," since in the commentaries on the fourth book of the *Metaphysics*, in the fifteenth division, he said that that which is not "in act" is not a being. <meta>This page continues the defense of the work "On Being and the One," specifically answering the 15th, 16th, and 17th objections raised by Antonio. It focuses on the classification of being, the definition of evil as a privation of good, and the mystical limits of language when speaking about God according to Dionysius the Areopagite.</meta>

# ON BEING AND THE ONE

...that the reasons are turned around. Secondly, even if it were granted to you for free that those powers were distinct, what would your reasoning prove? For a chimera <note>A mythological hybrid creature, used here as a standard philosophical example of an impossible or non-existent thing.</note> can by no means be called "being" on account of the power to produce itself which exists in God; for that power is so far from being able to be declared a chimera or anything intrinsic to a chimera that they are even infinitely distant from one another. You add, furthermore, that if the power of God and our own thought were excluded, a chimera would not be "evil," since evil is a privation which consists in a subject participating in goodness. I would respond to this with the same distinction used a little while ago: although a chimera does not look toward any subject but is absolutely "evil" <note>In this context, "evil" means a total lack of being or goodness.</note>—even though we can pronounce the notion itself of the chimera which we carry in our minds to be "something" and thus "good"—nevertheless, the chimera itself is neither something nor good. 

Furthermore, you seem to enjoy that what you brought forward was not disproved, and that the only response was that Simplicius <note>A 6th-century commentator on Aristotle.</note> did not say that. Likewise, you say you did not mean to suggest you felt Aristotle held every being whatsoever to be either "by its own nature" or "by accident" <note>original: "per se vel per accidens"</note>; nor that you ascribed anything false to Thomas [Aquinas] for that reason. Truly, although so many things have been said on this matter by the one we defend [Pico della Mirandola] that it does not seem necessary for me to speak further, and although I have proposed once not to retract things discussed by him in any way, I might say this much for my uncle <note>Referring to Giovanni Pico della Mirandola; the author is likely his nephew, Gianfrancesco Pico della Mirandola.</note> out of abundance: Simplicius, who has been summoned by you so often into judgment, has more often borne witness against you than my uncle has devised in his responses.

<margin>Solution to the fifteenth objection.</margin>

<margin>Aristotle. All these things are repeated a thousand times by Thomas.</margin>

Again, I would like to know whether you have undertaken to defend the idea that not every being is either "by accident" or "by its own nature" according to the mind of Aristotle. For he, in the fifth book of the *Metaphysics* <note>original: "primæ philosophiæ" - First Philosophy was the traditional name for Metaphysics.</note>, cuts that "being" into "being by its own nature" and "being by accident"; finally, they are cut into "substance" and "accident." These were contained in the first member of the partition, since that "by its own nature" is divided into ten categories <note>The "Predicaments" or categories of Aristotle (substance, quality, quantity, etc.).</note>: one of which is substance, the others are accidents. I would now most gladly be taught by you what kind of being that would be which is neither "by its own nature" nor "by accident." If perhaps you were to say that this division into "being by its own nature" and "being by accident" is an assignment of "complex being" <note>A "complex being" usually refers to a proposition or a compound statement (e.g., "the man is white"), whereas an "incomplex being" is a single concept or thing.</note> as you put forward in your first objections, I would not hesitate to respond that you truly cannot show that; neither any sentiment of Aristotle nor suitable reason supports your opinion. For in that place, Aristotle allows "being by its own nature" to have ten categories, one of which is substance and nine are accidents, which no one believes to be "complex beings" when they are distinguished against the complex.

<margin>Averroes.</margin>

And in that place, Averroes <note>The famous 12th-century Islamic commentator on Aristotle.</note> says that "being by its own nature" is divided by words signifying the categories; a word, however, is not a "complex being." In the sixth book of the *Metaphysics*, the same Averroes says that the first division of being is into "by its own nature" and "by accident." It could not be the first if a division of "complex being" preceded it; nor is it found in Thomas [Aquinas], in the fifth book of the *Metaphysics*, that "complex being" is divided as you asserted. Indeed, it cannot be believed—since being was first partitioned into "by its own nature" and "by accident," and that "by its own nature" was sub-partitioned into ten categories which we have shown to be "incomplex"—that an assignment of "complex being" is made in that place. These things have been said although they pertain little to the business at hand, since that dogma of yours seems to me at first glance to be consistent neither with the decrees of the Aristotelian interpreters nor with reason. But if perhaps you prove the contrary, it will be most pleasing to have learned something from such a serious philosopher as I certainly judge you to be. Furthermore, he [Pico] said that evil is a "privation" <note>A lack of a required good; e.g., blindness is the privation of sight.</note> insofar as privation was formally a 

<margin>Solution to the sixteenth objection.</margin>

negation, which you oppose by saying it is not established that there is one 

<column-break/>

opposition between affirmation and negation, and another between privation and possession <note>original: "priuationis & habitus" - "habitus" here refers to the presence of a quality or state.</note>; nor, for that reason, if evil were the privation of good, would "evil" and "non-good" necessarily be interchangeable. To which I would like it to be answered that the opposition of privation is one thing, and that of negation is another; and he did not put forward that they were the same. But for that reason, it still follows that if evil is opposed to good in a privative way, "evil" and "non-good" must be interchangeable. For privation, as Albert the Great says in the first book of the *Physics*, insofar as it is privation, is not "of itself" or "by itself," because it has "non-being" from itself.

<margin>Albertus Magnus. Aristotle.</margin>

Rather, it has even been asserted by Aristotle in the *Metaphysics* that privations are of the genus of "non-beings," since privation of itself is the other extreme of a contradiction. And therefore, since evil is the privation of good, and the consequence is "non-being" insofar as evil is evil, "evil" and "non-good" are also interchangeable. For "evil" and "nothing," as has been proved, are the same; "nothing" and "non-being" are the same; likewise "non-being" and "non-good" are the same because "being" and "good" are the same. Therefore, my uncle most correctly said that negation is a privation insofar as privation is formally a negation. For even if they differ in this—that one of them, namely contradiction, has no middle ground (as the Philosopher [Aristotle] says in the first book of the *Posterior Analytics*), while the other in one way may have one since it happens at the same time as the opposite concerning the same subject—nevertheless, as far as the proposal is concerned, they would be the same, since privation of itself is a negation and "non-being" and posits nothing, as 

<margin>Thomas.</margin>

Thomas [Aquinas] proves in many places, especially in the treatise *On the Four Opposites*. If truly non-being is evil, and evil is non-good, from these you can gather that "evil" and "non-good" are altogether interchangeable. And lest you believe that illustrious men were lacking who 

<margin>Aristotle.</margin>

asserted this: Hear Aristotle saying that "good" is said equivalently to "being." Add therefore, by the logic of contradictories, "evil" to "non-being." Hear the most celebrated theologian 

<margin>Anselm.</margin>

Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury, in his book *On the Fall of the Devil*, putting forward these words: "evil is nothing other than non-good," from which it is most consistently gathered that "evil" and "non-good" follow one another mutually.

There would have been no controversies between you and him in the seventeenth place if you had considered more diligently the little book *On Being and the One* itself, and if you had recalled to memory whatever was written in it when mention was made of those "grades" and of that very "cloud of darkness" <note>original: "caligine" - The "Cloud of Unknowing" or divine darkness, a concept from Pseudo-Dionysius where God is known by not knowing.</note> to which it is given to arrive for those contemplating. You would have seen that in those first three grades something can be enunciated about God, but in the fourth, not at all. There, the window of understanding the books of Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a highly influential Christian Neoplatonist.</note> was opened, by which you could most conveniently be moved concerning this. For he does not deny, nor could he deny, that this speech is true: "God is," in the way that we are able to both conceive and speak of God—namely, while situated in those first three grades. But he only denies that any predicate can truly explain the nature of God in that specific fourth grade of "darkness," which all right-thinking philosophers (not to mention theologians) would affirm. Since, however, this name "God"—which performs the duty of a predicate in this proposition "God is God"—not only fails to explain and declare the divine essence and nature, but is even infinitely surpassed by it, he denied that it could be affirmed of God, looking toward that fourth grade of darkness. Come then, let us examine the words themselves which will testify to the man's mind; afterwards we will bring forward some things so that it may be seen more clearly whether and how God can be spoken of by us; then we will show that your arguments against his words (even taken as they lie) conclude nothing. He had said it can be said in different ways that "God is God"; likewise, according to the opinion of Dionysius, he is above every name...

<margin>Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian theologian and philosopher of the late 5th to early 6th century, traditionally identified as a convert of St. Paul.</note></margin>
...had even said that God is greater than this very title, just as was held in his book *On Mystical Theology*. He said in another place that when you conceive of through this word "God" only that which is signified by the name, the word does not function as a **predicate** <note>In logic, the part of a sentence that says something about the subject.</note> but as a **subject**; for it is that about which one asks what can or ought to be stated about it, rather than being that which is stated about something else. For this reason, this was not unknown to Simonides <note>A Greek lyric poet famous for his wisdom.</note> when the Tyrant <note>Hiero of Syracuse, who famously asked Simonides for a definition of God.</note> consulted him; likewise, when he asked if God could not be called "God," or if it were something other than asking you what you conceived by this word "God" when you spoke of God: if you conceived nothing, you would not err, because you would be saying nothing. If you conceived something, you would be saying that God is something other than what you conceive and explain through this word "God," since He is above everything that can be conceived by us—these are his words. I believed it was clear to you from these words that the truest resolution of your doubts on this matter was evident. 

But you contend that Dionysius does not deny that God is God. Read, I pray, Dionysius in the final chapter of the book *On Mystical Theology* and the first epistle to Gaius, and it will become clear to you that God is greater than every name. Read him also in the second chapter of *The Celestial Hierarchy*, and you will understand that this divine man teaches us that the likeness of divine truth transcends all life and every subject; that no light can express it; and that all speech, all mind, and all reason is inferior to His likeness without any comparison. From these, I thought you could weigh my uncle’s <note>Referring to Giovanni Pico della Mirandola.</note> mind: namely, that it cannot truly be said "God is God" in such a way that the name "God," acting as a predicate, declares that which we attempt to conceive through the subject. This is not to say that "God is God" cannot be said in some way, just as it is said "God is good" or "God is wise," and other predications are allowed with which the sacred books are full, in which something is stated about God in some manner. But His nature is not explained by those concepts; He is infinitely distant from them. 

My uncle taught this clearly enough in the fifth chapter of his book *On Being and the One*. The passage you think is based on the words of Dionysius cited by Thomas [Aquinas] is actually based on those cited shortly before. Furthermore, Damascene <note>John of Damascus, a 7th-century monk and theologian.</note> writes in the first book of the *Sentences* of his theology that there are certain things said affirmatively of God that have the force of a "super-excellent negation." For example, if we say there is "darkness" in God, we do not mean literal darkness, but that He is not [merely] light; rather, we say He is "above light" and "beyond light" when darkness is absent. Discussing this opinion, the most learned and devout Chancellor of Paris <note>Jean Gerson (1363–1429), a prominent French scholar and reformer.</note> says: "Therefore, whatever we say affirmatively of God includes some negation." And a little later, he says that for this reason Dionysius denies that God is "being" <note>original: "ens"</note>, but affirms Him to be "above being." 

Aegidius <note>Giles of Rome, a 13th-century theologian.</note> says in his first book on the *Sentences* that God is "wise," but not in the way we understand wisdom. He says this is the reason why Averroes <note>The famous 12th-century Andalusian philosopher.</note> in the twelfth book of the *Metaphysics* pronounced that these predications we attribute to God are similar to mathematical propositions; in their manner, the things we understand are in the objects, but not in the way we understand them—just as we understand a line that is in matter, but not by the same logic by which it exists in matter. But why do I delay you with many words when I can make you certain of this truth we assert with even a few? Namely, that you may know that whatever we predicate of God signifies something far different than what we conceive and speak. Jesus Christ himself, the "power of God and the wisdom of God," and "Truth" according to the Gospel of John, says: "God is spirit." Dionysius, in his book *On Mystical*

By these final words, he teaches the reader that it is true that "God is spirit," so as to agree with the Gospel of Christ, and yet He is not spirit in the way we understand spirit, lest we believe that the nature of God can be truly expressed by us through any name.

Although I thought this was not hidden from you, since my uncle hinted in his responses to your objections that you did not very willingly admit the sayings of Dionysius during the dispute, I would have you know that he was the most faithful disciple of the Apostle Paul in the faith of Christ. By Paul's help, God willed that Dionysius, having left behind the errors of the gentiles, should recognize and follow the truth and be gifted with the crown of martyrdom for the faith of Christ. Gregory <note>Pope Gregory the Great.</note> spoke great things of his doctrine, as did Pope Martin in the synod celebrated at Rome against the heretics. Damascene and many others have praised him with the highest honors. His books, hidden by heretics for a long time, were concealed from the minds of the faithful. There is also a saying of Constantine the Philosopher <note>Better known as St. Cyril, missionary to the Slavs.</note>, who had committed all his books to memory: that if Dionysius had been held by more of the Fathers who fought great battles with the heretics and enemies of the holy Catholic Church, they would have achieved triumph over their enemies much sooner and more easily (which was later done by them only slowly and with great labors).

Solution to the
Eighteenth
Objection.

When you intend to prove that "God" can be called "God" because of the "reason of the name" <note>An argument based on the definition or etymology of the word.</note> which is predicated of the name, I say (my dear Antonio) that you labor in vain. For you are not stating something about God, but about this name "God." To understand this more clearly, I will explain at greater length: I ask you what you conceive as the "reason of the name" designated by "water." If you conceive nothing, you do not err (to use my uncle's words). If you conceive something, I ask again if you conceive it as that about which something can be stated. If in this way, you still do not err, because that "A" <note>A placeholder for the concept.</note> will hold the place of the subject, not the predicate. But if you conceived that which was stated about Him, you would wander far astray, since God Himself is infinitely greater than everything you can conceive. 

Even the Platonist Apuleius <note>A 2nd-century Latin writer and philosopher.</note>, in his book *On the Dogma of Plato*, calls Him "unutterable" and "innominable" [nameless]. Plato’s own words on this matter were rendered into Latin by Apuleius himself: "To find God is not easy; to understand Him is impossible." Therefore, let us say that all affirmations about God are improper, since whenever we wish not only to say but even to conceive anything, He exceeds it to infinity. Indeed, not only while we are held in this earthly prison of ignorance and misery, but even in the very enjoyment of God by which we are perfectly blessed in heaven, the faculty will be granted to us not to *comprehend* God, but to *apprehend* Him—to use the words of our theologians. 

Furthermore, you believe these propositions conflict with each other: namely, "God is above that which can be conceived" and "something cannot be affirmed of God." You say: let the definition of the name be "above that which can be conceived," and the argument will hold. But this is resolved: for when it is said that proper affirmations cannot be applied to God, it is understood that no predicate is found that represents the nature of God in its entirety. This phrase—namely, "above that which can be conceived"—signifies nothing other than that God cannot be conceived...

<margin>
Apuleius.
</margin>

## ON BEING AND THE ONE

...to be possible, and that what God is cannot be known. They say, therefore, that these words do not only describe what God is, but rather that it is impossible to know what He is. Thus, they possess the power of negation rather than affirmation. But even if they were used there to affirm something, your argument would not hold; otherwise, if someone asked about the essence of an unknown thing they desired to know, we could simply answer the inquirer: "It is that which we do not know, which we have not yet grasped, and which we cannot conceive." Would such a petition not seem unsatisfied? One would not be able to state anything affirmatively about that thing through this teaching, but only negatively—unless, perhaps, someone were found who could explain to others what that thing was, which, being entirely unknown to men and above the reach of all thought, could neither be known nor conceived even by himself. Therefore, both Simonides and the Tyrant <note>Hiero I of Syracuse.</note> who consulted him knew that the greatest name of God represented something; and yet one of them desired to know what God was, while the other denied that he knew. 

Furthermore, you use this connection: "God is above everything that can be conceived; therefore, God cannot be conceived; otherwise, He would be above Himself. Therefore, He cannot be loved or worshiped." I respond that God can be fully and perfectly conceived only by Himself, as He truly is, and by no other intellect. However, it does not follow from this that He cannot be loved or worshiped. For we conceive that the Deity is so great, endowed with such infinite omnipotence, and surpassing all creatures in every kind of virtue, that we cannot conceive Him except through His effects. Stirred and warmed by this admiration, we catch fire with love for Him. We conceive His effects, and we recognize that He is the supreme good; thus, we admire, worship, and love Him.

<margin>Themistius <note>A 4th-century Greek philosopher and rhetorician.</note></margin>
For once these effects which God created are known—to use the words of Themistius—He turns the minds and faces of all toward admiration and praise of Himself. Likewise, we read those things which have been divinely revealed, and being endowed with His grace, we conceive through faith that which we cannot fully conceive by nature. It is necessary for us to love Him above all things, so that finally, once the riddle of this flesh is broken, we may be able to contemplate Him as He is, with the greatest joy of both the inner and outer man, which is our ultimate happiness. Again, for us to love something, it is not necessary for it to be perfectly seen, known, or conceived by us; it is enough if we know that it exists, or that it is such a thing, even if that knowledge is confused and somewhat obscure. This knowledge comes either from faith or from effects; thus, even a small amount of preceding knowledge, of whatever kind it may be, is enough for us to love such a thing. For we can love any thing unless we are entirely lacking in knowledge of it; for from the things the soul knows, it learns to love the unknown, as 

<margin>
Gregory of Rimini.
Thomas.
Solution to the final objection.
John of Baconthorpe.
</margin>
Gregory <note>Gregory of Rimini (c. 1300–1358), an Augustinian theologian.</note> says. Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas.</note> also proves in the *Prima Secundae* <note>The first part of the second division of Aquinas's *Summa Theologica*.</note> that something can be loved perfectly even if it is not perfectly known, and he proposes God as an example among others. 

Finally, you say my uncle <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola.</note> thought the power of gold was so great that, whether we willed it or not, gold would by necessity drag God along with it, either in reality or as an axiom. But I would believe, my dear Antonio, that he did not merely think this, but was certain that it was not a "power" of gold, but rather an "impotence," such that gold could neither exist nor be understood if God were removed. I could refer you to John of Baconthorpe <note>An English Carmelite philosopher (d. 1346) known as the "Resolute Doctor."</note>, whom we mentioned in the resolution of the fifth objection. However, when you were recounting the arguments of my uncle—by which he asserted that "God does not exist" and "gold exists" are mutually exclusive—you said you did not wish to respond, lest you seem to be groping in the dark. My intention is to show in a matter clearer than light (even perhaps in your judgment) that it would have been worthwhile for you to undertake the dissolution of those arguments if you were able; if not, at least to put your hand to the work or frankly confess that his assertions were true. These are the arguments of my uncle, which

<column-break/>

I will now explain. It is impossible for anything to exist if Being itself <note>Latin: *ipsum esse*—the philosophical concept of pure existence.</note> does not exist; but God is Being itself; therefore, it is impossible for gold to exist if God does not exist. Furthermore, if God is not, then the Infinite is; if the Infinite is, then nothing is, because if the Infinite is, the finite is not, since the Infinite destroys itself—just as other things that contain a contradiction do. If "nothing" exists, then gold does not exist. It is impossible for anything to exist if Being itself does not exist, but God etc. 

Since Being itself, which is God (as no one denies), is that by whose participation not only are all things what they are, 

<margin>
Thomas.
Plato.
</margin>
but they also depend upon it and are preserved at every moment—as not only all theologians, and especially Thomas, teach most abundantly, but as is also asserted by Plato in the *Timaeus*—it is impossible for gold to exist except by the grace of His being and by participation in Him. 

Furthermore, if God is not, then the Infinite is. All beings besides God are finite and contained within certain limits. There is no doubt that they have and possess this limited nature through the work and grace of God. 

<margin>
Plato.
Book of Wisdom.
</margin>
For this reason, the followers of Plato say that he called God "The Limit" in the *Philebus*, because He limits all things by distributing forms like measures everywhere. But the Book of Wisdom also says that all things were constituted by Him in "weight, number, and measure." <note>Wisdom 11:20.</note> If, therefore, God—for whose sake all beings are finite—did not exist, nothing would be finite, and therefore everything would be infinite. If the Infinite is, then nothing is, because if the Infinite is, the finite is not, since the Infinite destroys itself, just as other things that contain a contradiction. Since it has been proven that there is one thing from which all things receive their being, if that one is removed, nothing exists and nothing is finite; for if it is "infinite," this means it is not limited or made finite by that First One by whose help all things both exist and are finished and limited. It follows that the infinite does not exist. Therefore, the infinite destroys itself, since saying "the infinite exists" in the sense used here is nothing other than saying "nothing exists." For if there is neither the finite nor God, it is beyond controversy that there is nothing at all. 

These, Antonio, are the points I have brought forward to clarify my uncle's opinion, which perhaps contains other teachings as well. For it is not within everyone's reach to attain what he had conceived. But I believe other meanings also lie hidden under the "bark of the words," and I am moved by the words with which he concluded his response: "These things, I believe, are sufficient for a man, however ingenious, but let us bring and hold onto what is inaccessible." These words, which I have written while performing the duty of an interpreter, satisfy me and shall close my response, after first bringing forward certain points that both strengthen my uncle's opinion and confirm and elucidate my interpretation of his words which I offered earlier.

<margin>
Reasons to demonstrate the proposition.
Aristotle.
</margin>
For if the First fails, it is necessary that all those things which proceed from it perish, as is gathered from Aristotle’s eighth book of *Physics*. But God, according to the testimony of the same philosopher, is the First Truth from which all other true things come. Therefore, if God were removed, it is necessary for all true things to perish. But if true things tend toward nothingness, beings are likewise not saved from destruction, since they move within the same boundaries.

<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
Likewise, if that which communicates both being and life to things were removed, who would not see that those same things would utterly perish? That God grants this to the things themselves is the opinion of Aristotle in the first book of *On the Heavens*, where he adds that this is communicated more clearly to some and more obscurely to others. Furthermore, whatever is ruled by the art of the First Cause will collapse if that cause perishes. 

<margin>Averroes.</margin>
Averroes <note>A 12th-century Al-Andalus Muslim philosopher, known for his influential commentaries on Aristotle.</note> testifies in the second book of the *Metaphysics* <note>Referred to here as "First Philosophy."</note> that this entire structure is safely governed and ruled by the First Cause, under which no one can doubt that gold is also contained and included. Many other things I could bring forward...

...from the sacred books, including much from the Gospel itself, much from the most sacred dogmas of the Apostle Paul, and very many things from <margin>Gregory, Augustine, Thomas, John Scotus</margin> others. I would do so very gladly, as I love you as a man, respect you as a philosopher, and revere you as a Christian. If you wish to put my feelings toward you to the test, you will find that my deeds outweigh my words.

### To the Illustrious Prince and his singular lord, Count Giovanni Francesco: Antonio of Faenza sends many greetings.

I have read the defenses sent to me regarding your uncle's writings, in which I clearly perceived great learning and an admirable sharpness of intellect. I was wonderfully delighted by your findings, not only because I see that the liberal arts will finally have excellent tutors and patrons by whom they may be rescued from darkness and barbarism, but even more because I easily promise myself something great and grand from you if you continue to philosophize. Posterity will see that I have measured nothing falsely, if you live; may God only grant you a long life. As for me, I do not disapprove of what you have written so subtly and acutely in defense of your uncle. For even if your uncle were still alive, I would not have protracted the debate already begun any further, just as I clearly testified to him in my last opposition. He replied through a messenger that he also would write nothing more. Therefore, let those who read be the judges of the case. But if you have decided that those things you have carefully meditated upon should be given to the printers, let it be done while keeping the honor of a friend safe and intact, as you promised. There are indeed some words in the booklet that have a bit of a sting <note>original: "aculei" — literally "prickles" or "stings," referring to sharp rhetorical barbs.</note>, and not just a little; you can easily temper these if you wish, without changing the meaning of the facts. If you do this, as I hope, it will not be unwelcome. I believe I have defended my cause sufficiently and abundantly, and could have easily continued to do so daily. But let there now be a limit to the dispute. Furthermore, illustrious Count, I want you to believe that I am yours and always will be, for you to use at your discretion. Farewell. From Ferrara, December 16, 1495.

### Giovanni Francesco Pico della Mirandola to the distinguished philosopher Antonio of Faenza, many greetings.

Your wishes have been fully satisfied, as have my promises to you, since I have removed all the words that seemed to carry any "sting" from my writings. One must excuse the impulse of the soul if, by chance, the argument was conducted more sharply than was proper. Something must be granted to a just defense—and all the more so because it is a common fault among those who, in their commentaries, either accuse someone or excuse themselves or their friends, to attack those to whom they write with insults, to pursue them with slanders, to provoke them with reproaches, and to perpetrate other such things foreign to the duty of a good man. From these things (with you as a witness and appointed judge), we have entirely abstained. At your hint, we have removed about ten or so somewhat sharp words, though the meanings remain intact. I would not have you believe I had any other purpose in laboring over this little commentary than to defend my uncle Pico without offending you. Indeed, I would have preferred that nothing had ever been debated between you, so that the path to writing about this matter would have been closed to me and every occasion removed. For the business of letters can hardly, or only with great difficulty, be conducted in an altercation while maintaining all the honor due to those being addressed. Add to this that such a task is rarely performed without a certain swelling of pride, which must be greatly avoided. As for what you say about the defense of your cause, we say the same about ours. But as you rightly wrote, let there be an end to the controversy; let those who read be the judges, provided they are learned and not biased toward either side—or, if they are held too ardently by love for one of us, let that love not cast a spell over their eyes. Furthermore, you attribute much to me, though I deserve little, and you promise great things of me if only I continue to philosophize. But I fear, my Antonio, that I may entirely temper or perhaps desist from this study of philosophy you mention. I will tell you what I feel about this matter: namely, that this pursuit, when too affected, brings us much harm and little profit. I do not say this to condemn or disparage the many truths, or at least the likenesses of truth, the knowledge of which we acquire by philosophizing. Rather, I blame the common use or (to speak more significantly) the abuse. Unless we strive greatly to avoid this, and examine our thoughts assiduously and with the utmost diligence, the poison of ambition creeps into the Christian soul, which later gives birth to deadly pride. From this, it often happens that the lovers of this wisdom in which we daily dwell entirely neglect that Wisdom which was begotten but is eternal, from which all this fleeting and temporary wisdom is derived—swollen and elated as they are by fading glory. But let us see, I pray, why we should be so puffed up in spirit, or why we value ourselves too highly. For how small is our knowledge? We possess the smallest science of natural things; and those very things we are ignorant of—which are both many and great—silently cry out that we profess or think ourselves learned in vain and falsely. By God, even a simple man, a farmer unskilled and entirely ignorant of letters, could ask many questions about things placed right before our eyes, for which a philosopher, otherwise very great, could not give a certain reason. In perceiving the very substances that are entirely separated from sensible matter, how far do we proceed in our knowledge? We see them only with bleary and nocturnal eyes of the mind. But what shall we say of divine things, at which we pant and are anxious not just to know but even to track down, blinking...

### ON BEING AND THE ONE

...that it is possible and yet what God is cannot be known. They say, therefore, these words not only regarding what God is, but that it is impossible to know what He is. They possess, therefore, the force of denying rather than affirming. But even if they were to affirm in that same place, your argument would not hold; otherwise, if someone asked about some unknown thing they desired to know and inquired about its essence, could we respond to the seeker: "It is that which we do not know, which we are not acquainted with, which we have not yet conceived in the mind, nor are able to conceive"? Would he not seem unsatisfied by such a request? This is so that, having received this teaching, he might be able to enunciate something about that thing affirmatively, rather than merely negatively—unless perhaps someone were found who could intimate to others what that thing was, which, being utterly unknown to men and above the reach of all thoughts, could not be known or conceived even by itself. Thus, both Simonides <note>The Greek poet Simonides of Ceos, who famously requested more time each day when asked by Hiero, the Tyrant of Syracuse, to define the nature of God, eventually concluding that the more he thought, the more obscure it became.</note> and the Tyrant who consulted him knew that the name of God represented the greatest thing, and yet one of them desired to know what God was, while the other denied that he knew. Furthermore, you use such a connection: "God is above all that can be conceived, therefore God cannot be conceived; otherwise He would be above Himself." Therefore, [you argue] He cannot be loved or worshiped. I respond that God can be conceived fully as He is only by Himself, and by no other intellect; yet it does not follow that He cannot be loved or worshiped. For we conceive the deity to be so great, endowed with omnipotence, surpassing creatures in every kind of power in infinity, that we cannot conceive of Him except through His effects. Stirred by this wonder, and becoming warmed, we burn with love for Him. We conceive His effects, and that He is the <term>summum bonum</term> <note>The highest good.</note>, and we wonder at, worship, and love Him. For when these things which God made are perfectly known—to use the words of <margin>Themistius</margin> Themistius <note>A 4th-century Greek philosopher and rhetorician who commented extensively on Aristotle.</note>—He turns the minds and faces of all toward the wonder and commendation of Himself. Likewise, we read those things which have been divinely revealed and, endowed with His grace, we conceive through faith that which we cannot fully conceive by nature; it is necessary at least that we love Him above all things so that finally, the enigma of this flesh being broken, we may be able to contemplate Him as He is, with the greatest joy of both the inner and outer man, which is our happiness. Again, in order for us to love something, it is not necessary for it to be perfectly seen, known, or conceived by us; it is enough if we know that He exists, or is such a being, even if confusedly and obscurely. This is either from faith or from effects. Thus, even a modest prior knowledge, of whatever sort it may be, is enough for us to love such a thing; for we can love any thing unless we are entirely lacking in knowledge of it. For from <margin>Gregory of Rimini. Thomas.</margin> those things which the soul knows, it is said to love the unknown, as Gregory <note>Gregory of Rimini (c. 1300–1358), a scholastic theologian.</note> says. Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas.</note> also, in the *Prima Secundae* <note>The first part of the second division of Aquinas's *Summa Theologiae*.</note>, proves that something can be loved perfectly even if it is not perfectly known, and he proposes the example of God among other things.

<margin>Solution to the last objection.</margin>
<margin>John Baconthorpe.</margin>
Finally, you say that my uncle <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola.</note> thought the power of gold was so great that, whether we willed it or not, or even if God were removed, it would by necessity draw God with it. But I would believe, my dear Antonius, that he did not think the power of gold was so great, but rather its impotence—indeed, he was made certain of it—so that gold could neither exist nor be understood if God were removed. And although I could refer you to <term>John Baconthorpe</term> <note>original: "Ioannem de bachone." A 14th-century English Carmelite philosopher known as the "Resolute Doctor."</note>, whom we mentioned in the resolution of the fifth objection, yet when you recounted my uncle's arguments—by which he asserted that "God does not exist" and "gold exists" are mutually contradictory—did you say you did not wish to respond lest you seem to grow dim-sighted in a matter clearer than light? It is my counsel (perhaps even in your judgment) that it would have been worthwhile for you to undertake their dissolution if you were able; if not, at least to apply your hands to the work or frankly confess that his assertions were true. These are my uncle's arguments, which I will soon clarify: It is impossible for anything to exist if <term>Being itself</term> <note>original: "ipsum esse." In scholastic philosophy, this refers to the pure act of existence, which is identified with God.</note> does not exist; but God is Being itself; therefore, it is impossible for gold to exist if God does not exist. Furthermore, if God is not, then there is the infinite; if there is the infinite, there is nothing, since if it is infinite, it is not finite, because the infinite destroys itself, just as other things which contain a contradiction do. If there is nothing, gold does not exist. It is impossible for anything to exist if Being itself does not exist, but God etc. Since Being itself, which is God (as no one denies), is not something in whose participation all things not only exist, but also depend upon and are preserved by at every moment—as not only all theologians, and especially <margin>Thomas. Plato.</margin> Thomas, most copiously teach, but even as was asserted by Plato in the *Timaeus*—it is impossible for gold to exist, since it exists by the grace of Being itself and by participation in it. Furthermore, if God is not, then there is the infinite; all beings besides God are finite and contained within certain limits. There is no doubt that they have and possess this limited nature which they hold by the work and grace of God. Wherefore <margin>Plato. Book of Wisdom.</margin> the followers of Plato say that he called God "the Limit" in the *Philebus*, because He limits all things by distributing forms like measures everywhere. But also the Book of Wisdom says that all things were constituted by Him in "weight, number, and measure" <note>Wisdom 11:20.</note>. If, therefore, God—by whose cause all beings are finite—were not, nothing would be finite, and therefore everything would be infinite. If it is infinite, it is nothing, because if it is infinite, it is not finite, since the infinite destroys itself, just as other things that contain a contradiction do. Since it has been proven that there is one thing from which all receive being, and that they are finite, with that one removed, nothing exists and nothing is finite; for if it is infinite, that is, not terminated and made finite by that first thing by whose help all things both exist and are finished and terminated, it follows that the infinite does not exist. Therefore, the infinite destroys itself, since to say "the infinite exists" in the manner it is accepted here is nothing other than to say "nothing exists"; for if it be neither finite nor God, it is beyond controversy that it is nothing at all. These are the things, Antonius, which I have brought forward to open the meaning of my uncle, which perhaps contains other dogmas as well; for it is not for everyone to attain what that man had conceived. But because I think other senses also lie hidden under the "bark of the words," I am moved by these words of his with which he ended his response: "These things, I believe, are sufficient for you, a man however ingenious, but let us move into the approach and hold those things which I have written by performing the office of an interpreter." Since these things are sufficient, they shall also close my response, having first brought forward certain things which both strengthen my uncle's opinion and confirm and equally elucidate my interpretation of his words which we produced before. For when the first fails, it is necessary that all those things <margin>Reasons to show the proposition. Aristotle.</margin> which proceed from it perish, as is gathered from Aristotle’s eighth book of the *Physics*. But God, by the testimony of the same philosopher, is the first truth from which all other true things are; therefore, if God is removed, it is necessary that all true things perish. But if true things tend toward nothingness, beings likewise are not rescued from destruction, since they move in an equal circuit. <margin>Aristotle.</margin> Likewise, if that one who communicates both being and living to things is removed, who would not see those same things as entirely about to perish? That God grants this to things themselves is the opinion of Aristotle in the first book of *On the Heavens* <note>De Caelo.</note>, who also adds that it is communicated more clearly to some and more obscurely to others. Furthermore, whatever is ruled by the art of the first cause falls down when that cause perishes. That this safe machine [of the universe] is governed and ruled by the first <margin>Averroes.</margin> cause is testified by Averroes <note>The 12th-century Andalusian philosopher known for his commentaries on Aristotle.</note> in the second book of the *First Philosophy* <note>Referring to Aristotle’s *Metaphysics*.</note>, under which no one can doubt that gold is also contained and comprehended. I could bring many other things into the midst...

It argues that God is the necessary source of all existence and limits, such that without God, even a material substance like gold could not exist or be understood.</summary>

# APOLOGIA

<margin>Gregory, Augustine, Thomas, John Scotus</margin>
...indeed from the sacred books, such as much from the Gospel itself, much from the most holy dogmas of the Apostle Paul, and very many things from others—such as from <term>Gregory<note>St. Gregory the Great (c. 540–604), a Church Father whose works Gianfrancesco cites to show that all creation depends entirely on God’s preservation.</note></term>, who said all things would fall into nothingness unless they were preserved by almighty God. I could also cite <term>Augustine<note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430); his work *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis* (De Genesi ad litteram) was a standard reference for medieval and Renaissance cosmology.</note></term> on Genesis, and Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas.</note>, and John Scotus <note>John Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a major scholastic philosopher.</note> in his treatise *On the First Principle*. However, I deliberately pass over these, since it is enough to have proven the matter by natural reasons—which you seemed to demand—and by the teachings of the gentile philosophers; a proof which you believed could not be achieved by such means. Therefore, regarding all these things we have stated, I should think that in the eyes of fine minds it will be beyond controversy that all my uncle's opinions have been sufficiently defended, perhaps even in your own judgment. Nevertheless, we wrote these things not to clash with you. We wrote them even reluctantly, as
<margin>Giovanni Mainardi, Cristoforo Sasolo</margin>
our friend <term>Giovanni Mainardi<note>Giovanni Mainardi (1462–1536) was a celebrated physician and humanist from Ferrara who worked closely with the Pico family.</note></term> and our fellow citizen of Mirandola, <term>Cristoforo Sasolo<note>A physician from Mirandola and a former student of Antonio Faventino.</note></term>, who was once your student, can testify. We also wrote without hatred; the greatest proof of this for you is that if you judge anything committed to these pages to be detracting from your honor in any part, I am ready to strike it out and remove it at your discretion before this response reaches the hands of others. I would do so very gladly, since I love you as a man, observe you as a philosopher, and cherish you as a Christian. If it pleases you to test my spirit toward you, you will perceive that my deeds outweigh my words.

->To the Illustrious Prince and his singular lord, Count Gianfrancesco, Antonio of Faenza sends many greetings.<-

I have read the defenses sent to me regarding your uncle's writings, in which I clearly perceived great learning and an admirable skill of mind. I am wonderfully delighted by your findings, not only because I see that the liberal arts will finally have the best guardians and patrons to rescue them from darkness and barbarism, but even more because I easily promise myself something great and grand from you if you continue to philosophize. Posterity will see that I have told no lie, if you live; may God grant you a longer life. As far as I am concerned, I certainly do not disapprove of what you have written with such subtlety and sharpness in your uncle’s defense. Indeed, even if your uncle were alive, I would not have drawn out the dispute already begun any further, as I clearly testified to him in my last opposition. He responded through a messenger that he too would write nothing more. Therefore, let those who read be the judges of the case. But if you have decided that those things you have rightly meditated upon should be given to the printers, let it be done with the honor of a friend safe and intact, as you promised. There are indeed some words in the booklet that have something of a "sting," and not just a little; from these you can easily abstain if you wish, without changing the sense of the matter at all. If you do this, as I hope, it will not be ungrateful. I seem to myself to have protected my cause sufficiently and abundantly, and could easily have protected it daily; but let there now be a limit to the disputation. For the rest, illustrious Count, I wish you to think of me as yours, now and always, to use at your discretion. Farewell. From Ferrara, the 16th day of December, 1495.

<column-break/>

->Gianfrancesco Pico della Mirandola sends many greetings to the distinguished philosopher Antonio of Faenza.<-

Your wishes have been abundantly satisfied, and my promises to you have been fulfilled, since I have removed all the words from our writings that seemed to carry any "sting." One must pardon the impulse of the soul if perhaps in some place it acted more sharply than was fitting. Something must be forgiven for a just defense, and all the more so since it is a common fault of those who, in their commentaries, either accuse someone or excuse themselves or their friends, to pursue those they strike at with insults, to attack with slanders, to provoke with reproaches, and to perpetrate other things of that kind that are foreign to the duty of a good man. From these things (I call you as witness and judge) we have entirely abstained, and we have removed about ten or so somewhat sharp words at your suggestion (while keeping the meanings intact). I would not have you believe there was any other purpose for laboring over this little commentary than to defend my uncle Pico without offending you. On the contrary, I would have preferred that nothing had ever been disputed between you, so that the path to writing on this matter had been closed to me and every occasion removed. For the business of letters can only with great difficulty be conducted in an altercation while maintaining all the honor due to those to whom the words are addressed. This task is hardly performed without a certain swelling of the spirit <note>i.e., pride or agitation.</note>, which is greatly to be avoided. As for what you say about the protection of your cause, we say the same about ours. But enough of the controversy; let those who read be the judges (as you rightly wrote), provided they are learned and not biased toward either side—or, if they are held too ardently by love for one of us, let love at least not create a deception in their eyes. Furthermore, you attribute much to me, though I deserve little, and you promise great things of me if only I continue to philosophize. But I fear, my Antonio, lest I entirely moderate or perhaps desist from this study of philosophy of which you make mention. I will tell you what I feel about this matter: namely, that much harm and little profit is brought to us by being too fond of this business. I do not say this to condemn or disparage the many truths, or at least the likenesses of truth, the knowledge of which we acquire by philosophizing. But I blame the common use or (to speak more significantly) the abuse of it. Unless we strive greatly to avoid this, and examine our thoughts constantly and with the greatest diligence, the poison of ambition creeps into the Christian heart, which afterwards brings forth deadly pride. From this it often happens that the lovers of this wisdom in which we are daily engaged entirely neglect—swollen and elated by fleeting glory—that wisdom which is begotten but eternal, from which all this flowing and temporary wisdom is derived. But let us see, I pray, from what source our spirits are puffed up, and why we value ourselves too much. For how small is our knowledge? Since we possess the smallest science of natural things, and those very things which we are ignorant of—which are both many and great—silently cry out that we either profess or think ourselves learned in vain and falsely. By God, even a rustic man, little skilled or entirely ignorant of letters, a farmer, could inquire about many things placed before our sight and eyes, for which a philosopher, otherwise the greatest, could not give a certain reason. Indeed, in perceiving those substances entirely separated from sensible matter, how far do we proceed in knowledge? We see them only with bleary and "night-owl" eyes of the mind. But what shall we say of divine things? Toward the knowledge of which, and even the tracking of them, we pant and anxiously go blind—

We must therefore boast of what is necessary: that we have learned the meditations of others, drinking them in as if from someone telling a history. But it is a history of nature; yet one placed in bitter altercations through diverse studies and agitated by varying opinions, and for that reason uncertain—which is most aptly revealed by the very name of "opinion" <note>original: "opinionis". But see how different the effect has been for our controversy compared to others, once the discussion—whether conducted by voice or by writing—was finished: quite often among those whose minds were in discord, hatreds and grudges are practiced; fraudulent wars are plotted; detractions of honor and reputation spring up from both sides. But you and our Pico <note>Referring to his uncle, Giovanni Pico della Mirandola.</note> were <term>godfathers<note>original: "compatres".
