Nevertheless, the former harmony of your minds has not been dissolved by this. I, however, was known to you only by name, nor were you to me while my uncle lived; this defense has brought it about that a certain treaty of friendship has been entered into between us. Take care that this remains stable as long as we shall live; and so that it may persevere eternally after this death which we await, by living rightly and piously, do what you can by whatever means; strive also to make that very thing easier. Meanwhile, let it not irk you to experience with what love I pursue you. Perhaps I shall provide in abundance what you have requested, more than I promised at the end of the defense. For there is nothing so arduous that I would not do for the sake of more readily deserving you (truly a most serious philosopher). From the castle of Mirandola, January 4, 1496.

->Gianfrancesco Pico of Mirandola, Count of Concordia,<-
->To the reader, Greetings.<-

Accept, reader, these "night-labors" <note>original: "lucubrationes". This refers to scholarly works produced by burning the midnight oil.</note> of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, works of lighter care, which perhaps he himself would not have published while living, nor would we have, unless stirred by the frequent encouragements of famous men. You will read first a most elegant oration, spoken indeed with youthful alacrity, but often admired by teachers for its peak of doctrine and eloquence. Let it not move you if many things are joined at its end which are also inserted in the preface of the *Apology*; for when he published the latter abroad, he always kept the former at home, making it common only to friends. You will see many teachings of the ancients, previously hidden in the wrappers of enigmas and fables, most ingeniously unlocked; and you will see how he shows, with effort, strength, and oratorical charms, how the "poetic theology" of the ancient sages served as a handmaid to the mysteries of our theology. Having untied certain knots of both, he invites men to literary wrestling-grounds; for in these he was most frequent during that time. These he later left behind as if they were playful preludes to more serious studies, turning his mind to those things which we have already issued,

<column-break/>

and which we are to produce in the future. You will also read some letters (for to have collected all would be most laborious), some familiar ones written in his tender age as well as in his more mature years; others, after he dedicated his whole heart to God, written full of most holy warnings. You will find that the former smell most copiously of both doctrine and eloquence; the latter you will perceive to savor of both in abundance, and beyond these, to breathe most richly the love of Christ.

# ORATION OF GIOVANNI PICO
# OF MIRANDOLA, COUNT
# OF CONCORDIA.

<margin>
The great proposition of Abdala the Saracen and Hermes must be noted: The dignity of Man.
</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative historiated initial 'L' depicting a landscape with trees and a building within a classical square frame.</image-desc>
I have read, venerable fathers, in the records of the Arabs, that <term>Abdala the Saracen<note>Likely referring to Abd Allah Ibn al-Muqaffa or a similar figure representing Arabic wisdom.</note></term>, when asked what was to be seen as most admirable on this, so to speak, worldly stage, replied that nothing is seen more wonderful than man. To this opinion agrees that saying of <term>Hermes<note>Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary Hellenistic figure associated with a body of mystical and philosophical texts.</note></term>: "A great miracle, O Asclepius, is man." When I thought about the reason for these sayings, those many things which are brought forth by many regarding the excellence of human nature did not satisfy me: that man is the intermediary between creatures, familiar with the higher beings, the king of lower things, the interpreter of nature by the sharpness of his senses, the inquiry of his reason, and the light of his intelligence. That he is the interval between stable eternity and flowing time, and (as the Persians say) the bond, or rather the marriage-song of the world, and according to the testimony of David, "a little lower than the angels." These are great things indeed, but they are not the principal ones—that is, those which may rightly claim for themselves the privilege of the highest admiration. For why should we not admire the angels themselves and the most blessed choirs of heaven more? At last, I seemed to myself to have understood why man is the most fortunate living thing, and consequently worthy of all admiration, and what precisely that condition is which he has been allotted in the order of the universe—an enviable state not only to the brutes but even to the stars and to minds beyond this world. A thing beyond belief and wonderful! Why not? For it is for this reason that man is rightly called and esteemed a great miracle and a truly admirable animal. But what that condition is, hear, fathers, and grant me this attention with kind ears, according to your humanity. Now the highest Father, God the <term>Architect<note>original: "architectus deus". A common Renaissance metaphor for God as the rational creator of the cosmic structure.</note></term>,
<margin>Constitution of the world.</margin>
had fashioned this worldly home which we see, the most august temple of divinity, by the laws of his secret wisdom. He had adorned the region above the heavens with minds; He had quickened the ethereal spheres with eternal souls; He had filled the excremental and drossy parts of the lower world with a crowd of animals of every kind. But, when the work was finished, the Craftsman desired that there be someone who might weigh the reason of so great a work, love its beauty, and admire its magnitude. Therefore, when all things were already finished (as <term>Moses<note>The Biblical prophet, traditionally the author of Genesis.</note></term> and <term>Timaeus<note>The title character of Plato's dialogue on cosmology.</note></term> testify),
<margin>Moses. Timaeus.</margin>
He finally thought about creating man. But there was nothing in the archetypes from which He might fashion a new offspring, nor in His treasures what He might bestow as an inheritance upon His new son, nor in the seats of the whole world where this contemplator of the universe might sit. All things were now full; all things had been distributed to the highest, middle, and...

<meta>This page continues the "Oration on the Dignity of Man" by Giovanni Pico della Mirandola. # GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA

distributed into the lowest orders. But it was not in the Father’s power to fail in this final birth, as if exhausted; it was not characteristic of His wisdom to waver in a necessary matter for lack of a plan; it was not characteristic of His beneficent love that he who was to praise divine liberality in others should be forced to condemn it in himself. At last, the best of artisans decreed that he to whom nothing could be given as his own should share in whatever had been private to each individual. Therefore, He received man, a work of indeterminate image, and having placed him in the middle of the world, He addressed him thus: "We have given you, O Adam, no fixed seat, no form of your very own, no gift peculiar to you alone, so that whatever seat, whatever form, and whatever gifts you yourself shall desire, these you may have and possess according to your wish and your judgment. The nature of all other creatures is defined and restricted within laws prescribed by us. You, constrained by no limits, shall define it for yourself according to your own free will, in whose hand I have placed you. I have set you in the center of the world, so that from there you might more easily survey whatever is in the world. We have made you neither celestial nor earthly, neither mortal nor immortal, so that as if you were your own arbitrary and honorable sculptor and modeler <note>original: "plaſtes & fictor"</note>, you may fashion yourself into whatever form you prefer. You will have the power to degenerate into those lower things which are brutes; you will have the power to be reborn into those higher things which are divine, according to the judgment of your soul." O supreme liberality of God the Father! O supreme and wonderful happiness of man! To whom it is granted to have what he chooses, to be what he wishes. Brutes, as soon as they are born, bring with them from their mother's womb <note>original: "e bulga matris" (literally "from the mother's pouch"), a phrase attributed here to the satirist Lucilius.</note> what they will possess. The highest spirits [angels] were from the beginning, or soon after, what they will be for eternal ages. But the Father implanted in man at his birth seeds of every kind and germs of every form of life. Whichever of these a man cultivates, those will grow and bear their fruit in him. If they are vegetative, he will become a plant. If sensual, he will grow brute-like. If rational, he will turn into a celestial animal. If intellectual, he will be an angel and a son of God. And if, content with the lot of no creature, he withdraws into the center of his own unity, having become one spirit with God in the solitary darkness of the Father, he who is set above all things shall stand before all. Who would not admire this chameleon of ours? Or who would admire anything else more? Not without reason did <margin>Asclepius the Athenian</margin> Asclepius the Athenian say that this shifty and self-transforming nature was symbolized in the mysteries by Proteus <note>A sea-god in Greek mythology capable of changing his shape at will.</note>. Hence those celebrated metamorphoses among the Hebrews and Pythagoreans. For even the more secret theology of the Hebrews transforms now the holy Enoch into that angel of divinity whom they call <unclear>Metatron</unclear>, and now transforms others into other divine beings. And the Pythagoreans transform wicked men into brutes and, if we believe Empedocles, even <margin>Empedocles</margin> into plants. Following these, Muhammad [Maumeth] often had this on his lips: that he who falls away from divine law becomes a brute—and rightly so. For it is not the bark that makes the plant, but its dull and unfeeling nature; nor the hide that makes the beast of burden, but its brute and sensual soul; nor the circular body that makes the heaven, but right reason; nor the separation from the body, but spiritual intelligence that makes the angel. For if you see someone devoted to his belly, a man crawling on the ground, it is a shrub you see, not a man; if you see someone blinded by the vain illusions of the imagination, as if by Calypso’s spells, and enslaved to his senses by a scratching lure, it is a brute you see, not a man. If you revere a philosopher discerning all things by right reason, he is a celestial animal, not an earthly one; if you see a pure contemplator, unaware of the body, relegated to the inner chambers of the mind: this is neither an earthly nor a celestial animal; this is a more august divinity clothed in human flesh. Who would not admire man?

<column-break/>

who is not without reason designated in the sacred Mosaic and Christian writings now by the name of "all flesh," now "every creature," since he fashions, fabricates, and transforms himself into the appearance of all flesh and the character of every creature. For this reason, <margin>Evantes the Persian</margin> Evantes the Persian writes, where he explains Chaldean theology: that man has no native image of his own, but many external and foreign ones. Hence that saying of the Chaldeans: <insert>[Space for Hebrew/Chaldaic text]</insert>
->That is, man is an animal of a diverse, multiform, and self-dissolving nature.<-
But why all this? So that we may understand that since we are born under this condition—to be what we wish to be—we ought to take care of this above all: that it may not be said of us that, while we were in honor, we did not know we had become like brutes and senseless beasts of burden. But let us rather remember that saying of <margin>Asaph the prophet</margin> Asaph the prophet: "You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High," lest by abusing the most indulgent liberality of the Father, which gave us free choice, we make that which is healthy harmful to ourselves. Let a certain sacred ambition invade our souls, so that, not content with mediocre things, we may pant after the highest, and (since we can if we wish) strive with all our might to attain them. Let us disdain earthly things; let us despise celestial things; and finally, setting aside whatever belongs to the world, let us fly to the court beyond the world, closest to the most eminent divinity. There, as the sacred mysteries hand down, Seraphim, Cherubim, and Thrones occupy the first places; <margin>Note on the representation of the super-celestial choirs.</margin> let us, incapable of yielding and impatient of second place, emulate their dignity and glory. We shall be in no way inferior to them when we wish. But by what method, or by doing what? Let us see what they do and what life they live. If we also live that life (for we can), we shall have already equaled their lot. The Seraph burns with the fire of charity; the Cherub shines with the splendor of intelligence; the Throne stands with the firmness of judgment. Therefore, if dedicated to an active life we undertake the care of lower things with a right assessment, we shall be strengthened by the steady solidity of the Thrones. If, resting from actions, meditating on the Creator in his work and the work in the Creator, we are occupied in the leisure of contemplation, we shall flash on all sides with Cherubic light. If we burn for the Creator himself alone with charity, we shall suddenly be inflamed into the Seraphic likeness by his fire, which is all-consuming. Upon the Throne, that is, the judge, sits God, the judge of the ages. Over the Cherub, that is, the contemplator, He flies, and as if by brooding, He cherishes him. For the Spirit of the Lord is carried over the waters—those, I mean, which are above the heavens, which in Job praise the Lord with morning hymns. He who is a Seraph, that is, a lover, is in God, and God is in him; indeed, God and he are one. Great is the power of the Thrones, which we attain by judging; supreme is the sublimity of the Seraphim, which we attain by loving. But in what way can anyone <margin>That we can attain to the super-celestial [beings].</margin> either judge or love things unknown? Moses loved the God whom he saw, and as a judge among the people, he administered those things which he, as a contemplator, had previously seen on the mountain. Therefore, the Cherub in the middle prepares us by his light for the Seraphic fire, and likewise illuminates us for the judgment of the Thrones. This is the bond of the first minds, the Palladian order, the presiding spirit of contemplative philosophy; this we must first emulate and strive for, so that we may be snatched up to the heights, and descend well-instructed and prepared for the duties of action. But truly, it is worthwhile if our life is to be formed according to the model of the Cherubic life, to have before our eyes and ready at hand what that life is and of what sort it is, and what are their actions and works. Since this is not possible for us to achieve through our own strength—because we are flesh and savor the things of the earth—let us go to the ancient fathers, who can provide us with most abundant and certain faith regarding these things, as they are familiar and kin to them. Let us consult...

<margin>The lifting up of Paul.</margin>
If we were to ask the apostle Paul, that "chosen vessel," what he saw when he was lifted up to the third heaven, he would surely answer (following the interpretation of Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite was a Christian theologian whose writings on the "Celestial Hierarchy" of angels deeply influenced medieval and Renaissance thought.</note>) that he saw the armies of the Cherubim being purified, then illuminated, and finally perfected. Therefore, if we wish to emulate the life of the Cherubim here on earth, we must first restrain the impulses of our passions through **moral science**; next, we must dispel the darkness of our reason through **dialectic** <note>Dialectic refers to the art of logical argument and reasoning.</note>, washing the soul clean of the filth of ignorance and vice. We do this so that our emotions do not rage out of control and our unguided reason does not occasionally wander into madness. Then, we should flood the well-ordered and purified soul with the light of **natural philosophy**, so that we may finally bring it to completion with the knowledge of divine things.

And so that we do not rely only on ourselves, let us consult the patriarch Jacob, whose image shines carved upon the throne of glory. This most wise father—who sleeps to the lower world but remains awake to the world above—will advise us. He will advise us through a figure (for all things happened to them in symbols) that there is a ladder extending from the lowest ground to the highest heavens, divided into a series of many rungs, with the Lord sitting at the summit. He saw the contemplative angels ascending and descending these rungs in turn. 

If we, who aspire to an angelic life, must do the same, I ask you: who would touch the ladder of the Lord with a dirty foot or with hands that are poorly cleaned? As the ancient mysteries teach, it is a sacrilege for the impure to touch the pure. But what are these "feet" and these "hands"? 

<margin>Commendation of the liberal arts, by which we can be made immortal.</margin>
<margin>Note.</margin>
<margin>The foot of the soul.</margin>
<margin>The hand of the soul.</margin>
The "foot" of the soul is surely that most lowly part by which the soul rests upon material things as if on the ground: I mean the power of nourishment and growth, the fuel of lust, and the teacher of pleasurable softness. And why should we not call "the hand" of the soul its capacity for anger, which fights as the defender of our desires, struggling for them and seizing its prey in the dust and heat? To prevent us from being rejected from the ladder as profane and polluted, let us wash these "hands" and "feet"—that is, the entire sensory part of the soul in which bodily allurements reside—in the living stream of **moral philosophy**, as if it were a river. 

But even this is not enough if we wish to be companions to the angels wandering on Jacob’s ladder, unless we are first well-trained and prepared to move properly from rung to rung, never straying from the path and performing the trip back and forth. When we have achieved this through the art of speech or reasoning <note>original: "artem sermocinalem sive rationariam"</note>, then, animated by the spirit of the Cherubim, we shall philosophize through the rungs of nature. We shall penetrate everything from the center to the center, sometimes descending, tearing the "one" apart like Osiris into a multitude by "Titanic" force <note>Pico uses the myth of Osiris being torn apart to represent the way human reason breaks down complex reality into parts</note>, and sometimes ascending, gathering the multitude like the limbs of Osiris into "one" by the force of Apollo <note>original: "vi phœbea"</note>, until at last, resting in the lap of the Father who sits above the ladder, we find our fulfillment in the happiness of **theology**.

Let us also ask the righteous Job, who made a covenant with the God of life before he was even brought into life, what the supreme God desires most among those ten hundred thousand who assist Him. He will surely answer: "Peace," according to what is written of Him: *He makes peace in the high places.* And since the middle order interprets the commands of the highest order to the lower ones:

<margin>Empedocles.</margin>
Let the philosopher Empedocles interpret for us the words of Job the theologian. He signifies to us that there is a double nature placed in our souls: by one, we are lifted upward toward the heavens; by the other, we are thrust downward toward the depths, through "strife and friendship" or "war and peace," as his poems testify. In these, he complains that he is tossed about, driven from the gods into the deep by strife and discord, like a madman. 

<margin>How the discord within us is to be settled. First cause.</margin>
Truly, fathers, there is a manifold discord within us; we have heavy and internal conflicts at home, worse than civil wars. If we wish to avoid these, if we aspire to that peace which lifts us so high that we are placed among

<column-break/>

<margin>Moral philosophy is what ends these conflicts.</margin>
<margin>Second: Dialectic.</margin>
<margin>Third: Natural philosophy.</margin>
<margin>Heraclitus. Homer.</margin>
the exalted ones of the Lord, then **philosophy** alone will entirely restrain and settle those conflicts within us. First, **moral philosophy** will quiet the rages of the many-headed beast and the quarrels, anger, and spirit of the lion, if our "inner man" seeks even a temporary truce with these enemies. Then, if we take better counsel for ourselves and desire the security of perpetual peace, she will be present and generously fulfill our prayers. Indeed, having "slaughtered both beasts" <note>Referring to the taming of the lower animal instincts</note>, she will strike an unbreakable covenant of holiest peace between the flesh and the spirit, like a ritual sacrifice <note>original: "quasi icta porca" - referring to a Roman custom of sacrificing a sow to seal a treaty.</note>. 

**Dialectic** will settle the disturbances of reason when it is tossed about in a tumult between conflicting arguments and the traps of logic. **Natural philosophy** will settle the disputes and disagreements of opinion which vex, distract, and tear the restless soul apart. But she will settle them in such a way as to command us to remember that nature, according to Heraclitus, is born of war, which is why Homer called it "contention." Therefore, she cannot grant us true quiet and solid peace in herself; that is the gift and privilege of her mistress, most holy **theology**. 

Theology will show the way to that peace and lead us there as a companion. Seeing us from afar as we hurry toward her, she will cry out: "Come to me, you who have labored; come, and I will restore you. Come to me, and I will give you the peace which the world and nature cannot give you." Called so softly, invited so kindly, we shall fly with winged feet like earthly Mercuries into the embraces of our most blessed mother and enjoy the longed-for peace: that most holy peace, an inseparable bond, a unanimous friendship by which all souls do not merely harmonize in one mind that is above every mind, but in an ineffable way become entirely "one."

<margin>The final end of philosophy according to the Pythagoreans.</margin>
This is that friendship which the Pythagoreans say is the goal of all philosophy. This is that Peace which God makes in His heights, which the angels descending to earth announced to men of good will, so that through it, men themselves ascending into heaven might become angels. Let us wish this peace for our friends, for our century, and for every house we enter. Let us wish it for our soul, so that through it, the soul itself may become the house of God. 

After the soul has shaken off its filth through moral philosophy and dialectic, and has adorned itself with manifold philosophy as if with courtly splendor, and has crowned the tops of its gates with the garlands of Theology, let the King of Glory descend; and coming with the Father, let Him make His dwelling within it. If the soul shows itself worthy of such a great guest (such is His immense mercy), she shall receive this beautiful guest—clothed in a golden garment like a wedding robe and surrounded by a variety of many sciences—not merely as a guest, but as a bridegroom. So as never to be separated from Him, she will desire to be separated from her people and her father's house. Forgetting herself, she will desire to die in herself so that she may live in her bridegroom, in whose sight the death of His saints is precious indeed. I say that death—if it should even be called death—is the fullness of life, the meditation of which the wise have said is the study of philosophy. 

Let us also cite Moses himself, who is only slightly lower than the holy and ineffable fullness of intelligence from which the angels drink their nectar. We shall hear this venerable judge proclaiming laws to us who dwell in the desert solitude of this body:

<margin>The study of philosophy is to be embraced from Moses as if from a law.</margin>
Those who are still polluted and need moral training should live with the common people outside the tabernacle, under the open sky, like the priests of Thessaly, while they purify themselves. Those who have already regulated their conduct may be received into the sanctuary, but they should not yet touch the sacred objects. Instead, as diligent Levites, they should first serve the sacred rites of philosophy through the service of dialectic. Then, once they are admitted to the rites themselves, they may contemplate sometimes the multi-colored (that is, the starry) courtly ornament of the palace of the supreme God, sometimes the celestial lampstand divided into seven lights, and sometimes the elemental coverings...

<margin>Greek secrets.</margin> Let them contemplate in the priesthood of philosophy, so that finally, through the merits of theological heights, having been received into the inner sanctuary of the temple with no veil of images intervening, they may enjoy the glory of divinity. These things Moses certainly commands us; and in commanding, he warns, excites, and exhorts us that we should prepare a path for ourselves through philosophy toward future heavenly glory while we are able. But truly, not only the Mosaic or Christian mysteries, but also the theology of the ancients shows us the benefits and dignity of these liberal arts about which I have come to dispute. For what else do the various levels of initiation observed in the Greek secrets mean? First, those who were purified through what we might call the "cleansing arts"—moral philosophy and dialectic <note>Dialectic is the art of logical reasoning used to clear away false beliefs.</note>—achieved the "reception of the mysteries." And what else can this be but the interpretation of nature's hidden secrets through philosophy? Then, finally, for those so prepared, there came that <term>Epopteia</term> <note>original: "ἐποπτεία" — the highest stage of initiation in the Greek mysteries, meaning a direct "beholding" or "inspection" of divine truths.</note>, which is the inspection of divine things through the light of theology. Who would not long to be initiated into such sacred rites? Who would not wish—by setting aside all human concerns, despising the goods of fortune, and neglecting the body—to become a guest of the gods while still dwelling on earth, and, drenched in the nectar of eternity, to be gifted with the prize of immortality while still a mortal creature? Who would not wish to be so inspired by those "Socratic frenzies" sung by Plato in the *Phaedrus*, that by the rowing of wings and feet, they might flee from here—that is, from this world situated in evil—and be carried in a swift course to the heavenly Jerusalem?

<margin>For Socrates is said to be the first of men to bring ethics down from heaven.</margin> We shall be driven, fathers, we shall be driven by these Socratic frenzies, which so place us outside of our own minds that they place our mind and our very selves in God. We shall be driven by them indeed, if we have first driven out what is within us. For if through moral philosophy the forces of our passions have been so stretched to their proper harmonies that they sound together in an unshakable accord, and if through dialectic our reason has moved in measured steps, then, stirred by the frenzy of the Muses, we shall drink in the heavenly harmony with our innermost ears. Then Bacchus, the leader of the Muses, in his own mysteries—that is, by showing the invisible things of God to us through the visible signs of nature—will intoxicate us from the abundance of the house of God. In this house, if we are as faithful as Moses, the most sacred Theology will approach and animate us with a double frenzy. For as we measure, from that most eminent height of contemplation, all things that are, will be, and have been in the indivisible flow of eternity, and as we gaze upon their primeval beauty, we shall become the winged lovers of those truths, like the seers of Apollo. Finally, stirred by an ineffable charity as if by a divine sting, and burning like Seraphim outside ourselves, full of the divine power, we shall no longer be ourselves, but He himself who made us. If anyone investigates the meanings of the sacred names of Apollo and the mysteries hidden within them, they show clearly enough that this god is no less a philosopher than a seer. <margin>Ammonius on the three Delphic precepts.</margin> Since Ammonius <note>Ammonius Saccas or perhaps Ammonius Hermiae, philosophers who commented on the divine nature of the Delphic maxims.</note> has followed this sufficiently, there is no reason for me to treat it differently now. But let three Delphic precepts <note>Maxims inscribed at the Temple of Apollo in Delphi.</note> govern the soul, fathers, which are exceedingly necessary for those who are about to enter the holy and most majestic temple—not of a fictional Apollo, but of the true Apollo who illuminates every soul coming into this world. You will see that these precepts warn us of nothing other than to embrace with all our strength this tripartite philosophy which is the subject of our present dispute. For that famous saying, <term>Nothing in excess</term> <note>original: "μηδέν ἀγαν" — meden agan.</note>, rightly prescribes the norm and rule for all virtues through the principle of the "golden mean," which moral philosophy treats. Then that saying, <term>Know thyself</term> <note>original: "γνῶθι σεαυτόν" — gnothi seauton.</note>, excites and exhorts us to the knowledge of all nature, of which the nature of man is the connector and, as it were, the bridge. For he who knows himself knows all things in himself, <margin>Zoroaster.</margin> as Zoroaster wrote, and after him,

<column-break/>

<margin>Plato. The precepts of Pythagoras and their explanation.</margin> Plato in the *Alcibiades*. Finally, illuminated by this knowledge through natural philosophy, and being already close to God, we shall address the true Apollo with the theological greeting "Thou art" <note>original: "εἶ" — Pico interprets the Greek word "ei" (thou art) as a recognition of God’s absolute being.</note>; thus we shall call upon him familiarly and happily. Let us also consult Pythagoras, the wisest man, who was especially wise because he never deemed himself worthy of the name of "wise man." He first commands us "not to sit upon a bushel"—that is, not to let the rational part of the soul, by which it measures, judges, and examines all things, lose its strength through idle laziness. Rather, we must direct and stir it up constantly through the exercise and rules of dialectic. Then he indicates two things to be avoided above all: "not to urinate against the sun" and "not to cut one's nails during a sacrifice." But after we have, through moral science, passed out the flowing appetites of overflowing pleasures, and have cut away the "nail-clippings" of the soul—the sharp prominences of anger and the stings of our passions—only then may we begin to take part in the sacred mysteries of Bacchus mentioned before, and devote ourselves to our contemplation, of which the Sun is rightly called the father and leader. Finally, he warns us to "feed the cock"—that is, to nourish the divine part of our soul with the knowledge of divine things as if with solid food and heavenly ambrosia. This is the cock at whose sight the lion—that is, all earthly power—trembles and feels awe. This is that cock to whom "understanding was given," as we read in the Book of Job. <margin>See the multiple interpretations of the cock.</margin> When this cock crows, erring man returns to his senses. This cock, in the twilight of the morning, daily joins in song with the morning stars as they praise God. To this cock, Socrates, when he was dying and hoped he was about to join the divinity of his soul to the divinity of the greater world, said he owed a debt to Aesculapius <note>Aesculapius was the god of medicine; Socrates’s final request to sacrifice a cock to him suggests that death is the "cure" for the sickness of earthly life.</note>—that is, the physician of souls—being now placed beyond all danger of disease. Let us also review the monuments of the Chaldeans, and we shall see (if they are to be believed) that the path to happiness lies open to mortals through these same arts. <margin>Zoroaster’s opinion on the soul.</margin> The Chaldean interpreters write that it was a saying of Zoroaster that the soul is winged, and when the wings fall off, it is carried headlong into the body; then, when they grow back, it flies back to the heavens. When his disciples asked how they might obtain souls with well-feathered wings, he said: "Water the wings with the waters of life." When they asked again where they might seek these waters, he answered them through a parable (as was the man's custom): "The paradise of God washes and waters all things with four rivers. From there, draw for yourselves the waters of salvation." The name of the river from the North:

Pay attention and consider diligently, fathers, what these dogmas of Zoroaster mean: surely nothing else than that we should wash away the filth of our eyes by moral science, as if by the western waves; then by dialectic, as if by a northern rule, we should align our vision toward "The Right." Then, in the contemplation of nature, we should accustom ourselves to endure the still-weak light of truth, like the dawn of a rising sun, so that finally, through theological piety and the most sacred worship of God, we may—like heavenly eagles—bravely endure the most brilliant radiance of the midday sun. These are perhaps those "morning, noon, and evening" knowledges first sung of by David and explained more widely by Augustine. This is that midday light which inflames the Seraphim to the limit and likewise illuminates the Cherubim. <margin>Note.</margin> This is that region toward which the ancient father Abraham was always journeying; this is that place where, according to the dogmas of both the Kabbalists and the Moors, there is no place for unclean spirits...

<meta>This page continues Pico’s argument that philosophy is a necessary healing stage for the soul. He has just finished discussing the Greek mysteries and now uses the imagery of Archangels to describe the soul’s progress through moral philosophy, natural philosophy, and finally, theology.</meta>

...they handed down these doctrines. And if it is permitted to bring any of the more secret mysteries into public view, even if only through a riddle: after the sudden fall from heaven dizzied the head of our "internal man," and—according to 

<margin>Jeremiah.</margin>
Jeremiah—death entered through the windows <note>A reference to Jeremiah 9:21, often interpreted by Renaissance thinkers as the senses letting in distractions that "kill" the soul’s focus.</note>, harming our vital spirit and its offspring, let us call upon Raphael, the heavenly physician. May he free us through moral philosophy and dialectic <note>The art of logical argument.</note> as if with healing medicines. Then, once we are restored to good health, Gabriel, the "strength of God," will dwell within us. He will lead us through the miracles of nature, pointing out the power and might of God everywhere. Finally, he will hand us over to the high priest Michael, who will crown those who have completed their service in the ranks of philosophy with the priesthood of theology, as if with a crown of precious stones. These, most worshipful fathers, are the things that have not only encouraged but compelled me to the study of philosophy. I certainly would not have said these things if I were not responding to those who are accustomed to condemn the study of philosophy, especially in princes or in those who live in even moderate circumstances. 

<margin>The great weakness of our time is proven by its constant contempt for the study of philosophy.</margin>
For it is now a common thing—which is the misfortune of our age—that philosophy is held in contempt and insult rather than honor and glory. A deadly and monstrous belief has invaded almost everyone's minds: that one should philosophize either not at all or only a little. It is as if they believe they already have the causes of things, the ways of nature, the reason of the universe, the counsels of God, and the mysteries of heaven and earth clearly explored before their eyes and in their hands. Nothing is done unless some favor can be gained or some profit made; it has come to the point (alas!) where men are not considered wise unless they make the study of wisdom a mercenary trade. One can see modest Pallas <note>Athena, the goddess of wisdom.</note>, dwelling among men as a gift of the gods, being cast out, exploded, and hissed off the stage. She has no one to love or favor her, unless she—prostituting herself, as it were, and receiving a small fee for her deflowered virginity—brings back ill-gotten money to her lover's small chest. I say all these things, not without the greatest grief and indignation, not against the princes of this time, but against the philosophers, who believe and preach that one should not philosophize because no 

<margin>Note.</margin>
rewards or prizes have been established for philosophers. As if they do not show by this very fact that they are not truly philosophers! Since their whole life is placed in either profit or ambition, they do not embrace the knowledge of truth for its own sake. I will grant this to myself and will not blush to praise myself in this regard: I have never studied for any other reason than to be excellent. I have never hoped for or sought any other reward or fruit from my studies and late-night labors than the cultivation of my soul and the knowledge of the truth I have always so greatly desired. I have always been so greedy for and such a lover of this truth that, leaving aside all care for private and public affairs, I have given myself entirely to the leisure of contemplation. No detractions from the envious, no insults from the enemies of wisdom, have been able to deter me in the past, nor will they be able to in the future. Philosophy herself has taught me to depend upon my own conscience rather than on external judgments, and to always think not so much about whether I am hearing bad things about myself, but rather that I myself neither say nor do anything bad. Indeed, I was not unaware, most worshipful fathers, that this very disputation of mine—which I wanted to be pleasing and delightful to all of you who favor the good arts and have honored it with your most august presence—would be heavy and troublesome to many others. I know there are those who have condemned my undertaking before now, and who condemn it currently on many grounds. It is common for those things done well and holily toward virtue to have no fewer—if not more—barking critics than those things done wickedly and wrongly toward vice. There are those who do not approve of this whole kind of disputing and this practice of debating literature in public, asserting that it is intended for the display of talent and the showing off of learning rather than for the gaining of erudition. 

<margin>At what age he proposed those nine hundred conclusions for debate.</margin>
There are others who do not disapprove of this type of exercise but do not approve of it in me. They argue that I, at this age—being only twenty-four years old—have dared to propose a disputation on the sublime mysteries of Christian theology, the highest points of philosophy, and unknown disciplines, in a most celebrated city, before a most ample assembly of very learned men, and in the presence of the Apostolic Senate <note>The high-ranking officials of the Catholic Church in Rome.</note>. Others, while granting that I may dispute, do not want me to dispute nine hundred questions, slandering the act as being as superfluous and ambitious as it is beyond my strength. I would have surrendered to their objections immediately if the philosophy I profess had taught me to do so; and now, since she is teaching me, I would not respond if I believed this discussion between us was intended for the purpose of quarreling and brawling. 

<margin>Plato.</margin>
Therefore, let all intent to insult and provoke—and that "envy" which Plato writes is always absent from the divine choir—depart from our minds. Let us examine in a friendly manner whether I should dispute, and whether I should dispute so many questions. First, I will not say much to those who slander this custom of public disputation, since this "fault"—if it is considered a fault—is shared with me not only by all of you, most excellent doctors, who have frequently performed this duty with the highest praise and glory, but by Plato, Aristotle, and the most esteemed philosophers of every age. They were certain that nothing was more helpful for achieving the knowledge of the truth they sought than 

<margin>How necessary disputation is: its very nature and glory are celebrated.</margin>
frequent exercise in debate. For just as the strengths of the body are made firmer through gymnastics, so without a doubt the strengths of the soul become far stronger and more vigorous in this "literary wrestling floor." I do not believe that the poets, when speaking of the weapons of Pallas, or the Hebrews, when they say that "iron" <note>original: "σίδηρον"</note> is the symbol of the wise, meant anything else than that these most honorable contests are absolutely necessary for attaining wisdom. This is perhaps why the Chaldeans <note>Ancient Babylonian astrologers and sages.</note>, in the horoscope of one who is to become a philosopher, require that Mars and Mercury be in a trine aspect—as if to say that if you take away these meetings, these "battles," all philosophy would become sleepy and drowsy. But truly, with those who say I am unequal to this task, my defense is more difficult. For if I say I am equal to it, I may be seen as immodest and having too high an opinion of myself; if I confess I am unequal, I may be marked as rash and ill-advised. See the difficulties I have fallen into, the position I am in, where I cannot promise something about myself without fault, which I then cannot perform without fault. Perhaps I could cite Job—that "the spirit is in all men"—and hear with Timothy, "let no one despise your youth." But out of my own conscience, I will say this: there is nothing great or singular in me. 

<margin>See how he defends himself.</margin>
I do not deny that I am perhaps studious and eager for the fine arts, but I do not take or claim for myself the name of a "learned man." Therefore, the reason I took such a great burden upon my shoulders was not because I was unaware of my own weakness, but because I knew that it is a peculiar feature of these literary battles that there is a gain in being defeated. Because of this, even the weakest person can and should not only not avoid them, but actively seek them out. For he who falls receives a benefit from the victor, not an injury; he returns home richer (that is, more learned) and better equipped for future battles. Encouraged by this hope, I, a weak soldier, have decided to engage with the strongest and most vigorous of all in such a...

<meta>This page continues Pico’s defense of his intellectual ambitions. Having established philosophy as a ladder to the divine, he now justifies the massive scope of his nine hundred theses, arguing that a true seeker of truth must study every school of thought—Latin, Greek, Arabic, and Hebrew—rather than being bound to a single master.</meta>

### ### JOHN PICO OF MIRANDOLA

<margin>
An excuse for the great number of conclusions. This varied collection of schools can be seen at the beginning of the book of "Theses," where this same point is repeated from the end of this speech on philosophizing.
</margin>

...I have not feared to decide on a heavy battle. Whether this was done rashly or not can be judged better by the outcome of the fight than by my young age. It remains for me to respond, in the third place, to those who are offended by the large number of things I have proposed, as if this burden rested on their shoulders and was not rather a labor to be exhausted by me alone, however great it may be. It is surely indecent and far too irritable to wish to set a limit on another person’s hard work.

<margin>
Cicero.
</margin>

And as Cicero says of this matter: in a pursuit that is better the greater it is, one should not desire mediocrity. In such grand attempts, it was necessary for me either to fail or to satisfy the challenge. If I satisfy it, I do not see why performing well in ten questions is considered praiseworthy, while doing so in nine hundred is considered blameworthy. If I should fail, they will have a reason to accuse me if they hate me, or a reason to excuse me if they love me.

Since in a matter so grave and so large, it will be more worthy of pardon than accusation that a young man, with limited talent and meager learning, fell short. Indeed, according to the poet, if strength fails, boldness will certainly be a merit; in great things, even to have willed them is enough. But if in our age many, imitating Gorgias of Leontini <note>A famous Greek Sophist known for claiming he could speak on any subject.</note>, have been accustomed to propose disputes—not without praise—concerning not only nine hundred but even all questions of all arts, why should I not be allowed to dispute, without blame, about many things indeed, but things that are nevertheless certain and determined? But they say this is superfluous and ambitious. I contend, however, that I have done this not only non-superfluously, but necessarily. And if they themselves would consider the method of my philosophizing, they would be forced to admit it is clearly necessary. For those who have devoted themselves to any one of the "families" <note>The different schools or "sects" of philosophy, like the Thomists or Scotists.</note> of philosophers—namely to Thomas or to Scotus, who are now most frequently in hand—they can indeed test their learning in the discussion of a few questions.

But I have so trained myself that, sworn to the words of no master, I have poured myself through all the masters of philosophy, examined every page, and acknowledged every family. Therefore, since I had to speak of all of them, I could not propose only a few things from each without the total number of things brought forward from all of them being very large, lest I should seem bound to one school while neglecting the defense of the others' private doctrines. Let no one condemn in me that I am "carried as a guest wherever the storm takes me" <note>A quote from Horace, meaning he is not bound to one single sect.</note>. For this was observed by all the ancients, that in rolling through every kind of writer, they passed over no commentaries they could read. This was true especially of Aristotle, who for that reason was called by Plato "the Reader" <note>original: "ἀναγνώστης" (anagnōstēs)</note>. It is surely a mark of a narrow mind to have confined oneself within a single "Porch" <note>The Stoa, or school of Stoicism.</note> or "Academy." Nor can one have rightly selected a personal view from all of them who has not first become intimately acquainted with all of them.

Add to this that in every family there is something distinguished that is not common to the others. And to begin with our own thinkers, to whom philosophy has most recently arrived: there is in John Duns Scotus something vigorous and analytical. In Thomas Aquinas, something solid and balanced. In Aegidius <note>Giles of Rome.</note>, something polished and exact. In Francis <note>Francis of Mayronis.</note>, something sharp and acute. In Albert the Great, something ancient, ample, and grand. In Henry of Ghent, it has always seemed to me, something sublime and venerable. Among the Arabs, there is in Averroes something firm and unshakable. In Avempace and Al-Farabi, something grave and thoughtful. In Avicenna, something divine and Platonic. Among the Greeks, philosophy is in general especially clear and chaste. In Simplicius, it is rich and abundant. In Themistius, it is elegant and concise. In Alexander of Aphrodisias, it is consistent and learned. In Theophrastus,

<column-break/>

it is gravely elaborated. In Ammonius, it is clear and graceful. And if you turn to the Platonists—to review a few—in Porphyry you will be delighted by the abundance of matter and his multifaceted religion. In Iamblichus, you will venerate a more secret philosophy and the mysteries of the "barbarians" <note>The term used by Greeks and Romans for non-Greek cultures, here referring to Egyptians, Chaldeans, and Hebrews.</note>. In Plotinus, there is nothing specific for you to admire, for he shows himself admirable in every way; the "sweating" Platonists can scarcely understand him as he speaks divinely about divine things and, with a learned indirectness of speech, far above man about human things. I pass over the more recent ones: Proclus, luxuriant with "Asiatic fertility" <note>A rhetorical term for a rich, flowery style.</note>, and those who flowed from him: Damascius, Olympiodorus, and many others, in all of whom that "divine" <note>original: "τὸ θεῖον" (to theion)</note>—which is the peculiar symbol of the Platonists—always shines forth. To this is added that if there is any sect that attacks truer dogmas and mocks good causes with the slander of its wit, it confirms rather than weakens the truth; like a flame shaken by movement, it excites the fire rather than extinguishing it. Moved by this reasoning, I wished to bring into the open the opinions not of just one school (as some preferred), but of every kind of doctrine, so that by this comparison of many sects and the multifaceted discussion of philosophy, that "splendor of truth" which Plato mentions in his letters might shine more clearly into our minds like a sun rising from on high.

<margin>
The honor of the Academy. Augustine.
</margin>

What would it be if only the philosophy of the Latins—namely Albert, Thomas, Scotus, Aegidius, Francis, and Henry—were treated, while the philosophers of the Greeks and Arabs were omitted? Since all wisdom flowed from the "barbarians" to the Greeks, and from the Greeks to us. Thus our countrymen have always thought it enough, in their method of philosophizing, to stand upon foreign discoveries and to cultivate the inventions of others. What would it be to have dealt with the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle.</note> regarding natural things, unless the Academy of the Platonists was also called upon? Their doctrine concerning divine things has always been held as the most sacred among all philosophies, as Augustine testifies; and it is now brought into public for the test of dispute by me for the first time—as far as I know (may the word be free from envy)—after many centuries.

<margin>
Seneca.
</margin>

And what would it have been to have treated the opinions of others, however many they were, if we, coming as if to a banquet of wise men without a "contribution" <note>Pico uses the term "symbolum," a contribution to a communal meal.</note>, brought nothing of our own, nothing produced and labored over by our own talent? Surely it is ignoble (as Seneca says) to be wise only from a commentary, as if the discoveries of our ancestors had closed the path to our own industry, or as if the force of nature in us were exhausted, so that it could produce nothing from itself which might, if not demonstrate the truth, at least point to it from afar. For if a farmer hates sterility in his field, and a husband in his wife, surely the divine mind joined and associated with the soul will hate an unfruitful soul all the more, since a far more noble offspring is desired from it.

<margin>
As quickly as possible. He found hidden doctrines. What Boethius and Simplicius promised.
</margin>

Therefore, not content with the common doctrines, I have added many things from the ancient theology of Hermes Trismegistus, many from the teachings of the Chaldeans and of Pythagoras, and many from the more secret mysteries of the Hebrews. I have also proposed for dispute many things discovered and meditated upon by us concerning natural and divine matters. We have proposed, first, the harmony between Plato and Aristotle, believed in by many before this but sufficiently proven by no one. Boethius, among the Latins, promised he would do this, but he is not found to have ever done what he always wished to do. Simplicius, among the Greeks, professed the same; I wish he had performed it as well as he promised. Augustine also writes in his *Against the Academics* that there were several who tried to prove the same with their most subtle disputes: namely, that the philosophy of Plato and Aristotle is the same. John the Grammarian <note>John Philoponus.</note> likewise says that Plato differs from Aristotle only among those who do not understand Plato’s words; nevertheless, he left the proof of this to posterity...

<summary>Pico defends the vast scope of his 900 theses by arguing that a true philosopher must be a "guest" in every school of thought, from the Latins and Greeks to the Arabs and Hebrews, to find the full splendor of truth. He also announces his project to prove the underlying harmony between the philosophies of Plato and Aristotle.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico’s defense of his intellectual program. He has just finished explaining why he has included so many diverse schools of thought in his nine hundred theses. Now, he transitions into his own original contributions, specifically his "new" dogmas, his revival of Pythagorean numerology, and his controversial defense of "Natural Magic" as a tool for understanding the divine.</meta>

### ### JOHN PICO OF MIRANDOLA

<margin>Note.</margin>
We have also added several points in which we assert that the opinions of the <term>Scotists</term><note>Followers of John Duns Scotus, known for his "subtle" logic.</note> and the <term>Thomists</term><note>Followers of Thomas Aquinas, the influential Dominican theologian.</note>, as well as those of Averroes and Avicenna <note>Major Arabic philosophers whose works were central to medieval European thought.</note>, which are usually thought to be in conflict, are actually in agreement. In the second place, we have set forth what we ourselves have devised in both Aristotelian and Platonic philosophy, as well as 
<margin>Note on the number of Pico’s dogmas.</margin>
seventy-two new physical and metaphysical dogmas. If anyone holds to these, they will be able—unless I am mistaken, which will soon be clear—to resolve any proposed question regarding natural and divine matters using a far different reasoning than that which is taught in the schools or cultivated by the doctors of this age. Nor should anyone wonder, fathers, that I, in my first years and at a tender age—during which it was barely permitted for me (as some boast) to read the commentaries of others—wish to bring forth a new philosophy. I would rather they praise it if it is defended, or condemn it if it is rejected, and finally judge not the age of the author, but rather the merits or demerits of the ideas. Moreover, besides that new 
<margin>A new method of philosophizing through numbers. Plato.</margin>
system of philosophizing through numbers which we have introduced, it is indeed an ancient one, observed by the earliest theologians—especially by Pythagoras, by Aglaophemus, by Philolaus, by Plato, and by the earlier Platonists. But in this time, like other noble things, it has withered away through the neglect of later generations, so that hardly any traces of it can be found. Plato writes in the *Epinomis* that among all the liberal arts and contemplative sciences, the chief and most divine is the science of numbering. Seeking also why man is the wisest animal, he answers: "Because he knows how to count." 
<margin>Aristotle. Abu Ma’shar.</margin>
Aristotle also mentions this opinion in his *Problems*. Abu Ma'shar <note>Original: "Abumafar," a famous Persian astrologer.</note> writes that it was a saying of Avenzoar of Babylon <note>Likely referring to a Babylonian sage or possibly the physician Avenzoar.</note> that he knew all things who knew how to count. These things can in no way be true if by the "art of numbering" they understood that art in which merchants are now primarily experts; for Plato also testifies to this, warning us with a loud voice not to think that this divine arithmetic is the arithmetic of merchants. Therefore, since I seem to myself after much study to have explored that arithmetic which is so highly praised, I have promised that I will publicly answer seventy-four questions—which are considered the principal ones among physical and divine matters—through the use of numbers.

<margin>Proficiency in magical theorems is not hidden from Pico. See more on the question of magic and Cabala.</margin>
We have also proposed magical theorems, in which we have indicated that magic is of two kinds. One consists entirely of the work and authority of demons; a thing, by God, to be cursed and monstrous. The other is nothing else, when well-explored, than the absolute perfection of natural philosophy. While the Greeks mention both, they do not deign to call the former by the name of magic, instead naming it <term>goeteia</term> <note>Original: "γοητείαν," meaning sorcery or witchcraft.</note>. The latter they call <term>mageia</term> <note>Original: "μαγείαν," meaning true magic or wisdom.</note>, as if it were a perfect and supreme wisdom. Indeed, as Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher.</note> says, in the Persian language "Magus" means the same as what among us is an "interpreter and worshiper of divine things." There is, however, fathers, a great—indeed, a massive—disparity and dissimilarity between these arts. Not only does the Christian religion condemn and curse the former, but so do all laws and every well-ordered state. The latter, however, all wise men and all nations studious of celestial and divine things approve and embrace. The former is the most fraudulent of arts; the latter is a higher and more holy philosophy. The former is useless and vain; the latter is firm, faithful, and solid. Whoever practiced the former always hid it, because it would bring ignominy and shame upon the author; from the latter, the highest literary fame and glory have been sought since ancient times and almost always. 

<column-break/>

No philosopher or man eager to learn the noble arts was ever a student of the former. But Pythagoras, Empedocles, Democritus, and Plato traveled across the sea to learn the latter; they preached it upon their return and held it as a chief secret in their records. As the former is proved by no reasons, so it is supported by no certain authors. The latter, honored by most illustrious parents as it were, has two primary authors: Zalmoxis, whom Abaris the Hyperborean imitated, and 
<margin>Authors of magic.</margin>
Zoroaster—not the one you perhaps think of, but that son of Oromasius. If we ask Plato what the magic of each was, he will answer in the *Alcibiades* that the magic of Zoroaster is nothing else than the science of divine things, in which the kings of the Persians educated their sons, so that they might be taught to rule their own commonwealth according to the model of the commonwealth of the universe. He will answer in the *Charmides* that the magic of Zalmoxis is the medicine of the soul, through which temperance is produced in the soul, just as health is produced in the body through medicine. In their footsteps later followed Charondas, Damigeron, Apollonius, Ostanes, and Dardanus. Homer also followed, and we shall one day prove in our *Poetic Theology* that he disguised this magic, like all other wisdoms, under the wanderings of his Ulysses. Eudoxus and Hermippus also followed. Almost all who searched into the Pythagorean and Platonic mysteries followed. Among the more recent men, however, I find three who have pursued it: the Arab Al-Kindi, Roger Bacon, and William of Paris <note>William of Auvergne, Bishop of Paris.</note>. Plotinus also mentions it, where he demonstrates that a magus is the servant of nature and not a craftsman. This most wise man approves and asserts this magic, while so loathing the other that when he was called to the rites of evil demons, he said it was more proper for them to come to him than for him to go to them—and rightly so. For just as the former makes man a slave and subject to wicked powers, so the latter makes him their prince and lord. Finally, the former can claim for itself the name of neither art nor science. The latter, full of the highest mysteries, embraces the deepest contemplation of the most secret things, and finally the knowledge of all nature. Calling forth into the light from their hiding places the virtues sown and scattered through the world by the kindness of God, it does not so much perform wonders as diligently serve nature as she performs them. Having searched more inwardly and deeply into the harmony of the universe—which the Greeks more expressively call <term>sympatheia</term> <note>Original: "συμπάθειαν," meaning "sympathy" or "co-suffering," the idea that all parts of the universe are interconnected.</note>—and having a clear perspective on the mutual knowledge of natures, it applies to each thing its own natural attractions—which the magi call <term>iynges</term> <note>Original: "ἴυγγες," ancient Greek magical charms or wheels used to draw something toward oneself.</note>. Thus, it brings into the public view the miracles lurking in the recesses of the world, in the lap of nature, and in the secret storehouses of God, as if it were itself the craftsman; and just as the farmer marries elms to vines, so the magus marries earth to heaven—that is, the lower things to the gifts and virtues of the higher. Thus, just as the former magic appears monstrous and harmful, the latter appears divine and salutary. For this reason especially, while the former subjects man to the enemies of God and calls him away from God, the latter excites in him that admiration for the works of God which is most certainly followed by spontaneous charity, faith, and hope. For nothing promotes religion and the worship of God more than the persistent contemplation of the miracles of God; when we have well-explored these through this natural magic of which we speak, we are more ardently animated toward the worship and love of the Creator. Then we shall be compelled to sing:
<margin>Note.</margin>
-> The heavens are full, and all the earth is full of the majesty of thy glory. <-
<note>Original: "Pleni sunt cæli plena est omnis terra maiestate gloriæ tuæ." A liturgical phrase based on Isaiah 6:3 and the Sanctus.</note>
And this is enough about magic, about which we have said these things because I know there are many who, just as dogs always bark at strangers, often themselves condemn and hate what they do not understand. I come now to those things which, from the ancient mysteries of the Hebrews...

<summary>Pico introduces his 72 original dogmas and his revival of Pythagorean "number philosophy" before launching into a famous defense of "Natural Magic." He distinguishes true magic (the "marriage" of heaven and earth) from forbidden demonic sorcery, arguing the former leads man closer to God.</summary>
<keywords>Scotists, Thomists, Pythagoreanism, Epinomis, Abu Ma'shar, Natural Magic, Goeteia, Sympatheia, Iynges, Zalmoxis, Zoroaster, Plotinus, Poetic Theology</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Pico’s defense of his intellectual sources. Having previously discussed the inclusion of various philosophical schools, he now moves into his defense of the "Cabala" (Jewish mystical tradition) and the "Ancient Theology" of figures like Orpheus and Zoroaster. He argues that these traditions contain hidden Christian truths.</meta>

->### JOHN PICO OF MIRANDOLA###<-

[These things] unearthed from the mysteries, I have brought forward to confirm the most holy and Catholic faith. Lest they be thought of as fabricated trifles or old wives' tales by those to whom they are unknown, I want everyone to understand what they are, where they come from, by which famous authors they are confirmed, and how secret, how divine, and how necessary they are for our men to defend religion against the persistent slanders of the Hebrews.

<margin>What the doctors of the Hebrews say.</margin>
Not only the famous doctors of the Hebrews write this, but also among our own, <term>Ezra</term><note>Referring to the biblical scribe; in this context, the author of the apocryphal 2 Esdras (or 4 Ezra).</note>, Hilary, and Origen: that Moses received on the mountain from God not only the Law, which he left to posterity written in five books, but also a more secret and true explanation of the Law. It was commanded to him by God to publish the Law to the people, but not to write down or make public the interpretation of the Law. Instead, he himself kept it, and then revealed it to the successive leaders of the priesthood under a great religious vow of silence. It was enough for the simple history to acknowledge now the power of God, now his wrath against the wicked, his mercy toward the good, and his justice toward all; and to be instructed through divine and salvific precepts toward living well and happily, and the worship of true religion. But to make public to the common people the more secret mysteries, hidden under the "bark" <note>original: *cortice*; meaning the literal outer layer or shell</note> of the Law and the rough garment of words—the secrets of the highest divinity—what was that other than giving what is holy to dogs and scattering pearls among swine? Therefore, it was by divine command, not human counsel, to keep these things hidden from the common crowd and share them only with the "perfect," among whom alone Paul says he speaks wisdom.

<margin>Plato says this same thing at the beginning of the *Heptaplus* <note>Pico is likely referencing his own work, the *Heptaplus*, which treats these same themes.</note>.</margin>
The ancient philosophers observed this custom most religiously. Pythagoras wrote nothing except a few small things which he entrusted to his daughter Dama as he was dying. The Sphinxes carved on Egyptian temples warned that mystical doctrines should be kept inviolate from the profane multitude through the knots of riddles. Plato, writing to Dion about the highest substances, said: "I must speak through riddles, so that if the letter should happen to fall into the hands of others, what we write to you may not be understood by them." Aristotle said that his books of *Metaphysics*, in which he deals with divine matters, were "published and not published."

<margin>Jesus Christ. Origen. Dionysius.</margin>
Why say more? Origen asserts that Jesus Christ, the master of life, revealed many things to his disciples which they were unwilling to write down, lest they become common to the crowd. This is especially confirmed by Dionysius the Areopagite, who says the more secret mysteries [were passed down] by the authors of our religion.

---

<margin>Cabala.</margin>
That is, from soul to soul, without writing, through the medium of the spoken word, he says they were transferred. In this very same way, when that true interpretation of the Law, divinely handed to Moses, was revealed by God’s command, it was called <term>Cabala</term><note>From the Hebrew *Qabbalah*, meaning "reception."</note>, which is the same among the Hebrews as "reception" is among us. Specifically, because one received that doctrine from another, not through written records, but by a regular succession of revelations, almost as if by hereditary right. But after the Hebrews were restored from the Babylonian captivity through Cyrus, and after the temple was restored under Zerubbabel, they applied their minds to repairing the Law. Ezra, then the head of the Church, after the book of Moses had been corrected, clearly recognized that through the exiles, slaughters, flights, and captivity of the Israelite people, the custom established by the ancestors of handing down the doctrine by hand could not be preserved. Realizing that the secrets of celestial doctrine granted to them by God would perish—since their memory could not last long without the intervention of commentaries—he decided that the wise men who then remained should be called together, and each should bring into the open what he held in his memory concerning the mysteries of the Law.

<column-break/>

And with scribes employed, they were reduced into seventy volumes (for there were about that many wise men in the <term>Sanhedrin</term><note>The supreme judicial and administrative council of the ancient Jews.</note>). Regarding this matter, fathers, do not believe me alone; hear Ezra himself speaking thus: "After forty days had passed, the Most High spoke, saying:

<margin>Ezra</margin>
The first things you wrote, put in public; let the worthy and unworthy read them. But the last seventy books you shall preserve, to hand them over to the wise among your people. For in these is the vein of understanding, the fountain of wisdom, and the river of knowledge." And so I did. These are Ezra's words, verbatim. These are the books of the science of the Cabala. In these books, Ezra clearly proclaimed with a loud voice that there is a "vein of understanding"—that is, an ineffable theology concerning the super-substantial deity; a "fountain of wisdom"—that is, an exact metaphysics concerning the intelligible and angelic forms; and a "river of knowledge"—that is, a most firm philosophy concerning natural things.

<margin>Sixtus IV.</margin>
Pope Sixtus IV, who immediately preceded the Pope under whom we live happily, Innocent VIII,

<margin>Innocent VIII.</margin>
took the greatest care and zeal that these books be translated into Latin for the public benefit of our faith. By the time he passed away, three of them had reached the Latins. Among the Hebrews today, these books are cherished with such religious awe that no one is allowed to touch them unless they are forty years old. When I had obtained these books for myself at no small expense, and had read them through with the greatest diligence and untiring labor, I saw in them (God is my witness) a religion not so much Mosaic as Christian. There is the mystery of the Trinity; there, the incarnation of the Word; there, the divinity of the Messiah; there, I read about original sin, its expiation through Christ, the celestial Jerusalem, the fall of the demons, the orders of angels, purgatory, and the punishments of hell. I read the very same things that we read daily in Paul and Dionysius, in Jerome and Augustine. In those things that pertain to philosophy, you truly hear Pythagoras and Plato, whose decrees are so akin to the Christian faith that our Augustine gives immense thanks to God that the books of the Platonists came into his hands. In short, there is almost no point of controversy between us and the Hebrews upon which they cannot be so refuted and convinced from the books of the Cabalists that not even a corner remains in which they can hide. I have a most weighty witness of this matter, Antonio Cronico, a most learned man, who with his own ears heard, when I was with him at a banquet, a Jew named Dactylus, skilled in this science, yield completely to the Christian view of the Trinity with "hands and feet" <note>An idiom meaning "entirely" or "unreservedly."</note>. But to return to myself and the topics of the debate to be reviewed: we have also brought forward our opinion on interpreting the poems of Orpheus and Zoroaster. Orpheus is read among the Greeks almost in his entirety; Zoroaster is read among them as a Magus, and among the Chaldeans more completely. Both are believed to be the fathers and authors of ancient wisdom. For, to say nothing of Zoroaster, of whom mention is frequent among the Platonists and always with the highest veneration,

<margin>Iamblichus of Chalcis. Pythagoras.</margin>
Iamblichus of Chalcis writes that Pythagoras had Orphic theology as a model, according to which he shaped and formed his own philosophy. For this reason alone, the sayings of Pythagoras are called "sacred," because they flowed from the institutions of Orpheus. From there came the secret doctrine of numbers, and whatever great and sublime things Greek philosophy possessed, they flowed from that first source. But (as was the custom of the ancient theologians) Orpheus so wove the mysteries of his dogmas into the wrappings of fables and disguised them with a poetic veil, that if anyone should read his hymns, they would believe nothing lay beneath them except trifles and the purest nonsense. I wanted to say this so it might be known what [it took for me]...

He also connects this to the "Ancient Theology" of Pythagoras and Orpheus, which similarly hid divine truths behind a veil of allegory and fables.</summary>

He then begins a letter to his nephew, Gianfrancesco, offering spiritual counsel on enduring the trials of a Christian life.</meta>

->### JOHN PICO OF MIRANDOLA ###<-

how great the difficulty of the labor was: to unearth the meanings of secret philosophy lying hidden within thickets of affected enigmas and the lurking places of myths—especially when no work or diligence of other interpreters assisted me in a matter so grave, so hidden, and so unexplored. And yet my "dogs" <note>Pico frequently refers to his academic critics as "barking dogs."</note> bark that I have accumulated certain tiny and trivial things for the sake of showing off a large number. As if all these questions were not of the most ambiguous and controversial kind, in which the principal <term>academies</term><note>Referring to the various competing schools of thought, such as the Thomists, Scotists, and Averroists.</note> clash; as if I have not brought many things—even to these very people who carp at my work and believe themselves to be the princes of philosophers—that are utterly unknown and unattempted. I am so far from the fault of which they accuse me that I have taken care to compress the dispute into as few headings as possible. If I had wished (as others are accustomed) to divide and tear these into their individual members, they would surely have grown into an innumerable number. To say nothing of the rest: who is there who does not know that one single dogma from the nine hundred—namely, that of reconciling the philosophy of Plato and Aristotle—could have been led by me into six hundred headings (if not more) without any suspicion of "affected numbers," by enumerating piece by piece all the points where others disagree and I believe they agree? But certainly I will say this—though neither modestly nor according to my natural disposition—I will say it nonetheless because the envious compel me, and my detractors force me: I wished through this assembly of mine to give proof, not so much that I knew many things, but that I know things which many do not know. So that this may now become clear to you in fact, most worshipful fathers, and to fulfill your desire, most excellent teachers (whom I see with great pleasure ready and girded, awaiting the battle), let my speech not delay us any longer. As if the <term>classicum</term><note>A Roman military trumpet call signaling the start of battle.</note> were sounding, let us now join hands in combat, and may it be happy and auspicious. ->End of the Oration.<-
