# THE LETTERS OF JOHN PICO OF MIRANDOLA,
## COUNT OF CONCORDIA.
### BOOK ONE.

->John Pico of Mirandola to Gianfrancesco, <gloss>his nephew, born of his brother.</gloss><-

<margin>This is consistent with the Virgilian poem in Book VII.</margin>
<image-desc>A large decorative initial "I" containing a figure of a scholar seated at a desk, surrounded by classical architectural motifs.</image-desc>
In Him who is true salvation: As you depart from me, you should not wonder, my son, that many occasions for evil are immediately offered to disturb you and oppose you for having taken up the purpose of living well. But neither should you grieve or be terrified. How much greater a miracle would it be if the way to heaven lay open for you alone among mortals without any sweat! As if the deceitful world and the evil demon had now for the first time ceased to exist, or as if you were not still in the flesh, which "lusts against the spirit." Unless we are vigilant and watchful for our salvation, the world deforms us into the monstrous shapes of beasts with its seductive and intoxicating Circean cups. But <margin>James.</margin> James affirms that you should rejoice when he writes: "Rejoice, brothers, when you fall into various temptations" (James 1:2). And not without reason: for what hope of glory is there, if there is no hope of victory? Or what place can there be for victory where there is no battle? He is called to the crown who is challenged to the fight; and especially to that fight in which no one can be conquered against his will, nor do we need any other strength to conquer than the will to conquer. <margin>Christian happiness</margin> Great is Christian happiness, when 

<column-break/>

<margin>Happiness to be noted.</margin> victory is placed within one's own judgment, and the rewards will be greater than every wish and every expectation of the victor. Tell me, I pray, dearest son: is there anything in this life among those things for which the lust of earthly minds is driven, for the sake of attaining which many labors must not first be undergone, and many indignities and miseries tolerated? The merchant thinks he has done well if, after a ten-year voyage, after a thousand inconveniences and a thousand dangers to his life, he has acquired a slightly richer estate for himself. Concerning the <term>militia of the world</term><note>original: *militia seculi*; referring to secular career service, often characterized by its "misery" and "servitude" in Renaissance thought.</note>, there is nothing I need write to you, for experience itself has taught you and continues to teach you enough of its miseries. In earning the favor of Princes, in reconciling the friendships of equals, in seeking honors—what a mass of troubles, how much anxiety, how much solicitude! I could sooner learn this from you than teach it to you; for I, content with my books and my little leisure, have learned since childhood to live within my fortune, and, dwelling as much as I can within myself, I neither suspect nor am ambitious for anything outside myself. Therefore, we barely achieve these earthly, falling, uncertain, and vile things—which we also have in common with the beasts—even while sweating and panting. Shall we then be drawn by the gods toward heavenly and divine things (which "eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered the heart of man") only while we are drowsy, sleeping, and almost against our will? As if God could not reign or those blessed heavenly citizens could not be happy without us? Truly, if earthly happiness were prepared for us while we were idle, someone might prefer to serve the world rather than God by shirking labor. But if we are fatigued no less—indeed, far more—in the way of sinners than in the way of God, whence comes that voice of the damned: "We are weary in the way of iniquity" (Wisdom 5:7)? It cannot but be the height of madness to refuse to labor where one goes from labor to a reward, rather than where <margin>An expression of passion.</margin> one goes from labor to punishment. I pass over how great that peace is, how great that happiness of mind to be conscious of no wrong and to grow pale at no fault—which undoubtedly far outweighs all the pleasures that can be possessed or hoped for in life. For what is desirable in the pleasures of the world? While <margin>The heart of the impious is like a boiling sea.</margin> they are sought, they exhaust us; when they are acquired, they sicken us; when they are lost, they torture us. Do you doubt, son, that the minds of the impious are agitated by perpetual cares? It is the word of God, who can neither be deceived nor deceive: "The heart of the impious is like a boiling sea that cannot rest" (Isaiah 57:20). For nothing is safe for them, nothing is peaceful; everything threatens fear, everything threatens cares, everything threatens death. Shall we then envy these people? Shall we emulate them? And, forgetting our own dignity, forgetting our fatherland—and our heavenly fatherland—shall we ourselves (though we were born free) voluntarily make ourselves slaves to these things? And, living miserably with them and dying more miserably, shall we at last be afflicted with eternal fires? <margin>Exclamation</margin> O blind minds of men! O blind hearts! Who does not see, clearer than light, that all these things are truer than truth itself? And yet we do not do what we recognize ought to be done; we still stick fast, unwilling to pull our foot out of the mire. Do not doubt, son, that in these places especially where you live, innumerable hindrances will occur every hour to deter you from the purpose of living holily and well, and (unless you are cautious) will drive you headlong. <margin>The company of evil men.</margin> But among all things, that most fatal plague is to dwell day and night among those whose life is not only in every part a lure to sin, but is entirely set upon the destruction of virtue. Under the commander the Devil, under the banners of death, and under the wages of Gehenna, such a life fights against heaven, against the Lord, and against his Christ. But you, cry out <margin>A saying of the Prophet.</margin> with the Prophet: "Let us break their bonds asunder and cast away their yoke from us" (Psalm 2:3). For these are the ones whom God "delivered into shameful passions and a reprobate mind, to do those things which are not fitting, full of all iniquity" (Romans 1:26-29).

# JOHN PICO OF MIRANDOLA #

<margin>The Apostle.</margin> ...filled with envy, murder, strife, deceit, and malice; whisperers, haters of God, insolent, haughty, boastful, inventors of evil things, foolish, rebellious, without affection, without loyalty, without mercy. Who, although they see the justice of God every day, do not understand that those who do such things are worthy of death—not only those who do them, but also those who consent to those who do them. <note>original: "tate plenos inuidia..." Pico is quoting Romans 1:29-32.</note> Therefore, my son, do not seek to please those whom virtue itself displeases. But let that word of the Apostle be always before your eyes: *one must please God more than men*; and that other: *if I pleased men, I would not be a servant of Christ.* Let a certain holy ambition invade you, and disdain to have those as masters of your life who rather stand in need of you as a teacher. For it is far more becoming that they should begin to be men by living well with you, than that you should wish to rot shamefully with them through the abandonment of your good purpose. 

<margin>Note our mere miseries and insanities.</margin> I swear by God that sometimes a kind of ecstasy and stupor seizes me when I begin to consider the pursuits of men—or to speak more significantly, their extreme insanities—and I know not whether to think on them rather than grieve, or to marvel at them rather than deplore them. For it is surely a great madness not to believe the Gospel, whose truth the blood of martyrs cries out, apostolic voices echo, wonders prove, reason confirms, the world testifies, the elements speak, and demons confess. But it is a far greater madness if you do not doubt the truth of the Gospel, yet live as if you did not doubt its falsehood. For if those things are true—that it is most difficult for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven—why do we pant daily for the accumulation of riches? And if it is true that glory should be sought not from men, but from God, why do we always hang upon the judgments of men? There is no one who cares to please God. And if faith is firm within us that the Lord will one day say: *Depart, you cursed ones, into* <margin>The words of the Judge at the end.</margin> *eternal fire*, and again, *Come, you blessed, possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world*, why is there nothing we fear less than hell, or hope for less than the kingdom of God? What else can we say than that many are Christians in name, but very few in reality? 

But you, my son, strive to enter through the narrow gate; do not attend to what the many do, but let the law of nature itself, reason itself, and God Himself show you what must be done. For your glory will not be less if you are happy with the few, nor your punishment lighter if you are miserable with the many. Moreover, there will be two remedies especially present for you against the world and Satan, by which, as if on two wings, you may be raised aloft from this valley of tears: namely, almsgiving and prayer. For what can we do without the help of God? <margin>Almsgiving and Prayer. Two most abundant remedies.</margin> Or how will He help one who does not call upon Him? But surely He will not hear you when you call, if you did not first hear the poor man calling to you. For it is not fitting that God should not despise you, a man, when you have previously despised a fellow man. It is written: *In the measure you have measured, it shall be measured back to you*; and elsewhere: *Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy.* 

When, however, I invite you to prayer, I do not invite you to that which consists of many words, but to that which, in the secret retreat of the mind, in the innermost parts of the soul, speaks to God with the very heart's affection; and which, in the brightest darkness of contemplation <note>original: "lucidiſſima contemplationis tenebra." This is a reference to "mystical theology," where the overwhelming light of God appears as darkness to the human intellect.</note>, does not merely present the mind to the Father, but unites it in certain ineffable ways known only to those who have experienced them. Nor do I care how long your prayer is, but how effective, how burning it is—interrupted by sighs rather than spread out in a perpetual series of words and rhythm. If your salvation is dear to your heart, if you wish to be safe from the devil's snares, from the storms of the world, from the ambushes of enemies; if you desire to be pleasing to God and finally happy, let no day pass in which you do not approach your God at least once through prayer, and 

<column-break/>

prostrate before Him with a humble and pious affection of the mind, cry out—not from the tips of your lips, but from the depths of your bowels—with the prophet: <margin>The manner of prayer.</margin> *The sins of my youth and my ignorances do not remember; but according to Your mercy remember me, for Your goodness' sake, O Lord.* Both the Spirit, who intercedes for us, and necessity itself will suggest to you every hour what you should ask of your God; and sacred reading will also suggest it. <margin>Sacred reading is necessary.</margin> I ask you again and again that, putting aside the fables and trifles of the poets, you always have this in your hands. You can do nothing more pleasing to God or more useful to yourself than if you do not cease to turn the sacred pages with your hand by night and by day. For there lies hidden in them a certain living and effective celestial power which (if only he handles them purely and humbly) transforms the mind of the reader into divine love by a certain marvelous power. 

But I have already exceeded the limits of a letter, drawn along by the subject matter itself and by a certain wondrous charity with which I have always followed you—especially from that hour when I was informed of your most holy purpose. Finally, I would wish you to be advised of that which I often spoke of with you when you were here with me: that you never forget these two things—both that the Son of God died for you, and that you also, even if you live long, will soon die. Driven by these twin spurs, the one of fear and the other of love, urge your horse through the short course of this momentary life toward the rewards of eternal happiness; for we neither should nor can set any other goal for ourselves than that we may enjoy the infinite Good without end, in the perpetual peace of both the inner and outer man. Farewell. And fear God. May 15, 1492.

# JOHN PICO #

...you can do what I can do. Farewell.

# John Pico of Mirandola to Lorenzo de' Medici, sends many greetings. Letter III. #

<image-desc>A large decorative initial 'L' containing a scene of a scholar seated at a lectern or desk, surrounded by books.</image-desc> I have read, Lorenzo de' Medici, your **Verses** <note>original: "Rhythmos." Here referring to Lorenzo's Italian poetry, likely his "Comento" or "Sonnets."</note> which the vernacular muses suggested to you during your tender years. I recognized in them the legitimate offspring of the Muses and the Graces; but the work of a "tender age" I did not recognize. For who, in your verses and the rhythmic joining of your lines, would not perceive the Graces dancing to the beat? Who, in your melodious style and modulation, would not hear the Muses singing? Who would recognize a mere youth in such unaffected charm, in such cheerful wit, in honeyed jests and fitting allurements, in such wondrous clarity? Who would see a young man in your prudent arrangement and in those most weighty thoughts drawn from the very inner chambers of philosophy?

I know for certain that I am not "on the white list" <note>original: "in hoc albo." A Roman idiom meaning a list of experts or those authorized to judge.</note> nor am I one who should ascend to such a height—that is, to the judgment of such things. But I wish it could be said without suspicion of flattery: I would declare that among the ancient writers, there is none in this genre of speaking whom you have not surpassed by a long interval. Lest you think this is said merely to please you, I will bring you my reasons for this opinion.

Among your people, there are two especially celebrated poets of the Florentine language: **Francesco Petrarch** and **Dante Alighieri**. Concerning them, let me first say generally that there are scholars who find substance lacking in Francesco and find the words lacking in Dante. <note>Pico summarizes a common 15th-century critique: Petrarch is all style, Dante is all grit.</note> But in you, whoever has a mind and ears finds neither lacking. In your work, it is impossible to see whether the matter is more illustrated by the speech, or the words by the ideas. 

But let us weigh the merits of each one individually, as if on a scale. If Francesco were to return to life, who doubts that regarding the thoughts themselves, he would willingly "yield the palm" to you? <note>original: "herbam tibi daturum." A classical expression for admitting defeat.</note> You are always so sharp, weighty, and subtle. He, however, snatching thoughts mostly from common sources, colors them with words; he makes ordinary things extraordinary through his style of speaking. In this, let us see how he stands against you and you against him: in some parts, he might appear sweeter. But to me, his sweetness (if I may put it this way) feels sweetly harsh and mildly bitter. He is flowing and smooth, soothing in an even way. You, with your majesty and a certain liveliness of speech, grip the soul. In him, there is an ambitious and excessive diligence; in you, a diligence that is neglected rather than affected. He is tender and soft; you are **masculine and muscular**. He is voluble and melodious; you are concise, full, firm, and modulated. He is perhaps more charming; you are certainly more ample and upright. He is more painted, but you are more vigorous. In him, there is much you could prune away; in you, there is nothing redundant and nothing cut short.

But perhaps I am a bit bold to say that something should be removed from him. It is certainly so, and it seems so to many in whose judgment I trust. For in my own view, one can often see him erring <term>just as</term> <note>original: "qp," abbreviation for "quemadmodum."</note> the Asiatics <note>The "Asiatic" style was a technical term for a rhetorical style that was overly flowery and wordy.</note> used to err—that is, stuffing in words as if to fill up cracks, and using full and harmonious voices not to decorate, but to support the poem like <term>props</term> <note>original: "tibicines." Literally "flute-players," but metaphorically referring to filler words used to maintain poetic meter.</note> so that the song does not limp. In you, all the words are no less necessary for the matter than they are pleasing for ornament, so that he who takes from you mutilates the work, while he who shears Petrarch merely prunes him.

Even if we were to grant (though I never will) that the things he wrote are more charming and more elegant than yours, it was easy for a man to excel who did not have to struggle and fight with the ideas themselves. But those sharp, subtle, and (to use your own word) **Laurentian** thoughts of yours can scarcely be described; they reject the "curling irons" <note>original: "calamistros." Metaphor for an overly artificial or feminine style.</note> and do not willingly admit those dyes which

<column-break/>

<margin>Castricius.</margin>
he [Petrarch] would have handled. If we had read those same ideas from him—whom we read as soft, polished, and pleasant—we would surely find them thorny, squalid, and ungrateful. For one can see that whenever Petrarch attempts something sharp, involved, or knotty, he fails in style as much as he rises in thought. But when he shows off his "furniture" of words—his ointments, his curls, and his flowers—he would often be warned, if **Castricius** <note>A reference to a figure in Porphyry’s "Life of Plotinus" who was warned not to be deceived by mere sound.</note> were present, as he warned regarding Greek: that we should not be deceived by a rounded sound and the flow of the verses. Rather, we should look at what lies beneath: what is the seat, what is the foundation, what is the depth of the words. If you do this there, you would sometimes see the "void of Epicurus" <note>A philosophical jab meaning the words contain nothing substantial, like Epicurus's empty vacuum.</note>—either no sense lies beneath, or it is cold and light. 

In that part which is the greatest, even if you do not surpass him, I do not see at all why he should surpass you for the sake of speaking. For 
<margin>Note.</margin>
the words in your work could not be more illustrious, and their arrangement is so fitting that they could not cohere better, nor flow more roundly, nor fall more rhythmically in any way.

But now let us weigh **Dante** with you, about whom perhaps more people will raise a controversy. For there are many who, in comparing writers, do not so much weigh their merits as count their years; they command others to read the ancients with reverence, while they themselves cannot read their contemporaries without envy. 

Certainly, as far as style is concerned, I think no one will deny you the first place. Dante is sometimes so rough, harsh, and lean that he seems quite crude and unpolished; even his "goldsmiths" <note>Devoted fans or scholars of Dante.</note> admit this. But they shift the blame entirely onto the age and the century in which he lived. You are altogether more cultivated in speech, and he is not "grander." 

"But," someone will say, "he is grander and more sublime in his thoughts." I ask you, what is the wonder in philosophizing when nature itself compels it and offers up thoughts? If he deals with God, the soul, or the blessed, he brings forward what Thomas [Aquinas] or Augustine 
<margin>Note.</margin>
wrote about these things. And he was as frequent as he was assiduous in treating and meditating on these matters; you, meanwhile, are occupied in conducting the greatest public and private affairs. It was not so much a glorious thing for Dante to have done this, as it would have been shameful not to have done it. 

But it was, without doubt, the work of a supreme genius—which you yourself provide—to make philosophical things out of things that are about love; and to make things that are somewhat austere in their severity become lovable by inducing "Venus" <note>Referring to the grace and beauty of love poetry.</note> over them. Thus, in your verses, the serious matters of philosophers are so mixed with the playfulness of lovers that the latter gain dignity and the former gain cheerfulness and grace. Through this bond, both have retained what was their own, and have so shared themselves with each other that both have individually what previously they both had together. 

But this is not as admirable as that which moved me most: these things are introduced by you not as if they were "brought in," but as if they were dug out from the very heart of the matter you are treating. From that very subject, as if you were directing the soil, they seem to blossom forth so that they appear native, not foreign; necessary, not imported; entirely genuine and not grafted on. This is what I cannot admire enough, and in this, you seem to me to have surpassed Dante. For even if he flies high, he is lifted by the "wings of his subject matter"; you, even when the subject resists and pulls downward, are raised on high by the **wings of your genius**. And you are raised in such a way that you do not depart from the subject, but you lift it up along with you. Your subject matter owes as much to you as Dante owed to his.

Now one can see the difference between you, Francesco, and Dante. To this I would add: Francesco sometimes does not live up to his promises, having that which allures at first sight but does not satisfy further in. Dante has that which sometimes offends upon meeting it, but pleases the one who penetrates more deeply. Your works have no less to hold the reader in their depths than they have at first spring to capture him. Add...

<meta>This page continues the letter from Pico della Mirandola to Lorenzo de’ Medici. Pico is comparing Lorenzo’s literary output to that of professional poets, arguing that Lorenzo’s achievements are more impressive because they were composed amidst the pressures of political leadership.</meta>

BOOK ONE 61

they wrote their poems in seclusion, in the shade, and in the utmost tranquility of study; you wrote yours amidst the tumults: the noise of the court, the clamors of the forum, and the greatest cares of turbulent storms, even while most occupied. For them, the muses were their ordinary and principal business; for you, they are a game and a kind of relaxation from cares. For them, poetry was their greatest exhaustion; for you, it is leisure when you are already exhausted. Finally, by relaxing your mind, you have reached a point which they, perhaps, had not reached even while straining every nerve of their souls. But what shall I say of my **paraphrase**? <note>original: "paraphrasi." Pico refers here to Lorenzo’s *Comento*, a prose commentary Lorenzo wrote to explain his own sonnets.</note> For why should I not call it mine? Either by the right of this title, which is mine, or why not mine because, although I revere it as yours, I love it as my own? I truly admire it and you within it; from this I realize how far I fell short of the true praise of your verses. Those things which were greatest and most illustrious in them—which I, with my "owl-like eyes," <note>original: "noctuinis oculis." A metaphor for dim-sightedness or failing to see what is obvious in the light.</note> had not looked into—I then saw revealed through you, who alone both could and should have done so. You owed it to yourself and to us, lest you defraud yourself of much glory and us of much pleasure. I read it (God is my witness), most great Lorenzo, not so much for delight as for instruction. 
<margin>Aristotle. Plato.</margin>
How many things are there from Aristotle’s *Physics*, from his books *On the Soul*, *On Ethics*, *On the Heavens*, and from the *Problems*! How many from Plato’s *Protagoras*, from the *Republic*, from the *Laws*, and from the *Symposium*! All these things, although I have read them elsewhere in those authors, I nevertheless read in your work as if they were new, as if they were better, and transformed by you into I-know-not-what form, so that they seem to be yours and not theirs, and in reading them I seem to learn something for myself. 
<margin>Note.</margin>
This is the greatest proof that you produce these things not so much from a commentary as from yourself. For many are accustomed to have more **intimate discourse** <note>original: "σαρίστεια" (oaristeia). A Greek term for familiar conversation or intimacy.</note> in letters than in their actual works; when they have written something, they hold philosophers as if they were technical experts suggesting certain dogmas to them, which they then thrust into their little books so that they might appear to be philosophers. But you may easily catch these people. For you see those things are neither rightly arranged nor coherent, and are not explained by the authors themselves, but rather entangled; and men who are otherwise eloquent appear most childish when speaking of those matters. But who would not see that you do not hold these things on loan, but as if you have the right and power over them to turn, act, and handle them at your will? These things (O happy genius!) you have achieved in the heat of the Republic and in an active life—things which we, who are not the disciples of philosophers but their "permanent residents" in a life of shadows and sedentary study, follow rather than attain. 
<margin>Caesar.</margin>
But what shall I say of the most sweet style of your paraphrase? It seems to me to be thoroughly like that of Caesar in the Roman tongue. For it is an oration not made by hand, not gilded, not twisted, but by its own nature upright, candid, and "square" <note>original: "quadrata." Meaning well-proportioned, solid, or stable.</note>; neither running out rashly but keeping its pace; neither luxuriant nor meager, neither wanton nor unpleasing; sweetly grave and gravely lovely. The words are chosen and not affected, illustrious but not disguised, necessary and not sought after—not just explaining the matter, but placing it before one's very eyes. I pass over how you always remember your own persona, and how the seeds and traces of that famous prudence of yours are scattered everywhere. I have seen these things, as have many others, and someone else might see far better things. But besides these, I saw two principal things which perhaps not many see, however eagle-eyed they may be: the first is that your style hides its own riches, so that it avoids envy; it holds flowers in its lap but does not flaunt them; it does not grow into tall plants but remains noble while sitting low, so that it appears smaller than it is. What the other thing might be, I do not see, for I am not so skillful; but I see that it is something (to speak most distinctively) "Laurentian." If someone were to see the gifts of Lorenzo’s genius and his excellence, he would see the whole Lorenzo graphically portrayed. But perhaps these things I have said are too many, even though I said them unwillingly, as the conviction of my mind dragged me sideways, as they say, into words. I will not pass over urging you with as much effort as I can that you occasionally steal a little leisure from governing the Republic to devote yourself to finishing the paraphrase.

<column-break/>

If you grant this, it will be to the honor of yourself and your native language, and to the use and pleasure of your citizens and all of us. At Florence, on the Ides of July, 1484.

->John Pico of Mirandola to his friend Hermolao Barbaro. Greetings. Letter IV.<-

<margin>In the ninth book of the letters of Angelo Poliziano, there is this and other youthful letters, especially the one in which he responds to this.</margin>
I certainly, my Hermolao, can neither be silent about what I feel concerning you, nor fail to feel those things which are owed to such a man, in whom all things are found in the highest degree, as if they were single traits. But I wish there were such a grasp of mind in me that I might feel toward you according to your merits; I wish there were such power of speaking that I might eventually be able to express what I always feel. I know that what I have conceived of you remains infinitely below the heights of your learning. You should know also that whatever we speak is far less than what we conceive; know that words fail the mind just as the mind does not fail the facts. And yet, do you believe I am so daring as to hope I can imitate your works, whose magnitude I cannot even estimate? All can admire you, but so few can imitate you that no one can find fault. And I wish that I had the good fortune that what I write might represent my Hermolao in some part. For (to say nothing of the rest) your very style, which you favor so little, affects me wonderfully; how much it delights me! It is so learned, grave, composed, erudite, polished, and ingenious. In it, nothing is unrefined, nothing is trivial, whether you look at the words or the thoughts. Our friend **Poliziano** <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), a brilliant Renaissance humanist and poet, and a close friend of Pico.</note> and I often read whatever letters of yours we have, whether to others or to us. Thus, those that follow always compete with the previous ones, and new graces flourish fruitfully during the reading, so that in a certain perpetual acclaim we have no room to catch our breath. But it is wonderful to say how you persuade, and drive the reader's mind wherever you wish. I have experienced this both at other times and especially in this most recent letter of yours to me, in which you attacked these **barbarian philosophers** <note>Pico is referring to the Scholastic philosophers of the Middle Ages, whom the Humanists criticized for their "rough" Latin.</note> whom you say are commonly held to be filthy, dull, and uncultivated—men who did not even live while they were alive, much less live now that they are dead; and if they do live now, they live for punishment and disgrace. Thus I was further moved; thus I was ashamed and weary of my studies. For I have already spent six years among them, so that I wish I had done no less than to have struggled so laboriously in a matter so worth doing nothing. 
<margin>Thomas. John Scotus. Albert. Averroes.</margin>
I have lost, I say, my better years, and such long vigils, among **Thomas**, **John Scotus**, **Albert**, and **Averroes** <note>Thomas Aquinas, Duns Scotus, Albertus Magnus, and Averroes: the pillars of Scholastic philosophy and Aristotelian commentary.</note>—years in which I might perhaps have become something in "good letters" [the humanities]. I thought to myself, to console myself, if any of those men should now come back to life, whether they—men otherwise full of arguments—would have anything with which to defend their cause by some reason, perhaps in this manner: "We lived renowned, O Hermolao, and we shall live hereafter, not in the schools of grammarians and in schoolrooms, but in the circles of philosophers and in the assemblies of the wise. There, the talk and dispute is not about the mother of Andromache, nor the children of Niobe, nor light trifles of that sort; 
<margin>By introducing the personification of 'barbarism,' Pico responds most sharply by refuting it with the barbarians' own arguments.</margin>
but it is about the reasons of human and divine things. In meditating upon, inquiring into, and unraveling these things, we have been so subtle, sharp, and keen that we might perhaps seem to have been sometimes too anxious and fastidious—if indeed anyone can be too fastidious or curious in investigating the truth. And indeed, if anyone should accuse us of dullness and slowness, come, I pray, whoever he is, let him join battle. He will find that the 'barbarians' had **Mercury** <note>The god of eloquence and wisdom.</note> not on their tongues, but in their hearts..."

<meta>This page transitions from the previous discussion regarding Lorenzo de’ Medici’s poetry to Pico della Mirandola’s famous defense of the "barbarous" philosophers (the Scholastics). He is addressing Ermolao Barbaro, a humanist who had criticized the unpolished Latin of medieval thinkers. # LETTERS

<margin>Praise of Latin philosophy.</margin>
It was not that they lacked wisdom; if they lacked eloquence, perhaps they are so far from blame for not joining it with wisdom that to have joined them would have been a sin. For who would not condemn and detest curls and rouge on an honest maiden? So great is the conflict between the duty of the orator and the philosopher that they could not be more opposed. For what else is the rhetorician’s office but to lie, to deceive, to circumvent, and to practice trickery? As you say, it is within your power to turn black to white or white to black at your whim; you can, by speaking, elevate, cast down, amplify, or diminish whatever you wish. In short, by the almost "magic" powers of eloquence (as you yourselves boast), you transform things into whatever appearance or habit you please, so that they do not appear as they truly are by their own nature, but as you would have them—not becoming so in reality, but appearing so to the listeners. Is this entire thing anything other than pure lying, pure imposture, and pure trickery? Since it always exceeds nature by increasing or falls short by diminishing, it offers a deceptive harmony of words—like masks and phantoms—to mock the minds of the listeners with flattery. Can there be any kinship between this and the philosopher, whose entire study is occupied with knowing the truth and demonstrating it to others? Add to this that no one will trust us if we affect a richness of vocabulary and charms, as if we did not trust the facts themselves; nor, relying on the truth, should we seek to pull men toward our opinion with these allurements. For this reason, it is better to read sacred matters written rustically rather than elegantly, for nothing is more inappropriate or harmful in any subject where the goal is knowing the truth than that entire elaborate style of speaking. That belongs to legal disputes, not to natural and celestial questions. It is not for those in the Academy, but for those engaged in the Republic, where things done and said are weighed on the popular scale, and where flowers far outweigh the fruit. Do you not know that not all things suit everyone in the same measure? Eloquence is an elegant thing (we admit this), full of allure and pleasure; but in a philosopher, it is neither becoming nor welcome. Who would not approve of a soft gait, expressive hands, and playful eyes in an actor or a dancer? But in a citizen or a philosopher, who would not disapprove, argue against, and abominate them? If we see a girl who is charming and witty in her manners, we will praise and kiss her; but in a matron, we would condemn and shun these same things. Therefore, it is not we who are foolish, but those who perform "Bacchanalia" <note>An ancient Roman festival of Bacchus, known for wild, unrestrained behavior.</note> at the feet of your [rhetoric]; who would dishonor the gravity and
<margin>Synesius.</margin>
chastity of philosophical matters with playthings and curling irons, as it were. Indeed, what Synesius <note>Synesius of Cyrene (c. 373–414 AD), a philosopher-bishop.</note> said of a youth can be aptly said of a speech: a "well-groomed" speech is always a "shameless" one. <note>original: "comatam orationē semper cinædā." Pico uses a term implying effeminate or sexually submissive behavior to characterize overly polished rhetoric.</note> Therefore, we prefer ours to be shaggy-haired, sturdy, and unencumbered, rather than beautifully groomed with the mark or suspicion of impurity. And even if nothing else remained, this is most true: nothing is further from the philosopher’s purpose in any matter than that which tastes of luxury or pride in any part.
<margin>Socrates.</margin>
Socrates used to say that Sicyonian shoes <note>A type of luxury footwear from the city of Sicyon, famous for comfort and elegance.</note> were handy and fit the foot; but a Socrates or a philosopher should use them for neither his table nor his speech. The philosopher uses these things only for necessity; the "civil man" uses them for grace as well. If the latter neglects grace, he is not a civil man; but if the former affects it, he will not be a philosopher. If Pythagoras could live without food, he would spare even the vegetables. If he could explain his thoughts by sight, or by some means less laborious than speech, he would not speak at all. He is so far from polishing and adorning his tongue; we must take care lest a reader, enticed by the "painted skin" of the text, lingers there and does not penetrate to the marrow and the blood—which we have often seen to be diseased beneath a face covered in white lead makeup. We have seen it, I say, in all these people, 

<column-break/>

for whom it has become a habit (since there is nothing inside that is not empty and vain) to detain the reader at the surface with varied modulation and harmony. If a philosopher should do this,
<margin>Musonius.</margin>
Musonius <note>Musonius Rufus, a Stoic philosopher of the 1st century AD.</note> would cry out that it is not a philosopher speaking, but a musician playing for you. Therefore, let it not be held as a fault in us that we did not do what it would have been a fault to do. We seek *what* we should write, not *how*; or rather, we seek a "how" that is without pomp or any "flowers" of speech. We do not want it to be delightful, charming, or witty, but useful, grave, and reverend—so that it achieves majesty through awe rather than grace through softness. We do not expect the applause of the theater because a balanced or rhythmic clause has soothed the ears, or because this part was clever or that part was elegant. Instead, we expect the silence of the few, moved by admiration as they look more deeply into something either unearthed from the inner sanctuaries of nature or brought down to men from the court of heaven. We seek something so sharp that there is no room for defense, and so well-defended that there is no room for argument. Let them admire us, moreover, for being keen in inquiry, circumspect in exploration, subtle in contemplation, grave in judgment, skilled in binding arguments, and easy in unraveling them. Let them admire in us a brevity of style pregnant with many great things: profound meanings full of questions and full of solutions hidden beneath plain words. Let them see how fit we are and how well-equipped to remove ambiguities, dissolve difficulties, and unfold the complex; and how we use soul-bending syllogisms both to weaken what is false and confirm what is true. By these titles, O Ermolao, we have vindicated our memory until now, and we do not doubt we shall vindicate it from oblivion hereafter. For if we are considered "sordid, rude, and uncultured" by the common crowd, as you say, this is our glory and not our shame. We did not write for the crowd, but for you and those like you. Just as the ancients used to keep unlearned men away from the mysteries with the wrappings of enigmas and fables, so we have been accustomed to deter them from our "feasts" (which they could not help but pollute) with a somewhat bitter "bark" of words. Those who wish to hide treasures, if they cannot put them away, usually cover them with trash or rubble so that passers-by do not discover them—unless they are people the owners judge worthy of the gift. It is a similar desire of philosophers to hide their affairs from the people; for since it is proper that they be not only disapproved of but not even understood by the crowd, it cannot but be harmful for them to write anything theatrical, plausible, or popular that seems to accommodate itself to the judgment of the multitude. But 
<margin>Alcibiades.</margin>
if you wish, I will sketch the "idea" of our speech. It is exactly like the Sileni <note>A reference to Plato’s *Symposium*, where Alcibiades compares Socrates to Silenus-statues: ugly on the outside but containing golden images of gods inside.</note> of our Alcibiades. These were statues with a shaggy, foul, and despicable exterior; but inside they were full of gems and rare, precious furnishings. Thus, if you look from the outside, you see a beast; if you look within, you recognize a god. "But," you will say, "my ears cannot bear it; now the texture is rough, now gaping, always discordant." You say you cannot bear "barbarous" names that are terrifying in their very sound. O delicate one! When you go to hear flute-players and harpers, take your ears with you. But when you go to philosophers, call yourself away from the senses; return to yourself, into the inner chambers of the soul and the recesses of the mind. Take up the ears of the man of Tyana, <note>Apollonius of Tyana, a 1st-century Neopythagorean philosopher.</note>
<margin>Thianeus.</margin>
who, when he was not in the body at all, heard not the earthly Marsyas, but the celestial Apollo, tempering the melody of the universe with ineffable divine strains on his lyre. If you taste the words of philosophers with these ears, they will seem as sweet as honey to you, to the envy of Nestor. <note>In Homer, Nestor is the wise elder whose speech flows "sweeter than honey."</note> But let us leave these things that soar perhaps too high; truly, to find a less-than-elegant style offensive in a man disputing most subtly is the mark of an insolent stomach rather than a delicate one. It is no different than if someone, while Socrates was teaching on ethics, were to take offense at a loose shoe or a gaping toga, or to get angry over a poorly trimmed fingernail.
<margin>Tullius.</margin>
Tullius <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero.</note> does not require eloquence in a philosopher, but only that he satisfy the subject matter and learning. Being a man as prudent as he was learned, he knew that our duty...

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's famous 1485 letter to the humanist Ermolao Barbaro. Pico is defending the "Parisian philosophers"—the medieval Scholastics—against the charge that their Latin was crude and "barbaric." He argues that the pursuit of truth requires a plain, technical style rather than the flowery, often deceptive language of traditional rhetoric.</meta>

# BOOK ONE

...to focus on the mind rather than the diction. We must take care that reason does not stray, even if the speech does. It is our duty "to save the logic" <note>original: "σώζειν τὸν λόγον"</note> rather than "the whole variety of ornament" <note>original: "τό πᾶν διαπρόφορα"</note>. It is praiseworthy in us to have the Muses in our souls and not just on our lips, lest anything in our speech sound too harsh through anger
<margin>Plato.</margin>
or too weak through lust. In short, our speech should not be discordant with that genuine harmony by which the soul itself is melodiously tempered. When Plato understood that such harmony was often corrupted by the theatrical style of poets, he banished all poets from his Republic, leaving it to be governed by philosophers—though even they were to be condemned to exile if they ever imitated the poets through a playful style of debating. But Lucretius will insist
<margin>Lucretius.</margin>
that even if philosophical meditations do not need the charm of speaking for their own sake, the harshness of the subject matter should be disguised by its application. Just as wormwood <note>Wormwood (absinthium) was a notoriously bitter medicinal herb.</note> dispels diseases, yet the rims of the cups are smeared with honey so that the "unwary age of boys" <note>A quote from Lucretius’s *De Rerum Natura*, suggesting that difficult truths must be sweetened for the uneducated.</note> might be deceived. Perhaps you had to do this, Lucretius, if you were writing for boys. If you were writing for the common crowd, you certainly had to do it—you who served up not just wormwood, but the most unmixed poisons. But we must follow a far different reasoning, for as we said before, we do not seek to entice the common crowd, but to frighten them away. We do not serve up foul wormwood, but
<margin>Lactantius.</margin>
nectar. Yet Lactantius <note>Lactantius (c. 250–325 AD) was an early Christian author known as the "Christian Cicero" for his polished Latin style.</note> will contend that it is well established that truth flows more powerfully into the minds of listeners, even older ones, when it is equipped with its own strength and adorned with the light of speech. If you had been as well-versed in the Sacred Scriptures as you were in fictional lawsuits, Lactantius, you would not have said this; perhaps you would have confirmed our position no less successfully than you destroyed the positions of others. Tell me, I pray, what moves and persuades more strongly than the reading of the Sacred Scriptures? They do not merely move or persuade; they compel, they agitate, they use force. You read words that are unrefined and rustic, but they are alive: they are animated, flaming, and sharp, penetrating to the depths of the spirit and transforming the whole man with a wonderful power. Alcibiades says that he was not moved at all by elaborate and brilliant speeches, but by the naked and simple words of Socrates. He adds that even if they are clumsy, he is carried into a frenzy, placed outside himself, and—whether he wants to or not—is driven to do
<margin>Three things that persuade most.</margin>
what Socrates commanded. But why do I waste words? It is a fact: unless the listener is a fool, what else can he expect from a dyed and painted speech but a trap? Three things persuade most: the life of the speaker, the truth of the matter, and the sobriety of the speech. These, Lactantius, are what will win credit for a philosopher: if he is good, if he is truthful, and if he seeks that kind of speaking which flows not from the pleasant groves of the Muses, but from that "dreadful cave"
<margin>Heraclitus.</margin>
in which Heraclitus said truth lies hidden. But someone will say: "Come, friend, let us examine these things without contention. Wisdom is something reverend and divine in itself, and it needs no foreign ornament. But what harm is there if ornament is added?" Who denies that things which are becoming in themselves might become more beautiful if adorned? I, my friend, deny this in most cases. There are so many things whose splendor you would ruin, not illustrate, if you added anything to them. They are in the best state in their own nature, such that they cannot be changed from it except for the worse. A marble house does not accept a painting. If you apply a coat of plaster <note>term: *opus albarium* (white-wash or decorative plastering)</note>, you take away from its dignity and beauty. It is no different with wisdom and the things treated by philosophers; they are not made clearer by a "plastering" of words, but are obscured. What more? Is it not common knowledge that beautiful faces are made ugly by white-lead makeup <note>term: *cerussa* (a toxic lead-based white cosmetic)</note>? In general, whatever beauty you impose upon a thing hides what it found and displays only what it brought with it. Therefore, if what was there before is better than the addition, the thing suffers a loss rather than a gain. For this reason, philosophy offers herself naked; she is conspicuous from every side; she desires to come entirely under the eyes and under judgment. She knows she has within her that by which she may please from every angle. However much you wish to take from her

<column-break/>

beauty, just as much do you take from her praise; she wishes to be perceived as sincere and unmixed. Whatever you mix in, you stain; you adulterate it and make it something else. It stands at a precise, indivisible point. Therefore, one must not play with metaphors or words, nor be too luxurious, nor wanton with translations, nor bold with invented terms in a matter so serious and of such great importance, where to take away, add, or change anything would be a crime. But you say: "Grant us this, that it is not your business to speak ornamentally. But surely it is your business—though you do not perform it—to speak at least in Latin, so that if you do not explain things with flowery words, you at least use the correct ones." I do not demand a polished speech from you, but I do not want a filthy one. I do not want it perfumed, but neither should it smell like a goat. It should not be "select," but neither should it be neglected. We do not ask that it delight us, but we complain that it offends us. Well then! Now you come over to our side. But please, let us investigate what this "Latinity" is, which you say philosophers alone owe and do not pay. If a philosopher says in an unpolished way, "An example: a man is produced by the sun" <note>original: "a sole hoīem [hominem] pduci [produci]"</note>, our critics will say: "The man is produced by the sun." You will immediately shout: "That is not Latin!" Up to this point, you are right; it is not spoken in the *Roman* way. This is even truer: therefore it is not correct? Your argument fails. An Arab will say the same thing, an Egyptian will say it; they will not say it in Latin, but they will say it correctly. For either the names of things are established by choice or by nature. If by chance—that is, by a community of men coming together in the same opinion to decree what each thing should be called—then among them, it is called correctly. What prevents these philosophers, whom you call "barbarians," from having conspired into one norm of speaking which is held as sacred among them as the Roman norm is among you? Why should you not call theirs "correct"? You call yours correct, but there is no reason for it if this imposition of names is entirely arbitrary. If you do not wish to dignify their speech with the name "Roman," call it "Gallic," "British," "Spanish," or as the common folk say, "Parisian" <note>original: "pissiesē" [parisiensem]</note>. When they speak to you, they will happen to be laughed at for many things and not understood in others; the same thing will happen to you when speaking among them. "Anacharsis makes a solecism among the Athenians, but the Athenians do so among the Scythians" <note>Anacharsis was a Scythian philosopher who traveled to Athens; the quote highlights that "correctness" is a matter of local custom.</note>. If the correctness of names depends on the nature of things, should we consult the rhetoricians or the philosophers—who alone have looked into and explored the nature of all things—concerning this correctness? Perhaps what the ears reject as being a bit rough, reason accepts as being more closely related to the facts. But why was it necessary for them to invent a new language, even if they were born among Latins, rather than speaking Latin? They could not, O Hermolaus <note>Hermolao Barbaro (1454–1493), the famous humanist to whom this letter is addressed.</note>, while they were reading the laws of the fates and the order of the universe in the heavens—while they were reading in the elements the cycles of birth and death, the powers of simple things, and the temperaments of mixtures. They could not, I say, at the same time annotate the properties, laws, and observances of the Roman tongue in Cicero, Pliny, or Apuleius. They were seeking what was repellent and what was accepted in nature; meanwhile, they did not care what the Romans thought. Truly, I now place you in a better position: I grant you that eloquence and wisdom have conspired together in a mutual bond. But the philosophers have separated wisdom from eloquence; the historians, rhetoricians, and poets have separated eloquence from 
<margin>Philostratus</margin>
wisdom—a separation which Philostratus <note>Philostratus (c. 170–250 AD) wrote the *Lives of the Sophists*, often discussing the relationship between rhetoric and philosophy.</note> lamented. You have no doubt that the latter will live with famous renown, while the former live only for punishment and insult. See what you are doing! 
<margin>Cicero.</margin>
Cicero prefers unpolished wisdom to foolish loquacity. In money, we do not ask by what mint it was struck, but what material it is made of. Nor is there anyone who would not rather have pure gold under a German mark than counterfeit gold under a Roman symbol. Those who create a divorce between the heart and the tongue commit a sin; but those who have no heart at all but are all tongue—are they not merely, as Cato says, "funeral glossaries"? <note>A "funeral glossary" (*mortuaria glossaria*) is a person who knows many words but has no life or substance behind them.</note> We can perhaps live 
<margin>Cato.</margin>
without a tongue, though not conveniently; but without a heart, we cannot live at all. He is not human who is ignorant of more polished literature; but he is not a *man* who is devoid of philosophy. Wisdom, however mute, can be of use; but foolish eloquence is like a sword in the hand of a madman—it can only do harm.

<sig>m ii</sig>

<summary>Pico della Mirandola argues that the "barbarous" technical language of medieval philosophers is superior to polished rhetoric because it focuses on the "heart" (truth and reason) rather than the "tongue" (ornament). He uses analogies of unpainted marble and unadorned beauty to show that wisdom shines brightest when it is plain and sincere.</summary>

# LETTERS

especially since it is not possible; therefore you will say that statues are commended not for their figure, but for their material. If Choerilus <note>A mediocre epic poet who wrote about Alexander the Great; often contrasted with Homer.</note> had sung the same things as Homer, and if Mevius had sung of the same things as Virgil, would they have been received equally among the poets? Do you not see the disparity in the similarity? We also used to assert that a thing is valued by its form, not by its subject. For a thing is what it is because of its form. But one person is to be received among the philosophers, and another among the poets. Let Lucretius write about nature, about God, about providence; let one of our own write about the same things. Let Johannes Scotus <note>original: "Io. sco."; referring to Duns Scotus, the famous medieval Scholastic philosopher often mocked by humanists for his "barbaric" Latin.</note> write, and indeed in verse so that he might seem more foolish: Lucretius will say that the principles of things are atoms and the void, that God is corporeal, and that He is ignorant of our affairs, and that all things are carried along blindly by the fortuitous collision of small bodies. But he will say these things in Latin and elegantly. Johannes will say that nature consists of its own matter and form, that God is a separate mind who knows all things and provides for all. Nor is He moved in the slightest from His own peace even though He sees and governs the universe, even the lowest things. But as is commonly said, "according to that which is no longer" <term>κατὰ τὰ μηκατι ειναι</term> <note>original: "κατὰ τὰ μηκέτι εἶναι"; likely a technical philosophical phrase regarding non-being or transcendence.</note>. But he will say it tastelessly, rudely, and not in Latin words. I ask you, who would doubt which is the better poet, and which the better philosopher <term>pħus</term>? It is beyond all controversy that Scotus philosophizes more correctly, even if the other speaks more ornately. But see what the difference is: the one has an insipid mouth, the other a senseless mind. This one is ignorant of the decrees of the grammarians, not to say the poets; that one is ignorant of God and nature. This most speechless man, in his speaking, perceives those things which cannot be sufficiently praised in speech; that man, in his speaking, most eloquently utters unspeakable things. These things, my dearest Ermolao, those men would perhaps bring forward in defense of their own "barbarism"—or perhaps they would bring much better things, given their subtlety. I do not fully agree with their opinion, nor do I think any noble or liberal person should agree. But I have exercised myself freely in this material as if in a well-known theme—just as those who praise a quartan fever <note>A common rhetorical exercise was to write a "paradoxical encomium" praising something typically considered bad.</note>—both so that my talent might be tested and with this plan: that just as Glaucon in Plato's work praises injustice not from judgment, but to stimulate Socrates to praise justice, so I have attacked the cause of eloquence with a somewhat more licentious sense and nature, so that I might hear its cause pleaded by you. For if I thought eloquence should be neglected or held second to the barbarians, I would not have almost entirely defected from them to it, as I recently did, turning to Greek literature and to your never-sufficiently-praised Themistius <note>Ermolao Barbaro was famous for his translation of and commentary on the Greek philosopher Themistius.</note>. To speak freely what I feel, certain grammarians move my stomach; when they have grasped two origins of words, they show themselves off so much, they sell themselves so much, they carry themselves about so boastfully that they think philosophers should be considered as nothing compared to themselves. They say, "We do not want these philosophies of yours"—and what wonder: you don't even like Falernian wine <note>A famous high-quality wine from antiquity.</note>. But let us close the letter with this end: if those barbarians earned some glory and a name for themselves through the knowledge of things alone, it is not easy to say what praise you should claim for yourself, you who are the most eloquent among philosophers and (to say it in Greek) the "most philosophical" <term>φιλοσοφωτατος</term> <note>original: "φιλοσοφώτατος"</note> among the eloquent. Florence, the third day before the Nones of June, 1485.

---

### To the Reverend Father in Christ, Brother Baptista Mantuanus <note>Baptista Spagnuoli Mantuanus (1447–1516), a famous Carmelite poet and humanist.</note>, of the Carmelite order, distinguished poet, philosopher, and theologian, etc.

->Your son, Johannes Mirandula. Letter V.<-

<margin>Glaucon.</margin>
Greetings, most beloved father. Regarding Apollonius the theologian, I feel no differently than you do; I shall write more to you on this matter when there is leisure and things that will perhaps not be unpleasing to you. Concerning the diversity of our translation from the Hebrew text in the third chapter of the book of Genesis, where it deals with Eve and the serpent, I think as follows: in the Hebrew it is as you write, "He shall crush your head," <note>Genesis 3:15. Pico is discussing whether the text says "He" (the offspring) or "She" (Eve/Mary) will crush the serpent's head.</note> and it refers to the seed of Eve, about which it had said, "I will put enmity between your seed and her seed." However, the Seventy <note>The Septuagint (Greek translation of the Old Testament).</note> and Jerome <note>The Vulgate translation.</note> translated it as "She shall crush your head." In both cases, however, the sense is the same:

<column-break/>

<margin>A most beautiful exposition.</margin>
For what is said as "He shall crush" regards not so much the person of Eve herself as it does Eve's posterity. Since she is said to be doing that which she is doing in her seed. But as for why they preferred to translate it as "she" rather than "he," I think the reason was to signify that since from Eve not only females but males were to be propagated, that which was said of the "seed" was to be referred only to the "feminine" seed. These are the things that come to mind on this matter. I am diligently working on the "Harmony of Plato and Aristotle" <note>One of Pico's major unfinished intellectual projects was to prove that the philosophies of Plato and Aristotle were ultimately in agreement.</note>; I give it its due every morning. After the midday hours, I give time to friends, to health, and occasionally to poets and orators; and if there are any studies of lighter work, they share the night with sleep. Sacred Scripture claims its part. Do not let me wait for your response any longer. Greet Beroaldus. Your Politian <note>Angelo Poliziano, the famous humanist and close friend of Pico.</note> is entirely yours. Farewell, and pray to God for me. Florence, the 20th day of March, 1490.

---

### Johannes Pico Mirandula to Aldus Manutius. Letter VI.

<margin>The same point here. Elsewhere.</margin>
I am sending the Homer that you desired; though later than you wished and I ought to have. I am so distracted by occupations, my dear Aldus, that there is no room even to catch my breath. I have bound myself (as you know) for a long time now to the service of letters; they, by their own command, so severely demand their task of reading and dictating that I can scarcely redeem my health. As for what you write that you will do: gird yourself for philosophy; but on this condition, that you remember there is no philosophy which calls us away from the truth of the mysteries. Philosophy seeks the truth, theology finds it, religion possesses it. Farewell. Florence, the eleventh day of February, in the year of grace 1490.

---

### Johannes Pico Mirandula to Ermolao Barbaro, Patriarch of Aquileia. Letter VII.

<margin>Three kinds of living.</margin>
I hear that you have been elected Patriarch of Aquileia. I congratulate those people for having the best pastor; the whole church for a most strenuous soldier; and you for the opportunity given to illustrate and amplify your virtue. There are roughly three kinds of living: the Civil, the Contemplative, and the Religious. In the first, we require prudence; in the second, learning; in the third, as if at the summit of the whole life, we require sanctity in addition to those other two. Your city has already experienced you as most diligent and prudent in managing the affairs of the Republic, and all scholars love and admire you as the patron and champion of the good arts. As for what remains, we know without doubt that you will do it, and we truly rejoice that the Church shall owe no less to you in the future than your city and literature have owed to you thus far.

---

### Johannes Pico Mirandula to his friend Ermolao. Letter VIII.

What shall I say this is, my Ermolao, that you burden me daily with new favors as if you owed me something—I to whom you have long owed everything? Our brother Antonius <note>Anton Maria Pico della Mirandola, Pico's brother.</note> came here recently, returning to our homeland. I ask, "What is Ermolao doing?" He says, "He does this: he loves you, praises you, raises you to the heavens in my presence, in the presence of others, and before the Pope himself; and he does this so constantly and so vigorously as if he had nothing else to do." Likewise, the friends I have there write to me sometimes, one especially: Cosimo Pactius <note>Cosimo de' Pazzi (1466–1513), later Archbishop of Florence.</note>, a man (to embrace his praises in a word) worthy of your unique love. Indeed, as often as he writes, he writes of your favors toward me, of your love, and of a certain wonderful inclination of mind, so that I may feel that you always speak of me most honorably. Oh, this unheard-of humanity of yours, which never thinks it has done enough for you...

### Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to Hieronymus. Greetings. IX.

Unless our "angel" <note>likely referring to their mutual friend Angelo Poliziano</note> were writing to you, I would have written more, but I do not want my "magpies" <note>original: "picas"; a play on his own name, Pico, which means magpie</note> to squawk against those Muses of yours, nor do I wish to be an importunate person who disturbs your pleasure. But if a man has bestowed a benefit who simply refrained from an injury he could have inflicted, you cannot help but credit this brevity of letters to me as a favor—for which you will be most beautifully rewarded if you return the longest letters for my shortest ones. For nothing is more pleasing to us than your letters; I pray you do not cheat me of them, otherwise if you are silent, I shall repay like for like. For then I will especially not be silent, for in that way I would retaliate against you very finely. Farewell: and greet our Hermolaus <note>Hermolao Barbaro, a famous humanist scholar</note>, the delight of the Roman tongue, most warmly in my name.

---

### Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to his nephew Gianfrancesco Pico. Greetings. X.

The reason I have not replied to your letters until now is this: certain Hebrew books have fallen into my hands, on which I have now spent a continuous week, day and night, so much so that they have almost made me blind. For a certain Sicilian Jew, who brought the books here, is to depart from here in twenty days; therefore, until I have extricated myself from them, do not expect even a letter from me. I cannot leave them for a moment, lest they perhaps depart before I have thoroughly examined them all. When I am free from this care, I will overwhelm you with letters, though you know I have a very busy mind. If you are ever going to do anything for my sake, take care by whatever means you can that the Prince of Carpi <note>Alberto III Pio</note> does not require my arrival there; for it would disturb all my studies, to which you know how devoted I am and how I care for nothing besides them. It is not clear enough to me whether it would be more troublesome for me to displease him or myself. Farewell, fear God, and think daily that you are going to die. Ferrara, May 30, 1492.

---

### Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to Marsilio Ficino. Greetings. XI.

Those who contend with friends for what they desire with many words do an injury to friendship, as if friendship itself could not achieve what the allure of speech can. Therefore, I will deal with you simply, as that benevolence which has long existed between us requires. At this time, the Platonist Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher from the 3rd century AD</note> is very necessary for my studies; if you send him to me, you will bind me to you in perpetual debt. He will be here for twenty days, or at most a month, and will be returned immediately by messenger. In the meantime, use both my library and all my things as your own. Farewell.

---

### Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to Angelo Poliziano. Greetings. XII.

My "loves" <note>A metaphorical way of referring to his writings or his favorite philosophical ideas</note> declare they have never been received more urbanely or cheerfully than in these past days at

<column-break/>

your home; and they have confessed quite amicably that while they congratulate themselves greatly, they also owe you much. For who would not wish to die by that sword? <note>Praising Poliziano's sharp wit and style</note> Yet they grieve that it was done more indulgently than was proper, and they are at the point where they doubt whether you, blinded by love itself for my "loves," acted as you did. And they doubt so much that they do not quite trust your otherwise very serious judgment in their own case. Yet they do trust, and now assert themselves to be free of bonds; they do not know how to stay at home, but securely demand liberty and the public stage. But what shall I say about the wit of your Epictetus? <note>Poliziano had translated the *Enchiridion* (Manual) of the Stoic philosopher Epictetus into Latin</note> O, what a humorous thing, worthy of a laugh from Cato! <note>Cato the Elder was famously stern and rarely laughed</note> He was scarcely on the threshold when, opening his robe, he said: "Behold the daggers <note>original: "obelos," a reference to Greek critical marks used to cut or mark text</note>, behold the arrows, if you do not know Greek. Behold me, if any of you is bold enough, ready to strike back." Who could restrain their laughter if a Stoic man joked so "stonily"? <note>A pun on *stoicus* and the Latin word for stone, *lapide*</note> We indeed abstained from weapons, both because he had threatened to repay the injury, and because his skin had become so calloused that it would not admit such light blows. Therefore, we received the old man with the veneration we owed him. When he finally sat down with us, he began to philosophize about morals, and indeed in Latin—not so much because he was among Latins (for there were those in that gathering who knew Greek), but because he himself, thanks to your gift, spoke more brilliantly in Latin. But he did not waste his effort, since he did not stop speaking until he had made Stoics out of us Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle's school</note>.
<margin>Equanimity is spoken of from Epictetus, and from the reading of the same, he progressed wonderfully and quickly.</margin>
And we all approved of that equanimity <term>original: "apathia"; in Stoicism, this is the state of being untroubled by passions or external events</term>. Now one may see men who a little while ago were delicate now made the most tolerant of all things—we who can indeed be provoked by others, but harmed only by ourselves; we who never struggle against fate, and finally wish that those things which are not ours should be just as God wills. Let us never blame or accuse Him; let us grieve for nothing, demand nothing, and not know how to be enslaved or conquered.
<margin>Learn true philosophy from here, whoever you are that reads.</margin>
Let us philosophize in deed, not in speech; and since we are novices, let us observe ourselves as adversaries. Let us neglect rather than reject the opinions of others about us and other external things of that kind. Let us care for the day as travelers care for an inn; finally, let us possess things and not be possessed by them. Let us love silence, lest anything be vomited up that is not yet digested. Let us rarely provide laughter for others, and never for ourselves. And—to embrace it in one word—let us abundantly learn the whole of Epictetus: both to endure adversity and to abstain from pleasures. See how, point by point, we have molded our life after your Epictetus; see how quickly we did so, lest in this part too we should not be Stoics, who want us to be warned
<margin>He fails as long as he does not make progress.</margin>
that a man fails as long as he does not make progress. I have admired this in others, but in myself most of all. I, who have always spent my time in the Lyceum or the Academy <note>Schools of Aristotle and Plato</note> and never in the Porch <note>The "Stoa," the porch in Athens where the Stoics taught</note>, was so conquered by the old man's speech that I came over to his opinion not just with my feet, but with my hands and my whole body. I am sending to you the list of Greek books staying here with me, along with Manuel's letter, as your letters requested. I likewise desire the list of your books. Say greetings in my name to the younger Lorenzo; I was going to write to him, but shame deterred me, lest I seem to pester the man with letters. Farewell.

---

### Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to Thomas the Physician. Greetings. XIII.

The fact that you dedicated your little story—and a festive and elegant one at that—to my name was proof to me of both your learning and your singular kindness toward me. Each is a serious cause urging and impelling me to love you; I know not which more, for as in love (as the proverb goes) a mutual return is not...

to have neglected such a highly praised man, even if not provoked, is a crime; to not have loved him is either the mark of a rustic wit or a truly wicked one. See, therefore, how you not only call but drag me toward friendship with (as they say) twin ropes, since in that tablet <note>Referring to a letter or manuscript</note> of yours there is nothing that does not smell of learning and genius. Nor could you have deserved better of me more splendidly than by so kindly and freely looking after my name in the dedication of that excellent fable <note>original: "fabella", a short story or witty tale</note>. I am so far from neglecting or criticizing its theme that I actually approve of it with the greatest effort. For it has always been my opinion—one I think no learned man will dispute—that it requires sharper wits to write these jests and fables, provided it is done (as you have most abundantly achieved) with erudition and elegance, than to discourse ornately on the gravest matters. Indeed, we consider it far more laborious to shape a graceful statue from mud than from bronze. Why then should it not likewise be considered remarkable to have spoken on humble rather than sublime material? It is certainly more work, and therefore even more praiseworthy. For the dignity of the subject matter lends charm to the work of the former; but for these writers, whatever worthy thing they bring forth is drawn entirely from the author's own store. The material itself contributes nothing, providing no share of the cost <note>original: "asymbola", a Greek term for a guest who brings no contribution to a communal meal</note>. Nature diligently assists the former; the latter certainly struggle against nature. Even if this is so, I will not deny that among these humbler subjects I mentioned, some remarkably surpass others, and there are some of that kind
<margin>

</margin>
so lowly and tasteless that they cannot be sufficiently raised or skillfully seasoned by any force or majesty of words. This flaw can never exist in these works, which are stuffed with the charming wit of jests. But truly, I think those should be placed in the front row which combine the grace of wit with a graphic description of ages and characters. They possess all the qualities of the comic poets, and you have imitated them most beautifully in that fable you sent me. What cleverness is there! What a timely and ingenious mixture of wit. How it delights! How charming and perfect it is in every way. Even if it appeared somewhat sordid or weak due to the humility of the subject, it raises itself by the light and dignity of the speech, assuming brilliance and strength. It is indeed (to speak briefly) a work that clearly demonstrates it came from a most literate man. But among all other things, that exquisite and suitable observation of manners, ages, and characters is especially dear to my heart; in which I see your unique wisdom—and no ordinary wisdom—as if from a watchtower in the distance. I wish you could see the laughter provoked in me by that eighty-year-old prelate, who, however much other things may succeed, constantly rolls this stone: to scrape together money from somewhere—a vice that has always been kindred and familiar to the elderly. What shall I say of our parasite, who, by feigning a familiar dinner, extorts a meal from a most parsimonious old man? Who, as they say, most uniquely "wipes the nose of a pumice stone" <note>A Latin idiom meaning to squeeze blood from a stone, or get money from a miser</note>. There is no word, my Thomas, in that fable that does not claim some peculiar prize for itself. But it is not my place to report everything I have "scented out," nor do I have the nose to smell everything. Let this be certain to you: nothing more pleasing or delightful has ever happened to me. Therefore, I have received the work within these walls and you yourself into my heart. You have, my Thomas, what (even if you asked for it) ought to have been asked by me: our friendship is mutual, which you yourself (as became a most excellent man) inaugurated with the Muses.

->Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, Count of Concordia, to his<-
->Nicolaus Leonicenus. Greetings. XIII.<-

I would have spoken with you by letter more often and at greater length, my sweetest Nicolaus, if your whereabouts had been known to me by messenger, letter, or rumor. I anxiously inquired of many, but received only doubtful answers from everyone. At last, in recent days, a letter from Antonio Faventino, a most serious philosopher, to Thomas Frignanus fell into my hands. From it, I learned that you were in Florence, which was then most pleasing to me. As soon as I understood this, I sent a letter to you in Florence by courier. The journey was in vain, for he did not find you there. I grieved exceedingly. Today Thomas indicated that you had departed from Florence and are in Bologna; I ordered these to be delivered to you there immediately. In them, I shall not strive to further reveal my goodwill or singular love for you; for you should not doubt our will toward you even a little, unless you thought me forgotten—which is not my nature—both of your outstanding virtue and your services to me. However, I could not help but wonder greatly that, when you snatched yourself away from the city's tumults to seek a place where you could live both peacefully and pleasantly, you either forgot or despised this little town of ours. You seemed, Nicolaus, to distrust either my will or my means. Truly, as the latter is less than your merits, so the former is greater than your opinion. It will be very pleasing if you advise me of your plan, and most pleasing of all if you do not disdain to share my home with me, to rest with me while others are busy with the "mother of business" <note>likely referring to urban commerce or politics</note>. I am sending you the rest of John the Grammarian <note>The 6th-century philosopher John Philoponus</note>, which was missing for many days but has now been found. I am yours and I wait for you. Farewell. At Mirandola, July 20, 1482. If you love me, take every care to get an index of all the books found in the library of Saint Dominic. Send it or bring it with you. Farewell again. I have built a suburban villa, pleasant enough given the condition of the place and region. I have composed a long poem about it; the house will be sweet to you, and the poem not unpleasant. Again, farewell.

<margin>
To whom the name
of "Learned" is fitting.
