Because you praised me so much in your last letter, I owe you as much as I am far from deserving that praise. For what is given freely is owed to the giver, not what is paid as a debt. Therefore, I owe all of what you write about me to you, since there is nothing of the sort in me. Since you owed this to me in no way at all, it was entirely the result of your kindness and singular goodwill toward me. For the rest, if you examine me, you will find nothing but what is thin, humble, and narrow. I am a newcomer and a raw recruit <note>original: "tirunculi", young soldiers in training</note> who has only just moved a foot out of the darkness of ignorance and has progressed almost nowhere. It goes well for us if we are even counted among the ranks of the studious; the name "learned" <note>original: "doctus"</note> implies something else that is peculiar to you and those like you. Such grand titles do not suit me, since I have not only not explored the chief things in literary studies, but have not yet even seen them except through a lattice window <note>original: "per transennam", an idiom meaning a fleeting or partial glimpse</note>. I will certainly strive (as I am doing now) to be such a person someday as you now proclaim me to be and either judge me to be, or certainly wish me to be. Meanwhile, I will imitate you, Angelo, who excuse yourself to the Greeks for being Latin, and to the Latins for "Greek-izing." I shall use a similar refuge, so that I may approve myself to poets and rhetoricians because I am said to be practicing philosophy; to the philos...

those who cultivate philosophy, rhetoric, and the muses, although for me it has happened far differently than for you. Indeed, while I wish to sit on "two chairs" <note>original: "geminis sellis sedere"; a proverb meaning to try to do two things at once and succeeding at neither</note> (as they say), I am excluded from both, so that in the end—to put it briefly—I am neither a poet, nor a rhetorician, nor a philosopher. You, however, fulfill both roles so well that it is hardly clear which you do better, for you embrace both the Greek and our own Minerva <note>Roman goddess of wisdom; here referring to Latin and Greek learning</note> so beautifully, like a swan of both languages, that what is "grafted" <note>original: "institia" for "insiticia", meaning acquired</note> and what is "natural" <note>original: "genuina"</note> cannot easily be discerned. For to say nothing of your Latin (in which you yield to no one), who would believe—as was said of Hadrian—that a Roman man could speak such perfect Greek? Our Emanuel <note>likely referring to a Greek teacher like Manuel Chrysoloras</note> swore while reading your writings that Athens itself was not so Attic. You are the one, my dear Angelo (let all flattery be cast aside), to whom only one or two of our men—not to say no one—can be compared. If there were more such men, this age would have no reason to envy antiquity. Apply yourself, I beg you, and rescue literature from neglect as much as you can, lest the brilliance of the Roman tongue completely fade away through the injury of time; always forge something new that may help and illuminate the Latin cause. And finally, let those works you have at home be published for the common benefit of students. I truly love you and all your works as I love yourself, and all the more because I have set you before me as a model to be imitated—even if you are one whom all ought to follow, but few can actually catch up to. Farewell.

->Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to Paolo Cortesi. Greetings. XVI.<-

<margin>The difference between an image and a letter.</margin>
**Y**ou think rightly, Paolo. Let us send letters frequently so that we, who are divided by distances of place, may certainly be joined by the exchange of letters. It is customary to lighten the longing for those who are absent: perhaps you have a statue or an image of someone at home. To me, however, there seems to be this difference between an image and a letter: the latter portrays the mind, the former the body; the former only sketches the outer limits, the latter clearly expresses and shapes even the innermost parts; the former represents as it were the friend's tunic and cloak, the latter represents the true friend to us; the former emulates the colors and figure of the flesh as best it can, the latter represents thoughts, plans, sorrows, joys, cares—in short, all affections. And those secrets of the soul which one hardly speaks even to oneself in person, one transmits most faithfully to an absent friend. Finally, the letter is a living and effective likeness, while the image is a dead and mute one. Let us therefore send these images of our souls to one another: you yours, which you can make of gold and silver; I mine, of bronze or clay. Thus we shall be beyond all injury of place and time, just as the power of the mind itself knows neither the distance of place nor the delays of time. But truly, how much I owe you, most dutiful Paolo, who first called me to this duty with such a letter as held and delighted me so much that I do not remember being more delighted by any reading for many days now. For it is full of eloquence, full of graces, full of love and benevolence—you were perhaps expecting me to say full of my own praises. Indeed, I was going to say that too. For I am not so iron-hearted, or (if you prefer it said this way) I am not so much a philosopher that I am not delighted by the praises of friends. If they are true, they commend me to myself; if false, they commend the friends' love and goodwill toward me. I will therefore easily obtain permission from my philosophy to read your letters frequently and with pleasure, even the parts where they praise me. But it is not so easy to appear sufficiently civil or not ungrateful in returning this literary duty. For an imperious mistress <note>likely referring to his philosophical studies</note> so distracts me, so demands her daily task, and so occupies me entirely that hardly anything of me is left even for myself. But such is your kindness that you will prefer even the bad letters we write, and you will take our silence in good part when we are quiet. Poliziano, our common delight, greets you. Farewell.

->Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to Troilo Malvezzi. Greetings. XVII.<-

**Y**our little book *On Lots* <note>original: "de fortibus", referring to divination or fortune</note> affected me with as much pleasure as usually comes to one who has met with the best fortune. I give you great thanks for making me a participant in your labors, especially such as these, in which both subtlety of disputation and a manifold knowledge of various things are clearly apparent. One of these deserves praise for genius, the other for diligence. I will give you my "trifles" <note>original: "nugas", a self-deprecating term for his writings</note> which you desire very soon. For it is uncertain whether it is more unworthy for you, a most busy legal expert, to be detained by reading them, or for a most friendly man to be kept in suspense by desire. Farewell and love me. February 29th, 1492.

->Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to Taddeo Ugolino. Greetings. XVIII.<-

<margin>Preparation for those nine hundred conclusions.</margin>
**Y**our most welcome letters were full of love, faith, and charity, not only because you remember me, but because in them you kindly warn me that I myself should remember my own studies and the expectations I must uphold. Indeed, being conscious of my own weakness, I would not dare to promise anything even mediocre about myself. But He from whom all good comes, the most merciful Father of Lights, just as He has previously given the means by which men might distinguish us, so He will give in the future so that we may not have held such a well-conceived opinion in vain. I am hurrying to Rome, where we shall put our studies to the test, even at some risk. If we profit anything, it is a gift from God; to Him be praise and thanks. If we fail in anything, it is our own weakness; let it be imputed to us. For the rest, I am yours, as one who, because of the integrity of your life and character, would hardly yield the first place in loving you even to our Jerome. Farewell, from Fratta.

->Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to Tommaso di Mezzo. Greetings. XIX.<-

<margin>Praise for Hermolaus.</margin>
**I** do not remember ever being more solidly delighted than recently while I was reading your *Epyrota* <note>a comedy written by Tommaso di Mezzo</note>, a little story undoubtedly most witty, challenging even the ancient comedies with the festive nature of its argument and the erudition of its style. For what shall I say of these modern ones, which are clearly inept and witless, easily declaring the "infancy" <note>clumsiness or lack of skill</note> of their authors? It was truly worthy of being dedicated to Hermolaus Barbarus <note>a famous humanist and diplomat</note>—I know not whether he is more yours or mine. I believe all literate men owe as much to him alone as they hardly owe to antiquity. That you did not cheat me of this work was done in accordance with your goodwill toward me, which has been very clear before now. There is nothing I possess of such value that, if I were to lend it to you like a fellow soldier, I would consider the favor abundantly returned. I am now waiting with open mouth <note>eagerly expecting</note> for the new comedy you promise me. There is nothing I desire more, except for one thing: your arrival here. Unless I had to depart from here within ten days (as I think you have learned from our Exita), I certainly would have obtained it from you by persistent asking. For it is possible to gather from what you have written what delight there would be in our familiarity, in our living together, and in our spoken voices; for they truly possess a hidden energy that delights the mind more deeply and affects it in wonderful ways, far outweighing all writings. But since this is not possible, in the meantime do not expect material for a comedy from me. I prefer that you bring forth both from your own store, so that Tommaso di Mezzo [Thomas "The Middle"] may not be middle-of-the-road...

...to have hated such a highly praised man, even if you do not provoke it, is either the mark of a rustic mind or a truly wicked one. See, then, how you do not merely call me to friendship, but drag me with "double ropes" <note>original: "geminis funibus"; a metaphor for being doubly compelled or pulled by two strong forces</note> (as they say). For there is nothing in that tablet of yours that does not smell of learning and genius. Nor could you have deserved better of me than to consult my name so kindly and freely in the dedication of that excellent little fable. I am so far from neglecting or criticizing its subject matter that I actually approve of it with the greatest effort.

For it has always been my opinion—and I think no learned man will object—that it takes a sharper mind to write these jests and fables, provided it is done with erudition and elegance (as you have most abundantly demonstrated), than to discourse ornately on the most serious matters. Indeed, we consider it a far more laborious task to fashion a beautiful statue from mud <note>original: "limo"</note> than from bronze or gold; why then should it not likewise be more difficult, and certainly more praiseworthy, to have spoken something remarkable on a humble subject rather than a sublime one? In the work of the latter, the dignity of the subject matter serves as a "lure" <note>original: "lenocinatur"; meaning the inherent importance of the topic makes the writing seem better than it is</note>; but in the former, whatever they bring forth that is worthy is drawn entirely from the writer's own storehouse. The subject matter itself contributes nothing, like a guest who brings no gift to a feast <note>original: "asymbola"; a Greek term for a guest who does not pay their share</note>. Nature diligently helps the serious writers, but these others certainly struggle against nature.

Even if this is so, I will not deny that among these humbler subjects I have mentioned, some are wonderfully superior to others. There are some of this kind so lowly and tasteless that they cannot be sufficiently raised or skillfully seasoned by any force or majesty of words. Such a fault can never be found in these works of yours, which are stuffed with the charming wit of urbanity. Truly, I believe those works should be placed on the highest benches which, along with the charm of wit, contain a vivid description of different ages and characters. Your work possesses all those qualities belonging to the comic poets, which you have imitated most beautifully in the little fable you sent me. How much cleverness is there! What an appropriate and ingenious mixture of wit! How it delights! How charming and perfect it is in every way! If any part appeared somewhat dirty or weak due to the humility of the subject, it raises itself by the light and dignity of your speech, assuming both brilliance and strength. It is, to put it briefly, a work that clearly demonstrates it proceeded from a most literate man.

But among all the rest, I especially cherish that exquisite and fitting observation of manners, ages, and persons, in which I see your unique wisdom—and no ordinary wisdom at that—as if from a high watchtower. I wish you could see what a laugh that eighty-year-old prelate provokes in me; no matter how other things go, he is constantly "rolling this stone" <note>original: "saxum voluit"; a reference to the endless labor of Sisyphus</note>: trying to scrape together money from somewhere, a vice that has always been kin and familiar to the elderly. What shall I say of our "parasite" <note>a stock character in ancient comedy who lives off others</note> who, disguising his intent, extorts a witty dinner from a most stingy old man? He "wipes the nose of a pumice stone" <note>original: "pumicem emungit"; a proverbial expression for getting something out of a person who is exceptionally "dry" or stingy</note>, so to speak, in a most singular way. There is not a word, my dear Thomas, in that little fable that does not claim for itself some peculiar prize. But it is not my place to recount everything I have "scented" out, nor do I have the kind of nose that can smell everything. Let this be certain to you: no more pleasing or pleasant thing has ever happened to me. Therefore, I have received the work within these walls and you yourself within my soul. You have, my dear Thomas, what was to be sought from me (even if you are the one asking): a mutual friendship between us, which you (as becomes a most excellent man) have inaugurated with the Muses. It remains that whenever you have need of my affairs (however small) or my labor, you should put my goodwill toward you to the test. Nor shall I, if any occasion is given, neglect any kind of duty toward you, just as you yourself were the first to act toward me at the very entrance to our friendship. Farewell.

-> Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, Count of Concordia, to his Nicolaus Leonicenus. Greetings. XIII. <-

I would have spoken with you more often and at greater length through letters, my sweetest Nicolaus, if your location had been known to me by messenger, letter, or rumor. I anxiously inquired about this from many people but received only doubtful answers from everyone. Finally, in recent days, a letter from Antonius Faventinus, a most serious philosopher, to Thomas Frignanus fell into my hands; from it, I learned that you were in Florence, which was then most pleasing to me. As soon as I understood this, I sent a letter to you in Florence by a courier. The journey was in vain, for he did not find you there. I grieved exceedingly. Today, Thomas informed me that you had departed from Florence and were in Bologna, so I ordered this letter to be delivered to you immediately.

In this letter, I will not strive to reveal my benevolence or singular love for you at great length; for you ought not to doubt my goodwill toward you even a little bit, unless you thought me forgotten (which is not my nature) both of your excellent virtue and your services toward me. I could not help but marvel greatly at how you have rescued yourself from the tumults of the city to seek a place where you might live both peacefully and pleasantly. You seem, Nicolaus, either to have forgotten or certainly to have looked down upon this little town of ours. You seemed to distrust either my will or my resources; but just as the latter is less than your merits, so the former is greater than your opinion. Nothing will be more pleasing than if you inform me of your plan, and most pleasing of all if you do not disdain to share my home with me, to spend your leisure with me while others are busy with the "mother of business" <note>original: "matre negociabuntur"; likely referring to the city or the marketplace</note>. I am sending to you the remainder of John the Grammarian <note>likely referring to the commentator John Philoponus</note> which was lost for many days and has now been found. I am yours and I wait for you. Farewell. At Mirandola, the 20th day of July, 1482. If you love me, take care with all diligence to have an index of all the books found in the library of Saint Dominic. Send it or bring it with you. Farewell again. I have built a suburban villa, pleasant enough given the condition of the place and region. I have composed a long poem about it; the house will be sweet to you and the poem not unpleasant. Farewell once more.

-> Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to Angelo Poliziano. Greetings. XV. <-

<margin>To whom the name of "learned" is fitting.</margin>
Because you praised me so much in your last letter, I owe you as much as I am distant from being deservedly praised. For that is owed to each person which is given freely, not what is paid as a debt. Therefore, I myself owe you entirely whatever you write about me, since there is nothing of the sort in me. Since you owed me this in no way, it was entirely the result of your humanity and singular benevolence toward me. As for the rest, if you examine me, you will find nothing but what is thin, humble, and narrow. We are novices and "young recruits" <note>original: "tirunculi"</note> who have only just moved a foot out of the darkness of ignorance and have advanced almost nothing. It is kindly dealt with us if we are counted among the ranks of the studious; the name of "learned" <note>original: "docti"</note> has something else about it which is peculiar to you and those like you; such great things do not fit me. Since of those things which are foremost in the study of letters, I not only have nothing fully explored, but have not even seen them yet except "through a lattice" <note>original: "per transennam"; meaning a brief or partial glimpse</note>. I will indeed strive (as I am doing now) to be such a person someday as you now proclaim me to be, or judge me to be, or certainly wish me to be. Meanwhile, I will imitate you, Angelo, who excuse yourself to the Greeks for being Latin, and to the Latins for "playing the Greek" <note>original: "graecisses"</note>. I shall use a similar refuge, so that I may approve myself to poets and rhetoricians because I am said to study philosophy; [and to] philoso- <note>The text cuts off here, continuing on the next page.</note>

...[philoso]pher than one who cultivates rhetoric and the muses, although it happened quite differently for me than for you. Indeed, while I wish (as they say) to sit on two stools <note>original: "geminis... sellis sedere"; the OCR reads "fellis federe," but this is a common Latin idiom for trying to do two things at once and succeeding at neither</note>, I am excluded from both, and it turns out at last (to put it briefly) that I am neither a poet, nor a rhetorician, nor a philosopher. You, however, fulfill both roles so well that it is hardly clear which you do better, you who embrace both the Greek and our own Latin <term>Minerva</term> <note>Minerva was the goddess of wisdom; here Pico uses her name to represent deep learning in both languages</note> so beautifully, like a swan of both tongues, that it is not easy to discern which is adopted and which is native. For to say nothing of your Latin (in which you yield to no one), who would believe—as was said of the Emperor Hadrian—that a Roman man could speak Greek so well? Our Emanuel <note>likely referring to Manuel Adramyttenos, a Greek scholar who taught in Italy</note> used to swear while reading your works that Athens itself was not so truly "Attic" <note>Attic refers to the purest, most elegant form of ancient Greek</note>. You are such a man, my Angelo (let flattery be far from here), that among our contemporaries only one or two, not to say no one, can be compared to you. If there were more such men, this age would have no reason to envy antiquity. Apply yourself, I beg you, and rescue literature as much as you can from neglect, lest the brilliance of the Latin language fade away entirely through the injury of time. Always forge something new to help and illuminate the Latin cause. And those works you have at home, let them finally come out for the common benefit of students. I truly love you and all your works, and I long for them; all the more so because I have set you up as the model after which I would be fashioned—even if you are the kind of man everyone ought to follow, but few can actually reach. Farewell.

### Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Paolo Cortesi, Greetings. Letter 16.

<margin>The difference between a portrait and a letter.</margin> You think rightly, Paolo. Let us send letters frequently so that we, who are divided by distances of place, may certainly be joined by the exchange of letters. It usually lightens the longing of those who are absent if you perhaps have a statue or a portrait of the person at home. To me, however, this seems to be the difference between a portrait and a letter: the latter portrays the mind, the former the body. The portrait outlines only the external features, while the letter clearly expresses and fashions even the innermost parts. The portrait represents, as it were, the tunic and clothing of a friend; the letter represents the true friend to us. The portrait emulates the colors and shape of the flesh as best it can; the letter captures thoughts, advice, sorrows, joys, cares, and finally all affections. And those secrets of the soul which one hardly speaks to another even when present, the letter transmits most faithfully to an absent friend. Finally, the letter is a living and effective image, while the portrait is a dead and mute likeness. Let us, therefore, send these images of our souls to one another—yours, to be sure, of gold and silver as you are able, and mine of bronze or even clay. In this way, we shall be beyond all injury of place and time. Just as the power of the mind itself knows neither the intervals of space nor the delays of time. But truly, how much do I owe you, most dutiful Paolo, who first called me to this duty with such a letter—one that held and delighted me so much that I cannot remember being more delighted by any reading for many days. For it is full of eloquence, full of graces, full of love and benevolence; perhaps you expected me to say it was full of my own praises. Indeed, I was going to say that too. For I am not so "iron-hearted" <note>meaning unfeeling or stubborn</note>, or if you prefer it said this way, I am not so much a philosopher that I am not delighted by the praises of my friends. If they are true, they recommend me to myself; if false, they recommend to me the love and goodwill of those who wrote them. I will easily obtain permission from my philosophy, then, to read your letters frequently and with pleasure, even the parts where they praise me. But it will not be so easy for me to appear sufficiently polite or not ungrateful in returning this literary duty. For a most imperious mistress <note>referring to his philosophical studies</note> so distracts me and demands such a daily task from me that there is hardly anything of myself left even for me. But such is your kind-

<column-break/>

-ness that you will take it well when I write even "bad" letters, and you will think well of my silence when I am quiet. Poliziano, our mutual delight, greets you. Farewell.

### Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Troilus Maluetius, Greetings. Letter 17.

Your little book *On Lots* <note>original: "de sortibus"; likely a legal or philosophical treatise on chance or inheritance</note> affected me with as much pleasure as a man usually feels when the best lot falls to him. I give you great thanks for making me a partner in your late-night labors, especially such as these: in which both the subtlety of your debating and your wide-ranging knowledge of various things are easily apparent. One of these earns praise for your genius, the other for your diligence. My "trifles," which you desire, I will give to you shortly. For it is uncertain whether it is more unworthy that you, a most busy lawyer, be delayed by reading them, or that a most friendly man be kept hanging in desire for so long. Farewell and love me. May 29, 1492.

### Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Thaddeus Ugolinus, Greetings. Letter 18.

I received your most welcome letters, full of love, faith, and charity, not only because you remembered me, but because in them you amiably warn me that I should remember myself—that is, my virtuous studies and the need to uphold the expectation I have given. Indeed, being conscious of my own weakness, I would not dare to promise anything even mediocre about myself. But He from whom all good comes, the most merciful Father of Lights, just as He previously gave the means by which men might distinguish us, so He will give in the future, so that we may not hold such a well-conceived opinion in vain. I am hurrying to Rome, where I shall make a trial of our 
<margin>Haste toward those 900 conclusions.</margin>
studies, even at some risk. If we profit anything, it is God's gift; to Him be the praise and thanks. If we fail in anything, it is our own weakness; let it be imputed to us. Furthermore, I am yours, as one who, because of the integrity of your life and character, would hardly yield first place to our Jerome in loving you. Farewell, from Fratta.

### Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Thomas Medius, Greetings. Letter 19.

I do not remember ever being more solidly delighted than recently, while I was reading your *Epyrota* <note>A Latin comedy written by Thomas Medius (Tommaso Mezzo) in 1483</note>, a little story that is undoubtedly most witty; with the festivity of its plot and the erudition of its style, it challenges even the ancient comedies. For what should I say of these modern ones, which are plainly inept and witless, easily declaring the "infancy" <note>meaning lack of skill or eloquence</note> of their authors? It was certainly worthy of being dedicated to Ermolao Barbaro <note>a famous Venetian humanist and diplomat</note>—I know not whether more by your name or mine. 
<margin>Praise of Ermolao.</margin>
I think all literate men owe him as much as they hardly owe to antiquity itself. That you did not cheat me of it was done out of your goodwill toward me, which has been well-seen before. There is nothing in my possession of such value that, if I were to lend it to you, I would think the favor had been abundantly returned. I am now gaping in expectation for the new comedies you promise me. There is nothing I desire more than those, except for one thing: your arrival here. Had I not to depart from here within ten days (as I think you have learned from our Seta), I certainly would have obtained it from you by demanding it. For one can gather from what you have written what pleasantness there would be in our familiarity and in our living together. Living voices truly have a hidden energy that affects the soul with a deeper pleasure in wonderful ways, far outweighing all writings. But since this is not permitted, in the meantime do not expect material for a comedy from me. I prefer that you bring forth both from your own storehouse, so that Thomas Medius is not "medium" <note>Pico is making a pun on Thomas's surname "Medius" (meaning middle or mediocre), saying he is anything but mediocre</note>.

...but the whole thing would taste of a mere fable. I fear, indeed, that by obeying you, the dullness of my wit would cause me a loss. ## Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Marsilio Ficino, Greetings. Letter 20.

<margin>Swiftness of talent.</margin>
You could not have asked for your Latin Muhammad <note>original: "maumettem tuum latinum"; Pico is likely referring to a Latin translation of an Islamic text or a polemic concerning Muhammad that Ficino had lent him</note> back at a more opportune time than now, when I hope to soon hear Muhammad himself speaking in his native tongue. For after I kept watch day and night for a solid month over the Hebrew language, I have now turned myself entirely to the study of Arabic and Chaldaic <note>In the Renaissance, "Chaldaic" typically referred to Aramaic or the language of the "Chaldean Oracles"</note>. I had no fear that I would make less progress in them than I did in Hebrew, in which I can—not yet with praise, but certainly without fault—compose a letter. See what the impulse of the soul can achieve! See what labor and diligence can do, even where the strength is somewhat weak. Moreover, certain books in both languages, which came into my hands not by chance or accident but by the counsel of God and a divine power favoring my studies, have encouraged me and even driven me to learn the letters of the Arabs and the Chaldeans while I was occupied with other things. Hear the titles, and you will give your pledge.

<margin>Chaldaic books given to him unexpectedly.</margin>
These Chaldaic books (if they are books and not treasures!) are primarily the oracles of Ezra, Zoroaster, and Melchior the Magi <note>Pico believed these "Chaldean Oracles" contained a lost, ancient theology that prefigured Christianity</note>, in which those very parts that circulate among the Greeks as corrupted and mutilated are read as whole and perfect. Then there is, in that wisdom of the Chaldeans, an interpretation—brief and rugged, indeed, but full of mysteries. There is likewise a small book on the dogmas of Chaldaic theology, then on those of the Persians, Greeks, and Chaldeans in that most rich and divine commentary. See, Marsilio, what unexpected goods have crept into my bosom! Why should I not seem to myself to have already obtained a <term>Cornucopia</term> <note>A "horn of plenty," representing an overflowing abundance of wisdom</note>? But what of the Arabic books? Among which there are many questions of the Muhammad of Toledo, the letters of Abugalem <note>Possibly a reference to Abu Ma'shar, the great Arab astrologer</note>—who heard Averroes—and (which will touch you more)

<margin>Ammonius, the teacher of Plotinus.</margin>
of a certain Adelard <note>Possibly Adelard of Bath, known for introducing Arabic science to the West</note> who philosophized in Egypt under Ammonius, the teacher of Plotinus. Good God, how <term>Pythagorean</term> <note>Referring to the mystical and mathematical philosophy of Pythagoras</note> they are, how full of the dogmas of the ancients and of secret discipline! An effective vow immediately seized my mind: to be able to unroll and examine these through my own efforts without an interpreter. And this I am doing now; this is the stone I roll with unwearied diligence. This, my Marsilio, is my desire; these are my fires, which promise me—and even now provide—a pleasure that is not fleeting or vain, but firm. It is a true image of the future glory which will be revealed in us. But I return to your letter. Your "Muhammad" is at Perugia; when I return there (for I am away due to a suspicion of the plague), it will go to you immediately. Regarding what you write about Plotinus, I do not quite understand; this I know: Plotinus has not escaped me, whom I have always judged—and judge still—not only to be held in one's hands but to be thoroughly learned. If you have complained of me at all, either to Mithridates <note>Flavius Mithridates, the Jewish convert who taught Pico Hebrew and translated Kabbalistic texts for him</note> or to Pierleone, it must be that an injustice was done to you by someone on my behalf, for I have never been unjust to you or your affairs in any way. What that might be, I still do not know—and I choose not to know. I am a Pythagorean, among whom nothing is more sa-

<column-break/>

-cred than friendship. If there is anything that can either weaken or diminish (as they say) the bond between us, let it vanish into the western winds. Farewell, and love me, for I am as much yours as I ever was. From Fratta.

## Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Girolamo Donato, Greetings. Letter 21.

By now, such is my negligence that I have written nothing to you for a long time. That alone was the cause of this silence of ours. I will allow myself to be judged by you for this crime—namely, negligence—but otherwise, I am neither a forgetful man nor a deserter of friendships. These friendships I establish—in opposition to that of witless friends—for a man such as Donato, not as temporary things, but as entirely perpetual.

## Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to his friend Ermolao, Greetings. Letter 22.

I sent a letter to you in recent days via your Sitanus. I do not know if it was delivered. Why you did not receive the commentaries on Aristotle that you requested, I have no doubt you understood from him. They will come as soon as I return to my library; I have come here at present to explore the libraries of others. Nor is there any reason for me to repent, for I have found so many things here, both Greek and Latin, that contribute to literature and learned philosophy. Indeed, on this very day when I gave this letter, there fell into my hands a fragment of Apuleius "On Interpretation"; it is a learned work and one that 

<margin>He doubts whether Apuleius "On Interpretation" is defective.</margin>
you would plainly recognize as being by Apuleius, but it is mutilated and defective. I would gladly know from you whether it is held to be complete anywhere that you know of. Although, when you publish those works of yours which you now have "under the anvil" <note>An idiom meaning a work currently in progress or being refined</note>, there will no longer be any reason for us to miss Apuleius. Regarding my studies, I have nothing to write to you except that I am constantly occupied with Hieronymus, and that for the greatest part of my nights, I keep watch over your Themistius <note>Ermolao Barbaro was famous for his Latin translation and paraphrases of the philosopher Themistius</note>. I recently diverted my path from Aristotle to the Academy <note>The "Academy" refers to the school of Plato</note>. But I went not as a deserter—as the saying goes—but as a scout. Yet (I will tell you, Ermolao, what I feel) I seem to recognize two things in Plato: both that Homeric faculty of eloquence that raises itself above prose, and—if one looks more deeply into them—an absolute commonality of meaning with Aristotle. Thus, if you look at the words, nothing is more combative; if you look at the substance, nothing is more concordant. If it is ever granted to me—which is the summit of my prayers—to philosophize with you for a few days, we shall discuss these things more widely in person, and we shall make some trial of this opinion of mine. Farewell, glory of our age. December 6, 1484.

## Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Brother Battista Mantovano, Carmelite, Greetings, etc. Letter 23.

Greetings, best of fathers. I have not written to you for some time, but in the meantime, I have read those things you wrote—namely, those divine and most holy poems of yours. In them, there is such majesty of matter and such splendor of eloquence that the words and the thoughts seem to vie with one another for the prize. Happy are you who desire the best things and are able to achieve them; happy are we to whom it is given not only to read what you have written but also to love you, see you, and speak with you. Here is rich material for me, which would fill not just a letter but a proper volume, if either my own weakness or your modesty would permit me to wander into the praising of your poems. I will say this one thing: that I am so delighted by the reading of your verses that almost every day, when either weariness or fatigue takes hold of me, I am accustomed to withdraw into them as if into a garden. From which such great pleasure always arises in my mind that it desires nothing more than to be fatigued again, so that it may again be refreshed. If you are finished with it, I desire the *Life of Apollonius* by Philostratus, and also the work of Zacharias the Philosopher, which you said you obtained in Rome...

...take care that I may eventually have a copy, and besides that, an index of your library in Bologna, if it can be done at your convenience. Farewell.

->Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to C. F. <note>original: "C. F."; likely a high-ranking official or a friend whose initials are abbreviated</note>, Greetings. Letter 23.<-

I debated for a long time within myself whether I should deal with you through silence or through letters. Since this matter had arguments on both sides, and my judgment swayed first one way and then the other, I have remained silent toward you until this very time. For it seemed no less shameless than inappropriate to make a noise with these light trifles before ears that are especially occupied; and there was nothing I could write to you that was entirely worthy of you. On the other hand, if I did not venerate a man distinguished by such dignity as yours—and one who has deserved the best from me—through letters when I could not do so in person, I was undoubtedly failing in my duty. While my mind wavered between these thoughts for a long time, devotion finally conquered shame, and it persuaded me that I should rather undergo the mark of being a bit bold and rash than that of a forgetful or negligent man. Receive therefore, Honorable Patron <note>original: "C.P." for "Clarissime Pater" or "Colendissime Patrone"</note>, my letters with that cheerful and open brow with which you always received me when I was there; they are indeed inept and unpolished, but they are a very serious testimony of my loyalty toward you and of my truly devoted will. Above all, I wish this one thing to be signified to you: there is nothing I desire more than to be given some occasion where I may clearly leave a witness with you of my loyalty, devotion, and respect toward you. Indeed, if you ever put our loyalty to the test, you will recognize that I am superior among those who are devoted to you, just as you wonderfully surpass the other leaders of your order in virtue, learning, and sanctity.

->Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Baldassarre Migliavacca <note>original: "Baldaffari millia vaccæ"</note>, Greetings. Letter 25.<-

You will wonder, and indeed not without cause, at a response from me to your letters even much later than you perhaps desired and than your letters themselves deservedly required. Hear in a few words why it happened so. A man—certainly honest, but previously unknown to me—was about to go to you on nearly the same days I received yours; he said he was doing business in Milan. I thought his departure a timely opportunity by which it would happen that my letter would be delivered to you by a faithful messenger and (which I desired most) without cost. But "the south wind blew" <note>An idiomatic way of saying things went wrong or were delayed</note>; for when that man had delayed his departure by procrastinating for a month, he finally left, but with me being entirely unaware. Because I had become more negligent regarding letters due to the hope of a certain messenger, the memory of them had almost slipped away. Now, finally, when your letter to me fell into my hands, it immediately roused me as if I were sleeping, and it warned me of the time passed without fulfilling my duty. I grieved—I call God to witness—not a little, and I still grieve now. Nor would I wish these things said to excuse me, but rather to accuse me; I will easily allow myself to be condemned for negligence, and even call for whatever penalty you prefer. Now to your letters: I received no small pleasure both from the letters themselves and from the Greek books for which you so liberally and in such a friendly way gave me access. This was not so much because the use of them did much for my studies, but because we have laid the foundations of a perpetual friendship. This alone I value more than the entire library of either Synesius <note>original: "Sunádii"; likely referring to Synesius of Cyrene, the Neoplatonist philosopher and bishop</note> or Ptolemy. For I am so far from neglecting the friendships of learned men that nothing is more a matter of care or closer to my heart. I know, moreover, what place you claim for yourself among learned men, since your letter was a most evident proof to me of your teaching, erudition, and humanity.

<column-break/>

Therefore, if I did not love you very much, I would surely have forgotten myself and acted far differently than I am accustomed to. I love you, therefore, uniquely, although I have never seen you. I love you so much from my heart that I love few others more, so that while our intimacy might eventually increase, our love cannot. And if anything can be added—that is, if it could grow—it will all be added by your arrival here. You promised this of your own accord in your letters, and we seek it so ardently that we desire it with impatience. If you obtain for me <term>John the Grammarian</term> <note>Also known as John Philoponus, a 6th-century Christian commentator on Aristotle</note> on Physics and Aristotle's *Metaphysics*, you will bind me to you in perpetual debt. For I do not have them with me, and I am in great expectation of them. Farewell.

->Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Giacomo Feltrino, Greetings. Letter 26.<-

Your letters, if ever they did, have now delighted me most of all. Through them, I have learned that your opinion of me is such that not even a wish could imagine anything better. One thing alone disturbed me: because you noted nothing in those things I wrote to you, you created a suspicion that you did not think everything was worthy of note. For I would have believed that most things pleased you only if you had indicated that some things displeased you. Thus it happens that I do not sufficiently trust your testimony in my own cause, even though it is otherwise most approved. For you love all our things just as we do; and since from the innate ease of your character you praise everyone, this happens to you especially in our affairs, because all that is in us has flowed from your own fountain. Indeed, I neither stop nor shall I stop emulating you and standing in your footsteps. I wish I might eventually catch up to you. But I grieve that because of the distance between our places, I am prevented from hearing you in person as you gravely treat the deepest points of philosophy, as is your custom. Even if those same things you say can be sent through letters—which I would most especially wish to obtain from you—nevertheless, the <term>living voice</term> <note>original: "viua vox"; the ancient educational concept that spoken instruction is superior to written text</note> has something, I know not what, that affects and forms a student more. Farewell.

->Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Girolamo Donà <note>original: "Hieronymo Donato"; a prominent Venetian scholar, diplomat, and philosopher</note>, Greetings. Letter 27.<-

I received your letters, which were truly sweet and erudite. I was delighted by them just as I once was by your company when I was in Padua, as often as the opportunity of enjoying it was offered to me. Indeed, I have always been eager and most hungry for it, even beyond your own opinion. For it was not hidden from me how sweet and pleasant the genius of Donà was, overflowing and stuffed on every side with all good disciplines and finally with every virtue. But it is certainly so, my Girolamo: it often happens to me that the easy and ready faculty of obtaining that thing which we most desire makes us lazy and negligent. For while we hope that what we pass over today can be done quite conveniently tomorrow, it finally happens that, from this supine procrastination of ours, the year flows away while we are blinking. But since the matter has turned out this way, you have done very beautifully; you have now roused me with your letters even as I was sleeping regarding this kind of duty. I shall use this against you more often in the future, and I would most especially ask that you do the same. As for your poems, they were with me for several days while I was in Padua, and I remember being greatly delighted by the charm of the little book and the most elegant composition of the verses. But unless I am mistaken, they were returned to Ramusio <note>Girolamo Ramusio, a physician and poet</note> before I departed from there. Concerning other things, whether they are in me or mine, consider it settled that you may use them as your own; otherwise, you would certainly be doing an injustice to both me and our friendship. Farewell.

### LETTERS

->Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Angelo [Poliziano], Greetings. Letter 28.<-

Since I have arranged my light verses—with which I played around regarding my love affairs as much as my age permitted—into five small books, I am sending you the first of them. I will send the rest once I have tested you in this one as a friend and not a flatterer. For they come to you under this law: that they be corrected and even "beaten," so that they may pay the penalty for their errors by both the fingernail and the mark of the spit <note>original: "vngue & obeliscis"; these were traditional marks used by ancient critics to denote deletions or corrections in a manuscript.</note>. Therefore, show yourself to them as a fair judge, not an unfair one—that is, be severe rather than indulgent. For what is greater unfairness than to deceive a friend who expects everything from you? I am not of such a delicate temperament that I loathe another's erasures; nor do I seem so beautiful to myself that I would either ignore or accuse my censor. Indeed, perhaps neither you nor anyone else would believe how much these works of mine fail to satisfy me, and how much I fear that even in those parts which please me more, I might be like that famous Suffenus <note>A character from the Roman poet Catullus, known for being a charming man who unfortunately thought he was a much better poet than he actually was.</note>. Truly, we are all deceived and do not see the knapsack that is on our back <note>A reference to Aesop’s fable where humans carry two bags: one in front for others' faults, and one behind for their own.</note>. Therefore, do not deny your effort in this honorable and noble matter to a man who is most friendly to you, especially one asking for it with such great zeal and from the bottom of his heart. If I were someone by whom a favor could be returned to you in a matter of this kind, I would not keep silent about that Greek saying concerning Lysippus and Apelles <note>original: "Lisippum appellis"; referring to the famous sculptor and painter of Alexander the Great who allegedly collaborated and critiqued one another's work</note>, and I would call upon the alternating works of Lysippus to be used in turn. Farewell.

->Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Angelo Poliziano, Greetings. Letter 29.<-

Since I was in Florence in previous years, I left four love elegies with you which, as happens, I had fashioned almost as a boy at that time for the sake of exercising my mind. They were somewhat tasteless, unlearned, and trivial, easily revealing the age and ignorance of their author. You, however, approved of them—not because the work deserved it, but out of your own kindness or indulgence. And for that very reason, to give proof that you approved, you asked for copies, certainly not unaware that such things are the sharpest incentives for the minds of youths toward virtue, so that, enticed by the desire for praise, they may soon strive to taste more deeply the glory they have sipped.
<margin>Despair crushes strength, but hope lifts the spirit.</margin>
For just as strength lies down and grows cold immediately in despair, no one doubts that it is lifted and set on fire by hope. But now the protection of my age is taken away; and those errors which were previously overlooked will now be turned into a fault against me, because I, now more mature in years, have neither purged them better nor deleted them. Therefore, whatever poems of mine are with you, if you love me, either send them back to me, or tear them up, or hand them over to the fire. All those poems, more carefully worked, and many others which have slipped from me in my leisure since I departed from there, will shortly be entrusted to your "file" <note>The "file" (lima) is a common humanist metaphor for the process of polishing and refining a literary work.</note>. In the meantime, let those which cannot live without the death of a friend be condemned by a capital vote. Furthermore, I would very much like you to send me your Epictetus, and what you have translated from Homer up to this day; likewise, what you composed concerning Giuliano de' Medici in our native tongue <note>Italian</note>, and whatever else you have composed in the Latin language. I ask this of you as urgently as possible: for I desire them as one who is most impatient. There is no reason for you to refuse because they perhaps have not yet been "brought to the navel" <note>original: "ad vmbilicum"; an idiom meaning to finish a book to the very end of the scroll</note>. For I announce and promise to you now that if this be your wish, everything will remain secret with me. Farewell.

->Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Marsilio Ficino, Greetings. Letter 30.<-

<margin>Hermes Trismegistus: what constitutes nobility of soul.</margin>
It has always been my judgment, most learned Marsilio, that one should labor in no matter more than this: that we should in no way degenerate through sloth or sluggishness from that nobility of soul by which (as Trismegistus <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom many mystical and philosophical works were attributed; a favorite source for Pico and Ficino.</note> witnesses) we are considered next after Jove.

<column-break/>

This has always been my chief concern: to acquire for myself, from wherever I could, the cultivation of the mind and the disciplines of the liberal arts. Although this plan of mine has been most constant since my childhood, your exhortations when I was with you in previous years greatly excited and inflamed me; and never more ardently than from that time until today have I devoted myself entirely to letters. For three years now, Marsilio, I have been occupied among the Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle.</note>, and I have omitted nothing within my power so that I might be admitted into the house of the Aristotelians as one not unworthy of their family. Although I have not achieved this in great abundance—in fact, I am scarcely in the entrance hall—I have nevertheless proceeded far enough that I would not hesitate to claim for myself the name of a "student," if not that of a "learned and erudite man" (which my age does not yet allow). But since it has also always been the opinion of you and of the most learned men that he who mixes the Academics <note>The followers of Plato.</note> with the Peripatetics will hold both sects more correctly and more richly, I thought I should take up this province: that now, according to the strength of my talent and with as much persistence and diligence as possible, I might compare Plato with Aristotle, and in turn, through alternating studies, Aristotle with Plato. But just as I previously needed you as a counselor, so now I need you as a helper. It will be a mark of your humanity and your goodwill toward me not to fail my purpose—and such an honest and noble one at that. I would consider this most fully accomplished by you if you would send me your book *On the Immortality of Souls*. With this as a sort of guide in the Platonic discipline, I am confident I shall make progress as I hope. For who would not promise himself the greatest things in that kind of learning from Ficino—in whom, if the opinion of the Pythagoreans were true, I would believe Plato had lived again? Only do not fail me. I would strive to obtain this from you with more words, except that the very principle of honor, which you value most highly, strives for this same thing from you. For if our Cicero, and Chilo the Wise, and Theophrastus the most serious philosopher, thought that one should turn somewhat from the path for the benefit of friends, would it not be a disgrace to have failed a most friendly man in such an honest petition? See to it, therefore, that what I have long pursued by your exhortation, I may finally attain by your help. For I have no one besides you who can help me in this matter, since—though many other things are beautiful and famous—care for Platonic matters has almost entirely faded away among the men of our age. Farewell.

->Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Hermolao [Barbaro], Greetings. Letter 31.<-

I write to you not because I have anything worthy of you to write, but only so that you may write back. Otherwise, I have no cause for writing, nor any subject matter. Indeed, I have always condemned the opinion of those who feel they must write to friends so that this might be paid as a sort of debt to friendship. For this whole business of writing and sending letters belongs to a friendship that is weak and somewhat chilly, which does not stand firmly enough supported by its own strength and seeks elsewhere for a way to stay standing. But what, I ask you, does a friendship need the support of letters for, once it has already struck roots deep within the very retreats of the soul? Therefore, Hermolao Barbaro, I shall give you my letters for this reason: to entice yours, which I desire most greatly. You, in return, lest mine be desired in vain, shall return yours as abundantly as possible. For just as it is the mark of a weak mind to use letters as "props" <note>original: "tibicines"; literally "flute-players," but used idiomatically to mean architectural supports or buttresses.</note> for friendship so it does not waver, so it is a mark of singular liberality and goodwill to show oneself easy toward friends and to grant a favor. Farewell; and [send] the *Music* of Ptolemy, if it is not inconvenient...

...provided it is not yours, hand it over to me to stay here for a few days. For what should I not boldly ask of you, to whom I have long since vowed and dedicated all my things?

### Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Hermolao [Barbaro]. Greetings. Letter 32.

**I** have never either pleased myself more or owed more abundantly than at this time, when a single letter of mine has called forth from you such sweet, such learned letters, so very like yourself. If the fact that you were away from Padua while I was there, and that I missed your company for two years, was the reason why you wrote these things to me, then I cannot help but find that situation—whatever it was—delightful now. So abundantly has this one letter of yours not only fulfilled my every wish but even surpassed it. For I shall remain silent regarding the elegance, charm, and erudition of the letter, the reading of which demands a reciprocal debt from the soul. How much do you think I value the fact that you give yourself to me as a friend so lovingly, so kindly, and so sincerely? I would not dare to wish for anything greater than that you so liberally promise your effort in honoring me in every way. Indeed, I would not blush to confess openly that this kind of service is not merely to be accepted but even sought after by me. For not even the Stoics themselves, nor our Arabs <note>Pico often refers to "our Arabs," meaning the great Islamic philosophers like Avicenna and Averroes whose works were central to his syncretic philosophy.</note>, disapprove of this; nor among those things which the Greeks call
<margin>freedom from passion [and] passions <note>original: "απαθια παθη" (apatheia, pathe). Apatheia was the Stoic ideal of being undisturbed by emotions.</note></margin>
can any affection be more praiseworthy or more honorable than this one—provided it is among those called the desire for a good name and glory. Truly, this can be provided to me by no one more richly than by you, in whom all the virtues, as if individually, compete to claim the prize for themselves. And I certainly have no one to whom I would more willingly be indebted. Therefore, this promise of yours is as pleasing and desirable to me as it is honorable; I rejoice in it most of all because it offers proof of your extraordinary love and most affectionate goodwill toward me. At last, I have what I have long desired; now I truly triumph. I have, I say, Hermolao Barbaro—the delight of the Latin tongue and the distinguished storehouse of all the good arts—not merely well-disposed toward me, but as a most intimate friend. You, likewise, have Giovanni Pico of Mirandola so devoted to you, so studious of your interests, that no one could be more devoted or more studious. In mutual duties toward you—since he can provide nothing grand or worthy of Hermolao—he will indeed be unequal; but if you look at his spirit, he will certainly be either your equal or your superior. Farewell.

### Giovanni Pico of Mirandola etc. to the same. Letter 33.

<margin>Plato and Aristotle said the soul is the seat of friendship.</margin>
**N**othing was sweeter to me while you were here with us than your company; likewise, nothing was more useful. Such is the sweetness of your character and such is your learning. But see how sweet and pleasing you were to me while I enjoyed your presence, since now, while you are absent, nothing is sweeter to me than the memory of you. But surely, if the seat of friendship is the soul, and we are primarily our souls—as Plato and Aristotle write—there is no reason why any distance of place or long interval of time should be able to create a separation between us. I was thinking just now whether there might be some
<margin>Love is the reason why the same thing both pleases and displeases.</margin>
other way I could achieve being with you, and nothing else came to mind but that my late-night work on the seven-fold explanation of the six days of Genesis <note>This refers to Pico's famous work, the *Heptaplus*, published in 1489.</note> should come to you. For if we give birth to books as if they were children, and the greatest part of a father is in his son, I too shall come to you in that which I have begotten. Receive, therefore, my little son coming to you, cheerfully and willingly as you were accustomed to receive me. It will please you, I know, because you love me. I know also it will displease you for the same reason: because you love me. For such

<column-break/>

is the nature of devotion, to look closely into the errors of those we love so that we may correct them, and having looked into them, to indulge them lightly so that we do not cause distress.

### Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to F. B. C. Th. Letter 34.

**G**reetings, most beloved father. Here is the *Apollonius* <note>Likely the *Life of Apollonius of Tyana* by Philostratus, a text popular among Renaissance Neoplatonists.</note> for you, which, even if I did not owe it to your virtue and your kindness toward me, I would certainly owe to those letters in which you demand it with such great love and humanity. For it is a mark of the highest love to call someone to that place where you have already arrived—namely, to the purging of the soul, which is true happiness. And it is the highest humanity to exhort me as an equal, though you could dictate the law to me as a son. But I wish it may happen eventually that in some retreat we might
<margin>O most wise man! O truly admirable Mirandula! <note>The writer of the margin note is making a pun on Pico's name, "Mirandula," and the Latin word "mirandus," meaning wonderful or admirable.</note></margin>
one day philosophize piously together. You will see that in my eyes nothing is more important than joining piety with wisdom. You will see that I am most convinced that there is no wisdom which blurs the image of the eternal wisdom within us and makes us like the foolish beasts. I have as my witness my companion angel <note>Pico is referring to the concept of a guardian angel or "genius" who guides the intellect and soul.</note>, by whose instruction I daily become stronger in purging my soul. All this handling of disciplines, and whatever letters can promise us, merely colors the skin and makes us appear more beautiful, as if with a painted face. But a healthy, firm, and robust
<margin>Integrity of mind is to be hoped for from God alone.</margin>
mind we cannot hope for from anywhere else but from integrity of life, from morals, and finally from divine religion. Therefore, you compel one who is already willing (so to speak) to be even more willing. But help me also with your sacred prayers so that I may be able to achieve what I myself desired and what you so greatly wish me to want. Farewell, most loving father, whom I love uniquely and hold most dear. Florence, January 13, 1490. I await all your news. My friend Poliziano <note>Angelo Poliziano, the famous poet and scholar who was Pico's closest friend.</note>, the delight of all literature, sends his greetings to you.

### Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Hermolao Barbaro. Greetings. Letter 35.

**I** remember that when I was deliberating which of the universities of Italy I should choose as my seat for the study of philosophy, although many things called me to Padua, I sought that place more willingly so that my love for you—which I had long nourished in my soul—might become clear to you through mutual company. I was in Padua for two years; yet, who would believe it? I neither saw Hermolao nor knew him except by reputation, as I had long before. Thus it often happens that while we despise an offered opportunity through a certain tiresome procrastination, it slips from our hands as if it were slippery. I have repented and still repent of this thing vehemently, and all the more because your learning in all matters, which I had previously known only by rumor, I have now recognized with these eyes and these ears: while I heard the Roman Themistius <note>Themistius was a 4th-century philosopher whose paraphrases of Aristotle were translated and championed by Hermolao Barbaro.</note> discoursing through your mouth concerning the nature of the soul, the first beginnings of things, and the science of reasoning. Good God, how much learning! What richness of expression! What
<margin>Hermolao honors Themistius by his translation.</margin>
purity! What cleanliness of speech! O most distinguished man! O express image of antiquity! It was my frequent wish that the writings of Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro, a Roman polymath whose massive works on "divine and human things" were mostly lost to history.</note> on divine and human things might one day live again, so that we might have someone from whom we could learn physical reasons in Latin. Truly, you, reflecting both him and all the most approved authors, have shown yourself to us such that nothing else remains for us to desire, except that by interpreting other Greek works you might both win more abundant praise for yourself and deserve even better of natural history and of all studious men. All these things, most learned Hermolao, look toward nothing else but that you understand that I am most friendly to you...

<meta>This page continues the correspondence of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, shifting from his dialogue with Hermolao Barbaro to a letter addressed to Andrea Corneo. The transition maintains the theme of the intellectual life, but here Pico defends his choice of private study over the active political life of a courtier.</meta>

### OF THE LETTERS

...bind you: your virtues so inflame me to love and respect you that I yield to no one, even among your own kin, in my affection. Let this letter be a covenant of friendship between us: so that we may continually engage in a most honorable contest of mutual love.

->Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Andrea Corneo of Urbino. Greetings. Letter 36.<-

<margin>Plautus. He judges and declares that the studies of philosophy, to which he has long been devoted, must never be abandoned.</margin>
**I** received your most recent letter, which you sent to me on the Ides of October. The one you write that you sent earlier never arrived; I would have replied at once had I received it, for I am tireless in writing and, whether by study or by nature, I am least of all a slacker in this duty. However, there was no reason why our friendship could be shaken by even a long silence; I am a perpetual friend, not a temporary one. A friendship is not firm enough if it requires these exchanges of letters like <term>props<note>original: "tibicines." In Roman architecture and theater (specifically in the plays of Plautus), these were literal supports or pipes used to hold up a sagging structure.</note></term> which (to use the word of Plautus) support a wavering and somewhat weak thing. But to come to what you write: you urge me toward an active and civic life, saying that I have philosophized in vain and almost in shame and disgrace for so long, unless I finally "sweat in the arena" of acting upon and handling affairs. And indeed, my dear Andrea, I would have wasted the "oil and toil" of my studies if I were now so minded that I could agree and assent to you on this point. This is that deadly and monstrous persuasion which has invaded the minds of men: either that the studies of philosophy are not to be touched by leading men, or that they should be tasted only with the "tips of the lips" for a display of wit rather than the cultivation of the soul, or perhaps for leisure. They hold that decree of Neoptolemus <note>A character from a lost play by Ennius; he famously said one should philosophize, but only a little, because "too much is displeasing."</note> as an absolute: either one should not philosophize at all, or only briefly. Now those things are accepted as trifles and mere fables. The sayings of the wise are that firm and solid happiness lies in the goods of the soul; that these external things of the body or of fortune pertain little or nothing to us.

<margin>Note.</margin>
But you will say, "I want you to embrace Martha in such a way that you do not, in the meantime, desert Mary." <note>A biblical allegory common in the Renaissance: Martha represents the active life of work and civic duty, while her sister Mary represents the contemplative life of prayer and study.</note> On this part I do not fight you, nor do I condemn or accuse those who do so. But it is a far cry from saying that passing from the contemplative life to the civic life is not an error, to saying that *not* passing is a disgrace or should be judged under the mark of fault or crime. Shall it therefore be turned into a vice, if someone should perpetually affect and pursue virtue itself for the sake of virtue, seeking nothing outside of it? Because, in scrutinizing the divine mysteries and the designs of nature, he enjoys this leisure as a despiser and neglecter of other things—since those mysteries can sufficiently fulfill the prayers of their followers. Shall it then be ungentlemanly, or not at all the act of a prince, to pursue the study of wisdom without seeking a reward? Who could bear or listen to this with an even mind? Certainly, he has never truly philosophized who philosophized so that he might one day be able—or willing—to stop philosophizing. Such a man has practiced trade, not philosophy. You write that the time is approaching for me to give myself over to one of the great princes of Italy.

<margin>Horace. What the true opinion of those philosophizing should be.</margin>
You do not yet know the opinion that those who philosophize have of themselves: who, according to Horace, think themselves "kings of kings." <note>Horace, *Epistles* 1.1.106–107. The Stoic paradox was that the wise man is the only true king, even if he is a beggar.</note> They do not know how to endure the whims of others or to serve; they dwell within themselves and, content with the tranquility of their own minds, they are sufficient unto themselves. They seek nothing outside themselves; things that are in honor among the common people are dishonorable among them, and they altogether neglect and despise whatever human lust thirsts for or ambition sighs after. This must be done without doubt by all, but especially by those upon whom fortune has so smiled that they can live not only comfortably and conveniently, but even splendidly. Those great fortunes indeed elevate and show off a man. But often, like a fierce and bucking horse, they throw the rider 

<column-break/>

<margin>The golden, best mediocrity [the middle way].</margin>
off. Certainly, they always trouble and vex rather than carry him. That "golden mediocrity" <note>original: "aurea mediocritas," Horace's famous "golden mean"—the ideal middle ground between luxury and poverty, or power and obscurity.</note> is to be desired, which carries us like a hand, more steadily, and, being patient of command, truly serves us and does not dominate us. Persisting in this opinion, I prefer my little cell, my studies, the delights of my books, and my peace of mind to royal courts, public business, your "bird-catching" <note>likely referring to the pursuit of courtly favors or "hunting" for status</note>, and the favors of the curia. Nor do I expect those fruits of my literary leisure to be that I should be tossed and fluctuate in the heat and tumult of public affairs. Rather, it is so that I may finally give birth to the children I am laboring over, and—may it be happy and auspicious—put something out into the public: if not learning, at least talent and diligence that "smells of the lamp." And do not believe that anything of our industry and labor has been relaxed:

<margin>The study of languages.</margin>
know that, after much work devoted to constant and tireless late-night studies, I have learned the Hebrew and Chaldean <note>Aramaic</note> languages; and I have now also applied my hands to overcoming the difficulties of Arabic. These I have always judged, and now judge, to be the pursuits of a leading man. But though I have spoken these things truly and even severely, I nonetheless so cherish and venerate those most excellent princes—and especially the magnanimous Ludovico [Sforza], Duke of Bari—that I value no one among the princes of Italy more. I understand that I owe him much for many reasons; and there is nothing so heavy, nothing so arduous, that (if the opportunity were given to me) I would not do for the sake of deserving his favor. But such is their greatness and my slightness: just as I cannot help but need them, so they can in no way need either my work or my arrival there.

I shall depart for Rome very soon to spend the winter there, unless either a sudden accident or a new falling fortune draws me elsewhere. From there, perhaps, you will hear what your Pico has profited by contemplating in his "shadowy and sedentary" life; or what finally (I shall say it, however arrogantly)—what, I say, he needs of the work of others in literary matters, since you promise him a wealth of learned men when he arrives there.

<margin>Plautus. The wit of Terence should be noted.</margin>
In Rome, and wherever on earth I may be, those princes will have someone to command: someone they may turn at their will like a "portable millstone" <note>original: "trufatilem... molam." A reference to a slave's work in a mill; Pico uses this ironically to describe being a "tool" or "gadabout" for the powerful.</note> as Plautus says. As for what you write about "marriage matters" <note>original: "re vxoria"</note>: I do not think it was said rashly or for no reason. But I am "given" [to my studies]; I am no Oedipus <note>The solver of riddles. Pico means he cannot solve the secret or riddle you are hinting at.</note>, nor if I were would I wish to be. Whatever that is: if it seems right, explain it more broadly; if not, let it be <term>Harpocrates<note>The Greek/Egyptian god of silence and secrets.</note></term>. I take counsel from my "arms" as things present themselves. There is no reason for you to long for my Tuscan rhythms [Italian poems]. Long ago we sent a dismissal to those "amorous playthings," having turned our minds to other things. But I also want you to be warned of this regarding your "Laura": if you were going to publish it, suppress it for a few more days. For perhaps very soon our people will read things about love (see what I am saying!) which they have not yet read. And you will be able to note many things which will be very useful to your work. Regarding Alibrana, I might say that he has poorly returned the favor to that well-deserving master. Nor is there any reason why he should cast or derive his flight upon anyone else but himself, since he owes to my household—which he cannot deny—almost no less than he owes to me. But this is not the first time, as you know, that he has either broken faith or mocked his master.

<margin>To make an edict.</margin>
I know what that man said against me and about me after he fled. But the "elephant does not care for the gnat." And I am willing to forgive you whatever that frivolous man has sinned before now; but let him not abuse my patience in the future, lest I be forced to eventually show myself to him in the same manner he has shown himself to me in his conduct.

<margin>Note.</margin>
As for your excusing that friend of yours whose love affair turned out badly before our Florianus, you did so out of duty. He indeed has means from history, from the poets, and even from philosophy itself, by which he may clear himself of the mark of crime; he has means from which...
