<header>BOOK ONE</header>

...he protects himself by the precedents of great men, like David and especially Solomon; not to mention Aristotle, who, while he often pined for certain mistresses, remembered nothing of his own moral precepts when he performed sacred rites for the woman he loved as if she were Eleusinian Ceres <note>Aristotle was famously accused of offering divine honors to his mistress Herpyllis or the concubine Pythias, treating her like the goddess of the harvest, Ceres.</note>. But your friend does not merely embrace or love these defenses and bulwarks of his misdeed; rather, he hates, rejects, and refuses them. He laments his loss rather than making excuses for his fault; he grieves that he has sinned, he does not defend it. And to me, he seems all the more deserving of excuse for the very reason that he does not excuse himself. Nothing is weaker than man; nothing is more powerful than love. Even the invincible and unshaken mind of Jerome <note>Saint Jerome, the 4th-century scholar, famously wrote about being tempted by visions of dancing girls even while living as an ascetic in the desert.</note>, while it clung entirely to heaven, was yet among the choruses of girls. What plague could infest or conquer him whom love will not tame? If love could do this in the wilderness, with limbs bruised upon the ground and during the fasts of the weeks, what can it not do amidst feathers, shade, and every abundance of delights? Add to this that he has now fallen for the first time, being otherwise unaccustomed to and ignorant of such a ruin. One may complain of Neptune who has suffered shipwreck only once. If he should stumble against the same stone a second time, let no one stretch out a hand; let no one take pity. Now, he cannot rightly be denied an excuse, for he so repents of the deed that he does not even judge himself worthy of the favor of an excuse. But enough of this, since your friend wishes the memory of such a deed not only to be recorded in some way in writing, but desires it to be entirely blotted out by his subsequent life. Farewell. Christopher was not present when I received yours; you will commend me in no ordinary way to your lord and to the entire Borromeo family, whom I have always loved and now love very much. At Perugia, October 15, 1486.

### Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to his nephew Giovanni Francesco. Greetings. Letter 37.

<margin>What is fitting and necessary for husbands to do with their wives. Paul.</margin>
Your letter was most welcome to me, not only because I had heard nothing from you for a long time, but also because it indicated things that delighted me wonderfully. Since these same things are pleasing to you, I do not doubt they are most pleasing to God; you too should have no doubt that if you continue on the path you have begun, your reward will be plentiful in heaven. I have not yet sufficiently explored whether I must go to Rome or not. As far as I can gather by conjecture, I believe it is more likely that I must go there; you know the reason. As soon as I am certain of this, I will let you know, lest if you should happen to come here (which I would otherwise greatly desire), you might not find me, or you might have to return to your homeland just as I am departing. In the meantime, you can remain at home, unless you feel otherwise. But remember this also: you have a wife, to whom you owe your body no less than you owe your soul to God. Her desire must be satisfied in some part; you must consider what she either desires or could desire based on her physical condition and age, and what she might not ask for out of modesty and virtue. For why should I be ashamed to write these things which the Apostle Paul also writes? <note>Referring to 1 Corinthians 7:3-4, where Paul discusses mutual conjugal rights.</note> There is almost no matter in which I suspect you could err more. Indeed, our men are very much deceived who think their wives are bound and devoted to them, but that they owe nothing to their wives, and that they can decide whatever they please concerning themselves according to their own will. In short, you cannot be entirely your own, you who once wished to belong to a wife by submitting yourself to the laws of marriage. Nevertheless, you can belong entirely to God, whom you will also win over for yourself when, in order to obey His law, you obey yourself less even in those things that are of God. But I have spoken of these things with you in person at other times. As soon as the air turns to spring—that is, during the first days of Lent—when I have extricated myself from these bundles of Greek books, I shall immediately

<column-break/>

come to Ferrara. In the meantime, devote yourself to sacred letters, especially the reading of the Gospels, which may repeatedly bring the soul back to God. For both the world with its allurements and the devil with his deceits do not cease day and night to lead the soul away from Him. Farewell, half of my soul, and pray to God for me. As soon as I have decided anything regarding my journey toward Rome, I will inform you. Florence, November 27, 1492.

### Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to his friend Iacopo Antiquario. Greetings. Letter 38.

Among the pleasures I took most from the company of Poliziano <note>Angelo Poliziano, the famous humanist scholar and poet.</note> when I was in Florence—a man who is, in my opinion, the most literate of all in our age—was no small pleasure that he used to give me your letters to read as soon as he received them, those letters of yours that were always weighty in substance and elegant in style. I was vehemently delighted by them, both by a certain singular wisdom in handling great affairs and business, and by the refinement and sobriety of your speech. Furthermore, because you made honorable mention of us in some of them, your letters not only pleased me, but I also pleased myself in them. To be sure, my conscience yielded to the testimony of such a great man; not entirely concealing what it felt, it was deceived almost willingly and without much struggle, as if betraying itself. Thus I was indebted to you on a double account: for your virtue, and for the service—or rather, the benefit—so often bestowed upon us. I thought more than once of thanking you by letter, lest I should seem ungrateful or perhaps uncouth toward you. However, since you and our Poliziano were carrying on a most beautiful exchange of letters between you, I did not want an intrusive Magpie <note>original: "Pica." A clever pun on his name, "Picus." He compares himself to a chattering magpie interrupting the song of swans.</note> to make a noise against the Muses, or like an ill-sounding goose, <margin>Note the simile.</margin> to disturb the swans singing to one another. Besides, I knew that my mind was open to you through our friend Poliziano; and being conscious of my own "infancy" <note>Here used in the classical sense of "speechlessness" or lack of eloquence.</note>, I used him as a most eloquent interpreter. Now your own letters have been sent to me by him, which you recently gave to Ricius, an ingenious youth. In them, you attribute so much to me that I would not dare to hope for it, let alone believe I deserve it. The magnitude of your kindness has broken my silence, which until now I know not whether to call boorish, but certainly not proud. I could not help but give you immortal thanks, not because you overwhelm me with immoderate praise which I do not recognize in myself, but because you love me so much that your judgment—otherwise constant and robust—has nevertheless wavered so much under the weight of love for us. I owe you, therefore, more than I can pay or you can easily believe; nor is anything so arduous or difficult that I would not do it for your dignity as if for my own salvation. You who possessed me through Poliziano until now, will now, without the reality having changed at all, simply unfold the name of Pico which was underneath, now for your own purposes. Farewell. From the Ferraran countryside, June 28, 1494.

### To the excellent and most learned man Master Iacopo Antiquario, as to a father. Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to Andrea Corneo. Greetings. Letter 39.

My wishes have been plainly and abundantly satisfied, my dearest Andrea. For I have learned from your letters to our most dear Christopher that you are living with both convenience and dignity. For this is, and always has been, my greatest wish for you: that you be well and happy; I have nothing greater to say in view of your merits. I never doubted that this would happen. And this one thing has always been certain to me, as long as your tongue survived...

<meta>This page continues the correspondence of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola. The text begins mid-sentence, concluding a letter (likely Letter 39) before moving into several new letters (40–43) addressed to various scholars and patrons in his circle.</meta>

...[wherever] you might be, you would be held in high esteem. I know (and let this be said without flattery) the nobility of your mind, which will endure nothing base or common. I know your virtues, your learning, your character, and your prudence—all of which will easily lead you wherever you aim. I only fear for your health, which, as you used to tell me, has been oppressed and weakened by so many illnesses from your early youth until this very day. Yet it is weakened rather than broken; indeed, your spirit has so moved your physical nature that it refuses to be conquered, but rather fights back vigorously against the blows of fortune with a certain perpetual inner strength. Cherish these qualities, for where life fails, nothing remains. As for the fact that you speak of me so honorably to everyone, you do so out of your own kindness and long-standing goodwill toward me, and for that, I owe you as much as any man could possibly owe another. 

But I fear you are unraveling your own web while you call into public view my follies and the trifles that flowed from me in my more tender years. For they are all quite foolish and unlearned—or even if one judges them most kindly, they certainly are not the sort of things that can sustain the opinion those men have perhaps conceived of me through your speech. Whatever they are, I decided they must be sent so that I might satisfy you even at the expense of my entire reputation. I would ask you, however, to regard all these as lighter works; for if you eventually desire my serious works, we have weightier things in hand which have not yet been finished <note>original: "ad umbilicum nondum ducta sunt" — literally "not yet led to the navel," an ancient idiom for finishing a book scroll</note>. Even these things we have sent required more polish and the file <note>original: "limam" — the 'file' refers to the process of refining or editing literary work</note>. But both the times and my studies in philosophy, which I watch over most carefully, have diverted me from the work. Nevertheless, we shall return to the Muses someday; and if we forge anything worthy of your ears, we will ensure it is brought to you immediately. Farewell.

### Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to R.C.C.S. Letter XL.

<margin>Note.</margin> **O**ur Matthew, a most dutiful man, gave me your warmest greetings and very clearly explained with what love and goodwill you follow me, promising moreover in your name your zeal and effort if I should ever happen to need them. I wish, most kind father, that I were equal to such duty. I have always both desired and hoped to be taken into your protection and numbered among your own. But to have you meet me of your own accord, approaching me so kindly with such friendly and liberal promises, and calling me, as it were, to your friendship (if I may say so—but through you I may), has surpassed my every hope and prayer. For what or how much is it to be invited by one by whom it would have been enough not to be excluded? Although you have done something worthy of yourself, if not of me—for I might not have been admitted based on my merits, yet I could not have failed to be called based on your kindness. 

Therefore, how much I rejoice for myself or how much I owe you, I cannot explain, as I cannot even conceive it. Certainly, I owe you all the more for these things because you owe them to me in no way at all. Nor are those things too grand or too numerous which both Matthew and my other friends have reported; they value me out of affection rather than judgment. But whatever or however great I may be—to say nothing of the rest—everyone honors and admires your virtues, through which one may see in you both what surpasses antiquity and what cannot be surpassed by posterity. I would say this deservedly, since nothing placed in honor, prudence, or learning is lacking in you; one thing alone ought to be desired by all: that through you, one day, according to Plato's prayer, supreme power might be joined with supreme wisdom <note>A reference to Plato's *Republic*, where he argues that human troubles will not cease until philosophers become kings or kings become philosophers</note>. But these things come from God. From you, meanwhile, I ask 

<column-break/>

and request this: not for the sake of returning a favor—for there is no room for that, given either your greatness or my insignificance—but that an occasion might present itself for testifying my mind toward you, and my loyalty and respect. You will find Giovanni Pico to be a man devoted and dedicated to you beyond all expectation, of whom you cannot promise yourself more; but you can make use of all things in him, such as they are, which you yourself will enhance with your own splendor when you use them. Things which cannot be great while they are mine will become great when they begin to be yours. Farewell.

### Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to his friend Alessandro Cortesi. Letter XLI.

**Y**our letter was most welcome to me, which you sent recently—not, as you think, as a stranger to a stranger, but as a friend and indeed an old friend to a friend, as a known man to one known. For you already knew me, as you write, and thought me worthy of your love. Likewise, I have often heard of your learning and virtue from many people, and especially from our friend Poliziano <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), the famous Renaissance humanist and poet who was a close associate of Pico</note>; and who would not trust his judgment? He has created faith in your integrity in me, just as he can confirm for you my goodwill toward you which began long ago. Although that goodwill was already very great, know that your letter added such heaps to it as few could even conceive in their minds. For what is sweeter than that letter? What more learned? How scholarly it is, how lovable! And when you subscribe so generously to our Pucci <note>likely Francesco Pucci, a Florentine intellectual</note>, who speaks of me more kindly than truly, certainly nothing more pleasing could come to me from you, nor anything more honorable than your opinion of me. For all these things, I give you the greatest possible thanks; and I confess that whatever I have, or whatever is in me, I owe to my friend Alessandro. I am sending you the letter you requested, our letter to Lorenzo de' Medici.

### Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to Domenico Benivieni. Letter XLII.

**G**reetings, my Domenico, chosen in the strength of the Lord. Your letter was welcome to me, but it was more welcome to learn both in person from your brother while he was here and through letters from our friend Pietro that you are in a stronger physical condition and have a better stomach. Take care of your health—if you care for us all, if you care for letters. I have always been and am concerned about it, not only because I love you (for I love you vehemently), but because I love learning, which I believe and certainly know is endangered along with you. If your brother has told you anything of our goodwill toward you, have the fullest faith in it; if he said anything regarding my praises, believe him as little as he loves me much <note>A classic trope of modesty: Pico suggests his friend's praise is biased by affection</note>. There is no reason for you to admire our little commentary; when we wished to be at leisure and do nothing at all, we did that, relaxing the mind rather than straining it. It is entirely a prelude to the commentaries we are contemplating on Plato's *Symposium* <note>The *Symposium* is Plato's famous dialogue on the nature of love; Pico wrote a significant commentary on a poem about love by Girolamo Benivieni based on these Platonic ideas</note>. <margin>Commentaries on Plato's *Symposium*</margin> In them, there will be something that you at least will love and praise, you who love and praise everything of ours. Regarding the council and the questions, as I think your brother has already reported why I wrote that I was working for you—what you ask of me I will most gladly do when I understand that you have been restored to your initial and desired health from that bodily weakness you have suffered until now. I pray and hope for this for you with the same spirit with which you pray and hope for the health of my soul for me. Farewell from Fratta. November 10, 1486.

### Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to Andrea Corneo. Letter XLIII.

**E**ven if I have sent letters to you either rarely or never, I have nevertheless thought of you and your affairs either often or always. But I do not wish to sell you hope, nor will I write to you about what I am doing for your benefit until I can write about what I have accomplished. But if never, on account of your or my misfortune...

# BOOK ONE

<meta>nio</meta>
<margin>Interpretation of the Hymns.</margin>
...[desti]ny <note>original: "nio," likely the end of a word like "destino"</note> should anything bad happen, believe me, I have desired nothing more than to have labored in your affairs—and not in vain. But perhaps fortune will be kinder to you than you yourself hope, or than she is accustomed to be. Regarding our poems, there is no reason for your "laurels" to wait, for they have been brought back to the anvil <note>original: "incudem" — a common metaphor in humanist writing for revising and refining a literary work</note> to be more precisely shaped; they do not dare go out in public with the face they currently wear. However, a pressing reason delays their correction: a new work I have in hand at the urging of Lorenzo de' Medici <note>The de facto ruler of Florence and a major patron of Pico</note>. In this work, I am not only illuminating the Davidic hymns <note>The Psalms</note> with a longer interpretation, but because the versions the Church sings were translated by the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note>, and the Hebrews prove that translation to be unfaithful in more than six hundred places, I am relying on the property of Hebrew and Chaldean <note>term: Chaldean — In the Renaissance, this usually referred to Aramaic</note> literature. I assert and defend them from all Jewish slander for the sake of the integrity of the meaning. There is nothing else to write, except that you should recommend me to Hermolao <note>Hermolao Barbaro, a Venetian scholar</note> with more than ordinary warmth whenever you see him. Likewise, make sure that the learned and serious man Jacopo Volaterrano understands he is greatly loved by me; if I can obtain the letters of Symmachus from him for a few days—only until they are transcribed—he will bind me to him by a perpetual favor. Farewell.
1489.

->Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Battista Guarino,<-
->his teacher. Greetings. XLIIII.<-

Why do you knit your brow? Is it because, contrary to what you instructed, and therefore perhaps wrongly, I have addressed you as "Teacher"? If you are not a teacher by right, then I do not stand by your instructions. If you are a teacher, I rightly call you "Teacher." But why do you refuse a student whom you praise so highly? These things are in conflict, unless perhaps one is a matter of love and the other of judgment; perhaps you praise him out of benevolence, while you fear his errors out of conscience—lest, naturally, those things which you can perhaps acknowledge as a praiser, you cannot acknowledge as a teacher, out of shame. But I beg you, receive me into the partnership of your discipline on this condition: that I may admit you into a partnership of our little glory, if there shall be any. I would endure the lashes alone. But why do I delay with cold jokes the ardor of my joy, which I conceived from your letters and from your so grave and honorable praise? Now at last, life smiles on me. Now my *Heptaplus* <note>Pico's famous work, a "seven-fold" explanation of the creation story in Genesis</note> is pleasing to me, since under your proclamation—as if under the shield of Pallas <note>Athena’s Aegis, representing divine protection and wisdom</note>—it now shows itself invulnerable to rivals. You urge me toward other writings of this kind, which you would do in vain were it not that you have already signed your name to my work and kindled sparks of good hope, making me far bolder in writing than I was before. Indeed, I trust so much in your judgment that the burden I have undertaken—of explaining the entire Old Testament, for which I am utterly unequal—I shall now bear far more strongly than usual. Regarding the books, perhaps I could satisfy you better if I had an index of those books which are with you, since many might suit your purpose which you might not otherwise need. Your aforementioned virtue has made you most highly commended to Lorenzo de' Medici. Never is there mention of the learned men of this age without "Guarino" being frequently on his lips, especially when our friend Poliziano <note>Angelo Poliziano, the renowned humanist poet and scholar</note> joins in (and he always joins in), who attributes as much to you as to no one else. Farewell, best and most learned of our friends; and bid greetings in my name to our shared delight among the painters as much as you can.

->Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Antonio Picimanno.<-
->Greetings. XLV.<-

<column-break/>

Nothing in my whole life has been more pleasant to me than the letters I recently received from you, full of love, duty, and kindness. As I hope to be happy, I do not deceive you—unless perhaps that day was more pleasant when you and Grimani <note>Domenico Grimani, a cardinal and famous collector of manuscripts</note> (I know not whether he is more yours or mine) met me as friends and greeted me so honorably. For although you took on personas other than who you were—as if presenting yourselves to me through some charming fiction of names—nevertheless, your sweetest wit, your singular learning, your amiable gravity, your liberal modesty, your noble face, and your most charming speech represented the true Picimanno and Grimani to me. Therefore, even if I could be deceived by the names themselves, I could not be defrauded of the pleasure which is owed to me from you. You were able to disguise your names, but you could not disguise your virtue, which betrays itself by its own brilliance and knows not how to remain hidden. That grave discussion of physical matters, those sharp and intricate arguments, those most refined judgments—whom else could they announce to me but yourselves? I congratulated myself silently when I heard you, thinking of our age, which had produced not just one Grimani and one Picimanno as I thought, but had brought forth two Grimanis and two Picimannos in its fertility. But when our friend Poliziano indicated who you actually were, I began to congratulate my own judgment rather than just my age; for I seemed to have recognized in you everything that I had learned from the most consistent testimony of all to be in those men—that is, in yourselves. But see how these praises of you carry me away and lead me from your letter; although the letter itself calls me to the same place even against my will. But I shall restrain myself, lest I seem to wish to satisfy you with mutual praise in return for the many praises you heaped upon me. Whether those came from an inclination of the soul or from judgment, I know not whether they bring me greater honor or pleasure. I owe much, my dear Picimanno, to that spirit of yours toward me. But I ask that you also make trial of my goodwill toward you whenever the opportunity arises. You will find a man so loving of your virtue and so studious of you that I shall not yield the first place in loving you even to your friend Grimani. Farewell. July 9, 1489.

make honorable mention; but I would not assert they are entirely the same as those read in the Latin codices, unless I had recently read the Greek copy, of which I have no supply here. To come to those things you desire regarding the letters of the Chaldeans <note>original: "chaldæorum" — In this period, this refers to the Aramaic language</note> and Hebrews, I have often questioned Mithridates <note>Flavius Mithridates, a Jewish convert and scholar who was Pico’s primary teacher of Oriental languages</note> and many Hebrews about what is read in Jerome’s <note>Saint Jerome, the 4th-century translator of the Bible into Latin</note> "Helmeted Prologue." There, he writes that the characters of the Samaritans and Hebrews were once the same, but that Ezra <note>The biblical scribe credited with restoring the law after the Babylonian exile</note>, after the restoration of the temple under Zerubbabel, invented other letters which are now in use. They all declare themselves ignorant of this change and (what is more) they take it for granted that both Moses and all the ancient patriarchs used the same Hebrew scriptural marks <note>original: "apicibus" — literally the 'horns' or tips of the letters</note> that we use now. To this opinion, as it now occurs to me, the science of the Kabbalah <note>Jewish mystical tradition</note> gives the greatest credit; its writers, who were in the synod with Ezra himself, believe and prove that Moses concealed divine mysteries under those very letter characters and figures in which we now have the law described. This would be in no way possible if Moses had used characters other than those we use now. However, I have one thing by which I might defend Jerome’s statement: I recently read it in the commentaries on the book that the ancient father Abraham published concerning Creation <note>The *Sefer Yetzirah* or "Book of Formation," an early Kabbalistic text</note>. While the authors are interpreting those thirty-two gates <note>The 32 paths of wisdom in the *Sefer Yetzirah*</note> which he mentions, they say that number consists of the ten numerations <note>The Sefirot, or divine emanations</note> and the twenty-two letters. Moreover, the remaining letters which are Mem, Sade, Pe, Kaph, and Nun—which are called "double" <note>These five Hebrew letters have different shapes when they appear at the end of a word</note>—their characters were added by the "watchmen" or overseers. Perhaps Jerome understood this; his testimony ought to be held in high regard by everyone in all matters, and it is certainly held most sacred by me. The 
<margin>Behold the unkindness of the Jews.</margin>
Chaldean alphabet you seek, you would not have obtained even from Mithridates; through him it is permitted that you obtain nothing from me, from whom you could obtain everything. For he would by no means teach me the Chaldean language unless I first swore an oath, and indeed in solemn words, not to hand it over to anyone. Our Girolamo Benivieni <note>A Florentine poet and close friend of Pico</note> can testify to this; when he happened to be present while he was teaching me, the raging Mithridates drove the man out. But so that you have not written in vain, you may have the Arabic alphabet as a substitute for the Chaldean, which is sent to you noted by my own hand. There is nothing else for me to write except that, whoever you are, it is impossible for you not to be most loving toward me, if I understand that you are most loving toward the noble arts. Farewell from Fratta. November 10, 1486.

<margin>To be ill-spoken of by the wicked is the greatest happiness for an upright man.</margin>
**Y**ou are happy, my son, when God grants you not only that you live well, but that while living well, you are spoken ill of by the wicked—most especially because you live well. For it is equal praise to be praised by the praiseworthy and to be disapproved of by the wicked. But I do not call you happy because this slander is glorious for you, but because the Lord Jesus, who is the Truth itself, affirms our future reward will be abundant in heaven when men speak evil against us and say all kinds of evil against us falsely for his sake. This, if you did not know, is an Apostolic dignity: to be considered worthy to be de-

<column-break/>

<margin>The example of living well through the Apostles.</margin>
-famed by the ungodly for the name of the Gospel. Thus we read in Luke <note>Acts of the Apostles 5:41</note> that the apostles rejoiced in the sight of the council because they were deemed worthy to suffer shame for the name of Jesus. Let us therefore rejoice also, if we are worthy of such great glory before God, that his glory may be made manifest in our ignominy. And if we suffer anything harsh or troublesome from the world, let that sweetest voice of the Lord console us: "If the world hates you, know that it hated me before you" <note>John 15:18</note>. If the world hated him through whom the world was made, shall we—vile little men, and if we repent of our crimes, most worthy of all reproaches—suffer it with difficulty if someone detracts or speaks evil of us? Shall we ourselves begin to act badly just so that he does not speak evil? Let us rather receive these curses eagerly. And if it is not our fortune to endure lashings, chains, prisons, and swords for virtue and truth, as our heroes once did, let us think we have done well enough if we suffer even the insults of wicked men, their detractions, and their hatred. Otherwise, if every occasion for merit is taken from us, no hope of reward remains. If men praise you for living well, then this virtue of yours, insofar as it is virtue, makes you like Christ; but insofar as it is praised, it makes you unlike him, who received as the reward of his virtue from men the death of the cross. Because of this, as the Apostle says, God exalted him and gave him the name which is above every name. It is more stable, therefore, to be 
<margin>Note.</margin>
crucified by the world so that you may be exalted by God, than to be exalted by the world so that you may be judged by God. For the one crucifies unto life, while the other exalts unto glory; the one exalts to heaven, the other judges to Gehenna <note>Hell</note>. Finally, if the world applauds you, it can hardly happen that virtue—which, directed entirely upward, ought to have only God as the one it seeks to please—does not incline itself a little toward the favor of applauding men. And even if it does not lose its integrity, it still loses some of its reward. When a reward begins to be paid on earth where all things are small, it will be less in heaven where all things are immense. Happy are the insults that keep us safe, lest the flower of justice wither by the pestilential breath of vain glory, or lest the wages of eternity be diminished for us by the empty payment of popular rumor. Let us embrace these insults, my son, and as faithful servants let us be proud with a most holy ambition for the ignominy of the Lord's cross alone. Paul says, "We preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block to the Jews and foolish-
<margin>What worldly wisdom may be.</margin>
-ness to the Gentiles, but to us the power of God and the wisdom of God" <note>1 Corinthians 1:23-24</note>. This wisdom of the world is foolishness before God, and that foolishness of Christ is what conquers the wisdom of the world, through which it pleased God to save those who believe. If you do not doubt that those who detract from your virtue are insane, and that they call the Christian life—which is wisdom—insanity: consider how great your own insanity would be to be moved from the path of a right life by the judgment of the insane. Every error should be removed by correction, not increased by imitation. Let them snarl, howl, and bark; you, proceed intrepidly on the path you have begun. And from their wickedness and misery, weigh how much you yourself owe to God, who illuminated you as you sat in the shadow of death. He has moved you from the company of those who, lost in the thickest darkness, rave here and there, and he has associated you with the children of light. Let that sweetest voice of the Lord sound always in your ears: "Leave the dead to bury their own dead; you, follow me" <note>Matthew 8:22</note>. For they are dead who do not live for God, and in this space of temporary death, they most laboriously acquire eternal death for themselves. If you ask them where they are going, or to what they refer their studies, works, and cares: what finally...

...[they think they] will be happy, they will either have nothing at all to say in response, or they will speak words that conflict with one another and contradict themselves, like the ravings of madmen. For they themselves do not know what they are doing; rather, like those who swim in rivers, they are carried along by the force of a poorly-acquired habit, as if by the rush of a torrent. From this point, their wickedness blinding them, and Satan goading them toward evil, they rush headlong into every crime—blind leaders of the blind—until an unforeseen death seizes them and says to them: <note>original: "Amice hac nocte repetēt aīam tuā a te"</note> "Friend, this night they will require your soul from you; and these things you have prepared, whose will they be?" <note>A reference to the Parable of the Rich Fool in Luke 12:20</note> Then they will envy those they once looked down upon, and they will praise those they once mocked. They will wish to imitate those they refused to follow when they were able, preferring instead to persecute them.

Look only to the judgment of God, who will render to each according to his works, at His revelation from heaven with the angels of His power, in a flame of fire taking vengeance on those who did not know God nor obeyed His gospel. These (as the Apostle says) <note>Referring to St. Paul in 2 Thessalonians 1:8-9</note> shall suffer the penalty of eternal destruction from the face of the Lord and from the glory of His power, when He comes to be glorified in His saints and to be marveled at in all who have believed. It is written: do not fear those who can kill the body, but Him who can cast the soul into Gehenna <note>Matthew 10:28</note>. How much less should you fear those who can harm neither your body nor your soul? If they now disparage you for your way of living, they will disparage you no less if you were to abandon virtue and be overwhelmed by vices—not because vice displeases them, but because the vice of disparaging others always pleases them. If your salvation is dear to your heart, flee; flee their company as much as you can.

Returning to yourself, pray often in secret to the most merciful Father, crying out with the Prophet: <note>original: "Ad te domine leuaui animam meam..."</note> "To you, O Lord, I have lifted up my soul; my God, in you I trust, let me not be ashamed," even if my enemies mock me. For indeed, all who hope in you shall not be confounded; let those who act iniquitously for no cause be confounded. How brief, uncertain, shadowy,

# SECOND.

->Brother Baptista Mantuanus, Carmelite, to Gianfrancesco Pico<-
->Count of Mirandola and Concordia. Greetings in the Lord. I.<-

<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'I' featuring a leafy, vine-like design within a square frame.</image-desc>
Illustrious Lord. Having recently heard of the death of Giovanni Pico, your uncle—a most distinguished and learned man—I was so stricken in spirit that neither my feet nor my mind could properly perform their duty. I nearly complained against both God and Nature: that they should so quickly remove such a light from the world, such an ornament of Italy, such a glory of our age, as if they envied the earthly republic its goods, having no regard for us. They have cut him down—cut him down, I say, while he was growing, while he was flourishing, while he was feeding everyone with the most abundant fertility of his genius. But remembering the sentence of Paul, in which he says "the judgments of God are a great abyss," <note>Romans 11:33</note> I restrained myself, lest I should think ill of God and His works with impious rashness. In the passing of this man, the study of letters, the knowledge of things, and the integrity of morals have suffered a great eclipse. For there was (as you know) in your uncle a linguistic erudition joined with such holiness of life, and a knowledge of both human and divine affairs, that in one and the same man I seemed to see Jerome and Augustine brought back to life. And if only he had finished that work on the Harmony of Plato and Aristotle before he departed! For its title promised the whole philosophy of the ancients and the opening of the most hidden things most worthy of being known. All his short works—those he completed and those he left unfinished—must be sought out with all zeal and diligence. For since they flowed from such a great happiness of genius, they cannot fail to be most worthy to be read, loved, and adored by all posterity. I would urge you to this duty, were I not certain that you are already sufficiently persuaded and inclined toward it. This immortal honor was lacking to your family: that alongside your most ancient nobility, your abundance of wealth and resources, and your glory in military affairs, there should also be placed the excellence of such great wisdom, so that all things which among mortals are worthy of the highest praise might flow together into your single house. Indeed, it befits you, Gianfrancesco, to strive with all your might to possess your uncle's virtue as an inheritance, and that his spirit may be doubled in you, just as the spirit of Elijah was in Elisha. This we expect of you; this we require. When you have collected his small works, I pray that you make me a participant in them as well; it will be worth the effort for me to come there for the sake of such great pleasure once I know they are ready. I subjoin a distich <note>A two-line poem</note> made on the spot in his praise, though it may not please. Farewell, best of princes, and love me. Mantua, November 27, 1494.

<meta>This page continues the correspondence following the death of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola in November 1494. The first letter is from the Carmelite poet Baptista Mantuanus to Pico’s nephew, Gianfrancesco, discussing a prophetic dream and the legacy of the late philosopher. # OF LETTERS

...I had begun to write them; your most desired, most ornate, and most pleasant letters arrived on the following night. I believe that because I had been thinking about it during the day, as I slept near dawn—the time when dreams are usually seen as true—the image of your uncle, who has already departed this life, seemed to appear to me. He discussed many things with me about the nature of angels; about the species, names, and offices of aerial, terrestrial, and even aquatic spirits, to the greatest pleasure of us both. And when I asked him why he was stuttering <note>original: "balbus"</note> (for he appeared to be a stutterer), he replied that it was a sign of imperfect and unfinished discourse, which he had begun long ago concerning the nature of things and philosophy. I seemed to be inflamed with a desire to inquire about many hidden things, which are marvelous and unknown to us mortals. Somehow, this first occurred to me: what use were amulets to infants, and corals, and other things of that kind which are tied around the necks of little children? He replied that there was sometimes some power in these things, and that this pertained to <term>natural magic</term> <note>A branch of science in the Renaissance that sought to understand the hidden powers of plants, stones, and stars without resorting to demonic intervention.</note>, but that for the most part they were condemned customs and superstitions. Having said these things, he vanished, and I, having woken up, thought long and hard about what we had discussed in the dream, because it seemed not to be empty but to have some weight. 

I write this not because I place any faith in dreams—for that is foreign both to my profession and my nature—but because I cannot wonder enough how it happens that those who sleep can dispute, teach, and learn, and often do things which are impossible or certainly difficult for those who are awake. Certainly our souls possess some spark of divinity, and if we lived skillfully and piously, and our minds were not driven about by so many winding paths of business, separated spirits would have great commerce with us. But enough of these things. 

Regarding your wish (as you write) to compose a life of your uncle: I both praise it and urge and beseech you to do it sooner. For that duty is most suitable for you, and it must be undertaken by you for many reasons; for you are very strong in both style and eloquence, which is a singular gift of nature, industry, and God. Likewise, because you are his kinsman and most closely related by blood to such a marvelous man, it follows that you cannot help but be a sharer in his glory. Nor should you in any way allow your most famous family to lose any of such ornament and splendor. Added to this is the fact that his life ought to be known to no one more than you, which you had long ago proposed to yourself to imitate; and indeed most wisely, for he was an extraordinary example of holiness and religion, in whom the light of all wisdom appeared. I will say to you, therefore, what Christ said to the apostles: "Gather the fragments, lest they perish," <note>original: "colligite fragmenta ne pereant" (John 6:12). Mantuanus uses this biblical quote to urge the preservation of Pico's unfinished writings.</note> and this must be done all the more studiously as it will be more profitable to us who survive and to future posterity. 

Undoubtedly, although I see that he is more to be congratulated who, after such a brief voyage, has gathered such great spiritual riches and reached port so happily, I cannot help but grieve with you over the loss of such a great man. The death of Giorgio Merula—first a fellow student, later my teacher 
<margin>
Who was a teacher of the Carmelite.
</margin>
(for we were companions under Gregorio Tiphernas)—affected me with sadness; but he was already old and, with old age weighing him down, now useless and having finished his duty. The lamentable fall of Hermolao and Poliziano, <note>Hermolao Barbaro and Angelo Poliziano, two of the era's greatest scholars, who both died in the early 1490s.</note> two illustrious men, brought heavy grief both to me and to all learned people; but another wound has struck deeper: the world of letters has suffered a far greater loss in our Pico. The fields of eloquence mourn; the studies of the mathematical arts have collapsed; all philosophy, and the highest speculations of metaphysics and theology, which he had already begun to expand and clarify

<column-break/>

will henceforth fall silent. But I stop now, lest I indulge too much in justified grief. We must take care rather that we turn out like him in the study and practice of the sciences and in integrity of character and religion, so that, enriched by a similar trade as he was, we may one day arrive where he now rejoices to have arrived. I will come as soon as I can so that I may see and venerate the immortal remains of his divine genius which are in your possession. Meanwhile, give your effort to writing his life, and love me. Farewell. Your lordship’s, to whom I commend myself. Mantua, the 3rd day of January, 1495.

### Hermolao Barbaro to Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, Greetings.

Indeed, Pico, you owe me nothing at all, whether in the name of silence or any duty of mine toward you; so much so that your letter was a great cause of blushing for me. You beg my pardon for your negligence, when I should have been the one to redeem my own negligence toward you at any price first. This is the goodness of your genius: your gift, your equity. You acknowledge the fault of another when you could either avoid it or certainly share it; you are anxious in a mutual transgression, you who could have been secure even before the accusation and with a better cause; either both are guilty or neither. Otherwise, as far as you are concerned, you have already cleared yourself. It remains that I also satisfy the debt. 

But what can I write to you most of all? Shall I exhort you to continue to love letters, in which you are most eminent? Shall I advise you to labor in virtue and good character, in which you have accomplished so much that it is difficult to know to which part of philosophy you have applied greater effort: that which contains the speculative and its instruments, or that which embraces the dogmatic and the moral? <note>original: "dogmaticē paræneticamq;"</note> Altogether it is supreme and greater than human capacity, what you—either by your genius or certainly by your own craftsmanship—have attained at such a tender age, which it would be most impudent to hope for in extreme old age. These things are not yours, Pico; they belong to nature, they belong to God; although if anything is yours, these are yours most of all. See how 
<margin>
Glory must be given to God the Best and Greatest, and the source of all.
</margin>
much less can the nobility of fortune, health, or beauty be called yours; in which goods you yield to no one, just as you do not in those which are more truly yours. I exhort you to turn yourself here; ponder this day and night: what a name you may be to Him who has enriched you to such an extent that you will never be able to repay or even account for the things you possess. Think how much He is able to do, He who willed that you be able to do those things; how much He loves you, He who chose you for Himself out of so many thousands; you who, as almost a boy, would surpass old men, and who, not yet a youth, would turn the circles of learned men to admiration of your learning. Unless you see this, unless you value it, I affirm to you right now and proclaim with a free voice that you are not as great as you are. 

It is immense and infinite, what I promised and do promise myself about you; but neither speech nor proclamation can reach the level of my preconceived opinion. I act as people usually do: the more they admire someone and wish to explain what they feel, the less they attain what they want; so that although they conceive something great in their mind, words nevertheless fail them and they seem to have been able to struggle rather than to speak. Therefore, do not listen to these things which I now write about you and bring forth; but understand those things instead which I speak about you alone and in silence within myself—by Hercules, they are as much greater as thought is than speech. Greet Marsilio <note>Marsilio Ficino, the philosopher who led the Platonic Academy in Florence.</note> and your Salvatus. There is no need for you to labor regarding Poliziano, because shortly (as I hear) he will be with me, than which nothing more pleasant could happen to me in this entire embassy. Build up the library there every day, larger and more ornate; I rejoice so much that nothing could be more; literature owes much to the Florentines, and among the Florentines to the Medici, and among the Medici to Lorenzo, who fosters this ancestral honor of his family with no less care...

## Hermolao Barbaro to Roberto Salviati. Sends Many Greetings. IV.

You are mistaken, Salviati, if you suspect anything other than my busy schedule has been the reason why I have not yet replied to you. This is a common and well-worn excuse for silence; but by Hercules, it is so true that unless you accept it, you would seem to do a disservice to my love, faith, and devotion toward you. All your letters are always most welcome to me, but that one was beyond measure in which the name and mention of my Mirandola appeared. There is nothing more wondrous than that one man in literature; there is no one whom I would rather see praised, honored, and raised to the heavens; no one from whose praise I can less easily depart. In this matter I am perhaps excessive, yet I would seem temperate to no one, for there is so much praise in him and it is so limitless that there is no longer room for ambition or flattery. I have read his *Apology* <note>original: "apologiam"; Pico's 1487 defense of his thirteen "heretical" theses</note>; and in it, why does he grant me so much, I who deserve so little? Why does he announce me with such an honorable preface—me, an ordinary witness, not to say a common one? 

Especially in that work, than which nothing is more subtle, more powerful, or more acute; regarding which, however, it is better that I defer my judgment for a while until I have read the whole thing clearly. Since you desire to hear what I am doing, what else can I say but that I am studying? Public business <note>Barbaro was serving as the Venetian ambassador to Milan at this time</note> certainly takes something away from my intensity—or rather, from my studies, not my intensity. For I press on more fiercely and exact my task more bitterly because the portion taken from me by this greater activity has struck me with more greed and eagerness for work. Therefore, all those holidays which a private citizen would give to his health, I distribute to public service; thus, what I lose from one cause, I gather back by another means. 

I believe I have written to you at other times, or said it to those who have heard it from me, that the *Instrument* of Aristotle <note>The *Organon*, or Aristotle's works on logic</note> (for so the Peripatetics usually call Logic), likewise the eight books on *Natural Audition* <note>Aristotle's *Physics*</note>, and his three books on *Rhetoric*, were translated by me into Latin long ago. My *Dioscorides* <note>Barbaro’s massive commentary and translation of the ancient Greek medical text by Dioscorides</note> is now finished; the final touch is being applied by me now; it is ready: it is a daughter’s dowry; it will be settled shortly. Then, relieved of that burden, I shall approach Aristotle entirely and as a whole; and unless God calls me elsewhere, he will go forth finished nearly two years after the edition of *Dioscorides*, at least in the Logic, and with him the commentaries which I have already completed on the *Posterior Analytics*. After these are released, I shall enter into natural and divine matters <note>Physics and Metaphysics</note>; likewise *Rhetoric* and *Poetics*, preparing all the volumes of that philosopher to the best of my ability, partly with commentaries and partly with annotations. For there are some things in the *Problems* and in the *History of Animals* that require clarity and light; I am prepared to flow past those quickly with the light of a brief note. I plan to undertake nothing new for the rest of my life; for indeed (I must restrain this greed, or rather this wickedness of my intellect, lest while it wishes to be considered correctable and fertile, it appear both laborious and ambitious), I experience more truly every day what is commonly said: that to embrace everything and to embrace nothing are the same. 

<margin>To embrace everything and nothing are the same.</margin>

Farewell. Milan, the 12th Kalends of November <note>October 21st</note>, 1488.

## Hermolao Barbaro to Giovanni Pico. Sends Many Greetings. V.

I read your *Heptaplus* <note>original: "Exameró"; Pico's work on the seven days of creation</note>, delivered to us three days ago by the effort of Salviati, so greedily that I drained the whole thing on the very first day, and not without inspiration. Three things in it delight me wonderfully: first, that your speech teaches and moves; a practice which it is well known the ancient theologians observed in Holy Scripture, and in 

<column-break/>

natural philosophy even the Pythagoreans and Platonists observed, while more recent men sweat only at teaching. Second, that in such a great abundance of material and such freedom to plunder, you have such chaste and innocent hands that in this genre of writing, you seem to have followed yourself and no other. And this is now common neither with the ancients nor with the moderns, but is peculiar and your own; in which indeed (I shall open my mind to you) I am so affected that since those earlier men did not say these things which you have said, they seem to me to have said almost nothing. Third, that I see you are initiated into the sacred mysteries not so much of Aristotle as of Plato and his sects; from there you have brought full drafts into this midnight study. I omit how many excellent things from Plotinus you have touched upon so cursorily and elegantly, so that you seem not so much to have read as to have mastered whatever the fifty-four volumes in six "nines" <note>The *Enneads*, the collected works of Plotinus, arranged into groups of nine by Porphyry</note> arranged by Porphyry contain. Nor can I pass over this: that 

<margin>54 volumes of Plotinus.</margin>

you conduct yourself as a middle ground between the new and old theologians, so that you neither hate their simple majesty nor are carried away by the ambitious subtlety of the others. Thus it happens that while you wish to imitate the one, you are able to do so for the other; you have plucked the best of both kinds, which I hope you will also do in the explanation of the Davidic poem <note>The Psalms</note> itself. Farewell. Venice, the day before the Nones of September <note>September 4th</note>, 1489.

## Hermolao Barbaro to Giovanni Pico della Mirandola. Sends Many Greetings. VI.

Greetings, most kind Mirandola. Indeed, I proclaim your name everywhere so 

<margin>Plato.</margin>

willingly that I do nothing with greater pleasure: not only because nothing (as Plato says) is heard more pleasantly than the truth, but also because, as Palaemon says, it is much more pleasant to speak the truth than to hear it. It happens that with no labor, as is often found in Aeschylus, Menander, and 

<margin>Aeschylus, Menander, Euripides.</margin>

Euripides, the truth comes forth even when not sought; it is often expressed even to the most unwilling man, not by questions but by its own force alone. This is that tyranny which you, following your own candor, interpret as humanity and goodness. And by Hercules, you are already so great that whoever does not praise you detracts from his own judgment and reputation. They act in their own interest; they consult their own reasons; they redeem their own fame—those who favor and desire yours. There are many names in your ledger that you do not know; your creditors owe you. Many follow the advice of Prodicus: they give so that they may receive; "hand 

<margin>Epicharmus.</margin>

washes hand," <note>original: "manus manum scabit"</note> as Epicharmus sings. Truly, the less you owe your creditors—that is, your praisers—the more you owe yourself, you who make them your creditors whether they like it or not. O unheard-of kind of debt, where the creditors are not the ones owed! But I am too busy to be able to play with you any longer. But you, how relaxed you are, good gods, that you allow anyone to be idle. I pray you have endured me this far; I do not ask you to admit some longer joke; I ask for a brief little yawn <note>original: "oscitaciunculam"</note>. Farewell, with my friend Poliziano. Rome, the Ides of August <note>August 13th</note>, 1490.

# LETTERS

...as Propericus says: would that it might one day be possible for me to live with you, to philosophize <note>original: "philosophari"</note> about nature, about God, and about holy morals. How much I desire this, and how much of an addition to my success I judge it would be if this should happen, I can neither express nor, if I could, would I wish to do so in this place. <margin>Every good in us depends on God alone.</margin>

Now there is a stupor and ecstasy of knowledge. You will read these things patiently, and your heart will not be exalted, nor will you have haughty eyes. For why should you be pleased with yourself, you who know that these good things you possess are not your own, nor from your own private savings, but are granted and belong to the Lord? Forgive me. The north wind of truth and the west wind of charity have seized me and carried me away. Farewell. Rome, the day before the Kalends of April <note>March 31</note>, 1491.

->Brother Baptista, Carmelite, to Giovanni Francesco Pico. Book VIII.<-

**I**llustrious Count and Lord, I have read your uncle’s <note>referring to Giovanni Pico della Mirandola</note> apology, or rather the prologue to the apology, of that most learned and eloquent man. I read it with as much pleasure of mind as it is supported by truth, as much as it shines with clarity, and with as much love and reverence as I have always pursued its author. But in reading it, while I desire to quench my thirst, another thirst has grown: the desire, namely, of seeing the rest. When I have obtained that by the gift of your favor, I will think myself to have attained a great part of happiness. In my judgment, your uncle Giovanni Pico has surpassed the philosophers of our entire age, chiefly for these reasons: while others waste their lives only on the dogmas of Aristotle and the Peripatetics <note>the followers of Aristotle</note>, he, with Herculean audacity, has scrutinized the sects and families of all philosophers, ancient and modern, with a marvelous vigor of genius. Furthermore, while the moderns follow no flower of oratory, he has so joined philosophy with eloquence that he can be said to have restored the ancient and true Academy <note>referring to the Platonic Academy of Athens, which prized both wisdom and beautiful speech</note>. These things are worthy of all the greater admiration because he ascended to such a height of virtue and glory with such swift study and in so few years. Nor does he seem to have sought knowledge, as others do, by labor and study and many late-night sessions, but to have found it all at once by chance—as happens to those who, while doing something else entirely, unexpectedly stumble upon a treasure. Happy is the land, therefore, illuminated by such splendor. Farewell, most worthy prince, and remember how much you must strive to be considered a worthy imitator of your uncle. I hate these distances between places. For I desire to be with you, so that we might share in your studies and I in yours. Again, fare well and fear God. Mantua, the 29th day of October, 1494.

->Matthew of Verona, Regular Canon. Rome.<-
->To Roberto Salviati. Sends Many Greetings. IX.<-

**T**he interpretation of the six days in which God created all things, written by our Giovanni of Mirandola, which you sent to me as a gift—inscribed and noted by him as the *Heptaplus* <note>original: "Heptaplus"; Pico’s 1489 work providing a seven-fold explanation of the first chapters of Genesis</note>—is clearly of such a kind that it cannot easily be scanned and understood simultaneously by a reader. Nevertheless, the beginning of the work so inflamed and drew me

<column-break/>

that, eager for the end and never catching my breath, I tasted that famous work. Certainly, I would have vowed to ruminate upon it with sharper study and a longer lamp <note>an expression for working late into the night</note> during a period of leisure. It seemed to me that our Giovanni here is not only skilled and wise in all philosophy and whatever is contained in the laws of nature, but he even raises himself above human things. He flies through sublime matters, and has turned the secret mysteries and heavenly sacraments toward mystical senses and allegory. These are things that those of our time who are considered wise and erudite scarcely notice or pass over entirely unattempted. He unshells the most difficult and heavenly things here and, as far as the subject allows, opens, discloses, and illustrates them more splendidly than the sun. And what is wonderful is that while still a youth and living in the secular world, he joins himself closely to the likes of Dionysius, Hilary, Damascene, Augustine, Ambrose, Jerome, and other such most holy and rare men of old. All posterity will admire him when envy has grown quiet and the slow passage of time has established his authority.

<margin>Display of Mirandola's genius.</margin>

What, O supreme God, should we think he will give us if a life equal to his mind is granted to him? Even with his first beard <note>in his youth</note>, he is already most learned in Latin and Greek letters—at which antiquity marveled in Origen and Jerome—and he is not ignorant of Hebrew. Furthermore, in sacred matters he can do so much that it is scarcely credible that anyone else could do the same. Truly, we expect whatever delights are coming next regarding the Psalms and the songs of David, which he has long been treating, interpreting, and explaining, having searched with infinite labor into what all the Latin, Greek, and Hebrew writers have left behind on them. I am glad that for the completion of this business, he has chosen leisure for himself in our monastery at Fiesole <note>original: "fesulano cęnobio"; the Badia Fiesolana near Florence</note> in this time of ours. It is plain happiness both to see and to hear these things. And so, Roberto, I give you as many thanks as I can, for you have taken such diligent and corrected care to have the work printed, which looks to the common utility and the praise of your noble mind; and also because you immediately presented me with it. So that I may seem grateful to you if I am able, accept this something of ours, which you may read in turn and perhaps taste. Otherwise, farewell, and live happily in Christ. From the Abbey of Fiesole.

->Hermolao Barbaro to Giovanni Pico. Sends Many Greetings. X.<-

**I**t does not escape me, nor did it ever escape me while you were living your life in Padua, Giovanni Pico of Mirandola, how great was the excellence of your genius and how great was your eloquence. You have indicated this more clearly in many things always, but especially in this, your most learned explanation of Moses. For, to speak of myself, it has not only confirmed the excellent opinion I had long ago conceived of you,

<margin>He highly praises the *Heptaplus*.</margin>

but it has also fostered and increased it in a wonderful way, and raised it to the very peak. Indeed, I was so delighted in reading this work of yours that I think nothing more excellent or more worthy could be had, which ought to be read or heard by everyone. For while many things in this most brilliant work of yours are known to be worthy of praise—which would be very powerful whether taken together or even individually—that which stands out foremost is that you have spoken with a divine mouth (as the saying goes), more like a divine being than a human one. Furthermore, you have attained such facility in explaining the enigmas of Moses that Jesus Christ seems to have granted it to you alone, who otherwise deserve well of Him. I am not unaware that this is rather a gift of some celestial nature than comparable to anything lower; indeed, it could not happen by human genius...

# BOOK THE SECOND

...anyone through these years of yours, which are few, to run through three languages <note>Latin, Greek, and Hebrew</note>—not to mention mastering them as you do. Then, understanding them so well as to unravel and interpret the hidden and secret meanings of Moses <note>Pico's *Heptaplus* interpreted the first chapters of Genesis</note>, and to do so not in a crude or barbaric way, but to speak and write in the Roman and Latin tongue, as you have undertaken. For few men "whom impartial Jupiter has loved" <note>original: "paucis quos aequus amauit iuppiter"; a quote from Virgil's Aeneid</note> are granted the ability to write as you have written. Therefore, posterity will commend you as a second Jerome <note>Saint Jerome was the 4th-century scholar who translated the Bible into Latin and was famed for his knowledge of the three biblical languages</note>, most skilled in languages. Accordingly, I congratulate you that you have rendered your name eternal and everlasting. For indeed, because of this most useful labor of yours, all students of letters will owe you as much—since you have given it to all to be read—as they confess they owe to Plato, Aristotle, and the entire school of the Peripatetics. I wish to be counted among their number, since I am, and always have been, most loving and devoted to you. Farewell, and I commend myself greatly to your excellence. September 20, 1489. Venice.

->Your Sebastian Prioli, son of the most illustrious Pietro, Procurator of Saint Mark.<-

### Hieronymus Donatus to Roberto Salviati. Greetings. XI.

I have been provoked by you with great charms of love, and a little while ago by the sweetest gift of the *Heptaplus*. Then, in your most recent, kind, and elegant letters: either of these by itself could have been enough to fulfill all the requirements of friendship. To this was added our Feruaticus, as honest in character as he is elegant in letters; for his sake also I must love you exceedingly. How much I owe to your kindness, I prefer to be conscious of within myself than to write to you. Pico's benevolence toward me, already seen before, deserves to be judged even more pleasing to me through the credit of your testimony. I know how much I ought to value being loved and praised by that man in whom the rewards of learning and character harmonize with the greatest glory of our age. It is more fitting to admire his *Heptaplus* than to judge it. That style of writing delights me wonderfully, because I see no richer harvest of doctrine and erudition from any source than from the Sacred Scriptures. But that boldness is successful in very few, among whom is my Pico; bid him greetings in my name as much as you can. For this very reason I am most dear to myself: because I love him vehemently. You, Salviati, shall promise yourself as much from me as is fitting to be provided by a most friendly and well-wishing man. Farewell. Milan, October 25, 1489.

### Battista Guarini to the most learned Prince Giovanni Pico della Mirandola. Greetings. XII.

Our Pictorius, with his rather quick step, brought me your little gift in recent days. Ha! Why did I say "little gift" because of the number of pages? It is rather a massive gift because of the broad and manifold knowledge and eloquence of your book. What point is there in me writing much about it, since it is already so regarded by the opinions of all those whose judgments are in the Register <note>The "Albo" likely refers to a list of approved or celebrated scholars</note>, so that it neither grows by praise nor is diminished by blame. I shall end with one word: since you wish it so, I have been made a disciple to you, my teacher. Therefore, beware of calling me by any other name hereafter. During the "halcyon days" <note>original: "halcedonia"; a time of peace and calm</note> of our lecture hall, I read through everything; I re-read and learned much; I mastered most of it. I loved you before as much as anyone possibly could. Now, because of this gift, I love you even more—that is, 

<column-break/>

beyond my strength—and I look up to your genius. Do this, my Pico: continue to deserve well of other men of letters and especially of students of sacred philosophy, which is to be considered the true and genuine philosophy. Rescue yourself from the delays of "devouring time" <note>original: "edacis aevi"; a common poetic trope for the destructive nature of time</note>. Know, moreover, that the greatest things are expected from you, as from one in whom everyone understands that the refined elegance of the humanities is joined with a philosophy more recondite than these times can bear. If there is any good book there which you think would interest my studies, let my mind participate in that food. You know the scarcity of books in this city; you know my "stomach" also—new things please me, yet great and ancient things <note>Greek: vσταλαια (palaia); ancient things</note> satisfy my hunger. You understand what these are. A few words to the wise. If any small opportunity is given to the great Lorenzo de' Medici—provided it can be done without troubling you—I ask that you commend me to him. For I admire the virtue of a man in such great fortune and learning, and I venerate him in silence. Farewell, glory of the Muses. Ferrara, November 1, 1489.

### Cristoforo Landino to Roberto Salviati. Greetings. XIII.

<margin>
Praise for the
Heptaplus
of Moses
</margin>

How grateful and how pleasant your most excellent gift was to me, I trust I could not sufficiently express even in another *Iliad*, given the magnitude of the matter. For what could more fittingly come from you, at once a most liberal man and a most learned gentleman—or what could be more expectedly brought to me, who am most greedy for letters—than that exact *Heptaplus* on the Genesis of Moses, wonderfully written by our Pico, who is easily the prince of all letters and doctrines in our age? For although among almost infinite Hebrews, many Arabs and Greeks, and not a few Latins, we see that matter treated so learnedly, distinctly, and eloquently that I believed not a single word could be added; yet he, beginning the whole matter with an almost new argument and arriving by an unusual path at things which seemed most worn and common to all, has so described them that even those who are most learned admire them as if they were new and unheard of. Therefore, I, who have never hitherto stepped outside the borders of Tuscany, have been carried through all the regions and tracts of the earth, though borne by no horse and moved by no beast of burden. If I was drawn along by the perpetual vehicle of his reasoning, I was moved without effort; and then, having left behind the dolphins of Arion—not to mention human ships—I was led through all the seas by his narration, as if carried on the chariot of Neptune. These things indeed 

<margin>A notable comparison.</margin>

can seem great and incredible to everyone. But other things are greater and worthy of greater admiration. For, lifted from the waters, I know not whether by swan's feathers or by Daedalian and Pegasean wings, I arrived through all the air and all the ether to the very highest summit of corruptible things, with him not only leading but carrying me up. It is a thing truly worthy of extreme amazement to have traveled through this lower and elemental world. But it is far greater to have reached the celestial world: to have penetrated first the orb of the Moon, then Mercury and Venus; to have seen the rays of the Sun; to have felt the fires of Mars; and finally to have known both the health-giving rays of Jupiter and the heavy rays of Saturn. Then, finally, to have observed that eighth sphere reflecting the burning stars, and all these heavens rotating not with a simple and uniform motion, but with a triple and triform motion. Yet who is ignorant that all these things fall within our senses? But he gave me the third world <note>The intellectual or angelic world in Pico's cosmology</note> to be so traversed that, with all senses put to sleep...

But the sharpness of his vision, like an owl blinking at the sun's rays, could not endure such great splendor. Therefore, whatever in this journey—or to speak more truly, this return to our homeland—either lay hidden from me or escaped my eyes, the guide himself is not to blame, if he to whom it was shown is easily found at fault.
