Indeed, as soon as I began to taste it, such a great thirst was stirred in me for what I had heard but once—and such a great love for feasting arose from the sweetness of this food—that, impatient with any delay, I commanded that nothing be left for later chewing, but like a most greedy youth, I devoured the whole solid mass at once. But when, through continuous reading, I had finished the entire thing, and like the same beast <note>Referring to a ruminant or "clean" animal from the Mosaic law</note> gathering it into the stomach and calling it back to the mouth I had more diligently ruminated upon it, then truly a marvelous sweetness appeared; then a wonder like never before stole over me. But you will say: did you not admire the man’s learning before? I did indeed admire how he was so engaged in all disciplines that he seemed to excel in each one.

<margin>
How well Pico is praised here.
</margin>

No topic in physics, no topic in mathematics escaped him when he disputed; in metaphysics truly, and in every kind of theology—whether you seek that which was stirred by Mercury <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of Hermeticism</note> and brought to perfection by Plato, or our own Christian theology, the most excellent and true of all—these our ages, and even several before us, have seen nothing more learned than him. But lest perhaps you think (a vice with which many of us have struggled) that he joined himself to wisdom by abandoning eloquence: does he not describe everything most gravity, most copiously, and moreover most elegantly? So much so that he can now, by his own best right, be numbered among those ancient orators. I have admired these things about him until now, thinking that nothing could be added to such an accumulation. Truly, I have begun to admire his *Heptaplus* <note>Pico's "Seven-fold" commentary on the six days of creation</note> more than those previous things I admired. Therefore, I would believe it happened not rashly nor by some chance, but by God’s command: that this divine man emerged distinguished by these three names. For *Ioannes* <note>John</note> is interpreted either as "the grace of the Lord," or "he in whom there is grace," or "one to whom a gift has been made by God." Who does not see that he could not have attained the learning with which he is endowed without the special and greatest grace of God? Moreover, in the *Picus* <note>The Latin word *picus* means "woodpecker." Donato is playing on the bird's reputation for drilling into wood</note> we know there is that hardness of beak, that strength of head, so that you will find no wood so bony (if I may say so), nor so like stone, that this bird does not pierce it; and in it, he carves out a hiding place for himself with craftsmanship, where he may retire and build a nest. In the same way, therefore, nothing from all disciplines is so difficult for human genius to know that he himself, by pounding, has not penetrated its hardest parts, built a nest, hatched his young, and brought them forth. Since all things in that man are to be wondered at, who would not think he should be called *Mirandulanum* <note>Mirandula, Pico's home, suggests the Latin *mirandus*, meaning "wonderful" or "to be wondered at"</note>? Therefore, as I congratulate you, who enjoy his constant friendship, so I grieve for myself; for myself, I say, who consider myself unhappy in this: that because of my many and necessary occupations, I am not permitted to cling to him day and night as I most ardently desire. For if it were permitted, I would never depart from his side—I do not say from the side of an old man, but of a youth; I speak of that youth in whom all wisdom and all learning is elderly and white-haired. You, however, to whom fortune has offered far greater leisure, and nature has bestowed an excellent genius—which, nevertheless, your long-standing exercise in all the good arts and frequent use has successively increased

<column-break/>

and polished—enjoy this good thing that has fallen to you from heaven. Drink from this most fertile fountain, or rather, this immense ocean; and drink so much that it might be enough to quench not only your present thirst but all future thirst. Consider yourself, therefore; calculate, and argue with yourself how few mortals have ever received so much good. That great Alexander <note>Alexander the Great</note> boasted that he lived in the times of so great a philosopher as Aristotle. But it has been given to you by your most happy lot to have lived familiarly with Aristotle and Plato at the same time—and such an Aristotle and Plato that in them, besides the ancient doctrine of the Academics and Peripatetics, we see our Pauls, Johns, Dionysii, Augustines, Jeromes, Thomases, and other lights of this kind shining back. Therefore, gather from these things how much you ought to love either yourself or him, best Roberto: to whom fortune itself has offered, and you in your providence have succeeded, in making yourself especially familiar to this man. Farewell. November 22nd.

### Alexander Cortesi to his friend Pico. Greetings. XIIII.

I have taken no greater pleasure in my whole life than recently from your letter. And although I had believed the highest things of you, you have nevertheless (I confess) surpassed my opinion; and you have surpassed it so far that I now think the boundaries of your glory, though spread far and wide, are yet too narrow. Let us speak more openly and far from flattery, from which illustrious souls have always shrunk: What in you is not extraordinary? What is not worthy of admiration? Individual traits could honor anyone, yet in you, they are all brought together equally; you have stolen (so to speak) all the Graces from everyone for yourself alone. And although your ancestors reached that point where only those born from them might easily arrive, you have nevertheless emerged so great that you seem to return a greater grace to them than you received. Age usually brings authority to others, but youth extols your dignity, and what others conquered by time, you have surpassed by invincible virtue. In my judgment, you are placed beyond any gamble of genius, and though I search through Greek praises, I find no one to whom I may deservedly compare you. In short, one may suppose that some equal to you existed at some time, but one cannot see such a person in this present time. Let all the ingenious men forgive me: all are greatly surpassed by the one Pico. Whom the kindness of nature has so cherished that it must seem even to her that such a great abundance of all praises has been gathered into one man. Why do you blush? Or do you think I am false? Indeed, I shall yield if you attribute it to Love, who is painted blind. But I have my witnesses, the Polizianos <note>Angelo Poliziano, the great humanist scholar and Pico's close friend</note>, who is deceived only regarding me; they are more reliable witnesses, even if he, as I hear, daily increases his riches of gold no less than those of speech. For this I congratulate him as much as I give thanks; I wish he may possess the horn of plenty, since he is unmindful neither of his guest nor of our old friendship. Concerning Pucci, that most loving of men, I shall speak another time. Who would not wish to be indebted to him? But I delay you too long while you are intent on higher studies. And I see Marsilio Ficino <note>The head of the Platonic Academy in Florence</note>, the prince of the philosophers of our age, laughing at these trifles. Why should he not laugh? He who weighs all mortal things no less than he despises them. Oh, for someone to place me in your academy and cover me with the great shadow of its branches! Especially because this sky belongs to Mars alone <note>A reference to the wars currently plaguing Italy</note>; no honor worthy of the plow remains; the fields lie neglected, the farmers being led away, and the curved sickles are beaten into rigid swords <note>A quote from Virgil's Georgics (1.506-8), describing the chaos of war</note>. But we are content with this Cato <note>Referring to Pico as a moral authority like Cato the Censor</note>. Meanwhile, gather from these scraps the fruit of my love, and do not make little of being loved by me, but return the favor. Longing...

->Girolamo Donato to his own Giovanni Pico, greetings. XV.<-

Those parts which should have been mine, you have taken for yourself, most learned Pico: accusing yourself of negligence toward me and seeking an excuse in that crime of which I am most guilty toward you. It seems insufficient to you to excel others in genius and erudition unless you also surpass not only others but yourself in modesty and humanity. But indeed, I pray you embrace the gifts of these virtues in such a way that you leave us some opportunity for performing our duty, lest while you claim all these parts for yourself, we be held inhuman and uncivilized. In this matter—such is my impudence—I no longer excuse my negligence, but I accuse your humanity, because you write that you have established not a temporary but a perpetual friendship with me. I understand that I owe you very much not only for that reason, but you also seem to have correctly defined friendship for me: which, since it is temporary, can no longer be friendship. Know that I have placed this among the choice of my ornaments. For what more distinguished thing can happen to me than to be not only praised but also loved by such a great man? Our Hermolaus <note>Hermolao Barbaro (1454–1493), a famous Venetian scholar</note>, through incredible tranquility of learning and care of <term>philoponia</term> <note>original: "φιλοπονια"—love of labor or industriousness</note>, I see to be most highly learned in utility—something supreme and rare which letters can hope for while he is safe. I preserve his company—which you envy me so much—in the same storehouse as your friendship. Furthermore, I think nothing so <term>thaumaston</term> <note>original: "θαυμαστον"—wonderful or marvelous</note> that you cannot attain it by genius and erudition, especially since I hear you have

->moved there: which plan<-

I so praise that I cannot praise it more. For "not even for a gathering of cattle would there be a display" <note>original: "ουδ’ αγελασ αν γεγονυμαι επιδειξις"—a Greek proverb suggesting that one should not show off their talents to those who cannot appreciate them (the "cattle" or the masses)</note>. I envy you [Angelo] Poliziano <note>A renowned humanist poet and friend of Pico</note>, a man of most fertile and eloquent genius, whose *Rusticus* I recently read; he seemed to me the splendor of our age and

->to whom I ask those things of me from you in my own<-

words: which can be expected from a most friendly man. I use you as a messenger in beginning my goodwill with him, relying on your humanity; however, through you, who are the <term>most supreme of the Muses</term> <note>original: "φ των μουσων κορυφαιοτατα" (the koryphaios or leader of the choir of Muses)</note>, it is fitting for me to be reconciled by you, who are the most learned. Farewell: and think nothing more pleasant to me than your letters. I will write more to you at greater leisure. Venice, December 16, 1484.

->Filippo Beroaldo to Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, greetings. XVI.<-

When I was about to dine at the house of Mino Rossi, who is most polished in the study of letters and the greatest ornament of our senate, I was reading the plays of Plautus, overflowing with the most urban wit, when your letter was brought to me—how literary, how refined, how "wiped clean" <note>polished</note>! Immediately, setting aside the comic charm, we began to read your most delightful writings in haste. Good gods, how

<column-break/>

much charm, how much erudition, how much majesty we recognized to be in them! Great fame had preceded Giovanni Pico; a greater man was found. Nothing worn out, nothing trivial resonates in your writings. Matter matches words and words match matter exactly; you speak Latin and use a pure, splendid, and magnificent elocution. You have a style full of pleasantness and candor; a most copious supply of the best words. You draw sentiments from the depths of your feeling, so that the immortal gods seem to have given to you alone what they have given to very few: namely, to feel best and to speak best, and you embrace this no less in verse than in prose. Livy and Homer write almost divinely that the gods did not grant all things to one man; hence it is that we often read that some flourished excelling in eloquence, others endowed with erudition; but very few have existed who were both eloquent and erudite at the same time. Hence the two peaks of the Roman tongue, Terentius Varro and Marcus Cicero, are cited: from one of whom the knowledge of things <note>facts/content</note> and from the other the knowledge of words was sought. One is called the most learned from every source; the other is called the most eloquent by all. Virgil, as Seneca best says, was abandoned by that felicity of genius in prose; Cicero wrote poems with no grace and no charm—the Muses being unwilling and resistant. But you are both most learned and most eloquent. You are powerful in prose and verse; you write things to be read; you know how <margin>See Apuleius, book 4 of the *Florida*.</margin> to write. You can rightly be called a foster child of the Muses: who have not, like many, drunk one or two musical bowls, but like another Apuleius, have drunk down all the bowls, and especially that clear and nectar-like bowl of philosophy, which very few touch with the tips of their lips, and barely salute from the threshold. O great fertility of mind! O most blessed abundance of immortal genius, which has hammered out such great virtues in Pico della Mirandola, still a boy, still a youth; has poured in such varied disciplines; has inserted such great gifts of soul! He who is a raw recruit in age is a veteran in erudition. Proceed, most learned man, where you have begun; ensure that as years increase, knowledge is augmented. Let genius mature, let memory become more vigorous and helpful. You who in youth are the glory of our age and an example of virtue: what will you be in old age? Papinian <note>A famous 2nd-century Roman jurist</note> is called by Spartianus the "asylum of law" and the "treasury of legal learning." You shall be called by us the "asylum of the liberal disciplines." Whenever anything hidden in inner letters occurs to us, you will be a treasury for us—or rather, to speak more truly, you are already a treasury now. All things, even the most profound in letters, are at your hand; all things occur readily. That "circle of learning" <note>the *encyclopedia*</note> praised by the learned seems to be in your service. Greek and Latin letters are your handmaids. You are permitted to refresh your genius now with this meditation, now with that, for one is the seasoning of the other. And as varied and changed seeds recreate and restore the lands, so the change of studies revives and delights minds. You are permitted to cheer your genius with the sweeter studies of poetry if ever it grows weary with the harsher dogmas of philosophy. You, finally, stand in the citadel and at the summit of the gifted disciplines, while we sweat on the first slope. You have ascended the narrow path of virtue with a giant's stride; we attempt to ascend with the gait of a tortoise or an ant, and we labor on rugged paths, repeatedly slipping, repeatedly nodding and stumbling. I write what I feel; I feel what I write; my pen agrees with my mind. I am affected by an incredible desire to visit you along with Poliziano; which desire within a few days...

# Bartolomeo Fonzio to Roberto Salviati. Letter XVII.

Greetings. Indeed, I read your Pico with the greatest pleasure last night, Robert. I read it for two reasons: both because it was sent by you, a most dear friend, and because I loved the author of the work for himself, whom I thought it would be shameful for me not to have read yet. Indeed, through your kindness, I have achieved what I most desired. I thank you for such a gift, and I heartily congratulate him for publishing such a great work to be celebrated by all Christianity. In it, I truly doubt whether to wonder more at the invention of so many great things, or at such incredible order in such variety, or at such elegance of speech in such laborious descriptions. For why should I mention in the *Heptaplus* <note>original: "heptaplo." Pico’s work providing a seven-fold explanation of the creation story in Genesis</note> those things which most commend the authors of works: that there is no wordiness, no swelling pride, and in all things a singular modesty without any suspicion of envy. I truly wish I could have returned a similar gift to this most sweet and desired present of yours, so you might see my spirit toward you more clearly. But what I could do, I have already done: I have sent to you, first of all, a speech I recently gave to King Matthias Corvinus <note>The King of Hungary and a significant patron of the Renaissance</note>. When you have read it yourself, you will also give it to your Pico to read. I judge him to be the most outstanding in every kind of learning of all those of our age whose writings I have seen so far. Farewell, and continue to love me as you do.

# Battista Guarino to the most learned prince Giovanni Pico della Mirandola. Greetings. Letter XVIII.

<margin>turning back on yourself <note>original Greek: αντιστρεφοντα (antistrephonta)</note></margin> I do not yet grant that the lawsuit ought to be decided in your favor, for I can easily turn those quibbles of yours back upon you. If I am your teacher, why do you not obey me? If I am not, why do you call me teacher? Nor do I refuse this name because I scorn you as a student, whom I assert to be my own teacher. Rather, it is because I both venerate and proclaim your learning. In this, I am aware that I have promoted you neither by my genius, nor by the mark of a crossed pen, nor by little wax tablets, nor finally by a dagger <note>original: "obelisco." A mark used by scholars to indicate a doubtful or superfluous passage</note> or an asterisk. But we have fallen, it seems, into a certain new kind of judicial case, while you strive to claim that possession for me which I try to claim for you. What single cause of the rhetoricians has ever had an actor or defendant of this kind? My dear Pico, I will never "hand over the grass" <note>original: "herbam porrigam." An ancient Roman idiom meaning to admit defeat</note> to you in this fight unless we first agree with good grace that since you do not succumb otherwise, each of us shall be judged equally as teacher and student to the other. But joking aside, let us act seriously: both your *Heptaplus* and you yourself can rightly be pleased with you. Since you have secured all the votes of learned men so thoroughly that no envy appears even in a hidden corner of the tablet. One must hope that the same will be more easily granted to you in your remaining writ-

<column-break/>

-ings, when experience is also added, which is accustomed to becoming the best master in writing. As for me, I rejoice greatly to be on the lips of Lorenzo <note>Lorenzo "il Magnifico" de' Medici</note>—a man praised and to be praised by everyone and everywhere—especially with the added "pebble" <note>original: "calculo." A stone used for voting; here meaning a vote of approval</note> of Poliziano. I so embrace his copious and secret reading of manifold discipline that I admire it; I so admire it that I do not cease to commend it. Thus it happens that I consider it like a triumph to be placed by him outside the "hazard" <note>original: "aleam." Referring to a game of dice; meaning he is beyond the risk of failure</note> of learning. As for your asking for an index of my books, that is laborious and useless for me; it will be enough if you serve my requests according to the occasion. Now I desire Martianus Capella <note>Author of an early medieval encyclopedia on the liberal arts</note> and Seneca’s *Natural Questions*, provided the codices are corrected; for those among us need the work of a Sibyl <note>A prophetess; implying the books are so corrupted they require divine inspiration to decipher</note>. If I can buy them printed, it will be more pleasing to me; if not, they will return to you after a short "right of return" <note>original: "postliminio." A legal term for someone returning to their original status or home</note>. Farewell, my hope and the hope of good disciplines, and continue to love me. Ferrara, the Nones of December, 1489.

# Angelo Poliziano to his own Giovanni Pico della Mirandola. Greetings. Letter XIX.

<margin>He gives thanks for the work *On Being and One* dedicated to him.</margin> I have burned almost always—perhaps too shamelessly—but I have always burned with a desire for your fame, so much so that glory conferred on me while alive was considered as nothing. But since what I was writing hardly promised even the antiquity of a name, you, Pico, stood forth and provided what I could not by dedicating to me, namely, your commentary *On the One and Being* (for so you make the title). In it, you recall those running through the Lyceum and the Academy back to a single head, and since philosophy is more "one" than "twin," you also join our theology to it. <margin>Allusion to a fable</margin> Therefore, why should I now seek the grass of Glaucus <note>A reference to a mythical fisherman who became immortal after eating a magical herb</note>, since I am to live eternally through you? But posterities will tell, both of you and with you, that there was once a certain Poliziano whom the great Pico himself—the light of all the learned—valued so much that he did not hesitate to name for him his most beautiful book on the highest matters. And so I give you thanks for immortality—but immortal thanks. Farewell.

# Marsilio Ficino, Florentine, to Germain de Ganay, President of Paris. Greetings. Letter XX.

<margin>In the year of salvation 1493 <note>Likely an error for 1494</note>, on the day King Charles of the Franks entered Florence in September, Giovanni Pico, Count of Mirandola, migrated from this shadow of life in his 32nd year, etc.</margin> You wish to be more certain about the death of Pico della Mirandola, which still seems uncertain to you; you certainly wish to grieve more heavily, Germain. For since you have grieved heavily until now in this ambiguous loss, once you are made more certain, you will, I think, soon grieve most heavily. Perhaps it was better to mourn a doubtful loss than to be tortured by a certain one. Alas, what you ask, my most longed-for Germain! I would rather remain in doubt myself. Nor can I, without tears, make you more certain at present. Last November, on the day when the great Charles, King of the Franks, entered our city of Florence <note>November 17, 1494. Charles VIII's invasion was a pivotal moment in Italian history</note>, our Mirandola deserted us. He affected the learned with almost as much grief as the King meanwhile brought joy to the city; thus the provident spirit of the place compensated for the joy of the people with the groans of the learned, and in place of the extinguished philosophical light, he meanwhile lit a royal light. Lest perhaps Florence should seem darker on that day, the light of the man of Mirandola, extinguished on earth, was returned to heaven. On that day, Pico migrated from this shadow of life with such cheerful security that he seemed undoubtedly about to return from exile into his heavenly fatherland. You desire, moreover, to know what Pico once composed, or what he was recently composing: he wrote the *Heptaplus*, the *Apologia*, and *On the One and Being*, as well as several letters. Whatever he had composed concerning love while his youth was still burning, he later condemned with a more mature judgment; and he wished it entirely...

<meta>This page continues the correspondence of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola and his scholarly circle. OF THE LETTERS.

...that the joined treaties may be understood without controversy: but I reserve the deeper repetition and more wordy explanation of this for another time. I come to you, my Robert <note>Roberto Salviati, a Florentine nobleman and close friend of Pico</note>, an excellent man indeed: whom I love uniquely from your writings. Although they are very few, they show such a specimen of your virtue that they promise no less a harvest of talent to come than the very pleasing hope of little flowers they now offer. Know, therefore, that your friend from Mirandola <note>original: "iunianum," likely a reference to Pico's family territory or a nickname used in this circle</note> is, and will be in whatever you send me hereafter of your writings, no less a herald of your affairs than a lover of you for that very reason. 

Victorius <note>Likely Victorio, a mutual acquaintance</note> therefore praises the excellence of your talent and your learned refinement in these letters, so that I am provoked to desire and praise the same. One thing, however, I ask: that since Victorius has invited me to love you with his charming encouragements, you do not cease to pursue me with that refinement which you profess and embrace. Therefore, you may expect my laziness to be overcome so that I write to you more often, provided you do not despise my efforts. And if, based on the words of our friend Victorius, you do not neglect my friendship, you will provoke me to follow you with every duty by the bond of our close relationship. For there is nothing I would prefer more than to contend with noble and learned men in mutual love and the exchange of letters. Give my love to your town of Mirandola—which you praise as a pillar of humanity and which I myself dare to call the delight of nature—and say that I am well. Farewell, from Naples, the day before the Nones of June <note>June 4th</note>, 1490.

### SUMMARY OF THE TWELVE RULES FOR LIVING WELL.

**T**he first rule: if the way of virtue seems hard to a man because we must continually fight against the flesh, the devil, and the world, let him remember that whatever life he chooses, even according to the world, he must suffer many adversities, sadness, inconveniences, and labors.

The second rule: let him remember that in worldly affairs, one fights longer, more laboriously, and more fruitlessly. In those things, labor is the end of labor, and at last comes eternal punishment.

The third rule: let him remember that it is foolish to believe that heaven can be reached except through a struggle of this kind, just as our head, Christ, did not ascend into heaven except through the cross; nor should the condition of the servant be better than the condition of the master.

The fourth rule: let him remember not only to endure this fight with difficulty, but even to desire it, even if no reward were to come to us from it, solely so that we might be conformed to Christ our God and Lord. Every time you resist a temptation or do violence to one of your senses, think of which part of Christ’s cross you are being made to conform to. When resisting gluttony you afflict your taste, remember that He was given gall and vinegar to drink. When you pull back your hands from stealing something that pleases you, think of His hands fixed for you to the wood of the cross. If you resist pride, remember Him who, although He was in the form of God, took the form of a servant for you <note>original: "formam servi." A reference to Philippians 2:7</note> and humbled Himself even unto death on a cross. When you are tempted by anger, remember Him who was God and the most just of all men, yet when He saw Himself treated like a thief, mocked, spat upon, scourged, afflicted with every insult, and counted among thieves, He never showed any sign of anger or indignation, but bearing all things most patiently, 

->Pleasure is brief and meager.<-
->The companions are disgust and anxiety.<-
->The loss of a greater good.<-

<column-break/>

responded to everyone most gently. And so, by running through each thing, you may find that there is no passion which does not make you conform to Christ in some part.

The fifth rule: that you should not trust in those twelve weapons, nor in any other human remedy, but in the power of Jesus Christ alone, who said, "have confidence, I have overcome the world" <note>John 16:33</note>, and elsewhere, "the prince of this world shall be cast out." Therefore, let us also trust in His power alone to be able to conquer the world and overcome the devil. And for this reason, we ought always to ask for His help through prayer and the prayer of His saints.

The sixth rule: remember that when you have conquered one temptation, another is always to be expected, because the devil always circles about seeking someone to devour. Therefore, it is necessary always to serve in fear and to say with the prophet, "I will stand upon my watch."

The seventh rule: that you should not only avoid being conquered by the devil when he tempts you, but that you should conquer him. This happens when you not only do not sin, but take the very thing he tempted you with as an occasion for some good. For example, if he offers you some good work of yours so that you might fall into vanity, you should immediately think of it not as your own work, but as a gift of God, humbling yourself and judging yourself to be poorly grateful to God for His benefits.

The eighth rule: that when you fight, you should fight as if by winning you would thereafter have perpetual peace. For perhaps God will give you this by His grace, and the devil will no longer return, confounded by your victory. But when you have won, conduct yourself as if you are about to fight soon, so that in the fight you may always have victory, and in victory, you may always be mindful of the fight.

The ninth rule: that although you feel yourself well-fortified and ready on all sides, you should nevertheless always flee the occasions of sinning, because as the wise man says, "he who loves danger will perish in it."

The tenth rule: that in temptations you should always meet them at the beginning and dash the "little ones of Babylon" against the rock <note>A common medieval allegorical interpretation of Psalm 137:9, where the "infants" are early sinful thoughts and the "rock" is Christ</note>. But the rock is Christ, for medicine is prepared too late when the illness has taken hold.

The eleventh rule: remember that although the fight may seem bitter in the conflict of temptation itself, it is nevertheless far sweeter to conquer the temptation than to go toward the sin to which it inclines you. In this, many are deceived because they do not compare the sweetness of victory to the sweetness of sin; instead, they compare the struggle to the pleasure. Yet a man who has experienced a thousand times what it is to yield to temptation ought to experience at least once what it is to conquer temptation.

The twelfth rule: because you are tempted, do not believe yourself to be forsaken by God, or to be little pleasing to God, or little just and perfect. Remember that after Paul saw the divine essence, he suffered a temptation of the flesh, which God permitted him to be tempted by so that he would not be tempted by pride. In this, a man ought to notice that Paul, who was a "chosen vessel" and caught up even to the third heaven, was nevertheless in danger of becoming proud of his virtues, just as he says of himself: "lest the greatness of the revelations should exalt me, there was given to me a thorn in my flesh to buffet me" <note>2 Corinthians 12:7</note>. Therefore, above all temptations, a man ought most to fortify himself against the temptation of pride, because pride is the root of all evils. Against this, the unique remedy is to think always that God humbled Himself for us even to the cross, and death will humble us—even against our will—so far that we shall be food for worms.

Twelve weapons of spiritual warfare which ought to be kept ready when the desire for sinning subdues the mind:

->Eternal reward, eternal punishment.<-
->The dignity and nature of man.<-
->The peace of a good mind.<-

M

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's spiritual reflections, moving from the personal "Twelve Rules" seen on the previous page to a formal commentary on Psalm 15 (Psalm 16 in modern Bibles). Here, Pico transitions into a more traditional scholastic exposition, though he maintains his characteristic blend of Platonic philosophy and Christian devotion.</meta>

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM 15 OF DAVID.

| | |
|---|---|
| Life is a sleep and a shadow. | The benefits of God. |
| Death is imminent and unforeseen. | The Cross of Christ. |
| The suspicion of impenitence. | Testimonies of the martyrs and examples of the saints. |

->The twelve conditions of a lover,<-
<note>While the heading promises twelve, the following list contains eleven distinct points of devotion.</note>

To love only one and to despise all things for him.
To consider him unhappy who is not with the beloved:
To suffer all things to be with him, even death. ->To adorn oneself to please him.<-
To be with him in whatever way possible: and if not in reality, at least in thought.
To love all things which pertain to him: all friends, the house, clothes, and images.
To desire his praises and to be unable to endure any shame toward him.
To believe all the highest things of him, and to desire that all others believe the same.
To choose even to suffer some inconvenience for him, and for that inconvenience to be sweet.
To weep with him often, whether out of pain if he is absent, or out of joy if he is present.
To always languish and always burn with desire for him.

---

To serve him while thinking nothing of a prize or reward. We are usually led to this service chiefly for three reasons. The first is when the service itself is desirable on its own; the second is when he whom we serve is in himself very good and lovable, just as we usually say we serve him <term>propter</term> <note>Latin: "on account of"</note> his virtues. The third is when he has bestowed many benefits upon you before you even began; and these three are found in God because <term>per</term> <note>Latin: "through"</note> his service nothing is newly received that is not already good for us, both regarding the soul and regarding the body, for to serve him is nothing other <term>than</term> <note>original: "quam"</note> to stretch toward him: that is, toward the highest good. Similarly, he himself is the best, the most beautiful, and the wisest; he possesses all the conditions that usually move us to love someone and serve him freely, and he has bestowed the greatest benefits upon us since he created us from nothing and redeemed us from hell through the blood of his son.

### Preserve me, O Lord.

<margin>Note:</margin>
If any perfected man wishes to examine his own state, he faces one danger: that he might grow proud of his own virtue. Therefore David, speaking in the person of the just man regarding his state, begins with this word "preserve me," which, if rightly considered, removes every occasion for pride. For he who can acquire something by himself can also preserve it by himself. He, therefore, who asks to be preserved by God in a state of virtue signifies by this <term>that</term> <note>original: "quod"</note> he did not acquire that virtue by himself from the beginning. Moreover, he who remembers that he attained virtue not by his own power, but by the power of God, cannot be proud of it, but is rather humbled before God according to that saying of the Apostle: "What do you have <term>that</term> <note>original: "quod"</note> you have not received? And if you have received it, why do you boast as if you had not received it?" <note>Referring to 1 Corinthians 4:7</note> There are, therefore, two phrases we should always have in our mouths: one is "Have mercy on me, O God," when we remember our sins. The other is "Preserve me, O God," when we remember our virtues.

### Because I have hoped in you.

<margin>Just and good things must be asked for, and so on.</margin>
This is the one thing that makes us obtain what we ask from God: namely, when we hope that we will obtain it. And if we observe these two conditions—that we never ask anything from God except those things which are healthy for us, and that we ask for what we desire ardently with a firm hope—then God will not fail to hear us, and our prayers will never be in vain. For when we do not know what to ask, as Christ says, and Jesus said "whatever you ask in my name will be given to you," this name "Jesus" signifies "Savior." Therefore, nothing is asked in the name of Jesus unless <term>that</term> <note>original: "quod"</note> which pertains to the salvation of the one asking. Otherwise, he does not hear: because if we ask for good things, we do not ask "well"—that is, with little hope. He who hopes timidly asks coldly; therefore James said: "Let him ask in faith, doubting nothing."

### I said to the Lord: You are my God.

After he has fortified himself against pride, he begins to de-

<column-break/>

scribe his state. The whole state of the just man consists in this phrase: "I said to the Lord: You are my God." Although this phrase seems common to almost everyone, there are few who can truly say it. For a person has <term>as</term> <note>original: "is... pro"</note> his god whatever he holds as his highest good. We hold that as our highest good which, if we possess it alone even if other things are lacking, we think ourselves happy; and which, if it alone is missing even if we have all other goods, we think ourselves miserable. Thus the greedy man says to his money: "You are my god," because even if he lacks honor, health, virtue, and friends, as long as he has money, he is content. And if he has all those goods we mentioned but lacks money, he thinks himself unhappy. Likewise, the glutton says it to his overindulgence, the incontinent to his lust, and the ambitious to his power or glory: "You are my god." See, therefore, how few can truly say, "I said to the Lord: You are my God," because he alone can say this for whom God alone is sufficient—so much so that if all the kingdoms of the world and all celestial and earthly goods were offered to him, he would not offend God even once to obtain them. In this saying, therefore, consists the entire state of the just man.

<margin>To whom the title "Lord" is truly fitting.</margin>

### Since you have no need of my goods.

<margin>Whence that saying of Plato: that we are not born for ourselves.</margin>
He gives the reason for his proposition: namely, why he says to the Lord alone, "You are my God." The reason is that God alone does not need our goods. There is no creature <term>that</term> <note>original: "quod"</note> does not need other creatures due to its imperfections, as philosophers and theologians prove; for if those other things did not exist, these would not exist. Because if one part of the universe is destroyed, the whole universe is destroyed; and if the universe is destroyed, all parts are destroyed. All creatures are parts of one universe, but God himself is not a part of this universe but its beginning, depending on nothing. For God acquired nothing from the fact <term>that</term> <note>original: "quod"</note> he created the world, and he would lose nothing if the whole world were annihilated. Therefore, God alone does not need our goods. We should be ashamed to hold him as a god who needs our goods, which is true of every creature. Furthermore, we ought not to have as God—that is, as the highest good—anything except that in which the "Total Good" resides; but in no creature is there every good. Therefore, to the Lord alone we must say: "You are my God."

<margin>Why the riches of the Saracens fall.</margin>

### To the saints who are in his land.

After God, we must especially love those who are most closely joined to God, such as the Angels and the blessed in the Fatherland <note>A common theological term for Heaven</note>. Therefore, after he said to the Lord, "You are my God," he adds that God—

### Has made his wills wonderful to mine.

That is, he made his loves and his desires wonderful toward the saints <term>who</term> <note>original: "qui"</note> are in his land: that is, in the heavenly homeland, which is called the land of God and the land of the living. And truly, if we consider how great the happiness of that homeland is, and how great the misery of this world...

<sig>o ii</sig>

<meta>The text cuts off mid-sentence, following the catchword "ta" (from "tanta") to the next page.</meta>

<meta>This page continues the formal commentary on Psalm 15 (known as Psalm 16 in modern Bibles). Following the previous page's introduction to the spiritual conditions of a lover of God, Pico now analyzes the biblical text verse by verse, contrasting the "infirmities" of idolaters with the "inheritance" of the faithful.</meta>

# EXPOSITION.

<margin>Metaphorically, the earth is called heaven to us.</margin>
Because of the goodness and brilliance of those citizens, we will always desire to depart from here so that we may dwell there. However, when we meditate on these and similar things, we must always take care that our meditations are not fruitless. Instead, from every meditation we ought to acquire some virtue. Specifically, from this meditation on the goodness of that heavenly homeland, we ought to acquire the virtue of bearing death not only bravely and patiently when our hour comes—or if we must face it for the sake of the Christian faith—but even to desire it willingly. We should long to depart from this valley of miseries so that we may reign with God and His saints in that happy homeland. Therefore, when the just man has described his state, which is entirely focused on God, and looks down from on high at the state of wicked men, he says: *Their infirmities were multiplied; afterwards they hastened.* <note>Psalm 15:4. Pico is using the Vulgate numbering.</note>

By "infirmities," however, he understands idols, and the Hebrew text holds this meaning as well. <note>The Hebrew word 'atsebōt' can mean both "sorrows/infirmities" and "idols."</note> For just as a good man has one God whom he worships, so the wicked have many gods and idols because they have many pleasures, many vain desires, and various passions which they serve. They seek many pleasures because they find none that can satisfy them; therefore, they wander in circles. He adds *afterwards they hastened* <note>original: "acclamauerunt" / "accelerauerunt"</note> because they rush headlong and without consideration after their desires. From this we are taught that we should run no less quickly toward virtues than they run toward vice, nor should we serve our Lord less diligently than they serve their lord, the devil. The just man, considering the state of the wicked, firmly resolves (as we always ought to do) to never follow them, saying: *through my lips.*

<margin>The custom of idolaters.</margin>
->I will not gather their meetings of blood, nor will I be mindful of the error of their names.<-

He speaks of "blood" partly because idolaters used to perform their ceremonies around the collected blood of victims, and partly because the entire life of the wicked follows sensuality—which is seated in the blood—rather than reason. He said that he not only refuses to sacrifice to idols but will not even name them, which is all that can be said or done. By this, he shows that a perfect man must abstain not only from illicit pleasures but even from licit ones, so that he may be carried more fully toward heaven and devote himself more purely to the contemplation of divine things. And because someone might believe it is foolishness to deprive oneself of all pleasure, he adds:

->The Lord is the portion of my inheritance and of my cup.<-

It is as if he says: do not wonder if I leave all other things to possess God, in whom all other good things are ultimately found. This ought to be the voice of every good Christian: "The Lord is the portion of my inheritance." Since we are Christians to whom God Himself is promised as an inheritance, we should blush to desire anything besides Him. And because it might seem like presumption to dare to promise these things to oneself, he adds:

->You are the one who will restore my inheritance to me.<-

As if to say: "Lord my God, I know well that since I am nothing in respect to You, I cannot ascend to possess You by my own strength. But You are the one who draws me to You by Your grace, and You are the one who will give Yourself to be possessed by me." Then the just man considers how great this happiness is, that God has fallen to him as an inheritance, and he adds:

<margin>The lot-casting of the ancients.</margin>
->The lines have fallen for me in excellent places.<- <note>The "lines" or "cords" refer to measuring ropes used to divide land into inherited plots.</note>

For in ancient times, portions and lots were divided by ropes. And since there are many who, although they are called to this happiness as all Christians are, nevertheless value it as nothing—often exchanging it for some light pleasure—he adds:
<sig>ii 6</sig>

<column-break/>

->For my inheritance is excellent to me.<-

As if to say: just as the inheritance itself is excellent, so I regard it as excellent. All other things in respect to it I count as dung, as Paul used to say. <note>A reference to Philippians 3:8.</note> Moreover, to have this light of the intellect so that a man recognizes the happiness given to him is a gift from God; therefore he adds:

->I will bless the Lord who has given me understanding.<-

Furthermore, because a man often judges according to reason that he should serve God, but the sensuality and the flesh rebel, a man is only then perfect when not only his soul but also his flesh are carried toward God, according to that saying: *My heart and my flesh have rejoiced in the living God.* <note>Psalm 84:2.</note> Therefore he adds:

->Moreover, even until night my reins have rebuked me.<- <note>The "reins" or kidneys were traditionally considered the seat of the emotions and lower desires.</note>

That is, the reins themselves, in which there is usually the greatest inclination toward lust, do not only fail to incline me toward evil, but rather "rebuke" me. This means they pull me back even "until night," meaning to such an extent that they even willingly afflict their own body. For affliction is often designated by the term "night." He then shows what the root of such great self-denial is, saying:

<margin>Just as night is the privation of light, so affliction is the cause of the privation of pleasure.</margin>
->I set the Lord always before my sight.<-

For if anyone always had God before his eyes as the rule for all his actions, and in all his works sought neither his own utility, nor glory, nor pleasure, but only to please God, he would shortly emerge as perfect. And because he who acts this way always prospers in all things, he says:

->Because he is at my right hand, I shall not be moved.<-

He then shows how great the happiness of the just man is: because he will be happy forever in both soul and body. Therefore he adds:

->Because of this my heart is glad and my tongue has exulted.<-

That is: my soul is joyful, knowing that after death heaven is prepared for it.

->Moreover, my flesh also shall rest in hope.<-

<margin>Whence (according to Thomas) happiness arises from hope.</margin> <note>A reference to Thomas Aquinas's theology on the theological virtue of Hope.</note>
That is: although the flesh itself does not rejoice as if it were to receive its state immediately after death, it nevertheless rests in burial with this hope: that it will rise again on the day of judgment with its soul, immortal and most splendid. He declares all of this in the following verse. For because he had said the soul was glad, he adds the reason:

->Because you will not leave my soul in hell.<- <note>The "underworld" or the state of the dead.</note>

And because he had said the flesh rested in hope, he adds the reason, saying:

->Nor will you allow your holy one to see corruption.<-

<margin>See how those things [pertain].</margin>
Because that which was corruptible will rise again incorruptible. And because Christ was the first who entered paradise and opened life to us, and was the first who rose again—and His resurrection is the principal cause of ours—therefore these things which we have said about the resurrection are understood principally regarding Christ (as the Apostle Peter declared) and secondarily can be understood regarding us, insofar as we are members of Christ. He alone did not see corruption because His body did not rot in the tomb. Since, therefore, the way of living well leads us to the perpetual life of soul and body, he adds:

->You have made known to me the ways of life.<-

And because the total happiness of this life consists in the open vision and enjoyment of God, he adds:

->You will fill me with joy with your countenance.<-

And because this happiness will last forever, he adds:

->Delights are in your right hand even unto the end.<-

He says "in your right hand" because our happiness is completed in the vision and enjoyment of the humanity of Christ, who sits at the right hand of majesty on high, according to that saying of John.

<summary>Pico provides a line-by-line commentary on Psalm 15, interpreting the text as a journey from the rejection of worldly "idols" to the hope of bodily resurrection through Christ. He emphasizes that true happiness is found in the "inheritance" of God, achieved through grace rather than human strength.</summary>

# EULOGIES FOR GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA BY MOST ILLUSTRIOUS MEN.

> This is the whole reward: that we may see God and Jesus Christ whom you have sent. The End. <note>original: "Hęc est tota merces vt videamus Deum & quem mi- sisti Ieſum Chriſtum. Finis." This is a reference to John 17:3.</note>

### From a letter of Hermolaus Barbarus to Giovanni Pico.

<image-desc>A decorative capital 'P' showing a scholar in a landscape, looking up toward the light of heaven.</image-desc>
Your genius is distinguished and clearly divine, Pico: for although those things which you write are the best, you nevertheless express and shape the "worst" writings of others <note>This refers to the medieval Scholastic philosophers, whom the Humanists called "barbaric" because of their rough Latin style.</note> in such a way that they seem to be your own—which are the best. For I consider it a greater feat to lower oneself and descend than to strive for the heights. For while the latter is more honorable, the former is certainly more laborious and a work of greater effort. Accordingly, whether you believe those writings of ours are such that you should spend effort imitating them, or whether you do this for the sake of earning my favor, I am deeply indebted to you in either case. I do not wish to say I will return the favor when I am able (for I will never be able), but rather when you yourself or your family <note>original: "vel tussi po i me putabis"</note> deem me capable. For such is the goodness and kindness of your family that you are accustomed to count as a benefit that which is not one. Therefore, it will be to my advantage if I leave both the manner and the time of repaying this favor to you, so that in the balancing of accounts every miscalculation—and the entire claim—may proceed not from me, but from you. Indeed, those things you wrote about the plan of your studies, which you wished to share with me, affected me with the greatest pleasure. I congratulated this century for a man of such great learning that he knows almost nothing of which he is ignorant, and such great care that he seems to know nothing at all. <note>A classic Humanist paradox: Pico's humility makes him seem like a beginner even though he knows everything.</note> I see you as an excellent poet and a most eminent orator. I notice that you, who were previously an Aristotelian philosopher, have now also become a Platonic one. I see that you have not merely learned but have truly "drunk in" Greek letters—which alone could have been missed in you, and without which you would have been nothing—and you did so with such ease and speed that you yourself do not remember, nor can you persuade others, that you were ever ignorant of Greek. This is something I proclaim about my friend Hieronymus Donatus no more gladly than I do truly. I would urge you toward these letters so that you might hold them as clearly and familiarly as Latin, but you do not need spurs; and so forth.

### From another letter of the same to the same.

Just recently, when I myself—in a certain corner of my letters to you, acting as if on another matter and in passing—had attacked the "barbaric" philosophers of our age, and when you wrote back that you also had become hostile to them and had sent them a formal "notice of divorce," you then seized this opportunity and sent us a work: an ancient dispute and controversy between us and them regarding the style of speaking used by philosophers, comprised and explained in many thousands of verses. <note>Pico's famous 1485 letter defending the Scholastics against Hermolaus's criticisms.</note> It is an elegant, learned, and elaborate work, finished with such speed that—had I not possessed the most perfect knowledge of your genius—I would have believed this argument had been prepared by you long ago so that you could bring it forth at the first opportunity. But so that the matter might turn out both more festive and more pleasant for me, you—a most witty, most kind, and most Latin-fluent man—defend a barbarian against a barbarian! You stand and pretend to act as a patron, as an enemy for an enemy, a companion against a companion, yourself against yourself; and so forth.

### From the same [letter] further down.

Now, if there is anyone so outstanding that he can grasp those things which you have said—provided as they are with such great cultivation, so many lights, and so many "emblems" <note>ornaments of speech</note> that dazzle the eyes of those who approach. Add to this so many stimulating thoughts, so many histories and examples of remote learning, like little flowers and altogether <meta>catchword: to</meta>

<column-break/>

which—if there are any of those people who are only slightly less "asses" (he wanted to say "unrefined" <note>original: "αμυσοι" (amusoi) - literally those without the Muses, meaning ignorant or uncultured.</note>), they only twitch their ears; the rest flee, reject them, detest them; and so forth.

### From another of the same.

Greetings. I have received Pico’s book on the narration of the seven days <note>Pico's *Heptaplus*, a mystical commentary on Genesis.</note>, a copy of which Jacobus Volateranus <note>Giacomo Gherardi, a papal diplomat and diarist.</note>, the envoy of the Supreme Pontiff, had also recently sent to me. I ran through the work as much as was permitted amidst the heat and dust. It is a creation worthy of a divine and admirable genius; truly, the "harvest" and material of the work do not demand a hasty opinion composed for the present moment. But at the same time, it can be said that it is almost a miracle that Pico, so learned, eloquent, and Christian, has achieved all these things at such an age. I owe you very much.

### From another of the same to the same.

Although I love these letters of yours because they flow, because they are not affected, and because they—I will not say they do not know care—but they reject it; that is, they do not receive it by design, and they exclude care when it approaches and desires to be inserted. Thus, there are indeed deep traces of diligence in them, but they are in a way repressed and repudiated. I am not so skillful that I can look into your genius and estimate its magnitude and fecundity. I seem to see this—and perhaps I am not deceived—where you are directing and aiming, and likewise where you will end up, and indeed very soon. Nothing is more noble than that character of yours, nothing more delightful <note>original: "risibilius"</note>, and let it be said once and for all, nothing is more promising, even if it seems a bit harsh—if indeed it should be called "character" which has produced fruits that should not be despised even by those of mature age and practiced learning. Come now, how great a spirit—as I hear—is in your poetry! What happiness, what vigor, and finally, what nobility and splendor in every act, especially in letters. What about when you act the philosopher? What memory! What great subtlety! What speed of mind, harmonizing with the vigor of the whole body! But I am carried away into your praises against my will—or rather, quite willingly—for everyone most desires that which turns them toward itself even when they are unwilling and reluctant. A time more suited to this duty will surely be given. Now I come to that [matter]; and so forth.

### From a letter of Angelo Poliziano to Pico regarding the dispute with Hermolaus.

Wherefore, my Pico, most learned of all learned men, I must now approach you—not indeed as a judge, but as an honorary arbitrator: namely, so that you may settle the suit between friends who are in disagreement.

### From the preface of the *Miscellany* of the same [Poliziano].

For regarding that man who is to be admired above all others—no longer a "Pico" <note>A pun on Pico's name: *Picus* is Latin for "woodpecker."</note> but (as I myself am accustomed to call him) rather a "Phoenix" who now nests in your laurel—my expectation is so great that I dare to sing along with Propertius: "Give way, Roman writers, give way, Greeks!" <note>original: "Cedite Romani scriptores cedite grai." A famous line from Propertius's Elegies praising Virgil.</note>

### From Chapter 14 of the same work.

The same is both prepared and shown by my Giovanni Pico of Mirandola, the one man of all who is utterly most blessed in every part. He shows this in a singular and admirable work in which he teaches that the Psalm translated by the Seventy <note>The Septuagint (the Greek Old Testament).</note> corresponds to the Hebraic truth <note>The Hebrew original.</note>, especially by the argument of those marks. Let the Jew no longer be able to object to us in an "un-saluted" way <note>rudely or without cause</note> that we sing those things in the temple every hour which we ourselves do not believe to be translated faithfully enough.

### From Chapter 90 of the same.

Such a man is also this Giovanni Pico of mine, from Mirandola. Among princes...

<meta>This page continues the "Eulogies" or testimonials from famous Renaissance scholars regarding Giovanni Pico della Mirandola. The previous page ended with a letter from Hermolaus Barbarus. This page concludes these testimonials and begins the "Prooemium" (Preface) to Pico's famous work attacking astrology.</meta>

...a most perfect work of nature, from which Latin philosophy—now preparing to speak—will, I believe, receive its highest peak.

### From Chapter 94 of the same. <note>original: "Ex Cap. eiufdem LXXXXIIII." Referring to Angelo Poliziano’s Miscellanea.</note>

Pico and I once ran through the ancient commentators of the Sacred Instrument <note>The Bible; "Instrument" was a common humanist term for the Testaments.</note> during our spare hours, specifically the Greek authors: Diodorus, Philo, Gennadius, Aquila, Origen, Basil, Didymus, Isidore, Apollinaris, Severianus, and many others of that kind. Like the opinions of the Latins, he compares all of theirs most diligently with the views of the Jewish and Chaldean <note>Usually refers to Aramaic or Hebrew interpreters.</note> interpreters, ventilating and weighing every detail: from which truth might be drawn out, obscurity removed, faith strengthened, or impiety refuted.

### From the conclusion of the same work.

Until this most noble prince, Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, returned to this city <note>Florence</note>, drawn both by the benevolence of Lorenzo de' Medici and by their similarity in virtue and genius. He is a man—or rather a hero—most filled with all the gifts of fortune, body, and soul. He is a young man of almost commanding beauty and eminent majesty of body; of the sharpest genius, singular memory, and tireless study, as well as clear and polished eloquence. It is uncertain whether he is more wonderful in his judgment or his character. Now, he is also most steeped in all philosophy and a diverse literature of languages; he is fortified and instructed by reasons and actions beyond the midday <note>An idiom for being "beyond his years" or "at the peak of his powers."</note>; finally, to sum it up at once, he is greater than any praise, etc.

### From the second Commentary of Filippo Beroaldo on Propertius, regarding the verse *Non tot Achemeniis*.

I read "Sussa" written instead of "Ethrusca" <note>This is a technical point of textual criticism. Pico suggested a correction to an ancient Roman poem by Propertius based on his own manuscripts.</note> in the book of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, who is a man worthy of the memory of ages, endowed with many diverse disciplines. He adorns the glory of our age. To him can be applied what Terentianus wrote of Varro: "Pico, a most learned man from every side." He not only likes but vehemently loves you, my Minus <note>Referring to the scholar Mino Rossi.</note>—as one most learned loves the learned, and one most noble loves the noble. He speaks honorably of you and thinks highly of you. After his more serious studies, he is accustomed to rest in the reading of Propertius as if in a most pleasant inn. He agreed with me reading this passage and showed me that in his book it was written "Sussa" and not "Ethrusca," etc.

### From the book of John, Abbot of Sponheim. <note>Johannes Trithemius, a famous German polymath and cryptographer.</note>

Giovanni Pico, an Italian by nation, Count of Mirandola and Lord of Concordia, is a man most studious of all good literature. Just as he is of noble blood, so too is he most noble by his divine genius. Surrounded by a great crowd of arts of all kinds, he is worthy and most deserving. The Muses follow his journey. He is the most learned philosopher of our age and a most sharp debater. He wrote in a most elegant style several things which our age will both approve and especially admire, through which he has made the memory of his name and glory not unworthily eternal.

### From the preface of the *Book of Recoveries* by Matteo Bosso.

With that same Poliziano, the distinguished and most famous Giovanni Mirandola read once and several times to the very end. Everyone is stunned by his genius, which is above human and all-encompassing learning. From his integrity and the brilliance of his soul, all delusion and blind confession is absent.

### From the Letter of Jacopo Antiquari to Angelo Poliziano.

# PREFACE OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA, COUNT OF CONCORDIA, TO THE DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGERS.

<margin>Homer. Caecilius.</margin>
Homer and Caecilius, the most ancient poets, proclaim that the worst enemies are those who circumvent us under the appearance of friends. No truer sentence can be said; no more healthy precept can be given. Why do we need the testimony of poets? Since divine truth, the teacher of life and morals, warned us to avoid wolves in sheep's clothing and cautioned us not to judge by appearance. Indeed, this is the one kind of enemy that can neither be turned away nor overturned, and whom we ourselves do not wish to overcome. Instead, we run to meet them, kiss them willingly, and receive them. We stand with them against ourselves, rather than against them as we ought. This deception, because it costs us dearly, must be looked into more deeply and examined longer; it should not be admitted rashly nor immediately put to flight. But where the fallacy is detected, it must be exploded all the more sharply, as it was sliding in for our destruction more covertly under the pretext of a benefit. Evils are no less to be thought of as such even if they do not seem to be the worst because they are sometimes mixed with good things—for they harm all the more fatally as they are more easily admitted through the appearance and mixture of good. Once admitted, they occupy the mind more tenaciously and retain it more powerfully. In the same way, if poison is drunk with pure wine, although the wine is most healthy by its nature, it nevertheless hides the malice of the poison with its flavor and drives it more quickly and deeply into the veins. This must be observed both in all life and especially in the arts and disciplines. Those are most ruinous which, being deceptions or some other kind of vanities, have nevertheless held out some allure for the lie, or claimed the name of science or art for themselves. Whether that allure was sought from antiquity through fictional authors, or from the lure of human curiosity and greed by great promises, or from some paint and appearance of probability—since sometimes false things are more probable than true ones.

<margin>Aristotle</margin>
With Aristotle as witness, this is especially true for the common people and the multitude who have not looked inside or explored, and whose nature it has always been to err, to be deceived, and to know nothing. What is more fatal? What is more impregnable? Than when error itself insinuates itself into us under the title of wisdom, so that we give effort to what the philosopher said: that we may "be insane with reason." This is nothing other than to dismiss counsel and the mind—whose innate power alone is to drive away falsehood—so that the lie emerges more honorable by its testimony, more robust by its power, and better protected by its defense. Furthermore, there is no hope left for health when nature itself aids the disease. This, as I was saying just now...

# PREFACE TO THE WORK OF DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGY

**Left Column:**

...happens through madness: which, under the appearance of either art or science, parades itself before the people and sells itself; it is no less a madness for the fact that it counterfeits wisdom on its very surface; indeed, the more deceptive it is, the more destructive.

<margin>Resolution of the arguments.</margin>
Just as among physicians, none rave—to put it so—more deliriously than those who maintain a serious face despite their delirium. This is the peculiar stain of all superstitions, of which no other profession has claimed a title for itself more than astrology; just as among those superstitions, of which it is rightly considered the mother and nursling, it holds the primacy.

<margin>A distinction of Astrology.</margin>
When I speak of true astrology <note>In the 15th century, "astrologia" could refer to both the scientific study of stars (astronomy) and the prediction of the future. Pico is careful to distinguish between them.</note>, I do not mean that which measures the masses and motions of the stars by mathematical reasoning—a certain and noble art, most honorable in its own merits, and greatly approved by the authority of the most learned men. Rather, I mean that which pronounces what is to happen from the stars through the fraud of mercenary lying—forbidden by both civil and church <note>original: "pontificiis"</note> laws, yet retained by human curiosity; laughed at by philosophers, cultivated by charlatans, and suspected by every excellent and prudent person.

<margin>Its professors.</margin>
Whose professors were once called by the ethnic name "Chaldeans" <note>Originally referring to people from Mesopotamia, but used in Rome as a synonym for astrologers.</note> or, from the profession itself, "genethliacs" <note>Casters of birth-charts or horoscopes.</note>; soon, so that they might be ennobled by a common name, they called themselves "mathematicians" and "astrologers," as if this too were one of the liberal disciplines which spoke of the stars with reason. They separated themselves from that true mathematics by this distinction alone: that the name "astronomy" was given to the former, and "astrology" to themselves—invading the title of another with excessive and wicked zeal. Indeed, "astrology" is the name of another art, as we have declared, but this "divining" art, always struggling with this ambition to be named after the stars, we shall deign to call by not just one, but both names. In emulation of that art which treats the motion of the stars, we shall quite fittingly and according to its merit call "astrology" astrology, and "astronomy" astronomy <note>The author is sarcastically noting how practitioners use the prestigious names of science to hide their superstition.</note>. Regardless of how the name is decided, I, supported both by reasons and the judgments of the wisest men, would not hesitate to affirm that there is no other among the deceptive arts that either more deceives the gullible and unskilled, or more harms those it has persuaded by its deception; it is all the more fatal than other superstitions because it seems to approach closer to the truth. For while other superstitions show the marks of their madness and levity on their first face and hardly impose on anyone except the utterly blind, this one, harboring madness in its bosom and nourishing it in its heart, presents the appearance and habit of wisdom. If you inspect it from afar or through a lattice, you are captured by its form; if you come closer, you see with an exploring eye that it is but a shadow or a mask, and in the open light you will loathe the fallacy of darkness. So it is, certainly; it shall become clearer than light through the most manifest reasons: there is no greater fallacy, none more ruinous. It displays from afar the heavens and the planets, whence you might easily believe that in such a sublime and lucid spectacle, nothing could fail to be foreseen most truly. Soon, when you have considered more attentively, you see that the mirror is so sublime that the images of earthly things do not ascend there, and it is so bright that our weakness grows dim at its splendor. Then, when you have come closer, you will see woven...

<margin>On which matter, above others, Hyginus shows the signs with the fables of the Greeks.</margin>
...into its robe, instead of heavenly things, monstrous effigies and stars transformed into animals <note>A reference to the constellations of the Zodiac being mythological creatures.</note>, and a sky full of fables—nay, a fabricated sky instead of the true one; a sky not made by God, but feigned by astrologers. Thus it seems equipped with every foundation of an approved dogma: it circulates books entitled with great names, and provides so many reasons for its decrees, and beyond reason, experiments corroborated by such long observations and diligent notes; then it is received by the use of so many centuries and the...

<column-break/>

**Right Column:**

...approval of so many ages. It is a wonder how, through these mists and clouds, it presents to the struck eyes of the unskilled an image of itself that is both beautiful, venerable, and full of serious authority. But when you have dispelled these shadows and tricks of reason with diligent treatment, you will see that in those books there is nothing balanced; in the authors, no authority; in the reasons, nothing rational; in the experiments, nothing harmonious, nothing constant, nothing true, nothing credible, nothing solid—but rather things fighting amongst themselves: false, vain, and ridiculous. One could hardly believe that those who wrote them had any faith in what they were writing. As for vanity, you would not easily find anything that proposes more hope, or which promises greater and more desirable things to its followers. It makes itself the preserver of prudence, whose conjectures about the future it stabilizes with certain foreknowledge; but also of philosophy, the greatest part of which—concerning the heavens, as they wish—is supposedly resolved clearly through celestial influence. It is not even worth mentioning medicine, navigation, or agriculture; for it not only foretells the future for these, but even draws down the powers of the heavens to earthly things. From this, the works of all arts are supposedly most effective, and the masters of all arts easily attain what they desire. And it has persuaded not only the ancients of this, but even the moderns <note>original: "neotericis"</note>: that it contributes—if it please the gods—the greatest authority and profit to religion (to all religions, but especially to Christianity). To put it simply, imitating its master <note>Satan</note>, it promises the kingdoms of the world to those who adore it, and to those who taste its wood <note>A reference to the forbidden fruit of the Tree of Knowledge.</note>, it promises an emulation of divinity and the knowledge of good and evil. Not only is it not useful for any life purposes as it promises, but it is the most pestilential of all frauds; for it is that very thing—as we shall demonstrate—which corrupts all philosophy, adulterates medicine, weakens religion, births or strengthens superstitions, fosters idolatry, takes away prudence, pollutes morals, defames the heavens, and makes men wretched, anxious, restless, slaves instead of free, and plainly unfortunate in almost everything they must do. Since I seemed to have explored and discovered this for myself, I thought I would be committing a crime that no sacrifice could expiate if I remained silent, if I concealed it, or if I did not attempt with all my strength to wrest this poison from the hands of the gullible—especially in this age, when more than any other, every age, rank, and sex is blinded by this fraud. Moreover, one must fight all the more for the truth as it is known to have more attackers; since we desire to benefit all, so we desire to please only the good. The judgment of the multitude holds no weight when reason stands against it with the consensus of the learned. We do not look for the popular breeze, but for the light of truth and the public utility.

->The Preface ends.<-

This prayer cannot fail to be greatly praised without fault, just as the supplication to the sun itself cannot be blamed; for the unlearned and rude common folk, by the innate light of knowing the truth, proclaim this everywhere—to omit the most powerful reasons and the divine eloqu...
