# PREFACE TO THE WORK OF DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGY
### 9

...testimonies. But if such a thing is to be wished for and even demanded from the Best and Greatest <note>original: "optimo maximo," a common epithet for God, borrowed from the Roman Jupiter Optimus Maximus</note>, they must undoubtedly rejoice exceedingly: those who have not only happened to recognize good men, but have even encountered and found these very men within their own family and bound to them by the ties of blood. From this, they may attain some of those fruits which the friendship of good men produces. I neither deny nor hide that this divine generosity has fallen to me, since I discovered within my own domestic walls Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, the brother of my father Galeotto—a man truly worthy of being sought out with eager scrutiny by Apollonius <note>Apollonius of Tyana, a 1st-century philosopher who traveled to India (crossing the Caucasus) in search of wisdom.</note> across the Caucasus and among the Brahmans, even to the opposite side of the world—and I have emerged overwhelmed by many kindnesses from him. While he was living with us, I judged that I should repay him as much as I could, equal for equal; but now that he is deceased, I have decided that these duties must be repaid all the more, since the usefulness of his studies and his glory were at risk, and the Church was suffering no small loss. For this reason, I have committed certain things to writing more than once, and I have taken care to pour his long-term labors and anxious investigations into many copies. 

I have labored most of all in restoring the books that fundamentally overturn all divinatory astrology. They were sketched in such characters (which was the man's habit) due to the speed of his writing and dictating, that they seemed to present the appearance of any language other than Latin. They were so smeared with erasures that it was not easy to distinguish what should be considered deleted and what should be considered corrected; furthermore, they were torn and mangled in so many parts that it was judged they could scarcely be transcribed even by the author himself. 

I thought long and hard with myself to whom I should destine and dedicate these books (if they are not treasures rather than books), now revived and recently rescued by us from destruction. You occurred to me, most sacred prelate <note>Referring to Cardinal Oliviero Carafa.</note>, from whom I wished by no means to depart. For to whom could I more fittingly and honorably dedicate the literary monuments of a most learned man and kinsman than to you? Especially those works which refute errors opposed to our Christian religion, since you are both powerful in letters and, on account of Giovanni Tommaso Carafa, Count of Maddaloni, my father-in-law (to whom you are bound by the closest kinship), you are also joined to me in close relationship. Moreover, you hold a role among the men of the religion itself which is next to the supreme office. Receive these, therefore, willingly; and when you steal some leisure from handling the greatest affairs, read them through, I beseech you. In the reading itself, you will at once learn and rejoice that the astrological art—or, to speak more correctly, the plague—which was raging to our destruction with a cruel and elevated madness (though hiding its poison behind a deceitful face), has been most powerfully extinguished by the help of my uncle Giovanni Pico himself.

->Farewell, most distinguished father. Mirandola, June 28 <note>original: "iiii. Kal. Iulias," the fourth day before the Kalends of July.</note>.<-

->Giovanni Francesco Pico della Mirandola<-

***

Let the lovers of truth rejoice; and you who are poured out with the desire for illustrating and amplifying that truth, gladden your hearts! Behold, there come forth into public the disputations of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola against the astrologers—of that Pico whose sublimity of mind and all-encompassing learning nearly the whole world has already stood in awe. Disputations, I say, which will force the haters and attackers of truth to grieve, and those who spend their effort on astrological vanity for the 

<column-break/>

sake of extorting money to either wail and burst with rage, or to abandon their error. Nor should it diminish our solid joy that he, called to God by a death untimely for us but late for him, neither wiped nor polished these books with the final file <note>A classical metaphor for the final editing of a literary work.</note>, nor brought the final epilogue (which was to be the conclusion of the whole work) from the anvil. That is perhaps lacking for the more exuberant ornament of the work, but not for the perfect benefit of the readers. 

And although this tree of vanity and all superstitions has indeed been exploded and detested by the oracles of the prophets, stripped of its leaves, hissed off the stage, and even struck in some part by the axes of our theologians and philosophers—Greek, Latin, and Barbarian alike—and though it has been torn up by the roots and displaced by imperial laws and pontifical sanctions, it has nevertheless been brought back often by human curiosity. It has been replanted in its former pit, propped up and strengthened, so that it was never entirely eliminated or led to destruction by the most powerful instruments of reason. But now, our Pico has utterly burned and reduced to ash this unlucky tree, from the root to the trunk, from the trunk to the branches, from the branches to the leaves, with the most scorching fire of true philosophy, true theology, and the inventions and meditations of his own incomparable genius. This ash he has scattered with such a rapid blast of eloquence that any supporter or practitioner of that art (unless he be out of his mind) must either wail in lamentation over its death or leap for joy at the rejection and contempt of that vanity. 

Therefore, you literate men of all nations, arm your minds with these reasons; support yourselves with these testimonies, both human and divine. With these, as if with the heaviest double-edged axes and ignited torches, strike down, crush, tear out, and exterminate any sprouts of the cut and extinguished tree that might perhaps sprout again, hiding within the bowels of the earth through the fault of a poorly cultivated field.

# THE DISPUTATIONS OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA, COUNT OF CONCORDIA, AGAINST ASTROLOGY.

## BOOK I BEGINS.

<image-desc>Decorative initial P containing a landscape scene with a building and trees.</image-desc>

First of all, I want the reader to know that it was not our own invention or boldness to reject and confute astrology. Rather, from the earliest antiquity, it has always seemed to good judgments that this is not a profession which should introduce so many inconveniences to men and so many insanities on every side under the pretext of science and utility. Hence, it is eliminated from cities by the laws of the Caesars and of prudent men as harmful to life. Hence, it is condemned by the oracles of the prophets, the sanctions of the popes, and the voices and doctrines of the holiest men as pestilential to morals and piety. Hence, by philosophers and mathematicians—whoever has learned to be wise from books and not just to talk—it is almost entirely struggled against or confuted as being false, not useful, not possible, and no friend to philosophy. This fact, which others either do not know or deny, we are about to declare in this book before the matter is even dealt with by reasons; so that after such accusers, this accusation may not bring envy upon us, but rather may serve as a defense for the modesty of honest men, if any should take it up. We shall make our beginning, however, from the philosophers, of whom the greater...

# THE FIRST BOOK OF DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGY.
### 77

<margin>
Testimonies of the philosophers: Theodoret, Laertius, Diogenes, Plutarch. The saying of Democritus. Favorinus, Panaetius, Seneca, Cicero.
</margin>
The authority of the prudent, which is sometimes even more common than that of the prophets, indicates that Pythagoras <note>A 6th-century BCE philosopher and mathematician.</note> did not place any faith in astrology; this is attested both by Theodoret and by Diogenes Laertius and Plutarch. From this comes that famous saying of Democritus: "no one looks at what is before their feet while they search the regions of heaven." <note>original: "ante pedes nemo spectat scrutaturque cœli plagas"</note> Favorinus the Academic and Panaetius the Stoic both attacked the practice; it was mocked by Seneca and refuted by Cicero. Moreover, who is ignorant of Carneades' <note>A skeptical philosopher known for his critiques of divination.</note> arguments against it, or that Bion was hostile to diviners? If there is any madness that surpasses all others—even one that the mad Orestes <note>A figure from Greek mythology driven mad by the Furies.</note> would not approach—it is the amount of insanity contained in astrology. Neither Epicurus, nor the great leaders of philosophy like Plato and Aristotle, could agree with its many ravings; they thought it unworthy of even a single word in their entire philosophy, condemning it more by their silence than others did with their voices or writings. Indeed, I ask those who think otherwise to respond: why, in the entire course of their commentaries—where they had to explain either the properties of heavenly bodies or the causes of lower things derived from them—did they never bring up anything astrological? Or did they not think that the primary and most noble parts of the universe, the bodies moved and the movers themselves, belonged to philosophy? These are the most effective causes, without which nothing in nature can happen or be understood—if one believes they are as the astrologers claim. If it were possible to know something specific about them, as the leaders of the philosophers wrote, then to know only generalities would be the mark not of a philosopher, but of an imperfect one. Why, then, did Aristotle leave his books *On the Heavens* so meager, where he could have said so many splendid things? If he was able, ought he not to have indicated to us the efficiency, properties, and knowledge of the stars and planets? Why, in his *Meteorology*, when investigating the causes of rains, comets, and winds, does he always forget astrological matters? Why, in his books *On the Generation of Animals*, does he not refer twins, nor portentous and monstrous births, nor the sex or number of offspring, nor their form or qualities, to the stars? Nor does he even mention in passing that they *could* be so referred.

<margin>Plato.</margin>
Why does Plato do the same in the *Timaeus*? Why, before Plato, did Timaeus the Pythagorean himself—the greatest philosopher and astronomer of his time in his book *On Nature*, as Plato says—do the same? Why also Ocellus Lucanus in his book *On the World*, who was himself most eminent in philosophy by the testimony of Plato? Did they despise these things as if they were trivial? Yet if they are true, nothing could be greater. Or did they not despise them, but were simply ignorant of them? Did they live in Egypt and Babylon and yet fail to understand these things that were chanted among those peoples, known to everyone in the streets? Certainly, they did not think it was outside their profession (as we have said), unless they were ignorant of their own profession; for it would be strange to think it a philosopher’s duty to seek the tiniest properties of bees and ants, but not those of Jupiter and Saturn. This is especially true if truth on these matters is taught not only by observation but also shown by reason—as the astrological writers so strongly contend. What else can be said, then, except that Plato and Aristotle were of the opinion that the celestial bodies are not the causes of the things astrologers claim? They believed that astrology was neither an art nor a science—of which mention would otherwise have to be made alongside others—but rather one of the pastimes or frauds of charlatans. It belongs to the same class as the illusions and incantations of geomancy <note>Divination by means of earth or markings on the ground.</note> and hydromancy <note>Divination by means of water.</note>, which none of the ancient philosophers counted among the sciences and arts. For if astrology were an art, it would depend on natural science, just as medicine does. Just as a doctor borrows from the philosopher the nature of shrubs, herbs, and animals which he uses to bring health to bodies, so the astrologer should learn from the philosopher the powers and properties of the stars which he uses, and which he himself teaches how to use for prediction. As for those who think that "divinatory" astrology is a part or an end of mathematical astronomy, and has more in common with it than with natural philosophy: we shall later declare how far they are deceived.

<margin>What is the role of the natural philosopher in sidereal matters, and what is the role of the astronomer?</margin>
For now, we only remind the learned of a point placed beyond controversy: it pertains to the philosopher to know whatever concerns the substance and order of the stars.

<column-break/>

<margin>and what the astrologer is able to perform.</margin>
The task of measuring their movements and masses is delegated to the astronomer, while the task of predicting the future from their condition and position is left to the astrologer—if, indeed, any such craftsman as an "astrologer" is even conceded to exist. Otherwise, the silence of Plato and Aristotle would have been utterly drowsy and inexcusable, as they would have failed to indicate things that they should have treated with the utmost exactness. One may marvel at this everywhere in Plato, who deals with a miscellaneous and all-encompassing doctrine, and especially in Aristotle’s *Problems*. In that book, while proposing questions about mathematics and all arts and disciplines, and bringing forth solutions from every kind of doctrine (even ancient ones), not a single astrological word is ever found to escape him. The same is true in the *Eudemian Ethics* where he discusses good fortune. If we are not moved enough by this evidence, let us hear the disciples of both philosophers, who testify to that same opinion which their masters spoke to us through silence. Plotinus <note>The 3rd-century founder of Neoplatonism.</note> is held to be of the primary authority in the Platonic family.

<margin>Porphyry</margin>
Porphyry <note>A student of Plotinus and a major philosopher in his own right.</note> writes that after Plotinus had given diligent work to astrology, and had finally discovered the vanity of the art and the falsehood of its predictions, he revoked all faith in astrologers.

<margin>Maternus.</margin>
For this reason, in a dedicated book entitled *On the Influence of the Stars*, he firmly laughed at and refuted the dogmas of the astrologers. Maternus <note>Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman who wrote a famous defense of astrology.</note> takes this badly and tells many lies about Plotinus's death, claiming that fate took punishment on him. However, that this is entirely false is easily understood from Porphyry himself, Plotinus’s disciple, who plainly and faithfully describes the type of disease from which he died, its cause, and why he departed from Rome.

<margin>Origen.</margin>
Origen "the Adamantine" <note>A major early Christian theologian and philosopher.</note>, who was most eminent in the philosophical sect as in all disciplines, frequently and with many arguments mocked astrological vanity—unless perhaps superstitious men give his testimony less weight because he was also a Christian.

<margin>Eudoxus.</margin>
But Eudoxus <note>A famous Greek astronomer and mathematician.</note> was not a Christian; he was a student of Plato, lived in Egypt, and was considered the prince of astronomers in his time. Yet he left it in writing that nothing should be believed of astrologers who predict the fates of men from their births.

<margin>Alexander.</margin>
Alexander of Aphrodisias <note>The most famous ancient commentator on Aristotle.</note>, the highest authority in Aristotelian philosophy, in writing his book *On Fate* to the Emperors Severus and his son Antoninus, rejected the necessity of fate and remained silent about astrological matters. The mention of fate usually draws people toward astrology, even against their will. Perhaps he had no other purpose in laboring over that commentary than to use philosophical reason to restrain the mind of the Emperor Severus, which was inclined toward that kind of superstition.

<margin>Averroes.</margin>
Averroes <note>A 12th-century Islamic philosopher from Spain, known as "The Commentator" on Aristotle.</note>, a celebrated philosopher in that same family and a serious evaluator of natural things, everywhere tears astrology apart, condemns it, and attacks it. For in his *First Philosophy*, he calls the opinion of astrologers concerning celestial images <note>The constellations.</note>—which they think resemble the figures of animals to which earthly things are subject—"fabulous" [mythical]. If this is removed, the greatest part of astrological superstition collapses. Likewise, in explaining the *Canticles* of Avicenna, he says in one place that they are contrary to philosophy, and in another that almost all the dogmas of astrologers are false; he calls the art itself universally vain and weak. Also, in his books against Al-Ghazali, he asserted that the "artificial images" into which astrologers think they can derive the virtues of heaven are entirely ineffective.

<margin>Avicenna.</margin>
Avicenna <note>An 11th-century Persian polymath and philosopher.</note>, a great man in all disciplines, proved with many arguments in the last book of his *First Philosophy* that the future cannot be foreseen by astrologers. Therefore, no faith should be placed in their predictions. I omit Henry of Hesse <note>A 14th-century theologian who wrote against astrology.</note> and many others, including illustrious moderns in the University of Paris, who pursued this vanity in dedicated works. Although the greatest part of philosophers despised it rather than refuted it—just as they did other charlatan and old-wives' arts, such as the tablets and ravings of illusionists—one should notice...

<summary>Pico della Mirandola lists an extensive "who's who" of ancient and medieval philosophers—including Plato, Aristotle, Plotinus, Averroes, and Avicenna—to argue that the greatest minds either ignored astrology as a fraud or actively refuted it as a false science.</summary>

# DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGY.

<margin>The precept of Eudoxus.</margin>
...rejected that art, which could not have happened except for their realization of its proven falsehood; otherwise, as men highly skilled in the motions of the heavens, they would have gained as much in knowledge, glory, and profit as astrology held in faith and authority. But that man whom we recently cited, Eudoxus of Cnidus <note>A 4th-century BCE Greek astronomer and mathematician whose work influenced Aristotle.</note>, was supreme in mathematics, and Aristotle relies on his judgment in astronomical matters. Yet he was also a most prudent legislator—for he wrote laws for his fellow citizens—and a distinguished physician under Philistion, and a philosopher under Plato. He warned us not to believe astrologers and committed this to writing, for mathematical reasoning had demonstrated this to him, and his teacher Plato had also persuaded him. Cassander and Archelaus, though they excelled in astronomy, never used this kind of prediction.

<margin>
Panaetius.
Hoychilas.
Nicole Oresme.
Giovanni Marliano.
</margin>
Panaetius <note>A Stoic philosopher who famously doubted astrology unlike many of his peers.</note> and Hoychilas of Halicarnassus, though most learned in all mathematics, nevertheless repudiated this entire genus of divining by the stars. Let us come to the moderns: Nicole Oresme <note>A 14th-century philosopher and scientist who was an early critic of astrology.</note>, a most sharp philosopher and highly skilled mathematician, attacked astrological superstition with great indignation in a specific commentary, judging nothing to be more deceptive, nothing more detestable, and nothing more a pestilence to all ranks of men, but especially to princes. Giovanni Marliano <note>A famous 15th-century physician and mathematician from Milan.</note> in our own age was, and was considered to be, supreme in mathematics. He not only always abstained from these predictions, but in his final years had begun to write about their falsehood, though as he was elderly, he was cut off by death and did not complete it. This man, who was not at all boastful, used to say that he possessed the most certain demonstrations against the astrologers. My friend Luchinus—himself an excellent mathematician—has told me this more than once.

<margin>Paolo of Florence.</margin>
Paolo of Florence <note>Also known as Paolo dal Pozzo Toscanelli, the famous geographer and mathematician who influenced Columbus.</note>, most learned in medicine but especially in mathematics in both Greek and Latin, whenever he was asked about that profession, he always asserted it was uncertain and deceptive. Among other things, he offered an evident experiment regarding himself: although he had already completed eighty-five years, he had found no "vital constellation" <note>A configuration of stars supposed to grant long life.</note> in his own birth chart, which he had examined most diligently. I could produce many others among those still living, both philosophers and astronomers, who feel the same way. But I do not know if they wish to incite the envy of those men who claim power over heaven and fate. Furthermore, our Marsilio <note>Marsilio Ficino, the head of the Platonic Academy in Florence and Pico's mentor.</note> wrote openly against them, following in the footsteps of Plotinus <note>A 3rd-century philosopher who argued that stars are signs, not causes, of human events.</note>. In interpreting and explaining Plotinus, Marsilio greatly aided, increased, and illustrated the Platonic cause. If, while consulting his health, he sometimes requests certain aids from the heaven, he desires that such things might be possible rather than believes they are. I can most faithfully testify to the mind of this man, with whom I am on intimate terms; I have had no one who more often or more effectively encouraged me to expose this deception. Whenever we were together, there was no richer occasion or harvest for laughter than over the vanity of astrologers—especially if a third party joined us, namely Poliziano <note>Angelo Poliziano, a brilliant humanist scholar and poet.</note>, who is always a wonderful "hisser-off" of all superstitions. Perhaps, indeed, the judgment of our friend Niccolò Leoniceno <note>A famous physician and scholar known for correcting errors in natural history.</note> on this matter should not be concealed. Since he possesses a faithful grasp of mathematics as he does all liberal sciences, he judges this prophesying astrology to be so vain that he does not even think those who wrote about it—especially the more learned ones—actually believed what they were writing.

<margin>Marsilio.</margin>

<margin>Niccolò Leoniceno.</margin>

<margin>What was the cause for the invention of the divining art?</margin>
If you ask the reason why they wrote it, he answers that it was produced partly by greed and partly by the ignorance of princes. For, he says, while those excellent men labored day and night in measuring the motions and bodies of the stars (which is what mathematics does), they received no profit from the princes, who certainly had no care for how large a celestial body was or with what speed it revolved through the spaces of heaven. When they saw this, lest they remain poor in earthly things while searching the heavens, they devised a charming deception by which they might bind the minds of princes to themselves and make them lovers of their profession. Therefore, they fabricated the idea that the fortunes of all men—but especially of princes—depend on these stars: namely, children, life, empires, victories, and health. They claimed that they, who had long observed the motions and natures of the stars, knew thoroughly and had explored exactly what good things they promised or what adversity they announced. Furthermore, they claimed to have remedies at hand by which foreseen evils could be repelled and good things confirmed. For if a "lucky hour" <note>term: *fœlix hora* — a specific moment in time deemed astrologically favorable for an action.</note> were noted, images could be forged from a material more closely related to those celestial natures. By wonderful mechanisms, a power drawn down from the stars into these images would make men most successful and powerful in affairs, easily attaining whatever they sought by the mere touch or wearing of them. To gain more trust for all these claims, they added that the more secret mysteries of this art had been divinely revealed to them—just as one reads in Maternus <note>Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century astrological writer.</note> that Petosiris and Aesculapius received many things from the most powerful deity Mercury. Then indeed, the unlettered and curious princes, being most greedy for the things promised, were easily led to believe; they supported the professors and encouraged these studies more and more each day with rewards. This is what our Leoniceno seriously speaks and feels, not far from the truth, regarding the astrologers. But we must be especially careful lest the astrologers sneak into our confidence by writing volumes falsely attributed to great authors—a practice they share with every superstition. For since the things they put forward cannot be confirmed by reason, whether they themselves believe them true or wish others to believe them, they title books of these fables with the names of the most famous and ancient men, hunting for credit for their own error from fictional authors. In this category is the book *On the Properties of the Elements*—in which great conjunctions and secrets are discussed—which they attribute to Aristotle <note>A medieval work falsely attributed to Aristotle to give it scientific weight.</note> through no fault or demerit of that good philosopher. Just so, the magi circulate Plato's books *On the Cow*, and works they call *Institutions*, filled with execrable dreams and fictions, as foreign to Plato as these beggarly scraps are distant from Plato's integrity and wisdom. Similarly, the heretics once called Gnostics used to show off books of Zoroaster, to make their heresy venerable with the antiquity of Zoroaster; Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote a famous treatise against the Christians and Gnostics.</note> demonstrated with many arguments that these were new and fabricated, not by Zoroaster. Those who are unrefined in humane letters, though otherwise learned, can easily be deceived and circumvented by these lies; whereas those who recognize the style and character of authors through those letters immediately discern the adulterated from the legitimate. However, the fictions of our astrologers and the superstitious arts currently in their hands shrink so far from any likeness to the truth that they are obvious even to a commoner. For who could be led to believe that *Ovid on the Old Woman* <note>original: *Ovidium de vetula* — a 13th-century poem falsely attributed to the Roman poet Ovid.</note> is by Ovid? In it, wonders are pronounced regarding great conjunctions and the Christian law, so much so that Roger Bacon, a great patron of astrology, uses the testimony of no writer more willingly—unless perhaps he prefers Artephius <note>A medieval alchemist/astrologer who claimed to be over a thousand years old.</note>, who mentions countless other secrets. Such is the claim that by inspecting not a star, but urine, one can know a man's life, character, and conditions; and finally...

<margin>Which books are falsely ascribed to Aristotle, Plato, and among those of Zoroaster.</margin>

<margin>Note. Roger Bacon.</margin>

# BOOK ONE.

...all to be foreknown as one. Thus, that ethical philosopher <note>original: "ethico philosopho"; likely referring to a pseudo-Aristotelian or Hermetic text common in the Middle Ages.</note> carries great weight with him; his book on cosmography is said to have been translated by Jerome. Yet the reading is so ridiculous that nothing could be more so, though it is frequently cited by our Roger [Bacon] in his letter to Clement. He almost introduces a certain little book composed by him titled *On the Errors of Students of Theology*. In this volume, he primarily accuses our theologians of error because they confirm the mysteries of religion more from Aristotle and other philosophers than from the authors we have just named: the Ethic, Artephius, Ovid in his poetic protection, and similar figures. Indeed, the book is ascribed to Albert [the Great], but most falsely, since he never mentioned these dreams in his theological writings; rather, it seems rightly attributed to Bacon. His other writings easily declare him to have held that opinion, as they are always overflowing with the testimonies and oracles of those authors. If he could believe them, it is no wonder he could also believe in astrology. Thus, this superstitious class of men has so scoured your sources that they even circulate books under the title of Thomas [Aquinas] concerning necromantic images. It is now less surprising that they forge I-know-not-what

<margin>
See the annotations.
</margin>
books of Ptolemy regarding rings, and even astrological books attributed to Ariston which Ptolemy never wrote. By such recklessness or ignorance, many also attribute a certain opuscule of a man from York to Albert, and mention books of Hippocrates written and explained by Galen, celebrated throughout all Greece. Or, if he knew them, he nevertheless set them aside as more secret things to be communicated only to those pure and rightly initiated. Furthermore, regarding rains and questions, Al-Kindi <note>An influential 9th-century Arab philosopher and astrologer.</note> and others commemorate Pythagorean and Aristotelian ideas; and those who write the book titled *Aristotle on Governments* <note>Referring to the "Secretum Secretorum," a popular medieval forgery attributed to Aristotle.</note> speak in such a way to the heavenly bodies. I wish that they had not attributed profane things even to holy men, and had not made the divine Jerome the translator of a certain book on incantations. Although, if they defamed angels, they can easily do so to men; for they say these delusions were handed down by the angel of Adam, those by the angel of Solomon, and others by the guardian of Tobias. But let us return to the astrologers, leaving behind those to whom a communion of error, as if bordering neighbors, has led us. Aristotle showed what he thought of this class of men in a single word when, in the *Problems*, he considered the astrologer alongside the mime and the prestidigitator <note>A street performer or "juggler" who performs sleight of hand.</note>. But you will say: if these philosophers wrote no such thing, yet those who did write them were philosophers: such as Albumasar, Ptolemy, Haly Abenzagel, Julius Firmicus, and countless other authors of astrology, both Latin, Greek, and barbarian—men most excellent in both learning and genius. You, my friend, have opportunely reminded me not to say only that astrology was neglected by philosophers. But also, whoever might have written on it, they either philosophized not at all or badly. Therefore, let you leave to us—if it pleases the gods—Pythagoras, Plato, and Aristotle; and keep for yourselves your Albumasars, Alchabitiuses, Avenezras, and Abenzageles. How far all of them were from a philosophical temperament will be openly demonstrated when we show plainly that they approach most fabulous things, grow accustomed to things that have no reason, say contradictory things, and overturn themselves. These are entirely different from the philosopher, whose most proper characteristic is to believe nothing and affirm nothing that cannot be demonstrated either by evidence or by reason. But come, let us say something here from which it may be established that the authors of astrology philosophized either too little or poorly.

<margin>
Such as Ptolemy in his books.
</margin>
Furthermore, they have easily conceded Ptolemy to be the prince of the others. For he is the most learned of the astrologers and, as far as pertains

<column-break/>

to mathematics, a man of most ingenious talent. However, regarding the casters of horoscopes <note>original: "genethliacos"; those who predict a person's life based on their birth chart.</note>, he is, as they say, the best of a bad lot. Therefore, with what judgment he treated philosophical matters, he sufficiently indicated both in the prefaces of the "Great Composition" (which they call the *Almagest*) and in the books of "Effects" <note>Referring to the "Tetrabiblos" or "Quadripartitum," Ptolemy's fundamental work on astrology.</note>. For, beginning his mathematical books, he divides philosophy into three

<margin>
The opinion of Ptolemy from Aristotle, Metaphysics Book 6.
</margin>
contemplative types according to the opinion of Aristotle: the theological, the natural, and the mathematical. Then, explaining the reason for the division, he says all things that exist consist of three: matter, form, and motion. These can be separated from one another in thought, but in reality, they cannot. From these three, therefore, those three types of philosophy are derived: from motion, the theological—since the cause of the first motion is none other than God; from matter, the physical; from form, the mathematical. This is the opinion of Ptolemy, in which no one even slightly learned would doubt that among good philosophers there are as many errors as there are words. For not all things consist of those

<margin>
Against Ptolemy.
</margin>
three. If, when he says "all things," he understands natural things, how will that philosophy itself be occupied with them, being then divided into those three types: physical, divine, and mathematical? But neither does anything consist of motion from among natural things, although it may not happen nor remain without motion. But let us give him this allowance of speech. How will Aristotle himself, whom he approves, grant him that the theological genus arises from motion? Since God himself, as the author and cause of the first motion, is investigated not by the theologian but by the [natural] philosopher. The rest are also either false or things you may easily see were uttered by a man little skilled or knowledgeable in philosophy. Now, from the books of "Effects" (which they call the *Fourfold*), there are more notable and more evident errors, as he believes the moon to be

<margin>
Against the same.
</margin>
more humid because a humid vapor ascends from the earth to it—being closer to the earth than the other stars; and by the same reasoning, that Saturn is dry because it is further removed from these vapors; and that the same is also cold because it is far from the heat of the sun; and Jupiter is temperate because it is placed midway between the icy Saturn and the burning Mars. And there are many other things of this kind concerning the properties of the stars, which philosophers will exhibit rather than refute. And even if his Arab commentator, blushing at the master's error, tries to transfer Ptolemy's words into another meaning, Ptolemy himself does not allow himself to be defended or excused, for he asserts and affirms these things so much, and repeats them so often, that no doubt of his meaning is left. You, indeed, learn all from this one, and judge the worse from the best. Almost first after Ptolemy is Albumasar;

<margin>
See the errors of the astrologers.
Ptolemy’s time.
</margin>
he was neither a philosopher nor a dialectician, and he was unskilled in mathematics. For he was a professor of the art of grammar and, as Averroes relates, he turned himself to astrology from the writing of histories. In this profession, you may know who he truly was even from this: that he thought the astrologer Ptolemy was among the Egyptian kings who succeeded Alexander, as if more than five hundred years did not intervene between them! Since the Ptolemaic kings flourished four hundred years before Christ, while Ptolemy the astrologer wrote under Hadrian and Antoninus. Behold the marvelous investigator of the deepest things and faithful observer: who in a matter so open could have such sleepiness or slowness of mind? We will later declare how much he erred in astrological matters and how he insisted on open and confessed lies as if they were truths. Why should I mention Maternus <note>Julius Firmicus Maternus, 4th-century author of the "Mathesis."</note>, hallucinating so in the rudiments of arithmetic that he writes Mercury determines something when it occupies the midheaven in a nocturnal birth-chart—as if Mercury could ever be more than forty or so degrees away from the sun, or the sun were not always more than seventy degrees away from the midheaven at night! I omit many other things in which you will find him a man of always much talk but always little wisdom. Now, if Manilius <note>Marcus Manilius, 1st-century author of the astrological poem "Astronomica."</note> were not a poet, good God, with what laughter would we pursue him! He says those heavenly images which he fashions are rather begun with a few stars than completed...

Pico argues that these "masters" are often little more than failed philosophers or grammarians whose foundational logic is flawed.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument from the previous leaf, concluding a thought about the "fires" of superstition before turning to a critique of specific astrological authors like Guido Bonatti and addressing the confusion caused by similar-sounding names of philosophers and astrologers. ### OF THE LETTERS.

...so that the world might not be set ablaze by an uncontrolled fire if too many torches were lit there. I do not even descend to the younger, common, and unlearned men, into whose hands almost the entire profession has now fallen. Among them, **Bonatti** <note>Guido Bonatti (c. 1210–1296), the most famous Italian astrologer of the 13th century, whom Dante placed in the eighth circle of Hell.</note> is considered the highest authority. He is not only ignorant of philosophy, but he was clearly out of his mind. Read his first book on astrological judgments, specifically where he writes his own introduction. I am a liar if you do not judge the man worthy of **hellebore** <note>original: "helleboro"; a plant used in antiquity as a treatment for madness or insanity.</note>. In those parts where he is less foolish, he constructs certain arguments to prove that astrology is true—arguments which I would call not merely false, but more childish and ridiculous than can be described. 

Indeed, the argument he thinks most effective is that the **quadrivium** <note>The "four ways" of mathematical learning in medieval education: arithmetic, geometry, music, and astronomy.</note> would be destroyed if astrology were removed. He claims it is one of the four mathematical arts. See how he does not even know the nature of the very thing he professes! For this divinatory astrology, which we are refuting, is as far removed from that which is numbered among the mathematical sciences as light is from darkness, or truth from a lie. While this practice—which usurps the prediction of the future—cannot stand if that first and truer science <note>referring to mathematical astronomy</note> is removed, the reverse is not true: it does not follow that if the divining part is taken away, the mathematical part is also destroyed. This is so clear, even to those who have touched the mere elements of these arts, that it would be superfluous to explain it further. **Ptolemy** himself, in the introductions to his *Apotelesmaton* <note>The "Tetrabiblos," Ptolemy’s foundational work on astrology.</note>, after speaking of a twofold astronomy, refers his discourse back to the first and mathematical kind, saying:

"However, if this profession has occasionally not displeased certain good men, it does not immediately follow that something is good just because a good man did not reject it. Good men are not always good in every respect, nor do the learned always achieve a perfect reputation in all matters; and if it must be said: not all the learned are always philosophers."

But it is also necessary to remember that there are certain truths against which our desires rebel. There are those truths in the first category which contain all matters of ethics and many theological points; in the second category is the greatest part of what concerns physical and mathematical things. Furthermore, it is manifest that this truth we are treating—concerning the **vanity of astrology**—belongs to the first kind. This is because the vice of curiosity, innate in man, rebels against it. Since this curiosity is the most powerful of all traits, being proper to man insofar as he is a human being, it sometimes results in many people either not having the time to investigate this truth, or even when it is found, they do not approach it willingly. Just as many, after hearing the most evident arguments of philosophy against greed, still pant for the accumulation of wealth; so too, many, even after it is established that what astrologers say is entirely empty, find that their innate curiosity is only torn away from the astrologers with great difficulty. Because we are greedy for new things, we even listen to fables willingly; we feel pleasure in things to come, and we even take pleasure in sensing the astrologers lying about them. Added to this is the fact that an excessive love of ourselves always infatuates us; we easily hope for or fear whatever pertains to our prosperity or adversity, and we are repeatedly solicited by a blind desire to seek those things out, even when we know they cannot be found. 

What can we say of this long-standing, widespread consensus, which acts as a prejudice? Many think that astrology must be *something*, yet it never enters their minds to look inside and see what foundation this thing has, or what solid firmament lies beneath it. Therefore, you will find that almost everyone held by this vanity was either too little a philosopher, or certainly too little an astrologer—the former so they would not see their errors, the latter so they would not judge them. Finally, it may have pleased some when merely tasted, but it never satisfied the palate of those who drank it deeply. For it has something on its face that allures, appearing great, plausible, and useful; but when you look deeper inside, you see that everything is false, uncertain, and fabulous...

<column-break/>

<margin>Most people err due to the similarity of names.</margin>

...born from either no conjectures at all or the weakest ones possible. We shall discuss these matters abundantly and at length in the following books. But this point might have deceived some: since the names of certain philosophers and astrologers are similar, it might be thought that those who wrote philosophical works were the same as those who wrote astrological ones. For instance, there is an **Albumasar** <note>Abu Ma'shar (787–886), a famous Persian astrologer.</note> among the philosophers and likewise one among the astrologers. Although the Latin language confuses these names, they are distinguished among the Arabs; for the one who is a philosopher is called *Albumasar*, but the astrologer is called *Aboasar*. **Abubater** <note>Abu Bakr al-Hasani.</note> also wrote on predictions of births (nativities), and there is another of the same name who wrote philosophical works, especially a book on how anyone might become a philosopher by himself, which we translated from Hebrew into Latin last year <note>Pico is referring to his translation of Ibn Tufayl’s *Hayy ibn Yaqzan*.</note>. But the latter was the son of Al-Tafail <note>original: "Altasibi," likely a corruption of Ibn Tufayl</note>, while the former was the son of Tripis. There is the same similarity of names in many cases, despite the great disagreement in their times and professions. But enough regarding the philosophers.

<margin>Testimonies of the prophets.</margin>

Let us pass to the prophets: that is, to the oracles of the Old and New Law, beginning with **Isaiah**. He, therefore, when threatening future destruction to the Babylonians (among whom this sect flourished most, which is why astrologers were also called **Chaldeans**), and when summoning **Cyrus**, King of the Persians—called "the anointed" even two hundred years before he was born—to fight against them, addressed the city of the Chaldeans which was to be desolated as follows:

<margin>The words of Isaiah.</margin>

> "Let now the astrologers <note>original: "augures coeli"; literally 'augurs of heaven.'</note> stand and save you, they who gazed at the stars and counted the months to announce what would happen to you. Behold, they have become like stubble; the fire has burned them. They shall not deliver their own soul from the hand of the flame."

And a few lines before this, he had rebuked them regarding this observation of the heavens thus: "This wisdom and your knowledge shall deceive you; evil shall come upon you, and you shall not know its rising; and calamity shall fall upon you which you shall not be able to atone for." In these words, the divine prophet accuses the twofold recklessness of the astrologers: one is to think they can foresee the future from the sky; the other is to think that, once foreseen, they can either ward off evils or confirm good things. "Evil shall come," he says, "of which you shall not know the rising"—that is, that neither Mars nor the cold star of Saturn signified it to you. Then, you will not be able to atone for the rushing calamity—that is, you will not be able to repel it from you by the "election of hours," by astrological images, or by other superstitious contrivances. 

It is worthy of notice that these words refute the responses of those who wish to be Chaldeans and Christians at the same time. For they are accustomed to say that astronomy <note>meaning astrology here</note> is not simply condemned by the saints and prophets, except insofar as they attribute either vices or virtues solely to the heavens, or bind human events to fatal necessity. They claim that since even "good" astrologers refute these errors, the saints do not hate the science of astrology itself, but only the mistakes of certain astrologers. Let **Pierre d'Ailly** <note>original: "Petrus aliacensis" (1351–1420), a French cardinal who attempted to reconcile astrology with theology.</note> and whoever defends themselves with this defense tell me then: did it pertain to "morals" or "character" that the King of the Persians brought war upon the Assyrians? And if it does not pertain to morals, why did the prophet judge that it could not be foreseen even by the greatest astrologers? Even if they had been in the error of thinking that what was to happen would happen by necessity, it would not be held against them that the coming calamity could not be atoned for by them; for they themselves would not hope it could be atoned for if they believed it would happen by necessity, like everything else. But no good art is condemned by a right judgment just because some evil people abuse it. Otherwise, the reading of the Sacred Scriptures would have to be condemned first, from which so many heresies and so many insanities were confirmed by certain unlearned and proud men. Philosophy would likewise have to be condemned, since this philosopher says the soul is mortal, and that one says there is only one soul in all men; some deny that God provides for men, others deny any at all...

<summary>Pico della Mirandola distinguishes between mathematical astronomy and divinatory astrology, critiquing practitioners like Guido Bonatti for their ignorance. He uses the prophet Isaiah to argue that even non-moral events (like war) cannot be predicted by astrologers, refuting those who try to harmonize astrology with Christianity.</summary>
<keywords>astrology vs astronomy, Guido Bonatti, quadrivium, curiosity, Isaiah, Chaldeans, Pierre d'Ailly, Albumasar, biblical critique of astrology</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the refutation of astrology by addressing common defenses used by its practitioners. ### AGAINST THE ASTROLOGERS. BOOK II.

<margin>Objections.</margin>
...to be religion at all. But by this reasoning, all good things would be overturned, since there is nothing so good that the nature of men cannot abuse it. Therefore, those who defend themselves in this way are indirectly and gravely slandering the judgment of the Church—which they are ashamed to openly despise. But they can be completely forced to either repudiate this vanity or admit they cannot deviate to the left from the path of their ancestors, the leaders of the Church. For by whatever reason those leaders condemned astrology, I ask you: did they condemn it justly or unjustly? They do not wish to say "unjustly"; if "justly," then why do you not likewise condemn it along with them? "But," they will say, "we too shall condemn those errors for which astrology was displeasing to them." But I ask this: why is it not displeasing to you for those same reasons? For it is clear, and we shall soon show, that they did not forbid astrology only to a certain extent, but pursued and abominated it entirely. You contend that this was done because of certain errors—so be it—but answer this: was the whole practice rejected by a right judgment because of those errors? If by a right judgment, why do you not do the same? Instead, you approve what they condemned; you defend what they attacked; you disseminate what they forbade; you teach publicly what they wished not to be known. Or is it as **d’Ailly** <note>original: "Alliacensis"; Pierre d'Ailly (1350–1420), a French cardinal who argued that astrology was compatible with theology if used correctly.</note> says: that because it could hinder the growing faith, the first doctors of the nascent Church attacked it, but now that the Church is mature, it does not harm—indeed, it even profits greatly?

<margin>Whether philosophy, like astrology, is to be condemned.</margin>
But this shall be refuted later; for we shall clearly demonstrate that it is as pestilential now as it was then, which experience itself now demonstrates. But [they argue] it was not the art that should have been condemned, but its abuse. Why, then, did they not condemn philosophy, but only the impiety of certain philosophers? And why did they not likewise condemn astrologers, but astrology itself? Certainly because in philosophy, if there is any error, it is the fault of the teacher; in astrology, the very profession is the fault. Following their authority along with reason when disputing against the impious, we have refuted not philosophy, but the errors of philosophers. Here, however, we refute not astrologers, but astrology, because astrology is itself an error. But let us return to the testimonies of the prophets. God speaks to us through Moses in this way: "The nations listen to soothsayers and diviners; but you have been instructed otherwise by the Lord your God." <note>Deuteronomy 18:14</note> For the word we read as "soothsayers," the Hebrew has <gloss>me'onen</gloss> <note>original: מעונן</note>.

<margin>Achinnas.</margin>
**Achinnas** <note>likely referring to a Jewish authority such as Rabbi Akiva</note>, the greatest doctor of the Hebrews, says that by this word are understood those who calculate times and observe lucky and unlucky hours; for that word is derived from <gloss>onah</gloss> <note>original: עונה</note>, which signifies a "time" or "hour." Jerome translated it as "soothsayers." But we have also seen astrologers called "soothsayers" in Isaiah. For the specific name of "astrologers" is not found throughout the Sacred Scriptures. Indeed, the practice itself has various names, and this superstition has been assigned different titles at different times. For formerly they were called **Chaldeans** and **genethliacs** <note>casters of birth charts</note>; in the time of Augustine, **mathematicians** and **planetarians**; now they are commonly called **astrologers**. 

<margin>Avenezra. Jeremiah.</margin>
As for what Jerome translated as "diviners" in that place and elsewhere, the Hebrew has <gloss>kesem</gloss> <note>original: קסם</note>, which **Avenezra** <note>Abraham ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167), a famous Jewish scholar and astrologer</note> himself—though he was an astrologer—says is a term common to all diviners, but is more properly the name for astrologers. And who is ignorant of that saying of Jeremiah: "Be not afraid of the signs of heaven, which the heathens fear"? <note>Jeremiah 10:2</note> Why then does a Christian man either rejoice or grieve at the judgments of astrologers? From them, according to Isaiah, nothing is to be hoped; according to Jeremiah, nothing is to be feared. Indeed, through both, the Divine Truth affirms to us that the whole of what they profess is, as **Ambrose** says, absurd to seek, since

<margin>Ambrose. Job.</margin>
the things they promise are impossible. Whence the Lord of heaven says in **Job**: "Do you know the laws of the heavens, and can you set their rule over the earth?" and further: "Who shall declare the accounting of the heavens?" <note>Job 38:33, 38:37</note> For the error of astrologers is twofold: one, that they subject many things to the heaven which do not depend upon it; the other, that even those things which the heaven does effect cannot be foreseen by them as they suppose,

<column-break/>

which the words brought forth in the midst of Job show us. And since the doctors of the Church reject both errors equally, how can it be said that they only disapprove of that which takes away free will or introduces the necessity of fate? 

<margin>Testimonies of Augustine.</margin>
Does not **Augustine’s** famous argument regarding twins tend toward taking away all foreknowledge of the future from them? Does he not, in his *Enchiridion*, say that the mere observation of times—such as thinking this day auspicious and that one inauspicious—pertains to a great sin? This is so even though in this selection of hours and days we are exercising our freedom rather than having it taken away. But it is certainly true that astrology was displeasing to them in every respect, though especially in that part by which it subjected religion and morals to the sky. For this reason they cursed it, everywhere they refuted it; for this they judged it impious, everywhere vain; for this blasphemous, everywhere superstitious; for this abominable, everywhere ridiculous. Wherefore Augustine, in his book *On Christian Doctrine*, said it pertains to a pernicious superstition—those who are called **genethliacs**—not only because they think our actions, but also the outcomes of our actions, proceed from the stars. And in the book of *Confessions*, speaking of **planetarians**—that is, astrologers—he says that "Christian and true piety expels and condemns them." Explaining that passage in Moses, "The stars were placed for signs and times," <note>Genesis 1:14</note> he says he does not mean signs which it is vanity to observe, but those necessary for the uses of life, such as sailors, farmers, and craftsmen of that sort observe. In the same place, **Basil** called it a most busy

<margin>Basil. Ambrose. Theodoret. Chrysostom.</margin>
vanity; **Ambrose**, useless and impossible; **Theodoret**, refuted even by the philosophers; **Chrysostom**, vain, false, and ridiculous. Let us read Bardesanes, Eusebius, Didymus, Apollinaris, Tertullian, and countless others, even many **Apostolic men** <note>early Christian figures directly influenced by the Apostles</note>; and what more? We see that the Hebrews, the heretics, and the gentiles—this same class of men—have been pursued by this censorial rod. Thus it was that Augustine wondered, since these testimonies rebuking astrologers were read with such frequency in the churches, yet the assemblies were full of our own people who took the timing for their affairs from the "mathematicians." When the same man was preaching to the people on the sixty-third psalm, he produced a penitent "mathematician" who had renounced his profession, just as if a Jew or some ethnic person had received the bath of regeneration. How beautifully the same man, interpreting John, warns us of our infancy: that we enter as free men to the astrologers only to exit as slaves, and we pay out our liberty to them for purchased lies. In his book *On the Nature of Demons*, he expressly says that after Christ, it is permitted to no one to interpret any person's birth chart from the sky. **Jerome** says that to seek the courses of the stars and to search out the outcomes of the future from them is among the "reproaches of Egypt"—that is,

<margin>Jerome. Severian.</margin>
the remnants of idolatry. **Severian** <note>Severian of Gabala (d. after 408)</note>, in the book he wrote *On the Seven Arts*—which Roger [Bacon] falsely cites as if it were by Cassiodorus—after speaking of true astronomy, then says: "Those things which pertain to foreseeing the future ought to be so unknown that they should not even seem to be written; for they are without doubt contrary to our faith." These are his words, verbatim. If the opinion of such great and excellent men moves no one, let at least the Papal authority deter them, which so forbids this profession to our people that **Alexander III**, the Supreme Pontiff, wished a certain priest to abstain for an entire year from the ministry of the altar because he had scrutinized an astrolabe to investigate a theft from a certain church—even though, as the same Pontiff testifies, he had admitted no magic or other superstition there. In the **Synod of Martin** <note>The Council of Braga (561 AD), often associated with Martin of Braga</note>

<margin>Synod of Martin.</margin>
it was written: they are not truly Christians who observe either the courses of the moon or the stars, or the empty deception of signs for the sake of building a house...

# DISPUTATIONS
<sig>q</sig>

or observing marital unions, but also under the name of "haruspices" <note>Ancient diviners who originally read omens in animal entrails, but the term was often used broadly in medieval law to include astrologers.</note> anathema is pronounced by the decree of Gregory the Younger <note>Pope Gregory II (r. 715–731).</note>, and in the Council of Toledo: If he himself be a priest or deacon, let him be banished to a monastery to pay the penalties of his crime there in perpetual detention.

<margin>Gregory</margin>
<margin>Augustine</margin>
For, as Augustine teaches in his book *On the Nature of Demons*, they are accustomed to be designated among us under the name of "haruspices": those who observe days and hours in the conduct of business and works; here that part of astrology which concerns "elections" <note><term>Elections</term>: The astrological practice of choosing the most auspicious moment to begin an undertaking.</note> seems especially noted. Who then, being a Christian man (for my speech is now addressed to those who have been "digested" or initiated into the faith), would dare to defend, follow, or extol astrology—prohibited by law, condemned by prophets, mocked by saints, and interdicted by pontiffs and most holy synods?

<margin>Defense of Albert</margin>
But if you should oppose me with Albert <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a prolific theologian and scientist.</note>, that most outstanding theologian and supporter of astrologers: I will first remind you that many things are attributed to Albert which are not Albert’s, as we touched upon above. Then, if you should perhaps object to the book *On Licit and Illicit Things* <note>Often titled *Speculum Astronomiae*, a work then attributed to Albertus Magnus which defended certain astrological practices.</note> in which he rejects magi but approves astronomical authors: I will respond that although many estimate that work to be Albert’s, neither Albert himself nor the inscription of the book everywhere signifies this, since the author himself, whoever he may eventually have been, deliberately and professedly hides his name. Why so? Because in it many things are read that are unworthy of a learned man and a good Christian—such as the claim that "images" <note>Astrological talismans or seals believed to capture planetary power.</note> can be made by which not only one man, but even an entire city might become unhappy or unfortunate; or that books of magic are not to be cast away because they might one day be useful to the Church. For this is plainly contrary to the judgment of the Church itself, which commands those books to be entirely exterminated wherever they are found. For by what reason will it be useful to keep whole books which it would have been most useful never to have written? These things Albert certainly either did not write, or if he did, it must be said with the Apostle: "In other things I praise him; in this I praise him not" <note>A paraphrase of 1 Corinthians 11:22: "What shall I say to you? Shall I praise you in this? I praise you not."</note>. But just as it is the mark of envy to seek in great men what you may damn rather than what you may extol, so it is the mark of madness to refuse to damn them where they have failed, rather than to merely imitate them.

<margin>The disgrace of Pierre d’Ailly</margin>
I shall praise in Pierre d’Ailly <note>Petrus Aliacensis (1350–1420), a French cardinal and scholar who attempted to harmonize astrology with theology and history.</note> his zeal for letters, his experience in affairs, his wide reading, and that he wrote and treated certain theological matters with skill and subtlety. But that he wished to reconcile astrology with history in one small work, and with theology in another—so that he might prove it a true system in the former and a pious one in the latter—this I plainly do not praise, but damn, execrate, and detest. For we can defend no position that is either more false or more adverse to religion. Regarding this matter, since we shall discourse widely in the following books, nothing more need be said in this place: for there we shall leave it abundantly witnessed, even to his supporters, that those booklets are both enemies to religion and full of so many historical and astrological errors that our saying might apply: "If you wish to remove the error, remove the book."

<margin>Testimonies of Civil Law</margin>
We have spoken of philosophers and prophets; there remain the civil laws—that is, the commands and judgments of the Caesars and the learned jurists. Their end is chiefly to look after the utilities by which the life of men may be passed well and blessedly. Since life is most aided by good arts and disturbed by harmful ones, they have cared with the greatest zeal that the former should abound and the latter (as far as possible) should be nonexistent in cities. To achieve this, they decreed rewards and honors for the professors of the former, but public ignominy and increasingly grave punishments for the latter, according as they judged those arts to be more harmful.

<margin>Justinian</margin>
What they thought of astrologers, therefore, no one is ignorant who has read the legal codes of the Emperor Justinian. In these, the "art of mathematicians" (for so the astrologers used to call themselves) is forbidden as abominable, with the Emperor commanding that no one

<column-break/>

should consult a mathematician; rather, let curiosity of judgment be perpetually silent for all. If anyone should consult a mathematician, the penalty of death (which is the ultimate punishment) is pronounced against him. Surely the most wise Emperor would not have established this, with the use and judgment of so many wise men and laws, unless experience had demonstrated that profession to be not only useless for life, but ruinous to men. The most fortunate Justinian himself so shuddered at this race of men that if any mathematician were caught in his company, he would pay the penalty for his rashness with the highest tortures, even unto the rack.

<margin>Conclusion of this book</margin>
Then finally, speaking of this superstition, the Emperor pronounces that those who teach these things and those who learn them are kindred in the same guilt. Even before Justinian, do we not read that all mathematicians were often expelled from the city of Rome? This we shall openly demonstrate at the end of these disputations. For if all right reason is either governed by prudence, perfected by philosophy, or illuminated by the rays of divine splendor, astrology will surely be banished by every right judgment—an art which the most prudent legislators have exterminated, the most learned of philosophers have refuted, and divine and most holy men have abominated.

# GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA’S
## DISPUTATIONS AGAINST
## THE ASTROLOGERS.
### BOOK II BEGINS.
### Chapter I. That this art is uncertain, even by the judgment of its own leaders.

But lest we fight by authority alone, we shall demonstrate throughout this whole work, by certain reasons, that this superstition has been rightly rejected by the saints as being most adverse to religion; usefully interdicted by laws as being useless to life (nay, rather, exceedingly harmful); and rationally refuted by philosophers as something they recognized to be false and uncertain. And although it seemed we should begin by demonstrating it to be false (since it was thereby immediately rendered useless as well), I thought I should act otherwise: namely, that before I disputed its falsehood, I would show the lovers of astrologers that even if this profession were such as they make it out to be and affirm, no benefit comes from it to the "outer man," while to the "inner man" it brings not only the greatest detriments but even fatal ones. Before we approach this, we must preface certain things from which we may understand how much the supreme leaders of the astrologers themselves attribute to their own profession. Ptolemy, therefore, in the first book of the *Apotelesmatika* <note>Known as the *Tetrabiblos*, the foundational text of Western astrology.</note>, after he said that the judgments of astrologers are often lies because of the defect of prediction, then adds these things word for word, which we have wished to translate—for they are poorly rendered in the common translation, and worse in the translation of Averroes, and poorly explained by him; but when they are faithfully translated, they will need no explanation. "But this much is clear: even if one has properly tracked these disciplines as far as possible, it is nevertheless necessary that he should very often stumble; it is not valid for those reasons we stated above, but rather because of the very nature of the matter, or because our weakness is greater than our ability to be equal to the magnitude of so great a profession. For since all contemplation involving the affections of matter seeks the probable rather than deciding anything for certain truth... further, this is most characteristic of it: that it is composed, as it were, confusedly from many dissimilar things, and depends upon the ancient figures and aspects of the wandering stars; because those things which were observed by the ancients regarding the events of things, we accommodate to our own age whenever the situation holds in the same manner..."

<summary>Pico concludes his appeal to religious and legal authorities—citing Pope Gregory, St. Augustine, and the Emperor Justinian—to justify the condemnation of astrology. He then begins Book II by arguing that even astrology's founders, like Ptolemy, admitted the art was prone to error and uncertainty.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico's systematic dismantling of astrological theory. # AGAINST ASTROLOGY. BOOK II.

... we observe. Furthermore, who does not see that this can happen: that the celestial figures and their aspects may become more or less similar to one another over long circuits of time? However, it seems we should not even hope that the exact same harmony of all things in the heavens—especially if you include the Earth as well—will ever truly return. To believe otherwise would be to boast vainly and gloriously about comprehending things that either cannot be fully understood by their own nature, or certainly cannot be grasped within the span of time granted to human senses. Consequently, because the examples proposed are never identical, errors occur whenever one tries to predict the future. 

In observing the natural world that surrounds us, nothing is overly difficult; however, in the case of individual births and the private circumstances of every person, causes arise that are neither small nor light by which each person’s character is shaped. For the differences in "seeds" <note>original: "seminu differētiæ" — Pico refers to the biological nature or species of a being.</note> have the greatest power over the properties of a genus. Even if the surrounding heavens and the horizon are the same, each seed carries immense weight in the universal formation of its specific shape—whether it be a human, a horse, or any other creature. 

The locations of birth also bring no small degree of difference. For even if the seeds are of the same genus—namely, human—and the state of the heavens surrounding all things is the same, those who are born still differ greatly in body and mind due to the diversity of their regions. It also matters greatly for the various acts of life, even if all other things are equal, what food a person eats or what customs they follow. Unless one argues that each of these factors is contained within the cause of the surrounding heavens (which would imply the heavens are the primary force), then these factors must be considered a significant part of the cause for why things are the way they are. 

This is where those who think they can know everything should hesitate: for things are clearly not the same, yet they try to discern them solely from the motion of the celestial bodies. On this point, Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century author of the *Tetrabiblos*, the foundational text of Western astrology.</note>, speaking of the science of astrology in the first statement of his other book titled *The Fruit* (commonly called the *Centiloquium* <note>A collection of 100 astrological aphorisms falsely attributed to Ptolemy in the Middle Ages.</note>), says: "It is impossible for one who is knowledgeable to pronounce the particular forms of things, just as the senses do not perceive a particular form but rather a general form of a sensible thing; therefore, the practitioner must use conjecture. Only those inspired by a deity predict particulars." These are his words verbatim, though they are found differently, and often corrupted, in common manuscripts. 

But even among the Arabs and Hebrews who write on astrology, it is an undisputed opinion that whatever a star has promised might still not come to pass. This is either because the "matter" <note>The physical recipient of the star's influence.</note> is not suitable for receiving the influence, or because human affairs depend largely on our own free will, or because a particular fate may be overcome by the power of a more universal opposing fate. Furthermore, Divine Providence—which is more powerful than any fate and greater than the heavens—sometimes orders things to happen differently than the ordinary revolution of the sky would have effected. While these ideas are scattered throughout the works of astrologers, you may read them all together in Abraham ibn Ezra <note>original: "Auenazram" — A famous 12th-century Jewish scholar and astrologer.</note> in the first chapter of his *Book of Nativities*.

## Chapter II. That Auspices, which they call Elections, are Useless: by the testimony of one astrologer, by reason, and by experience.

Now, if these things are true, let the astrologer show what benefit life gains from his predictions. He will perhaps answer that the benefit is twofold: first, that he teaches the hour in which we ought to "auspicate" <note>Begin an undertaking under favorable omens.</note> our actions so that what we are about to do happens successfully. Second, when he predicts what is to come, there is this utility: that we may abstain from those things in which we know we shall be unhappy, and conversely 

<column-break/>

<margin>Auspices are useless.</margin>
attack those tasks in which the natal hour promises us success. 

But come, let us examine both claims, beginning with the first. And since our dispute is with the astrologers, let us use the very assumptions they consider most true. Either the natal constellation of your birth made the heavens favorable to the thing you are about to do, or adverse. If it is adverse, then "auspication" <note>Choosing a lucky starting time.</note> is of no use according to Ptolemy’s own opinion; therefore, you will always approach that task unsuccessfully, and you would be better off always abstaining from it. If the heavens are favorable, there is no need for an "election" of hours; your own choice is sufficient, for you will undertake that task most successfully whenever your own mind invites you to it. 

For to be fortunate (if anyone is made fortunate by the heavens) is nothing other than having our imaginative faculty, the servant of reason, moved by the heavens in such a way that we undertake each thing at the times and in the ways that our wish can be most successfully fulfilled. Regarding this, Aristotle <note>Referring to the *Eudemian Ethics* or the pseudo-Aristotelian *Magna Moralia*.</note> said that counsel does not benefit the fortunate man in the matter for which nature shaped him, lest perhaps counsel distract and lead him away from that natural impulse of the mind where he was being called.

<margin>Aristotle. Haly. From Critias.</margin>
I pass over the fact that Haly <note>Haly Abenragel, an 11th-century Arab astrologer.</note>, the interpreter of Ptolemy, says this part of astrology concerning "elections" is frivolous and ineffective. I pass over the evidence of experience itself, than which nothing is more certain or constant. For daily experience makes it manifest that those who observe this vain distinction of times are the least successful in conducting their affairs. On the contrary, those who reject such superstition and use only their own choice and prudence as guides are far more successful.

<margin>To whom success and to whom failure is born from Astronomy.</margin>
Who, in our age, was more fortunate than Francesco Sforza? <note>The mercenary who became Duke of Milan (1401–1466).</note> Through military success, he secured for himself the vast and flourishing Empire of the Insubrians <note>The Duchy of Milan.</note> and left it increased and confirmed to his descendants. Yet he always held all astrologers either in hatred or contempt, never employing them as advisors in his military or domestic affairs. Among the ancients, who was more powerful in astrology, magic, and every superstition than Zoroaster? And yet Ninus <note>The mythical founder of Nineveh.</note>—who was certainly neither an astrologer nor a mage—conquered and killed him in war. 

Pompey placed the greatest faith in the responses of diviners; Caesar placed none. To the former, fortune was adverse; to the latter, it was happy and joyful. Who is unaware that Justinian—the exterminator of astrologers, as we have seen—was most successful at home and in war? The Emperor Julian <note>Julian the Apostate (r. 361–363).</note>, the enemy of the Christian name and the most curious observer of all superstitions: how briefly and how unhappily he lost both his life and his impious [rule]! 

I could name one or two learned astrologers, familiar to me, whose faith in this vanity—to which they devoted their way of life—resulted in their ruin or significant detriment. But I do not wish to defame men who are otherwise good, nor to violate the laws of holy friendship in a matter not strictly necessary for the truth. But I wish this vanity had not taken away one man's patrimony, and another's country and life! It has made many fools and madmen through vain hope, and many miserable through fear. 

As God may not see my sins, I have seen no one more lacking in those things which astrology promises to its followers than those who have devoted themselves entirely to astrology, hunting for the favor of the heavens every single hour. A certain great man known to me changed his way of life after suffering a significant loss of his former fortune; he did this based on astrological hope, believing that in a new profession he would achieve great happiness through celestial favor. But when he experienced worse fortune every day in that new life, he used to say he had been "deceived by Mars," not wanting to say what was more true: that he had been deceived by astrological vanity. The same man died shortly after in a very miserable death, which he himself had not foreseen from the heavens. For he was preparing many...

<sig>p ii</sig>

<summary>Pico argues that perfect astrological prediction is impossible because celestial configurations never truly repeat and human variables (biology, location, habit) interfere. He also mocks the practice of "elections," citing historical figures like Sforza and Caesar who succeeded by ignoring astrology, while those who followed it, like Julian the Apostate, met ruin.</summary>
