<meta>This page continues Pico’s critique of the practical application of astrology. He transitions from discussing the personal tragedies of those who trusted stars over medicine to a broader logical argument: if astrology contradicts reason or professional expertise (like medicine or statecraft), it is dangerous; if it agrees, it is redundant.</meta>

->DISPUTATIONS<-

...and he was undertaking great projects, as one who had still set for himself long boundaries of life. I could recount many instances of this kind, but my mind recoils from the narration of those things which I can scarcely remember without tears. Since these misfortunes befell my dearest friends, they demand compassion from me rather than reproach. Yet I hope that this reluctant rebuttal—in which I have suppressed the names of my old friends—may benefit my living friends. By all the rights of friendship that exist between us, by their fortunes, and by my prayers for their happiness, I warn and ask them again and again: never entrust their affairs to the counsel of that vanity <note>Meaning astrology.</note>. Let them regard it (if they like) as a poetic fable over which they may laugh, play, and joke; but let them not hold it as a leader or a mistress of life. Instead, when the health of the body must be considered, let them consult physicians. When external matters must be foreseen, let them use the eyes of prudence and reason. Divine wisdom teaches us both: it says that the physician was created by the Most High for our necessity <note>A reference to the Biblical book of Sirach/Ecclesiasticus 38:1: "Honor the physician... for the Lord created him."</note>, and it says that prudence must be preserved by man so that he may be rescued from the evil way. We find no such thing written about astrology. We have proven its profession to be so useless that we would grant it only as much as the astrologers themselves think should be granted. For once it has been proven that it possesses no truth, it will be beyond all controversy—as we have endeavored to prove here—that it is most dangerous to trust our affairs to the counsel of astrologers. If ever something happens correctly according to their predictions, it should be attributed not to reason (of which they have none) but to recklessness and chance.

### Chapter III. Astrology is not useful in deciding what should be done or what should be avoided.

<margin>Note the destructions.</margin>
**A**nother benefit of astrology can be imagined, as we mentioned above: namely, that we should pursue a matter which the astrologer has ordered us to follow, or conversely, avoid those things which he forbids. We have demonstrated that this is either superfluous or harmful. For what he predicts pertains either to the body or to external and fortuitous matters. Regarding those things which pertain to the body, if they concern health, I ask whether the judgment of the physician agrees with the judgment of the astrologer, or whether it differs. If both feel the same, the astrologer contributes nothing to you that the physician could not provide alone. If they disagree, which of the two do you think should be followed? Surely, if you commit yourself to the astrologer while rejecting the physician, you will pay the penalty for your madness. Similarly, in conducting affairs, I ask whether prudence advises the same action that astrology advises. Or do these judgments thoroughly oppose one another? If they agree on something within our reach, why should we seek it so far away in the heavens? If they disagree, who could rightly or rationally defend the choice to abandon prudence—which is nothing other than the right reason for doing things—in the conduct of affairs? But these points will be clearer with examples. Suppose an astrologer predicts that Mars threatens you this year with a tertian fever <note>original: "tritæum" — a fever that returns every third day, historically associated with an excess of "yellow bile."</note>. He claims it will stir up bile through the power it holds in the annual revolution. Therefore, you should use cooling remedies and arrange your way of life against the heat of Mars. Now, will this very thing which he predicts from the heavens be demonstrated by the signs of your own body—from which the conjectures of physicians are drawn—or will it not? If they do demonstrate it, this will be enough evidence for you to guard against future ill health. If they do not demonstrate it, I ask whether you think it right to act when there are no observable signs from the heat. But a <unclear>whitish and thick</unclear> urine, sluggish pulses of the veins, a face

<column-break/>

deformed by paleness, lethargy of the limbs, and other such things which physicians use as signs, will indicate the dominance of phlegm, not bile. Yet you would evacuate bile because an astrologer imagined Mars threatening you from the sky! What if even a wise astrologer cannot advise you? For even if he speaks truly about Mars, your natural temperament, the universal disposition of the year itself, or your own way of life may have turned you toward the opposite for as long as you practiced it. Finally, while the astrologer sees only one cause that can effect this—and a remote and universal one at that—the physician judges not only from personal and immediate causes but perceives the matter itself through the senses. He holds the truth that results from the combination of all causes simultaneously, through the evidence of present nature itself. <margin>An example in external affairs.</margin> I pass over the fact that even those who favor the judgments of astrologers are not so insane as to think they are less prone to error than the judgments of physicians. Let us propose a similar example in the handling of external affairs: suppose a mathematician <note>In this period, "mathematicus" often referred specifically to an astrologer or someone who calculated horoscopes.</note> advises a prince not to enter into war with enemies because Mars is not sufficiently favorable to him. I ask whether, at the time he gave this advice, the prince had no just cause for war, or no occasion and opportunity for winning. Or rather, was there both a just cause for war and all the instruments for victory at hand? If you grant the first, he will rightly not go to war, but with prudence alone as his guide, even if the mathematician remains entirely silent. If the second, not even the astrologer himself (unless he has a personal stake) would judge that one should abstain from war. And if he did abstain, what would that be other than abandoning sense and evidence for the sake of mere conjecture?

### Chapter IV. Astrology is not useful for religion; a view held by Roger Bacon and Pierre d'Ailly for a twofold reason.

<margin>Reasons by which d'Ailly affirmed astrology to be necessary.</margin>
**B**ut if it is useless for life, is it perhaps useful for religion? This is what both Roger Bacon and Pierre d'Ailly <note>Two prominent medieval scholars who argued that astrology could be reconciled with Christian theology.</note> seem to have thought. The latter did so for two main reasons. First, that the truth about the number of years from Adam to Christ—about which there is such great debate among ecclesiastical books—could be obtained from the astrological calculation of the "Great Conjunctions" <note>Significant alignments of planets, especially Jupiter and Saturn, believed by some to mark great historical and religious shifts.</note>. Second, that the oracles of the prophets could be confirmed if the testimony of astrological prediction were added to their predictions. For since all truth is in harmony with all truth, they argue the truth of astronomical science must necessarily be in agreement with theological truth. Indeed, they claim it should serve that truth as a handmaid to a mistress above all other sciences, since the invisible things of God are perceived through the visible things he has made. And since nothing among those things is more noble than the heaven, hence that saying of David: *The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament announces the work of his hands.* As if to prove this opinion through his work, d'Ailly wrote a small book divided into twenty theorems, which he calls "words." The title is *On the Concordance of Astrology and Theology*, as if he had never read Paul exclaiming: *What fellowship has light with darkness? Or what part has Christ with Belial?* In that work, he strives to achieve those two things we mentioned: namely, to show that what the prophets predicted by divine inspiration was also prefigured by celestial constellations, and then to investigate the calculation of years from Adam to Christ from the dogmas of the astrologers. He adds another small book to this on the *Concordance of Astronomy and History*, in which, noting seven "greatest conjunctions" since the beginning of the world, he strives to relate them to the great and wonderful events collected from histories in the intervening times, intending to confirm the dogma of the astrologers that from those great conjunctions...

<summary>Pico argues that astrology is redundant when it agrees with medical or practical wisdom and dangerous when it contradicts it. He also begins to refute the claims of Roger Bacon and Pierre d'Ailly, who attempted to use astrology to calculate biblical timelines and validate prophecy.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's systematic dismantling of astrological authority, shifting from personal anecdotes to a focused critique of Pierre d’Ailly, a high-ranking churchman and scholar who attempted to harmonize astrology with Christian history.</meta>

### AGAINST ASTROLOGY BOOK II.

<margin>
The cause of d’Ailly’s error.
</margin>
...they claim that great changes in human affairs, both of laws and of kingdoms, are always occurring. Indeed, I would have preferred that he had written things I could praise rather than refute; for I love him as a man of literary talent and I venerate the high office he held in the Church. Yet perhaps I shall even be doing him a kindness: if what he wrote—thinking, with little caution, that he was helping the Church—is found to be undoubtedly false and harmful, it is better that it be wiped out by this just correction. What led this otherwise learned man into such error was, above all, an ignorance of astronomy. Having exercised himself in theological studies at the most famous University of Paris, he began as an old man to get a mere "taste" of astronomy. He was lured by the magnificent appearance of that art which discusses the greatest matters—things human curiosity desires to know above all else. Before he reached the point where he could detect the weakness of its dogmas through deep examination, he too hastily wrote those two small works. Later, having become a little more skilled, he revised them; then he wrote much in that booklet he calls the *Elucidarium* <note>Latin: *Elucidarium*, meaning "The Elucidator" or "The Bringer of Light."</note>, though there is much darkness in it. If someone ignorant of astronomy reads these books, he will marvel at them all the more because he understands them less. But anyone who has made even moderate progress in that art will judge him to have been a writer rather than an astronomer; he will see that whatever he says was merely read by him, rather than understood "to the marrow." Almost everything he writes is taken word-for-word from Roger Bacon, Abraham the Jew <note>Likely referring to Abraham ibn Ezra, a famous 12th-century scholar.</note>, Henry Bate of Mechelen, Albumasar <note>Abu Ma'shar, a highly influential Persian astrologer.</note>, and some summary by a certain John of Britain <note>Referring to John Eschenden, a 14th-century English astrologer.</note>. That he was merely a listener and lacked skill in astronomical matters can be known from this: in the *Elucidarium* itself (his most polished work), in chapter eleven, he says that we were (when he was writing) in the year of Christ 1404, and that we were in the "aerial triplicity" <note><term>triplicity</term>: In astrology, the twelve zodiac signs are divided into four groups of three based on the elements (Fire, Earth, Air, Water).</note> and would remain so for sixty-one more years until the year 1465. He claimed that a "great conjunction" <note><term>great conjunction</term>: A rare alignment of the planets Jupiter and Saturn, which astrologers believed signaled major historical shifts.</note> of Saturn and Jupiter would then occur, with a change from the aerial to the watery triplicity. In truth, however, that change had already occurred nearly forty years earlier, in the year of Christ 1365; at that time, on the twenty-ninth day of October, Saturn and Jupiter were together in the seventh degree of Scorpio. From then on, they have always joined in watery signs up to these times. Our friend d’Ailly was waiting for something to happen in the future that had actually happened nearly a hundred years before!

<margin>
Where he took his dogmas. D’Ailly’s ignorance exposed.
</margin>

<margin>
The book on the true calculation of time.
</margin>
As for the other benefit he thought came from astrology—namely, gathering the true count of years—we have abundantly refuted this in that book we wrote *On the True Calculation of Time*. Even if astrology helped the Christian commonwealth in that regard, it would not belong to the kind of astrology we are refuting here (which deals with predicting the future), but rather to true astronomy. Astronomy is one of the liberal arts, whose job it is to calculate times and measure the motions of the stars by mathematical reasoning. But this is not the place to refute his errors; we shall do that in the following books. There, regarding the "concordance of philosophy and theology," we shall show that things announced by the prophets are neither caused nor signified by the heavens. Thus, even if astrology were true, the prediction of those religious events would not belong to it. As for those who claim that such things are outside the heavens' power insofar as they are supernatural, yet are caused or "persuaded" by the heavens insofar as they have a natural element, we shall show that they say nothing, even though they seem to be saying something. Indeed, far from the prophetic oracles being usefully confirmed by the decrees of astrologers, nothing could be more effective or powerful in 

<column-break/>

weakening religion. Furthermore, those who have tried to do this have always been found to be liars; they are unskilled in astronomy and wander far from the truth in their historical profession. Generally, not only regarding laws and divine miracles, but also regarding other changes in human affairs which many have wished to predict from "great conjunctions," we shall there expose their vanity and the falsehood of their dogma. There we shall struggle for the truth against Albumasar (the author of that error), his interpreter Hermann, Abraham the Israelite, and John of Exeter. We shall so thoroughly unweave d’Ailly’s book—in which he tried to do the same regarding the "concordance of astrology and historical narrative"—from beginning to end, that as we run through every conjunction he notes from the first to the last, we shall show that he said nothing sound or close to the truth regarding either heavenly or earthly matters. Not one of those seven conjunctions he notes happened at the time he thinks it did; the actual narrative of the times (that is, of recorded history) and the true calculation of dates are vastly different. But let us see if those arguments he brought later carry any weight: namely, that "all true things harmonize with each other" and "the heavens declare the glory of God" <note>A quote from Psalm 19:1.</note>.

<margin>
A great discovery regarding d’Ailly.
</margin>
Certainly, that first statement is most true; but the conclusion to be drawn is that since astrology is false, it cannot harmonize with theological truth. The Apostle Paul teaches that the testimony of David <note>Referring to the author of the Psalms.</note> should be applied to the "heavenly minds" of the Apostles, who announced that glory of God about which it is later written: "the law of the Lord is spotless, converting souls." But even if the quote refers to the visible sky, what kind of logic is this: "if the heavens declare the glory of God, then the heavens support the fables that astrologers tell about God's glory"? But "His invisible things," it is said, "and His power and divinity are understood through visible things" <note>A reference to Romans 1:20.</note>. This is understood by the *philosopher*, whose proper task is to climb from the order, motion, and nature of the heaven to the invisible, divine Maker of the heaven. The astrologer, if the heaven is anything, looks at it unwillingly; he turns his eyes away from heaven down to the earth. Only the philosopher contemplates invisible things from the visible.

<margin>
Praise for the philosopher.
</margin>

### Chapter V. How harmful and pestilential astrology is to the Christian religion.

Indeed, as I survey everything around me and scout the enemies of the Church, I do not see any source that provides more troops and more weapons against the truth than this profession. From here, there is a headlong and very easy slide into impiety, into bad religion, into heresies, into vain superstition, and into ruined morals and irredeemable malice. From where else will impiety arm itself against the weapons of religion than by claiming that divine miracles (by which all religion is chiefly confirmed) must be referred back to the heavens? If you bring up the martyrs who despised death, or the few, poor, unlearned Apostles who subjected the world to the law of the Gospel, or even people called back from the dead—things too great to be human and too good to be done by a demon—they will tear away the power in these things unless it is something that only the course of a star or a "heavenly breath" could do. If someone says this, is he not moving a saw against the roots of religion? If he persuades others, is he not examining and utterly uprooting it? Now, if you say that this is not a vice of the *art* but of its *professors* who err in their own profession, I will admit that is so. I was not saying this was an inherent error of astrology, but rather that it is an easy slide from astrology into this error. Even if astrology were true, it would not cease from this duty: to keep away from that danger...

-> OF THE DISPUTATIONS <-

...to turn men away: since no truth is to be confirmed by lies. Instead, since astrology is false, its falsehood should be usefully exposed; for if it were thought to be true, it could generate so grave a plague in the minds of rulers. Indeed, if you see the professors of any art holding such vanities, it is almost impossible for the fault not to be truly attributed to the art itself. Truly, I have read none among the chief writers of astrology who does not subject religion and all laws—as they do all other human affairs—to the constellations of the stars. Ptolemy, in the second book of his *Apotelesmaton* <note>The *Apotelesmaton* is better known today as the *Tetrabiblos*, Ptolemy’s foundational 2nd-century work on astrology.</note>, 
<margin>Ptolemy.</margin>
understands that the fact that one deity is worshipped among one people and another among another arises from no other source than the various natures of the stars and signs ruling over those peoples and nations. Not far from that passage, a certain Greek interpreter of Ptolemy says that the miracle of Moses—who crossed the Red Sea with his people on dry feet—occurred because he observed the ebb and flow of the sea. As if the Hebrew people could pass through those same waters unharmed while Pharaoh was submerged along with his own astrologers! Or as if Joshua did not cross the Jordan on dry feet, where no tide and no reciprocity of waves is imagined by them! But we have sufficiently refuted all these and similar trifles elsewhere. Albumasar,
<margin>Albumasar</margin>
the Arab, derives the law of the Saracens <note>The term used historically for Muslims.</note>, his own law, and our own—indeed, all laws equally—from the heavens. He pronounces which constellation created each one, and for how many years each is to last, based on that same constellation. We shall later declare how little astrology and how little truth is found in these matters. His interpreter, Henry 
<margin>Henry.</margin>
of Mechelen, was so delirious that he even "found" a ship in the sky after which Noah was to build that Ark of his—an "invention" which d'Ailly greatly admired as if it were divine. Finally, it can be known from this that they reduce Law to the order of those things which happen by a natural course and the changing of the heavens. They want to know from the sky how many revolutions of years will occur from the "ascent" of a law until its "fall." And Haly Abenzagel,
<margin>Haly.</margin>
to say nothing of the others, pronounces the prosperity or sterility of the year from this: if the "ascent" of the law falls in the place of Jupiter or Venus, it will be a fertile year; conversely, if it falls in the places of the unlucky stars. Abraham the Jew—not the one called 
<margin>Abraham.</margin>
Avenazra <note>Abraham ibn Ezra, a famous 12th-century Jewish scholar and astrologer.</note> as d'Ailly falsely believed, but the one they call the *Nasi*, that is, the Prince—did he not attempt to refer the Mosaic law, the departure of the Jews from Egypt, and whatever happened to the people under the Law to various conjunctions, in a manner both inept and ridiculous? But would that only those we have mentioned had failed to see the light of this truth amidst the darkness of a bad religion! Would that our own men were not so blinded in the splendor of the Gospel, and did not think worse of our religion and theirs than those others did! That insane man Bonatti <note>Guido Bonatti, a 13th-century Italian astrologer.</note> says that the Lord Jesus used the "election of hours" <note><term>Electional astrology</term>: the practice of choosing a specific moment in time to begin an action based on the position of the planets.</note> when, responding to the apostles who advised Him not to return to Judea, He said there are twelve hours in a day. For Bonatti says He chose an hour for Himself in which they could not harm Him—as if He did not prostrate them when He willed, or as if He were not hidden from them while passing through their midst in the light of day. I pass over the reckless and blasphemous things he says about the divine family of Francis <note>Referring to the Franciscan Order.</note>, fabledly claiming that the miracle of divine love was the work of Mars. But why do we look for remote examples? In those things which are daily spread abroad in public prophecies regarding the events of the years, do they not say that the Christian law was perfected by the doctrine of Christ and Mercury, and that the religion of Jupiter receives its purity from a Virgin? Thus Christian men read these things with eyes that are not indignant. And in the prefaces of some "theory" or other, disputing much against Gerard, is it not even 

<column-break/>

written—when treating the election of a new Pope—that one should devoutly pray that the "Mercurial star" might temper him with its holy ray? For they say our Law is subject to Mercury, and therefore he called Christian men "men of Mercury"—something I do not know how any Christian man can hear with level ears. 
<margin>Roger Bacon.</margin>
Roger Bacon was carried so far that he did not hesitate to write that Christians err by not resting on the Sabbath and by working according to the Jewish rite, since that is the day of Saturn, a star considered little suited or lucky for conducting business. In these words, he accuses not only our people, but Moses; indeed, he openly turns the prophet into an astrologer, teaching that the decrees Moses made concerning the Sabbath rest were based not on any divine mystery, but on astrological dogma. If anyone weighs all these things with a correct examination of judgment, he will see that the piety of true religion is offended by no error more than this; for it is equally impious to think there is no religion at all as it is to derive it from the heavens by some fatal necessity. Indeed, if an astrologer is to embrace any religion, to what will he be more inclined than to 
<margin>What the Manichean heresy is.</margin>
idolatry? For he would especially worship and revere those "gods" from whom he thinks all things, both good and evil, proceed for men. Now, the Manichean heresies <note>The Manicheans were followers of a dualistic religion that often taught a form of determinism.</note>, which take away the freedom of the will—where else do we think they emanated from, if not from this false opinion of the astrologers regarding fate? Regarding superstitions, 
<margin>See Varro on superstition.</margin>
there is no controversy that they all proceed from astronomy; Varro confirms that they are all contained by it like foster-children. All writers of geomancy <note><term>Geomancy</term>: divination by means of lines and figures or geographical features.</note> call it the daughter of astrology. The Magi think the use of this art is so necessary to them that they call astrology the "key to magic." Chiromancers <note>Palm readers.</note> fashion seven "mounts" in the palm of the hand according to the number of the planets, from which the future may be foreseen by the lines seen there. But we shall pursue these follies in detail later, after we have trampled upon the rest of the crowd of superstitions as their mistress and queen. But it is manifest enough from this that they are all born from it and cannot stand without it: for there is no superstition that does not use the "election" of days and hours, in which only astronomy instructs them. Thus, that saying of Ecclesiastes can be said of astrology: "Vanity of vanities, astrology and every superstition is vanity." It is not necessary to say more about morals, since it is clear enough that no greater patronage can be given to vice than if the heavens are thought to be its author; there is nothing that makes us fear Hell less or hope for happiness less. If these things are undoubtedly true, even if this profession were true, would it not be more useful for the truth to be ignored? And since it is false, how much more usefully is its falsehood attacked? This is a province I hope to fulfill with as much vigor as the desire with which I have embraced it for the sake of helping religion and defending the truth.

### Chapter VI. That this art is deceptive, if it exists at all, both because of many factors and because of the disagreeing opinions of astrologers.

Thus far we have shown that astrology is usefully refuted, and that its patronage is unworthy of both a philosopher and a Christian. Now, before we engage hand-to-hand with the astrologers to begin our refutation, let us see how much the facts and events themselves repel it. For how many things happen that were predicted by them? Or if something does happen, why did *that* happen rather than something else? Thus, I am often amazed by those who, when disputing against this art, always object: "If their art is not true, why then are their predictions true?" They have clearly done well for themselves...

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s second book against the astrologers. He is currently arguing that astrology is unreliable not only because of its internal logic, but because its greatest practitioners constantly contradict one another and admit to the art's uncertainty.</meta>

# AGAINST THE ASTROLOGERS, BOOK II.

<margin>Ptolemy.</margin>
<margin>Porphyry.</margin>
<margin>A remarkable and manifold disagreement among astrologers.</margin>
<margin>First disagreement.</margin>
The astrologer thinks he has accomplished much if he can offer some defense when we confront them with the falsehood of their predictions; yet he is so far from being able to take an argument against us from this place, even if he thinks he can. We have cited above the words of Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the most influential astronomer and astrologer of antiquity.</note> attempting to resolve this very question: in which we saw that he rejected the lies of astrologers not only by blaming the practitioners for being unskilled or careless, but by blaming the art itself, which he claimed is uncertain and highly prone to deception. Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher and critic of popular religion.</note> himself said that the responses of oracles were often found to be false; for this reason, those spirits predicted things based on celestial causes which they had investigated. However, any prediction based on such things is fallacious. But if even the demons themselves—from whom nothing of celestial matters is hidden—are deceived when they look into the future from that source, what, I ask you, shall we judge of men? Among whom, even those who were the most excellent in that art (if it is an art at all) never touched even a thousandth part of it. Finally, among all the arts—all of which are prone to fall away from the truth—there is none whose judgment is more uncertain; nor, I believe, will the astrologers themselves deny this. For they say that a man's own choice <note>Free will</note> causes many things to happen differently; and the flux and mobility of matter often frustrates the workings of celestial actions; and one fate is turned or hindered by another. 

<margin>Second [disagreement].</margin>
If you examine human affairs diligently, you will find almost nothing in which something of what we have said does not change the outcome, even if that outcome was truly foreseen from the heavens. For it is proper for men to arrange their affairs by choice and reason; and that which is connected and bound to matter on all sides is vehemently subject to change. Furthermore, since nothing exists in isolation, almost all men depend on one another in turn, such that there is no one whose fortune cannot be harmed or helped by the fortune of another. Thus, a fortunate son will obtain a fortunate outcome from the good fate of his parent, despite a father’s misfortune. And a servant, though his own birth-chart is less fortunate, will fare happily under a fortunate master. So too the fate of a soldier depends on the fate of his commander, and the fortune of the sick man on the physician—and conversely, that of the physician on the sick man—happening now one way, now another. 

<margin>Third [disagreement].</margin>
<margin>Note.</margin>
From all these things, it is declared how often it is necessary for that which the mathematician <note>In this period, "mathematicus" was often used as a synonym for "astrologer."</note> predicted for someone not to happen, even if that profession were true—let alone that the truth of the profession could be proven by the true predictions of the professors. What of the fact that there is such great dissension in dogma among the authors of this art? It makes it necessary that either all or the greatest part of them are telling lies about the future. They themselves greatly admire and venerate certain Egyptians, Persians, Indians, and Babylonians as if they were priests of celestial mysteries, and they sound their names daily into the ears of the unskilled with puffed-out cheeks, as if they were gods. But if you were to speak the truth, O astrologers, you cannot tell us which of them you follow, as you possess only the books of the younger writers, who differ in every way from that ancient discipline. For Ptolemy, your "father," everywhere censures and tears apart the astrology that belonged to the Egyptians, sometimes saying it is not consistent with reason, other times attacking it with other proofs, as is easily seen by anyone reading the books of the *Apotelesmaton* <note>original: "apotelesmaton"—referring to Ptolemy’s *Tetrabiblos*.</note>. Nor did Ptolemy only differ from them; those others disagreed among themselves equally: the Indians from the Chaldeans, the Egyptians from both each other and from these, the Indians from all of them, and the Persians from all the rest. Greek astrology is no less discordant with itself than the foreign varieties; for the things that Ptolemy rejects, Dorotheus <note>Dorotheus of Sidon, a 1st-century astrologer.</note> embraces; Paulus <note>Paulus Alexandrinus.</note> feels one way, Hephaestion <note>Hephaestion of Thebes.</note> another, and others think differently still. Nor will you find any among them who does not claim the weight of experience for the reliability of their outcomes. Do not the Arabs also fight with each other and with the Greeks? Furthermore, just as Ptolemy rejects that ancient astrology, so Albumasar <note>Abu Ma'shar, a famous Persian astrologer.</note> rejects the astrology of Ptolemy, to the point that he says nothing can be read in his books that is found to be consistent with either reason or experience. Conversely, Avenrodan <note>Ali ibn Ridwan, an Egyptian physician and astrologer.</note> says there was no place in astrology consistent with reason except for Ptolemy, and that if you look at the sayings of others, you will find them far removed from the truth, whereas the sayings of Ptolemy can in no way be found false. The Hebrews also disagree; and the first of the Hebrews, Abraham Ibn Ezra <note>original: "Abraam Auenazra"</note>, disagrees with Ptolemy and often tore Albumasar to pieces; indeed, they reject and repudiate his entire book, which in Latin is titled *On Great Conjunctions*. 

If, therefore, the followers of Ptolemy are truthful, must not the ancient Arabs, their followers, necessarily be lying? And if those books were—as they boast—admired by everyone because they brought forth the truth, must not Ptolemy and Albumasar have been objects of laughter in their own centuries? And others similarly, deviating entirely from their decrees. And yet you will find it was always כך <note>Original Hebrew: "so" or "thus"—Pico likely uses this to emphasize the continuity of the error.</note> that in every nation and every age there were always men who said true things were predicted by astrologers, which happened not by the truth of their dogmas but by chance; nor was there ever a lack of those who held this fallacy in mockery and contempt, or even hatred. But whatever may have been the case in former centuries, surely in this time of ours the truth of the dogma cannot be confirmed by the professors, since they follow mostly bad authors and do not understand the good ones; moreover, they perform this duty so negligently that they are ignorant of many things they ought to know, and omit even more that should be considered, sparing themselves the labor and hurrying toward monetary gain. If I had intended to teach astrology here rather than confute it, I would pour out a hand against the errors of the younger men professing this art, but that is not my plan. Nevertheless, it will perhaps be worthwhile to note some things, so that it may become more manifest that they cannot predict the truth even if the dogmas of the astrologers were most true.

---

### Chapter VII. On the ignorance of the astrologers of our age.

<margin>Ptolemy.</margin>
<margin>John of Ashenden.</margin>
Those predictions regarding men are either universal—as when they predict future good or evil for the whole world from the chart of the year, from eclipses of the sun and moon, or from the conjunctions of the superior stars—or they are particular, such as when they divine something about a man's fate from his own specific birth-chart <note>original: "genitura"</note>. In the first category, nothing is more effective than an eclipse of the luminaries, from which, as if from the most universal causes, the most universal changes of inferior things occur. In the second category, nothing has greater weight than the "equalization" <note>A technical term in astrology for calculating the length of life.</note> which is usually done for the span of life and the number of years. It is amazing how much the modern and foreign writers err in both of these; it is their authority that is most used among our astrologers. Ptolemy writes in the second book of the *Apotelesmaton* that in a solar eclipse, two things are primarily to be observed: the place in which the sun is eclipsed, and the "angle" which follows that place most closely. For example, if the eclipse occurs in the ninth region of heaven, the angle of the tenth place should be observed; if in the eleventh or twelfth, the angle of the rising <note>The Ascendant</note>. However, because the Greek text there says "of the following angle," the common translation <note>The Latin Vulgate translation of the text.</note> has "of the preceding angle," from which an entirely opposite sense is derived. This gave the foreign writers an occasion for error, such that John of Ashenden <note>An 14th-century English astrologer and physician.</note>, in that work which is commonly called the *English Summa* <note>A massive compilation of astrological lore.</note>—which carries the highest authority among our people—after he tormented himself with a long and argumentative investigation, finally defined, according to the opinion of Ptolemy, that he ought to observe the angle...

### NINTH DISPUTATION

<margin>An error in Ptolemy.</margin>
...not one that follows, but one that precedes the place where the eclipse of the luminary <note>The "luminaries" are the Sun and the Moon.</note> occurred. It is entirely clear that this is contrary to the opinion of Ptolemy from what we have said, namely because the Greek word <insert>preceding <note>original: προηγούμενος (proegoumenos)</note></insert> was written—meaning "that which follows"—and not <insert>following <note>original: ἑπόμενος (epomenos)</note></insert>—meaning "that which precedes." But because a little later Ptolemy himself, explaining which angles these are, named the meridian and the rising angle of the sun, the Greek interpreter reminds us that the angle of the setting sun is omitted. This angle cannot follow the place of the eclipse unless the sun were obscured beneath the earth; and when that happens, they do not believe it has the power to produce future effects. However, if the "preceding" angle were to be observed, then the "rising" angle should have been omitted by Ptolemy, since it cannot precede the eclipsed sun unless it is beneath the earth; and the "setting" angle should have been included, which would always be found to run ahead of and precede the eclipse, whether it fell in the eighth or ninth house of heaven. From this error, the entire method of prediction is changed, since in predicting they respect nothing more than the nature and state of the stars, both at the location of the luminaries and at that dominant angle. When one angle is taken for another, there will also be one ruler instead of another. And according to the diverse nature of the ruling star, the pronouncement about future events will always be varied—indeed, even contradictory. Regarding the foreseeing of the span of life—about which these little diviners see nothing—I will show in a few words that Haly Abenragel, <margin>Haly Abenragel. What the Hylegh is.</margin> the oracle of the astrologers of this age, says in the fourth part of his work that, according to Ptolemy’s opinion, there are five <term>Hylegh <note>From the Persian 'haylaj,' the "Giver of Life"; a point in a birth chart used to determine the length of a person's life.</note></term>. For this is how they speak: the Sun, the Moon, the Ascendant <note>The "horoscope" or the point of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon.</note>, the "Part of Fortune," and the place of the full moon or new moon immediately preceding the birth. Besides these five, they say the planets holding power and authority in those five places must be considered. In the next chapter, speaking of what they call the <term>Alcocoden <note>From the Arabic 'al-kadhkhudah,' the "Giver of Years"; a planet that determines the specific number of years a person will live based on the Hylegh.</note></term> (who is the "giver of years"), he says: "Ptolemy says the Alcocoden is the planet that has the most authority in the Hylegh, whether it aspects it or not." <margin>What the Alcocoden is. A most evident error of the astrologers.</margin> And so thereafter he repeats many things about this Alcocoden according to the "opinion of Ptolemy." Our astrologers, who follow him and other barbarians <note>Pico uses "barbarians" to refer to non-Greek sources, particularly Arabic and Medieval Latin authors.</note>, persist in the same error. They search through every birth chart for what the Hylegh is and what the Alcocoden is, according to the "opinion of Ptolemy." But in truth, in Ptolemy himself, this "Alcocoden" is as much a non-entity as a <term>goat-stag <note>A 'hircocervus,' a standard philosophical example of a mythical creature used to represent something that does not exist.</note></term> or a chimera. Read all his books, read all his interpreters, read even the barbarian translations, and you will not find that word or any word corresponding to it in his writings. For that opinion—making the Hylegh one thing in a birth chart and the "giver of life and years" (which they call the Alcocoden) another—belongs to later writers. Neither Ptolemy nor those older than him ever held such an opinion. He first names places that we might call "dismissory" <note>Places from which the "course of life" is released, like runners from a starting gate.</note>, so called because the course of life takes its starting point from there, as if from the gates of a racecourse. These are known to be above the earth, connected by some affinity to either the setting or the rising horizon. Then he establishes the <term>aphetas <note>Greek for "releaser" or "sender forth."</note></term>, which are the "releasers" themselves, who, from those places as if from gates, bestow the impulse of life by their "breath," so to speak. He wants these to be the Sun, the Moon, the Ascendant, the Part of Fortune, and the wandering stars <note>The planets.</note> predominating in those places. Besides these, all of which are counted as Hyleghs, he makes no other distributor of years—except that he thinks the gifts of these "releasers" can be increased or exhausted by the influence of lucky or unlucky stars. Yet the barbarians and our own countrymen believe that, besides these "releasers" (whom they call Hylegh), there is another who decrees the span of life according to Ptolemy's opinion, whom they call the Alcocoden. Regarding this matter,

<column-break/>

as I was saying, Ptolemy himself says nothing anywhere; yet based on his supposed opinion, they inquire, dispute, and define many things about it. Nor do they err only in this, upon which the whole sum of the matter depends, but also in the very enumeration of the Hyleghs themselves. <margin>Haly.</margin> For Haly says that the place of the preceding new moon or full moon is placed among them by Ptolemy. However, Ptolemy never thinks this should be done, whether the birth chart is for night or day. What of the fact that this Haly accuses Ptolemy of being inconsistent with himself, and greatly boasts over this assessment of Ptolemy—in which he says no one has ever opposed him—and gives great thanks to God, the revealer of secrets? He says Ptolemy contradicts himself because he does not count the eighth house among the Hyleghs since it does not "aspect" <note>An "aspect" is a specific geometric angle between celestial bodies; astrologers believed planets only influenced points they could "see."</note> the Ascendant. Yet in choosing the Alcocoden, <margin>The error of Haly.</margin> Haly thinks it does not matter whether it aspects the Hylegh or not. Why are you so foolish, you barbarian? Or what are you dreaming? Where did you read about the "Alcocoden" in Ptolemy? But I know what deceived him and the rest. Ptolemy places the ruling planets of the remaining Hyleghial places among the Hyleghs; these men think that the planets are a separate thing from the Hyleghs—as if only the other four (the Sun, Moon, Ascendant, and Part of Fortune, to which they falsely added the new and full moon) should be considered Hyleghs, while the planets ruling those places should "decree the years." And since Ptolemy nowhere said it was necessary for the ruling planets to "aspect" the Hyleghial places, they wondered why he did not think those two—which they believe are two distinct things, namely the Hylegh and the Alcocoden—should be joined by the association of an aspect. Yet it is no fault of Ptolemy if he did not seek an association of aspect between things that are one and the same. For in his work, whenever the Sun or Moon are Hyleghs, there will never be another planet besides them as the disposer of life. He only uses a ruling planet when the other Hyleghs do not have authority in the granting of years. When this happens, no "vital commerce" can be left to a life-giving planet with any of the Hyleghs, because none is found besides it. I do not know how these men failed to understand this from Ptolemy's words, or why no one among them detected it. But they have all gone off into this error in a herd, so that there is no one who does not go looking for the Alcocoden and the Hylegh "according to the opinion of Ptolemy." See how they uphold the true dogmas of the astrologers, and how they can predict the truth about the span of life! Especially when a massive error is added to those we have mentioned: that they prescribe the number of years, even "according to Ptolemy’s opinion," to a planet as if it were the giver of life, according to that common saying among them that there are "greater," "lesser," and "middle" years of the Sun, so many of the Moon, so many of Mars, and so on for the other stars. Yet Ptolemy both rejects this Egyptian opinion, saying it has no rational basis, and when he speaks of the span of life, he calculates the years not from the nature of the planets, but from the number of degrees of the equatorial circle. He does this according to the "place of life" (that is, the divider) and another "lethal" or "interfering" place, at which the course of a now-failing life first heavily strikes the native. For example, when the "releaser" is located between the boundary and the heights of heaven, that progression is observed which the Greeks call <insert>ray-projection <note>original: ἀκτινοβολίαν (actinobolian)</note></insert>. But when it has declined from the height toward the west, we use a reckoning drawn in both directions which they call <insert>horary <note>original: ωριμαν (horiman)</note></insert>, as we might say "hourly." Our astrologers are so ignorant of all these things that if they were to read them, I have no doubt they would think they were hearing of monsters. And yet we, in our wretchedness, are too credulous of their predictions when they promise us a <term>Nestorean old age <note>A reference to Nestor, the long-lived hero of the Iliad; meaning an exceptionally long life.</note></term>...

<header>AGAINST THE ASTROLOGERS, BOOK II.</header>

...and we forget the voice <note>A reference to the biblical command to be "ready" for the hour of death, which is unknown to man.</note> commanding us to be prepared; yet we, who do not know the day of our own passing, are tortured by anxiety day and night if they threaten us with a short life. The voice of a single loudmouthed babbler <note>original: "rabulæ"</note> strips away all the joy of our life. Haly says that if a lucky planet is in the <term>horoscope<gloss>the Ascendant, or the point of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon</gloss></term>, it adds its "minor years" to the years of life according to the opinion of 
<margin>Ptolemy’s ignorance.</margin>
Ptolemy. And yet, as I was just saying, in Ptolemy's work there are no "major," "middle," or "minor" years for the planets. When Ptolemy speaks of adding years, he follows an entirely different path using the partition of hours, which Haly, I believe, did not understand. But it is not necessary to pursue every single detail, otherwise this book would grow to an immense size. Now, in those very questions which they call <term>interrogations<gloss>Horary astrology, where a chart is cast to answer a specific question</gloss></term>, do they not also err so signally that the entire logic of their response is perverted by a single error? For it is a common proverb among them that the seventh house of the <term>theme<gloss>the birth chart or figure</gloss></term>—that is, the West—is given to the "thing sought." And yet, Ptolemy commands that this place be given not to the seeker or the thing being consulted about, but to the Mathematician <note>In this period, "Mathematician" was a common term for an astrologer.</note> who is being consulted. The Indian mathematicians also observed this; so much so that when the West and the "lord" of the West were in a bad state, they would not answer the question, fearing an error. I could list six hundred errors of this kind if I were not aiming instead to show that the entire profession is an error. Indeed, recently, when comparing Ptolemy’s books with Barbarian <note>Pico uses "barbaris" to refer to Arabic and Islamic sources.</note> and Latin authors, almost everything had to be "pierced with spits" <note>An idiom meaning to mark something as faulty or to be discarded.</note>.

### Chapter VIII. On the laxity of the astrologers of our age, which is so great that even if astrology were true, they themselves could not be true.

<margin>Bonatti.</margin>
Now, consider how great their laxity is. You will find few, even among those who have the method for calculating (which the majority of them lack), who do not flee to <term>ephemerides<gloss>Pre-calculated tables showing the daily positions of celestial bodies</gloss></term> to find the true position of the stars. 
Bonatti <note>Guido Bonatti (c. 1210–1296), a famous Italian astrologer.</note> testifies to this in a certain place with these words: "The wise men of this art," he says, "use the *Almanach*"—for that is what the Arabs call the ephemerides. Those who do this must necessarily speak wrongly and omit much, whereby all the truth of their predictions is weakened. For there, there is almost never any indication of the <term>latitude<gloss>The distance of a planet north or south of the ecliptic, the Sun's apparent path</gloss></term> of the planets. If this is ignored, where will the astrologer not err? Where will he not lie? If we consider the true decrees of this art, they believe the stars have the greatest power when positioned at the start of the twelve "houses" of heaven, especially the <term>cardinals<gloss>The four most powerful houses: the 1st (Ascendant), 10th (Midheaven), 7th (Descendant), and 4th (Imum Coeli)</gloss></term>. But the man who only observes a star's forward progress and does not look at its sideways declination will think a star is in those places when it is not, and think it is not there when it is. For when a star veers toward the north or the south, it both rises later and is always placed more swiftly in that part of the sign where it is located. Thus, you will sometimes think a planet is above the earth when it is below it, or that it has already set when it is still visible above the horizon. While this produces error in every prediction, it makes them fall away from the truth even more when they investigate the hour of birth from the hour of conception. If the moon happens to be near the west, it could be thought to have already set when it is still above the earth; and conversely, thought not yet to have submerged when it is hidden below the east. This will cause one to wander off by many days from the true hour of conception. Who could correctly determine the "radiations" of the planets if the latitude is unknown? Who will correctly measure the "walking of a star"? For that is what it is called in Greek, though commonly it is named a "direction." Since every 

<column-break/>

deviation of a star to either side of the sun’s path makes the event of a matter faster or slower by some years. Hence, what a great slip there is in arranging the <term>fixed stars<gloss>The stars that do not move relative to each other, as opposed to "wandering stars" or planets</gloss></term>, since they are commonly placed in that spot to which they are carried in a straight-line progression. Yet they do not consider at all with which part of heaven they rise in various regions, or upon which beginnings of the other houses they shine. What of the fact that the location of the planets is often poorly calculated—sometimes due to the scribe, but often due to the author who was not diligent or skilled enough? I pass over the fact that different astronomers use different tables, which are sometimes inaccurate, or even when one has made his own diary, they deviate from the truth—greatly so in this current age. But now all reject the tables of Ptolemy; a great part of the more learned follow the <term>Alfonsine Tables<gloss>13th-century astronomical tables named after King Alfonso X of Castile</gloss></term>, in whose "roots" <note>The base data used for calculation.</note> it is now clear there is evident falsehood. Nor are they any less "sleepy" <note>meaning lazy or negligent</note> in choosing the horoscope and in grasping the beginnings of the twelve other celestial places. I have seen many people of no small skill and of good name in that profession use some little table of their own for distributing the twelve "houses" (as they call them), regardless of the sky under which the person whose birth they were inspecting was born. If they ever wish to be diligent, they barely investigate anything more exact than the difference of <term>climates<gloss>Zones of latitude</gloss></term> which Alfonso alone showed them. Now, as for the declinations from the equator, the circumferences of the planets, their various "sublimations" in the smaller circle, or the fluctuations of latitudinal movements in the <term>eccentric<gloss>A circle whose center is off-set from the Earth</gloss></term>—who observes these now when judging birth charts? How many things do the younger generation not know about "equalizing the days"; how many things they say wrongly! We have said all this so that it may become manifest that this art of foretelling cannot be confirmed by the reliability of its predictions. Even if the art were established as perfectly true in theory, the truth about the future could still not be known due to the fault of the practitioners—that is, either their ignorance or their negligence. If we cannot persuade people that astrology itself should not be trusted, let us at least persuade them of this, as it is said in the epigram:

->Trust should not be placed in astrologers.<-

### Chapter IX. That the things astrologers say rarely happen, which he shows by both external and domestic examples.

If they were healthy and true, they would not only be not entirely ejected from cities and held in mockery by every prudent man, but they would have been held in the highest honor in every age among all nations. For so great is the curiosity of men to know the future, especially what pertains to themselves; and for those who provide this, there is rightly a great reputation and esteem. And yet we read of statues being erected and public honors decreed for philosophers, physicians, poets, and generals. They are even turned into the people's fables, so that the allegories of myths—which are usually drawn from common sense and life—contained a critique of this vanity among the ancients. For those who explain Homer allegorically say that astrologers are signified by that story of Icarus, who, committing himself to the thinner sky with artificial wings, was plunged into the sea. 
<margin>Interpretation of the story of Icarus against astrologers.</margin>
For astrologers, lifting themselves into the sky on the wings of a rash profession, fall into a sea of lies when they are about to predict from their celestial dogmas (by which they seem to be raised up). Why do we need other testimonies or conjectures, when daily experience itself shows us this?

He concludes by comparing astrologers to Icarus, falling from the heights of their pretensions into a "sea of lies."</summary>

# OF THE DISPUTATIONS

<margin>
Giovanni Pico’s observations regarding the useless rules of the astrologers.
</margin>
...even though experience itself testifies to the truth, especially in a matter where, if astrology has any power at all, it ought to show its greatest strength: in predicting <term>changes in the air<gloss>weather patterns</gloss></term>, such as rain, drought, heat, cold, winds, hail, and earthquakes. In these matters, they are found to be so false daily that the actual state of the weather almost never corresponds to their predictions for any given day. I observed this during the winter at my suburban villa, where I wrote these words. I noted every significant change in the weather each day, keeping the decrees of the astrologers right before my eyes. Meanwhile, the heavens favored me with such healthy weather everywhere that, in a continuous observation of over one hundred and thirty days, I saw no more than six or seven days that turned out as I had foreseen in their books. I believe my friend Pandolfo Collenuccio still remembers—a man learned in the law, but most ingeniously educated in all branches of literature—how much laughter a certain mathematician in Bologna gave us on this subject. That man commanded us to expect the heaviest rains on a day which the sun rendered most luminous, bright, and serene.
<margin>
Ambrose
</margin>
Ambrose, in his *Hexameron* <note>original: "Exameron"; a famous theological work by St. Ambrose on the six days of creation</note>, says that when there was talk some days prior about a coming rain that would be useful, someone remarked, "Behold, the <term>new moon<gloss>neomenia</gloss></term> will bring it." And yet, no rain fell until it was granted through the prayers of the Church, making it manifest that rain is not to be hoped for from the beginnings of the moon, but from the providence and mercy of the Creator. These are his words, by which both the vanity of astrology and the efficacy of religion are proven by the facts themselves. Therefore, those who are less capable of following complex reasons and have surrendered their faith to these men can assert their freedom in this way: let them repeatedly ask these astrologers about the state of the air. When they find that these men speak falsely almost every time, they will easily realize that if these "cloud-catchers" <note>original: "nebulones"; a pun in Latin meaning both worthless fellows and those concerned with clouds/mist</note> lie so much about the clouds, they will predict even more falsely when judging the fates of men and nations. For in the latter case, they are predicting things that are less subject to the heavens and far more difficult and laborious to foresee. As for the stories they fabricate daily in their mercenary prophecies regarding men’s <term>birth charts<gloss>genituris</gloss></term>, who has examined them? One will see that they lie far more there than when they answer regarding the quality of the air. And if I did not fear committing the very fault of the fools while I pursue the follies of others, I could bring forward many birth charts of living and deceased men—unlucky charts for the happy, and the most happy charts for the miserably poor. In this matter, I surely tell no lie, for I know that the Divine Truth, in whose service this expedition fights, neither needs nor delights in our falsehoods. But I will be content with certain domestic examples, by which I particularly wish to warn those who, having a promise of long life from the mathematicians, forget the Gospel voice <note>Matthew 24:42 or Luke 12:40</note> warning us to watch, lest the day of the Lord catch us unprepared. To Prince Pino Ordelaffi of Forlì, to whom my sister 
<margin>
Since he has so far sought examples of many people deceived by the delusions of astrologers, he now looks to his own relatives.
</margin>
Lucrezia was married: in the year he died, Girolamo Manfredi—an astrologer singular in our age—had promised him total safety of life. Yet it is no wonder he failed to foresee the deaths of others, since he did not even foresee his own. For although he died the following summer, in his public prophecy for that very year (which was his fatal one), he promised more than once that he would have many wonderful things to say in the following year. I do not know how he can now redeem his pledged word, unless perhaps he looks down upon earthly things more truly from heaven than he once looked up at heavenly things from the earth. Pietro Attendolo, an ingenious youth who married Eleonora, the daughter of my brother Galeotto, died last year, killed by the distress of a sudden and unexpected disease; yet the astrologer in whom he placed the greatest trust had predicted no such thing, but had promised him security of life.

<column-break/>

Costanza, the most loving wife of my brother Antonio, who died at Rome two years ago amidst the public mourning of almost the entire city—did she not testify to us the vanity of this art? In the very year she left us longing for her, she had received a promise from an astrologer not only of prosperous health, but even of a most happy life. Having forgotten none of this, while she was drawing her last breath and holding the hand of her weeping husband, by whom she was uniquely loved, she said: "Behold, how true are the prophecies of the astrologers!" On the other hand, what evils, what heaps of troubles, and how many dangers did astrology threaten my brother Antonio with this year? And yet, having experienced no injury from the heavens, he has lived with his family safe, his property intact, and his health whole, tossed by no shaking of misfortune or danger. And lest you think only our modern astrologers lie, you should know that the same happened to the ancients. Seneca, in a certain passage mocking the "most blessed" Claudius Caesar <note>A reference to Seneca's satire *Apocolocyntosis*, or the "Pumpkinification" of Claudius</note>, introduces Mercury among the gods procuring his death. To knock down that vanity in passing, among the other reasons by which Mercury

See the ridiculousness.
</margin>
persuades them of the Emperor's death, he says: "Out of pity, you should let the Chaldeans <note>A common term for astrologers in Rome</note> be right for once, who have already been burying him for so many years." For the mathematicians used to predict every single year that Claudius would die, yet he did not die. When I read this, I thought of our own little diviners who likewise "bury" the Roman Pontiff every single year. Cicero writes that it was 
<margin>
Cicero.
</margin>
predicted by the Chaldeans to Pompey, Crassus, and Caesar that none of them would die except in old age, at home, and in glory. For which reason, the orator says it seems a marvel to him that any prudent man exists who believes those whose predictions he sees refuted daily by reality and events.

### Chapter X. Why astrologers sometimes predict the truth.

But it happens, nevertheless, that they occasionally predict things that come true. Yet since there are many more things that do *not* happen, why should we not conclude that they have stumbled upon the truth by chance? What of the fact that there is no "old wives' tale" or art of such vain superstition that it could not be proven true by the same argument—namely, that what was predicted from it occasionally happens? For there is no art that does not achieve this, even if you yourself were to invent a reckless and haphazard one. Therefore, let those who are moved by this reasoning tell me: do they think every divining art is true, or rather that many are vain and false? If many are false, I will prove those "false" ones to be "true" by the same argument: because occasionally what they predicted happens. If they say all are true, I will demonstrate that they believe in contradictions, because different divining arts do not give the same answer about the same things. For I have tested it often, a hundred times over: when I had cast both a <term>geomantic<gloss>Geomancy: divination by interpreting marks on the ground or patterns formed by tossed handfuls of soil/rocks</gloss></term> figure and an astrological one for the same question, one outcome appeared to me in the marks and another in the stars. If someone does not believe this, let him try it himself: let him consult a <term>Chiromancer<gloss>Palm reader</gloss></term>, an Astrologer, and a Geomancer regarding the fate of the same man, and you will see that almost always what is designated in the lines of the hand is not the same as what is pronounced from either geomantic marks or astrological planets. And if he looks at the actual outcome of the matter, he will find the truth more often where he least expects it. This is either because chance has more power where there is less reason, or because in those arts spiritual wickedness more willingly mocks us. Yet a manifold fallacy assists the predictions of astrologers, explaining why they seem to be proven true to many people more often than their <term>astrological outcomes<gloss>apotelefmaton</gloss></term> are actually verified. For if they must speak of the past, to show that such things have happened as...

We wished to address the question
of the people who are constantly
gaping at astrologers: why is there
faith in their responses if there is no
solidity in their profession? I called
it a question which, of course, the
more accurate and learned do not
use. To them it is known that the things astrologers say do not happen often, but rather rarely and, as it were, by accident. Nor, if they do happen, can it be concluded that the art is necessarily true, just as it is not necessarily false because they very often lie in their predictions. Indeed, false things can be pronounced from true precepts—not so much because of the total falsity of the art, but because of its speculative and conjectural uncertainty, to say nothing of the ignorance or indulgence of the practitioner. Likewise, on the contrary, true things can be pronounced from false ones, not by the truth of the dogma, but by the cunning of the speaker, or by luck, or by chance, or by the hidden promotion of foreknowing spirits who predict them, or for other reasons which we sufficiently explained in the previous book. If anyone cannot be persuaded of this, let him recall to memory how much I discussed just a moment ago regarding the carelessness and the errors of the astrologers of our age—would that we could discuss this without hatred or envy. Unless he desires to be deceived, he cannot be led to think that whenever they attain the truth, it was found by them rather than stumbled upon. This following treatise will entirely settle this dispute. In it, it will be demonstrated that the things they predict from the heavens do not have causes or signs there by which they are produced or indicated. Or, if they are produced from there, they are produced differently than the astrologers believe. Or if they are produced in that way, it is not from these causes in the heavens nor from these beginnings of things on earth. Then, even if all these were granted as certain, it will be shown that these beginnings and causes cannot be grasped by men; or if they can be grasped, they have not yet been grasped. When all of this has been demonstrated, I think it will be beyond controversy for good minds that whenever an astrologer happens upon the truth, this can be reduced to no cause more truly than to anything *but* the truth of the profession. This profession will appear clearly false for so many reasons already named, supported by no rational truths, but rather manufactured and deceptive, and therefore by its very nature a liar. Therefore, let us now approach the refutation itself, examining first that which contains the sum of the whole business: whether...

...the heavens, let us see what these diviners pronounce from the heavens. This will be treated by us in such a way that in this book we defend that the heavens act upon us only through motion and light. Beyond these, other more occult influences are imagined in vain. From that light and motion of the stars, nothing else is communicated to the receiving matter except motion, light, and heat—heat, I say, which both consumes bodies in a general state of flux and disposes bodies capable of life toward life and its functions. This heat flows from all stars, although it is not universally admitted that the outflows of all planets reach us. That the stars bestow anything beyond these upon lower things is neither proven by reason, nor demonstrated by experiments, nor persuaded by the authority of the leaders of philosophy. Indeed, we understand that all these things stand in the way, and that the power of the celestial bodies does not pertain to <term>sublunary<gloss>under the moon</gloss></term> bodies in any way beyond these common influences. Therefore, the peculiar properties of things—even corporeal ones, whether they follow the species or the particular thing—do not have their origin in the stars (except by way of a universal principle), but from the proper nature of the things themselves and from their proximate and related causes. And we shall make this opinion of ours more certain and probable by no other means than the very arguments which the astrologers use against us. When this has been sufficiently explained, we shall come in the fourth book to this: even if we grant to the astrologers that occult powers exist in the rays beyond the effect of light and heat, from which humans and the rest of nature might uniquely receive various gifts and powers, we will prove beyond doubt—by the clearest reasons and the consensus of all the most illustrious philosophers and theologians—that those powers they imagine do not exist in the stars. Once this is sufficiently completed and each of their prophecies about the stars is reconsidered, we should add and leave this most well-attested principle: those things which are not caused by the heavens are not signified by the heavens; that is, those things of which the celestial bodies are not the causes, they are also not the signs. Therefore, there is no reason why they could be foreseen from the heavens. Now, performing what we first proposed, let us see with what arguments they attack us—those who contend that all things are bound, led, and governed by the stars—so that we may soon not only repel them but, relying on divine aid, drive them back against our adversaries with greater force than they brought.

### Chapter II. Five reasons by which astrology
### seems to be strengthened.

The reasons by which the astrologers try to persuade us that all changes of the sublunary world—and indeed the diversities of all things, as well as fortuitous events and the characters and wits of men—depend on the stars, are chiefly these:
The voice of theologians and philosophers is one: that the 
<margin>Aristotle, Augustine</margin>
lower world is governed by the heavens. This is taught by that most common sentiment of <note>Aristotle's *Meteorologica* 1.2</note> Aristotle, that this lower world is necessarily contiguous to the superior motions, so that all its virtue is governed from there. Thus Aurelius Augustine also said that these grosser bodies are ruled and moved by the subtler ones. Who then, they ask, would doubt that any changes whatsoever in earthly things are caused by the motions of the superior bodies? Experience itself also demonstrates this by the changing seasons of the year, from the approach of the sun to us and its retreat; from this, the condition and habit of all living things is varied, while the heavens temper the fields, and while they vary and return the crops. But even in the daily revolution, the sun changes the qualities of the air: more or less

<column-break/>

heating and drying at noon, morning, and evening, leaving it to moisture and cold. Who is ignorant that the moon also has power over all bodies, especially the more fluid ones? It moves the tides <note>original: "estus oceani"</note> of the ocean, rising and falling; it stirs the sea and sends it into the lands. Moreover, those animals enclosed in the prison of shells <note>A common medieval belief that shellfish grow and shrink with the phases of the moon.</note> change their bodies according to the motion of the moon. The "critical days" <term>crises<gloss>crismi</gloss></term> observed by doctors follow the motions of the moon and sun. We see that storms are often stirred and humors agitated in bodies at the new and full moon; hence many observations about the motions of the moon have been accepted by shepherds, sailors, and farmers, and proved by manifold experience over many past centuries. Why then, if we perceive the more manifest impressions of the <term>luminaries<gloss>the sun and moon</gloss></term> and their authority in changing lower things, should we believe the rest of the stars to be inactive and ineffective? Or that their powers (however much more hidden) do not reach us, by which the bodies subject to them are affected in various ways? Those who are skilled and prudent in these things can foresee certain more secret future events, just as doctors, shepherds, farmers, and sailors divine the weather. Furthermore, no one would deny that the state of the air and the weather vary according to the state and position of the stars, since heat, cold, dryness, moisture, and whatever impressions occur on high are generated by celestial motions and influences. If the drier vapors enclosed in the bowels of the earth move the earth, and if causes in the air—from the exuberance or defect of those four qualities—produce 
<margin>For in his "Problems," the philosopher [Aristotle] posits that diseases are caused by the abundance or defect of those qualities; hence Peter of Abano confirms it. Ptolemy.</margin>
scarcity of grain, or if excessive moisture or dryness occurs when crops are gathered or sown, then a moderate and opportune state of the air brings fertility. Who will deny that from the stars come not only changes in the weather and earthquakes, but also plagues and various kinds of diseases in men and cattle, the healthiness of regions, and fertility or sterility? Then, if we also consist of these same qualities, and the character and wits are varied by the temperament of the body (while maintaining full freedom), why can it not be that dispositions in us toward anger or mildness, and toward other good and bad effects, are caused by the stars—either by rousing or restraining the bile, blood, phlegm, or black bile <note>The four humors of Hippocratic medicine.</note>, which those affections usually accompany? Why can it not likewise be that the dry and hot impressions of the heavens, sharpening the bile in us, can excite us to strife, brawls, insults, and enmities? From whence come wars, slaughters, and devastations; from whence empires and kingdoms are changed. After this, Ptolemy concludes thus: if the stars create a diversity of body and mind, this is then derived toward those things which are external but have an affinity with them—such as a wife and resources have with the body, or dignity and honors with the mind. This is the chief reason of Ptolemy; nor does he prove the power of the stars as the effectors of all things in any other place except from the efficiency of the primary qualities, by producing which they consequently produce all other things. Therefore, he brings no other causes for why Saturn does this, Jupiter that, or Mars the other, than that Jupiter is a hot and moist planet, Saturn is dry and cold, and Mars is more dry and burning. He feels the same about the <term>fixed stars<gloss>non erraticis</gloss></term> as about the <term>planets<gloss>erraticis</gloss></term>, judging the fixed stars by the nature of the planets based on the nature of the primary qualities. Indeed, others, having left behind the primary qualities, might flee to more eminent and occult powers, which it is not fitting to doubt exist in the celestial bodies as many and most effective.
