# AGAINST THE ASTROLOGERS, BOOK III.

<margin>Fifth Reason.</margin>
When we behold unique and excellent talents, we are accustomed to considering them gifts of the heavens, rather than qualities of the elements from which these bodies are formed; we believe they instead obtain a virtue infused into them from the sky. How much more, then, will these most noble bodies—so bright in light, so vast in mass, and so rapid in movement—not lack such powers and properties? Or in what way, if they are transmitted to the earth along with motion and light, will they not produce wonderful effects among us? Finally, the course of human affairs—over which the astrologer’s divination claims the greatest power of heaven and fate, seemingly persuading us from every side even against our will—is characterized by its very familiarity and frequent variety. We see many things happen that are beyond the strength of our mortality, many things beyond reason and merit, and most things beyond the order and established condition of human existence. These seem to have no possible causes elsewhere than in the heavens. This man is born with an aptitude for philosophy, that one for poetry; another, scorning literature, handles civil business or arms more willingly and successfully. From where does this variety of natural talents arise? There is the man who thinks nothing of riches, and the man who would sell his soul for profit; this one is sober, that one is a rogue; this one is bold, that one is fearful. Why is there such great dissimilarity in character?

<margin>Alexander</margin>
Alexander <note>Alexander the Great (356–323 BCE).</note> conquered the East as quickly as he saw it: a single impetus of such great good fortune. What power unlocked the secrets of nature for his teacher Aristotle, for Plato, and before them for Pythagoras, Socrates, and the rest? This reason seems too great for them to be believed to have merely sprouted from the earth.

<margin>The course of fortune to be observed.</margin>
Again, who would not ascribe these things to the fortuitous paths of the stars: that an innocent man is condemned while a guilty one is rewarded with prizes; that the industry, skill, talent, and learning of so many are neglected? Meanwhile, the idleness and wickedness of others are enriched. A pirate, bloodied by slaughter, after a thousand dangers of sea and land, finally ends his life at home among his own people in old age. Yet a most gentle and ready man is mindlessly cut down by swords, even by those who did not wish to do it. Then there are certain portents of talent and monsters who either delight in foul things or, to put it simply, wander outside the laws of humanity. Do they not seem to testify to some force and necessity of fatal power? Since the life of mortals is full of such things, they persuade many that these successions of good and evil—whether deserved or undeserved, like the variety of things themselves—are caused by the movements of the stars, against whose impulses fragile and fleeting mortality can hardly ever struggle.

### Chapter III. The first reason is turned back, and it is shown that the heaven is a universal cause and not to be referred to the variety of individuals.

<margin>Turning back the first reason.</margin>
We have strived not merely to weaken these reasons of the astrologers, but to strengthen them, lest they complain they have been cheated. First, however, I wish the reader to know that even if these reasons were granted, it would not follow that there could be any such science as astrology (as will become clear in the following books). But we do not grant them these points; rather, we take from these very same premises strong arguments against them. For regarding the first reason: as soon as the astrologers say that every lower motion depends on the motion of the heaven, they immediately contradict their own dogma. From this follows a point well-worn among philosophers: that the heaven is the *universal cause* <term>universal cause<gloss>A general force that powers all things equally, like the sun providing light to both a rose and a weed, without choosing the nature of either.</gloss></term> of lower effects. A universal cause, however, does not distinguish between effects, nor is it asked why *this* happens or *that* happens. That is the role of *proximate causes* <term>proximate causes<gloss>The immediate, specific causes of an event, such as biological parents or personal choices.</gloss></term>, which are varied and different according to the difference and variety of the effects. Since among these proximate causes one does one thing and another does another, the universal cause does all things with everyone. Because this

<column-break/>

is clearly apparent in things that are different in nature and species, it is a wonder how they do not understand that the same must much more be believed regarding the variety of individuals. The more an individual is particular and draws its origin from matter, the less it can be referred back to a cause that is primarily formal and universal. Who does not see that the heaven generates a horse with a horse, and a lion with a lion? Is there any position of the stars under which a lion is not born from a lion, or a horse from a horse? Why, by the same reasoning, will the same heaven not produce different children from different parents, even if under the same or a similar constellation? This is proven by experience itself, since we sometimes see those born in the same hour, and under the same inclination of the heaven, yet who are most different in fortune, talent, and body.

In this matter, the astrologer cannot dodge the blow. For when the birth of twins is thrown in their faces, they usually flee to "Nigidius’s wheel" <note>original: "nigidianam rotam." A famous anecdote about the scholar Nigidius Figulus, who argued that the sky moves so fast that even a tiny delay in birth results in a different horoscope, illustrating this by marking a spinning potter's wheel.</note>, on which it is impossible to mark the same spot twice with ink. But even here they explain themselves poorly, since they themselves cannot track that difference of a rapid moment, from which nevertheless arises—so they claim—such a great difference in fate. Thus, while they try to defend the efficiency of the heaven, they fall into other snares, so that they are forced to admit they cannot have knowledge of that very efficiency. Furthermore, we do not only present them with twins (where the small delay as one comes out after the other offers them a little loop-hole for an answer). We also point to those born at the same moment from different parents, yet within the same latitude and longitude of the same region. The astrologer must describe the same celestial theme and pronounce the same things for these people—both regarding what will happen after the hour of birth and what happened to them even within the mother's womb—so that just as they were born at the same hour, they are considered by him to have been conceived at the same hour. What, I ask, will the astrologer answer regarding these? When the constellation is exactly the same, yet the fate of each appears different? Unless he is insane, can he say anything else than that those celestial influences—universal in virtue and power—are determined and distinguished by proximate and secondary causes?

If this is so, how can they promise that they will provide the cause for every variety of individual once the hour of birth has been explained by the stars? For instance: why this man is snowy-white and that one black; this one short and that one tall; this one slow-witted and that one clever; this one pleasing to all and that one annoying; this one born for philosophy and that one for trade; this one rich and that one poor; this one short-lived and that one long-lived? All this variety of individuals within the same species is far less dependent on the heaven than the diversity of species within the same genus—such as whether a lion, a human, a donkey, or an elephant is produced. Just as all these things follow the specific difference of proximate causes, so do those individual traits follow either the difference of seeds (if we consider bodily qualities), or the difference of education and will (if we consider animal qualities), or the parents' faculties, private choices, prudence, and opportunities (if we consider fortuitous and external things).

### Chapter IIII. How the heaven acts by motion and light, and is the universal cause of meteorological, mineral, and living elements.

Therefore, just as a universal cause is more divine and eminent than particular causes, so do we think more truly and more honorably of the heaven than the astrologers do. So that this reasoning of universal efficiency may shine more brightly, and so that it may be more clearly explained what the heaven does and does not do, we must begin from a deeper point regarding the nature of the heaven and its actions toward lower bodies. The heaven is a natural body of all bodies...

# DISPUTATIONS
<meta>catchword: and those</meta>

<margin>What heaven is.</margin>
...of natural things, the most perfect. Since a natural body is defined by both its motion and its perceptible quality, it follows that the most perfect of natural bodies must possess the most perfect motion and the most perfect perceptible qualities. No motion is more perfect than circular <note>original: "orbiculari"</note> motion, and no quality perceptible to the senses is more perfect than light. These, therefore, shall be the 
<margin>Perfection in circular motion.</margin>
properties of the celestial body. Consequently, the heaven is also of an unfading substance, since its motion and its quality have no contrary; and because it is the most perfect body, it must also occupy the primary—that is, the supreme—place, to which the first motion is owed. Now, that which is first in any genus is the cause of the remaining things contained within that series, even if not all things relate to that cause in the same way. Therefore, that which is moved by the first motion moves the rest of the things that are moved; nor, if that motion were to cease, would the others continue to move—just as in the <term>microcosm</term> <note>literally "the smaller world," referring to the human body as a reflection of the universe</note>, if the motion of the heart should cease, it is necessary that all motions of the living creature perish. For this reason, Aristotle rightly said in the eighth book of the *Physics* <note>original: "physicæ auscultationis"</note> that the first motion of the heaven is "life" for all things, since the most evident and common operation of life is internal motion. Therefore, this is the unique dignity and efficacy of the heaven toward the lower world: that by its tireless agitation, all other 
<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
<margin>The action of the heaven is through universal motion. How the heaven acts upon us through light.</margin>
motions are both ordered and excited. That this efficiency is universal—and does not distinguish between lower motions by this logic alone—is evident enough; for just as the heaven co-operates with a clod of earth falling downward, so it does with a flame moving itself upward, and with all other kinds of motion equally. 

The heaven has another prerogative regarding light; for since light is the highest quality of bodies, and the first stage of life for a corporeal nature—and since the highest points of a lower order always reach toward the lowest points of the higher order—it follows necessarily that light possesses a certain "perfecting" power over bodies and contains something vital within it. This is not because light itself lives or brings life, but because it most excellently prepares and disposes a body capable of life for the reception of life. For there follows from light, as if its own property, a certain heat—not of fire, nor of air, but celestial, just as light is the heaven's own quality. This heat, I say, is most effective and most healthful, penetrating all things, fostering all things, and moderating all things. This is the chief gift of the heaven by which bodies are perfected and living things are disposed toward life, beyond the agitation of circular motion. This motion is necessary not only to carry this light and heat down to us and to impart it to the lands in greater or lesser degrees with wonderful timing, but also so that we, being moved, might be made more fit for the heat which flows continually from a perpetually moving body. 

We perceive the power of this most beneficent heat in the entire world of "corruptible" things <note>the Earthly realm, where things are born and die</note>, both in things beginning and things completed, in things with souls and things without. For it contains and preserves the elements as if it were their place and form—like a craftsman surrounding all things, yet also diffusing himself intimately through all things. And just as it is the privilege of the first motion that other motions would falter without it, so it is with the first perceptible quality <note>light/celestial heat</note>: without it, other qualities could achieve nothing. Therefore, if they were deprived of celestial heat, coldness could not act as cold, nor could heat act as heat. For that stellar heat is not "contrary" to cold in the way that fiery or airy heat is; rather, it contains all elemental qualities by a "simple eminence," just as the nature of the heaven contains every body, just as circular motion contains all motions, and just as light contains all colors. 
<margin>For Pythagoras was diligently engaged in mathematics and especially in arithmetic.</margin>
This is what the Pythagoreans meant when they said that "Unity contains all numbers." Thus, those who deny that cold elements can be preserved by the heaven—unless the stars also flow with coldness in addition to heat—are mistaken. They would have a point if the heaven preserved hot things with a heat of the same nature and logic; but instead, it preserves all things—hot, cold, moist, and dry—equally 

<column-break/>

by that quality of its own. Just as that celestial quality is none of those four elemental qualities, it nonetheless encloses them all within itself—not as they exist in the elements, but as a "multiplicity concluded in unity" by a principal virtue. Through this virtue, the heaven rules the elements so that it overcomes each one by preserving it, keeps the whole together by moderating them all, and creates new things from them by mixing them all. 

Truly, the name "heat" is deceptive; when we hear it, we immediately think of a thing opposed to coldness. But elemental heat is indeed closer in nature to that celestial heat than elemental coldness is, just as it is more perfect; yet nothing 
<margin>From whence the derivation came. A suitable comparison.</margin>
prevents that celestial quality, being exalted above the properties of both elements, from embracing the virtue of both. It is as when we speak of "brightness" <note>original: "candorem"</note>: we see it as something opposed to dark and black colors. And yet, no one would deny that the color black is both preserved and made effective by the brightness of light, even if another color, closer to the nature of light, shares a common name with it (as when something is occasionally called "white"). In short, if the substance of the heaven, as the "first body," contains every body most perfectly in power, its own quality must necessarily contain every corporeal quality in power and perfection. This is what we call "celestial heat"—the offspring of light. We call it "heat" both because it warms things in a way that gives life, and because among all the properties of the elements, heat is the one that approaches it most closely. Thus, when it 
<margin>Celestial heat, along with all the closest heats of bodies, produces qualities.</margin>
departs from its celestial condition, it exercises this operation most of all, as we shall declare later. 

Therefore, if this heat contains all qualities of lower bodies by its perfection and virtue, it will generate and nourish them all along with their proximate causes. It acts much like "seminal heat," which, although it is called heat and rules the matter of the fetus, nevertheless governs, digests, preserves, forms, and moderates all parts of the offspring, whether they be hot or cold. Therefore, if anyone asks me whether the heaven produces coldness "by itself" <note>term: "per se" - essentially or directly</note> or "by accident" <note>term: "ex accidenti" - incidentally or indirectly</note>, I shall reply: If you ask what the heaven does by itself with no intermediate cause, it produces only heat, and the other qualities "by accident" (just as heat itself can make things cold by accident, as we will show in the next chapter). But if you ask what it does as a "universal cause" acting with "secondary causes," then it produces both coldness and heat, dryness and moisture, by itself. In this way, it is no less involved when water generates water than when fire generates fire; nor could water generate water without the heaven any more than fire could generate fire. When it generates the substances of the elements, it also generates the properties that follow them; therefore, it makes coldness with water and heat with fire. 

And if we were to deny that anything other than heat is produced "by itself" by the heaven in this way, those absurdities mentioned by Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> would follow: 
<margin>Thomas's argument.</margin>
that coldness, dryness, and moisture do not exist "by themselves" in the universe, but only "by accident," and that not all substantial forms of lower bodies are contained within the virtue of the celestial bodies. But these absurdities do not follow at all when we deny that the heaven, by itself and from itself alone, makes the air or other lower bodies cold. Thus, those arguments of Thomas prove not what we deny, but exactly what we assert. 

We have seen what the heaven does to the elements, and we have proven its universal 
<margin>How celestial heat is the cause of meteorological phenomena.</margin>
efficiency here first; let us now descend to other things made from the elements. That same heat—the son of light—raises vaporous breaths from earthly bodies. By thinning them and dissolving thick and foul dregs, it gives birth to those things created on high, varying according to the diversity of the matter that is lifted up. For if vapor is raised from a fluid body, it creates "moist impressions" <note>rain, mist, etc.</note> in the middle or lowest region of the air. But if the evaporation is raised from dry and earthy matter, it becomes a "fiery evaporation" <note>meteors, lightning, etc.</note> toward the higher parts adjacent to the <term>ether</term>, where it necessarily grows hot from its proximity to the motion and the fire. All these things, therefore, that same celestial heat produces, whether they be cold...

<summary>Pico explains that the heavens influence the Earth through two primary physical mechanisms: universal motion and "celestial heat" (an offspring of light). He argues that this celestial heat is a superior, universal force that contains and regulates all four elemental qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) without being identical to them.</summary>

Therefore, heat is the cause of all things, and universally so; their distinction and variety do not come from a variety of constellations, as the astrologers fabulate, but rather according to the matter and the place in which they are generated. This is made known from the books of Aristotle’s *Meteorology* <note>original: "metheorologic Arist. lib."</note> and Plato’s *Timaeus*. For this reason, 
<margin>
The exhaustion of the Aristotelian interpreters.
</margin>
in his treatise on this part of nature, Aristotle produced that common saying: that the lower things are continuous with the superior ones, so that all their power is governed from there. While this can be accepted more generally and truly from what we have said regarding celestial motion and heat—by which all things are moved and nourished—it was nonetheless said by Aristotle specifically because of the "meteorological impressions" <note>the term for atmospheric phenomena like rain, wind, or comets</note> which he was then primarily discussing. Therefore, to prove or explain what he had said, he added that the "matter" of all these things is the inferior elements, while the "efficient cause" is the heaven. I marvel, however, that certain interpreters exhaust themselves to defend Aristotle from the calumny that he might have said every inferior power is governed by heaven—as if our own freedom <note>original: "nostra quoque libertas"</note> were endangered in these words! They fail to see from the context of the words that what is said pertains only to the elements. For when he says "the world" there, he calls the elementary bodies filling this sublunary space "the world," not including the living things that inhabit that world along with the elements. This is most evidently clear from the sequence of the speech; for after he said it was determined by him in earlier books that there are four bodies below the heaven—Fire, Air, Water, Earth—he then joins it thus: "Since, therefore, around the whole earth the world consists of these bodies, whose affections we are about to describe, this world is of necessity continuous with the superior rotations, so that all its power is governed from there." Thus, the "world" whose every power he said is governed by the superior body is this very mass of the four elements, since no other world is continuous with the superior rotations; nor was he about to discuss the "affections" of any other world in that book, in which certainly no mention is made of plants or animals, but only of those things which occur in the elements, such as comets and other "impressions," and whatever are the common passions of air and water, as he himself prefaced in the introduction shortly before. Therefore, let our diviners cease to use this testimony of the philosopher in their annual prophecies as a kind of decoration and strength for their fraud, when in that very book the most prudent Aristotle detracts from astrology, since he seeks the causes neither of rains, nor of earthquakes, nor of other effects of this kind in the stars, but in matter—according to whose variety (not the diversity of the constellation) the heat of the sun affects them in one way or another. Such, then, is the state of affairs regarding meteorological impressions.

The remaining things are those which live by the breath of that heat. Indeed, as we gathered a little while ago, since this quality <note>heat</note> holds the highest rank among bodies so that it perfects the bodies themselves (as we have said), it is thus placed immediately beneath life. It joins the extremes together, binding the life to the body and the body to the life. For this reason, in all living things, between this which is seen as a coarser dwelling <note>the physical body</note> and the soul, which is the fountain of life, there is a medium which we call the "spirit" <note>original: "spiritum"</note>. This is a most thin and invisible body, most closely related to that celestial light and heat; 
<margin>
Spirit is a certain medium between body and soul.
</margin>
it is in this spirit that life is chiefly present, and through it, the soul explains and diffuses its powers into this visible and earthy body. Thus, in the seminal matter, this kind of spirit lies hidden, whose mystery that more divine power—the craftsman of vital works—uses in the first place. Acting in the place of the soul, it flows down and propagates the likeness of the generator into the matter it has occupied. However, these spirits are not useful for either begetting bodies, or preserving them, or performing the duties of the senses, if they are destitute of the aid of the "celestial spirit" (that is, the heat we have described). Because it is more mobile, pure, and effective, and therefore closer to life, it strengthens the weakness of the inferior spirit and, through its commerce, renders it more related to the soul. Thus, it is no longer an argument that the heaven "lives" simply because it quickens 
<margin>
Heaven is not proven to be alive because it quickens living things.
</margin>
living things with its rays; for all these things live through their own souls, and they are propagated through the power of the soul implanted in their seeds, with the heat of the heaven assisting them—not as something life-giving itself, but as something most conveniently and closely disposing them toward life for the reasons we have stated. No one would say that the power of seeing, which comes from the soul, is "in" the light or "through" the light, even though we do not see without light. Whether the life of the heaven can be proved by other reasons has been disputed by us in the *Harmony of Plato and Aristotle*. Thus it is clear that in the corporeal world nothing indeed happens without the heaven; nevertheless, that *this* or *that* happens is not from the heaven, but from second causes, with all of which the heaven makes such things as they themselves were born to make, whether those causes pertain to the species or to the individual.

### Chapter V. Beyond the common influence of motion and light, no peculiar power exists in the heavens.

<margin>
Do the celestial spheres act on us through heat?
</margin>
Moreover, the pouring out of this heat is common to all stars, since it follows the universal celestial nature just as light does. But whether it belongs to the *spheres* is doubtful; for if they are not luminous, they are not propagators of this heat. If they are luminous, the question is whether their light, by its rarity, is invisible and becomes ineffective toward us, as Avicenna writes in his book *On the Heaven*. Regarding the stars themselves, whatever comes under our sight cannot be doubted, unless we equally take away from them their celestial nature and the gifts of light. Therefore, beyond motion and light, and the life-giving heat that proceeds from light, no other influences descend from the stars to us; nor is there any evidence from experience (as we have seen and will see more clearly in what follows) that other corporeal "effective qualities" exist in them, since the heaven seems able to fulfill its duty everywhere through motion and heat-producing light. Thus, Aristotle never said we were affected by the heaven in any way other than by motion and heat—which Averroes and Plotinus, great men each in his own school, asserted most firmly. And indeed...

# OF THE DISPUTATIONS

<margin>The opinion of some,</margin> regarding "cooling influences," reason seems to strongly deny such a thing. For those who hold the opposite view—when they are convinced that all light is a producer of heat—usually argue that while all stars, because they shine, produce heat by a general property common to all, they then possess their own specific powers. Thus, they claim one star bestows dryness, another cold, another humidity, and another something else. They argue that nights during a full moon are warmer because the more abundant light heats more, but that this does not prevent the moon, by its own specific influence, from either cooling or moistening the air. I therefore ask them: do they believe this heat, which they admit is common to all stars just like light, is the kind we have described—containing most excellently all four qualities <term>the four qualities: heat, cold, moisture, and dryness, which were thought to compose all physical matter</term>—and therefore productive of all things through secondary causes, yet in itself only a spreader of heat? Or do they believe the other properties are not contained within it, but only heat, while cold (as a thing distinct from heat) flows from some other specific power of a star? Whichever they choose, they fall, unless I am mistaken, into no small difficulties.

<margin>An effective reason.</margin> If they choose the first, I will argue that a specific nature cannot be less perfect than the general nature from which it comes. A quality that contains *every* quality is more perfect than one which is only effective at producing cold. Therefore, if that universal heat is granted to the stars by a general condition, a specific cooling influence cannot be granted to any star by its own nature. Thus, the other side of the argument remains, in which they must inevitably get stuck: for nothing belongs to a specific nature that is repugnant to the properties it receives from its general nature. For example, if it belongs to man insofar as he is an "animal" to have sensation, he cannot have "insensibility" <note>original: "stupiditas," here meaning a lack of sensory function</note> insofar as he is a "man." Or if it belongs to him to have the principle of internal motion insofar as he lives, it cannot be that his specific nature as a living thing should agree with the immobility of inanimate objects. Rather, the specific level refines what is in the general nature. If a living thing moves from within, a human (a species of living thing) must have an even more specific internal operation, such as reason. By this same example, if life-giving heat follows celestial nature because it is celestial, then a specific power to produce cold and dryness—qualities contrary to life—will not follow the nature of any particular star. Thus we argue against them.

<margin>Solution to the arguments of the opposing side.</margin> As for the reasons for the opposing opinion, they are partly solved already and partly will be dissolved in their proper places. They thought it would follow that the "cold elements" (like water and earth) could not be preserved by the heavens, and that other qualities would arise from heat only by accident, and that it would not be true that all "substantial forms" of bodies are contained in the power of celestial nature. All these things we have already dismantled in the preceding sections. We have also addressed the idea that many things are generated here by celestial action even where the light of heaven does not reach. Two points remain: first, that the air cannot be changed so suddenly from heat to intense cold unless it is believed to be the work of a new "constellation" <note>a specific alignment of stars</note> bringing cold; second, how the moon, when carried beneath the earth and even under the depths of the earth, moves the tides of the ocean, to which the lunar 

<column-break/>

rays undoubtedly do not reach at that time, unless it acts through an "influence" separate from both light and the heat that follows light. These points will be resolved later: the first in Chapter 13, where we will treat the changes in lower things caused by the sun; the other where the cause of the ebb and flow of the ocean will be discussed at length by us. Here, we will only satisfy those who ask how the moon affects us during the "interlunium" <term>the period of the new moon when it is invisible</term>, since at that time it does not illuminate us at all. Galen asserts that just as it does not illuminate, so it does not affect us in any way when in "conjunction" <note>when the moon and sun are aligned from Earth's perspective</note>. For this reason, he makes the month consist of twenty-six days and twelve hours—the days when the moon’s light reaches us with efficacy—while it remains hidden under the sun’s rays for about three days. However, the moon acts upon us when joining the sun in the same way a person acts by doing nothing: for by depriving bodies of its light, it harms them; but as it grows, it nourishes them more fully and fills them with moisture. If we believe the moon has its own light, however dim and thin—which is why it does not entirely vanish from sight during conjunction—one could believe it retains some efficacy from that light as well.
<margin>Galen.</margin>

### Chapter VI. The light of the Moon, like that of the Sun, is vital: and neither produces cold or humidity except by accident.

---

The celestial heat is, therefore (to bring together everything we have said), the universal craftsman of all bodily things. There is no reason to believe that different "breaths" are inspired into earthly bodies by the stars, nor should we give more to those superior bodies or less to the inferior ones than is proper. Let the reader only recall this: whatever is shared from a better nature to a lesser one must necessarily become "other" in some way, according to the capacity and condition of the receiver. It becomes "worse" than its first origin because it is mixed with a foreign and alien nature. Because the lower nature is affected by many other impressions from elsewhere, it necessarily infects and confuses the "influence" it received from the better place with a heap of many other conditions. Therefore, there is no doubt that this happens to celestial heat whenever it is received into the "sublunary mass" <term>the Earth and its atmosphere, located "under the moon"</term>: it fails in its natural action and perfection. This happens in two ways: first, although it is always healthy in its own nature, it sometimes becomes harmful due to the weakness of the receiver; and second, although it produces none of the "elementary qualities" (being different from them by its own property), it nevertheless degenerates in an elementary nature toward the actions of the elements—especially heat, to which it is closest in name and nature. Therefore, it often acts not so much as celestial heat, but as "igneous" <note>fiery</note> and elementary heat usually does. That this does not happen by its own nature but by a fault of the matter is evident (to set aside reason) because when it finds matter kindred to itself among sublunary bodies, it is always found to be beneficent and life-givingly warm. Indeed, nothing is more like it than the "spirit," especially the human spirit, which is a thin, clear, mobile, "sanguine vapor" <note>the vital breath or 'pneuma' believed to travel through the blood</note> that corresponds in proportion to the heaven, as Aristotle and Avicenna write. The heat of heaven always cherishes and strengthens this spirit, such that the heat is to the spirit what the spirit is to the thick body. If it harms it sometimes, it does so for no other reason than the infirmity of the receiver; the sign of this is that the same ray hurts the weak and strengthens the robust. Thus, even here it is true that "to him who has, more shall be given, and from him who has not, even what he has shall be taken away." Therefore, what harms one person does not come from the sun, since to another 
<margin>Aristotle. Avicenna.</margin>

<summary>Pico argues that planets do not possess individual "personalities" (like cold or wet) but influence Earth through a universal life-giving heat. Apparent cooling or harmful effects are actually caused by the weakness or corruption of the earthly matter receiving that heat.</summary>

### AGAINST THE ASTROLOGERS, BOOK III.

<margin>
Why Aristotle, in his book *On Generation and Corruption*, correctly understood the power of the sun. Hippocrates and Aristotle.
<note>original: "Aristote. in lib. de generatione & corruptioe"</note>
</margin>
...would not have benefited another; rather, it is from the weakness of the matter, which faints under the weight of such goodness due to its own "sickness" <note>By "sickness," Pico means the inherent instability or unsuitability of earthly matter to receive pure celestial influence.</note>. Otherwise, things that are equal to the sun’s rays would gain more vigor and life the more they were exposed to them. Therefore, no one should think that either a "devouring heat" or its opposite, "dryness," flows directly from the sun; just as one should not think a "stifling flux" or excessive "moisture" and "numbing cold" flow from the moon. If this were the case, the moon’s growing light would not assist the innate "procreative force" <term>vital power used for reproduction and growth</term> in things, by which bodies are nourished and grow along with the moon itself. Nor would the full moon be useful for those conceiving—as Hippocrates writes in his book *On the Eight-Month Birth* <note>original: "Hippocrates... in lib. de octimestri partu"</note>—by making both the female and male fertile. Nor would it be true, as Aristotle says, that the moon is a principle like a "second, smaller sun," contributing to all generation and perfection. For how could these things be true if the moon's light were not by its own nature white, vital, and fertile, just like the light of the sun and other stars? For all stars, this light is their essence, just as the celestial property is common to them all. But (as we were saying), although this celestial heat may sometimes be excessive relative to the weakness of the recipient, when it descends into the "elemental nature" of our world, it becomes almost like elemental heat. Thus, you would not easily recognize it as celestial, except in those "spiritual small-bodies" <note>Likely referring to the "pneuma" or "spiritus," a subtle substance thought to bridge the gap between soul and body.</note> which we have explained are most similar to the heavens among all bodies.

<margin>
Note on the effects of the sun.
</margin>
When infused into these, the heat completes every mixture and everywhere serves to fulfill the works of the soul. However, when it falls upon hard, rough, thick, watery, or dreg-filled bodies, it degenerates from its celestial property and acts much like elemental heat itself. If this heat is powerful, it burns, dries, and reduces things to ash. Conversely, if it is thin and weak, it causes a "flux" and dissolves moisture. This is what happens to celestial heat depending on the condition of the matter it hits. This is the source of the opinion that the sun’s heat is "burning" while the moon’s is "tepid." Yet, in suitable and "kindred" subjects, the sun’s rays will not dry out healthy moisture, nor will the moon generate useless or harmful humidity. Rather, each star will perform the same work according to its nature, though the moon does more weakly what the sun performs more intensely. The fact that they seem to act differently—the sun drying and the moon moistening—happens "by accident" due to the contamination of foreign matter. For when the sun's rays are closer to us (as in northern signs) or hit us at direct angles (as at midday), or when they are squeezed together in hollow or rough surfaces and bounce back, they acquire a "fiery property" through such violence or infection. Thus, they dry and scorch the bodies they strike. In turn, the moon, with its tiny and thin heat, if it touches a moist and fluid body, dissolves the moisture it finds there and makes it more fluid. The moon does not bring that cold and watery humidity itself; rather, with its heat, it dissolves the moisture it finds in a cold, watery body and draws it out, spreading it around. For this is the nature of heat: if it is strong, it consumes the moisture it draws out of bodies; if it is weaker, it merely draws it out. Because it is the same heat—that is, a healing heat—but is weak, it fails in the effort and does not consume the moisture it has drawn out. Thus, "by accident," the moon moistens excessively and the sun dries. But both can also produce cold "by accident." For as Aristotle writes:

<margin>
Aristotle.
</margin>
Both are principles of cold and heat, and their movement governs the limits of both the beginning and the end of these qualities. How this is to be understood, the same author explains elsewhere. For he says the sun produces winter and summer throughout the year, and the moon does the same through the month. But the difference is that the sun does this through

<column-break/>

<margin>
The origin of the coldness of the sun and moon. Aristotle.
</margin>
its approach and departure <note>Closer in summer, further in winter.</note>, whereas the moon does it not in this way, but rather through its increasing and decreasing light. Thus, when the sun departs far from us, it leaves us to the cold, and so it is said to "make cold." Likewise, the moon, when its light is stripped away at the time of conjunction <note>The New Moon, when it is aligned with the sun and appears dark.</note>, is said to make things cold—not because it brings cold, but because it protects us less than usual from the night’s coldness. Furthermore, it is worth examining that Aristotle, in those same books *On the Generation of Animals*, says the times of the waning month are more humid and colder. Yet, it is commonly admitted that as the moon ages, moistures dry up. I would resolve this as follows: when the moon is waning, humidity thrives not because it comes *from* the moon, but because the moon—weakened in its heat and hiding for the greater part of the night below the horizon—offers less resistance to the "lower elements" <note>The Earth and Water below.</note>. Therefore, that moisture is watery, unhealthy, and "excremental" <note>Waste-like or surplus fluid.</note>. Hence, as the New Moon approaches, many vapors rise, rains fall, and "monthly flows" <note>Likely referring to both biological menstruation and general natural cycles of fluids.</note> generally flow more fully, as Aristotle writes in his *Histories* and *On the Generation of Animals*. But as the moon grows, the moisture also grows—either the kind found in bodies that has been made more fluid, or a more life-giving moisture that increases through the benefit of the moon's heat. For

<margin>
What arises from lunar increases.
</margin>
Aristotle believes that because of lunar increases, "sea urchins" <note>original: "echinnos"</note> and similar living things become fuller. This is for no other reason than that, although they are cold (as they lack blood), when they are fostered by the moon's more abundant light, they grow stronger and digest better. Consequently, they necessarily become more succulent and robust. Therefore, moistures flow both when the moon is waxing and when it is waning, but they are different kinds: good moisture when it waxes, and bad when it wanes. This clearly shows that the moon does not "moisten" because it is cold and wet (for such humidity increases when the moon wanes), but because it is healthily and life-givingly warm. When its light is abundant, bodies become more moist and robust—moist not in any other way than by the power of heat assisting the nourishing force and drawing humors from the depths to the surface. For this reason, bloodletting is also most conveniently done at this time. Thus,

<margin>
Haly Hamec.
</margin>
the astrologer Haly Hamec <note>The Latinized name for the medieval Arabic scholar Ali ibn Ridwan.</note> was greatly mistaken when he said veins should be cut when the moon is failing. Let us conclude, then, by asserting that the moisture which increases along with the moon—and therefore increases by its influence—is a most healthy moisture. it does not relax bodies into a "flux" or kill them with cold, but makes them firmer and more lively. This is attested by the experience and faith of all physicians: those who fall ill at the beginning of the month bear the brunt of the disease more strongly, and those who are already at death's door can scarcely lose their life while the moon is ascending. Both the sun and moon can make things cold, not only by leaving us without light, but also by affecting us (though

<margin>
Another cause of solar and lunar cooling.
</margin>
this too is "by accident"). The sun cools while it either kills through excessive drying, or calls the vital heat outward, or generates rain from the sea’s vaporous breaths (which it raises more than it can dissolve), or by stirring up winds. The moon cools by opening and thinning the pores of the body with its weak heat, allowing the night cold—also thinned by its rays—to enter us more abundantly. This is the source of the error for many who think the moon is cold: that numbness and coldness felt by those sleeping under the moon's rays. The star's weaker ray merely makes a path into the body for the cold of the earth and water that occupies the air at night. In this way, they "make cold," and the stars' rays—which by their own nature only provide healthy warmth—sometimes dry things out when they hit hard bodies, and sometimes moisten things when they hit watery thicknesses. They are also sometimes harmful, not by their own fault, but because of the weakness of the one receiving them.

<summary>Pico argues that the sun and moon are naturally warm and life-giving; their perceived "cooling" or "moistening" effects are actually accidental results of how their light interacts with the Earth's environment and various materials.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s systematic dismantling of astrological theory. On the previous page, he argued that the Sun and Moon do not possess "elemental" qualities like cold or moisture, but rather produce heat and light that interact with earthly matter. Here, he addresses the theories of the medieval scholar Abraham ibn Ezra regarding the heat of the stars.</meta>

# OF THE DISPUTATIONS

### Chapter VII. The dogmas of astrologers cannot be defended in the way Ibn Ezra thought, even if all stars are considered hot.

<margin>The opinion of Abraham ibn Ezra regarding the heat of the stars.</margin>
But someone will say that it is enough for the astrologers if, by some means, this star produces dryness and that one moisture, or another star produces other qualities. For even Abraham ibn Ezra <note>original: "Abraam auenazra," a famous 12th-century Jewish polymath and astrologer</note>, a great figure in the astrological profession, contended that stars are only producers of heat; he believed nothing else could be true of bodies that are bright and in perpetual motion. He argued that certain stars are called "cold" only because they do not provide as much heat to us as is required for our temperament. Thus, Saturn is accused of coldness because, being positioned far from the earth and being smaller than Jupiter, it fosters the lower nature more lukewarmly than it ought. Therefore, when Saturn is the "Lord of the Geniture" <term>the planet ruling a person's birth chart</term>, it signifies death not because of an impressed coldness, but because of a lack of heat.

<margin>Pico's opinion against Ibn Ezra.</margin>
I, for my part, praise Ibn Ezra for thinking correctly about the heat of the stars, but he loved his profession too much and did not see that its dogmas necessarily conflict with that truth. For even if his reasoning regarding Saturn holds—that it is considered cold because it is only slightly warm and therefore "kills"—this reasoning does not work for the other stars, nor does it work entirely for Saturn. As we have already explained, a planet that provides little heat causes moisture "by accident" <term>indirectly or as a side effect</term>, but it does not cause dryness; yet the astrologers contend that Saturn is dry. Furthermore, would it not immediately follow that all the fixed stars—especially those below the first magnitude—are colder than Saturn, since they are both smaller than it and more remote from the earth? If a star is only cold because it has little heat, then "the Heart of the Lion" <note>original: "cor leonis," the star Regulus</note> would be a cold star; yet it is judged by astrologers to be the most blazing of all. Even among the planets, if we were to examine which star heats us more or less according to this principle accepted from Ibn Ezra, we would find nothing consistent with the sayings of the astrologers.

<margin>What factors produce heat in the stars, and which ones do so.</margin>
For there are roughly three things that create the intensity of heat: the magnitude of light, density, and proximity. However, it has not been clearly explored how much magnitude outweighs density, how much density outweighs magnitude, or how much proximity outweighs either or both. Therefore, for those wishing to reason through this, the matter remains uncertain. Our senses cannot judge it, since they perceive no rays except those of the Sun and the Moon. This is the first obstacle for the astrologers: their art is nothing if the powers of the celestial rays remain ambiguous. To those willing to follow conjecture, it will appear to be something entirely different from what the astrologers have determined. For if we consider mass, the rays of Mars would be thought less hot than those of Saturn and Jupiter. If they respond that Mars is hotter because it is closer and its light comes from a more compact body, I would say it is in no way credible that this could achieve so much. Furthermore, given the smallness of its disk, it would be strange if Saturn, which is nearly fifty times larger, should be numb with cold while Mars is parched with heat. Otherwise, if the smallness of a body detracts so little from the efficacy of its light, then the abundance of light combined with proximity should mean we are warmed more by Venus than by any star except the Sun and the Moon. When the "nourishing Cytherean" <note>original: "citherea," a poetic name for the planet Venus</note> smiles from on high, she shines widely with a nectar-like glow, so that she alone among all the stars casts a shadow. Nor is there a star closer to the earth—at least according to the common opinion that the sphere of Venus does not exceed the size of the earth. And yet, most astrologers condemn her as cold, just as they do not doubt that Jupiter and Mars far surpass her in heat. In this, if they refer back to the appearance of the body, it is done with little logic: since Jupiter's disk does not exceed that of Venus by much, considering such vast distances, nor is it much closer to the earth than Saturn, they nevertheless define it so that Jupiter warms far more than Venus, and Saturn far less. Indeed, they say the bodies of Venus and Jupiter nourish, while Saturn kills with coldness.

<column-break/>

<margin>The star of Venus... <note>The marginal note is cut off at the column break.</note></margin>
...kills.

### Chapter VIII. An objection against what has been said.

"But," someone will say, "even if the differences in rays are not known to astrologers and cannot be known, that belongs to another question. Now we must see whether such a diversity can exist in the rays: that is, while all are hot by their nature and life-givingly hot, could one be called cold and contrary to life when compared to another, due to an abundance or lack of light, or its thinness or efficacy? And could one be dry and another moist, and could a star do this by its own nature without the contamination of elemental matter?" For if this is possible, what is to stop it? Since the heaven is a "universal cause" <term>a primary force that influences all things</term>, yet because of its continuous motion, it behaves differently at different times. Due to the varying positions of the stars, it cooperates differently with the "lower causes" <term>earthly forces</term>. Thus, not all variety of effects comes from the lower things, but also from the various dispositions of the universal cause itself. This is especially true if stars differ from one another not only in the quality or quantity of light, but in their other gifts and peculiar properties—which the fourth argument claimed against us. For then it seems possible that through motion and heat (which are common to all stars insofar as they are celestial), that common effect is owed to the heaven. But through "influences" <term>specialized celestial energy</term> that follow the particular natures of the stars, something more specific might happen. Through the various positions and habits of the same star in relation to other stars, locations in the sky, and earthly bodies, the work of the lower causes might be changed significantly. Thus, the first argument of the astrologers would still stand, tracing the very diversity of effects back to the heavens.

### Chapter IX. The objection is solved, and it is shown that neither specific nor individual differences of things depend on the movement of heaven.

<margin>While the heaven acts by motion, how many and what things it does.</margin>
This is a timely objection that brings to mind many things we might object to them; and it is almost always the case that a bad cause reveals itself more the more it defends itself. Truth, by contrast, is like fire: the more it is shaken, the brighter it shines. Therefore, we shall satisfy the objection. We will first declare what diversity exists in celestial influence, whether due to the diverse nature of the many stars or due to the varied and volatile changes of the same star. We will say what evidence or natural reason prescribes regarding these through necessary demonstration. For the ways in which our adversaries err require more work than can be completed in passing. Therefore, it will be treated in the following books. Here, since it will have been sufficiently explained how much one constellation can differ from another, we shall see how much authority that diversity has in varying the effects on lower things. From this, what we intend will be confirmed: that the primary substantial distinction of things comes almost entirely from secondary causes. The fallacy of the astrologers, who profess to predict such distinctions from celestial causes, will be further exposed. We have said that the heaven acts upon us through motion and light. Through motion, it is believed to do three things: to move, to heat, and to bring light. This third point must be treated later when we discuss light. But as for their claim that it heats by motion, that is a difficult question and must be considered separately...

<meta>This page continues Pico’s critique of the physical mechanisms of astrology. Having previously discussed whether stars are inherently "hot" or "cold," he now turns to their motion and light as potential sources of influence on Earthly affairs, citing classical and medieval authorities to show the lack of consensus among experts.</meta>

# AGAINST THE ASTROLOGERS, BOOK III.

to be discussed in the books of philosophy: for it matters very little to the astrological business. Indeed, we have explained above how it moves by motion: namely, while all motions depend on the first motion <note>The *Primum Mobile*, or the outermost sphere in the medieval cosmos that drives the rotation of all other spheres.</note>, just as the movements of an animal depend on the motion of the heart. Let us see, therefore, as far as motion is concerned, whether different stars move differently, and whether the same stars move differently at different times; then we shall look at their light.

<margin>
The difference in the motion of the stars.
Aristotle.
</margin>

The motions of the stars differ for three reasons: First, because some move faster and others slower. Second, because some move with many motions and others with fewer. Third, according to the position of the region in which they move, because some occupy higher seats than others and traverse wider spaces. Aristotle does not think that the multitude or fewness of motions pertains to a diversity in the things effected or moved. Rather, it happens according to the dignity of the movers: that which is more noble achieves its end with few motions, while the less noble requires many. Concerning their speed and slowness, nothing has been sufficiently explored.

<margin>
Macrobius.
Ibn Ezra.
Al-Bitruji.
</margin>

For Aurelius Macrobius <note>A 5th-century Roman provincial writer whose work on Cicero's *Dream of Scipio* was a primary source for medieval cosmology.</note>, imitating the ancients, affirms that all planets proceed at an equal pace <note>original: "pari passu"</note>, an opinion which Abraham Ibn Ezra <note>The 12th-century polymath previously mentioned.</note> supports, placing the Sun, Venus, and Mercury in the same sphere, separated only by the positions of their epicycles <term>epicycle: a small circle on which a planet moves, which itself moves along a larger circle</term>. However, those who make their speeds unequal disagree among themselves. For Al-Bitruji <note>original: "Alpetragius," a 12th-century Spanish-Arabic astronomer known for challenging Ptolemaic models.</note> asserts that those which seem faster are actually slower; others, on the contrary, observe the "time of restoration" <gloss>the orbital period</gloss>. This must necessarily be deceptive unless one examines the proportion of their delays and spaces more painstakingly. But however the matter stands: if they cause heat through motion, they would cause more heat with faster motion.

As for that "principality of motions" <note>The idea that certain motions are primary or govern others.</note> we were speaking of, this can produce no variety since the lower motions depend on the motion of the heaven. Insofar as that first and circular motion is concerned, it does not matter if it is slower or more rapid. A stone would not move downward, nor fire upward, if the heaven were at rest; but the stone does not descend more quickly, nor does the fire ascend more quickly, simply because the heaven revolves more rapidly. It receives from the heaven only the fact that it moves at all, as if from a universal nature that animates every motion. It derives the *type* of motion from its own substance, but it receives its intensity or relaxation from the mover, from impetus, from its shape, and from other similar conditions.

Therefore, Saturn will not move us differently just because it moves more slowly than Mars, which is considered faster. For what the astrologers say—that slower planets bestow their gifts later—will be refuted afterward. For now, we maintain that nothing else is given by them through motion except that we ourselves are moved; this certainly does not happen differently from them, whether they are driven around slower or faster. Furthermore, regarding the same planet, there is no reason to doubt that we are moved by it in different ways because it moves differently at different times; for it is a firm dogma of the philosophers that celestial motions are always similar to themselves and equal to themselves. The stars are not permitted to suppress or turn their course, even if it seems so to us—a fact which mathematicians attribute to eccentric circles, or to different motions striving against one another, or to other things of that kind.

<margin>
Note.
</margin>

The only possible diversity is that, when carried through the lowest parts of their epicycles, they might affect us more favorably as they are nearer; yet this is more discordant with the decrees of astrologers than in agreement with them, as will be explained more widely in what follows. Concerning the dignity and rank of the movers or the bodies that are moved, the question is: do they all do the same thing equally in these things that happen, or does one mover do one thing and another do another?

<margin>
Question.
Opinion.
</margin>

For there are those who think that everything that happens is done by the proximate <gloss>nearest</gloss> cause, and that the higher causes do nothing else but move that proximate cause to act. They believe so many intermediate causes are placed by nature not so that one does one thing and another does another, but so that the thing may be effected in its proper order. This is because an effect cannot be produced except by a known cause, and that cause is too in-

<column-break/>

-effective, due to the bonds of matter by which lower things are more strictly bound, to move unless it is itself moved. Since the lower cause cannot be moved directly by the most noble and supreme causes, it was necessary for as many intermediate causes to intervene as there were ranks of dignity in the order of causes. Therefore, these thinkers believe that the same thing is done by so many causes, not because one claims one part of the work and another claims another—since they are bound together by an essential mutual connection—but because, in order to act as one, one is necessarily moved by another across a triple series.

<margin>
Another opinion.
</margin>

There are others, on the contrary, who wish for the higher and lower cause *not* to do the same thing in what happens. Instead, according to the degrees of perfection contained in a substance, they believe the work also depends on causes graduated by their level of perfection. Therefore, the more general aspect of a common work pertains to the more general cause; that is, in the act of producing something, the more excellent the cause, the more universal it is. Thus, things that are made have the fact that they "are" from God; they have the fact that they are "substances" from the next cause in line; again, they have the fact that they are "bodies" from the cause that follows, until one arrives at the thing's own species <gloss>specific type</gloss> and nature, which is referred to its own proximate cause. Whichever of these views we hold, it is clear that neither the individual differences nor even the specific differences of things come from the heavens, insofar as we are considering this efficiency of motion.

---

### Chapter X. That stars other than the sun and moon either do nothing to us, or certainly very little.

We have spoken of motion; it remains to speak of light. But we must first note certain differences between the action of the stars upon us through motion and the action through light. The power of the former comes from the mover rather than the soul, and from the moved body <note>original: "actionem stellarum in nos per motum ab ea quæ fit per lumen: illius virtus a mouente magis anima quàm a moto corpore"</note>; the power of the latter comes from the body of the planet itself. The former is believed to belong to the spheres rather than the stars; the latter to the stars rather than the spheres.

<margin>
From the mover rather than the soul; for in the first book of Physics it is said that the substantial form is active motion while matter is passive, thus in both motion is found.
</margin>

In the case of motion, the lower things depend on the higher, since no one doubts that the planets and the sun are driven around by the motion of the first sphere. Regarding light, on the contrary, it is thought by almost all philosophers that not only the moon but also the remaining stars are illuminated by the sun. Likewise, things that are higher move us more, since the others move by their power; but regarding the influence of light upon us, if other things are equal, the influence is more powerful from a nearer place. 

Furthermore, it is not even clear—as we shall demonstrate—whether the lights of the superior bodies act upon us at all, or whether only the lights of the sun and moon do, while the others do not reach this far with any efficacy because of the smallness or distance of the shining bodies. Concerning motion, there is no doubt that the higher bodies are more powerful. From all this, it can be gathered what is said by philosophers: that the series and, as it were, the chain of causes hang from one another in a certain essential order downward. This pertains mostly to the efficiency of motion, since this army and order of causes is understood more in the moving souls than in the bodies. It is characteristic of this order that the second depends on the first, and the higher cause has more strength and power than any of the lower ones—so much so that if the higher ceases, the lower cannot act. 

However, we do not deny that the heat of the sun has the nature of a superior cause in the essential order relative to seminal heats <note>The "vital heat" believed to be inherent in seeds and living organisms.</note>, but that order does not extend further. Therefore, there is not here that "conspiracy of causes" <note>A Stoic and Neoplatonic concept (*sympatheia*) where all parts of the universe are interconnected.</note> traced from the first to the lowest through intermediate steps of which people speak; rather, it is found more completely in the series of movers insofar as they are movers. Yet, in both cases, one may observe a nearly fourfold progression: in motion, the first place is held by that sphere, or the universe itself, which is revolved by the daily agitation; from which the others...

<meta>catchword: ...revolve</meta>

<meta>This page continues Pico’s investigation into the physical influences of the heavens. # MOUNTAIN OF DISPUTATIONS

<margin>Plato.</margin>
this motion is also communicated. There follows the choir of the planets running along the poles of the zodiac in the opposite direction; and in this, there are no further degrees to be distinguished, since they neither move nor are moved by one another in turn. Therefore, as if a single movable thing is swept along by the first mover <note>The *Primum Mobile*, the outermost sphere of the heavens</note>, it also moves by its own motion—which is called the "motion of diversity" by Plato—it moves the ether, into which it moves the highest air, from where, in a fourth degree, motion reaches us and the lower bodies. While they are quickened by this, all the particular motions of natural things arise from it.
<margin>Influence, of the Sun, action.</margin>
In light—and when I say this, I always mean the heat flowing forth from light—the sun is the eye of the world and the source of all influence. This sun illuminates the moon; the moon affects the air; the air is that in which all bodies live that exist under and within the air. But there is this diversity: we are moved by the first mover through the planets, and we are illuminated by the sun differently than by the moon. We recount all these things for this reason most of all: so that before a discussion of the difference of astral flows is held, we may know it is not established whether those superior influences, of whatever kind they may be, reach our region. Instead, what is believed by astrologers about certain smaller stars can also be believed about all the planets except the sun and moon. Since the primary objection to this opinion could be that celestial bodies are the essential causes of inferior things (an order in which nothing can be idle), I wanted to declare that this order pertains not so much to the illuminating bodies, but rather to the moving powers. For astrologers cannot say that the stars were created in vain by God if their breath is not perceived; lest they be in vain, the astrologers themselves freely confess this very thing. Otherwise, perhaps this sublime candelabra, radiating with so many lights, was not first made so that, bringing light to our nocturnal eyes, it might illuminate the dens inhabited by light-shunning moles. But you will ask, why so many stars, if the sun alone and the moon suffice for us? This was fitting for celestial nature; the order of things and the perfection of the entire universe demanded this. Nor does it follow that if they do not all illuminate us, there can be no other use and benefit for us from them.
<margin>Doubt. Solution. The reasoning of Averroes and Aristotle.</margin>
Averroes <note>A 12th-century Andalusian philosopher known for his commentaries on Aristotle.</note> argues thus: The sun and moon act upon us, therefore the others do as well, since they are all of the same nature. This species of argument is pleasing, and it tastes of Aristotle, who also argues thus: the moon is not moved by its own motion but with its sphere, as its spots declare; therefore, the same must be judged concerning the others, since the nature of all celestial things is one. Wherefore, following in these same footsteps, we shall conclude thus: The sun heats, therefore the moon does as well, because they are all of the same nature. And we indeed conclude rightly, since reason proves this much: that the conditions of all are the same insofar as they are considered absolutely in themselves. But when you compare them to other things, since they are not compared in the same way, reason wavers. For if the sun is going to do the same thing by its own nature as Saturn, it does not follow that both do the same thing toward us, because one is compared to us as near, the other as remote.
<margin>See how Pico summarizes against the astrologers. Argument. Note.</margin>
Thus, those who would say that only the sun and moon act upon us have reasons they may bring for their suspicion, even though there is the same nature in all celestial bodies. For three conditions of a shining body chiefly make the action of light effective upon us: size, density, and proximity. These all concur preeminently in the sun; for it is nearest to us, especially if it is placed above the moon, which the ancients and, after Ptolemy, Geber <note>Jabir ibn Aflah, a 12th-century astronomer.</note> and Theon <note>Theon of Alexandria, a 4th-century commentator on Ptolemy.</note> contend. And it is of such a vast body that it surpasses the largest of the stars by more than a ratio of one and a half <note>original: *plus sexqualtera propositione*</note>. Furthermore, it is seen with the densest light, the most radiant of all. The moon is so close to our regions that it cannot fail to affect those things which it even touches.

<column-break/>

From this, its light is necessarily effective, which is nearly no different than solar light. You would not find these conditions in others in such a way that what you granted concerning the moon and sun, you would be unable not to grant concerning the rest. But perhaps in the lights of the eighth sphere <note>The sphere of the fixed stars.</note>, even the greatest of them, distance itself will stand in the way; the same will stand in the way for the stars of Saturn and Jupiter, which, just as they are farther from the earth, are also reported to be smaller than those others. For the most fixed stars are said to contain the mass of the earth one hundred and seven times; but Jupiter ninety-five times, and Saturn only ninety-one times. These things, however, are not said with the utmost precision. And if we follow experience, we see that the rays of those fixed stars, even though of such vast magnitude, are not perceived at night, even if Saturn and Jupiter irradiate us along with them above the horizon.
<margin>The quantity of the Sun.</margin>
Mars decreases far more in body than it approaches in position, for it has a proportion to the earth a little greater than one and a half, so that one sun might contain nearly one hundred Marses. For the sun is larger than the earth one hundred sixty-six times. Therefore, why would he have said the most absurd things who, with the senses witnessing that the powers of the sun are blown into bodies, believes it can happen that the powers of the star of Mars do not reach these things, being so much smaller and more remote from the earth? Let him believe the same concerning the star of Venus, perhaps even more remote from us than the sun is; certainly much smaller than even the earth itself, of which it is thought not even a twentieth part. For Mercury is smaller than the moon just as it is also more distant from us. Therefore, what wonder is it that this is also felt so little, since it is also so rarely seen, though astrologers are accustomed to attribute very much to it.
<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
But Aristotle also seems to support those who think this way. Indeed, when he deals with motion, he mentions all of them, as in his book *On the Heavens*, and especially the highest motions, as in the last part of his *Physics*. This is because, clearly, all bodies are moved by these motions. But when he speaks of that life-giving heat that cherishes the generation of things and brings them to perfection, he mentions either only the sun (as when he said a man is generated by the sun and a man) or the sun and the moon (as in his books *On the Generation of Animals*). Thus, if someone should contend that this was the opinion of Aristotle, he could be refuted by no sayings of that philosophy.
<margin>Pico's Opinion.</margin>
We do not assert that so much as this: whatever reaches down from the other stars is so meager that if perhaps the air is softened a little by the nightly lights of the stars so that it becomes more suited for generation, even if someone should refer all generation to the sun alone as the recipient, he might decide thus: what the sun performs by day with its light, it also performs at night through that light reflected to the moon as if to a mirror, from where it is reflected back to the earth. Nature, in its great wisdom, disposes these turns because earthly weakness could not endure the rays of the sun almost continually. Therefore, let the earth receive them at night through the moon, through reflections that are weaker and therefore more suited to its infirmity. Thus it is neither entirely deserted by vegetal light nor does it faint, as it were, under the fullness of that light again. In this way, the sun returns to us more healthfully in early spring after it has been far away all winter, than if it had dwelt near us constantly and diligently. Indeed, our fragility is so overwhelmed by the good of heaven if it be too much, that not even the moon itself always pours back the solar rays in their entirety, but now more sparingly, now more abundantly, according to its configurations relative to the sun. Divine care ordained them thus for that utility, since for that reason it did not fill the star nearest to us with its own light.
<margin>The opinion which was asserted above is most aptly placed here.</margin>
If, therefore, you look around at all of nature, you will see no sign given by it that inferior things are cherished by any other heat than that of the sun. While we do not defend this point stubbornly, we also do not refuse to admit the stars into the partnership of this duty, as many philosophers have opined.

<summary>Pico argues that while the heavens share a common nature, the physical influence on Earth is dominated by the Sun and Moon due to their size and proximity. He uses astronomical measurements and Aristotelian philosophy to suggest that other planets are too small or distant to exert a significant effect on terrestrial generation.</summary>
