# AGAINST ASTROLOGERS, BOOK III.

<margin>Note.</margin>
In this way, we refute the astrologers who believe that in any given birth chart <note>original: "genitura"</note> (if human births are indeed tied to the stars) the primary influence is sometimes owed to other planets while the Sun or Moon are neglected, whether the birth occurs by day or by night. They even think the Sun itself can be "oppressed" by the rays of others and negatively affected, as if it were merely one of many in a rank. We shall deal with these matters later; for now, we simply warn that those who believe the stars have more power than the Sun in governing lower things are more strongly refuted by clear evidence and the senses than those who contend the stars have almost no power at all. These latter thinkers attribute the entire illumination and growth <note>original: "vegetationem"</note> of the lower world to the "Phoebean lamp" <note>The Sun, associated with the god Phoebus Apollo</note>, from which the "lunar lamp" is also lit for us throughout the night.

### Chapter XI. How the same stars can act on us in different ways.

<margin>Paul the Apostle.</margin>
**B**ut let us grant the astrologers—and we ourselves do not greatly deny it—that something flows down from all the stars. It remains for us to examine what their objection demanded: whether the same things always grant the same effects, or whether the same things grant diverse effects. If they are not the same, let us see whether the lower effects are varied by that diversity. In the fourth argument, they try to prove that every star has its own particular powers beyond motion and light, based on the nobility of the heavens and the powers of certain bodies thought to come from the heavens. We will dismantle those arguments there. Here, they only offer the diversity of the stars as a reason: since one star differs from another, and light and motion are common to all, they must necessarily have certain unique properties by which they differ from one another. But Paul said: "Star <margin>Opinion.</margin> differs from star in clarity." <note>1 Corinthians 15:41</note> What then if, just as circular motion is common to all yet they differ in motion (some moving faster, some slower), they also differ in the conditions of their light—even if we agree they all possess light? One star's light might be denser and more abundant, while another's is rarer or thinner. Indeed, there are those who believe a star differs more from its own celestial sphere than one star differs from another; yet they differ only in rarity and density. If this is accepted, it follows that their action upon us varies only in that those which are denser, larger, or closer pour out more light and heat, while those that are rarer, smaller, or more distant pour out less. Ultimately, the "breath" <note>original: "spiramen"</note> from all of them is the same: a luminous heat of warm light, which provides health, life, and nourishment to bodies. The only difference is that from some it is breathed more thinly, from others more abundantly; from some nearby, and from others from afar. Furthermore, what shall we decide about the same star, given the perpetual revolution of its motion? <margin>What the Peripatetics thought.</margin> It is the opinion of the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle</note> that stars do not change their quality, only their location—except for the Moon, which, shining with borrowed light, is illuminated more or less depending on its orientation to the Sun. Therefore, because of the turn it makes away from the Sun, it pours back light to us more or less abundantly, and with its light, its heat. Thus, it almost deserts us at the New Moon when the side facing us is deprived of light; it nourishes and warms us more at the Full Moon. Just as it grows when waxing and lessens when waning, such variety cannot exist in the other stars that shine with a stable, intrinsic light. For this reason, if there is any celestial cause for the changes that frequently happen to bodies, it is usually attributed to the Moon; because it is mutable not only in position but in quality, it affects us most closely. For the other planets, change occurs only through the motion of their locations, from which arises a variety

<column-break/>

of influence—not of a different kind, but merely in how intensely or weakly they affect us, insofar as they become nearer or farther from us as they migrate here and there. They have a double motion: universal and proper. The universal motion carries them above the earth to us daily, and daily snatches them away, leading them toward the setting. From this arises the first diversity of action: when they are at their peak <note>the zenith</note>, they hurl the strongest rays because they fall more directly and perpendicularly. Therefore, the closer they approach the summit, the more powerfully they affect us; the more they descend from there, the more weakly. We must discuss whether or not they can have any effect on us when they are submerged beneath the earth. For when they are near the horizon <note>original: "finitorem"</note> and not yet fully taken from us, <margin>Whether stars submerged under the earth can have any power over us.</margin> they can certainly do something, however small, since their rays still reach us at an angle. But when they are hidden deep in the shadows of the earth and removed far from us, if I believe they have no power, my senses will support me and reason will not object. Indeed, how could it be believed otherwise? If what we have defended so far is true—that nothing reaches us from heaven except by the vehicle of light—then this follows. Avicenna <note>A famous Persian polymath and philosopher</note> also said this <margin>Avicenna. Albertus.</margin> in his books on meteorology, calling light the "vehicle of all celestial virtues"; and Albert <note>Albertus Magnus, a prominent medieval scholar</note> confirmed this in his book *On Sleep and Waking*. Therefore, just as light does not reach us then, neither will any power reach us. We say that only the Sun is "present" to us at night for the reason that it makes its sister <note>the Moon</note> its deputy, shining upon us through the splendor impressed upon her. Unless, perhaps, it could also be said that since this upper air is continuous with the lower air, the presence of the Sun there warms this air as well, so that it would be colder if no Sun at all illuminated any part of the air. But if this effect is anything at all, the eyes and the facts will testify that it is almost nothing. Astrologers will renounce their status if they do not admit that the virtues they have dreamed up—which the entire mass of the earth does not block—are at least not so delirious that they wouldn't grant these virtues are impressed upon us more purely and effectively when poured through the air surrounding us than when the dense thickness of the "brute earth" must be entirely perforated by them. When they do not concede this, who could defend them from insanity? For they think the powers of the stars in the "twelfth house" (which is closest to the eastern horizon and rising) are sluggish, ceasing, and weak, yet they think those same stars in the depths of the earth <note>the 4th house</note> have the most vigor and efficacy. But we will deal with their errors later; now we only discuss what ought to be decided by reason. We have spoken of universal motion. By their "Proper Motion," the planets are carried sometimes to the south and sometimes to the north—which the fixed stars are also believed to do, according to the opinion of the younger thinkers. The Sun does the same, not by bending from its once-occupied orbit, but because that oblique path makes it now closer to us, now more remote: closest in the north, remote in the south. From this is born another variety of influence, since there is greater efficacy in rays inclining toward us and less in those receding toward the south. Beyond these or similar things, any diversity imagined in the action of the stars is utterly vain and irrational—such as the astrologers' belief that the same star acts differently according to twelve locations, or the signs it passes through, or the stars (fixed or wandering) to which it is joined by certain intervals. <margin>Intervals of the stars are called aspects.</margin> These intervals they call "aspects," and they think the stars acquire very different powers for influencing us through them. The entire sixth book will arm itself against this error. Here, at the beginning of this chapter, we will only object to them with the authority of the Peripatetics, who deny any change in the stars except for position, except in the Moon. For if they only excluded destructive and harmful change, it would not have been necessary to exclude the Moon...

<summary>Pico argues that celestial influence is strictly physical, operating through light and heat. He rejects the astrological "houses" and "aspects" as irrational, noting that if light is the vehicle of power, stars beneath the earth should have no influence.</summary>

## DISPUTATION NINE

<columns>
...be excluded, when the Moon itself is not changed in that way by the Sun. Furthermore, as we shall see, astronomers do not even free the stars from harmful changes that weaken—if not their substance—at least their powers and faculties; but more on this later. This, however, is a point of 
<margin>Whether the moon receives the rays of other planets like those of the sun.</margin>
doubt: does the moon receive the rays of other planets just as it clearly receives those of the sun? It seems probable because the moon is, by its nature, a vessel <note>original: "susceptaculum"</note> for incoming light rather than being a source of light itself; and as the lowest of all the spheres, it seems most prepared for this. Yet, neither the authority of the great thinkers nor our own senses support this. Indeed, when the moon is in conjunction with the sun, if it is then positioned opposite the rays of Jupiter or Mars—from which it ought to reflect their light more fully to us—it is found to have no rays or light at all. We touch upon this question because if the moon did draw light from the others, the planets would become more effective toward us for this reason: they would be joined to the moon, and their power—which perhaps reaches here less on its own—would be transmitted through it to us. But if this did happen, it would happen in a completely different way than the astrologers think. For they believe the moon transmits the rays of that star with which it is currently found. I, however, have no doubt that the further the moon moves away from a star, the more light from that star is communicated to us through it; and the closer they are, the less light is reflected—reaching a minimum or nothing at all when they are together. I am moved by 
<margin>Why the moon’s conjunction with the stars signifies the opposite of the astrologers’ annoying claims.</margin>
evident experience: when joined to the sun, the moon does not transmit the sun’s rays to us, as the mass of its body is the greatest obstacle. How much less, then, could it transmit the rays of others, which are far thinner than solar rays and more distant from the moon? See how greatly they are deceived who believe a day or a birth chart <note>original: "genituram"</note> is "fortunate" when the moon meets with benefic stars <note>In astrology, Jupiter and Venus are typically called "benefics."</note>, or "unfortunate" when it meets with malefic ones <note>Saturn and Mars are traditionally called "malefics."</note>. In truth, for the moon to meet them is nothing other than for their influence to be cut off from us by the moon's density. Perhaps there is also a reason that a morning planet <note>A planet that rises before the sun.</note> has some advantage in changing things below, because by rising before the sun, it claims the air for itself before the air is entirely occupied by the sun. But if this effect exists, it can have no great importance. It remains to be examined whether a new effective force, capable of producing a 
<margin>Question. Plotinus.</margin>
new work, arises from the mixture of rays—a force that individual rays alone could not produce. Plotinus <note>A major Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 204–270 AD).</note> denies that such a "tempering" or blending can happen to rays so that a new power or "form" springs forth from their combination. I believe this is because rays are not bodies (like liquids) nor qualities fixed to bodies. Because of their nature, they are not received into bodies in such a way that they are stained by them or changed from their own state in any way. Therefore, it is likely that for this philosopher, rays do not undergo what happens to many qualities: that from some combination or mixture they are sometimes changed into a different form emerging from all the parts. This is especially true since such a change usually happens only with the destruction of the simple and particular qualities flowing together—a concept one cannot easily imagine applying to rays. Even if we grant to astrologers that rays are mixed, or that the heat flowing from rays is mixed, we assert that *all* rays are *always* being mixed. They are not "un-allied" <note>original: "a symbolos," from the Greek "asymbolos" meaning non-contributing or separate.</note> or incapable of uniting with others except through what the astrologers now call "aspects." Therefore, the mixture of the present hour, moment, year, month, or day does not vary from the radiant mixture of another time, except for those reasons we have already explained for the variation of the stars' actions: namely, that the "tempering" <note>or balance of qualities</note> is one thing by night and another by day; one thing when the stars recede to the south and another when they incline to the north. From this arises only the intensifying or lessening of heat.

<column-break/>

### Chapter XII. Which effects can be traced to the heavens and which cannot.

<margin>In the mixture of rays in the air, there is again both a substantial and accidental part.</margin>
**L**et us consider the mixture of all rays in the air. In this mixture, there is something you might call "substantial" and something "accidental." <term>Substantial</term> <note>Meaning essential or foundational to the nature of the thing.</note> is the fact that there is a single light or a single heat gathered or resulting from all the lights of heaven; and this is perpetual and unchanging. But the fact that one specific ray is more intense in it now, and another more relaxed, is <term>accidental</term> <note>Meaning incidental or a non-essential variation.</note>; it changes constantly according to the continuous movement of the celestial bodies. The reason for our distinction is easily seen. In the heavens, which we know to be the source of this heat, something can be called substantial: just as we say things are substantial which follow the substance of a thing inseparably. Such things are the celestial body's inability to decay, its circular shape (the first of all shapes), its movement in a circle, and the light that, along with its heat, gives life to all things. And if indeed the stars have their own powers, those rotations of the stars are also substantial. Again, there is something in the heavens and stars that is variable, and thus accidental—such as the change of position in all the stars, and the changing phases of light in the moon. Therefore, those things in the mixture of rays that follow the substantial things of heaven, we call substantial; those that follow the accidental, we call accidental. For instance, the fact that the mixture includes the power of Saturn, Jupiter, the Sun, and the rest is in there substantially. But that these powers have certain intensifications or lessenings according to the variety of rays is said to happen accidentally. Thus, Socrates <note>Used here as a generic example of a human being.</note> was aided by that superior power—which is not a changeable power, otherwise it would not always be present in the causes that do everything, as it is seen to be—and aided by it, the power generates a human being insofar as he is human. And it generates *this* human being from this woman and from this matter. Therefore, if you look at the substantial condition or nature or individual character of the effect, any constellation is indifferent. But it is from the diversity of the constellation—that is, the various positions and relationships of the stars to the earth—that more or less heat is poured into the air. From a different mixture of rays, a new proportion and measure of warm light springs forth. That is, the accidental change in the heavens produces an accidental diversity in the things produced. For example, if someone says that a better conception occurs during a full moon, or 
<margin>Note.</margin>
that a fetus grows more as the moon waxes, or that seeds are better affected under a temperate state of the sky and therefore better offspring are produced—this kind of diversity can indeed exist in generating substances due to the varying positions of the heavens. We call this "accidental" and "external" because, as we have declared, the specific and substantial character of the conceived fetus depends on its own most immediate principle and its own substantial matter. Furthermore, the accidents of the woman and the matter contribute more to accidental properties than the external disposition of the surrounding air does, as they are more related, more immediate, and more internal. Daily experience makes this manifest: so much so that if a son is not shaped according to the seeds of his parents and does not derive his likeness from them, 
<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
Aristotle says he must be counted among "monsters" <note>original: "monstris." In natural philosophy, a "monster" is a biological anomaly that deviates from the parental type.</note>. Accordingly, nothing shall stop us from making the stars only universal causes and seeking the distinction of effects from secondary causes. The varying arrangement of the stars can, in some way, vary the disposition of the air, or the bodies already born or about to be born, since as we said, this is an external and very general change. But that which pertains to the substance and the most internal qualities comes more closely from the [own...]
</columns>

-> AGAINST ASTROLOGY, BOOK III. <-

It undoubtedly draws its origin from these; therefore, it can in no way be foreseen from the heavens. This is indeed true in the case of physical bodies which are complete substances, all of which have nearby efficient causes—or something proportional to them—as in those things generated from decay and inanimate mixtures, which we shall discuss in the solution to the fourth argument. But since the heavens can produce changes in the air regarding heat, cold, moisture, and dryness without any intermediary, it does so universally. Because the heavens, by their own nature, provide only a healthy warmth, other effects happen by accident <note>The term "by accident" here refers to the Aristotelian concept of *per accidens*, meaning an unintended side effect based on the recipient's nature rather than the cause's intent.</note> according to the condition of the matter—just as by one and the same heat, clay hardens while wax melts; and under the same sun, linens turn white while they are washed, yet the face of the one washing them is darkened in the meantime. 

Furthermore, since this accidental change is very powerful, it is what we have called "accidental" in a celestial constellation: namely, the positions and attitudes of the stars, from which the strength of the rays is intensified or weakened. Because of this, heat acts more or less upon the air; for this very reason, the four seasons of the year vary according to the various paths of the sun, as do the rising and setting, and the ascending and descending, which produce nearly the same four changes within a single day. 

Among these primary qualities of bodies are meteorological impressions—inanimate mixtures that hold a middle place. The efficient cause of these is also the heavens, while their matter is from below; hence their diversity depends more on celestial arrangement than do perfect substances. Thus, thunder usually occurs in spring and autumn, hail in summer, and snow and rain in winter—though less so than the four absolute qualities themselves, since the sun’s ray produces these qualities in matter by its own power, whereas meteorological events are indeed moved by the ray, but are formed from the matter below. For this reason, they vary greatly according to the condition of that matter, as we shall explain more 
<margin>
Augustine inserts what follows in the fifth book of *The City of God*.
</margin>
broadly in the treatise on the third argument. 

But perfect substances, which possess not only matter but also their own specific efficient cause, receive whatever is substantial and proper to them (to repeat the same point often) from their own specific causes. The heavens act as a universal cooperating cause through their unchanging influence, while their changing influence causes some external, general mutation. Regarding this, however, astrologers can say nothing at all, since it depends neither on the celestial causes they have established, nor on the hour of birth, but on other principles, as we shall later declare. For now, we are investigating only what the heavens do and what they do not do. 

Understanding these things which we have discussed, Aurelius Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a foundational Christian theologian who famously argued against astrology in his work *The City of God*.</note> did not say it was entirely absurd to think that certain "stellar breathings" <note>original: "afflatus... sydereos"</note> had power over the differences of bodies alone. He did not assert it was so, nor did he accuse those who thought otherwise; rather, he lightened the blame of those who held such an opinion, pronouncing it not so much an "absurd" opinion as one that was "not entirely absurd." However, he added an explanation of which bodily differences were to be understood: just as we see the seasons of the year vary with the sun’s approach and retreat, and certain kinds of things increase and decrease with the moon’s waxing and waning—such as sea urchins, shellfish, and the wondrous tides of the ocean. 

In these words of his, you see nothing listed that contributes to the generation of any perfect substance. He immediately adds a warning that the diversities of these substances—though they are highly physical—should not be referred to the stars, but to proximate causes. What is more "of the body" than the sex of a body? And yet, under the same position of the stars, twins of different sexes can be conceived. Confirming this same 

<column-break/>

view a little earlier, he had approved of Hippocrates <note>The famous Greek physician often called the "Father of Medicine."</note> giving a reason from specific and secondary causes as to why two brothers were sick at the same time and recovered at the same time. 
<margin>
Hippocrates.
</margin>
<margin>
Posidonius.
</margin>
But he did not approve of Posidonius <note>Posidonius of Rhodes, a Stoic philosopher who tried to find physical links between the stars and human biology.</note> referring this to the similarity of their constellation. A "medical conjecture," he says, is much more acceptable: that as the parents were affected in their bodies while they lay together, so the beginnings of those conceived could be affected. Thus, having followed the first developments from the mother’s body, they were born with equal health. Then, nourished in one house with the same foods—where medicine testifies that the air, the position of the place, and the quality of wine and water matter greatly for the body to be received well or poorly—and accustomed to the same exercises, they bore such similar bodies that they were moved similarly by the same causes even to falling ill at the same time. But to refer this to the constitution of the heavens or stars when they were conceived or born, I know not what kind of "insolence" <note>original: "insolentiæ"</note> that is. 

These are the words of our Augustine which we have quoted. Many people, understanding only this much from him—a point often used by our own writers—think that Augustine believed all physical diversity comes from the heavens because he said it was "not absurd" that bodily differences relate to stellar breathings. Consequently, they think that because Augustine agrees on this, astrologers can prophesy. They are little mindful that nothing can be so rightly called "physical" as the temperament of the body itself; yet Augustine brands those who seek the causes of that temperament in the heavens with the title of "insolence."

### Chapter XIII. That the Sun performs many actions which astrologers think are done by other stars.

<margin>
A recollection of the preceding points.
</margin>
**R**etorting the first argument of the astrologers back upon them, we have declared in a long but necessary digression what the heavens and celestial action do to us, and how it varies whether we consider the stars themselves or the receiving matter. From this, it has been made clear that the heaven is a universal cause, and the distinction of effects—especially regarding principal and substantial nature—is not to be sought there. 

Now, in the proper order, as if taking a step through the things we have disputed, we shall set our hands to solving the second argument. Because, they say, the dispositions of lower bodies are found to vary according to the sun and moon’s various relations to us, they contended that the same should be believed regarding other things and planets. For they say the cycles of the four seasons vary through the sun’s turns, and the state of all bodies is changed both by that cycle and by the moon’s waxing and waning. 

What then? There are two things they think can be gathered from this. First: that just as we see sea urchins, shellfish, the ocean, and the moisture of bodies changed according to the moon’s courses—and generally the earthly mass according to the sun’s annual and diurnal revolution—so we should agree that all other things are bound to the stars and governed by them. Second: that the manifest power of the sun and moon in changing sublunary matter should force us to believe the same about the rays of other stars—that is, that although their power is more hidden, a great force still exists in them for changing things and affecting them in many ways. 

We shall make it clear that neither can be concluded. In fact, these very things they bring forward for themselves actually favor those who suspect otherwise. Before that happens, we shall give 
<margin>
The perseverance of the disputation.
</margin>
an account of all those observations from the principles already established, so that it may be evident that we are led neither by arguments nor by experiments to feel anything different about the efficiency of the stars and the change of celestial virtues than what we have so far prescribed under the guidance of natural reason. In the meantime, I will not cease to expose the many...

<meta>This page continues Pico’s argument that celestial effects are the result of physical proximity and heat rather than the "mystical" natures of the zodiac signs. # OF THE DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGY

<margin>
What follows and what he refutes.
</margin>

...their fallacies, mocking many of their errors in passing. Let us begin, therefore, with the works of the Sun alone: the approach and retreat of the Sun changes the seasons of the year. This we shall affirm even under oath if necessary. Yet this is caused by the tilt of the zodiac itself, not the nature of the signs. It is not for this reason that the Sun blazes in Leo: because it is the sign of Leo, or the "house of the Sun," or a "hot sign," as the astrologers fabricate. Rather, it is because the Sun is positioned there and is closer to our air, having already heated it for six months prior. Otherwise, it is also most fervent in Cancer, even though Cancer is not—even according to them—the Sun's house or its exaltation, nor is it a fiery sign, but an aquatic one. 

Similarly, in Aries, the Sun restores the world, calling forth flowers and increasing seeds; this is because, returning to us for the first time, it breathes a fertile and favorable temperature into bodies. It is an astrologer’s fable that Aries is the Sun's "exaltation," <note>original: "exaltationem." In astrology, an exaltation is a specific sign where a planet's influence is thought to be strongest.</note> as if the Sun did not do the same in Libra for other peoples—which is the opposite of Aries—as it does for us in Aries. That is, while it departs from here, it approaches them. Therefore, the sole cause of all the variety that occurs with time is the greater or lesser distance of the Sun from the lands we inhabit. From this, we receive more or less heat from it. 

<margin>
Why thunder happens in spring; *alphos* is called *morphea*.
</margin>

From this also, thunder occurs in the spring: because when the Sun reaches Aries, the winter moisture is dissolved by the heat of the air. From this, much evaporation is lifted upward into the air—a "harvest of clouds," so to speak—from which thunder and lightning proceed. If astrologers also understand this, then what is this sleepiness or desire to deceive? To define Aries as a sign that "stirs up rain and thunder," as if the nature of that sign produced it? Why then would they not say that the Moon also causes thunder in Aries? They would not say this by any means if they were able or willing to notice that this happens not by the power of the sign, but by the action of the Sun reaching that sign. 

They write with a similar fallacy—as seen in Ptolemy’s books of *Apotelematon* <note>original: "apotelematon." This refers to Ptolemy's *Tetrabiblos*, the foundational text of Western astrology.</note>—that the Moon in Aries, if it causes disease, causes especially *vitiligo* (which the Greeks call *alphous* and is commonly called *morphea* <note>A skin condition involving white patches or scales.</note>); in Cancer, it causes *mentagra* (which the Greeks call *lichenas* and is commonly called *impetigo* <note>Sores around the mouth or skin rashes.</note>); in Libra, leprosy; in Capricorn, freckles. This was drawn from the state of the air when the Sun is carried through those signs: that is, from the quality of Spring when the Sun is in Aries; of Summer when it is in Cancer; of Autumn when in Libra; and of Winter when it traverses the sign of Capricorn. Indeed, those types of diseases fit the conditions of those seasons. 

*Vitiligo* belongs to Spring, which easily invades and occupies the top layer of the skin due to the humors <term>Humors: In ancient medicine, the four fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) that governed health.</term> overflowing at that particular part of the year. *Mentagra* belongs to Summer, arising from drier and sharper matter. Leprosy belongs to Autumn, since it is considered an infection of black bile. Freckles belong to Winter, generated from the prevailing colder and more humid conditions. Therefore, it is the height of nonsense to ascribe to the signs—under which the Sun is carried during those times—the things that are handed down as being caused by the Sun heating the air more or less according to its position. 

<margin>
Why not all summers are equally hot.
</margin>

Or, if they understand this but pretend not to, they think that other planets in those same signs produce the same effects. Let us conclude immediately that the diversity in the seasons of the year comes from nowhere else than the approach and retreat of the Sun according to the tilt of the zodiac. If not all summers are equally scorching, nor all winters equally freezing, this can happen due to the "disposition of matter," <note>Pico argues that local conditions on Earth (matter) are more important than the stars (the cause).</note> which has the greatest momentum in the air, according to the testimony of Seneca and Ptolemy. Nor is it necessary to refer this to the heavens, except as a universal cause of every corporeal thing, as one may understand from Aristotle’s books on *Meteorology*. Thus, in the same summer, the heat is more intense on some days and duller on others; yet the position of the Sun itself does not demand this. A change in the lower regions causes it—namely, a wind stirred up somewhere, or a flood of rain.

<column-break/>

...or something else of this kind which can happen far away from us, such that we do not see the cause itself, though we nonetheless experience its force overflowing even to our own sky with an effect. If the planets are some hotter than others, those that are less hot can—by accident—generate rains and veil the sky with clouds from dissolved humors that have not been consumed. From this, heat fails and cold is intensified. Conversely, those that are more fervent lead to dryness and heat. It is not far from our principles that the dominance of various stars contributes something to the change of the air, provided we do not understand "dominance" here as anything other than that a star is closer to us or illuminates us with more direct rays. 

However, since we suspect that whatever reaches us from the higher stars is entirely thin—especially regarding these sensible qualities—the causes of storms are usually not found in the heavens, whether we think of the stars according to the astrologers' opinion or as we philosophers define them. It seems that this whole matter, which subtracts from or adds to the actions of the luminaries, should rather be referred to the "matter" <note>The physical environment on Earth.</note> itself. As for the luminaries themselves, one changes only by position, the other also by light; neither changes according to the nature of the signs they traverse, the places where they stand, or the planets with which they are configured—as will be made manifest in what follows. 

<margin>
The source of the sea's disturbance and calm; how the sailors' observation of seasons is useful, not superstitious.
</margin>

Therefore, the fact that the clear sea is agitated by waves and swells when the Sun enters Virgo—and especially when it reaches Sagittarius—and again becomes calm and navigable when the Sun is carried to Pisces and especially Gemini; and conversely, that the Indian sea is calm under Virgo and Sagittarius and navigable under Pisces and Gemini; this arises not from the "quality" of the signs but from the position of the Sun and the condition of the matter. Even astrologers confess this. Thus, a sailor’s observation of these times, taking the sea into account, is useful and not superstitious. 

Regarding those who sail and predict days on which one must abstain from navigation: if they have any cause from the heavens, they cannot have it from anywhere else than the Sun. Because their observation of these days is fixed and perpetual, it can only be referred to the Sun, whose attitude is almost always exactly the same at the same times. It can in no way be referred to other constellations, which are never found in the same positions. For example, the days usually suspended for sailors are always the 1st, 7th, 15th, 17th, 19th, and 25th of March; the 6th, 5th, 6th, 12th, and 20th of April; the 6th, 12th, 15th, 17th, 19th, and 20th of February. They always use this invariable observation. They say that during these days, great changes in the sea usually occur, either toward tranquility or toward storm. Since the outcomes are uncertain, those who abstain act more securely, lest the change happen for the worse. 

<margin>
There can be a double cause for the badness of those days.
</margin>

Therefore, this cannot be reduced to the positions of the stars that astrologers note and command to be observed, since those similar parts do not return during the same periods of the year, but rather very dissimilar ones. An astrologer would sometimes pronounce those very days—which are always suspected by pilots—as harmless for navigation and most happy; and those which the pilots do not much fear, he would call most dangerous, as the mixed ranks of the Sun and planets present themselves in varying states in that hour. Therefore, the sailor will not approve of such rules, as they are most hostile to his own principles. Since these rules are confirmed daily by long experience and the use of a sublime art, they provide the wealthiest evidence of the astrologers' vanity. These days can have a double cause: one from the Sun, and the other from the water—just as the humors in our body have their own periods by which they are moved.

He highlights how sailors rely on consistent solar cycles for safety, proving that complex astrological charts are irrelevant to real-world experience.</summary>

### AGAINST ASTROLOGY, BOOK III.

...just as the tides follow, so the ocean has its movements: it is recognized by clear evidence that the Sun, according to the moments of its approach to or retreat from us, changes the disposition of the sea and of all bodies. The reader should be reminded that this variety of seasons is denoted by those who write on farming and seafaring through the setting and rising of fixed stars, such as Arcturus, the Pleiades <note>original: "Vergiliarum," the Latin name for the Pleiades constellation, often used as a marker for the start of spring or autumn.</note>, the Hyades, and others similarly. This is not because these stars themselves are the ones whose influence is feared or expected—otherwise, even the astrologers would not say this, for they hold that these stars are ineffective on their own unless they occupy the "pivotal points" <note>original: "cardines," referring to the four most powerful points in an astrological chart: the Ascendant, Descendant, Midheaven, and Imum Coeli.</note>. Rather, it is so that there might be a visible sign for the unlettered and unlearned masters of those arts to distinguish that time; they could find no better sign, at once perpetual and conspicuous, than the emergence and setting of the stars.

Furthermore, there is that which gains more authority and observation among the unrefined common folk: that which is written by physicians—that winter illnesses are resolved in summer, and summer ones in winter; sometimes those that attack in winter fade in spring, or those of spring depart toward autumn; and finally, those occurring in any season are terminated in a different one. This happens, of course, because the quality of these times differs according to the proximity or distance of the Sun from the lands. What they say about the Moon regarding "critical days" <term>crismis diebus: In ancient and medieval medicine, these were specific days during an illness when a decisive change (the "crisis") was expected, often linked by astrologers to lunar phases.</term> is vain and irrational; but we shall speak of this later when we discuss the Moon. 

From these same progressions of the Sun comes the varied affection of things, both those lacking life and all living creatures, under the different inclinations of the heavens. Not all lands produce the same things, and the customs of peoples and the habits of bodies vary in different regions. Nor is it necessary for us to imagine other constellations, other signs, or other planets to which those places are subject, besides the Sun. The Sun always travels between Cancer and Capricorn. Therefore, whoever lives between the equinoctial circle <note>The Equator.</note> and the summer solstice necessarily lives in a very hot region; those positioned far to the north, being furthest from the Sun, live in the coldest; and those in the middle live in a temperate one. And since the eastern part of the heavens is the "right" side and more effective, the power of the Sun is greater there than in the west. From this, a reason can be given for all things reported concerning the unique properties of things, as far as it pertains to a celestial cause.

<margin>Man is born everywhere.</margin>
For gems, spices, and all such things that require more celestial heat are produced toward the East and the South. Likewise, lions, tigers, and elephants are produced in those same lands, along with other animals that require powerful heat to be generated, to live, and to remain in their vigor. Man alone is born and preserved in every part of the earth because of the ample "latitude" <note>Here meaning a wide range or adaptability.</note> of his nature under a multiform habit; though some philosophers have vainly suspected that the specific differences between men were due to some other force.

<margin>Southerners,</margin>
Those who inhabit the southern part, therefore, the more they breathe hot air, the colder they are inside. For this reason, they are timid, effeminate, and—as proven by ancient and modern experience—born for servitude. This happens because immoderate heat so relaxes the body that it draws out and consumes the greatest part of the internal heat; thus, being drawn to the surface of the body and deserting the inner depths, it leaves blackness on the skin and timidity in the heart.

<margin>Northerners,</margin>
Conversely, those who live under a cold sky toward the North are spirited, brave, and fair-skinned, for the opposite reason. But both races—whether the one most under the sun or the one furthest removed from it—have little of the "human" about them and are not very sociable 

<column-break/>

due to the exuberance of heat or cold, through which they depart from that moderate temperament in which our nature is chiefly situated. Both races are also fierce and wild, both for the common cause we mentioned and specifically because one is ferocious while the other is fearful.

<margin>The error of the Greek astrologers.</margin>
It is not, therefore, as the Greek astrologers fabulate—that because the harmful planets Saturn and Mars dominate the extreme climates <note>climatibus: Ancient geographical zones determined by the length of the longest day of the year.</note>, those peoples are more monstrous; nor that because Saturn rules the Southerners, they are timid and short-lived; nor that because Mars rules the Northerners, they are more warlike. This is a fiction in which even other astrologers do not agree, as some do not put Mars over the Northerners, but the Moon. 

Using neither Mars nor the Moon, we derive the reason for the conditions of both races from the Sun alone. To dream of any other cause is for a trifler rather than a philosopher. They say Saturn also rules in India; and yet people there are long-lived. Why then are Southerners supposedly short-lived because of Saturn's "excessive cold"? Why timid? For even there, the most ferocious beasts are born, though Aristotle writes that all creatures in the North are more "masculine." But human moderation endures extremes with great difficulty. Just as bellies are hotter in winter than in summer, so those people under excessive outer heat grow cold within; they are barely finished with their thirtieth year of life before being consumed by old age, as Avicenna relates.

<margin>Aristotle in his books on animals. Avicenna.</margin>
Those in the North, under a frozen seat, burn most deeply within, with heat trapped in their principal organs and with much thicker blood. They are as much stronger than the Southerners as the latter are more ingenious due to the refinement of their spirits and blood. The middle nations, being dull neither from a lack of blood nor from its thickness, are more prudent and wise; thus, they are made for ruling and are, so to speak, "more human." This is the general variety of the inhabitants of the earth caused by celestial circulation, to which are added many particular variations from the sublunary disposition of lands, air, and water—such as whether a place is marshy, near stagnant water, or high in the mountains. I have perhaps held you longer than necessary on these points; these factors pass from the earth to the air, and the air itself has its own properties in different places, which, as Panaetius <note>A Stoic philosopher who influenced Roman thought and was skeptical of certain astrological claims.</note> says, are not sought from heaven but are held from their own principles. No one is ignorant that inhabitants can be changed by these influences, or that food becomes harmful or healthy based solely on the condition of the water and air.

<margin>Panaetius. Whence the variety of characters and customs arises,</margin>
Hence, the primary diversity of bodies comes from the celestial impression of the Sun, followed by other factors. But the variety of characters and customs depends both on the habit of the body and on education—the foundation of habit, which rivals the forces of nature. To these are added laws, which have the greatest momentum in this matter; so much so that if they are rightly applied, they can render fierce nations most mild. Conversely, they can enervate the strongest, and easily turn the best into the bad if the laws themselves are bad. From this, the freedom of the will is most evidently declared against all "natural necessity."

<margin>An example regarding the Gauls.</margin>
The Gauls <note>The people of France.</note> were once infamous for the "love of boys" <note>A reference to pederasty or homosexual practices in antiquity.</note>, if we believe Ptolemy and Aristotle; yet now, through the benefit of Christian law and the most holy prince, King Louis <note>Likely referring to Louis XI (reigned 1461–1483), known for his legal and administrative reforms.</note>, they abhor such a crime. No nation under heaven abhors it more. Nor is it right for a single people...

-># DISPUTATIONS<-

<margin>The quality of a region does much to help one acquire skills. The response of the astrologers. A refutation.</margin>
...one can rely on examples, since the preaching of the Gospel changed the morals and institutions of almost the entire world, which had been established from the earliest times. Moreover, the quality of a region can do much to help one grasp arts and masteries: for instance, whether one is first destined by lot to devote oneself to trade and navigation because the city is conveniently located by the sea; or to letters because it is near an academy; or to military service if it is agitated by hostile neighbors or internal civil factions. There are those whom fertility and abundance make idle and pleasure-seeking, while scarcity and sterility make men hardworking, industrious, and diligent. 

But perhaps one of the astrologers will say: "We do not deny these things, but we assert and proclaim them along with you. However, we contend that there are other properties in these places arising from private influences and a peculiar constellation—according to the <term>trigonum</term> <note>original: "pro trigono"; in astrology, a 'trigon' or triplicity is a group of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element (Fire, Earth, Air, Water).</note>, the planet, or the sign under which the region falls; or according to the disposition of the heavens under which the foundations of the city were laid, or under which its empire, king, or tyrant rose to power." 

Thus, even if what you say is true, it does not follow that our claims cannot also be true. But I, most excellent diviners, do not believe it follows from the things I have mentioned that your fictions cannot exist; rather, we should understand that a full explanation for the all-encompassing diversity of places and peoples can be given through the natural causes we have stated, such that seeking other causes is not at all necessary. For the subsequent arguments will demonstrate that the causes you astrologers have introduced above are both false and fabulous. 

Truly, as we were disputing against those things to which you yourselves attribute the diversity of peoples and regions, someone might have asked what the cause of such great variety actually was. Therefore, before we overturned the false causes, it was necessary to demonstrate the true ones; thus, your unnecessary claims may be understood as such, which will later be refuted as fictional and impossible. So, we did not introduce that life-giving heat of the heaven (about which we discussed so much above), nor the efficacy of the sun, nor the way the rays are intensified or weakened by the distance or proximity of the stars, simply to tear down your views. Rather, before we refuted your fabricated nonsense—and showed how absurdly you imagine a change in stellar power based on places, signs, and aspects—I wanted to make it known that whatever force the heaven exerts upon us can be perfectly explained (by the authority of philosophers, the testimony of the senses, and the judgment of reason) through the common influence of light, which is healthily warm and flows continually from a body in perpetual motion. Therefore, to imagine other powers or "stellar influences" acting upon bodies, as you have imagined, is no longer merely superfluous, but insane.

### Chapter Fourteen. How the power of the Moon varies, and that certain days of the moon are observed through legitimate observation.

<margin>Ptolemy’s opinion on the operations of the moon.</margin>
We have shown that the dogmas of the astrologers are not necessarily proven by the works of the sun. The same must be done regarding the works of the moon. Ptolemy, in his *Apotelesmata* <note>Ptolemy’s famous astrological work, commonly known as the *Tetrabiblos*.</note>, says that from the new moon <note>original: "interluniio"</note> until it is half-full, the moon is more effective at producing moisture; from then until the full moon, it produces heat; from then until it is half-full again, it produces dryness; and finally, until the conjunction <note>the dark moon or new moon</note>, it produces coldness. Thus, he claims the moon has the nature of spring and 

<column-break/>

air in its first quarter; of summer and fire in its second; of autumn and earth in its third; and of winter and water in its fourth; and that it most especially excites these qualities of the seasons in bodies at those times. 

This division is more beautiful to describe than it is natural or true. For the condition of heat is such that when it is weak, it does not move moisture—being hardly felt; when it has some efficacy, it begins to release and dissolve moisture as it spreads; and the more powerful it is, the more it increases, until it eventually consumes the moisture it caused to flow. For then it dries out rather than moistens. But the heat of the moon, being very thin, is never so intensified that it dries things out; rather, it increases within those limits where it moistens bodies with heat, but does not parch them. Thus, the more light the moon has, the more moisture it produces, just as it produces more heat; conversely, as it is deprived of light, it likewise moistens and heats less. 

Therefore, it follows the nature and quality of spring from the first quarter to the full moon, rather than from the new moon to that first quarter—if indeed the nature of spring is defined as moist. Nor can it represent winter from the second quarter to the conjunction, or autumn from the full moon to that same quarter; for autumn is dry and winter is moist. Truly, after the moon has been full until it is half-full, it moistens; and from then until the conjunction, it dries out, namely because its moistening ceases. For this reason, timber intended to last is cut at that time. 

<margin>Ptolemy in the *Book of a Hundred Aphorisms*. Experiments.</margin>
Therefore, Ptolemy himself spoke much more correctly in his *Book of a Hundred Aphorisms* <note>original: "Centum enunciationum," referring to the *Centiloquium*, a collection of 100 astrological secrets attributed to Ptolemy.</note> when he said that the moisture of bodies flows from the first quarter of the moon (from the time it departs from its meeting with the sun) until the second quarter, but decreases during the remaining times. Indeed, beyond the reasoning we have given, experience itself bears witness to this: for as the moon waxes, there is an increase in moisture, and as it wanes, there is a decrease. This is because it is not just the location that works this quality, but also the moon's motion toward increase or decrease. 

Around the time it departs from the sun and begins to rise until its half is illuminated, it moistens and heats more than when it possesses the same amount of light in its second half-phase as it tends toward the conjunction; this is because in the former case the light is growing, while in the latter it is failing. This is the whole of lunar astrology: usefully and naturally observed by doctors, farmers, and sailors. 

<margin>Why the time of the waxing moon is suitable for planting. Why the waning moon for cutting timber. Verification of certain sayings of Hesiod and Plutarch. Explanation of a certain passage of Virgil.</note></margin>
For in general, they have judged the time of the young moon to be suitable for planting, because seeds, fed by more abundant moisture, also grow more quickly themselves. But the time of the waning moon is for cutting timber, since then all wood is drier and thinner; therefore, it does not rot so easily or get consumed by decay. Conversely, if any wood is taken when the moon is increased in light, the moisture then overflows, and it easily putrefies and is ruined. 

For this reason, Hesiod rightly praises the ninth day of the moon for planting trees, as well as the thirteenth; for as Plutarch says, the power implanted in the roots is now spread more fully by the light. He makes the same day inconvenient for sowing seeds, because the sown seed desires rain more, so that it may rot and germinate. Furthermore, he denies that the seventeenth day is fit for planting because the failing light does not sufficiently call forth the sprouts. Therefore, what Virgil said—"the seventh after the tenth is lucky both for planting vines" and what follows—cannot be understood to mean the seventeenth day; for this day is least lucky for planting vines due to the diminished light. Rather, he means either the first seventh day that occurs after the tenth...

->### AGAINST THE ASTROLOGERS BOOK III.<-

...he judged the tenth day better, that is, the fourteenth, on which—under a full moon—vines are planted quite successfully. Or, as is more consistent with reason, he praised two days, the seventh and the tenth, but the tenth more so; which is why he says that after the tenth, the seventh is lucky. For this is how it stands: on the seventh day, the half-moon provides enough heat and moisture for the roots of plants, but the tenth day does the same even more abundantly. The seventeenth day could only be denoted out of ignorance or error, as it is suitable not for planting trees but rather for cutting them; a fact that <term>Hesiod</term> <note>Hesiod was an ancient Greek poet whose work *Works and Days* serves as a guide for farming based on the calendar.</note> also records for the reason we mentioned: the decrease of moisture. For this reason, timber for building ships is prepared then, as ships must last a long time. As for why the Greek poet orders crops to be brought to the threshing floor at that time, 
<margin>Proclus</margin>
<term>Proclus</term> <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote commentaries on Hesiod.</note> writes that the reason is that winds are usually stirred up after the full moon, by which the grain itself is separated from the straw and the husk. Just as the cause and reason for these tasks are easily understood on these days, so other lunar days can be more convenient for certain works for reasons that are not so manifest, though they arise from those same natural principles we mentioned. Indeed, a portion of such great light can harmonize with one thing in a fitting proportion while disagreeing with another. Perhaps this is why Hesiod commands that lambs be castrated on the sixth moon, oxen and pigs on the eighth, and mules on the twelfth; and that the sixth and sixteenth are more opportune for begetting males than females, but the tenth for females. In truth, he orders calves to be castrated in autumn during a waning moon for a known reason: for those who emasculate animals fear the flux of humors <note>In ancient medicine, 'humors' were bodily fluids believed to control health; moisture was thought to increase or decrease with the moon.</note>, and therefore require both a dry season and a "dry" moon. For this reason, they even forbid the procedure when the moon is large. Thus, there is an evident reason why Hesiod says the sixth and sixteenth are more opportune for begetting males than females, but the fourteenth for females; since, as we have 
<margin>Exposition of the opinion of Hesiod.</margin>
frequently found, moisture increases with the light. Therefore, at the full moon, the "excrements of generation" will flow more moistly, from which female offspring are more likely to result than male. In this manner, you can reduce other things handed down by Hesiod to natural causes. He does, however, mix in a few things from old superstition—but nothing that supports the astrologers. Likewise, from these shifts of the light reaching the moon, 
<margin>Sailors</margin>
sailors can usefully observe many days without superstition, since that variation of light has great power in changing the state of the air. Therefore, they wisely abstain from sailing during the new moon and full moon, when storms are usually stirred up. 
<margin>Physicians</margin>
Physicians also rightly advise the sick by observing the days of the moon’s increase, lest the flowing humors escape their notice, especially in an afflicted body which, deprived of its own strength, is more vulnerable to external harm. For example, it might be better to open a vein as the moon grows. Conversely, <term>cupping</term> <note>original: "ventosa"; a medical practice of using heated glass cups to create suction on the skin.</note> might have its reason during a waning rather than a waxing moon, since the incision of a vein expels while suction attracts. Therefore, when humors are boiling and pushed to the extremities of the body at the start of the month, perhaps more material would be drawn out than is proper—unless one says that the works of art are always more successful when they harmonize with the progression of nature. But let these matters be left to the judgment of 
<meta>tur.</meta>

<column-break/>

physicians. Whatever they observe beyond these things, however, possesses manifest vanity, as will be made clear in what follows.

### Chapter Fifteen. The tides of the sea can be referred to a cause other than the moon; even if they are so referred, astrology is not helped by it.

<margin>See the similar reasoning of Adelard.</margin>
There is a manifold question regarding the flux and reflux of the sea, since it seems to everyone that this proceeds from the moon. <term>Adelard</term> <note>Adelard of Bath, a 12th-century scholar who introduced many Arabic scientific concepts to the West.</note>, following the opinion of the <term>Saracens</term> <note>Medieval term for Muslims/Arabs.</note>, both narrates and approves of this cause for the sea's approach and retreat. For he says that when the arms of the sea—which, thrust into the land, divide its masses—hasten to meet and flow together with rapid impetus, it happens because of the intervening mountains and the layout of the land itself. When they fail in that course, they are carried back to where their paternal and natural motion impels them; they are recalled by the position of the place itself. The moon is not the cause. Otherwise, this same thing would happen in the seas closer to the torrid zone, since they are no further from the moon—so why would they not feel its force?—and they are no less moist by nature. And yet, there is no reciprocation of tides there, specifically because the cause we mentioned is missing: the concurrent parts gapped by the mass of the terrestrial layout. This opinion of his is not greatly abhorrent to the likeness of truth, since the parts of every element are carried by a natural propensity toward their own integrity. What wonder is it, then, if the parts of the ocean, separated by lying lands, strike the shores as they approach in their desire to run together, and are likewise driven back by the obstacle? When this cause is removed (as happens in the southern sea), we see that these tides do not appear. Thus, someone might say that this manner of approaching and receding is natural to water, not insofar as it is water, but insofar as it has parts of a principal element directed and separated by the obstacle of the terrestrial mass. If this 
<margin>Another opinion.</margin>
reasoning does not satisfy someone, let him hear another: astrologers admit that such recursions do not happen in all waters, even marine ones, but only in those where the deep earth is hard, rough with frequent mountains, and uneven; and where there is much water, which neither increases by the addition of rivers nor decreases by their departure, but has held its seat there for a long time with thick density. Around such a place, a receptacle is formed, a breeder of many vapors that are neither thin nor easily dissipated. These vapors derive that well-known bitterness and saltiness from their parents—that is, watery earth and earthy water—and from the heat of the sky. Because other waters do not have these conditions, they say these tides do not appear in them. From this, a sufficiently clear and sufficient cause for the marine reciprocation might appear to anyone: for from such earth and water, vapors and winds are repeatedly stirred up, as we have said. From this, wind and tumult arise in the water, especially because it grows hot from that motion and impulse and the mixture of vapors; therefore, it seeks a wider place in which to spread itself. A third cause of motion is added: the reflection of winds nipping at the surface of the water toward its lower parts. These winds, entangled with the winds blowing from below, push the waters into the upper regions; then the waters necessarily overflow and swell as they erupt, and are rejected and pushed back in equal measure. Having rolled back, they seek their own...

# FOURTH DISPUTATION

...they produce the rising tide. Conversely, when that force catches fire among the dissolved vapors, they subside and are leveled; and by contracting themselves in narrow spaces, they depart from the occupied places. This generation of vapors and winds, according to the nature of the sea, seems to be a sufficient cause for the continuous ebb and flow, just as there is almost a perpetual generation and a perpetual dissolution. From this, the cold water returns, which had previously arrived as temperate; this is what <term>Adelard</term> <note>Adelard of Bath (c. 1080–1152) was a 12th-century English scholar known for translating Arabic scientific works into Latin.</note> indicates to us. And those defending this opinion can indeed give a reason why certain larger seas do not have an ebb and flow, even though winds and exhalations are present. For the effect is surely the same for them, but the vastness of the open sea and the distance of the shores removes the appearance of rising and falling; so it is better said that the waters seem to do this rather than alternating—that is, it is a fluctuating surge rather than a receding one. If these things harmonize with natural reason and experience, why should they be judged improbable? Or why is it necessary to add, besides these causes, the motion of the moon, pulling the waters downward and even upward with itself? Especially since those things do not correspond which must correspond: such as that when the moon is increased in light, when it is faster in its course, when it is closer to the earth, when it is declining toward the north from the path of the sun, or when placed in notable northern positions—then the rising tides should become more abundant. On the contrary, they are thinner when it is otherwise than what we were saying. Furthermore, it does not seem that anything can be objected to those who think this way, except for the harmony of the waters themselves with the moon in both rising and falling. Which (if what 

<margin>Abu Ma'shar</margin> 
<term>Abu Ma'shar</term> <note>original: "Aboaşar"; Abu Ma'shar al-Balkhi (787–886), a famous Persian astrologer.</note> admits is true) I do not know how it can even be raised as an objection. For he writes that the beginnings of the rising and falling are not the same everywhere, even where there is no variation in the horizon; but sometimes it happens in practice that at the time when the waters recede in one place, they begin to rise in another. He himself does not hide the fact that this has given many people a reason to suspect that those motions do not depend on the movements of the moon. Although he tries to give a reason for this diversity to defend the moon as being no less the cause, it follows from this that an argument for the moon cannot be taken from it. 

<margin>Another opinion of Alpetragius. That this question is irrelevant to astrology.</margin> 
Whence rather an occasion for contradiction is provided: and these things differ greatly among themselves: that the lunar cause is evidently confirmed by the times of the tide, and that it is not evidently refuted by them. <term>Alpetragius</term> <note>Nur ad-Din al-Bitruji, a 12th-century astronomer from Al-Andalus who proposed a non-Ptolemaic model of the universe.</note> brought forth the cause of this celestial motion: not from the moon, but from the daily motion by which all things are moved—but the lower things less so. For the sphere of fire is rotated in a circle, and an uncoordinated motion occurs in the air, which ends in the water as rising and falling. Indeed, I dispute all these things more as a philosopher investigating the true cause of that effect than to contradict the astrologers, since nothing here is added to or taken away from astrological matters, whether we refer these rising and falling tides to the cycles of other stars or to the moon. 

<margin>Favorinus</margin> 
Since this itself is (as <term>Favorinus</term> <note>A 2nd-century philosopher and polymath.</note> most truly said) more a fallacy of the astrologers: who, when they have seen that certain earthly things situated among men are moved by the sense and guidance of celestial things—such as that the ocean, like a companion of the moon, ages and grows young along with it—from this, clearly, they prepared an argument for themselves to persuade us to believe that all human affairs, both small and great, are guided and ruled by the stars and constellations. For even if they were from the moon, which we ourselves also freely and easily believe: what does that prove for the astrologers, or against us? Nor, as some 

<column-break/>

think, is it understood from this that the stars act not only by motion and light but also by hidden influences: since the moon, positioned below the bottom of the earth, might move the waters, yet its light could not then reach the waters. <term>Roger Bacon</term> <note>original: "Rogerius Baccon"; 13th-century philosopher and scientist.</note> in a letter to Pope Clement V <note>Pico writes "Clement V," but Bacon’s famous scientific correspondence was with Clement IV (1265–1268).</note> wanted to give a cause from light in this manner. 

<margin>Opinion of Roger Bacon.</margin> 
For when, he says, the moon rises over the sea of some region, the lunar rays fall at oblique angles; therefore they are weaker, and thus they stir up vapors from the depths of the sea which they cannot consume (the vapors, I say), flooding the waters with billowing noises, so that they are extended from their channels, just as fire placed under a pot of soup evaporates the water, and the lips of the vessel foam over. Therefore, while that attraction of boiling vapors lasts, it flows water from its seats. But when the moon nears its peak, the rays become the same because they are straighter, and therefore stronger; specifically, as much as it ascends further: which at last become strong to the point that they are equal to dissolving the vapors. Therefore, says Roger, the rising tide becomes slower as the moon approaches the south (the zenith); and when it declines, the waters also immediately decline, just as in that same pot: when the heat has become stronger and the vapors are consumed, the liquid subsides and retreats into the bottom of the vessel. After this, he raises the proposed question as to how, moving from the west to the bottom of the earth, the moon retains its power of moving. For then the waters rise equally as the moon hastens from its rising to the summit. Yet, as he confesses, no power of rays can penetrate the middle of the earth. 

<margin>Explanation of the dissolution.</margin> 
This, therefore, he himself thus explains <note>original: "dissoluit," playing on the concept of solving a problem and the dissolution of vapors.</note>. The highest heaven, he says, whether the eighth or the ninth, is necessarily dense, since it terminates sight, which is only terminated by something dense. Accordingly, it is necessary for the lunar rays extended there to be reflected to the opposite part; therefore, if the moon is moved from the west to the bottom of the earth, its power will flourish in another opposite quarter of the heaven and acts with a reflected ray, as it did when proceeding from the east to the summit. This is Bacon's discovery, in which he is so pleased with himself that he boasts he was the first to have given a reason for the rising and falling tides in opposite quarters, although there are as many shameful errors in his words as 

<margin>Refutation of Bacon. First, Second, and Third reasons.</margin> 
there are words. First, he contradicts—I would not say experience—but certainly Abu Ma'shar, whose interpreter he makes himself; who teaches that the vigor of the rising tide is when the moon has reached the summit of heaven, and it is not released until it begins to descend. On the contrary, Bacon thinks that the closer the moon approaches the summit, the more the tide is released because the vapors are dissolved by the hotter light. Nor did he see that the light of the moon is never so intensified that it can consume sea exhalations—never mind stir up as many as are needed to set the tides in motion. But if he should obstinately deny this, he must admit, even against his will, that for several days around the new moon there would be no tides in the ocean; since at that time, there is either no lunar light or it is so thin that none could be said, however impudently, to be equal to creating so many vapors in the sea and also 

<margin>Fourth reason.</margin> 
dissolving them. Finally, why are the rays of the descending moon not stronger than those of the ascending one? Why does the descending moon recall the waters, while the ascending moon pours them out? And why are those slightly declining from the summit not weaker than those just then rising? Why does it cause a recession there and a rising here?

He argues that even if the Moon influences the tides, this physical relationship does not validate the spiritual or predictive claims of astrologers.</summary>

# AGAINST THE ASTROLOGERS, BOOK III.

<margin>Fifth argument.</margin>
Indeed, just as he himself perceives, the vigor of the rays suppresses any approach with more intense heat, since the weakness of those same rays increases it. Finally, who would believe that in the reflected rays of the moon running beneath the earth, there is such great power that they can even consume the stirred-up vapors? Or, if they cannot do that, what is the cause of the moon's retreat when it is brought below the horizon at the foundation of Bacon's <note>original: "Bocconis"; referring to Roger Bacon (c. 1214–1292), the English philosopher and friar who wrote extensively on optics and tides.</note> argument? Why, when the moon sets, do the waters recede, while those which approach from the east rise? Therefore, let Bacon keep these inventions of his for himself. If such an effect pertains to the moon at all, let us refer it to its motion, which the movement of the ocean imitates by a silent consensus of nature; thus, it rises with the rising moon and falls with the falling moon.
<margin>Opinion of Thomas.</margin>
The one who says this seems to favor the view of Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274) in his work *De occultis operibus naturae* (On the Hidden Operations of Nature).</note> in his book on the hidden works of nature. Nor should we think that these tides are an increase or decrease of the waters themselves. Rather, the very words "access" [flow] and "recess" [ebb] express not an increase or decrease in volume, but the rising of the sea as it extends itself and its contraction as it descends. Moreover, we say these things regarding the tides of the night and the day. For if there are any seas (as has been written by some) that are always in a state of rising while the light of the moon increases—that is, from the conjunction <note>The "coitus" or meeting of the sun and moon; the New Moon.</note> to the full moon—and again in recession when it is diminished from the full moon until the conjunction, those seas do not follow the motion of the moon in its sphere, but rather the motion (so to speak) of the light in the moon as it increases and decreases in equal measure. This variation can also somewhat vary the daily tide. But the observations handed down on this matter do not agree. For both the Egyptians and those who sail to the West used to say that the flow is strengthened from the noon of the first day of the lunar month until the eleventh day, and weakened from the eleventh to the eighteenth and part of the following day. Then, from the eighteenth to the twenty-seventh, it is intensified again, and subsequently slackened until the start of the month. Whenever the flow is greater, the ebb is smaller, and vice versa by an exchanged ratio. There are some who say this is truly observed in the waters of rivers flowing from springs, which on the aforementioned days are extended, and on others are contracted at their heads. Regarding the sea, however, it is reported differently by the Easterners, who do not even agree among themselves. For there are those who report that in the first and last <term>decan</term> <note>A ten-day period or a ten-degree segment of the zodiac.</note> of the month, the flow is diminished and increases in the middle; this seems to have the rationale that they grow with fuller light and decrease with its failure. Others say it is not a perpetual state over several days—that the flows either increase or fail—but that it happens on one or another day, whether when they are intensified or when they are slackened.
<margin>Abu Ma'shar.</margin>
Abu Ma'shar <note>Ja'far ibn Muhammad Abu Ma'shar al-Balkhi (787–886), a leading Persian astrologer and astronomer.</note> makes four shifts in this manner: the first after the conjunction when the moon begins to move away until it is half-full; then he says the flow is diminished in that proportion by which the moon departs from the sun, so that when it comes to the <term>quadrangle</term> <note>A 90-degree angle or "square" aspect in astrology.</note> they are weakest. The second shift is from then until the full moon, during which time they are gradually intensified so that the tide reaches its peak at the full moon. The third is from the full moon until it is halved again, with the flow decreasing along with the light. The fourth is from then until the conjunction. At that time, however, he claims the flows become increasingly more violent, so that they are most violent when the
<margin>Against Abu Ma'shar.</margin>
moon is in conjunction. But this can have no logical basis, since this difference of light (as far as the proposal is concerned) involves much or little light, increasing and decreasing. If the flow occurs with much or increasing light, the fourth observation is false; if with little or decreasing light, the second is false; if with much but decreasing light, the third is false; if with little but increasing light, the first is false. Truly, whichever of these traditions is accepted, it is clear that we are not forced to devise any new power in the moon besides motion and light as to why it moves the sea, since all the reported

<column-break/>

diversities in the flows and ebbs of the sea can most evidently have their cause either from the diversity of the motion of the rising or declining star, or from the losses and increases of its light.
