### Chapter XVI. The opinion of Galen, who refers critical days to the moon, is refuted.

<margin>The twofold influence of the moon: one from the sun, the other from the signs of the oblique circle.</margin>
I certainly do not doubt that <term>crismos</term> <note>From the Greek *krisis* (judgment/turning point). Pico refers to medical "crises" or "critical days" where a disease was thought to reach a turning point.</note>—which you might call "judgment days" in Latin—are referred to the moon as falsely as they are superstitiously, which must be declared more broadly. Galen, the author of this opinion among physicians, mentions a twofold lunar influence in the third book of *On Critical Days*. One of these comes from the sun, from which the moon receives light; the other from the signs of the <term>oblique circle</term> <note>The Zodiac or Ecliptic.</note> through which the moon passes each month by its own motion. Then, following the opinion of the astrologers as if it were tested and proven by experience, he posits that great commotions are excited by the moon in opposite places and quadrangles. He contends this is true both in its relationship to the sun and also toward the zodiacal signs, with no regard for the sun. Toward the sun, because when the moon is halved (which happens in places nearly quadrangular to the conjunction) and again when it is filled (which is in opposite places), it changes the state of the air and the weather. Toward the signs, it works in this manner: whatever begins while the moon is positioned, for example, in Taurus, a change always occurs when the moon subsequently reaches Leo, Scorpio, and Aquarius, which are locations at a right angle [square] or opposite to Taurus. He confirms this
<margin>Note on the Egyptian opinion.</margin>
by the authority of the Egyptians, who assert that if happy stars <note>Benefic planets like Jupiter or Venus.</note> are seated in someone's birth chart in Aries (used as an example), the person born will be well off whenever the moon passes through either Taurus, the square signs, or the opposite signs; conversely, they will be poorly off if the stars are unhappy. From this, Galen thinks the cause of "critical days" becomes most evident. For the seventh and fourteenth days are especially critical. The moon arrives on the seventh day at the fourth sign from the one it held at the beginning of the illness, and on the fourteenth day at the opposite sign, since it completes its restoration <note>Its sidereal orbit.</note> in twenty-seven days and nearly a third part of a day. Therefore, since the moon excites commotions in these places—namely the quadrangular and opposite ones—it causes the tumult of the disease to be excited on these days (the seventh and fourteenth), on which those places are reached. This results in a prosperous outcome toward health, or a deadly one toward death. However, because Galen thought the twentieth day was critical and not the twenty-first (which
<margin>Archigenes.</margin>
Archigenes <note>Archigenes of Apamea (1st/2nd century AD), a prominent physician of the Eclectic school.</note> believed), he labored to provide a reason for how the twentieth day was also a "seventh" day.
And first, he showed this by a proof that was neither absurd nor difficult. For the course of the moon is completed in twenty-seven days with eight hours added. If you divide this into four weeks, any given week will consist of six days and twenty-one hours. Therefore, three weeks will have twenty days and twelve hours. For this reason, the twenty-first day—which is the third weekly marker in the lunar course—will pertain partly to the twentieth natural day and partly to the twenty-first. For twelve hours of it will terminate the twentieth day, and the remaining hours will begin the twenty-first. And thus, a critical commotion will occur on the twentieth day when the moon reaches the second quadrangle, specifically in the third week. And again, it will not escape the same logic if it is deferred to the twenty-first natural day, which usually happens in acute illnesses; just as in longer-lasting ones, the cycle occurs in equal turns...

# DISPUTATIONS

...running through those odd numbers. After Galen himself had said this, which <margin>Pietro d'Abano</margin> <note>original: "Apponensis"; referring to Pietro d'Abano (c. 1250–1316), a famous physician and astrologer who sought to reconcile Greek medicine with Arabic astrology.</note> later reported as his own discovery, Galen devised a new explanation. Through this, he sought to distinguish himself from <term>Archigenes</term> <note>Archigenes of Apamea, a prominent Greek physician of the 1st–2nd century AD.</note> regarding the "cretic" <note>original: "cretico"; from "crisis," referring to the critical turning points in a disease.</note> influence pertaining to each day. His goal was to prove that the entire twentieth day was a critical day, while the twenty-first was not. Thus, he devised a period of time in which the moon returns to its conjunction with the sun: twenty-nine days and twelve hours, which is generally considered a month by the common people. Let us subtract the days during which the moon does not appear, being overwhelmed by the rays of the sun, since it then has no power to change lower things. There will remain twenty-six days and twelve hours, for it is hidden for roughly three days. Let us then add these days of the glowing moon's duration to the days in which it traverses the <term>signs of the zodiac</term>, which he calculates as twenty-four days and twenty hours. The sum will be fifty-three days and twenty hours, the half of which is twenty-six days and twenty-two hours.

Galen considered this span of time to be a not unreasonable measure for the placement of critical days. He saw that this was half of the days in which the moon both permeates the zodiac and is illuminated by the sun, as if it then encompassed the powers of lunar influence twice within itself: both that which comes from the signs and that which comes from the sun, both of which were likely to cause commotion in diseases. <margin>What may be called the "Medicinal Month."</margin> This number was later called the "medicinal month" by those following Galen’s authority. This is distinct from the month of twenty-nine days based on conjunction, the month of twenty-six days and twelve hours based on visible appearance, or the month of twenty-seven and one-third days based on the moon's transit through the zodiac. 

However, through this invention, Galen achieved what he wanted against Archigenes. For if the whole month consists of 26 days and 22 hours, the individual <term>weeks</term> <note>original: "ebdomadae"; from the Greek word for a seven-day period.</note> of this month will each consist of six days, seventeen hours, and a half-hour. In fact, half of the month would be thirteen days and eleven hours. Therefore, from the first hour of the seventh natural day until the seventeenth, they will also pertain to the seventh day of the medicinal month. Because of this, they will be critical days. The rest of the day will belong to the eighth medicinal day. The fourteenth natural day will have only the first eleven hours from the end of the fourteenth medicinal day, whose preceding thirteen hours will be counted with the thirteenth natural day. Truly, as for the third medicinal week, since any week is six days and seventeen and a half hours, it is clear that it terminates on the twentieth natural day, with only four and a half hours overflowing into the twenty-first. And so, what Galen primarily desired was achieved, and for the sake of which this whole invention was fabricated: that the twentieth day should be considered critical far more than the twenty-first, following the logic of the weeks. Galen took up this labor for himself for no purpose. For it was not necessary; the twentieth day was sufficiently defended as critical by the delay of the transit through the zodiac—especially since he himself does not deny that the twenty-first is also critical, indeed frequently so in acute diseases. Nor have we reported these things to act as a judge between Archigenes and Galen, going beyond our purpose, but rather so that—when we have demonstrated that critical days cannot be referred to the moon, whether we consider its power received from the sun or from the signs—no one should think we have not fully answered the matter simply because Galen introduced a kind of "mixed influence" which might specifically stir up critical days. For Galen perhaps did not do this; or if he did, he could not have done it reason-

<column-break/>

<margin>First reason.</margin> ably. For if we say with him that the moon stirs up commotions when it is in <term>quadrate</term> <note>A 90-degree astrological aspect considered tense or challenging.</note> or opposite signs to some primordial position, and again when it is illuminated by the sun’s rays in quadrangles and oppositions: we cannot expect these events from the Moon except at those times in which it behaves in one of those ways, if the outcome is expected from those causes. For if it produces such effects at both times according to the habit and constellation of each time, are we to believe that the power of both constellations is mixed at a time when neither of those constellations is found? This is supported by no other argument than that the time is half the sum of both times counted together. We do not know this; we are not even consistent. 

Therefore, if Galen thinks this stirring power exists in the weeks of this "medicinal month" and its midpoint—but not in the weeks or the midpoint of the month in which the moon is either illuminated by the sun or surveys the signs of the zodiac—he brings upon us a problem. This devised "month" cannot be reduced to any astrological influences; that is, neither to quadrate or opposite signs, nor to the quadrangular or opposite configurations of the moon with the sun. For to claim that the virtue of these things is preserved and fused together at a time when they do not exist is, as I said, too absurd and fictitious. Nor could those who wished to defend Galen and simultaneously adapt critical days to the moon's cycles stand by their promises. Now they defend this point, now that; never both at once. For if it is asked why the fourteenth day is critical, they will retreat to the month of the moon's cycle and transit, because on that day the moon arrives at the opposite signs. This reasoning does not fit the medicinal month's calculation. Indeed, its second week falls back into the 13th natural day, and only 11 hours remain from it pertaining to the fourteenth. For as we said, any week of Galen's month is six days and seventeen and a half hours; therefore, the thirteenth day should be called "more critical" than the fourteenth, since the former has thirteen critical hours and the latter only eleven. Here, then, having abandoned the power of the "mixture" and the artificial month, they will flee to the spaces of the zodiac traversed. 

<margin>Second reason.</margin> On the other hand, to make the twentieth day critical, they use Galen’s month, not the transit month. Furthermore, if someone should fall ill the day before the Moon's conjunction and have a critical seventh day, how will that result from the influence of power received from the sun as well as from the signs? For during the greatest part of those days, as the Moon was not seen, it would not have affected us with solar power, according to Galen himself. It is necessary, therefore, that here too they turn back to the signs, whose influence alone, by the power of the quadrate, would have made that seventh day critical for him. <margin>Third reason.</margin> I set aside the fact that Galen's month is entirely artificial and not struck from the mint of nature. For it is forged as if the Moon were always hidden by the sun for three days. But it is sometimes seen in the morning before the sun rises, and in the evening of that same day with a crescent face; both experience indicates this and <term>Alfraganus</term> <margin>Alfraganus.</margin> <note>Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Kathir al-Farghani, a 9th-century Persian astronomer whose works were a primary source of astronomical knowledge in Medieval Europe.</note> testifies to it. Then, he determines the span of lunar motion as if it always moved at the same pace, and not sometimes faster and sometimes slower, as is demonstrated in astronomical calculations. Therefore, let Galen keep his month for himself. Lest he thrust it upon us too importunately, let us grant to those he prefers that there are critical days, while rejecting those of Archigenes; yet I firmly assert that they are governed by no cycles of the moon. Whether we estimate the power as received from the sun or from the signs, for that which is from the sun is solid and natural (as 

<meta>catchword: we have declared</meta>

He asserts that medical crises are not actually governed by lunar positions or solar illumination.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s critique of the astrological theory of "critical days" in medicine. He is specifically refuting the idea that the internal cycle of a disease is dictated by the Moon's movement through the zodiac signs or its phases relative to the sun.</meta>

# AGAINST THE ASTROLOGERS, BOOK III.

...as we have declared) but critical days cannot belong to the Moon unless diseases always attacked us at the new moon. Otherwise, the half-moon would not correspond to the seventh day, nor the full moon to the fourteenth—the points at which the <term>square and opposite configurations</term> <note>These are astrological "aspects" or angles: a square is 90 degrees and an opposition is 180 degrees, both considered stressful or "challenging" alignments.</note> of the sun stir up the <term>humors</term> <note>The four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—which ancient medicine believed governed health.</note>. This leaves the theory regarding the zodiac signs. This theory is actually nothing at all, as the following points will show; and even if it were something, it would in no way relate to critical days in the way they claim.

<margin>
Refutation of the argument.
</margin>

For if they argue from experience, a "commotion" occurs on the seventh day. Again, one occurs on the fourteenth, and on these days the Moon is in square or opposite signs. Therefore, they claim these commotions follow from this change of signs.

We, on the contrary, argue thus: a commotion occurs on the seventh day and again on the fourteenth, yet on these days the Moon is frequently neither in square nor opposite positions. Therefore, that commotion is not stirred up by this change of signs. Which side relies on truer assumptions is a matter of doubt to no one who is not entirely ignorant of lunar motions. For when the Moon travels through the lower parts of its <term>epicycle</term> <note>In the Ptolemaic system, an epicycle was a small circle on which a planet moved, while that circle itself moved along a larger circle.</note>, it is carried with great speed and reaches the square signs on the sixth day, and sometimes the opposite signs on the thirteenth. But when it is carried more slowly through the upper parts, it does not reach the square position until the eighth or ninth day.

<margin>
The opinion is falsely ascribed to Galen, Hippocrates, Avicenna, Celsus, and Asclepiades. Galen is mocked by Avicenna and Maimonides. Thus also by Averroes, it is argued he did not speak naturally regarding the "fourth figure."
</margin>

Now, if they respond that for this very reason those other days sometimes become "critical," they might have a point if the humors were stirred on the eighth or ninth day specifically when the lunar course is slow, or on the sixth when it is fast, or on the seventh when it is somewhere in the middle. But observation does not teach this. Instead, it frequently happens in practice that even when the Moon is slower, the seventh day gives the "judgment" (and sometimes the sixth), while when the Moon is faster, the commotions are delayed until the eighth or ninth. Noting this, many physicians have denied that this order preserved by nature in diseases depends on lunar cycles. Nor were those who taught otherwise led by anything other than a love for astrological matters or the authority of Galen. We shall soon say how much weight his authority actually carries in this matter.

Furthermore, some of the "moderns" <note>original: "Neotericis"; referring to recent medieval or Renaissance commentators.</note> falsely report that <term>Avicenna</term> <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the influential Persian polymath and physician.</note> and <term>Hippocrates</term> <note>The famous Greek "Father of Medicine" (c. 460–370 BC).</note> held this opinion. For Hippocrates never said a word about this.

Rather, Hippocrates attributed this order to the power of numbers, which nature is accustomed to observing gladly—a point noted by <term>Celsus</term> and <term>Asclepiades</term> <note>Aulus Cornelius Celsus (c. 25 BC–50 AD) and Asclepiades of Bithynia (124–40 BC), major figures in Roman medicine.</note>. Avicenna, when he recalled the opinion attributing these things to the Moon, said, "There is much ambiguity in these sayings." Then he rejected the question as one whose investigation did not concern the physician—indeed, it would rather be an impediment to him.

Therefore, let Galen's authority prevail among us where it is decided which days are critical and in what manner the patient should be treated when they appear or are foreseen. For this is the duty of the physician, in which profession we—along with the consensus of the learned—approve and admire the truly divine Galen as preeminent.

But when the *cause* of those days is investigated—since this is the work of a deeper philosophy—Galen's opinion should be treated neither as a definitive judgment nor even as a testimony of great weight. For as <term>Moses the Egyptian</term> <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), the great Jewish philosopher and physician.</note> and Avicenna (great men and great supporters of Galen in medicine) report, he clung more to the branches of the other sciences than to their roots.

Indeed, his "fourth figure" of syllogisms is laughed at by logicians, and in philosophy he is so often terrified and fails to perceive the strongest reasons that many find a lack of philosophical judgment in him.

He cannot understand how the soul, being surviving and immortal, can cease from its work when the brain is not yet dissolved; he says he was exhausted by this question from a certain Platonic philosopher—as if, when a ship is broken,

<column-break/>

the surviving sailor does not cease from his sailing. Nor does he understand what is demonstrated by philosophers: that universal notions of things are grasped only by our intellect and not by the capacity of brute animals. This is not the time to recount his hesitation in the knowledge of time. For we have only sampled these points about Galen’s philosophy here to confirm the judgment of Maimonides and Avicenna regarding him, and simultaneously to warn anyone against letting Galen's authority impose upon them the acceptance of superstition. For in this very astrology of which we treat, the calculation of lunar motion shows him to be poorly skilled.

Nor does <term>Pietro d'Abano</term> <note>original: "Apponensis."</note> defend him otherwise than by saying that in Galen's age, the ratio of celestial motions had not yet been clearly explored.

Let that faith in him regarding medicine be as great as possible; but regarding other doctrines, let us remember to act more cautiously with the man. We must examine more diligently what he has handed down: whether it harmonizes with experience, with reason, or with the opinions of others. And indeed, we have proved that what he produced concerning critical days agrees very little with the facts themselves; and it will become clear to those who look that these ideas do not even have the color of reason. For what reason is there that the Moon, when it reaches the fourth or seventh sign from the place it occupied when the disease struck, should stir up an agitation in the humors?

Galen refuses to give a reason, but instead holds up the authority of the Egyptians. We will remind him of his own sixth book *On Simple Medicines*, in which he marks the Egyptians as delirious. Why their authority falters among us will become known in the final two books.

For now, let us say this: the changes of bodies according to these lunar courses could not have been faithfully observed by the Egyptians, to whom the lunar courses were not faithfully known.

<margin>
Hipparchus. The reasoning of the moderns.
</margin>

For <term>Hipparchus</term> on the island of Rhodes was the first to observe them with greater certainty, although he did not reach the truth. <term>Ptolemy</term> later came closer to it, though he did not satisfy the desires of later astronomers. The "moderns" have devised a reasoning that not only fails to harmonize with the truth, but is inconsistent with the position they defend and with Galen's own following words.

It is of this sort: square or opposite signs have contrary qualities. Square signs are discordant in either both qualities or at least the active ones. For instance, Aries differs from Cancer in both qualities, since Aries is a hot and dry sign, while Cancer is moist and cold. Taurus differs from Leo not in both qualities (for they agree in dryness), but it disagrees in the active quality, Taurus being cold and Leo being hot. Likewise, opposite signs always disagree in at least one quality. Then they say it is a common refrain among astrologers that square and diametrical radiations are contrary and fighting. Given these premises, they conclude: when the Moon reaches locations hostile to those it held when the disease struck, it follows that a fight arises between the disease and nature.

<margin>
Opposition to the reasoning.
</margin>

But we, accepting their premises, shall address them thus: you think the cause for why the Moon makes critical days is this: if it was in Taurus, for example, when the disease occupied the body's nature, it must be that when it comes to a contrary place, it creates a contrary effect. It will therefore cause nature to rise up against the disease; hence the fight and the "judgment" as the victory leans toward one side or the other. Now, it will be in a contrary place when it reaches Leo or Scorpio. It will reach Leo on the 7th day, and Scorpio on the 14th. During these days, then, it sounds the battle-trumpet for disease and nature. But why will it not do the same on the 3rd day, when it reaches Gemini, which differs from Taurus more than Leo does? Why not on the 12th or 13th day when it reaches Libra, with which Taurus again agrees less than...

<summary>Pico refutes the astrological basis for medical "critical days," arguing that the Moon's speed is too inconsistent to match clinical observations and that the qualities of zodiac signs do not logically explain disease crises.</summary>

### DISPUTATIONS

# BOOK III

...with Scorpio: Why does not the fifteenth degree entering Sagittarius differ from Taurus in the same way that Scorpio differs from Leo? I know what they will answer: that there is no connection of <term>aspect</term> <note>An "aspect" is a specific geometric angle between celestial bodies or signs, believed by astrologers to transmit influence.</note> between these signs. But I did not wish to lead them elsewhere for any other reason than this: not to object that this logic of aspects is non-existent (which we shall do in the sixth book), but to show that even if it were something, it still does not serve the question at hand. For that logic is clearly observed between two planets, whose rays they believe cannot come together to fulfill an effect—whether they agree or disagree—unless they are shaped by specific intervals from one another: the <term>sextile</term> <note>original: "exagono"; a 60-degree angle.</note>, the <term>trine</term> <note>original: "trigono"; a 120-degree angle.</note>, the <term>square</term> <note>original: "quadrangulari"; a 90-degree angle.</note>, and the <term>opposition</term> <note>original: "diametro"; a 180-degree angle.</note>. But here, we are not configuring the Moon with other planets; we are only observing that it is carried to a place contrary to the one it previously occupied. Although astrologers will deny that a star placed in Gemini is linked by an aspect to a star placed in Taurus, they will not deny that this location is contrary to the other. Now, if the Moon produces an effect contrary to the first because it has arrived at a place of contrary quality, why is it that if it excited a disease while in a cold and dry sign, it does not excite nature against the disease when placed in hot and moist signs? Whether that sign is counted as the sixth, or the second, or by any other number you prefer? This is altogether ridiculous, and not something that could be said by a man who looks toward the truth rather than merely defending a pre-conceived position. But if they contend that the power consists in these aspects, they must consequently also concede that the Moon, when it reaches the <term>square</term> signs, will strengthen the disease; for just as square signs disagree, so trine signs agree. Why then, if trine signs stir nature by a quality contrary to the sign of the sickness, will those same trine signs not excite the disease by a quality that is in harmony with it? Since the Moon is carried to these on roughly the eleventh day, the eleventh day ought to be judged harmful; yet it is numbered by physicians among the healthy <term>critical days</term> <note>original: "creticas"; days when a disease was expected to take a turn for better or worse.</note>. Finally, it will be most manifest to anyone considering the matter that the observations of critical days handed down by physicians cannot have their logic from the motion of the Moon. For they say that bad disturbances occur on these days: the sixth, eighth, twelfth, tenth, sixteenth, and eighteenth. Let them give a reason for these from the Moon if they can! For it would be more fitting for the sixth and eighth to frequently be good days, as we were saying, since the Moon arrives at the squares through these days. But why is the tenth or twelfth bad at all, on which the Moon is not in places linked by any aspect with the sign of the sickness? Why are the seventeenth and thirtieth numbered among the healthy ones? And what logic is there that, according to the Moon, every fourth day has power before the twentieth, but after the twentieth, it is every seventh day and not every fourth? Such as the twenty-seventh, the thirty-fourth, and the forty-first—which, when passed, the twentieth critical days are found, such as the sixtieth and eightieth, along with the hundred and twentieth. Why then the circuit of months and years? Just as all these things do not have a cause from the Moon, so they cannot have one from the Sun, nor from any other constellation. For on those fixed days, the constellations are not found to be fixed or similar or in harmony, but they vary in a marvelous way. Nor do they keep any order that could respond to this order in the disturbances of diseases, which is for the most part preserved by nature. Thus, one may marvel at the one who adds that the malice of the sixth day (which Galen

<margin>
See the shameful error of Peter of Abano, the Conciliator.
</margin>

compares to a tyrant, just as he says the seventh can be reduced to a king) can be attributed to the Moon arriving more swiftly at the square. He is too forgetful of himself, having said that illnesses become healthy on the seventh day

<column-break/>

on account of the nature of the square, which would presumably oppose the sign of the disease.

<margin>
The process of nature through sevens. Avicenna, Galen.
</margin>

How then does he now also give a reason for the malice of the sixth day from the square? It is clear, therefore, that all these things have other causes. But it deceived those to whom it seemed to agree on the seventh and fourteenth days—though even there, as we have said, it does not truly agree. But we see this progression by sevens observed elsewhere in the works of nature, where there is no suspicion of the motion of the Moon or the Sun. For instance, in the very periods of diseases: just as they are acute on the seventh day, so are long-lasting ones; as <term>Avicenna</term> <note>A famous Persian physician and philosopher (c. 980–1037).</note> writes, they are often settled in the seventh month, the seventh year, the fourteenth, or the twenty-first. I do not, however, approve of those who superstitiously observe numbers here; rather, I say that the courses of nature are mostly fulfilled in things not because of constellations appearing at these times (for they are not found), but because of a hidden property and condition of those things which usually happen this way. For we see it so arranged by nature—as <term>Galen</term> <note>A Greek physician (129–c. 216 AD) whose work dominated Western medicine for centuries.</note> himself writes—that acute diseases are moved through odd days, while the slower and longer-lasting ones through even days. Trace these to the Moon, trace them to the Sun and stars if you can! Why then should we refer the disturbance on the seventh day in acute diseases to the square signs through which the Moon is carried? Especially since that is not a permanent rule. Moreover, some of the younger physicians, against the opinion of Galen and others who flee to the Moon, say this: If someone falls ill with the Moon placed in Aries, they ought to have the eighth day as a critical day, because the Moon then arrives at the square of Cancer. He would answer that it ought to happen that way if one considers the lunar motion, but that the disturbance happens on the seventh because of the nature of the disease which, when it is acute, moves through odd days until the fourteenth day. Lastly, what has been truly observed by medicine concerning critical days is not only not confirmed by the art of astrology, but is weakened by it. This is the greatest argument that the affections of bodies do not depend on the causes which the astrologers introduce. For if there were no status or order in these days—but now this day were critical, now that one, and again

<margin>
Galen: If critical days were caused by the heavens, they would not be immutable.
</margin>

among the critical ones another was found harmful at one time and healthy at another—no wonder would rouse us to investigate the cause, since the changeable diversity of matter alone would satisfy us. But since certain days are not always, but yet for the most part, critical—and some for the most part lead to life, some to death—this order seems to require a cause that is certain and rarely changeable. Galen concludes from this that the cause is in the heavenly bodies, which are bodies moving in a fixed and stable order, because they can produce a fixed and stable effect. To me, on the contrary, it seems clear from this that a cause of this kind cannot even be from the heavens; because if it were from there, different days would be critical at different times, and the order that appears in them would not be preserved. For if the Moon were joined to Mars or the Sun, it would stir a disturbance of influx; if to Saturn, it would delay it. Furthermore, the conjunction of the luminaries immediately preceding the day of the disease would have to be inspected; and then if the ruler of that place where they joined held the ascendant, the disturbance would happen quickly; late, if it held the setting. Moreover, stars proceeding in direct motion or placed in movable signs would sound the trumpet of war for the disease and nature more swiftly; conversely, those moving backward or located in fixed signs would do so more slowly. These things would not happen similarly for every sick person, even if they shared the same constellations; but differently for different people according to the condition of their own birth. I pass over the "figure" whose angles <term>Ptolemy</term> <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century author of the *Tetrabiblos*, the foundational text of Western astrology.</note> commands us to observe, whether they are derived from fortunate or unfortunate rays, so that we may prophesy concerning the disease—something which certain very ignorant people believe pertains to critical days,

<summary>Pico argues that the medical concept of "critical days" in an illness is a natural biological cycle (often following patterns of seven days) rather than a result of the Moon's movement through zodiac signs or its geometric aspects. He uses contradictions in astrological theory and the authority of Galen and Avicenna to show that celestial alignments do not consistently match observed medical realities.</summary>

...pertain. If physicians received all these rules from astrologers, they would not generally find what the medical art has determined; instead, different people would have different "critical days." Nor would it be a fixed rule that the sixth day kills with "tyrannical cruelty" while the seventh liberates with "royal kindness." <note>Pico is referencing a traditional medical proverb about the timing of a disease's turning point.</note> Instead, the seventh day might be counted as harmful under bad constellations, and the sixth as healthy under favorable ones. If such a thing occasionally happens, it should not be said to come from the heavens—where they seek a cause for something that occurs with regularity and almost always—but should rather be attributed to the physical matter and some particular quality of the suffering person.

### Chapter XVII. The cycles of the humors are not to be attributed to the movements of the stars.

<margin>First method.</margin> NOR should anyone believe that the cycles of the <term>humors</term> <note>In ancient medicine, the four humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—were believed to control health and temperament.</note> in fevers are to be referred to the movements of the stars. For example, some say <term>black bile</term> <note>Associated with melancholy.</note> ceases for two days and is stirred up on the fourth because it is under the influence of Saturn, whose movement is slower than others. But by what logic do astrologers think <term>blood</term>, which they link to Jupiter, putrefies continuously without pause? Jupiter is not the fastest of all; rather, if we measure the time it takes to return to its starting point, it is the slowest of all after Saturn. Why, likewise, is the movement of <term>red bile</term> <note>Also called choler; associated with anger and heat.</note> ascribed to Mars? Its cycle is a little slower than that of black bile, for it ceases for six fewer hours: while the former is quiet for forty-eight hours, the latter is quiet for thirty-six. Yet the star of Mars is much faster than Saturn. Furthermore, it is a decree of the astrologers that the works of slow-moving stars are more long-lasting the slower they are. Therefore, if the movement of <term>phlegm</term> <note>original: "pituita"; the cold, moist humor.</note> returns more quickly than that of red bile—for the former returns after six hours and the latter after thirty-six—because the movement of the Moon exciting the phlegm is faster than the movement of Mars exciting the choler, why does the agitation of choler not last longer than that of phlegm? The former lasts only twelve hours, while the latter lasts eighteen. If we follow the precepts of the astrologers, the works of Mars should be longer-lasting than those of the Moon, since the Moon is faster than Mars. But if, again, we wish to refer all these cycles to the Moon alone—as if it dominated all humors—the astrological reasoning upon which they lean will falter no less. For they say that because phlegm has a kinship with the Moon and water, it imitates the movement of the waters, which flow and ebb with a middle delay between them, but a small one, such as

<margin>Second [method].</margin> necessarily falls between direct movements. Thus, phlegm leaves only six full hours. But this could have suited blood more, in which a continuous tide is found, just as in water, where the small delay separating the flow from the ebb does not well correspond to an interval of six hours—in which the entire flow or ebb itself is driven. But in blood there could be a greater similarity, for the supporters of this opinion do not deny that its movement is interrupted in perceptible delays.

<margin>Pico’s opinion</margin> But let us pursue the rest. They say black bile, because it differs most from the nature of water, moves in a way contrary to phlegm: namely, ceasing for the most part up to the entirety of two days. But it seems to me that water has more in common with earth than with fire, whether you consider location, quality, or movement—and no other condition can outweigh these. Therefore, the judgment regarding humors linked to the elements will be the same: that the movement of red bile ought to be more different from the movement of phlegm than the movement of black bile is. Indeed, none of the illustrious and ancient physicians referred the circuit of fevers to these causes.

<margin>On Peter of Abano.</margin> <term>Pietro d'Abano</term> <note>original: "Petrus Apponensis" (1250–1316); an Italian physician and astrologer often criticized by Pico.</note> was the first to attempt this—a man born to collect many things rather than to digest them. Indeed, the more unlearned a person is, the more they are accustomed to admire him intensely where he trifles the most.

<column-break/>

### Chapter XVIII. The misfortune of an eight-month birth is not to be ascribed to Saturn.

WHILE we are treating these matters, it comes to mind that astrologers are accustomed to ascribe the misfortune of an eight-month birth to Saturn. This must be discussed here, but briefly, lest it seem that by not refuting it, we are compelled—even against our will—to concede that the rays of the most hostile stars are not perceived. Just as I willingly grant that, I do not willingly grant that we are "seized" by them so as to be held fast. Indeed, I feel that things glide down from heaven in such a way that I do not think anything harmful proceeds from it. The sum of the matter is this: astrologers are deceived if they believe that those born in the eighth month do not live because a single planet presides over each month of gestation in the womb, and therefore, because Saturn rules the first month, he also rules the eighth—a planet that is cold and dry, qualities contrary to life. For first, those traditional "shifts" of the planets' dominance have no basis in reason (as will be said elsewhere in its proper place); and that an eight-month birth does not survive has an entirely different reason.

<margin>The cause (as provided by astronomers) of the eight-month birth, from Hippocrates.</margin> There are those who think the fetus tries to exit in the seventh month and is injured in the attempt; if it then comes out in the eighth month—as it has not yet been restored to its health—it is not usually viable. But I agree rather with <term>Hippocrates</term> <note>The famous Greek "Father of Medicine."</note>, who in the treatise he wrote on the eight-month birth says the cause why it usually does not live is that in that month, gestation in the womb is difficult. For then pregnant women find themselves in a more serious state, and the womb suffers certain heavy and inconvenient things. If they give birth then, oppressed by the double labor of both the birth and the illness, they become extremely weak; and of necessity, the fetus itself, having been made more feeble, rarely lives long. This opinion is attested by the fact that if any women are found to be more vigorous and strong, they are accustomed to give birth to survivors even in the eighth month—such as those <term>Avicenna</term> <note>The famous Persian physician (Ibn Sina).</note> writes are found in Spain, and <term>Aristotle</term> in Egypt. I have subjoined the Greek words of Hippocrates on this matter—lest it be believed we fabricated it since this book is not commonly held: *On the Nature of the Eight-Month Child* <note>original: "ΠΕΡΙ ΟΚΤΑ ΜΗΝΟΥ ΦΥΣΙ"</note> and what follows.
<margin>Avicenna, Aristotle</margin>

### Chapter XIX. Why sailors, physicians, and farmers predict the truth more often than astrologers.

THERE were roughly three objections in that second line of reasoning of the astrologers. The first was from the changes of lower things based on the cycles of the Moon; from this, they gathered that both the action of other stars upon us and the changes of other things should be conjectured from them. The second was from the testimony of the good arts of medicine, agriculture, and navigation, which use astrological observations in their own resources. We have rejected both of these by turning their own weapons against them, showing (as I was saying a moment ago) that from the works of the Sun and Moon, and from the observations of those arts, it is gathered that what they deny is true rather than what they affirm. There remains the third point, which was taken from the predictions of those same craftsmen and the common people themselves. It is as if we were being too unfair by granting no foreknowledge of the future to astrologers—who are experts in the whole heaven—while even crude teachers and anyone from the common crowd sometimes speaks to it. Thus, we see many things about rains, illnesses, cattle, and the price of grain predicted daily by the common people with reliable results. Why, then, they ask, cannot those who know the celestial causes more exploratively predict those things more correctly, along with other secrets? This is what we must now dissolve, or rather, as is our custom, reject.

<summary>Pico refutes the astrological links between bodily humors and planets and rejects the idea that Saturn causes the deaths of eight-month-old infants, favoring biological explanations from Hippocrates. He argues that practical experience in medicine and farming is more reliable than astrological theory.</summary>

### DISPUTATIONS OF PICO AGAINST ASTROLOGERS

...against them, which we shall easily and briefly explain. For if they predict true things without taking any account of the rules of astrology, who would not say that their conjecture is flimsy? Those things they omit or are ignorant of are not necessary, but superfluous; they are not more "secret," but more false; they are not doctrines, but fictions. But <margin>Ptolemy.</margin> astrologers are more often wrong. It follows, therefore, that astrologers know less about astrology than those who are not astrologers at all. For it cannot be denied that what physicians say about the sick, <gloss>that</gloss> farmers about the harvest, sailors about storms, and shepherds about their flocks, corresponds more closely to reality than the predictions made about these things by astrologers. The reason is immediately obvious: since the astrologer looks at signs that are not signs, and speculates on causes that are not causes, he is therefore deceived. For <margin>From these two points, it is concluded that the astrologers’ reasons are not reasons but fables and imaginations.</margin> he looks at the celestial arrangement, which is only a universal cause and does not produce variety in lower things except according to the condition of the matter and the lower efficient causes. Yet, it is not even that celestial arrangement he looks at, but a fictional arrangement in the heavens made by him through the most vain and fabricated rules; it is established not by nature, but by the whim of astrologers. Indeed, as we shall demonstrate, that Father of men and God of gods did not create in the heavens the <term>images</term> <note>Referring to the constellations envisioned as creatures or figures.</note>, <term>signs</term>, parts, <term>antiscia</term> <note>Points on the zodiac that are equidistant from the tropics.</note>, <term>dodecatemoria</term> <note>The division of each zodiac sign into twelve smaller parts.</note>, <term>houses</term>, and other such things they use. Rather, it is the astrologer, the deceiver of men and slanderer of the heavens, who has lied about these things being in the sky. Therefore, it is no wonder if this art can foresee no future event by any certain reason. But the craftsmen we mentioned—doctors and sailors—rely on true, natural, proper, and proximate causes and indicators. For this reason, they rarely miss the truth; through true premonitions of the future, they give credit to their methods and practice their arts with success and good fortune. Read the books of <term>prognostics</term> by **Hippocrates** <note>The famous Greek physician often called the "Father of Medicine."</note>; you will never find him seeking the future state of a patient among the stars. He knew that these things are better sought from <term>urine</term> <note>original: "lotio"</note> than from a star, and are known more certainly from the pulse of the veins than from the motion of the spheres. <margin>Whence this kind of art is based on observations rather than fictions—for (as Aristotle says in the first book of the Metaphysics) experience creates art, while inexperience creates chance.</margin> Skilled pilots do not foresee storms by Jupiter, Saturn, Venus, Mars, or Mercury, but from the clouds, the winds, and the overall condition of the air. Their skillful discipline is confirmed everywhere by experience: from the breath of the slightest breeze or a barely visible cloudlet, they understand an imminent storm, of which no omen or sign was yet visible to the eyes of others. Not only do they understand that a storm is coming, but from which direction it will be stirred up, how it may be avoided, and how it can be overcome—matters about which all the wisdom of the astrologers will be utterly blind. So too shepherds and farmers, and often even the unlearned common folk, foresee the state of the weather—not from the stars, but from the disposition of the air itself and from the <term>impressions</term> <note>Atmospheric phenomena like halos or meteors.</note> that occur on high. For this reason, they are rarely wrong, judging the air from the air, just as doctors judge the sick person from the sick person—that is, from their own proper principles. They do not do what the astrologers do, who judge from remote and universal things, or rather—what is worse—from fictional, imaginary, and fabulous ones. Therefore, let no one think that farming will be better, medicine more effective, or navigation safer if these tasks are handled by men inquiring after and observing astrological signs. That would rather be the decay and destruction of those arts, as they would be called away from certain rules to uncertain ones, from true ones to fabrications; and the solidity and truth of every discovery already proven by experience would be undermined by the mixing in of false dogmas. Even if the reasons by which the vanity of astrology is made known were not yet

<column-break/>

understood, one could be sufficiently persuaded by this: what we said at the beginning of the work, that the greatest masters of those arts, who were especially successful in practicing them, not only did not apply astrological observations to their works but even held them in contempt or refuted them. **Columella** <note>A prominent Roman writer on agriculture (1st century AD).</note>, whom we have cited elsewhere, that most exact writer on rural matters, in the place where he is about to hand down the rules for observing the seasons, mentions his own study written against the astrologers. He says that these things we have treated with "plain common sense" <note>original: "pingui Minerva" – a Latin idiom for rough, practical wisdom.</note> are true, but those things which the most imprudent <term>Chaldeans</term> <note>A common historical term for astrologers.</note> promise are false and have been refuted by us elsewhere. Therefore, when **Ptolemy** reasons thus—that farmers foresee much about the state of the air, and therefore we foresee more and more certain things insofar as we excel them in the knowledge of celestial matters—Columella would deny that this leads to the attainment of truth. This is because this "astrological wisdom" in which they supposedly excel farmers is not wisdom, but folly. That is, they do not know more than farmers; they simply invent more things, using the magnitude of the subjects they lie about as a screen for the mockery of their profession. Without a doubt, if it truly made agriculture, medicine, and navigation better, life would have accepted it in the most honorable place alongside other arts. But its vanity and fallacy, detected so often by the wisest lawmakers, forced them to banish it from cities with the strictest prohibitions, as we declared in the first book—lest it infect both good minds and good arts with its hidden poisons. How much it is surpassed in the foreknowledge of the future by these common arts we mentioned can be seen from this: among sailors, farmers, and shepherds, there is a wonderful agreement in their prognostics, but among astrologers, there is none at all. <margin>A saying made.</margin> So much so that **Abu Ma'shar** <note>An influential Persian astrologer (787–886 AD), often called Albumasar in the West.</note> does not hesitate to begin a journey without a <term>traveling hat</term> <note>original: "petastus" – a wide-brimmed hat used for protection against sun and rain.</note> on the very day that Ptolemy predicted a flood of waters.

### Chapter XX. Not everything predicted by astrologers depends on the primary qualities.

-> We now wish to examine what things can depend on the primary qualities, <-
-> since the third argument of the astrologers seemed to demand it. <-
-> Ptolemy proves that whatever happens occurs through the stars in no other <-
way, as his books on <term>judicial astrology</term> <note>original: "apotelesmatici" – referring to the *Tetrabiblos*, Ptolemy's work on the effects of the stars.</note> declare. All astrologers always retreat to this point whenever they defend themselves by saying they speak nothing superstitiously, or nothing that does not proceed through the tracks of nature, or again, nothing for which a manifest reason cannot be given. They almost always flee to these "qualities" whenever they are asked why Jupiter does this, Saturn that, or another planet does something else. In that part of the work where the reasons of the astrological doctrine are refuted, it will be shown that they speak in a way that is consistent neither with themselves nor with the truth. Indeed, many things declare that they prepare this refuge for themselves in vain, beyond what we have already said. <margin>First reason.</margin> Among these, the first point that occurs is that the season of the year in which someone is born will have a greater effect on the lot of their fate than any other diversity of the constellation. This is because the season does more for the intensity or lessening of the **primary qualities** <note>Heat, cold, moisture, and dryness.</note> than any other position of the stars or mixture of rays. Thus, summer days are always hotter than winter ones, even if Saturn is as stiff and sluggish as you like in summer. Conversely, winter days are always colder than summer ones, even when Mars is burning and rages in flames in the middle of heaven. If the difference in fate arises from heat, cold, dryness, and moisture prevailing more or less, it follows that whoever is born in winter is absolutely condemned to an always cold fate...

<summary>Pico argues that practical arts like medicine and farming are more accurate than astrology because they rely on real physical causes. He notes that even the greatest ancient authorities, like Columella and Hippocrates, rejected astrological methods in favor of observation and experience.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s systematic dismantling of astrological theory. Having argued on the previous page that practical observers like sailors and doctors are more accurate than astrologers, he now addresses the "naturalist" defense of astrology—the idea that stars influence us simply by changing the physical temperature and moisture of the air.</meta>

<header>AGAINST THE ASTROLOGERS, BOOK III.</header>

<margin>The second argument.</margin>
...those born in winter would be [vastly different] compared to those born in summer, especially if (as they must necessarily defend) these people follow the quality of the air as affected by the heavens more than they follow the condition of the seed and the immediate matter of their conception. Furthermore, if Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century author of the *Tetrabiblos*, the foundational text of Western astrology.</note> maintains—as he does for the very foundation of his "natural astrology"—that the rays of the planets act through the primary qualities <note>The "primary qualities" are Heat, Cold, Moisture, and Dryness, which were believed to be the building blocks of all physical matter.</note>, then he ought not to prophesy about human character or fortune from any other source than from that constellation which creates and demonstrates the physical habit of the body, since all things would follow from this. Likewise, in universal prophecies, only one thing would need to be inspected: what the future state of the air will be. Once this is inspected, the rest would be revealed, since all other things are arranged according to the measure of heat and cold, or dryness and moisture. But neither others nor Ptolemy himself do this; for they often say things about character in a private birth chart, or things about accidental events, which do not correspond to the temperament of the body by that logic through which all other things are usually referred to it. Nor will the things they pronounce about the seasons of the whole year agree with what they say about character, or about plagues, grain prices, or wars. Therefore, they investigate these things from the most diverse constellations—a fact that will be easily established for anyone reading both astrological books and the prophecies of astrologers. Thus, they should not hold out a "mask" or the "honorable decoration" of a natural method for their superstition, claiming that they only subject human affairs to the stars insofar as the disposition of the air and the body depends on the heavens through the primary qualities. For while Ptolemy said this when entering the art and asserting it as if it were possible, in the process and explanation of his dogmas, he neither observed it, nor could he have observed it while keeping his professional oaths. Otherwise, as I was saying, astrology would consist of very little: one would only have to speak about the disposition of the air and the habit of bodies. Anyone from the crowd could guess the rest for themselves from these few given rules. But there are countless things in the books of Ptolemy and others which can in no way derive their origin from the primary qualities of matter.

### Chapter XXI. Neither the harm caused by the elements nor the damage to our bodies originates from the heavens.

From these things we have just said, that point which was brought forward in the third place above in defense of astrology can easily be rejected. For when it is said that if the changes of the air come from the stars, then so too do plagues, floods, conflagrations, and high grain prices, we deny it. Indeed, it does not follow; rather, he who says this is ignorant of what the "heaven" <note>original: "cœlum"; Pico uses this to mean the celestial sphere and its influence.</note> is. For what else is it in the whole of corporeal nature, other than the very force that contains the whole—just as in any particular body—so that it does not flow away or dissolve? Just as the heart in an animal is the source of that power by which integrity and the order of the mixture are preserved, and the injury of invading members is repelled: let him know, therefore, that whoever attributes the excesses of the elements (from which fires and floods happen, and from which high prices, disease, and plague arise) to the heavens, errs no differently than one who refers the diseases, vices, and ailments of our body to the ruling power of nature itself—whose role is to cure those things, not to cause them; to soothe them, not to excite them. If these things are true, another point is clear: it is one thing for the primary qualities to exist, and another for the withdrawal or detriment of primary qualities to happen because of the heavens—unless we were to deny that the laws and magistrates of a city are one thing, and the crimes committed against them (which do not originate from the work of a good prince) are another. Thus, while the philosopher may grant that whatever is orderly and natural in the elements has the heaven as its author, I do not know by what logic he would

<column-break/>

concede that those things which fail, or which vary from nature’s prescription and laws, also come from there. For it is rather a dogma of the philosophers that the elements remain within their boundaries and content with their own rights—not causing trouble for the world—because of the celestial nature that rules and moderates the fluid and wandering number of corruptible things. <margin>Objection.</margin> But you will say: "When you have conceded to me that some stars cause coldness and others heat, does it not follow that when the cold stars predominate, the cold elements grow strong, and when the hot stars do, the hot elements do? And if this is said, does it not also happen that by a great convergence of cold constellations, the coldness of the waters so overflows that the earth is submerged in floods?" <margin>First response. Second response.</margin> "Conversely, when the hot stars are very powerful, conflagrations occur." The response is easy, and not just one: first, the "dominion" of planets and signs which the astrologers have invented will be demonstrated later to be false. Why, I ask, would any planet so command the heavens as to produce monstrous things—especially evils—in this world? Since the work of the heaven results from the conspiracy <note>In the sense of "breathing together" or harmonious cooperation.</note> of all the lights, that entire superior harmony is always so tempered that, just as all things are consonant within it, so nothing through it is ever dissonant in the lower world. Whenever an unharmonious, harsh, or discordant sound is heard in the lower world, it should not be referred to the touch of the heaven, but to those four strings of the sublunary lyre <note>The "sublunary lyre" refers to the four elements of Earth: Earth, Water, Air, and Fire.</note> which, being made of unordered and impure matter, are sometimes found to be stubborn when touched by the celestial plectrum <note>A tool used to pluck a stringed instrument.</note>, even though it always moves them toward rhythm and concord. <margin>Third response.</margin> After this, it must be more subtly considered that if various stars are set over various elements, they are set there so that the elements themselves might be perfected. Therefore, will not each element be more perfect when touched by its presiding star, the more powerful that star is? If the perfection of the parts does not conflict with the perfection of the whole—indeed, since the parts fall when the whole falls—it will not belong to the perfection of an element for its nature to transgress its order and occupy the others. Rather, it will be perfect when it has deflected nothing from the order and course of nature; from which, certainly, it can deflect as much by exceeding as by failing. Therefore, if Mars presides over fire, since it is not fitting for anything to be done by a star in a subject quality that does not agree with the good order and laws of nature, it would be the duty of the celestial prefecture no less to restrain the tumultuous than to rouse the sluggish. It can therefore be conceded that the four primary qualities are from the heaven, yet their "excesses," transgressions, and tumults are not from the heaven, but from the unordered motions of matter, which does not obey the laws of celestial discipline in every respect. For this reason, I believe that neither Plato in the *Timaeus* nor Aristotle in the <margin>Plato, Aristotle: Damages to bodies do not have causes in the heavens.</margin> *Meteorology* ever referred these temporary tyrannies of the elements to any force of the constellations. It is established, moreover, by these words, that not only the harms of the elements but, by the same logic, the damages to our bodies and to other living creatures do not have their causes in the heavens. That which is the most excellent among all bodies, distinguished by titles of order and beneficence, ought not to effect those things which are rather the works of tumultuous or failing matter. Therefore, what we have said about the elements can likewise be said about the humors <note>In ancient medicine, the four "humors" (fluids) corresponded to the four elements.</note> in our body that correspond to them: if Saturn presides over black bile <note>original: "atra bilis"; associated with melancholy and the element of earth.</note>, Mars over red bile, another over blood, and another over phlegm <note>original: "pituita"</note>, the work of these planets is nothing other than to bridle these qualities and contain them under a harmonious disposition of life. Nor, when Saturn is very powerful, will black bile be stirred up to destroy the rest and cause the whole to fail; rather, it will behave in a more orderly, composed, and better fashion. The same must be said of red bile when [Mars] reigns...

<summary>Pico argues that the heavens act as a harmonizing force rather than a source of chaos. He contends that natural disasters and bodily illnesses result from the "stubbornness" of earthly matter failing to follow celestial order, rather than the stars themselves causing harm.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico’s critique of the "naturalist" defense of astrology. He previously argued that the stars influence the air through physical qualities; here, he refutes the idea that the stars are responsible for death, biological "monsters," or the complex outcomes of human history like war and wealth.</meta>

# DISPUTATIONS

<margin>Death does not come from the heavens.</margin>
Since the rays of the planets and their very nature are beneficial and life-giving, they do not act like a destructive fire. Instead, just as our internal "vegetative" heat <note>The "vegetative soul" was believed to manage basic biological functions like growth and nutrition.</note> works correctly under the guidance of the soul toward a certain end for the safety of the living being, so too those vital lights—the instruments of the mind of the heavens—never act for destruction, but always for the benefit and well-being of the bodies subject to them. Saturn, even if it presides over black bile <note>original: "atram bilem"; one of the four humors, associated with melancholy.</note>, will never influence it in a way that is disordered or non-vivifying. Therefore, it will not stir that bile toward the destruction of the animal, but will moderate it for its preservation. Nor will the humors receive from their stars a power to act more violently when those stars prevail, but rather to act more moderately and more livelily. Death never comes from heaven, but from matter with its own defect, or when some quality has so degenerated that it can no longer sustain the discipline of the presiding star, either wandering immoderately or failing through weakness. Yet our diviners—who make themselves both the interpreters and the patrons and defenders of heaven—attribute to the stars not only diseases caused by an excessive irritation of the primary qualities <note>The "primary qualities" are Heat, Cold, Moisture, and Dryness.</note>, but even vices themselves, such as blindness and deafness. What is even more detestable, they attribute even "monsters" <note>In the Renaissance, a "monster" (*monstrum*) referred to any biological birth defect or abnormality.</note> to them. Nothing more absurd can be said or thought; for what are monsters other than the "sins" of nature? No philosopher has ever referred these to an efficient cause—especially one that does not fail—but all refer them to the matter. Nor has anyone been so delirious as to say that monstrous births occur through a fault of the "informing power" <note>The "virtus informans" is the biological force believed to shape the embryo in the womb.</note>.

<margin>For even the counsel of physicians affirms that monstrous births do not happen except from some impediment of nature.</margin>
For those things done by the hand of God do not fail; rather, they accuse the matter, which—by its position, quantity, or quality—is poorly formed and stubborn or rebellious toward its maker. It is a far greater insanity to condemn the power of heaven than the power of the seed. The power of heaven is so much less likely to err or fail as nature herself is more powerful, and closer to the mistress and the craftswoman <note>Referring to the Divine intelligence guiding nature.</note>, by whom this lower "seminal" power is ruled and formed. It is therefore beyond absurd to think that the motions and configurations of the celestial bodies—even if those configurations change the efficiency of the planets—ever proceed or are composed in any way other than what the natural tenor and ordered course of lower things requires. Otherwise, where would that "order of nature," the transgression of which constitutes a monster, actually reside? Where would it have its origin, if not in heaven? Or how can those people be heard who ascribe something evil, disordered, and unnatural—the origin of which is defect and weakness—to the first causes of nature, which are the best, most ordered, and most powerful of all?

<margin>Indeed, not only astrology but all "mathematics" <note>In this context, "mathematici" refers to astrologers who calculated charts.</note> were always mocked by Averroes.</note>
Therefore, Averroes <note>The 12th-century Andalusian philosopher Ibn Rushd, famous for his commentaries on Aristotle.</note> said truly: anyone who believes that Mars or any other star, however positioned, harms bodies, believes things foreign to all philosophy. But it is certainly true that no profession does more injury to heaven than astrological superstition. Whatever we do outside of reason by the fault of our will, and whatever happens in matter outside of order by the fault of chance or unstable matter—astrology seeks to impute all of it to the stars. It does not think their dignity is safe unless even the most unworthy things are credited to them.

### Chapter XXII. The variety of talents and characters does not depend entirely on the primary qualities.

But even if the stars do not cause the bad affections of bodies, perhaps they at least cause the *diversities* of bodies—not the diseased or vicious or sickly ones, but those within the limits of nature's integrity, differing from one another by the ratio of their temperament. For this seems to follow logically: if the stars are the authors of the four primary qualities, then perhaps from Saturn are born or conceived bodies that are 

<column-break/>

drier and colder; warmer under Mars; more humid under Venus; and so on for the rest. This diversity of temperaments is usually followed by a diversity of talents and affections of the soul—not those by which we are compelled, but those by which we are provoked. But this topic will be treated more extensively later. Let us see, however, whether the dissimilarity of talents and morals can be born from this. For while it is true in some way, it is false in another. For the measure of the prepotent qualities in the body does indeed result in some affections: for example, boiling bile <note>Yellow bile, associated with the "choleric" temperament.</note> makes one prone to anger; phlegm <note>original: "pituita"</note> makes one sluggish; blood makes one more cheerful; and black bile makes one sad. But this is entirely too general and does not always correspond to the evidence, nor does it satisfy the more hidden and specific conditions of one's natural character. I say it does not always correspond to the evidence because one can sometimes find men very similar in bodily temperament, yet very different in their pursuits—not by choice, but by natural propensity. I have seen a beastly cruelty beneath a virginal face; and beneath a grim and scornful countenance, a mild and lovable gentleness. Others, by the grace of their brow and the beauty of their face, show perpetual joy, while inside they seethe with sorrows and are a loathing to themselves. Others, whom you would judge to be plain slaves of Saturn <note>Saturn was associated with gloom and "melancholy."</note>, brighten everything with cheerfulness and wit. Many other powers and "sprouts" can follow from the primary qualities by the general consensus of philosophers: that is, things that are neither the primary four qualities nor their direct "daughters" or appendages. We shall declare shortly that many things prophesied by astrologers regarding the diversity of character cannot be referred to these qualities at all, as they depend on things much further removed than primary qualities.

### Chapter XXIII. Neither wars nor external things depend on primary qualities.

Indeed, it is quite ridiculous to suggest that if the stars can produce cold, heat, and other qualities, they can also produce wars and seditions, or that they can overturn cities and change empires. The reasoning for this position is no less ridiculous. They say that when the bile is stirred in the bodies of kings and princes by a more flaming heat of the soul, they become more greedy to either avenge or inflict injuries. O blessed Italy, flourishing in perpetual peace—if only it were permitted to you to have princes full of phlegm! This great and divine good could be achieved at a small cost: a single small ounce of an <term>electuary</term> <note>A medicinal paste or syrup, often used here to purge "excess" humors like bile.</note> that draws out bile, if distributed properly to those princes who are more warlike, would pacify the whole world for us. Who would refute these things rather than laugh at them? As if this were the only cause of wars! As if they were not caused more by greed than by anger; or by desire, or the opportunity and hope of seizing power. Do not rivalries and hatreds—which astrologers attribute to Saturn rather than Mars—or sometimes the love of justice itself stir up wars and tumults? As if the mind of kings is not more often moved by God than by bile—God sometimes training the good toward virtue, sometimes punishing the wicked through the ministry of other wicked men, whom He holds as executioners for the cleansing of the state, like visible demons. Truly, although the astrologers say ridiculous things here, they seem

<margin>External things.</margin>
at least to be saying *something*. But as for external things, which do not vary at all according to our humors: how will they refer to those four qualities things like exile, honors, riches, poverty, children, a wife, friends, and enemies? Ptolemy says they have an "affinity" with the soul and the body. For example, honor and dignity have affinity with the soul; a wife and riches with the body.

<margin>Ptolemy's question and the solution.</margin>
What is this "affinity," O Ptolemy? That these fortuitous things should follow the condition of the soul or the body? Or is it as you usually say: that if the influence of Mars makes someone bilious, it also brings him wounds and—

<summary>Pico argues that the stars are naturally beneficial and cannot be the cause of death or biological deformities, which instead arise from the defects of matter. He further mocks the astrological claim that complex social events like wars or personal fortunes like wealth and marriage can be reduced to the physical "humors" or temperatures of the body.</summary>
