<meta>This page continues Pico’s argument that the heavens do not directly cause the specific "accidents" of human life, such as social status or the manner of death. He now moves to a deeper philosophical critique of Ptolemy’s logic and the supposed "occult" powers of the stars.</meta>

# AGAINST ASTROLOGY BOOK IV.

...and inflicts a violent death: since the heat of the bile incites one to quarrels and to arms, in the midst of which death itself is a familiar inhabitant. But we are most accustomed to think of this as the work of the stars when a man, living in the gentlest leisure and insulting no one, is nevertheless drawn into dangers, into swords, and into enmities by some fatal force, as if against his will. Likewise, a warlike man—and a "disturber of hornets," <note>A Latin idiom (*crabronum irritator*) meaning someone who stirs up trouble or provokes dangerous people.</note> as they say—might die full of days, unharmed, at home among his own people. Why, then, does the former man, who lacks Martian heat, succumb to the sword (which is the work of Mars), while the latter dies in peace, even though he is almost hotter than Mars himself? Furthermore, some things of this sort might display a bit of a connection with what is within us, such as the condition of the body; but by what reasoning could stars influence the differences of body and soul regarding a <margin>Refutation</margin> wife, riches, honors, and other things of this kind? Truly, one is not even allowed to dream of such a thing. For this reason, <margin>Ptolemy</margin> Ptolemy himself, in the first chapter of his book *Apotelesmaton* <note>Known today as the *Tetrabiblos*, Ptolemy's foundational work on astrology.</note>—where he builds his reasoning regarding the efficacy of the stars—concludes nothing other than that the diversity of the body, and of the soul insofar as it is attached to the body, proceeds from the stars. Regarding fortuitous things <note>External events or "accidents," such as wealth or luck, that are not part of one's physical makeup.</note>, he adds nothing in that place; for he writes: "Anyone will be able to say what the state of the ambient air surrounding us will be at any given time." He also understands the specific habit and temperament of any man based on the argument drawn from the state of the air when he was being formed. Therefore, he will be able to say what kind of body and what kind of soul one might obtain. Then, he foresees how one will fare in the progress of time: namely, that a future disposition of the air, being suitable to a body of such a temperament, might lead to its safety, or if discordant, might provide the occasion for disease and sickness. These are Ptolemy's words, in which, as is apparent, there is no mention of external things. Soon after, however, in the next chapter—where he repeats his points so as not to be [redundant] in what follows—he adds external things as if he had proven them as well, perhaps thinking the reader could be deceived if the logic from which those points were supposedly deduced and proven had already slipped their mind. Therefore, even if we grant to Ptolemy that the primary affections of matter (moisture, dryness, cold, and heat) are changed according to the condition and state of the stars, we are by no means going to concede that the various accidents of men are caused by the stars.

<margin>Chapter 24. That occult powers do not exist in the heavens through which they might produce occult properties in lower things: but only heat and life-giving light.</margin>

### Chapter 24. That occult powers do not exist in the heavens through which they might produce occult properties in lower things: but only heat and life-giving light.

<margin>Refutation</margin> It remains to be discussed whether, besides the power of producing these [four] qualities, there are more hidden and eminent powers in the stars through which they can do many things that they cannot do through those primary qualities. For example: a magnet attracts iron by its own property; the peony <note>In ancient and medieval medicine, the peony root was famously used to treat the "falling sickness" (epilepsy).</note> helps those with the falling sickness; and in other things, there are other powers, both nobler and more effective than the primary affections of matter themselves. The fourth argument contended this, asserting that stars could in no way lack such virtues if (as is said by almost all philosophers) earthly things obtain such gifts by the benefit of the stars—and since they are the noblest of bodies, they must necessarily be endowed with the noblest gifts. But neither the nobility of these bodies, nor the fact that hidden and wonderful powers of earthly bodies are said to come from them, is an argument by which we are forced to believe that such virtues—that is, some power in the celestial nature beyond the life-giving heat we mentioned—exist. For, to address the last point first, they do not correctly understand what is

<column-break/>

said when it is claimed that lower bodies obtain powers from heaven by which they do things that cannot be achieved through the four primary qualities. Those gifts and powers flow from the innermost principles of the bodies themselves: that is, from their forms or, if you prefer, their essences. Furthermore, just as heaven gave the form which that motion follows, so it is said to give them such virtues. However, the diversity of these virtues arises from a diversity not of the constellation, but of the mixture <note>The specific "recipe" or proportion of elements in a physical object.</note>, from whose varying proportion one form or another springs forth. And this pertains to the dignity of the heavens themselves: for those things which are divided into a multitude in the lower order are possessed by the superior order in a single and more eminent act. Therefore, if this sublunary, multifaceted, and numerous crowd of perishable bodies—weak, tumultuous, particular, and narrow—is compared to the celestial body—eternal, indefectible, simple, vast, and universal—it is most consistent with reason that whatever strength or perfection is cut up and distributed among the lower things proceeds from that first body. All of them together, however, though so various and manifold, are granted [their powers] by the celestial bodies through their unique gift of light and heat. This gift, communicated more or less through the series of the stars, creates their order among themselves rather than a diversity [of nature]. Nor should we search far for what this gift is, or what this property is; we have said often that it needs no one to demonstrate it, for it demonstrates itself and all other things with it: namely, light, evident to all. Flowing from a moving body and breathing forth heat, it indicates to us a nearly hidden mystery of <margin>The great dignity of light: God is the true light.</margin> divinity: power in motion, wisdom in light, and it figures love in heat. By these, He moves, illuminates, creates, perfects, and preserves all things: that first God, the first of all, I say, just as heaven is the first among all bodies. Beyond this prerogative of a triple efficacy hanging in a certain order from one body, what do we desire in heaven? Or what does it seem to lack for the highest perfection of corporal nature and the mastery of the lower world? To be marked and distinguished by manifold properties is a claim to dignity for an imperfect nature, but it detracts from a perfect one. For it is proper to the perfect nature (as I said) to possess all at once in one thing what lower things possess separately and partially. This privilege would not belong to either if it did not suit both the perpetual motion of the body and the heat-producing light. Aside from this, one would have to search for something else in heaven that could embrace the virtue of any corruptible bodies whatsoever through a most simple act. But if this is fully found in [light and heat], there is no need for the labor of inventing other things. It is found undoubtedly, since without it, no corporal thing can generate, nor can those already generated perform their operations. For take away the heaven and its heat, and the peony will not help the falling, nor will the hyacinth <note>A gemstone (possibly zircon or sapphire) believed in lapidaries to have the power to stop bleeding.</note> stop blood, nor will rhubarb draw out bile. And just as the efficacy of any things that act upon us would cease if they were not stirred by the fuel of our own internal heat, so too would the virtue of those bodies cease, and the very heat of living things, unless it were both cherished separately and joined together by celestial heat. Therefore, the act and perfection of whatever strengths are implanted in earthly things is this very heat-producing light, insofar as it indeed heats—just as the perfection of all color, in turn, is insofar as it shines. And just as neither colors can be seen, nor eyes see, except by the benefit of that light, so neither can the gifts of any bodies whatever consist of themselves, nor can they affect each other, if they are destitute of the help of that motion and heat. Therefore, as it pertains to dignity and beauty...

<summary>Pico argues that celestial influence is limited to universal heat and light, which merely "activate" the specific properties already inherent in earthly things, rather than the stars possessing thousands of unique "occult" powers for every specific human event.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico’s philosophical argument that the heavens act as a unified whole rather than a collection of independent, specialized powers. He uses analogies of light and political order to explain why celestial influence is universal in scope.</meta>

# NINTH DISPUTATION

belongs to the heaven: just as they might shine with a single splendor of the nature of light despite such a great diversity of colors, so too it would have possessed a single power for the manifold number of material virtues—and one more noble than all of them. Just as light precedes all colors, and is their perfect constitution, so light is the perfect constitution of all colors. Nor should we think it detracts from the dignity of the heaven if we deny these particular gifts to the stars, any more than we believe the heaven itself is yellow, or blue, or green, or purple. Just as this is a beautiful and necessary variety in earthly things, so it is neither possible nor becoming in the stars.

### Chapter XXV. Even if a specific and proper power is granted to each star: that power is nevertheless universal.

Now, if someone should contend that, in addition to this property of motion, light, and heat common to all, each star has its own proper influence, I would not greatly resist him, though I could. But I will advise him that these diverse virtues by which they differ among themselves nevertheless agree in this: that they are all celestial virtues. Furthermore, whatever is in the heaven—even if it is something particular when compared to the celestial whole—is nevertheless universal when it is referred to sublunary things <note>The "sublunary" world refers to the Earth and its atmosphere—everything below the orbit of the Moon—which was believed to be the realm of change and decay.</note> (even if it were very narrow). When I say "universal," I wish it to be understood in such a way that it encloses the entire perfection of the corruptible world within itself. Otherwise, it would not be celestial, as has been declared in part already and will soon be explained more broadly. If this is granted, these peculiar gifts of the stars will not help the cause of astrology at all. There will indeed be one property for Jupiter and another for Saturn; but for that reason, Jupiter will not effect anything different among us than Saturn. Therefore, both will be able to do all things equally through their own property. I will not deny that the virtue of Jupiter differs from the virtue of Saturn. But there is no virtue of the lower bodies which the virtue of Jupiter does not contain as much as that of Saturn, and Saturn’s as much as Jupiter’s—generating it, preserving it, and making it effective and perfect. I will say first why this is so, and then how this diversity remains in both property and action alongside this commonality. The nature of the heaven seems unable to be explained more clearly and briefly than if you say that the heaven is the **unity of all bodies**. Surely there is no multitude which does not depend on its own unity; nothing in the universe is <margin>An Analogy.</margin> not derived from one source-like head. And just as in an army any legion is referred to its own prefect, and the whole army to one Commander, so any series of things agreeing among themselves by a common nature has its own principle from which it is led, by which it is nourished, ruled, and contained. Since there are many such principles—a sort of manifold unity—they are finally reduced to the simplest unity of the first principle. Moreover, just as every number is in a way contained in unity, a whole city in a king, and a whole army in a Commander, so in its own principle is found all the virtue and perfection of its own "flock," so to speak. But that which is divided, maimed, unformed, and undetermined in that "gregarious" condition (if I may call it that), thrives in the head within the singular embrace of a certain undetermined unity: pure, effective, and perfect. Thus it is said that nothing of the following body is in the head, and yet again, the whole body is in the head. So it is with the first among all things that exist, the ineffable God: He is none of the things that exist, and yet again He is all things by a certain eminence of His primary nature and all-encompassing power.

<column-break/>

From what principle, therefore, will the corporeal genus depend, rather than from the first body in place and dignity? This, however, is the Heaven. What we were saying is therefore true: the Heaven will be the unity of all bodies, of which all things that belong to other bodies can be denied, and yet all can also be affirmed. They can be denied, certainly, because that which is formed in those lower bodies has various limits—what is discrete, manifold, and imperfect—does not have those characters of form nor that same diversity in the heaven. They can be affirmed because it encloses all those things at once, not by the power of matter, but by the amplitude of its virtue and the sublimity of its original nature. If this is the nature of the heaven, it surely belongs to every celestial body. Nor should it be thought that while the whole Heaven contains the whole perfection of the lower bodies, a part contains only a part. That would be no privilege of the heaven; rather, any part of the heaven is the entire lower world, except for those things which are *in* the world but not *of* the world. This is what the <margin>Note: An allegory on the opinion of the Pythagoreans.</margin> Pythagoreans <note>Followers of the ancient philosopher Pythagoras, known for their mystical and mathematical view of the universe.</note> seem to have signified by a certain allegorical opinion of theirs, by which they were accustomed to affirm that this entire sublunary region is one single "star"; and that in any star of the Heaven, all things exist which are seen in this region of ours. Thus in the Moon, there are the distinctions of the four elements, as well as of valleys and mountains, and also the plants and whatever living things are among us; so too in Venus, in Mercury, and in the rest of the stars. By this figure, they certainly declare nothing else to us than what we wanted to establish: that there is no star in the Heaven which does not encompass all that is below the moon. Otherwise, those stars would not be of a celestial nature, if it were not a true—and proven—supposition that nothing is more truly called "celestial nature" than the unity of corporeal nature. Then, this would be a privilege worthy of the heaven: that with such vastness and an innumerable number of lights, it finally encompasses the goods of the sublunary narrowness. Therefore, in the virtue of any star, there is every virtue of the transitory bodies. Nor do the virtues of different stars differ in that some are in charge of some things and others of others—since they are all in charge of all things. Nor does one that is higher excel a lower one by a broader embrace (that is, of more things), but by a more noble one, containing the same things that the lower one contains, but in a far more unified and eminent way. This same thing <margin>A distinction between ambiguous terms.</margin> can be seen in the separate minds and in the cognition of living beings. For just as every body depends on the heaven, so every power that shares in cognition depends on the intellect. I do not mean "intellect" like ours, which is called reason; but that of the angels, whom the philosophers call "minds" and "intellects." <note>original: "mentes & intellectus". Pico is distinguishing between human discursive reason (ratio) and the immediate, intuitive understanding of angelic beings (intellectus).</note> This intellect is sufficient unto itself for understanding; it looks into nothing below itself, nor into anything below itself does it inspect what it understands. It is not deceived; it does not labor. And that which excels in every kind of cognition—distributed among various powers—it possesses through a single power far more excellently than it is in them. In itself, it beholds the truth and touches it as present with the certainty of sense. It holds within itself that which is in fleeting things through an imaginary faculty; it perceives the causes and species of things, both corporeal and incorporeal, by a rational perspicacity—not that he is rational, or sensual, or imaginary, but through an intellectual property of a more noble condition, gathering what is perfect in them and rejecting what is imperfect. For in us, physical knowledge is one thing, mathematical another, and divine another. For reason follows physical knowledge with sense; mathematical with the "phantasia" <note>The "phantasia" or imagination was seen as the faculty that bridges sensory data and abstract thought.</note>; divine with the mind and intellect. <margin>The order of things is also set down in book 6 of the [Platonic] Theology; noteworthy.</margin> Furthermore, there is no mind, even the most lowly, which does not see every truth in its own light, which we certainly either reach for or pant after through those sciences and arts. Come then, let us compare those things to corporeal ones: these arts and sciences are in us; they are varied in the whole of knowing nature...

<summary>Pico argues that the heavens act as a unified, universal force where every star contains the potential of all earthly things, rather than being limited to specific "astrological" influences. He uses the analogy of light containing all colors and the angelic intellect containing all forms of knowledge to illustrate this celestial unity.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s argument against the specialized powers of planets. He has been arguing that the heavens act as a universal cause, and any diversity in effects on Earth comes from the diversity of the receiving matter, not from the stars having specific "jobs" like departments in a government.</meta>

# AGAINST ASTROLOGERS, BOOK IV.

...various kinds of cognitions, just as in the mass of bodies there are various privileges of different virtues. Every cognition is a certain participation in intellectual light; every bodily virtue is a certain participation in celestial faculty. However, just as the former shines more clearly in reason, so the latter shines more perfectly in the spirit of the heart. These things having been established, come, let us see whether anyone has correctly said that if intellectual rays flow down from those minds <note>original: "mentibus," referring to the celestial intelligences or angels believed to move the spheres</note>, some would be those that make men physicists and not mathematicians; others mathematicians and not theologians; others theologians rather than physicists or mathematicians. Thus, this light would be like these studies, according to the diversity of the nature of the breathing minds, and not from rays proceeding from the same mind according to its own counsel and will. I think he will judge more correctly who believes that there is nothing of this kind: because any one of those minds is able to give generously, and they do not give by their own freedom, in the manner of the stars, but by nature. And if it happens that this gift is received from there rather than that one, it should be said to be referred not to the giver—who is equally liberal in all things—but to the capacity and condition of those receiving.

If the relationship of a star to a corruptible body is as we have described—which pertains to our present purpose—just as the mind is related to a falling cognition, it must likewise be said that any star can give of itself whatever the subject body, whatever it may be, is born to receive. Thus, the diversity of the "hidden breath" <note>original: "afflatus occulti," referring to an invisible influence or inspiration</note> is not caused by the star that breathes, as the astrologer thinks, but by the diversity of the material that is breathed upon. I said "hidden breath" because the action of a star through light and heat can be diverse according to the intensity or relaxation of the ray, as we explained above. But in these hidden properties through which the star propagates itself, and pours out its own (so to speak) species and images: just as that intensity and relaxation do not appear there, so we are not persuaded to 

<margin>The effect of the power of the stars is equal.</margin>

place any diversity of action in them. But, you will say, is the power of Jupiter and that diffused species not certainly different from the power of Saturn? I admit it: but it will not for that reason produce a different thing, since there is no thing in the sublunary world <note>The region below the moon, i.e., the Earth, characterized by change and decay.</note> that either of them cannot produce. What, then, is the diversity of action? Each does the same thing: but one does the same thing in another way—the more noble star in a more noble and eminent way. Although I do not know if we should decide this about those virtues: perhaps an inferior power is more effective in us, not because it is closer in place, but because it is more related in nature. But this inquiry is for another work. Here we only assert that if a property is granted to each star besides light and heat, they can all be defended as universal in such a way that they create no diversity among inferior things by themselves. We could, however, grant them some particular force by contracting the celestial power. And even if we granted this, it would still not help the astrologers at all: as if we were to grant that all stars always work the same in all things, but not all things are granted in all; rather, one thing in another according to this example: Any bodies consist of matter and form. Someone might therefore think that the matter is handled by the three lesser stars: the Moon, Venus, and Mercury. With their duties divided, the Moon would rule the matter itself; it would be disposed toward form by Venus and Mercury—by Venus through quantity, providing order, shape, composition, and due beauty in the parts; by Mercury through quality, while it puts on appropriate affections for receiving form through a shapeable mobility. And the enduring forms are from the superior 

<column-break/>

three stars in this manner: that a thing has form from Saturn; that it is given being and life (in those things that live) from Jupiter; and that it is moved within and excited to action from Mars. Moreover, that any thing diffuses itself, and through that diffusion makes itself known and propagates, will be referred especially to the Sun, whose work seems to be as much to overcome the matter from which it produces something like itself, as are generation and manifestation themselves. What if, therefore, the works of the planets differed—which we even grant of our own accord—not by reason, nor by the faith of experiments, nor compelled by the authority of Plato or Aristotle: even then, all diversity of inferior things would be not from the heaven, but from inferior causes. That celestial cause always acts in the same way in all things, but the work is varied both by the proximate causes and by the disposition of the matter. It is better to place particulars in the stars rather than universal virtues when no reason persuades us of the latter. One might suspect otherwise about certain things without offense, and even with the authority of learned men, I do not deny it: but as the following book will show, if there are such powers, they are not those which the astrologers describe, nor are we affected by them in the way they believe.

### Chapter XXVI. Epilogue of this book, with a rejection of certain astrological arguments, turned back upon those who use them.

We have examined all the natural changes of inferior things which seem to be the works of the heaven; for we shall speak of the fortuitous accidents of men in the solution of the fifth reason. We have found nothing in them that favors the astrologers; rather, the occasion was given to object to many things, so that they might repent of having stirred up this "tracing back" <note>original Greek: "anagoge," the process of tracing earthly effects back to celestial causes</note>. For what else do we gather from this than that sublunary bodies are affected by the rays of the luminaries? But they are affected by no other influence than heat, and by no other heat than the vital kind, and its action is not changed otherwise than by the position of the star, radiating upon us more either from nearby or directly. From these principles, we have given an account of all the effects which they brought forward from the testimony of experience in support of their dogma. In giving this account, astrology was not confirmed by those observations, but was sought to be weakened; and where they either failed or were deceived was everywhere uncovered. Thus it appeared false to believe that the Sun has a drying power, or the Moon a less healthy moistening and cold power; it is falsely imagined that the Moon has a hidden power besides motion and light which draws back and pours out the sea; it is false that Saturn is made the culprit for the harm of an eight-month birth; it is falsely ascribed to the signs, as if they were of diverse virtue and power, whereas the ray of the sun works only according to the variety of position; it is false that critical days and the periods of fevers 

<margin>Astrological argument. Another argument. He retorts the first with Aristotle.</margin>

are referred to the motions of the Moon or other stars. Finally, it was so far from being the case that an argument for the faith of the decrees of astrology could be taken from these changes of the Sun and Moon, that from them it is brought into no small suspicion of falsehood. For they argued thus: if anyone lies under the Moon, numbness seizes his limbs, and at the same time, sea urchins <note>original: "echinni." Aristotle noted that sea urchins grow fuller during the full moon, a common ancient "proof" of lunar influence.</note> are filled; therefore it cools and moistens. Sensation attests that the Sun is scorching, therefore it is dry. We, on the contrary, press them thus: the Moon fills the sea urchins, therefore it is hot. We have demonstrated these things from Aristotle: those sleeping under it are numbed by cold, therefore it is hot. We have declared this by clear reason, namely, in what way it happens. In the full moon it favors conceptions, nourishes bodies, and as it grows it strengthens and enlivens: therefore it is hot. We have proved from...

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s critique of the specific "powers" of planets. He has just finished arguing that the diversity we see on Earth comes from the variety of the material receiving celestial influence, not from the stars having specialized "jobs" or characters. Here, he addresses specific counter-arguments regarding the Sun, the Moon, and the lives of great men like Aristotle.</meta>

->OF THE DISPUTATIONS<-

<margin>
Hippocrates.
Solution to the second argument.
</margin>
According to Hippocrates, this is clear from the evidence itself. Regarding the sun, we likewise appeal to experience, through which it is clear that all the life of the spirit is vitalized by its rays. This, however, does not come from a "power of dryness," <note>Astrologers categorized planets by qualities: the Sun was hot and dry, the Moon cold and moist.</note> but from a health-giving warmth. Nor was it difficult to show how the sun might dry or burn—or even cool—by mere accident. The moon is said to be the cause of cold and moisture, even though both stars, by their own nature, are the authors of nothing but life-giving light and heat.

<margin>
Another argument of the astrologers.
</margin>
They also used to gather evidence this way: we see that our bodies are manifestly changed by the sun and moon; therefore, we should not doubt the influences of the other stars. Yet this very observation about the sun and moon is what makes us doubt the others. We see how the disposition of bodies varies because of them, and this leads us to judge the remaining stars as symbols <note>Signs or indicators rather than active causes.</note> rather than active participants in the work. Indeed, when the light of the moon decreases, the moisture in bodies is always thinned, and it increases whenever the moon grows.

<margin>
The error is uncovered.
</margin>
Why then, if what the astrologers think about the power of the other stars is true—why, I ask, do the "low-lying" planets, <note>The planets below the Sun in the traditional geocentric model: Mercury and Venus.</note> when they are dominant, not make up for the loss of lunar light and increase moisture? If they could, we might occasionally, by the benefit of the stars, enjoy succulent oysters even during the new moon. <note>Ancient naturalists believed shellfish grew and shrank in sync with the moon's phases.</note> Conversely, why does the "dryness" of Saturn and Mars—who usurp the laws of the sky in the astrologers' introductions—never desiccate bodies or protect cut wood from rot when the moon is full? Therefore, these observations actually favor those who take away the power of the planets rather than those who assert it. They favor those who attribute no efficacy to the Zodiac signs over those who attribute much. Otherwise, if the sea is moved by the moon (as they claim and we do not deny), why does the moon move the tides no more when placed in "watery" signs than in "fiery" ones? Why no less in "dry" signs than in "moist" ones? Or why does the moon not produce richer tides when joined to "wet" planets than to "drying" ones? And if their predictions about the twelve places (which they call "houses") were true, how does it harmonize with the fact that as the moon climbs from its rising and approaches the summit, it acts more strongly on the ocean? This means it acts more strongly from the 12th house than from the horoscope <note>term: horoscope; here referring to the "Ascendant" or the 1st house at the eastern horizon.</note>—yet they claim that the power of all stars languishes and becomes weakest in that 12th house. These experiments, therefore, stand with us against them, rather than allowing their opinions to claim victory over the truth. 

<margin>
Favorinus.
</margin>
It is as *Favorinus* <note>A Roman-era skeptic and philosopher.</note> used to say, as we touched upon earlier: because the ocean acts as a companion to the moon, ebbing and flowing with it, they think this is an argument to persuade us that all human affairs, both small and great, are led and ruled as if bound to the stars. But this is a far cry from the truth. As Favorinus used to boast while mocking the astrologers, it is quite inept and absurd to think that just because the ocean tides follow the moon's course, a lawsuit about a water-pipe <note>original: "de aquæ ductu," a reference to mundane civil litigation.</note> before a judge is also governed from heaven as if by a rein.

### Chapter XXVII.

It remains for us to dissolve the final argument, which is sought from human events. Some things in life so exceed our strengths, or happen so far beyond merit and reason, that they seem to prove the force of a fatal decree and celestial power. We shall resolve this for now by showing that all these things have their own causes among us through fate, and nothing appears in any of them that requires the heavens as an author. That is to say, there is nothing in the course of human affairs that should give rise to the suspicion 

<column-break/>

that the deeds of men are ruled and governed by fates. For at the beginning of the next book, no longer merely solving problems but actively arguing, we will teach that these events can in no way be caused by heaven—even though these people think they recognize the force of fate in them. These events fall into two great categories: the great and the small (or the good and the evil). Let us speak first of the "great" things, which pertain either to the mind or to external circumstances. For they have objected to us both the success of *Alexander* [the Great] and the genius and learning of his teacher [Aristotle]. 

<margin>
Why Aristotle was a consummate philosopher.
</margin>
Let us begin then with the things that pertain to the mind. You admire the consummate knowledge of natural things in *Aristotle*; I admire it just as much as you do. You say the cause is heaven and the constellation under which he was born. I do not agree. I do not agree for the common reason that many people born under that same star were not Aristotles, but also because—beyond the heaven, which acts as a "universal cause" under which both the dull Boeotians and the brilliant Athenians sprout alike—the "proximate causes" <note>Immediate, specific causes.</note> are proper and peculiar to Aristotle himself. It is to these that we should refer his singular progress. First, as he himself said, he was allotted a "good soul." This certainly did not come from heaven, since the mind is immortal and incorporeal, as he himself demonstrated and even the astrologers do not deny. Then, he was allotted a body suitable to serve such a soul. This too did not come from heaven (except as a common cause of all life), but from his parents. He *chose* to philosophize: this was the work of those principles we mentioned—the mind and the body—and of his own free will. He progressed in philosophy: this was the fruit of his chosen purpose and his own industry. You might ask why he succeeded more than the many others who philosophized with equal study and labor. The cause was the teaching of his master [Plato] and the "happiness of the age" in which he was brought forth, which was full of the monuments of the ancients, yet not so complete that there was no labor left for him to start or perfect the arts. He accomplished far more than his contemporaries and his disciples because he was allotted not a better *star*, but a better *genius*. And genius is not from a star, since it is incorporeal, but from God—just as the body is from the father, not from heaven. We speak of God with as much more honor than the astrologers as a "universal cause" is more divine and eminent than "particular causes." If the capacity of human genius in *Aristotle* or any other philosopher exceeded the norm, the cause will be something not at all inferior (like a celestial body), but something better—that is, divine. Just as *Socrates*, the greatest of all philosophers in my opinion, attributed his wisdom not to his birth-stars, but to an assisting divinity [a *daemon*]. 

Thus, we give more to heaven than is proper if we derive the divinity of our minds from those material rays, and we give it less than is proper if we attribute the bodily differences of private individuals to it as a specific cause. But we give it altogether less than is becoming when we ascribe our very deformities and the stains of our minds to the stars. This is one of the main reasons people are moved to "flee to the stars": because they see in many men certain discordant appetites that break the laws of humanity. These seem to have an extrinsic cause rather than an intrinsic human one, and because that cause is powerful, they assume it is stellar. 

I would ask them, then, why a pregnant woman sometimes prefers to eat earth and coals rather than every kind of exquisite food. If they find the cause of that monstrous desire in the fetus rather than a star, I will remind them that the cause of the things they wonder at should likewise be sought in the temperament of the body rather than in heaven. I might even suggest the influence of demons among the wicked, but that would lead them away from physical causes. 

<margin>
See the portentous example of lust.
</margin>
Certainly, beyond the habit of the body, I can declare by a very true example how much habit and custom contribute to such portentous affections.

He further argues that human genius, like that of Aristotle, stems from the soul, upbringing, and God, rather than the stars.</summary>

He then transitions into Book IV, beginning his more technical refutation of astrological principles.</meta>

AGAINST THE ASTROLOGERS BOOK III. 205

<columns>
There still lives a man known to me of a monstrous and unheard-of <term>lust (libido)</term><note>Pico uses this case to argue that extreme behavioral deviations are learned through habit, not imprinted by the stars.</note>. For he is never moved to passion unless he is beaten: and yet he contemplates this wickedness in such a way, and so desires the raging blows, that he rebukes the one striking him if she deals with him too gently. He is not fully satisfied in his prayer unless blood breaks out, and the more violent whip leaves the limbs of an innocent man who is yet most guilty. That miserable man demands this service with the greatest pleas from whichever woman he approaches; on the day before, he provides her with a whip hardened for this duty by an infusion of vinegar, and as a suppliant he begs to be flogged by the prostitute. The harder he is struck by her, the more fervently he grows hot, and he hastens toward pleasure and pain with equal step. Here is a man found who finds bodily delights in the midst of torture! Since he is not otherwise a bad man, he recognizes and hates his disease; and because he has been familiar to me for many years now, he freely revealed what he suffered. When I diligently asked him the cause of so unusual a plague, he said: "I grew accustomed to it this way since I was a boy." And when I asked again for the cause of this habit, he said he was raised with the most wicked boys, among whom it had been agreed that they would sell their mutual shame to one another in a shameful exchange, using this license of striking as a kind of price. I have not suppressed this fact, though it may be heavy for noble ears, so that we might recognize by this very evidence how much power <term>habit (consuetudo)</term> has over these affections. We should not immediately accuse heaven because we think they can have no earthly cause. For if an astrologer heard this, he would say that Venus was condemned in the man’s birth-chart, and perhaps whipped by the adverse or otherwise threatening rays of Mars. 

Let us come to external matters, in which Alexander was preeminent:
<margin>Whence such great fortune for Alexander in warlike matters.</margin>
it is asked from where such great and sudden happiness had its origin, if he did not have it from heaven? The answer is easy: from the virtues of Alexander, of which he had many necessary for a commander: fortitude, liberality, endurance of labors, skill in military affairs, excellent learning, and others which it is not necessary to list. It came from the army which he obtained, most practiced under his father Philip, and most warlike by the benefit of their region, and most loving of him because of his liberality and example of virtues. It came from the cowardice of the peoples whom he overcame, whence he was said by his uncle to have "fought with women." It came from Fortune, which rules most of all in warlike matters. 

When I say Fortune, 
<margin>Fortune.</margin>
I do not mean heaven, but that cause which Aristotle mentions in the second book of his *Physics*: that which we commonly call fortune and are accustomed to express with these words: "it turned out so," "it happened so," "it fell out so." It is by this that those who play claim they either throw what they want or what they do not want. This is that blind cause: it made the Caesars, the Syllas, the Augusti, the Alexanders. This cause does not depend on heaven by itself, nor is it the same thing as fate, nor does it detract from divine providence. What it may finally be or not be must be discussed at length in the next book; it is not necessary to say here, where we shall overwhelm the astrologers with no better weapons than those of 
<margin>Thomas.</margin>
Thomas Aquinas, whom these men think favors them most highly. But as for what is principally treated here: I deny that anything on earth becomes or appears so great that it deserves heaven as its author. For the miracles of the soul, as we have said, are greater than heaven; but the miracles of fortune and the body (however great they may be), when compared to heaven, are found to be very small. As Favorinus rightly said:
<margin>Favorinus.</margin>
"Nothing is great on earth except man; nothing is great in man except the mind and the soul." If you ascend to this, 

<column-break/>

you transcend heaven; if you incline toward the body and look up at heaven, you see yourself as a fly, and something less than a fly. But just as in that black line of ants, there are those who excel others in strength or size; there are victories, wars, peaces, duties, labors, poverty, and riches. To us who contemplate them, these things are all tiny and, with no distinction, are nothing. So too these little bodies of ours, our fortunes, our kings, our provinces, wars, treaties, and marriages: if compared to heaven, they are nothing at all. Compared to heaven, the whole earth—of which men divide one tiny portion among themselves with fire and sword—is an indivisible point. Therefore, the magnitude of earthly things is not such that they cannot be the work of anything other than heaven. If those things which are considered worthy among us are not worthy of heaven, how much more unworthy will be those things which are even done unworthily by us? Such as the wicked being raised to dignity, Socrates perishing by the judgment of "star-worshippers," <note>original: "stellicotoris" — Pico likely refers to the judges influenced by superstition or those who "cook" or manipulate the stars.</note> and many enormous things of that kind which we see and suffer daily. 

In these matters, Maternus <note>Julius Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century astrologer.</note> says that fate and the necessity of celestial decree shine forth most of all. I would gladly ask him and other astrologers: why do they so eagerly seek to impute our errors to the stars? Why, when we ourselves sin, do we more willingly accuse heaven than ourselves? As if it were a wonder that we err—we who have been prone to evil from youth—or as if those stars could ever err, which serve the unchangeable order of the best and most just God. They say the innocent are condemned and the wicked are gifted with rewards. By which princes, I ask? Just or unjust? If by the just, then even heaven will not be enough for such a miracle; if by the unjust, what need is there of heaven, when malice—the despiser of heaven—is enough? 
<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
Aristotle asks in his *Problems*: why are the good almost always the poor? Although he brings forward many causes, both true and witty, he brings forward none from heaven; for he knew that the earth, not heaven, germinated thorns and briars. 

But a cautious and prudent man falls into the very danger he most avoided; another escapes a peril to which he had rashly exposed himself quite often. Why should we wonder at this? Since it should be held as no less a miracle that these things *never* happen than if they happen *often*. When these things occur, one must first seek the proximate cause. If this is missing, then the more remote and hidden cause. Since for the rare and fortuitous, no other cause is to be investigated, if we remember well enough what the most wise Aristotle left written for us in the second book of his *Physics* and the sixth of his *Metaphysics*.

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s systematic dismantling of astrological theory. Having previously discussed historical figures, he now addresses the physical arguments involving the Sun, Moon, and the origins of human genius and vice, specifically responding to the "evidence" cited by Hippocrates and Favorinus.</meta>

# DISPUTATIONS

<margin>
Hippocrates.
Solution of the second [argument].
</margin>
According to Hippocrates, this is evident from the facts themselves. Regarding the sun, we likewise appeal to experience, which shows that every spirit of Life is vivified by its rays; this power is not merely "dry," but healthfully warm. Nor was it difficult to declare how the sun might, by accident, either dry things out, burn them, or even make them cold. The moon is said to be the cause of cold and moisture, even though by their very nature both luminaries are authors of life-giving light and heat. Thus the astrologers likewise gathered their evidence: we see that our bodies are manifestly changed by the sun and moon; therefore, we should not doubt the influences of the other stars. But this very fact about the sun and moon is what draws us into doubt: because we perceive the dispositions of bodies are varied by them in such a way that we judge the remaining stars to be "symbolic" rather than active participants in the work. Indeed, when the light of the moon is decreasing, the moisture in bodies is always thinned, and it always increases as the moon waxes.

<margin>
Another reasoning of the astrologers.
</margin>
Why then, if what the astrologers think about the efficiency of other stars is true—why, I ask, do the "lowly" planets, when they dominate during the loss of lunar light, not make up for it by increasing moisture? This would allow us, by the benefit of the stars, to feast on succulent oysters even during a new moon <note>Oysters were traditionally thought to grow or shrink with the phases of the moon; Pico argues that if planets had the power astrologers claim, they could override this lunar cycle</note>. Why, conversely, does the "dryness" of Saturn and the "law of the sky" belonging to Mars—who usurp power according to astrological laws—never desiccate bodies or protect felled timber from rot when the moon is full? Therefore, these observations actually support those who take away the power of the planets rather than those who build it up. Likewise, they support those who attribute no efficacy to the <term>signs (zodiacal constellations)</term> rather than those who attribute much. Otherwise, when the sea is moved by the Moon (as they claim and we do not deny), why does she not move it more when positioned in "watery" signs than in "fiery" ones, or no less in "dry" signs than in "moist" ones? Or why does the moon not produce more abundant tides when joined with "moist" planets than with "drying" ones?

<margin>
The error is uncovered.
</margin>
And how, if what they predict regarding the twelve places—which they call <term>houses</term>—is true, does this harmonize with the facts? For as the moon climbs from the horizon, the closer it approaches the highest point, the more strongly it acts upon the ocean. Thus it acts more strongly from the twelfth "house" than from the <term>horoscope (the ascendant)</term>; yet they affirm that in that place, the power of all the stars languishes and becomes the weakest of all. Therefore, these experiments stand with us against them, rather than allowing them to arrogantly claim evidence against the faith. Unless it is as Favorinus used to say (as we touched upon above): because the ocean, as a companion of the moon, grows old and young along with it, they think this is an argument to persuade us that all human affairs, both small and great, are led and governed as if bound to the stars and constellations.

<margin>
Favorinus.
</margin>
But it is far different, and as the same Favorinus used to boast when mocking the astrologers, it is too inept and absurd: just because the tide of the ocean agrees with the course of the moon, should we think that a legal dispute a man might have with his rivals before a judge regarding a water pipe is also governed from heaven as if by a rein?

### Chapter XXVII.

It remains for us to dissolve the final argument sought from human events: in which some things so far exceed our powers, or happen so far beyond merit and reason, that they seem to build a case for the force of a fatal decree and celestial power. We shall solve this for the present by showing that all these things have their own causes among us, and nothing appears in all of them that requires "Heaven" as an author. That is to say, there is nothing in the course of human affairs from which a suspicion ought to arise

<column-break/>

that the deeds of men are ruled and governed by fates. For at the beginning of the following book, no longer merely solving [problems] but arguing [the case], we will teach primarily that these things—in which those men think they recognize the force of fate—can in no way happen from heaven. Those things are two great categories: namely, the "great" and the "bad." Let us speak first of the "great" things: these pertain either to the mind or to external things. For in this way they threw in our faces both the good fortune of Alexander and the genius and learning of his teacher [Aristotle]. Let us begin, therefore, with those things pertaining to the mind. You admire in Aristotle the consummate knowledge of natural things; I admire it equally with you.

<margin>
Why Aristotle was a consummate philosopher.
</margin>
"The cause is heaven," you say, "and the constellation under which he was born." I do not agree. Not only for the common reason that many born under the same star were not Aristotles, but because, beyond heaven (which acts as a universal cause, just as Boeotians and Attic philosophers sprout equally under it), there are proximate causes proper and peculiar to Aristotle to which we may refer his singular progress. First, as he himself says, a good soul is more powerful; and this soul is certainly not from heaven, since the mind is immortal and incorporeal—as he himself demonstrated and as the astrologers do not deny. Then, a fit body is more powerful to serve such a soul; and this is not from heaven except as a common cause, but from the parents. He *chose* to philosophize: this was the work of those principles we mentioned—that is, of the mind, the body, and his own free will. He progressed in philosophy: this was the fruit of the purpose he embraced and his own industry. "But many others philosophized with equal zeal and labor." The cause was the teaching of his master and the good fortune of the age in which he was produced, which was full of the monuments of the ancients—though not so finished that there was no labor left for beginning and perfecting the good arts. "But he perfected far more than his contemporaries and his disciples." He was allotted not a better star, but a better <term>genius (ingenium)</term>. Nor is genius from a star, since it is incorporeal, but from God, just as the body is from the father, not from heaven. We speak of this with as much honor as the astrologers, insofar as a universal cause is more divine and eminent than particular causes. But if the reach of human genius exceeded even that of Aristotle or another philosopher, the cause will not be something inferior (like all bodies, including celestial ones), but something better—that is, divine. Just as Socrates, in my opinion the greatest of all philosophers, attributed his wisdom not to his natal stars, but to an assisting <term>divine spirit (numen)</term>. Therefore, we give more to heaven than is proper if we derive the divinity of souls from those corporeal rays; and less, if we attribute corporeal differences regarding private matters to it as a particular cause. But we give it altogether less than is becoming when we ascribe our very deformities and the stains of our minds to the stars. This is one of the things by which they were most moved to flee to the stars: that there appear in many men certain discordant appetites, beyond the laws of humanity, which seem to have not an intrinsic human cause but an extrinsic one—and because it is powerful, they think it is celestial. But I would ask them why a pregnant woman eats earth and charcoal more willingly than every kind of exquisite food? And if they find the cause of this monstrous desire to be the fetus and not a star, I will remind them that the cause of the things they marvel at should likewise be sought in the temperature of the body rather than in heaven. I might also mention wicked demons, but that would lead them away from corporeal things.

<margin>
See the [monstrous] excess of lust.
</margin>
Certainly, besides the habit of the body, I can declare by a most true example how much custom contributes to these kinds of portentous affections.

# DISPUTATIONS II

The most they can demand: let us show that even if we grant what we have declared can be rightfully denied, it still follows in no way what they believe. For in this way, the very matter under dispute is explored more particularly through all its parts, and the opponent understands how many things he accepts for free, and how little certainty or how absurd an opinion he defends. Since these things are false for so many reasons, or at least doubtful, and however things may stand, it is impossible for them not to be entirely false. Keeping to this custom, we will first defend against the astrologers that only the rays of the sun and moon have the power to change inferior things. The other stars influence us in no way, 
<margin>Order of the disputation</margin>
either due to the distance of their rays or their weakness. Secondly, if it were granted to them—not because they extort it, but because we allow it—that something flows down from all the stars into us, let us show that this flows from all of them only with a difference in intensity and relaxation; that is, light with life-giving heat. However, cold, moisture, and dryness do not emanate from them. Thirdly, if they did produce the <term>four primary qualities <note>The basic building blocks of matter in ancient science: hot, cold, wet, and dry.</note></term>, it does not follow that the diversity of impressions made in the atmosphere comes from them; or if this were so, it is still not from them that plagues, floods, or conflagrations arise: **much less are external matters, subject to chance and fortune, governed by the stars through the power of those primary four qualities.** Fourthly, if the stars were believed to be the authors of the primary affections—that is, having the power to heat and cool, and to moisten and dry—no other gifts should be attributed to them besides these, through which they might effect many things that cannot be done by the force of those qualities. Finally, whatever virtues and properties the stars might have, they are so universal that there is none that does not embrace the true condition and power of all inferior bodies. Therefore, they act upon all things with all their power, which is the property of a universal cause. However, the diversity of what happens and what occurs takes its entire origin from proximate causes, whether they be free, natural, or fortuitous.
<margin>The weakness of astrologers;</margin>
All of these points we have undertaken to defend with the intention that astrologers might understand that when they think and assert otherwise, they are not speaking of things agreed upon and manifest, but of things which are confirmed neither by any certain reasons, nor by evident experiments, nor by the authority of Plato or Aristotle. Instead, placed in ambiguity, just as they are defended by some, so they are attacked by many. If all of astrology relied on these points and did not place itself upon even more unfaithful foundations, it would not be utterly ruined in my eyes, but merely tottering: that is, it would waver as much as it would fall in my opinion. But even if we give to the astrologers as much as <term>Thomas Aquinas <note>A hugely influential 13th-century theologian who attempted to reconcile Aristotelian philosophy with Christian doctrine.</note></term> and very many theologians and philosophers contend can be given—without reason greatly rebelling—they would still receive far less than is necessary for them to receive if any astrology is to be defended, not only among us but by its own nature, even among the angelic minds themselves. 
<margin>The authority of Thomas. That there is no astrology even if that is conceded.</margin>
For Thomas will give them what can most greatly be given without an open slander of the truth: namely, that the outflows of all the planets reach us with power, and that different stars have different properties, not only for heating, cooling, moistening, and drying, but more hidden ones. From these, the crowd of earthly things might obtain various gifts, so that not every property which humans and the rest of inferior corporal nature possess is held from their own proximate causes, but some even from the celestial ones. Granting all of this precariously to the astrologers, we will show that this art will nevertheless be nonexistent: 

<column-break/>

rather, it prophesies most about those things from the stars which cannot be done or indicated by them, even if all those things we mentioned were to happen. Thus, astrology, which was shaken or brought to destruction in the previous book, will be utterly overturned by the present disputation, with no hope of peace or indulgence remaining.

### Chapter II. Fortuitous events are not from the heavens.

<margin>Prediction of subjection.</margin>
Fortuitous things—those for whose good or bad outcome we call men "fortunate" or "unfortunate"—are primarily those which are thought to be fated and dependent on a celestial decree, and thus they are the greatest part and most powerful subject matter of astrological predictions. For those things which have proximate causes in themselves, such as conditions of the mind and body, do not seem to require a higher and more hidden cause as much as those things which we say happen by chance and luck, since they seem to occur without a proximate cause. Such things include: sailing fortunately or unfortunately; traveling; trading; a man digging the earth and finding treasure; encountering robbers or beasts; pleasing a king; 
<margin>Mortal outcomes.</margin>
escaping danger; obtaining good or bad luck; entering a house that is soon to collapse; and other things of this kind which happen to wretched and truly sick mortals beyond counsel or expectation. It is about these things—which are entirely outside our hand and come upon us from the outside—that we most desire to hear the opinion of the astrologers. Otherwise, one might know the habit of his body from a mirror or a doctor, just as he might know the quality of his mind from himself, if only he has a mind. And what we call "fortuitous" are the things which human curiosity especially seeks through the divining arts. We will prove, therefore, before all else, that these can in no way be foreseen from heaven, using no other reason than that which Thomas Aquinas uses, 
<margin>Where St. Thomas compares his reasoning to prediction,</margin>
especially in that passage where he seems to favor the opinion of the astrologers: that is, in the third book of *Against the Gentiles*, where his reasoning that men are made fortunate and unfortunate by heaven is as follows: The power of a celestial body does not act by intellect or choice, but in the manner that nature acts. It is the property of nature to tend toward one thing. Therefore, an effect which is not "one" cannot be from a natural cause <term>per se <note>Latin: "by itself" or "directly." Pico is distinguishing between a direct result and a side effect.</note></term>. But those things which concur by accident and happen to meet each other are not truly "one," but only "one by accident." Therefore, a coincidence of this kind, which we are accustomed to call "fortuitous," can have no natural cause *per se*, but rather a natural celestial cause, as we were saying. And therefore, there can be no *per se* cause of such fortuitous things. He adds to these an 
<margin>Example of the same.</margin>
example, which simultaneously declares how heaven is not the *per se* cause of such events, but only by accident: someone, he says, is instigated by heaven to dig a grave; it happens to him that there is treasure in the grave. Therefore, while digging the grave, he finds treasure. This was not from heaven so that he would find the treasure, except by accident; for it is by accident that the same place is both a grave and the location of a treasure. 
<margin>Note.</margin>
For to instigate a man to the digging of a grave in which treasure lies hidden, *so that he may find the treasure*, belongs to a rational and intelligent cause, whose property is to relate and order one thing to another. It does not belong to a natural cause, which is carried only toward one thing, as we said, and no one will deny that a celestial ray is such a cause.

### Chapter III. How God is the cause of fortuitous things: how angels are, how heaven is, how we are, how fortune is.

Since mention is made of fortuitous things, it will be worthwhile to explain more deeply what their causes are...

Pico is arguing that what astrologers call "luck" from the stars is actually either a logical coincidence or the result of divine providence and guardian angels, which the stars cannot control.</meta>

### AGAINST THE ASTROLOGERS, BOOK IV.

among philosophers and theologians: for from what we have said so far, it might be estimated that we refer those events only to chance and rashness. Now we must disprove the astrologers who attempt to maintain order and certain causes even in these extraordinary events, as if nothing in nature happens rashly or without a legitimate cause. If any cause must be imagined, the one the astrologers choose seems most prominent: the heavens. Namely <note>original: "s." for "scilicet"</note>, since no power below the heavens is judged so potent—that is, over all things that happen under the sun—nor do they speak of anything above the heavens. This is because many things seem to happen unworthily, beyond merit and reason, which argue for a certain necessity of a physical cause rather than the providence of a chooser. Therefore, to push out these doubts, it will be useful to discuss these matters more broadly. After we have shown that these things cannot be governed by the heavens, we shall reveal from where and how they are governed. We say that "fortuitous" things are those
<margin>From where fortuitous things arise. An example.</margin>
which happen beyond the intention of the actor. For this reason, fortune is spoken of only in human affairs, as they alone are done with counsel and reason. An example, like the one we used above: a farmer proposes to dig the earth, thinking of cultivating the soil, not of treasure. It happens that he finds a treasure; we say this is by chance, and we give no other cause for the finding of the treasure than fortune. Indeed, we do not understand fortune
<margin>Note how fortune is excluded.</margin>
to be a deity, or nature, or any thing that is the cause of such an outcome. Rather, we exclude a cause by saying it was done by fortune, as if we were to say: "It happened by chance, not from any specific cause." For the digging of the earth cannot be called the cause; it does not produce the treasure, insofar as the earth is merely the location. But it happened that the same place was both the earth and the hiding place of the treasure. Therefore, if you ask by what cause it happened that he dug up that treasure, there is none to bring forward. It was not one cause, but a fortuitous meeting of many causes that produced this. Therefore, those were in error who denied that fortune exists in things; an opinion which Aristotle 
<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
shattered in the second book of his *Physics* <note>original: "physicæ auscultationis," the standard title for Aristotle's lectures on nature</note> and the sixth book of his *Metaphysics* <note>original: "primæ philosophiæ," or "First Philosophy," the name Aristotle used for what we call Metaphysics</note>. However, they erred not because they thought that things unforeseen and fortuitous to us could be known and foreseen by higher minds—for nothing is fortune in an absolute and simple sense—but because they thought such events necessarily have a proximate cause in themselves. They did not understand how that which is "one by accident" <term>one by accident <note>A logical term for two unrelated things happening at once, like a baker who also happens to be a singer. There is no single "cause" for him being both; they are two separate paths that happen to coincide in one person.</note></term> requires no single cause in itself. For example, there is no single cause for the same man being both a musician and a warrior. Otherwise, if they were together because of some cause, they would have an order between them derived from that cause. But things that happen to one another rashly—as for a warrior to be a musician, or a musician to be a warrior—it is clear they have no order between them. Therefore, such things have no "per se" acting cause, but only an "accidental" one. Thus the <term>Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle, named after the "covered walkways" where they studied in Athens.</note></term> correctly defend chance and fortune in things, excluding necessity. But some among them err more detestably than those who take away chance by denying it. Namely, they claim these things happen in no other way than by chance—that is, by no counsel of a higher cause, and no providence. This most pestilent error sprouts from the root of impiety, by which it is believed that human affairs are either not known, or if known, not cared for by the powers above. This will be refuted by reasons elsewhere, where there will be a dispute against impious philosophers. Now, let it be rejected as a judged falsehood, by the authority of all theologians and the entire family of philosophers,
<margin>Another detestable error</margin>
and of Aristotle, the prince of the Peripatetics, in his books on ethics, both where he discussed happiness and where he discussed good fortune. For there he asserted most clearly that men, and especially the wise, are a care to the gods; and here he asserted that all sensible things, past

<column-break/>

and future, are known to God, and that we are directed by Him in these matters. He also confirmed this in the book *On the Universe* <note>original: "de mundo," a treatise formerly attributed to Aristotle</note>, a book certainly 
<margin>Commendation of Aristotle's book "On the Universe."</margin>
worthy of Aristotle's wisdom, which he ended with that Platonic sentiment concerning divine justice as if with the finishing touch of an oracle. If, therefore, the gods care for human affairs—for thus we speak, so that we may include the guardian angels and the order of intelligent causes serving the counsel and providence of the true God—if, I say, this is true, no one will doubt that men, incited by them, often do things which are not foreseen or foreknown by the man, 
<margin>In what way they are understood and are causes of fortuitous things.</margin>
but are arranged by those beings with most wise foreknowledge. A most common example is that of servants sent to the same place by a master so that they might meet, yet they are ignorant of the master's will. Their meeting and gathering is unexpected and fortuitous to the servants themselves, but foreseen and prearranged by the master. In this way, a guardian angel can provide for the utility of a poor farmer, inviting him by hidden impulses to dig in that place where the angel knows a treasure is; so that what was fortune for the poor man was nevertheless a plan for the angel. 
<margin>Augustine.</margin>
Regarding this, Aurelius Augustine says in the fifth book of *The City of God*: "We do not say that the causes which are called fortuitous (from which fortune also takes its name) are non-existent, but that they are hidden, and we attribute them either to the will of the true God or of any spirits whatsoever." He said "of any spirits whatsoever" because this can be done by both good and evil angels, although the evil ones cannot do all that the good can, nor is the end of both the same. For the good of men is the common goal for the good spirits, but for the evil, it is harm; yet the divine goodness frustrates their malice while it orders and reduces into good whatever might have been committed by them with an evil will. But more on this elsewhere. Proclus the Platonist, in his commentaries on the *Timaeus*, 
<margin>Definition of fortune assigned by Proclus.</margin>
defined fortune by the same reasoning for which Augustine did: as a "daemonic power" <note>In the Platonic sense, "daemonic" refers to intermediary spirits or divine forces, not evil demons.</note> bringing together causes that were divided from each other. Nor does this differ from the Peripatetic determination which says that fortune is a cause producing something by accident in human choice. One looked to the more remote and hidden cause, the other to the proximate and known one. For Proclus spoke of a "daemonic power" as the Platonists call all minds placed between humans and the higher intellects, 
<margin>Example of the aforementioned points.</margin>
removed from the particular and proximate knowledge of our affairs. Let us declare with examples how these things happen, so that we may understand what the heavens do in them. Lucius was at home, and indeed had nothing to do outside, but the thought of going out settled in his mind anyway. As soon as he stepped out of the house, the house collapsed. You would call him fortunate to have thus avoided the imminent danger. If you ask the cause of this from an impious philosopher, he will answer—as a bad philosopher—that it happened by chance, and no other cause should be sought. If you ask an astrologer, he refers this to some benign reasoning of a "fortunating" planet, by whose help the man was defended from the ruin. However, he is deceived by the reasoning narrated above. Since inciting Lucius to exit so that he would not perish under the ruin is the work of a cause that is intelligent and acting with counsel and reason—and no ray of Jupiter or any other star is such a thing—the most that could come from the heavens was that Lucius's mind was more prone to movement than to rest. Just as this could also come from the habit of the body itself, from which some men are more sedentary and others more prone to walking. Thus, if any constellation were the cause of this good, it would be among those which make us vigorous and better at seeking things (such as they call the "Martian" qualities), not because they are "pious" or "defenders" against evils, as we were previously invoking. For thus it is helpful to order those things in turn by rea...

He uses the example of a man leaving a collapsing house to show that such timing requires an intelligent mind, not a mindless planetary ray.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument that "fortune" or "luck" is not a product of celestial influence. Pico uses the example of a man named Lucius escaping a building collapse to distinguish between a simple physical urge to move (which an astrologer might claim to predict) and the providential timing of that move (which only God knows).</meta>

# NINTH DISPUTATION

...the day <note>original: "dius", likely continuing a sentence about a specific day or time from the previous page</note> cannot provide the exit, namely, and the protection from ruin. Just as for Lucius, who chooses to go out for the sake of a walk, it is a matter of chance that by leaving he escapes the danger of death; so too for a constellation—if we even grant that such a thing exists—that helps him toward movement, it is entirely accidental and fortuitous that it frees him from ruin. It follows that even if an astrologer knows what the heavens are influencing at that time, he knows nothing other than that Lucius will be eager for movement and walking. But that he would flee both the house and the danger at once, neither the horoscope <note>original: "thema"</note> nor any logic allows to be foreknown by him. Therefore, only one cause remains for which this could be foreseen and not a matter of chance: namely, the Divine, plucking at Lucius’s mind from within and instigating him to leave, so that he does not perish under a house soon to fall. For that same divinity understands both that the house will fall and can ordain Lucius's departure for that end. Regarding a physical ray <note>an influence from a star</note>, neither can be said. For this reason, no philosopher has ever defined fortune by a celestial constitution or a birth-chart <note>original: "genituram"</note>, or derived any such thing from the dogma of the astrologers. Instead, they either referred themselves to chance itself and the unexpected clashing of causes, or to intellectual causes reconciling things among themselves by their own counsel, which have escaped the boundaries of our providence.

<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
Thus that great leader of philosophers, Aristotle, distinguishes very widely between what is good fortune and what is bad, and what it is to be fortunate or unfortunate. Not only does he avoid mentioning celestial constellations when deciding these matters, but he does not even do so when inquiring or disputing. This is because he did not think the opinion of the <term>genethliaci</term> <note>casters of birth horoscopes</note> was even worthy of a philosopher’s doubt; rather, like the other delusions of charlatans, it should be numbered among fables and trickery rather than among the controversies of philosophy. Aristotle himself, therefore, in that treatise <note>likely the *Eudemian Ethics*</note>, after a diligent examination of the whole question, defines it thus: when something good happens to us by chance, it usually occurs in two ways. It happens either by us stumbling quite unknowingly into that which produces a good outcome, or by being led toward it by an impulse of the mind, though not by counsel or deliberation. We are so ignorant of the reason for this impulse that we go down with "oar and sail" <note>an idiom meaning with all one's might</note> toward wherever it carries us with the greatest obstinacy. He thinks the first should be referred to chance, and the second to a divine motion, since the mind is inclined by those hidden inner impulses. Those who have experienced this are accustomed to say: "My mind forebodes I know not what," "I cannot will otherwise," or "I am snatched in this direction," while the mind does not agree with other thoughts. And so, although they can give no reason for their own plan, they nevertheless assert that it was so pleasing to them and so fixed in their mind with persistence.

<margin>Aristotle correctly on God and the soul.</margin>
In this passage, the philosopher Aristotle affirms both that all things are known to God (as we said above) and that nothing is higher than God from which our will can be moved—which he asserts is a great argument for immortality.

<margin>The ambiguity of human affairs.</margin>
From all these points it can be gathered that some human affairs happen by chance, some by nature, some by choice, and some by divine counsel. For although nothing happens outside of God’s counsel, we divide them so that we say those things are done "divinely" which human minds, if left to themselves, would not achieve, but which they do when moved by a peculiar impulse of the divinity. This is beyond that general assistance of the Supreme Power which stays with all things, without which nothing can exist or be done, however small. Thus, although it is proper for a human to act by choice, they are nevertheless sometimes ruled by nature when, surrendered to the movements of bodily affections, they do not wait for the judgment of reason. These things are declared by one example: a king declares war on a neighbor. Perhaps the cause is the king’s nature, which is warlike, greedy, and restless; perhaps he is led not so much by passion as by reason or by the right

<column-break/>

of claiming what is his, or of repaying an injury, or for other reasons. Beyond all these, a special counsel of God can intervene, which is always just and always rational, even if its justice or reason is not always open to all. I mean the counsel of God, and of the living being <note>the King</note> taking up war, and the free arming toward victory. In this way He speaks through the prophet Jeremiah: "Behold, I will send and take all the families of the north, and Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon, my servant; and I will bring them against this land, and against its inhabitants, and against all the nations that are round about it." And in Isaiah: "O Assyrian, the rod of my anger and the staff in his hand is my indignation. I will send him against a deceitful nation, and against the people of my wrath I will give him a charge, to take the spoil, and to take the prey, and to tread them down like the mire of the streets. But he will not think so, nor will his heart so intend."
