->Chapter IV. That it should not be referred to the heavens if anything<-
->is done by us that seems to exceed our strength: but<-
->rather to either angels or to God. And<-
->therein much about fate, and how divine providence<-
->does not take away our liberty.<-

<margin>Those condemned to popular applause.</margin>
When something is done by a human that seems to exceed their strength, our mortality is usually shaken by unusual and admirable events. Overcome by the magnitude of the things, we suspect the force of a more powerful cause acting in the person and through the person, which exceeds the human capacity of faculty. And indeed, by this suspicion, those who have only eyes of flesh are snatched toward the heavens, than which they see nothing greater or feel nothing more powerful. They are so possessed by a bad mind that they refer this to a mindless cause devoid of knowledge <note>the stars</note>, for which they believe even the whole counsel of the human mind is not sufficient. But if they respond that those things are indeed disposed and ordained by God, but completed by God through the heavens and the stars, whose power and efficacy is so great, they are proved to speak most absurdly. For these intervening causes between God and us, just as they are lower than God, so they ought to be more sublime than humans. Nor is it fitting for the First Author to dispose through irrational bodies those things which are carried out by reason and counsel, such as our affairs are. Just as He rules and moderates the elemental mass (being inferior) through the celestial mass (which is better), so it is fitting that human affairs be governed not by bodies, but by the mystery of angels, who mediate by nature and dignity between us and God. Therefore, when you descend from God to the earth, descend through the heavens; when you descend from God to man, descend through the angels.

<margin>That angels intervene between God and humans is confirmed by the opinions of many.</margin>
Thus we see the Angel of the Persians, of the Greeks, and of the Hebrew law in the prophets, providing for their own peoples. And in Plato and all the Platonists, we see local gods set over cities, kingdoms, and men. Mention of these was also made by Aristotle, and the elder Isidore, and after Isidore, Clement of Alexandria in the *Stromata* <note>Miscellanies</note> remembered them. Nor should it disturb us that certain things sometimes seem to us to be done unworthily or unjustly, so that we might more willingly run back to a cause acting by natural necessity rather than counsel. For the common slaves of a city would be truly ridiculous if they presumed to judge the counsels of the Prince; much more is our own temerity either ridiculous or rather sacrilegious, claiming for itself the judgment of the first order of divine wisdom. This wisdom looks to the utility not of one man, or one family, or one city, but of the whole world; not for the present age, but for all things equally...

<summary>Pico argues that extraordinary human events and "good luck" are the result of direct divine intervention or guardian angels rather than the stars. He uses the philosophy of Aristotle and biblical examples to show that God uses rational spirits (angels) to guide humans, while the heavens only govern lower, irrational matter.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico’s argument that "fortune" or "fate" is not a product of the stars, but either natural cause, human choice, or Divine Providence. He has just finished using the example of Lucius escaping a collapsing building to show that while stars might influence a general physical urge to walk, they cannot account for the specific, providential timing that saves a life.</meta>

### AGAINST THE ASTROLOGERS, BOOK IV.

Equally throughout the ages, He extends the eye of providence and the ray of His goodness. We little men—no, rather owls and moles, truly asses and oxen, and seventh-rate judges at that—
<margin>A common rebuke.</margin>
shall we call God to account? We, who more often judge not with what little reason we possess, but rather from a sickness of the soul, complain that whatever happens is an injustice simply because we did not wish it to happen. And who would not have persistently cried out that "God is sleeping" when the righteous Joseph was sold by his brothers? <note>Referring to the biblical story in Genesis where Joseph’s brothers sell him into slavery in Egypt.</note> Who would not even say "there is no God" when that same man received prison as the reward for his chastity? But see him soon after as a king in Egypt, or second only to the king. See him redeeming his father and his whole family from famine. See him as a noble prophet; then you will not deny that those earlier events were orchestrated by God, through which he was brought in due order to these later heights. 

Indeed, if you look deeper, you will understand how things were brought from that impious slave-trade to this: that the entire people descending into Egypt, after being long oppressed by the Egyptian kings, were so gloriously asserted into liberty by Moses. The power of God was confirmed by so many portents and manifested by so many oracles: in Pharaoh, in Egypt, and in the people of the Hebrews through the Law. Through so many miracles of divine majesty—now through beneficence, now through justice—these events foreshadowed the ineffable mysteries of the future divine incarnation under Jesus. <note>Pico is using "typology," a common Renaissance method of reading Old Testament events as "figures" or symbols that predict the life of Christ.</note>

Surely even a madman could not be led to suspect that anything in human affairs happens without reason, and therefore believe they are governed not by the best and wisest Being, but—as the Manicheans claim—by an evil demon; or—as the astrologers claim—by the necessity of the stars’ revolution; or—as many poor philosophers claim—by random chance and recklessness. 

Furthermore, whenever you see wars being stirred up, slaughters, the wasting of cities, and the overthrow of kingdoms, you should not imagine the cause to be a "mixture of two rays" or a "light placed between the sun and moon" <note>An eclipse or planetary alignment.</note> as those charlatans do. Rather, consider it the counsel of God, either punishing the wicked or testing the good. This is why one was called the "Scourge of God" <note>Likely Attila the Hun, often called "Flagellum Dei."</note> and another, closer to our own age, said he was not a man, but the "wrath of God and the devastation of the world." <note>Likely referring to Tamerlane (Timur), the Central Asian conqueror.</note>

That wise man in the writings of Herodotus spoke rightly to a Theban who was dining with him.
<margin>Herodotus</margin>
The Theban revealed a future slaughter of his people, which he had foreknown through some kind of premonition. When the Theban urged that this be reported to the commander of the army to discourage an undertaking that would have such an unhappy exit, the wise man replied that what God has ordained to happen is inevitable for man. Therefore, even if he warned the commander, he would not be believed, since God had so decreed it. Consequently, he too followed Mardonius <note>The Persian general at the Battle of Plataea (479 BCE).</note> (for that was the leader’s name), bound by necessity. 

I find it pleasing that he spoke of the necessity of "divine counsel" rather than of the "stars." If anyone calls this "fate," as Augustine says,
<margin>On Fate, Augustine. Fate is accepted in a fourfold meaning. The first mode:</margin>
he will find his meaning is more accurate than his terminology. However, as far as can be gathered from the monuments of the ancients, this word "fate" has been accepted in a fourfold sense:
1. Fate as nature itself.
2. Fate as a series and order of causes producing all things by a necessary connection.
3. Fate as the constitution of the stars at the moment something is born, conceived, or begun.
4. Fate as the execution of divine counsel—a certain and inevitable outcome.

In the first sense,
<margin>Alexander</margin>
it is accepted by Alexander of Aphrodisias <note>A famous Greek commentator on Aristotle (c. 200 CE) who wrote "On Fate."</note> in his book *On Fate* dedicated to the emperors Severus and Antoninus. He allows that fate exists in the sense that nature itself is fate; nature is a principle distinct from our choice. Thus, by "fate," fire heats, water is wet, and the sun illuminates. Furthermore, when someone dies from a breakdown of the body’s balance, they die by fate. If, however, they are thrown from a horse or killed by swords, they do not die by 

<column-break/>

fate. In this way, Virgil says of Dido
<margin>Virgil</margin>
as she prepared a violent death for herself: "But because she perished neither by fate nor by a deserved death." <note>Quoting the *Aeneid*, Book 4. Dido committed suicide, which was viewed as "breaking" her natural lifespan.</note>
<margin>Demosthenes. Aristotle. The Second [mode].</margin>
The astrologers, however, would have rejected that kind of death most of all as being part of fate; so too Demosthenes. In this way, no one would deny that fate exists, just as no one denies nature exists. 

In this sense, Aristotle, in the fifth book of his *Physics*, spoke of "fatal generations"—that is, those which happen according to nature. There is no doubt that when we understand fate this way, many things happen *outside* of fate, just as many things happen outside of nature, either by chance or by our own choice,
<margin>Alexander. Confutation of the second mode.</margin>
or, as Alexander of Aphrodisias says in the same place, by the counsel of the gods. 

Those who introduced the second opinion [determinism] thought that in nature itself, nothing happens that is not necessary, provided one could embrace all causes at once. For those who say many things happen outside of necessity defend this view in both natural and voluntary things. In natural things, because not everything that happens naturally happens by necessity (since a work of nature can be hindered). In voluntary things, because our choice and judgment are free. 

The determinists, on the other hand, insist that in natural things, if something is hindered, it is hindered *necessarily*, because that hindrance comes from a natural cause, which must eventually be traced back to the supreme nature—that is, the heavens. They claim the heavens act necessarily. But they are deceived. For although the hindrance was indeed a natural cause, it was a cause that could itself either not exist or be hindered while it was acting; therefore, that hindrance was "contingent" <note>In philosophy, "contingent" means something that could be otherwise; it is the opposite of "necessary."</note> and not necessary. 

If you press us again with that hindrance, claiming it was a natural cause that was itself necessarily hindered, I respond (if you believe the world is eternal or proceeds infinitely from one contingent cause to another, among which the order is always accidental) that you will never arrive at a single "first necessary cause" from which necessity is forced upon the subsequent things. There is no such cause among natural things, since even the celestial cause is easily obstructed by both matter and the interplay of lower causes. 

If, however, you agree with theological truth regarding the creation of the world, you will arrive—through that persistent regression—at the first contingent institution of things, from which necessity is removed. They attempt to impose necessity on our choices much more irrationally, arguing that the will chooses nothing that has not been pre-judged by reason, and that it is not in our power to will or judge thus. But they rely on false assumptions, as has been declared by others elsewhere and will be by us. For these matters require separate, specialized treatises. 

Nor do these points greatly pertain to the refutation of the astrologers.
<margin>The third mode of fate, to be refuted in this entire work.</margin>
Theirs is that *third* definition of fate, which must be refuted throughout this whole work. It differs from the first opinion because it makes the celestial nature the origin not only of natural things, but also of fortuitous ones (as we see). This view is mistaken about lower causes and is at its worst regarding the heavens. For although the heavens are natural, those "constellations" they invent from the positions of stars—through places, signs, houses, and other such things—are not natural causes, but fictitious ones. The operation of the heavens does not depend on a single initial moment [the birth], nor does it dictate those things which 
<margin>Approval of the fourth acceptance of fate.</margin>
are proper to lower causes, as we have already declared and as the following pages will further clarify. 

There remains the fourth, theological meaning of fate. Like the first, it is more "physical," but both are true: it denotes the series and order of causes depending on Divine Counsel. Under this counsel, our liberty is not endangered. For we are among these causes ourselves; in this "dance of fate," we do not merely suffer [passively], but we act. Whether we call it God’s foreknowledge or His providence...

<summary>Pico distinguishes between different definitions of "Fate," rejecting the astrological view that the stars control human destiny. He argues that while nature and God’s plan exist, they do not destroy human free will or the "contingent" (accidental) nature of worldly events.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s philosophical assault on astrology. Having previously argued that God’s providence works through hidden, non-celestial ways to protect the virtuous, he now addresses the classic theological problem: does God’s foreknowledge of the future (and His planning of it) destroy human free will? He concludes that it does not, before turning his focus to the logical absurdities of birth charts (genitures) that claim to reveal a person's past or the lives of their relatives.</meta>

# NINTH DISPUTATION

<margin>God's foreknowledge and providence do not take away our liberty. The opinions of Damascene and Gregory of Nyssa are explained.</margin>
Whether you consider His mind, which foreknows all things, or His will, which disposes all things according to His own pleasure: let there be no prejudice against our free actions. For if we consider His foresight, why should I not freely do what God foresaw I would do? For if that which He foresaw is to happen, I shall certainly do it freely, because He foresaw that I would do it freely. And because it will be what He willed: and He willed that I should be free, I shall act freely in whatever I do, unless He Himself should take my liberty away from me. Certainly, God not only foreknew our wills, but also pre-ordained them. When <term>Gregory of Nyssa</term> <note>A 4th-century Christian theologian and bishop.</note> and <term>John Damascene</term> <note>An 8th-century monk and polymath.</note> seemed to deny this, they did so only to offer a warning: that while other things are governed by divine will alone, our choices are disposed by that same will in cooperation with our own. This is so not only for the outcomes of our thoughts, but for the thoughts themselves: the very plans, the very purposes. Not only the hearts of kings, as it is written, but the hearts of all men are in the hand of God, who alone governs all things. Now, in those matters which pertain neither to vice nor virtue, He inclines the will wherever He pleases, if the fulfillment of one of His decrees requires it. At other times, He works virtues in us, both beginning the work with us and perfecting what was begun. Sometimes, when men move from virtue toward vice, He changes them back toward justice, or applies the "rod of the pedagogue" <note>A metaphor for divine discipline; a pedagogue was a slave who supervised and disciplined children.</note> out of mercy, or crushes them as if they were struck by lightning for the sake of justice. He always makes all things either good or, certainly, opportunities for good. We have said this much concerning fate, providence, and the governance of human affairs, as these things are useful to know in themselves and necessary for demolishing the vanity of astrology. Thus, when we see something happen that seems either greater or more orderly than can be attributed to human chance, let us understand it not as the force of physical "rays" from the stars, but as the care and power of divine counsel and angelic ministry working alongside human liberty. It is clear from what we have said how future things are both foreseen and, when they are evil, can be avoided by us. For if human affairs happened only by chance, no foreknowledge of the future would be possible. But since they occur by both human and divine counsel, human reason can conjecture something about them, while only those inspired by the Divine can foresee them with absolute certainty. This is confirmed by the predictions and oracles of the prophets; though wise men may be "proximate" to the prophets, it is only by a very long interval. Hence that saying of <term>Euripides</term>: <note>A famous Athenian playwright.</note> 

<margin>Euripides.</margin>
"He who conjectures well, let him be the best diviner." <note>Original Greek/Latin: *Qui bene coniectauerit is vates optimus esto*.</note> Thus, in seeking a happy outcome and avoiding misfortunes, the most important thing is to win God's favor through purity of soul, pious works, and most holy vows. After this, a man should consult his own prudence. For although fortune has much power in many things—or rather, the disposition of the certain divine will has the most power, or indeed everything—nonetheless, the right way of living must have great weight in these matters; otherwise, we would say this gift was bestowed upon us by God in vain. Therefore, that author rightly said that "no divinity is absent if there is prudence," but rather that "it is we who make Fortune a goddess and place her in heaven." <note>Pico is likely referencing Juvenal’s Satires (10.365-66): *Nullum numen habes, si sit prudentia: nos te, nos facimus, Fortuna, deam caeloque locamus*.</note> 
<margin>Plato.</margin>
For this reason, Plato, in his letter to the Syracusans, recalled that Homeric saying: "The gods took away his mind," <note>Referring to *Iliad* 6.234.</note> implying that men themselves rather threw away the mind that had been granted to them. This is confirmed by that sentiment of Euripides, who said that "fortitude is the daughter of the soul." Therefore, by arranging our lives prudently through natural reason, and then by preparing divine benevolence for ourselves through pious religion, let us avoid all superstitious vanity. Otherwise, he who hopes either to foresee the future or to avoid evils through astrological observations will hear <term>Isaiah</term> 
<margin>Isaiah.</margin>
saying to him: 

<column-break/>

"Evil shall come upon you, and you shall not know its dawning; and calamity shall fall upon you, which you will not be able to atone for." <note>Original Latin: *Veniat super te malum et nescies ortum eius...* from Isaiah 47:11. This biblical passage specifically mocks Babylonian astrologers.</note>

***

### Chapter V. Neither the past nor things pertaining to others can be foreseen from any constellation.

If the astrologers have some response regarding matters of chance—though they can have nothing that is either true or even likely—what, I ask, will they answer concerning those things that precede the hour of birth? That is to say, in what way will they think an efficient cause can be later than its own effects? What of those things which are not only prior, but also belong to others, and therefore have their causes not in the constellation of *this* birth, but elsewhere? For instance, when they pronounce judgments on the natures and fortunes of parents, ancestors, and elder brothers based on the hour a son is born. These things are both prior to the constellation and foreign to it; they already have their own order of fate and dependency from their own specific constellations in the past (if, indeed, we were to believe there is such a thing as fate from the sky). Furthermore, regarding the one who is being born, how does the birth-constellation cause that which he received many days before his birthday? For they predict from the "birth chart" <note>Original Latin: *themate geniturae*.</note> whether the one being born is male or female, crippled or whole, beautiful or deformed. The "die was cast" on all these bodily conditions long before the infant was committed from his mother's "pouch," <note>Original Latin: *bulga*. Pico quotes the satirist Lucilius here to refer to the womb.</note> as **Lucilius** says. By what logic do astrologers claim the prediction of all these things? A cause cannot be later than its effect, nor can things be foreseen from heaven in any way other than how an effect is foreknown from its cause. 
<margin>Haly Abenrodan's imagination concerning births.</margin>
<term>Haly Abenrodan</term>, <note>Ali ibn Ridwan, an 11th-century Arabic commentator on Ptolemy's *Tetrabiblos*.</note> narrating the astrological books of Ptolemy as if he wished to solve this question of ours, wanted to show how the fates of parents could be foreseen from the birth charts of brothers or sons. He says: "A woman does not conceive every time she joins with a man, but only then when that hour falls whose constellation agrees with the constellation of the parents." And since things that agree with another thing must necessarily agree with each other: if the birth charts of all the children agree with the constellations of the parents, they will also be in harmony with each other. Therefore, they will mutually signify each other's fates; thus the nature and fortune of the parents are demonstrated from the birth chart of a brother or a son. 

<margin>Refutation. First reason. Second. Third.</margin>
For my part, I do not know which part of this astrological "subtlety" to refute or mock first. He says a woman does not conceive unless the position of the stars at that hour agrees with the stars of the parents. If that is so, the fates of the parents should be foreseen from the hour of *conception*, not from the hour the boy is *born*. Furthermore, since the father was born under one sky and the mother under another, how can a single constellation correspond to two such different constellations? Or if they think this can happen through some diversity of the stars, how will the charts of so many children correspond to the charts of the father and mother at the same time? Especially since the "signification" of the parents must be sought from the same stars and the same regions of the sky in every case. The lot of the father and mother is investigated from the 4th and 10th houses of the sky, and likewise from the Sun, Saturn, Venus, and the Moon. The arrangement of these in the charts of births is almost always varied and manifold according to the variety of the children; do you think all that variety can fail to vary from the constellations of the parents? It is as if something could fail to disagree with another thing when it already disagrees with itself! Or as if it were impossible for the same father to necessarily be both lucky...

<meta>The catchword "natus" (born) indicates the next page will likely discuss a father being "born" or having children born under different fates.</meta>

<summary>Pico argues that divine providence does not override human free will and mocks astrologers for claiming they can predict a person's past or their relatives' fortunes from a birth chart, specifically refuting the medieval scholar Haly Abenrodan.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s systematic dismantling of astrological logic. Having previously argued that birth charts cannot logically account for the lives of relatives, he now transitions into a critique of how astrologers explain the timing of events and the practice of "elections"—choosing "lucky" moments to begin tasks.</meta>

<header>AGAINST ASTROLOGERS, BOOK IV.</header>

<margin>The response of the common crowd of astrologers.</margin>
...one may be born lucky and another unlucky: simply because one son has his "fourth house" <note>The astrological "house" associated with parents and ancestry.</note> illuminated by favorable rays, while the other's is besieged by unfavorable ones. To avoid the absurdity of this, the common crowd of astrologers is accustomed to say that the fates of the parents are not foreseen from the <term>genitures</term> <note>A birth chart or "nativity" calculated at the moment of birth.</note> of all the children, but only from the one who is the eldest. Yet that refuge—their claim about the genitures of brothers—is immediately taken away from them; for they used to show that these charts agreed with one another precisely because they all harmonized equally with the constellations of the parents. But why bother to laboriously refute something so evidently frivolous? For what reason can defend this: that a woman cannot conceive unless the one being conceived is destined to be born at an hour whose constellation will be of such a kind that it can signify the lot and nature of the parents to an astrologer? It is as if the heavens and all of nature were at their service, and nothing can happen in the universe unless it happens in a way that allows an astrologer to divine it. Furthermore, how do they solve the point where the whole force of our argument lies: that something cannot be caused by the hour an infant is born which has already occurred in the brothers or parents long before? As for the opinion of those who say things are not *caused* by this but only *signified* by the stars: we shall prove them wrong later. For now, we dispute against those who believe the heavens are the *cause* of those things predicted from the sky—which is what <term>Ptolemy</term> <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the most influential ancient authority on astronomy and astrology.</note> and all the leading masters of this art believed.

## Chapter VI. Future events occurring much later cannot be caused by a present constellation.

<margin>Attacking the vanity of astrology by its own claims.</margin>
What of the fact that—if we consider it rightly—not only past events, but even those occurring much later in time, cannot be caused by a present constellation? Yet this is a very common and familiar feature in the predictions of astrologers. For where do we not read among them that an "oriental" planet <note>A planet rising in the east before the sun.</note> provides what it promises in the first part of life, while an "occidental" one <note>A planet setting in the west after the sun.</note> does so in the last? They claim that whichever planet occupies the <term>horoscope</term> <note>original: "horoscopum"; here referring to the Ascendant, the sign rising on the eastern horizon.</note> or rules the horoscope gives its gifts quickly; a little later comes the one possessing the rights of the "tenth house"; later still the one present in or presiding over the west; and latest of all the one placed in the "bottom of the sky" <note>original: "imo caelo"; the Imum Coeli or the lowest point of the chart.</note>. There are countless other rules of this kind, all attesting to this: that constellations do not produce what they are going to do when the constellations themselves exist, but rather many years after they have passed. An example of such a marvel is seen in no other natural power or action (which they confess the celestial power to be). It is as if a cause were thought to be more effective when it is *not* there than when it *is*. Furthermore, the celestial influence does not remain in the body like a medicine. <margin>The Response.</margin> But perhaps they will respond that even if that position of the stars passes away, the power infused into us from it nevertheless endures, which will finally bring its effects to light in its own time, according to the nature of the agent and the suitability of the material. <margin>The Refutation.</margin> I, however, would object that while the nature and condition of an effect do vary according to the condition and varied power of the agents, it is a rule common to all causes that they produce their effects more when they *exist* than when they have already ceased to be for a long time. Regarding "material," if they say a person is not immediately made a king or a philosopher at birth—even if the heavens promise it—because their age prevents it, this might seem not to be absurd. But when the person reaches an age capable of receiving those gifts which the birth stars promised, why does it still not happen? The sufficient cause has already preceded it, and 

<column-break/>

the material is ready and fit. But they either say the effect ceases for as many years as the planet was distant from a certain place by degrees of the signs, or that because it held such a position in the heavenly theme <note>A birth chart.</note>, it cannot provide its benefits except late. <margin>Note the failure of prediction.</margin> This sounds like the behavior of a rational nature, dispensing its gifts at whatever time it wishes according to its own choice and judgment; it is not, and cannot be, the behavior of a natural cause. Furthermore, if the heavens would give what they promise immediately, but the "disposition of the material" causes the delay, it will not be the astrologer's job <margin>Note.</margin> to foreknow the timing of events by looking at the heavens. Rather, it would be the job of someone who knows the state and condition of the "material" <note>The person's physical or social circumstances.</note> to hear from the astrologer *what* is going to happen, and then show the astrologer *when* it will happen. Likewise, regarding their response that a force derived from the heavens is preserved after the constellation passes, I would like to know from them: where is it preserved? Surely either in the "material" or in lower and secondary causes. Whichever they prefer, they should know that the celestial power cannot remain the same and stable for such a long time, neither in the tide of flowing and ebbing matter, nor in such a varied and changeable multitude of particular causes.

## Chapter VII. Concerning the "auguries" which they call "elections": how vain and impossible the astrologers' opinion is.

I would also like to ask them about that part of astrology which is thought most useful for life: "auguries," which the common people call <term>elections</term> <note>The practice of choosing a specific moment to start an undertaking to ensure success.</note>. That is, in what way do they understand it to be caused by the heavens that what we undertake to do at this hour happens happily, but what we do at another hour happens unhappily for us? For just as they say all these things easily—and it has an appearance of probability at first glance—so too, when they are examined more diligently, they are discovered to be vain and impossible. They say: if someone begins a journey under such a constellation of the sky, he will have a convenient trip, be kindly received by a king, and increase his family's wealth. Conversely, if he mounts a horse or boards a ship at another hour, he will experience difficult journeys and dangerous navigation, and will fail to achieve the goal <margin>See by what arguments "elections" are refuted.</margin> for which he undertook the journey or voyage. Here, I confess I do not see how these things are caused by the sky; let them teach me if they can. Suppose Jupiter hurls his rays to the earth from the ninth region of the sky; they will call it a lucky constellation for starting a journey. I ask them: does this fortunate breath or influence affect the men themselves who are about to start the journey, or rather the very *action* of the men traveling—that is, the mounting of the horse, the leaving of the house, or some such necessary beginning of a journey? If they answer the first, the men would be affected even if they did not start the journey then, whenever the purpose of starting a journey occurred to them—especially since, in the astrologers' own opinion, a constellation does not provide what it promises most when it *is*, but often after a long interval of time. If they answer the second, they will certainly be forced into many delusions to defend their position, as they explain to us how that "Jovian" mounting of a horse makes the road soft for the feet, drives away robbers from the path, and clears the clouds to make a peaceful sky with diffuse light. Nor will they have any less trouble in explaining how this "outflow" is maintained while a journey of many days is being completed, when there is a strong suspicion that the power does not descend from the sky for the one mounting the horse...

<summary>Pico critiques the logical gaps in astrological timing, arguing that natural causes should be most effective when present, not years later, and ridicules "elections" (lucky timing) for attributing miraculous powers to simple actions like mounting a horse.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s critique of astrology by contrasting divine providence with the supposed "fate" of the stars. He argues that while God knows the future, He does not strip humans of their free will, whereas the mechanical "fate" of astrologers would render human choice meaningless.</meta>

-># THE NINTH DISPUTATION<-

<margin>
Human freedom is not removed by God’s foreknowledge or providence. The opinion is explained.
</margin>
Whether you consider His mind, which foreknows all things, or His will, which disposes all things according to His pleasure: no prejudice is done to our free actions. For if we consider His foreknowledge, why should I not freely do what God has foreseen I would do? For if what He foresaw is to happen, I will certainly do it freely, because He foresaw that I would do it freely. Furthermore, because what He willed shall come to pass, and He willed me to be free, I shall act freely in whatever I do, unless He Himself were to take my freedom away from me. Indeed, He not only foreknew our two wills <note>likely referring to the human and divine will, or the capacity for choice</note> but also pre-ordained them. When Gregory of Nyssa <note>a 4th-century Church Father</note> and John of Damascus <note>an 8th-century theologian</note> seemed to deny this, they did so only to remind us that while other things happen through divine will alone, our choices are disposed through His will *along with* our own will. Thus, it is not only the outcomes of our thoughts, but the thoughts themselves, the counsels, and the intentions—not only of kings, as it is written, but the hearts of all men—that are in the hand of God, who alone governs all things. Now, in those matters which pertain neither to vice nor to virtue, He inclines the will wherever He pleases, if the fulfillment of one of His decrees so requires. At other times, He works virtues in us, both beginning them within us and perfecting them once started. Sometimes He turns those moved from virtue toward vice back to justice, either applying the "pedagogue’s rod" <note>a metaphor for corrective discipline</note> out of mercy, or crushing the delusional out of justice. He always makes all things either good or, certainly, occasions for good. 

We have said this much concerning fate, providence, and the governance of human affairs because these things are useful to know in themselves and necessary for demolishing the vanity of astrology. Thus, when we see something happen that appears too great or too orderly to be attributed to chance or man, we should not perceive there the force of physical rays from the stars. Instead, we should understand the care and power of divine counsel and angelic ministry working alongside human freedom. 

It is clear from what we have said how future things can be both foreseen and—when they are evil—avoided by us. For if human affairs happened by chance alone, there could be no foreknowledge of the future. But since they happen by human and divine counsel, human reason can conjecture somewhat about them, while those alone who are inspired by the Divine can foresee them with absolute certainty. This is confirmed by the predictions and oracles of the prophets. Even if they are separated by a vast interval, those who are prudent are closest to the prophets. Hence that saying of Euripides <note>original: "Qui bene coniectauerit is vates optimus esto"</note>: *He who guesses well, let him be the best seer.* Thus, in seeking a happy outcome and avoiding misfortunes, the most important thing is to win God’s favor through purity of mind, pious works, and most holy prayers. After this, a man should look out for himself with his own prudence. For although "Fortune" <note>chance</note> can do much in many things—indeed, the disposition of the certain divine will is everything in all things—it is nonetheless necessary that a right way of living carries great weight in these matters; otherwise, we would say this gift was bestowed upon us by God in vain. Therefore, that author <note>Juvenal, though attributed here to a general 'he'</note> rightly said that "no divine power is absent if there is prudence," but that it is we who make Fortune a goddess and place her in heaven. 

<margin>
Plato.
</margin>
For this reason, Plato, in his letter to the Syracusans, recalled that saying of Homer: *The gods took away his mind.* He argued that it is men themselves who cast away the mind that was granted to them. This is confirmed by that sentiment of Euripides, who said that bravery is the daughter of the soul. Therefore, by arranging our lives prudently through natural reason, and by preparing divine benevolence for ourselves through pious religion, let us avoid all superstitious vanity. Otherwise, he who hopes either to foresee the future or to avoid evils through astrological observations will hear Isaiah 

<column-break/>

saying to him: *Evil shall come upon you, and you shall not know its source; and calamity shall fall upon you which you will not be able to expiate.* <note>Quoting Isaiah 47:11, a common passage used to rebuke diviners.</note>

---

### Chapter V. Neither the past nor things pertaining to others can be foreseen from any constellation.

If they perhaps have some response regarding matters of chance—though they can have nothing that is either true or even likely—what, I ask, will they answer regarding those things which precede the hour of birth <term>geniture</term> <note>the specific alignment of stars at the moment of birth</note>? That is, in what way will they think an efficient cause can be later than its effects? What of those things which are not only prior, but also belong to others, and therefore have their causes not in the constellation of *this* birth, but elsewhere? For instance, when they pronounce judgments on the natures and fortunes of parents, grandparents, and elder brothers based on the hour a son is born. These things are both prior to the constellation and foreign to it, having their own order and dependence of fate from their own constellations long ago. (This is assuming, of course, we believe there is such a thing as "fate" from the sky). Furthermore, in the one being born, how does the birth-constellation cause that which he received many days before the day of birth? For they predict from the <term>theme of the geniture</term> <note>the birth chart</note> whether the one born is male or female, crippled or whole, beautiful or deformed. The "die was cast" regarding all these bodily conditions long before the infant was released from the mother's <margin>Lucilius</margin> "pouch" <note>Latin: *bulga*; a reference to the satirist Lucilius using the word for the womb</note>, as Lucilius says. By what logic do astrologers claim the prediction of all these things? A cause cannot be later than its effect, nor can things be foreseen from heaven in any other way than how an effect is foreknown from its cause. 

<margin>
Haly Avenrodam on genitures.
</margin>
Haly Avenrodam <note>Ali ibn Ridwan, an 11th-century Egyptian physician and astrologer</note>, in his commentary on the <term>apotelesmatic</term> <note>pertaining to astrological effects</note> books of Ptolemy, wanting to solve this question of ours, tried to show how the fates of parents could be foreseen from the birth charts of their children. "Whenever a woman joins with a man," he says, "she conceives; but only then when an hour occurs whose constellation accords with the constellation of the parents." And since things that agree with a third thing must necessarily agree with each other, if the birth charts of all the children agree with the constellations of the parents, they will also be in accord with each other. Therefore, they will mutually signify each other’s fates; thus the nature and fortune of the parents are demonstrated from the birth charts of the brothers and sons. 

<margin>
Refutation. 
First:
Second:
Third.
</margin>
Truly, in this astrological "subtlety," I do not know what I should first refute or mock. He says a woman does not conceive unless the position of the stars at that hour agrees with the stars of the parents. If that is so, the fates of the parents should be foreseen not from the hour of *birth*, but from the hour of *conception*. Furthermore, since the father was born under one sky and the mother under another, how can a single constellation correspond to two such different constellations? Or, if they think this is possible through some diversity of the stars, how will the birth charts of so many children correspond to the charts of the father and mother simultaneously? For the significance of the parents in all these charts must be sought from the same stars and the same regions of the sky. They investigate the lot of the father and mother from the fourth and tenth houses of the sky, and likewise from the Sun, Saturn, Venus, and the Moon. The arrangement of these in the birth charts is almost always varied and manifold according to the variety of the children. Do you think all that variety can avoid diverging from the constellations of the parents? As if something could agree with another thing when it first disagrees with itself! Or as if it were not the case that the same father must necessarily and fortunately—

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s systematic dismantling of astrological logic. Having previously argued that divine providence does not override human free will, he now turns to the internal contradictions of astrological practice, specifically regarding the timing of "fate" and the absurdity of "elections"—choosing lucky moments to begin tasks.</meta>

-># AGAINST THE ASTROLOGERS, BOOK IV<-

...one might be born fortunate and another unfortunate: because, for example, one son has his fourth house <note>In traditional astrology, the "fourth house" or "fourth place" represents one's parents, home, and hidden things</note> illuminated by lucky rays, while the other's is beset by unlucky ones. <margin>The response of the common astrologers.</margin> To avoid this problem, the common crowd of astrologers are accustomed to saying that the fate of the parents is foreseen not from the birth charts of all children, but from that of the firstborn. 

But that refuge is immediately taken away from them concerning the siblings' horoscopes, which they used to show must agree with each other because they all resonate equally with the parents' constellations. But why spend more effort refuting something so obviously frivolous? On what grounds is it defended? That a woman does not conceive unless the one then conceived is to be born at an hour whose constellation will be such that it can signal to the astrologer the fate and nature of the parents? As if the heavens and all of nature were at their service! As if nothing can happen in the universe unless it happens in a way that allows an astrologer to divine it. 

Furthermore, how do they solve the core of our argument: that something which happened long ago to siblings or parents cannot be caused by the hour an infant is born? We will later refute the opinion of those who say the stars do not *cause* these things but only *signify* them. Now, we are arguing against those who believe the heavens are the *cause* of what is predicted from the sky—a view held by Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century author of the *Tetrabiblos*, the foundational text of Western astrology</note> and all the masters of this art.

### Chapter VI. Future events occurring much later cannot be caused by a present constellation.

<margin>An attack on astrological vanity through its own claims.</margin> What if we consider that not only past events, but even those far in the future, cannot be caused by a present constellation? Yet this is a very common and familiar claim in astrological predictions. Where do we not read among them that a planet in the east promises results in the first part of life, and one in the west in the last? That whoever occupies the <term>horoscope</term><note>The rising sign or Ascendant, the point of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at birth</note> or rules it gives their gifts quickly; a little later, the one possessing the rights of the tenth house; then late, the one present in or presiding over the west; and latest of all, the one placed in the "bottom of the sky" <note>The *Imum Coeli*, the lowest point of the chart</note>? They claim countless other things of this kind, attesting that what the constellations are going to do does not happen when the constellations themselves are present, but rather many years after they have passed. 

Yet no example of such a marvel appears in any natural power or action (which they admit the heavens are): that a cause should be thought more effective when it is *not* present than when it *is*. Nor does a celestial influx remain in the body like a dose of medicine. <margin>Response.</margin> But perhaps they will respond that even if that celestial alignment has passed, the power infused into us from it remains, which will eventually bring its effects to light in its own time, according to the nature of the acting cause and the suitability of the material. 

<margin>Refutation.</margin> As for the nature of the "agent" <note>The acting cause, in this case, the stars</note>, I object to them as I did before: while the nature and condition of an effect vary according to the power of the agents, it is common to all causes that they act more powerfully when they *are* present than when they have been absent for a long time. Regarding the material: if they say a newborn does not immediately become a king or a philosopher even if the heavens promise it because their age prevents it, this might seem reasonable. But once the person is of an age capable of those duties promised by the birth stars, why does it still not happen, since the sufficient cause has already preceded it and

<column-break/>

the material is ready and suitable? But they either say the effect is delayed by as many years as the planet was distant in degrees from a certain place, or that because it held such a place in the celestial <term>theme</term><note>A "theme" refers to the map of the heavens or birth chart</note>, it cannot grant its favors except late. This sounds more like the nature of a rational being dispensing gifts at a chosen time according to its own will, rather than a natural cause; it is not, nor can it be, a natural cause. 

Furthermore, if the heavens would give what they promise immediately, but the "disposition of matter" <note>The physical readiness of the person or object</note> is the delay, then it will not be the astrologer—who considers only the sky—who foreknows the time of the event, but rather the person who knows the state and condition of the material, so that he might hear from the astrologer *what* will happen, while he himself shows the astrologer *when* it will happen. 

Likewise, regarding their response that the power derived from the heavens is preserved after the constellation passes, I would like to know from them: where is it preserved? Surely either in the matter or in inferior and secondary causes. Whichever they choose, let them know that neither in the tide of flowing and ebbing matter, nor in such a varied and changeable multitude of particular causes, can a celestial power remain the same and stable for such a long time. <margin>Note the failure of fore-calculation.</margin> <margin>Note.</margin>

### Chapter VII. Concerning the taking of omens, which they call "elections," and how vain and impossible the astrologers' opinion is.

<margin>See the arguments by which "elections" are refuted.</margin> I would also like to inquire about that part of astrology which is thought most useful for life: the taking of omens, which they commonly call <term>elections</term><note>The practice of "Electional Astrology," choosing a specific time to start a task—like a wedding or a war—to ensure success</note>. That is, how do they understand the heavens to cause what we begin at this hour to turn out happily, while what we begin at another turns out unhappily? For they say all these things easily, and at first glance they have a look of probability; yet when examined more closely, they are found to be vain and impossible. 

If someone, they say, begins a journey under a certain constellation of the sky, he will have a convenient pilgrimage: he will be kindly received by a king; he will increase his family wealth. Conversely, if he mounts a horse or boards a ship at another hour, he will experience difficult paths and a dangerous voyage, and will not ultimately achieve the purpose for which he undertook the journey. 

I confess I do not see how all these things are done by the heavens; let them teach me if they can. Suppose <term>Jupiter</term><note>In ancient and Renaissance astrology, Jupiter was the "Great Benefic," the planet of luck, wealth, and success</note> hurls his rays to earth from the ninth region of the sky: they will call it a lucky constellation for starting a journey. I ask them: does this fortunate "breath" affect the men themselves who are about to start the journey, or rather the very *action* of the men traveling—that is, mounting the horse, or leaving the house, or some such thing that is a necessary beginning of a journey? 

If they answer the first, the men will be influenced by the benefit of the star even if they do not start the journey then, whenever they intend to set out—especially since, in their opinion, a constellation does not provide what it promises most when it is present, but often after a long interval of time. If they answer the second, they will certainly be forced into many delusions to defend their position, while they explain to us how that "Jovial" mounting of a horse spreads a soft path for the feet, drives thieves away from the road, and makes the sky peaceful with diffused light after the clouds are chased away. Nor will they have a small task in explaining how that flow is retained while a journey of perhaps many days is completed, since there is a well-founded suspicion that no power descends from the sky into that man mounting the horse, just as, by the same logic...

<summary>Pico critiques the logical inconsistencies of astrology, specifically attacking the idea that stars can cause events years after a person is born or influence the success of a journey based on the exact moment one "mounts a horse." He argues that natural causes should be strongest when present, not delayed, and that "elections" (picking lucky times) attribute impossible powers to the stars.</summary>

-># DISPUTATIONS etc.<-

<margin>The example of Ptolemy to be refuted.</margin>
...from which it descended, it should return to heaven again: and that traveler <note>The soul is often described in Neoplatonic thought as a traveler descending from the stars into the body.</note> would always need a new Jupiter <note>Pico is mocking the idea that a soul needs a specific planetary alignment to "ride" back to heaven.</note> upon whose horse he must sit. For to dream of some primordial force consistent nowhere, rooted in nothing—which smoothly and happily completes the entire journey for you—is the talk of sleepless, even delirious men; they do not weigh what they say, but give off a futile sound without a mind behind it. Let us see again if these same men fall into difficulties in the holdings of Ptolemy: if in the founding of a city Mars occupies the midheaven, the leaders of that state will mostly perish by the sword. Let Ptolemy explain to us where that bloody radiation of Mars is received, which is to kill so many leaders in succession over the course of time? If he wants it to be received in the prince who is then building the city: I will ask how those stones, cast and buried in the earth by the prince's command—namely, the foundations of the city—can bend and divert the celestial rays of others toward that prince. By what path does this harmful power descend to his posterity and successors of the realm, as if by hereditary right, when its recipient has perished and its origin has passed? Truly, I do not see how they can respond to us when we ask such questions without blushing. 

<margin>If such a plague of slaughter hides in the foundations of the city and is eventually to be emitted as a noxious vapor, then it is said it would also kill the poor.</margin>
He will say, perhaps, that the plague is received not in the prince himself, the founder of the city, but rather in the city itself: in those first stones upon which it is to be raised. By a kind of pestilential breath of Mars, it will then breathe upon all the leaders of that city. Surely a war-like discovery to be confirmed even by the testimony of Moses, who once showed us the purification of a leprous house by prophetic inspiration! <note>A sarcastic reference to Leviticus 14, where Moses gives laws for "leprosy" in the walls of a house.</note> But I fear that the earth piled on top, and the nearby stones packed in, might not prevent that Martian <term>miasma</term> <note>original: "mephitin," referring to foul-smelling, poisonous vapors believed to rise from the earth.</note> from exhaling; or if it exhales at all, that it would not rather invade the needy and the poor, who are more susceptible to plague, than the prince of the state himself. If the prince happens to live in some suburban villa, I believe he will not perish by the sword—especially if it is separated from the city by many miles, so that the Martian vapor, meanwhile choked on all sides by lime and rubble, cannot reach there intact and effective. But the glory of the philosophers Plato and Aristotle will be at risk here; in their books on the Republic and Politics, where they perceived so much about founding and ruling a city happily, they left us nothing written about such a useful and necessary caution. If we weigh all these things seriously and not as a joke, we will see that Haly <note>Likely Haly Abenragel, a famous 11th-century Arab astrologer.</note>, the commentator on Ptolemy, though a supreme astrologer, rightly judged this part of astrology concerning "elections" <note>The practice of choosing an auspicious time to start an undertaking.</note> to be frivolous and ineffective.
<margin>Haly.</margin>

### Chapter VIII. That Astrologers subject our minds to the heavens, though they are clever enough to try and hide it.

Thus far it has been demonstrated that no corporeal and temporary thing—over which the heavens are thought to have the most right—depends on the heavens in the way the astrologers imagine. For neither those things which are accidental, nor those which pertain to others, nor those which are either past or far in the future, nor even the greatest part of those things which people begin under certain observations of the hours in order to succeed, are governed by the stars. If the heavens do not effect these things such that they can be foreseen from the sky, how much less so those things which are incorporeal—about which, nevertheless, astrological superstition does not blush to pronounce judgment. For in 

<column-break/>

this category are contained the diversities of characters and talents, and whatever works and properties belong to our soul; it includes things pertaining to demons, to higher minds, to God, to the efficacy of prayers, to the secrets of conscience, to the state of the future life, and other things of this kind. Concerning all of these, they babble a thousand dogmas of prediction, and this breed of men divulges them with the most arrogant rashness. Indeed, I would begin with the movements which they think are different in men according to the variety of such-and-such a constellation. 

<margin>The cunning of the astrologers.</margin>
But when they are pressed on this point, they are accustomed to hide what they truly feel. Pouring out many words about the freedom of the will, they warn us to be careful lest we think our liberty is compelled by the stars, from which we only have some "inclination" or "invitation" which it is our choice to follow or decline. I will therefore first uncover the 

<margin>Astrologers subject our mind to the heavens.</margin>
fraud of this defense, bringing forward many of their own dogmas from which it is clear that they subject the mind itself to the heavens, even where it does not depend on the body. Afterward, we will declare that the diversity of characters and talents cannot be referred to celestial causes even in the way they claim. Therefore, if they do not think the differences of the human soul come from the condition and position of the stars in any way other than the soul’s operation being somewhat changed by the body being affected, then how can they contend that Mars, happily placed in the ninth region of the sky, can grant us such power that we might expel demons from possessed bodies by our mere presence? This is not a feat of a soul merely leaning toward the body, but of one living in the body in such a way—filled with God and inhabiting the inner chambers of the mind—that it does not even feel itself living in the body. 

<margin>Second [argument].</margin>
In the same way, how do they presume to judge the secrets of the conscience of one who is born toward God and men from the "part of the Sun"? <note>A specific mathematical point in a birth chart used in ancient astrology.</note> Nothing in these matters is placed in anyone's hand but our own liberty; they are not open even to the knowledge of angels, nor are they subjected to their power. Finally, if the partnership of the body connects the soul to the heaven, 

<margin>Third [argument].</margin>
why do they pronounce judgment from a celestial constellation concerning the soul's state when it has been released from the body? For it is common among them that there are two planets who are authors of happiness, Venus and Jupiter, but with different duties: Venus bestows the happiness of the present life, and Jupiter the happiness of the future. 

<margin>Maternus.</margin>
Maternus <note>Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Latin author of a massive astrological manual.</note>, after he recounted many of these things which are granted by Saturn when positioned in Leo, then adds this: "But when they have attained all these things, they will die at a great age, and their soul will pass to heaven, joined to the gods." For Saturn placed in Leo recalls the souls of those who have conducted themselves thus on earth, freed from innumerable straits, back to heaven and to the beginnings of their origin. Thus he says. 

<margin>An empty dogma, mere smoke for discussion.</margin>
By this, I want it understood not only how far this astrological superstition spreads—even to the suspicion of impiety—but how much faith can be placed in the writers of this art, as if they had committed to letters only what was tested and proven by experience. For we know without a doubt that when they were writing, they had no experience of the future life. If they perhaps learned these things from their departed associates, they might better have understood which constellation sent one to the underworld rather than to the heavens. For although they think that by praying at a certain hour they can obtain what they want from God, I would not easily believe—unless they changed their dogma—that they will obtain eternal happiness from Him. And they certainly believe what we have said. 

<margin>Fourth [argument]. Albumasar.</margin>
For that most fabulous Albumasar <note>Abu Ma'shar, a famous Persian astrologer whose works were central to medieval European astrology.</note> writes: "he who prays to God when the Moon is joined to Jupiter along with the Dragon's Head <note>The ascending node of the moon.</note> will obtain from God whatever he asks." And will there still be philosophers, will there be theologians, who find these things pleasing? And who think that they and those whom they follow...

-># AGAINST THE ASTROLOGERS, BOOK IV.<-

...who follow the astrologers do not yet sufficiently understand what God is, or what prayer is. Such insanity does not need to be refuted here so much as it needs to be cursed, since it has already been sufficiently refuted by the arguments we have disputed elsewhere concerning prayer against the impious. But as for Peter of Abano <note>Petrus Apponensis (c. 1250–1316), an Italian physician and astrologer who was often accused of heresy and magic.</note>, whenever I read his writings, that saying of Heraclitus <note>A pre-Socratic Greek philosopher known for his cryptic and often pessimistic sayings.</note> comes to mind: **"Much learning does not teach understanding."** <note>original: "πολυμαθια νοον ουφερει" (polymathia noon ou pherei)</note> He himself wrote that at the very hour I was just speaking of, he sought knowledge from God and that after that day, he made great progress in it. 

<margin>Peter of Abano. Heraclitus.</margin>

I do not have the time to measure how much this "new Solomon" <note>Pico is being sarcastic, comparing the astrologer to the biblical King Solomon, who was famed for divinely granted wisdom.</note> actually progressed in it. I certainly believe that whatever progress he made was no more than what can be reached by human steps. But however the matter stands, I would advise this Peter to credit whatever he achieved to his own industry and talent, rather than to that "supplication to Jupiter" of his. He should not stubbornly defend such a claim, lest men of good judgment be forced to deny that he made any progress in good literature at all, rather than believe he ever assented to such vain superstition. I would likewise give this general advice to all astrologers: since Jupiter is so favorable to them, they should use a single prayer at a lucky hour to acquire so much wealth and resources for themselves that they no longer need our money. Then they might finally stop mocking the minds of the unlearned with so many daily lies for the sake of swindling their cash.

### Chapter IX. Human morals are not made by the heavens.

<margin>Refutation of the opinion of certain people.</margin>

**L**et us see regarding morals: can it be defended by right reason that their cause is also somehow in the heavens? For perhaps one might think that if the rational part of the soul suffers no violence from the sky, and our freedom of will is not coerced, then there is no reason why either philosophy or piety should deny that the various interests of men and the multiple properties of their talents arise from the different influences of the stars. This would be similar to how the condition of the body affects us, while the dignity of the soul and the freedom of choice remain safe. 

But anyone who thinks this way is greatly deceived. For the idea that the sensory part of the soul is so affected by the sun as to have a propensity toward some disgrace—something contrary to reason—is greatly opposed to piety. For whatever is done by natural causes (especially those that unchangeably follow the laws prescribed for them by the Creator of nature) must be attributed both to the Author of nature who established it and to nature itself. Yet, by the consensus of both philosophers and theologians, God, the beginning of nature, endowed the stars with whatever virtue or property they possess. 

Even the foolish hardly deny that God is most good and wise; but what kind of "goodness" or "all-powerful wisdom" would it be for the hand of heaven to bend a man—who, though free, is nevertheless weak—toward that side where you would least want him to turn? It would make the best servants <note>The stars, seen here as God's "servants" or tools.</note> into the authors and ministers of evil. Thus, while the stars themselves never transgress the King’s commands, they would be the ones primarily inviting and impelling others to transgression. Finally, what kind of natural order, what harmony, what wise institution would this be? That which the reason of nature would not want to happen is nonetheless diligently brought about by those very parts of nature that are great, powerful, excellent, and primary. 

Furthermore, one who sins does not "act" in a positive sense, but rather "fails" or "falls short." Therefore, one who invites another to sin invites them to fail—which does not suit superior "efficient" causes, which are always active and never "deficient" <note>In Scholastic philosophy, God and the heavens are "efficient causes" (bringing things into being). Sin is a "privation" or a "deficiency" (a lack of good), so Pico argues a perfect cause cannot produce an imperfect failure.</note>. Therefore, it is a most absurd dogma of the astro-

<column-break/>

-logers to think that we have an inclination toward theft from one position of the stars, toward incest or fraud from another, or toward murder from another. Since all of nature—especially the superior part joined most closely to the Divine Mind—may perhaps favor the observation of natural and divine law, it can in no way hinder or oppose it. 

Therefore, let them shut their profane mouths! Let them not say that Venus coupled with Mars excites one to adultery or "nefarious" <note>Commonly a euphemism in this period for homosexual acts.</note> intercourse between males; or that Mars occupying the ninth part of the sky makes men irreligious; or that other constellations entirely irritate us toward other disgraces. Let them impute their crimes to themselves, not to their heaven, nor to "foul matter"; and let them not think that the filth of an unjust soul flows from the purest fountains of nature. 

But can this objection perhaps be solved? Some think so, saying that the powers of all the stars are good and healthful, but when they are received in us, they degenerate due to the "vice of matter." Thus, influences that were beneficial sometimes turn out to be harmful and malicious. For example, they say that Mars provides fortitude of soul and Herculean effectiveness; but either due to a vice of the body (in which red bile might excessively boil) or the fault of the soul abusing the celestial gift, those impulses are sometimes twisted into cruelty and injustice. Likewise, they say Saturn infuses depth of mind, profound counsel, investigation of hidden things, and a love of contemplation. Yet, because these same things find a sluggish vessel—or by the fault of the will of the person in whom they are received—they make the soul deceitful, filthy, unrefined, superstitious, and imaginative to the point of being driven mad. Similarly, from Venus we are made prone to cheerfulness, benevolence, and civil elegance, but we abuse that instinct for wickedness, luxury, and dishonesty. We are incited by the Sun toward magnanimity, but we abuse that impulse for ambition—and so on for the rest. 

<margin>A solution proposed by some.</margin>

However, such things would be said by a "defender" of astrology rather than by an actual "astrologer." For among the very first principles of the astrologers—and the one most widely confessed—is that some planets are good and others are bad <note>The "Benefics" (Jupiter, Venus) and the "Malefics" (Saturn, Mars).</note>. If what these defenders said were true, then all planets would be called equally good by their nature, and all would be called equally bad by the same reasoning. For there is no influence so healthful that the "matter" and condition of the recipient cannot infect, change, and disturb it. 

<margin>Reproof.</margin>

Furthermore, if the astrologers themselves want to claim that there is no planet so bad that great goods cannot come from it, and none so good that great evils cannot come from it, they still do not attribute this diversity of effect to the "matter" or the recipient of the ray. Instead, they refer it to the various conditions and positions of that same star in the heavens. 

This is why they say that if Saturn holds his own "house," his own "exaltation," or his own "bounds" <note>Technical terms for the specific positions in the zodiac where a planet's power is supposedly strengthened or modified.</note>; if he is mixed with good radiations; if the birth occurs during the day—then he makes men contemplative, pious, and wise. But truly, if he is received in a less favorable position, they say that same planet degenerates into this evil condition. If he is poorly placed, joined to Mars, or in bad "schematisms" <note>The geometric relationships (aspects) between planets.</note> with the Sun, they say he makes men demonic, filthy, envious, and liars. Nor do they ever contend that when Saturn is in such a state in the heaven, any good can be expected from him. Therefore, he who defends astrology in that way <note>i.e., by blaming human matter rather than the star's inherent nature.</note> is clearly ignorant of what he is defending. What we have said about Saturn should be understood as being said about all; for concerning Mars, when he is unhappily disposed, they are accustomed to say...
