<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s argument that even if the heavens possessed specific powers, they would not function in the way astrologers claim. He is transitioning from a critique of astrological "elections" to a broader philosophical rejection of celestial influence over human choice and chance.</meta>

<page-num>110</page-num>
<header>AGAINST ASTROLOGY, BOOK IV.</header>

...choice <note>original: "electionem". In astrology, an "election" is the practice of choosing a specific moment to act based on the stars.</note>: and even if we were to grant that the heavens possess powers capable of producing specific qualities, they are certainly not of the kind that astrologers prophesy. For there is no rational way to link chance events to natural causes, nor evil things to the best of authors, nor things proceeding from reason and deliberation to principles acting out of natural necessity. Nor can we link incorporeal rays to physical bodies, nor things already past or far in the future to a present constellation, nor things pertaining to others to our own birth chart. Furthermore, it is utterly absurd and most foreign to all philosophy to see the proper, manifest, and sufficient causes for things right here among us—in the powers of lower bodies, in the diversity of souls, in emotion, deliberation, opportunity, and habit, and in the varied intersection of things and causes flowing together from every side—and yet seek their origin in the stars. Such an origin is neither found there, nor is it possible for it to be there, given the nature and condition of the things that happen or of the heavens that would supposedly effect them. For this reason, all philosophers whose labor is spent investigating the causes of things borrow true causes from medicine, mathematics, and every art and science, 
<margin>No true philosopher has ever placed any astrological reasoning in his own works.</margin>
yet they never use astrological causes. I pass over Favorinus, Carneades <note>A skeptical philosopher famous for arguing against the possibility of certain knowledge, including astrology.</note>, Posidonius, Timaeus, and Pythagoras; but as we declared at the beginning of this work, this same rejection was practiced by Aristotle himself, by Plato, by Plotinus, by Averroes, by Avicenna, and by the worthy followers of both their schools.

### Chapter XII. The heavens cannot be a sign of a thing for which they are not the cause.

<margin>The first refutation.</margin>
**B**ut perhaps someone will say that even if it is granted that these varieties and outcomes of human affairs are not caused by the stars, it does not immediately follow that they cannot be foreseen and predicted from the heavens. After all, things the stars do not cause they can nonetheless signify and portend. Indeed, there are those who have held this opinion: that while lower matters are not produced by the power of the celestial bodies (except in the sense of a general influence), and while they depend on their own immediate and proper causes, they are nonetheless indicated by the heavens before they happen. Thus, through the transit, station, and retreat of the planets, future events might be known, just as birds signify the future by their flight or their song without knowing it themselves. But in truth, neither the most distinguished astrologers ever believed this, nor does any reason permit us to believe it. For a thing that is a sign of something else by nature (rather than by human convention) and is a physical body must be one of three things: the cause of the thing it signifies, the effect of it, or a sign because both it and the thing signified proceed from the same common cause. If someone thinks a fourth option should be added—a necessary and inseparable connection and accompaniment—this cannot happen by any other means than the cause producing one thing from itself while it effects another, or that whatever stimulates the cause to act also rouses this sign at the same time. This, as we have granted, refers both back to a common cause. Come then, let us see which of these most fits the heavens if the future is signified by them. Certainly, the motions and arrangements of the heavens are not the *effects* of lower things, and the astrologers in this argument deny they are the *causes*. It remains for them to say that the state and arrangement of the heaven, and what is believed to be indicated by it, proceed from the same common cause—just as a rainbow sometimes portends clear weather, not because 

<column-break/>

it makes the weather clear, but because the cause of the rainbow is also the cause of the clear weather. But no physical cause can be considered "superior" to the heavens that could simultaneously produce the arrangements of both the heavens and the lower world. 
<margin>Divine minds are not the causes of lower events without the activity of the heavens. Arguments 1, 2, 3, and 4.</margin>
Will the remaining cause be incorporeal? For perhaps it might seem possible to say that the events of human affairs are produced by those same divine minds <note>Referencing the "Intelligences" or angels that medieval and ancient philosophy often claimed moved the planetary spheres.</note> that revolve the celestial bodies; and while these events happen, they are indicated to us by the state and position of the very heaven they move, as if by certain nods of the head. Truly, whoever says this is surely close to the fables of the poets. How will he avoid the inconvenient conclusion that those divine minds produce things that men themselves cannot do without the guilt of a crime? For this would mean they urge and impel one man to murder, another to adultery, and another to theft. I leave aside the fact that all philosophy should loathe the idea of physical things being produced by incorporeal causes without some mediating physical cause. Furthermore, why are those born at different hours born with a different fate, if the author and cause of fate is considered to be the Creator of the heavens—who is always equal to Himself, similar to Himself, and immobile—rather than the position of the heaven which varies by the hour? 
<margin>Thomas.</margin>
Finally, as Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential Dominican theologian.</note> argues: when the effects of the same cause indicate one another because they come from the same principle, they also proceed in the same manner. But the motion of the heavens and the arrangement of lower bodies and affairs do not come from the higher causes in the same way. The former follows an immutable and necessary order, while the latter follows a variable order that can fall either way by chance, according to the nature of the things being moved and governed. Divine principles do not change these natures but preserve them; otherwise, they would not be guiding nature, but destroying it. Therefore, the heaven cannot signify lower things except insofar as a cause indicates its own effect. Thus, those who are defeated by reason and admit the heaven is not a cause, yet still contend it is a sign, do not even know what they are saying. 
<margin>Thomas.</margin>
And this Thomas Aquinas—a man of the weightiest judgment who was not accustomed to asserting anything rashly—pronounced with certainty in his *Summa Theologiae*. One might say this about comets, shooting stars, and other things of that kind that occur high in the air: that being stirred up by stars that produce something, they do not cause but rather signify what their cause is about to do. But this can in no way be said of the stars themselves, since, as we were saying, no physical cause superior to them can be found. 
<margin>The second major argument.</margin>
But those who hold this opinion also introduce the necessity of fate, even if they do not wish to. For if the stars are the *causes* of lower things, it is possible that what is intended by their influence might not happen, because either the matter resists or some particular cause diverts the general influence elsewhere. But if they are *signs*, since they were instituted by nature for the purpose of signifying, their significance will be as true as their true nature. Otherwise, why were they instituted by God to signify, if His works, which are perfect, deceive and lie? But if they do not lie, that which is signified by them as the future must necessarily come to pass. 
<margin>Third argument.</margin>
Finally, if they are numbered among causes, it does not contradict their condition to be in that order of causes which can be hindered, changed, or overcome. But if they are considered signs, they cannot be held to be lies, lest He who wrote the notes and "letters" of the future in the celestial volume (as they say) be either deceptive or ignorant. 
<margin>Fourth argument.</margin>
Lastly, if the heaven does not indicate things by causing them, but indicates things it does not cause, it must be that it indicates what other causes are doing. Therefore, it either indicates what *all* causes do, or only what *some* do. If only some, why, I ask, does it indicate the works of these and not those? If indeed it indicates all equally, then there will be no remaining causes through which the thing demonstrated could be prevented from happening. Therefore, what was portended will necessarily happen. But if we say this...

<page-num>103</page-num>
<header>DISPUTATIONS</header>

...toward ambition, toward lack of self-control, and to stimulate a lust for tyranny. This is not because the vital spirit of the newborn is excessively hot or cold, thereby making the beneficial fire of heaven either sluggish or devouring. Rather, it is because Saturn, Mars, and the Sun—when they are positioned in the heavens in such a way—infuse these types of evils according to their own nature and properties. This is what astrologers write and believe. Nor does anyone defend astrology any better by denying this than a person who tries to "correct" a book with a sponge; as we have shown, if the truth of every prediction does not depend on the observation of celestial influence, then the dogma itself is wiped away. Furthermore, the disposition of matter does not merely diminish or increase celestial influence, but completely alters and changes it.

### Chapter X. Bad laws, like good ones, are not subject to the heavens.

<margin>Ptolemy</margin>
This refutes the opinion of those who deny that good laws are subject to the heavens (arguing instead that they depend on divine power) but concede this for bad laws, as if bad laws have nothing about them that exceeds the forces and capacity of nature. Yet, just as the lofty excellence of good laws prevents them from being subject to physical causes, the wickedness of bad laws prevents them from being attributed to the highest causes, which are most obedient to the best God. Indeed, experience itself sufficiently demonstrates that religions, both good and bad, do not depend on the heavens. For some people attribute the origin and variety of religions to the stars ruling over cities and provinces by their own right (as they believe). Others attribute them to what they call <term>Great Conjunctions</term> <note>The alignment of the "superior planets," Saturn and Jupiter, which occurred every 20 years and was thought to signal major historical and religious shifts.</note> of the higher planets, especially Saturn and Jupiter; this is the opinion followed by the Arabs and by the Latins who follow in the footsteps of the Arabs. Ptolemy seems to have approached this view, although (as we will show later) he never made mention of those "Great Conjunctions." However, in the second book of his *Tetrabiblos* <note>original: "apoteleşmaton". This is the Greek title of Ptolemy's foundational work on astrology.</note>, he says that those among the inhabitants of the world who lean toward the East and South worship Venus and Saturn because they fall under the "triplicity" of the dry quality—that is, Virgo, Taurus, and Capricorn—which he believes are ruled by Saturn and Venus. Again, he says those who live between the South and the West hold Venus and Mars as deities because they are subject to the "watery triplicity," over which he places Mercury and Venus along with Mars. But both opinions are refuted by the sheer evidence of history and events. For if a religion is born by the power of some Great Conjunction, that religion ought to be abolished once that power is extinguished. However, there is no conjunction of stars whose power is imagined to last as many years—even by astrologers—as the worship of idols, the Mosaic religion, and the Christian religion have endured. For about five thousand years, the world was darkened by the worship of idols. What conjunction, I ask, or what "Great Year" of any star, can claim so many spans of years for itself? The rites and observances of the Mosaic law still flourish among the Hebrews today, and have flourished for three thousand years or more. What constellation is so strong and so long-lasting that it does not allow a religion to be extinguished even when its empire has fallen? The theologian will give the true causes for these things, consistent with his doctrine; the astrologer can give none from the heavens. If that variety of religions were derived from the stars, we would see them vary every day and change more frequently. Even the astrologers themselves, thinking this and gathering it from the principles

<margin>No religion is subject to the conjunctions of the stars.</margin>

<column-break/>

of their own science, set "terms" or expiration dates for every religion. Yet, by outliving those dates, religions have demonstrated by the very evidence of the facts that they depend on something other than the stars. Now, that opinion of Ptolemy’s—which imagines that various religious rites exist in various places because different stars rule different lands and nations—is even more thoroughly refuted by experience. The same stars rule over those provinces lying between the East and the South today as ruled over them in the past. Yet, Venus and Saturn are no longer worshiped there as they once were. For why did these deities rule over them? Surely, as Ptolemy himself writes, because the "earthly triplicity" (consisting of Taurus, Virgo, and Capricorn) presides over those regions, and Venus and Saturn preside over that triplicity. That was his opinion. But this division of the world and its regions, distributed under various triplicities, is perpetual, not temporary. Therefore, the stars will always be the same as they once were. Why then, O Ptolemy, does the same religion not still endure today in those same places? Finally, let us conclude this entire dispute by asking Ptolemy himself: if different stars were worshiped by different nations in the past due to the varying presidency of the stars, by the power and force of which star is it brought about that almost no stars are worshiped in any region of the whole world today?

<margin>Derision of Ptolemy.</margin>

### Chapter XI. Physical dispositions are not caused by the heavens.

If all those points have been sufficiently refuted, there remains only the physical disposition of the body, about which an astrologer might be able to pronounce—if indeed he can speak on matters effected by the heavens. But not even a birth constellation can effect this, since a child already possesses the habit and shape of the body he carries with him in the womb before he leaves the womb. Therefore, this must also be numbered among those things we spoke of in the fifth chapter: things that cannot be predicted by the birth chart used by astrologers, because they precede the birth. They should rather be predicted by the moment of conception or the disposition of the seed. But the seed is not formed at the moment of birth; therefore, the constellation under which the seed was formed ought to be looked at instead. (We will deal with this later.) If, therefore, the disposition of the body can be foreseen and pronounced upon, it could certainly be done better from the hour of conception than from the hour of birth—though it cannot be done at all. Whether it can even be done from conception will be examined in the following books. Now, we are demonstrating that astrologers err when they pronounce, from the hour of birth, whether someone will be born with a short or tall body, fat or thin, strong or weak, maimed or whole, legitimate or monstrous. For he acquires all these conditions long before he is emitted into the public as a fully formed and finished being from his mother's womb. Therefore, just as these traits are not created by a constellation that they clearly preceded, they cannot be predicted by a mathematician’s observation of that constellation. We have discussed the time of conception elsewhere; for now, we want the reader to know that the greatest astrologers believed that things pertaining to the "temperament" of the body depend on immediate causes lower than the heavens. As Haly <note>original: "Haly". Likely referring to Haly Abenragel, a famous 11th-century Arabic astrologer.</note> writes, they asked to be pardoned if they failed to reach the truth in predicting the body’s disposition. Let us therefore sum up this entire dispute on the efficiency of the heavens: if heaven is a universal cause, then the variety and distinction of particular things do not come from it.

<margin>Haly.</margin>
<margin>Epilogue.</margin>

Having previously argued that the heavens do not exert specific physical control over human morality or the rise of religions, he now turns to a common "fallback" argument used by astrologers: that even if the stars do not *cause* events, they might still act as *signs* or omens of them.</meta>

<margin>
Of angels and human souls.
</margin>
<margin>
That no philosopher has placed any astrological reasoning in their works.
</margin>
...[reasoning]: and even if we grant that in the heavens there are powers capable of producing particular properties, they are nonetheless not of the kind that astrologers prophesy from the sky. It appears that there is no rational way to attribute accidental events to natural causes; nor things that are evil to the best of authors <note>original: "optimos auctores," referring to God or the celestial intelligences</note>; nor things that proceed from reason and deliberation to principles acting by natural necessity; nor incorporeal rays to physical bodies; nor things already past or far in the future to a present constellation; nor things belonging to others to our own <term>nativity</term> <note>the specific configuration of stars at the moment of birth</note>. Furthermore, it is utterly absurd and most foreign to all philosophy to see the proper, manifest, and sufficient causes for things right here among us—in the powers of lower bodies, in the diversity of minds, in emotion, counsel, opportunity, and habit, and in such a varied confluence of things and causes flowing together from every side—and yet seek their origin in the stars. Such an origin is neither there, nor is it possible for it to be there, given the nature and condition of the things being done or of the heaven that acts upon them. For this reason, all philosophers whose study and labor is spent in scrutinizing the causes of things—though they borrow true causes from medicine, mathematics, and every art and science—never make use of astrological causes. Setting aside Favorinus, Carneades, Posidonius, Timaeus, and Pythagoras, we declared at the beginning of this work that this was also the practice of Aristotle, Plato, Plotinus, Averroes, Avicenna, and the good followers of both their schools.

### Chapter XII. The sky cannot be a sign of a thing for which it is not the cause.

<margin>
First reason of the confutation.
</margin>
But perhaps someone will say that even if it is granted that these varieties and outcomes of human affairs are not *caused* by the stars, it does not immediately follow that they cannot be foreseen and predicted from the sky. For the stars can signify and portend things that they do not actually cause. Indeed, there are those who have held this opinion: that lower matters are not produced by the power of the celestials (except in matters of general influence), but while they depend on their own immediate and proper causes, they are nonetheless indicated by the sky before they happen. Thus, through the transit, station, and retreat of the planets, future things are known—just as birds, either by flying past or by standing still, signify future things with their wings or voice without knowing they are doing so. But in truth, neither have the distinguished astrologers ever believed this, nor does any reason agree that we should believe it. For a thing that is a sign of something else by nature (not by human convention) and is a physical body, is either the *cause* of the thing it signifies, or its *effect*, or else both the sign and the thing signified proceed from the same common cause. If someone thinks a further category should be added—distinct from those I have mentioned—such as a necessary and inseparable connection or accompaniment, this can happen in no other way than that the cause either produces the sign from itself before it effects the other thing, or that whatever rouses that cause to act also rouses the sign at the same time. In both cases, we concede they refer back to a common cause. Come then, let us see which of these most fits the sky if future events are signified by it. The motions and dispositions of the heavens are not the *effects* of lower things; and our opponents deny they are the *causes*. It remains for them to say that the state and disposition of the sky, and what is believed to be indicated by it, proceed from the same cause—just as a rainbow <note>original: "iris"</note> sometimes portends clear weather, not because it *makes* the weather clear, but because the cause of the rainbow is also the cause of the clear weather. But no physical cause can be considered superior to the sky that could produce the dispositions of both the heavens and the lower world.

<margin>
Divine minds are not the causes of lower events without the efficiency of the sky. First reason. Second. Third. Fourth.
</margin>
Or will the remaining cause be incorporeal? For perhaps it might seem possible to say that human events are caused by the divine minds <note>the angels or spiritual movers of the spheres</note> that revolve the celestial bodies; and while these events are happening, they are indicated to us by the very state and position of the heaven they move, acting as if by certain nods or gestures. Truly, whoever says this is very close to the fables of the poets. How will he avoid the following problem: that things are being done by divine minds which men themselves cannot do without the guilt of a crime? Such a view implies that these minds urge and impel one man to murder, another to adultery, and another to theft. I set aside the fact that all philosophy find it abominable that physical things should be produced by incorporeal causes without an intermediate physical cause intervening. Furthermore, why are those born at different hours born with different fates, if the cause and author of fate is considered to be the mover of the sky—who is immobile, always equal to himself, and like himself—rather than the position of the sky, which varies by the hour?

<margin>
Thomas.
</margin>
Finally, as <term>Thomas [Aquinas]</term> <note>the 13th-century theologian whose views on astrology were highly influential</note> argues: when the effects of the same cause indicate each other, they proceed from the same principle in the same manner. But the motion of the sky and the disposition of lower bodies and affairs are not from superior causes in the same manner: the former is by an immutable and necessary order, while the latter is by a variable order that falls contingently on either side, according to the nature of the things that are moved and governed. Divine principles do not change these natures but preserve them; otherwise, they would not be guiding nature, but destroying it. Therefore, the sky cannot signify lower things except insofar as a cause indicates its own effect. Thus, those who, defeated by reason, confess it is not the cause but still contend it is a sign, do not know what they are saying.

<margin>
Thomas.
</margin>
And Thomas Aquinas, a man of the weightiest judgment who was not accustomed to asserting anything rashly, pronounced this with certainty in his *Summa Theologica*. This "sign-without-cause" argument might be said of comets, shooting stars, and other such things that occur in the upper air, as things stirred up by the stars that produce them; they do not *make* what their cause is about to do, but they signify it. But this can in no way be said of the stars themselves, since, as we were saying, no superior physical cause is found above them.

<margin>
Second main reason.
</margin>
But even those who think this way introduce the necessity of fate, whether they want to or not. For if the stars were the *causes* of lower things, it might happen that what their influence seeks to produce is not achieved, because either the matter resists or a particular cause diverts the general influence. But if they are *signs*, since they were instituted by nature for the purpose of signifying (which is their true nature), their signification will be as true as their nature. Otherwise, why were they instituted by God to signify, if his works—which are perfect—deceive and lie? If they do not lie, then what is signified by them must necessarily happen.

<margin>
Third.
</margin>
Finally, if they are numbered among causes, it is not repugnant to their condition to be in that order of causes which can be hindered, changed, or overcome. But if they are considered signs, they cannot be held among lies, lest he who described the marks and "letters" of the future in the celestial volumes (as they call them) be either deceptive or ignorant.

<margin>
Fourth.
</margin>
Lastly, if the sky does not indicate by acting, but indicates what it does not do, it remains that it must indicate what *other* causes do. Therefore, it indicates either what all causes do, or only what some do. If only what some do: why, I ask, does it indicate the works of these and not those? If it indicates all equally, then there are no remaining causes through which that which is demonstrated might be prevented from happening. Therefore, what was portended will necessarily occur. If we say this, however...

<sig>cij</sig>

<summary>Pico argues that the heavens cannot act as signs for human events if they are not also the causes of those events, as natural signs must share a causal link with what they signify. He further contends that treating stars as infallible divine signs would eliminate human free will by making the future a matter of absolute necessity.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s Ninth Argument against the astrologers. He is currently dismantling the specific branches of astrology, moving from general principles to the specific practice of "interrogations"—the habit of asking an astrologer a question and having them "read" the answer from the sky at that exact moment.</meta>

# NINTH ARGUMENT

<margin>Astrologers have denied the necessity of fate.</margin>
We shall oppose not only the truth, as we have demonstrated elsewhere, but even the astrologers themselves. For the Egyptians, Ptolemy, and every one of the most celebrated astrologers have always thoroughly denied the necessity of fate <note>original: "fati necessitatem," the idea that every event is strictly predetermined and unavoidable</note>. They declare this to be their view especially in their treatises on <term>interrogations</term> <note>the practice of seeking answers to specific questions by looking at the stars at the moment the question is asked</note>. Since they say that not every question is "legitimate," but only those which proceed from an impulse of the soul moved by the heavens—and since they concede that very few such impulses exist, as most are born from our own reason and planning—they openly declare that they do not admit the necessity of fate. Furthermore, if fate were introduced, the entire utility of astrology would perish, as its value is placed primarily in this: that by foreseeing evils we might avoid them, and by foreseeing good things we might confirm and increase them. Finally, if the stars are merely signs and not the causes of lower things, that part of astrology commonly called <term>elections</term> <note>the practice of "electing" or choosing the best time to start a project based on the stars</note> is removed beyond controversy; for in that practice, one seeks celestial favor to bring something about, not merely indicators for the sake of curiosity.

<margin>Thirteenth.</margin>
### Chapter Thirteen. Whether the stars are signs or causes, that part of astrology concerning interrogations is void.

<margin>The foundation of astrological questions.</margin>
Whichever opinion the astrologers might prefer—that is, whether they want the stars to be the causes of lower things or merely signs and not causes—that branch concerning interrogations, which they use most frequently, would necessarily be utterly destroyed. For the foundation of that branch is this: that our minds are moved by a celestial <term>constellation</term>, at least in the part of our imagination. They claim that when the mind is incited from there to a desire to know some thing, and then consults an astrologer, the configuration of the heavens at the hour of consultation portends that which the seeker desired to know. Therefore, they claim the astrologer can give true answers to those asking about all things for which a question is made. Let us then ask those who claim to resolve every question: are the stars only signs of lower things, or are they also causes that signify by *acting*? If they are signs only, then the impulse of our desire does not come from the stars; rather, just as those who hold that opinion say other things happen by their own proper causes (even if they are indicated by the stars), so too the movement of desire would take its origin and strength not from a celestial constellation, but from the power of imagination itself, our own choice, the seeking power of the mind, and things from the outside that provoke the sense and the soul. But if they respond that the stars are causes and that lower things are signified by them just as an effect is demonstrated by its cause, how on earth will they defend the idea that the constellation appearing at the hour of consultation is the *cause* of those things about which the astrologer answers the questioner? Since those things may have happened long ago, or may never happen at all, they ought to have no cause in the present sky. Truly, Mars will be in the west, which will not allow them to be told the truth! But if they can obtain from him that they might at least hear the truth, I shall respond to these questions with the absolute truth, even for those who do not ask. It seemed to the astrologers that too little glory and—what urged them more—too little profit was being gained if they pronounced fates to each person only from the time of their birth <note>original: "genituræ," or nativity</note> or from the annual revolution of the year. For to understand these, it was only necessary to visit them once in a lifetime or only once a year. Yet our curiosity desires to know many things daily, about which they could answer nothing. From this, much authority among the unlearned—

<margin>A very witty mockery.</margin>
<margin>Where this branch of astrology was born.</margin>

<column-break/>

—and much money for the practitioners was being lost. Hence, they persuaded themselves (or at least others) that they could clearly foresee whatever was asked from the hour of the question—provided that the one asking was moved by a "natural impulse" and not by their own choice. In this way, of course, they beautifully vindicate themselves from every infamy of falsehood. For if what they answered was refuted by the reality of the event, they would say it was not because the astrologer was untrue, but because the question was not "efficacious" <note>the astrologer's "get out of jail free" card: blaming the questioner's lack of sincerity for a wrong prediction</note>. If the answers matched the events, what could then stand in the way of having oracles here on earth? With these arts and fallacies, this breed of men mocks the unskilled; for nothing more discordant with reason can be said or thought than what they have devised concerning this fallacy of interrogation. For even if I grant them that my desire to know about someone who is absent comes from the heaven, what kind of logic is it that the configuration of the sky at the very hour I explain this desire to an astrologer should show me the state of that absent person? Where does this agreement or alliance between our desire and the thing we wish to know come from?

<margin>The response refuted.</margin>
If they should perhaps answer that the same celestial power which effects that thing far away from us also tweaks our mind and, as it were, warns us of the thing being done—firstly, it would follow that these desires would only seize us at the very moment the event itself occurs. And yet they think that "efficacious" interrogations can be made about things that happened long ago, or will happen a long time in the future, or will never happen at all. Furthermore, if we say this, we should not look at the configuration of the sky at the hour we question the astrologer, but at the very first moment the lust for questioning invaded us. For surely it is that same or similar constellation which both produces the event and arouses in us the desire to learn of it. Certainly, if one must be "rationally insane," it would be far more rational to say that than what the astrologers say—namely, that we must observe the time of the inquiry, not the time when the care of inquiring first solicited us. Then, as we were saying, if any kinship or consensus can exist between these things, it can only be if the thing that happened and our desire can both be seen to refer to the same or a similar constellation. But the hour in which we actually consult the astrologer can vary for a thousand reasons: we might meet the astrologer later or sooner; his house might be far from us; someone might delay us on the road; and other things of this sort occurring by chance which postpone the hour of the question. Why would a question made then answer more certainly? Moreover, these delays change the configuration of the heaven upon which he is to answer, making it one thing and then another. But the astrologers care nothing for these things; it has long been familiar to them to always say and feel things that have no reason or stability at all.

### Chapter Fourteen. Divine miracles are neither performed nor signified by the heaven, but the nature of miracles is indicated from natural things.

Truly, I wish they were only insane to this extent, and did not also think that divine miracles—which exceed the capacity of all nature—were performed by the natural rays of the superior bodies. We have shown above that they wallow in this error, declaring that divine religion is referred by them to the power of the stars; and...

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s critique of astrology, specifically focusing on how astrologers wrongly attempt to claim divine miracles and sacred history as products of the stars. In the previous section, he argued that the stars are merely signs, not causes, and here he extends that to show that even as signs, they cannot predict the supernatural.</meta>

# AGAINST ASTROLOGY BOOK IV.

<margin>Greatest madness.</margin>
<margin>A book against the impious.</margin>
...law: both that which God once promulgated to the Hebrew people through Moses, and that which Christ later revealed to the world through the apostles. Thus, they have also ascribed to their own constellations that Great Flood <note>original: "eluuiolnem," referring to the Deluge</note> in the time of Noah, and other divine miracles of this kind which sacred history brings forth. In this matter, they undoubtedly appear more like children than those who simply refuse to concede that these events ever happened. For the astrologer believes that such things occurred as they are narrated, yet claims they were effected by natural causes. No greater madness can be imagined than to think that something done *above* nature was achieved by the *forces* of nature. Moreover, we have proved, in disputing against the impious, that the Divine Law is among those things which exceed the powers of nature. The same can easily be demonstrated regarding the universal Cataclysm <note>The Great Flood</note>, since nothing is more contrary to nature than that she should engineer her own destruction. Therefore, nature would never inflict such an injury upon herself, from which she could not assert her own recovery by her own power. If it could not happen through a natural course—that the waters should surpass the peaks of all the mountains by fifteen cubits, or that Noah with his family and every kind of animal, enclosed within a single ark for twelve months, should escape that shipwreck—then it was certainly not the purpose of nature to submerge the entire earth in a flood of water for the destruction of all living things. And if these things do not happen because of the heavens, they cannot be foreseen from the heavens either. Since the heavens do not *make* these things happen, they do not *signify* them either, as we proved a little while ago.

<margin><unclear>To elude our reasoning</unclear></margin>
Nevertheless, they have a specific logic for why such things are not portended by the stars, even if we were to grant that other things which do not exceed the capacity of nature are either caused or indicated by the heavens. For, as we have declared elsewhere, the order of things instituted by God for the natural course is so enclosed within its own limits, and so separated from those things which happen through divine power and will *beyond* nature, that if all these supernatural things were removed, nothing would be missing from the nature of things, and nothing would be redundant. The heavens, however, and whatever happens in the heavens in their common course, are among those things which are according to nature. Therefore, if the motion of the stars or the arrangement which is due to them from their natural condition signifies anything in the future, this significance and indication must be held and numbered among natural things.

<margin><unclear>This also happens if the astrologer imagines signs for waters that are outside nature</unclear></margin>
But if we say that any of these signs portend things that will happen *above* nature, an absurdity follows: if God were to leave nature to its own conditions and do nothing above it, then nature itself would be found false and lying. In such a case, God would have instituted something in the stars in vain and superfluously, since there would still be signs in the stars of future things which would nevertheless never happen—because the things signified are things beyond nature which we supposed were removed. The signs themselves are things according to nature; it must be said that even if supernatural events are removed, the signs are neither taken away nor deprived of any perfection due to them. Therefore, it is not the case that if God disposed from eternity to perform some miracle, he inserted the indications of that miracle into natural things in such a way that this significance belonged to the natural logic of the stars. Rather, He willed that natural signs should signify natural things, while preceding miracles should signify miracles. He willed that the Cataclysm, which was to happen by the miracle of divine justice, be signified to the world by Noah, who was divinely inspired and to be divinely preserved. The liberation of the Hebrews from Egypt and the giving of the law to them were testified to more by the miracles performed through the divine rod of Moses than by the magicians <note>original: "magis," here likely referring to the court magicians of Pharaoh</note> and astrologers of the Egyptians. The fact that the Promised Land was to be subjected to the people of God, and the wonders God was to perform in it above the laws of nature, was not indicated by some natural configuration of the heavens, but by the most rapid motion of the sun being restrained by the hand 

<column-break/>

of the Creator. I shall pass over the crossing of the Jordan on dry feet and the walls of the city destroyed by the sound of trumpets; yet the life of Hezekiah, prolonged by divine power, was demonstrated not by a favorable irradiation of Jupiter running its course in the correct order, but by the miracle of the sun moving backward. The prodigy of the Word made flesh and the Virgin's child-bearing were announced when the oracles of minds divinely inspired beyond the nature of the human mind spoke; when a thousand prodigies were testified to in the celestial and earthly bodies themselves while that immense new covenant for the Lord arose. And when He was failing on the cross, the Sun failed while the Moon was full, contrary to the order of nature. By these signs, divine miracles are both demonstrated and confirmed—things which can neither be done by the natural state of affairs, nor is it fitting for them to be indicated by it.

---

### Chapter XV. That no constellation can be understood as the Star of the Magi: and an explanation of certain scriptures which might seem to the unskilled to support astrology.

Now, since we have come to mention the star which showed the Magi the newborn Jesus, it would not be out of place to warn the reader lest he suspect this star somehow favors the opinion of astrologers. As if it were nothing other than a celestial constellation—an index of a born prophet—known and explored by those men from the East who were, as is thought, quite skilled in celestial science. The very letter of the Gospel most evidently leads us away from this error, for speaking of this star it says: *And behold, the star which they had seen in the East went before them, until it came and stood over where the child was.* No one but a madman would think this should be understood as the stars or configurations of the sky <note>Because actual stars do not move independently to guide travelers and then stop over a specific house</note>. That was, therefore, a created and temporary star, not a perpetual and natural one established for that duty by the Creator, through which the birth of the King of the Jews was to be signified. Perhaps the Magi understood it in the same way they were later warned in their sleep to avoid Herod and return to their country by another way.

<margin>Paul.</margin>
But we must likewise beware lest we be disturbed by certain phrases in the Scriptures: as when we read in Paul that the Son of God was sent "in the fullness of time," or in the Gospel when the Lord says, *Now is your hour and the power of darkness*, and elsewhere, *My hour has not yet come*. For the superstitious man will think that constellations of hours and times are being signified. But you should ask him: when he is hungry, does he think it is "the time for eating"? Whatever the constitution of the heavens might be at that time? And when the body is worn out by hardships, is it "the time for healing"? And when he has slept enough, is it "the time for waking"? If he says all these things have their own time, it is not because of the constellation of that time, but because of the nature of the thing itself which is done, and because of the occasion and opportunity for doing it. So it is with other things which God does above nature, and which men do by their own freedom. Although they require no constellations to happen, it is nonetheless necessary that they happen at *some* time, and more fitting and convenient that they happen at this time rather than that. It was fitting for the Son of God to be sent at the time He was sent; it was not fitting before. The cause is not in the heavens, but in the purpose of God and the requirement of things, about which theologians write much, insofar as they were permitted to penetrate the secret of divine counsel through the indications of Scripture. It was likewise fitting that after He was born, He should not immediately...

He concludes Book IV by refuting Pierre d’Ailly’s attempts to find "natural" components in miracles and begins Book V with a direct attack on the theory of "Great Conjunctions," citing the failed predictions regarding the end of Christianity.</meta>

...slain: but at the time it was expedient, he surrendered himself into the hands of the wicked, and that hour was the power of darkness. The same must be understood in other matters, as is clearly declared to us from a single passage in the Book of Genesis. For there, when God promised the land of promise—so called from the event—to Abraham, He then said: "Know that your seed shall be a stranger in a land not their own, where they shall be afflicted for four hundred years; but in the fourth generation they shall return here." If the text had ended there, the astrologer would boast that the divine promise could not be fulfilled until, after the passage of so many years, a certain heavenly alignment was reached which would bring about that event. But look at what the prophet adds from the person of God: "For the iniquities of the Amorites," He says, "are not yet complete up to the present time." See then, what was being waited for? Not a conjunction of Jupiter and Saturn <note>original: "f. Iouis & Saturni"</note>, or any other stellar constellation, but the fullness of iniquity among the Amorites. By this, divine justice—by whose laws human affairs are governed, not by fatal necessity—would deservedly expel them and introduce the seed of faithful Abraham.

### Chapter XVI. That the powers of nature which are exceeded—even regarding what they contain of nature within themselves—cannot be signaled by the heavens.

<margin>
What Girolamo asked. A reply to the error of Pierre d'Ailly.
</margin>
It has now been sufficiently demonstrated, unless I am mistaken, that divine miracles are neither created nor signaled by the heaven; although, as far as their efficiency is concerned, the very names of these events indicate this, and it requires no further proof. However, very recently, Girolamo Benivieni <note>A Florentine poet and close friend of Pico</note>—a man of sharp and piercing wit—asked: since in those things that happen above nature there is sometimes something that is also natural, could they perhaps be signaled by the stars from that perspective? For instance, if a constellation could not indicate the incarnation of God, could it nonetheless show a "law-giving man" who was about to promulgate good laws? I replied that even in this way, those things cannot be signaled by the stars; nor does it happen in the way that d'Ailly <note>Petrus de Alliaco, or Pierre d'Ailly, a 14th-century cardinal who tried to reconcile astrology with theology</note> thought. For he believed there was no other way to defend those who sought the causes of such miraculous and divine things in the stars from a charge of impiety, unless they said these things depend on heaven not insofar as they are *above* nature, but insofar as there is something natural in them. But he who says this, says nothing. It is just as meaningless as someone who says a man is made by a certain constellation, but that a "rational nature" is not made by it. For if the stars do not create the part of a man that is rational, there is no reason why they should be said to "make a man" any more than a lion. If, therefore, you take away from divine miracles that which is unique to them, and leave only those things they have in common with countless other things, there is no reason for you to so studiously seek a singular cause in the heaven. Indeed, those who investigate the birth <note>original: "genesim"</note> of Jesus do not strive to know why he was in the womb for nine months like other men, or why he was in good physical health, or had long hair, or was poor, or was a Jew—since every mortal life is full of such conditions. Rather, they seek the cause in the stars for those things which were primary and singular in Him, which they believe to be both exceptional and unique. But those works of God are already above nature, not of the heavens: that He was born of a virgin; that He was both man and God; that He was Lord in His own realm yet a stranger in the flesh; that He was a worker of miracles; the rightful Lord of the world; the judge of the living and the dead; the author and dispenser of divine grace; the expeller of idolatry; the conqueror of demons; the author of virtues and the driver-out of vices;

<column-break/>

the peace of the world; the manifester of truth. If you do not seek these things, you seek nothing; if you seek them [in the stars], you seek impiously. Therefore, there is no refuge provided by d'Ailly for astrologers to say that divine miracles are made by the heaven, but "not insofar as they are miracles." For such things cannot even be signaled by the stars for the reason our friend Girolamo was asking: because if the order of things proceeding from God above nature were removed from the equation, these heavenly signs would still remain, pointing to those effects in some part (as we were saying); yet there would be no effect. Therefore, those signs would be vain and deceptive, and it has been demonstrated above that nothing in the nature of the heavens is like that.

## THE DISPUTATIONS OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA AGAINST THE ASTROLOGERS. BOOK V BEGINS.

### Chapter One. That the decrees of astrologers concerning "Great Conjunctions" are usefully refuted; and how deceitful those have been found who wished to judge great changes in lower things through them.

<margin>
Heretical opinion of astrologers.
</margin>
<margin>
It is impossible to know the future through experience by the rules of astrologers.
</margin>
But many are led away from the truth by the fallacy of astrologers who persuade the unskilled that there was never any change of laws, no coming of prophets, no admirable event in human affairs that a "Great Conjunction" <note>A rare alignment of the outer planets, Jupiter and Saturn, believed by medieval astrologers to trigger major historical and religious shifts</note> of the higher stars—especially Saturn and Jupiter—did not precede. Regarding this matter, when they bring it before their colleagues or the more uneducated as if it were a certain and confessed fact in their charts, and running through so many thousands of years, they say: "This is the constellation that caused the Flood; this one produced Moses; this preceded the coming of Jesus; this preceded the law of Muhammad." There is almost no one who is not moved, and who is not forced either to descend into their "science" or at least to harbor some doubt. Therefore, since this profession attacks religion most strongly in this part, I wish to counter this pestilence before we tear up the foundations of the whole art. For the astrologers err so much in this place that even if they were correct in all other things, they could not be defended here. This is not only because they predict things which it is doubtful are subject to the heaven at all, but because the very rules they use in predicting contain the most manifest errors in both history and astrology. Before we show this by reason, experience itself can make it certain enough for those who may not fully see the force of our arguments. For all who wished to divine anything regarding the failure of laws or the change or success of things from these constellations have been found to be liars and deceivers. Long ago, when the faith of Christ began to sprout, the "mathematicians" <note>A common term for astrologers in the late Middle Ages and Renaissance</note> said it would not last more than 400 years; yet from its beginning, the one thousand four hundred and ninety-fourth year is already passing.
<margin>
Now the year 1494 has passed. The error of Albumasar.
</margin>
Albumasar <note>An influential 9th-century Persian astrologer</note>, either the author or the inventor of this error, said this same law—that is, our own—would remain for 1,460 years, because, forsooth, there are that many years in what they call the "Greatest Years of the Sun." Those years have passed, and the law itself has not passed; for indeed, "heaven and earth shall pass away, but the words of the Lord shall not pass away." Nor however...

# AGAINST ASTROLOGY, BOOK IV.

<meta>Catchword: du-</meta>

<margin>Abraham’s Error.</margin>
...yet he predicted more truths concerning his own law, that is, the law of Muhammad <note>Muhammad, the prophet of Islam.</note>. Abraham the Jew <note>Likely referring to Abraham ibn Ezra, a famous 12th-century scholar and astrologer.</note> said, based on astrological observation, that their Messiah would arrive in the year of Christ 1464. He claimed <term>q̄</term> <gloss>that</gloss> at that time, the same positioning of the stars would first return as that under which Moses once led the people out of Egypt and gave the law to those he had led. I was born in the year immediately preceding that one, and since I am now in my thirtieth year, I have learned by experience the falsehood of that prediction.

<margin>Arnald’s Error.</margin>
Arnald the Spaniard <note>Arnald of Villanova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist.</note>, a noble physician indeed but slightly too prone to superstition based on astrological vanity, threatened us with the arrival of the Antichrist in the year of grace 1345, along with many other additions. From that time, more than one hundred and forty-eight years have already flowed by, and as of yet, there is no Antichrist, except for the kind that were already numerous in the time of the Apostles. How often have younger men announced to us the arrival of a false prophet based on some conjunction of the superior planets? This was especially the case regarding the conjunction of Jupiter and Saturn in Scorpio ten years ago; nevertheless, no false prophet has yet appeared to the world except for those same men.

<margin>The error of d’Ailly and the astrologers of his time.</margin>
Pierre d'Ailly <note>Alliacensis, a prominent 15th-century theologian and cardinal who tried to reconcile astrology with theology.</note> himself writes that in the year the General Council of Constance <note>Held from 1414 to 1418 to end the Western Schism.</note> was celebrated, astrologers predicted there would be no future peace in the Church. Instead, they claimed the destruction of religion and dissensions within it were signaled, because Jupiter was retrograde in the first house in the figure of the year. Yet that great schism—greater than any which had ever been in the Church, and more lasting, having already been confirmed for forty years—was first extinguished in that very year, with the Church's customary peace and tranquility restored. This certainly should have been enough to move d'Ailly himself to no longer place any further faith in that vanity; for he himself, perhaps persuaded by them, feared that the schism would bring the Antichrist to us shortly thereafter. There were other predictions of theirs regarding laws and sects that I might recount, which were subsequently proved false by the outcome itself; but I think these will suffice, as there are no others in that art of such great authority as these are held to be among all astrologers. We have declared their predictions to be refuted by the experiments of reality; now let us descend to the arguments.

---

### Chapter II. By what powers astrologers pass judgment on greater matters: and a rejection of the Great Cycles.

<margin>Where astrologers especially aim in their investigation of things. The opinion of astrologers concerning Great Cycles.</margin>
Astrologers are accustomed to investigate great changes in lower things by four primary ways through the superior planets—especially Jupiter and Saturn when they are together, which they call a "Great Conjunction." They also look through Great Orbs <note>Also called "Great Cycles" or "Firdaria," these are long-term planetary periods believed to govern historical eras.</note>, through Saturnian revolutions, and through the progression <term>atq;</term> <gloss>and</gloss> recession of the eighth sphere. We shall show all these ways to be irrational, false, and non-viable. From this, we shall achieve not only what we first sought here—that the impious temerity of what they publish concerning religion and laws be proven false—but also every judgment concerning the great changes of the world will be weakened. I shall begin, however, with the refutation of the Great Orbs and the revolutions which they call Saturnian; so that once these are rejected—which requires less effort—the entire remaining dispute of the present book may wander freely against the Great Conjunctions.

<margin>Under which cycle we live according to them.</margin>
They imagine that each of the planets, and likewise each of the signs, holds empire over the world for three hundred and sixty years. When these are finished, they say a new "Great Orb" begins, over which both the planet closest to the previous one and the sign which follows next after the previous sign preside equally. Thus, whatever the nature of the dominant sign and star may be, such things occur in that space of years; and when a new Orb is begun, many things in the lower world are also renewed, and the condition of our affairs is always changed according to the nature of the ruler. Then, if anyone asks them where we are, or in which Orb we now live—that is, under which ruler—they answer: under Leo and the Moon. They prove it in this way:

<margin>Aoniar</margin>
For Aoniar <note>An Arabic source, possibly Al-Andarzaghar.</note> writes in his book on nativities that a new Great Orb began at the time of that conjunction of Jupiter and Saturn by which they claim the Great Flood <note>The "cathaclysmus" or biblical Deluge.</note> was pre-signaled. That conjunction preceded the Flood by two hundred and seventy-nine years, as they say. Aoniar says that Saturn presided over this Orb among the planets, and Cancer among the signs; which Albumasar <note>Abu Ma'shar (787–886), a highly influential Persian astrologer.</note> also said in the first book of *Great Conjunctions*, the first distinction.

<margin>Aoniar [and] Albumasar</margin>
Therefore, using these things as the hinge of their entire calculation, they conclude from the number of years he provided that the Lord Jesus was born when the one hundred and forty-first year of that Orb was turning. This would be the fifteenth cycle since the one we mentioned under which the Flood occurred, over which Leo presides among the signs and the Moon among the planets, and which is to be ended in the year of grace 1659. This is the entire opinion of the astrologers; you will not see anyone who, in public prognostications of the years, if he makes mention of the Great Orb, does not appoint Leo and the Moon as the rulers and governors of the world. I could object here to how slight a conjecture moves them to call a space of as many years as they have imagined parts of the heavens a "Great Orb," and by what lack of reason the governing power of a single planet is said to endure for so many years, especially that of a lower planet. Nevertheless, nothing of the sort was ever devised by Ptolemy nor by any of the ancients; rather, it is a fiction of the Arabs and the moderns. But leaving these things aside, let us first press them with necessary reasons which they cannot avoid if they wish to stand by their own principles and not renounce their dogma.

<margin>Reasons to be brought forward: First, Second, Third.</margin>
Let them tell me, therefore: if these Great Orbs are to be established, do they make the beginning of a new Orb at the very first constitution of the world (upon which all agree), or do they not? If I say they do not, what could they say that is more absurd? If they do, I shall now rescind by mathematical deduction whatever they have determined above regarding Great Orbs, showing that it is impossible for those things they were saying to be true if the beginnings of the new Orbs commenced with the constitution of the world.

<margin>Albumasar</margin>
For Albumasar, upon whose authority they chiefly lean, counts two thousand two hundred and twenty-eight full years from the beginning of the world to the Flood.

<margin>Eusebius</margin>
Although Eusebius’s <note>Eusebius of Caesarea, a 4th-century historian known for his chronological tables.</note> calculation exceeds this number by sixteen years, it makes no difference what we say, since in disputing with astrologers we use their own opinions especially. Let it be established, therefore, that the number of years from Adam to the Flood according to the opinion of Albumasar (against whom we dispute) is clear from that conjunction which they say pre-signified the Flood; and since the new Orb began at the same time, there remain one thousand nine hundred and forty-seven years back to the creation of the world, since the conjunction itself preceded the Flood, as we said, by two hundred and seventy-nine years. Let us therefore divide that number by the number of the Great Orb: that is, by three hundred and sixty parts. It will be plain that five full Great Orbs are composed therefrom, and then there remain one hundred and forty-seven undivided years. Therefore, the beginning of a Great Orb must necessarily be set in the year of the world 1408. If this number of years is part of another preceding Orb, it must necessarily be said that the years of that Orb passed...

->DISPUTATIONS<-

...died; but at the time it was expedient, he surrendered himself to the hands of the impious, and that was the hour and the power of darkness <note>A reference to Luke 22:53: "But this is your hour, and the power of darkness."</note>. The same must be understood in other matters, as is clearly declared to us from a single passage in the Book of Genesis. For there, when God promises the land of promise—so named from the fact—to Abraham, He then says: "Know that your seed shall be a stranger in a land not their own, where they shall be afflicted for four hundred years; but in the fourth generation they shall return here." <note>See Genesis 15:13–16.</note> If only this much had been written, the astrologer might mockingly claim that the divine promise could not be fulfilled until that span of years had passed to reach a certain celestial disposition that was to bring about that event. But look at what the prophet adds from the person of God: "For," He says, "the iniquities of the Amorites are not yet full up to the present time." See, therefore, what was being waited for? Not a conjunction of Jupiter and Saturn, or any other stellar constellation, but the fullness of iniquity in the Amorites. By this, divine justice—by whose laws human affairs are governed, not by fatal necessity—would deservedly expel them and introduce the seed of faithful Abraham.

### Chapter XVI. That things which exceed the powers of nature cannot be signified by the heavens, even in regard to the natural elements they contain within themselves.

<margin>What he sought. Jerome to Pico. Pierre d'Ailly's error.</margin>

It has now been sufficiently demonstrated, unless I am mistaken, that divine miracles are neither caused nor signified by the heavens; although as far as their efficacy is concerned, their very names indicate this, and it needs no proof. However, very recently Jerome Benivieni <note>Girolamo Benivieni (1453–1542), a Florentine poet and close friend of Pico.</note>, a man of sharp and perceptive intellect, asked: since in these things that happen above nature there is sometimes something natural, could they perhaps be signified by the stars from that perspective? For instance, if a constellation could not indicate the incarnation of God, could it nevertheless show a law-giving man who would promulgate good laws? I replied that even in this way, those things cannot be signified by the stars, nor—as Pierre d’Ailly <note>Pierre d’Ailly (1350–1420), a French cardinal and theologian who tried to reconcile astrology with Christianity.</note> thought—could they be caused by them. For he thought there was no other way to defend from a charge of impiety those who seek the causes of such miraculous and divine things in the stars, than by saying that these things depend on the heavens, not insofar as they are above nature, but insofar as there is something natural in them. But what he says is nothing. Just as he says nothing who claims a man is made by a constellation, but that a rational nature is not made by it; for if it does not make in the man that which is rational, there is no reason why it should be said to make a man more than a lion. Therefore, if you take away from divine miracles what is proper to them, and leave only those things which they have in common with countless other things, there is no reason why you should so studiously seek a singular cause for the effect in the heavens. But surely those who investigate the birth of Jesus do not strive to know why He was in the womb for nine months like other men; why He was in good bodily condition; why He had long hair; why He was poor; why He was a Jew; since these conditions abound in the lives of all mortals. Rather, they seek the cause in the stars for those things which were chief and singular in Him, and which they think are also chief and singular; but those are works of God above nature, not of the heavens: <gloss>that</gloss> He was born of a virgin; <gloss>that</gloss> He was man and God; <gloss>that</gloss> He was Lord in His own realm and a stranger in the flesh; <gloss>that</gloss> He was the worker of miraculous deeds; <gloss>that</gloss> He was by right the Lord of the world; <gloss>that</gloss> He was the judge of the living and the dead; <gloss>that</gloss> He was the author and dispenser of divine grace; <gloss>that</gloss> He was the expeller of idolatry, the conqueror of demons, the author of virtues, and the expeller of vices;

<column-break/>

the peace of the world, and the manifester of truth. If you do not seek these things, you seek nothing; if you do seek them, you seek impiously. Therefore, there is no refuge provided by Pierre d’Ailly for astrologers to say that divine miracles are caused by the heavens, though not insofar as they are miracles. Nor can they be signified by the stars for that reason (as our friend Jerome was asking of us). For if the order of things that proceed from God above nature is removed, there will still remain, as we said above, these signs of the heaven, pointing in some way (as we were saying) to those effects; but the effect will no longer exist. Therefore, those signs will be vain and fallacious, and it has been demonstrated above that nothing of the sort exists in celestial nature.

<margin>Reduction to the impossible.</margin>

## THE DISPUTATIONS OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA
## AGAINST THE ASTROLOGERS.
## BOOK V BEGINS.

### Chapter I. That the decrees of astrologers concerning great conjunctions are usefully refuted, and how they are caught out as liars who wished to judge the great changes of lower things through them.

<margin>The heretical opinion of the astrologers.</margin>

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'S' showing a man's head in profile inside a floral border.</image-desc>

But many are led away from this truth by the fallacy of the astrologers, who persuade the unlearned that there has never been a change of laws, no coming of prophets, and no wonderful event in human affairs that a great conjunction of the superior stars—especially Saturn and Jupiter <note>A "Great Conjunction" occurs when Jupiter and Saturn align. Medieval astrologers believed these cycles dictated the rise and fall of religions and empires.</note>—did not precede. Regarding this matter, when they bring forth tables before those present, or onlookers, or the more unrefined, as if speaking of a certain and admitted fact, and running through so many thousands of years, they say: "Behold, this is the constellation that caused the Flood; this one gave birth to Moses; this one preceded the coming of Jesus; this one preceded the law of Muhammad." There is almost no one who is not moved, and who is not forced either to descend into their science or at least to doubt. Therefore, since this profession attacks religion most in this area, I wish to counter this pestilence before we pull up the very foundations of the art itself. For the astrologers err so much in this place that even if they thought correctly in other matters, they could not be defended here. This is not only because they predict things which it is doubtful are subject to the heavens, but because the very rules they use in predicting contain the most manifest errors in both history and astrology. Before we show this by reasons, experience itself can make it certain for those who will less clearly perceive the force of reasons: for all who have wished to divine anything from these constellations regarding the failing of laws and their change or success have been found to be false and liars. Once, when the faith of Christ began to sprout, the mathematicians <note>In this context, "mathematici" usually refers to astrologers.</note> said it would not last more than 1,464 years; yet from its beginning, the one thousand four hundred and ninety-fourth year has already passed. Abu Ma'shar <note>Albumasar (787–886 AD), an influential Persian astrologer whose works were widely read in Latin translation.</note>, either the author or the inventor of this error, said that this same law—that is, ours—would remain for 1,460 years, because, forsooth, there are that many years in what they call the greatest years of the sun. Those years have passed, and the law itself has not passed; for indeed, heaven and earth shall pass away, but the words of the Lord shall not pass away. Nor yet...

<margin>Abraham’s Error.</margin> ...nevertheless, he predicted more truth regarding his own law—that is, the law of Muhammad <note>original: "Maumetis"</note>. Abraham the Jew, in the year of Christ 1464, claimed their Messiah would come based on astrological observation. He argued that the specific position of the stars under which Moses had once led the people out of Egypt and given them the Law was then due to return for the first time. I, having been born in the year immediately preceding his prediction and being now in my thirtieth year, have learned by experience the falsehood of that prediction. <margin>Arnaldus’s Error.</margin> Arnaldus of Spain <note>Arnaldus de Villanova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist who wrote on the coming of the Antichrist.</note>, a truly noble physician but somewhat too prone to superstition through astrological vanity, along with many other additions, threatened us with the arrival of the Antichrist in the year of grace 1345. More than 148 years have now flowed by since that time, and still no Antichrist has appeared, except such as were already many in the time of the Apostles. How often have the younger astrologers announced the coming of a false prophet to us based on some conjunction of the superior planets—especially from that conjunction of Jupiter and Saturn in Scorpio ten years ago! Yet, no false prophet has appeared to the world besides those already present. Pierre d'Ailly <note>original: "Alliacensis"; Pierre d'Ailly (1351–1420) was a Cardinal who attempted to harmonize astrology with theology.</note> himself writes <margin>Error of d'Ailly and the astrologers of his time.</margin> that in the year the General Council of Constance <note>Held 1414–1418 to end the Great Schism in the Church.</note> was celebrated, astrologers predicted there would be no peace in the Church. They claimed the destruction of religion and dissensions were signaled because Jupiter was retrograde in the first house in the chart of the year. And yet, that great schism—than which none was ever greater or more long-lasting in the Church, having been confirmed for forty years—was finally extinguished in that very year, and the accustomed peace and tranquility were restored to the Church. This certainly should have been enough to move d'Ailly himself to no longer place any further faith in that vanity; he himself, perhaps persuaded by them, had feared that the schism would bring us the Antichrist shortly thereafter. There were other predictions of theirs regarding laws and sects which I could recount that were subsequently refuted by the actual outcome; but I think these will suffice, as there are no others in that art of such great authority as these men are held to be among all astrologers. I have shown their predictions to be refuted by actual experience; now let us descend to the arguments.

### Chapter II. By what powers astrologers judge major affairs; and the rejection of the "Great Circles."

<margin>The ways astrologers especially tend toward the investigation of things. The opinion of astrologers concerning the Great Circles.</margin> Astrologers are accustomed to track the great changes of lower things through four main ways involving the superior planets—especially Jupiter and Saturn when they are together, which they call a **Great Conjunction**. They also use "Great Circles" <note>Cycles of 360 years where a planet and a sign rule human history.</note>, Saturnian revolutions, and the "accession and recession" <note>A medieval theory of the oscillation of the equinoxes, also called trepidation.</note> of the eighth sphere. I shall show all these ways to be irrational, false, and dead ends. From this, we shall not only achieve what we first sought—to prove that the impious claims they broadcast with such temerity regarding religion and laws are false—but every judgment concerning the great changes of the world will also be weakened. I shall begin with the refutation of the Great Circles and the revolutions they call Saturnian, so that by rejecting these lesser works, the entire remaining dispute of this book may move freely against the Great Conjunctions. They imagine that each of the planets, and likewise each of the signs, holds dominion over the world for 360 years. When these are finished, they say a new Great Circle begins, over which both the planet closest to the previous one and the sign that follows the previous sign likewise preside. And so, whatever the nature of the dominant sign and star is, <column-break/> such things occur in that span of years. When a new circle starts, they claim many things are renewed in lower affairs, and the condition of our world is always changed according to the nature of the ruler. Then, if one asks them where we are now, or in what circle—that is, under which ruler we live—they respond: under **Leo** and the **Moon**. This they prove in the following way. <margin>Abu Ma'shar</margin> For Abu Ma'shar <note>original: "Aoniar," a corruption of the name Abu Ma'shar, the influential Persian astrologer.</note> writes in his *Book of Nativities* that a new Great Circle began at the time of that conjunction of Jupiter and Saturn by which they claim the Great Flood <note>original: "cathaclismum"</note> was foreshadowed. That conjunction preceded the Flood, as they say, by 279 years. <margin>Abu Ma'shar, Albumasar.</margin> Abu Ma'shar says that Saturn presided over this circle among the planets, and Cancer among the signs; which Albumasar <note>The same author as above; Pico uses both names found in his sources.</note> also said in the first book of *Great Conjunctions*, first distinction. Taking these things as the hinge of their entire calculation, they conclude from the number of years he provided that the Lord Jesus was born when the 141st year of that circle was turning. This circle was the fifteenth from the one we mentioned under which the Flood occurred; Leo would rule among the signs and the Moon among the planets, ending in the year of grace 1659. This is the consensus of the astrologers. You will not see any of them, in their public year-prophecies, make mention of the Great Circles without establishing Leo and the Moon as the rulers and governors of the world. I could here object to how flimsy a conjecture moves them to call a span of as many years as they have invented parts of the heaven a "Great Circle," and how it is said by no reason that the governing power of a single planet lasts through so many years—especially an inferior planet. Furthermore, nothing of the sort was ever devised by Ptolemy or any of the ancients, but it is a fiction of the Arabs and the moderns. But setting these aside, let us first press them with necessary reasons which they cannot avoid if they wish to stand by their own principles and not renounce their dogma. <margin>Reasons to be brought forward: First, Second, Third.</margin> Let them tell me then: if these Great Circles must be established, do they make the beginning of a new circle at the very first constitution of the world (upon which everyone agrees), or do they not? If they say they do not, what could be more absurd? If they say they do, I shall now strike down whatever they determined above regarding Great Circles by mathematical deduction, showing it is impossible for their claims to be true if the start of the new circles began with the constitution of the world. <margin>Albumasar.</margin> For Albumasar, the author they chiefly rely upon, counts 2,228 total years from the beginning of the world to the Flood. <margin>Eusebius.</margin> Although Eusebius’s calculation exceeds this number by sixteen years, it makes no difference what we say, since in disputing with astrologers we should use their own opinions most of all. Let it be established, therefore, that the number of years from Adam to the Flood—according to the opinion of Albumasar against whom we dispute—is set; and since a new circle began 279 years before the Flood, that leaves 1,947 years from the creation of the world until that circle began. Let us therefore divide that number by the number of the Great Circle—that is, by 360 parts. It will be clear that five full Great Circles are formed therefrom, with 147 years remaining undivided. Therefore, the beginning of a Great Circle must necessarily be set in the year of the world 1408. If this number of years is part of another preceding circle, it will necessarily have to be said that the years of the circle passed...
