# DISPUTATIONS

<column-break/>

<margin>How delirious the astrologers are.</margin>
...one hundred and thirteen years before they even existed—that is, before the very beginnings of the world itself. From this, it is clear enough that nothing more delirious can be said. But certainly, there is nothing more reckless than this class of men; nothing is more prone, by nature or profession, to lying and deceiving. They invent things for themselves just to make their dogmas cohere and to perform trickery upon the unlearned. This is a product of their malice and vanity. Yet, it always happens by the power of truth that something either false or entirely impossible follows from their claims—or something repugnant to their own dictates. Failing to notice this, these men—who are equally forgetful and deceitful—nevertheless produce and spread these claims; this is clearly a vice of ignorance and of their tradition. We have an example at hand in the very matter we are discussing. To persuade people by any means possible that the Great Flood <note>The biblical Deluge of Noah.</note> proceeded from heaven, they added a childish fiction of a "Great Conjunction." They claimed a "new orb" <note>term: "Orb" (orbis). In this context, it refers to a vast astrological cycle or "Great Year" believed to govern eras of history.</note> began with it, under which the world was to be renewed. To ensure nothing was lacking for the deception, they put Saturn and Cancer in charge of that orb—since the former among the planets and the latter among the signs are considered the authors of moisture and cold. And this

<margin>How slow and ignorant they are.</margin>
indeed, as I said, stems from their malice and vanity. But their stupidity, sluggishness, and ignorance are also apparent: first, because they did not see the delirious consequences of this—such as when the novelty of an "orb" would not actually have the start of a new world—and second, because if Saturn and Cancer presided over that orb, we must necessarily conclude that Mars and Aquarius presided over the first entire orb of the world. They will never be able to defend by any reason why the empire of the world should have begun under those two. For if they said this of the Moon, they might offer some reason, such as her being closest to the Earth; if they cited Saturn for the orb's height, or the Sun for the power of virtue, or Jupiter or Venus for the benevolence of nature, it might stand. But in Mars, they will find no reason why he should deserve the first government of the world. Likewise, there is nothing in Aquarius, since it has no primary prerogative such as Cancer, Libra, and Capricorn are thought to have. But

<margin>How lying and forgetful they are.</margin>
why do we wander through more examples? One can see plainly and clearly from this how lying and forgetful they are. For they say, as we have shown, that Cancer and Saturn presided over that orb before the event of the Flood, because this confirms their dogma that a great inundation of waters proceeded from a moist and cold planet. On the other hand, since it seems fitting that we should begin the government of the world from the Sun among the planets and from Aries among the signs, they say the planet of the world was the Sun, and the sign was Aries. Indeed, Haly Abenzagel <note>Alboazen Haly Abenragel (d. 1037), an Arab astrologer.</note> writes this, and even

<margin>Haly Abenzagel. Albumasar.</margin>
Albumasar <note>Abu Ma'shar (787–886), the most influential astrologer of the Islamic world in the Middle Ages.</note> himself in the first book of *On Great Conjunctions*. And yet, these claims fight against each other so much that they cannot be true at the same time. For since there are five complete "Great Orbs" before the orb of the Flood back to the beginning of the world (or six imperfect ones), whether we count five or rather six, it is impossible for Aries to dominate the first orb while Cancer dominates the fifth or sixth. Or, if the Solar star ruled the first orb, that Saturn should be placed over the orb of the Flood. For if Aries and the Sun presided over the first, then Taurus and Venus presided over the second; Gemini and Mercury over the third; the Moon with Cancer over the fourth; but neither in the fifth nor sixth did Cancer and Saturn rule. Rather, Saturn with Leo ruled the fifth, and Jupiter with Virgo the sixth. How, then, are they not ashamed to leave these writings to posterity—manifest testimonies of such great ignorance or dullness? But the authors of astrology are almost always of this character. So too did some man named Oclination <note>Likely a corruption of a name or a reference to a specific work on "inclinations" or cycles.</note>, inventing other Great Orbs for himself, wish to show that both the

<column-break/>

constitution of the world and the birth of Jesus had the beginnings of a "new orb," and that the same sign—Aries, the head of the signs—presided over both. When this did not otherwise work out for him, he said that 4,320 years must be counted from Adam to Christ. If we count that many, it would indeed be exactly what he wanted. But no history accepts that number! It differs from the Greek and Latin writers by almost nine hundred years, from the Hebrews by five hundred, and from other astrologers even by one thousand one hundred. But he preferred that reality should not be what it was, rather than renounce his beautiful fiction.

<margin>See a very beautiful Aristotelian example.</margin>
They are just like those ancients mentioned by Aristotle: once they had decided that all things were distributed by the number ten, but could not find more than nine spheres in the universe, they said there must necessarily be another "Counter-Earth" <note>original: "antichthon". A hypothetical planet in Pythagorean cosmology.</note> so that their number ten might be filled. This is done in a sort of imitation of divine wisdom, which does not shape itself to things, but rather shapes the truth of things to itself. Finally, we must not pass over the fact that if these Great Orbs were a necessary reality (which the astrologers claim), then their own theory would have to be false, since they err so greatly in calculating them. For they think that this current cycle—which they claim is in its 195th year—is the nineteenth orb from the first, and the fourteenth from the one under which the Flood occurred; for this reason, they place Leo and the Moon in charge of it. But this cannot be unless we count 

<margin>Our true calculation of the years from the beginning of the world.</margin>
6,838 years from the world to us. This exceeds the true calculation of years by more than 1,400 years, as we have proven in our treatise *On the True Calculation of Time*. And even if we follow other histories—namely the Latins, who calculate more years—we still find fewer than those these men scrape together to complete their "orbs," since no history exceeds 6,700 years or thereabouts. Yet they are caught adding nearly 140 years to that number to defend their arrangement of orbs, which I think is sufficiently refuted even for those who are not experts.

### Chapter III. That the Saturnian revolutions found by Albumasar contradict both history and reason.

It remains to speak of the Saturnian revolutions. These seem to have been invented by Albumasar alone; those after him do not use them much. But let us see what they are, what moved Albumasar to invent them, and how much he erred in these (as is his custom). When Saturn has completed ten periods—which takes about three hundred years—he thinks great things then happen in human affairs. He was moved to this conjecture because in his other histories he sometimes found that something remarkable happened after this number of years. From this, he established the dogma that ten revolutions of Saturn bring a change to inferior <note>Earthly/sublunary</note> things. But look how he erred in this historical conjecture itself. He says that 300 years after Alexander [the Great], Aielasor son of Bel appeared and established the Persians; and after another 300 years, the leader Jesus (that is, our Lord) appeared. By this reasoning, there would be

<margin>Years from Alexander to Christ.</margin>
600 years from Jesus to Alexander. This is established beyond all controversy as being utterly false, since no history counts even 400 years between Christ and Alexander; even Alphonsus <note>King Alfonso X of Castile, sponsor of the Alphonsine Tables.</note> in his astronomical tables counts no more than 311. Let us now see how these principal...

# AGAINST THE ASTROLOGERS, BOOK VI

<margin>An attack through reason.</margin>
...the principal authors of astrology: from which foundations they support their marvelous dogmas. This same Albumasar <note>Albumasar (787–886 AD) was a highly influential Persian astrologer whose works shaped medieval European thought.</note> says that after Jesus, once ten Saturnian revolutions were completed, a law <note>In this context, "law" (lex) refers to a religion or sect.</note> arose which is midway between the Nazarenes and the pagans (for so they call the gentiles). But we certainly know that no law arose after Christ before Muhammad; but I think those Arabs meant the sect of the Manichaeans, who are also called *Minim* among the Talmudists. <note>original: "Minim." A Hebrew term used in the Talmud to refer to heretics or sectarians.</note> This heresy gained strength not only after ten revolutions were completed, but even before the ninth revolution of Saturn was finished. If he had brought all this faithfully from history, it would still not be a reason to make a dogma out of the idea that ten periods of Saturn produce such things; otherwise, I could invent a thousand such dogmas for myself. For the Hebrews also say the first temple built by Solomon lasted for four hundred or a few more years; then the one built second under Darius lasted no more than ten [additional] years—that is, four hundred and ten. From its desolation, they devised their laws for themselves in Babylonia for almost as many years. Shall we then make a dogma from this: that the fourteenth revolution of Saturn always brings a great change to the Saturnine people of the Jews? We would be saying things more probable than Albumasar, who chooses the number ten for himself. From whom I would also gladly ask: where indeed does nature begin these revolutions? And under what part of the heaven will he assert the beginning of the logic of this period? I ask, why did he prefer that part over the others? But we must not labor any longer in refuting these trifles, especially since they seem to have satisfied few other astrologers besides Albumasar. 

<margin>Pierre d'Ailly.</margin>
Indeed, even Pierre d'Ailly <note>original: "Alliacensis." A 14th-century French cardinal and scholar who attempted to reconcile astrology with theology.</note>—who had made great use of these in his treatise *On the Harmony of History and Astrology*—confessed in his explanation that they have no foundation; reversing his pen, he bit back at a large part of his own little book, having found them to be false.

# Chapter IV. The order of things to be said: the conflicting opinions of astrologers concerning great conjunctions.

<margin>The order of arguments.</margin>
There remains the approach and retreat of the eighth sphere and the ninth sphere; <note>Refers to "trepidation," a disproven theory that the fixed stars moved back and forth.</note> there remains the matter of "great conjunctions." But let the former be examined in the following book; for now, let us turn to the great conjunctions. It will be worthwhile to first present what they themselves think about these, so that what we bring forward in refutation may be more easily understood. This narration itself will not be without use for the refutation, as we shall see them disagreeing so much on these matters that it is not yet clear among astrologers which is the *greatest* conjunction, which is the *major*, and which is the *middle*. In this matter, the controversy is not only about the name; from it arises a great diversity of predictions, as some command us to expect events from the greatest, others from the middle, and others from the minor conjunctions.

<margin>Common opinion. The Great Conjunction.</margin>
The common opinion, therefore, which Alchabitius <note>A 10th-century Arab astrologer.</note> and Leopold <note>Leopold of Austria, a 13th-century astronomer.</note> hand down, and Albumasar before them, is of this sort: that it is a **Great Conjunction** when Jupiter and Saturn are joined together, which always happens after twenty years. 

<margin>The Major.</margin>
It is a **Major Conjunction**, however, when a migration is made from one triplicity to another and they meet on the threshold of the new triplicity; <note>term: "Triplicity" (triplicitas). A group of three zodiac signs sharing an element—Fire, Earth, Air, or Water. Astrologers believed history changed when conjunctions moved from one element to the next.</note> and this happens roughly after two hundred and forty years. For within the boundaries of one trigon <note>A triangle formed by the three signs of a triplicity.</note> they are coupled twelve times, and then the transition is made to the sign of the next trigon—which is not the first sign from the one in which they joined, but the second. For example, if both departed from Capricorn, they are received first not in Libra, but in Aquarius 

<column-break/>

in that triplicity. There is a **Middle Conjunction** between these 
<margin>The Middle.</margin>
due to the cause that it is completed every thirtieth year by Saturn and Mars in Cancer. The **Greatest** of all is that of Jupiter and Saturn in Aries, which occurs after nine hundred and sixty years. 
<margin>Greatest, Best, Middle, Greatest.</margin>
Mashallah, <note>original: "Messala." An 8th-century Persian Jewish astrologer.</note> disagreeing with these in his book *On Conjunctions*, says that the **Greatest Conjunction** is that which is made of the three superior planets: that is, Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars. From this, he expects the change of sects, the transfer of kingdoms, and the arrival of prophets—not from that which is made by Jupiter and Saturn in Aries, as the common crowd of astrologers believes. He makes the next conjunction after this one that of Jupiter and Saturn; 
<margin>Major, Middle, Great.</margin>
the third, Saturn and Mars; the fourth, Jupiter and Mars. Let us now see how much both positions err.

# Chapter V. Planets joined in great conjunctions are no more powerful than when separate: and those great conjunctions are a new invention born from a poor understanding of Ptolemy.

<margin>First reason.</margin>
First, I would like to know from them why they think Jupiter and Saturn do greater things when they are together than when they are separate, each performing and exercising its own powers. For the mixture of rays of various natures does indeed produce a new result that a separate and distinct influx would not; but we cannot find a reason why it should produce a *greater* result. Rather, we are inclined to believe that something *lesser* happens from it than if each of the planets acted separately as it is able. For if the planets that come together were of the same property, and had powers producing the same effects, then surely by the addition of a double ray, the effect would also be doubled. But since they are of contrary and repugnant natures—as are Jupiter and Saturn—necessarily one hinders the other. While they mutually curb and fetter their powers by the diversity of the mixture, the result is that we can expect nothing from them except something mediocre, just as all things are which result from a mixture of extremes. It is just as they themselves are accustomed to say when Saturn and Mars are together: although both are harmful and both are "malefics," because they have different powers of harming, no greater or more marvelous evil arises from their conjunction. Instead, the powers of one are broken and weakened by the other, so that neither can harm while both strive to harm according to the condition of their nature. Therefore, it is not fully certain—even if earthly events were subject to the heavens—that greater and more durable things happen when the superior stars are joined than when some one of them, with the others weakened, perhaps obtains more power and authority than usual. Even if we granted them that joined planets do more than separate ones toward the great changes of this world, 
<margin>Second reason.</margin>
we would not grant that this must be referred to the conjunction of Jupiter, Saturn, or Mars. We shall prove both by reason and by the authority of the highest astrologers that other stars hold the primary power in these matters. For never did any of the ancients judge universal changes of the world by these things which these men call "great conjunctions." Maternus says nothing of these, though he was a most curious investigator of astrology; nothing from Paul, nothing from Hephaistion, nothing from Theophilus, nothing from Aftaxarebus, and nothing from Ptolemy himself. <note>Pico lists the heavyweights of ancient astrology—Firmicus Maternus, Paul of Alexandria, Hephaistion of Thebes, and Claudius Ptolemy—to show that "Great Conjunctions" are a later Arabic invention not found in the original Greek tradition.</note> His testimony alone will be enough for us, lest we use witnesses poorly known to them against them. He, therefore, in the second book of the *Apotelesmaton* <note>The *Tetrabiblos*, Ptolemy's foundational work on astrology.</note>, teaching by what way general and world changes may be foreseen...

<summary>Pico critiques the Arabic astrological theory of "Great Conjunctions," arguing that planetary cycles are historically inconsistent and that planets of opposing natures (like Jupiter and Saturn) should logically cancel each other out rather than amplify their power.</summary>

### NINTH DISPUTATION

...refers all [major effects] only to the eclipses of the Sun and Moon; nor can anything more rational be said, for universal and great effects ought to be referred to those causes which are most universal and effective. 

<margin>
Ptolemy’s implementation.
</margin>

It is admitted by everyone that among the planets only two possess universal efficiency: namely, the Sun and the Moon, whose light is nothing other than the Sun’s light carried to the earth through the Moon as if through a mirror, so to speak. Therefore, if any celestial power ought to be considered the origin and cause of universal and great effects, none should be more highly considered than these stars. As for what Messahallah <note>original: "Messalla." Ma'shallah ibn Athari (c. 740–815) was a Persian Jewish astrologer whose works on conjunctions were central to medieval astrology.</note> says—that great things are done by Jupiter and Saturn because they move more slowly—he proves what he denies rather than what he affirms, since it is the unanimous opinion of all that a faster motion is owed to a nobler and more powerful body. On account of this, those who defend the roles and dignity of the superior stars—lest they be thought weaker because they are restored to their place more slowly—usually try to prove from the proportion of the orbits they encircle that they are actually faster than many others, even though they appear slower due to the length of their periods. But I know what they will say about Ptolemy: that this was left out by him in the book *Apotelesmata* <note>The *Apotelesmata*, better known as the *Tetrabiblos*, is Claudius Ptolemy's 2nd-century foundational work on astrology.</note> lest he betray the "mystery." For so writes Haly <note>Ali ibn Ridwan, an Egyptian physician and astrologer who wrote famous commentaries on Ptolemy.</note>, his interpreter. 

<margin>
Refutation.
</margin>

But they claim that in the *Centiloquium* <note>A collection of 100 aphorisms once attributed to Ptolemy, though Pico correctly suspects it is a later forgery.</note> (for so they call it) he gave many proofs of this matter, when in the fiftieth word <note>Aphorism.</note> of that book he commands that we do not forget the conjunctions of the planets, in which there is great efficacy; and likewise in both the fifty-eighth and sixty-fourth words, he warns us of the same things, handing down great precepts about them, distinguishing between the "Greatest," "Middle," and "Least" conjunctions. I, however, would wish for nothing more than for them to answer: so that it might become plain to everyone from this that whatever of their dogmas seem more significant or admirable have sprouted either from vain opinions or from a false understanding of ancient authors. For as to their saying that Ptolemy kept silent about this in the *Apotelesmata* lest he betray the mystery, I am far from denying it—so much so that I do not even believe it was "betrayed" by him in the *Centiloquium*, in which he certainly spoke no more of these conjunctions than he did of the death of Priam or the Trojan War. We shall soon reveal how they perverted many of that author’s pronouncements and how many errors were propagated one after another from a single source. 

This is the fiftieth word of Ptolemy, as it stands in their vulgate edition: "Do not forget that there are one hundred and twenty conjunctions among the wandering stars; for in them is the greater knowledge of things that happen in this world, regarding increase and decrease." In Greek it is thus: "Nor let us overlook the one hundred and nineteen conjunctions." For in these is placed the conjunction of those things which happen in the world, both of generation and corruption. First, the "barbarian" <note>Pico uses "barbarous" to refer to Arabic and medieval Latin translations he considers linguistically or intellectually inferior.</note> interpretation attributes more to these conjunctions than Ptolemy does, for whom it is not the case that there is no greater knowledge of things happening in the world than that which comes from them. 

<margin>
Ptolemy’s opinion.
</margin>

Furthermore, even if we omit that, the meaning of the pronouncement is nothing other than that we should not look only at the property of each individual star. But let us know that from their conjunction various effective powers of various things arise, which no one denies must be conceded by all astrologers. But that we should refer the greatest changes of inferior things specifically to the conjunctions of the superior stars—Ptolemy certainly did not say this. Rather, if his words are read and understood correctly, they will indicate to us the contrary opinion. For he did not say that these conjunctions were one hundred and twenty (as is commonly read), but only one hundred and nineteen. 

<column-break/>

<margin>
The corrected passage of Ptolemy in his book the Apotelesmata.
</margin>

The reason for this is that he does not count the conjunction of the Sun and Moon among them. Because they have such peculiar privileges and a singular prerogative in great and universal changes, he reduces all the rest into a heap in number and order, as if none of them excelled the others by any singular condition. The "barbarian" expositors, not noticing this, thought it was a scribal error and added the conjunction of the Sun and Moon back in, thinking it should read one hundred and twenty instead of one hundred and nineteen, which all the Greek manuscripts have. Not content with perverting the sense, they also corrupted the integrity of the text. 

Let us pass to other matters. Ptolemy writes in word 58: "Inspect this manner of the place of conjunction, in which place it is from the ascendant of the year; for if the profection <note>A technique in astrology where a point is moved forward by a certain number of degrees over time.</note> reaches that point, then will be the time." And word 64 is of this kind: "In the difference of the least conjunction, the middle conjunction, and in the middle, the difference of the greatest conjunction." The Arabs and Latins think that in both places, by "conjunction," Ptolemy means the conjunction of Saturn and Jupiter. 

<margin>
Bad understanding of the 57th and 64th aphorisms.
</margin>

But no one would be so deceived if they had ever read the Greek authors of astrology, especially Ptolemy, with attentive eyes. For what we call "conjunction," in Greek is *synodus*—a word which, when used on its own, is always taken for the coupling of the Sun and Moon, unless it is specified whose conjunction it might be (such as Venus and Mercury, or Jupiter and Saturn). Therefore, since in both pronouncements Ptolemy said *synodus* absolutely, adding nothing further, it is most manifest to all who are not entirely unfamiliar with Greek readings that Ptolemy is talking about the conjunction of the lights [the Sun and Moon], and not of other stars. 

<margin>
The meaning of the 58th aphorism.
</margin>

And thus the meaning of the first (the fifty-eighth) word is: that once the sign and place where the conjunction of the Sun and Moon occurred in the revolution of the year is diligently observed, we should expect the effect when the "profection" of the year (distributed through the months of the year, by which one sign succeeds another in power according to the order of the constitution) reaches that place; since that conjunction of the Sun and Moon which preceded the turning of the year will have signaled it to us. For Ptolemy especially uses these meetings of the luminaries to investigate the outcome of the entire year, as no one who has turned the pages of his *Apotelesmatic* books is ignorant. 

<margin>
Errors of the vulgate translation in the 80th and 57th. Explanation of the 74th aphorism.
</margin>

However, in the translation of this word, many things have been added, omitted, and interpolated. For instead of "conjunction," they read "minor conjunction," even though no distinction of greater or minor is added in the Greek copies. And the term of the profection is extended to many years, though there is no mention of this in Ptolemy, who speaks only of the events of a single year. 

<margin>
Under what condition Ptolemy is to be followed.
</margin>

Finally, regarding that pronouncement where "greatest," "middle," and "least" conjunctions are distinguished: many do not understand such a difference in the conjunction of the luminaries. But this is easy and open to those who have sometimes kept watch by Ptolemy’s lamp without yawning. For since he, as we said, attributes everything to the conjunctions of the Sun and Moon, he then distinguishes them into a threefold kind and order. 

<margin>
What the greatest is.
</margin>

For those that cause an eclipse of either luminary he places in the first rank, through which the outcomes not of one year, but sometimes of many, can be foreseen. These we shall call "greatest" <note>original: "Sion." This appears to be a printer's error for "synodos" (conjunctions).</note> because the stars are then most closely joined, since they differ neither in longitude of place nor in latitude, and they portend the most distant future events. 

<margin>
What the middle is.
</margin>

Conversely, the "least" for him are those which occur in individual [months]...

Having previously argued that astrologers misinterpret Ptolemy, he now focuses on the distinction between "mean" (mathematically averaged) and "true" (actually observed) celestial positions, proving that the cycles astrologers rely on are based on convenient fictions rather than reality.</meta>

AGAINST ASTROLOGERS BOOK V. 114

occur every month: and they indicate to us the disposition of only a single month. Intermediate among these are those conjunctions which immediately precede the entry of the sun into the four tropical signs: Aries, Cancer, Libra, and Capricorn. From these, the whole following time of the year is indicated to us: whether it be spring, summer, autumn, or winter. Since, therefore, the following particular disposition distinguishes and determines what the universal disposition indicates, he [Ptolemy] said that the "mean" conjunction is the greatest difference <margin>Which are the mean [conjunctions].</margin> and the "middle" is the least. For example: if the conjunction of the Moon and Sun immediately preceding the vernal equinox shows us the coming quality of spring, we should know that this whole quality is diminished or increased according to the nature of the conjunctions that occur in each following month by a fixed revolution. And the relationship that these monthly conjunctions have to those four seasonal ones is the same relationship those three-month ones have to the larger and fewer <margin>In what way the barbarians <note>Pico uses "barbarians" to refer to non-Greek, specifically Arabic and medieval Latin astrologers whose works he considered intellectually crude compared to Classical sources.</note> erred in their understanding of Ptolemy, while our Pico has so acutely detected it.</margin> conjunctions and meetings of the receding stars. This is Ptolemy's opinion regarding the greatest, middle, and smallest conjunctions. But these barbarians, not understanding this, have fabricated the most beautiful dreams for themselves about the conjunctions of Saturn and Jupiter: the greatest of which return after 960 years, the middle after 240, and the smallest after 20 years. This cannot even be consistent with their own pronouncements (beyond what we have already said), because for them, the "greatest" conjunction encompasses the "middle" and "smallest" ones. Therefore, the effect of a greatest conjunction could not be determined by those smaller ones through which that great cycle is driven over many centuries of revolution. What, therefore, did Ptolemy mean by saying the "mean" is the difference of the "greatest," and the "middle" is the "smallest"? This is that fiction born from a false understanding of a single author [Ptolemy], which these men boast of so much. By this they judge themselves, full of glory, claiming that all religion is bound to the stars. By this they most fanatically subject the law of the prophets, the coming [of Christ], and divine miracles to the powers of the stars and the fates. Certainly, nowhere do they show themselves more childish or are found more ignorant and ridiculous.

### Chapter VI. That the leading astrologers used mean conjunctions, not true ones; and their other errors concerning the same.

<margin>The response.</margin>
But perhaps one of the astrologers will say: "Suppose we did not understand Ptolemy; yet if this error has led us to the truth—just as a storm sometimes drives a ship into port—then whatever Ptolemy and others thought, experience has confirmed that no great change of laws or kingdoms has ever happened without some conjunction of the superior stars preceding it. Nor has any such conjunction ever occurred that was not followed by changes of this kind in inferior things." They are doing well if they admit to being in a storm, provided they remain in that port while they attempt to prove these lowliest things by experience. We shall first declare this in a general sense, and then we will show more clearly than daylight that whatever "Great Conjunctions" any of the astrologers have marked and related to the events of marvelous things are both false and falsely calculated, <margin>First reason.</margin> and falsely related to effects. To begin with, all authors of this dogma do not use *true* conjunctions, but *mean* ones—that is, fictional and imaginary ones. So that everyone may understand this clearly, I will say what "true motion" is and what "mean motion" is. The wandering stars [planets] do not pass through the Zodiac at a steady pace—that is, they do not always cross an equal part of it in an equal interval of time.

<column-break/>

<margin>What true motion is and what mean motion is.</margin>
Therefore, those who wished to measure their movements and arrange them into numbers devised a "uniform motion" for each planet. They did this so that from this fictional and uniform motion, they might more easily track that unequal and "true" motion. Ptolemy calls that fiction "periodic," <margin>Ptolemy.</margin> while the younger [modern] authors call it "mean" [average], because they use it as a middle-point to investigate the true motion. When we seek the location of a planet from the calculation of its movement, we sometimes use the mean motion and sometimes the true motion—not because that "mean" indicates the actual place where the planet stands, but so that we may seek its true seat from it by an easier method and logic. For a planet is never actually where it is found to be through mean motion, because it never moves in that [uniform] way. But as I said, this was devised by astrologers so they might reach the truth more surely by a certain order. I was saying, therefore, that those who judge the future through "Great Conjunctions" use mean conjunctions, not true ones. For when they say that Jupiter and Saturn join after 20 years, and meet at the beginnings of the triplicities <note>A "triplicity" is a group of three Zodiac signs belonging to the same element (Fire, Earth, Air, Water).</note> after 240, and then convene at the boundaries of Aries after 960—this is completely false if we look at true motions. It is "true" (though not even then exactly) if we look at those mean ones—that is, those fictional and false ones—devised by mathematicians for ease of teaching. Moreover, what is called "mean motion" is so different from what we reach through the "true" that even the sign of the conjunction might change. For example: a conjunction might be assigned to Pisces, when it actually occurred in Aquarius. And the time varies so much that if we are dealing with conjunctions that happen after 240 years, the "true" conjunction sometimes precedes the "mean" one by as much as a hundred years. It is apparent from the tables to anyone calculating correctly that in the year of grace 1236, Jupiter and Saturn, migrating from the Earth triplicity to the Air triplicity, met in Aquarius. According to the logic of mean motion, they were supposed to remain in that [Air triplicity] for 240 years; and yet after about 140 years—that is, in the year of grace 1365—the change having been made from the Air to the Water triplicity, they met in Scorpio. Found together always in the Water signs thereafter, they did not return to the Air signs. <margin>The insanity of the astrologers. That the leading authors of astrology used mean conjunctions.</margin> What insanity is this, then, to fight against open truth and to use things so impudently false and fictional, that by their own consensus they refer the outcomes of human affairs to a constellation that is entirely non-existent? To think that something which is not, nor was, nor ever will be, is the cause of things that *are*—surely nothing is more delusional than that vanity. Yet in this, all the leading authors of astrology have slipped. For Albumasar, <note>Abu Ma'shar (787–886), a Persian astrologer whose work *On the Great Conjunctions* was the standard text for medieval mundane astrology.</note> the prince of this dogma, in that book titled *On the Great Conjunctions* which is much celebrated among astrologers, always used mean conjunctions, never true ones. Furthermore, Abraham, <note>Likely Abraham bar Hiyya (c. 1065–1136), whose *Megillat ha-Megalleh* (Scroll of the Revealer) calculates the coming of the Messiah via astrology.</note> in that work titled *Redemption*, although he seeks one or two conjunctions from true motion, then flees always to the mean ones, making no mention at all of the true ones. <margin>D'Ailly.</margin> Alliacensis, <note>Pierre d'Ailly (1351–1420), a French theologian and cardinal who wrote on the "concordance" of astrology and history.</note> in his treatise *On the Harmony of History and Astrology*, although he cites seven "greatest" conjunctions, cites them all as mean, and none as true. Many others do the same, always suffering from the same disease, whom we shall discuss individually later. And indeed, these things ought to suffice for us to show that what they say is nothing, if the constellation itself from which they predict is nothing. <margin>The fiction of the astrologers.</margin> For since even those mean ones (which are non-existent in reality) do not correspond for them—that is, they do not fall in those times in which they would most like—they seek another refuge for themselves...

<meta>This page continues Pico's systematic takedown of "Great Conjunctions." After criticizing the general logic of astrologers, he turns his focus to Pierre d’Ailly, a famous cardinal and scholar who attempted to use astronomical cycles to create a universal timeline of history.</meta>

-> NINTH DISPUTATION <-

...they plot through a new folly to defend their prior madness. For they have imagined that the things portended do not follow immediately after these conjunctions, nor even quickly: but after many years indeed—a hundred, or two hundred, or even more.

<margin>Refutation.</margin> 
I say, look at how greatly they are deceived; for it is not the nature of a powerful and effective cause to begin what it is meant to produce lately; rather, it ends lately. It should begin either immediately or quickly. Therefore, the power of these conjunctions is either effective or weak. If it is effective, it cannot cease for long without acting; if it is weak, it cannot last long enough to act eventually after a long delay. A great force tames and overcomes what prohibits and resists it.

<margin>Another refutation.</margin> 
A weak force vanishes: and it dissolves itself through the passage of time by its own extreme thinness. Furthermore, why is it that in this interval of time, new conjunctions are always supervening? Their nature, as the astrologers themselves say, is to obliterate the previous ones, since a supervening constellation strikes down the preceding one. Hence, if an eclipse of the luminaries <note>The "luminaries" refers to the Sun and the Moon.</note> happens at a certain time of year, they are accustomed to saying that the fate which was received from the beginnings of the annual conversion ceases. Why, therefore, does it not cease with a following conjunction, especially one different in property and nature? Why would it not expunge that first one? Yet they want effects to belong to that first conjunction even three hundred years later, despite so many various intermediate constellations occurring in between. No one would say this—not even a philosopher or a man of the slowest wit. This error is increased in a wonderful way by another inexpiable error: for in the very calculation of time, they err so significantly that sometimes they think a conjunction preceded an event by, say, two hundred years, when in truth it preceded that event by one thousand four hundred years. This will be demonstrated in the following chapters of this book. In these matters, they are caught as unlearned and ignorant liars. But see also how cunning these most "beautiful" diviners are: for so that the opportunity for deceiving might never fail them, they have continued their doctrines in such a way that whatever happened at any time that was somewhat admirable, they could refer it back to some antecedent conjunction. To achieve this, they said the force of one conjunction lasts until the very hour of the next; and thus, whatever intervenes in the middle can always be referred back to some conjunction. Nor did they see their own ruin in this fallacy: since if things return in cycles for them so that no great effect happens without a great conjunction, and no great conjunction appears without an effect, while they maintain that causes are never absent from such events, they necessarily make it so that such causes are often exhausted without any such events. For great and wonderful things do not always happen because of them—in fact, they do not even frequently happen—and yet, as they themselves wish, the force that produces them remains always uninterrupted by succession. These points are made generally against those who speak with impious boldness about future events from these great conjunctions; now let us examine everything point by point.

### Chapter VII. Which order is to be followed, and that d'Ailly <note>Petrus de Alliaco, or Pierre d'Ailly (1351–1420), was an influential French theologian and cardinal who sought to harmonize astrology with history.</note> felt one thing at one time and another at another.

<margin>D'Ailly contradicts himself.</margin> 
Let us begin with the greatest conjunctions which d'Ailly collects in his treatise on the harmony of history and astrology. From this, he confirms the astrologers' claim that such conjunctions never occur without a great change in inferior things <note>In the Aristotelian worldview, "inferior things" refers to the sublunary world—the Earth and everything on it—which was believed to be governed by the "superior" heavens.</note>. And indeed, he 

<column-break/>

himself disagrees with all his own "harmony" in his *Elucidarium* <note>The *Elucidarium* was another of d’Ailly’s works where he revisited his earlier theories.</note>. Although in that work he uses both Saturnian revolutions and the greatest conjunctions, he openly confesses once that the former have no foundation and that the latter were not calculated by him. It is all the more wonderful that he has a praiser in this matter, considering he did not even approve of himself. But because he sometimes raised arguments against himself that were not entirely true—since some are unnecessary and several are poorly expressed—let us collect a few but effective ones by which that entire treatise may be plainly torn down. Then we shall proceed to refute the other conjunctions which Abraham <note>Abraham Ibn Ezra, a 12th-century Jewish polymath and astrologer.</note>, Albumasar <note>Abu Ma'shar, a 9th-century Persian astrologer whose works were foundational for Latin astrology.</note>, and many others brought forth, and whom d'Ailly followed in his *Elucidarium*. But since we must often speak of the calculation of time, we thought it necessary to preface a few things. First, it should be shown that when time is in doubt, the judgment of this matter does not belong to the astrologers, as d'Ailly thinks, but to history. Furthermore, when there is a variety among historical writers, we must determine which ones should be followed by right. We will say only a few things here in passing, since we have disputed this at length in a specific work we wrote on the true calculation of time. <margin>To be observed in the *Prodromus* <note>Pico is referring to a "forerunner" or introductory work he intended to publish or had written.</note>.</margin>

### Chapter VIII. The timing of events is to be sought from history, not from astrology as d'Ailly thought.

<margin>Opinion of d'Ailly.</margin> 
In his book on the harmony of astrology and theology, d'Ailly thinks that the number of years from the beginning of the world until these times can be detected by astrological reasoning and reduced to the truth, correcting the various sacred or foreign histories that have been produced on the subject. For, he says, if you have investigated the "theme" of the world's own birth <note>Essentially, the "birth chart" or horoscope of the creation of the universe.</note>, you will be able to collect from it the first conjunction of Saturn and Jupiter from the beginning of the world by calculation. If you then search for another conjunction closest to your own years, the interval of time that was in the middle between that first and last one will be elicited from the calculation of the occurring conjunctions.

<margin>His opinion on the same.</margin> 
These were indeed his feelings at that time; but in the *Elucidarium*, he plainly confessed that there is no astrological way by which we may find anything certain concerning the doubtful number of years. He adds that not even the greatest astrologers ever attempted this or promised it from their art. But while he says this, I do not know why he persists again in that opinion that the ultimate question concerning the reckoning of time should be referred to astrologers, and that whatever is found in histories concerning the year of the world that differs from them ought to be amended and corrected according to their opinion.

<margin>Conclusion of d'Ailly.</margin> 
We will show briefly that this can be defended by no reasoning. For an astronomer can indeed—if he has some true position of the stars that existed once, and again another known position nearby—determine by most certain reasoning how much exact time necessarily passed between them. But how will this help him? Is the time of some performed action uncertain? For suppose someone says three thousand years have flowed from Christ to us; let another say one thousand four hundred. In settling this dispute, what will be the office of the astronomer? You will say he will show that between the position of the stars under which Christ was born and that which is held now, three thousand years cannot have passed, but only one thousand four hundred. But what is this sluggishness, what is this dullness: that you do not see you are positing as certain the very thing which is under question? For under what position of the stars was Christ

## Chapter IX. Summary of the opinion of Pierre d'Ailly in the book which he titled "On the Harmony of Astrology and History."

<margin>Ridiculous</margin>
After we have briefly laid these foundations concerning the true calculation of times, let us come to those "Greatest Conjunctions" of the astrologers—that is, to their greatest insanities—beginning from those which 
<margin>Foundations of d'Ailly's harmony.</margin>
d'Ailly collects in his treatise *On the Harmony of History and Astrology*. In that work, he used this order: he assumes two principles: one concerning the number of years from Adam to Christ; the other concerning the theme of the world’s own birth chart. He says there flowed from Adam to Jesus five thousand, three hundred and forty-four years: namely, from Adam to the Flood, 2,249 years; from the Flood to Jesus, 3,102. In the first constitution of the world, the stars were so placed in the sky: for the first part of Cancer made the horoscope <note>The Ascendant or rising sign.</note>; the highest peaks of heaven <note>The Midheaven.</note> possessed the first part of Aries. Mercury was in the fifteenth part of Gemini, occupying the twelfth region of the sky; Venus was in the eleventh part of Taurus; both luminaries <note>The Sun and Moon.</note> were indeed in the sky: the nocturnal one in Taurus, while the diurnal one in the nineteenth part of Aries shone in the middle and highest part of the sky. <margin>The first greatest conjunction.</margin>
These things having been so placed, he gathers with no effort that there was a first "Greatest Conjunction" of Saturn and Jupiter at the beginning of the world, specifically in the beginning of Aries, after three hundred and twenty years. After this, he enumerates six others, always with nine hundred and sixty years intervening (by the error of mean motion); and so it follows that the seventh Greatest Conjunction from the beginning of the world happened in the year of grace 735. After which the eighth will follow in the year 1693. These being so distributed, he gathers from histories the main points of more memorable things which happened in that middle space of time which is required between one greatest conjunction and another: that is, through those nine hundred and sixty years. In this interval of time, whatever happens that is notable and memorable they think must be referred back to the preceding conjunction, since it occurred after it. Because he always finds some great and memorable deed in this span of years, he thinks it is confirmed that these greatest conjunctions do not happen without a great motion of inferior things. He seems to himself to have fulfilled what he promised in another book: to show that the truth of history harmonizes with astrological truth. This is the summary, the order, and the foundation of his whole book.

### Chapter X. That d'Ailly erred in many ways: and even if everything he supposes were granted, he still does not prove what he intends.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
**F**irst of all, even if we accept his claims about the conjunctions, the timing of events, and the "birth chart of the world" <note>original: "mundi genitura," a hypothetical horoscope calculated for the moment of the world's creation</note>—if we grant him everything he demands—what kind of historical confirmation for astrology is this? Even if we show that in the last nine hundred and sixty-five years there was some great movement of births or a change in the human condition, the world would have seen it. I ask you to describe this span of years from different starting points, not, for example, from the year of the world 460,

<margin>Second, Third, Fourth, Fifth, Sixth [conclusions].</margin>
which was the time of the first conjunction. Instead, start from the year 500 of the world: count those nine hundred years that revolve from one conjunction to another. You will find no fewer varieties: wars, laws, prophets, plagues, and a diverse and varied range of events occurred in that long stretch of time. Why did you not always reduce the series of those deeds by two hundred years to the time of your conjunction?

<margin>The birth chart of the world described by d'Ailly is false and impossible.</margin>
This logic is far too crude <note>original: "pinguis hic nimis minerua," an idiom for dull or clumsy reasoning</note> if we are to harmonize astrology with history in this way. But those conjunctions are not even real; they are "mean" <term>mean conjunctions|calculated averages of planetary positions rather than their actual observed positions</term>, which is to say they are false and non-existent; and even if we accept them as averages, they should not be referred to those times. Nor is the number of years from Adam to Christ what he thought it was, but the true calculation exceeds it by more than 1,400 years. Furthermore, those deeds or events did not happen at the times he thought they did. The "birth chart of the world" he describes is demonstrated to be not only doubtful or false, but plainly impossible by astrological reason. Therefore, that entire book can be corrected with a single strike of the pen. No one is ignorant of the fact that those are mean conjunctions, not true ones, nor does he deny it himself.

<margin>Refutation of another birth chart of the world by Abraham. Note the greatest error.</margin>
But if the birth chart of the world, from which all others are derived, is impossible, then by necessity the one calculated according to the "mean motion" <note>the average speed of a planet</note> will also be false. If you want to know if it is impossible, let Mercury be your interpreter: in that figure, he is placed fifty-six degrees away from the Sun. Yet Mercury would swear by all the gods and goddesses that he has never moved even a fingernail's breadth further than twenty-nine degrees <note>Mercury is always close to the Sun; its maximum elongation is about 28 degrees. Placing it 56 degrees away is a physical impossibility in astronomy</note>. This is an obvious and unpardonable error. He also thinks the primordial figure of the world, which d'Ailly presents in his *Elucidarium*, is burdened with wondrous illusions. For it is attributed to the Chaldeans and Ishmaelites, whom he claims the Divinity made privy to this mystery. In it, Mercury is placed in the first part of Gemini, and the Sun in the first part of Aries; this results in Mercury being sixty degrees from the Sun. No astronomer will deny that this is plainly impossible. But let us return to those conjunctions which (as I was saying), once the first figure of the heavens is removed, are all found to be false and impossible.

<margin>Error in Abraham's time.</margin>
Added to this is the fact that after nine hundred years, that conjunction is not in Aries at all (as Abraham the Spaniard <note>Abraham bar Hiyya, also known as Savasorda, a 12th-century Jewish mathematician and astronomer</note> teaches in his sixth book titled *The Redemption of Israel*). Furthermore, the events he relates to them did not occur at the times he thinks. For the years from the creation of the world to the Flood were not 2,252 as he reports, but 1,656, as will be declared later. Therefore, that third "Greatest Conjunction," which he says preceded the Flood by two years (occurring 2,250 years from the world's constitution), actually happened 674 years after the Flood itself.

<margin>The true calculation of years from the Flood to Christ.</margin>
Likewise, in the 942nd year after the Flood, he notes a fourth "Greatest Conjunction," and says that sixteen years before it, the patriarch Abraham was born. Yet Abraham, seeing the day of the Lord and exulting, lived 680 years before the conjunction of this time. For he was born in the 292nd year after the Flood. But from the Flood to Jesus there are not as many

### Chapter XI. That astrologers disagree both among themselves and with the truth regarding the conjunction of the Flood; and even if they get what they ask for, they still do not prove what they contend.

**L**et us pass to the other Great Conjunctions, noted a little more diligently by others, but not so that they avoid the mark of madness, let alone error. Regarding this, we shall first see how conflicting and contrary the astrologers' own views are, and how they tax and rebuke one another; then, how they all clearly wander from the truth. Finally, even if their opinion were true, it does not achieve what they want—namely, the confirmation that such conjunctions do not happen without a great change in the lower things <note>the earthly realm</note>.

<margin>Disagreement of astrologers. Common opinion according to Aoniar.</margin>

### Chapter XII. How crazy the Jew Abraham is regarding the conjunction of Moses and the prophecy of the Messiah.

<margin>
Abraham the Prince was the teacher of Abraham ibn Ezra.

# NINTH DISPUTATION

<margin>Thirdly.</margin>
In such a great calamity, in which the glory of divine justice might delight mankind, yet men suffering such extremes would feel commiseration and grief: this is the Messiah; this is that redemption which Abraham <note>Abraham bar Hiyya (c. 1070–1136), a Jewish mathematician and astrologer</note> promised them from the "Mosaic constellation." Lest he be believed to have divined past events any better than future ones, let us see how plainly false and ridiculous he is regarding that conjunction to which he attributed the arrival of Moses. For that conjunction, through which he believed Moses was born, occurred many years after Moses’ death; and even if we grant him the timing, it signified nothing of the sort he imagines. Let us look at the timing, but 
<margin>Third.</margin>

### Chapter XIII. Various "mean" conjunctions to which the Christian law is ascribed by various people, even without astrological reason.

<margin>The Christian law is not said by them to be ruled by "means."</margin>

# AGAINST ASTROLOGERS, BOOK IV.

The positions are more than five fingers apart; therefore, this "migration" <note>referring to the shifting of astrological signs over time</note> can be dismissed with almost no effort. But we have laughed enough at this, and we have sufficiently refuted those "middle conjunctions" which we have now completely removed from the center of discussion. There is no reason to spend more labor against them, since it has been sufficiently shown that calling them "middle" is no different than saying they do not exist. That which does not exist certainly cannot act, nor can it indicate things that are. For if they assert some true conjunction occurred after the birth of Christ, I shall wonder at nothing unless we are to believe that the heavens stood still after He was brought into the light. Otherwise, it was necessary for Jupiter, Saturn, and the other planets to meet and move apart from one another frequently. But no astrologer has ever said that these conjunctions have power over things that have already passed. Rather, it is reasonably said that their effects precede them by many years, but never follow them. For if things are brought about by an effect, the cause cannot be later than the effect; and if they act as signs, it is pointless for the celestial signs to signify something that has already happened.

### Chapter XIV. That the commonly cited birth chart of Jesus is not true: nor does it indicate that He would die a violent death or that He was a great prophet.

<margin>The impious fiction of Albumasar.</margin>
However, some people are often disturbed by the trifles these little diviners babble regarding the birth chart of Jesus himself. For they say He was born while the "first face" of the Virgin (as they call the decans <note>subdivisions of zodiac signs</note>) was rising. About this, Albumasar <note>Abu Ma'shar, a famous 9th-century Persian astrologer</note> writes that in this sign there is a beautiful virgin holding two ears of grain in her hand and nursing a boy, whom a certain people calls "Jesus." Thus they think the miracle of the Word made flesh is confirmed by the science of astrology, which supposedly found the Virgin and Jesus among the images of the sky. Here, I am not particularly angry with them, since they are accustomed to confirming their own dogmas with such testimonies; therefore, they think we will also gladly receive these things to corroborate our own teachings. But Christian truth has no need for these fables and dreams; in the eyes of Christian truth, even the "holidays" of the philosophers are almost fables. Who saw these images? To whom did a more hidden reason reveal them while the senses were silent? Where did Ptolemy or any ancient author ever make mention of them? They are the purest nonsense and the fictions of the Arabs—even if they attribute them to the Indians—against which we shall dispute more extensively in the following book. Furthermore, the Lord Jesus was not born while that "Virgin" (as they say) was rising. <margin>First reason. Second reason.</margin> Otherwise, He would have appeared in the light nearly two hours before midnight, whereas we have received from the tradition of the Church that He was born at midnight. Therefore, it was not the third part of Libra (as someone says), but rather the tenth, which occupied the ascendant <note>the point of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon</note> when He, the most desired of all children, was born. From this, it is also shown to be false what they spread with blasphemous voices: that Mars was in the "house of death" in that birth chart, <margin>Mary was not in the [shrine/temple]. Objection. Solution.</margin> which is why He had to die by the punishment of the cross. For Mars could not have been in that place unless we make the Virgin the ascendant, which we have shown to be far different from the actual hour of His birth. But someone will insist: if we remove Mars from that part of the sky, we will have to place him in the West, where he would still threaten the dangers of a violent death. <margin>A violent death was not predicted by the birth chart of Jesus.</margin> I, however, without departing at all from their own decrees, will show that a violent death was not pre-signified by that birth chart. Although Mars in the seventh house might bring a person born then into life-threatening danger, Maternus <note>Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman astrologer</note> writes that this misfortune is lessened if the birth is nocturnal; likewise, if Mars is in his own house, or his own borders, or at his

<column-break/>

<margin><unclear>marginal note illegible</unclear></margin> own height. Moreover, if he were found in the eighth house, from which no clearer sign of death can be drawn, the benevolence of Jupiter would nevertheless resist the malice of Mars—provided Jupiter is in the ascendant, and the ascendant itself is in the house of Jupiter or Venus (a prosperous star that joins itself to Jupiter by its radiation). Out of these conditions, not one or two, but clearly *all* of them are found in the birth chart of Jesus. For He was born by night, not by day; and Mars was in Aries (that is, in his own home); and the ascendant was Libra, the house of Venus, which Jupiter nevertheless illuminated almost specifically. Furthermore, Venus, positioned in Aquarius, was joined by the friendly fellowship of a trine aspect <note>an angle of 120 degrees, considered harmonious</note>. If you add to this the Moon, which rules the night and is happily situated in a nocturnal birth, you will see that a "good death" must necessarily be pronounced from that position of the stars, even though the Moon held the house of death. For she was in Taurus, which is her exaltation, and she was increased in light; and in the place where she rejoices (the eighth house), she was flowing toward Venus with a most happy gaze from the Sun, being hosted by her and infested by no rays from either Mars or Saturn. She was neither departing from them nor going toward them—that is, she was bound to them by no link of fellowship. Add to this that Venus, the mistress of both the house of death and the ascendant alike, was struck by no hostile radiation from Mars or Saturn, but was cherished by the rays of Jupiter, promising a good end for herself. Therefore, He was "offered up because He willed it," <note>Isaiah 53:7</note> not because the fury of the heavens drove Him to the punishment of the cross.

But an occasion for babbling can never be lacking for rash men of no shame. For imagine that Mars had been in any place at all; they would have found a handle for raving in some way regardless. If he were placed in the ascendant, they would say that his face—slapped, beaten with fists, and defiled with blood—referred to that Martian man, and they would say he brought the sword of destruction upon himself. If he were in the second house from the ascendant, they would claim it meant poverty and the lack of all things. If in the third, no brothers. If in the fourth, no patrimony—as one who, though the Son of David, did not obtain even a temporary kingdom. If in the fifth, no children. If in the sixth, all his servants given over to slaughter. If in the seventh and eighth houses, you already know what they would say. If in the ninth—O blessed astrologers!—since Maternus says that he who has <margin>Blasphemous dogma of Maternus.</margin> Mars in his own house in the ninth region of heaven will be a man who is a terror to good demons, and from whose arrival the spirits of evil demons flee, and who frees suffering men from them not by a word, but by his mere presence. How much shouting and applause do you think the astrologers would follow and spread if the star of Mars had happened to be there at the Lord's birth? But if it had held the heights of heaven (the midheaven), they would immediately pronounce the empire of the world subject to His laws, especially since Jupiter occupied the first pivot. If they had caught him in the eleventh house, they would have brought forward the Charleses and Constantines, and all the Caesars who fought for the Church of Christ. If in the twelfth, they would complain of the traps of enemies—among whom they would even find themselves. Thus, as the saying goes, an occasion for jumping in is always ready for the insane.

But hear also what they say about Saturn: for he was in the ninth <margin>What the astrologers say about Saturn.</margin> region of heaven in the sign of Gemini. They say this "makes prophets and priests." But what of the fact that he was in retrograde? This ought to diminish those promises entirely. It might make him a prophet, but it could not make him *more* than a prophet, such as John the Baptist was. Could it then make him the divine inspirer of all prophets? Saturn was positioned in that same place and in the same sign when Eleonora was born, <margin>Refutation of their errors.</margin> the daughter of Galeotto’s brother; she was indeed a modest virgin of the most upright character, but she was no Anna, nor Deborah, nor...

# NINTH DISPUTATION

<margin>
Refutation by example:
Cassandra.
</margin>
Cassandra <note>Pico likely uses the name of the Trojan prophetess here to mock the astrologers' claims to foresight</note>. But persist, I pray, you admirable astrologers, in your proposed dogma, and let us see what Saturn might signify there in his birth. Your Abraham <note>Abraham Ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167), a celebrated Jewish scholar and astrologer</note> writes in his *Book of Nativities* that whoever has Saturn positioned in the ninth region of the heavens will be a "bad Christian"—but how could someone be a bad Christian if they were never a Christian at all? O, what ridiculous men, surely never mocked enough! <margin>The madness of Cecco d'Ascoli.</margin> That superstitious Cecco d'Ascoli, who is called a magus, says that Jesus was born in a stable because Capricorn held the bottom of the sky <note>The *Imum Coeli*, or the lowest point of the chart, associated with one's foundations and home</note>; and another says he was "King of the Jews" because his horoscope was in Libra, for the Hebrews belong to Saturn, and Saturn’s "exaltation" is in Libra. As if many people are not born every single month under these same conditions who are neither born in stables nor recorded as kings of the Jews! But enough about these worthless clouds of men.

### Chapter XV. That what Abu Ma'shar said about Muhammad has been found false by experience.

<margin>Abu Ma'shar is false.</margin> Abu Ma'shar <note>Latinized as Albumasar (787–886), a highly influential Persian astrologer</note>, an Arab, attributes the arrival of his Muhammad and that Saracen <note>A common medieval term for Muslims</note> law to a conjunction of Jupiter and Saturn which occurred in Scorpio fifty-two years before that law was published. He does not need to be refuted with many words, since experience itself has already refuted the things he prophesied from that same constellation regarding that law. Finally, as we have already said above, at whatever time good or bad prophets might come, a conjunction can never be lacking to which their arrival might be attributed, since, as we said before, after twenty years <margin>A similar conjunction to Muhammad’s which produced no new religious law.</margin> Saturn and Jupiter always meet. But such meetings are neither a sign nor a cause for why prophets of this kind come. This can be sufficiently shown by the fact that often, at other times, similar or even more powerful constellations for that same purpose return; yet after them, no prophet, no new law, and no change of religion follows. They say Muhammad came after Jupiter and Saturn joined in Scorpio; why then did not another Muhammad come after the year of grace 1065, at which time Jupiter and Saturn were together under a similar condition, with the triplicity <note>A group of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element; a major shift in astrological "ages"</note> even having changed? And what did not happen in that conjunction of Muhammad occurred in that year: Mars joined them in the same sign by its body. Yet, if we wish to read histories, we shall read of no institution of a new religion through those times which drew nearly a third of the world into its laws.

### Chapter XVI. That in the prophecy of the Antichrist, some have already appeared as liars, and others will be liars in the future.

<margin>Arnaldus.</margin> If we have found them to be false, vain, and ridiculous in the things they have said about past religions, we should not think that more faith should be given to their trifles when these scoundrels talk with a certain "prophetic authority" about the Antichrist, the end of the age, and other future things of this kind. For even now, the outcome has refuted some of them: such as Arnaldus <note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova (c. 1240–1311), who predicted the end of the world based on astrology</note> and several others who say that in the year of our Lord 1345, because of that conjunction of the three superior planets in Aquarius, or in the year 1464, because of Jupiter and Saturn joined in Pisces, some threatened the Messiah of Abraham, and others the Antichrist. I do not doubt that others who have pushed these things further into the distance will be refuted by posterity with the same argument,

<column-break/>

because the reality of the situation will refute their prophecy until that day comes which is unknown even to the angels. When our Lord Jesus denied that it was ours to know this, He, as Augustine says, "unloosed the fingers" <note>An idiom meaning He stopped the calculations or "counting on fingers" of the curious</note> of all bold men with a single voice. <margin>Augustine.</margin>

### Chapter XVII. How weakly the astrologers prove there can only be six religions; and that the Hebrew law should be called Jovian or Solar rather than Saturnine.

But hear by what a "beautiful" fiction they gather all past religions and the one that will be under the Antichrist into one bundle (so to speak). They say Jupiter signifies religion, but one or another type of religion arises from its embrace with various other stars. There are six planets besides Jupiter, and therefore there are six types of religion, of which there will be neither more nor fewer. For Jupiter with Saturn makes the religion of the Jews; with Mars, that of the Chaldeans, who worship fire; with the Sun, that of the Egyptians, who worship the "host of heaven" (that is, the stars); with Venus, the Saracen religion; with Mercury, the Christian; and with the Moon, that which is to be the last of all under the Antichrist. This is that "subtle and profound" invention which Roger Bacon <note>Medieval English philosopher and friar (c. 1214–1292)</note> used especially in his letter to Clement, and which Pierre d'Ailly <margin>Roger Bacon. Pierre d'Ailly. Evaluation of this logic's lies.</margin> also used in his treatise *On the Concordance of Astrology and Theology*. In this, I first marvel that they have so forgotten their own dogma: they who were always accustomed to say that religions are made or signified only from the meeting of the superior stars—especially Saturn and Jupiter—now descend all the way to the Moon, claiming she will bring us some Antichrist. Moreover, if they wish to count the types of religion according to the number of planets, they must either remove one planet from the sky or beg for more from somewhere else; otherwise, the number will not correspond. For they either accept "idolatry" as one religion, or they want to accept every single type of idolatry separately in that number according to various rites and worships. If they prefer the first, they must remove one planet from the middle; since the religion of the Egyptians and that of the Chaldeans will not be different, but one and the same: that is, idolatry. Therefore, there will only be five religions: the Mosaic, the Christian, the Muhammadan, and (so to speak) the Antichristian. If they command the types of idolatry to be taken separately, there are hardly as many stars in the sky as there are religions on earth. If they think these can be reduced to "heads" <note>Major categories</note> where one is fire-worship and the other star-worship, they deserve a great evil from the demons for being passed over in that partition—the demons would be indignant, since they are the ones worshipped chiefly and almost exclusively in idolatry. For "all the gods of the gentiles are demons"; therefore, they must necessarily make at least three types of idolatry: of the heavens, of demons, and of elements. They are forced to seek one "error"—I mean to say "error," that is, a planet <note>A pun: the Greek word *planetes* means "wanderer" or "error"</note>—from their friends somewhere so that eight may be found to match the number of religions. But they are always poorly skilled in all the things they speak of. <margin>Tertullian, Iamblichus.</margin> For the worship of the celestial bodies was proper to the Chaldeans, as Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD)</note> writes, while the Egyptians were more occupied with the worship of demons; therefore, they ought to procure the Sun for the Chaldeans instead of Mars, and some "diabolical" planet in the meantime for the Egyptians. It would be easy to show that they fight against the truth everywhere, for they have always been very little friendly to it. But why do they so often disagree with themselves? For if they consult reason, they will not find enough in their own dogmas to explain why the Hebrew law is Saturnine...

->AGAINST THE ASTROLOGERS, BOOK VI.<-

<note>original: "Saturnia fit potius quàm christiana"</note> It should be called Saturnian rather than Christian; but [the Jewish religion] should rather be referred to the Sun or to Jupiter, while ours [Christianity] should be referred to Saturn. For Saturn, as some say, does not bestow bodily goods but takes them away; instead, he gives spiritual things and those which are not seen. The Mosaic law <note>The religious law of the Hebrews</note> both promised and bestowed bodily goods; our law [Christianity] takes these away rather than displaying them, and it promises and provides spiritual things and whatever is not seen. Saturn does not create kings of the people, commanders of armies, wealthy men, nobles with many offspring, or those who are womanizers by nature—the sorts of leaders found in all the Hebrew religions: Abraham, Jacob, Moses, Joshua, Solomon, David. Instead, he makes people ignoble, poor, hermits, haters of pleasures, those meditating on eternity, and those who despise bodily things. If such a person is to be numbered among others, it is our leader and commander Jesus Christ; such were the apostles, martyrs, monks, and Christians, by whose life, teaching, and blood our religion was increased, born, and confirmed. Therefore, if we had to speak in a way consistent with their [the astrologers'] decrees, we should be called "Saturnians," and the Hebrews should be called "Solarians" or "Jovians" <note>followers of the Sun or Jupiter</note>. 

But they were drawn into that opinion by the worship of the Sabbath; because that day is considered by them to be the day of Saturn, it seemed most fitting to them to say that the people were "Saturnian" because they venerated the day of Saturn above all others. Led by a similar conjecture, they are also accustomed to say that our religion is "Solar," because we observe the day of the Sun, which we call the Lord's Day. But why should we not rather be assigned to the day of Mercury, since they also subject us to Mercury? For he [an astrologer] gave the Sun to the Egyptians and Mercury to us. 

<margin>Abu Ma'shar.</margin>
And Abu Ma'shar <note>The influential Persian astrologer Albumasar (787–886)</note> says that Jupiter with Mercury signifies the Christian law, although he also said the same about the Sun. Indeed, it is not considered a vice to err or change one's opinion among those who are so constantly focused on the errors and movements of the planets; for while they are stunned by inspecting that rapid whirling of the heavens, they can scarcely ever stand firmly on their feet. But however it may be, they have marvelous reasons with which to confirm these discoveries of theirs. For they did not refer us to Mercury at random; but because, as Roger Bacon <note>A 13th-century English philosopher and friar interested in science and astrology</note> says, Mercury has manifold movements that are difficult to know, he claims for himself the Christian religion, whose dogmas are almost incredible and most difficult to find and recognize. Other younger men have thought up some other nonsense: namely, that because Mercury is the "Librarian" <note>original: "Librarius"</note> of the gods, and there is a great abundance of books among Christians, therefore they say this religion ought by right to be judged "Mercurial." This is the "admirable wisdom" of the astrologers—they have evidently forgotten the libraries of the pagans, and they have seen almost none of the books of the Arabs and Hebrews until now.
