# THE DISPUTATIONS OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA AGAINST THE ASTROLOGERS: BOOK SIX BEGINS.

### Chapter One. In what order we must proceed in tearing down the foundations of the astrologers. Likewise, that it is impossible for all the stars to eventually be restored to the same places in which they once were.

**W**e have exceeded the order and plan of our commentary, in which the roots of the astrologers should have been torn up before we cut down those "lofty heights" of the great conjunctions, the great orbits, and other things of that kind; for once the roots are removed, those things must necessarily collapse. For who would place faith 

<column-break/>

in those who pronounce judgments on the change of kingdoms and religions through "great conjunctions" <note>Rare alignments of Jupiter and Saturn thought to signal major historical shifts</note>? It would already be established that those signs—the Rams, Lions, Crabs, and Archers <note>Aries, Leo, Cancer, and Sagittarius</note>—in which they think Jupiter and Saturn meet to cause these things, are non-existent, or if there are any such things in the heaven, they are not where they are calculated to be. Furthermore, Saturn, Jupiter, and the rest of the planets would not produce events and the changes of lower things. Even if they did produce them, nevertheless nothing has been discovered about their efficiency, nature, or property, either by reason or experience. And since one thing comes from one conjunction and another from another (if indeed anything comes from them at all), it cannot be distinguished among those for whom the very first principles of that art are still in doubt. 

For we shall see in the things that will be disputed later that it has not yet been agreed upon what hour should be considered the beginning of the year of the conjunction: whether in the year when it happens, or rather in the year when the stars themselves meet. Furthermore, we shall see that they can attain neither of these times; therefore, the horoscope of the conjunction is left in doubt. Likewise, even if the horoscope were established, nothing is yet certain regarding the method of arranging the "theme" <note>The birth chart or figure of the heavens</note>, but it is uncertain where the beginnings of the twelve "houses" <note>The twelve divisions of the sky in an astrological chart</note> are correctly established. And even if those were established, it is not clear to them what the power of the place itself is—what is the beginning, what is the middle, and what is the end. When these things are ignored, just as it is unknown in what region of the heaven they are joined, so it cannot be known what the conjunction is going to do, since almost every variation of what is signified is reduced to the nature and property of the places they call "houses." 

And because in those specific conjunctions they are accustomed to observe which planet is "exalted" above the other, we shall see that they do not yet know what that "exaltation" is, which they commonly call "elevation." And since it also matters greatly which planet rules primarily over the place itself, or the coupling of the superior stars, or the eclipse of the luminaries, we shall see that all these rights, empires, and authorities of the planets are so controversial that there is scarcely any part of any sign found about whose prince and lord anything certain is held among astrologers. But it is not necessary to enumerate here the foundations of this art which will be torn down later. With these foundations (as I said before), everything must also fall which they dare to pronounce regarding divine miracles through great conjunctions and other such things. Truly, since they would especially offend the character of religion with this part, every delay seemed like a loss in removing this pestilence—especially since the entire astrological system seemed most effectively refuted, and not at all weakened in other respects, if this part about great conjunctions were proved false and they were defeated there where they seem greater and stronger. Now returning to where we digressed, we shall proceed to root out the first foundations of that art in the following order.

<margin>The error of Abu Ma'shar and others.</margin>
Nor truly should we pass over in silence a common error among astrologers, into which Abu Ma'shar and many others fell, thinking that eventually all the stars would be restored to the same places so that a completely similar disposition of the heaven and the position and relationship of all heavenly bodies to one another would be found as it once was. From this, they think it will follow that the same things will exist among us as once were: the same men, the same events, the same beasts, and a completely identical condition for all lower things. Certain astrologers, examining these things more deeply, are accustomed to whisper in one's ear: "This is that resurrection of the Christians, which the Hebrews and the 

<margin>An impious, execrable dogma.</margin>
Mahometans <note>Followers of Muhammad; Muslims</note> also hope for." Surely those were the greatest prophets...

->DISPUTATION ON NUMBERS<-

<margin>Haly and Ptolemy</margin> Astronomers: but they hid this mystery from the common people and the unlearned. For they thought there was a common number of years for the world and days by which the positions of the planets and stars could be certified. They believed that when that number was complete, all the stars would return to the exact same point; because of this, they thought all things would return to the state they once were <note>This refers to the "Great Year" or the "Platonic Year," the idea that history repeats itself when the stars return to a starting configuration</note>. For us, however, it is not necessary to refute this insanity with many words, since Haly himself—in his exposition of the first book of the *Apotelesmatika* <note>original: "apotelesmatum"; Ptolemy’s work on the effects of the stars, commonly known as the *Tetrabiblos*</note>, following the opinion of Ptolemy himself saying the same—indignantly rebukes that idea. He says there is no one skilled in arithmetic to whom this error would not be evident. <margin>Nicole Oresme</margin> Then, after him, Nicole Oresme <note>A 14th-century philosopher and mathematician</note>, a most sharp philosopher and diligent mathematician, demonstrated in his treatise *On the Ratios of Ratios* <note>original: "de proportionibus proportionum"</note> by mathematical reasoning that this opinion was false and impossible—the belief, that is, that the same position of the heavens and stars that once existed could ever return. Since he sufficiently fulfilled this task, I thought the reader should be directed to him, so that we do not do again what has already been done—something we have nowhere done until now.

---

### Chapter II. By what means astrologers say the influences of the stars vary, and how utterly absurd these are in general.

<margin>The opinion of astrologers on the variation and powers of the stars</margin> Unless I am mistaken, great—or more truly, all—foundations of astrology are removed if it is sufficiently proved that nothing is caused or indicated by the heavens of which the astrologers profess a prediction from celestial observation. Now, among the reasons we used against them, one was most powerful: concerning the momentary change of celestial virtues which they invent. We touched upon this in the previous disputation, but we rightly deferred its explanation until this place; for it needs a specific and proper treatment of its own, and it carries great weight in tearing down astrology. For from this, not only is that confirmed which has been proved so far—namely, that the stars do not cause the particular changes of lower things—but also that if those changes did come from heaven, they would come in a way other than what could be grasped or signified by any celestial observation.

Therefore, what the astrologers say is this: that the virtue and power of the stars and planets is different at every single hour and moment, as they are either in other places of heaven (which the moderns call "houses"), or are found in other signs (of which they invent twelve), or the planets themselves, being distant from one another by a certain interval of space, are joined by various mutual radiations which they commonly call the "aspects" of the planets. These are the principal ways (to omit certain more recent ones) by which they think the flow and virtue of celestial things are changed: namely, the diversity of the house, the sign, and the aspect. Indeed, unless they defend these things, they cannot maintain their dogma about the efficacy of the stars—that every change and diversity of lower things proceeds from the stars. For if those stars always possessed the same and immutable virtue (as we believe of all except the Moon), then necessarily either the same or similar effects would always proceed from them. For they cannot refer the diversity of effects to "lower causes" <note>Earthly factors</note> as we do, unless they also confess with us that they can divine nothing from heaven concerning this diversity, since its author and cause would not be held within their system. <margin>The variety of things cannot be attributed to the multitude of stars.</margin> Therefore, it is necessary for them to find as much diversity of causes in heaven as there is variety in the effects of lower things. In this matter, the multitude of the stars

<column-break/>

does not help them at all: because however many stars and planets there may be, they are all present to everyone being born. Therefore, no reason could be given why they would grant different things to different people and not the same to all, unless they invented something whereby the virtue and efficiency of the stars is one thing at one time and another at another. From this, it could then easily be gathered why things happen or arise at different times: namely, because he who was born when the state of the stars was different received a different condition from heaven, which they themselves can pronounce upon, having explored the state of the stars at whatever time it was.

This, however, is what we refute in the present book, since nothing can be thought more absurd or more remote from all reason than that there should be such inconstancy and mutability in the nature of the higher bodies <note>the stars and planets</note>—more than is seen even in lower things, though these are by their nature most fluid and changeable. <margin>General refutation.</margin> For what is this so "shifty" change and Chameleon-like inconstancy, that even in a brief interval of time those most divine bodies are never found to be like themselves or endowed with the same gifts? Let them say, I ask, what they think those properties of the sidereal flows are: do they proceed from the nature and substance of the stars themselves, or rather from some force sent in from the outside? Whether drawn from the twelve places of heaven, or from the signs, or from their mutual radiations. If they answer the first, they cannot change those properties unless the substance of the stars itself is changed—which I think they will not concede. If they prefer the second, the celestial bodies will be the most ignoble of all bodies, doing almost nothing from their own nature, but doing everything according to a force and affection attacking them from the outside. For a corporal substance is more perfect the more the operation flowing from it emerges from the innermost substance of the one acting.

And these things we have said in a universal and general way; for the insanity of the opinion will shine forth most clearly when we soon examine in detail the things by which they think the virtues of the stars are changed. In running through these, we shall preserve the sequence of their errors and fables.

Let us now begin to do this, starting from the twelve houses of heaven, for whose diversity they most fabulously devise that the flow of both signs and stars is not only intensified or weakened, but rendered entirely and utterly different.

### Chapter III. How the "Houses" of the astrologers are supported by no foundation: and how the astrologers fight among themselves in explaining their powers.

No one who is not entirely ignorant of this art is unaware of the twelve houses celebrated among astrologers; to these, it seems to me, almost every signification and property of the flows is finally referred by them. For if you ask about the nature of any planet—what it might effect, or of what thing it is considered the giver and author—they will answer nothing definite or certain, except according to the nature of the house in which the planet is found. Thus, almost everything they usually say in common about the properties of the planets seems to fall under that which has a manifold meaning under a common word. For what is more general in the nature of a planet than that it be "good" or "bad"—that is, the author of happiness or unhappiness? And yet even this is not firm and always the same in the stars. <margin>What a good and bad planet might work.</margin> But a "good" planet in a "bad" place hurts, and a "bad" one in a "good" place is thought by them to help. Finally, to name one for all, Jupiter, when placed in the East, differs so much from himself...

# AGAINST THE ASTROLOGERS, BOOK VI.

<column-break/>

...itself, when it has moved a little above the eastern horizon into that which they call the twelfth place of heaven, if fire differs as much from air or from water as a hare does from a donkey, or a donkey from an elephant. For in the east, it always decrees the greatest goods; yet in the twelfth house, which is adjacent to the east, it often decrees great evils. It is especially characteristic of Jupiter to bestow wealth and riches; nonetheless, when placed in the third or eighth house, it frequently dissipates one’s inheritance, even though its own nature is to make men noble and wise. If it holds the eighth place, it will make them ignoble, and those whose fury—as Maternus <note>Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman lawyer and astrologer who wrote the *Matheseos libri octo*</note> says—results in insanity. Finally, what is more characteristic of Jupiter than that it is thought to give the benefit of its own nature, since it is called both the most fortunate of planets and the "great happiness of the sky"? Yet, when positioned in the third place, Maternus says it is neither good nor bad. Even when placed in the sixth place, it decrees the greatest evils. Giving the reason for this, 
<margin>Maternus.</margin>
Maternus adds: "For the festive place <note>original: "locus festus"; a technical term in ancient astrology for certain houses</note> has its own prerogative of malice, and whatever star is in that place—that is, the sixth—will borrow the greatest power for decreeing evils from the defect of that location." These are his words. Let us therefore ask the astrologers: from where does such a sudden and perpetual "flood" <note>original: "diluuio"; likely used here metaphorically for a washing away or total change of character</note> in divine bodies come? Bodies which, by the firmness and immutability of their substance, should rightly be believed to be most tenacious of their own nature and always similar to themselves. Surely only two ways can be imagined by which this could happen. One is if we understand various powers and authorities to be implanted in those places, which they then flow into the stars positioned beneath them; this is what the quoted words of Maternus seem to signify. The other way is if we think the planet itself neither receives anything from elsewhere nor is affected differently in different places, 
<margin>Refutation</margin>
but rather that the projection of its rays varies according to the different positioning of the star relative to the earth. From this, we might believe the power and efficiency of the rays are also varied. Whichever they choose to say, they will be proven insane. For if they answer that powers of this sort flow from the "place" to the planets, we shall ask what they think a "place" actually is? Is it what some ancients thought, that place is a space 
<margin>
Definition of place. Aristotle, *On Physics*.
</margin>
void of bodies and separate from them? Or is it what Aristotle calls the "outermost surface of the surrounding body"? <note>Aristotle defined "place" (*topos*) in his *Physics* as the inner boundary of the containing body</note> If it is a space or an interval, let them admit along with those same philosophers that such an interval has no virtues or properties, since natural forms follow actual matter, not mere dimensions and empty gaps. If it is the outermost surface of a surrounding body, some power could indeed reside in this "place"—namely, the power of the body whose surface it is—by which the body being surrounded is subsequently affected. But what are these bodies? Whose edge will be considered the "place" of the stars? Certainly, whatever they are called—whether the outermost sphere of all, or the one joined and closest to each individual star—there will be no part of such bodies that does not surround the east, the west, the highest point of heaven, the lowest, and all other places in a single day's revolution. Therefore, if the power comes from those parts, the power of the east will not always be the same, nor will that of the west. Rather, according to the nature of the body currently present there, the power itself will be changed. Finally, this cannot be said by them because the twelve signs <note>The constellations or divisions of the Zodiac</note>, which are said to be in the houses besides the houses themselves (just as planets are in houses and signs), are described by them as being in the highest sphere of all. These signs are also said to borrow their powers and nature from the house in which they are, just as the planets do. For they say that Aries does not do the same things in the east as it does in the west; and the same for other signs that are perceived in the eighth sphere, or in that which is considered the highest sphere. Since these are 

<column-break/>

surrounded by no other body, there is nowhere we can imagine this "power of the houses" to be, except in immobile space and the interval which is occupied by bodies. But that is either nothing (if we believe Aristotle), or if it is something, it is marked by no character of efficacy or property. Therefore, to imagine different powers in those places—that is, in the different positioning of signs and planets—by which the stars placed therein are affected, is utterly foreign to all reason. Nor will they say anything less discordant or ridiculous if they use the second part of their defense: namely, that because of the diversity of position, the planets look at us with a different face, and their rays are sent down to earth differently, and from this diversity of effects is born. How absurd this is, anyone who has even tasted the rudiments of optics and philosophy will easily understand. For there is no one who does not know that the quality of an effect is distinguished by the quality of the ray and the nature of the radiating body, not by the different circulation of the ray. This [positioning] can be the cause of the same thing happening more or less. The Sun's ray, in whatever way or position it is directed toward us, always heats and always illuminates; but when it is closest or on a direct line, it illuminates more and heats more. When it is slanted or refracted, or descends from a more remote place, it does the same things as the direct and near ray, but it does them less. No other diversity in effect can occur except that which follows the actual intensification or weakening of heat and light. It is therefore an insane dogma of the astrologers to think that the twelve signs of heaven and the planets, when placed here, bless our brothers or make them miserable, yet when they have moved a little further from there, they have no power and no significance regarding brothers, but either give or take away riches; in one place they provide friends, and in another they stir up adversaries against us. Nothing of the nature of the sign or planet has changed, but only a variety of position has occurred. However, as we have said, whether this variety makes the rays closer to us, or pulls them more powerfully to the earth, or joins or separates them from the east, or mixes them more or less with the vapors of the earth: it can perhaps sharpen or blunt the power of the ray, but it certainly cannot change its nature. Therefore, it cannot change the thing the ray produces; rather, the effect—without its species being changed—will perhaps operate with some different disposition, perhaps more firmly and effectively, or perhaps more weakly. Since virtues and properties, whether those of the elements or those more occult, follow the nature and species of a thing, if that nature is not changed into another, the properties themselves cannot be changed so that they become different things. But if they respond that they have experienced it to be so, some faith might perhaps be held—if an experiment could be prepared regarding these things (which will be refuted below), or if they agreed among themselves on the same opinion. But since different men ascribe different properties to the same places, they deprive their own observations of the authority of faithful testimony. The Arabs, and the Latins following in the footsteps of the Arabs, 
<margin>
Arabs and Latins.
Egyptians and Ptolemy.
Discord in [houses] 5 and 10, etc.
</margin>
contend that the quality of servants is indicated by the sixth house. The Egyptians and Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century foundational figure of Western astrology</note> look for adverse health—whether a defect or a disease—from that house which is most distant of all from the sixth, that is, from the twelfth. Ptolemy does not seek it from the sixth house as much as from the seventh and the first; for he never uses the sixth in his prognostications <note>original: "apotelesmatis"</note>, whereas he always uses these others. Conversely, the common crowd of astrologers, omitting those, seek every significance of this kind from the sixth house. Whoever is to have children, the Arabs and Latins pronounce from the fifth house; Ptolemy from the tenth and eleventh; and for those for whom life is not extended, he uses the fifth as well...

### DISCUSSION VII.

<margin>Paulus, Manilius, Porphyry.</margin>
...fourth. This is the same thing that Paulus of Alexandria <note>A 4th-century astrological writer</note> observes. Manilius <note>The text spells this "Mallius," referring to the 1st-century Roman poet Marcus Manilius</note> suspends the fortune of those born in the east and the prayers of parents upon the fourth house. Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote a commentary on Ptolemy</note> says that children are primarily signified by the tenth house: because from that part of the sky, souls are sent down into bodies; and thus he beautifully confirms one fable with another fable. The same Manilius puts Saturn in charge of the fourth place, against the opinion of others who put it in the twelfth.

Indeed, if we unroll the works of Manilius—who says he occasionally imitated the dogma of the ancients, and than whom no older narrator of celestial matters (or, more truly, of fables) has existed among the Latins—we find a system of the twelve places so different from every opinion now reported that the entire method of predicting is utterly changed. For instance, he placed Mars in the setting sun, while others decreed the first seat below the setting for it. What of those other twelve places of heaven handed down by Manilius? Are they not different from all the astrology now in our hands? Do they not vary every reason for predicting?

> Now oppressed, the stars and the world warn accordingly.
> No other seats, nor time, nor kind of healing
> Should it demand for itself: or in whose time it may offer
> Help: and to mix the healthy juices of life.
<margin>The Twelfth.</margin>
> The last, concluding the whole sum in order,
> Is the labor in acquiring things, which contains all
> The effects of prayers, and what studies and arts
> Each man proposes for himself; that these may not be in vain,
> Whether he brings duty: it flatters every nod,
> Or whether he attempts harsh disputes through litigation in the forum:
> Whether he seeks fortune on the sea and follows the winds.
> Whether he seeks full grain and a harvest surpassing the granaries,
> Or returns to Bacchus through the flowing, rich must.
> In this part, the days and these moments will be given.
> If the stars following through the signs will agree well.

So far Manilius, whose opinion is clearly at odds with all the astrology now in use. Yet I think he has been understood by none of those who today make themselves the interpreters and followers of Manilius. In this great variety of opinions, what trust can there be in experience? For a greater problem arises: the very manner in which the beginnings and ends of the houses <note>The "cusps" of the houses</note> ought to be divided has not yet been established. Different people feel differently, as we have declared in another book. This ought to have been explored before any observation regarding their properties was instituted as an experiment. It is so far from being certain or factual that no observation can even be claimed which would force us, by true and compelling reasons, to yield our assent. We conclude—regardless of what Ptolemy and the others believed—that it is ridiculous and false, as the evidence of reason compels us, to think that there are any properties in those places, or that the flow and efficiency of the planets are changed by their diversity.

### Chapter IV. Concerning the twelve signs, that they were invented by mathematicians for ease of calculation. Likewise, that astrologers have erred in many ways concerning them.

**I**ndeed, they observe this division and the boundaries of the signs as if they were prescribed by the laws of nature. They think two planets have more in common if they are separated by twenty degrees but placed in the same sign, than if one holds the last parts of Aries and the other is found in the beginnings of Taurus, even though they are separated by the narrowest space. Between these latter two, not even the width of a finger falls as an interval. But if anyone should contend that this number of signs is from nature, and not invented by mathematicians

### AGAINST THE ASTROLOGERS, BOOK VI.

<columns>

<margin>Against Albumasar.</margin>
...for the ease of calculation, but established by a philosophical reason such as the one Albumasar <note>Abu Ma'shar (787–886 AD), a highly influential Persian astrologer and astronomer.</note> asserts: namely, that there are twelve signs because there are four elements, each of which is divided into three parts—the middle, the first, and the last. I could indeed respond that this reasoning is no less ridiculous and frivolous than the mathematical one.

<margin>Haly, Aben Ezra.</margin>
But it can be easily demonstrated by reason that the authors of this division were not moved by such conjectures at all, just as we declared above through the testimony of Haly <note>likely Ali ibn Ridwan, an 11th-century commentator on Ptolemy</note> and Aben Ezra <note>Abraham ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167), a Jewish polymath and astrologer.</note>. For even if that conjecture holds for the signs, what will be said about the distribution of the signs into thirty parts <note>degrees</note>? What about the portioning of the parts into sixty minutes? What philosophical reason will he provide for these? Or how will they justify the fact that mathematicians, considering no properties of nature there, instead sought numbers more suitable for calculation? From this comes the error of the astrologers, or a certain opportunity for deception, as they decree these things as if they possessed entirely separate powers—not divided by human choice, but rather by nature. It is well known how they ascribe various properties to different parts and even minutes of the same sign. Thus, they proclaim some parts as "bright," others as "dark," others related to the Sun, others to Mars, and others to different planets. They even tell fables about the minutes themselves; for example, Aesculapius wrote the *Myriogenesis* <note>original: "miriogenem"; a lost work on the 36,000 divisions of the zodiac</note>, 

<margin>Aesculapius. Maternus.</margin>
which Maternus <note>Julius Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman astrologer</note> concealed as a mystery, in which he claimed that every single minute had a specific property through its "outflowing." Yet, just as the mathematical calculation was made by human will alone, so too the primary division of the entire Zodiac into twelve signs received its origin from nowhere else. We have already declared that however the division of these signs is understood, they have no efficacy. Thus, the insanity of the astrologers is refuted here, as they believe a planet is changed according to the condition of the sign it has traveled through. For they establish the houses and exaltations <note>original: "altitudines"; the "peak" of a planet's power</note> of the planets according to these signs, not according to the constellations <note>original: "imagines"; the actual visual shapes of the stars</note>, which we showed in the previous book can only be imagined and have no physical solidity. This is perhaps why the Chaldeans <note>The ancient Babylonians/astronomers</note>, who did not use these mathematical signs, also made no "houses" for the planets; for among them, Leo was not the home of the Sun, nor Cancer of the Moon, nor Libra and Taurus of Venus, nor Pisces and Sagittarius of Jupiter, and so on for the rest. Instead, they observed only the "exaltations" of the stars, not in relation to the signs, but to the actual constellations. Thus, for them, Saturn possessed nothing in Capricorn or Aquarius, but held authority only in Libra and Scorpio. For although these are two signs, they are judged as a single constellation among the Chaldeans. Otherwise, if Ptolemy and others were to refer the houses of the planets to the constellations (which they do not), the logic would not fit: for Mars has a very great affinity with the stars that make up the constellation of Taurus—more than any other planet—yet he is said to be "detrimented" <note>fallen or weakened</note> in the sign of Taurus. Therefore, they take the houses, exaltations, terms, triplicities, degree-rulerships <note>original: "monomirīas"</note>, decans <note>ten-degree divisions</note>, faces <note>original: "hydropoſopias"</note>, and the rest of the planetary affinities with the parts of the Zodiac from these signs. Since these things are entirely imaginary, not natural, and not effective, no power can come from them to the planets. This, I think, has been sufficiently proven. One must wonder at those who wished to bolster astrological opinion with the idea of "planetary similarity," saying that planets take on the qualities of the Zodiac (in which the seeds of things are scattered) just as plants take on the flavor of the soil. That comparison is quite flawed, since plants are nourished by the earth and therefore reflect its flavor; the planets are not nourished by the Zodiac, even though 

<column-break/>

every kind of animal <note>A reference to the *Zodiakos*, or "circle of animals"</note> shines there. Not only are the planets not attached to the Zodiac like the roots and branches of plants to the earth, but they are separated by an immense chasm and interval. For this reason, Panætius <note>A Stoic philosopher (c. 185–109 BC) who rejected astrology</note> and Plotinus <note>The founder of Neoplatonism (c. 204–270 AD)</note> especially mock them, thinking it impossible for "contagion" to pass from the Zodiac to the stars across such a vast gap of space. We are moved not so much by the space that lies between, which is immense, but by the nature of the things themselves: since real and natural bodies cannot be affected by imaginary ones, and shining stars cannot be changed by non-shining ones (not to say by things that don't exist at all). But it is easy to see 

<margin>Panætius. Plotinus.</margin>
<margin>Where they were deceived.</margin>
what deceived them here as well. Because the Sun, when positioned in Leo, heats the earth more violently, and the same Sun, when coming to Aries, restores the world, as it were, it seemed to them that it had a kinship with Leo and Aries. Since the Sun is rendered stronger while traveling through those signs, and we experience its greater power every year, they established Leo as the home of the Sun and Aries as its kingdom. Led by this conjecture regarding the Sun, they thought the same should be decreed for the other signs: that a planet could do more in one sign and less in another. And with "most beautiful" logic, they distributed two houses to each planet, except for the Sun and the Moon, for whom one royal house each would be enough. Regarding the Sun, since they had decided for the reason given that it should be allotted Leo as its home (in which it exercises its greatest power in the blazing heat), it seemed reasonable that the next house should be thought of as belonging to the Moon, which is closer to us. Indeed, its circle is also most proximate to us; therefore, they assigned Cancer as the domicile of the Moon. However, according to the position of the spheres in which the planets are carried, they distributed two to each, one on either side. Thus, to Mercury, which is believed to be adjacent to the Moon, they gave Gemini on one side and Virgo on the other; to Venus, Taurus on this side and Libra on that; to Mars, Aries here and Scorpio there; to Jupiter, Pisces and Sagittarius; to Saturn, Aquarius and Capricorn. With these persuasions, they founded their dogmas—which have been handed down by posterity with such authority that they are accepted almost as if they were great oracles—without even the weight of rhetorical probability. In these matters, see how criminal and full of both ignorance and sluggishness is the first principle upon which the rest depend! For the fact that the Sun heats us more in Leo does not come from the nature of the sign it traverses, 

<margin>The foundation is destroyed.</margin>
but happens because of its position and placement, because from that location it strikes the earth more directly in the regions closest to us. Otherwise, if a quality received from the sign caused this, it would do the same among all nations, since the same signs exist for everyone. But at the same time that the Sun burns the lands situated to the North while positioned in Leo, it is cold for those who inhabit the South; for them, it is hot when coming to Aquarius, under which for us it pours out ice and rain. This is clearly because the more it approaches us, the more it is distant from them, and conversely, it turns its path toward them whenever it departs from us. But if they contend that they were led not so much by this as by other experiments, through which it was observed that a planet could do more or less in different places—perhaps some faith might be given if the founders of the art had handed down consistent information. Where, then, are the "experiments" of the Chaldeans? I speak of the masters who, they proclaim, observed the heavens for so many thousands of years in the open plains; yet they gave no credence to these "houses," as we said above. Why, then, in such diligent and long-lasting observations, did they never find Mars to be strong in Scorpio and weak in Taurus, or Saturn powerful in Capricorn and weak in Cancer? The same should be understood for the rest. And since the same sign is divided into so many "terms" and so many...

He points out that the Sun's strength in certain signs is due to geographical perspective and the angle of light, not the "quality" of the sign itself.</summary>

Among the Egyptians, this is the title of the second house. The same Mallius puts Saturn in charge of the fourth house, against the opinion of others who put him in the twelfth. If we unroll the works of Mallius—who says he has sometimes followed the dogma of the ancients, and than whom no older narrator of celestial things (or to speak more truly, teller of fables) exists among the Latins—we find a system of the twelve houses so different from every opinion now reported that the entire method of predicting is utterly changed. He placed Mars in the setting [the West], where others decreed the first seat under the setting for someone else. Are not those other twelve celestial houses handed down by Mallius different from all the astrology now in hand? Do they not vary every reason for predicting?

Thus far Mallius, whose opinion is clearly at odds with all astrology now in use. But yet, I think he has been understood by no one among those who make themselves interpreters and followers of Mallius. In such a great variety of opinions, then, what is the reliability of experience? Especially when another greater problem is added: the manner in which the beginnings and ends of the houses ought to be divided has not yet been established. Others feel differently, as we declared in another book—yet this ought to have been explored before any observation regarding their properties was instituted. It is so far from being certain that any observation could finally be claimed that would compel us to turn away from the truth and toward these persuasive reasons. We conclude it is ridiculous and false—no matter what Ptolemy and the others believed, even if the evidence of reason forced them to it—that there are either any properties in these places, or that the influence and efficiency of the planets are changed by their diversity.

### Chapter IV: On the twelve signs, which were invented by mathematicians for the ease of calculation. Likewise, that astrologers have erred in many ways concerning them.

**T**hey observe this division and the boundaries of the signs as if they were prescribed by the laws of nature. They think two planets have more "commerce" <note>Astrological connection or relationship.</note> even if they are twenty degrees apart, provided they are placed in the same sign, than if one holds the last parts of Aries and the other is found in the beginnings of Taurus—even though the former are separated by a vast space and between the latter not even a finger's breadth of an interval falls. But if anyone contends that this number of signs is from nature, and not a fiction by mathematicians for the ease of...

He argues that these houses are arbitrary mathematical inventions rather than natural realities.</summary>

# OF THE DISPUTATIONS

Furthermore, concerning the deans <note>original: *decanis*; 10-degree divisions of a zodiac sign</note>: there are as many among the Egyptians as there are "single-degrees" <note>original: *monomiriis*; a system assigning a planetary ruler to every individual degree</note>: and among the Chaldeans, "twelfth-parts" <note>original: *dodecathemoriis*; divisions of 2.5 degrees</note>. Nor is there any agreement among them regarding the boundaries. Ptolemy ignores the deans, whom the Indians divide one way and the Egyptians another. The Arabs do not know the "single-degrees," while the Greeks mock them, yet the Egyptians use them in every prediction. I pass over the use of the "twelfth-parts," which are used by many; yet, as Firmicus Maternus <note>A 4th-century Latin author of the *Matheseos libri octo*, a major astrological compendium.</note> writes, a planet provides more when in its own boundaries than it provides in its own house, or in its dean, or certainly provides things most similar and close to these. Since these things are so, I ask: what reliable and consistent experience can there be regarding which part of the Zodiac a planet travels through or is exiled in, or whether it is found powerful or weak? Add to this the various opinions about the signs when they are referred either to the "new orb" <note>Referring to the contemporary calculations of the zodiac</note> or rather described by the "eighth sphere" <note>The sphere of the fixed stars</note>; one man wants Saturn to rule in the same part where another wants Jupiter, and another wants a different planet. And here, indeed, some use those signs which they think move, while others use those that do not move. Regarding these opinions, nothing is so settled or 
<margin>Abraham.</margin>
pre-judged that Abraham <note>Referring to Abraham Ibn Ezra, a famous 12th-century Jewish scholar and astrologer.</note>, in his *Book of Nativities*, did not command that a double "theme" <note>A birth chart or horoscope.</note> be made: one for the moving signs, and another for the fixed signs. By this variation of the chart, the entire logic of the predictions is changed. Thus, the authority of every experiment is weakened; and as will be shown later, no certainty can be had about these matters—or if it could be had, it has not yet been achieved.

### Chapter V. What the opinion of astrologers is concerning aspects, and how little rational it is.

We have already refuted the opinion of astrologers regarding the signs and the twelve places of the heavens; there remains the third way by which they falsely claim that powers and "outflows" <note>original: *defluxus*; the planetary influence flowing down to Earth</note> are altered, which is commonly called the **aspect**. For they think that if Saturn, for example, is distant from Jupiter by 60 degrees—that is, by two entire signs—it affects and moves the lower world differently than if it were distant by 90 degrees from the same star, which is an interval of three signs. In the first distance, they say Saturn "looks upon" Jupiter with a hexagonal radiation, which they call the **sextile** aspect, because the space between them is the sixth part of the Zodiac; in the other, they say they behold each other from a **square** <note>original: *ex quadrato*</note>, because they are separated from each other by a fourth of the Zodiac. Similarly, they say there are other properties of both stars if one is distant from the other by 120 degrees, from which the triangular radiation—that is, the **trine** aspect—emerges. Others occur if they are simultaneously opposed from the diameter <note>an **opposition**, or 180 degrees</note>, or meet in the same position or place <note>a **conjunction**</note>. And what we have said of Jupiter and Saturn should be understood as said of all, so that their power and efficiency are changed according to their varying distances from each other. Indeed, they say they are changed so much that when they are distant by certain intervals—that is, trine, or sextile, or opposite <note>Pico notes later that some consider opposition good and some bad; here he is summarizing their general claims.</note>—every outflow is good and healthy. Again, positioned at another distance—that is, either the square or the opposite—they have the most harmful rays, or certainly always little benefit. They claim that from this diversity of intervals, not only the goodness or malice of the outflow is changed, but also the very type and logic of the effect. These are the ravings of the astrologers concerning the aspects of the planets, which a philosopher, upon hearing them, will condemn immediately even without a counter-argument, since the nature and property of two causes working toward the same end cannot be so fundamentally changed by the mere diversity of distance and interval. First, I ask them this: do they wish these things they say about 

<column-break/>

aspects to be referred to the planets themselves, or only to the effects of the planets? That is, when they say that Jupiter is 
<margin>A two-part argument.</margin>
provoked by Mars with "square" rays, or Venus is cherished by the "trine" radiation of Jupiter, do they mean that the bodies of the planets themselves are moved by these kinds of good or bad affections? Or do they mean that the planets suffer nothing from each other and feel no such mutations, but rather that this manner of speaking signifies what they do to us and how they move the subject bodies <note>i.e., people and objects on Earth</note>? Whether they answer this way or that, they fall into a thousand snares and a thousand difficulties. For if they think the planets are 
<margin>That the stars do not harm each other.</margin>
moved by each other and, as if exercising friendships and hatreds, now cherish each other in a friendly embrace and now pursue and attack each other in a hostile manner with the points of their rays—not only will 
<margin>Job</margin>
divine Job cry out against them, in whose book we read that God "makes peace in his high places" <note>Job 25:2</note>, but so will the 
<margin>Aristotle</margin>
entire family of the Peripatetics with their Aristotle. Among them, it is certain that the superior bodies are changed only by the variety of their locations. Those qualities found below the Moon <note>The "sublunary" sphere of change and decay</note> neither reach up there nor depart from there. If they wish to concede those qualities, certainly as far as harmful qualities are concerned, they seem fit to be exploded from the entire assembly of philosophers; for they seem to be entirely ignorant of the nature of the celestial homeland who think there is anything in it that could do injury or endure it. Therefore, if any "passion" <note>In the philosophical sense of being acted upon or changed</note> is to be admitted in the stars, it is at least none other than what should be called a perfection rather than a passion—such as when the Moon is illuminated by the Sun, she does not "suffer" from him in any other way than one who receives a benefit suffers from the benefactor. To suggest, then, that a star is harmed by a star, or besieged, or infected, or made weaker or worse—rendered harmful instead of beneficial, or infirm instead of powerful—is as remote from all truth as all nature of the celestials is remote from all evil. If the stars could suffer injury, surely the nobler and more perfect ones should not suffer it from the ignoble; thus, at the very least, it would follow that not all things can be mutually affected and moved by all things, but only some by others, so that some only act and some only suffer. Otherwise, how do they not blush? They take the Sun, the 
<margin>The Sun's power.</margin>
ruler and king of the planets, the supreme celestial fountain of power as he is of light, and yet reduce him to such a rank and order that even he, conquered by the rays of others, either languishes or turns out to be of little health; and since every virtue of the planets is derived from him, he would "suffer by his own weapon," as the saying goes. But let us dismiss all these things which perhaps do not seem absurd to them, and let us suppose, as they wish, that the planets are affected and moved: let them answer what reason they have that stars which are very close do not move each other, but when they are made more distant, they begin to feel each other and suffer mutually? For this is how they usually define things when they speak of aspects. If Jupiter holds Cancer and Mars holds Leo, between which signs 
nothing lies, they say the stars of Jupiter and Mars are "unlinked" <note>original: *asyndeta*; a Greek term meaning "not bound together"</note>—that is, joined by no coupling of rays or aspects. But then, when Mars has moved further away from Jupiter into Virgo, they will think that Mars participates in Jupiter, and Jupiter in Mars. What could be said that is more absurd or more remote from all philosophy? For it is a most common principle that everything which acts upon another does so more effectively the closer it is to the one suffering the action. Therefore, this thing which the younger astrologers call an "aspect," since it is nothing other than "radiation" (as it was also named by the ancients)—that is, the propagation of one's light and virtue onto another (and, so to speak, a certain "shining-forth")—how [can it be...]

<summary>Pico attacks the internal divisions of the zodiac signs as contradictory and unscientific, then begins a philosophical critique of "aspects," arguing that celestial bodies are immutable and cannot logically be "harmed" or "weakened" by geometric angles.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s Book VI, where he attacks the foundations of astrological theory. In the previous pages, he discussed the lack of consensus regarding the divisions of the zodiac signs. Here, he turns his focus to "aspects"—the geometric angles between planets—arguing that these mathematical relationships have no physical mechanism to influence the natural world.</meta>

# AGAINST ASTROLOGERS, BOOK VI.

<margin>That different radiations do not produce different effects.</margin>
...none upon bodies which are nearby, but will be effective upon those most remote: as if anything could persuade them that just as a ray <note>original: *radius*; in astrology, this refers to the influence projected from a planet at a specific angle</note> is poured out from a more remote or nearer distance, it thus turns out to be of one nature or another. Since (if we follow true reason) no other diversity can arise from this than that the ray is broken more weakly or more strongly upon the planet receiving it. Why its property should also be changed, no cause can be imagined or devised. For even if, due to the diversity of the interval, either the number of intervening parts is varied, or the planets themselves obtain a different positional figure among themselves: nonetheless, that inefficiency of natural things is not varied according to the diversity of numbers and figures: because natural virtues do not proceed from numbers and figures, but from natural forms. It is according to the diversity of these forms that the figures themselves are stable and natural—not like those adventitious <note>Occurring by chance or external motion rather than essential nature.</note> ones that arise from motion; they are moved and varied.

Nor do smaller difficulties arise if they think the diversity of radiation should be considered not in the bodies of the planets, but in their effect; namely, if they say that the stars <note>original: *sydera*; often used generally for any heavenly body, including planets.</note> suffer nothing from each other, but the varying ratio of distance between them causes the flowing rays to be mixed differently, and therefore various effects arise from the diversities of the mixture. For if they answer this, we could first object on the authority of **Plotinus** <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher who argued that stars were signs, not causes, of earthly events.</note> that rays flowing from heaven cannot be mixed with each other in such a way that a new virtue or form arises, since they are neither bodies, nor liquids, nor qualities fixed to bodies. Because of this, they are not received into bodies in a way that they would be "infected" by them, or changed in some way from their state according to the condition of the substance. Therefore, it remains likely to that philosopher that what happens to many qualities—namely, that they are sometimes changed by a certain concretion or mixture into another form coalescing from them all—does not happen to rays. This mixture also usually occurs only with the destruction of the simple and particular qualities flowing together; one will not easily imagine such a thing happening in rays.

But let us grant them that rays are mixed; provided they show us how rays are mixed differently because they flow together from stars that are distant from each other in one way or another. For only this diversity (as we said above) can arise: that those which emanate from closer and more joined bodies will be mixed better and more intimately, while conversely those which proceed from separate and more remote bodies will cohere with more difficulty. This, however, does not please those astrologers who allow no "commerce" between the rays of planets located in adjacent signs; yet they allow it most of all between those that emanated from the most distant signs. Furthermore, if the ratio of either diametric opposition, or quadrangular, or triangular figure creates a diversity in the property of the rays, this cannot be defended unless we say that the bodies of the planets change their condition based on that variety of figures: since the virtue and property of the ray comes from nothing else than the nature of the radiating body.

<margin>Where the variety of figures exists.</margin>
Nor is that variety of figures anywhere else than within the bodies themselves from which the rays descend to us. The more they recede from there, the less they preserve that relationship of figures among themselves, until, touching the earth, they unite into one: so that those which flowed from opposite sources flow together into a unified coalition here with us. Therefore, when they are mixed, they are no longer folded together in triangular or quadrangular schemes <note>original: *schematis*; the geometric patterns or "aspects" formed between planets.</note>, so that the reason for the mixing could be changed by that variety of schemes. But astrologers will have to turn to saying that there is such a property in the rays by which the stars from which they emanated were composed by such a relationship of figures among themselves. And so, finally, they will either say that the stars vary their nature according to the variety of configurations—which has been refuted—or if the stars themselves do not vary, they will be forced to confess that the virtue of the rays flowing from them is also the same and unchanged.

### Chapter VI. Various theories of aspects are recounted and refuted.

<margin>Refutation</margin>
The ancients, whom **Maternus** <note>Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century astrological writer.</note> imitates, brought forward a theory of aspects based on numbers. They said stars were "joined" or separated by a specific number of parts which, when multiplied by another number, would equal the total parts of the heaven. Therefore, a "diametrical" <note>Opposition; an angle of 180°.</note> radiation is made by an interval of 180 parts: because that number doubled makes the whole number of 360 parts. Likewise, a "trine" <note>Trine; an angle of 120°.</note> consists of 120 parts: because if you triple these parts, you again complete all the parts of the heaven. A "quadrate" <note>Square; an angle of 90°.</note> radiation requires 90 parts, which if you quadruple, you gather the sum of 360. A "hexagon" <note>Sextile; an angle of 60°.</note> is computed at 60 parts, which are the sixth part of all the parts. But this theory is too drowsy and too lazy. For by the same reasoning, they should make an aspect at 72 degrees: because multiplied five times, they complete 360 degrees; and they should do the same at 45 degrees, since this number is the eighth part of all the degrees of the heaven.

But, says **Aboasar** <note>Abu Ma'shar, a highly influential 9th-century Persian astrologer.</note>, those numbers have another prerogative, because they not only count the parts of the heaven but also the number of the signs when multiplied. For in a hexagon there are two signs; in a trine four; in a quadrate three; in a diameter six are computed. For twice six, and three times four, and four times three, and six times two all complete the number of twelve signs.

<margin>Rejection of the theory</margin>
But that confirmation is also frivolous. For by similar reasoning, stars that are distant by 30 degrees would be configured with each other: because if you look at the number of parts, you have a twelfth part of the heaven's parts; if you look at the signs, you have a twelfth portion of them as well.

<margin>Ptolemy's mathematical arguments.</margin>
Finally, the causes brought forward by **Ptolemy** regarding geometric figures do not prove the point, since those harmonies of figures do not produce different properties in natural things. But those who use them fall into that error condemned by **Aristotle**: that mathematical arguments are used to treat physical things.

<margin>Avenrodan.</margin>
Perhaps seeing this, **Avenrodan** <note>Ibn Ridwan, an 11th-century Egyptian physician and commentator on Ptolemy.</note> says that Ptolemy, after bringing forward the mathematical theory of aspects, brought forward another from nature.

<margin>Ptolemy's natural theory.</margin>
The theory he brings forward is of this kind: that sextile and trine radiations are beneficial because they are from signs of the same genus, either masculine or feminine. That is, the planets bound together by those schemes are so disposed that if one is in a feminine sign, the other is also in a feminine one; if one is in a masculine, the other is likewise in a masculine. Conversely, square and opposite radiation are harmful because they emerge from signs of different genera.

<margin>First reason. Second.</margin>
This theory of Ptolemy is not only weak but it destroys itself: first because those signs are in reality nothing, which we will reveal in the following books; second, even if they are something, [they are noted] by those marks of qualities or sexes...

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s systematic dismantling of astrological theory in Book VI. Having previously argued that the physical distance and geometric angles (aspects) of planets have no natural mechanism for influencing human affairs, he now examines the specific logical inconsistencies in how astrologers—including Ptolemy and Abu Ma'shar—justify why certain angles are "good" or "bad."</meta>

### FIFTH ARGUMENT

<margin>Third, Fourth</margin> The third and fourth signs are not distinct in such a way that some can be called masculine and others feminine, or some fiery and others airy; this has already been sufficiently proven above. Finally, whatever their condition may be, the planets cannot be changed by them, as we have demonstrated below. For now, let us not dispute these points. Instead, let us demonstrate how these ideas, like all their theories, are clearly in conflict with one another. If what they assume is true, then the "opposite" radiation <note>original: *oppofita radiatio*; in astrology, the "opposition" is an angle of 180 degrees, traditionally considered very difficult or "malefic."</note>—which is considered the most harmful—ought to be numbered among the good ones, since it also occurs only between signs of the same genus. For Aries and Libra are of the same genus; likewise Cancer and Capricorn, and all others that look upon each other from across the diameter. It is truly quite strange that Ptolemy did not see this; that a man otherwise so ingenious would hallucinate in a matter so obvious and clear. If he had remembered what he himself wrote elsewhere, he would have seen that his reasoning does not hold, but is actually contrary to his own precepts.

<margin>Fifth.</margin> For in the third book of that same work <note>referring to Ptolemy's *Tetrabiblos*</note>, he thinks that between signs not only of the same sex but even of the same quality, the configuration is sometimes not "hexagonal" <note>original: *exagonam*; the sextile aspect of 60 degrees, considered harmonious.</note> (that is, good) but "quadrate" <note>original: *quadratam*; the square aspect of 90 degrees, considered tense or bad.</note> (that is, bad). This happens when they are "oblique," meaning signs of short ascension. <note>Signs that take less time to rise over the horizon due to the angle of the ecliptic.</note> Likewise, those signs which are of a different genus might not have a quadrate relationship, but rather a hexagonal affinity. Thus, he would compose a quadrate radiation between Gemini and Aquarius, but a hexagonal one between Taurus and Aquarius. If this is true, how can the goodness or malice of the configurations arise from the affinity or discord of the signs? This is a difficulty that must be faced by all those who measure the spaces of radiations not by the parts of the zodiac, but by the parts of the equator—a practice observed by the majority of astrologers. Yet all of them (as they are incredibly thoughtless) still reason about the malice or goodness of these effects based on the kinship or diversity of those signs.

<margin>Another reason. Abu Ma'shar.</margin> Abu Ma'shar <note>original: *Aboafar*; a 9th-century Persian astrologer influential in the West.</note> brings forward another reason for the aspects which he thinks is based on nature. He says that the **opposition** is confirmed by the fullness of light which the Moon achieves when it is opposite the Sun. He claims the **quadrate** (square) power appears in the motion of the planets from their "apse" <note>the highest or lowest point in a planet's orbit (apogee/perigee)</note>, from which they change their course when they are ninety degrees away. The **trine** <note>original: *trigonum*; a 120-degree angle, considered very lucky.</note> is seen in the "superior" planets <note>Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.</note> which, when removed from the Sun by one hundred and twenty degrees, move backward (if they were moving forward) or move forward (if they were moving backward). The quantity of the **sextile** (hexagon), he says, corresponds to half the diameter of a circle, and also to the distance of the "houses" <note>The zodiac signs traditionally ruled by specific planets.</note> of Venus from the houses of the luminaries <note>The Sun and Moon.</note>. Thus, he has poorly stitched together a single patchwork quilt from a thousand scraps: seeking the opposition from the Moon, the square from the apse, the trine from the superior planets, and the sextile from Venus.

<margin>Refutation</margin> And everything is done poorly by everyone. For what reason is there that, because the Moon is filled with the Sun's light across the diameter, all planets should be linked by this distance—not only to the Sun, but also among themselves? And if the superior planets change their course at a trine from the Sun, why should this interval have the power to change the strengths of planets that are not only superior but also inferior? And why should it apply between the planets themselves, rather than just in relation to the Sun? Furthermore, that rule for superior planets is not even constant.

<margin>Paul and Porphyry.</margin> For Mars, as Paul <note>Paul of Alexandria, a 4th-century astrologer.</note> and Porphyry <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher.</note> write, sometimes stops itself to go backward when it is only eighty-four degrees away from the Sun in the preceding signs—not only failing to wait for the trine, but not even completing the square. But if they derived the power of the trine from that change of the superior planets in trine to the Sun, then it should have been numbered among the bad radiations rather than the good ones.

<column-break/>

<margin>Another reason for aspects devised by the moderns.</margin> For every superior planet in trine to the Sun is "unhappy," if we believe Paul and Heliodorus. For they all say they "become star-like" <note>original: *asteristerizontai*; a Greek term used to describe a planet becoming stationary and appearing like a fixed star, which was considered a moment of weakness or "bad luck" in ancient astrology.</note>; that is, that all stationary planets are bad and unhappy, whether they are in their first or second station. But all these things are more obvious examples of frivolity than they are worth refuting at length. Finally, another reason was devised by certain "moderns" concerning musical consonances, from which they teach that the rays of the planets either harmonize or clash with one another through a certain similarity to musical harmonies. For they say it is proven among musicians by reason and experience that the third and fifth notes harmonize with the first, but the fourth and seventh do not at all. What if, therefore, planets distant from each other by equal spaces are found to be sometimes in good harmony and sometimes in bad? The sextile (hexagonal) radiation corresponds to the third note; the trine (trigonal) to the fifth; and the square (quadrate) to the fourth, since there are as many signs mediating there as there are intervals of notes here. These things are certainly "pretty" and have an appearance of probability to those who have only greeted philosophy from the doorstep <note>meaning those who have only a superficial understanding of philosophy.</note>.

<margin>Refutation.</margin> We, however, setting aside such similarities between such different kinds of things, shall declare that this reasoning has no efficacy and that the comparison and similarity do not hold. For among musicians, if a note does not harmonize with another, it is dissonant; but among astrologers, many spaces are (so to speak) "mute" to each other: that is, they neither harmonize nor clash. For example, the second note is counted among the dissonant ones by musicians no less than the fourth, seventh, or eleventh. But among astrologers, the second sign emits no voice at all in relation to the first, rather than a discordant one. The fifth and seventh signs emit a certain voice, but not a concordant one. Furthermore, there is an even greater discrepancy: the sixth note among musicians harmonizes just as well as the third; yet among astrologers, the sixth sign is completely distinct from the first. Then, in music, the eighth note harmonizes as if it were the same <note>the octave</note>; but the eighth sign does not recognize the first, nor can the eighth note represent the appearance of a "conjunction," which instead the notes of the same tone represent. Therefore, in this "pretty" similarity, one finds entirely more dissimilarity than similarity.

### Chapter VII. What deceived them: and that no experience has been had concerning aspects.

Truly, however, those who first invented that dogma were not even led by reasons of this kind; rather, a certain conjecture based on the Moon deceived them. For when they observed the Moon changing its light from the Sun according to its different position relative to the Sun—whether it was very close or receding—it varied its shape. They transferred this same idea to the rest of the planets, so that all of them, based on their different distances not only from the Sun but also from each other, would change their condition and state. You may easily notice that they were taught this opinion from no other source.

<margin>Five phases of the Moon in relation to the Sun</margin> Thus they established neither more nor fewer, nor any other configurations of the planets among themselves, than those which the Moon undergoes relative to the Sun, which depends more on the diversity in the signs. There are five celebrated configurations of the Moon to the Sun: when it is seen either joined to the Sun <note>New Moon</note>, or crescent-shaped, or halved <note>Quarter Moon</note>, or gibbous <note>mostly full</note>, or full. Just as many configurations were devised by them in the planets to correspond to these: when they are together, or sextile (hexagonal)...

### Chapter VIII. What is said concerning "obsession" contradicts what is said about "aspects."

<margin>*Emperichesis* <note>Greek term for enclosure or besiegement.</note></margin>
<margin>Response and refutation.</margin>
There are, moreover, besides these figures and

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s systematic dismantling of astrological techniques. Having previously criticized the "aspects" or angles between planets, he now turns his attention to the Lunar Nodes (the "Head and Tail of the Dragon") and the concept of "antiscia" (mirrored points of equal light), arguing that these are merely abstract mathematical concepts with no physical power to influence human life.</meta>

<header>AGAINST ASTROLOGY BOOK VI.</header>

<margin>What the Head and Tail are</margin> They invent and make up many things in the heavens that serve mathematical numbers and measurements, yet are founded on no other stability of nature. We showed this regarding the signs which Ptolemy considers immovable, being defined by the solstices and equinoxes; we shall show it again in the discussion of the divisions of the signs into small parts. Now the same will appear regarding the "Head and Tail" <note>These are the Lunar Nodes: the points where the Moon's orbit crosses the ecliptic (the Sun's path).</note>, for they are nothing other than the intersections of two circles. They are mere points, the nexus of two lines conceived in the mind, introduced by mathematicians so they might discern the locations of eclipses. There is, however, no power there, no quality or natural efficacy that could somehow be transferred to the practice of casting birth charts <note>original: "genethlicam".</note>. Certainly, they can do nothing unless some planet positioned there might decree something better or worse for the benefit or disadvantage of that place; but these points, noted separately by themselves, can have no power to rule or change physical bodies.

<margin>Abraham Ibn Ezra</margin> The astrologer Abraham Ibn Ezra <note>A famous 12th-century Jewish scholar and astrologer.</note> saw this regarding the signs as well, for in the first book of his *Reasons for Astrology* he writes: "They also said the Head of the Dragon is exalted in Gemini, and the Tail in Sagittarius. But this is vanity, since the Head and Tail signify neither good nor evil. For they are connections of two circles; however, the Moon is observed when she is in them. For when placed in the Head, she is more invigorated for this reason: because she is closer to us. Conversely, she is weaker in the Tail because, turning toward the south, she is further away from us. The same happens to the rest of the planets when they are found in the Head and Tail, except for the Sun, which has no declination to either side. But when you see the Head and Tail noted separately in the tables of the law, know that they neither harm nor help, though many think otherwise." Thus he spoke.

<margin>Maternus</margin> But Ptolemy never uses them in prediction, nor will you find the ancients using them, as seen in Maternus <note>Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman astrologer.</note> in whose work there is no mention of the Head and Tail of the dragon. If the ancients spoke of them at all, it was only as a location or position. Hence, there was a diverse opinion among them: for the older authors saw both places as evil because of the "ecliptic path" <note>original: "viam eclypticam"; the path where eclipses occur, historically viewed as ominous.</note>; therefore, they categorized both equally among the unlucky places.

<margin>Heliodorus. The opinion of the moderns</margin> Heliodorus, in the treatise <term>On Children</term> <note>original Greek: "περι τεκνων" (Peri teknon).</note>, says: "If the places signifying children are free from the unfortunate planets and the ecliptic nodes—that is, the Head and Tail—it is lucky." The more modern astrologers say that if the Head is in the house of children, they will pronounce children to be "like young olive shoots around the table" <note>A biblical allusion to Psalm 128:3.</note>, led by that other conjecture we cited above from Ibn Ezra: that planets are more effective in the Head because they are closer to us. Truly, that reasoning might hold when a planet is actually in the Head; however, a planet declining toward us even before the Head should be considered stronger by the same logic. But when no star is found in that spot, what can a point give or take away? For it is designated only by our minds. As for the fact that some suspect a certain power is "left behind" there by the Moon, no astrologer has said this, nor is it physical—if you consider the nature and light of the heavenly bodies—nor is it astrological, since the Moon travels through the Tail just the same.

<margin>Discord among astrologers</margin> Therefore, it is merely a site and a pure position, about which, however, both the Arabs and the Latins eventually decided as if it were some kind of star. Thus, they think this "Head" can even add years to a life, govern a certain portion of one's age, be "exalted" in Gemini, and possess the nature of Venus and Jupiter; conversely, they give the Tail the nature of Mars and Saturn. In this matter, we see how much they disagree with the truth itself. But it is a wonder how much they even disagree with themselves, as when they called it the bond and link of all celestial happiness. Elsewhere, how-

<column-break/>

<margin>Alchabitius</margin> -ever, they say it is good with the good, and evil with the evil, increasing whatever it finds. Elsewhere they speak of it as if it were entirely evil. For Alchabitius <note>A 10th-century Arab astrologer.</note>, with whom the rules we just recounted also reside, commemorates this among the misfortunes of the planets: if they are "with their heads." For according to the Arabs, every planet has its own head and tail, called <term>genzauar</term> <note>A Persian-derived term for the lunar nodes, used in medieval Arabic astrology.</note>; or when they are with the Head and Tail of the dragon—which is the specific name for the Moon's Head and Tail—in which they are held to be as malicious as when in the Head. In his book on births, the same author says a "climacteric" <note>A critical or dangerous period in a person's life.</note> Moon is one that is approaching the Head; indeed, he counts this Head and Tail among the principal places of life. Abraham Ibn Ezra, as we noted, affirms that the Moon is invigorated when located in the Head. We saw Heliodorus above counting them among the unfortunate signs. The same author, in his treatise on the climacteric, counts them alongside the Sun, the Moon, the Ascendant, and the Part of Fortune. Thus, it seems that what they have brought forth concerning this "Head" was brought forth with no "head" (intelligence) or certainly no heart. Everywhere, however, they maliciously call it the "Head of the Dragon" so that it might sound in the ears of the gullible with greater reverence, as if possessing the authority of a god.

***

### Chapter XII. The origin of antiscia: that Ptolemy did not use them in forecasting: and how much Maternus and Haly erred in these matters.

<margin>The origin of antiscia</margin>
<margin>Hipparchus</margin>
<margin>Repudiation of antiscia</margin> Taking an opportunity from the words of a certain mathematician, they have likewise erred regarding <term>antiscia</term> <note>Mirrored degrees of the zodiac that have equal day length because they are equidistant from the solstices.</note>. For because there are degrees in which the Sun is positioned where days are equal to days and nights to nights, Hipparchus and the ancients called them "antiscia"—as if you were to say "equally opposite"—due to the responding equality of days and nights on both sides. Our little diviners have claimed these degrees are equal in power and potency. Anyone can recognize this as supine ignorance: that from the physical equality of days and nights that occurs when the Sun traverses them, they have transferred themselves to an "equality of power."

<margin>Maternus was most ignorant of mathematics, as seen elsewhere. Ptolemy does not use antiscia in judging.</margin> But it is pleasing to accuse Maternus above all others as the propagator of this error, although pardon must be granted to him as one most ignorant of all mathematics. He says that Ptolemy attributes the highest importance to antiscia in his decrees. I am not surprised, for though I have read through all of Maternus diligently, he has nowhere given me an indication that he himself had read Ptolemy. As far as antiscia are concerned, Ptolemy never uses them in deciding or pronouncing, whether you look at his *Hundred Sayings* <note>The *Centiloquium*, a collection of aphorisms falsely attributed to Ptolemy.</note> or his *Apotelesmata* <note>The *Tetrabiblos*, Ptolemy's foundational work on astrology.</note>. Only in the first book of the *Apotelesmata*, where he recounts the opinions of others <term>On the Sympathy and Appearances of the Zodiacal Signs</term> <note>original Greek: "περι της συμπ. εκφασεων ζοο διοιων" (Peri tes sympatheias ekphaseon zoon dion).</note>, did he use these words during his introductory lessons: "Again, they say that whatever points are equally distant from either of the tropics are of equal power, because when the Sun is placed in them, it makes days equal to days and nights to nights." Once he had said this, as if forgetting it afterward—since he obviously did not approve of it—he never brings it up again. He never mentions not only the name "antiscia"—which otherwise appears nowhere in his work—but not even the thing itself: that is, this affinity and consensus of parts equally removed from the tropics. As for the fact that in the *Hundred Sayings* he says in a certain place that a planet often extends its powers where it is not, to want to transfer this to antiscia and <term>dodecatemoria</term> <note>The division of each zodiac sign into twelve smaller parts.</note> is too forced and licentious. Especially since in all his teaching, Ptolemy laughs at the one (the dodecatemoria and other things of that kind) and neglects the other (the antiscia of which we speak). Indeed, by that precept, he wished to indicate nothing else to you...
