<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s critique of astrological technicalities. After dismissing the "Head and Tail of the Dragon" (Lunar Nodes) as mere mathematical points without physical power, he now turns his attention to "antiscia" (shadow-points) and "exaltations," arguing that these concepts arose from linguistic misunderstandings and errors in copying ancient texts.</meta>

# ON THE DISPUTATIONS

...rather, they consider "configuration" <note>original: "σχηματισμόν" (schēmatismos). This refers to the geometric arrangement of planets.</note>, which is the power of arrangement and radiation. Through this, according to the opinion of astrologers—and especially Ptolemy—planets act effectively even in places where they are barely present; for in his study of the constellations, Ptolemy observes almost nothing other than their phases and shapes—or certainly, nothing more than those.

<margin>Maternus did not understand what antiscia are.</margin>
But even our Maternus <note>Julius Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century author of a major astrological handbook, the *Mathesis*.</note> did not understand what **antiscia** <note>Antiscia (from the Greek for "opposite shadows") are pairs of points in the zodiac that are equidistant from the solstice points (the start of Cancer or Capricorn). Astrologers claimed they "mirrored" each other's influence.</note> were meant to be. He promised to explain their hidden logic elsewhere, as if the matter were either not already explained to any mathematician, or as if it could not be explained in three words. You can detect his ignorance from the fact that he uses the terminology itself quite unskillfully. He claims that Mars, positioned at the fifth degree of Gemini, "sends an antiscium" into Cancer; he would not speak this way if he understood what an antiscium actually was. For an antiscium is not a ray or a light that is "sent," nor is "sending an antiscium" anything other than a planet occupying a degree of equal standing. Therefore, a skilled person would rather say that the **epoch** of Mars—that is, the position it occupies—is the "antiscia" to such a part of Gemini, or (which amounts to the same thing) that Mars is in the antiscium of Gemini. Anyone who says Mars "hurls" an antiscium into Gemini will be hissed at and mocked by mathematicians.

<margin>The error of Abenzagel.</margin>
But Abenzagel <note>Likely referring to the 12th-century Jewish scholar Abraham Ibn Ezra (often called Abenzare or Abenzagel in Latin sources), though Pico frequently critiques his reasoning.</note> also slipped up in many ways. In the first book of his commentaries, while explaining certain aphorisms, he writes that degrees equidistant from the equinoxes have equal power, just as those equidistant from the tropics (Cancer and Capricorn) do. However, the ancients did not say this regarding distance from the equinoxes, but only from the tropics; it was to the latter that the name "antiscia" was given. Abenzagel should not have failed to see this, since circles described on either side of the equinoxes are indeed equal. It is necessary that parallels equidistant from them are equal to each other, but the half-circles <note>original: "hemicyclia"</note> are not equal to each other in the same way as occurs with those equidistant from the tropics. From that comes the "agreement" of the antiscia.

<margin>The error of our own and the "barbarian" astrologers.</margin>
He also errs, along with many others, in counting the relationship of a degree to its antiscium degree among what they call **aspects** <note>The geometric angles (like squares or trines) believed to transmit planetary influence.</note>. From this, they conclude that a star placed in one of these points has power in the other as well, just as it does in hexagonal, tetragonal, trigonal, and opposite positions <note>These are the sextile (60°), square (90°), trine (120°), and opposition (180°) aspects.</note>. This error arose because the Greeks used the word **figures** <note>original: "σχήματα" (schēmata).</note> for what the "barbarians" <note>A term often used by Renaissance scholars for non-Greek or Arabic sources.</note> and our own people call "aspects." Among the Greeks, signs are said to "look at" each other not because they are configured toward one another—which is how our people use the word "aspect"—but because, in Greek, they **emerge and set from the same visible points** <note>original: "ἐκ τῶν φανερῶν σημείων" (ek tōn phanerōn sēmeiōn).</note>. Since this occurs in signs equally distant from the tropics (for they are on the same parallel), the majority of astrologers call those signs which are antiscia **seeing** <note>original: "βλέποντα" (bleponta).</note>. Later, the Arabs—and then the Latins—accepted this meaning, but they misuse the name "aspect" to describe it.

<margin>Often an error in words gives birth to an error in things.</margin>
And so it happens: often an error in wording gives birth to an error in reality. It has thus been sufficiently shown how varied the observation of antiscia is among astrologers when explaining fates (if any fates were to be granted), and how much both the Arabs and the Latins have dreamed up regarding these things, contrary to the opinion of the ancients.

### Chapter XIII. That astrologers are equally deceived regarding "commanding" and "obeying" signs.

Of this same sort is that observation—of clearly twin-like dullness or deception—concerning "commanding" and "obeying" signs. Mathematicians called the signs in which the Sun is positioned to make the days lon-

<column-break/>

-ger than the nights **commanding** <note>original: "προστάττοντα" (prostattonta).</note>, when compared to signs where light is overcome by darkness in equal proportion. These latter signs, which conversely portend darkness over day, they called **obeying** <note>original: "ὑπακούοντα" (hypakouonta).</note>. Moved by the literal sound of these names, practitioners of **genethlialogy** <note>The branch of astrology concerned with casting birth charts.</note> decreed that a person whose birth chart had a commanding sign on the horizon <note>original: "horoscoparet".</note> would command anyone who had an obeying sign as their rising sign. They acted as if that nickname of "commanding" and "obeying," established by mathematicians, actually pertained to human status, rather than merely indicating the inequality of days and nights occurring under those signs.

### Chapter XIV. A refutation of the reasons certain astrologers have assigned to the "exaltations" of the planets.

<margin>Praise for Pliny, Book II, Chapter XVI.</margin>
Regarding where this opinion about the "heights" or **exaltations** <note>A sign in which a planet is thought to be particularly powerful.</note> of the planets originated, and how they similarly rushed headlong into this through a mathematical misunderstanding, I have been reminded by that most diligent writer of natural history, to whom all antiquity and all posterity is indebted: who rescued the former from barbarism and the latter from death <note>Referring to Pliny the Elder, author of the *Natural History*.</note>. In his second book, treating the question of why the same stars appear higher at some times and lower at others, he adds the following: "Another cause for their heights is that they have their highest **apses** <note>A term for the point in an orbit furthest from the center (apogee).</note> from their own center in these signs: Saturn in the 20th degree of Libra, Jupiter in the 15th of Cancer, Mars in the 28th of Capricorn, the Sun in the 19th of Aries, Venus in the 26th of Pisces, Mercury in the 15th of Virgo, and the Moon in the 4th of Taurus." Thus, anyone who is not too slow-witted can gather that in the past, those devoted to stellar science either found or believed that the stars placed in these mentioned parts were removed to the highest point from the center of their apses. For this reason, those degrees or parts were called the "heights" of the planets.

<margin>An error in Maternus.</margin>
This gave the birth-chart casters an opportunity to misuse the term. They kept the name "height," but treated it as a height of nature and power rather than a height of physical location. For astrologers say the planets are "exalted" in no other parts than those where, as we have shown from ancient astronomy, they were thought to be at their greatest physical distance from their centers. However, the reader should know that a flaw is found in the common manuscripts of Pliny; the words following were introduced with swapped numbers, as the mark for ten owed to Venus was transferred to the Sun. Thus, one incorrectly reads the 29th part for the Sun instead of the 19th, and the 16th for Venus instead of the 26th.

<margin>Porphyry.</margin>
There is also a fault in Maternus, where we read that Venus is exalted in the 27th part of Pisces. It should be written as the twenty-sixth, according to Porphyry <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote on astrology.</note>. There is also some variation regarding the Moon: ancient astrology assigns her the 4th part of Taurus, but a later age assigns the 3rd. This is either a diversity of opinion or the fault of librarians <note>i.e., scribes/copyists.</note> who very often hallucinate when noting numbers. Similarly, for Saturn, one should read the 20th, not the 21st, on the authority of the same Porphyry.

Indeed, I have no doubt it is now clear to sound minds how the "exaltations" of the planets crept into divinatory astrology. But when the dogma reached later generations, and the reasoning for that dogma was rendered obsolete by changes in the theoretical discipline of the stars, posterity invented other reasons for themselves to justify why the earlier ones were persuaded. Some thought one thing and some another—as usually happens with a lie—but their reasons were trivial and ridiculous.

<margin>Ptolemy's Reason.</margin>
Ptolemy says the Sun is exalted in Aries because, when it reaches that sign, its power begins to appear more greatly.

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s systematic dismantling of astrological technicalities, specifically the "exaltations" (signs where planets supposedly exert their greatest power). He argues that these associations are not based on the physical reality of the heavens but on the arbitrary and contradictory reasoning of astrologers like Ptolemy and Abu Ma’shar.</meta>

# AGAINST ASTROLOGERS, BOOK VI.

<margin>Refutation</margin>
...to appear. Truly (as we said above when speaking of the houses), it is not the quality and nature of the sign that produces this effect, but the location. It is not because the Sun traverses Aries that it begins to be stronger, but because it begins to approach us. Therefore, it is not by arriving at that sign that it pours out a time or hours of hope—as if it were being raised to its kingdom—simply because it is placed in its "height" <note>original: "altitudine." In astrology, "exaltation" or "height" refers to the specific zodiac sign where a planet's influence is most potent.</note>. In other regions, the Sun would certainly be "cast down" in that same sign, since it is further away in Aries and closer in Libra for those people. But let us look at the other planets. They say the Moon’s exaltation is Taurus, because 
<margin>Refutation</margin>
if she is joined with the Sun in Aries, her power will first appear in Taurus. O, what a "most effective" reason! As if, if she were to meet the Sun in Taurus, the same result would not happen in Gemini; and if they met in Gemini, the same in Cancer; and if in Cancer, the same under Leo, and so on for all the rest. One can only marvel at Ptolemy, who was not ashamed to write such things. Truly, there are other reasons given: that the Moon is closest to the Sun and that Taurus is the Moon's "triplicity" <note>original: "trigonum." A group of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element.</note> partner. But Ptolemy does not think the Moon is closest to the Sun; nor should we guess at an exaltation based on a triplicity, nor a house from a triplicity or height, nor terms or "decans" <note>original: "decanum." A subdivision of a zodiac sign into ten-degree increments.</note> from any of those. These things are so unmixed that each should be granted its own proper authority in its own sphere. Furthermore, if the argument of the triplicity carries weight, why would Mercury not be exalted in Gemini rather than in Virgo? For in Gemini, it would also fit that he is closest to the Sun’s exaltation, from which he is usually not far distant.

<margin>Abu Ma’shar</margin>
<margin>On the exaltation of Mars.</margin>
This is what Abu Ma’shar <note>original: "Aboasar." A famous 9th-century Persian astrologer and astronomer.</note> also tries to maintain in his reasoning for these exaltations. But, says Ptolemy, Virgo suits Mercury because he is dry, and under Virgo, the dryness of autumn appears. Yet we have already said that this change of the four seasons does not proceed from the nature of the signs; therefore, the Sun positioned in Virgo will produce in other regions what it does not do for us when positioned in Taurus. Furthermore, if this were being observed, why was Mars not decreed to rule in Cancer? For under Cancer, the world swelters, just as under Virgo it begins to dry out. Mars is a "most burning" planet, yet they want him to be exalted in Capricorn, under which we are constrained by cold, frost, and ice. "But," they say, "Capricorn turns toward the South, and the southern part is warmer." This is exactly what we charge you with, astrologers: this lightness and inconsistency of your arguments (if indeed these should be called arguments). For you discuss the same sign according to your convenience and whim—now as if it were hot, now as if it were cold. And soon you will call the same sign neither hot nor cold, but rather moist or dry. In the partitioning of signs, you make Capricorn earthy, and therefore dry; but when it is transferred to Mars, it is counted as an 
<margin>On the height of Jupiter</margin>
intermediary. And when it is called the domicile of Saturn—the coldest of stars—it is recorded that snows and rains happen under it. But if Capricorn is granted to Mars as if it were a "hot" sign, then by the same reasoning, Cancer ought to be considered the "coldest"; therefore, it surely will not have Jupiter as its king, who is most powerful in "life-giving heat," as they say. But they have a hiding place ready to crawl into. 

<margin>Ptolemy</margin>
For, says Ptolemy, Jupiter stirs up the northern winds; therefore, a sign positioned toward the north suits him. But other astrologers cannot flee here first, as they deny that such winds are stirred by Jupiter. Furthermore, Ptolemy is not excused: by similar reasoning, he should have sent Mars to the West, not the South, since he thinks "westerly" winds, not southern ones, are excited by Mars. I leave aside that Gemini and Leo incline toward the north; why

<column-break/>

therefore is Leo not rather the exaltation of Jupiter? Averroes <note>original: "Auenrodam." Likely referring to the commentator Averroes or a related astrological source.</note> says the heat of Leo does not suit Jupiter—on the contrary, it suits him much more than the coldness of Cancer! Add to this that Leo is Jupiter's "triplicity," a "daytime" and "masculine" sign; Jupiter is likewise masculine and daytime. Cancer is designated among the "feminine," "nocturnal," and "aquatic" signs, all of which are removed from the nature of Jupiter. Therefore, Leo suits him entirely more than Cancer.

<margin>On the exaltation of Venus and Saturn.</margin>
Concerning Venus and Saturn, they rave no less. They say Libra is the height of Saturn because Saturn is "contrary" to the Sun. They say Venus is exalted in Pisces because she is moist, and the moisture of spring begins under Pisces. But we have often said already that these qualities of the seasons do not follow the nature of the signs, but rather the position of the approaching and receding Sun. Regarding Saturn, they speak as they usually do for their own convenience: here they make him opposite to the Sun, elsewhere they proclaim him to be "consonant" <note>original: "σύμφωνον" (symphōnon). Meaning in agreement or of the same character.</note>—that is, of the same condition. They claim that both signify the father, and both are "oriental" (rising in the east). Both are masculine; both are of the day. But I would certainly have too much to say if I pursued all other such matters point by point. Some, having little confidence in these arguments, devised a new reasoning—shorter, to be sure, but entirely ineffective: that the exaltations are the "trine" <note>120 degrees apart.</note> or "sextile" <note>60 degrees apart.</note> aspects of the houses, except in the case of Mercury. But if you ask why they preferred the sextile for the Moon, Venus, and Mars, and the trine for the others, they answer that the trine suits the daytime and more powerful planets better; but the nocturnal ones, which they say are of the "sect" <note>original: "haeresi." Here used in the astrological sense of "sect" (planets belonging to a day or night team).</note> of the Moon—or as the Arabs say, "due to the weakness of the ray" <note>original: "οἵα τὸ σθένος τῆς ἀκτῖνος."</note>—suit the sextile.

<margin>Rejection</margin>
Truly they are mistaken regarding Mars; he is not numbered among the nocturnal planets because he is "weak," but rather so that the vigor and efficacy of the Martial ray might be restrained by the nocturnal cold. Nor can he be said to be of the "sect" of the Moon, since he is a masculine planet. Both qualities of Mars disagree with the Moon; he is considered nocturnal for a reason entirely contrary to the Moon. For she is nocturnal due to a similarity of nature; Mars due to a dissimilarity. He is adverse to the Lunar sign and Cancer in Capricorn, just as he is opposite Taurus in Scorpio. But even if this conjecture were allowed, let them answer this: why a "right-hand" trine rather than a "left-hand" one? Why a left rather than a right? Indeed, why is it left-handed for Jupiter, but right-handed for Saturn and the Sun? And since the planets have two houses, why is the trine taken from one rather than the other? For instance, since Jupiter dwells in Sagittarius and Pisces, why should he be exalted in Cancer rather than in Leo? Especially since he has more affinity with Sagittarius, as astrologers say—and also (as I said before) Leo suits him far more than Cancer does. Finally, so that you may understand that all such conjectures were fabricated by later writers, and were not at all the foundation upon which the first originators of this dogma built: notice that they give no reason why a planet is said to be exalted in a *specific part* of a sign rather than just in the sign itself. We have shown the cause of this above from ancient astrology.

<margin>Abu Ma’shar</margin>
Wherefore Abu Ma’shar says that this was difficult for the whole community of astrologers to find. He himself, lest he say nothing at all, twisted many anxious thoughts on this matter with a far too perverse and mythical subtlety. Therefore, it is clear without a doubt that this dogma regarding the "heights" of the planets was accepted by practitioners of "genethlialogy" <note>The casting of birth charts.</note> from the occasion we mentioned: the ancient discipline which thought that in these degrees, the planets were at their greatest distance from their centers. Anyone can now see how vain the observation of these heights is, not only because they transmit to nature and power whatever was the status of the place...

->FOURTH DISPUTATION<-

<margin>Apogees.</margin>
...name. But since ancient astronomy was perhaps deceived in this matter—being too fallible and insufficiently explored in its infancy—even if a true system had been decreed then, it would not suit posterity now, as the apsides <note>The points in an orbit where a planet is nearest or furthest from the body it orbits.</note> and what are called the "apogees" <note>The point in the orbit of a planet or the moon where it is furthest from the Earth.</note> of the wandering stars have shifted.

### Chapter XV. The reasons of astrologers concerning trigons and the rulers of trigons are refuted; and, in passing, the gender of the signs is also debunked.

Indeed, we should not think that astrologers rave only when an opportunity is given; they are too "sharp-sighted" to be able to wander off without a guide. They prevaricate most often where there is no one to lead them astray. For they almost owe it to these mathematical "exaltations" that they are insane—though we should not, out of a sense of justice, defraud them of the credit, as they are mostly responsible for their own delusions. But as for what are commonly called "trigons" <term>Trigons: Also known as triplicities, these are groups of three zodiac signs associated with one of the four elements: Fire, Earth, Air, or Water.</term> or triplicities, they sired these themselves, and mathematics did not help them at all in this place. Since the matter depends on this—that certain signs are "fiery," some "earthy," some "airy," and some "watery"—we shall first compel them to give an account of these things; then we shall examine how they define this trigon as belonging to this planet, and that one to another.

<margin>Elementary qualities cannot be ascribed to the signs.</margin>
Tell us then, O most wise men and interpreters of the heavens: by what reasoning do you distribute those qualities of the elements to the signs in the sky? Averroes <note>original: "Auenrodam." Referring to the 12th-century Andalusian philosopher Ibn Rushd.</note>, a great figure in your discipline, refers the nature of the signs either to the Sun or to the stars. To the Sun, in that the nature of a sign is said to be whatever the effect of the Sun is while passing through that sign. By this logic, the "movable" signs are the equinoxes or solstices, and the rest are "fixed" or "common." If referred to the stars, the virtues of the stars residing there are attributed to the sign. I see neither reason fitting your fourfold partition. For if we follow the works of the Sun, Cancer would be fiery, not Aquarius—just as Sagittarius would be watery rather than fiery. Aries would not be fiery but airy; Taurus would abound in moisture and heat rather than cold and dryness; and thus the condition of almost all signs would be changed. Nor would they be permanent (as you desire) if they refer to stars that are constantly migrating from their seats. Or do you think the reasoning of Al-Kindi <note>original: "Alchindi." A 9th-century Arab philosopher and astrologer.</note> is better? He assigned the four primary qualities of the elements to the four principal signs of the Zodiac: fiery to Aries, watery to Cancer, airy to Libra, and earthy to Capricorn. Then, because the radiation of the "trigons" falls upon corresponding places, the signs forming a triangle on either side of any sign are rightly judged to have obtained a similar nature. But even this reasoning does not square. In referring the four properties of the elements to the signs, there could have been a twofold reason for that order: one based on the kinship of the sign and the element, and the other based on the position of the elements themselves—so that the first is given to the first, the second to the second, and so on. If they observed the first rule (matching hot to hot and cold to cold), they should have given Fire to Cancer (as I said) and Air to Aries. If they followed the second, they should have given Air to Cancer, which is the second from Fire.

<margin>Against the reasoning of Al-Kindi.</margin>
But Al-Kindi says that opposites, heat and cold, must be given; therefore, cold should be given to the sign of the second season, which is Cancer—or rather, to Libra, which is opposite Aries. But if they say water should be preferred to air because it is more effective, they will now be making themselves "wiser" than nature itself. Furthermore, if an "active" quality like coldness (rather than a "passive" one like moisture) belongs to Cancer, how is it categorized by them among the feminine and nocturnal signs, rather than the diurnal and masculine? They observe this in the planets as well, 

<margin>Al-Kindi's reasoning, Refutation</margin>

<column-break/>

reasonably acknowledging gender in the celestial bodies for no other reason than the distinction between active and passive qualities. For this reason, they called the Sun and Mars (in which heat excels) and Saturn (in which cold excels) masculine; they called the Moon and Venus feminine because they are moist. Thus, even among the Egyptians, water and fire were called masculine for the stated reason, while air and water <note>Pico likely meant air and earth here, or is pointing out a contradiction in the Egyptian source.</note> were feminine. Thus, the signs they established as watery should have been numbered among the masculine by the astrologers, not the feminine—yet they did the latter for all of them: namely Cancer, Pisces, and Scorpio. Conversely, they decreed the airy signs to be masculine, even though moisture is the proper quality of air. Astrology, therefore, fights against itself in these matters and overthrows itself, raving here as it does everywhere else.

<margin>That there are no masculine or feminine signs.</margin>
And—not to wander too far from the subject at hand—what of these most trivial trifles: discerning gender in the heavens? It was by such a conjecture that they were moved to establish six masculine and six feminine signs, making the first male, the following female, and so on through the ranks, always one man and then one woman. If this was to be done, it ought to have been done according to the nature of the signs, not by a fatal and vain sequence of "first, second, and so on." Hear from Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century author of the *Tetrabiblos*, the foundational text of Western astrology.</note> what "reason" this has: "Night," he says, "follows day, and women cling to men; therefore, a feminine sign must be placed next to a masculine one." One should not dispute such reasoning, but laugh at it—unless perhaps it is a serious matter to see whether night comes before day or day before night, such that perhaps the nocturnal signs should have been placed first, since day follows night rather than night following day. For it is written: *And it was evening and morning, one day* <note>A reference to Genesis 1:5.</note>; for which reason the Hebrews established the beginnings of time from the night. But you are too busy for me to play the fool with many words.

<margin>See the [point] instilled, The reasoning for the genders.</margin>
And yet, even in Ptolemy himself, this diversity of genders carries much weight; he considers it no small matter whether planets are found in masculine or feminine signs. If they contend that this dogma is proven by experience, I ask: by whose? Their own, or the ancients'? If their own, they are not yet old enough to have such authority. If the ancients', then a great part of the ancients felt otherwise. Many determined the order from the *horoscopus* <note>The rising sign or Ascendant.</note>, so that the rising sign was always masculine and diurnal, and the rest were divided by turns in the following order. Others made four signs diurnal: Aries, Cancer, Leo, and Sagittarius; four nocturnal: Gemini, Libra, Capricorn, and Aquarius; and four "promiscuous" <note>Mixed or neutral.</note>: Taurus, Virgo, Pisces, and Scorpio. Indeed, antiquity used to explode the received opinion. Hence this verse from ancient astrology:

> There are those who like the signs that rise as masculine to be diurnal,
> And the feminine to rejoice in the happy darkness of the night.
> Who, with no one showing them, speak many things to themselves.

In this place, it is amazing how much a certain trivial interpreter of that poet raves. He is far more "rational" (if one must occasionally be insane with reason) who called all the fiery and watery signs diurnal, and the remaining six (the earthy and airy) nocturnal. Likewise, if—as Ptolemy likes—masculine and diurnal follow one another, those will be masculine and these feminine. Thus he sang:

<margin>It is read more truly in [variant note]... rare diligence...</margin>
> For the sign of the Archer and the swift Lion
> And the one looking back at his own back with a golden fleece <note>Aries the Ram.</note>,
> Then the Fish, the Crab, and the Scorpion joined to the Crab,
> Whether neighboring in place or at equal intervals,
> All are said to be diurnal under a similar lot;
> The others share neither the number nor the turn of their seat.

There were also those who felt otherwise, which is why he adds:
"Indeed, they even said six continuous ones were diurnal."
The turns of Castor <note>A reference to the constellation Gemini.</note> are those which start from the leading sign,
The Wool-bearer <note>original: "Lanigeri"; refers to Aries the Ram.</note>; six from the Scales <note>Libra</note> are seen as nightly.
Let them therefore cease to claim the reliability of ancient observations, from which they differ as often as all astrology differs from the truth. Moreover, this objection could also be raised: if they judged that a masculine sign should be established in the first place, it will remain uncertain which sign is truly the first and masculine one, just as it is uncertain which sign is the initial one, as we declared above. For to some, Cancer seemed first; to others, Capricorn; yet both of these are feminine among those men. But perhaps it was not necessary to mock these fables with so many words—although it was worth the effort to refute in passing that fable of discerning celestial signs by sex. We turned aside to this point for a reason: to show that they contradict themselves regarding Cancer, which they make watery and feminine, even though "coldness" is among the active qualities, not the passive ones <note>In Aristotelian physics, active qualities (heat/cold) were thought to drive change, while passive ones (moisture/dryness) were acted upon; Pico is pointing out a logical inconsistency in their elemental assignments.</note>. But even if that first partition is granted to them in the tropical and equinoctial signs, the logic of distribution will not hold in other signs. For they demonstrate in a "circle"—which is a disgrace in logic—whenever they try to prove the signs of a trigon share the same nature. They take as their argument that the triangular radiation comes from places that agree with each other, and then they turn around and prove the radiation agrees because it falls on places of the same nature. Let Al-Kindi <note>A famous 9th-century Arab philosopher and astrologer.</note> be silent now. The rest

<margin>The reasoning of Abraham Ibn Ezra</margin>
is the opinion of Abraham Ibn Ezra <note>original: "Abraham auenazræ"; a 12th-century Jewish scholar and astrologer.</note>, who derives the reasoning for these qualities from the shapes of the images and the properties of the animals depicted therein. Thus, Pisces, Cancer, and Scorpio are called cold because they represent the names and likenesses of aquatic creatures. The sign of Leo is hot because of the nature of the Lion, and so on for the rest. But this reasoning is either non-existent—if there are no such images in the stars, as we have demonstrated—or it is false if there are images, in which case the images are confused with the signs themselves, a thing we also rejected above.

<margin>The Rulers of the Trigons, whom they call lords of the triplicities, are nothing.</margin>
Finally, since the shapes vary by location, this distinction of the signs will be temporary, and not—as all astrologers and Ibn Ezra himself want—immobile and perpetual. Nor will Aries be a "fiery" sign in our time, since the image of Pisces has occupied almost the whole of it, the image of Aries having already shifted into its twenty-fifth part <note>Pico is referring to the precession of the equinoxes, which causes the physical constellations to shift away from the zodiac signs over centuries.</note>. Now, if there are no trigons, there are also no <term>Trigonocratores</term> <note>Lords or rulers of the triplicities.</note>—that is, the "lords of the triplicities," as they call them. Yet even if these were granted, they still define them, as is their habit, beyond all reason. For they will not deny that if a planet is well-placed in some sign, it must be poorly placed in the sign diametrically opposite; this is clear in the "houses" of the planets and clear in the "exaltations." If this is widely confessed among them, how did they forget their own astrological dogma and decide that the same three planets should rule in opposite trigons? Specifically, in the earthy and the watery trigons, they place Mars, Venus, and the Moon. Taurus is opposite to Scorpio; Virgo is opposed to Pisces; Capricorn resides in the region across from Cancer. And yet, those who dominate in Taurus, Virgo, and Capricorn rule with the same trigonal power in Cancer, Pisces, and Scorpio. If you ask these astrologers why Mars is weakened in Cancer, they will answer only that it is because he is exalted in Capricorn; and why he is weakened in Taurus? Because, they say, he has his home in Scorpio. Thus, all these things fight against each other and prove themselves false. Add

<margin>Albumasar and Al-Qabisi</margin>
to this that in the first triplicity, Albumasar <note>The Latinized name of the Persian astrologer Abu Ma'shar.</note>, Al-Qabisi <note>original: "Alchabitius"; a 10th-century Arab astrologer.</note>,

<column-break/>

and all the Latins <note>Medieval European scholars writing in Latin.</note> decree that Saturn dominates along with Jupiter and the Sun. Yet in this triplicity, Saturn is exalted in Leo, falls in Aries, and recognizes nothing of his own in Sagittarius. "But," they will say, "he is a daytime planet like Jupiter and the Sun." True, but he is also cold, while both of the others are considered hot. And if, when dealing with exaltations, they assigned Libra to Saturn only because it was opposite to the nature of the Sun, why is he now associated with the Sun in Aries as a lord of the triplicity, as if he were most compatible with the Sun's nature? There are many things of this sort, but to pursue each one would perhaps be unnecessary, and certainly for me it is bothersome and nauseating. Even if we turn here to the reliability of experience, I point again to the discord among such "experiments," since the Egyptians make only two rulers of the trigons, as can be understood from the <term>monomeria</term> <note>Individual degrees of the zodiac assigned to specific planets.</note>. The rest establish three, who then disagree among themselves. For in the first triangle, Albumasar, Al-Qabisi, and the Latins want Saturn to dominate; Ptolemy <note>The 2nd-century mathematician and astronomer whose 'Tetrabiblos' was the standard astrological text.</note> wants Mars. Conversely, in the second triangle, Ptolemy chooses Saturn; the Arabs and almost all the Latins choose Mars. In the fourth, Ptolemy makes Mars the lord, with two secondary lords, the Moon by night and Venus by day. Others equal Mars with Venus in lordship, and do not want Mars to command except by night, and Venus by day, with the Moon second both night and day. This is their authority. More recent authors say the opinion of the Arabs and Latins is confirmed by experiments. Ibn Rushd <note>original: "Auenrodan"; likely referring to the commentator Ali ibn Ridwan, though sometimes confused with Averroes.</note> himself (not to mention the Greeks) affirms that all effects support the opinion of Ptolemy. I omit many points on which they clash over these same triangles, since they were discussed above. It is clear from this that even the "Great Conjunctions" <note>Rare alignments of Jupiter and Saturn used to predict major historical shifts.</note> are dissolved, insofar as they depend on the migration through the trigons—not to mention other dogmas of the astrologers that derive their credibility and origin specifically from these trigons.

<margin>Ptolemy.</margin>

### Chapter XVI. Concerning the faces, terms, and the dodecathemories of the Babylonians; and how little the ninths and degrees hold up, even by the testimony of Ptolemy himself.

It remains to refute the "faces" and the "terms," so that everything regarding the affinity of planets with the signs may be addressed. For we have already overturned the houses, struck down the exaltations, and erased the trigons; there will be no trouble in confounding these remaining points. For there are no "faces" <note>Also known as Decans; 10-degree subdivisions of a zodiac sign.</note>, even according to Ptolemy; likewise for the Greeks, who call them "decans." There are decans of the signs, but "faces" of the planets. Ptolemy despised these faces, thinking them unworthy of mention or of ever being used in his <term>apotelesmata</term> <note>Astrological forecasts or outcomes.</note>. Since they can support these with no reasons, they might perhaps claim "experience"—if only harmony did not desert them in this place as well. For the Indians want certain faces of the planets, the Babylonians (whom the Arabs imitate) want others, and Maternus <note>Julius Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman astrologer.</note> wants others still. The first decan of Taurus, according to the Babylonians, bears the face of Mercury; according to the Indians, Venus; according to Maternus, Jupiter. The second decan, according to Maternus, is of the Moon; according to others, Mercury; according to still others, Mars. The first of Gemini belongs to Jupiter for the Chaldeans, to Mercury for the Indians, and to Mars for Maternus. To avoid listing them all in detail: the Babylonians followed a method where they gave the first decan—the beginning of Aries—to Mars, since Aries belongs to Mars; then, following the order of the spheres, they gave the first decan of any sign to the "head of the household" (the lord of the house) and the remaining two...

<margin>In Ptolemy, there are many faces.</margin>
<margin>Various faces of various authors. The first decan of Taurus, the second. The first of Gemini.</margin>

->DISPUTATION FOUR<-

<margin>Apogees <note>The point in an orbit farthest from the Earth.</note></margin>
...appellation. But since old astronomy was perhaps too mistaken in its beginnings—faltering and insufficiently explored—even if a true calculation had been decreed then, it would not suit posterity now, since the "apsides" <note>points of least or greatest distance in an orbit</note> and what are called the **apogees** of the wandering stars have shifted.

### Chapter XV. The arguments of astrologers concerning trigons and the rulers of trigons are refuted; and, in passing, the sex of the signs is also debunked.

<margin>That elemental qualities cannot be ascribed to the signs.</margin>
Nor should we think that astrologers only rave when they have been given the opportunity to observe, as if they could not go astray without a guide. They prevaricate most often precisely where no obstacle stands in their way. For regarding these mathematical "exaltations" <note>specific degrees where a planet is thought to be strongest</note>, they almost owe it to themselves that they are mad—though we should not cheat them of their due, as they owe it more to themselves than to any injury from us. But as for what they commonly call **trigons** or "triplicities," they gave birth to these themselves, and in this matter, mathematics did not help them at all. Since this system depends on making certain signs "fiery," some "earthy," some "airy," and others "watery," we shall first compel them to give an account of these things, and we shall examine how they define this trigon as belonging to this planet, and that one to another.

Tell us then, O wisest men and interpreters of the heavens, by what reasoning did you distribute these qualities of the elements to the signs in the sky? Averroes <note>original: "Auenrodam"; a famous 12th-century Andalusian philosopher</note>, a great figure in your discipline, refers the nature of the signs either to the Sun or to the stars. To the Sun, in that a sign's nature is said to be whatever effect the Sun produces while passing through it—by which reasoning the "movable" signs are called equinoctial or solstitial, and the rest are called "fixed" or "common." To the stars, if the virtues of the stars residing there are attributed to the sign. I see neither reasoning fitting your partition. For if we follow the works of the Sun, **Cancer** would be fiery, not **Aquarius**; just as **Sagittarius** would be watery rather than fiery; **Aries** would not be fiery but airy; **Taurus** would abound in moisture and heat rather than cold and dryness. Thus the condition of almost all signs would be changed, and they would not be perpetual (as you wish them to be). If it is referred to stars migrating repeatedly from their seats, do you think the reasoning of Al-Kindi <note>original: "Alchindi"; a 9th-century Arab philosopher and astrologer</note> is better? Since there are four principal signs in the Zodiac—two equinoctial and two solstitial—he assigned the four primary qualities of the elements to these four: fiery to **Aries**, watery to **Cancer**, airy to **Libra**, and earthy to **Capricorn**.

<margin>Against the reasoning of Al-Kindi.</margin>
Then, because the radiation of the **trigons** falls in congruent places, the signs forming a triangle on either side of any sign are rightly judged to have obtained a similar nature. But even this reasoning does not fit. In assigning the four properties of the elements to the signs, there could be two ways of ordering them: one based on the kinship of the sign and the element, and the other based on the position of the elements themselves, so that the first is given to the first, the second to the second, and so on. If they observed the first rule—that hot things correspond to hot, and cold to cold—they ought to have given Fire (as I said) to **Cancer** and Air to **Aries**. If they followed the second rule, they should have given Air to **Cancer**, which is second after Fire.

<margin>The reasoning of Al-Kindi. Refutation.</margin>
But Al-Kindi says that opposites—heat and cold—must be given to the sign of the following season, that is, to **Cancer**. On the contrary, they should therefore be given to **Libra**, which is opposite to **Aries**. If they say Water should be placed before Air because it is more "effective," they make themselves wiser than nature itself. Furthermore, if an active quality like coldness, rather than a passive one like moisture, belongs to **Cancer**, why is it categorized by them among the feminine and nightly signs, and not rather among the diurnal and masculine ones? They observe this in the planets, where they recognize sex in the celestial bodies for no other

<column-break/>

<margin>That some signs are not masculine and others feminine.</margin>
more rational reason than the presence of active and passive qualities. For this reason, they called **Jupiter**, the **Sun**, and **Mars** (in which heat excels) and **Saturn** (in which cold excels) "males"; they called the **Moon** and **Venus** "females" because they are moist. Thus, Water and Fire were also called males by the Egyptians for the reason mentioned, while Air and Water <note>Pico is highlighting a contradiction in their elemental gender assignments</note> were called females. Thus, the signs they established as watery ought to have been numbered among the masculine by the astrologers, not the feminine—yet they did the same for all of them: namely **Cancer**, **Pisces**, and **Scorpio**. Conversely, they decreed the airy signs to be masculine, even though moisture is the proper quality of air. Therefore, astrology fights with itself in these matters and overthrows itself, raving here as it does everywhere. 

For—not to stray from the matter at hand—what of these most trivial trifles of discerning sex in the heavens? Specifically, the conjecture by which they established six masculine and six feminine signs, setting the first as male, the next as female, and so on through the ranks, always one man and one woman. If this was to be done, it should have been done according to the nature of the signs, not by a fatal and vain sequence of "first" and "second."

<margin>See below for Ptolemy's reasoning.</margin>
Listen to Ptolemy <note>the 2nd-century foundational authority for Western astrology</note> on what logic this has. "Night," he says, "follows day, and women cling to men; therefore, a feminine sign must be placed next to a masculine one." One should not dispute against such reasoning, but rather laugh at it—unless, perhaps, it is a serious matter to see whether night comes before day or day before night, so that perhaps the nightly signs ought to have been placed first, since day follows night rather than night following day. For it is written: *And there was evening and there was morning, one day* <note>A reference to Genesis 1:5; Pico uses the Bible to show the arbitrary nature of the "day-first" assumption.</note>. Because of this, the Hebrews established the beginnings of time from the night. But you are too busy for me to play the fool with many words.

Yet even in Ptolemy himself, this diversity of sexes carries great weight; he considers it very important whether planets are found in masculine or feminine signs. If they contend that this dogma is proven by experience, I ask: whose? Theirs, or the ancients'? If theirs, they do not have the gray hairs of long experience for their authority to be so great. If the ancients', then a large part of the ancients thought otherwise. Many made the order from the "horoscope" <note>the Ascendant sign</note>, so that the rising sign was always masculine and diurnal, and the rest were divided in alternating order. Others made four signs diurnal: **Aries**, **Cancer**, **Leo**, and **Sagittarius**; four nightly: **Gemini**, **Libra**, **Capricorn**, and **Aquarius**; and four promiscuous <note>neutral or mixed</note>: **Taurus**, **Virgo**, **Pisces**, and **Scorpio**. Indeed, antiquity used to explode the now-accepted opinion. Hence this from ancient astrology:

> Some prefer that those which rise masculine be diurnal,
> And that feminine signs rejoice in the happy shadows of night.
> They who speak many things to themselves with no one to guide them.

In this place, it is amazing how much a certain trivial interpreter of that poet raves—and he is far more rational (if one must occasionally be insane with reason) who called all the fiery and watery signs diurnal, and the remaining six—the earthy and airy ones—nightly.

<margin>A more true reading is found... [Pico notes textual variants in the Latin sources].</margin>
Likewise, if what pleases Ptolemy is that masculine and diurnal follow each other, those will be masculine, and these feminine. Thus he sang:

> For the sign of **Sagittarius** and of the rapid **Lion**,
> And the one looking back at its own back with a golden fleece <note>Aries the Ram</note>,
> Then **Pisces**, **Cancer**, and the sting of **Scorpio**,
> Either neighboring in place or at equal parts,
> All are said to be under a similar diurnal fate,
> The others sharing neither the number nor the turn of position.

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s systematic deconstruction of the technical "dignities" of planets—the specific positions in the zodiac where they are supposedly strengthened. Having previously questioned the general logic of these systems, he now focuses on the internal contradictions between different astrological schools (Egyptian, Babylonian, Arabic, and Greek) regarding trigons, decans, and the "faces" of the signs.</meta>

<header>AGAINST THE ASTROLOGERS, BOOK VI.</header>
<columns>2</columns>

Nightly intervals are spread between as many places. There were also those who felt differently, which is why he adds: 
"Indeed, they even spoke of six continuous daytime signs." 
They claimed these were the turns of Castor <note>A reference to the mythological twin who shared immortality with his brother by alternating between the upper and lower worlds; astrologers used this to explain signs alternating between day and night natures</note>, which, starting from the leading sign of the **Ram** <note>original: "Lanigeri" (the Wool-bearer), referring to Aries</note>, see six signs as nocturnal starting from the **Scales** <note>original: "libris," referring to Libra</note>. Let them, therefore, cease to appeal to the "faith of ancient observations," from which they differ as often as the whole of astrology differs from the truth. 

Furthermore, this objection could be raised: if they judged that a masculine sign must be established in the first place, it remains uncertain which sign is truly the first and masculine one, just as it is uncertain which sign is the "initial" one, as we declared above. For to some, the **Crab** <note>Cancer</note> seemed first; to others, **Capricorn**; yet both of these are considered feminine by these very men. But perhaps there was no need to elude so many fables—though it was worthwhile to briefly refute that fable of distinguishing celestial signs by sex. We turned aside to this point for this reason: to show that in the sign of the **Crab**, they fight with themselves. They make it "watery" and "feminine," even though "coldness" is among the active qualities, not the passive ones. 

But if the primary division is granted to them in the tropical and equinoctial signs, the logic of distribution will not hold in the other signs. For they demonstrate in a circle <note>A logical fallacy where the proof assumes the conclusion</note>, which is a disgrace in dialectic; since in this place they prove that the **trigons** <note>groups of three signs belonging to the same element</note> are of the same nature, they assume this argument: because a trigonal radiation <note>an aspect of 120 degrees</note> belongs to places that agree with each other. Conversely, to prove that trigonal radiation is in agreement, they assume it falls upon places of the same nature. Let **Al-Kindi** <note>original: "Alchindus," a 9th-century Arab philosopher and astrologer</note> be silent now.

<margin>The reasoning of Abraham Ibn Ezra.</margin>
There remains the opinion of **Abraham Ibn Ezra** <note>original: "Abraam auenazræ," a 12th-century Jewish polymath</note>, who derives the reason for these qualities from the figures of the images and the properties of the animals depicted there. Thus, **Pisces**, **Cancer**, and **Scorpio** are called "cold" because they represent the names and likenesses of aquatic creatures. The sign of the **Lion** <note>Leo</note> is hot because of the nature of the Lion, and so on for the rest. But this reasoning is either void, if there are no such images in the sky (as we have demonstrated), or false if there are images, because it confuses the images with the signs—a thing we also rejected above. Finally, since the figures vary by location <note>due to the movement of the stars</note>, this distinction of the signs would be temporary, not "immovable and perpetual" as all astrologers—including Ibn Ezra himself—desire. Nor would the **Ram** <note>Aries</note> be a fiery sign in our time, since the image of **Pisces** has occupied almost the whole of it, the image of the Ram having already shifted into its twenty-fifth part <note>A reference to the precession of the equinoxes, where the constellations no longer align with the seasonal zodiac signs</note>.

<margin>The Trigonocrators, whom they call the lords of triplicities, are nothing.</margin>
But if there are no trigons, there are also no **Trigonocrators**—that is, the "lords of triplicities" as they call them. Even if those trigons were granted, they still define these lords, as is their custom, outside of all reason. For they will not deny that if a planet is well-situated in a certain sign, it must be ill-situated in the sign diametrically opposite to it. This is clear in the "houses" of the planets and in their "exaltations." If this is a most confessed point among them, how did they forget their own astrological dogma when they willed that the same three planets should rule in opposite trigons—namely, in the Earthly and Watery ones: **Mars**, **Venus**, and the **Moon**? **Taurus** is opposite to **Scorpio**; **Virgo** is opposed to **Pisces**; **Capricorn** resides in the region across from **Cancer**. And yet, those who dominate in Taurus, Virgo, and Capricorn all rule with trigonal power in Cancer, Pisces, and Scorpio. If you ask an astrologer why Mars is weakened in Cancer, he will give no other answer than that he is exalted in Capricorn; and why is he harmed in Taurus? Because they say he has his home in Scorpio. Thus, all these things fight against each other and mutually convict themselves of falsehood.

<margin>Albumasar, Al-Qabisi.</margin>
Add to this that in the first triplicity, **Albumasar**, **Al-Qabisi** <note>original: "Alchabitius," a 10th-century Arab astrologer</note>,

<column-break/>

<margin>Albumasar, Al-Qabisi, the Latins.</margin>
and all the **Latin** writers decree that **Saturn** dominates along with **Jupiter** and the **Sun**. Yet in this triplicity, Saturn is exalted in **Libra**, weakened in the **Ram** <note>Aries</note>, and recognizes nothing of his own in **Sagittarius**. "But," they say, "he is a daytime planet like Jupiter and the Sun." True, but he is also cold, while both of those others are held to be hot. And if, when discussing exaltations, they assigned **Libra** to Saturn only because it was opposite to the nature of the Sun, why then is his kingdom in Aries? Why, as a lord of the triplicity, is he associated with the Sun against the very nature of those signs, as if he were most congruent with the Sun’s nature? There are many more things of this kind, but to pursue every single one would be perhaps superfluous, and certainly troublesome and nauseating for me. 

If we look to the "faith of experience" here, I point again to the discord of such experiences. For the **Egyptians** make only two Trigonocrators, as can be understood from the *monomeria* <note>individual degrees of the zodiac</note>. The rest constitute three, who then disagree among themselves. For in the first triangle, Albumasar, Al-Qabisi, and the Latins want Saturn to rule; 

<margin>Ptolemy.</margin>
**Ptolemy** wants **Mars**. Conversely, in the second triangle, Ptolemy wants Saturn, while the Arabs and almost all the Latins want Mars. In the fourth, Ptolemy makes Mars the lord, with two almost secondary lords: the Moon by night and Venus by day. Others equate Mars and Venus in lordship, but only want Mars to rule by night and Venus by day, with the Moon being second by both night and day. 

<margin>The more recent: Ibn Rodan.</margin>
Authority rests with them: the more recent writers say that the opinion of the Arabs and Latins is confirmed by experiences. **Ibn Rodan** <note>original: "Auenrodan," referring to Ali ibn Ridwan</note> himself (not to mention the Greeks) affirms that all "effects" support the opinion of Ptolemy. I pass over many points in which they cross swords over these same triangles, since they were discussed above. It is clear from this, however, that even the "Great Conjunctions" are dissolved, insofar as they depend on the shift between trigons <note>Astrologers believed history was shaped by Jupiter and Saturn meeting in signs of the same element for 200 years before moving to the next element</note>—not to mention other astrological dogmas that derive their faith and origin from these very trigons.

### Chapter XVI. On faces, terms, the dodecathemoria of the Babylonians, and the "nines" and "ones" <note>original: "monomirijs"</note> which stand on little evidence, even by the testimony of Ptolemy himself.

<margin>According to Ptolemy, there are many faces.</margin>
It remains to refute the "faces" and the "terms" <note>subdivisions of zodiac signs</note>, so that everything regarding the affinity of planets with the signs may be addressed. Since we have already overturned the houses, cast down the exaltations, and obliterated the trigons, there is no trouble in refuting these. For there are no "faces," even according to Ptolemy; so also with the Greeks, who call them **decans** <note>ten-degree segments of a sign</note>. But the decans belong to the signs, while the "faces" belong to the planets. Ptolemy spurned these faces, thinking them unworthy of mention or of ever being used in predictions <note>original: "apotelesmatis"</note>. Since they can support these with no reasons, they might perhaps pretend they are based on experience—if only harmony did not desert them in this place as well.

<margin>Various faces of various authors. The first decan of Taurus, the second. The first of Gemini.</margin>
For the **Indians** want certain faces to belong to the planets, the **Babylonians** (whom the Arabs imitate) want others, and **Maternus** <note>Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman astrologer</note> others still. The first decan of **Taurus**, according to the Babylonians, wears the face of **Mercury**; according to the Indians, **Venus**; according to Maternus, **Jupiter**. The second decan belongs to the **Moon** according to some, to Mercury according to others, and to Mars according to others. The first decan of **Gemini** belongs to Jupiter for the **Chaldeans**, to Mercury for the Indians, and to Mars for Maternus. Not to pursue them all individually, the Babylonians followed this method: they gave the first decan—the beginning of the **Ram**—to Mars, because it is his sign; then, following the order of the spheres, they gave the first ten-day period <note>decury</note> of any sign to the "head of the family" (that is, the lord of the house), and the remaining two...

<summary>Pico exposes the logical circularity and massive contradictions between Greek, Egyptian, and Arabic astrologers regarding who rules the "trigons" and "decans" of the zodiac. He argues that if these "experts" cannot agree on basic planetary rulers, the entire system of celestial influence is a groundless invention.</summary>

<header>DISPUTATIONS</header>

<column-break/>

<margin>On the Babylonian dodecathemoria.</margin>
...the lords of the signs of that triangle. The commentary of Maternus <note>Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman astrologer</note> is entirely arbitrary and relies on ancient tradition; anyone who weighs it should recognize that these men did not decree these dogmas through true observations or the reliability of experiments, but through weak and trivial conjectures of this sort. We will later dispute these experiments more extensively below. Just as the Egyptians devised "decans" <note>Ten-degree divisions of a sign</note> by dividing a sign into three parts, the Babylonians used **dodecathemoria** <note>Twelve-fold divisions of a sign, where each 2.5-degree segment is assigned to a different zodiac sign</note> by cutting a sign into twelve parts. However, they did not use the version Maternus ascribes to them; the authors Manilius and Porphyry 

<margin>Porphyry.</margin>
mention them, as does Ptolemy, though he does so mockingly. These dodecathemoria are called **topoi** <note>original Greek: "τοπους", meaning "places"</note>. Likewise, Albumasar, 

<margin>Albumasar, Avenazra, of Seville.</margin>
Avenazra <note>Abraham ibn Ezra</note>, and John of Seville mention only this dodecathemoria, not the one handed down by Maternus, Alchabitius, and Heliodorus, about which we shall speak in its proper place. 

<margin>The Saxon error.</margin>
The Saxon <note>Johannes de Saxonia, a 14th-century commentator</note>, in his commentaries on Alchabitius, was deceived by the similarity of names and confused the two. The Indians, also making up their own fictions, divided any sign into nine parts <note>Known as Navamsas in Vedic astrology</note>, decreeing that the first part belongs to the lord of the sign that is "moveable" within that trigon. For example, the first ninth-part of Aries belongs to Mars, because Aries is a moveable sign; the first part of Leo is again Mars, because the "moveable" sign of the fiery triplicity 

<margin>On the monomoirias.</margin>
is Aries. They place the following parts in the series of the subsequent signs: so if the first belongs to Mars, whose house is Aries, the second belongs to Venus, and the third to Mercury, since Venus has Taurus and Mercury has Gemini as their houses. The Egyptians, on the other hand, numbered each individual degree, which they called **monomoirias** <note>From the Greek for "single part"</note>; they assigned 

<margin>Of the Egyptians. A refutation of all these by words.</margin>
these to the planets by the order of the trigons. Specifically, the first part of any sign would be the monomoiria of the planet that is the lord of that trigon—a nocturnal planet if the birth was at night, or a diurnal one if by day. The second part would belong to the second lord of the same trigon, the third to the lord of the following trigon, and so on; however, they ensured that the same planet would not obtain a monomoiria twice in one sequence. I shall refute all these "anatomies" and dissections using no other words than those of Ptolemy himself, who said that all these things are **unnatural, empty, and mere talk** <note>original Greek: "ἀφυσικὸν ἀλλὰ κενὸν καὶ λόγον"</note>; that is, they have no physical 

<margin>Ptolemy.</margin>
reasoning, but are only for vain ostentation. He could not have defined these matters more correctly. For the more these things possess rashness and are fabricated with greater license, the more they appear marvelous and great to the unrefined and unskilled. There was no other reason why Aboafar <note>Abu Ma'shar</note> was 

<margin>Why Aboafar is considered great in astrology.</margin>
considered a great man in astrology—though otherwise ignorant of mathematics—except that nothing seemed even slightly unreasonable to him. He heaped together the fables of everyone at once, rejecting and scorning nothing. Thus, he seems to have produced more "secrets" than others simply because he recorded more fables. 

What remains are the "bounds" <note>term: **Fines** (or Terms); specific degrees within a sign where a planet is said to have influence</note>, which I shall refute just as briefly by pointing out the discord among those still litigating over them. For Ptolemy prescribes some, the Egyptians others, the Babylonians others, the Indians others, and some other astrologer mentioned by Albumasar 

<margin>Albumasar.</margin>
others still. In his *Great Introduction*, Albumasar puts forward wonders: the younger astrologers stick to the Egyptians, the Greeks follow Ptolemy (and with them Ibn Ridwan), while others have their own followers. Therefore, not only are the signs themselves nothing, but if the signs *were* something, these affinities of the planets with the signs—where a planet has a "house" here, a "dominion" there, and "bounds" elsewhere—are frivolous, fabulous, conflicting, and fabricated. Nor do only the Latins disagree on these things, but also in 

<column-break/>

the comparison of the dignities themselves. For the common crowd gives the first rank to the house, the second to the exaltation, the third to the bounds, the fourth to the triplicity, and the fifth to the "face" <note>A five-degree or ten-degree division</note>. Ptolemy places the house in the first spot, the triplicity in the second (as Haly <note>Ali ibn Ridwan</note> prefers), the exaltation in the third, and the term (bound) in the fourth; he ignores the "face" entirely. The Chaldeans do not have houses. The Egyptians add monomoirias to everything, the Indians ninth-parts, the Babylonians dodecathemoria. They do not place triplicity with the houses. Maternus attributes more to "height" <note>Exaltation</note> than to bounds, and more to bounds than to houses. "For," he says, "the stars rejoice when placed in the first rank in their height; in the second rank in their bounds; in the third rank in their houses." These dogmas of the astrologers are therefore most vain; they neither strengthen them with reasons nor with experiments. When they play with these trifles, they cannot reach any agreement.

->### Chapter XVII. On feminine, bright, and dark degrees, and others of that kind, which Ptolemy despised, and on which other astrologers do not agree.<-

<margin>Ptolemy, Haly, Maternus</margin>
We have refuted those divisions of the signs that they relate to the planets—such as Mars being "exalted" here, and the Sun elsewhere; or that this is the "face" of one, and that the face of another; or this is the "monomoiria" of one, and that of another. Likewise for trigons, bounds, ninths, and dodecathemoria. Now we must treat those things which they have handed down concerning the degrees themselves in absolute terms: such as some being "bright," others "dark," others "fortunate," others—as they say—"well-like" <note>term: **Puteales** (pit degrees); degrees thought to be debilitating or "deep" like a well</note>, others "sickly" (which they call *alzemena*), some masculine, and some feminine. 

But this has been largely satisfied above; now we shall add this: Ptolemy despised all these things too. His interpreter, Ibn Ridwan, seems to grant them only this much: that they should be observed *if* truth is found to be in them through experiments. But what faith can there be in an experiment when six different opinions are carried about regarding masculine and feminine degrees? For you will read them described one way in Firmicus, another way in Albumasar, another in Ibn Ridwan, and another in Alchabitius. Abraham <note>Ibn Ezra</note> varies in many points; then those who make every twelfth part of a sign alternately masculine and then feminine, starting from the gender of the sign, disagree entirely with all of these. I pass over those who place twelve degrees out of thirty into the sex of the sign, the next twelve in the opposite, and then divide the remaining six equally. 

Regarding the bright, dark, and obscure degrees, there was another opinion among the ancients based on the position of the stars; they called that part "bright" in which there was a star, and they believed this to be permanent because they thought the stars did not move. Therefore, these men were in error. We later thinkers, although we agree with Hipparchus, Ptolemy, and the rest regarding the origin of the dogma, and even though we contend that the stars *do* move, still determine the "bright" and "dark" degrees to be the same ones the ancients defined. In this matter, such confusion has arisen among them, and such perversity of things and words (as explained above), that nothing could be less true than their "experience" in these matters. 

The same error was made by them regarding the degrees they say "increase fortune"; we have declared that there, too, you will find them noted one way in Alchabitius, another in Albumasar, and another in Avenazra. The same diversity exists in the "well-like" degrees, which none of the ancients established. Nor can Aboafar help but lie when he says he follows the opinion of the Egyptians while describing them; for many of the degrees that Aboafar makes into "wells," Hephaistio of Thebes (who was skilled in all Egyptian astrology) counts among the "bright" degrees—such as the sixth degree of Aries.

<margin>Firmicus, Albumasar, Alchabitius, Abraham.</margin>
<margin>Men.</margin>
<margin>Aboafar, Hephaistio of Thebes.</margin>

### AGAINST ASTROLOGY, BOOK VI.

degree: the fifth of Taurus, the thirtieth of Gemini, the twenty-second of Cancer, and many others in other signs. What of a certain Dorian astrologer who called himself "The Scrutinizer" <note>original: "perscrutatorem"</note>? Regarding these properties of the degrees, he feels entirely differently than all the ancients. Nor does he allege anything for his dogma other than the "reliability of experience"—namely, that events do not respond to the sayings of the ancients. But should they respond to his own? Therefore, the various observations of the degrees are vain; they are not only unfaithful and inconstant according to us, but were even condemned by Ptolemy himself.

### Chapter XVIII. The "Parts," where they originated, and how much astrologers fight among themselves in measuring them.

Now, as for the **"Parts"** <note>Also known as "Arabic Parts" or "Lots," these are mathematical points calculated by the distance between two planets and projected from the Ascendant</note> which they use in every prediction: are they not a mere fiction and a vain thing? A voluntary dogma? "Count," they say, "the degrees intercepted between this planet and that one, and when you have traversed as many degrees from the horoscopus <note>The rising sign or Ascendant</note>, where the number ends, there will be a **Part** <margin>Refutation</margin> signifying some matter." This point is to be observed no differently than a planet or a star. What could be imagined more delirious than this precept? Not only because natural power in the heavens exists where there is no star, no light, nor any other natural quality—as there certainly is none at that degree where the count ends—but because this calculation is fashioned according to their whim and can have no physical reason. 

Abu Ma'shar <note>original: "Aboasar," a 9th-century Persian astrologer influential in the Middle Ages</note>, that most trifling man, wished to give a reason <margin>Abu Ma'shar's Reason.</margin> for these kinds of parts, which none of the ancients had done. But he spoke in such a way that, in the midst of his extreme wordiness, he says nothing. For the sum of his words is finally this: when there are two planets signifying the same thing, the distance between them also has the power of signifying; but that power must be measured from the horoscopus. Because things to come, whether good or bad, are known through the location where the significator of those things arrives from the horoscopus. 

For example, since the Sun and Saturn are the stars of parents, the interval by which they are separated from each other is to be counted from the ascendant. In the degree where that number falls, the future signification regarding parents will be found, as if the power of the Sun and Saturn were joined there in a certain way. This is the "subtlety" of Abu Ma'shar, in which that which is denied is assumed, and which we especially mock: namely, that such a distance has a power such that the end of a similar interval drawn from the ascendant has any power to effect anything. He ought to have given a reason for how this is so; since he fails to do so, it is not a reason for an opinion, but a mere story. As we have seen, this is not only ineffective (since it proves nothing about the matter in question) but it is false and repugnant to the principles of the astrologers themselves. This is because the original authors of the "Parts" (as we just said) made the primary parts belong to the planets themselves, not to things and events; that was something devised later by their successors. 

Furthermore, let us see what place Abu Ma'shar's reasoning holds regarding the Parts of the planets. He says the parts are taken from the interval of two planets signifying the same thing—even though the distance of no planet except the Sun and Moon is taken on its own <margin>Hermes, first author of the Parts.</margin> by Hermes. Hermes was the first author of these parts in that book to which he gave the title *Panaretos* <note>original Greek: "παναρετω", meaning "The All-Virtuous"</note>. But a part is taken from the planet whose part is sought and the part of one of the two luminaries. For he takes the Part of Venus from the Part of the Sun and Venus (where we noted in the first book that Abu Ma'shar and Al-Qabisi <note>original: "Alchabitium"</note> were deceived) <margin>Abu Ma'shar. Al-Qabisi.</margin>. He takes the Part of Mercury from the Part of the Moon, which is called "of Fortune," and Mercury itself (where they also wandered). He takes the Part of Mars from Mars and the Part of Fortune; the Part of Jupiter from the Part of the

<column-break/>

Sun and Jupiter; and the Part of the Sun and Moon from each other, as is manifest to everyone. Nor does he wish other things to be signified through the parts than what each planet (whose part it is said to be) signifies. 

Add to this that the "Parts of things" are not taken from the planets that signify those things among the astrologers. For indeed, Mars signifies brothers among all of them; and yet the "Part of Brothers" is taken from Jupiter and Saturn; it is never taken from Mars. And all the ancients collect the "Part of Marriage" from Saturn, a planet which they claimed had no union with weddings. Therefore, the commentary of that Abu Ma'shar is not only light and trifling (assuming the very thing under dispute), but it is alien to the opinion of the authors of this dogma. 

For something else moved them than what that trifler dreamed up after so many centuries. The first occasion of this error was as follows: it seemed to the ancients that the rising degree—that is, the horoscopus—corresponds to the Sun. Therefore, since the Moon is considered to be almost a second Sun above us, they wanted there to be a second horoscopus for the Moon, corresponding in proportion. They judged that it should be placed in no other location than one that was as far from the East as the Sun was distant from the Moon in any given birth. They called that place the *Kleron Tyches* <note>original Greek: "κληρον τυχης"</note>, that is, the "Lot of Fortune," for the reason we shall mention shortly. 

Ptolemy himself teaches this in the third book of his *Apotelesmatika* <note>Ptolemy’s "Tetrabiblos" or Four Books on the Influence of the Stars</note> <margin>Where the name of the Lot and of Fortune comes from.</margin>, reminding us also that all antiquity agreed that the Part of Fortune should be as far from the horoscopus as the Moon is from the Sun. Nor does the opinion of those who, in nocturnal births, compare from the Moon to the Sun rather than vice-versa, vary; because they turn themselves by the same amount from the ascendant toward the preceding signs. Therefore, they define it in the same place as those who, counting from the Sun to the Moon, number according to the sequence of the signs. 

I suspect the reason for the name is this: since they had made two "horoscopes," as it were—one of the Sun and one of the Moon—to the true and solar one they attributed the lot of the body and mind; but to the lunar and accidental one, they attributed the "Lot of Fortunes." That is, the things that are outside of us. Thus, from the first, we would receive our nature, and from the second, our fate regarding the things that are ours. For this reason, the lunar horoscopus was called the "Lot of Fortune," and for no other reason does Ptolemy judge fortunes from it. Generally, these "Lots" are called "Parts," but they are called "Places" in <margin>Here Hermes the Egyptian is criticized in the book he titled Panaretos.</margin> Maternus. 

When this was already accepted, a certain Hermes the Egyptian, having poorly considered the reason for the previous institution, thought that "Lots" should be made for all planets by a similar example. And so he established the Lots of Saturn and the rest in the book titled *Panaretos*. He called the Part of the Sun the *Agathos Daimon* <note>original Greek: "αγαθον δαιμονα", meaning "Good Spirit" or "Good Divinity"</note>; the Part of Jupiter, *Nike* <note>original Greek: "νικην", meaning "Victory"</note>; the Part of Mercury, *Ananke* <note>original Greek: "αναγκην", meaning "Necessity"</note>; the Part of Venus, *Eros* <note>original Greek: "ερωτα", meaning "Love"</note>; the Part of Mars, *Tolma* <note>original Greek: "τολμαν", meaning "Audacity"</note>; and the Part of Saturn, *Nemesis* <note>original Greek: "νεμεσιν", meaning "Retribution"</note>. 

In ordering these, he observed this method: he took each part from the distance of the planet itself (whose part it is) to the part of either the Sun or the Moon. He used the Sun's part for Venus and Jupiter, and the Moon's for the others. Where the Sun's part was to be used, the computation would be made from it in a day birth; but in a nocturnal birth, from the planet to the part. The opposite was done where he used the Part of Fortune. But he also ordered the count for all of them to be led from the horoscopus, because he saw that done by the ancients in the Part of Fortune. By its example, he imagined the rest. He paid little attention to the fact that the conjecture (whatever it may be) that moved the ancients to establish a Lot for the Moon does not apply to the remaining planets. For the other planets do not have that same parity or kinship with the Sun that would make it necessary for something to correspond to them in place of a horoscopus, just as the rising East corresponds to the Sun.

<summary>Pico criticizes the "Arabic Parts" or "Lots," arguing they are mathematical fictions with no physical basis. He specifically traces the "Lot of Fortune" to a flawed analogy between the Sun and Moon, which was then baselessly expanded by later astrologers like Hermes to include all the planets.</summary>

Later, being ignorant of the origin of the dogma, they fabricated fables there, such as those Abu Ma'shar <note>original: "Aboasar," a famous 9th-century Persian astrologer</note> relates. If they say they were moved by experience rather than reason, I will respond as I have always done: there is no authority in "experiences" upon which men of equal authority do not agree. Moreover, this happens with the "parts" as it does in every astrological dogma. First, almost every author sets the Part of Fortune itself in a different place. For Ptolemy commands it to be computed from the Sun to the Moon, whether the birth <note>original: "genitura"</note> was by day or by night. Others affirm the **Part of Venus** should be computed from the Moon to the Sun in a nocturnal birth. Heliodorus and Maternus start from the

Opinion of Heliodorus and Maternus. Opinion of Alchabitius and Abu Ma'shar. Another by Ibn Ezra, the opinion of the Arabs.
</margin>
**Part of the Spirit** <note>original: "parte daemonis"</note> to Venus by day, but the opposite by night. Alchabitius, following Abu Ma'shar, goes from the Part of Fortune to the Part of the Spirit at night; by day, from Spirit to Fortune. Ibn Ezra <note>original: "Abenzagela"</note> takes it from Venus to Fortune, equally by day and by night. For the **Part of Parents**, the Arabs take it from the Sun to Saturn in a daytime birth, and from Saturn to the Sun in a nocturnal birth.
<margin>
Another by Heliodorus.
