Heliodorus says if Saturn is hidden by rays, whether it be night or day, one proceeds from Mars to Jupiter. For the **Part of Brothers**, Maternus uses Jupiter to Saturn at night. The Greeks use the same at night, but by day they go from Saturn to Jupiter. Regarding **Marriage**, they disagree in a marvelous way: for if you seek the Lot of the Husband, Alchabitius always counts from the Sun to Venus; Heliodorus goes to Venus indeed, but starting from Saturn. Maternus, following the opinion of the ancients, commands that by day we go from Saturn to Venus, but at night we begin from Venus; he testifies that he himself (as others also prescribe) proved in many nativities that one should always compute from the Sun to the Moon in both day and night births. If we examine the birth of a woman, Maternus orders it to be computed from Mars to Venus by day, and from Venus to Mars at night. Others always go from Venus to Saturn, which Ibn Ezra claims is the opinion of Hermes. Alchabitius says it should always be taken from the Moon to Mars. Others always from the Sun to Mars; thus they disagree on the rest, but it is tedious to follow them all. For the **Part of Travel**, the Arabs start from the lord of the

ninth house to its first minutes; the Greeks go from the Sun to Mars. For the **Part of Inheritances**, the former go from Saturn to the Moon, while the latter go from Saturn to Venus. For **Servants**, the former from Mercury to the Moon, the latter from Mars to the Moon. All the ancients compute the **Part of the Mother** from Saturn to the Moon, then reckoning the number from the ascendant, as the ancients were accustomed to do in everything. But the Arabs seek it from the Moon to the first minute of the eighth house, adding as many degrees as Saturn has traveled through the sign in which he is located; and whatever sum the calculation makes, they count that much from the beginning of the sign in which Saturn is through the following signs. But we are not so idle as to record the fables of everyone; it can certainly be clear to anyone that these are not based on faithful experiences, but that each person has fashioned dogmas for himself according to his own whim.

->### Chapter XIX. The theory of the Dodecathemorium is exploded and its Egyptian authors are rejected along with their climacteric years.<-

<margin>
What is being dealt with here regarding the Dodecathemorium.
</margin>
There is a similar insanity regarding **Dodecathemoria** <note>The division of a single zodiac sign into twelve 2.5-degree segments</note>, and for the same reason they should be hissed off the stage as the "parts" were. I do not mean that Dodecathemorium which we mentioned above, which is simply the twelfth part of any sign. Rather, I mean what is handed down by Maternus and the Greek writers in this manner: of whatever planet you wish to find the Dodecathemorium, they say, calculate its degree twelve times—whether that planet be in the tenth or fifth degree of the sign, or any other number. Then, whatever the sum of the comparison makes, you divide them among the individual signs, allotting thirty to each. But you shall take the beginning from the start of the sign in which the star is whose Dodecathemorium you seek; and in whatever sign the last number falls, that sign shows you the place of the Dodecathemorium. Take an
<margin>
Example.
</margin>
example: the Sun is in the fifth degree and fifth minute of Aries. If you multiply five by twelve, there will be sixty degrees; the minutes will make one degree, and thus there will be sixty-one degrees. You will give thirty to Aries (in which we said the Sun was), thirty to Taurus, and the Dodecathemorium will be found in the first degree of Gemini. Once this is found, what could be imagined more vain or futile? Since through those numbers, no power of the planet and no quality is transmitted into that part. But if it is said that "observation" corresponds to the outcomes, I will object that Paul of Alexandria—a most serious author among the Egyptians, whose
<margin>
Refutation of Paul of Alexandria because he added a different calculation to the Egyptian one.
</margin>
invention this primarily was—testifies that such an observation was found to be false. For he himself introduced a new method against the opinion of all the ancients: that the degrees should not be multiplied by twelve, but by thirteen. Clearly, the ancient computation was not succeeding for him, as it was false and fabricated. And since sometimes by multiplying by thirteen he achieved what he was seeking, after the manner of astrologers he established a dogma from a single success. These are those "mysteries" of the Egyptians, whose opinions the superstitious common folk adore like oracles, though their doctrine possesses nothing of divinity but is ridiculous even to the half-learned. For if there were any astrology, the Egyptians would deserve the name of astrologers least of all, for they were ignorant of the movements of the true and natural things in heaven—that is, the constellations and stars—as we shall say below; and in predicting, they used these deceptive dreams more than the stars and planets. Heliodorus writes that Hermes Trismegistus, who first found the "parts" of the planets, opened the way whereby, through those parts alone and with nothing else respected, predictions could be made.

Having previously argued that astrology has no basis in physical reality or experience, he now begins a new line of attack: even if celestial influences existed, they would be impossible to calculate because the "starting moment" of any event is impossible to define with certainty.</meta>

AGAINST ASTROLOGY BOOK VII 127

regarding all the single-degree divisions <note>original: "monomeriis," a system where each degree of a zodiac sign is assigned to a specific planet</note> and the twelfth-parts <note>original: "dodecathemoriis," the division of each 30-degree zodiac sign into twelve 2.5-degree segments</note>, it is surprising how much weight they attributed to them in every prediction. For this reason, Ptolemy <margin>Ptolemy, the wisest of the astrologers.</margin>—the wisest of the astrologers—noting them indirectly, says that his own doctrines are being handed down, which are free from all "whispering of irrational lot-casting" <note>original Greek: ψυθιακῶν κληρισμῶν ἀνοήτων λογήτων</note> and are free from "parts prattled about by the masses that possess no reason" <note>original Greek: μέρους ὑπὸ τῶν πολλῶν φλυαρούμενα καὶ μηδαμῶσιν ἔχοντα λόγον</note>. That is to say: not through parts and ineffective numbers that have no basis in cause or reason, which many people fabulate superfluously with no logic to persuade others. When he speaks of "numbers," he is noting both the twelfth-parts which we represent here, and those who calculate "climacteric years" <note>Critical years in a person's life thought to bring great change or danger, traditionally multiples of 7 or 9</note> from the observation of numbers alone, such as the multiples of nine and seven. This is why many old men are troubled by a superstition regarding their sixty-third year; they dread it more than a snake or a tiger. But the common folk sin in these matters with a pardonable error; yet who could excuse those who wish to be considered philosophers?

# THE DISPUTATIONS OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA AGAINST THE ASTROLOGERS. BOOK SEVEN BEGINS.

## Chapter One. What has been discussed so far, and what is to be discussed in this book.

<margin>The continuation of this book with the preceding ones.</margin>
Up to this point, it was demonstrated that astrology is non-existent by removing the efficiency of the stars; we showed that this could be reasonably asserted based on philosophy, the dignity of the stars, the condition of lower things, and the reliability of experience. Then, even if the stars did effect what astrologers imagine, we proved why they would do so differently than what has been devised by them, and consequently, that no knowledge of this efficiency or of future things is possible for them. Now we must act so that, even if we grant that these things occur from heaven, we may declare that the way it is constructed by them—that is, that all things receive their fates from heaven from the primordial hour—cannot be known by them. For this is first necessary for them to achieve: they must have explored with total certainty what the fatal hour is for each thing; we shall teach in the disputation of the present book that this can neither be known, nor is it certainly known by them. And since various principles are established for various things, we shall first dispute regarding the beginning of man, declaring that it is in ambiguity and that, whatever it may be, it is certainly not what is thought by the astrologers.

## Chapter II. That the fatal hour is ambiguous, if such a thing exists in all matters which are not completed in a moment but over time, and especially in all those in which the birth-chart seems to have little strength.

<margin>The question regarding the beginning of a thing.</margin>
<margin>A thing receives its fate when it begins to be made.</margin>
There is an inextricable question in determining the beginning of any thing that is not consumed in a moment but over time: whether that fatal time is when the craftsman first moves to make it, whatever efficient cause it may eventually obtain? Or rather when it is finished? Or when it is not indeed all required at once, but is finished in parts, so that there are different fates for the different parts? For whatever we say has its own reason to support it. For if the craftsman puts his hand to it successfully, how can the work be unsuccessful when the craftsman works successfully? Since the success of both the worker and the operation is ultimately that the work turns out both well and according to the worker’s wish. Then, if fate comes from the stars efficiently and not just significantly, when ought a thing rather receive its fate than when the stars effect it through other intervening causes? It seems, therefore, that fate depends on that hour in which the craftsman first moves to make the thing. On the contrary, how shall a thing receive a fate before it exists? Or how shall it be said by us to exist when it first begins to be made so that it might exist at some point? Finally, a thing is what it is because of its species and form, which arrives at the final moment of completion. Therefore, is not that moment rather fatal to it when it first begins to be what it is, and when it can stand by its own nature and firmness, separate from the cause from which it was made? We shall therefore more reasonably herald the fates of things not from the hour in which they begin to be *made*, but the hour in which they begin to *be*. Again, if different parts are completed at different times, why shall not each part obtain the decree of its fortune from its own time? Especially since it is proven by experience that things turn out differently for various parts of the same thing: for even in the body of the same man, sometimes some members are well and others are poorly; and some part of the same city will be subject to ruins and fires while nothing of the sort happens to the remaining parts. Why is it not, therefore, more reasonable for each thing to be moved and governed by its own constellation, rather than drawing the condition of its subsequent fate from some past and perhaps abolished principle? And let these things be said in general about all things; now let us examine the same in man specifically, regarding whose fatal primordial beginning (if there is such a thing) a great and necessarily inextricable ambiguity arises. <margin>What hour deserves to be called the fatal hour of man; the various beginnings of man.</margin> For what shall we rather establish, when so many of his principles are seen, and all of them worthy of being considered a beginning? Do we judge that fatal point of time to be the one which is first in time among all: that moment when the man first joins with the woman? Or not that, but when the seed from the male grows into the womb? Or rather are these merely preludes and necessary antecedents? Shall we establish the first beginning of human formation as when that seminal power attacks the purest part of the female excrement <note>A reference to the Aristotelian view of menstruation as the material for the fetus</note> and constitutes it—that is, drives it into a fetus, just as milk is united and condensed by rennet? Or is it not yet the beginning of a man, but only when all parts of the body are present in potential within the conception? Or when it is now covered by its own fruitful membranes? Or does nature begin the man when the heart is first actually separated, by whose virtue that which is begotten—now like a son emancipated from his father—begins to be governed by itself, as <margin>Aristotle, the interpreter of nature.</margin> Aristotle, the interpreter of nature, taught. For great weight and authority are owed to this principle, since the heart is the first thing that is formed, and in the distinguishing of the other parts, both the movement of all and the growth are distributed from the heart. Thus (if we must play along with the astrologers' fables), just as the power implanted in the heart then unfolds the whole man with the other parts acting together, so too the solar virtue first drank into the heart would then unfold the entire power of fate. Or rather, is the principal fate of the heart and life from here, but the disposition of any individual member depends most of all on the hour in which it is disposed, undergoing the condition of its own private fate? For to those considering all things rightly and deeply, it appears very reasonable that—if, for the sake of argument, the "luminaries" <note>The Sun and Moon</note> as they say, preside over the eyes—the habit and mixture of the eyes should depend rather on the disposition of the luminaries when the eyes are being disposed, than either from that which preceded long ago when the seed filled the womb, or that which is to follow later when, the eyes having long been completed, the infant is about to come forth from the mother’s womb—a thing which is said of the remaining members by the same reasoning...

<summary>Pico della Mirandola begins Book VII by critiquing the "fatal hour" in astrology, arguing that it is impossible to pinpoint the exact moment a person or object begins, thereby making astrological charts fundamentally unreliable.</summary>

# DISPUTATIONS
## AGAINST DIVINATORY ASTROLOGY
### Book VII

<margin>A new way of defining the beginning from several mixed elements.</margin>
...should be understood. But if, setting aside all these things we have mentioned, we search for another beginning that is more outstanding in authority and efficacy, what more reasonable one could we propose than the moment when the soul is shared with the fetus? For it is then that a human being begins to exist; having attained the complete definition of "substance," he is then constituted from his own matter and form. And if fate proceeds from the hour in which a thing first exists, no hour would surely be considered more "fatal" for a man than this one. 

Yet if we must depart from that opinion, there is great probability in the view that the things of the body should be referred to the seminal beginning (conception), the things of the soul to animation itself (the entry of the soul), and the things that are external or related to "fortune" to that momentous time when a man, exiting the enclosures of the womb, first enters this field in which fortune plays. 

Finally, the "divine philosophers"—who rely only on reasons to explain themselves—cannot correctly extricate themselves from this varied and knotty ambiguity concerning the human beginning. If philosophy is to affirm anything, it will affirm nothing less than what the astrologers have decreed: that the fates of a man depend on the hour of his birth. Astrologers were led to this opinion not by reason, but because they saw they could more easily grasp this specific moment; therefore, they granted it the primary role. 

This is why, after the birth, they are also accustomed to granting something to the moment of conception, hoping that they might occasionally be able to know something about it. But they have rejected the other, most powerful beginnings—especially the moment the fetus is animated—entirely. They rejected them because these moments were completely unknown to them. If they admitted that human fate depended on those moments, they would no longer be able to claim for themselves any power of divining fate. 

But, to pass over the rest, by what reason do they prefer the birth over the conception and the animation of the fetus? If we give the primary role in establishing fate to the beginning that is first in time, there is no beginning prior to the seminal one (conception) from which all other things proceed. If, however, a beginning is preferred not because it is first in time but because of its efficacy and dignity, then the time of the fetus's animation must be preferred over all others. The birth is later than all of them and has little or no efficacy; it does not start the human, nor make him, nor complete him; it only shows him to the world after he has already been started and completed.

### Chapter III. That Ptolemy attributed more to conception than to birth, and that Ptolemy's own reasoning proves nothing should be attributed to birth.

<margin>Ptolemy gave more weight to conception than to birth.</margin>
If the words of Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), whose *Tetrabiblos* was the "bible" of medieval and Renaissance astrology.</note> himself are weighed seriously, we will see that he, led by the force of reason, gives more weight to conception than to birth, although he tried to build a case for the efficacy of birth to favor his own profession. His words in the third book of the *Apotelesmatika* <note>The *Apotelesmatika*, better known as the *Tetrabiblos*, Ptolemy's four-book treatise on astrology.</note> are as follows: "When some temporal beginning of a man is established, by nature indeed that beginning will be when the seed is admitted into the genital womb; but in potential and by accident, it is the hour when the infant emerges at birth. Therefore, for those who have caught the hour of the admission of the seed by chance or observation, it is more fitting to follow that hour in distinguishing the properties of the body and soul, after considering the configurations of the stars active at that time. For once the seed is disposed with a certain quality from the state of the surrounding air at the beginning—even though the timing of its formation varies thereafter—it naturally adopts only ma-

<column-break/>

terial that is proper and related to itself, and when it is fully developed, it will be even more assimilated to the disposition of its first quality." 

These are Ptolemy’s words, quoted verbatim. Here it seems to me he declares—as clearly as possible and without any bit of doubt—that the first, most natural, and most effective beginning of a man is the admission of the seed. He says we should cling to this especially when recognizing the shifts in a man's life, both regarding the body and the soul. Once he asserted this, he then accurately and anxiously tried to resolve the objections that could be raised about the change in the seed. 

But, because he knew his art would be in danger if he denied the ability to pronounce on human fate from any other source, he added the following to what we have said: "However, for those who are ignorant of the hour of the seminal beginning—which is usually the case—it is necessary for them to follow the beginning of the birth." 

Let us weigh these words before we add others. He says the hour of birth should only be used when the hour of conception is unknown. Regarding the hour of conception, he used the word *ephaptesthai* <note>original Greek: ἐφάπτεσθαι</note>, which means "it is fitting" or "it is proper." But regarding the hour of birth, he did not say it "is fitting," but rather *anankaion* 
<margin>Necessity</margin>
<note>original Greek: αναγκη</note>, which means "it is necessary." It is as if he is saying that for those who do not know the hour a man was conceived, but who still want to divine his fate, they must "of necessity" flee to the birth. 

Thus, it appears clearer than light that Ptolemy did not enter into this opinion willingly, but was forced by necessity, using the hour of birth as a "second plank after a shipwreck" <note>A classical metaphor for a desperate backup plan.</note>. And having spoken thus far according to reason, he soon tries as hard as he can to demonstrate that the beginning at birth is also valid, so as not to abandon his profession. Therefore, he adds: "And this is also a major beginning, falling short of the first only in this: that from the conception, those things can also be foreknown which happen before the birth. Furthermore, if one calls the former 'the beginning,' then the latter is the *katarchē*
<margin>Inception</margin>
<note>original Greek: καταρχή - a term in astrology for a starting point or an 'inception' used to predict the outcome of an undertaking.</note>, that is, the 'after-beginning.' It will indeed be second to the first in time, but perhaps it will be more perfect in power. For by almost every right, the former will be called the generation of the human seed, but the latter the generation of the human being, since the infant then receives many things it did not have in the womb, and those things are proper to human nature. Moreover, although the hour of birth seems to contribute nothing to making the child turn out this way or that, it nonetheless makes him come into the light under a configuration similar to the one that measured him [at conception]. For nature, after it has perfected him, gives the impetus to exit only when the disposition of the stars is similar to the figure that formed the fetus at the beginning. It is reasonable, then, that the disposition of the stars at the hour of birth also has significance for these things—not because it causes them, but because by natural necessity it is similar in power to the configuration that did cause them."

These are Ptolemy's words, faithfully recited by us. In them, the first thing to see is that what the interpreter Avenrodan 
<margin>Avenrodan's Error</margin>
<note>Avenrodan is the Latinized name of Ibn Ridwan (c. 988–1061), a famous Arabic commentator on Ptolemy.</note> says is entirely false: that Ptolemy speaks hesitantly in the first words where he discusses the efficacy of conception, but assertively in these last words where he demonstrates that the hour of birth has the power to signify. On the contrary, in the first part he affirms everything without exception or doubt, whereas here he speaks with constant qualifiers, inserting "almost" and "perhaps." Finally, when he finishes his whole argument, he has no other reason to defend the hour of birth as a signifier of fate than to argue that it is *similar* to the seminal beginning. He is so far from denying that the authority for deciding what a person will be like resides in the conception, that he concedes nothing more to the birth...

<summary>Pico argues that while birth is the only "beginning" astrologers can easily measure, even their greatest authority, Ptolemy, admitted that conception is the true natural starting point. Pico critiques the logical leap astrologers make by using birth as a "second-best" substitute for the unattainable moment of conception.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico’s critique of the "beginning" of life in astrology. # AGAINST ASTROLOGY. BOOK VII.

<margin>The common opinion is criticized.</margin>
...yield to the birth chart, so that it might be found similar and in agreement with the conception. For that common opinion among astrologers—believed even by the <term>interpreter of Ptolemy<note>Pico is likely referring to the Arabic commentator Ali ibn Ridwan (Avenrodan), who wrote a famous commentary on Ptolemy's *Tetrabiblos*.</note></term>—claims that the hour of conception signifies only what happens to the fetus in the mother’s womb. This idea was born from a false understanding of Ptolemy’s words; for Ptolemy did not say that *only* those things are signified by conception, but also those things which the birth chart cannot show. Ptolemy says that the conception is superior to the birth chart <gloss>through</gloss> the fact that by it, even things that happen before birth can be foreseen. But if it only showed those things, it would never have been necessary to add it, nor should we think the first principle (conception) superior to the second (birth) for that reason, since the span of a whole life is far greater than governing the first stages of a fetus that is still raw and unformed. Therefore, if Ptolemy hesitated on these points—and if he trusts the spoken word that the power of the second principle (birth) is perhaps more effective than the first, and that the first is the beginning of the human seed while the second is rather the beginning of the man—he clearly disagrees not only with reason but with himself. He disagrees with himself because, as I was saying, he could not defend the authority of fate at the beginning of birth unless he devised an affinity between birth and the seminal beginning. Furthermore, when he later gives instructions for foreseeing sex and other conditions of the one being born, he says these are better known from the conception than from the birth. He disagrees with reason both for many things we have said above, and because it is utterly beyond reason for us to call conception the beginning of the seed and birth the beginning of the man. For when the seed has filled the womb, it does not "become" itself, but rather begins to be abolished as nature sets her hands to the task of building a human being. Therefore, just as that moment is the beginning of generating a man, it is likewise the principle of the seed’s destruction. <gloss>As if</gloss> you should call birth the beginning of a man: for a man then has many things for the first time which he did not have in the womb. Yet those things do not pertain to his substance (which is already made and complete), but only to the management of certain actions which are not even unique to humans. If we were to start a man’s fate from these actions, fate would only begin long after birth—namely, when the infant begins to think, deliberate, and reason. For immediately at birth, a human has nothing unique to his species except his wailing. Therefore, Ptolemy, the most prudent of astrologers, surely would not insist on these false and frivolous points, although he may have put them forward hesitantly so as not to be seen as a total deserter and betrayer of his profession. Nor indeed can these arguments—by which birth is preferred to conception—have any firmness, nor even those which attribute some power in decreeing fate to the birth chart. For the sum of their entire argument is referred back to the "consensus" or agreement that exists between the birth and the conception. But what is this consensus? What is the similarity? Haly <margin>Refutation of Haly.</margin> answers that the Sun at the hour of birth is always found in a sign that is either the seventh, ninth, or tenth from the sign it was in at the hour of conception. Is this, then, that "similarity"? O, what ridiculous vanity! As if any time would not "agree" with another time by this logic, since the Sun, at whatever time it may be, must necessarily be some number of signs away from where it was at another time. Or is that which is brought up concerning the Moon more probable? They claim that the position of the Moon when we are born was the <term>horoscope<note>In ancient astrology, the "horoscope" referred specifically to the Ascendant—the degree of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon—not the entire chart.</note></term> of the conception, and whatever the position of the Moon was then, that becomes the horoscope of the birth. However, it will be demonstrated later that this is false and a fiction of the astrologers. And Haly <margin>Ibn Ridwan</margin> Avenrodan, explaining Ptolemy in his treatise on the present question, says that he has found this to be sometimes true and sometimes false. But come now, even if it were true, that fabricated consensus of both hours could be more clearly refuted by no other way: be-

<column-break/>

cause if you investigate the hour of conception according to that rule of the astrologers, and set up a <term>theme<note>A "theme" (thema) is a technical term for an astrological chart or map of the heavens at a specific moment.</note></term> for that time, you will find that the disposition of the heavens and stars is always different from it, and a signifier of entirely different things than what will appear to those calculating the hour of birth. But why do we waste more words in refuting trifles? Haly, the distinguished astrologer, in the book he wrote on <margin>Haly says the efficacy of fate is in the hour of conception.</margin> <term>elections<note>"Elections" or "Electional Astrology" is the practice of choosing the most astrologically auspicious moment to begin an undertaking.</note></term>, openly confesses that the efficacy of decreeing fate is in the hour of conception. But because this hour is unknown, he says that astrologers have fled to the hour of birth. And when they themselves are pressed regarding the birth of twins—whose fortunes are different—they are accustomed to say that sometimes a difference in their conceptions varies their fortune. Yet, if the hour of conception only disposes those things which happen inside the womb, it would follow instead that those whose conception is different could have a similar fortune, but their birth could in no way be the cause.

### Chapter IV. By what ways astrologers track universal fates, and how little they are based on reason.

We have spoken of how the beginning of a particular fate is uncertain, and how it is established by astrologers through false reasoning. It remains to speak of "universal" fate: from where, for instance, the fates of cities, nations, kingdoms, and the world in general are pronounced, and how this too (if any such thing be granted to exist) is nonetheless in an ambiguous and uncertain state, and incorrectly defined by our astrologers. They are accustomed to <margin>The triple path of astrologers for predicting universal things.</margin> proceed by roughly three ways to predict universal changes: either from the great eclipses and conjunctions of the higher stars or the luminaries (the Sun and Moon); or from the disposition of the heaven when the Sun enters the very first minute of <term>Aries<note>This refers to the Spring Equinox, which astrologers considered the "natural" beginning of the year.</note></term>, which they have established as the beginning of the year; or from the peculiar beginnings of cities, kingdoms, and nations—that is, from the hour in which a city is built, a kingdom instituted, or a law given to a people by which they live and are governed. All of these things are largely frivolous, as has been shown above, not only where the entire influence of the stars was struck down, but even when we weakened the entire logic of predicting from "great conjunctions." Whether from those conjunctions or from the eclipses of the luminaries, we declared it vain to expect anything a long time after they occurred. Then we exposed the <margin>The madness and impiety of astrologers.</margin> impiety and madness of the astrologers, who subject the heaven to fate and the laws of nations to the fate of their own "laws" <note>original: "fato suæ legis gentes subijcientium"</note>, and we showed how vain it is to decree a "birthday" for a built city or an accepted kingdom as if it were a natural thing. Now, even if we were to grant that there is some fate for all things, we are going to show that nothing certain can be defined regarding the fatal beginning of these things, nor has anything been defined by astrologers thus far. First, <margin>The fates of a city are not reasonably begun from the laying of the first stone.</margin> indeed, in auspiciously starting the fate of a city from the "throwing of the stone" (the foundation), by what reason are they moved? Since they are investigating the fates of a *society* rather than just a *city*, that moment should rather be observed when the built city first began to be inhabited and to be ruled and contained by its own laws. Likewise, regarding the fortune of a king, there is great discord among them: some think it depends on the hour in which a king is instituted or chosen. Others think the enthronement or coronation should rather be inspected. But let us pass over these as if they were smaller details, since even Haly believes that the fates of nations, cities, and kingdoms depend not so much on those things we were mentioning as on the principles of the great and universal constellations; we shall soon dispute with them on these matters in close combat.

<summary>Pico critiques the astrological reliance on birth charts by arguing that the "moment of beginning" is logically inconsistent, specifically refuting the "Trutine of Hermes" and other methods used by Haly and Ptolemy to link conception and birth. He then turns his critique toward "universal" astrology, questioning how one can determine the "birth" of a city or kingdom.</summary>

# DISPUTATIONS

...the very degree in which the <term>ascendant<note>Original: "horoscopus." In ancient astrology, this refers to the point of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at the moment of birth.</note></term> is located: for this reason, if a good planet is in that degree, either by its body or its rays, it will bestow its benefits in that year. Conversely, if a malevolent planet is there, it brings misfortune. In the second year, the second degree from the first corresponds; in the third, the third, and so on. Therefore, if Saturn, for example, occupied the twenty-first part from the ascendant, since that part corresponds to the twenty-first year of age, it would follow that this year will be infested by Saturn’s rays. When they wish, therefore, to foresee in what year some good or evil will happen to the person born, they measure the degrees between the principal places of the birth chart and the body or rays of a good or evil star intercepted between them; and for every degree, they prescribe a year of time after which that event should be expected. This is their position on <term>directions<note>A predictive technique where the positions of planets are mathematically "moved" to determine the timing of life events.</note></term>, from which the crowd of astrologers pronounces the span of life and all the falls and turns of fortune. 

<margin>Response.</margin>
<margin>Refutation.</margin>
<margin>First reason.</margin>
<margin>Avicenna in the Meteorology.</margin>
What could be more trivial than this? What could be imagined more irrationally? For first, that distribution of degrees to years: can it be fashioned more out of whim? It is conceived with no foundation of science or reason, especially since they say these degrees indicate sometimes years, and sometimes days (as it happens to suit them). This might perhaps have some probability if the partition of degrees itself were from nature; but it depends entirely on the will of the mathematicians, who divide the signs into thirty parts rather than twenty for no other reason than that the number thirty is more convenient for arithmetic divisions—as will be demonstrated to us in the next book by the testimony of the astrologers themselves. But how could Saturn harm me, found in the sixth part of Virgo (as was recorded) when I was being born, even if we grant them that its influence pertains to me in the twenty-first year of my life? For when it pertains to me, Saturn will not be there; and when Saturn is there, that part will not pertain to me. If they should say—perhaps like clothes infected by a plague do not lose their poison for some time—that it happens similarly to the parts of heaven, which retain for a long time the contagion received from an evil star, and that for this reason the degree already infected by Saturn when I was born pours back that noxious power into me after many years: they will be defending their position very prettily and subtly. Yet, if the conversation were with philosophers, I would bid them remember that the affection of light does not stick to the subject but departs with the body from which it is diffused. 

As <note>original: "Auicenna"</note> <term>Avicenna<note>The Latinized name of Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath whose works on Aristotelian science were standard university texts.</note></term> says in his *Meteorology*, light is both the vehicle and the fuel of all celestial impressions. But let them answer me: when there is an encounter of other planets at that same degree during so many intervening years, do they think that "ingrained" power can be abolished or diminished by the arrival of beneficial lights? Furthermore, if qualities received and taken up from planets endure in the regions of heaven, it will not only be necessary to observe which planet is found in which place in the heaven—either in the revolving year or the hour of birth—but also those who traversed the same places in preceding years. Finally, that fiction of "directing" is nothing other than subjecting things not only to those constellations that *are*, but those that *could be*. For what else is it to say that the Moon, which was struck by <term>sextile rays<note>Original: "exagonis radijs." An aspect where planets are 60 degrees apart.</note></term> from the Sun at my birth, will nevertheless eventually produce misfortune there from a <term>square aspect<note>Original: "quadrato aspectu." An aspect where planets are 90 degrees apart, traditionally considered difficult or "unfortunate."</note></term> of the Sun? She was not under that aspect when I was born; she would have been if she had been positioned further from the Sun with more parts of heaven placed between them—those parts across which she was distant from the square radiation. 

<margin>Second, Third, Fourth [reasons].</margin>

<column-break/>

When she has traversed those parts after so many years, that calamity will be inflicted there. But that constellation did not exist at my birth, and if it is to exist at some point afterward, it is nothing to me; for if there is any fate for me, the past disposition of the heaven gave it. It is clear, therefore, how absurd, how false, and how inconsistent is the position of "directing" which astrologers use daily. For what foundation do they have from which it is derived? They have not yet, I think, called it into consideration and examination. 

<margin>Other ways by which astrologers think the times of events can be foreseen.</margin>
<margin>Opinion of the Egyptians and the Mathesis.</margin>
Besides directions, they use the "rulership" of planets in predicting the times of events, having invented a system where planets take up the empire of life in a certain order. From this come the "centers" of the Chaldeans, the <term>fardaria<note>Original: "fridariæ." A system of planetary periods used in Persian astrology.</note></term> of the Persians, the "nines" of the Indians, the <term>tecates<note>Likely a reference to a division of time or planetary power mentioned in Ptolemaic traditions.</note></term> and "profections" of Ptolemy, the decennials of the Egyptians, the <term>chronocrators<note>Original: "cronocratores." Time-rulers; planets that govern specific periods of a person's life.</note></term> of the Arabs, and whatever other things of this kind others have dreamed up according to their whim. All these err in this unseemly way: they define the stars such that this planet rules us for so many years; when that time is consumed, it hands over the "rudder" of government to the succeeding planet as if by hand, according to the order of the spheres or the climate. This planet, in turn, having administered its jurisdiction through the time granted to it, yields the right and power to the next star. This is entirely alien to all natural reason. For no other cause can be rationally assigned why *this* planet rather than *another* should dominate lower things at this time, other than either the disposition of the matter (being more suitable for the impressions of one rather than another) or a more effective relationship of the star itself to us—such as when it is carried above the earth while others are placed below, or by turning toward the north it becomes closer to our regions, or shoots more direct rays into the earth. Although we might agree with the astrologers regarding the good or bad condition of things based on the diversity of places, signs, and radiations of that planet which holds more authority and power in heaven at that time: this is the *only* thing that can be said according to natural method. 

But the rest are fictions and fables: for example, to say that Jupiter now presides over earthly things because Saturn presided in the preceding years (whom Jupiter follows in the order of the spheres), and that Taurus rules this year because Aries ruled the previous one—as if the turns of earthly magistrates were found among the stars! If they say this has been proven by experience, some faith might be granted if they agreed among themselves on this distribution of times. But when one attributes the same years to the Moon, another to Mars, and another to Jupiter, should not the credit of "experience" be denied to all equally? For each one pretends it for his own opinion amidst such a variety of opinions. The Egyptians, whom <note>original: "Firmicus"</note> <term>Firmicus<note>Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman author of the 'Mathesis', a major astrological compendium.</note></term> follows, give the administration of life to each of the stars in an equal partition of 10 years and 9 months in this order: in a daytime birth, the Sun takes the first decennial; in a nighttime birth, the Moon. After that decennial, the planet found in the second place in the birth chart through the course of the signs takes over; then the third who was after the second, and the others in a similar way. But whoever is allotted the decennial, although he is the master of the whole time, divides the entire substance of the decennial among all the stars, beginning from himself and handing it over to those placed in order after him—specifically to whoever is found second in the <term>theme<note>The birth chart or horoscope layout.</note></term>. According to their opinion, the sum of the years that the seven planets moderate is seventy-five, with months added; when these are completed, a return is made again to the first planet. They collect the same number of years starting from the Sun if someone was born during the day, or from the Moon if born at night.

<summary>Pico critiques the mathematical systems astrologers use to predict the timing of life events, arguing that "directions" and "planetary periods" are arbitrary human inventions rather than natural physical influences. He mocks the idea that a planet's "contagion" lingers in a specific degree of the sky long after the planet has physically moved on.</summary>

### AGAINST ASTROLOGERS, BOOK VII.

...they participate: they also establish one principal lordship of times, but make others participants in the governance through a vicarious succession. They call this distribution the **firdaria** <note>Original: *fridariam*. A system of planetary periods used in medieval astrology, likely of Persian origin.</note>. From this comes that common saying among the younger astrologers that someone is a "participant in the firdaria of Jupiter." However, they differ greatly from the Egyptians; for in the sequence of the planets, they do not observe the places of the birth chart's theme, but rather the order of the celestial spheres, placing the Sun in the middle. Furthermore, they do not assign an equal amount of time to each planet: but rather ten years to the Sun, eight to Venus, thirteen to Mercury, nine to the Moon, eleven to Saturn, twelve to Jupiter, seven to Mars, three to the <term>Head<note>The North Node of the Moon.</note></term>, and two to the <term>Tail<note>The South Node of the Moon.</note></term>. Even **Abraham ibn Ezra** <note>Original: *Auenazra*. A famous 12th-century Jewish polymath and astrologer.</note> himself, in his book on astrological matters, confesses he does not know what reasoning could justify this. On the other hand, in appointing a participant in the governance, the Persians give an equal portion to any of the planets, so that the leading planet governs the first seventh part of its time alone, the second part with the planet following it, and the third with the third. But the Egyptians make this distribution unequal, decreeing nineteen months for the Sun, thirty for Saturn, twelve for Jupiter, fifteen for Mars, eight for Venus, twenty for Mercury, and twenty-five for the Moon. They subdivide these again: for example, out of his thirty months, Saturn imparts six days to the remaining planets, and the others do the same with their months, as **Hephaestion** <note>Hephaestion of Thebes, a 4th-century astrologer.</note> teaches and **Maternus** <note>Firmicus Maternus, author of the *Mathesis*.</note> ignored. But there was this disagreement between the Persians and the Egyptians: the former include the Head and Tail among the <term>chronocrators<note>Original: *cronocratoris*. "Time-lords" or planets that rule a specific period of life.</note></term>, while the Egyptians do not. From all of which it is clear that after the first ten-year period,

<margin>Ptolemy’s Opinion.</margin>
the governor of the years will rarely be the same among the Persians as among the Egyptians. **Ptolemy** differs from both, making them "lords of the ages": he has the Moon govern the first four years, and Mercury the ten following years. Yet in the following order: Venus eight, the Sun nine <note>Ptolemy usually assigns 19 years to the Sun in this system; "novem" (nine) may be a transcription error in the original Latin text or a specific variant Pico is reading.</note>, Mars fifteen, Jupiter twelve, and Saturn for the remainder of life. However, when he seeks the exact and particular distribution of times for each birth, he adds annual, monthly, and daily rulers to those principal chronocrators. But in these matters, the entire hinge of fate for Ptolemy revolves: where he censures those who make a single chronocrator for life (hinting at the Egyptians and **Dorotheus**), and yet if anyone follows Ptolemy’s opinion, they will define times in a way that is always vastly different from the 

<margin>A notable error of the astrologers of our age.</margin>
Egyptians and Persians. This makes it all the more pleasant to mock the astrologers of our age, who—not understanding that Ptolemy’s <term>ages<note>Original: *tecatis*. Likely a derivation from the Greek *dekata* or a corruption of *aetatis*.</note></term> and chronocrators, the Persians' firdaria, and the Egyptians' decades all pertain to the same thing—have tried to use all of them at once, as if they were not diverse and contrary opinions on the same subject. But concerning different matters, their opinions are least of all in agreement. **Indian astrology** knows neither firdaria, nor decades, nor ages, nor chronocrators; instead, it partitions life not into seven parts as the others do, but into nine members. Regarding these, it pronounces an order according to the disposition of the places in the birth chart: so that the first part of the years is ruled by the constellations belonging to the <term>twelfth house</term>, the second by those in the <term>ascendant</term>, the third by those in the second house, the fourth by the ninth, the fifth by the tenth, the sixth by the eleventh, the seventh by the sixth, the eighth by the seventh, and the ninth by the eighth. Nor do they disagree with others only in this dispensing of time, but also in the very partition of the houses. Dividing these according to the degrees of the zodiac (which they call equal), the Arabs—imitating **Andruzagar**—judge three parts of life through the <term>triplicity lords<note>Original: *trigonocratores*. The planets that rule the "triplicities" or groups of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element (Fire, Earth, Air, Water).</note></term>:

<margin>The Opinion of the Arabs.</margin>

<column-break/>

so that regarding the matters signified by each of the twelve places, they judge the state of the beginning and future from the first lord of the triplicity, the middle state from the second, and the final state from the third. But if there are only two lords for one triangle (as we mentioned in another book), or perhaps only one disposer for a single birth—although there will be one for a day birth and another for a night birth—a large part of life will be left without a governor. But neither do these triplicity lords truly exist; and even if three thousand of them were granted, that "vicarious succession" in governing a life is utterly ridiculous. But the inventions 

<margin>The Opinion of the Chaldeans.</margin>
of the **Chaldeans** are very different from all of these; they use neither ages, nor decades, nor firdaria, nor the nines of the Indians, nor triplicity lords, but rather the "angles" <note>The four most powerful points in a chart: Ascendant, Midheaven, Descendant, and Imum Coeli.</note> of the birth chart. They investigate the first part of life from the first angle (the East), the middle from the height of the midheaven, and the final part from the West; then, they pronounced on death and even on those things that happen after death from the fourth place of the theme. But they also partitioned that earlier three-part division again, so that the <term>cadent<note>Original: *apoclima*. A house that "falls away" from an angle.</note></term> of the ascendant indicated the pains of labor and what happens while the mother carries the womb; the ascendant itself indicated the birth and the first years; and the <term>succedent<note>Original: *epanophora*. A house that "rises up" toward an angle.</note></term> of the ascendant indicated the last remaining part of the first age. Again, the cadent of the midheaven indicated the first parts of middle life; the midheaven itself the middle; and its succedent the final parts. They did the same in the fourth house: so that the house declining from it signified the things preceding death, the fourth house itself signified death, and the succedent signified what might happen after death. I have set out to explain these opinions so that the conflict between them might be recognized, and therefore no faith should be placed in their "experience." Simultaneously, the vanity of these arbitrary dogmas, resting on the flimsiest conjectures, is exposed. For how shall we give the first part of life to the East and the middle to the midheaven, since middle age succeeds the first, but the midheaven does not follow the East, but precedes it? <note>Pico is pointing out a logical flaw: if you follow the daily rotation of the sky, the Midheaven reaches its peak *before* the stars behind it rise in the East.</note> But one must not labor in refuting these opinions, which refute and destroy themselves. Indeed, if I were to continue recounting the dreams of everyone, there would be no end. **Messahallah** <note>Original: *Messala*. An 8th-century Persian-Jewish astronomer and astrologer.</note> governs the first half of life from the 

<margin>Messahallah's Opinion.</margin>
rising Sun, and the second from the setting Sun. **Hemus** does it otherwise: he gives the first half to the planets 

<margin>Hemus's Opinion.</margin>
located in the upper hemisphere (whether they are oriental or occidental) and the second to all those beneath the earth. **Vellius**, with another fiction, ascribes the first part to the Moon and the second to the lord of the second house. **Abu Ma'shar** <note>Original: *Albumasar*. The most famous medieval Islamic astrologer.</note>, the most fabulous of them all, says that the first part should be referred to the "Lot of Fortune" and the second to the lord of that Lot. Others have it other ways, but it is not necessary to pursue them all. Read **Abenzagel**, and besides those we have recounted, you will find many other opinions there, fighting among themselves on this matter. Therefore, everyone composes his own fable according to his whim. Finally, being too credulous, as if toward oracles and the responses of prophets, we hand over our faith to these most trifling and deceptive peddlers, entrusting them with our hopes, fears, anxieties, joys, and—what is more ruinous—the very instruction and steering of our whole lives.

### Chapter VIII. Just as they adopt ineffective things, so they omit necessary ones; and how much they err concerning the fixed stars.

But just as they adopt many fictitious things such as we have mentioned—which have no nature and thus no influence, such as the signs, houses, images, the Tail, and...

<meta>This page continues Pico’s critique of the inconsistent methods used by astrologers. After discussing the Persian and Egyptian systems of planetary periods (firdaria), he now moves to a broader critique of why astrologers prioritize the seven planets over the "fixed stars" and the logical inconsistencies in their reasoning regarding planetary power and movement.</meta>

# AGAINST ASTROLOGERS, BOOK VII.

<margin>First reason.</margin> I contend against those asserting that greater effects can be provided by the planets than by the fixed stars. For the more sublime position of the "non-wandering" <note>Original: *non errantium*, referring to the fixed stars as opposed to the "wandering" planets.</note> stars does not indicate a less sublime nature: especially since the Sun, the moderator of all things—which certainly surpasses all other bodies except perhaps the Moon—has many stars placed far above it. Furthermore, let this be the argument for why they judge the planets to excel the fixed stars: that many spheres serve a single planet, while only one sphere serves many fixed stars. Thus, they argue the entire army of these stars is overcome by the power of a single celestial body. Yet, individual stars cannot surpass individual planets. <margin>Second.</margin> If you look at the magnitude of their bodies, the Sun is beyond controversy the largest of all; likewise, Jupiter and Saturn are larger than all others, unless you except certain principal fixed stars. Although, greater power is not necessarily <margin>Third.</margin> understood from the vastness of the bodies. For it is not proven that Jupiter is more powerful than Saturn just because he is larger; and although Mercury is the smallest of all the heavenly bodies, he nevertheless possesses (as they themselves wish) the most power in every birth chart. Nor do they place Venus before the Moon, even though she is exceeded by the Moon in the <margin>Fourth.</margin> vastness of her body. Finally, that bright star located at the Heart of the Lion <note>The star Regulus.</note>, which is called "The Little Queen" by the Latins and *Basiliscus* <note>Original: *basiliscus*, meaning "little king" in Greek.</note> by the Greeks: although it is not of the first magnitude, it is nonetheless judged by them to be of the first authority and power. They certainly make it more noble because it does not deflect from the path of the Sun; by the same reasoning, the planets would be more noble than the stars because they decline less from that same path in either direction. There is also the <margin>Fifth.</margin> testimony of antiquity, which calls the planets *cosmocratoras* <note>Original: *cosmocratoras*, from the Greek for "world-rulers."</note>, as if you were to say "rulers of the world"—a title they did not deign to give the fixed stars. But if only they would at least maintain their dogma! Instead, they frequently speak of these same planets (whom they make the creators of miraculous works) as if they were weak and feeble. For they say the planets effect nothing unless they occupy the "angles" <note>Original: *cardines*, the four most powerful points in a horoscope (Ascendant, Midheaven, etc.).</note> or at least the beginnings of the "houses," or are joined to one of the two luminaries <note>The Sun or the Moon.</note>. And so, to those to whom they attributed so much above, they here detract so much from their virtue that the planets effect nothing by themselves unless they are supported by the vigor of their location or the help of a most powerful celestial body. For this they offer neither a cause nor any probable reason, but have perhaps fallen into error from a false understanding of some <margin>How astrologers have erred.</margin> ancient saying. For the ancients, as Maternus <note>Julius Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Latin astrological writer.</note> teaches, said regarding the signs of the zodiac that when they were found "naked" of stars, they had no efficacy, except for those occupying the four angles. This teaching, which was intended for the signs (as the mansions and inns of the stars), they transferred to the individual stars themselves. Or perhaps they craftily established this dogma so that if they had to explain the calculation of fate from *all* the stars, they would not be wretchedly tortured by an inextricably difficult task. Nor could they easily persuade the credulous that such a task could be mastered by a man. Otherwise, what is the reason for this opinion? Is it because they are in a more remote place? But how much closer to us is Saturn? Or what is so great a prerogative of an "angle" that in it <margin>The error is revealed by logic.</margin> the stars do not just act, but do admirable things, despite the vastness of the distance—yet as soon as they decline a little from it, or have not yet reached it, they do nothing at all? This is even when the eleventh place <note>The 11th house, associated with "Good Spirit."</note>, rising toward the heights of heaven, seems more powerful for action than the fourth place, located under the middle of the earth. But it is certainly as I was saying: labor deterred them, and they did not want the art to appear so difficult that it might easily be judged impossible. For as for the slowness of motion they usually cite, slowness provides no support; a star's ray is fixed all the more strongly and clings more constantly the longer the star itself lingers in the place from which it is sent. Furthermore, these things are self-contradictory: for the dogma concerning a slower star is that it gives

<column-break/>

late whatever it gives, but that what it has given endures and remains for a long time. Conversely, they decree concerning the non-erratic stars: they usually say that those with the slowest motion bring the greatest happiness, but they eventually conclude these with calamities. Therefore, their gifts do not stay long, just as they are not preserved for long. Thus, just as they are always far from the truth, they are everywhere in disagreement with themselves—though we do not even pursue all their contradictions. For someone might also ask them: why did they not consider the "aspects" <note>The angular relationships (like square or trine) between celestial bodies.</note> between the fixed stars, or between the fixed stars and the planets, just as they do among the planets themselves? Johannes Regiomontanus <note>Original: *Ioannes de Regio monte*. A famous 15th-century German mathematician and astronomer.</note>, noticing this, says that the aspects of the fixed stars might perhaps be more perfect than those of the planets, because they are not fleeting and momentary like the planets, but rather stable and perpetual. Other objections could be raised on these points, but let us run through the following matters.

### Chapter X. That astrologers are also deceived regarding the planets: and a repetition of what has been discussed so far.

How much they are deceived even regarding the planets themselves has been sufficiently demonstrated above. They think that the properties and powers of the planets (wherein they seem to err as they do with the fixed stars) are not only intensified or diminished, but actually become different and diverse from time to time based on the variety of their locations, the condition of the signs, their configurations, and the manifold relationship of all things among themselves. They also categorize them based on the various names of their motions: as "standing still," "proceeding," or "stepping backward" <note>Stationary, prograde, and retrograde motion.</note>. We have very clearly shown (unless I am mistaken) that these things are said far from all truth, far from reason, and far from the dignity and nature of celestial things. We also criticize that they prescribe a certain empire over different things and times for those planets and those twelve signs, ruling by turns—an administration passed down as if by hand through the right of succession. Clearly, they are not so much measuring celestial things as they are inventing lies about them based on human affairs. Furthermore, we have laughed at and—along with Plotinus <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote against the astrologers.</note> and his contemporaries—struck out the idea that <margin>Plotinus also contends against the astrologers.</margin> they command one to wait for the effect of some planet for as many years as it happened to be distant in degrees from some place in the sign. They devise a thousand false things like this, conceived with no foundation of science. Therefore, let us summarize this entire previous dispute: it seems indeed that astrologers say probable things when they say lower things are ruled by celestial ones, but they are soon caught as false, vain, and detestable. That is, they are neither pious nor philosophers when they believe, preach, and assert that particular evil things can be produced by universal causes, small things by great, reckless things by orderly, incorporeal things by corporeal, arbitrary things by necessary, artificial things by natural, and past things by present ones. Even if all these things were produced by the heaven, the astrologers assign no causes less "celestial" than their own: for they are silent about the powers of the true stars and constellations that are in the heaven, yet they accept many properties from things that are not real. Holding only a tiny part of the truth, they themselves add many fictional things such as we mentioned in the preceding book: places, houses, images, nodes, *antiscia* <note>Points on the zodiac equidistant from the solstice points.</note>, *dodecatemoria* <note>The division of each zodiac sign into twelve smaller "micro-signs."</note>—fictional, ineffective, imaginary things with no solidity of nature. If a wise man can place faith in these things as if they consisted of the true solidity of nature and therefore ruled us, then I confess I have not yet understood what it means to be wise.

<summary>Pico argues that astrologers inconsistently prioritize planets over fixed stars and use illogical criteria like physical size or "angles" to determine celestial power. He concludes by summarizing their systems as a collection of fictional constructs—like houses and nodes—that lack any basis in natural philosophy.</summary>

<meta>This page marks the beginning of Book VIII. Having previously challenged the logic of planetary influence in the preceding book, Pico now shifts his critique to the fundamental physical uncertainty of the heavens. He argues that if astrologers cannot even agree on the number of celestial bodies or spheres that exist, their entire system for determining "fate" is built on a foundation of guesswork.</meta>

<header>DISPUTATIONS</header>

# THE DISPUTATIONS OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA AGAINST ASTROLOGERS, THE EIGHTH BOOK BEGINS.

## Chapter One. That the number of celestial bodies, in whose power fate is decided according to astrologers, is uncertain.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'I' featuring floral and foliate motifs.</image-desc>

Among all the things that a man who professes the science of the stars ought to know, the matter we are about to discuss might be considered almost the easiest: namely, how to judge the fatal hour of any given event. But if astrologers have neither attained this knowledge, nor can they attain it, how can they hope for more difficult things? For how much more difficult and laborious an effort is it to have grasped the number of celestial bodies from which the force of fate reaches us, so that in describing a "fatal constellation," <note>A "fatal constellation" refers to the specific arrangement of stars at a person's birth believed to dictate their destiny.</note> nothing fabricated is admitted and nothing true or effective is omitted. Otherwise, this would be a useful and necessary thing for them to know, and yet we shall reveal in the disputations of this present book that it cannot be known. Thus, not only can they not predict the truth because they do not clearly see the movements and positions of the stars—and because they have by no means investigated all of them (as we shall argue in the following books)—but also because it is not yet clear to them which bodies these are whose positions must be inspected and whose properties must be investigated. They are so far from having achieved everything their profession promises that they do not even know which things are necessary for their own knowledge. For if they say we are deceived or that we hurl these charges out of malice, I shall challenge them with a divine voice and ask them to tell me something about the number of the stars. When I question them, I realize not only that the stars that *are* seen are not fully counted by them,

<margin>
Favorinus against the casters of birth-charts, Gellius.
</margin>
but it is not even certain whether there are other stars in heaven besides those we see, escaping both our senses and our reason. The philosopher Favorinus, in that elegant speech of his against the <term>genethliacs</term> <note>From the Greek *genethliakos*, those who cast birth charts based on the moment of birth.</note> found in Aulus Gellius, said he wondered how it could be clear to anyone as a precept that the planets (which Nigidius calls "wanderers") are no more numerous than the common people suppose. For it could be that there are other planets of equal power which men cannot see because of an excess of either brightness or distance.

<margin>
Alpetragius.
</margin>
Certainly, as Alpetragius <note>Al-Bitruji, a 12th-century Spanish-Arab astronomer who challenged the Ptolemaic system.</note>—a most wise man in celestial matters—says, it has not yet been discovered by any observation of the art to which body that particular motion most belongs. This is attested by the many and various movements of the celestial bodies devised by more recent thinkers, which were unknown to the ancients (as they themselves believe) and were finally discovered through long-lasting observation. By this example, it is made manifest that other movements, by their own slowness or obscurity or some other appearance, might still be hidden from mathematicians, which posterity will eventually come to know through even longer observations. I do not wish to speak of <term>epicycles and eccentrics</term> <note>Geometric models used to explain why planets appear to speed up, slow down, or move backward.</note> or the multitude of spheres serving the planets, which remains uncertain among all astronomers. Perhaps they will deny that the power to decide fate resides in these bodies. But concerning the spheres above the planets, how much ambiguity there is—and how much uncertainty is thereby cast upon this "divinatory" astrology—must not be passed over in silence. For some make the eighth sphere, which is illuminated by the fixed stars, the outermost; others have placed a ninth above it; others even a tenth.

<column-break/>

<margin>
The Egyptians and Chaldeans.
</margin>
The astronomers of the Egyptians and Chaldeans thought there was nothing above the eighth sphere; they were followed by Plato, Aristotle, Hipparchus, and Ptolemy. Perhaps the more recent writers did not think so, but that is how the matter stands. There is no ninth sphere in Ptolemy, which can easily be understood from his *Great Composition* <note>Original: *Magna Compositione*, better known by its Arabic title, the *Almagest*.</note>. Many, however, are deceived because they think that everyone who has discovered that the eighth sphere moves from west to east must necessarily fall into the opinion of a ninth sphere. Therefore, since both Ptolemy and Hipparchus admit this, they do not doubt that the invention of a ninth sphere belonged to those who first noted that motion.

<margin>
Their reason.
</margin>
It is added that Ptolemy uses both movable and immovable signs, since he makes the constellations of the eighth sphere movable and says the planets are located according to immovable signs.

<margin>
Another [point].
</margin>
Therefore, it seems certain and beyond doubt to them that, besides the signs of the eighth sphere which move, there are other signs in Ptolemy which do not move except by the motion of the whole world, and these are imagined to be nowhere else but in a ninth sphere above the eighth.

<margin>
Where Ptolemy has the immovable signs.
</margin>
But they are very much mistaken. For the motion of the stars from west to east does not necessarily lead to the conclusion of a ninth sphere. And as for what he proposes regarding immovable signs, it is most clearly declared that Ptolemy was content with the eighth sphere alone. I wonder that this was not noticed and understood by them! For Ptolemy describes these immovable signs in the eighth sphere itself, which he would not do if he had devised another higher one. His words in the second book of the *Great Composition* are these: <note>original: "Abutemur autem signorum nominibus..."</note> *We shall use the names of the signs for the twelve parts of the oblique circle themselves; and as if their beginnings were taken from the tropical and equinoctial points: thus we shall call the "dodecathemorion"—that is, the twelfth part—which is from the vernal equinox toward the following parts of the whole sphere, "Aries"; the second "Taurus," and so on according to the order of the twelve signs handed down by us.* So says Ptolemy, who also teaches the same in the first book of the *Apotelefmaton* <note>Better known as the *Tetrabiblos*, Ptolemy's work on the effects of the stars.</note>: that the parts of the zodiac to which the planets are referred begin and are determined by the solstices and equinoxes as principles. Since these four points are fixed and unmoved, the partition of the signs established by them is also fixed and immovable, even though the constellations from which those names were transferred move continually, and in the course of time their ends and beginnings are found in various places. Therefore, these immovable signs in Ptolemy are not in a higher sphere, but are described from four fixed and immovable points of the eighth sphere; if he had imagined another above it, he would never have remained silent about this great discovery in his *Great Composition*.

<margin>
John of Saxony.
</margin>
I am inclined to mock John of Saxony <note>A 14th-century astronomer known for his commentaries on the Alfonsine Tables and Alchabitius.</note>, who in his expositions on Alchabitius <note>An 10th-century Arab astrologer.</note> tries to prove that one must use the signs of the ninth sphere according to the opinion of Ptolemy.

<margin>
From the first part of the second [book].
</margin>
In confirmation of his opinion, he brings forward certain words of Haly, the interpreter of Ptolemy, concerning "bright and dark degrees," which he thought were the words of Ptolemy himself, not Haly. However, they are the words of the commentator, not the author, which anyone can easily understand not only from the Greek copies but even from the common translation. See what faith can be placed in these men regarding celestial things, when they are caught examining their own authors with such sleepy and half-blind eyes.
