<meta>This page continues Pico's critique of the physical structure of the heavens as understood by astrologers. He focuses on the debate between the "ancients" (who followed Ptolemy's eight-sphere model) and the "moderns" (who introduced a ninth and even a tenth sphere). Pico uses this lack of consensus to argue that the entire foundation of astrology is unstable.</meta>

<header>AGAINST ASTROLOGERS, BOOK VIII.</header>

<margin>The reason by which the modern scholars were moved.</margin>
Consider that not only Ptolemy, but no one who followed him for more than a thousand years, found a use for a ninth sphere. Alphonso <note>Alfonso X of Castile, who sponsored the Alfonsine Tables in the 13th century.</note> was the first to calculate the positions of the planets relative to a ninth sphere, and all the modern scholars have adhered to him. The ancients used only eight spheres. Even Leo the Hebrew <note>Also known as Gersonides, a prominent 14th-century Jewish polymath.</note> and Proclus the Platonist—both most excellent mathematicians—contend that the eighth is the highest of all. From this opinion, the moderns differ, asserting by a far from empty conjecture that there is another sphere higher than the eighth. They argue that two motions toward diametrically opposite parts cannot exist within the same body by its own nature. Therefore, since it has been discovered by true observation that the "erratic stars" <note>The planets.</note> move from the west to the east, and yet that sphere along with the rest revolves from the east to the west, they think it must follow that the former motion (which is completed in a single cycle over many thousands of years) follows the proper nature of the sphere of the stars. The other motion, however—which is completed in the space of a single day—is communicated to the eighth sphere from another and therefore higher globe, just as it is to the planets. This higher globe sweeps everything with it from east to west, even the stars which are carried by their own proper motions from west to east.

<margin>Various solutions.</margin>
This suspicion was not born of nothing, yet it is refuted by others in many ways. For there are those who deny that the stars move from west to east; though there are certainly both observant men and mathematicians who say that the diurnal motion of the ether is a single motion, not divided into spheres but continuous. They claim that all the stars, both fixed and wandering, are carried by their own motions from west to sunrise.

<margin>
First.
Second.
Leo the Hebrew.
Third.
Fourth.
</margin>
Leo the Hebrew attributes that motion to a certain inferior sphere, not a superior one. Others, viewing the whole heaven as a kind of living animal—constituting the various spheres as if they were limbs—say there is a different mode: one motion belongs to the whole heaven from a certain "universal motor," and other motions belong to individual spheres according to their diversity, owed to their own distinct motors. Therefore, that motion which we call "diurnal," since it is common to the other spheres, belongs no more to the eighth than to any other; rather, it exists from a common motor of the celestial universe. For this reason, one need not fabricate another sphere to which that motion is proper, nor does it follow that the same sphere has two proper motions, since one arises from what is common with the rest of the parts of heaven, and the other from its own nature, granted by a different motor. Let us place all these arguments in the middle, affirming only this: nothing certain or beyond doubt can be asserted regarding these things. The entire dispute returns to "probable arguments" <note>original: "probabiles locos," referring to dialectical arguments that are plausible but not demonstrably certain.</note> and interpretations which, being many and ambiguous on both sides, leave us at last in uncertainty. But if we think we must concede to the reasoning by which a new sphere is confirmed, then we must also agree with those who devise a tenth above the ninth; the logic for both dogmas is nearly the same. For those men, in order to stubbornly defend the idea that more than one motion does not suit a single sphere by itself, introduced a ninth; then, having detected a double motion there, they were led by the same conjecture to introduce a tenth.

<margin>
Alphonso.
Campanus.
Leopold.
Messahala.
</margin>
This is what Alphonso, Campanus, Leopold, and Messahala <note>A group of influential medieval astronomers and astrologers from various traditions.</note> believed; they also refer this opinion—though falsely, as did Albert <note>Likely Albertus Magnus.</note> who followed them—to Ptolemy.

### *Chapter II. If there is another sphere above the eighth, ancient astrology is false; if there is none, modern astrology is false; and even if there is a new one, it must necessarily collapse.*

From this so varied and manifold variety of opinions, it is easy to see how uncertain the "divining" astrology

<column-break/>

<margin>All ancient astrology collapses if there are two spheres.</margin>
becomes. For if there are two other spheres above the eighth, all the astrology of the ancients is false, for they relied on useless and imperfect observations while being ignorant of the most powerful parts of heaven. Those higher spheres cannot be ineffective, since the highest excels the rest in the rapidity of its motion, and both excel in the sublimity of their location and the vastness of their mass. If, on the other hand, there is no sphere beyond the eighth, then all the astrology of the moderns is also nothing, for it describes the twelve signs in the ninth sphere. If that sphere does not exist, what authority will it have in decreeing fate? <note>original: "in fato decernendo"</note> Yet, whether there is some ninth sphere or none at all, all the astrology of our age is known to waver; it speaks not only with inconstancy, but with controversy and conflict. For let them answer me this: do they think that influences reach us from the whole heaven, or only from those parts which flash with visible light? First, if they concede the former, then not only the planets but the very spheres that carry the planets will be received into participation of the "fatal decree"; <note>The "fatal decree" refers to the astrological determination of a person's destiny.</note> yet astrologers do not observe the spheres in this way, acting as if they have no power to change things below. On the other hand, if they answer that such power exists only in the stars shining with a ray of visible light, then they must also concede that no "outflowings" <note>original: "defluxus," referring to celestial influence or emanation.</note> from the ninth sphere reach here. That sphere is either endowed with no light or invisible light, and is distinguished neither by stellar rays nor by any variety of lights; it is either entirely transparent—whence it is called the "aqueous and crystalline heaven"—or it is diffused with a thin and rare light, such as many believe can and does exist in the other globes.

<margin>Bonatus.</margin>
Therefore, either every sphere must be observed, or that ninth sphere, even if it exists, must be disregarded—which is what Bonatus <note>Guido Bonatti, the most famous astrologer of the 13th century.</note> believed, affirming that nothing placed above the eighth sphere pertains to the astrologer. And yet, the twelve signs are described by everyone as being in that ninth sphere; these signs have not just some, but the greatest authority in the constellation of the year—not only for what they grant by their own powers, but because the primary role in changing the powers of the planets is assigned to them by everyone. Thus, whichever way they turn, they fall into inextricable snares: they either omit many spheres that should not be omitted, or, by admitting one that is ineffective, they adulterate the truth of every constellation. Even if they could somehow extricate themselves from this, they would be held by an unresolvable bond: even if we granted as much power and efficacy to the ninth sphere as you wish, and raised no further dispute about the other spheres, the predictions of all the moderns would be proven utterly false. It cannot be denied that the power and property of that sphere must be different from the influences of the eighth; yet they, treating them as if they were the same, have handed down nothing regarding the signs of the ninth that was not handed down regarding the signs of the eighth by the ancients. This was surely a matter of great dullness or malice—either they did not see that the nature of different spheres cannot be the same, or seeing this, they nevertheless wished to persuade others of it. For it appears likely enough that they managed to deceive others. Once the ninth sphere was devised, if they had to deal with the influence of a different world, their profession would have had to cease for many ages while the nature of that newly discovered world was being proven by many experiments. These swindlers and ambitious men could by no means allow this. Therefore, they transferred to the parts of the ninth sphere the same names that the ancients called the parts of the eighth, as if nature itself were communicated along with the name. They said exactly the same things about them as the earlier writers said of the eighth.

<summary>Pico argues that astrologers cannot agree on the basic physical structure of the heavens, specifically whether there are eight, nine, or ten spheres. He points out that if the "modern" ninth sphere exists, ancient astrology is void, but if it is invisible and characterless, it cannot logically exert the astrological influence moderns claim it does.</summary>

<header>DISPUTATIONS</header>

<margin>The difference between the ninth and eighth spheres is no less than the difference between Jupiter and Saturn.</margin>
They have put forth these dogmas. Thus, they describe Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, and the rest of the signs as being in the ninth sphere, and they claim these signs perform the same functions that the ancients wrote were performed by signs of the same name, but in a different sphere. Clearly, they are defending a total imposture based solely on a shared set of names. If they do this to deceive, it is a crime; if they are themselves deceived, it is madness. For they err no differently than if they were to transfer the name of Jupiter to Saturn, believe that Saturn had become Jupiter, and then, when a prophecy concerning Saturn was required, they pronounced those things which the ancients taught that Jupiter portends. For the difference between the eighth and ninth orb should be considered no less than that between Jupiter and Saturn, if we evaluate the quality of their motion and light, by which celestial bodies are primarily distinguished. For between those two planets, the only apparent differences are that one is slower than the other, and that the light of one is either darker or brighter than the light of the other. But how much greater is the distance between those orbs, where one is moved by its own nature with the slowest motion, while the other is carried by the most rapid motion of all? The former is radiant and conspicuous with a manifold army of stars; the latter, possessing either no light or an invisible light, does not fall under our gaze or eyes. Finally, if they say that parts of the same sphere—and even tiny fractions of them—have vastly different effects, how can the effect of two different spheres be the same? And if two spheres have the same nature, did God, the architect of nature, not create the second one in vain? And if, as I have said, they do not agree in motion, light, position, or mass, what other communion of nature is there for them? Let the machine of the universe be looked upon from every side: in all the globes of the elements or the heavens, a manifest diversity will always appear. Therefore, if there is a ninth orb (beyond the others they have devised), it is necessarily of a different nature from the eighth. Thus, the rules that Ptolemy and other more ancient writers laid down concerning the signs and parts of the eighth orb cannot be ascribed or applied to the signs of the ninth sphere. Since all the moderns do this nonetheless, their prophecies—even if they claim to practice a true art—can only strike upon the truth by mere chance.

### Chapter III. That the constellations differ from the signs, although they agree in name.

In truth, whatever is decided about the number of spheres, we shall briefly demonstrate that the twelve signs themselves—to which both the ancients and the moderns attributed so much that the sum and pivot of the entire astrological prediction turns upon them—are fictions and non-existent. Furthermore, even if they were real, the astrologers have passed down false and conflicting dogmas about them; therefore, those divinations which depend on them (and all of them do) are utterly deceptive. But the reader must first be warned that the twelve signs are one thing, and the images <note>constellations</note> are another, although they agree in number and name. I say these are entirely different things, even among those who, either ignoring or neglecting the ninth sphere, make the division of signs in the same place where the forms of the images are imagined. For the signs are established as unmoved and fixed, bounded by the equinoxes and solstices, so that the beginnings of the sign of Aries are always taken from the vernal equinox. The image <note>the actual group of stars</note> of Aries, however, has its beginnings calculated in different places at different times, just as the stars from which it is formed are continually moved from west to east. In this matter, a great part of the astrologers have slipped, thinking that those who refer the planets to the eighth sphere must necessarily use moving signs. For they have not understood the words of Ptolemy in the first book

<column-break/>

of the *Apotelesmatika* <note>original: "apotelef." — referring to Ptolemy's *Tetrabiblos*</note>, who teaches the opposite. His words in Latin are as follows: "Let us not overlook this, which is worthy of note: that it is reasonable to make the beginnings of the borders or terms of the *dodecatemoria* (that is, the twelve signs) from the tropical and equinoctial points. This is what the writers have most clearly indicated. From those things we said above, it is clear that their natures, powers, and relationships have their cause in the tropical and equinoctial principles, and not from any other source. Therefore, if we establish other principles, we shall either be forced not to use their natures in predictions, or by using them, we shall fall away from the truth, having omitted and changed the intervals of the zodiac from which their powers proceed." These are the words of Ptolemy, whose opinion had to be revealed before it was refuted, since it has been poorly understood or noticed by so many.

<margin>The second difference.</margin>
The first difference between images and signs is therefore clear: the former move, while the latter do not. Even if they are described in the eighth sphere, there is another very evident difference: images have unequal magnitudes, while signs are equal to one another. For each of the signs contains thirty degrees, whereas some images stretch through fewer spaces and others through more.

<margin>That there is no difference of signs, etc.</margin>
Since, therefore, signs are one thing and images are another, we shall refute both by their own logic. First, we shall ask regarding the signs what logic demonstrated to them that there are twelve natures there, distinct in power and properties—no more and no fewer. Abraham ibn Ezra <note>original: "Abraam auenazra"</note>, at the beginning of his book of *Astrological Reasons*, says that some things said about the signs are proven, while others are established by arbitrary choice. He immediately declares what those things are that are brought forward as arbitrary, mentioning the division of the zodiac. He asks why the divisions of the signs are only into three hundred and sixty parts: "Because this number is more convenient for divisions." Haly Abenrodan <note>original: "Haly Auenrodan"</note> also writes this when explaining the *Apotelesmatika* of Ptolemy: "We divided the circle into twelve parts which are called signs, and each of the signs into thirty parts called degrees, and each thirtieth part into sixty minutes, because these numbers are found to be more suitable for divisions." By what better means, then, should we refute them than by their own words? They are ignorant of the nature of things and the consequence of reason. Since those who measure the motions of the stars divided the circle into twelve parts for the convenience of the number for dividing, the astrologers then established a dogma that those twelve parts have diverse powers and properties—as if their distinction arose not from the arbitrary choice of mathematicians, but from the nature of heaven. It happens that if they are described in the eighth sphere—as Ptolemy, the Egyptians, and all the masters of the signs intended—no physical reality or natural solidity corresponds to them; they can only be thought of and conceived in the mind.

<margin>Origen.</margin>
For this reason, Origen, imbued with the doctrine of the Egyptians, called those signs "intelligible" and perceptible by reason alone. For there is no part of the eighth sphere where either an equinox or a solstice always occurs; rather, it occurs in one part after another, if that sphere is carried by its own motion from west to east as they believe.

<margin>The uncertainty of the art.</margin>
Therefore, the points in which we understand the equinox or solstice to always occur depend in reality on nothing but our own thought. These points can certainly serve mathematicians for finding motions and calculating the positions of planets, but they cannot be established as the origins of virtues or the principles of any influence. Perhaps the Chaldeans, considering this, [gave influence] to the images alone, and not also...

<meta>The text cuts off mid-sentence with the catchword "etiam" (also), preparing for the next page's discussion on the Chaldean perspective.</meta>

<summary>Pico argues that the mathematical divisions of the zodiac (the signs) are arbitrary conventions created for the convenience of calculation rather than physical realities with natural powers. He highlights the confusion between fixed mathematical signs and moving stellar constellations, asserting that astrological predictions are based on fictional structures.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s systematic dismantling of astrological theory. Having previously argued that shifting from an eight-sphere to a nine-sphere model makes traditional astrological "influences" logically impossible, he now focuses on the confusion between mathematical "signs" of the zodiac and the physical "images" or constellations of stars.</meta>

-> ### NINTH DISPUTATION ### <-

Are the signs mobile, or do they move along with the images? If they answer that they are mobile, then they are already moved away from their own markers. After all, initiating summer, autumn, winter, and spring is a property of immobile signs, not mobile ones. The very qualities they assign to the signs—that they are mobile, fixed, or double <note>In astrology, "double" or "mutable" signs like Gemini or Pisces mark the transition between seasons.</note>—are derived from the aforementioned variation of the seasons. Therefore, these qualities cannot belong to any signs other than those which are conceived as forever unmoved in those specific locations on the circle. 

But if they say the signs are immobile, it follows that they do not coincide with the location of the images; for the images, along with their stars, have repeatedly changed their positions. If this is the case, how can properties derived solely from the *shape* of the images be attributed to these other "signs"? For instance, they call *Aries* <note>The Ram</note> a "mobile" and "equinoctial" sign of "short duration"—all of which are conditions of an immobile sign. Yet, in the same breath, they call it a "four-footed animal," "lustful," and "weak-eyed"—traits that belong to the image of the animal, not the mathematical sign. They use the same name, even though the nature, location, and properties are entirely different.

And so I do not need to follow every detail. The entire crowd of astrologers divides the signs, saying some are "common," some "fixed," and others "mobile"; again, some are "straight" and others "oblique." These, as I have said, are conditions of immobile signs. Likewise, they use these distinctions: some are "human," some "wild," some "aquatic," others "earthy"; some are "mute," others "vocal," some "sterile," others "fertile." All of these belong to the *images*, not the mathematical signs, because they do not follow any position on the circle, but rather the nature, form, and likeness of the constellation's image. 

<margin>See this exclamation!</margin> What is this great sluggishness or sleepiness? Do they not see that they are mixing diverse things and confusing them, deceived only by a shared name and not by the nature of the things themselves? For even the idea that one sign is "hot," another "earthy," another "airy," and another "watery" was taken from the images and transferred with the same recklessness to the signs. If the state of the circle is considered from immobile points, Aries should be judged as "airy"—that is, hot and moist—rather than "fiery" (hot and dry), since spring opens with a hot and moist quality. 

Furthermore, **Ptolemy**, <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century foundational authority for astronomers and astrologers.</note> giving the reason why we usually begin the year at Aries in a circle that has no real beginning, answers that in the first age of all things, moisture abounds, which is the quality of the spring that we begin from *Aries*. So then, O **Ptolemy**, if the first sign is *Aries* because moisture is owed to the "first age," do you think it is a dry sign or a moist one? If it is dry, then it is not the first; if it is moist, why is it called "fiery" by your people? 

Finally (which is what I wanted to prove), these differences of cold, dry, hot, and moist distributed among the signs seem to be taken from the condition of the images rather than the signs. <margin>Ibn Ezra.</margin> Even **Ibn Ezra** <note>Abraham ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167), a celebrated Jewish scholar and astrologer.</note> confesses this in his *Book of Astrological Reasons*. For they established *Cancer*, *Scorpio*, and *Pisces* as "cold" after considering the nature of the animals whose names they bear. They called *Aries*, *Leo*, and *Sagittarius* "hot" for the same reason. They called *Gemini* and *Aquarius* "airy" because of their human likeness, as that quality is most dominant in humans. Thus, they made *Taurus*, *Capricorn*, and *Virgo* "earthy," both by the power of their sex and by reason of the ear of grain <note>The star Spica.</note> that the Virgin carries in her hand. 

They have therefore attributed to the signs a power taken from the diverse properties of the images. In this matter, the good **Ptolemy** is not just nodding off, but is utterly exhausted, shifting himself from the sign to the image within the same context. I shall demonstrate this clearly, along with the unpardonable error of **Haly** <note>Ali ibn Ridwan, an 11th-century Arabic commentator on Ptolemy.</note> in explaining **Ptolemy’s** words. His words in the second book of the *Apotelesmaton* <note>Ptolemy’s *Tetrabiblos*.</note> are these: the <term>dodecathemorion</term> <note>From the Greek meaning "twelfth-part"—referring to one of the twelve 30-degree signs of the zodiac.</note> of *Aries*

<column-break/>

is generally "thunderous and hail-producing" <note>original Greek: "brontodes kai chalazodes"</note>... more specifically according to the property of the stars that are in it and below it. <note>Pico is quoting a corrupted or specific Latin translation of Ptolemy's Greek.</note> That is to say: "These things happen more or less in detail according to the nature and property of the stars which are in it." And he adds: "for its preceding parts cause rain and wind; the middle parts cause a tempering of the air; and the final parts cause heat and pestilence. Then, those parts which turn toward the north cause heat and corruption, while those toward the south are icy and somewhat cold." 

I take these words of **Ptolemy** as follows: what he pronounces about Aries in general refers there to the immobile sign. This cannot be denied, since that is where the equinox occurs, and for that reason, **Ptolemy** said it was "thunderous and hail-producing," because all these things usually stir up before the springtime. However, as for what he adds subsequently regarding the different effects of its parts according to the nature of the stars existing therein: **Haly** believes this is also said about the parts of the *sign*, as I shall soon show. But I will demonstrate that it is clearer than daylight from **Ptolemy** himself that this was said about the *image* (constellation). As great as **Ptolemy** was in establishing doctrine, **Haly** was just as great in erring while explaining him. 

**Haly** thinks **Ptolemy's** words should be taken to mean that the stars he says are in those parts were in those parts of the *sign* he is talking about at the time he was writing. He thinks that property belonged to the sign then, but as the stars move to another place over time, the property is transferred elsewhere. This interpretation of **Haly's** would appear plausible if **Ptolemy** had done in other signs what he does in *Aries*, and had provided no names for the stars he places in those parts. But when he explains certain stars by name in *Taurus*, he manifests both his own error and that of his interpreter; for those stars, in **Ptolemy's** time, were not in the part of the *sign* in which he arranges them, but rather in the part of the *image*—where, of course, they were and will be. 

His words concerning *Taurus* are these: "The sign of *Taurus* generally brings both qualities of air, but it is somewhat warm. Specifically, its preceding parts, especially where the **Pleiades** are, stir up earthquakes, winds, and clouds; the following parts, where the **Hyades** are, produce lightning and thunderbolts." 

<margin>Ptolemy, Hyades, Vergil.</margin> Now then, who does not see that these things are said by **Ptolemy** about the *image*? In its preceding parts are the **Pleiades**, which our people call the *Vergiliae*; in the following parts are the **Hyades**, for which the common translation reads "Aldebaran." For although the **Hyades** are in the forehead, horns, and the whole head, and the **Pleiades** are between the end of its body and the tail of *Aries* (the place they call the "severing"), the former occupy the "following" parts and the latter the "preceding" parts, because *Taurus* sets and rises backward. 

But truly, if these things are referred to the *signs*, there will be no truth in his words, since in **Ptolemy's** time the **Pleiades** were not in the *sign* of Taurus, but in Aries—as is easy to recognize from his *Great Composition* <note>The *Almagest*.</note>. Since **Haly** ought to have read this, and did not doubt that the same man was the author of both works, I cannot marvel enough that he hallucinated in such an obvious matter. He explained **Ptolemy’s** words as being about the locations of stars in the signs, and left it written that the **Pleiades** were in the first parts of *Taurus* during that time. This error was followed by **Haly**, **Leopold**, <note>Leopold of Austria, a 13th-century astronomer.</note> and **Ascandensis** <note>John of Eschenden, author of the 14th-century *Summa Anglicana*.</note> in the "English Summary" as they call it, and finally by later men like **Bonatus**. <note>Guido Bonatti, the most famous astrologer of the 13th century.</note> But their greater error is that they follow **Haly** in saying **Ptolemy** spoke...

speaking about the stars positioned in those parts: and yet they do not change. But they say the same thing as Ptolemy, even though since his time the stars have shifted by more than twenty degrees. It is therefore evident what we intended to prove: that astrologers imprudently contradict themselves by mixing the properties of signs and images (if they have any at all) as if they did not differ in location, nature, and parts.

### Chapter V. The images of the Chaldeans <note>The "Chaldeans" was a common Renaissance term for ancient Babylonian astrologers.</note> are mere fictions; what led them to invent them; and how the error of these artificial images gave rise to many others.

Truly, even if we grant that the signs have no power, are the images themselves anything at all? For perhaps here the astrologers will not seem to rave; perhaps they do not lean upon fabricated and arbitrary things when they claim that those images—composed of their own lights, stars, and rays—possess great power according to the nature of the stars. I, however, have no doubt that the astrologers are raving here as well. For even if the stars from which the images are fashioned are both real and natural, the very construction of images from those stars is neither real nor natural. Rather, it is false, entirely imaginary according to the whim of the creators, and lacks any trace of probability. For who would not immediately judge that if the power of one star is great, the power of many stars conspiring together in one should be greatest of all? But when reason returns to itself, it sees that there is no "conspiracy" of stars there except the one we have imagined. For there is certainly no physical merging or growing together there; how then do many stars, distinct in nature and separated by the immense vastness of great distances, combine into a single property? I know what they will answer: that they meet in the likeness of a single image, which is evidence of some hidden affinity. Just as a figure is drawn from a single species, they say, so a single natural property of that same thing exists in them all. Now, this might be something—even if it did not achieve what they want—if those images appeared there as perfectly expressed and distinct signs. But since they are fashioned according to our own whim (as I shall show), and it is just as easy for anyone to form tigers and elephants for himself as it is to see dogs and hares (as they prefer), it is clear that the argument taken from the figure is, like the rest of the astrologers' claims, vain, arbitrary, and mythical. 

If they contend that those figures exist there not by the whim of the observers but by nature, I will appeal not so much to the evidence of experience as to the reasons and testimonies of the astrologers themselves. For Abraham <margin>Avenazra wrote two books on the methods used by astrologers.</margin> Avenazra, <note>Abraham ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167), a celebrated Jewish scholar and astrologer.</note> a man of great authority among them, in his second edition on astrological methods (for he wrote two books on the same subject), gave this explanation for these images. He writes in these words:

"What we have translated into Latin according to the sense, Ptolemy calls the 'falling vulture' and others the 'lyre.' Nor is it a surprise, since just as anyone can change the shape for himself, so can he change the name. For the heaven is spherical, and therefore there is no reason why you should establish the beginning of anything in one place rather than another. But just as different stars are joined together according to the judgment of the eyes, so different images are made. We, therefore, shall describe them in the manner they have been handed down." Thus he spoke. He could not confirm my opinion more truly or effectively. For if there is no beginning or end in the parts of a circle, you can begin an image from whatever 

<column-break/>

star you prefer, and end it at whichever you wish. There is no doubt that, depending on the diversity of the starting and ending points you prescribe for yourself, and the number of stars you either include or exclude, you will fashion various images from them. This is especially true since different people represent different forms to themselves from these same stars, as Abraham declared regarding the vulture and the lyre, and as he could likewise declare for others. 

Indeed, they did not even agree on the number of the most famous images of the zodiac. While <margin>Different people fashioned different images for themselves in the same place.</margin> others counted twelve, the Chaldeans made them eleven, making one out of Libra and Scorpio. For what forbids it, since in this celestial painting, the same power of hearing <note>Likely a reference to interpreting or "reading" the sky.</note> is granted to everyone? Even Albumasar <margin>Albumasar.</margin> himself—who professes that he will provide the reasons for the dogmas of astrology in all things—when he comes to the images, brings no other reason than that Aratus <margin>Aratus.</margin> described them so. <note>Aratus (c. 310–240 BCE), a Greek poet whose work *Phaenomena* described the constellations.</note> As if Aratus were not the most mythical of writers! As Cicero says, Aratus wrote about astrology while being utterly ignorant of astrology. If you compare the <margin>The Hebrew alphabet-sphere depicted in the sky.</margin> sphere of Aratus with the "barbaric" sphere, <note>The "Barbaric Sphere" refers to non-Greek (Egyptian, Persian, or Indian) astronomical traditions.</note> you will see that they mostly disagree and clash with one another. 

Since these images are clearly fashioned by whim and rest on no solidity of doctrine or reason, the masters of the Hebrews try to find their own "alphabet" in the stars—that is, the characters and elements of their own language—just as the astrologers find their images. If they find credulous eyes, they can persuade people of this with no less probability than the astrologers do with their images. Why say more? Where all forms and all likenesses are possible, there are actually no forms and no likenesses; all exist by the power and will of men, while in nature and truth, none exist. 

If only our little diviners had fashioned there some likenesses of venerable and sublime things! I might then be more easily led to believe they were the works of God rather than human inventions against nature. But when I consider His counsel and wisdom, I do not see why that temple of divinity, those courts of heaven, could not or would not be adorned with better images than those of irrational animals, monsters, or even lifeless things. For what is there besides bears, dragons, hares, and dogs? And things that are empty, like arrows, ships, and triangles? Add to this the severed heads of myths, and a virgin banished to punishment—not to mention the hydra and the centaur. <margin>Observe this excellent madness.</margin> If nature does not allow such things, yet they have described the archetypes of them in heaven! Indeed, I think it is a madness beyond all others to be led to believe that these were formed there by the design of nature and divine counsel. A good priest or a high-minded king would be ashamed not to have better paintings in his temple or palace. 

Otherwise, what was the purpose of nature in establishing these? Was it so that through these "superior" images, she might govern "inferior" bodies of the same kind? That through the celestial Lyre she might breathe musical melody into whichever men she chose? That through the animals there, those which are among us—being born and perishing daily—might be generated and preserved? And are monsters appropriate there, which exist nowhere in nature? Why are countless animals not described there? For what special privilege do dogs and bears have, that they should have two leaders or overseers in heaven, while elephants, tigers, and innumerable species of animals have no divinity in heaven by which they may be ruled? But I have said too much of these things; to a philosopher, it is not only shameful to believe them, but even undignified to refute them. If anyone asks me why, in this license of invention, the supporters of astrology turned to these images rather than others, I will reply that he asks a question based on reason...

For I think the names of the images <note>In this context, "images" refers to the constellations of the zodiac.</note> which are ascribed to the parts of the zodiac are derived from the works of the sun, which primarily occur when it is found in those parts. For example, that part of the zodiac-bearing circle <note>original: "signiferi"</note> in which the sun is located when it begins to move backward, in the manner of a crab, received the name **Cancer**. The next part is **Leo**, because of the excess of immoderate heat. Similarly, another part is called **Taurus** because when the sun reaches it, the earth is plowed by oxen <note>original: "bobus"</note>. **Gemini** follows, because then, by doubling all things, they are doubled <note>original: "geminando omnia geminantur"; Pico is playing on the Latin root for 'twins' and 'doubling,' referring to the peak of the growing season.</note>. Under **Virgo**, the earth, scorched by the sun's heat, produces nothing. Under **Aries**, the fields are clothed in a fleece of flowers, for which reason they placed that animal in charge of it, also because of the similarity to a head of hair <note>original: "capitā... de capilamenti similitudine"</note>. **Libra** equals out the nights and days, as if they were weighed against each other in a balance. When the sun reaches **Scorpio**, then for the first time the air stings with cold; soon, under **Sagittarius**, it provokes us with the stings of more vehement cold and winds. In **Capricorn**, the reason is manifest: for from that point the sun begins to ascend again like a goat. In **Aquarius** and **Pisces**, it pours forth rains and fish in abundance. Driven by similarities of this kind, they were able to manufacture these images rather than others in various parts of the sky, easily drawing the stars into the shape of that nature whose name they intended to impose on that part for some reason. To this were added the fictions of the poets, who invent many things for pleasure or favor; just as

What Conon the Egyptian saw.

Conon the Egyptian, the mathematician, was the first to see monsters and the lock of hair from the head of Berenice <note>Conon of Samos famously "discovered" the constellation Coma Berenices (Berenice's Hair) to flatter the Egyptian Queen Berenice II.</note>. Thus, let me finally define these inventions correctly: they arose from corrupt philosophy and the fables of poets. Yet all astrologers attribute so much to them, as if they were the truest things and formed (if I may say so) by the very finger of God, that it is scarcely credible into what superstitions this madness has led them. "Do not give a remedy," <note>original: "pharmacun"</note> they say, "when the Moon is located in Taurus, because that animal ruminates; therefore it will cause the medicine to be vomited back up." "When you build a house, beware lest Scorpio occupy the fourth place, because scorpions will abound in that house." He who is procreated when the Crown <note>The constellation Corona Borealis.</note> is rising will be a king; he who is born under the Lyre <note>The constellation Lyra.</note> will be a musician; and a thousand other things of this kind, from which you can see they are most convinced that the true likenesses and natures of all these things exist in the sky, from which powers flow down to us to determine our fate in a wonderful way. Finally, that entire superstition of manufacturing talismans <note>original: "fabricandarum imaginum," referring to astrological "images" or seals engraved on metal.</note> sprouted from this madness: so that, with a similar image formed in some metal, they think the virtue from the celestial image is breathed into the metal. Yet these things are not in the sky, nor if they were would they descend from there because of that carved image; and even if they did descend, as Averroes <note>The 12th-century Andalusian philosopher.</note> proves against Algazel <note>The Persian theologian Al-Ghazali; Pico refers to their famous debate on the limits of philosophy and causality.</note>, they would be of no profit to us. But we shall discuss these things more extensively in a specific treatise later.

### Chapter VI.
> That the invisible images are known neither by sense nor reason, and that their authors—who were not Chaldeans or Indians, but only Arabs—disagree among themselves.

**A**nyone could certainly marvel at the madness of astrologers in manufacturing the most fabulous images which we have attacked thus far, unless they had dreamed up others far more ridiculous. For they report that in each and every decan <note>term: <term>decan</term> — A division of a zodiac sign into three parts of 10 degrees each, also called a "face."</note> or

<column-break/>

face of any sign there are certain images, which are indeed invisible, but consist most truly of the solidity of nature. Those who approach these descriptions cannot help but break into laughter. For they are of this kind: in the first face of Cancer, he says, there ascends a handsome youth, well-clothed, but having something of crookedness in his face and fingers, with the rest of his body like a horse and an elephant, with white feet, and hanging above himself various species of grain and leaves of trees. In the first face of Leo there ascends a tree with a very deep root, in whose branches sits a dog, and a man clothed in noble but dirty garments, weeping and sad about his parents. Other similar things are described by them in the other decans of the signs, all of which are mentioned as most effective things by
<margin>Aboafar</margin>
Abu Ma'shar <note>Abū Maʿshar, the influential 9th-century Persian astrologer known to the West as Albumasar.</note> in the sixth book of his *Great Introduction*.
<margin>Auenaz</margin>

<margin>Pietro d'Abano, Michael Scotus</margin>
Pietro d'Abano, Michael Scotus, and the Arab astrologers, and many among the Latins. When I heard something of these things long ago, I thought that through these images they were indicating what the decan of each sign produced; not that they thought there were actually figures there in the sky. But approaching their books, I recognized it was far otherwise. For they think and assert and contend that these images in those decans are most truly the producers of wonderful effects among us. Indeed, Abu Ma'shar says they sometimes produce things similar to their forms, but often other things entirely different. Certainly, if lynxes <note>Legendary for their keen sight.</note> had established this dogma, it would lead me in some way to doubt whether things had been open to their eyes which escape our gaze. But I find nothing that could build faith in these men who broadcast such admirable mysteries, since they have no other eyes than those men usually have, and men do not see these things. Nor do we read that they were snatched into heaven like the Apostle <note>A reference to St. Paul's vision of the third heaven.</note>; nor could any reason demonstrate these things to those located on earth. Let those who call themselves philosophers blush; yet they are not ashamed to write down these trifles which a storytelling old woman could scarcely persuade a two-year-old infant to believe. Add to this that they do not all imagine the same things, but some imagine one set of images and others imagine another. Here one says that in the first face of Aries a woman ascends resplendent with brightness and the tail of a sea fish. Another says there is no beautiful woman there, no fish, but an Ethiopian; though it is disputed whether his eyes are black or rather red, but who is certainly of tall stature and wears a white cloak. In the third face of Gemini, some say there arises a golden flute, a barking dog, and a dolphin. Others contend that none of these things are there, but a man seeking arms with which to clothe himself, protected by a shield and equipped with a quiver. In the third face of Scorpio, the Arabs say there is a horse and a hare. The Indians say neither a horse nor a hare, but a dog, a boar, and a leopard. Others say no beast, but a man curved on his knees—perhaps (if one may interpret the mysteries) praying to God on behalf of the astrologers, that He might at last free them from madness by restoring their minds. For what else are they but insane, who devote themselves to such fallacious and impossible trifles, and believe and support them? Seeing these things,
<margin>Abraham mocks them.</margin>

The Egyptians say nothing of them; nothing the Chaldeans; nothing the Greeks; nothing the ancient Latin writers of astrology. But this is a peculiar habit of the Arabs: whatever commentaries they invent themselves, they assign to them the names of illustrious authors, many of which we mentioned in the first book of these disputations. Therefore, although there are certain writings of Petosiris <note>An ancient Egyptian priest-astrologer often cited as a founding authority</note> still among the Egyptians, who was a master of astrology; and although there <margin>Ephestion.</margin> exist, besides Maternus, the works of Ephestion and the <margin>Thebanus.</margin> Theban commentator, and Paul of Alexandria—all of them interpreters of astrology—one can easily learn from them that there is no mention of those specific images in Egypt. The same is clear <margin>Tenyrus, Babylonian</margin> regarding the Chaldeans, on the authority of Tenyrus the Babylonian, who wrote on the *results of the decans* <note>original: "apotelesmata decanorum," referring to the 10-degree subdivisions of the zodiac</note> and the images that rise along with them. It is also clear from the testimony of Porphyry, who wrote astrological instructions according to the opinion of the Chaldeans—not to mention Manilius and Maternus, who in various ways pass down to us the dogma of the Chaldeans. Regarding the Greek authors, only those who have not read Greek can have any doubt, for nowhere in any Greek writer is there mention of those images. Thus, we ought to greatly accuse Haly <note>Ali ibn Ridwan, a medieval Arabic commentator on Ptolemy</note>, who ascribed this error to Ptolemy. For when, in the ninety-fifth aphorism of the book titled *The Fruit* <note>The Centiloquium, a collection of 100 astrological aphorisms attributed to Ptolemy</note>, Ptolemy says that the <term>symptomata <gloss>co-risings</gloss></term> <note>original Greek: "συμπτώματα"</note>—that is, the things that rise together with the individual decans of the signs—indicate the will of the newborn and what art they will practice, the commentator Haly thinks that those invisible images we have spoken of are meant by "co-rising images." He was ignorant of what the Greeks call <unclear>symptomata</unclear>, which means "co-risings." For among them, those thirty-six images outside the zodiac are called by this name, fifteen of which are to the south and twenty-one to the north. Ptolemy writes about their properties and nature in the first book of his *Judicial Astrology* <note>original: "apotelesmaton," referring to the Tetrabiblos</note>. Neither in that place nor anywhere else does he ever mention other images besides those fashioned from the visible stars, against which we argued in the previous chapter. He uses the same word in the following sentence when he says that the <unclear>symptomata</unclear> <gloss>co-risings</gloss> must be considered in the eclipses of the lights. He handles this same opinion in the second book of his *Judicial Astrology*, indicating what kind of things these "co-risings" are. When he says that the will and the craft of the newborn are indicated by them, he teaches what Manilius, Maternus, and the Greek writers explained: such as that one born when the "Ship" is rising will be a sailor; one born under the "Lyre," a musician; under "Heniochus" <note>Auriga, the Charioteer</note>, a driver; and so on for the rest. Furthermore, Porphyry, in his *Introductions*, says that the <term>type <gloss>figure and form</gloss></term> of the <term>zodiacal signs <gloss>the animals in the zodiac</gloss></term> <note>original Greek: "των ζῳδιων"</note> consists of the <unclear>symptomata</unclear> <gloss>co-risings</gloss>, that is, the arrangement of the stars. From this, we understand that these things called "co-risings" are no other images than those composed of stars. I have been rather lengthy in declaring this because I hear that George of Trebizond, a Greek man (though his book has not reached us), followed Haly’s exposition in his commentaries on Ptolemy’s *Centiloquy*. The barbarian Albumasar <note>Abu Ma'shar, a famous Persian astrologer</note> could have diverted them from this error; he affirms that, according to Ptolemy’s opinion, no images rise with the decans except the visible ones composed of stars situated to the south and north. It is worth recalling what we said in the fifth book against those who say the Lord Jesus was born when the first face of the Virgin was rising, in which there is a virgin nursing a boy who is called Jesus. For it is established that this image of a virgin nursing a child

<column-break/>

comes from these fabulous images that we have mocked. Although even there, no such image exists; rather, as Albumasar reports, the Indians invented a different one. Anyone who considers how vain and ridiculous this invention is will be ashamed to want to confirm the truth of the Gospels with these astrological delusions. This was procured by the demon for no other reason than that this plague might be received as if it were a friend and supporter of religion. But let them keep their trifles to themselves; by summoning such things, the Christian truth is not confirmed, but rather weakened and defiled.

# THE DISPUTATIONS OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA 
# AGAINST THE ASTROLOGERS. 
# THE NINTH BOOK BEGINS.

## Chapter I. A summary of what has been
## accomplished so far, and what must be done in the
## following books, and where we should begin.

It has been demonstrated so far that astrology is nothing, because the things it pronounces upon do not depend on the heavens, except by accident or as a remote and universal cause—neither of which produces a particular knowledge of events. It has likewise been declared that even if these things were caused by the heavens, it would not be in the way astrologers imagine: that is, from a certain initial moment. Furthermore, even if this were granted, it certainly would not be from those causes they use in predicting, none of which are true or natural if we subject them to a certain test. For although they use stars and planets, they increase, diminish, and change them according to places, signs, intervals, and other things of that sort, which we have declared to be false and ineffective. Therefore, they either introduce bad causes—that is, fabulous ones—or they stain good causes by mixing in bad ones. Now we must act to declare that even if all these things were consistent, they are nevertheless of such a kind that they cannot be known by them; or if they could be known, that knowledge has not yet been obtained. Three things are necessary to know if true predictions about future things are to be made: First, that the initial hour of each thing be faithfully kept. Second, that we exactly comprehend the state of the heavens and the position of the stars at 그 hour. Lastly, that we understand through true reasons or observations from unfailing experiments what that position of the heavens and stars actually does. In the two following books, we will reveal that none of these things can be known, or that no one has existed so far who knew them. We shall begin with the primordial hour <note>The moment of birth or beginning</note>, the knowledge of which is especially necessary, nor can the rest be correctly established if anything in it is either doubted or mistaken. Whether they begin from the birth of men, or of cities and kingdoms, or from the constellations of the year, let us start with births <note>original: "genituris"</note>.

---

## Chapter II. An astrologer can neither always 
## know the certain hour of birth, nor explore it through a true rule.

An astrologer cannot have the moment in which someone is born explored and certain, unless perhaps he stands ready with an <term>astrolabe <gloss>a tool for measuring the heavens</gloss></term> as the infant comes forth to measure the celestial bodies. But this happens very rarely. Nor can it always happen even when we wish it, such as at night, or in cloudy weather, or when no mathematician is present. Furthermore, it is very easy to slip up, as Avenezra <note>Abraham ibn Ezra, a Spanish Jewish scholar and astrologer</note> testifies in his commentaries on Ptolemy. For if the instrument is not most exact, as perhaps it might—

<sig>z iij</sig>

<summary>Pico della Mirandola argues that the "extra-zodiacal" images used in astrology are historical fabrications and linguistic misunderstandings of Greek texts. He begins Book IX by stating that even if astrology were theoretically sound, it is practically impossible due to the inability to accurately record birth times or interpret planetary influences.</summary>
<keywords>Petosiris, Ephestion, Porphyry, Haly, George of Trebizond, Albumasar, decans, symptomata, co-risings, astrolabe, birth hour, Centiloquium</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s critique of the technical foundations of astrology. Having previously dismissed the constellations as arbitrary human inventions, he now moves to the practical impossibility of determining the "horoscope"—the exact degree of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at the moment of birth—which is essential for casting any astrological chart.</meta>

-># NINTH DISPUTATION<-

never is it the case that an observation at the moment of emergence <note>The moment of birth</note> corresponds exactly to the truth: the calculation of the specific degree of the horoscope will waver. Even if there were a true investigation of the hour by means of an astrolabe, this happens very rarely, as we were saying. What is frequent and almost constant is that parents, or the master of the birth, tell the astrologer what they believe the hour of birth was; yet not even astrologers deny that such reports should not be trusted, for they are mostly deceptive. For this reason, they call it the "estimated" or "suspected" hour, because there is suspicion about it and no certainty. For sundials lie, and even mechanical clocks <note>original: "horologia," referring to water-clocks or early mechanical timepieces</note>, though they may not fail entirely, do not show the intervals that fall between the hours. Add to this that the common hours do not begin from sunset, which the logic of mathematicians requires, but rather when the air begins to darken. This happens when the sun has long since sunk below the horizon, especially when the sun is placed in "oblique signs" <note>Signs that rise at an angle to the equator, making twilight longer or shorter</note>; since these signs linger longer in the west, night may sometimes have already claimed an hour before the air grows dark. Finally, the astrologers admit this along with us, but they have applied a remedy so that their divination might not be endangered by it. For even if that which they call the estimated hour is not the true one—provided it does not differ too much from the truth—they claim to have a method for finding the true hour, so that the initial uncertainty does not hinder them. If these men were wise, we would object only this: that no art or science can be given by which a particular fact may be known to have occurred or not. There is, therefore, no method by which we can be made certain of the exact moment John or Paul was brought into the light. But these things do not seem absurd to them, and perhaps neither does the fact that in any day, and even any hour, there are many small particles of time in which it can be demonstrated that no one can be born in a certain region. For if I am said by my parents to have been born at the first hour of the night, and the astrologer says that hour does not fit his method, I ask why? Could someone else have been born under that same inclination of the sky at the first hour of the night? If they deny this could happen, it follows, as I said, that there are many parts of any hour in certain places where a human being cannot be born. I say "many parts" of any hour because almost no birth time given by those seeking advice fits the rules of the astrologers; it is always changed by them into either a preceding or subsequent part of the hour. If they grant that another could have been born during that time in that region—even though I was not born then—let us say Anthony was born at the first hour of the night. I then ask: if we establish a true hour for Anthony's birth and he gives it to the astrologer, will the astrologer judge it true or false? If he judges it true, he ought by the same logic to have judged mine true when it was offered, since it fits his method no better now than when John offered his. If he judges it false, then Anthony was established as being born at that hour; therefore, the dogma is false through which a very true hour is rejected as if it were false. Furthermore, those who handed down this type of precept say the sign ought not to be changed from what the estimated hour shows, but only that the specific *part* of that sign should be declared by the method. Yet the estimated hour often lies about the sign itself, especially when a person is born with the very last or very first parts of a sign ascending. In those cases, the method will not correct the error, but confirm it. It is clear from these reasons that there is no way of tracking down the horoscope when it is uncertain. Now let us show, if any method could perhaps be devised, that those which the astrologers have handed down are most clearly deceptive.

<column-break/>

### Chapter III. The dogma of Ptolemy, which they call the "Almufeli" or "Animodar," is refuted by both authorities and reason.

**P**tolemy, in the third book of his *Tetrabiblos* <note>original: "apotelefinatorum lib.," Ptolemy’s fundamental work on astrology</note>, hands down a dogma of this kind. He instructs that one should observe the New Moon or Full Moon immediately preceding the birth. Then, one finds the planet that has the most authority in the degree where that conjunction or opposition occurred. Finally, with the chart already laid out, to whichever "angle" <note>The four critical points of a chart: Ascendant, Midheaven, Descendant, and Imum Coeli</note> that planet is closer, they set that place to the same degree and minute that the dominant planet held in its sign. They fashion this as the "angle" of the entire birth. All astrologers decree this as the foundation of all judicial astrology. This is the decree they call the *Almufeli*, or sometimes the *Animodar* <note>A method for "rectifying" a birth chart to find the exact minute of birth</note>. We have seen above how much the younger astrologers err in misunderstanding Ptolemy’s meaning. Now Ptolemy himself is examined, against whom I can primarily oppose a great weight of authorities. For Abraham the Jew <note>The scholar and poet Abraham Ibn Ezra, c. 1089–1167</note> says that he observed many births with the most exact astrolabes in regions whose longitude and latitude were known and explored, yet he never found any planet whose degrees and minutes in the signs it occupied responded to the degrees and minutes of the eastern horizon or the mid-heaven; nor did they vary by less than half an hour from the birth time already perceived by the senses to be most true. Truly ridiculous are those who say that Abraham Ibn Ezra <note>original: "Avenazra"</note> did not write these things with a judged mind, as if he were fighting with Ptolemy over a kingdom—he who lived nine hundred years later and who, in determining the year and the giver of years and many other things, does not prefer his own opinion to Ptolemy’s. But Alchabitius also writes in his own commentary that he has demonstrated that the true rising degree can in no way be found through that calculation. Henry Baten <note>A 13th-century astronomer and disciple of Albertus Magnus</note>, examining his own birth chart—though concealing his name and calling himself "a servant of God"—says, "Let us set aside the *Animodar* of Ptolemy, which is rejected by the wise." They do not erase such a dogma but "correct" it, as Aoniar <margin>Aon.</margin> does, who differs somewhat from Ptolemy. Others fight over the understanding of it: when they ask which place the planet is "closer" to, some want to observe "discrete quantity" <note>counting degrees</note> and others "continuous quantity" <note>measuring time</note>, like Antonio de Monte Ulmo. But setting aside the authorities who oppose Ptolemy, I am accustomed to declare the falsehood of the dogma thus: Let Lucius be born in Rome and Fabius in Florence at the same hour and same moment. It is clear to astrologers that the horoscope will not be the same for both because of the different inclination of the sky under which they are born. And yet, if we follow the calculation from Ptolemy’s precepts, we will make the horoscope the same for both, since the preceding Full or New Moon occurred in the same part of the sky for both regions. Therefore, the same dominant planet, possessing the same degree of a sign in the chart for both, will define the "angles" in each birth by the same numbers. But this is refuted by the evidence of the facts and the senses; therefore, the dogma is false, which I am surprised that Ptolemy, a supreme mathematician, did not see through.

### AGAINST THE ASTROLOGERS, BOOK IX.

...that the location of the Moon at birth was the horoscope <note>The "horoscope" here refers to the Ascendant, the specific degree of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon.</note> at the time of conception. Conversely, they hold that the location of the Moon at conception is the horoscope of the birth. Based on this premise, they pass down a method by which they believe they can seize upon the Moon’s location at the moment the seed filled the womb. Having found this, they conclude that a similar degree
<margin>The occasion of their error: a faulty translation of Ptolemy.</margin>
rises at the hour of birth. However, the occasion for their error was a faulty translation of the books of Ptolemy. For he never wrote about this specific *degree*, but rather only about the *sign* <note>In astrology, a "sign" covers 30 degrees, while a "degree" is much more precise. Pico is arguing that the ancient source was much more general than modern astrologers claim.</note>. His words in the place mentioned above are these: "where..." <note>original Greek: "ἔνθα"</note> and what follows.

Translated word-for-word into English, it says: "where that sign of conception is at the time of birth, you should establish the horoscope; where that sign was at conception, make that the horoscope of the delivery, or the one opposite to it." Thus, Ptolemy did not think the horoscope could be found precisely <note>original: "partiliter," meaning degree-by-degree</note> by this path. Therefore, in his books on *Judicial Astrology* <note>original: "apotelesmaton," referring to Ptolemy’s *Tetrabiblos*</note> where he investigates this matter, he makes no mention of this specific decree. Otherwise, if he had understood it to refer to the *degree*—which we have shown to be false from his own words—he would have thought it very easy to find the hour of conception. Today’s younger astrologers, with no great effort, provide this to anyone who asks, using the method they claim belongs to Ptolemy. Yet how is it that Ptolemy himself, in the third book of his *Judicial Astrology*, says the seminal beginning is "mostly" <note>original Greek: "ἐπίπαν λέον"</note> unknown? He says that when knowledge of it is obtained, it is either "by chance" <note>original Greek: "συμπτώματι"</note>—that is,
<margin>None of the ancients handed down a way of tracking the moment of conception for women.</margin>
by a stroke of luck—or by observation. Surely he ought to have added "by technical art" <note>original Greek: "τεχνικῶς"</note> if he truly believed it could be seized upon by some art or method. Furthermore, the Greek interpreter explains how it is known by "chance" or "observation": by chance, when it happens that a woman feels a sensation when the seed is received (as Cleopatra <note>Likely referring to a pseudo-anonymous medical writer of the time</note> teaches); by observation, if a man intentionally notes the time when he had intercourse once and then abstained thereafter. Then the following months would reveal the timing of the conception. Besides these, no one among the ancients produced any other way of exploring that time clearly, much less did they wish to investigate the hour of birth from it. As for what the Arabs say—that Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary Hellenistic figure to whom many astrological works were falsely attributed</note> commanded this—it is a fable (like many other things which, as we noted in the first book, they most lyingly attribute to the same author). For regarding what the Egyptians handed down on this matter,
<margin>Ephestion, Porphyry.</margin>
Ephestion reports it, as does Porphyry. They say that this very precept read in Ptolemy was the invention of Petosiris the Egyptian, using these words: "Thus says Petosiris..." <note>original Greek: "ὁ δὲ Πετόσιρις"</note> and what follows.

---

<margin>Petosiris.</margin>
Petosiris says that the sign in which the Moon was at the time of conception becomes the horoscope at birth, or its opposite; and that which the Moon occupied at the time of birth was the horoscope of conception. But in the same passage, Porphyry <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote on astrology</note> records two other methods from the opinion of Antiochus and certain others for tracking the sign in which the Moon was at the hour of intercourse, but never is any mention made of the *degree*. Indeed, the very chapter in which this is written is titled "Concerning the seminal sign" <note>original Greek: "περὶ τοῦ σπερματικοῦ σημείου" (OCR: "περι περι μισιμείκ")</note>; that is, about the lunar sign of the seed, because the Moon held that sign when the seed was released into the genital place. Ephestion of Thebes also recounts three other methods of the Egyptians, different from these (which Porphyry mentions), by which they might investigate this same thing: namely, which sign was rising at the hour of intercourse. There, in express words, Ephestion warns us that one does not arrive at the precise horoscope through those paths, but tracks it "by indication" <note>original Greek: "τεκμηρίως"</note>; that is, by "rough logic" <note>original: "crassa Minerva," a Latin idiom for unrefined or plain common sense</note>, as is

<column-break/>

customarily said. He says there is only one reason for determining the degree: the one which Ptolemy handed down in the third book of the *Judicial Astrology*. It is the very one we refuted in the previous chapter. But as we said, the younger astrologers fell into error because, in the Arabic translation followed by the Latins, the translators incorrectly put "degree" instead of "sign." Furthermore, whatever those authors might have written, what is the logic
<margin>The error of the younger generation.</margin>
of this dogma? Or by what observation could this be grasped? They answer: "The calculation responds." They claim that from the location of the Moon at the hour of birth, one understands how many days the infant was in the womb. If you count those days backward, you arrive at the hour of conception, and through that time you will find the location of the Moon to be the same as the one rising at the time of birth. But I ask this: who taught us to define the time of stay in the womb from the location of the Moon? Not Ptolemy, nor any of the ancients; not even your Hermes produced this. Your only answer is that those stays *must* be defined that way if the dogma about the exchange of the ascendant and the Moon's location at conception and birth is true. You are therefore moving in a circle, proving the truth of the dogma
<margin>The dogma is refuted by experiments.</margin>
by saying it happens because of the observed stays, and then saying the stays must be observed that way because the dogma is true. In no other way will the dogma be "true"—it is certainly easy for anyone to "confirm" dogmas that way! If perhaps you dare to assert it by experiment, having observed and compared the times of birth and conception together, you may lie with impunity since the act was done without witnesses. However, those of your own number who strive the most deny that the precept corresponds to the truth based on experience. For Abraham Ibn Ezra <note>A famous 12th-century Jewish polymath and astrologer</note> says he observed this five times,
<margin>Abraham Ibn Ezra.</margin>
and it failed three times. He blamed this once on Mars, once on Venus, and once on Mercury. I think if he had observed it ten times, he would have accused the other planets just the same. For Immanuel the Hebrew, a follower of Ibn Ezra, experimented
<margin>Immanuel.</margin>
twice and found that it varied from the true time of birth by seven days. Abu Ma'shar <note>The most influential Arab astrologer of the Middle Ages</note>, the prince of astrologers, believes this method can be deceived by five degrees, as his disciple Sedis relates. If that is so, it does us no good, as we are concerned with the specific degree. Likewise, Ibn Ridwan <note>An Egyptian physician and commentator on Ptolemy</note>, a great expositor of Ptolemy among them, testifies that the method often lies. The Saxon translator of Alchabitius <note>Johannes Saxo, commenting on the 10th-century astrologer al-Qabisi</note> thinks it is entirely false and
<margin>Sedis, Ibn Ridwan, Johannes Saxo.</margin>
vain, affirming it to be useless as well, stating that it is impossible for an uncertain degree of the horoscope to ever be made certain through it—which he demonstrates at length with the example of a proposed birth chart.

### Chapter V. The fiction of Messahala, along with five other modes of exploring the horoscope recited by Paul of Alexandria, is refuted.

THESE are mostly the methods accepted by astrologers. Messahala <note>Masha'allah ibn Athari, a leading 8th-century Persian-Jewish astrologer</note> devises another fiction, but it has been rejected
<margin>The fiction of Messahala.</margin>
by everyone and seen for its vanity. For he commanded that the time of the Moon from the new moon to the full moon (or vice versa, from the full moon to the dark moon) be considered as if it were one hour. Then, whichever of those preceded the birth, the space that fell between it and the time of birth should be compared to the total distance of the Moon’s waxing and waning. Whatever the proportion of the intervals was, one should take that portion of the temporal hour—provided we observed that a male should not be born in an even hour, nor a female in an odd one.
<margin>See the beautiful deduction of the astrologers' folly.</margin>
The following age laughed at this, discovering by experiment that males and females are born at the same hour. I, however, do not merely consider the vanity of this one decree, but judge that whole Messahala by it. For as he slipped into error...
