# DISPUTATIONS IX

...to be deceived is indeed a human trait; yet to write such shameful things, to rely on ridiculous matters, to present fables as if they were dogmas, and to say things that are everywhere refuted by the evidence of reality—this is certainly not the mark of a human, if reason is the defining gift of humanity. But I am not judging Messalla <note>likely referring to Mash'allah ibn Athari, a famous 8th-century Persian Jewish astrologer</note> alone so much as I am judging all astrologers through him. Among them, he is of the first rank, and you will not easily find anyone wiser in that family of thought. For the Egyptians, those wonderful priests of this "sacred" discipline, what great fairy tales they have invented regarding this matter! Paul of Alexandria 
<margin>Five other methods of the Egyptians, recounted by Paul of Alexandria.</margin>
relates five different methods (beyond the three already mentioned) which they use to investigate the truth of the horoscope <note>the specific degree of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon</note> down to the exact degree. Good God, how vain, crude, futile, and false they are! <margin>First.</margin> The first is of this kind: they say to look at the "epoch" <note>the position or starting point</note> of the Sun in a birth during the day, and of the Moon in one at night. Whichever planet’s "single-degree" <note>original: "monomiria," a system where each degree of a sign is assigned to a planet</note> it falls in, you should make the horoscope the single-degree of that same planet that is nearest to the suspected degree of the ascendant. <margin>Second.</margin> The second, whether it be day or night, looks only at the epoch of the Moon, but is otherwise similar. <margin>Third.</margin> The third, which gave Ptolemy the occasion for his own dogma, considers the full moon or the new moon nearest to the birth. Then, one looks for the "house-ruler" <note>original: "despotem"</note> and the "limit-ruler" <note>original: "onocratorem"</note> of the sign where that moon occurred. One sees which of these is stronger in the birth constellation and which possesses more authority; from that, one calculates the rising degree. <margin>Fourth.</margin> The fourth merely inspects the supreme ruler of the degree in which the Sun and Moon either joined or were opposite before the infant truly came forth. However many "limits" <note>terms or subdivisions of a zodiac sign</note> that planet possessed in the rising sign, they think that many degrees of that same sign had already appeared in the east. <margin>Fifth.</margin> The last observes not only the birth but the conception—that is, the time that preceded either the full moon or the new moon. Then, it commands that the "twelfth-parts" <note>original: "dodecathemoria," a division of a sign into twelve 2.5-degree segments</note> of the degrees in which those occurred be made and observed, seeing which of the planets' single-degrees they fall into. Whichever planet is better positioned in the chart has the authority to measure the horoscope. Heliodorus <note>an ancient commentator on astrology</note>, writing on how they investigated the time 
<margin>Heliodorus.</margin>
of conception, says they would count back nine months from the birth, as if the time spent in the womb is always equal—showing these most "divine" Egyptians to be the most ignorant people everywhere. I could object to many things in which these dogmas are peculiarly flawed. But this one reason is enough for those who desire brevity (by which we also rejected Ptolemy's dogma): whichever method we follow from those predicted above, we will always create the same horoscope for those who were born at the same time but in different regions—yet it is an established fact for all mathematicians, beyond any controversy, that their horoscopes are different.

---

### Chapter VI. The beginnings of cities, kingdoms, factions, and laws are unknown, and the astrologers have passed down no art by which they can be investigated.

It is clear from these points that the hour of birth is never known with clarity except by chance, and since it is prone to error, it cannot be restored by any art. But since that "truth" was never true, the truth of the prediction cannot stand. Therefore, nothing true can be said by the "nativity-casters" <note>original: "genethliacis"</note> who testify with one voice that the specific degree of the horoscope is the hinge of the birth, the structure of all fate, and the foundation of all predictive astrology <note>original: "apotelesmaticae"</note>. Nor is there any better reliability in the beginnings of cities and kingdoms. The knowledge of these is far more difficult to pin down than that of births. For who recorded these? What writer of histories observed them? A historian whose reliability and diligence could provide the exact day a city was restored or founded would be considered far too legendary. It was the custom in Rome to celebrate the city’s birthday, but nothing more is established for the astrologers than that the Moon was in the sign of the Scales <note>Libra</note> when it was
<margin>Paolo of Florence.</margin>
founded. In the notebooks of Paolo of Florence <note>Paolo dal Pozzo Toscanelli, a 15th-century polymath</note>, a physician and mathematician, I found two different times noted for the restoration of the city of Florence: one in the year of grace 801, the other in 802. From this, the arrangement of the stars is entirely different. I would also believe that many constellations of cities commonly cited are actually fictions based on later events—just as Julius Firmicus 
<margin>Julius Firmicus.</margin>
invents charts for the ancients like Paris and Plato and others, which he himself admits regarding the birth-chart of the world that he provides. Furthermore, they want that moment to be of great importance when a new thing arises among the common people: when civil discord is born, when a foreign nation invades a kingdom, when new laws are established, or new decrees promulgated. Who but a diviner could provide the horoscope for these things? Yet one must have these before we can divine anything. Finally, even if some moments of these times could be had, they certainly will not deny that they are perhaps less exact and less certain than those of individual births. Therefore, if they think those births need "correction" and shouldn't be trusted otherwise, this is much more necessary for these events. Yet they teach no method for correcting these, for the methods we mentioned are applied only to human births. Therefore, all their forecasting about the fates of cities and kingdoms was crippled and deceptive, since they want these to depend on those primordial moments—which they either completely ignore or have received through traditions that are neither faithful nor precise. Therefore, let men no longer fear death, exile, or poverty, nor let cities fear destruction or plague, when these most audacious triflers threaten such things in their widely available annual booklets.

---

### Chapter VII. It is still uncertain among astrologers how the houses are to be divided, how far their powers extend, and which signs are to be used.

It remains to speak of the beginnings of the year, great conjunctions, and eclipses. For by observing the moment these occur, they prophesy the fates of republics and universal matters. It must be shown, therefore, that such times cannot be grasped by them without falling into error. This will become clear from the following sections, where we will show that the movements of the planets are still uncertain and not encompassed by blameless calculation. Thus far, we have spoken of how uncertain the fatal hour is for any given thing—if indeed there are "fatal hours" for the things astrologers most highly value. For we demonstrated above that none are fatal, and if any were, they would be different from what they think. Now let us make it public that even if they could obtain the correct times for beginning a prediction, they still cannot know the position of the stars or the state of the heavens at that hour. 
<margin>Discord among astrologers regarding the houses.</margin>
First, then, is the task of arranging the chart into the twelve places they call "houses." No one who has touched the books of mathematicians is unaware of the darkness in which the astrologers are plunged here, and how much they stab at one another over things entirely unproven. Some distinguish these places with six circles, one of which, rotated through the point of the east, makes the seventh "hinge" <note>the Descendant</note> and the horoscope <note>the Ascendant</note>; another, the meridian itself, outlines the highest and lowest points of the ether. Others say the division arcs—the half-day and half-night arcs—intercepted in the four middle places through four points and marks, are divided into three equal portions. But all these circles...

# AGAINST THE ASTROLOGERS. BOOK IX.

<margin>Abraham,</margin>
...these circles pass through the poles of the world: an opinion generally accepted which we refuted above. *Abraham Ibn Ezra* <note>original: "Abraā Auenazra," a famous 12th-century Jewish polymath and astrologer</note> teaches in his work on the construction of the astrolabe, and elsewhere, how to divide the "houses" <note>the twelve divisions of the sky in a horoscope</note> by designating six circles. One of these is the horizon, another is the meridian itself; from these, the four "angles" <note>the ascendant, descendant, midheaven, and lower midheaven</note> are immediately established. He orders the other four to be drawn through the intersection points of the horizon and meridian, and through the divisions of the parts of the equator falling between the east and the meridian—divided, I say, into three equal portions. This method is highly approved, though the author's name is suppressed. *Johannes Regiomontanus* <note>Johannes Müller von Königsberg, a leading 15th-century mathematician</note>, 
<margin>Johannes Regiomontanus.</margin>
the most learned mathematician of our age, was highly esteemed, yet he did not satisfy *Campanus* <note>Campanus of Novara, 13th-century mathematician</note>, who also brought his own new reasoning to this partition. Campanus followed *Ibn Ezra* in most things, but differed greatly in this: instead of the equator, he used a certain artificial circle which he called the "vertical circle," from which a different measurement and different boundaries of the houses emerge. *Johannes* also wrote an extensive defense of his dogma, relying on many mathematical proofs and the authorities of ancient astrologers. Others allow different methods; and our friend *Ludovico the Hermit* <note>original: "Ludouicus heremita," likely Ludovico da Gazzuolo, a contemporary mathematician</note>, a diligent and most exact calculator, used to prove that none of the methods we have mentioned agree with the sayings of *Alchabitius* <note>a 10th-century Arab astrologer</note>. Furthermore, many believe these same houses should be divided by the degrees of the zodiac (which they call "equal houses"), either using this path alone (which we noted above that the Indians frequently did) or accepting both divisions equally: both the one that varies by planetary risings <note>original: "anaphoris"</note> and the one that respects the degrees of the zodiac. 
<margin>Ludovico the Hermit, a most exact calculator.</margin>
<margin>Abraham the Spaniard. Henry.</margin>
*Abraham the Spaniard* <note>Abraham bar Hiyya</note>, the teacher of *Ibn Ezra*, and *Henry of Mechelen* <note>original: "Henricus valensis"</note> observe this, pronouncing judgment based on the place where a planet is found by equal degree distribution no less than where the divisions are marked in the common manner. Furthermore, if it were certain where the beginnings and ends of the houses should be placed, there remains another doubt that calls everything back into uncertainty: for they do not agree whether the power and efficacy of a house is enclosed within the designated space. *Ptolemy* starts it five degrees before the actual boundary of the sign. Others extend it by only three parts. The sages of the Egyptians wanted the beginning of the house (which is commonly called the "cusp") to be not the start, but the middle and a sort of center of power. Therefore, they believed its influence spread fifteen degrees above that point and just as many below it. If we notice that all these varieties of opinion are supported by almost equal reasons or authorities, we must confess that this uncertainty alone leaves the entire system of pronouncing judgment by the stars (if such a thing exists) in ambiguity. For when the divisions of the houses are varied, the entire constellation is varied; since (as we criticized above) the stars change their nature, influence, and properties according to the astrologers’ change of house. And what is most significant, they assign these houses conditions that are primarily conflicting and contrary, even though they are joined and coherent in position. For what could be more different than the first house and the twelfth, which follow one another? Or the sixth and seventh? Or again, the fifth and sixth, or the eleventh and twelfth, or the ninth and eighth, and so on? It often happens that one mathematician will place a planet in the sixth house, while another will contend it is in the fifth—which completely changes the entire prediction. One will decree a planet is in the ninth, while another says it belongs to the eighth. Thus, this whole distribution of houses, the root and foundation of all predictive astrology <note>original: "apotelefmaticæ"</note>, remains in uncertainty. Following this is the

<column-break/>

concern regarding which signs we ought to use. Here arises a tangled and inexplicable question concerning the "movable" and "immovable" signs, and the eighth, ninth, and tenth spheres—a matter we need not discuss here, as it was treated extensively above. *Abraham the Jew* <note>Ibn Ezra</note> commands that "two charts" <note>original: "duplex thema"</note> be made, as one who clearly believed the controversy could not be decided. From this doubt, it will be uncertain which signs are owed to the planets; and from what we treated before, it is uncertain which houses. Yet every astrological pronouncement hangs on this; therefore, every such judgment is doubtful, uncertain, and unproven.
<margin>Abraham the Jew makes a double chart.</margin>

---

### Chapter VIII. It teaches that attaining the truest positions of the planets is most laborious due to the deception of instruments.

<margin>Andreas Summarius</margin>
**W**ith the houses divided and the signs distributed, there remains the labor of establishing the "epochs" of the constellations and stars: that is, indicating at which degrees and minutes both the fixed and wandering stars are found. The unrefined and unskilled think they can perform this duty very easily; the most learned hesitate and lack confidence. To the latter, it is well known how great the difficulty is in truly attaining the positions of the planets—something judged by many to be not just laborious, but impossible. *Andreas Summarius*, a serious mathematician, begins his book thus: "Whether the motions of the stars can be known, I do not know; but that they have not yet been known, I hold for certain." He offers this reason for his opinion: those who measure the motions of the stars must necessarily first define the position of a star where they see it with the help of an instrument. Having "found" the position of the star, they use it as a premise to calculate its course. If the position is truly caught, the future calculation of motion will be true, for they rely on mathematical reasoning, which does not fail. But the detection of the position is not reliable everywhere, simply because the instrument fails. For no mechanical instrument, no matter how vast, can have divisions perceptible to the sense and act that are sufficient to avoid error—especially when one considers the distance of any star from the observer and the ratio by which the circumference of the entire universe exceeds the circumference of the instrument. Therefore, since the senses cannot grasp the relationship between the parts of a very small instrument and the parts of the whole universe (which are immense), the position of a star cannot be observed without deception. Perhaps the error will lie hidden, but with the passage of time it will become evident, as the star always moves further from its "true" position with each revolution.
<margin>Confirmation by the opinion of Haly.</margin>
*Ptolemy* confirms this, and for this reason, he orders astronomical numbers to be renewed every two hundred years because of the deception of instruments. He argues that in that span of time, the faults of old observations are revealed; thus they must be corrected by new observations, which themselves will not be faultless, but will at least be free of the error then perceptible to the senses. When these again deviate significantly after many cycles, they will be brought back to the truth by a new correction, as best as possible. Thus the tables of *Ptolemy*, the prince of astrologers, have been considered useless for many years now. Indeed, the studies of more recent men constantly correct observations because, as we said before, no construction of any instrument is so skillful or subtle, nor any size so vast, that it can report the position of a star with faultless faith. *Abraham the Jew* reports in his book on the use of tables concerning two astrolabes made with the highest reasoning and of such great size that the diameter of each extended nine palms <note>roughly 6 or 7 feet</note>. And when the two Berfechit brothers...
<margin>Abraham the Jew. Astrolabes with a diameter of nine palms.</margin>

the instrument designers, observing the Sun’s altitude at the moment it entered Aries, found that each instrument did not report the same result: they differed from each other by two minutes. Henry Baten of Mechelen <note>A 13th-century astronomer and philosopher</note>, a master in this art as in all mathematics—for he wrote a noble treatise on the construction of the astrolabe—believes it is either impossible, or as he says, next to impossible, to create an instrument that is in no way deceptive. He reports that even in Paris, he saw the maximum altitude of the Sun observed at the midday of the summer solstice using two wonderfully crafted, massive quadrants: one instrument recorded sixty-four degrees and forty-two minutes, while the other recorded the same degrees but zero minutes. Thus, there was an error in one of them of forty-two minutes. See <margin>An error of forty-two minutes. The eyes can be deceived in many ways.</margin> how even those who calculate the horoscope of a birth by an instrument can be deceived; we have already testified that Ali ibn Ridwan <note>original: "Auenrodan," an 11th-century Egyptian astrologer and physician</note> warned us of this above. Likewise, the same Baten whom I just cited proves in his *Mirror of Natural Things*—through many thousands of verses—that neither Ptolemy, nor Geber <note>Jabir ibn Aflah, a 12th-century Spanish-Arabic astronomer</note>, nor Albategni <note>al-Battani, a 9th-century Arab astronomer</note> can investigate the size of the diameters of the Sun and Moon more certainly than through eclipses; for the reliability of instruments on that matter will always be suspect. <margin>Levi invented a new instrument.</margin> I omit the many ways in which Ptolemy in the *Almagest* <note>original: "magna compositione," the Great Composition</note> and Alhazen <note>Ibn al-Haytham, a 10th-century physicist</note> in his seventh book on optics teach that the eyes can be deceived when observing the positions of the stars. For even if the air is considered clear and cloudless, what prevents a wind from blowing that is not felt? Yet the philosopher Aristotle writes that when the east wind blows, the stars appear larger. Levi ben Gerson <note>original: "Leo hebræus," also known as Gersonides</note>, a distinguished man and famous mathematician, as if trusting the ancients too little, invented a new instrument <note>The "Jacob’s Staff" or "Staff of Levi," used to measure angles between celestial bodies</note>; we have seen his mathematical rules for it, which are excellent in their subtlety. Nevertheless, when he observed two fixed stars twice in the same year with it, he says the second observation differed from the first by two degrees, which he believes must be attributed to the state of the atmosphere.

### Chapter IX. Various opinions on the motions of the planets: the inequality of the year: and the maximum declination of the sun.

<margin>Because of the ancients.</margin> From this, perhaps, was born such a great diversity of opinions among authors regarding the motions of the stars; for if they had detected the true positions with non-deceptive instruments, they would not have erred or disagreed with one another in measuring the period of time it takes for a planet to return to its starting point. Ptolemy, in the *Almagest*, calls the motion of the Sun the most manifest of all, by which we ought to measure the others as if by something better known; yet nothing shows us more certainly how little it has been explored than the wildly conflicting traditions written about it by the princes of astronomy. <margin>Another opinion of Hipparchus.</margin> Those more ancient than Hipparchus <note>A 2nd-century BCE Greek astronomer</note> maintained that the solar cycle which constitutes a year consists of 365 days plus more than a quarter of a day. <margin>Ptolemy's opinion.</margin> Others added exactly a quarter part. Hipparchus, writing in the 178th year after the death of Alexander <note>c. 145 BCE</note>, calculated from his own and the Chaldean observations that less than a quarter of a day should be added, though he did not determine exactly how much was lacking. <margin>Albategni's opinion.</margin> Two hundred and eighty-five years after him, Ptolemy defined that missing part as the three-hundredth part of a day. Seven hundred and forty-two years after Ptolemy, Albategni, observing the heavens, found the motion of the Sun to be faster, <margin>Thebit's opinion.</margin> because it fell short of that quarter part by the one-hundred-and-sixth part of a day. Thabit ibn Qurra <note>original: "Thebit"</note> said the year consists of 365 days, 6 hours, 9 minutes, and 12 seconds. Then there is that great diversity because

<column-break/>

<margin>Ptolemy. Alfonso. Arzachel. Baten. Isaac.</margin> some, like Ptolemy and Alfonso <note>King Alfonso X, sponsor of the Alfonsine Tables</note>, think all years are equal in length. Others think they are unequal, such as Arzachel <note>al-Zarqali</note>, Baten, and Isaac Israeli the Younger <note>A 14th-century Jewish astronomer</note>, who are followed by others of the more recent generation. They argue that the Sun returns sometimes sooner, sometimes later, to the place from which it departed. They claim the cause of this inequality is that the eighth sphere <note>the sphere of the fixed stars</note> does not always move from west to east, as Ptolemy and many others think, but sometimes is carried from east to west <note>This refers to the theory of "trepidation," a mistaken idea that the precession of the equinoxes oscillates back and forth</note>. Therefore, when the Sun moves in the same direction as the sphere's motion, its motion becomes faster; when in the opposite direction, slower. Hence, at different times, the year has been observed to be now longer, now shorter. And the Isaac we cited, in the book titled *Yesod Olam* <note>original: "iesodolam," meaning "Foundation of the World"</note>—he wrote it in the year of grace 1400, which was the Hebrew year of the world 5100 <note>The Latin text says 5700, likely a scribal or printing error for 5100 (5100 AM = 1340 AD, close to Pico's dating)</note>—thought that in his time the years were at their shortest, so that they could not be shortened further; but that the time was now appearing when they would begin to gradually lengthen by the motion of the eighth sphere. He claimed that between the longest possible year and the shortest, the median duration is 365 days and five hours; then, dividing the hour into 1080 parts <note>A standard unit in Hebrew astronomy</note>, it has 996 parts, and then 48 minutes, each of which is the 76th part of one of those 1080 parts. I remember reading this same meticulous calculation in the work of a very ancient Hebrew writer, Rabbi Ada bar Ahaba <note>original: "rabi adabaraba Adani Abrax filium"</note>. Finally, how ambiguous the Sun’s motion is can be seen by solar eclipses, which precede the time noted in the tables by more than half an hour—as Andreas Sumarius reports, and as is declared daily by the evidence of the senses. Henry of Mechelen also, in the book he titled *The Mirror of Natural Things*, asserts that in detecting eclipses, whether you look for the location, the hour, or the magnitude, anyone who follows the numbers for the motions given by either Ptolemy or Albategni will err.
<margin>Paolo of Florence.</margin> Paolo dal Pozzo Toscanelli <note>original: "Paulus Florentinus," the famous 15th-century cosmographer and mathematician</note>, a distinguished mathematician, having observed the Sun’s entry into Aries with the most diligent notes, found it to be faster by a third of an hour than the time defined in the tables. Pierre d'Ailly <note>original: "Alliacensis"</note> also reports in his *Elucidarium* <margin>D'Ailly.</margin> that when the Sun’s entry into the spring equinox was observed in Paris in the year of our Lord 1363, it was found that the Alfonsine tables deviated from the truth. But if they stumble in such clear light—that is, in the motion of the Sun, the most manifest of all, where if any error is made, it is necessary to err in all the rest—what will become of the motion of Mercury? It almost never shows itself to mortal eyes. Sosigenes, the teacher of Alexander of Aphrodisias, reports it can be no more than twenty-two degrees distant from the Sun; <margin>Various opinions on the distance of Mercury from the Sun.</margin> Theon, Paul, Heliodorus, and Porphyry say twenty-three; Ptolemy even says twenty-eight. Regarding the motion of this planet, a distinguished mathematician once confessed that he had discovered nothing certain. Furthermore, I have noticed that Mars is slower than they think by nearly one part in thirty. The same man published that the maximum declination of the Sun from the equator observed by him was twenty-three degrees and thirty minutes; whereas Ptolemy recorded it as the same degrees <margin>Ptolemy. Albategni.</margin> but fifty-one minutes; Albategni as thirty-six minutes and thirty seconds; and Arzachel <margin>Arzachel. Abraham Ibn Ezra.</margin> proposed it as more than twenty-three. Finally, Abraham Ibn Ezra <note>original: "Abraā Auenazra"</note>, the supreme mathematician, affirms in his sixth book on *Revolutions* that it is impossible to find which degree is in the horoscope at the moment the Sun enters the first part of Aries. This is because the time it reaches Aries cannot be grasped clearly, neither by a certain calculation of motion, as he says, nor by any kind of instrument.

He argues that if the motion of the Sun—the most obvious celestial body—cannot be agreed upon, the foundations of astrology are entirely unreliable.</summary>

-> AGAINST ASTROLOGY, BOOK IX <-

<margin>Ali ibn Ridwan</margin>
...which Ali ibn Ridwan <note>original: "Auenrodan," an 11th-century Egyptian physician and astrologer</note> also openly confesses when explaining the *Prognostic*. The same frequently cited Abraham ibn Ezra <note>original: "Auenazra," a 12th-century Jewish polymath</note>, whenever he was about to calculate something with refined logic, would employ three types of canons <note>Standard tables of planetary motion</note> as he writes: those of Ptolemy, the Persians, and the Indians. These all varied from one another and determined the positions of the planets differently. <margin>Plutarch. Aemilius.</margin> Plutarch—writing after Ptolemy and a contemporary of the Roman Aemilius, a supreme mathematician under the Emperor Trajan—states in his *Roman Questions* that even in this era, when astrology has reached its peak, the inequality of time has nevertheless defeated the skill of the mathematicians; it very often fails and escapes their numbers and calculations.

### Chapter X. An error of a single degree, or even a single minute, produces many errors: the astrologer cannot judge through annual revolutions, nativities, or great conjunctions.

<margin>The bounds change.</margin>
From this uncertainty of celestial motions, who does not see that the entire art of divinatory astrology is undermined? For if it slips by a single degree, it must necessarily fall away from all truth. If the part of the sign where a star is found changes, the "bounds" <note>original: "fines," specific subdivisions of a zodiac sign</note>—to which <margin>Exaltations. Monomoriae. Decans. Sign.</margin> some attribute equal power to the "houses," others more, and all admit have the greatest influence—will often be swapped. Certainly the *monomoriae* <note>the individual influences of each of the 360 degrees</note> will always vary, as will sometimes the borders of the "decans" <note>ten-degree segments of a sign</note>. If a planet holds the final parts of a sign, an error of a single part can transfer it from one sign to another. Thus, the Moon that should have been in Taurus might be placed in Gemini; yet it is considered fortunate in Taurus and unfortunate in Gemini. Furthermore, it will change from a masculine part to a feminine one, from a bright part to an opaque one, from opaque to dark, from a "pit" <note>a degree of difficulty or debility</note> to a "height," and from "full" parts to "empty" or "sickly" parts to the most fortunate ones. Finally, since every single degree has a different property among astrologers—and even the individual minutes, whose distinct properties Aesculapius <note>referring to a legendary Hermetic text on "Myriogenesis" or the creation of ten thousand things</note> <margin>Aesculapius.</margin> handed down—how can the virtue and influence of a star not be greatly changed by an error in its location by a degree or even minutes? Just as an error of a degree sometimes changes the sign, so an error of a minute sometimes changes the degree. Even regarding the "houses" <note>the 12 sections of the local sky</note>, a slip of one degree will sometimes cause a failure: a star that might be in the West could be placed under the earth, and one that belongs to the *horoscopus* <note>the Ascendant or 1st house</note> could be thrust back into the darkness of the 12th house. In the *dodecathemoria* <note>the division of each sign into twelve smaller parts</note>, an error of one degree will cause a wandering of twelve degrees. Nor, if the epoch <note>the starting point for a calculation</note> of a star is held incorrectly, can any of the "lots" (which they call "parts") be correctly established. Add to this the fallacy in "rays" <note>the geometric aspects or angles between planets</note> caused by a variation of only one part: it produces one effect if the ray is "partile" <note>exact to the degree</note>, another if it is "applying," and yet another if it is "separating." Add the gravest sin of all in "directing" the rays of the planets: if the astrologer slips by one part, an error of a whole year of life will result. These are the highest and most flagrant outrages in that profession; yet, if you compare them to other errors, they will seem small. For they must necessarily run into these when they take the initial hours of the year from the motions of the planets—a point we mentioned earlier and deferred to this <margin>Beginnings of the year.</margin> place. Suppose the beginning of the year is to be set at the entry of the Sun into the first minutes of Aries; if, as we have seen, they are off by more than half an hour, the entire constellation is lost, so great a variation will occur. The same will happen if they do not start the year from the Sun's entry into Aries, but rather from the preceding full moon or new moon.

<column-break/>

And I do not see why Abraham ibn Ezra and <margin>Error of Ibn Ezra and Ibn Ridwan.</margin> Ali ibn Ridwan think an error can be avoided in the latter case but not the former, since the hour of "conjunction" <note>the meeting of Sun and Moon</note> cannot be clearly grasped unless the motion of both stars is correctly held. Indeed, Ibn Ezra even objects to this in his work against Mashallah <note>original: "Macliucfis," likely referring to the 8th-century astrologer Mashallah ibn Athari</note>. Likewise, how can they not define annual revolutions of a birth incorrectly when they are ordered from the return of the Sun to the same place, given that the time of its restoration is unexplored? How correctly will they establish the "ascendants" of "great conjunctions" <note>rare meetings of Jupiter and Saturn used to predict historical eras</note> if the motions of Jupiter and Saturn are not exactly understood? Abraham ibn Ezra thinks we are so far from a perfect knowledge of these planets that he pronounces it a "great thing" if we even know the *day* on which they ought to be found together. John of Saxony <note>original: "Saxoniensis," a 14th-century astronomer</note> agrees with this opinion, and for that reason <margin>John of Saxony.</margin> calls it "foolish" to use the ascendant of the great conjunction itself; instead, he uses the ascendant of the beginning of the year in which the conjunction happens. Thus they defend one error with another. But the ascendant of a conjunction does not cease to be what it is just because it is unknown to us. Therefore, it should have been said that what the conjunction will produce cannot be known because the "horoscope" <note>the rising degree</note> cannot be known, rather than inventing a false one because the true one is ignored. What does a conjunction have to do with the ascendant of a year that perhaps happened many months prior? Or what reason is there that we should observe the ascendant of eclipses but not of conjunctions? Finally, even if we grant that the ascendant of the year has power over a conjunction, they cannot deny that the specific ascendant of the conjunction is of equal or greater importance. Since a completely different constellation arises from that unknown ascendant, they must necessarily waver in predicting the effects of the conjunction. I will pass over the fact that <margin>Ibn Ezra.</margin> the ascendant of the year is equally uncertain, according to the same Abraham ibn Ezra. From all this, the shameful error of Abu Ma'shar <note>original: "Aboafaris," the 9th-century Persian astrologer</note> is evident; in the first book of his *Greater Introduction*, he said it does not matter if an astrologer errs by one degree. By this word, he showed that he plainly did not understand the very astrology he was defending. Thus, it is not true, as many say, that astrology is accused only out of ignorance; rather, it is only condemned once it has been thoroughly examined, and it is only loved by those who have greeted it from a distance and from the threshold.

### Chapter XI. Differing opinions on the motions of the eighth sphere: the distance of the "Head of Aries" of the eighth from the "Head of Aries" of the ninth; and the apogee of the Sun.

Up to now, we have spoken only of the motion of the planets, which are perhaps better explored. But who will faithfully report the motion of the "fixed stars"? All astrology confesses that these have great, indeed primary and miraculous, power. Who, I ask, will correctly place the fixed stars in a chart? Or who will deny that an error of a single degree has no significance, when there is only one degree in which they are believed to be effective (that is, at the "angles" of the chart or with the luminaries)? "But," they say, "we have it all in our astrolabes and described everywhere in common tables of numbers." This is exactly what I warned of when we began this dispute: these things seem very easy to trivial astrologers whose doctrine spans only a few centuries. But to masters and experts, they are inextricable. When these experts consult slightly older writings, they see that masters of equal authority disagree on these matters as much as the East is distant from the West. The Egyptians, the Chaldeans, and indeed every ancient opinion thought that the wandering stars moved with only a single motion...

He highlights the internal contradictions and admissions of failure by major figures like Ibn Ezra and Abu Ma'shar regarding the precision of their data.</summary>

# DISPUTATIONS

-> AGAINST ASTROLOGY, BOOK IX <-

<margin>The work of Hipparchus.</margin>
...what we call the diurnal <note>The daily rotation of the sky from East to West.</note> motion: Hipparchus introduced another motion by which the stars are carried, like the planets, from West to East. Here, then, is the first controversy: whether they move by their own motion or not. More recent authors will say there is no controversy at all, since it is not surprising that later observers noticed what the ancients could not yet have detected. Yet there are even among the moderns those who defend the opinion of the ancients, and do not doubt that those who thought otherwise were deceived. Proclus <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher and mathematician.</note>, who lived long after Ptolemy, 
<margin>Proclus, most skilled in all mathematics.</margin>
was most expert in all mathematics, as is easily shown by his astronomical hypotheses, his treatise on the sphere, his work on the construction of the astrolabe, his commentaries on Euclid, and many other things he wrote. In his commentaries on the *Timaeus*, and elsewhere, he rebukes Hipparchus and Ptolemy for thinking that the "unwandering" stars <note>The fixed stars, as opposed to "erratic" stars or planets.</note> revolve around the poles of the zodiac toward the East, completing one degree every hundred years. Instead, he argues we should believe the Egyptians and Chaldeans, who, despite centuries of observation, recorded no such thing—especially since our senses testify to this ancient tradition so clearly that Proclus believes anyone who disagrees must be blind. For if they moved 
<margin>Proclus rebukes Ptolemy and Hipparchus.</margin>
upon the poles of the zodiac as Hipparchus and Ptolemy believe, it would necessarily follow that in these regions the Great Bear would verge considerably toward its setting; yet since the time of Homer, it has been called "never-setting." <note>In the *Iliad*, Homer describes the Bear as the only constellation that never bathes in the ocean (never sets below the horizon).</note> Furthermore, the star Canopus would eventually cease to be visible, although it performs a brief circuit above the horizon for those living in the third climate <note>A geographical zone in ancient mapping.</note>; while for those 
<margin>Poseidonius.</margin>
who inhabit Rhodes, it grazes the eastern horizon, as Poseidonius <note>A Stoic philosopher and astronomer (c. 135–51 BCE).</note> writes. Since, therefore, the Bear appears the same now as it did so many centuries ago—always visible—and Canopus has preserved the same position, it is proven false by the evidence of the senses that the stars have the motion introduced by the moderns. If they should object that the calculations for planetary motions are correctly gathered by the testimony of the senses by those who arrange the numbers and the canons <note>Astronomical tables.</note> assuming the motion of the fixed stars, Proclus says this objection is dissolved in two ways:
<margin>A double response.</margin>
First, that those who omit that motion of the fixed stars when calculating the planets also say things consistent with appearances, and in establishing the canons for the revolutions of the stars—even though they make the "unwandering" stars immobile—they nevertheless arrive at a most true correspondence with reason. Secondly, it is well known that a true result can be gathered from false calculations; therefore, the fact that a result corresponds to the senses does not prove the truth of the calculations themselves.
The most learned philosopher and mathematician Abraham 
<margin>Abraham ibn Ezra.</margin>
ibn Ezra <note>original: "Abraam Auenaz." A 12th-century Jewish polymath.</note>, though he often mentions both opinions—the one that they are mobile and not "unwandering," and the other that they are easily immobile (which he ascribes to the Indians)—never makes a final judgment. He leaves the matter in the middle, such that in his *Book of Nativities*, he commands that two charts be made: one as if they moved, and the other as if they did not. And although I define nothing on these matters beyond this—that nothing certain can be defined—it is nevertheless most true that this favors the opinion of the ancients: namely, that the supporters of the opposite dogma agree on nothing among themselves. For Ptolemy, following Hipparchus, 
<margin>Ptolemy, Hipparchus, Arzachel, Isaac, Thabit.</margin>
thinks they always move from West toward the East. Arzachel the Moor <note>Al-Zarqali, an 11th-century Andalusian astronomer.</note> thought that after they had proceeded a certain distance, they returned from East toward the West—which Isaac the Israelite <note>Isaac Israeli ben Solomon, a 9th/10th-century physician and philosopher.</note> follows, saying it was observed through most true experiences. Thabit ibn Qurra <note>original: "Thebit benchorat," a 9th-century Sabian astronomer.</note> strikes out that motion and devises another which verges toward the South and North. Moderns, approving of Thabit's discovery, also admit the opinion of Ptolemy, dividing the eighth sphere into a triple motion. Furthermore, those who agree with Ptolemy that they progress toward the East and 

<column-break/>

do not change course, nevertheless clash over the speed of that course. They think it false that one degree is completed in a hundred years, as had been handed down. For Maimonides <note>original: "Auen. Moses aegyptius."</note> and Ibn Ezra state that a space of one degree is traversed every seventy years. Al-Battani <note>original: "Albategni," a 10th-century Arab astronomer.</note> 
<margin>Al-Battani.</margin>
says after sixty-six years, making them faster than Ptolemy by nearly a sesquialter ratio <note>A ratio of 1.5 to 1.</note>. Paolo of Florence <note>Paolo dal Pozzo Toscanelli (1397–1482), a famous mathematician and cosmographer.</note> 
<margin>Paolo of Florence.</margin>
used to assert they revolve even faster than Al-Battani said. Who shall judge between these opinions? The younger men say: "We have detected their locations with faithful instruments, therefore we cannot be deceived." What, then, deceived those ancients, who did not lack instruments, nor had less skill in the art than you? It is commonly said at this time that the "mobile Aries" <note>The vernal equinox point.</note> is distant from the "immobile Aries" <note>The actual constellation of Aries.</note> by twenty-eight degrees. But Ibn Ezra, in his book of 
<margin>Ibn Ezra.</margin>
astrological matters, records that the distance was eight degrees when he was writing; for he wrote in the year of grace 1153, which preceded our own times by more or less 340 years. Therefore, if we follow the motion handed down by Al-Battani, which is faster than the others, the stars would have proceeded no more than five degrees in the years since Ibn Ezra; thus the distance today would not be 25 degrees as they say, but thirteen. Was Ibn Ezra then deceived, for whom both reason and instruments provided calculations? Maimonides, in that book 
<margin>Maimonides.</margin>
titled *Mishneh Torah* <note>original: "misthethora." Pico glosses this as *deuterosin* (Greek for "repetition") or "the second law."</note>, says at the beginning of the first part that at the time of the Flood <note>The Cataclysm.</note>, the mobile Aries coincided with the immobile one. 
<margin>Years of the flood.</margin>
Then afterward, the eighth sphere always moved toward the East by one degree every seventy years. Since the waters flooded the earth in the year of the world 1656, and now—as the more true calculation teaches—nearly 5,300 years have passed since the world's founding (it does not matter here to be perfectly exact), there will be about 3,600 years or so from the Flood to us. Therefore, the eighth sphere will have moved in those years by more or less fifty-two degrees, which would be the distance of the mobile Aries from the immobile. Isaac the Israelite writes that both signs coincided in the year 560 after the birth of Christ. Pierre d'Ailly <note>original: "Petrus alliacensis."</note> in his *Elucidarium* records that this happened in the year of Christ 260; this calculation disagrees with the former by three hundred years. Angelus Mantuanus 
<margin>Angelus Mantuanus.</margin>
and many moderns contend that the same occurred in the 15th year of grace, with a few months added. He also mentions a certain younger man, Isarith <note>Likely referring to a specific Jewish astronomical source.</note>, who 
<margin>Isaac.</margin>
after calculating the positions of the Sun and Moon relative to the eighth sphere, found the new moon of the month of March—after 5,224 years from the beginning of the world—to be near the fourteenth part of Pisces. But Angelus himself, calculating that new moon relative to the immobile signs (since he used the tables of Immanuel <note>Immanuel ben Jacob Bonfils, author of the astronomical tables *Ba’al Kanafayim* ("Lord of the Wings").</note>, which he titled 
<margin>Tables of Immanuel.</margin>
*Ba’al Kanafayim*), found it in the twenty-eighth degree of Pisces; if he followed the Alfonsine Tables, it would be in the twenty-seventh degree and fourteen minutes. From this, it would be gathered that the mobile signs were distant from the immobile ones by thirteen or fourteen degrees. This man wrote a few years before our age, which is why he says it is a marvel to him that the Oxonian Tables <note>Tables produced at Oxford in the 14th century.</note> record the star situated between the horns of Aries (which is the beginning of the mobile Aries) as being distant from the immobile Aries in the year of grace 1360 by twenty-four degrees and fifty-seven minutes—around which time I find it was actually forty years more.

Pico uses these contradictions to argue that astrology is built on a foundation of scientific uncertainty and guesswork.</summary>

# AGAINST ASTROLOGY, BOOK IX

<margin>The time when Isaac and Roger Bacon flourished; a summary of the argument.</margin>
...at that time both the famous Isaac <note>Likely Isaac ben Sid, a 13th-century Jewish astronomer who worked on the Alfonsine Tables.</note> and Roger Bacon flourished. Both of them believed that in their own age the "immobile Aries" <note>The vernal equinox, or the point where the celestial equator and ecliptic cross.</note> had varied from the "mobile Aries" <note>The actual constellation of stars called Aries.</note> by no more than ten degrees. Both followed Azarquiel <note>A 11th-century Arab astronomer from Toledo, also known as al-Zarqali.</note>, who estimated the maximum possible distance between them at ten degrees. Isaac claimed that this limit had been reached in his own time, and that the motion would soon begin to move backward toward the West. Therefore, let us consider: either their horoscopic instruments <note>original: "organa thematica"</note> deceive them, or they do not. If they do not deceive, how is it that Isaac and Roger, while observing the stars, judged that the mobile Aries was removed from the equinox by no more than ten degrees? Yet, if the opinion of the Oxford tables <note>The "Tabulae Oxonienses," likely the 14th-century tables of William Rede or similar English astronomical works.</note> or more recent ones is true, the stars were moved more than twenty-three degrees from that point. This reveals an error of thirteen degrees! If their instruments *do* deceive them, how can our contemporary astrologers know they are not also deceived, when the leading men in this art differ with such a great variety of opinions? Among these views, if anyone thinks he can judge the truth, he does so by brute impulse rather than by a sound judgment of the heavens. Thus, anyone who offers an opinion on the locations of the "unwandering" <note>Fixed</note> stars might not err by pure chance, but he certainly cannot reach the truth through reason.

<margin>Proclus, Ptolemy. Leo the Hebrew agrees with Proclus.</margin>
Nor should we overlook the fact that Proclus and Ptolemy deny that the Sun's apogee and perigee <note>The points where the Sun is furthest from and closest to the Earth.</note> move. However, more recent writers claim they do move—using the "barbarous" <note>Medieval Latin astronomical terms often derived from Arabic.</note> terms *auzem* <note>original: "augem," meaning the highest point or apogee.</note> and its opposite. These moderns are rebuked by Leo the Hebrew <note>Levi ben Gerson, also known as Gersonides (1288–1344).</note>, who defends the true opinion of Ptolemy. I will not even mention how little they know or how much they fight over the "equation of days" <note>The correction needed to convert solar time into uniform clock time.</note>, from which arises the greatest uncertainty in casting a horoscope.

### Chapter XII. On the "directions"—how numerous and varied are the opinions of astrologers.

<margin>The work of the moderns; Regiomontanus against it.</margin>
Beyond all this remains the inextricable task of arranging the "rays" and calculating what Proclus calls *aphetes* <note>The "giver of life," a point in the birth chart used to determine lifespan.</note> and the common folk call "directions" <note>A technique for "moving" a planet's position forward in time to predict the year a certain event will happen.</note>. Here, the mathematicians stab one another with mutual wounds. No authority is so balanced against another, nor has the experience of so many ages been able to settle any single matter. The opinion of the moderns is that the most exact "radiation" is composed of direct, oblique, and mixed "ascensions" <note>original: "anaphoris," referring to how signs rise over the horizon.</note> according to the variety of locations. But it follows from this that if someone is born in a region where the pole is raised forty-eight degrees and the first part of Capricorn is rising, a "trine" aspect <note>A 120-degree angle, considered harmonious.</note> would occur in parts of Cancer—even though we know Cancer is diametrically opposite to Capricorn <note>An "opposition" is 180 degrees, the opposite of a trine.</note>. Henry Baten <note>A 13th-century astronomer from Mechelen.</note> observes this configuration of planets based on location, so that a trine is whatever occupies the fifth house from the horoscope <note>The rising sign.</note>, regardless of the signs involved; he does the same for the other aspects.

<margin>The opinion of Albategni.</margin>
Albategni <note>Al-Battani (c. 858–929), a major Arab astronomer.</note> counts the intervals by the degrees of the zodiac, which they call "equal degrees," unless a star deviates to either side in latitude—though this varies the number very little. Indeed, it varies by no more than thirty minutes even if the star deviates by ten degrees. Johannes Regiomontanus <note>The famous 15th-century German astronomer (1436–1476).</note> followed this method, which was also taught by Abraham <note>Abraham bar Hiyya.</note>, the prince and teacher of Ibn Ezra.

<margin>Johannes Regiomontanus.</margin>
If you say that experience has shown that these schemes should be composed through "ascensions," Ibn Ezra <note>original: "Auenazra"</note> will stand against you; having long denied this through many observations, he will say it is recorded that they must be established through equal degrees. There are some who always use "direct ascensions,"

<column-break/>

which we have already shown above was falsely attributed to Ptolemy. Add to this that Ptolemy does not observe latitude <note>The distance of a planet north or south of the ecliptic line.</note> except in the case of planets in conjunction.

<margin>Abenzagel and Albumasar.</margin>
Abenzagel <note>Abu al-Zarqali.</note>, however, observes it in every "radiation" except the diameter. Albumasar <note>original: "Aboasar," a 9th-century Persian astrologer.</note> observes it even in the diameter, for which others criticize him. I will pass over the great disagreement regarding how far the "force" of a radiation extends. Some say three degrees; some say five; for the Moon, some say up to twelve degrees, and some even say thirteen, as Porphyry <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher.</note> says. It is an equal question for mathematicians

<margin>Porphyry.</margin>
and an inexplicable dissension concerning "directions" (to use their own terminology). For the Egyptians always used the ascensions of the specific region.

<margin>Dorotheus.</margin>
Dorotheus <note>Dorotheus of Sidon (1st century AD).</note>, in directing the first part, always used "direct ascensions"—which Abraham testifies very often corresponds to experience.

<margin>Abraham, Ptolemy.</margin>
Ptolemy and almost all later authors use the region’s ascensions when a star is in the East or West; when placed in the fourth or tenth house, they use the ascensions of the equator; for the intermediate places, they use a mixture. Al-Ma'mun <note>original: "Almeon," the 9th-century Caliph and patron of astronomy.</note> holds the same view in the seventh chapter of his fourth treatise on directions.

<margin>Al-Ma'mun. Opinion of Albumasar.</margin>
Albumasar directs through the degrees of the zodiac. Thus, in the eighth "difference" of the second treatise of his book *On the Great Conjunctions*, he directs the Moon to the place of conjunction with the unfortunate stars.

<margin>Ibn Ezra. Another opinion.</margin>
Ibn Ezra holds the same view in the book titled *The Beginning of Wisdom*, confirming it also by the authority of Albategni. There are those who think that both methods should be used—that rays should be extended and stars directed both by the degrees of the zodiac and by the proportion of the ascensions.

<margin>John of Seville.</margin>
This seems to be what John of Seville <note>A prolific 12th-century translator of Arabic astrology into Latin.</note> wanted in his *Isagoge* [Introduction]. For in the second part of his *Quadripartite*, in the chapter on the first house, he carried out the same. Others extend the rays by zodiacal degrees but direct by ascensions; this is what Messahalah <note>An 8th-century Jewish-Arab astronomer.</note> and also Ptolemy seem to have ascribed to Ibn Ridwan <note>original: "Auenrodan," an 11th-century Egyptian physician and astrologer.</note>.

<margin>Another [opinion] of Ibn Ridwan. Abraham the Jew. Another discord.</margin>
On the other hand, Abraham the Jew <note>Ibn Ezra.</note> brings the same reasoning to both operations, arguing that the charts should be composed by equal degrees and directed by them. I will omit how much they disagree on which direction a planet should be led. One can see in the *Apotelesmata* <note>Ptolemy's *Tetrabiblos*.</note> where Ptolemy differs from others, with Ibn Ridwan explaining some of it. But neither

<margin>Averroes.</margin>
do we discuss here the great difficulty for those who think mixed ascensions should be used in executing these doctrines. For the most learned men have judged that Ptolemy taught this neither correctly nor sufficiently.

<margin>Paul the German.</margin>
Paul the German <note>Paul of Middelburg (1446–1534), a scientist and bishop.</note>, a distinguished mathematician who now lives with Guidobaldo, the Duke of Urbino <note>A major patron of the arts and sciences in Renaissance Italy.</note>, a most literate prince,

<margin>Guidobaldo, Duke of Urbino.</margin>
once wrote that he had never seen anyone who could correctly direct a star to a trine position. Furthermore (as should have been said earlier), he denies that the commonly circulated tables for the latitudes of the planets are reliable. From all this, one can see how wide a door is opened to errors: in seizing the initial hours of births, cities, or constellations; in arranging the chart; in establishing the "angles" of the houses; in defining locations or dividing signs; or in assigning seats to the stars, whether fixed or wandering. Mathematical certainty on these matters still lies hidden, unexplored, in the cave of Heraclitus <note>A metaphor for a place where truth is deeply obscured or hidden away.</note>.

<summary>Pico details the chaotic lack of consensus among the world's greatest astronomers regarding the basic measurements of the stars and the methods for calculating astrological "directions." He argues that because these masters disagree by as much as thirteen degrees, the entire "science" of astrology rests on a foundation of guesswork and error.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico’s critique of the technical foundations of astrology. Having previously discussed the inaccuracies in calculating the zodiac's position, he now moves to the physical ordering of the planets and the symbolic (and in his view, absurd) logic used to assign meanings to the "houses" of a horoscope.</meta>

# NINTH DISPUTATION

<margin>The question of the sun: serious authors disagree whether it is placed first or second from the moon.</margin>
The placement and order of the middle planets <note>The "middle planets" refers to those between the Moon and the outer spheres—Mercury, Venus, and the Sun.</note> are entirely uncertain. For the ancient dispute still remains before the judge: is the Sun second after the Moon, or is it more central? The Egyptians believed it was closest to the Moon; the Chaldeans placed it in the middle. Ptolemy and a crowd of more recent thinkers also think it is in the middle. However, not only did Jabir ibn Aflah <note>original: "Heber," a 12th-century Spanish-Arab mathematician and astronomer.</note>, that most sharp-witted mathematician, dissent from his master, but even Theon—the Greek interpreter of Ptolemy—believed it should be placed immediately above the Moon. Plato and Aristotle also affirmed this. It is no wonder that the greatest authors disagree on this matter, for while many common arguments are exchanged on both sides, no certain reasoning can be devised. For when you remove parallaxes <note>original: "parallelares," referring to the displacement or difference in the apparent position of an object viewed along two different lines of sight.</note>—that is, the differences in observation—mathematics indicates nothing about which of two stars is higher. Nor is there ambiguity regarding the Sun alone; it exists also for Venus and Mercury. As the <margin>The Summary,</margin> *Summary* <note>Likely a reference to a specific compendium of the era, such as the *Summarium* of Richard de Furnival or a similar astronomical digest.</note> says: it is established that Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn are all above the Sun, yet in what order is neither known nor can it be known. This is because there is much diversity in their appearance (as they say), and whatever reasons you may construct will be empty and dialectical—drawn from common assumptions—rather than specific and mathematical. Take, for instance, that reasoning of Ptolemy’s <margin>Ptolemy’s reasoning is frivolous and Alpetragius’s is weak.</margin> which places the Sun conveniently in the middle of the planets because some are "summoned" by it in longitude (as Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars do) while others always follow it (like Venus and Mercury). This is a frivolous conjecture that does not hold up, because the Moon departs from the Sun just as much as the superior planets do; therefore, the Sun is not a "middle" between those that depart and those that do not. The reasoning of Alpetragius <note>original: "Alpetragij," referring to al-Bitruji, a 12th-century astronomer who challenged Ptolemaic models.</note> is equally weak, suggesting that the lower planets are faster in motion, even though he tries to prove those that *appear* faster are actually slower. In his view, the position of Venus, the Sun, and Mercury would be higher than the others—a claim everyone resists with equal force. More weight seems to be given to the reasoning of the ancients who decided the Sun was closest to the Moon because it is never snatched from our sight by the intervention of Venus or Mercury <note>Meaning, we do not see Venus or Mercury eclipse the Sun.</note>. But this too is solved in many ways: it might happen with Mercury because of its smallness, or with Venus because it is occupied and intercepted by the Sun's rays due to its proximity. Thus, it cannot block the path of the rays descending to us, whereas the more distant Moon can. Furthermore, perhaps these bodies are thin and lack the earthy density of the Moon, so they do not block the rays. They might even have their own light, so that when they take the place of the removed solar light, they do not snatch light away but merely exchange it; hence, no eclipse is perceived. Averroes, in his <margin>See the note of Averroes the Great.</margin> *Large Paraphrase* of Ptolemy’s *Almagest* <note>original: "magna compositionis Ptolemæi," the Syntaxis Mathematica.</note>, says that he once noticed two blackish spots on the Sun, and when he had calculated the numbers, he found that Mercury was positioned opposite the Sun’s rays at that time. Therefore, Maimonides <margin>Moses the Egyptian,</margin> <note>original: "Moses ægyptius."</note> correctly pronounced the placement and order of the planets to be uncertain, citing also the testimony of Ibn Bajja <note>original: "Abubachefis," also known as Avempace.</note>. For while we know the Moon is lower than all others and is the "vestibule of heaven" because of its greater parallax (which necessarily indicates a smaller ratio of the Earth's radius to the sphere's radius), the true state of the other three—the Sun, Venus, and Mercury—is uncertain. Likewise, it is certain that these four stars are closer to us than the other three (Mars, Jupiter, Saturn), but reason does not demonstrate the order of those three among themselves. Therefore, since general conclusions depend on an order of this kind, the consequences rest first on a falsehood, and even if it were true, on an uncertainty. One may object the same regarding the signs of the zodiac, since (as we have sufficiently demonstrated) there is either no starting point in the zodiac, or four equal ones. Having spoken of the first type of argumentation, they also try to prove things by "parabolic similarity" <note>Metaphorical or symbolic analogy.</note>: the tenth house lies open at the high summit of heaven, while the fourth is hidden

<column-break/>

in the depths of the earth. Since more is known by everyone about their mother than their father, they claim it is fitting that the mother be judged through the tenth house and the father through the fourth. This method is so flawed it requires no refutation other than its own title. For whatever arguments are sought from these similarities are not only unworthy of philosophers who teach, but are not even fit or useful for logicians in dispute; indeed, they are not even suitable for the persuasions of rhetoricians. They are empty poetic fancies that display a sense of play rather than the proper authority of any serious proof. I was saying that they argue as mathematicians when they poorly turn the sound decrees of mathematics to their own predictions—such as the divisions of the zodiac into signs, signs into parts, and <margin>Third type, Fourth type, Fifth type.</margin> parts into minutes which we mentioned above. Likewise, when certain signs are called "straight" and others "oblique" by astronomers because of the unequal time they take to rise, the astrologers transfer this to the nature of "straightness" or "obliquity" in human character. They gather from astrological principles whenever they make one astrological dogma the starting point for confirming another. They use dialectics <note>Formal logic.</note> if they ever assume common and probable propositions from nature or first philosophy—but this is extremely rare. I do not remember ever reading a reason among them that carried the weight of logical probability.

---

### Chapter V. Arguments derived from metaphorical similarity, by which the properties they assign to the "houses" are refuted.

We have spoken in general; now let us descend to recounting the fables in detail (for I would more truly call them that than arguments) by which they asserted the properties of the "houses," beginning with those taken from the position and conditions of the signs. There is an argument from metaphorical similarity of this sort: a father loves his sons, and the fifth house has a "friendly" radiation because it looks upon the ascendant <note>original: "horoscopo," the 1st house.</note> through a triangle <note>A "trine" aspect (120 degrees), considered harmonious.</note>; therefore, the fifth house signifies children. So that we may show whether this method of arguing—which is clearly ridiculous—is correctly gathered as they contend: they say the first house signifies the newborn himself because he comes forth from darkness into light. Likewise, the ascendant—behold the metaphorical similarity—is also the reason why the same house represents "short journeys," such as when one goes from one district of a city to another, or from the city to the suburbs, or from a house to the open space just outside the walls. For they want the cause of these movements also to be in the stars, as portended by the disposition of the first house, as Bonatti <margin>Bonatti</margin> <note>Guido Bonatti, a famous 13th-century Italian astrologer.</note> says. Furthermore, let us see if the similarity holds in the remaining houses. The property of the second house <margin>Zael the Israelite,</margin> is over wealth; because, they say, nothing is closer to a man than his wealth. Therefore, being attached to the first house, the second house will signify riches. This is a "necessary" reason for those who value nothing more than riches, but in truth, many things are closer and more internal to a man: for instance, the gifts of mind and body, wisdom and health. Therefore, these should have been signified by the second house rather than the sixth or ninth. What of the fact that among external things, parents, wives, friends, children, and glory are preferred to money? These are more important and "closer," except perhaps to one class of men who call themselves astrologers. Then, why does the same house also denote letters <note>written correspondence.</note>, as Sahl ibn Bishr <note>original: "Zael israelita," a 9th-century Jewish astrologer and mathematician.</note> says, unless perhaps in the horoscopes of scribes, to whom the stylus and writing tablets are always attached? Now let us proceed to the rest. They want brothers to be indicated by the third house; for the fifth, we mentioned the reason for children...

<summary>Pico critiques the lack of consensus among astronomers regarding the physical order of the planets and mocks the "metaphorical" logic astrologers use to assign meanings to the twelve houses, such as linking wealth to the second house simply because it is "close" to the self.</summary>
<keywords>astronomy, planetary order, Ptolemy, Averroes, Maimonides, astrological houses, metaphorical similarity, Guido Bonatti, Sahl ibn Bishr, Jabir ibn Aflah</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s systematic dismantling of astrological theory. Having questioned the physical order of the planets on the previous page, he now turns his critique toward the "houses" of the horoscope—the twelve divisions of the sky that astrologers use to predict specific life areas like siblings, children, health, and death. He mocks the internal contradictions and arbitrary logic used by various authorities to assign meanings to these divisions.</meta>

# AGAINST THE ASTROLOGERS, BOOK X.

<margin>
Ptolemy
Ibn Ridwan
Porphyry
</margin>
The logic regarding brothers is similar because the third place is joined to the ascendant by a hexagonal aspect <note>original: "exagona radiatione." In astrology, a "hexagonal" or sextile aspect occurs when two points are 60 degrees apart, traditionally considered a harmonious or "friendly" alignment.</note>. Since a hexagonal coupling is friendly, but a triangular one <note>A "trine" aspect, 120 degrees apart.</note> is better, the latter is given to children (whom we love more) and the former is given to brothers. For the same reason, they say the eleventh place belongs to friends, because you look upon it likewise with a hexagonal aspect from the ascendant. But I ask them: why will the ninth place not signify children, since it also "falls" <note>A technical term for a "cadent" house, which astrologers often viewed as weak or declining.</note>? I ask again: which is better, the third or the eleventh? A father, by the same reasoning, would prefer the eleventh because the third "falls." Why then was the third house not assigned to friends and the eleventh to brothers? Unless, perverting the order of nature, they think friends should be preferred over brothers.

That point about children is further disturbed by another rule: for they say parents are judged by the fourth house. But between the fourth and the ascendant is a square aspect <note>original: "tetragonus aspectus," a 90-degree angle, traditionally considered a source of tension or conflict.</note>, than which no judge of enmity is greater. How then do they connect the newborn and his children with a "friendly" radiation, yet connect that same newborn with his own parents through an "unfriendly" one? Furthermore, it pleases Ptolemy, all the Greeks, and Ibn Ridwan <note>original: "Auenrodan," a 11th-century Egyptian astrologer and physician.</note> that children should be judged by the tenth place rather than the fifth. Porphyry proves this is right because he believes souls are sent down into bodies from that point. <margin>The descent and ascent of souls.</margin> But we can oppose Porphyry’s fables with another fable: for it is claimed that souls glide downward through the sign of Cancer and ascend through Capricorn. However, Cancer is a northern sign which, according to Ptolemy, corresponds to the "bottom of the earth" <note>The Imum Coeli or 4th house cusp.</note>, not the top. Yet they also begin predictions about children from the fourth and eleventh houses equally.

<margin>
Al-Qabisi
Andragazar
Vellius
Adla
</margin>
What about the fact that Al-Qabisi <note>original: "Alchabitius," a 10th-century Arab astrologer.</note> and the Hebrew Andragazar want messengers to belong to the fifth house? And they add what Vellius says: that it includes rumors, news, and the fame that remains after one’s ashes. And what Adla writes: clothing. By what reasoning is this? They provide none. It is truly irrational that the sixth place—which he calls <margin><term>apraktos</term></margin><term>apraktos</term> <note>original: "απρακτον," a Greek term meaning "idle," "ineffective," or "unproductive."</note>, as if you were to say torpid, ceasing, sluggish, or ineffective—they attribute to servants, whose labor and industry nonetheless nourish the leisure and laziness of their masters. <margin>Opposition to the mockery of Ibn Ridwan.</margin> But look at the "most beautiful" reason Ibn Ridwan <note>original: "Auenrodan."</note> gives for this dogma: "The seventh place," he says, "signifies equals, but subjects are removed from equals (these are his own words) by as much as the sixth house is removed from the seventh." Therefore, they designated the sixth as the house of subordinates. This is what he says—statements that should be laughed at rather than refuted, lest we be too heavily rebuked by Aristotle for wasting time on them.

For regarding what they say about the seventh signifying "equals," see how little truth and consistency they themselves find there. For they refer to this same house a wife, partners, and open enemies—and what is more combative than these? <margin>Abraham Ibn Ezra.</margin> But Abraham <note>Abraham Ibn Ezra, a famous 12th-century Jewish scholar and astrologer.</note> defends it in this manner: since the seventh place is opposite the first, it signifies lawsuits and wars; but because it also supports the rising horoscope <note>The 1st house.</note>, it signifies a wife. Finally, because the time of its descent <note>Setting in the West.</note> is equal to the time of the ascensions of the first place—which is a kind of agreement—it therefore signifies equals and partners. Thus everything can be "confirmed" easily, since there is nothing which cannot be imagined as similar or dissimilar to something else by some argument of this kind. Where does such logic not succeed, if symbols for opposite things are placed in the same spot as if they agreed? But they "agree," he says, for this reason: because the times of emerging in the ascendant and falling in the west are equal. I admit that is well said—if you also concede that, by the same example, water is similar to fire, since water possesses as many degrees of coldness as fire has of heat. For I think they are perhaps as opposed (let it not be said 

<column-break/>

too scrupulously) as descent and ascent, or heat and cold. <margin>Ptolemy.</margin> Does not a wife more certainly belong to the second house, being always next to the man and succeeding him as almost his equal? And especially since they want one sign to be male and the other female, for as Ptolemy says, women are attached to men. <margin>Vellius.</margin> But let them also give a reason why the same place signifies thieves and fugitives (as Vellius pleases), and also purchases and sales, and what others claim are "moderately long journeys." <margin>Guido Bonatti.</margin> Then there is what Bonatti <note>original: "Bonatus," a prominent 13th-century Italian astrologer.</note> writes: that it signifies the worship of pure divinity and the foreknowledge of the future.

Surely death was more rightly assigned to this place than to the eighth, since one descends here equally from light into darkness, just as one goes from darkness into light in the ascendant. <margin>Ibn Ezra.</margin> But it did not please him, says Ibn Ezra <note>original: "Auenazra."</note>, because the descendant is "not unlike" the ascendant—namely, by such a similarity as that by which we just proved water to be similar to fire. <margin>Dorotheus.</margin> But Dorotheus also judged death from this place rather than the eighth, observing the "lord" of that house for the purpose. 

Let them likewise answer why the eighth place signifies wars according to <margin>Abu 'Ali, Al-Khayyat.</margin> Abu 'Ali, and why Al-Khayyat <note>original: "Alchainil."</note> says it signifies the stewardship of a villa. Others want usury here; they even say inheritances are foreseen from this spot. I do not see how the heir and the dead man "agree." It would be better, then, if the eighth house judged death and the ninth signified inheritance, as it follows the eighth. <margin>Ibn Ezra.</margin> But Ibn Ezra says inheritances are related to the eighth because it corresponds proportionally to the second house, to which wealth belongs. This is that "harmony of opposite things" that I have already laughed at so often. For what similarity will there be in opposite places besides their dissimilarity? If they always spoke of them as if they were similar, the error might perhaps be forgiven; but now they treat them as similar, now as most dissimilar, and indeed as true opposites—evidently just to help themselves out of a logical hole.

Thus, locations are taken as if they were contraries: while we are nourished and preserve life in the second and fifth houses, the eighth signifies death and exile. Yet soon, that same eighth house signifies inheritances and wealth, as if it were similar and related to the second. Truly, those who die *make* heirs; they do not *become* them—unless perhaps they become heirs of heaven, which certainly is not subject to the physical sky <note>Pico is making a philosophical point: the human soul (heir to heaven) is not governed by the material stars.</note>. There would be other things to object to, but I fear that by refuting such trifles, I too might become a trifler. <margin>Wittily said.</margin>

What they say about the ninth house cannot be passed over, for it gives the reader so much to laugh at that he may be relieved from the boredom of their wordiness. The ninth house, they say, signifies long journeys. Listen to the reason: because the Sun, placed in the tenth house, moves by descending toward the ninth. <margin>Ibn Ezra.</margin> Ibn Ezra wrote this in the first and second books of his *Book of Reasons*. This is a work where there is entirely more need for laughter than for logic <note>original: "chachinnis potius quam syllogismis."</note>, as if the Sun were not moving from one place to another in *all* houses! And what if the Sun descends with that motion? I suppose the ninth house then will not signify journeys by which we climb mountains and high places? For who would not joke when arguing with such ridiculous people? 

Add also that fable about the twelfth house: that animals upon which we ride are signified by it because it is "joined" to the ascendant whenever the same sign extends through both houses. Elsewhere they say that darkness and prisons are portended through the same place because it is "most distant" from the ascendant. Thus they measure everything with as little memory as truth. For if they say that place is joined to the horoscope when the same sign occupies both seats, but disjoined when the signs are different, it follows that the house should not *always* indicate both riding animals and prisons; indeed, never both at once, but only when the same...

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s critique of the "houses" or domiciles of the planets.
