### NINTH DISPUTATION

...winter cold. Therefore, **Libra** is ill-suited to **Venus**, for while it is defined by many as hot, it is defined by all as moist. I am not a little amazed at **Ptolemy** <margin>Ptolemy</margin> for saying these signs suit Venus because they are, so to speak, highly generative and fertile. For while this might be said of **Taurus**, it can in no way be said of **Libra** <note>Libra is an autumnal sign associated with the "falling" of nature, while Taurus is a spring sign of growth.</note>. In what way does the logic hold for **Jupiter**? He has no commonality with **Pisces** and **Sagittarius**. If the time of year is judged by those signs, one ends the winter and the other is the end of autumn. Therefore, the former will resist Jupiter through coldness, and the latter through dryness—though even the moisture of Pisces does not match the vital, life-giving moisture of Jupiter.

Ptolemy refers to this harmony by saying that both of these signs produce winds and possess generative power; therefore, he claims Jupiter, a temperate planet, resonates with them. In refuting these points, I would think I was performing a useless task, were it not that Ptolemy—whose authority can easily deceive the unlearned—had put them forward. Otherwise, these claims are like things that scholars sometimes say in jest to one another: "They stir up the winds, therefore they are like Jupiter." <margin>Ibn Ridwan: On the delusions of the astrologers.</margin> **Ibn Ridwan** <note>original: "Aueroadan." Likely Ali ibn Ridwan, a medieval Egyptian astrologer and commentator on Ptolemy.</note> provides a reason: because Jupiter presides over the generation and seeds of living things, and their vapors and breaths are somewhat similar to winds. O, what marvelous wisdom, by which even dry things can be defended as similar to moist ones! For philosophers (unless I am mistaken) make all winds dry, contrary to the nature of generation, which is entirely moist.

They also call these signs fertile because when the **Sun** is placed in them, seeds sprout and things arise. Oh, if only they could have attributed this to human semen; it would have been much more fitting for them to take it from **Aries**. But they could not give Aries to Jupiter because **Mars** had already occupied it—though entirely by injustice. For what does Mars have to do with the beginning of spring? His parched dryness shares nothing with the warmth and prolific, generative moisture of that season. With equal audacity, he seized **Scorpio** with no right at all—a sign that is clearly cold and autumnal. Therefore, if we follow this logic, the partition of the houses is hardly fair.

Let us examine other reasons taken from the configurations of the luminaries <note>The Sun and the Moon.</note> and the number of the spheres. But since they gather these by their relationship to the houses of the luminaries, we must first examine the reasoning by which the houses of the luminaries themselves are established. <margin>Ptolemy’s Logic.</margin> This is the sort of reasoning that Ptolemy brings forward: **Cancer** and **Leo**, out of the twelve signs, turn most toward the north and come closest to our zenith; for this reason, they were given to the two greatest and principal stars—that is, the luminaries. Leo was given to the Sun because it is a masculine sign; Cancer to the Moon, as it is feminine. First, the assumption is false: for the signs closest to us are Cancer and **Gemini**, not Cancer and Leo. Secondly, even if it were true, what logic dictates that signs closer to us should suit the greater stars? The ancients could have said this by the analogy that those planets are also closer to us. But Ptolemy cannot say this, for he places the Sun in the middle of all the planets. Or was it done because the Sun heats more in Leo? But it has been said many times that this happens because of its position, not the property of the sign. Thus, for other nations, the Sun does in Libra what it does for us in Leo. If the powers of the other stars were so spread out in truths and reasons that we had experience of solar heat, we would find the same for the rest as for the Sun: that we are more affected by them when they approach Leo than when they are found far from us in other signs. Does the Sun harmonize with Leo for other reasons? Certainly, because it is a hot and dry sign, and also masculine—but this is not unique

<column-break/>

to Leo; it is common to Aries and Sagittarius. There remains one condition mentioned by that most serious author, **Abu Ma'shar** <note>original: "Aboasar," the influential Persian astrologer Albumasar.</note>. <margin>Abu Ma'shar's logic.</margin> For just as he says the Sun is the middle of the planets, so Leo is the middle sign of summer. Unless he tied it together with this logic, I would not have conceded that **Phoebus** <note>The Sun.</note> is better hosted by Leo than by any other beasts of the sky. But Abu Ma'shar—truly the protector and sweet glory of the astrologers—convinced me, for he thought of a most beautiful thing regarding the Moon's kinship with **Taurus** as well. Ptolemy, however, cited distance, saying that Cancer is the feminine sign closest to Leo. <margin>Another reason for Cancer.</margin> Not content with this, Abu Ma'shar added another reason: that Cancer signifies the beginnings of things for the Moon. Let Cancer be the beginning of summer—who would not concede to this demonstration?

**Ibn Ridwan** <margin>Ibn Ridwan</margin> did not see this, using another reason: that the Moon's house is rightly placed next to the Sun's house because the Moon always follows the Sun. But he should see how this might be more rightly said of **Venus** and **Mercury**, whose houses nature made closest to the Sun—if we believe Ptolemy, whose interpreter is the Ibn Ridwan we cited.

However, let these be the houses of the luminaries. What logic does Ptolemy bring for distributing the others? Primarily, that the houses of the "evil" stars, such as Mars and **Saturn**, should behold the houses of the luminaries with a hostile aspect <note>original: "inimica radiatione," referring to planetary aspects like squares or oppositions.</note>, while the houses of the "good" ones, like Jupiter and Venus, should be friendly, and Mercury should be placed closest to them. Thus, Aries and Scorpio were rightly given to Mars as a square aspect <note>original: "quadrangulares," a 90-degree angle, traditionally considered stressful.</note> to Cancer and Leo. Saturn was given **Capricorn** and **Aquarius**, which are opposite to them. Jupiter was given the trine signs <note>original: "triquetra," 120-degree angles, considered harmonious.</note>, Pisces and Sagittarius. Venus was given the sextile signs <note>original: "exagona," 60-degree angles, considered friendly</note>, Libra and Taurus. Mercury was given the closest ones, Gemini and **Virgo**.

But neither is the assumption true, nor is the conclusion correctly drawn from the assumptions. <margin>Refutation.</margin> For we say a house is rationally established as one in which a planet is well-situated when placed there. But the square aspect of those signs is equally harmful to Mars and the Sun; likewise, the opposition is harmful to Saturn, both because of the adversity of the opposition and because of retrogradation. If what Ptolemy himself teaches is true—that all planets are fortunate at that distance from the Sun in which their houses are distant from the Sun’s house (which the Greeks call <term>idiotropia</term> <note>original: "υδϱοποπιαμ" (likely a corruption of idiotropia), meaning a planet's specific solar phase or individual relationship to the Sun's light.</note> and the Arabs call <term>al-mugea</term> <note>An Arabic astrological term for a planet's specific distance from the Sun.</note>)—it would follow that Saturn opposite the luminaries and Mars square to them are "fortunate." This contradicts the opinion of all astrologers, who decree great misfortunes and calamities from such configurations.

Finally, it is evident that the conclusion does not match the principle. For when they say these or those houses are trine or square, they take it in this way: they are compared to Leo for those signs that follow it in order toward Capricorn, and to Cancer for those in reverse order toward Aquarius. Thus, one half is called the Sun's dominion and the other the Moon's. Otherwise, the houses of Venus could be called both square and trine, since Libra is square to Cancer and Taurus is square to Leo; and the houses of Mars would be trine, since Scorpio is trine to Cancer and Aries is trine to Leo. Therefore, the collateral house should be compared to the house of each luminary as if located under that star's jurisdiction. If this is done, it will be found most false that the houses of Saturn are opposite the luminaries, as Ptolemy says; for neither is Aquarius opposite Cancer, nor is Capricorn opposite Leo. Therefore, no one would say they are the houses of Saturn because they face the luminaries diametrically, but rather because they hold the sixth place from the Sun or the eighth from the Moon—which Ibn Ridwan also confesses. <margin>Ibn Ridwan: Logic by the number of spheres.</margin> Another reason is taken from the number of the spheres: once Cancer and Leo are defined, the planets closest to the Sun and Moon in the order of the spheres are given the next...

He specifically mocks the logic used by Ptolemy, Abu Ma'shar, and Ibn Ridwan to justify the geometric relationship between planetary houses and the Sun and Moon.</summary>

# AGAINST THE ASTROLOGERS, BOOK 10

The closer <term>houses</term><note>The "houses" or "domiciles" are the zodiac signs where a planet is said to be most "at home" and powerful.</note> were assigned: thus they establish that **Mercury** is given **Gemini** on one side and **Virgo** on the other; then follow those of **Venus**; then those next to **Mars**; then **Jupiter**; and finally **Saturn**. We have already declared that all these arguments, derived from the sequence of the celestial spheres, are false; and even if they were true, they would still be uncertain. Rightly, therefore, **Abraham Ibn Ezra** <margin>Ibn Ezra</margin> <note>original: "Auenazra"</note> says in his second book of *Reasons*: "I have searched in the books of the wise concerning the signs for the reasons for the houses, and I found nothing good in them; they turn only to the reliability of experience." So says he. In this book, we shall dismantle their reasons, and in the next, we shall dismantle the "experiences" of the astrologers.

### Chapter X. The reasons for the Faces and Bounds have already been rejected.

<columns>2</columns>
<margin>Division of the faces.</margin>
The <term>Faces</term> <note>Also known as "Decans," these are three 10-degree segments within each zodiac sign.</note> of the planets, which everyone uses, are similarly divided according to the sequence of the celestial orbs. For when they decree the first parts of **Aries**, they give them to the master of that house; they give the following parts to the following planets according to the order of their positions and spheres: namely, the first to the **Sun**, the second to **Mars**, the third to **Venus**, and so on
<margin>Another division of the Indians.</margin>
thereafter. The **Indians** <note>Meaning Hindu astrologers.</note> gave the first face to the master of the house, and the other two to the masters of the signs in the same <term>triplicity</term> <note>A group of three signs belonging to the same element (Fire, Earth, Air, or Water).</note>. But since we have already sufficiently refuted the triplicities and the arguments based on the number of the orbs, there is no need for new arguments against such theories. Regarding the <term>Bounds</term> <note>Also called "Terms," these are specific degree-ranges within a sign assigned to different planets.</note>, they disagree so much that they have produced five different opinions on them; thus, the reasoning of one is argued against and mocked by the other. Indeed, they are all so weak and infirm that everyone changes their own "boundaries" by some new law and invades the territory of others. From the order of the triplicities, the **Chaldeans** organized their bounds so that the signs of the triplicity were divided similarly. The method of partition was that the master of the triplicity occupied the first parts, then the ones following who have power over the subsequent signs of the triplicity, with the numbers always decreasing from eight to four.
<margin>The Egyptians of Ptolemy.</margin>
The **Egyptians**, as **Ptolemy** objects against them, observe no consistency in their method: sometimes they look to the triplicities, sometimes to the "kings," sometimes to the "heads of the household," beginning occasionally with those who possess no authority in the sign—such as starting with **Mercury** in **Capricorn**. Ptolemy approves of another division, the reasoning for which anyone may readily read in the first book of the *Apotelesmaton* <note>Ptolemy's *Tetrabiblos*.</note>. However, it depends on the masters of the house, the <term>exaltation</term> <note>The sign where a planet is said to be at its highest functional strength.</note>, and the triplicity. Yet Ptolemy should not have approved of it unless he wished to contradict himself, since the author of that division prefers the exaltation to the triplicity, and the triplicity to the house. Ptolemy, however, prefers the house above all else, and puts the exaltation last—which in that other division is preferred above everything. The Indians divide the masculine signs similarly through all things, and the feminine signs likewise 
<margin>Afotol.</margin>
by the same example; but in both cases, no reason for the example is known. **Afotol** <note>A reference to a source or author in the medieval tradition.</note> even gave "terms" to the luminaries (the Sun and Moon), and to each planet an equal number of parts: the first to the master of the house in the "order of the prophets," and the rest to the others. Since we have already removed this foundation—as well as the houses, exaltations, and triplicities—or proved them to be uncertain, every reason for defining the "Bounds" collapses (if indeed any such bounds are even granted to exist). Furthermore, even if the truth about triplicities, houses, and heights were discovered, it would still not be proven that the bounds should be decreed in this way rather than that. This is the source of the variety of opinions: while one way seemed more probable to some, another seemed so to others.

<column-break/>

<margin>Aristotle makes seven parts of the body. Nicomachus, ten. A medical note.</margin>
...they derive their origin from a mocked-up order of numbers: namely, that the first sign is placed over the first part of the body, the second over the second, and the third over the third. However, they also err in this partition: not so much because they make Aries the first of the signs—treating such an ambiguous (not to say false) thing as an established fact—as because there is no reason to persuade us that the body should be divided into exactly twelve parts, limb by limb. **Aristotle** made seven parts; **Nicomachus** made ten. Let the astrologers explain why they give twelve! We see a rather absurd thing: they force the shoulders, arms, and hands into a single part subject to one sign, yet they subject the feet, shins, knees, and thighs—four large parts—to four separate signs. Furthermore, if one were to make such a distribution, hot signs should have been compared to hot parts, and cold to cold, rather than just the second sign to the second part and the third to the third. One should observe the shared qualities of nature rather than a mere counting of position and order. Perhaps they would not be laughed at for subjecting the feet to **Pisces**—the only creature among the celestial signs that lacks feet! Doctors should therefore be careful; for if they are occasionally persuaded by this futile dogma, they might fear to lance a vein in the arms if the situation requires it, simply because the Moon is traveling through **Gemini**, since Gemini supposedly rules the arms. They should not delay a life-saving remedy because they are led by a vain superstition. Neither **Hippocrates** nor **Galen**,
<margin>The studies of all doctors dissent from this.</margin>
nor **Avicenna**, nor **Paulus**, nor **Oribasius** <note>Ancient and medieval medical authorities.</note> did this themselves, nor did they command others to do it. Nor did those who, in our own time (as we have said elsewhere), have practiced this art successfully and prudently. Therefore, let all insane superstition of this kind cease. If it is proven to have no reason, it can have no strength of experience. This is both because no truth harmonizes with a lie, and because of the many things we shall prove in the following book, and because of the contradiction among those who propose these things. For **Ibn Ezra** gives the testicles to **Sagittarius**; **Abu Ma'shar** gives them to
<margin>Abu Ma'shar. Alchabitius. Porphyry.</margin>
**Scorpio**; **Al-Qabisi** gives the diaphragm (which in Latin is the *septum transversum*) to **Virgo**. **Porphyry** gives the belly to **Leo**, which the Arabs give to **Virgo**. There are those who give the knees to **Sagittarius**, which both Arabs and Latins usually give to **Capricorn**. **Eleazar**
<margin>Eleazar.</margin>
**of Worms** <note>original: "Heliazer garnozensis"</note>, a Hebrew man, in his *Book on the Soul*, assigns the hands and feet to **Cancer**; yet others give the hands to **Gemini** and the feet to **Pisces**. Others subject the legs and feet to **Libra**, though for a different reason than for Cancer: for they say the legs are like Libra (the Scales) because in walking they are raised and lowered like a balance. Others say no such thing of Libra, but give the legs to **Aquarius**, the feet to **Pisces**, and subject the buttocks, kidneys, and loins to **Libra**. Eleazar says the bile corresponds to **Scorpio** and nature to
<margin>Eleazar.</margin>
**Sagittarius**, but others give the genitals to **Scorpio**. Now, if anyone says that astrologers have observed that a blade should never be brought to a limb when the Moon is sitting in its sign, I reply: first, in such uncertainty as to which sign is said to rule which limb, no constant and confessed experience can be had. Nevertheless, however it may happen, a wise man has observed the opposite. For
<margin>Nicole Oresme.</margin>
**Nicole Oresme**, a grave philosopher and mathematician, writes that he had often seen bloodletting performed healthily in the foot when the Moon was in **Pisces**, and likewise in the arms when it was traveling through **Gemini**.

<meta>This page continues Pico’s systematic dismantling of the "proofs" astrologers use to justify the qualities of the zodiac signs. He moves from the logic of planetary "houses" to the physical imagery of the constellations and then initiates a sharp critique of Ptolemy’s physical theories regarding the planets.</meta>

# OF THE DISPUTATIONS

<margin>The first type of proof.</margin>
These arguments are applied absolutely: they are taken from a threefold type of proof. The first is derived from an affinity with the planets, which has already been refuted. The second is from the figure of the animal for which it is named. The third is from the effects produced by the Sun when it is positioned under them. They argue from affinity with the planets when they make the nature of a sign the same as the planet that rules it. For example, when they say **Aries** signifies the hiding places of thieves and wicked men because it is the <term>house</term><note>The "house" or "domicile" is the sign where a planet is traditionally said to be most powerful.</note> of **Mars**, who signifies that kind of person. They argue from the work of the Sun when they designate signs as "moveable," "fixed," or "common," according to whether the Sun, in those signs, changes the season, stabilizes it, or tempers it with a mixed quality.

<margin>The second.</margin>
Regarding the figure of the signs, they say some breathe mild manners into those being born, while others breathe wild manners, according to the image they all bear. For instance, **Aquarius**, **Gemini**, and **Virgo** [are human]; others are beasts, like **Leo**, **Taurus**, and **Capricorn**. Likewise, they say some are beautiful and others deformed. They call "beautiful" any signs conceived in human likeness—except for **Aquarius**, because it is the lodging of the aged **Saturn**, as if an old and deformed man could not either need or take pleasure in a beautiful lodging. Similarly, they call those with a brute likeness "semi-vocal" and the human ones "vocal"; those resembling aquatic creatures they call "mute," because that genus of living things has no voice. **Rufus** <note>Possibly Rufus of Ephesus, a 1st-century physician.</note> also notes that aquatic signs are very fertile, while human ones are sterile. They place the rest in a middle condition, following the nature of the living creatures whose images they are believed to be. The arguments we discussed above have sufficiently overturned these modes of positioning.

<margin>These things are refuted. The third.</margin>
When they make conjectures about the "domiciles" and character of a planet, they argue from astrological principles which we refuted a little while ago. When they argue from the work of the Sun, we have shown how much they either deceive or are deceived; for the nature of a sign should not be judged by what the Sun does while located in that sign. That effect does not come from the nature of the sign, but from the Sun's position and its distance from the Earth. Furthermore, what happens regarding the seasons and changes in the air is transferred by a most fallacious conjecture to other things. For example, they claim that because the moveable sign of **Aries** changes the season, it also makes the character of one born under it "moveable"—not persevering, and better suited for beginning things than finishing them. Not only do they errantly carry properties from the quality of the air to diverse events and characters, but they imagine that what is observed in the Sun also happens in other stars. For example, why should we think the **Moon** placed in **Aries** would do the same as the **Sun**, which, when placed in **Aries**, causes the spring equinox and stirs up lightning and thunder? They fall into no other error than referring things to the nature of the sign that actually proceed from the Sun’s variety of position.

<margin>Where the images originated.</margin>
In the eighth book, we spoke abundantly about the figures of these images—how they are non-existent, vain, and fictional. They are not the works of God, but of men; they did not proceed from the reason of nature, but were fashioned by the recklessness of the poetic mind. As has been most truly said, astrologers are never more false than when they elicit the properties of signs from these images. As we demonstrated widely above, images even in the <term>eighth sphere</term><note>The sphere of the fixed stars.</note> differ from the [zodiac] signs not only in position and movement but also in the dimension and quantity of their parts. Finally, with a dull, futile, and lazy sluggishness, they contradict themselves while seeking the condition of the same signs from both the work of the Sun and the image. For by common consent, the former qualities apply to the fixed signs, while the latter apply to the moveable ones.

<column-break/>

### Chapter XIII. Ptolemy is criticized for speaking of the planets as if they consisted of elements; the reasons of others who try to prove planetary qualities are likewise refuted.

So much for the reasoning regarding the signs, which are remarkably irrational; in the planets, one finds the same falsehood—indeed, a greater one, and greater recklessness. To show that **Ptolemy** philosophized poorly concerning errors, we previously pointed out those things by which he investigates the nature of the planets. For he speaks of them as if the planets consisted of <term>elements</term><note>The four elements: Earth, Air, Fire, and Water.</note> or the passions of elements. He discusses them as if they not only exchange heat or cold with each other but are also changed by the vapors of the Earth.

<margin>The words of Ptolemy.</margin>
The **Moon**, he says, is moist because, being nearest to the Earth, she becomes damp from the Earth's vapors rising up toward her. The star of **Saturn** is primarily cold and moderately dry; it is cold because it is positioned far from the Sun, and it grows dry because it is raised far above the vapors of the Earth. **Mars**, scorched by proximity to the Sun, is dried out. **Jupiter**, being in the middle between the cold of Saturn and the fervor of Mars, becomes temperate; but because he is carried above the hot spheres of Mars and the Sun, he primarily heats things. **Venus** is moist just like the Moon, for by the abundance of her light, she draws many of the Earth's vapors to herself; she also has the power of heating from the Sun, to which she is close. **Mercury** has the property of drying from the Sun, to which he is always attached, and the power of moistening from his proximity to the Earth and the border of the Moon. Thus Ptolemy reasons in the first book of the *Apotelesmaton* <note>original: "apotelesmaton"; better known as the "Tetrabiblos," Ptolemy's foundational work on astrology.</note>.

<margin>Note.</margin>
If he cannot be persuaded by the <term>Peripatetics</term><note>Followers of Aristotle, who believed the heavens were made of a "fifth element" (ether) and were not subject to earthly decay or qualities like "wet" and "dry."</note> that the heavens are free from these affections, he should at least understand from his own demonstrations that the Earth is too far from the Moon for Earthly vapors and breaths to reach her.

<margin>Learn physics.</margin>
Physicists believe these vapors are lifted no higher than sixteen <term>stadia</term><note>A stadium is roughly 600 feet; 16 stadia is about 2 miles, far below the reach of the Moon.</note> upward; they certainly do not reach the Moon, Venus, or Mercury intact. Furthermore, Venus should be more dry from her proximity to the Sun than moist from the clouds of the Earth, since she is closer to the Sun than to the Earth; nor can the power of Earthly moisture be compared with the potency of the Sun. Add also that Mercury, being closer to the Earth and therefore more distant from the Sun [at times], should be more dry than moist. How then does he agree with himself, granting Venus a humidity equal to the Moon’s, given that Lunar fire is so close and heats so little that it is considered cold by many? And if Saturn is stiff with cold from being less distant from the Sun, would not the entire multitude of fixed stars, being even further from the Sun, be constricted by the sluggish ice of cold? Yet they pronounce many of them to be of a fiery nature. Therefore, Ptolemy's reasoning is not only false but inconsistent with itself—which often happens with false arguments. Others argue from the colors of the planets, a point Ptolemy also touched upon regarding Mars. These men say the philosophers lie when they think the elements have no part in color or taste. They claim the color of water is white and its taste is sweet; that the color of earth is dark and its taste bitter (though others deny this, contending it is sweet, for if it were bitter, the earth would sprout nothing). Then they confess fire has no taste but is red in color. They say air lacks both color and taste but admits various foreign colors. They say the planets have no tastes, but multiple colors, from which we can easily explore their nature. For they say the darkness in **Saturn** shows an Earthly property... and the redness in **Mars** is evidence of a fiery quality and red bile...

<summary>Pico refutes the symbolic and seasonal logic used to define zodiac signs and begins a physical critique of Ptolemy’s theory that planets are affected by Earthly vapors and elemental qualities.</summary>

->AGAINST THE ASTROLOGERS, BOOK X.<-

...to judge: that Venus, shining with saffron and white, is understood to be hot from the saffron and moist from the white; and since these qualities are not equal, they indicate a temperament of nature like a <term>sanguine condition</term><note>The "sanguine" temperament was one of the four humors in ancient medicine, associated with blood and a balance of heat and moisture.</note>. They make a similar conjecture about Jupiter. In the case of the Moon, they claim its whiteness shows moisture, while its touch of darkness shows it to be cold. The color of Mercury, they say, changes repeatedly: now appearing green, now dark, now turning to some other aspect; however, it most often favors a dark hue, which they would confirm belongs to earthly dryness. They reason in this way—quite beyond all reason—for colors follow the mixture of elements, and there is no such mixture in the celestial bodies. Nor does Aristotle say 
<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
that celestial things participate in color, except insofar as light is a kind of color. Moreover, even if color indicates some property of a mixture, light will not indicate the nature of a shining body, since a conjecture about color is based on how various colors are thought to emerge from a variety of mixtures. Therefore, since color is nothing other than the manifestation of light—more or less bright, emanating not from a compound but from a simple body—it can give us no indication of the nature of the illuminating body. Furthermore, there could be no certain investigation of the celestial bodies from their colors even if they were endowed with true colors, because of the intervention of such a vast space, which would further disturb our confidence in a color that appears in so many forms.
<margin>Plato.</margin>
I did not even wish to object to them by citing Plato, who writes in the *Phaedo* that the bodies of the stars we see are not the stars themselves, but certain reflections of rays in the air, mirroring a likeness to the star—just as fish living in the deep see not the stars themselves on the surface of the water, but images of the stars, or what I might call "radiant shadows." But whether we are looking at these reflections or the stars themselves, no one initiated into the sacred mysteries of philosophy is unaware that colors vary in a wondrous way through the intervention of multiform bodies. Finally, there is a doubt among 
<margin>Galen, Averroes.</margin>
physicians as to whether the powers and properties of herbs can be known from их smell, color, taste, and touch, as Galen thinks. Averroes demonstrated this to be false through both reasoning and experience. Furthermore, no one has ever suspected that we could attain this knowledge through color alone—I mean even of those things which we can keep under our eyes and observation for whole days, where neither movement, nor distance, nor a multitude of light interferes with our diligent study. Who, then, would listen to such a promise regarding the heavens? Even if the colors of those bodies were reported to us most truly—unmixed, sincere, and pure. The whiteness of lime is hardly surpassed by snow, yet there is a great deal of heat in lime, while in snow, by contrast, there is a great deal of cold.
<margin>The error of Avenrodan.</margin>
Moreover, <term>Avenrodan</term><note>Ali ibn Ridwan (c. 988–1061), an Egyptian Muslim physician and astrologer.</note> errs most impudently: he believes we are deceived by color in earthly things but not at all in celestial things, because earthly things are mixed from elements while celestial things are not. For this is exactly how we know that no faith should be placed in the colors regarding the nature of the heavens: because they are not mixed from elements. Color can only indicate the nature of a body insofar as it shows us the manner of its mixture. Besides (as we were just saying), the multitude of bodies in the intervening vast region cannot help but pervert and alter whatever colors might be imagined there; this is proven by the very variety of opinions born 
<margin>Various opinions on the colors of the planets.</margin>
concerning these colors. For <term>Aboasar</term><note>Abu Ma'shar (787–886), a leading Persian astrologer in the Abbasid court.</note> denies that the celestial colors of the planets are such as we described above, which were believed by those who judged the stars by their colors. Indeed, he believes the star of Saturn reflects the color of lead rather than one representing the darkness of the earth;

<column-break/>

nor is there whiteness in Jupiter, nor is brightness the specific property of Venus. Furthermore, if Mars is called hot because it is red, a red color ought to be much more attributed to the Sun, which is hotter than Mars. No one who is not blind would think the Moon is white. The accounts found in the records of the ancients in natural history concerning the colors of the planets seem somewhat different: there, Saturn is white, Jupiter is clear, and Venus is now falling when called <term>Lucifer</term><note>The "Light-Bringer," or the Morning Star.</note>, now shining when she has the name of the Evening Star. Mercury is described with radiant rays and the Moon with a mild color. As for the claim that Mercury varies in colors—and is therefore of a multiform and changeable nature—this arises from a deceptive appearance. For Mercury does not become this way itself; rather, because it is always seen very close to the horizon, the various vapors and moisture of the earth (as Ptolemy testifies) create "chameleon-like" appearances and represent the colors of the stars as wandering in many ways. Therefore, none of these stories about colors, says Aboasar in his commentary, is colored with the credit of probability—even though, as he says, the entire community of astrologers depends on them. Aboasar himself, rejecting the aforementioned reasons, thinks the nature of the planets can be known from the primary qualities they produce, as Ptolemy also advised. Thus, Saturn is found by experience to be the author of cold and dryness; for these qualities flourish in bodies when he is the 
<margin>Refutation of Aboasar's error.</margin>
ruler of the year. The same is observed of Mars and the others: whatever elementary affection each one influences in bodies. From these effects, the whole nature of the planet is conjectured. Since the works of cold and dryness of Saturn are hostile to life, Saturn is decreed an unlucky and <term>malefic</term><note>In astrology, a "malefic" planet is one thought to have a harmful influence, while a "benefic" one is helpful.</note> star. Mars is also called malefic because of its parching heat and immoderate dryness. On the other hand, Jupiter and Venus are said to be benefic stars because of their nature of heat and moisture, qualities by which life is preserved. He argues similarly for the others, referring everything to those four qualities: cold, moisture, heat, and dryness. But this kind of reasoning is ashamed of its own "experiments." For he does not prove by reason that Saturn produces effects of cold rather than heat (as those we just refuted were trying to do), but rather by "experience," as if it were a fact found by the evidence of the senses. This is considered utterly false by many philosophers who assert that no star is a producer of cold and dryness—as if it were even agreed among them which star is the worker of which quality! This is certainly ambiguous in the case of the Moon and Venus.
<margin>Abenzagel, Alchabitius, Aboasar, Ptolemy.</margin>
For both <term>Abenzagel</term><note>Abu al-Salt (c. 1067–1122), an Andalusian polymath.</note> and Alchabitius consider Venus to be cold; Aboasar, along with Ptolemy, thinks she is hot. Aboasar wants the Moon to be so. If an observation has been made, how can they disagree on it? Especially when there is such an ambiguity of opinions over choosing the "Lord of the Year," such that there are almost as many future "Lords" as there are astrologers to pronounce them.

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s systematic dismantling of the physical and philosophical foundations of astrology. # ->AGAINST ASTROLOGY, BOOK XII.<-

He [the astrologer] insists that Mercury is dry by its own nature and partakes more of the nature of earth than other planets. Therefore, if he follows his own principles, he ought to number it among the harmful planets. However, others disagree among themselves and especially with <margin>Aboafar.</margin> **Aboafar**; for a great many make the Moon, the Sun, and Mercury "middling" <note>Neutral or intermediate in influence.</note> between the harmful and the beneficial, whereas Aboafar makes them all beneficial. <margin>Heliodo. Paulus.</margin> **Heliodorus** and **Paulus** also count Mercury among the salutary stars. <margin>John A.</margin> **Ptolemy** makes the Moon salutary, but he makes Mercury and the Sun of a "middle" condition. Thus, this discord among them quite overturns their opinions and exposes the uncertainty of their art. Furthermore, if that supposition about the <term>primary qualities</term><note>The four basic building blocks of matter in ancient physics: heat, cold, moisture, and dryness.</note> were true, it would follow without controversy that six of the twelve celestial signs are unhappy and unfortunate—namely, all the fiery and all the earthy signs—since they abound in those qualities for which they accuse **Mars** and **Saturn** of being unfortunate. <margin>...chindu</margin> Indeed, nine signs rather than six would be unfortunate, since in the watery signs, they think a dryness exists alongside the coldness; even if there is moisture, it is not like that of the airy signs—which in **Jupiter**, **Venus**, and the "airy" planets is vital and prolific—but is instead aquatic and flowing. This is absurd for two reasons: first, the heavens, which are the most beneficial of all bodies, would be condemned in their greatest part; and second, "unhappy" signs would be the "houses" <note>The specific signs of the Zodiac where a planet was thought to be most powerful.</note> for "happy" stars. For instance, **Pisces** and **Sagittarius** are the houses of Jupiter, and **Taurus** is the house of Venus; yet these should be distributed according to a kinship of nature. Finally, if they call some planets "fortunes" and others "infortunes" because the vital primary qualities come from the former, while the corruptive and harmful ones come from the latter, they would achieve no more (to settle the matter most generously with them) than to say this happiness or unhappiness pertains only to the condition of the body, which is tempered and balanced by those primary qualities. But how will they defend deriving external and "accidental" successes from this? Unless those arguments we brought against that opinion above are incredibly weak. Lastly, even if all we have said amounted to nothing, there is no doubt that those who wish to explain the "influences" of the stars by these primary qualities act with too little skill and consideration. Yet every astrologer does this; even those who boast that they can provide "natural causes" for the dogmas of this art turn at last to nothing other than these elemental affections. But in truth, if there are any specific and particular "breathings" or influences of the stars, these do not follow such qualities, but rather the hidden and truly celestial properties of each star. <margin>...ple.</margin> In earthly things, people are also accustomed to refer to these hidden properties whenever things seem to rise above elemental nature (though still within the limits of a body). In such things, we sometimes see many gifts and virtues that do not arise from a mixture of elemental qualities but actually disagree with them. For example, <term>myrobalans</term><note>A type of dried fruit used in medieval medicine, thought to have astringent and life-extending properties.</note>, with their cold and dry temperament, would seem by their nature to lead more toward death than toward life; yet, by a privilege of a more secret nature, they are believed to have a wonderful efficacy for prolonging and refreshing life. <margin>...ole, Aboafar,</margin> Much more so should both Jupiter and Saturn, and all superior nature, be thought to influence us (if they influence us at all, as astrologers think), not through these qualities—even if one planet is judged cold and dry and another hot and moist—but through other hidden powers of their rays. Furthermore, their nature is better suited to this, since the works

<column-break/>

attributed to them by astrologers cannot, as we have demonstrated, be referred back to those elemental qualities and affections. If it is clear that they cannot be grasped by reason—which we have undertaken to prove in this place—there remains the path of experience, about which we shall dispute at length in the following book.

### Chapter XV. The reasons of astrologers regarding the lords of days and hours, and the years of the planets, are ineffective; and that astrologers often use circular demonstrations.

We have refuted every way in which they trust they can prove the universal properties of the planets: whether from the locations of the spheres and the position of the Earth, or from the colors of the stars, or from the influence of the four primary affections. There remain the arguments by which they gather certain more specific conditions of the planets; these are elicited either from parabolic similarity, or from astrological principles, or from the order of the spheres. From the spheres, for example, they derive the lordship of days and hours: for giving the first hour of the day to the Sun, for instance, they give the rest to the planets that follow in order from the position of the spheres. From this, the distribution of the days is born: the day is ascribed to that planet which happens to fall on the first hour of the day according to the preceding hourly division. These things are amply refuted by what was said above: where we declared how futile this mode of arguing is, how the order of the orbs is still placed in ambiguity, and how the "succession of command" in the heavens is a vain invention. Besides this, we can also ask the astrologers: what reason demonstrated the "first day" of all time to the **Chaldeans** and **Egyptians**, the authors of this superstition? For they cannot use the authority of the Mosaic Law unless they believe that they, along with every diviner, should be utterly exterminated according to that same law. <margin>Refutation</margin> They reason from astrological principles when they say some planet grants so many years of life because it possesses that many "bounds" <note>Subdivisions of a zodiac sign, each ruled by a different planet.</note> in the Zodiac. But what is taken from "bounds" is just as uncertain as what is to be proved from them regarding years. Even if what they claim about the bounds were true, there is, according to **Ptolemy**, no reason for the consequence: that the spans of our lives are determined by that number. They also often sin by using "circular proof," gathering the number of bounds from the number of years in one place, and in another place gathering years from the bounds. <margin>The beginning of the year. Why the Moon grants 108 and the Sun 120 according to [Aboafar].</margin> They start the year from **Aries** because it is the "first" of the signs; yet they usually show it is the first in a continuous circle because we begin the order of time from it. Likewise, they argue that the "second house" <note>The astrological house traditionally associated with wealth and possessions.</note> corresponds to Jupiter because he "makes and portends wealth," and that Jupiter "makes and portends wealth" because he corresponds to the second house. You will find many such examples in their books, but even far more ridiculous ones, especially if you happen upon the books of **Aboafar**. I was recently reading in his work that the Moon grants one hundred and eight years, <margin>Aboafar. Why the "minor years" of the Sun are 19.</margin> and the Sun grants one hundred and twenty. He says the Moon falls short of the Sun's life by twelve years because it has no power until it has been elongated from the Sun by twelve degrees. It is no wonder, then, that Aboafar boasts of having fully provided the "reason" for astrological dogma. Since nothing is so irrational that it does not seem like "reason" to him. There is equal insanity when they say the shorter years of the Sun are nineteen, because through this number the luminaries [Sun and Moon] are joined in their mean motion—where there is absolutely no...

...common: nothing is connected; nothing follows from what preceded it; yet they argue in this way: after this number of years, the Sun and Moon meet in <term>mean motion</term><note>The theoretical average speed of a celestial body, as if it moved in a perfect circle.</note>. Therefore, the Sun gives that same number of years when it gives the fewest: for it is just as if one were to say a man is born with two eyes, therefore he is also born from two parents. They use metaphorical analogy in this way; the Moon is the gate of heaven. Therefore it signifies the mouth: for the door is roughly the mouth of the house, and the mouth is the door for food and speech. Likewise, the beard pertains to the same star because, like the Moon, it is renewed time and again. Furthermore, the ears are subject to **Saturn**: because they hold the highest parts of the head, just as Saturn himself is highest in the heavens; for the same reason—namely, because he is the supreme planet—he produces tall men: although this does not fit his nature, since he is judged to be dry and cold. These are the reasons of the astrologers by which their celestial dogmas are supported: reasons I would call not arguments, but rather opportunities for erring or playing. When these are heard, the vanity of the dogma is as obvious as the firmness of truth usually becomes when heard. Therefore, it was better for them to cover these things with a veil or a chest, as if they were <term>mysteries</term><note>original: "orgia", referring to secret religious rites</note>, leaving behind a superstition of mystery; instead, while they wish to seem rational, they subscribe to their own accusation with their own hand by their own reasons: for hearing them is nothing other than understanding what led the astrologers into error.

<column-break/>

Whenever a star has first breathed upon anyone, it will be as uncertain to you as the unique condition of that primary matter is utterly unknown: but even if someone makes the <term>seminal hour</term><note>The moment of conception.</note> fatal, the astrologers themselves will not deny that the opportunity for observation would be far too hidden. But even granted that the time of birth is sufficiently observed: in what way would it be a reliable observation? If it has not been explored, as we have declared, how many and what celestial causes are involved: what form, what habit, what position can be determined with faith at every single moment? Then they can neither have the exact hour of birth from the "lord of the geniture" <note>The planet ruling the birth chart.</note> nor can they correct what is wrong by any method. Furthermore, if they fail in these things (and we have shown they always fail), the authority of the entire observation must necessarily fall: now, even if they do not fail in those matters, we shall demonstrate in the present book that no experiments can be made upon the heavens.

# JOHN PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA'S
## DISPUTATIONS AGAINST
### THE ASTROLOGERS. BOOK
### XI. BEGINS.

->Chapter one. From what has been proven so far, it is clear that astrology is not confirmed by experiments; then the same is proven by many reasons.<-

---

<margin>With what mask on their face do the astrologers dare to come out into the open?</margin>
<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'S' depicting a figure in a classical landscape with buildings in the background.</image-desc>If they could not reach the nature of the celestial bodies by reason—which we have demonstrated—could they do so by experience? And although they may be ignorant of why it happens, have they nonetheless learned through observations that it happens, so that if it cannot have the name of a "science" of astrology, it can at least have the prerogative of an "art" and a true tradition? Thus, they might also predict true things, whether this was achieved by logic or by experiments. For it does not matter for the purpose of divining, provided the result is achieved. Now, astrologers—like every miraculous art—usually defend themselves mostly under the title of experience: into which they retreat as if into an asylum whenever they speak or promise something beyond belief and beyond reason: thinking themselves immediately extricated from all the snares of all arguments if they say they have "experienced" it so. We shall therefore take away this refuge from them—which those who are more accustomed to speaking with their lips and hearing with their ears than with their heart think is something valid. For if anyone has explored and meditated upon what experience is: and by what ways it might be obtained regarding the influence of the stars, he will certainly not doubt that the peculiar powers and proper operations of the stars are as inscrutable to man by experiments as they are by reasons. And indeed, this can be clear enough from the preceding: since if there is either no fate from heaven, or if there is fate but it does not depend on the initial hour but on the kinship of matter: it is clear that no path is left for experiments,

<sig>dd</sig>

<column-break/>

Whenever a star has first breathed upon anyone, it will be as uncertain to you as the unique condition of that primary matter is utterly unknown: but even if someone makes the seminal hour fatal, the astrologers themselves will not deny that the opportunity for observation would be far too hidden. But even granted that the time of birth is sufficiently observed: in what way would it be a reliable observation? If it has not been explored, as we have declared, how many and what celestial causes are involved: what form, what habit, what position can be determined with faith at every single moment? Then they can neither have the exact hour of birth from the lord of the geniture nor can they correct what is wrong by any method. Furthermore, if they fail in these things (and we have shown they always fail), the authority of the entire observation must necessarily fall: now, even if they do not fail in those matters, we shall demonstrate in the present book that no experiments can be made upon the heavens. Let us grant, then, to the <term>genethliacs</term><note>Casters of birth charts.</note>: that they hold the hour of birth faithfully, and the state of the heavens at that hour as faithfully as possible; I ask by what way they think they have achieved knowledge of what the decree of heaven or such a constellation makes or signifies through experience? Since experience is gathered from multiple and often repeated observations of the same thing: but the same constellation, as the more learned prove, either never returns, or—as the ancients believed—it will not return except after many thousands of ages. Perhaps he might respond that partial constellations return and are repeated more often, even if the restoration of the whole and absolute constellation does not occur; therefore, they can obtain knowledge of those partial ones by repeated observations, from which, once experiments are collected, future things may be faithfully foretold. <margin>Exemplification.</margin> Let this be declared by an example. Someone is born with **Aries** on the horizon, the star of **Mars** placed therein, and **Saturn** occupying the seventh point. Then another will be born in his own way, with the rest of the birth chart dissimilar, but similar regarding Mars and Saturn: the astrologer will be able to make an observation of that part twice, even if not of the whole constellation. Since this happens more often, the more often repeated observation will create an "experiment." <margin>Refutation.</margin> Thus they perhaps defend themselves, but with little truth and little consistency even with their own principles. First, because the same partial constellation works entirely differently in another "whole"; second, because the substance of the entire decree does not come so much from the parts as from the whole: that is, from the harmony of all parts together, producing something peculiar and proper, which no part alone, nor even all of them together <note>Without the specific harmony of the whole.</note>, would produce. For the parts are one thing, and that which results from the proportion of the mixture of all is another. Such an observation, by which they collect their experiments, will therefore be imperfect. For that which is imperfect regarding the whole is in no way deceptive in considering the same part but not in the same whole. This reasoning has strength from no other place more than from the precepts of the astrologers themselves, who assert that everything happens because of the mixtures of the stars, and the lot of fate is produced not from their own individual powers but from the embrace of all of them together and the union of their society. Therefore, if in one or another birth you have seen the lord of the geniture distracted by calamities when Mars and Saturn looked at each other diametrically in the primary points: you will not be able to announce calamities as if by a completed experiment when the same happens elsewhere: since nothing prevents that constellation, under a different tempering of other stars, from combining in such a way that it either does no harm, or perhaps even produces something entirely different than it did in other births from...

<meta>catchword: "births from" (Latin: turis ex)</meta>

<summary>Pico begins Book XI by arguing that astrology cannot be based on experience because celestial configurations are so complex and rare that they never truly repeat. He refutes the idea that "partial" observations of planets like Mars or Saturn can lead to reliable predictions, as the influence of the whole sky always outweighs the individual parts.</summary>

# AGAINST THE ASTROLOGERS, BOOK XII.

## bb ij

...produced from the various mixtures of rays: so that if we agree with the astrologers that human affairs happen by fate, it could be pointed out here that experience daily discovers the birth-charts of the most unfortunate people to be the most "fortunate," and conversely, those of the fortunate to be most "unfortunate." This is because, although particular constellations might seem to portend good or bad luck based on past observations, the total harmony of the temperament itself—never before seen, unknown, and unexplored—can now produce something entirely different from what those stars portended elsewhere, either separately or in another mixture. Noticing this, the most ancient astrologers handed down the dogmas of this art in no other way than by explaining the singular birth-charts they themselves had observed in detail and comparing them to the eventual outcomes; thus, they judged not just what **Saturn** or **Jupiter** did, but what <margin>Maternus</margin> such an entire constellation had brought forth. <term>Maternus</term><note>Julius Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman lawyer and astrologer who wrote the *Mathesis*, a major astrological compendium.</note>, following the example of the Egyptians, attempted this in some way in the sixth book of his commentaries. However, <margin>Ptolemy</margin> <term>Ptolemy</term><note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century scholar whose *Tetrabiblos* became the foundational text for Western astrology.</note> accuses them of not reducing the art to a method and of pursuing an infinite and incomprehensible matter. Therefore, he turned himself toward explaining universal precepts and the simple powers of the stars, believing that once these were known, a <term>genethliacal</term><note>A practitioner of natal astrology, from the Greek "genethlialogia," the study of birth charts.</note> could finally judge the particular mixture by his own conjecture. But although <margin>Ptolemy is to be accused</margin> he rightly accuses the ancient astrologers, he himself is no less rightly to be accused. For those ancients saw correctly what needed to be done, but they erred in thinking that it was something that *could* be done; since it is infinite, it can be reduced to neither art nor method. Furthermore, there is no use for it: for that same constellation is never restored <note>original: "restituta", referring to the concept that the exact same planetary alignment never repeats perfectly.</note>. Thus Ptolemy, considering what *could* be done rather than what *ought* to be done, wandered too far if he thought true predictions could be made from such precepts. From this, perhaps, occurred what <margin>Avenazra</margin> <term>Avenazra</term><note>Abraham ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167), a Jewish polymath whose astrological works were highly influential in the Middle Ages.</note> writes: that the precepts of Ptolemy never agree with actual outcomes and experiments. But Ptolemy is less to be blamed for this because, as we showed in the second book, he clearly confessed that this art is based on opinion, conjecture, doubt, and deception. Therefore, with the <term>theme</term><note>The "thema" or layout of a horoscope.</note> brought into the open, let us press the astrologer. Here is something, O Astrologer, if the rest be granted to you, that is powerful and primary in producing effects: namely, the specific effect of the whole harmony, upon which the fortune of the newborn most properly depends. Since neither reason nor observation has given you knowledge of this, how can you explain the truth of fate? For you are deceived if you think the efficiency of the whole is nothing more than the collection of what the individual parts produce. This would be true only in things that are merely heaped together or adhering bodies or qualities; it is not so where they are mixed and dissolve into another form—which all astrology believes happens with the rays of the stars. Just as one has not experienced the property of <margin>Example</margin> <term>theriac</term><note>A famous ancient medicinal "all-cure" or panacea made of dozens of ingredients; its final effect was thought to be a unique emergent property different from its individual components.</note> who has merely observed the powers of the ingredients from which it is made, so too does he fail to understand what the present array of the heaven effects if he has only had experience of its parts separately at other times. For it is not only the relation of part to part—that is, star to star—but the state and habit of absolutely *all* stars among themselves that produces what is unique to the newborn. Just as the unique characteristics of an individual are not born from a mere confluence of accidents, but are the private lot of an incommunicable or peculiar substance. <margin>Reason</margin> What of the fact that they cannot even achieve knowledge of a single star through experiment? For nothing ever operates alone, but everything always works with others; by which not only is it such that

<column-break/>

any star can only be defined by its relationship to others, but it cannot in any way be discerned by knowledge separated from the others. For from the whole constellation, you will see the sequence of such a life and such outcomes arise; but since all stars are acting on all things, you will not be able to know which star was the author of which thing, unless you have first grasped the nature of each star separately, either by reason or some other way. And if you say you will observe in this way: that for those men you see having some similar fates, <margin>Solution</margin> you argue that the event arises primarily from that part where their charts agree, and that this is established by frequent observation. <margin>Confutation</margin> I will answer that this way of conjecturing is far too deceptive. First, because a similar state of a star can produce a different thing in a different mixture, and a dissimilar state can produce the same thing. Second, because the same lot might not have the same cause, since in the opinion of astrologers, there are almost innumerable causes in heaven for the same effect. All of this will be clearer with an example: **Peter** is born with **Jupiter** placed in **Pisces**; **Paul** is born with Jupiter in a similar position; their remaining constellations being entirely dissimilar, they live with a disparate lot—in character, talent, and health—sharing only an equal fortune in accumulating wealth. From this, is it permitted to conjecture that Jupiter, placed in a fertile spot in Pisces, is the giver of riches? Certainly not. For that which was common in their fate—namely, the abundance of riches—could have come from different celestial causes, not from common ones. If in one's birth the lord of the <term>horoscope</term><note>The "dominus horoscopi" or the planet ruling the sign currently rising on the eastern horizon.</note> bestowed power upon the Sun occupying a <term>cardinal point</term><note>The "angles" of a chart—East, West, North, and South—where planets are thought to be most active.</note>, while in the other's birth the <term>Part of Fortune</term><note>A specific mathematical point in a horoscope used to determine prosperity.</note> held the East joined to its lord by a favorable radiation; or if in one birth a fortunate planet shone at the first cardinal point, and in the other **Mercury**, situated in that place, had its power changed by a fortunate or cardinal planet. And even if **Venus** was residing in the fifth house at Peter's birth and held power, while at Paul's birth the <term>luminaries</term><note>The Sun and the Moon.</note>, weakened by no debilities, looked upon each other amicably—the same fortune of riches would exist for both according to the opinion of astrologers, yet not from the same "face" of the stars. Different lots can happen from various things, even if the "craftsman" star was in a similar position in their birth charts. Furthermore, the position of one star cannot be entirely the same unless the whole constellation is exactly the same. Also, a contrary power could have been present in the other person's chart, either overwhelming or blunting the efficiency of that star. It is clear, therefore, from the conjunction and promiscuous influence of the stars, that we cannot discern through any observation what each star specifically bestows. Consequently, we cannot define the powers and natures of the stars as being known through experiments. <margin>Third reason</margin> Another reason for this insurmountable difficulty arises even if each star acted separately. Since the effects of the stars or of lower and surrounding causes can occur in many ways, no one who is not reckless and lacking in judgment would assert: "this happened because that star was positioned so; therefore, when it is positioned similarly another time, a similar outcome is to be expected." For perhaps that star was going to produce a different thing by its own nature, but the work was changed by a private fate, or the universal fate of the region, the year, the rulers, the city, the family, or the household; or by an antecedent, such as parents, grandparents, or great-great-grandparents; or the will of the person born; or the disposition of the air through which celestial influences are transmitted; or stubborn matter; or...

<summary>Pico argues that astrology cannot be an empirical science because the infinite variations in planetary "mixtures" prevent anyone from isolating a single star's influence or creating a reliable method. He highlights the failure of Ptolemy's universal rules and contrasts them with the equally flawed case-study approach of earlier astrologers like Maternus.</summary>

->DISPUTATION NINE<-
dd
<meta>catchword: Chaldeans</meta>

...a lesser cause is not suitable: it is not fit for the superior motions. Since all these things can change the efficiency of the stars as they wish, how can the <margin>Refutation of a silent solution.</margin> argument be safe if we interpret the nature of the stars based only on what happens? This is especially true since the things we have mentioned are always so connected to the operations of the stars that an event cannot be referred back to a star as its sole origin, even if we have noted its occurrence many times. They seem to fall into an unpardonable error because they think that what they observed in their own regions—for example, the observations of the **Egyptians**, **Chaldeans**, or **Arabs**—holds the status of a universal dogma. They believe these rules will be equally valid in every region, when in fact it is necessary for things to happen entirely differently, even if the traditions they hand down were true and demonstrated by the reliability of life and experience. For we see this clearly in changes of the weather: from the same constellation, different storms occur in different places—here they are calm, there they are violent; here it snows, there it is clear; in one place there are winds, and in another, rain. It is therefore quite inconsistent to suggest that in the birthing of human bodies or in the success of business (if indeed these things come from heaven) the stars would not work differently due to the diverse curvature of the sky, even if they are the same stars in different places. **Favorinus** <margin>Favorinus, Paul of Alexandria.</margin> also objected to them on this point, which we will confirm by the authority of **Paul of Alexandria**. For in his *Introduction to Astrological Effects* <note>original: "isagogis apotelesmaton"</note>, he writes that lucky <term>birth-charts</term><note>Latin: "genituras." A map of the sky at the moment of birth used to predict a person's fate.</note> in Egypt are especially those when **Aquarius**, holding the principal places, is well-affected; this is because the region of Egypt is said to be subject to **Aquarius**. From this, perhaps, comes the idea that **Mercury** in **Aquarius** breathes fortunately upon the talents of the Egyptians, though it is recorded by <term>Maternus</term><note>Julius Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman astrologer.</note> that in every house of **Saturn**, **Mercury** is humbled and fares poorly. It is clear, therefore, by the testimony of an outstanding astrologer, that the same observations will not be equally valid in every region (even if reliable observations could be made in any one region), a point which we have already demonstrated to be impossible for many reasons. And if **Hippocrates**, the father of physicians, <margin>Hippocrates.</margin> said that "experiment is deceptive" <note>A reference to Hippocrates' first aphorism: "Life is short, art is long, opportunity fleeting, experiment deceptive, judgment difficult."</note> in medicine, no one but the most unlearned would deny that it is utterly fallacious in astrology.

### Chapter II. If any experience could be had regarding astrological dogmas, it has not yet been obtained.

Up to this point, we have been arguing that no length of time, and no industry or learning of any men, can provide an experimental basis for the more secret powers of the stars. Now, if perhaps that has not been fully persuasive, we will demonstrate this at least most evidently: if any such experience could be gathered, it has not yet been gathered. For by our previous reasons, it is certainly established that we must admit knowledge of all these things is extremely difficult, and cannot be perfected over many revolutions of ages. Therefore, we will first refute those lies of the astrologers by which they—neither as Christians, nor as experts, nor as truth-tellers—proclaim that they possess observations from many thousands of years; then we will declare that whatever observations they do have are fallacious based on their own words. **Favorinus** <margin>Favorinus, Cicero.</margin> the philosopher, as quoted in **Gellius**, says: "That discipline of the **Chaldeans** is not of such great antiquity as they want it to seem." And **Cicero**, following the authority of **Panaetius**, says: "For when they say that the **Babylonians** spent 470,000 years in testing and experiencing whatever boys were born, they are lying. For we have no author who either says it can be done or knows that it was done." So says he; we, starting from a deeper point, shall expose their impudence.

<column-break/>

Whether the world is eternal, as certain philosophers wish, or created in time, as the Divine Truth teaches, let us leave this as most well-attested: no observations older than four thousand years could have reached those who handed down the science of the stars. For it is certain even to those philosophers who believed in the eternity of the world that by certain great changes of the elements, the seas receded and the lands were flooded; and as the dwellings of lands and men were exchanged, the ocean came to be where there was land, and land where the ocean had been. Not only the sacred historians, but also the philosopher **Plato** <margin>Plato.</margin> and external writers, have often mentioned floods and fires of this kind. It makes no difference whether the world is new or if a total change robs us of the memory of past things. Let us therefore examine from histories how old these celestial observations could be. **Varro**, <margin>Varro</margin> the most learned of the Romans, when about to weave together the most ancient history possible, began from the kingdom of the **Sicyonians**. **Trogus**, <margin>Trogus. Note on the calculation of time.</margin> who was either slightly earlier or a contemporary, began his work from **Ninus** himself, who warred with **Zoroaster** and was a few years older than the patriarch **Abraham**. Thus, those who write that **Zoroaster** flourished five thousand years before the Trojan War are caught as tellers of fables, since not even that many years are counted from **Abraham** to our own times. What, then, is the reason why both **Trogus** and **Varro**, professing to write the most ancient histories, did not start from an earlier point? It is because, due to the world's newness or at least its renovation, earlier records are either non-existent or utterly obliterated. For although they wished to write ancient and even primary histories, they wanted to write true ones, not fables like those of **Herodotus** and **Diodorus**. <margin>Note on the fables of Herodotus and Diodorus.</margin> The most imprudent tellers of tales sometimes use the words of these men to bolster their "observations of so many thousands of ages"—as if **Diodorus** by his own title, and **Herodotus** by the consensus of all literature, were not considered the most fabulous of writers. 

But let us set these things aside as a mere prelude; there is the most evident testimony of **Porphyry** <margin>Porphyry.</margin> regarding our subject. He says that the annotations about the stars which **Callisthenes** sent to Greece from **Babylon** in the times of **Aristotle** and **Alexander** contained only 1,903 years of observation. If you count those years back from **Alexander**, you will find they end at the time of the patriarch **Abraham** or slightly earlier. **Hipparchus** and **Ptolemy**, <margin>Hipparchus, Ptolemy.</margin> the princes of astronomy, when they bring forward observations of the ancients to establish a dogma, bring forward none older than those made among the **Egyptians** or **Babylonians** under King **Nabuchodonosor** <note>Reference to the Era of Nabonassar (747 BCE), which Ptolemy used as a chronological baseline.</note>. **Hipparchus** flourished nearly six hundred years after his reign, and from his time to our own, no more than 1,600 years or so have passed. Therefore, they lie and tell fables when they boast of having observations from so many centuries; and that the ones they do have are necessarily false is easily demonstrated. For either they began from the times of **Ptolemy**, or they fell to those who preceded **Ptolemy**. If the course of these observations began after **Ptolemy**, there has not been enough time to perfect the observation—which they themselves will not deny. If it relies on the experiments of the ancients—namely, those which either the **Egyptians** or **Chaldeans** handed down—who again will doubt that it is fallacious? For there can be no reliable observation of the heavens among those who did not correctly grasp the motions of the heavenly bodies. In these matters, the **Chaldeans**...

He uses classical authorities to show that Babylonian and Egyptian records only go back about 1,900 years, not the hundreds of thousands of years claimed by astrologers.</summary>
