<meta>This page continues the argument that the foundational observations of ancient astronomers were flawed, making the astrological systems built upon them unreliable. It transitions from Book 11 to the start of Book 12.</meta>

->AGAINST ASTROLOGY, BOOK XII.<-

No one who has touched the books of the mathematicians is unaware that both the Chaldeans and the Egyptians erred greatly. Ptolemy critiques them everywhere in his *Great Composition* <note>original: "magna compositione," the work commonly known as the *Almagest*</note>; Hipparchus critiques them too, and no one would easily believe <gloss>how</gloss> late it was when mankind truly began to understand anything about the movements of the heavenly bodies. According to Eudenius, **Thales** <margin>Eudenius, Callimachus</margin> was the first to predict solar eclipses, and **Callimachus** says <gloss>that</gloss> he was the first discoverer of the Little Bear <note>Ursa Minor</note> by which the Phoenicians sail. He also divided the year into three hundred and sixty-five days. **Plutarch** <margin>Plutarch, Euripides of Chios</margin> asserts that the obliquity of the Zodiac—the very first rudimentary step of sidereal science—was devised by **Pythagoras**, although **Euripides of Chios**, who was younger than Pythagoras, boasted that it was first discovered by himself. Before **Solon** flourished in Greece (and he flourished about six hundred years before the time of Christ), everyone thought the lunar month was exactly thirty days. Solon was the first to correct this error, <margin>Proclus, Ptolemy</margin> as **Proclus** writes in his commentary on Plato’s *Timaeus*. Now, if they were erring so remarkably in the motion of the moon—which is so easy and familiar to us—what should we think about the motions of the other stars, which are more hidden and slower? But there is no need for guesswork here. Let Ptolemy's book titled *The Great Composition* be read, and it will be clear beyond suspicion that all the ancients were entirely "out by a whole heaven" <note>original: "toto vt dicitur cœlo," a Latin idiom meaning "completely wrong"</note> regarding the movements of the heavens. Concerning the movement of the nearer star <note>the moon</note> which we were discussing, you will learn there that nothing found by the ancients was true, nor even close to the truth. <margin>In what time Hipparchus [lived].</margin> **Hipparchus** was the first, on the island of Rhodes about two hundred years before Christ, to observe the course of the moon more accurately. Yet even he did not reach total clarity, which is why he is corrected by **Ptolemy**, who indeed came closer to the truth than Hipparchus, but still did not fully grasp it, as he was later corrected by the Spanish astronomers <note>likely referring to the Alfonsine Tables produced in Toledo</note>. Regarding the motion of the sun, by which they measure all others, they are still "groping in the dark" even now, let alone in antiquity. The Egyptians stray far too much, thinking the solar return happens after three hundred and sixty-five days and a quarter, with a thirtieth part added; for later and truer observations have taught that even the quarter-day is not fully completed. How, then, could the wisdom of the Egyptians have produced reliable experiments regarding the fate of the year, when they were so mistaken about its very beginning? There too they were ridiculous <gloss>because</gloss> they inaugurated their year, <margin>Theophilus, Favorinus</margin> as **Theophilus** relates, whenever the Nile first flooded Egypt. **Anaximander**, as **Favorinus** writes in his *Universal History*, was the first to invent the Gnomon <note>the part of a sundial that casts a shadow</note>, by which he might mark the solstices and equinoxes. No one who has read his books is unaware that the astrolabe was the invention of Ptolemy. **Pythagoras** was the first to say that the Evening Star and the Morning Star <note>Lucifer</note> were the same star, on the authority of <margin>Parmenides</margin> **Parmenides**. Pythagoras did not precede Christ by more than five hundred years. But let us return to those motions so poorly explored by the ancients; regarding the motions of the five planets (excluding the sun and moon), **Hipparchus** said <margin>Hipparchus</margin> that so few observations by the ancients existed that he could not affirm anything he himself had discovered that would command belief. Ptolemy was the first who seemed to say something certain about them, although a later age corrected him in many places thanks to the benefit of time. In the numbering of the ascensions—which the Greeks call *anaphoras*—how far from the truth were all those in Egypt who used the stars for divination! **Ptolemy** in the first book of his *Apotelesmaton* <note>Ptolemy's astrological work, the *Tetrabiblos*</note> and **Apollinarius** in his commentaries <margin>Ptolemy, Apollinarius</margin> have testified to this. <margin>Apollonius</margin> And **Apollonius of Laodicea**, in a five-book work dedicated to the subject, mocked their errors. Who, then, 

<column-break/>

considering these things, could doubt? No true experience of the influences of the stars could have been held among the Egyptians or Chaldeans, since they had explored neither the ascensions of the signs (upon which the greatest part of this art depends) nor the motions of the planets. How could they faithfully test what any planet was doing in a certain place when the planets were always in a location other than where they thought they were? This is not even to mention the fixed stars, whose motion, if we believe Ptolemy, was entirely unknown to them. If they erred, as is undoubtedly clear, then the Greeks err who follow them; the Arabs err who follow the Greeks; and the Latins err who follow the Arabs and the Greeks, pronouncing what is to come based on their rules and "experiences." For they think nothing gives them greater authority than <gloss>that</gloss> which they confirm by the authority of the Chaldeans and Egyptians. Hence they scatter names like **Aesculapius**, **Hermes**, **Nechepso**, and **Petosiris**—names that are entirely empty, like clouds before the readers—as if those men were not the most ignorant of the science they professed, if the things handed down to us by Hipparchus and Ptolemy (the chief authors of astrology) are true. Why, then, in the first book of his *Apotelesmaton*, as if to gain belief for his words, does Ptolemy turn to the experiments of the ancients? He himself could scarcely begin to find the truth in his own time, when sidereal science was then for the first time tolerably <margin>Peter of Abano, Galen</margin> investigated. **Peter of Abano** excuses **Galen** for wandering into error regarding the motions of the moon thus: "Galen did not write these things exactly, for they had not yet been understood." Yet Galen was not prior to Ptolemy, but a contemporary. <margin>Ptolemy, his time.</margin> Therefore, let us conclude this entire dispute: if the astrology that has been written down relies on the experiments of the ancients, it is fallacious, because they lacked the proper theory <note>original: "ratio"</note>. Since these things are still in doubt for the moderns, as we showed above, much less could they have been manifest to antiquity—and the astrology of the younger generation is even more fallacious, for they lack both theory and the necessary passage of time.

# THE TWELVE BOOKS OF DISPUTATIONS BY GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA AGAINST THE ASTROLOGERS BEGIN.

---

## Chapter One. That faith should not be given to astrology as if it were a revealed science.

If astrology is not supported by the fables of the astrologers, and if no faith can be placed in it from empirical experiments, what is left? Why should a wise man surrender himself to it? Shall these things be thought of as oracles? <margin>First reason.</margin> And shall we look up to as "divine" those things which we have refuted as being scarcely rational? Shall we <margin>Second reason.</margin> imitate the astrologers, who, if anything is done by men beyond reason, refer it to the stars? Shall we then, by a similar example, refer the ravings of men to the stars? But if by chance this persuasion has seized anyone, let him know that such "divine revelations" are of no use to him, seeing as—as we have seen—there is such great disagreement in the decrees of astrology. It has not yet been revealed whether the "true" astrology breathed upon us by the gods as a singular gift is that of the Chaldeans, or the Egyptians, or the Jews, or Ptolemy, or the Arabs. This divine beneficence does us no good as long as that "most true" wisdom received from heaven lies hidden in the dregs of our lies. Nor has any Lydian stone <note>a touchstone used to test the purity of gold</note> <margin>Third reason.</margin> been sent down from heaven by which the legitimate might be discerned from the adulterous...

He concludes that astrology cannot be trusted as an empirical science or a divine revelation due to these historical errors and internal contradictions.</summary>

### OF DISPUTATIONS

<margin>Fourth Reason.</margin>
...if I were to argue with Christians, I would ask whether they think this art was revealed by God, or rather by a demon. It cannot be said to come from God, since the Holy Scriptures—the interpreters of the divine voice—forbid it. If they respond that it comes from a demon, then no faith can be placed in a demon, whom God called the "father of lies." From this, the madness of those who fabricate the story that this science (like all others) was granted by God to **Adam**, and from him passed down to **Noah**, is refuted.

<margin>Methodius</margin>
The author **Methodius** reports that Noah's son **Jonicus** predicted many future events through this art. They claim that through the sons of Noah who survived the **Deluge** <note>original: "Cathaclismo," referring to the Great Flood</note>, it reached the patriarch **Abraham**, who (according to **Josephus**) taught it to the Egyptians; from the Egyptians it passed to the Greeks, and from the Greeks to the Latins. In this way, these people invent a "very pretty" succession for themselves, well-suited for ensnaring the unlearned, but recognized as false and deceitful by the more learned everywhere. For regarding what they say about Adam: unless this too was revealed by God, by what testimony do they prove it? Does it follow that because we believe he excelled in all sciences by God's gift, he also possessed this one? Certainly, it would follow if this were actually a science, and not something vain, false, ridiculous, and repugnant to the principles of true doctrines—not to mention repugnant to God, as we were saying. It is not even worthy of a human inventor.

<margin>Methodius is an ignoble author of empty doctrine.</margin>
Let us come to Jonicus. Methodius does write about him, but he is a hardly suitable authority. For he is not the **Saint Methodius** <note>Methodius of Olympus</note> whom **Saint Jerome** mentions among illustrious men; this one was from Patara <note>likely referring to the author of the "Revelations of Pseudo-Methodius"</note>, and the other is entirely different, occasionally cited by **Peter Comestor** <note>a medieval historian</note>, in whose work no one even moderately learned would fail to notice a lack of selection of good authors. Furthermore, Methodius does not even say that Jonicus predicted anything. Besides, what weight can the authority of an ignoble writer have regarding this Jonicus, when **Moses** the prophet himself counts only three sons of Noah: **Shem, Ham, and Japheth**?

<margin>Josephus, Philo</margin>
Neither Josephus, nor **Philo**, nor any Hebrew author, nor any compiler of annals, nor any expositor of the Mosaic law mentions anyone else besides these. We might believe Josephus when he says Abraham passed on **astrology** to the Egyptians; but he did not mean this superstitious, divining kind, which was more frequent among idolaters than among the worshipers of the true God. The "God of Abraham" was invoked by Moses and the prophets, who professed to follow the tradition and precepts of Abraham.

<margin>What kind of astrology was Abraham’s?</margin>
In truth, that was rather the mathematical science of the movements of the stars, the use of which was frequent and necessary for the Hebrews to observe the fixed times of their ceremonies. Hebrew records show that the tribe of **Issachar** <note>original: "Hyssachar"</note> was delegated to this study. This cannot be learned without **arithmetic**, since it consists almost entirely of numbers and measurements. 

<margin>Josephus</margin>
Josephus writes that Abraham demonstrated this alongside astrology to the Egyptians. If Josephus had intended to mean this "divining" art instead, he would be entirely mistaken, especially since he says the Egyptians received this astrology (which Abraham first showed them) from the **Chaldeans**. It is clear from earlier points that the Egyptians created their own astrology for predicting the future, which has almost nothing in common with the dogmas of the Chaldeans. 

<margin>Ptolemy</margin>
However, **Ptolemy** teaches in his *Great Composition* that in the study of the movements of the stars, few Chaldeans practiced it, and from them it flowed to others. Therefore, Josephus understood nothing other than this mathematical astronomy.

<margin>Aboufar. Fifth reason.</margin>
Furthermore, **Aboufar** <note>likely Abu Ma'shar, a famous Persian astrologer</note> is to be laughed at. In his own work, he says that when the sons of Noah came into Chaldea, they disseminated this science, which he claims was received from heaven; yet he himself rejects the Chaldean opinion regarding the "terms" <note>specific degrees of a zodiac sign</note> of the planets. But one should not spend so much effort in refuting these trifles, since everyone but the most slow-witted understands that these are the ravings of men who surrender their faith to their own dreams. Because they cannot produce any rational proof for what they say,

<column-break/>

<margin>How the study of astrology ought to conduct itself.</margin>
they confirm it by repeating its authority back to Adam. For let them answer this: why did other arts and sciences not reach us through this same succession? Instead, they were devised by the talents of later men and brought to perfection by diligent study. Did we receive this gift of divine providence in astrology alone, as if it were the most useful? Truly, that providence is not usually so sleepy as to fail to notice that this "divining" art is preserved for us in vain unless the **mathematical** art were also preserved, without which we cannot use the former correctly. For it does no good to have the powers and natures of the stars discovered unless you can mark, by exact calculation, the conditions, form, and position of the stars at every single hour. Since only mathematics provides this, it too should have been passed down to us as an inherited tradition from our first father, if divine providence did not want us to lack the use of such a "salutary" divination in our lives.

## Chapter II. What kind of people the Egyptians and Chaldeans were, among whom astrology was born.

<margin>The Chaldean and Egyptian nations, and what they studied diligently.</margin>
Thus, those who worship these trifles—fictions so unworthily and falsely made up about the heavens, yet treated as if they came from heaven—are rejected. When anyone reads this with insight, they see the nature of it so clearly that no suspicion of "celestial inspiration" remains. I think this is evident enough even to the dullest person from what has already been said. Nevertheless, it will not be useless, reader, to consider in a single view how this plague was born and spread through the world: that is, by which authors it arose, by what persuasions it was accepted, by what authority it was confirmed, and by what fuel it has been increased to persist to this day. For this will not be entirely ineffective in stripping away its credit and exposing its vanity. It was born, then, from Chaldean and Egyptian parents, about whom something must be said before we speak of their vanity. Both nations were, above all, studious and skilled in two things: **idolatrous religion** and **mathematics**. They were invited to the latter by the suitability of their location, for they inhabited open fields and broad plains, which provided an easy and more accurate view of the stars. As for the former—that is, why they were occupied with and honored for vain and superstitious ceremonies more than other nations—it was due to their antiquity. Because of this, they were the first to practice the worship of gods, acting as parents and necessary teachers of religion to others. Furthermore, they embraced monstrous things elsewhere due to their ignorance of natural philosophy <note>original: "physicæ," meaning the study of nature</note> and the rudeness of their minds.

<margin>What does mathematics contribute to philosophy? A solution to the doubt.</margin>
For mathematics does not make men wise; that is why the ancients considered it a study for boys. Indeed, while it paves the way for philosophy if tasted moderately and with reason, if someone gives themselves entirely to it alone, it produces the greatest occasions for error in philosophy, as **Aristotle** testifies. Therefore, the Egyptians and Chaldeans were—as far as I can gather by conjecture—of a talent little suited for wisdom. This is still seen in the people of those regions today; even if the chance of study had been taken away, nature should not have been. Nor should we be deceived by what once deceived me in my youth: the wisdom of the Egyptians and Chaldeans so celebrated by the ancients and even by **Plato**. It is recorded that **Pythagoras, Democritus, Eudoxus, Plato**, and many others traveled there for no other reason than to acquire wisdom. But those people claimed that famous and divine name of "wisdom" for themselves solely based on their knowledge of ceremonies and the worship of the gods, which was found among all nations...

<summary>Pico refutes the myth that astrology was a divine science passed down from Adam and Noah, arguing instead that it is a superstitious byproduct of Egyptian and Chaldean cultures who, while good at basic math, lacked true philosophical wisdom.</summary>

->### NINTH DISPUTATION<-

<margin>Retrograde motion.</margin>
<margin>Eclipses of the luminaries.</margin>
...you should despise it; for if you touch it with your hand, you would break it apart and dissolve it. Descendants expanded upon the invention of their fathers, though the fabrication was even older than that, growing more robust through the hidden fraud of its origins—as always happens when age bestows authority. Truly, we have not said everything, but have only demonstrated the method of invention—that is, the slippery path of error. The rest of their claims follow that same pattern: everything is based on the most trivial conjectures and supported by thin and poorly matched analogies to earthly things. For example, they claim that planets are "fortunate" when they move forward and "unfortunate" when they move backward <note>original: "retrocedunt," referring to retrograde motion</note>, or even when they are believed to stand still. It is as if they think that by moving backward, the planets deny what they promised; by moving forward, they fulfill what they pledge; and by lingering while standing still, they delay what they bestow. They also claim that eclipses <note>original: "Deficientem," literally "failing" or "fainting"</note> of the Sun and Moon produce great calamities. These things terrify people primarily because their cause is unknown—as if the gods were either deserting us or rejecting us. They claim that a star is "exalted" when it is placed at its apogee <note>original: "apogeo," the point in orbit furthest from Earth</note> because that place is the highest. They even go so far as to assign influences to the parts of the Moon, then to other stars, and finally even to oats and beans—the errors of whoever introduced these things were explained in Book VIII. After they established these dogmas upon such conjectures, they began to observe the birth charts <note>original: "geneses"</note> of newborns. If their dogmas happened to match reality by chance even once or twice, they granted them total faith and the greatest authority. For instance, if by chance some famous man was born while Mars occupied Scorpio and excelled in war, it was held as an indubitable fact that Scorpio was the "home" of Mars—as if it were not one thing for Mars to be positioned thus, and quite another for a warlike person to be born. As we have said, nothing could be faithfully tested in the motions of the heavens by those who err so greatly. They would note what happened to the subject of a specific horoscope <note>original: "themate"</note> and from there establish rules and canons. Since this was not a path of true experimentation, but rather relied on chance and rashness, it happened differently for different observers—and even for the same observers at different times. Thus, as many systems of astrology emerged as there were observers, leading to that confusion and conflict of opinions which we examined at length in the previous book.

### Chapter VI. By what fuels it grew and how it was propagated.

<margin>The dogmas were confirmed through the "astrological Apollo." The name of "Demon" was commonly used.</margin>
Thus, having arisen from trifling conjectures, it grew through deceptive experiments, fueled by the vice of the age and nourished by human curiosity. There is no one who is not greedy to know the future, and to believe those things are most truly sought from heaven. For how few among the common people—or even among scholars—recognize how incorrectly these things are sought from the sky? Added to this were the interests of princes, who believed everything out of ignorance and hoped for everything out of greed. If ever happiness was pronounced for them from the heavens (and it was always pronounced), they no more wanted astrology to be overturned than they wanted that promised happiness to be lost. Sometimes they predicted the truth—now by chance, now by cunning, now with a demon's support in the ways we have explained—for who could not succeed occasionally when predicting many things? Yet their successes brought applause and cheers, while a thousand lies were immediately buried in oblivion. Moreover, they gained much faith and authority from oracles, which not only approved of this art but practiced it. When Apollo was asked whether a male or female would be born, he answered "a female," because at the time of conception the Moon was moving toward Venus. What greater testimony could a profession have than to have the gods as its authors? Of course, the wicked demons knew this—demons so named not only by our people, but also by the Platonists—

<column-break/>

<margin>He shows that all liberal arts, such as Theology, Philosophy, and Medicine, as well as religion itself, are contaminated by this superstition.</margin>
they knew, I say, how much poison they were administering to the world under a single superstition. Once this poison had penetrated deep into the veins, it first stripped away faith in religion (the greatest good of mankind), as if everything depended on a fatal necessity from heaven—as if there were no miracles and no divine foreknowledge of the future, but everything happened by the force of the constellations. Then, it provided a defense for vices, claiming they descend upon us from heaven—and perhaps it even tainted good things (since all things from nature are good). Finally, it infected the noble arts of medicine and philosophy; though it did not overturn them entirely (any more than it did theology), it nonetheless contaminated them. It turned philosophy away from true reason toward fables, and medicine away from natural and effective remedies toward vain observations and the delusions of old women. Thus, it became a single plague of perverse superstition, fatal to both body and soul at once. They saw prudence go to ruin, for instead of using wisdom, people consulted astrology on what to do, at what time, and by what means—so that a most foolish vanity sat at the helm of life. Finally, they hoped for what actually happened: that an art which claimed authority from heaven and mathematical calculations would cover up the more obvious fraud and painted weakness of other superstitions. They hoped that these other superstitions would not be thought vain if they were followers, appendages, and foster-children of "celestial doctrine." For as we showed in Book I, there is no superstition that does not recognize astrology as its ally, parent, or leader. Was it not worthy, then, for the most harmful demons to act as astrologers themselves? Would they not provide everything necessary so that this pestilential persuasion might daily possess the senses and interests of men? Even Porphyry <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher</note> tells us that we must believe demons used the rules of astrologers in their oracles for no other reason than to deceive—that is, to give credibility to a fallacy. <margin>Porphyry.</margin> For Porphyry himself says those oracles were lying when they responded based on astrological dogmas; this would not have happened if the art were true, since the demons—who are most skilled in natural things—could not have failed to see the future if it were hidden there. Nourished by these fuels, astrology grew and deeply occupied the Egyptians and Chaldeans with many predictions. Immediately among them, a superstitious form of medicine arose. <margin>The origins of superstitious Medicine.</margin> For **Nechepso** <note>original: "Necipsus," a legendary Egyptian King associated with early astrology</note> wrote in Egypt about which "decan" <note>a 10-degree segment of the zodiac</note> caused which disease, and which decan’s power could cure it. This matter was held in secret and among the mysteries, as if that partition of decans were not arbitrary (as we have demonstrated), though it was later mocked and utterly neglected by Ptolemy. From this source, magic immediately emerged—which is nothing other than an embrace of idolatry, astrology, and superstitious medicine. We have refuted these one by one in our books on the True Faith against the seven enemies.

### Chapter VII. How Astrology passed from the Egyptians to others.

<margin>The evil of the Greek schools is spread by this kind of superstition.</margin>
Astrology passed from the Egyptians and Chaldeans to the Greeks, but through ignoble authors. For except for the houses of traveling performers, it did not enter the Lyceum or the Academy. It did not even enter the Stoa, although Thales tried to arrange its admission. Nor could Epicurus believe in astrology, since he believed in atoms and the void. The first man of good literary reputation to cultivate it was **Ptolemy**, in the 140th year after Christ. Yet he did so more sparingly than others, so that he seems not so much to favor this madness as to have wished to set a limit upon it. Nevertheless, the authority of this one man—always a mathematician, rarely a philosopher—influenced so many...

# AGAINST ASTROLOGERS, BOOK XII.

[philoso]phy. So many prejudices of famous men in mathematics and philosophy stand in the way, yet it slips back in. The name of Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century astronomer whose work "Tetrabiblos" became the foundation for Western astrology</note> snatched some Greeks into error who were otherwise prone to superstition, such as Porphyry, 
<margin>Note.</margin>
whose excessive concern for the cult of demons and the scent of superstitions was condemned by both his teacher Plotinus and his disciple Iamblichus. From the Greeks, it devolved to the Arabs with even greater authority, as they marveled at whatever they found written by the Greeks and looked up to that vain appearance of antiquity in the names of the Egyptians and Chaldeans. However, just as the most prudent of astrologers, Ptolemy, purified and pruned that tradition as best he could after receiving it from the barbarians, so too did 
<margin>Abu Ma'shar on the decades.</margin>
a certain grammarian named Aboafar <note>A Latinized name for Abu Ma'shar, a famous Persian astrologer</note> take it from the Greeks; as a writer of history, he filled it with innumerable trifles and fables. He made astrology almost as much worse than Ptolemy’s astrology as astrology itself is worse than the good arts. He was a man made for empty loquacity, almost entirely unskilled not only in philosophy but also in astronomy, and was mocked by every learned astrologer. Yet, he was pleasing to the masses, among whom he who says the most is considered great, rather than he who says the best. During those times, the study of mathematics—and indeed of all philosophy and disciplines—grew in Spain. 
<margin>Note, by what path this art reached the Italian kingdoms. Note.</margin>
In that land, while Alfonso <note>Alfonso X of Castile, known as "The Wise," who commissioned the Alfonsine Tables</note> reigned, he was most diligent in mathematical numbers and the calculation of celestial motions, but he also loved the vanity of divination, being otherwise uninitiated in philosophical studies. For his sake, many monuments of that art from the Arabs and Greeks reached us, primarily through John of Seville and Michael Scot <note>A medieval scholar and "magician" at the court of Frederick II</note>, the latter being a writer of no weight but much superstition. Albert <note>Albertus Magnus, the "Universal Doctor"</note> first embraced these things as they were new—for he was born during those times—but I believe he did not approve of them as an old man as much as he did as a youth. Just as he published magic when he was a young man, he detested it in his mature age, living a most holy and blameless life in the monastery. However, as time went on, through the long duration of tradition, the multitude of writers, and a certain affinity between mathematical astronomy and astrology (both in name and subject matter), it almost came into dispute whether it was a science without deceit or a superstition. Truly, although it was accepted for so many centuries by the multitude (whose nature is to know nothing) and cultivated by the superstitious (whose knowledge is madness), and sought by the curious with no judgment, it was always—as we warned in the first book—laughed at, refuted, and driven out by the prudent, by philosophers, and by the most holy men. For at the time when the cult of idols was maturing in Egypt and Chaldea along with the insanity of all vanities, it was condemned among the Hebrews, the worshipers of the true God, through Moses, Isaiah, Jeremiah, and other prophets by voice and by writing. When it came to Greece, it did not please Pythagoras, according to Diogenes and Theodoretus. The Platonists and Peripatetics 
<margin>Diogenes, Theodoretus. Eudoxus.</margin>
did not even think it worthy of words, except to treat it as one of the "mountebank" <note>original: "circulatrices," referring to wandering tricksters or street performers</note> arts. Eudoxus of Cnidus, a most prudent legislator (for he wrote laws for his citizens) and a great philosopher under Plato—and by the consensus of all, the prince of mathematicians of his age—affirmed that astrologers should in no way be believed and left this in writing. Several years later, Cassander and Archelaus, distinguished mathematicians, did the same; as did Panaetius and Carneades, grave and true philosophers. Whenever these diviners came to Rome, whether from Egypt or Babylonia, 

<column-break/>

<margin>How little astrology is valued.</margin>
that Roman providence removed them from the city with the most severe laws. Thus under Tiberius, Vitellius, Diocletian, Constantine, Gratian, Valentinian, and Theodosius, they were forced either to desert their profession or pay the penalty for it. It is clear enough why Hadrian was delighted by their deceptions, for by a certain natural inclination he loved Egypt so much that nothing Egyptian could fail to please him. Yet at that same time, Favorinus openly and Plutarch obliquely mocked them with the gravest judgment. 
<margin>He raises a doubt.</margin>
Soon after, under Ptolemy, when astrology seemed to gain a little respectability, it was immediately defamed by the judgments of Plotinus the great Platonist, Alexander of Aphrodisias the distinguished Peripatetic, and Origen, who was most eminent in all disciplines. When it came to the Arabs, it did indeed detain Abenzageles and Aboafares, who were neither men of logic nor philosophers, but it did not detain Averroes and Avicenna. When it first appeared at the University of Paris, it was barely prevented by the curious from being utterly destroyed by fire. When some years later Roger Bacon and certain others tried to honor it, most learned men resisted them: William of Auvergne, Bishop of Paris; and after him, Nicole Oresme, an excellent mathematician; and Henry of Hesse; and Jean Gerson; and the Briton Brynllywarch <note>original: "Brenlanlius," likely referring to a medieval British critic</note>. They detested astrology not only where it harms religion, but entirely, as something vain and false. Therefore, the name of the "art" never gained such standing as to become an established rule. For there was always some patron of truth who spoke against it.

-> TO THE READER. <-

<margin>In the year of Christ 1488.</margin>
<image-desc>A rectangular woodcut historiated initial 'I' showing a scholar sitting in a study or library, surrounded by books and a desk.</image-desc>Giovanni Pico, born of the noble family of the Princes of Mirandola, was a greedy explorer of the secret things of nature. He applied such tireless effort that he was, and was considered to be, a consummate Theologian and Philosopher while still a youth. In the twenty-fourth year of his age, he traveled to Rome, and there he proposed these nine hundred questions concerning natural and divine matters, culled not only from the writings of the Latins and Greeks, but tracked down from the mysteries of the Hebrews, and the secrets of the Chaldeans and Arabs—many items also regarding ancient and obscure philosophy, many from the Kabbalah, and many also from natural Magic. He posted all these in public places so they might be more easily spread, promising that he would pay the expenses of those who came from distant places to dispute them. However, because of the envy of some, he was never able to ensure that a day for the debate was set. And when they could do nothing against his learning, they attacked thirteen out of the 900 as being suspected of heresy. But he, not enduring these losses to his reputation, published an "Apology" <note>A formal defense of his positions</note> which you will find above on Folio 13. He beseeched his readers to read that first, since in the little book of unexplained conclusions, many things were contained which he intended to be discussed not everywhere in public, but only in secret meeting among the learned. Many things were also proposed there not from his own opinion, but as they were believed by those in whose name he always added them. If you read that Apology diligently, you will easily discover that the conclusions themselves are filled with the knowledge of many things. Farewell.

Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, Count of Concordia, will debate publicly nine hundred written conclusions concerning Logic, Morals, Physics, Mathematics, Metaphysics, Theology, Magic, and Cabala—both his own and those of the wise 
<note>original: "placitis"</note> 
Chaldeans, Arabs, Hebrews, Greeks, Egyptians,

In reciting these, he has not imitated the elegance of the Roman tongue, but rather the style of speaking used by the most celebrated Parisian debaters <note>Pico refers to the "Scholastic" style of the University of Paris, which favored technical precision over Renaissance rhetorical flourishes</note>, because nearly all philosophers of our time use it. Furthermore, the dogmas to be debated are set apart when they concern specific nations or the leaders of heretical sects, but are mixed together when they concern branches of philosophy, presented as a miscellany <note>original: "per satyram," referring to a literary medley or variety</note>.

->Conclusions according to the doctrine of the Latin philosophers and theologians Albert the Great, Thomas Aquinas, Henry of Ghent, John Duns Scotus, Aegidius Romanus, and Francis de Mayronis.<-

### Conclusions according to Albert. <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a Dominican friar and teacher of Thomas Aquinas known as the "Universal Doctor."</note> Number: 16.

1. Intelligible species <note>The mental representations or "images" that allow the mind to understand objects</note> are not necessary, and to posit them is not consistent with the views of good Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle</note>.
2. Even if all individuals of the human species were destroyed, this statement remains true: "Man is an animal."
3. This statement is in the fourth mode of essential predication <note>A technical logical term for how properties are predicated of a subject</note>: "Man is man."
4. In every point of matter, there are—by a potency of inchoation <note>The "seeds" or beginnings of forms</note>—the essences of all natural forms; these are co-eternal with matter according to the philosophers, but created together with it according to the Faith.
5. Form, in its intensification and relaxation <note>The way a quality like heat gets stronger or weaker</note>, does not vary according to its essence, but according to its being.
6. The separated soul understands through species created together with it from the beginning of its existence, which it uses rarely or never while it is in the body.
7. Sound is carried according to real being all the way to the start of the auditory nerve.
8. Light has only an intentional being <note>A non-physical, representational existence</note> in the medium.
9. The organ of hearing is the nerve expanded at the cavity of hearing.
10. The object of the common sense <note>The faculty that integrates information from the five individual senses</note>, in itself and properly, is magnitude, as Avicenna rightly said.
11. It is possible for the species of something we are said to remember to be totally lost.
12. The vegetative soul is not introduced before the sensitive, nor the sensitive before the rational, but the whole is introduced at once.
13. Although the sense concurs passively to receive the species, it concurs actively to judge the thing sensed.
14. The mobile body is the subject of natural science.

<column-break/>

15. The consideration of the body (in that it is a body) belongs to the Metaphysician.
16. The relational potency <note>original: "potentia respectatiua"</note> of matter does not add a physical thing to matter, but only a rational distinction.

### Conclusions according to Thomas. <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the "Angelic Doctor," whose work synthesized Aristotelian philosophy with Christian theology.</note> Number: 45.

1. If the Spirit did not proceed from the Son, he would not be distinguished from the Son, neither in himself nor in the plurality of Persons.
2. The temporal procession of the Holy Spirit is regarded according to the gifts of sanctifying grace.
3. The contingent existence of things that are, will be, or have been, was known infallibly by God from eternity because it was present to His eternity.
4. The contingency of future things known by God is compatible with the infallibility of divine knowledge.
5. Whatever contingent thing God knew would be in the future, He necessarily knew that it would be in the future.
6. The reason for the predestination of some and the reprobation of others can be found in the divine goodness, and the divine will alone is the reason why He rejects some and chooses others for glory.
7. Although God's consequent will <note>God's will as it responds to the actions of creatures</note> is always fulfilled, it does not necessarily impose necessity on the things willed.
8. One who has grace cannot—even by the absolute power of God—be not accepted by God for eternal life, nor can one lacking grace be accepted.
9. A work formed by the soul in charity merits eternal glory by condign merit <note>A merit that God, by his promise, treats as equal in value to the reward</note>.
10. The three divine Persons could have simultaneously assumed one nature.
11. The moral and cardinal virtues will remain in the heavenly homeland after the resurrection.
12. Beatitude <note>Supreme happiness or the state of the blessed</note> consists essentially in an act of the intellect.
> Corollary: Beatitude does not essentially consist in the remaining acts of the will.
13. The sacraments of the New Law are the cause of grace, not only as a necessary condition <note>original: "sine qua non"</note>, but also as the instrument through which it is given.
14. The true body of Christ is in heaven locally, and on the altar sacramentally.
15. The impassibility <note>Incapability of suffering or decay</note> of bodies after the resurrection will result from the soul's full dominion over the body.
16. Christ in the final judgment will judge not only in His human nature, but also according to His human nature.
17. Although it can be defended in some way that a creature can create, it is more rational to believe that the power of creating cannot be communicated to a creature.
18. The *Aevum* <note>The mode of time for eternal beings like angels, distinct from temporal time and eternity</note> is subjectively in the more blessed angel.
19. There cannot be sin in the will unless there is a defect in the reason.
20. The same body cannot be in different places at the same time through the power of God.
21. There is no multiplication of angels within the same species <note>Aquinas held that every individual angel is its own unique species</note>.
22. God is not seen in the homeland through a species, but He Himself is applied to the intellect as an intelligible species through His own essence.
23. The "One" adds nothing to "Being" except the privation of division.
24. The subject and its proper property <note>original: "passio"</note> are really distinct.
25. Form is generated accidentally.
26. Matter signed by quantity <note>original: "materia signata"</note> is the principle of individuation.
27. A quality is numerically the same from the beginning of an alteration until its end.

<header>GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA</header>

28 All liberty resides essentially in reason.
29 In substantial generation <note>The process of a new substance being created, such as a plant growing from a seed</note>, there is a breakdown until one reaches prime matter <note>The most basic, formless substrate of all physical reality</note>.
30 Being immediately expresses ten concepts <note>The ten Aristotelian categories: substance, quantity, quality, relation, etc.</note> so united among themselves that they do not belong to one single thing, but are directed toward one.
31 Essence and existence in any created thing are really distinct from one another.
32 Regarding the same thing, contradictories can in no way be proven true if that thing is actually distinct outside the mind.
33 Matter implies no positive entitative act <note>In Scholastic thought, matter is "pure potentiality" and has no independent "act" or existence without form</note>.
34 No moral virtue except justice is subjectively located in the will.
35 This proposition, "Man is capable of laughter," does not belong to the "second mode" of essential predication <note>A technical distinction in Aristotelian logic regarding how properties relate to a subject’s definition</note>.
36 Two accidents differing only by number cannot exist in the same subject.
37 Heavy and light things are moved by no other motor than either the one that generated them or the one that removes an obstacle to their motion.
38 Heavy things are moved by themselves, rather than *from* themselves.
39 The phantasm <note>A mental image or sensory impression</note> is a secondary and instrumental agent in the production of an intelligible species <note>The abstract concept formed by the mind</note>.
40 The difficulty of understanding can arise both from the nature of the intellect itself and from the nature of the thing being understood.
41 The powers of the soul are really distinct from the soul itself.
42 Specific quiddities <term>quiddity: the "what-ness" or essential nature of a thing</term> are considered by the Metaphysician.
43 It implies a contradiction for matter to exist without form.
44 The "idea" of prime matter is not to be placed within the mind of God.
45 The ideas of genera <note>General categories, like "animal" as opposed to "human"</note> are not to be placed in God.

### Conclusions according to Francis. Number VIII.
<note>Francis de Mayronis (c. 1280–1328), a French Scholastic philosopher known as the "Master of Abstractions."</note>

1 This proposition is false: "The Essence generates," because essence is ultimately abstract, and "to generate" is predicated formally <note>A technical distinction in Trinitarian theology regarding whether the divine essence itself acts to produce the Son</note>.
2 The divine essence can be perceived without the Persons of the Trinity, and one Person can be seen without another.
3 The will cannot fail to enjoy an object shown to it as "enjoyable."
4 Being is spoken of God denominatively <note>Describing God by His attributes rather than His hidden essence</note>.
5 Quiddities possess their own formal being from eternity of themselves, not from anything external.
6 No definition perfectly matches the thing defined.
7 A plurality of "formalities" <note>The distinct aspects of a thing that are not separate "parts"</note> is compatible with a single real identity.
8 "To be" is not part of the quiddity of God, but is attributed to Him in the second mode.

### Conclusions according to John Duns Scotus. Number XXII.
<note>John Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), one of the most important High Medieval theologians, known as the "Subtle Doctor."</note>

1 Charity is not a habit distinct from the habit of grace, through which the Holy Spirit dwells in the soul.
2 The "idea" of a stone is nothing other than the stone produced by the divine intellect in "intelligible being"—which is a secondary kind of existence—existing in the divine mind like a known thing within the knower.
3 Whoever says that the Persons in the Godhead are distinguished by absolute properties does not contradict Catholic truth.
4 In Christ, there were two "beings" <note>Two distinct existences or acts of being—one human and one divine</note>.
5 Praxis <note>Practical action</note> is the operation of a power distinct from the intellect, naturally suited to be drawn forth in conformity with right reason so that it may be considered "right."
6 Every individual is an individual through its own individual difference, which is called haecceity <term>haecceity: the "this-ness" or unique property that makes an individual different from all others of the same species</term>.
7 "Being" is said of God and creatures univocally <note>Meaning the word "being" has the same basic sense when applied to both</note> in its essence.
8 Being is not predicated quidditatively <note>according to its essence</note> of its own attributes and ultimate differences.

<column-break/>

9 In Christ, there was no "acquired" knowledge <note>Knowledge gained through sensory experience and learning over time</note>.
10 Virtues are to be placed in the higher appetite <note>The rational will, rather than animal instincts</note>.
11 Grace is subjectively located in the will, not in the essence of the soul.
12 The body of Christ was, of itself, impassible <note>Incapable of suffering or decay</note>.
13 By God’s absolute power, it is possible for original sin to be deleted without the infusion of grace.
14 After the Passion of Christ, the ceremonies of the Old Law could be observed without sin.
15 By these words alone, "This is my body," without the preceding words being expressed (namely, "the day before he suffered"), the consecration cannot be performed.
16 The relation of a creature to God is really the same as its foundation, yet formally distinct and distinct by the nature of the thing.
17 Every relation other than its foundation is really distinct from it.
18 A thing can move itself from a "virtual" act to a "formal" act.
19 The act of understanding is caused by both the object and the intellect, acting as two partial agents.
20 The act of understanding is caused in a nobler way by the intellect than by the object—no matter what the object is, provided it is not the vision of God.
21 Substance is not known through its own "species" <note>The mental representation or image</note>.
22 A habit produces an act as a partial effective cause.

### Conclusions according to Henry of Ghent. Number XIII.
<note>Henry of Ghent (c. 1217–1293), a prominent philosopher at the University of Paris who often disagreed with Thomas Aquinas.</note>

1 There is a light higher than the light of faith, in which theologians see the truths of theological science.
2 Paternity is the principle of generating in the Father <note>Within the Trinity</note>.
3 The processions in the Godhead are distinguished according to the intellect and the will.
4 This proposition is not to be granted: "The essence is the father of the son."
5 Demons and sinful souls suffer from fire insofar as it is hot, with an affliction of the same kind as that which afflicts bodies.
6 The operations of angels are measured by "discrete time" <note>A time made of distinct moments rather than a continuous flow</note>.
7 Angels understand through a scientific "habit" <note>A disposition or skill</note> that is natural to them.
8 The "irascible" and "concupiscible" powers <note>Anger-based and desire-based impulses</note> are distinguished in the higher appetite just as they are in the lower.
9 Having a quidditative and definable reality is common to both imaginary things and real things.
10 Friendship is a virtue.
11 The formal "certainty" <note>or "ratitudo"</note> of any created thing is a relation.
12 For there to be a real mutuality of relation, it is required that the foundation be ordered by its nature toward another as toward its own perfection.
13 Relation is not really distinguished from its foundation.

### Conclusions according to Giles of Rome. Number XI.
<note>Giles of Rome (Aegidius Romanus, c. 1243–1316), a student of Thomas Aquinas and Archbishop of Bourges.</note>

1 The power of generating in the Godhead is neither the divine essence taken precisely and absolutely, nor a relation or property, nor something composed of both... but is the essence with a mode of revelation.
2 Theology is neither practical nor speculative, but affective <note>Related to the emotions and the love of God</note>.
3 God, under the aspect of "Glorifier," is the subject of theology.
4 The Father and the Son can be called not only "two breathing" but also "two spirators" <note>Referring to the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and Son</note>.
5 Angels were not created in a state of grace.

6 Therefore, an angel is obstinate and unrepentant because special divine impulses have been withdrawn from it.
7 A higher angel illuminates a lower one, not because it presents a luminous object to it, or because it breaks down and divides what is unified within itself for the lower one, but because it strengthens and fortifies the intellect of the lower angel.
8 The sense of taste, as taste, perceives not only what is flavorful, but also what is moist.
9 Heat, if it were to exist even in a state of separation <note>meaning existing without a physical body</note>, would be able to generate fire.
10 For one science not to be subordinate to another, it is sufficient that it reduces its arguments to principles that are self-evident within its own level of abstraction.
11 Given a vacuum, if something were to move within it, it would move in an instant <note>Pico is debating a classic Aristotelian problem: without the resistance of a medium like air or water, motion would theoretically have no duration</note>.

## Conclusions according to the doctrine of the Arabs, who for the most part profess themselves to be Peripatetics <note>original: "Peripatheticos"; followers of Aristotle, who famously taught while walking about</note>: Averroes, Avicenna, Al-Farabi, Avempace, Isaac, Abumaron, Moses, and Muhammad.

### Conclusions according to Averroes, 41 in number.

1 Prophecy in dreams is possible through the illumination of the Agent Intellect <note>The "active" part of the mind that allows us to understand universal truths</note> upon our soul.
2 There is only one single intellective soul for all human beings <note>A controversial Averroist doctrine suggesting a single shared human consciousness at the highest level of thought</note>.
3 The ultimate happiness of man occurs when the Agent Intellect is joined to the "Possible Intellect" <note>the individual human capacity for thought</note> as its form. This "joining" was perversely and erroneously understood by the Latins I have read, and especially by John of Jandun, who corrupted and depraved the doctrine of Averroes not only in this, but in almost every question of philosophy.
4 Even while holding to the unity of the intellect, it is possible for my soul—so specifically mine that it is not shared with everyone—to remain after death.
5 Every abstract being depends on the First Abstract Being <note>God</note> in three types of cause: formal, final, and efficient.
6 It is impossible for the same species to be generated both from reproduction and from decay <note>original: "putrefactione"; the medieval belief that some life, like maggots, arose spontaneously from rotting matter</note>.
7 God moves the "First Mobile" <note>the outermost sphere of the universe</note> not only as its goal or "final cause," but as its true "efficient" and proper mover.
8 Every mover of the heavens is the "soul" of its own celestial sphere, forming a more substantial unity with it than the soul of an ox forms with its physical body.
<margin>¶ Corollary: The soul of the heaven gives the sphere its mobile and perfect being before it gives it motion.</margin>
9 The heaven is a simple body, not composed of matter and form.
10 Three "modes of essence" are useful for logical demonstration: the first, the second, and the fourth.
11 In every demonstration, except for the "absolute" demonstration, circular reasoning can occur.
12 Heavy and light things move themselves "by accident" by directly moving the medium <note>such as air or water</note> through which they travel.
13 The heavens are not identical in "genus" while differing in "species," as Avicenna believed.
14 No science can prove that its own subject exists, nor can it prove the existence of the primary part of its subject.
15 Universals exist within the object only potentially; they exist actually only through the operation of the soul.
16 "Indeterminate dimensions" are co-eternal with matter, preceding any "substantial form" within it.
17 Every Intelligence <note>a celestial being or angel</note>, except for the First one, understands nothing except the First.
18 There is no way to prove the existence of an abstract being in an absolute sense

<column-break/>

except through the argument of the eternity of motion.
19 Whatever belongs to a "genus" <note>a general category or class</note> is subject to corruption.
20 The subject of metaphysics is "being insofar as it is being."
21 Definitions of natural substances mention matter only as a consequence of their form.
22 The proof in the seventh book of the *Physics*—that "everything that is moved is moved by another"—is a demonstration based on a sign, not a cause.
23 No active power that is purely neutral and indifferent to acting or not acting can be determined by itself to perform an action.
24 One of two related things is most appropriately defined by the other.
25 Aristotle’s example in the second book of the *Metaphysics* regarding the night-owl's eyes in respect to the sun denotes difficulty, not impossibility; otherwise, nature would have acted in vain.
26 The "necessary proposition," which Aristotle distinguishes in the *Prior Analytics* from the "possible" and "contingent" proposition, is that which is composed of necessary terms.
27 For a term to be considered "necessary," it must be a term that is essentially one.
28 When Aristotle said that a necessary conclusion follows from a "necessary major premise" and a "contingent minor premise," he meant a minor premise that is contingent in itself, but necessary by accident.
29 There can be no natural habitation for living things beneath the equator <note>original: "æquinoctiali"</note>.
30 There is a natural "right side" in the heavens, and it does not change, even though the parts of the celestial sphere change position.
31 Whoever claims the soul is merely a "form of temperament" <note>the balance of physical humors</note> denies the existence of an "acting cause."
32 The "One" in metaphysics signifies the privation of divisibility—not actually, but in potentiality.
33 The "One" of metaphysics is the foundation for the "One" of arithmetic.
34 Number is found in abstract things exactly as it is found in material things.
35 The essence of any thing and its existence are really the same. <note>Averroes famously argued against the distinction between essence and existence, a point where he differs from Thomas Aquinas</note>.
36 Quiddity <note>the "what-ness" of a thing</note> and essence are different in every being except for the First Being.
37 Substance is prior to accident, not only in nature but in time.
38 The physicist considers matter insofar as it is matter.
39 The essence of any Intelligence is substantially "relative to" something.
40 Even if we assume the impossible—that there could be a type of matter that was not a source of corruption—if the heaven were truly composed of such matter and form, it still could not be eternal.
41 An "end" <note>a goal or purpose</note> does not act as a final cause according to how it is conceived in the mind, but according to its real existence.

### Conclusions according to Avicenna, 12 in number.

1 Besides the categorical and hypothetical syllogism, there is a genus of "composite syllogisms."
2 Although no syllogism that is actually or potentially categorical can reach a conclusion from two negative premises, this can happen in a composite syllogism.
3 There is matter in the heavens of the same nature as the matter of lower <note>earthly</note> things.
4 There cannot be an intelligible concept in the soul without the actual act of thinking.

<meta>This page continues the presentation of Pico della Mirandola’s 900 Theses. Having concluded the section on "Arabic" thinkers (like Averroes), Pico now moves to the ancient Greek commentators on Aristotle (Simplicius, Alexander of Aphrodisias, Themistius) and the Neoplatonic tradition (Plotinus and his followers), bridging them with his "Arabic" sources.</meta>

->C O N C L V S I O N S<-

### *Conclusions according to Simplicius, numbering IX.* <note>Simplicius was a 6th-century philosopher and one of the last great pagan commentators on Aristotle.</note>

1 To know its own act is not common to every external sense, but is special to human senses.
2 Aristotle, in the third book of *On the Soul* <note>original: "de anima"</note>, treats only of the rational part.
3 When the soul perfectly returns into itself, then the agent intellect <note>The "Active Intellect," the part of the mind that produces universal concepts</note> is liberated from the possible intellect <note>The "Passive Intellect," the part that receives information</note>.
4 The same rational part, as it goes out from itself, is called the possible intellect; but as it is such that it can perfect itself (as far as it is possible), it is called the agent intellect.
5 The same rational part, as it goes outside itself and proceeds, is perfected by the species <note>The mental forms or images of things</note> which are in it; as it remains, it is called the intellect in habit.
6 One can know from the preceding conclusions why the agent intellect is sometimes likened to art, sometimes to a habit, and sometimes to light.
7 Passion caused by a sensible object is received in the physical organ alone; sensation is received in the soul alone.
8 Just as light does not make colors colors, but makes pre-existing colors (which are visible in potential) actually visible, so the agent intellect does not create species <note>concepts</note> as if they did not exist before, but makes pre-existing species (which are knowable in potential) actually knowable.
9 When Aristotle says that one does not remember after death because the passive intellect is destroyed, he understands the "possible intellect" by "passive intellect."

### *Conclusions according to Alexander of Aphrodisias, numbering VIII.* <note>A 2nd-century commentator known for his "materialist" interpretation of Aristotle's soul.</note>

1 The rational soul is immortal.
2 To every heaven, besides the soul that moves it efficiently, there is a proper intelligence that assists it and moves it as an end, which is entirely distinct in substance from such a soul.
3 According to Aristotle's opinion, matter does not enter into any definition, not even a natural one.
4 God understands neither evils nor privations.
5 The number of abstract things of which Aristotle treats in the twelfth book of the *Metaphysics* is not the number of movers, but the number of intelligences which are the ends of motion.
6 When Aristotle says in the ninth book of the *Metaphysics* that separate and divine things are either totally known by us or totally ignored, this must be understood regarding that knowledge which happens to those who have already reached the highest activation of the intellect.
7 Just as the first intellect among all intellects understands itself first and other things secondarily, so the last intellect among all intellects understands things other than itself first, and itself secondarily.
* The metaphysician and the dialectician dispute equally about all things, but the former does so demonstratively while the latter does so by probability.

### *Conclusions according to Themistius, numbering V.* <note>A 4th-century philosopher who attempted to harmonize Plato and Aristotle.</note>

1 Possible intellects, which are only illuminated, are many; active ones, which are shared, illuminating, and illuminated, are also many; but the active, illuminating intellect alone is one.
2 The active intellect that only illuminates is, I believe, what Themistius calls that which is Metatron in the Kabbalah <note>Metatron is a high archangel in Jewish mysticism; Pico is famously attempting to link Greek philosophy with Jewish secret tradition</note>.
3 The science of the soul is the middle ground between the natural and divine sciences.
4 Besides the two types of demonstration which Aristotle puts forward, 

<column-break/>

a third type must be established, and it is when one property is demonstrated through a coeval <note>equal in age or duration</note> property.
5 A proposition is "through itself" <note>original: "per se"</note> when either the subject defines the predicate, or the predicate defines the subject, or both are defined through the same third thing.

## *Conclusions according to the doctrine of the philosophers who are called Platonists: Plotinus the Egyptian, Porphyry the Tyrian, Iamblichus, Chalcidius, Proclus the Lycian, and Adeland the Arab.*

### *Conclusions according to Plotinus, numbering XV.* <note>Plotinus was the founder of Neoplatonism; his "Enneads" are the source for these points.</note>

1 The first intelligible <note>the object of thought</note> is not outside the first intellect.
2 Not the whole soul descends when it descends <note>into the body; Plotinus believed a part of our soul remains in the divine realm</note>.
3 All life is immortal.
4 The soul that has sinned, whether in a terrestrial or an aerial body, lives the life of a brute beast after death.
5 The irrational soul is the idol <note>image or reflection</note> of the rational soul, depending on it just as light depends on the sun.
6 Being, life, and intellect coincide as the same thing.
7 The ultimate happiness of man is when our particular intellect is fully joined to the total and first intellect.
8 Civil virtues <note>social/political ethics</note> are not to be called virtues in the simple sense.
9 Assimilation to divine things does not happen through the virtues of even a purified soul, except as a preparation <note>original: "dispositive"</note>.
10 In the reason, there are likenesses and species of things, but in the intellect are the beings themselves.
11 It is the mark of consummate virtue to cut away even the first impulses <note>referring to instinctive reactions before they become conscious thoughts</note>.
12 It is improperly said that the intellect "inspects" or "looks at" ideas.
13 Things which are necessary to an animal can be called necessary, but not good.
14 Just as accidental happiness requires focused attention, substantial happiness is not only not lost through a lack of attention, but is actually strengthened.
15 A man who has already attained happiness is not hindered from it by frenzy or lethargy <note>mental illnesses or physical conditions of the brain</note>.

### *Conclusions according to Adeland the Arab, numbering VIII.* <note>Likely referring to Adelard of Bath, or a misunderstood Arabic source.</note>

1 The agent intellect is nothing other than the part of the soul which remains above and does not "fall" <note>into the material world</note>.
2 The soul possesses the species <note>forms</note> of things within itself, and is only awakened by external things.
3 To complete the preceding conclusion, which not only Adeland but all the Moors say, I say those species are actually and substantially in the part that does not fall, and are received anew and accidentally in the part that falls.
4 The greater part of things which become known in dreams become known either through the purgation of the soul, or through namelessness, or through the mere revelation of the spirit.
5 What Thabet the Chaldean <note>Thabit ibn Qurra, a 9th-century mathematician and astronomer</note> writes about sleeping on the liver regarding the revelation of dreams will be rightly understood if we harmonize his saying with the words of Plato in the *Timaeus*.
6 Because, as Abdala <note>Likely referring to a Sufi or Arabic commentator</note> said, seeing dreams is the strength of the imagination, but understanding them is the strength of the intellect; therefore, he who sees them for the most part does not understand them.
7 The soul is outside of motion and is the governor of matter.
8 All the sages of the Indians, Persians, Egyptians, and Chaldeans believed in the transcorporation <note>reincarnation</note> of souls.

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s "900 Theses," moving from the Greek Aristotelian commentators into the Neoplatonic tradition. Here, he presents "conclusions" or philosophical propositions drawn from Porphyry, Iamblichus, and Proclus—three of the most influential figures in late antique philosophy. Pico’s goal is to show how these pagan insights align with his own syncretic worldview, even finding connections to Christian scripture and the physical traits of European nations.</meta>

->JOHN PICO OF MIRANDOLA<-

### Conclusions according to Porphyry, numbering XII. <note>Porphyry (c. 234–305 AD) was the student of Plotinus and a key systematizer of Neoplatonism.</note>

1 By "father" in Plato, we should understand the cause that produces the entire effect from itself; by "maker," the one who receives matter from another.
2 The maker of the world is a super-mundane soul.
3 The "exemplar" <note>The perfect pattern or blueprint of the universe</note> is nothing other than the intellect of that maker-soul.
4 Every soul participating in the Vulcanian intellect <note>Referring to Vulcan/Hephaestus, the god of the forge, often associated in this context with the "crafting" intellect</note> is sown into the Moon.
5 From the preceding conclusion, I deduce why all Teutons <note>The Germanic peoples</note> are of good stature and white color.
6 From the same conclusion, I deduce why all Teutons are most reverent toward the Apostolic See <note>Pico is suggesting a metaphysical/astrological reason for the religious devotion of the Germans to the Papacy</note>.
7 Just as Apollo is the solar intellect, so Aesculapius <note>The god of healing</note> is the lunar intellect.
8 From the preceding conclusion, I deduce why the Moon in the ascendant gives health to the newborn.
9 There are two kinds of evil demons: one kind are souls and substantial demons; the other are material powers and accidental demons.
10 The two kinds of demons mentioned in the preceding conclusion according to Porphyry, we believe to be nothing other than the "law of the members" and the "powers of this darkness" spoken of by Paul <note>Pico is identifying Porphyry’s demons with the spiritual struggles mentioned by St. Paul in the New Testament (Romans 7:23 and Ephesians 6:12)</note>, although I do not believe they agree on the essence and substance of these powers.
11 Plato, at the beginning of the *Timaeus*, determines only the extremes: that is, that which truly "is" and is in no way "begotten," and that which is truly "begotten" and in no way "being"; he says nothing of the middle states, one of which is "being and begotten," the other "begotten and being."
12 God is everywhere because He is nowhere; the intellect is everywhere because it is nowhere; the soul is everywhere because it is nowhere. But God is everywhere and nowhere with respect to all things that come after Him. The intellect is indeed in God, but is everywhere and nowhere with respect to those things after it. The soul is in the intellect and in God, but is everywhere and nowhere with respect to the body.

### Conclusions according to Iamblichus, numbering IX. <note>Iamblichus (c. 245–325 AD) emphasized theurgy, or ritual, as a way to unite the soul with the divine.</note>

1 The speculative intellect is a "separated form" in both its essence and its mode; the practical intellect is separated in essence but joined in its mode; the rational soul is joined in essence but separated in its rational mode; it is joined in both essence and mode.
2 The maker of the sensible world is the seventh of the intellectual hierarchy.
3 Corporeal nature exists in the intellect immovably; in the soul, it is primarily mobile by itself; in the animal, it is mobile by participation; in the heavens, it is moved orderly from another source; below the Moon, it is moved disorderly from another source.
4 The elements are found twice in the eight celestial bodies in a "celestial manner," which one will find if they proceed in a retrograde order in that double numbering.
5 Above this world, which theologians call *ideaton* <note>original: ἰδεατὸν, "made of ideas"</note>, is another which they call *noēton* <note>original: νοητὸν, "intelligible" or "perceived by the mind"</note>, and above this yet another, which they call *noeron* <note>original: νοερὸν, "intellectual" or "possessing intellect"</note>.
6 When the soul is excellently assimilated to the intellect, a perfectly circular motion occurs in its vehicle <note>The "astral vehicle" or "spirit-body" that Neoplatonists believed carried the soul</note>.
7 No power of the celestial stars, in and of itself, is malevolent.
8 He who understands the final cause of floods and great fires will call these "purifications" rather than "destructions."
9 When Plato says the soul is placed in the middle of the world, it should be understood as the "unparticipated soul," which he says is placed in the middle because it is equally present to all things, freed from every particular regard and specific habit.

<column-break/>

### Conclusions according to Proclus, numbering LV. <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was one of the last major Greek philosophers; his complex, systematic Neoplatonism deeply influenced medieval Christian theology.</note>

1 What exists in "intelligible terms" as the infinite, exists in "intellectual terms" as male and female; in the super-mundane, as identity and alterity, similarity and dissimilarity; in the soul, as the circulation of the "Same" and the circulation of the "Other."
2 The Gods who are "containing" and "perfecting" are exempt from the laws of Saturn. The Saturnian Gods are exempt from the laws of Jupiter.
3 Every soul living intellectually is exempt from the laws of Fate. However, all things obey the Law of Adrastia <note>Adrastia was a goddess of inescapable destiny; Pico suggests that intellectual life grants a degree of freedom from common fate, but not from the highest divine law</note>.
3 The title of "God" belongs simply and absolutely to the One, who is the God of gods; simply but not absolutely to any of the super-substantial beings according to their essence; to the intellectual beings according to their participation; to divine souls according to their contact and union; and to demons according to their dissimilarity to human souls.
4 The "containing" property belongs to the middle order of the second trinity, which in the *Phaedrus* is called the "celestial circuit."
5 In the intelligible realm there is not "number" but "multitude," and the paternal and maternal cause of numbers; but in the intellectual realm, there is number according to essence and communicative multitude.
6 The term "alterity" in the *Parmenides* is the same as the "super-celestial place" in the *Phaedrus*.
7 Regarding the "One," the "Many," "Whole," "Parts," "Finite," and "Infinite" which we have in the *Parmenides*: understand these according to the order of the trinities in the intelligible and intellectual realms, following the threefold division of that order.
8 What is called the "back of heaven" in the *Phaedrus* is called the "One" in the *Parmenides*; what is "the depth of heaven" there is "the whole" here; what is "the axis of heaven" there is "the limit" here.
9 Plato expresses the third order of the second trinity through three terms: the "extremes," the "perfect," and that which is "according to figure."
10 The Intellectual Gods have their "unions" from the first One; their "substances" from the intelligible realm; their "perfect, containing, and generative lives" of the divine from the intelligible and intellectual realms; and their "intellectual property" from themselves.
11 Just as the intelligible Gods produce all things uniformly, so the intelligible-intellectual Gods produce them trinally, and the intellectual Gods produce them hebdomadically <note>In groups of seven</note>.
12 Between the extreme paternal Gods, Saturn and Jupiter, Rhea necessarily mediates through the property of "fruitful life."
13 The second trinity of the intellectual "hebdomad" (group of seven) is the trinity of the "Curetes," whom theology calls the "untainted gods."
14 The proper role of the Curetes is to render the work of the paternal trinity immaculate: the "staying" of the first, the "proceeding" of the second, and the "illumination" of the third.
15 The tragic "slaughter of the gods" described by theologians designates the seventh distinctive unit in the intellectual group of seven.
16 The same goddess who is called Rhea (as she coexists with Saturn at her summit) is called Ceres when she produces Jupiter and, along with Jupiter, the total and partial orders of the gods.
