<meta>This page continues the "900 Theses" of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, specifically moving into the section of "Conclusions according to Proclus." These propositions explore the complex metaphysical hierarchies of Neoplatonism, bridging the gap between the "One" (God) and the physical world through various orders of gods, angels, and demons.</meta>

-># CONCLUSIONS<-

<meta>catchword: that which</meta>

17. Although, as theology teaches, the divine hierarchies are distinct, it must be understood that all things are in all things in their own way. <note>original: "omnia in omnibus esse modo suo." This is a famous Neoplatonic maxim meaning everything in the universe reflects the whole, but at its own level of existence.</note>
18. Just as the paternal property exists only in the intelligible realms, so the "founding" or "productive" property exists only in the gods. There is a "paternal-and-founding" intellection <term>noesis</term>; in the intelligible pattern <note>The ideal blueprint of the world</note> it is "founding," and it is "paternal" in the works of the craft.
19. Whatever operations belong to either the gods or nature are twofold: immanent <note>remaining within</note> and transient <note>passing out to others</note>. Through the immanent, each thing contains itself and the internal principles <term>rationes</term> that are in it; through the transient, it turns toward external things.
20. After the intellectual heptad <note>A group of seven divine powers in Proclus's system</note>, one must immediately arrange the super-mundane gods <note>Gods existing "above the world" or outside the physical cosmos</note> who are exempt from the parts of the universe and are not coordinated with this world, but encompass it from all sides as its cause.
21. It is characteristic of the super-mundane gods to liken things to themselves and to pass on to beings that "compassion" <note>A technical term for the sympathetic resonance between different levels of reality</note> and mutual communion which they possess from the likeness of one to another.
22. Although the power of assimilation is characteristic of the "leader-gods" mentioned in the previous conclusion, it is specifically assigned to the middle order of their trinity, since its first order is immediately joined in substance to the intellectual gods, and its third order mixes with the lower kinds.
23. The Jupiter mentioned in Plato's *Gorgias* is not the universal third "founder" among the intellectual gods, but the highest and first among the leader-gods.
24. In the "leader" trinity, Jupiter is the giver of substance, Neptune is the giver of life, and Pluto is the one who "turns back" <note>conuersiuus; the power that leads souls back to their divine source</note>.
25. The act of making <term>fabrica</term> is fourfold: the first adorns the universals of universals entirely; the second adorns universals but in a particular way; the third works according to things divided by universality; the fourth weaves particular parts into universals.
26. Jupiter, Neptune, and Pluto, who divide the kingdom of Saturn, do not receive that kingdom from Saturn except through the medium of Jupiter the Founder.
27. Under the first member of the "leader" trinity <note>Jupiter</note> is substantial being: every noble soul not subject to birth, the "first mobile" sphere of fire, the upper part of the air, things that grow upon the earth, and the Eastern part of the world.
28. Under the second member of the "leader" trinity <note>Neptune</note> is life and generation: every soul coming into birth, the wandering spheres <note>the planets</note>, water, the lowest part of the air (which is in caves and mines), earthquakes, the middle part of the earth, and the area around the center.
29. Under the third member of that same order <note>Pluto</note> is the "turning back" of specific divisions: the purification of souls, the sphere of active and passive elements, the earth and terrestrial things near Tartarus <note>the underworld</note>, and the Western part.
30. Even if the entire second trinity of super-mundane gods is called Proserpina, its first unity is called Diana by the Greeks, the second Persephone, and the third Minerva; among the non-Greeks <term>barbaros</term>, however, the first is Hecate, the second Soul, and the third Virtue.
31. Following the previous conclusion, one can use the works of Proclus to interpret one of the sayings of Zoroaster according to the Greek reading, though among the Chaldeans it is read and explained differently.
32. The third trinity of super-mundane gods is called Apollo, and the power of "turning back" is assigned to him.
33. The trinity of Proserpina is accompanied on its side by the trinity...

<column-break/>

34. The twelve gods mentioned in Plato's *Phaedrus* are intermediate gods between the super-mundane and the mundane <note>world-dwelling</note> gods, serving as their bond.
35. The gods mentioned in the *Phaedrus* are to be distinguished into four trinities: the crafting, the guarding, the vital, and the "turning back" <term>conuersiuam</term>.
36. There are four armies of "junior gods": the first dwells from the first heaven to the beginning of the air, the second from there to the middle of the air, and the third from there to the earth.
37. To each of these corresponds, proportionally, a fourfold army of angels, demons, and souls.
38. In the "Living-Being-Itself" <note>The Platonic 'Animal'—the intelligible world containing all life-forms</note>, there first appears a quaternary of the One Being, the "One of Being," and the "Being of the One."
39. The Crafter <term>Opifex</term>, looking toward the quaternary of the "Living-Being-Itself," fabricates the four principal parts of the world.
40. Inasmuch as the Crafter looks toward the pattern <term>exemplar</term> of the "Form of the One" in the Living-Being-Itself, he makes the first part of the world's body.
41. Inasmuch as the Crafter sees in the "Form of the One" the "One of the One's Essence," he makes the mundane gods of that part; inasmuch as he sees the "Being of the One's Essence," he makes the angels in that same part; inasmuch as he sees the "One of the Unity of Being," he makes the demons there; and inasmuch as he sees the "Existence of the Unity of Being," he makes the animals there.
42. The Crafter makes the other parts proportionally to the patterns of their forms, as was said regarding the first part; there is no need to explain this further, as anyone who knows the method of reasoning by analogy will be able to deduce it for themselves.
43. We ascend to the wise, beautiful, and good Lord through intellect, love, and faith.
44. Just as the faith that is "credulity" is below knowledge, so the faith that is truly faith is super-substantially above knowledge and intellect, joining us immediately to God.
45. Just as not every body participates in the soul, but only a perfect one, and not every soul participates in the intellect, but only a perfect one, so all things participate in the One.
46. Just as they differ by the scope of their causality, so they exceed one another in the height of their nature and rank in this order: Soul, Intellect, Life, Being, and the One.
47. Every order of the world remains stably in what precedes it and strengthens what follows it in itself.
48. Just as the first trinity after the One is to measure all things intelligibly and in the form of a "Limit," so the second trinity is to measure all things vitally, truly, and in the form of "Infinity"; the third is to measure everything according to the property of the "Mixture" and in the form of Beauty.
49. The first trinity only "remains"; the second "remains" and "proceeds"; the third, after "proceeding," "turns back" <note>original: "conuertit"</note>.
50. Eternity <term>Æuum</term> is above the "Living-Being-Itself" in the second and middle trinity.
51. Just as intelligible things are the causes of all species, so intellectual things are the causes of divisions according to common genera: super-mundane things differing by species, and mundane things differing by individual.
52. By "the place above the heavens," we are to understand that which in the second trinity is more intelligible than intellectual; by "the hollow beneath the heavens," that which is more intellectual than intelligible; by "the heaven," that which...

It emphasizes the "triple" movement of divine principles—remaining, proceeding, and returning—and places a mystical "true faith" above even intellect and knowledge as the means of union with God.</summary>

# GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA

...that which participates equally in both.
53. Whatever is stated affirmatively about the "super-celestial place" in Plato’s *Phaedrus* <note>original: "Phedro." Plato's dialogue *Phaedrus* discusses the soul's journey to a realm beyond the heavens.</note> is said of it not as the "simply first" principle, but as it possesses higher categories above it in which it participates. Whatever is stated negatively is said of it because of how it relates by analogy to the "First Good," which is the absolute head of all things, not restricted to this or that specific order.
54. Ambrosia is analogous to the "Limit," and nectar to the "Infinite." <note>Pico is interpreting Greek myths of the gods' food and drink as metaphysical principles of boundary and expansion.</note>
55. Just as the perfect intellect is to be sought from the "intelligible" things, so must we seek the "upward-leading virtue" from the intellectual powers, "absolute operation" (separated from matter) from the "beyond-worldly" beings, the "winged life" from the worldly beings, the "expression of the divine" from the angelic chorus, and the "fullness of inspiration" from the good spirits <term>demons</term> <note>In the classical sense, "daemons" were intermediary spirits, not necessarily evil.</note>.

->### Conclusions according to the Mathematics of Pythagoras. Number: 14.<-

1. The One, "Otherness," and "That-which-is" are the causes of numbers: the One causes unified things, Otherness causes generative things, and That-which-is causes substantial things.
2. Among participated numbers, some are the species of numbers, while others are the "unions" of those species.
3. Where the point-like unity falls into the "otherness" of the number two <term>the dyad</term>, there the triangle first exists.
4. Whoever understands the order of 1, 2, 3, 4, and 6 will hold the exact distribution of Providence.
5. Through the numbers one, three, and seven, we recognize in Pallas <note>The goddess Athena, representing wisdom.</note> the power of the intellect that unifies distinctions and acts as both cause and source of bliss.
6. The triple proportion—Arithmetic, Geometric, and Harmonic—indicates to us the three daughters of Themis <note>The goddess of Divine Law.</note>: Judgment, Justice, and Peace, existing as symbols for those who are peaceful.
7. The "foot" <note>A geometric or measuring term.</note> is the secret of the straight, reflected, and refracted ray in the science of optics <term>perspective</term>; it reminds us of a triple nature: intellectual, animal, and corporeal.
8. Reason has the proportion of an "octave" <term>diapason</term> to desire.
9. The spirited part of the soul <note>The "irascible" or emotional faculty.</note> has the proportion of a "fifth" <term>diapente</term> to desire.
10. Reason has the proportion of a "fourth" <term>diatessaron</term> to the spirited part.
11. The judgment of the senses should not be employed in Music, but only the judgment of the intellect.
12. In the numbering of forms, we must not exceed the number forty.
13. Every equilateral plane number symbolizes the soul.
14. Every linear number symbolizes the gods.

->### Conclusions according to the opinion of the Chaldean theologians. Number: 6.<-

1. The principal order of "separated beings" is not the first, as the Egyptians think, but above it is the "fountal" order, which is uniquely exalted above all.
2. Fate <term>Fatum</term> is not the necessity of the primary female power, but is an intellectually participated disposition of the "animal reasons" <note>The guiding principles of living things</note> that does not decline from higher things and is inevitable for lower things.
3. The substantial qualities of visible things do not result from a specific separated power, as the Egyptians believe, but result dependently from the first "receptacle of the fount of lights" through a living splendor.
4. Partial souls are not illuminated by intellectual splendor immediately, as the Egyptians say, but through the mediation of total "daemonic" souls

<column-break/>

[illuminated] by intellectual splendor.
5. The "intelligible coordination" is not within the "intellectual coordination," as the Egyptian Amosis <note>Likely referring to Ahmose or a legendary Egyptian sage.</note> said, but is above every intellectual Hierarchy, hidden impartially in the abyss of the first Unity and under the gloom of the primary darkness.
6. Whatever is above the Moon is pure light, and that is the substance of the worldly spheres.

->### Conclusions according to the ancient doctrine of Hermes Trismegistus the Egyptian.<-

1. Wherever there is life, there is a soul. Wherever there is a soul, there is a mind.
2. Everything moved is corporeal; everything that moves is incorporeal.
3. The soul is in the body, the mind is in the soul, the Word <term>Verbum</term> is in the mind, and God is the father of all these.
4. God is around all things and through all things; the mind is around the soul, the soul is around the air, and the air is around matter.
5. Nothing in the world is devoid of life.
6. Nothing in the universe is capable of death or corruption.

->#### Corollary: Everywhere there is life, everywhere there is providence, everywhere there is immortality.<-

7. God announces the future to man in six ways: through dreams, portents, birds, intestines <note>Referring to the ancient practice of haruspicy, or reading entrails.</note>, spirit, and the Sibyl <note>A prophetess.</note>.
8. The True is that which is unperturbed, undetermined, uncolored, unfigured, unshaken, naked, transparent, comprehensible by itself, the immutable good, and entirely incorporeal.
9. Within every person there are ten "avengers": ignorance, grief, inconstancy, greed, injustice, luxury, envy, fraud, anger, and malice.
10. The deep contemplator will see that the ten "avengers" (of which the previous conclusion of Hermes spoke) correspond to the evil ten-fold coordination in the Kabbalah and its prefects; I have stated nothing about these in my Kabbalistic conclusions because it is a secret.

1. Just as the lower man and priest sacrifices the souls of irrational animals to God, so Michael, the higher priest, sacrifices the souls of rational animals <note>Meaning human souls; Pico is referencing the mystical idea of the Archangel Michael offering the souls of the righteous in the heavenly Temple.</note>.
2. There are nine hierarchies of angels, whose names are: Cherubim, Seraphim, Hashmalim, Hayyot, Aralim, Tarshishim, Ophanim, Taphsarim, and Ishim.
3. Although the "Ineffable Name" <note>The Tetragrammaton, the four-letter name of God.</note> is the property of Mercy, it must not be denied that it also contains the property of Judgment.
4. The sin of Adam was the "pruning of the kingdom" from the other plants. <note>original: "truncatio regni." This is a Kabbalistic metaphor for separating the last Sefirah (Malchut/Kingdom) from the rest of the divine tree, causing a rift in reality.</note>
5. With the Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil, in which the first man sinned, God created the world <term>seculum</term>.
6. The "Great North" is the source of all souls simply, just as other "days" are the source of some and not all.
7. When Solomon says in his prayer in the Book of Kings, "Hear, O Heaven," we must understand "Heaven" as the "green line" which circles the universe. <note>Pico is likely referencing the *Kav ha-Yarok*, a mystical line of light or the "void" that surrounds creation in Kabbalistic cosmology.</note>
8. Souls descend from the "third light" to the "fourth day," and from there to the "fifth"; departing from there, they enter the "night" of the body.

<meta>This page continues the "Conclusions according to Proclus," a series of metaphysical propositions derived from the Neoplatonic philosopher Proclus. Pico is outlining a complex hierarchy of divine beings—from the "Intellectual" gods down to the "Worldly" gods—using the names of Greek deities as symbols for abstract cosmic principles. This section focuses on the "supermundane" gods who bridge the gap between pure thought and the physical universe.</meta>

# CONCLUSIONS

->### CONCLUSIONS ACCORDING TO PROCLUS<-

17. Although, as theology teaches, the divine hierarchies are distinct, it must nevertheless be understood that all things exist in all things in their own specific way. <note>This is a fundamental Neoplatonic maxim: the entire universe is reflected in every part of it, but according to the capacity of that part.</note>
18. Just as the "paternal" <term>paternal: the source or fatherly principle</term> property exists only in the intelligible realms, so the "creative" or "making" property exists only in certain gods who are both paternal and creative: creative in the intelligible archetypes, and paternal in the works they produce.
19. Whatever operations belong to either the gods or to nature are twofold: "immanent" <term>immanent: remaining within</term> and "transient" <term>transient: passing out toward something else</term>. Through immanent operations, a thing contains itself and the rational principles within it; through transient operations, it turns itself toward external things.
20. Immediately after the "intellectual week" <note>In Proclus's system, a group of seven intellectual deities.</note>, the "supermundane" <term>supermundane: existing above the physical world</term> gods must be ranked; they are exempt from the parts of the universe, cannot be coordinated with this world, and yet embrace it from all sides according to their role as its cause.
21. It is characteristic of the supermundane gods to assimilate and pass down to all beings that "compassion" and "shared communion" which they possess based on the likeness of the One to the "Other."
22. Although the power of "assimilation" belongs to the "leading" gods <note>original: "ducalium." These are the gods who guide the lower orders.</note> mentioned in the previous conclusion, it is specifically attributed to the middle order of their trinity: the first order is immediately joined in substance to the intellectual gods, and the third order mingles with the lower generations.
23. The Jupiter mentioned in Plato's *Gorgias* is not the universal creator who holds the third rank among the intellectuals, but rather the highest and first among the leading gods.
24. In the "leading" trinity, Jupiter is the principle of "substantial being," Neptune is the principle of "life-giving," and Pluto is the principle of "conversion" <term>conversion: the act of returning or turning back toward the divine source</term>.
25. The "fabrication" of the world is fourfold: the first adorns the universals of universals entirely; the second adorns the universe but in a particular way; the third acts according to things divided by their universality; and the fourth weaves the parts together particularly within the universals.
26. Jupiter, Neptune, and Pluto—who divide the kingdom of Saturn—do not receive that kingdom from Saturn except through the mediation of Jupiter the Creator.
27. Under the first rank of the leading trinity <note>Jupiter</note> is "substantial being," every noble soul not subject to birth, the "first mobile" <term>first mobile: the outermost sphere of the heavens</term>, fire, the highest part of the air that grows above the earth, and the Eastern part of the world.
28. Under the second rank of the leading trinity <note>Neptune</note> is life and generation, every soul coming into birth, the "wandering spheres" <term>erraticae sphaerae: the planets</term>, water, the lowest part of the air, the middle part of the earth, and the region around the center.
29. Under the third rank of the same order <note>Pluto</note> is the "conversion" of specific divisions, the purification of souls, the sphere of active and passive things, the earth along with terrestrial things near Tartarus <note>The deep abyss of the underworld</note>, and the Western part of the world.
30. Even if the entire second trinity of supermundane gods is called "Proserpina," its first unity among the Greeks is called Diana, the second Persephone, and the third Minerva; among the "barbarians" <note>original: "barbaros." To Pico, this refers to the ancient Persians or Chaldeans.</note>, however, the first is Hecate, the second Soul, and the third Virtue.
31. According to the preceding conclusion and the mind of Proclus, one of the sayings of Zoroaster can be explained as it is read among the Greeks, although it is read and explained differently among the Chaldeans.
32. The third trinity of supermundane gods is called Apollo, and the power of "conversion" is attributed to him.
33. The trinity of Proserpina is accompanied on its side by the trinity...

<column-break/>

34. The twelve gods mentioned in Plato's *Phaedrus* are the "intermediate" gods between the supermundane and the worldly, serving as the link between them.
35. The gods in the *Phaedrus* are to be distinguished into four trinities: the creative, the protective, the vital, and the converting.
36. There are four "armies" of junior gods: the first lives from the highest heaven down to the beginning of the air; the second from there to the middle of the air; and the third from there down to the earth.
37. To each of these, there corresponds proportionally a fourfold army of angels, demons, and souls.
38. In the "Living-in-itself" <note>original: "per se viuente." The Platonic archetype of all life.</note>, there first appears the "fourness" <term>quaternitas</term> of the "One-Being," the "One-of-Being," and the "Being-of-the-One."
39. The Creator <term>Opifex</term>, looking toward the fourness of the "Animal-in-itself," crafts the four principal parts of the world.
40. Insofar as the Creator looks to the archetype of the "Form of the One" in the "Living-in-itself," he makes the first part of the worldly body.
41. Insofar as the Creator sees the "One of the One-Essential" in the form of the One, he makes the worldly gods of that part; insofar as he sees the "Being of the One-Essential," he makes the angels in that same part; insofar as he sees the "One of the Being-of-the-One," he makes the demons there; and insofar as he sees the "Existence of the Being-of-the-One," he makes the animals in that same place.
42. The Creator makes the other parts proportionally to the archetypes of their own forms, just as was said of the first; it is not necessary to explain further, because anyone who knows the method of reasoning by analogy will be able to deduce it for themselves.
43. We ascend to the wise, beautiful, and good Lord through intellect, love, and faith.
44. Just as the faith which is "mere belief" is below science <term>science: certain, logical knowledge</term>, so the faith which is "truly faith" is supersubstantial, above science and intellect, joining us immediately to God.
45. Just as not every body participates in the soul, but only a perfect one; and not every soul participates in the intellect, but only a perfect one; nevertheless, all things participate in the One.
46. Just as they follow the scope of causality, so too by the sublimity of their nature and rank do these things exceed one another in order: Soul, Intellect, Life, Being, and the One.
47. Every middle order remains stable in the one that precedes it and strengthens the one that follows it.
48. Just as the first trinity after the "Unity" is to measure all things intelligibly and in the form of the "Limit," so the second trinity is all things vitally, truly, and in the form of the "Infinite"; the third is everything according to the property of the "Mixture" and in the form of "Beauty."
49. The first trinity only "remains"; the second "remains and proceeds"; the third, after "proceeding," "converts" <note>This describes the Neoplatonic cycle of *manene* (staying), *procedere* (emanating), and *revertere* (returning).</note>.
50. Eternity <term>aeon</term> is above the "Animal-in-itself" in the second and middle trinity.
51. Just as the "intelligibles" are the causes of universal species, so the "intellectuals" are the causes of divisions: supermundane things differ by genus, worldly things differ by species, and worldly things also differ by individual.
52. By the "super-celestial place," we are to understand that which is more "intelligible" than "intellectual" in the second trinity; by the "sub-celestial cavity," that which is more intellectual than intelligible; by the "heaven"...

    *   *43-44:* Ascent through intellect, love, and faith. Distinction between belief (creduality) and "true faith."
    *   *45-46:* Participation: Body/Soul/Intellect/One. Hierarchy of causality: One > Being > Life > Intellect > Soul.
    *   *47-50:* The stability of orders, the properties of the trinities (finitude vs infinity), and "Aeon" (Eternity).
    *   *51-52:* Intelligibles vs Intellectuals, and the "Supercelestial place" (from Plato's *Phaedrus*).

    *   *Check summary and keywords.*<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's "Conclusions according to Proclus," a series of philosophical propositions based on the Neoplatonic system. Having established the general nature of divine hierarchies, Pico now moves into specific "orders" of gods (supermundane, ruling, and worldly) and their roles in the creation and governance of the cosmos. He increasingly uses the names of Olympian gods (Jupiter, Neptune, Pluto, Apollo) as symbols for abstract metaphysical principles.</meta>

# CONCLUSIONS

->### CONCLUSIONS ACCORDING TO PROCLUS<-

17. Although, as theology teaches, the divine hierarchies are distinct, it must nevertheless be understood that all things exist in all things in their own specific way. <note>This is a fundamental Neoplatonic maxim: the entire universe is reflected in every part of it, but according to the capacity of that part.</note>
18. Just as the **paternal** <term>paternal: the source or fatherly principle</term> property exists only in the intelligible realms, so the **creative** or **making** property exists only in the gods known as paternal and creative: creative in the intelligible archetypes, and paternal in the works they produce.
19. Whatever operations belong to either the gods or to nature are twofold: **immanent** <term>immanent: remaining within</term> and **transient** <term>transient: passing out toward something else</term>. Through immanent operations, a thing contains itself and the rational principles within it; through transient operations, it turns itself toward external things.
20. Immediately after the **intellectual week** <note>In Proclus's system, this refers to a group of seven intellectual deities.</note>, the **supermundane** <term>supermundane: existing above the physical world</term> gods must be ranked; they are exempt from the parts of the universe, cannot be coordinated with this world, and yet embrace it from all sides according to their role as its cause.
21. It is characteristic of the supermundane gods to assimilate and pass down to all beings that compassion and indicative communion which they possess from the likeness of the **One** to the other.
22. Although it is characteristic of the **ruling** <term>original: ducalium</term> assimilations mentioned in the previous conclusion, this property is nevertheless appropriated to the middle order of their trinity, which is immediately joined in substance to the intellectual gods in its first order, and mixes itself with the various kinds in its third order.
23. The **Jupiter** spoken of in the *Gorgias* <note>Referring to Plato's dialogue, the *Gorgias*.</note> is not that third universal Maker among the intellectual gods, but the highest and first among the ruling gods.
24. In the ruling trinity, Jupiter is the **substance-giver**, Neptune is the **life-giver**, and Pluto is the **converter** <term>converter: the one who turns souls back toward their divine source</term>.
25. The "workshop" of creation is fourfold: the first fully adorns the universals of universals; the second adorns universals but in a particular way; the third according to things divided by universality; the fourth weaves parts into universals in a particular way.
26. Jupiter, Neptune, and Pluto, who divide the kingdom of **Saturn**, do not receive that kingdom from Saturn except through the mediation of Jupiter the Maker.
27. Under the first of the ruling trinity (Jupiter) belongs **substantial being**, every noble soul not subject to generation, the first moving sphere of fire, the highest part of the air, things that grow upon the earth, and the eastern part of the world.
28. Under the second of the ruling trinity (Neptune) belongs **life and generation**, every soul coming into generation, the water of the wandering spheres, the lowest part of the air (which is beneath the mountain-recesses), earthquakes, the middle part of the earth, and the area around the center.
29. Under the third of the same order (Pluto) belongs the **conversion of specific divisions**, the purification of souls, the sphere of active and passive things, the earth with terrestrial things (those around Tartarus), and the western part.
30. Even if the entire second trinity of supermundane gods is called **Proserpina**, its first unity is called **Diana** by the Greeks, the second **Persephone** <note>original: Persephosinne</note>, and the third **Minerva**; however, among the "barbarians" <note>Usually referring to the Chaldean or Persian traditions in this context.</note> the first is called **Hecate** <note>original: Mechate</note>, the second **Soul**, and the third **Virtue**.
31. According to the preceding conclusion and the mind of Proclus, one of the sayings of **Zoroaster** can be explained according to how it is read among the Greeks, although it is read and explained differently among the Chaldeans.
32. The third trinity of supermundane gods is called **Apollo**, and the power of conversion is appropriated to him.
33. The Trinity of Proserpina is accompanied at its side by a trinity that is

<column-break/>

**guarding** and **preserving**.
34. The **Twelve Gods** mentioned in the *Phaedrus* <note>Plato’s dialogue on the soul and beauty.</note> are the "middle gods" between the supermundane and the worldly, serving as the bond between them.
35. The gods mentioned in the *Phaedrus* are to be distinguished into four trinities: **creative**, **guarding**, **vital**, and **converting**.
36. There are four armies of **junior gods**: the first dwells from the first heaven down to the beginning of the air; the second from there to the middle of the air; the third from there down to the earth.
37. To each of these there corresponds proportionally a fourfold army of **angels**, **demons**, and **souls**.
38. In the "Self-Living Being" <note>The archetype of all life.</note> there appears first a **quaternity** <term>quaternity: a group of four</term> of the one being, the one "be-ing-ly," and the "one-ly" being.
39. The **Maker** <term>original: opifex</term>, looking toward the quaternity of the "Self-Living Being," crafts the four principal parts of the world.
40. Insofar as the Maker looks toward the archetype of the "Form of the One" in the Self-Living Being, he makes the first part of the worldly body.
41. Insofar as the Maker sees the "One of the One Essential" in the Form of the One, he makes the **Worldly Gods** of that part; insofar as he sees the "Being of the One Essential," he makes the **angels** in that same part; insofar as he sees the "One of the One-ly Being," he makes the **demons** there; and insofar as he sees the "Being of the One-ly Being," he makes the **animals** there.
42. The Maker makes the other parts proportionally to the archetypes of their own forms, just as was said regarding the first; there is no need to explain further, as anyone who knows the method of **analogy** will be able to deduce it for themselves.
43. We ascend toward the wise, beautiful, and good Lord through **intellect**, **love**, and **faith**.
44. Just as "faith" which is merely belief is below knowledge, so **Faith** which is truly Faith is "supersubstantially" above knowledge and intellect, joining us immediately to God.
45. Just as not every body, but only a perfect one, participates in a soul, and not every soul, but only a perfect one, participates in intellect, so nevertheless **all things participate in the One**.
46. Just as they differ according to the scope of their causality, so they exceed one another in order according to the sublimity of their nature and rank: **Soul**, **Intellect**, **Life**, **Being**, and **the One**.
47. Every "middle order" remains stably in the order that precedes it and strengthens the order that follows it.
48. Just as the first trinity after the "Unity" is to measure all things intelligibly and in the form of a **Limit**, so the second trinity is to measure all things vitally, truly, and in the form of **Infinity**; the third is all things according to the property of the **Mixture** and in the form of **Beauty**.
49. The first trinity only **remains**; the second remains and **proceeds**; the third, after the process, **converts** <term>converts: returns things back to the source</term>.
50. **Aeon** <term>Aeon: Eternity</term> is above the "Self-Living Being" in the second and middle trinity.
51. Just as the **Intelligibles** are the causes of universal species, so the **Intellectuals** are the causes of divisions according to common genera: the supermundane gods for those differing by species, and the worldly gods for those differing by individual.
52. By the **"supercelestial place"** <note>A famous image from Plato’s *Phaedrus*.</note> we are to understand that which is more intelligible than intellectual in the second trinity; by the "sub-celestial cavity," that which is more intellectual than intelligible; by "heaven" [it is the mixture].

It concludes by describing how the human soul ascends to God through faith and how the physical world is modeled on divine "quaternities."</summary>

that which participates equally in both.
53 Whatever is stated affirmatively about the "supracelestial place" <note>original: "supercœlesti loco"</note> in the *Phaedrus* <note>Plato’s dialogue on the soul and beauty.</note> is said of it not as the simply primary thing, but as having superior types above it in which it participates. Whatever is stated negatively is said insofar as it relates by analogy to the primary Good, which is absolutely the head of all things and not of this or that determined order.
54 Ambrosia is analogous to the "limit," and nectar to the "infinite."
55 Just as the perfect intellect must be sought from the "intelligibles" <note>purely mental forms</note>, so the power that leads upward is sought from the intellectual beings, an operation absolute and sequestered from matter from those beyond the world, a winged life from the mundane, the expression of the divine from the angelic choirs, and the fulfillment of that aspiration which belongs to the gods from the good demons <note>term: "demons" (daemones) - in the Greek sense, these are guiding spirits or intermediaries, not evil beings.</note>.

### Conclusions according to the Mathematics of Pythagoras, number 14.

1 Unity, "otherness" <note>original: "alteritas"</note>, and "that-which-is" are the causes of numbers: unity for the united, otherness for the generative, and that-which-is for the substantial.
2 In participated numbers, some are species of numbers, while others are the unions of those species.
3 Where the unity of the point falls into the otherness of the "binary" <note>the number two</note>, there the triangle first exists.
4 He who understands the order of 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 12 will exactly grasp the distribution of Providence.
5 Through the numbers one, three, and seven, we recognize in Pallas <note>Athena, representing divine wisdom</note> the power that unifies discernment and the power that causes and blesses the intellect.
6 The triple proportion—Arithmetic, Geometric, and Harmonic—indicates to us the three daughters of Themis <note>Goddess of divine law</note>, existing as symbols of Judgment, Justice, and Peace.
7 Through the secret of the direct, reflected, and refracted ray in the science of optics <note>original: "perspectiva"</note>, we are reminded of a triple nature: the intellectual, the animal, and the corporeal.
8 Reason holds the proportion of the *diapason* <note>an octave</note> to desire.
9 The spirited/angry part of the soul <note>original: "Iraicibilis"</note> holds the proportion of the *diapente* <note>a perfect fifth</note> to desire.
10 Reason holds the proportion of the *diatessaron* <note>a perfect fourth</note> to anger.
11 The judgment of the senses must not be employed in music, but that of the intellect alone.
12 In numbering forms, we ought not to exceed the number forty.
13 Any equilateral plane number symbolizes the soul.
14 Any linear number symbolizes the gods.

### Conclusions according to the opinion of the Chaldean theologians, number 6.

1 The principal order of "separated beings" is not the first, as the Egyptians think, but above it is a "fontal" <note>source-like</note> order, exalted in its unity.
2 Fate is not the necessity of the primary "seminal power," but is an intellectually participated habit of "animal reasons" <note>the vital principles of living things</note>, unswerving from those above and inevitable for those below.
3 The substantial qualities of visible things do not result from a particular separated power, as the Egyptians believe, but result dependently from the first receptacle of the "fountain of lights" through an "animal splendor."
4 Individual souls are illuminated by intellectual splendor not immediately, as the Egyptians say, but through the mediation of universal "demonic" souls 

<column-break/>

5 The "intelligible coordination" is not within the "intellectual coordination," as the Egyptian Amosis said, but is above every intellectual hierarchy, hidden impartially in the abyss of the first unity and under the gloom of the primary darkness.
6 Whatever is above the Moon is pure light, and that is the substance of the worldly spheres.

### Conclusions according to the ancient doctrine of Hermes Trismegistus the Egyptian, number 10.

1 Wherever there is life, there is soul. Wherever there is soul, there is mind.
2 Everything moved is corporeal; every mover is incorporeal.
3 The soul is in the body, the mind is in the soul, the Word <note>original: "verbum"</note> is in the mind, and the father of these is God.
4 God is around all things and through all things; the mind is around the soul, the soul is around the air, and the air is around matter.
5 Nothing in the world is devoid of life.
6 Nothing in the universe is capable of death or corruption.
7 **Corollary:** Everywhere is life, everywhere is providence, everywhere is immortality.
7 <note>The original text repeats the number 7.</note> God announces the future to man in six ways: through dreams, portents, birds, intestines, spirit, and the Sibyl <note>a female prophet</note>.
8 The Truth is that which is unperturbed, undetermined, uncolored, unfigured, unshaken, naked, transparent, comprehensible by itself, the immutable Good, and entirely incorporeal.
9 Within each person there are ten "punishers": ignorance, sadness, inconstancy, desire, injustice, luxury, envy, fraud, anger, and malice.
10 The ten punishers, about which the preceding conclusion of Hermes spoke, the profound contemplator will see correspond to the evil "denary coordination" <note>the ten evil counterparts to the divine emanations</note> in the Kabbalah and its prefects, about which I have placed nothing in my Kabbalistic conclusions because it is a secret.

4 The sin of Adam was the "cutting off of the kingdom" from the other plants.
5 With the Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil, in which the first man sinned, God created the world.

8 Souls descend from the third light to the fourth day, and from there to the fifth; departing from there, they enter the "night of the body."

<meta>This page continues the presentation of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola’s "900 Conclusions." Having discussed Neoplatonic and Pythagorean ideas on previous pages, he now moves into a series of Aristotelian and Scholastic "Conclusions," engaging with the major commentators of the Middle Ages—Averroes (the "Commentator"), Avicenna, Thomas Aquinas, and Duns Scotus—to refine definitions of logic, physics, and the nature of being.</meta>

we assert, and it is in harmony with the sayings and opinion of Averroes.

29 Logic is practical.
30 The "common sense" <note>the faculty that integrates information from the five senses</note> is not distinct from the senses of sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch.
31 There are no "intelligible species" <note>term: "intelligible species" — the mental concepts or "blueprints" of things</note> abstracted from phantasms <note>mental images</note>; we assert this as the true opinion of both the Commentator <note>Averroes</note> and Albert <note>Albert the Great</note>.
32 In every question that can be known through demonstration, one must first know the "whatness" <note>original: "quid"</note> of the subject and its properties; by this "whatness," we should not understand merely the meaning of the name <note>original: "quid nominis"</note>, as other expositors do, but the essence of the thing itself <note>original: "quid rei"</note>.
33 It is possible to reason backward from effect to cause without the "negation" imagined by Burley <note>Walter Burley, a 14th-century English logician</note>.
34 Those who hold that there are "natural minima" <note>term: "natural minima" — the smallest possible unit of a substance that still retains its properties, similar to an early concept of atoms</note> in qualities do not therefore have to deny that the motion of "alteration" <note>change in quality</note> happens successively over time.
35 It is necessary to hold, following Averroes, that the form of a "genus" <note>a general category</note> is really distinct from the form of a "species" <note>a specific type</note>; the opposite view is inconsistent with the principles of his doctrine.
36 Aristotle’s demonstration in the seventh book of the *Physics*—that everything which is moved is moved by another—proves none of those things intended by Thomas <note>Aquinas</note>, Scotus, Giles of Rome (whom John of Jandun follows), Gratiadeus, Burley, or others I have read. Rather, it proves only what the Commentator <note>Averroes</note> said best (though misunderstood by all Latin expositors): that in anything moved, the mover is distinct from the thing moved, either by its nature or by its subject.
37 The demonstration in the seventh book of the *Physics* proves evidently that the heavens are not moved by themselves, given the principles of Averroes, which are indeed true and most firm.
38 The order of the books of natural philosophy handed down by Aristotle is this: the *Physics*, *On the Heavens and the World*, *On Generation*, the *Meteorology*, the *Minerals*, *On Plants*, *On the Generation of Animals*, *On the Parts of Animals*, *On the Progression of Animals*, *On the Soul*, and then the books called the "Short Physical Treatises" <note>original: "parui naturales"</note>.
**Corollary.** Those who call the book *On the Soul* a "text of physics" disagree entirely with the mind of Aristotle.
39 Every way of defending Aristotle's statement that eastern winds are warmer than western winds—except for the theory that the heavens are "animated" <note>possess a soul</note>—is frivolous and worthless.
40 Neither the reasons brought by Aristotle nor those by his expositors regarding the saltiness of the sea are sufficient; nor can any reason be assigned that is more sufficient (especially standing by the "Mosaic truth" <note>Biblical truth/the Book of Genesis</note>) than the causality of that same Universal Providence, which also worked the uncovering of the dry land.
41 No part of the heavens differs from another in being "luminous" or "non-luminous," but rather in being more or less luminous.
42 The method given by Aristotle for how the lower things are heated by the higher things appears in no way to be correct.
43 These two points stand together, and I believe both to be true: that Averroes’ reasoning in the final comment of the first book of the *Physics* against Avicenna is conclusive, and yet Avicenna’s reasons for proving the "first principle" <note>God</note> are good and effective.
44 If Thomas says that "Intelligences" <note>angelic or celestial beings</note> exist within a "genus" according to Aristotle, he contradicts himself no less than he contradicts Aristotle.
45 If the unity of a genus exists not only in the mind of the one conceiving it, but also in the thing conceived, then it is necessary that whatever things

<column-break/>

are in the same Logical genus must also be in the same Physical genus.
46 Knowledge is a real relation, while the "knowable object" is related to it only by accident.
47 Following the common method of the Doctors—namely, that something may be formally predicated of God—I state two related conclusions, of which this is the first: That God alone is so much a "substance" that He is in no way a "non-substance."
48 Second: God is not in a genus because He is "substantially substance."
49 To place a difference between "limitation" and "whiteness," or similar accidents, by claiming that one is separable and the other inseparable from a certain subject, is a fiction.
50 Any difference that appears between the aforementioned accidents originates solely from the voluntary assignment of names.
51 It is necessary to say, following Averroes, that "substance" belongs to the intrinsic essence of an "accident" <note>a non-essential property</note>, and this opinion is most in harmony with both Aristotle and philosophy.
52 In the definition of natural substances, "matter" should not be included; this opinion is consistent with both Averroes and Albert.
53 If Thomas said that according to Aristotle there are accidents in the "Intelligences," he contradicts not only Aristotle but himself.
54 These propositions are to be granted as entirely true: "Prime matter is an ass," "an ox," and similar things. <note>This is a technical logical point: because prime matter has the potential to become anything, it can be described in terms of those potentials.</note>
55 In a material composite, there are not two precise and distinct entities, but one single entity.
56 I say that sound is caused not by the motion of air trapped between two striking bodies (as Aristotle and his expositors hold), but from the "contactual" nature of such-and-such bodies.
57 The reasons the Peripatetics <note>Aristotelians</note> bring to prove that there is no infinite regress in "essentially ordered causes" do not necessarily prove that the opposite is false.
58 The "sensitive power" of the common sense—just as it does not differ from the sensitive powers of the external senses (as stated in conclusion 30)—likewise does not differ in subject (that is, in reality) from the sensitive powers of the "internal senses" (the phantastic or imaginative, the cogitative, and the memorative); we assert this as the true opinion of both Aristotle and Plato.
59 I say that all "matching" qualities <note>original: "symbolas"</note> of the elements are of different species.
60 If a "fourth figure" of syllogisms is to be used, it should be the one Galen proposed, not the one childishly devised by Francis of Meyronnes and Peter of Mantua; however, it is more correct to propose none at all.
61 We must say, according to Aristotle’s doctrine, that the Metaphysician treats matter insofar as things are made from it *in themselves* <note>original: "per se"</note>, while the Physicist treats it insofar as things are made from it *by accident* <note>original: "per accidens"</note>.
62 An exclusive expression added to one relative term does not exclude its correlate.
63 It should not be granted that a "part" within a "quantitative whole" is in any way actually distinct from its whole.

<meta>This page continues Giovanni Pico della Mirandola's "900 Conclusions." Having just discussed Aristotelian logic and the nature of "genus" and "species," Pico concludes his section on Aristotelian and Scholastic philosophy and transitions into his own "Paradoxical Conclusions," where he proposes his most original and provocative ideas.</meta>

### GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA

...that each thing is "one" through an intention added to its essence, if it is not necessarily true, it is nonetheless probable and will be defended by me.
<margin>65</margin> Although the intellectual power in us is an "accident" <note>original: "accidens"; a non-essential property, like the color of a shirt</note>, in angels it is their "substance" <note>original: "substantia"; the very core of what they are</note>.
<margin>66</margin> Formality is the "actuality" fit to perfect the "possible intellect" <note>term: "possible intellect" — the human capacity to receive and process universal concepts</note> by its own nature.
<margin>67</margin> If a mixture is made from the meeting of elements, in whatever way the elements are said to remain, the result in the mixture will be a composite formed from the elements, as if from matter digested by a spiritual, vaporous heat raised from them.
<margin>68</margin> In all things below God, matter is the same according to its essence, but diverse according to its "being" <note>original: "esse"</note>.
<margin>69</margin> The "whatnesses" <note>original: "quiditates"; the essential nature of a thing</note> of physical natures can be conceived as a proper and adequate concept without their accidents, whether they are considered by a metaphysician or a physicist.
<margin>70</margin> The organic body which is the matter of the soul, and is placed in its definition by Aristotle, is a body and organic through a form essentially distinct from the soul that perfects it.
<margin>71</margin> According to all philosophers, it must be said that God necessarily acts in whatever He does. <note>This was a controversial claim, as it seemed to limit God's free will</note>.
<margin>72</margin> He who doubts that a more true and substantial unity is formed from the "intelligible" and the "intellect" than from matter and material form, is no philosopher.
<margin>73</margin> Holding the opinion on the intellectual soul which the Commentator <note>Averroes</note> holds, it seems to me reasonable to hold that such a soul is the subject of no accident; I will defend this position as true, though whether he himself held it, I do not define.
<margin>74</margin> I say that, according to Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note>, it must be said that our ultimate happiness consists in the "reflexive act" of the intellect.
<margin>75</margin> The definition of celestial nature is inclusive, and the word "and" is taken conjunctively and not disjunctively.
<margin>76</margin> Just as every philosopher has to say that the sensitive powers are in the heart, so every physician has to say they are in the brain. <note>Pico is highlighting the disagreement between Aristotelian philosophy and Galenic medicine</note>.
<margin>77</margin> What is said by the common school of all Latin philosophers regarding the "first operation of the intellect" <note>the simple grasping of a concept</note> is an error, because there is no operation of the rational part other than those two which they call the "second" and "third"—namely, composition and discourse <note>logical reasoning</note>.
<margin>78</margin> Accidents should in no way be called "beings," but rather "of a being."
<margin>79</margin> The "Six Principles" <note>a reference to a medieval logical text often attributed to Gilbert de la Porrée</note> are absolute forms.
<margin>80</margin> If there is any primary and non-causal language, it is clear from many conjectures that it is Hebrew.

---

->Seventy-one paradoxical conclusions according to my own opinion, introducing new dogmas into philosophy.<-

<margin>1</margin> Just as the "being" of properties is preceded by "quidditative being" <note>the being of a thing's essence</note>, so quidditative being is preceded by "unial being" <note>original: "esse vniale"; a higher level of unity specific to Pico’s metaphysics</note>.
<margin>2</margin> We cannot say that anything is predicated of a thing, when taken most precisely, by "predication" properly so called.
<margin>3</margin> He who reaches a thing in its definition, reaches the thing in its "alterity" <note>original: "alteritate"; its difference from other things</note>.
<margin>4</margin> Only he who reaches a thing in the precision of its "union" reaches the thing as it is itself.
<margin>5</margin> The more eminent any mode of cognition is, the more imperfect and useless it becomes in a disproportionate intellect.
<margin>6</margin> Just as knowledge gained through demonstration is the most perfect knowledge for a human in the common state we experience here, so simply speaking among all modes of knowledge,

<column-break/>

it is the most imperfect.
<margin>7</margin> Just as God is simply the knowledge of "all being," so the intellect is the definition of "all being," and the soul is the science of "all being."
<margin>8</margin> If theology is treated theologically, its primary subject will be that which is "unially one," and anything else according to its "unial being" will be a secondary subject.
<margin>9</margin> True metaphysics, treated metaphysically, is about whatever is "true form" as its primary subject, and about whatever exists according to its "formal being" as a secondary object, neglecting the method of demonstration.
<margin>10</margin> Just as in a creature the logical consequence "it is a being, therefore it exists" <note>original: "est ens, ergo est"</note> is invalid, so in God the consequence "He exists, therefore He is a being" <note>original: "est, ergo est ens"</note> is invalid.
<margin>11</margin> The same thing in a creature is called "being" <note>original: "esse"</note> by reason of its actuality, and "essence" <note>original: "essentia"</note> by reason of its determination.
<margin>12</margin> Just as an angel is necessarily composed of essence and being, so the soul is necessarily composed of substance and accident.
<margin>13</margin> Contradictories are compatible within an intellectual nature.
<margin>14</margin> Although the preceding conclusion is true, it is more properly said that in an intellectual nature there are no contradictories, rather than saying they are compatible.
<margin>15</margin> Contradictories coincide in "unial" nature.
<margin>16</margin> Aristotle reasonably posited in his sciences the first principle: that of anything, one of two contradictories is said, and never both at once.
<margin>17</margin> In the intellect there is "this and that," but there is not "this outside of that."
<margin>18</margin> Therefore, the impossibilities of contradictories appear in the soul because the soul is the "primary quantity" that places "part outside of part."
<margin>19</margin> Everything in an intellectual nature possesses from its "intelligible unity" both the power to unite everything to itself, and the power to keep its own property immaculate and unmixed.
<margin>20</margin> The "selfhood" <note>original: "ipseitas"</note> of each thing is then most truly itself when all things are in it in such a way that all things are it.
<margin>21</margin> Through the aforementioned conclusions, one can understand what the *homeomeria* <note>term: "homeomeria" — the theory that substances are made of parts that are the same as the whole; original Greek: "omiomeria"</note> of Anaxagoras is, which the Creator Intellect distinguishes.
<margin>22</margin> Let no one wonder that Anaxagoras called the intellect "unmixed" even though it is "most mixed," because the greatest mixture coincides with the greatest simplicity in an intellectual nature.
<margin>23</margin> Just as "substantial forms" in the "second world" <note>likely the celestial or intellectual realm</note> exist in the manner of accidents, so "accidental forms" exist in the "first world" <note>the divine realm</note> in the manner of substances. Corollary: Just as in the first world there is not "white" but "whiteness," so in the second world there is not "fire" but "fiery."
<margin>24</margin> It cannot be said that in the intellect the ideas of, for example, fire, water, and air are three ideas; rather, it must be said they are a "ternary" <note>a single set of three</note>.
<margin>25</margin> Unless we destroy intellectual nature, we cannot understand ideas to be numbered except through the intimation of the "idea of number" through the rest, as each is through all.
<margin>26</margin> From the preceding conclusions, one can understand what the "formal number" is, which Pythagoras said was the principle of all things.
<margin>27</margin> Five primary "predicaments" <note>categories</note> are to be posited: The One, Substance, Quantity, Quality, and Relation <note>original: "ad aliquid"</note>.

<summary>This page concludes Pico's engagement with traditional Scholastic debates—touching on the soul, angelic substance, and the differing views of Averroes and Aquinas—before introducing his own "Paradoxical Conclusions." In these personal theses, Pico explores high metaphysics, proposing that in the highest intellectual and divine realms, contradictions coincide and unity transcends the basic categories of human logic.</summary>
<keywords>Pico della Mirandola, Paradoxical Conclusions, intellectual nature, unial being, Thomas Aquinas, Averroes, Anaxagoras, Pythagoras, coincidence of opposites, essence vs existence, Hebrew language, homeomeria</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Giovanni Pico della Mirandola's "900 Conclusions," specifically the section of "Conclusions according to his own opinion." Having discussed logic and the nature of "genus" and "species" on the previous page, Pico now moves into metaphysical categories, the nature of the soul, and his provocative claims about Hebrew and mystical theology.</meta>

### C O N C L V S I O N S

<meta>catchword: 69 Rational</meta>

28 The diversity of beings is more correctly reduced to the five previously written than to the ten which Archytas first, and then Aristotle, proposed; or the five which Plotinus <note>Plotinus (c. 204–270 AD) was the founder of Neoplatonism.</note> proposes, or the four which the Stoics propose.

29 The principle of a single category <note>term: "predicament" or "category" — a fundamental classification of things that exist</note> is absolute precision from everything external.

30 The principle of the category of substance is the unified perfection of unparticipated substance.

31 The principle of the category of quantity is the external positioning of part to part.

32 The principle of the category of quality is the truth of denomination through inherent participation.

33 The principle of the category of relation <note>original: "ad aliquid"; literally "toward something"</note> is to be an imaginary being.

34 There is no unparticipated formal predicate that cannot be partially predicated of an intelligence.

35 Just as it is truly said of the intellect alone that it is fire and that it is water, that it is motion and that it is rest, so it is truly said of the soul alone that it grows cold, that it grows hot, that it stands still, and that it moves.

36 Just as the intellect of God multiplies unity, so the soul quantifies and extends the multitude of the intellect.

37 The first intelligible coincides with the first intellect, and the first thing knowable with the first knower.

38 In souls of a lower sort, reason exists after the manner of sense; in more sublime souls, sense exists after the manner of reason.

39 That wondrous saying of that barbarian, the companion of nymphs and demons, concerning the 184 worlds in a triangular figure with three units at the angles and one placed in the middle, is most correctly understood if we understand from the intelligible unity a trinity that is intellectual, animal, and seminal, and a computation of the principal parts of the world through the first spherical number. <note>This refers to an obscure Pythagorean or Hermetic myth regarding the structure of the universe.</note>

40 Not only the Platonic philosophers, but also those among the Peripatetics <note>Peripatetics: followers of Aristotle</note> from whom it seems least likely—the followers of Averroes—must concede that the soul can, through the purgative way, without any other study or investigation, through only a modest and very easy gathering and attention upon the intelligibles it already possesses from above, acquire a perfect knowledge of all things knowable.

41 Just as the common sense behaves in the cognition of accidental qualities and material quantity, so reason behaves in the cognition of substantial qualities and formal quantity—maintaining the proportion that the former acts sensually and the latter rationally.

42 The infinity of God can be proved through "superexcellence" <note>The idea that God's attributes are infinitely beyond human concepts</note> regarding intellectual being and the way of mystical theology, and every other way is ineffective for proving it.

43 The act by which the angelic and rational nature is made happy with ultimate happiness is neither an act of the intellect nor of the will, but is the union of the unity which is in the "otherness" of the soul with the unity which is without "otherness."

44 Aristotle, in the book of *Metaphysics*, does not treat God except in the final chapter of the twelfth book, which begins: "It must also be considered in which of two ways the universe possesses the good."

45 The order of the books of *Metaphysics* after the *Physics*, in the way Aristotle ordered them, cannot be correct according to any process, whether of composition or resolution.

46 Given any practical object, the operation which puts it into practice is nobler than the one which contemplates it, all other things being equal.

<column-break/>

47 The text of Aristotle which says that every soul is immortal can be better defended than the one which says every soul is mortal.

48 Besides the three kinds of demonstration—"that," "on account of what," and "simply"—which Aristotle and the Commentator <note>The "Commentator" usually refers to Averroes</note> propose, there is a fourth kind of demonstration which can be called the "demonstration of convertibility," which is stronger than all the aforementioned.

49 It is said more improperly of God that He is "intellect" or "understanding" than it is said of the rational soul that it is an "angel."

50 Matter alone suffices to explain that for the sake of which Aristotle and other philosophers placed "privation" <note>term: "privation" — the absence of a quality that should normally be present</note> among the principles of nature.

->Corollary: Privation is not to be placed among the principles of nature.<-

51 There are three principles of natural things: matter, motion, and form.

52 The science of God, man, and primary matter is the same; and he who has knowledge of one will also have knowledge of the others, maintaining the proportion of extreme to extreme, middle to extremes, and extremes to the middle.

53 He who denies primary matter neither contradicts the senses nor denies physical reason.

54 To prove that primary matter exists, either the way of numbers or the way of universal philosophy <note>original: "catholicæ philosophiæ"; here meaning "universal" rather than specifically Roman Catholic</note> provides more certainty than any physical reason in which the senses have an entry.

55 He who holds the order of the Hebrew language deeply and fundamentally, and knows how to maintain it proportionally in the sciences, will have the norm and rule for perfectly finding any knowable thing.

56 Besides the distinction of "thing" and "reason," a third distinction must be placed, which I call "inadequation."

57 The types of enmity which are multiplied from the wolf to the "estimative power" <note>The animal faculty that perceives intent, like a sheep sensing a wolf is dangerous</note> of the sheep are not species of any accident, but species of substance.

58 Formality is the adequate object of the intellect.

59 Wherever there is a nature composed of several natures remaining in it in act, one of them is always substantially nobler and the others accidentally so.

60 The soul understands nothing in act and distinctly except itself.

61 The entire substance of the rational soul is the intellectual part.

62 The soul always understands itself, and by understanding itself it understands all beings in a certain way.

63 Although there is in the soul an intellectual nature in act, through which it agrees with the angel, just as there is a rational nature through which it is distinguished from the angel, nevertheless nothing is intrinsic to it through which it can understand something distinct from itself without its own species.

64 The intellectual nature which is in the rational soul, above the rational nature, differs precisely from a pure intellectual nature as a part differs from the whole.

65 Because the animal intellect differs precisely from the intellectual intellect as a middle part, not just as a part, it is therefore more equalized to the intellectual totality.

66 The soul can, through external information, come to this: that it understands all things indivisibly through its own substantial form.

67 One pure intellect corresponds to each series of souls.

68 All celestial souls <note>The souls associated with the stars and planetary spheres</note> are one in the first intellect.

<vocab>Aristotle, Plotinus, Stoics, Peripatetics, Averroes, Metaphysics, rational soul, primary matter, Hebrew language, formality</vocab>

<summary>In this series of theses, Pico della Mirandola challenges traditional Aristotelian categories and hierarchies, arguing for the soul's innate ability to reach total knowledge through purification and self-understanding. He notably asserts that a deep understanding of the Hebrew language is the key to all science and that God's nature is best approached through mystical theology rather than standard logic.</summary>

<keywords>Aristotelianism, Neoplatonism, Category Theory, Nature of the Soul, Hebrew Language, Mystical Theology, Averroes, Primary Matter, Metaphysics, Intellectual Unity</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Giovanni Pico della Mirandola's "900 Conclusions." Having previously discussed logic and the nature of the soul, Pico now transitions into specific philosophical paradoxes involving the Presocratics and the Sephirot, followed by a major section of his own highly controversial "Theological Conclusions." This section contains many of the "heretical" propositions that led to his conflict with the Papacy, particularly his views on the Eucharist and the nature of Hell.</meta>

->GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA<-
dd
<meta>catchword: happy</meta>

<margin>69</margin> It is reasonable, according to philosophy, that every animal lineage finds its ultimate happiness <note>original: "beatificari," to be made blessed or happy</note> within its own specific intellect; however, let this be said as a probability rather than an assertion.

<margin>70</margin> Although there were three thinkers who said that "all things are one"—Xenophanes, Parmenides, and Melissus—anyone who carefully examines their words will see that Xenophanes’ "One" is that which is simply one. Parmenides’ "One" is not the absolute One as is commonly believed, but rather "Being as One." Melissus’ "One" has an ultimate correspondence to the One of Xenophanes.

<margin>71</margin> Through "Strife" and "Friendship" in the soul, Empedocles <note>A Greek philosopher who proposed the four elements and the cosmic forces of Love and Strife.</note> understands nothing other than the powers within the soul that draw it upward and downward. I believe these are proportional to "Eternity" and "Beauty" <note>original: "æternitati & decori"; these correspond to the Sephirot Nezach and Tiferet in Jewish mysticism</note> in the science of the Sephirot <note>term: "Sephirot" — the ten attributes or emanations in Kabbalah through which the Infinite reveals itself.</note>.

### Twenty-nine conclusions in theology according to my own opinion, differing significantly from the common way of speaking among theologians.

1. Anyone who says that an "accident" <note>term: "accident" — in philosophy, a property (like color or smell) that cannot exist without a substance (like bread).</note> cannot exist unless it exists within a substance will still be able to hold the sacrament of the Eucharist, even while maintaining that the substance of the bread does not remain, as the common path holds.

2. If the common path is held regarding the possibility of "supposition" <note>term: "suppositation" — the theological act of a divine person taking on a nature, such as the Word becoming flesh.</note> in respect to any creature, I say that without the conversion of bread into the body of Christ <note>original: "conuersione panis"; referring to transubstantiation</note> or the annihilation of the "bread-ness," it is possible for the body of Christ to be present on the altar according to the truth of the sacrament of the Eucharist; this is said regarding what is possible, not what currently is.

3. We hold with theological truth that the "Ideal" and formal patterns of things are found effectively by God, formally and primarily, in the First Created Mind.
**Corollary:** Where ideas exist "ideally," they do not exist "formally"; where they exist "formally," they do not exist "ideally."

4. If we assume that God knows creatures as a "secondary object" of his intuition, as is commonly held, I say that the Father produces the Word <note>The Logos or second person of the Trinity.</note> before He knows creatures.

5. The "attributal perfections" in God, taken in themselves according to their essence, do not imply different concepts that can be directly and principally defined or described.

6. The gaze of divine knowledge does not formally terminate at creatures as if they were primary or secondary objects (as the common school of theologians says). Instead, by gazing only at Himself and nothing else outside Himself, He knows all things primarily and secondarily in a unifying, eminent, and more than equivalent way.
**Corollary:** There is no "multitude" of things understood in God, nor do creatures, as understood things, add to the number of the divine essence as an understood thing; rather, it is entirely one most simple "understood."

7. The three "transcendentals" <note>Usually referring to Truth, Goodness, and Unity.</note> in which the Image <note>of God</note> consists do not imply different concepts that can be directly and principally defined or described.

8. Christ did not truly and in terms of real presence descend into Hell, as Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the most influential medieval theologian.</note> and the common path maintain, but only in terms of his effect.

9. Although it seems probable to me, it should not be stubbornly asserted that the soul of Christ could not have descended into Hell by another mode unknown to us.

<column-break/>

10. Those words, "This is [my] body," etc., which are spoken during the consecration, are held "materially" and not "significatively." <note>Pico is suggesting the words act as a ritual formula rather than a descriptive statement.</note>

11. If the common path is held—that God is reached by an act of the intellect—I state the two following conclusions, the first of which is: those seeing the Word by the same act by which they reach the divine essence do not reach creatures, except in an eminent way equivalent to formal knowledge—an equivalence not of the act, but of the object.

12. The Blessed <note>Those in Heaven.</note> have a double knowledge of creatures that reaches them formally: one is inferred from that by which they reach the Word, and the other is that by which they contemplate the creature in its created reality.

13. I do not agree with the common opinion of theologians who say that God can "suppose" <note>take on or inhabit</note> any nature; I concede this only regarding a rational nature.

14. Neither the Cross of Christ nor any image is to be adored with the adoration of "latria," <note>term: "latria" — the highest form of worship, which the Catholic Church teaches is reserved for God alone. Pico's denial that it applies to the Cross was highly controversial.</note> even in the way that Thomas Aquinas maintains.

15. If Adam had not sinned, God would still have become incarnate, but He would not have been crucified.

16. In the same light in which John saw the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation.</note>, he did not understand the Apocalypse in that same light.

17. The first sin of the angel was a sin of omission; the second, a sin of lust; the third, a sin of pride.

18. I say probably—and were it not for the common way of speaking among theologians, I would firmly assert the opposite—that just as no one thinks something is a certain way precisely because he *wants* to think so, so no one believes something is true precisely because he *wants* to believe it is true.
**Corollary:** It is not within a person's free power to believe an article of faith is true when it pleases him, and to believe it is false when it pleases him.

19. Were it not for the sayings of the Saints, which in the literal surface of their speech seem to say the opposite, I would firmly assert this and the following conclusion; however, I offer them as being probable and capable of being rationally defended. The first is that mortal sin in itself is a finite evil.

20. The second is that for a mortal sin of a finite duration, an infinite punishment in time <note>i.e., eternal damnation</note> is not owed, but only a finite punishment.

21. Not every "will of God's good pleasure" <note>original: "voluntas beneplaciti"; a technical term for God's hidden or sovereign will.</note> is effective.

22. The saying of the Apostle <note>St. Paul, in 1 Timothy 2:4</note> that "God wants all men to be saved" is to be understood positively regarding the antecedent will of his good pleasure.

23. "Antecedent will" can be described thus: the antecedent will of God is that by which God gives to someone natural or preceding gifts by which they can achieve something, with which God is ready to cooperate if the other person wills it; nor will He manifest the contrary to him with a command or counsel of execution, permitting him to freely will to act toward the attainment of his salvation.

24. Holding the common path of theologians that happiness consists in the intellect or in the will, I state two conclusions: the first is that the intellect would not reach happiness unless there were an act of the will, which in this case is more powerful than the act of the intellect itself.

25. The second conclusion is this: Although the act of the intellect that formally makes one happy reaches the essence of the object, nevertheless, that his act regarding that act is happy...

62. Although Plato’s reasoning in the *Phaedo* <note>Plato’s dialogue on the immortality of the soul.</note> regarding the cycle of opposites does not conclude absolutely, it does conclude something specifically when presented to the character Cebes as an "argument to the man" <note>original: "ad hominem," an argument based on the specific person's beliefs rather than universal truth</note>.
